notes.text: a regional verb here meaning to butt or ram with the head; the contest escalates from making a dent to driving a head shoulder-deep into the rock.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: the Alpine and Swiss name for hard conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones resemble nail heads; the giants test their skulls against a wall of it.

notes.label: Dümpfe
notes.text: a regional word for a dent, hollow, or depression; the first giant leaves one in the Nagelfluh wall, though the precise size implied is unstated.

notes.label: Schnapsack
notes.text: the source's historical form for a small traveling or provision bag; the tailor secretly reaches into it instead of picking up a stone.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd, commonly made from the whey left after ordinary cheese making; its moist ball lets the tailor pretend he has crushed water from a stone.

notes.label: Reispappen
notes.text: thick rice pap or rice porridge; it is the giant's favorite food and the substance used for the final deceptive eating contest.

16462d93a064fd7320fe8a8406c2178b963f5d10.summary: A king tests his three sons, and the youngest receives help in a contest for the kingdom.

notes.label: three sons
notes.text: A contest among three brothers gives the youngest repeated chances to succeed with supernatural help. The structure links inheritance and marriage to tests of worth.

46817578eaa6a2c2440b6149da7fb486db9cefda.summary: Three sons set out from Kandersteg to determine who will inherit their parents’ property.

notes.label: three sons
notes.text: The parents’ small holding makes inheritance a practical problem. The brothers’ journey turns the division of family property into a fairy-tale contest.

1437b7ef9cdb477ae3407b103ba9d8d61e9bf112.summary: A quest for three golden apples sends a king’s sons toward danger, betrayal, and healing.

notes.label: apples
notes.text: The golden fruit is the object of a healing quest. Its value comes from the promised cure, which draws the sons away from home and tests their loyalty.

44515194125d6ce51131c4fbb60c3be541bcec45.summary: A prince travels in search of the fairy of the three golden apples and must recognize her through deception.

notes.label: three golden apples
notes.text: The apples connect the bride’s identity with a magical object. Recognizing the right person through deception becomes as important as finding her.

392ddc236ddac6891054d51f6ea8d58ea80293cd.summary: A boy learns the languages of animals and discovers that his unusual education can change his life.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the central Catholic act of worship. The doves supply the words that the newly chosen pope cannot yet say.

e4ecdf959955c869b27d59cf81c4aea86d9c1382.summary: A belief from Uri warns that calling a Toggeli victim by name may wake the person dangerously quickly.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Alemannic name for the oppressive night-being associated with nightmares, chest pressure, and sleep paralysis; speaking the victim’s baptismal name releases the pressure here, though an abrupt awakening is feared to be fatal.

47c0d034d6bed56e7bb1d88986b3f8a9f4b19c08.summary: A companion must use the full baptismal name to release someone oppressed by the Toggeli.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for the nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; speaking the sufferer’s full baptismal name is said here to break its attack.

6459b0f84550e7003ceab6128bc87e26aee2d327.summary: A night visitor in Davos sees a ghostly coffin procession follow the route of a later funeral.

notes.label: Davoser
notes.text: a person from Davos; the local man witnesses the spectral procession that foretells a real funeral route.

notes.label: Heimgarten
notes.text: a traditional evening social or courting visit in a home; here the young man is on his way to spend the evening with his sweetheart.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” a spectral company or procession of the dead whose route anticipates the later funeral procession.

c5015c64a814b57be05a12692c882b64b50c9851.summary: Two young men outside Kessler’s pharmacy witness the Totenvolk and suffer the effects afterward.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” the regional name for a spectral procession or company of the dead whose appearance here foretells a death in the village.

6c2ac635032b20327b751418b12be3f7cd8e4697.summary: A Laufenburg carter’s intended prank becomes a gift of gold when frogs change inside his sack.

notes.label: chrome
notes.text: a regional verb meaning to bring someone a small present or treat from a market or journey; its related noun Chrom is the expected gift that the mischievous husband replaces with frogs.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Chrom
notes.text: the regional market gift or treat brought home for someone; in this story the apparent frog-prank becomes a gift of gold coins instead.

841b3c5e06e156429bbd61a5ccae36d0b5c4d0a1.summary: Rochholz’s carter brings home frogs that turn to gold and change a quarrel with his wife.

notes.label: Zwilchsack
notes.text: a sack made of strong Zwillch or twilled cloth, suitable for hauling goods; the carter uses it to contain the six frogs he intends as a prank gift.

notes.label: Goldfüchse
notes.text: literally ‘gold foxes,’ a playful or colloquial old expression for gold coins; the narrator uses it for the money into which the frogs have transformed.

2f909f02a6e4251e50c45a29f6c028117540fecd.summary: Lienert follows a proud hunter into the company of the Türst and the storm-driven supernatural hunt.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: in Lucerne and central Swiss tradition, the Türst is a leader or embodiment of the nocturnal Wild Hunt; the figure’s exact origin and relationship to other regional Wild Hunt names are uncertain.

notes.label: Sträggeln
notes.text: here Sträggeln is the valley’s name for the wild huntress who is taken into the Türst’s company; the word’s precise etymology and whether it originally denoted a witchlike being are uncertain.

464626346ab047cfe9553afc7bbb8c954cfcd70a.summary: Lütolf links the Türst and Sträggele to forbidden hunting, uncanny animals, and the dangers of their pursuit.

notes.label: Sträggele
notes.text: a Swiss female night or storm spirit associated here as the Türst’s wedded companion in the Wild Hunt; the closest sense is a frightening hag-like being, but her form and relationship to other regional Sträggele traditions vary.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a regional name for the leader or embodiment of the Wild Hunt, heard with dogs and horses and sometimes appearing as a sow; ‘wild huntsman’ conveys part of the role, but the figure’s form and the name’s derivation vary across central Switzerland.

cda30055fb57f0ad06c73bdcc41019ff9d89a62f.summary: A woman’s recurring Good Friday dream leads her to treasure in a Laufenburg ruin, but doubt intervenes.

notes.label: Good Friday
notes.text: Good Friday commemorates the crucifixion of Jesus. The repeated Friday dreams and the specified hour give the treasure search a ritual calendar.

0f8bbb607399bc8ace4c2d1efa83f385feb3d96c.summary: Rochholz connects a woman’s treasure dream with Laufenburg’s ruin and the religious obligations of its dead.

notes.label: Jahrzeit
notes.text: an endowed annual Catholic memorial observance for the dead, normally centered on a Mass; anniversary service alone does not convey the ongoing foundation described here.

0f0498570b98dfea956d56778dd835e6922fada4.summary: A father’s final encounter with his son ends in punishment that continues among the glaciers.

notes.label: eternal penance
notes.text: The punishment extends a family obligation beyond death and gives it a visible home in the glaciers. The landscape becomes a reminder of the son’s treatment of his father.

871a49790eb66c56994802e7c05aa649f484654b.summary: Kohlrusch explains Zug’s sunken streets through a water maiden’s love and the fate of the town.

notes.label: Wasserfräulein
notes.text: literally a ‘water maiden,’ a feminine lake spirit; this one marries a human and transforms two Zug streets so their inhabitants can join him underwater.

notes.label: Nixe
notes.text: a Germanic female water spirit or water nymph, potentially alluring and dangerous; the source uses it interchangeably with Wasserfräulein.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial seasonal movement of cattle and herders between valley farms and high Alpine pastures, accompanied by distinctive dress, bells, and communal celebration.

notes.label: Paternoster
notes.text: the Latin name for the Lord's Prayer; the boatmen recite it when sacred music rises from the drowned church.

fadd3437afc72bb06329de025416fd71266e6583.summary: Lütolf’s water maiden demands that her beloved join her beneath the lake, and Zug suffers the consequences.

notes.label: Wasserfräulein
notes.text: literally ‘little water lady’ or ‘water maiden,’ a female water spirit or nymph; here she marries a human and magically brings part of Zug beneath the lake so he can rejoin his family.

notes.label: Ratschreiber
notes.text: the clerk or recording secretary of a town council; here the office identifies the human lover's father and social position.

5acbc32e524559b09dc920d7355e8a8c789235d8.summary: Lienert’s hunters pursue white chamois into a fatal mountain landscape remembered as Rieggi’s Path.

notes.label: Gemsjäger
notes.text: literally a “chamois hunter,” a hunter specializing in the dangerous pursuit of chamois in Alpine terrain; here it carries the cultural image of an exceptionally daring mountain marksman, not merely any game hunter.

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally “ridge animals,” a regional poetic name for chamois as creatures of mountain ridges; the word’s range may include other high-country game in some usage, but here it clearly refers to chamois.

notes.label: Käsernalp
notes.text: the named seasonal Alpine pasture where the narrator heard Marty’s stories; Alp denotes a high grazing and dairy landscape, while the place-name’s precise derivation and boundaries are not explained.

notes.label: Föhnsturm
notes.text: a violent storm associated with the warm, dry Alpine Föhn wind; here it exemplifies weather too dangerous to deter Rieggi, though the source gives no meteorological detail.

notes.label: Stutzen
notes.text: a short, sturdy hunting rifle traditionally used in German-speaking Alpine regions; it is Rieggi’s trusted firearm, but the text does not identify its caliber or mechanism.

notes.label: Felsenkarren
notes.text: plural of Felsenkarren, sharp grooves and fissured forms weathered into exposed limestone; the term evokes difficult karst terrain high on the mountain, though the passage uses it descriptively rather than geologically.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; here they preserve the local name Rieggi’s Path, while their individual roles are not given.

774b0df251b5dcd68a03ef9a89a8f2af65b9804b.summary: A hunter from Quinten shoots at white chamois despite a warning and the protections of a game reserve.

notes.label: Freiberge
notes.text: protected mountain hunting grounds where taking game was forbidden or specially regulated; the hunter violates both the legal sanctuary and the supernatural taboo attached to the white chamois.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, heavy hunting rifle traditionally used in the Alpine regions; its bursting turns the hunter's forbidden shot back upon his own body.

027c387d1909cc5c20a1ca1c6014757387cf5dce.summary: Big Lerjen pursues a white chamois against his priest’s advice and is found dead below an abyss.

notes.label: verwahren
notes.text: although the ordinary German verb can mean ‘to keep safe,’ in this Valais Catholic context it denotes a priest attending a gravely ill person with the church’s final sacraments, closest to administering the last rites; the passage does not identify the precise sacrament or rites performed.

4e11252902ee502f98a4c34776baf52d9f4c19c6.summary: A sacristan in Altdorf fulfills a dead man’s request, and a white dove marks the soul’s release.

notes.label: Sacristan
notes.text: A sacristan looks after the church and prepares what worship requires. His early bell-ringing brings him into contact with the figure asking for spiritual help.

7ded2ee1411c807faf68fa6f21b5df7a7a225a20.summary: A widow and her son protect travelers at a remote inn and receive thanks for their help.

notes.label: Säumerkarawanen
notes.text: caravans of Alpine pack-train carriers and their laden horses or mules; their weekly halt and horse change explain the isolated inn's regular traffic.

notes.label: welsch
notes.text: from a German-speaking Swiss viewpoint, Romance-speaking, Italian, French, or more broadly non-German; here the universities lie across the mountains, the robbers use the welsch language, and the next sentence identifies Italian in particular.

notes.label: Schlag
notes.text: a pigeon loft, coop, or enclosed compartment in which the newly given dove is still being kept; its position above the living space lets the widow hear the bird cooing.

0d70f7bc1d65c9066db8f571ca2692b4e43785d9.summary: Sooder records the winter Wild Hunt as a rushing host passing over the landscape near Rohrbach.

notes.label: Chutt
notes.text: a dialect word for a mass, troop, or pack; its exact nuance in this description of the Wild Hunt is uncertain.

notes.label: Guger
notes.text: a local dialect name or figure followed by the spectral troop; it may also carry associations with Gugger, the cuckoo, but the intended referent is uncertain.

d5146c4ce9ee5cc6a1271aac27179997ee609147.summary: Two men returning from a social visit test an apparition’s hand and suffer for the contact.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: an evening social gathering held in a Stube, often involving company, music, courtship, or shared work; the two young men encounter the spirit while returning late from one.

cd3497f6304f3e47f4be8035272a0ad6e4d8fb93.summary: A man at Rynächt challenges a tall ghost and pays for his boldness with a swollen leg.

notes.label: ghost
notes.text: The apparition is described through familiar local dimensions, including the fence rails. The man’s challenge turns a sighting into a dangerous physical encounter.

55e3904f993698138d91edfdf579eab7a6eda077.summary: Accounts from St. Gallen describe impossible stable chains and the rituals used to free their occupants.

notes.label: Mistfurke
notes.text: a manure fork or pitchfork, retained from the regional wording of the charm.

notes.label: Furke
notes.text: dialect form of ‘fork,’ referring to the same implement in the alternate ritual.

810365e86541d70fb08b6e6d37cf06e72767ce03.summary: Tscheinen and Ruppen collect strange stable events and memories of the vanished Zerdile family.

notes.label: livestock
notes.text: Cattle were a major part of a household’s livelihood. An unexplained event involving chains or stalls could therefore become a sign about the household’s security.

1a2f4144ed506f7df5c7adfb460b29a710011aff.summary: A fiddler’s late arrival at a woodland dancing ground leads into an uncanny account of the dance.

notes.label: fiddler
notes.text: A fiddler provided dance music for a local gathering. The tale ties an ordinary paid performance to a place and hour with uncanny associations.

0d627361c3e24860a675193975125a7142f04e7b.summary: Unseen work near a chapel is vouched for through an oath drawn from the familiar world of card playing.

notes.label: Chüäne
notes.text: cows in the local dialect; the neighboring verb in the transcription is uncertain and was interpreted as loosening them.

notes.label: Stumpä
notes.text: probably a tethering stake or stump being driven in; the precise agricultural referent is uncertain.

notes.label: Bur
notes.text: the Bauer or Under card in a regional card game, retained because its rank and role vary by game.

notes.label: Trumpfsächsi
notes.text: the trump six in a regional card game; the saying asserts certainty through game play, but the exact game and move are not identified.

d6f9180e83886a45cc58238908d28c1931981c23.summary: Grimm recounts Tell’s confrontation with the hat on the pole, the apple shot, and his escape across the lake.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor ruling on behalf of an external sovereign; Grißler uses that office to demand submission and punish Tell.

notes.label: Grißler
notes.text: the name used in this early Tell version for the tyrannical governor better known as Gessler; spelling varies across Tell traditions.

notes.label: Göller
notes.text: a close-fitting upper garment, collar-piece, or leather jerkin into which Tell thrusts the spare arrow; the exact historical cut is uncertain.

notes.label: Tellen Platte
notes.text: literally ‘Tell's slab,’ the lakeside rock ledge traditionally marking Tell's leap from the Landvogt's boat; it is now commonly associated with the Tellskapelle site.

notes.label: schattenhalb
notes.text: literally ‘on the shadow side,’ the shaded or less sun-exposed mountain route through Schwyz; the source itself glosses it as the dark mountains.

notes.label: hohle Gassen
notes.text: literally ‘hollow lanes,’ the sunken or enclosed road near Küssnacht where Tell waits in ambush; the plural wording is retained from this source version.

109df4445f70b8906ab5cb77d8e6687e66f75223.summary: A short oral recollection adds a family visit above Sisikon to William Tell’s journey toward Küssnacht.

notes.label: Küssnacht
notes.text: This is a brief local addition to the William Tell legend. It records a family connection and a visit during the journey toward Küssnacht.

8c928101dd8b5d4b9ac41fdbbd9a8f157c11629a.summary: A place above the Malunbach is remembered as a dancing ground for witches and their uncanny leader.

notes.label: Egli
notes.text: the local name of the site between Schuhegg and the Malunbach above the waterfall where the witches dance; its precise literal sense is not established by the source.

5589197de69e98d0e69439d3689e551e4a55ac5a.summary: Accounts from Uri place witches’ dances near the Gotthard road and in other familiar local landscapes.

notes.label: Schinhüte
notes.text: the source’s name for the witches’ hats; their exact historical form is not explained, though the term is associated here with the dancers’ distinctive headwear.

notes.label: bärsianenen
notes.text: an Uri textile adjective describing the woman’s short skirt; its exact fabric is uncertain from the source, so the original form is retained rather than assigned a specific material.

46b5790de80ee2d8c377a8e46eecac3588cee293.summary: Women use a deception about heavenly signs during the defense of Mülenen, leaving names on the local landscape.

notes.label: angels
notes.text: The defenders turn a belief in heavenly intervention into a military deception. The account also explains the names Engelburg and Faltschen through that event.

14aab07f8abc94cde6d766c41e4cf75a5ba0868f.summary: A wife in old Chur uses a household clock to expose the time of her husband’s late return.

notes.label: Curia
notes.text: an old Latin-derived name associated with Chur; Jecklin calls the gathering place the “old Curia,” but the approved passage does not identify more precisely whether this means a named establishment or a playful name for the town setting.

notes.label: Schwarzwälderin
notes.text: literally a “Black Forest woman,” a humorous feminine nickname for the ticking Black Forest clock that the wife asks her late-returning husband to stop.

298ffbb0d40cc2e0f666a142b7f221895f5a4cf2.summary: A poor farmer’s wife finds a way to defeat the Devil’s building bargain before the rooster crows.

notes.label: Teetschipürli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive glossed by the source itself as a downtrodden or oppressed little farmer; it conveys both the man's humble status and his pitiable condition, while the word's exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, often violent Alpine downslope wind; here its force threatens to collapse the family's decaying hut.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small Gaden—typically a barn, storehouse, or modest outbuilding; the Isental and Reuss-valley variants identify the promised structure this way, but its exact residential function is not specified.

d09829985ef3a6427d35b0b5f3e4439b5fdee97d.summary: Lukas Manhart, a herder of many years, relates: ‘On evenings before snowstorms break in during late autumn and force the herders to descend from the Alp with the herd, I often saw a little man in a white cloak who called very strangely but entered nowhere.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its pastoral operation; snow forces the herders and cattle to end their season and descend.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Nepermannli
notes.text: literally ‘little Neper man,’ the local name used on the Prod Alp because the being is thought to inhabit the Neperwald; Neper appears to be a place-name whose deeper meaning is unstated.

notes.label: 's Schneemannli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘the little snow man,’ a white-cloaked weather apparition whose range foretells the next day's snowfall; it is not the modern snow figure built by children.

b12e25a5da5453c6e99008b819ea1e5ce9351448.summary: Schaan (Oberschan) is far and wide the oldest village. Many, many years ago—so long ago that the forebears could not remember it—a tiny little man would now and then come into the village; nobody knew where it came from.

notes.label: Tufmannli
notes.text: the compact local name for the tiny adviser and helper associated with Tuf; it behaves like a village spirit, but the story does not assign it a more specific supernatural class.

notes.label: Spötterbank
notes.text: literally ‘mockers' bench,’ apparently a customary gathering place for the village scoffers who provoke the Tufmannli; whether it was an official bench-name or the narrator's descriptive label is uncertain.

notes.label: 's Tufmannli
notes.text: dialect for ‘the little man from Tuf,’ using the Swiss German diminutive -li; Tuf is presented as the place from which the helpful being descends, although the source does not explain that locality's name.

notes.label: Nochber
notes.text: Nochber is Bernese dialect for ‘neighbor,’ here the hostile man suspected of listening through animal forms; the accusation’s basis beyond the storyteller’s suspicions is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Müsli
notes.text: Müsli is the dialect diminutive for a little mouse, believed here to be the neighbor’s spying form; whether the tale imagines bodily transformation or a familiar spirit is uncertain.

1fac312781b1b458f19c2c0d7cb993c4c08715ac.summary: Consisting of four men and three women, the group came one evening to Tresch's house in the Wyler at Gurtnellen and asked for lodging for the night, which was hospitably granted to them according to old custom.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: Swiss German for butter; here it is clarified or cooked, stored in cellar pots, and used in flour soup, but the source does not describe its preparation further.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a historical German slur often applied to Roma people but also used indiscriminately for itinerant outsiders; it is retained only to identify and contextualize the source's language, not as a reliable statement of the group's ethnicity.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans,’ a historical othering label applied here to itinerant strangers accused of magic; the source does not establish their religion, ethnicity, or identity, and the term reflects the narrator's prejudice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tällibörter
notes.text: a Valais place-word in the warning cry, referring to the slopes or ledges down which the invaders approach; the exact local topography and singular form are not explained by the source.

5bdf0c0ae572b8e5b13de03eb17b9a5b8f1eb5d2.summary: In Giswil, Canton of Obwalden, a rock called the Giswilerstock rises sheer from an Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated working landscape, not merely an Alpine mountain; the Giswilerstock rises from such a pasture, whose exact ownership and use are unstated.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Wilde
notes.text: literally “wild ones,” supernatural wild folk imagined as living in the mountains outside human society; here the collector treats the name as an alternative to Bergmännchen, though local traditions can distinguish such beings.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally “little mountain man,” a diminutive supernatural mountain dweller that guards animals and knows hidden treasure; it overlaps with dwarfs and wild folk, but the source does not define its kind more precisely.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

a8ddfd3d4952e01718edc436da382f85f8efe366.summary: In the municipality of Menzingen, three farmsteads bear the names Mangeli, meaning want, Sparen, meaning saving, and Hungerhältli.

notes.label: Hungerhältli
notes.text: a diminutive farmstead-name suggesting a place that ‘keeps hunger’ or barely holds it off; it belongs to a trio of names evoking scarcity and thrift.

notes.label: Herdmanndli
notes.text: the source's dialect name for the little supernatural suitor; it appears to mean a diminutive earth- or hearth-man, but the spelling leaves the first element genuinely ambiguous.

notes.label: Hinecht choche-n-es Chrütli
notes.text: the first line of the dwarf's Swiss German rhyme, ‘Tonight I cook a little herb’; the song betrays his secret name.

notes.label: Senfchörnli
notes.text: literally ‘little mustard seed,’ the dwarf's hidden name; discovering and speaking it frees the prospective bride.

notes.label: Gänsefuss
notes.text: literally ‘goose-foot,’ a contemptuous or creature-like designation for the unwanted supernatural suitor; the second variant does not explain its precise folkloric sense.

notes.label: Gragörli
notes.text: the second dwarf's hidden diminutive name; its literal derivation is not explained, but knowing it breaks the compelled marriage.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally a ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like supernatural being associated with mountains or underground dwellings; the title uses it for the name-demanding suitor.

6f1b1b7482de19a72eb9a55c6c4a419b5aa5bd09.summary: About thirty years ago, one evening, boys and girls from the Kulm valley between ten and fourteen years old were playing close below Trostburg Castle near a little bee house.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like being associated with mountains, underground places, and nearby castles; this brief sighting describes only its cautious appearance and does not establish whether it is a miner spirit or another kind of little folk.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

288bc476ca7cda750b55f59381ca442290b0ced1.summary: A man from Altbüron had to drive a millstone at night from the Stalten into the village of Altbüron.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

f084917f13e98fc178c90e3039a4c012629af323.summary: from Altdorf wanted to bind a Gespenst in a mountain area of Bürglen. But it told him flatly that it had nothing to do with him, since it was not one of his parishioners.

notes.label: Gespenst
notes.text: a ghost or spectral being; its claim to belong to a particular parish makes ecclesiastical jurisdiction part of the binding ritual.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: verbandisierte
notes.text: the narrator’s playful or dialectal verb for formally banishing or magically binding the Gespenst; its exaggerated formation is preserved rather than normalized.

notes.label: Ruossdiele
notes.text: an Uri house term for a soot-darkened upper wooden floor or loft space; the Gespenst is bound there, though the source does not specify the house's precise internal arrangement.

037541650f0a38509a533df0e1441f82a3f77b21.summary: is buried in the ground at Bauen in Big Kari's Hostet. Every year it moves one ell farther away from the house, but unfortunately no one knows in which direction.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a Swiss German orchard or tree-planted homestead ground; here it identifies the land belonging to the person called Big Kari where the treasure is buried.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large cauldron, especially the kettle used in Alpine dairying to heat milk for cheese; here the vessel serves as a buried treasure container, and its exact size or material is not stated.

b315840de315c34e061058f633b6a550ec35a931.summary: The Herger Tonis from Spiringen were spending the grazing season on the Brunni Alp.

notes.label: Herger Tonis
notes.text: a collective house or family designation for the Herger people associated with Toni or an Antoni line; the source treats it as a plural household name, not as one person’s ordinary forename and surname.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, dairy work, and community, not simply a mountain peak; the family is living and working there during the grazing season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tafäla
notes.text: a small votive plaque, painted tablet, or ex-voto promised to a pilgrimage chapel in thanks for divine aid; the exact material or image intended here is not stated.

notes.label: Büebli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little boy; here it affectionately identifies the roughly five-year-old Micheli in the reported questioning.

notes.label: Ronä
notes.text: a felled or fallen tree trunk; the source explicitly explains that this one was laid across the stream as a makeshift bridge.

notes.label: g'fätterlet
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb for a child’s small-scale make-believe or fiddling play; Micheli says he did it with snail shells and stones, but the exact game is not described.

notes.label: Schnäggähüslänä
notes.text: Uri dialect diminutive plural for little snail houses or snail shells, the objects Micheli uses in his unexplained game.

notes.label: Steindlänä
notes.text: Uri dialect diminutive plural for little stones, paired with the snail shells as the abducted child’s playthings.

notes.label: Pfahr
notes.text: an Uri dialect form associated with Pfarrer, a priest or clergyman; it becomes Micheli’s nickname because local belief held that abducted children would enter the clergy.

43c20d926019f84be8f7f9623f340d7accc138e2.summary: Around Christmas come the Sträggelennächte. At Fischbach, an old village between Zell and Grossdietwil, there is a farmstead called Tschägglen.

notes.label: Sträggelennächte
notes.text: these central Swiss winter nights around Christmas were associated with the roaming Sträggelen and dangerous masquerade or Wild Hunt traditions; their exact calendar span is uncertain.

notes.label: Sträggelen
notes.text: this is the witchlike female being invoked to frighten the child and then said truly to abduct it; her precise relationship to the Wild Hunt is uncertain.

4bce8eab7707833745a9dbce8757b4475083e673.summary: The following story was on everyone’s lips in the eighties of the previous century and was generally held to be true.

notes.label: Stäfeli
notes.text: a diminutive Alpine pastoral place-name, often denoting a small seasonal grazing station or terrace with huts; here it identifies the family’s occupied station in Niedersurenen rather than merely any little stable.

notes.label: Stygi
notes.text: the local name for the narrow, extremely steep path and adjoining place where Wyseli was found; its dialect name suggests a steep ascent or stair-like way, but the source does not define its precise topography.

7dd453dd65c90b1553fa66bbe1fb579beb7ddc27.summary: Nuschi-Hansi in the Winkel at Altdorf had lost his wife. When they carried her to the church for burial, Hansi entrusted his child, a girl not yet seven years old, to the care of the wife of his neighbor Peter Walker.

notes.label: Nuschi-Hansi
notes.text: the local byname by which the widower Hans is identified; the source does not explain the Nuschi element or provide a fuller surname.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small private room or parlor; the sleeping child remains visibly there while her double is seen in the funeral procession.

e92296ee327239a1693fdc66f2873c8a2f26d49e.summary: In the mountains around Ursern, people sometimes hear a mournful child’s cry.

c9b2e46912b377331c3f16c5f997cbfa1b793644.summary: According to legend, a city once stood where the little hamlet of Oberrindal lies today, although no trace of it can now be seen.

notes.label: Heidengasse
notes.text: literally ‘heathen lane’ or ‘pagan alley,’ a present street name interpreted as a memory of the vanished city; the source provides no archaeological or linguistic derivation.

36a6fd878be510903f632111cbb4dc2580280485.summary: At Läntergen, Father Imhof was altogether as much at home as in his own house.

3a7d67b9b9b23a75d0ab48b8cf7fafaa244aef88.summary: Two men from Gurtnellen—I could give you their names and families—once went crystal hunting in the Fellital.

notes.label: About this telling

8609da42a95bb8f33a0093da1825bab86abe5ab8.summary: Once, in a farmhouse, a corpse lay in state on a bench in the main room while all the watchers were taking a snack in the adjoining Stübli.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small heated parlor or sitting room adjoining the main Stube; here the funeral watchers withdraw there for food.

22aa0fca8361f0851a5ed8166b5ca6b22ed132f2.summary: Just as Zug and Unterwalden have their most notorious witch in Lisi Bossard, so the old land of Schwyz had its own in the Kastenvögtin from the Muotathal, who lived around the middle of the previous century.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kastenvögtin
notes.text: the female title or byname by which the notorious Muotathal woman was known, formed from Kastenvogt; the source does not establish whether it refers to her own office, her household, or a family byname, so it is retained without forcing one interpretation.

b66905d9b93db710a3b77874747f2a4ea8986c06.summary: Within living memory, two brothers or friends lived in the Schmidgasse at Wassen and promised one another that after death they would come and call, ‘I am dead.’ Later one of them emigrated to America.

3cfbb7927e6216570c766e15c047cabe1938ef24.summary: 1. Old Rubi of Attinghausen had often watched the children of his neighbors in Hohl; he had the time, after all, and was no longer capable of other work.

notes.label: Holzwitteren
notes.text: the regional name of the place or kind of work where the farmer was occupied with wood; the source does not describe its exact setting or task, so it is retained rather than narrowed to a specific workshop or forestry operation.

notes.label: Waldstätten
notes.text: literally ‘forest states,’ the traditional collective name for the early central Swiss cantons; the historical passage speaks of four and identifies Uri as von Beroldingen’s homeland.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or presiding officeholder of a Swiss canton or rural polity; the exact powers of Andreas von Beroldingen’s historical office are not specified here.

92ef2a72e19a4ad26b1700b2ccf4324498f03673.summary: At Törelen in the Schächen Valley, Josefa—the good, caring mother of the household and wife of Councilor Kaspar Herger—had died.

notes.label: tifig
notes.text: an Uri dialect adjective conveying liveliness, quickness, capability, or alertness; the two youngest children are praised by this term as well as for being well behaved, but no single English adjective carries every shade.

a737654f7d0618dc12f6b9888fd710c745ca06ad.summary: For years old Babä-Sepp of Golzer had spent the grazing season at Hohlen Balm in the Maderanertal.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a Swiss and Alpine regional word for a shallow cave, rock shelter, or overhang; here the overhanging rock provides the pastoral workers’ shelter and gives the Alp its name.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the seasonal Alpine dairying and cheesemaking work carried out on an Alp; here the rock overhang supplies the bare shelter needed for that work, not shelter for a person named by the noun Senn.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live and work seasonally on an Alp, especially its herders and dairy workers; here the plural describes those sleeping beneath the rock shelter.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts or shelters, livestock, and dairy-working landscape, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: chlotterte
notes.text: an Uri dialect form meaning ‘rattled’ or ‘clattered’; the unseen force makes this noise among the hanging carrying frames and shakes them to and fro.

notes.label: blügg
notes.text: Uri dialect for frightened or timid; saying Babä-Sepp was not blügg emphasizes his composure before the omen.

notes.label: Gabele
notes.text: an Uri carrying frame or fork-shaped back-carrier used for loads; the source glosses the plural Gabelen as Rückenreff, and the same implement becomes the child’s bier.

notes.label: So, wenn-d'si witt ha, sä magschi nu einisch chu holä!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘There! If you want it, you may just come and fetch it once more!’; Babä-Sepp defiantly addresses the unseen force shaking the carrier.
notes.anchor: So, wenn-d'si witt ha, sä magschi nu einisch chu holä!

9f8882a4f0b669941e5536bc052669899543afe0.summary: It is told from Gasenried in St. Niklaus that, for a whole year, a young man named Peter Joseph was met by the shadow or spirit of a deceased person everywhere and every time he was outside his dwelling after sunset.

56b63b86b9842fae15112a6274e1b2d716718ed8.summary: As at Gibelflüh, there was such a Doggelistein—perhaps it still stands—about a quarter of an hour from Winikon beside the forest road to Reiden, near the edge of the woods.

notes.label: Doggelistein
notes.text: literally a ‘Doggeli stone,’ a conspicuous boulder associated with small supernatural beings called Doggeli; the parallel Gibelflüh tradition describes such a stone as their dwelling, while this brief notice records only its location and pyramidal form.

367d507de174837649df0a9384f85e0b9b6dc169.summary: The Schlierenbach in the Wägital region of Schwyz, dangerous in general, had swollen greatly during a terrible storm, but the neighboring landowners made no effort to contain it.

notes.label: Fahriger
notes.text: a regional form related to Fahrender, a wandering outsider credited with occult or specialized powers; here he offers to control the Schlierenbach, though his exact social identity is uncertain.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetian’; in Alpine lore it can denote a mysterious foreign prospector or magician, and the narrator uses it here as an alternative label for the Fahriger rather than necessarily a native of Venice.

c5456b482426ef2efc8d0351129c6cd46d607d7e.summary: Wherever Süffibalzi went or stood, he is said to have said a prayer beforehand.

notes.label: nywä Wägg
notes.text: Uri dialect for the ‘new path’ or ‘new way,’ the local route where the man from Bristen stages his unsuccessful fright.

notes.label: Bisch ä Geischt, sä säg's
notes.text: the opening of Balzi's Uri dialect challenge, ‘If you are a spirit, say so’; he continues that a spirit can then be addressed, while an ordinary prankster should be taken away by the Devil.

notes.label: abtättsch
notes.text: an uncertain Uri dialect expression for a rough supernatural encounter, fright, or knocking-about; the source makes clear that the prankster later fared badly, but does not specify exactly what happened.

notes.label: St. Antoni-Chappäli
notes.text: the dialect name for the little Chapel of St. Anthony; it marks how far the uncanny presence accompanied or pursued the man, though the sentence leaves the manner uncertain.

notes.label: Alpknecht
notes.text: a hired male farmhand serving on an Alp, with livestock and dairy duties; the attribution identifies Gamma's seasonal occupation rather than domestic service.

9f91309006e61bd04c18692da2646235b6a2b763.summary: In Basel there was a burgher of an old and distinguished family: Adelbert Meyer.

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a ‘black artist,’ an alleged practitioner of the black arts such as sorcery, necromancy, or occult magic; the historical accusation is broader and more sinister than the modern English word ‘magician,’ and the source applies it to Meyer and later to his daughter and son-in-law.

notes.label: verganten
notes.text: a Swiss legal and administrative verb meaning to put property up for public auction, often in a compulsory sale; here Meyer's household goods are sold during his dispute with his former wife.

notes.label: verbannisiert
notes.text: an unusual historical form meaning roughly ‘banished’ or placed under a restriction of residence; the passage confines Meyer to a house in Basel's Lesser City, but it does not make the precise legal status clear.

6a620b8e20d919995d255006d83017c2cdb53389.summary: Chliser is a small, difficult-to-reach Alp enclosed among rocks on the southwestern slope of the Bristenstock.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its grazing rights, buildings, livestock, and work, not simply a mountain peak; Chliser once formed part of the Felli Alp’s cattle operation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Oberstafel
notes.text: the upper grazing station or level within a multi-stage Alp system, generally used later in the summer; Chliser formerly served this role, though its exact buildings are not listed.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: hay cut from uncultivated, often steep and remote mountain grassland; gathering it is a distinctively Alpine and potentially dangerous form of seasonal work.

adfb37e2eac0be09993157041dce557b6f642be1.summary: More than 100 years ago, a chaplain from Göschenen once stayed much too long with his parish priest in Wassen and did not set out for home until late in the evening.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: gwandet
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb for being supernaturally stopped, confined, or spellbound so that one cannot move forward or back; the source itself explains the experience as feeling enclosed by four walls, but does not name the force responsible.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d27d016a976cacd45734db920e8e6a2c8d0f8907.summary: In the house in the Hostet (Helgossingen) at Spiringen, a Maitschi often had to gaumen the younger children while the parents were away.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a Swiss German orchard or tree-planted homestead ground; here it forms part of the house’s local place designation at Helgossingen.

notes.label: Maitschi
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a girl or young woman; she is old enough to care for younger siblings, but her exact age is not given.

notes.label: gaumen
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to tend, watch over, or care for people or animals; here it specifically means minding the younger children.

7f390f235b2ad3a00a3071b931634bb2bed08f6d.summary: At Erlinsbach, a Wöchnerin had died and been buried. The churchyard, however, does not lie on the same side as the orphaned house but beyond the stream dividing the village into two parts.

notes.label: Wöchnerin
notes.text: a woman in the weeks immediately after childbirth; the legend extends this culturally important six-week postpartum period beyond death, during which the mother must return to her infant.

ec5936e85612a68f4a6a440ac305698097544d32.summary: At nightfall a few decades ago, the Älpler of Gufern in the Maderanertal once saw a forearm bearing a torch float through the darkness.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live and work seasonally with livestock on an Alp, especially its herders and dairy workers; here the Gufern pasture community witnesses the omen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: weisser Tod
notes.text: literally the ‘white death,’ an Alpine name for death in snow or avalanche; the floating torch and cries prefigure the later avalanche-recovery procession.

a92b6e21240a216f92aa39e20b04b9f05bd13e61.summary: On Arni above Silenen, a solitary Manndli lived all winter in an old little house, where a ghost disturbed him.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a little or humble man; here it describes the solitary winter resident rather than a clearly supernatural being.

notes.label: syg näiwä näiwis-i'ds Hüsli chu
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘something or other came into the little house’; the deliberately vague phrase emphasizes that the visitor’s form was unknown.

notes.label: Dem gah-n-i ga lotzä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I shall go and lie in wait for that’; the Manndli decides to ambush the nightly apparition.

notes.label: Nachtchibel
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a night pail or chamber pot; the ghost humiliates the challenger by forcing his head into it.

notes.label: Hämmli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a shirt or nightshirt; the ghost drives the man outside wearing only this light garment in the severe cold.

notes.label: häig'm dr Grind i Nachtchibel innä gsteckt und häig-ä-n-im Hämmli zum Hüsli üss'tribä-n-i diä greescht Chelti üsä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the ghost put the man’s head into the night pail and drove him from the house in his nightshirt into the bitterest cold; Grind is a rough word for ‘head.’

ca1b2b394aeac78703bc3e01b419cb54b9ccb7ee.summary: Josef Maria Tresch in Bristen, called ‘schwarz Tresch,’ went to visit his sweetheart one evening.

notes.label: schwarz Tresch
notes.text: literally ‘black Tresch,’ Josef Maria Tresch's local distinguishing nickname; the source does not explain whether it refers to complexion, hair, clothing, temperament, or a family branch.

notes.label: erdrohlet
notes.text: an uncertain regional verb for being killed by tumbling, rolling, or falling on steep ground; the context establishes a fatal Wildheu accident but not its exact mechanics.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: wild hay cut on steep, uncultivated mountain slopes, a hazardous traditional Alpine occupation; the girl's death while doing this work fulfills the earlier double apparition.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a Bernese/Alemannic name for a nightmare-like nocturnal pressing or tormenting spirit, sometimes understood as a witch or person moving in spirit form; diminutive and creature associations vary by locality, so no single English monster-name is exact.

eb0634ac0520f32e73225e47296dda926bfc9fc9.summary: In former times several houses stood in Tscharina above Untervaz. Katharina, the daughter of a family living there, stepped outside one morning but quickly ran back into the house with the words that everything around it was covered with Rahm. — It had been snow.

notes.label: Rahm
notes.text: cream; the girl interprets the unfamiliar white covering around the house as cream rather than snow.

09a931c506f54d057900e6b13a31a1d249f478b8.summary: We were still living at Holzerberg in Bürglen. Our mother had died, and her sister, Bäsi-Nänni, was our housekeeper.

notes.label: Bäsi-Nänni
notes.text: Bäsi is an Alemannic kinship term that can denote an aunt or female cousin, while Nänni is the woman's familiar name; the story identifies her specifically as the deceased mother's sister.

notes.label: Gwandlatte
notes.text: a dialect word for a wooden wall slat or rail at the house on which the mysterious knocking sounds; its exact architectural position is uncertain.

notes.label: Bäsi-Anna
notes.text: Bäsi is an Alemannic term for an aunt or female cousin; here it refers to the same maternal aunt elsewhere called Bäsi-Nänni, although the variation in her familiar name is left as given by the source.

c1c22e143a42ed6638551c8c844fca6f90c283f2.summary: The goblin-like people called ‘Gottvärinen’ or ‘Gottwärinen,’ who sometimes associate with the inhabitants of the valley, are distinguished by their small stature and are kindly and helpful toward humans.

notes.label: Gottvärinen
notes.text: a Valais dialect plural for the small household- or work-helping beings described here; the source records several spellings, suggesting an oral regional name rather than a standardized category.

notes.label: Gottwärinen
notes.text: an alternate spelling of Gottvärinen in the same source; it denotes the same helpful little people, with the v/w variation reflecting unstable transcription or dialect pronunciation.

notes.label: Gottvärinne
notes.text: the source's singular spelling for the particular little being who works at the Täsch mill; it appears beside the title form Gottvärine, and the doubled n is retained as recorded.

notes.label: Gottvärine
notes.text: the title's Valais dialect singular for one of a small, helpful, goblin-like people; its literal origin is uncertain, and it should not be flattened into a single modern fantasy creature type.

5a6c6cfde22493174f117135c2cf7da53b90f443.summary: Once a Senn intended no longer to pray the Ave Maria and therefore remained in the hut at the appointed time, where he mocked the prayer with the other farmhands.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and dairy production on a seasonal Alp; here the title identifies the man in charge at the hut, although the story later calls him a farmhand.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: guot chu
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect meaning “come out well” or “turned out fortunately”; in the warning it means the Senn was lucky, and the spelling reflects speech rather than a standardized phrase.

notes.label: usglu
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect meaning to omit, leave out, or skip; the apparition says the man’s safety depends on having omitted not a single word of the prayer.

notes.label: Gstüpp
notes.text: a regional word glossed by the source as waste tow from processing hemp and figuratively understood here as light mist dispersed by the sun; the comparison is uncertain because the collector himself says “probably.”

db5d8c031457e6faabc1f6c02dda6f957972c0d8.summary: A great black man without a head encountered my aunt—who lived to be nearly 80 years old—once as she walked from the large Lusser house high in the village along the little path toward the Höfli.

notes.label: Höfli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a small farmstead, courtyard, or named little property; here it functions as the local destination of the path, whose exact built form is not described.

ff0019b92850c7f6afc17a2254f5a0ae62f7d623.summary: The Teiffigaden at Talachern in Bürglen was also unghyrig—haunted. Once the farmer's wife wanted to bring feed to a Fährlisau, but she could not get through to the Krummen at all until she began to curse.

notes.label: Teiffigaden
notes.text: the named Gaden at Talachern; a Gaden is a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding, and this one is the setting of the obstruction.

notes.label: unghyrig
notes.text: Uri dialect for uncanny, haunted, or troubled by an unseen supernatural presence; the force prevents the farmer's wife from reaching the animal until she curses.

notes.label: Fährlisau
notes.text: a regional term for a breeding or nursing sow associated with Fährli, piglets; the source does not say whether she currently has a litter.

notes.label: Krummen
notes.text: a named or descriptive part of the farm space that the woman cannot reach; the source does not establish whether it is a crooked passage, a pen, or another local feature, so the exact form is retained.

3e6e15936f75d2c286efebe24092c9d5a10a3395.summary: The former house in Riedmatt, in the parish of Amsteg—the predecessor of the present house—was a Heidenhaus.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Heidenhaus
notes.text: literally a ‘heathen house,’ a folk-archaeological label for a building believed exceptionally ancient or attributed to pre-Christian or otherwise unknown earlier inhabitants; it is not reliable evidence of the occupants’ religion or identity.

473766aadb701c485a816eedd282887a9457d268.summary: Glarus and Bünden had once fallen out, and quarrels and friction often arose between them.

notes.label: Bünden
notes.text: a historical shortened name for Graubünden, the territory opposed to Glarus in the cattle raid.

notes.label: Flimser-Stein
notes.text: the great rock face or mountain landmark at Flims; the tale explains its red streak as the dying herdsman’s blood.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen whom the raiders kill in boiling milk.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the old Swiss political order; the warning identifies his brown lead cow.

notes.label: Chua
notes.text: Graubünden dialect for ‘cow’; in the warning verse it is the Landammann’s brown cow with the largest bell.

notes.label: Schälla
notes.text: dialect for a large livestock bell; its sound marks the stolen herd’s direction.

notes.label: Glarnerland
notes.text: the territory of Glarus toward which the raiders are driving the stolen cattle.

notes.label: guga
notes.text: the dialect verb ‘to blow or sound a horn’; the Senn repeats it in the line ‘Ih guga, ih guga’ while making his desperate warning call.

notes.label: Guga
notes.text: the dialect noun for the horn in the verse; the line ‘Mi Guga verspringt’ says that his horn will burst.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and milk work; the lone survivor sacrifices himself to warn Flims.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Schellen
notes.text: plural of Schelle, livestock bells; the rescuers hang every bell on one bull to make the raiders believe the whole herd remains nearby.

03aa3eeea62e21a465a1796b641cb22ecb3f7a06.summary: A hunter from Bärschis went hunting in the nearby mountains. He caught sight of a fox but could not get a shot, although several times he came close to the animal, for the fox always managed to slip away in time through a bush or a crevice.

5fc6588e159aa5f9abe983788ac7157a1a78f83b.summary: Once a tailor sat mending at his table. He had the remains of his midday meal beside him, and a swarm of flies descended upon the scraps.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese with several regional forms; the source itself glosses it broadly as a soft cheese or herb cheese, and here its moisture lets the tailor pretend to squeeze water from a crystal.

6149957540f5160382e3686c984cdf2295bc563b.summary: At Riederberg in the territory of Saint Niklaus, there once lived a man who reached a hundred years of age, all in the same house.

notes.label: Totu-Prozessio
notes.text: Valais dialect for the ‘procession of the dead,’ a nocturnal passage of deceased people that living witnesses may recognize; it is a folkloric procession, not an ordinary funeral.

notes.label: Hundert Jahr nur eine Nacht
notes.text: German for ‘a hundred years, only one night’; the title expresses the legend’s comparison between an entire human lifetime and a single night when measured against eternity.

42bfa6850158a14bd90b3f8815906839801afbb0.summary: Around the time of All Souls, a hunter once spent the night at Rindermatt. As was his custom, before lying down in his bed he intended to recite the Gospel of St.

notes.label: Nischt
notes.text: the sleeping nest, bunk, or bed space in an Alpine hut; the bearded stranger climbs into the same sleeping place, but the source does not describe its exact construction.

notes.label: Geissgädemli
notes.text: a diminutive for a little goat barn, shed, or stable; the hunter flees to this separate outbuilding rather than share the Nischt with the apparition.

6f203e0fe7f520a2204cbd682b39eecfe6604a57.summary: Even courageous hunters, who sometimes look death in the face in the high mountains, are not always free of superstition and magic.

d42a3d1375fce129da7f13d34d11b4153b40317a.summary: An eyewitness related several details from the days of the Pfynkrieg of 1799—glorious for the Upper Valais but laden with disaster—that had not previously been put on paper.

notes.label: Pfynkrieg
notes.text: the ‘Pfyn War,’ the 1799 fighting in and around the Pfyn forest during the French invasion of Valais.

notes.label: Oberwalliser
notes.text: people or fighters from the Upper Valais, the local defenders through whose viewpoint the account is told.

notes.label: Pfynwald
notes.text: the Pfyn forest along the Rhône near Siders, used as the Upper Valais defensive position.

notes.label: Ballen
notes.text: an older term for cannonballs or other fired balls; the narrative applies it to the projectiles exchanged across the Rhône and from the batteries.

notes.label: Wart Bub! dem bist du's nit
notes.text: Valais-flavored speech meaning ‘Wait, lad! You are no match for that man,’ the father's warning before he faces the French horseman himself.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, stout rifle associated with Alpine hunters and marksmen; the narrator fires his before retreating from the collapsing defense.

d5852d6c61df21d4c5ae9a5a5e878aa895824fe7.summary: Once a boy at Compadiels was tending goats on a scree slope of Pic Gliems. While his animals grazed or leaped about, he sat on a rock and thought how much rather he would have gone to church than tended goats.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

ef5a189d136f39d6743d4db809d76701d546966d.summary: By the lake near Meggen, a small holding is called die Ewigkeit. A witch once lived here who thoroughly understood everything belonging to her trade, including making weather and such arts.

notes.label: die Ewigkeit
notes.text: literally ‘eternity,’ the name of the small lakeside holding near Meggen where the witch is said to have lived.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Herd
notes.text: literally ‘hearth’ but used here in the older sense of firm ground or earth; contact with it restores the witch's power to escape.

notes.label: Hofbrücke
notes.text: the historic covered bridge by Lucerne's Hof district, used in the legend as the place where pursuers can seize the witch away from open earth.

notes.label: Schneidergret
notes.text: a folkloric name or type for a cunning witch, probably combining Schneider, ‘tailor,’ with Gret, a familiar form of Margareta; the exact local reference is uncertain.

952e936fe056aaa4cd2c8091e4beedba17d51399.summary: At Weissemmen near Escholzmatt, there was a Kindbetterin who, on her first church-going for the purpose of the Heraussegnens, refused to let a second person accompany her.

notes.label: Kindbetterin
notes.text: a woman confined in childbed after giving birth; the historical role carried ritual expectations during the postpartum period, not merely the modern sense of a patient in bed.

notes.label: Heraussegnens
notes.text: literally a ‘blessing out,’ the churching or ritual blessing by which a woman formally returned after childbirth; the tale treats going without an escort as dangerous.

30bdc89d7a0a377ff0851b2446333efc0a6dd612.summary: From Grunikon in the Willisau ravine, not far from Hohlisrüti, a Kindbetterin set out for church early in the morning to undergo the churching rite.

notes.label: Kindbetterin
notes.text: this historical term denotes a woman still in the period of confinement after childbirth, here traveling to be ritually churched; the exact length of her confinement is unspecified.

notes.label: Heiligstöcklein
notes.text: this diminutive denotes a small roadside devotional shrine or wayside holy marker at the disappearance site; its exact form, dedication, and survival are uncertain.

eff76ca8bc862db492fb1ef77a34c03fbb80ddb5.summary: Around unser frowen tag zur Lichtmäß in the mccccc und viii jar (1553), a Kurtisan came by night to Sursee and asked for a servant who would ride with him for pay as far as Lucerne, for, as he said, he had to be in Rome within four days or lose great benefices.

notes.label: unser frowen tag zur Lichtmäß
notes.text: early New High German for ‘Our Lady's Day at Candlemas,’ the Marian feast associated with Candlemas in early February.

notes.label: mccccc und viii jar
notes.text: the chronicle's Roman-number wording literally indicates the year 1508, while its supplied parenthesis reads 1553; both forms are preserved without resolving the discrepancy.

notes.label: Kurtisan
notes.text: the title's historical form for a courtier or court-connected traveler; the body spells it cortisan, and his clerical benefices suggest a court cleric.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin; the traveler promises six and advances three as payment for the servant's ride.

notes.label: Halta halta!
notes.text: the traveler's old-dialect cry meaning ‘stop, stop!’ just before horse and rider rise into the air.

8662ad122966c79b3cd67a10dd73465083fedacb.summary: In ancient times, only two Sennhütten stood on the Langerberg. There was no other human being for miles around.

notes.label: Sennhütten
notes.text: plural of Sennhütte, seasonal Alpine dairy huts where herding families live and process milk during the summer pasture period.

notes.label: Langerberg
notes.text: the locally named high pasture landscape near Lenk where the two isolated dairy huts stand.

2d0955578b6f48b5cad63f0ebe6fe7074f2b6a26.summary: A man from the Teiler family of Gurtnellen, a lineage extinct for centuries, owned the whole Stalden and drove his sheep onto the now almost inaccessible Stafel of Saas in Gornern.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a seasonal station, level, or cluster of buildings within an Alpine pasture system; Saas is the named, difficult-to-reach grazing station at issue in the dispute.

a1276379322ceb1af0f547be2318b3e2c0b29c99.summary: The belief is widespread in Uri that fatal accidents—especially those occurring while felling timber in the forest or gathering litter and Wildheu—‘announce’ themselves beforehand through lights.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: hay cut from uncultivated, often steep and remote mountain grassland; gathering it is a distinctively Alpine and dangerous seasonal occupation, which is why the belief links it to fatal falls.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of a traditional German-speaking house; the prophetic lamp is first seen there and is later physically placed there during mourning.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a smaller parlor or side room adjoining the main Stube; the light’s movement between the two rooms is repeated by the memorial lamp’s later placement.

notes.label: Dreissigstlichtlein
notes.text: literally the ‘little thirtieth-day light,’ an oil lamp kept burning for a particular deceased person through the Catholic thirty-day memorial period.

notes.label: Dreissigsten
notes.text: the traditional Catholic thirty-day mourning and memorial period following a death, often culminating in a commemorative Mass; the account describes the lamp but not the complete local observance.

afccb6c0184fbbc845b46b4d3eca30c1786869d2.summary: A prosperous farmer had gone up the mountain with his thirty cows to the Vorsäss.

notes.label: Vorsäss
notes.text: an intermediate seasonal pasture and settlement used between the valley farm and the high Alp; it forms a distinct stage in Alpine transhumance.

notes.label: Melkstuhl
notes.text: a small milking stool, often with one leg and strapped to the milker’s body so it could be carried from cow to cow.

notes.label: Blag
notes.text: a burdensome, sickly, or wretched creature; the farmer uses the dismissive word for the thin cow that seems unlikely to thrive.

notes.label: Schelle
notes.text: a livestock bell, here valuable enough that the farmer initially wishes to remove it before lending the cow; bell forms and sounds also identify animals within a herd.

notes.label: Lehenzins
notes.text: the payment or interest owed for the Lehen; the inexhaustible little cheese becomes the dwarf’s return for use of the cow.

notes.label: Lehen
notes.text: a loan, lease, or entrusted holding; the dwarf borrows the cow for seasonal use rather than buying it.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: wie die Seide am Zapfen
notes.text: literally ‘like silk on the Zapfen,’ a comparison for the cow’s extraordinary sheen; Zapfen probably denotes a peg, bobbin, or spool holding silk, but the precise local object is uncertain.

notes.label: Sömmerung
notes.text: the seasonal keeping and grazing of livestock on mountain pasture over the summer, including their care and dairy use.

notes.label: Bratkäslein
notes.text: a small cheese intended for heating or roasting; this one magically restores itself as long as a final piece remains.

notes.label: Thio und liog!
notes.text: an old or dialectal imperative glossed by the source as ‘Do as you were told, and you will see!’; its exact word-by-word derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: the customary arrangement in which itinerant craftspeople such as a tailor or shoemaker worked in a customer’s home, often receiving food and lodging while completing the job.

a1625853ee4340792733cacf5cd1a00920c0307c.summary: On a beautiful day in late autumn, the hunter A. of Langwies went hunting with a companion.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

notes.label: gestellt
notes.text: the past-participle form used when A. and his companion have been magically halted and cannot step forward.

notes.label: sich lösen
notes.text: literally to release or free oneself; here it is the counter-charm by which A. breaks the magical binding.

notes.label: stellte
notes.text: the verb form used when A. retaliates by placing the same immobilizing enchantment on the other hunters.

notes.label: gelöst
notes.text: released or freed from the binding; the adversaries eventually undo A.'s counter-spell and reach the hut.

notes.label: Kugel von sich abzuwenden
notes.text: literally ‘to turn a bullet away from oneself,’ a separate magical art that prevents the shot from striking A.

notes.label: stellen
notes.text: literally to set, stop, or staunch; applied to blood, it means preventing wounds from bleeding until the victim reaches open air.

notes.label: Verstellen
notes.text: in this tale, supernatural binding or immobilization rather than ordinary disguise; hunters magically prevent rivals from advancing.

6d28036109e2f34c16d746f7bd52b8657b258ea5.summary: In ancient times, the people at Beroldingen in Seelisberg had to go all the way to Erstfeld to attend church—or, according to others, to Buochs.

7ddfe0dfd6a4076154d817f37213b9f6bfc4005f.summary: Two simple, innocent spouses once came to a priest with a book and said guilelessly that it was surely a curious book: when one read from it, all locks sprang open.

59366057504f697ca433c62954d5be745093686e.summary: Two years ago Franz Biner dreamed that his late mother came to his bed and told him that the following day he should give a thirsty person something to drink on her behalf; later in his life, on a high mountain, she would then help him.

notes.label: Vergeltsgott
notes.text: a contracted German Catholic expression meaning “may God reward you,” traditionally offered as thanks for a gift or charitable act; here it makes the drink an explicitly pious kindness rather than an ordinary transaction.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope wind of the Alps, often associated with rapid warming and dangerous snow conditions; here “Föhn weather” softens the snow, though the source does not give meteorological details.
