92810237d64d7adf02fe9890a23dac863886302e.summary: The family statistics of Zermatt relate that once a Zermatt midwife was summoned to a Zigeunerin who was in labor.

notes.label: Zigeunerin
notes.text: the historical German feminine exonym used in the source for a Romani woman; the word is now widely recognized as derogatory, and its retention identifies the source's wording rather than endorsing it.

notes.label: Vorschoss
notes.text: a regional word for the front part of an apron or the apron itself, used here to hold the midwife's payment of coals.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: the historical German masculine exonym used in the source for a Romani man; it is now widely regarded as derogatory and is retained only to represent the source faithfully.

notes.label: Meh zat — minder hat.
notes.text: a dialectal saying whose closest contextual sense is ‘the more [you] scatter, the less [you] have’; it warns that each discarded coal reduces the miraculous gold retained.

notes.label: Godwerdjimutter
notes.text: the local name or title of the wealthy supernatural mother in the Saas Valley version; Mutter means ‘mother,’ but the source does not explain the first element, so the precise derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Kindbetterin
notes.text: a woman confined after childbirth or lying in childbed; here it describes the immensely wealthy supernatural mother whose golden cradle is hidden.

notes.label: Bodmen
notes.text: a local place-name near Wiesen; names of this family commonly refer to level ground or valley-bottom land, but the poem treats Bodmen as an established name.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: a pack-train carrier who transported goods and led laden animals over Alpine routes; the six-horse journey is commercial travel, not a pleasure ride.

notes.label: Veltlin
notes.text: the historical German name for Valtellina, the Alpine valley in present-day northern Italy.

notes.label: Plurs
notes.text: the historical German name for Piuro, a prosperous settlement on the Alpine trade route whose catastrophic burial is the event recalled by the poem.

5826b4b9a5f9d0148ebcffcaf7fc96a3011c90fc.summary: In former times, the old house at Talachern stood farther west than the present one.

notes.label: Fuhrerin
notes.text: an occupational or household byname related to Fuhr, carting or transport; the narrator identifies the elderly woman by this name but does not say whether she herself drove loads or belonged to a carter’s household.

notes.label: Moore
notes.text: in this Bernese dialect tale, Moore means a sow and represents the dead mother who returns with her children; the word’s exact local pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Färli
notes.text: this Alemannic plural denotes piglets, corresponding to the nine murdered children; the precise dialect form and symbolic transformation are uncertain.

notes.label: fahrende Schüler
notes.text: the source’s phrase fahrende Schüler denotes a wandering scholar often credited in legend with ritual or occult knowledge; his training and identity here are unspecified.

notes.label: Dünns
notes.text: this dialect noun denotes a thin or weak drink, likely small beer or a diluted beverage offered to travelers; its exact preparation is uncertain.

notes.label: banisiert
notes.text: this dialect verb means banished or magically confined, here into the threshold; the precise rite and derivation of the form are uncertain.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Zum Chehrumtürli
notes.text: literally something like ‘to the little turn-around door,’ a dialect expression for reaching a narrow turning point, reversal, or close call; the woman's fright reverses her disbelief, but the exact idiomatic image is uncertain.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: literally ‘little woman’ or ‘little lady,’ an Alemannic diminutive used here for the skeptical woman rather than necessarily a supernatural being.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: a female seasonal or cautionary figure associated by name with Faschte, fasting or the Fastnacht period; the source assumes local familiarity and does not clearly distinguish whether she personifies Lent, Carnival discipline, or another winter custom.

notes.label: Tusigsdiller
notes.text: a comic or emphatic oath approximately ‘by the thousand-thaler,’ used while wagering that the mocker will be frightened; it is not presented as an actual coin payment.

notes.label: Chiltobe
notes.text: an evening social gathering associated with visiting, courtship, and household work such as spinning; local forms of the custom varied, and this scene supplies no further details.

6f5fbd58635c4df07e98531537f747c0435f748c.summary: 1. In late autumn, a hunter from the Schächental spent the night at Alplen, went into the hut, and cooked himself some warm soup.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop used across distance, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; in both episodes, an answering Jauchzer summons or reveals an uncanny companion.

3263dffd5cae86670b9f02706b234ccd443380a7.summary: In the year 1607, during the summer at night, a wondrous and terrifying specter allowed itself to be seen several times in the city of Lucerne.

notes.label: Ekkststägen
notes.text: this early-modern Lucerne place-form appears to name steps leading up from the Eggk toward the square; its modern identification and the source spelling are uncertain.

notes.label: furen
notes.text: this early-modern route-name or topographic term lies between the square and Cappellplatz in the specter’s course; its capitalization, exact meaning, and modern location are uncertain.

57c6710c4c96d4490ceb8b5c6d0cbf6866db668b.summary: According to a belief current in the Freiamt, a person who dies through his own fault must wander restlessly until the full number of years allotted to his life has elapsed.

notes.label: Gumpen
notes.text: a regional word for a deep hollow or pool in a stream, often scoured beneath falling or fast-moving water; sudden mountain runoff makes this one dangerous.

notes.label: Loosbücher
notes.text: historical spelling of Losbücher, ‘lot books’ or divination manuals consulted to answer questions by drawing or interpreting lots; their statement of the drowned man's destined lifespan belongs to folk belief, not official recordkeeping.

notes.label: Tagelöcher
notes.text: literally ‘daylight holes,’ small window-like openings admitting light into a simple structure; the ghost is seen looking through one of them.

notes.label: Nothhaus
notes.text: an older spelling of Nothaus, literally a ‘house of need’ or emergency shelter; here it is a tiny protective dwelling built for the restless spirit of a drowned person, not a rescue station for living swimmers.

a61baedcf866c4d098c44bcccd9678736cd20493.summary: A poor man who had spent the entire day gathering brushwood in the forest was returning home late in the evening with the heavy bundle on his back, lamenting his great poverty.

notes.label: Hexenmeister
notes.text: literally a male ‘master of witchcraft,’ a man accused of harmful magic; retaining the term signals the historical demonological charge that sends him to the stake.

541da658edf94bf78b341ec9cd69afa9c8344243.summary: In Saas, devout mothers tell the following legend to children who are always eager to listen to little stories:

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

307f18e7bd76d92195c4194a68c5d5e86f61f5b0.summary: A Cistercian convent formerly stood at Ebersecken, founded in 1274 by Jakob von Fischbach and Rudolf von der Balm.

ce11169daeac5f4fe056ac73e667df41c9603840.summary: In the time of Maximilian the First, an exceedingly devout and God-fearing priest lived in the Rhaetian Alps.

notes.label: Wegzehrung
notes.text: literally ‘provision for the journey,’ the Catholic Viaticum—Communion brought to someone near death as spiritual sustenance for the final journey; the consecrated host exposes and disperses the witches' illusion.

c37eed7300d4484e115463369c5a2572864d5e88.summary: Two young men had arranged to meet in the evening beneath the honey-pear tree—it was a Hingler—in the so-called Seelenmätteli by the rectory in Erstfeld.

notes.label: Hingler
notes.text: the local name used for this honey-pear tree or its pear variety; the parenthetical wording identifies the particular tree, but does not define the variety further.

notes.label: Seelenmätteli
notes.text: literally ‘little meadow of souls,’ the local name for a small meadow by the Erstfeld rectory and cemetery; the name strengthens the tale's association with the dead.

notes.label: So, so, bisch dü scho da
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Well, well, are you here already?’; the familiar greeting shows that the young man initially mistakes the apparition for his expected companion.
notes.anchor: So, so, bisch dü scho da

notes.label: Hed äso 'tätschlet
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that he clapped or smacked his hands together in that manner; the gesture is presented as a challenge from within the cemetery.

notes.label: Ich dänkä, der uf'm Friedhof wär de fir-nä g'sy
notes.text: Uri dialect for the informant's conjecture that the being in the cemetery was ‘there for him’; the phrase may imply that it meant to lure, seize, or otherwise confront the young man, but its precise threat remains unstated.

2c88cb0a92662769e0bd75d053d548df5ecc9cc7.summary: At the time when the plague was in Graubünden under the name "the Black Death" and claimed countless victims, so that entire farms died out and many municipalities no longer had room in their cemeteries to bury the dead, people discovered that no wild little men or women died of this dreadful disease.

aee2667609817b290558574a317a441840e41012.summary: 1. According to a fahrender Schüler, a salt spring is to be discovered in the Brändwald above Intschi.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning and secret knowledge; here he knows the existence and future opening of a hidden salt spring, not merely ordinary school knowledge.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its grazing rights, huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; the prophecy says the felled forest will be converted into such pastureland.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bissen
notes.text: an unexplained regional object imagined as a plug, bit, or wedge stopping the salt spring; the third account’s paradoxical ‘golden iron Bissen’ does not establish its material or exact shape.

notes.label: Trychelkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Trycheln, the deep-toned sheet-metal livestock bells used in Swiss pastoral culture; the source describes them as two gray cows and gives two white bulls as an alternate version.

59b184aaccd5793f6923746e2ece7c787069c161.summary: There was once a woman who could not bear to give the poor anything. Whenever little leftovers of cooked food or other dishes or meat were brought out, or whenever she had buttermilk or whey that she did not need, she diligently threw everything into the Schwi’s trough and refused to share anything with beggars.

notes.label: Schwi
notes.text: Saas Valley dialect for a pig or swine; the repeated dialect word keeps the animal at the center of the woman’s punishment, and it does not specify the pig’s sex.

notes.label: Chepfu
notes.text: Saas Valley dialect plural meaning “heads”; the second head seen eating is understood as the dead woman’s supernatural presence, not a physically two-headed animal.

notes.label: Chrommu
notes.text: Saas Valley dialect for the pigpen or enclosed place where the pig is kept; the closest English sense is “sty,” while the source gives no construction details.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

59cac4273d505293ee96dfe4463f388035d02843.summary: a) A distinguished pilgrim to Rome from the German lands spent the night at an inn in Amsteg.

notes.label: Trullihegel
notes.text: an Uri dialect name explicitly glossed by the source as a pocketknife; it is the chance-found weapon with which the traveler or servant defends himself, but the source does not describe its particular form.

notes.label: Ankenwage
notes.text: literally the ‘butter scales,’ a named butter-weighing or market point in Altdorf; the pilgrim is confined at a house there, though the source does not identify the site’s exact institutional arrangement.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

6013b75265582ebef8248e8ef3502759b01df753.summary: A farmer at Grosshaus in Gurtnellen had a servant who sometimes performed the greatest and heaviest tasks without effort and without growing tired.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn bay, hay store, or farm outbuilding in Alpine German usage; here it is the storage space into which the enchanted hay flies, while the exact building form is not specified.

notes.label: Heuer
notes.text: a haymaker or farm worker engaged in cutting and gathering hay; in Alpine agriculture the role is tied to the urgent seasonal hay harvest, not modern wage hiring.

506a8736a9001efd57e0702b9cafbf867764dff4.summary: In one of Werdenberg Castle’s cellars, three very old skulls were formerly displayed.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

9823e570cd7cf30a261f36dd50ab6a0b0af3b34b.summary: A father and mother left their house in Flüelen for the dance floor without first blessing the little child whom they left utterly alone in its cradle.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small barn, stable, storage building, or farm outbuilding; the councilmen hear the child inside one, but its exact construction is not specified.

notes.label: Wäuti
notes.text: an Uri name for an uncanny being, threatening apparition, or nocturnal bogey; here it is the broader label for the chest-pressing creature.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for a nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; the narrators offer it as a possible identity for the Wäuti sitting on the child’s chest rather than as a certainty.

notes.label: Getti
notes.text: a Swiss German kinship term for a godfather or male godparent; the councilman is the child’s Getti, and that relationship is said to protect him from the spirit.

e4ddcbf4947b35423e2e1c9e9deca8331b30f5d3.summary: A boy of about ten, who told me the story himself five years ago as a 70-year-old man, was often visited at night by a spirit in the form of a large man wearing a white Hirthemd, who lay down beside him on the wall side of the bed.

notes.label: Hirthemd
notes.text: the source’s form for a white herdsman’s or shepherd’s shirt, used here as the spirit’s distinctive garment; its precise cut and whether it carries any funerary significance are not described.

6922a8870169bbf9b8fcf61be50e282d1bc4bbbd.summary: Anyone who goes from Grossdietwil to Eppenwiler comes to the Schartenhöhle.

notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

861b7815923f07ccc65fe1504ef1c8f103c7a7f6.summary: Above the Devil's Bridge in Uri, the name Reuss Valley ends, and its continuation is called the Göschenen Valley.

notes.label: Göscheneralp
notes.text: the high Alpine valley and seasonal pasture landscape above Göschenen from whose glaciers the Reuss headwaters emerge.

notes.label: Dammafirn
notes.text: the named firn or perennial glacier-snow field toward the head of the Göschenen Valley; firn is old compacted snow that feeds a glacier.

notes.label: Samiklausen
notes.text: a local form built from Sami Chlaus, ‘Saint Nicholas’; here it names the remote chapel also called Sankt Niklausen.

notes.label: Urseren
notes.text: the historic high valley region around Andermatt adjoining the Göschenen route; its residents also affirm the chapel's antiquity.

notes.label: Waldbrüder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brothers,’ religious hermits or lay ascetics believed to have lived at the early Christian site.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

89d3eb5214833ca02a72257e452af45013714cab.summary: In the year 1402, a great star with a fiery tail was seen in the sky, which was called a comet.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

5526ee5e237d639dddb54093c29213cf284bf123.summary: In the year 1566, on the feast of Corpus Christi, a Sterbent broke out. By the end of autumn, 650 people had died in the entire Kilchhöri of Walenstadt, 1100 in Flums, and many in Quarten as well.

notes.label: Sterbent
notes.text: an archaic regional noun for a great mortality, epidemic, or pestilence; here it denotes the deadly outbreak beginning on Corpus Christi in 1566, without identifying a specific disease.

notes.label: Kilchhöri
notes.text: Swiss German for the territory or community belonging to a parish, literally those who ‘hear the church’; here it defines the wider Walenstadt parish area counted in the death toll.

95760ce729441774e6429e55156e21967a4e40b1.summary: A man named Heding was walking one morning, while it was still dark, on a Thomas-Markttag with several other traveling companions out through the Forst—the area between the so-called Clus and Marschlins—toward Cur.

notes.label: Thomas-Markttag
notes.text: the day of a local market associated with St. Thomas; Heding begins his journey on that market morning.

notes.label: Forst
notes.text: ordinarily “forest,” but the source uses it as the local name for the area between the Clus and Marschlins.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical form used here for Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Geisshirt
notes.text: a goat herder; Geiss is Swiss German for goat.

notes.label: Jesmen
notes.text: a regional noun for plaintive crying, moaning, or lamenting; the source itself glosses it as Lamentieren.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully, often cut by a torrent.

notes.label: Medicus
notes.text: the historical Latinizing designation for the physician who must amputate Heding’s frostbitten legs.

3e2d4db1c1b19674e32d1bdf8993711cd023c283.summary: The following happened to a Traubenwächter at the so-called Kreuzgasse on the Masanser-Strasse near Cur.

notes.label: Traubenwächter
notes.text: a vineyard guard appointed to protect ripening grapes before the harvest; his recognized office and duty protect him from the apparition.

notes.label: Masanser-Strasse
notes.text: the historical spelling of the road toward Masans near Chur; it locates the Kreuzgasse and vineyards in the story.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical German spelling used here for Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

cffc60e9b875c6a494849142e6ff3fc335ff893b.summary: ‘And once something damned curious happened to me too. I was lying in wait for the fox in a little Gädemli at the back of the Intschitobel.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a diminutive of Gaden, an Alpine barn bay, hay store, livestock shelter, or farm outbuilding; the hunter uses the small structure as a blind, while its exact layout is not specified.

notes.label: Wychwadel
notes.text: an Uri form of Weihwedel, a holy-water sprinkler or aspergillum, often brush- or tuft-shaped; the shredded, bent muzzle of the gun barrel is compared to one.

notes.label: Rung Bluet
notes.text: a dialect expression for a visible quantity or trace of blood; it may suggest a streak, runnel, or pool, while the hunter’s ability to follow it favors ‘trail’ in this context.
The dialect phrase Mannli machen denotes a hare sitting upright.

5aedc270a7a4bc377a18317aa196762bfabc9032.summary: A young Closterser had enlisted for service in Holland. — But he did not like it in Holland; he could not forget his distant homeland, the familiar meadow valley with its sunny farmsteads—and still less could he put from his mind a little flower he had left at home, namely his sweetheart, whose…

notes.label: Closterser
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling for a person from Klosters in the Prätigau.

notes.label: s'Schätzlein
notes.text: a dialectal affectionate diminutive meaning “the little sweetheart” or “your dear one”; the landlady uses it for the soldier’s beloved.

notes.label: s'Schätzchen
notes.text: a second affectionate diminutive for the sweetheart, parallel to s'Schätzlein in the landlady’s speech.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Pardenner-Bödeli
notes.text: a small level tract or meadow near Klosters; Bödeli is a Swiss German diminutive of Boden, and the place serves as a recognizable landmark on the magical flight.

notes.label: Lus-Bühl
notes.text: a local hill named among the familiar landmarks below the flying hide; Bühl is a regional word for a hill or rise.

notes.label: Mönch-Alpe
notes.text: the Alpine pasture called Mönch-Alpe; Alpe denotes the managed high grazing area rather than only a peak.

notes.label: Nasenspiegel
notes.text: a humorous historical word for spectacles or eyeglasses, literally a “nose mirror”; the mother holds the large optical aid while opening the family Bible.

notes.label: Zimmerrapport
notes.text: the soldier’s required barracks-room report or morning accountability procedure; the precise military routine is not described, but returning in time for it proves the journey fit within one night.

7d2edd3ebe8eb629e137e1136ef0b75ac69f061f.summary: Long ago, a man from Ausserberg was sent by his municipality to Sion to visit an experienced Schüler and ask him to sell and give them a spring or well, for their mountainside suffered a great shortage of water.

notes.label: Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘scholar’ or ‘student,’ a learned magical practitioner in Alpine legend who can command hidden natural forces; the adjective ‘experienced’ distinguishes the role from an ordinary schoolchild.

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a practitioner of the ‘black art,’ meaning a magician credited here with packaging and transferring a spring rather than merely a stage conjurer.

notes.label: Brummel
notes.text: the source's name for the large buzzing or humming creature that flies from the box and enters the ground, releasing the spring; its exact species and supernatural nature are left uncertain.

b37e092a1bcfd7353821df62809a03a6c9a75bed.summary: At Unterschächen a father had a clumsy, oafish child. One day in anger he called the child a Toggel.

notes.label: Toggel
notes.text: a dialect insult for a clumsy fool, oaf, or lout; the father’s angry use of the word is distinct from, yet magically summons, the supernatural Toggeli.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for a nightmare or pressure spirit believed to creep onto sleepers and oppress the heart; this account gives it the tiny bodily form of an enchanted child that can be trapped in bedding.

notes.label: Lylachen
notes.text: Uri dialect for a linen bedsheet; tightly wrapping it around himself allows the father to trap the Toggeli until morning.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for departed souls still needing prayer and release, often understood as souls in purgatory; the father prays for them before giving the tiny body to the cemetery.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

4675c69127b69b60a4a9008fe63f58a1e4cfd167.summary: At Gurtnellen in the canton of Uri, a Venediger once acted like the one in Sörenberg.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine legend, a name for supposedly Venetian or southern prospectors credited with secret knowledge of mountain ores and magical travel; ‘Venetian’ gives the geographic association but not this regional folkloric role, whose historical basis is uncertain.

4011828d45b56e94ffbf14f518a76ef86e649184.summary: Years ago, Venice took pride in a number of men who possessed a magnificent art: they understood how to make gold.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a Venetian, Venediger here also carries the Alpine folkloric association of secretive mineral experts and gold-makers; whether the fugitive is historical or a stock alchemist is uncertain.

4174b9e80c17aba1acd237f434c5a8a9616d22a1.summary: Halten-Sali of Isental once spent the night with cousins in Bürglen while on pilgrimage to the Rieder Valley.

notes.label: Zeintli
notes.text: a diminutive of the regional Zeine, a handled carrying basket often made of wicker; the apparition wears one on her arm, but its contents, size, and construction are not stated.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name for a nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; here it appears as a female figure whose weight causes paralysis and near suffocation until a hidden sign of the cross drives it away.

5cfc182693be7bffaaf30b3b1dd92705ba3ce1da.summary: In Eggen at Grächen there was a house past whose windows the Volchgang passed especially on the Tempertagen.

notes.label: Volchgang
notes.text: a Valais name for a spectral procession or passage of the dead, literally suggestive of a “folk-going”; here it reveals those doomed by the plague, while the word’s exact etymology and relation to other dead-procession traditions are uncertain.

notes.label: Tempertagen
notes.text: a regional form of “Ember Days,” the quarterly Catholic fast and ordination days associated in folklore with heightened supernatural activity; the story does not specify which of the four seasonal sets is meant.

06137cea6c0510f412178570fe5d5efb79226693.summary: Once in Kippel three cobblers were working auf der Stör. They were merry and in good spirits, amusing themselves in all sorts of ways and telling Schnurren and Bozengeschichten while they beat the leather and pulled the Pechdraht.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: itinerant work performed by a craftsperson at a customer's home or premises; the three cobblers are working away from their own shop.

notes.label: Schnurren
notes.text: comic anecdotes, tall tales, or entertaining yarns exchanged while the cobblers work.

notes.label: Bozengeschichten
notes.text: stories about Bozen, frightening apparitions or bogey-like spirits; here they foreshadow the night's encounter.

notes.label: Pechdraht
notes.text: strong shoemaker's thread treated with pitch or wax and pulled through the leather.

notes.label: Trinkelkuh
notes.text: the leading or bell cow wearing a Trinkel or Trychel, a traditional livestock bell; the wager's reward is the finest such cow in the Lötschental.

notes.label: Guggialp
notes.text: the named high pasture where Simud must complete the wager.

notes.label: Quatembersamstag
notes.text: an Ember Saturday in the traditional Christian quarterly fast; the tale treats it as an especially uncanny time.

notes.label: Guggialphütte
notes.text: the working hut on the Guggialp, reputedly haunted from ancient times.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Quatembernacht
notes.text: the night associated with the Ember observance, when the remote hut and route are believed especially dangerous.

notes.label: Reissens und Beissens
notes.text: literally “tearing and biting”; the apparition's riddling formula alludes to Simud's protective horse and saber without assigning each word unambiguously.

notes.label: Geweihtes und Gewagtes
notes.text: literally “something consecrated and something daring”; the formula points to the consecrated candle and the daring traveler.

notes.label: Chluistein
notes.text: the narrow rock or constriction in the Guggischlucht where the fiery being sits astride Simud's path.

notes.label: spinnen rein
notes.text: literally “spin finely” or “spin cleanly”; in the apparition's threat it is an ominous idiom whose precise intended punishment is not explained.

notes.label: Horrou
notes.text: a local place-name on Simud's route toward the Guggischlucht; the source gives no further geographical gloss.

notes.label: Knieholz
notes.text: literally “knee wood,” here a curved wooden implement or specialized shoemaker's knee-wood sturdy enough to strike the creature; the source does not define its precise construction.

0c9b0793ad0f2457827abf80ad5848b7eb84b4bb.summary: At Emmetten, in the house on the Rubi, all ten fingers of a person—or, in another version, the three fingers used in swearing an oath—can be seen burned into a window.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d41f08fda83e518ca51faeda6c74db7a808082da.summary: a) Older people still knew a poor woman from Attinghausen who had the reputation of being an old witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations

notes.label: Müess-ech äu eppä chu hälfä?
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Do you perhaps need me to come and help?’; the suspected witch offers assistance with the urgent hay harvest before the localized storm.

notes.label: Nä-näi! mer hennt nytt z'pressiärä, mer chennet's machä ohni ych!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘No, no! We are in no hurry; we can do it without you!’; the workers' dismissive refusal provokes the warning and selective rain.
notes.anchor: Nä-näi! mer hennt nytt z'pressiärä, mer chennet's machä ohni ych!

notes.label: I weiss nitt! äs chennt de nu gleitiger chu, as iähr meinet
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I do not know! It may come more quickly than you think’; gleitiger conveys sooner or more swiftly, and the next storm makes the remark prophetic.
notes.anchor: I weiss nitt! äs chennt de nu gleitiger chu, as iähr meinet

notes.label: Heidenmüetterli
notes.text: literally a ‘little heathen mother,’ a regional label for an ancient, non-Christian, or otherworldly female being; the older variant makes her more than an ordinary human witch.

75135acbb48d09274a1d4a59ba027b157c3f1072.summary: On both sides of the road from Herzogenbuchsee to Bützberg, a beautiful beech forest extends alongside it for a quarter-hour's walk.

notes.label: Zwingherrenschloss
notes.text: literally a castle of a Zwingherr, an oppressive feudal lord who exercised coercive local power; the term casts the vanished stronghold and its still-hunting owner in the moral world of tyrannical lordship.

notes.label: Widlichorb
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a basket woven from willow or similar rods, literally a wicker basket; because such a basket should not hold water, Frau Faschte returning it full makes the object the tale’s supernatural proof, while its exact weave and form are unspecified.

notes.label: z’chilte
notes.text: the traditional Swiss practice of evening or nighttime courting visits, often involving a young man visiting a young woman at her home; here the maid intends to continue all night, but the story does not describe who she visits or the precise local rules of the custom.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally ‘Lady Fast’ or ‘Mrs. Fasting,’ an uncanny female personification connected here with a night that should be kept ritually safe; the text does not make clear whether she represents Lent, a particular fast day, or an older seasonal being.

notes.label: Prattig
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a printed calendar or popular almanac used to identify dates and observances; here it warns about Frau Faschte’s night, though the exact almanac and wording are not given.

eb9ce6cd8f8a43e54718669c026811fcea9ac2ee.summary: In the Furka mountains between Ursern and the Upper Valais, one sometimes encounters patches of snow that look as red as though soaked with red wine, and the color reaches fairly deep beneath the surface.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: pack-train drivers who transported goods across Alpine passes, here condemned for losses of entrusted wine.

notes.label: Saumrossen
notes.text: packhorses used by Säumer to carry barrels and other loads along mountain routes.

2d59ea48ad37556ea047c6c817c33cdc8a785ccb.summary: A woman once came to a house in Wassen and rubbed her body against the front door.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

8050630a9978184c20eb4ad02a0935acafe87a3d.summary: a) ‘Our father,’ relates a man from the Schächen valley, ‘and I and another half-grown lad from Balm had been logging over there at “bim Stei.” It may be nearly 40 years ago.

notes.label: bim Stei
notes.text: literally ‘by the stone,’ a quoted local microtoponym for the logging place; the account does not identify the particular stone or its history.

notes.label: Wyssä Gand
notes.text: a local place-name whose second element, Gand, denotes a slope or tract of coarse rock, scree, or rubble; the spelling is retained because the exact named terrain is not identified more narrowly.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine German term for a slope, field, or tract of scree and coarse rock; here it is the place where the boys rest and imagine confronting the witch.

notes.label: d’Bäch
notes.text: literally ‘the streams’ in Uri dialect and presented in quotation marks as a local terrain designation; the account does not identify which watercourses or tract the speakers mean.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Risel
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a fine but driven fall of rain or precipitation; here it develops into a heavy downpour after the woman passes.

notes.label: Boden
notes.text: literally ‘ground’ or ‘level land’; here it is a shortened local designation for Urnerboden, the high valley floor below the Klausen Pass.

notes.label: Schallächüeh
notes.text: an Uri dialect compound for a bell cow, likely a prominent cow wearing a Schelle; here it is Hanssepp’s finest cow, but the animal’s precise herd role is not stated.

notes.label: Prigel
notes.text: the source’s local name for a log causeway across the swamp on Urnerboden, explicitly glossed there as a Prügelweg.

notes.label: Biächäli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive meaning a little book or booklet; the accused witch has it sewn secretly between the lining and outer cloth of her skirt, but its contents are not described.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: a Swiss German term for cream, especially rich cream skimmed from milk; here the stranger drinks it and mysteriously pours some into a closed coat.

notes.label: Ambäck
notes.text: a local word for a bench, ledge, or seat in front of the Alp hut; its exact construction is not stated.

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: an Uri form of Tschoope, a traditional short coat, jacket, or smock; here it is black, buttoned shut, and nevertheless receives the poured cream without leaking.

notes.label: Schwirrli
notes.text: literally a little whirring, swirling, or sudden stroke in Uri dialect; in the woman’s threat it appears to mean an uncanny blow, spell, or burst of weather, but the exact idiom is uncertain.

a3d932f6444b4eff709b05457dd920bf2861ad3c.summary: A woman once lived in a village in the canton of Glarus. This woman was a witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

bff325e22528514464ac921ba7ef7ac70eb1afd6.summary: who often occupied herself with making weather was popularly called the ‘Nägälimüetter’—the Carnation Mother.

notes.label: Nägälimüetter
notes.text: literally ‘Carnation Mother’ in Uri dialect, the local byname of the weather-making woman; the source explains the literal sense but not why carnations are associated with her.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small Gaden—typically a barn, shed, storehouse, or simple farm outbuilding; the witch lodges there, but its exact use is not described.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Ryffen
notes.text: an Uri river-landform word for a reef, gravel bar, stony shallows, or exposed strip within the Reuss; the source does not determine its exact composition or whether it was above water.

e7f639ce0e5779e0b20e2c9baca97b8b1bc10aac.summary: 1. A Wybervolch in Schattdorf had a reputation—Gott b'hiätis darvor!—for being an old witch.

notes.label: Wybervolch
notes.text: an older, dismissive Alemannic expression for a woman or female person, literally ‘woman-folk’; the collector’s neuter grammar and pejorative tone are culturally significant and are preserved.

notes.label: Gott b'hiätis darvor!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘God preserve us from it!’; it is a protective spoken aside against the danger of naming someone as a witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Da wett-i etz doch äu nu lüegä, was d'r diä chennt a'tüe?
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘Now I would just like to see what she can do to me’; the shoemaker’s inward challenge provokes the infestation.
notes.anchor: Da wett-i etz doch äu nu lüegä, was d'r diä chennt a'tüe?

notes.label: Bim Eich, das isch än alti Häx!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘By my oath, that is an old witch!’; Bim Eich is a softened oath, and even the unspoken judgment is followed by lice.
notes.anchor: Bim Eich, das isch än alti Häx!

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a little, slight, or humble woman; it can sound familiar or belittling depending on context, and here marks the wandering stranger.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: the diminutive of Wybervolch, an older and dismissive term for a female person; its smallness does not make the suspected witch harmless.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Mänenen
notes.text: a regional plural for heads of livestock, probably pack or draft animals in this journey over the Klausen; the passage does not identify the animals’ species securely.

notes.label: Weibervolk
notes.text: an older, dismissive expression for a woman or female person, literally ‘woman-folk’; the source treats the uncanny traveler grammatically as neuter.

notes.label: vergaumen
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to watch, tend, supervise, or look after someone; the family cannot leave the stranger unwatched while everyone works in the field.

notes.label: der Brügg
notes.text: Johann Baumann’s local byname or house-name, literally something like ‘the one of the bridge’; the source does not explain the precise reference.

1ad26ebbd8f05535bd89eb627a2a8367d744ce99.summary: In ancient times a farmer lived in Ems; he was called “Gschworne Christof.” He had a maidservant from the Oberland.

notes.label: Gschworne Christof
notes.text: dialect for “Sworn Christof”; Gschworne suggests a man who had taken an official oath, such as a local sworn officer or juror, though the tale does not state his precise office.

notes.label: Mayensäss
notes.text: a seasonal mountain-pasture holding with meadow and buildings, used between the valley farm and the higher summer Alp; Christof goes there for the hay harvest.

notes.label: Mensch
notes.text: in this older regional context, a familiar and often disparaging label for a young woman or female servant; Christof uses it while secretly spying on his maid rather than as the neutral modern word “person.”

notes.label: Hexenmensch
notes.text: a historical pejorative meaning approximately “witch-woman” or “witch-creature”; it records the accusation used to justify the maid’s arrest and execution, not a neutral modern description.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a Bernese name for a nightmare or chest-pressing night spirit; here people obstruct it with sharp objects, while its exact imagined form and the name’s literal origin remain uncertain.

notes.label: Chlungere
notes.text: a Bernese regional name for masked or costumed carnival figures who performed ritual house visits; the source identifies their protective sweeping role at Belp, but the term’s precise costume and literal derivation are not explained.

3f90dd4249ceb74471de08612daf0bc8cd561ba8.summary: Frau Pfarrer B . . in N . . . once related:

notes.label: Frau Pfarrer
notes.text: a historical German-speaking Swiss form of address for a pastor’s wife; the initials and place are deliberately anonymized in the source.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical German spelling used here for Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Anneli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Anna, with -li marking smallness or endearment.

b10121464c0860a8f3b693c457dc210dfebf543e.summary: In the southern part of the canton of Fribourg lies the Bellegarde Valley, watered by the Jaunbach.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its associated livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; Les grosses Combes is the named working landscape afflicted by the snakes.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: a seasonal pasture station, level, or group of working huts within an Alp; the source says the snakes entered it but does not identify a single building, and the exact physical sense varies regionally.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd product made from whey left after ordinary cheesemaking; it is listed separately from bread and cheese among the dairy foods stolen by the snakes.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; here they are the Alpine community that asks the monastery for help, although their individual duties are not specified.

notes.label: Schlossen
notes.text: a regional German word for large hailstones; the story’s nut-sized Schlossen form part of the supernatural storm and are said, unusually, to be mixed with human hair.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the specialist Alpine dairymen and herders responsible for cattle and milk work on a high seasonal pasture; the tale does not distinguish their individual roles within the group.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Mönchstritt
notes.text: literally ‘monk’s step’ or ‘monk’s footprint,’ the footprint-like mark in limestone attributed to Abbot Hugo and presented as material proof of both the miracle and the annual vow.

notes.label: Zatte
notes.text: a Bernese agricultural word for a row or swath of cut crop laid by mowing; here an unseen force lifts the Zatte far through the air during harvest, though the exact crop is not identified.

notes.label: Tauner
notes.text: a land-poor rural laborer or day worker in the older Bernese social order, often dependent on hired agricultural work; the narrator cites such a man as an eyewitness, but gives no detail about his household status.

notes.label: Vierbeiner
notes.text: literally ‘four-legged one’; in ordinary German it can mean any quadruped, but here the narrator uses it as the unexplained name of a human-headed animal apparition.

notes.label: Vetter Üel
notes.text: dialect for ‘Cousin Ueli’; Vetter can mean a male cousin or a familiar older kinsman, and Üel is a local form of Ueli or Ulrich.

notes.label: Grünge
notes.text: the dialect place-name from which Vetter Üel walks; it likely represents Grünen, but the translation retains the storyteller's exact form.

notes.label: Widigschbärg
notes.text: the dialect destination or direction named in the account; its exact standard spelling is uncertain, so the source form is retained.

notes.label: Marchstei
notes.text: Swiss German for a boundary stone, the liminal landmark beside which the Vierbeiner appears.

123c16903f125061b538615b20311af0c597b20a.summary: Near the Scharten Cave by Eppenwil, there is said to have been a so-called gate in a pasture that opened and closed by itself for everyone who passed through.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Alrune
notes.text: the feminine form used in this Bernese legend for a mysterious money-producing toad kept in a cellar; it draws on mandrake and household-spirit traditions but here denotes the animal-shaped spirit specifically.

notes.label: Chrott
notes.text: Swiss German for a toad, usually standard German Kröte; here ‘stuffing the Chrott’ is an obscure euphemism for tending or feeding the money-producing Alrune.

notes.label: Alraun
notes.text: the German name for the mandrake root and for a carved root-spirit believed to bring wealth; the explanatory passage distinguishes this older plant tradition from the tale's feminine Alrune toad.

notes.label: alrûna
notes.text: an Old Germanic form cited by the source for secret-working mythical beings; it is presented as an etymological relative of Alraun, though the passage does not settle the folklore's historical development.

notes.label: rûna
notes.text: the Gothic word glossed in the source as ‘secret’; it supplies the proposed hidden-working sense behind the Alraun name rather than naming a creature in this story.

notes.label: Heckemännchen
notes.text: literally a ‘breeding little man,’ a small figure credited with multiplying or producing money; here it is compared with a strangely formed root found while watering.

notes.label: Alräunchen
notes.text: a diminutive of Alraun for a little mandrake-root figure or spirit; here it is another comparison for the root found by Bergresli.

notes.label: Gäldschiesser
notes.text: literally ‘money-shooter,’ the dialect name within that expression for something that produces money; its tone is colloquial and figurative rather than a formal creature category.

notes.label: Mi sött e Gäldschiesser ha
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for roughly ‘one ought to have a money-shooter’; the source interprets this wish for an inexhaustible producer of cash as a survival of Alraun belief.

notes.label: Brueder Chlaus
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘Brother Klaus,’ the popular Swiss name of Nicholas of Flüe; prophetic sayings were traditionally attributed to this national saint and hermit.

notes.label: Dokter Fuschti
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘Doctor Faust,’ the legendary scholar-magician bound to the devil; the altered local name places the international Faust tradition in oral Swiss storytelling.

notes.label: Tüfel
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘devil’; he serves and ultimately captures Dokter Fuschti in this compressed local Faust legend.

notes.label: Mäss
notes.text: a regional measure of capacity, related to Mass; Fuschti scatters one Mäss of millet as an impossible sorting task, but the exact historical volume is uncertain.

b837aefd92f20cf6358b9ec52a83dcea1720d775.summary: Beneath the Weisse Nossen above Butzen opposite Amsteg—namely in the Breiten Wald near the Schmidigberg1—a treasure is said to be buried.

notes.label: Gutterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small bottle or flask; an unidentified object attached below it is tapped three times as a treasure test, but the device and its contents are not described.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the older Swiss political order, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; the footnote identifies Heinrich Dietlin by this title.

4bc7244cd5c41c5c7116ff45d2b18a9fb647916f.summary: The farmer at Katzensternen in Oberintschi lay in wait for a marmot. It came and peered out of its burrow.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source’s regional name for the marmot’s hat; elsewhere in the corpus it denotes a conspicuous hat, but its exact historical shape and the word’s literal derivation are uncertain.

notes.label: Chüeiher
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German occupational name formed from Chüe, ‘cows,’ for a cowherd or cattle keeper; here the man also practices book magic and flies on a broom, so the ordinary job title acquires a sorcerous role.
The dialect verb pföselet was rendered as snuffles; it can suggest wheezing, fussing, or making an unattractive breathing noise.

50f4835ced8ded9c4d391c8d896fa9fa14e5ede5.summary: I once heard a story told about the Toggeli. But all I remember is that it transformed itself into a little pig, a horse, and a cow.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name for a bogey, oppressive spirit, or uncanny being; here the fragment remembers only its transformations into a little pig, a horse, and a cow, so its exact nature and relation to nightmare spirits remain uncertain.

c4635221cd00300f1d5dd3bee8c046710ec081d0.summary: About the Vögeli in the Tree

notes.label: Vögeli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Vogel, ‘bird’; here the little bird is recognized as the murdered boy's living soul or soul-carrier.

notes.label: Trögli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Trog, meaning a small chest, trough, or lidded storage box; here it contains apples and its lid becomes the murder weapon, while the exact household form is not specified.

notes.label: Guggus
notes.text: a dialect rendering of the cuckoo's call and, by extension, the cuckoo itself; here the alternate refrain supports the editor's interpretation of the bird as the boy's soul-animal.

notes.label: Wärber
notes.text: Bernese dialect for military recruiters, here men enlisting those present into the king’s guard under a coercive midnight rule; the story does not identify the king or whether the recruitment was formally lawful.

notes.label: Chimpetti
notes.text: a Bernese childbed observance or gathering connected with a recent birth, apparently held or paid for at the inn; the brief account assumes the custom and does not specify whether it was a meal, drinking party, or other celebration.

notes.label: Chimpettima
notes.text: literally the ‘Chimpetti man,’ apparently the new father or male host responsible for the childbed gathering and its payment; his exact family relationship is implied rather than stated.

b917ac8109ac131e6bef6b1233b9360b3278ec61.summary: Witches—or, as an 80-year-old woman from Seedorf calls them, Pfaffenkellerinnen—must cause five shillings' worth of damage every day; they have this commission from the Evil One.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Pfaffenkellerinnen
notes.text: a historical, disparaging regional label for clergymen's female housekeepers, often implying illicit partners; this informant extends the term to witches, so it should not be read as a neutral modern occupational name.

notes.label: So nimm's i Gottsnamä
notes.text: a dialect almsgiving formula meaning ‘Then take it in God's name’; a disguised witch is believed unable or unwilling to accept a gift explicitly offered under divine protection.

90d768444ad795997c026662a4979f9f14617334.summary: Frisians once came into the land and established their homes in Frutigen. One day, a Frisian boy was grazing his herd in this region.

notes.label: Bergstatt
notes.text: a mountain holding, enclosure, or shelter where livestock can be secured; the source does not describe its exact structure.

notes.label: Geissbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘goat spring’ or ‘goat fountain,’ named in the legend for the spring where the herder finds his missing goats.

notes.label: Adelboden
notes.text: the settlement and valley name, literally suggestive of ‘noble ground’; the tale associates its naming with the valley's exceptionally rich pasture, but does not present a linguistic derivation in detail.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally ‘goat boy,’ a boy who herds goats; the term identifies the young discoverer whose dream foreshadows the future church.

c06f9c93145933fa35350bf9bd9d443cc2efc89c.summary: Among the more remote Alpine pastures behind Escholzmatt was one that had long been shunned and ill-reputed.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine dairy hut where a Senn tends cattle and makes cheese during the high-pasture season; here it is fully operating despite having no visible workers.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here the abandoned-looking Alp continues to be supernaturally managed.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gäumer
notes.text: a regional word for a keeper, attendant, or person who watches over something; here the intruder jokingly addresses an imagined worker behind the cheese cauldron, and the precise occupational nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: halbviertliges Mäss
notes.text: a small traditional measure, literally a ‘half-quarter Mäss’ and therefore likely an eighth-sized vessel or quantity; the exact local capacity varied, and here the object accompanies a shovel and light into the cellar.

notes.label: Wandler
notes.text: literally ‘one who walks’ or ‘wanderer,’ used here for the restless spirit performing its penance; it implies a revenant or haunting being without naming a single fixed folklore type.

e8d4a2ad0c93159f645a36a1c891285a82947507.summary: Two witches—or, according to others, three—on the Vierschröt intended to break off a piece of the rock and smash the chapel in the Riedertal with it.

notes.label: Witch accusations

notes.label: Noch, Lunnä, stosset!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Again, Lunnä, push!’; Lunnä appears to be the name or byname of one witch, but the source gives no further identification.

notes.label: Ich mag nimmä, d'Agäthä schrytt.
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘I cannot anymore; Agatha is crying out’; Agatha personifies the chapel bell—probably through its saintly dedication—and its ringing breaks the witches’ effort.

2c8fbdac4de7f6600e127cb7eca0898fc3fa7630.summary: Agatha von Hohnau was a virtuous and beautiful maiden who flourished in the aforementioned castle about 430 years ago.

a0c77d0db98d7f43c72bf35d36187dfae8622fdf.summary: Nesa of Brunberg had strayed from the path of simple and pure conduct upon which she had seen her parents and siblings walk.

notes.label: Nesa
notes.text: the name used throughout the source text for the woman called Agnes in the title; the difference is retained rather than silently regularized.

notes.label: Fetzwaldung
notes.text: the source's first spelling for the woodland around Brunberg in which Nesa hunts; later passages use Fesswald, so the historical variation is preserved.

notes.label: Fesswald
notes.text: the local forest-name used for the haunted crossroads where Nesa dies and remains bound as a spirit.

notes.label: Fessfräulein
notes.text: literally the ‘little lady’ or ‘maiden of the Fesswald,’ the local name for Nesa's misleading apparition; Fräulein carries an older sense of an unmarried young woman rather than the modern form of address.

0c13326b26caa4ed1fec603cc9a892983ef04951.summary: There, where the dark rock cave known as "the Hunter's Hut"—a refuge for chamois hunters—opens wild and eerie in a deep icy crevasse of the Aar Glacier between the Lauteraarhorn and the Wetterhörner, was the resting place of Ahasuerus whenever, on his eternal wandering, he came to Switzerland, the…

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

b97893e8d11b2f0c1b45bfa01881bad539bae7be.summary: When Ahasver crossed the Alps for the first time on his eternal wandering, shortly after his curse, he chose the Grimsel as his crossing place.

notes.label: Ahasver
notes.text: the German name Ahasverus used for the Christian folkloric figure commonly called the Wandering Jew, cursed to wander until the end of time; the figure belongs to a historically anti-Jewish legend tradition, not to Jewish teaching.

notes.label: Grimsel
notes.text: the high Alpine pass connecting the Haslital with the upper Rhone region; the legend uses repeated crossings there to imagine enormous environmental change.

notes.label: Maienwand
notes.text: the named steep slope on the Grimsel route; it marks the threshold at which Ahasver discovers the transformed landscape.

notes.label: Haslital
notes.text: the Hasli valley in the Bernese Oberland on the north side of the Grimsel, toward which Ahasver descends.

0695001d3bb499f1bb4cc1ce74e8ed90466ec328.summary: Old Mingli im Fäld was also a sort of half-sorcerer; he could drive away Muschelä, boggermint!

notes.label: Muschelä
notes.text: an uncertain St. Gallen dialect word for creatures or pests the sorcerer could drive away; the exact animal or phenomenon cannot be identified confidently from context.

notes.label: boggermint
notes.text: an emphatic dialect exclamation or mild oath reinforcing the claim about Mingli’s power; its precise derivation and force are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations

notes.label: Trüllwind
notes.text: a Swiss dialect word for a whirling wind or dust devil, imagined here as the place where witches dance.

notes.label: zum Pfister
notes.text: retained because the dialect/OCR form is uncertain; context strongly suggests ‘out through the window,’ contrasting improper disposal of combed-out hair with burning it in the fire.

f6f610715ba94da0451ce4d4ce2f0ece6743532c.summary: About 6–7 years ago in the municipality of Göschenen, a Geissbub repeatedly encountered at a particular spot near Abfrutt ‘än altä tügg-lychätä-grawä Ma i bluttä Fiëssä, ohni Tschopä’—‘an old dark-and-light-gray man, barefoot and without a jacket.’ He came to believe it was an arme Seele and, on…

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally a goat boy, a young Alpine herder charged with tending goats.

notes.label: än altä tügg-lychätä-grawä Ma i bluttä Fiëssä, ohni Tschopä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘an old dark-and-light-gray man, barefoot and without a jacket’; the compounded color description is unusual and is not narrowed beyond its literal elements.
notes.anchor: än altä tügg-lychätä-grawä Ma i bluttä Fiëssä, ohni Tschopä

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for a departed soul undergoing purgatorial suffering and awaiting release through prayer or restitution.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosed property boundary; here it is moved a handbreadth each year to steal common land.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land whose members possess shared use rights; moving a private boundary into it is both theft from the community and a religious offense in the legend.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Göttigeld
notes.text: money given by or associated with a Götti, a godfather; the goat boy sacrifices his own godparent gift money to help pay for the Masses.

aed8073b09aecb75f37e25eebb87b94f450cb0dd.summary: In the mountains near Flums lives a giant called the Alpheuer. When the weather changes, he can be heard above, shouting for joy and yodeling.

notes.label: Alpheuer
notes.text: literally suggestive of an ‘Alp haymaker,’ the local name of a mountain giant whose calls and yodels announce a change in weather; the brief source does not explain whether the name describes an occupation or preserves an older being-name.

46b06d6684dc048b6442221b108c0780201c6d77.summary: Several hunters came to an abandoned dairyman’s hut on the Oberalp near Urseren.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

5f7c40241bd4d640d5abb72138a045c8f47e4cf2.summary: It is well known that much magic was formerly practiced with the Alraun root.

notes.label: Alraun
notes.text: a shortened historical form of Alraune used here both for the magical root and for the catlike being; the passage deliberately shifts between plant, carved charm, and animal.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: the German mandrake and, by extension, a magically potent figure made from its anthropomorphic root; the Werdenberg belief unusually also imagines the Alraun as a real catlike household luck-bringer, so ‘mandrake’ alone does not cover the full sense.

notes.label: Alti Brüch
notes.text: literally ‘old customs’ in Bernese dialect, Alti Brüch labels the protective livestock practices and the collector’s interpretation of them as diminished sacrifice; their age and historical continuity are uncertain.

notes.label: Schofhirt
notes.text: Schofhirt is the dialect form of ‘shepherd,’ cited as advising that docking lambs’ tails protects them from birds; the species of bird and the belief’s exact rationale are unspecified.

707dfd02f77ac0044c332d4ba9f3ce1cc561d259.summary: Aluegen isch gnue! — A Look Is Enough!

notes.label: Aluegen isch gnue!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘A look is enough!’; it summarizes the belief that the evil eye can harm a child without touch or spoken spell.

notes.label: drei höchschte Näme
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the three highest names,’ a protective written formula placed beneath a child’s head; the source does not identify which three sacred names were used.

3bc62e221ff18ce66c41ecbb6385b5451d167b3c.summary: a) While the bubonic plague raged, a man on the Guggern in Iberg cut off his swelling as soon as he developed it, bored a hole in the wall, put the swelling inside, and nailed the opening shut.

5e92cbeb03def887d6e11f7de8813c3af7fec551.summary: In olden times, people always bored Wasser-Teuchel—wooden-log water pipes—from only one side, and so the Teuchel were naturally very short.

notes.label: Wasser-Teuchel
notes.text: hollowed or bored wooden logs used as water pipes; this traditional Alpine water-conduit technology explains why boring from both ends is the Männlein’s guarded craft secret.

notes.label: Teuchel
notes.text: regional German for a bored wooden pipe or conduit, especially one carrying water; English ‘wooden pipe’ gives the function but not the locally named craft object.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ used here for the wild, dwarf-like forest beings who possess superior craft knowledge; the text leaves their more exact supernatural identity unspecified.

notes.label: volle Bare
notes.text: literally a full feeding trough or manger, used here as an image for growing up with constant abundance and therefore not knowing hardship; the regional noun Bare can refer to a trough or feeding rack.

notes.label: Frau Faschten
notes.text: literally suggestive of Lady Fast or Lady Lent, the named supernatural woman who warns the washerwomen to stop their late-night labor; her precise identity and connection to fasting-season or work-taboo traditions vary regionally.

notes.label: Chornritere
notes.text: a Bernese German grain sieve, handed to Frau Faschten as an impossible vessel for fetching water and thus as a delaying trick; the construction and local spelling of such sieves vary.

848119caf82b217fbc48460a93252204d812fccf.summary: a) A fahrender Schüler once came to Amsteg. With a mysterious air, he spoke of the treasures of the Bristenstock and hinted at its wealth of gold.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar,’ a traditional folkloric figure credited with occult learning, treasure knowledge, and magical power rather than simply an itinerant student.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: uff dry goldig Stitt
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘upon three golden pillars’; retaining the boast preserves the repeated number word and the traveler’s claim that the gold-rich Bristenstock deserves a fabulous support.

notes.label: Stäg
notes.text: the Uri dialect short form associated here with Amsteg and its inhabitants; the repeated place-name anchors the taunting prophecy.

notes.label: Schinderloch
notes.text: literally a ‘flayer’s’ or ‘knacker’s hole,’ a harsh insult applied to Stäg in the verse; it suggests a wretched place rather than naming a documented occupation there.

notes.label: Stägerloch
notes.text: literally the ‘hole of the people of Stäg,’ an insulting variant name for Amsteg in the verse.

notes.label: Bristä-See
notes.text: the Uri dialect name for Lake Bristen in the verse; its waters are imagined sweeping away the people of Stäg.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally a ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd; in variant c he hears the disembodied taunting prophecy.

notes.label: Sinderloch
notes.text: the spelling in a variant of Schinderloch; its exact force may be affected by dialect or transmission, but it serves as the same insulting rhyme-name for Stäg.

notes.label: Chärschäläbach
notes.text: the local Uri name for the stream more often standardized as the Kärstelenbach; the verse imagines it sweeping Amsteg away.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: literally a ‘boundary stone,’ a marked stone defining a territorial or property border; here it stands at the municipal boundary where the traveler meets the apparition.

notes.text: Franz Zgraggen’s local byname; the source gives no derivation or reason for it, so it is retained without treating it as a surname.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; the abandoned hut and vacated pasture station rule out such a worker as the figure’s identity.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a seasonal Alpine grazing level or station with its working ground and often huts; this high, wild one has already been cleared at the end of the pasture season.

notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

c39efdf68430d8485d712c27173dcc0b0472fc73.summary: Our father († 1923, 84 years old)—he often told this story—was looking out for the neighbor's kids one evening and was standing at the Riggäport at Gufern in the Maderanertal.

notes.label: Riggäport
notes.text: an exact Uri place or farm-feature term at Gufern, probably a gate or passage on a ridge; the source does not describe its construction, so the physical sense remains uncertain.

notes.label: hählä Schachä
notes.text: an Uri dialect place-description for the named patch of Schachen ground, likely open, light, or sparse riverside woodland; the source gives it as a local designation and does not define it.

notes.label: Ruossdiele
notes.text: literally a soot-darkened loft floor or boards above the hearth area of an Alpine hut; the apparition climbs the ladder and lies down there, though the hut's exact interior arrangement is not described.

notes.label: Tuolen im Nätsch
notes.text: an Uri dialect phrase for two distinct hollows, impressions, or sleeping places in the bedding; the visible paired marks convince the narrator that the ghost slept beside his father, but the exact meanings of Tuolen and Nätsch remain regionally uncertain.

notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply a mountain summit; the wanderer ends the night far above Attinghausen in the remote Waldnachter Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock-and-dairy working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; here the entire valuable pasture property is exchanged.

notes.text: the German name for the Alpine valley also known in Italian as Val Bregaglia; Bondo lies within it.

notes.label: Bergellerin
