f02e1ad61d9307f786d0b7f4f7f02a7a6a428949.summary: In olden times, the people of Gundis, subjects of the Duke of Savoy, quarreled for a long while with the citizens of Savièse over possession of the Hochalpe Berzé in the Sanetsch-Tale.

notes.label: Hochalpe Berzé
notes.text: the named high summer pasture at the center of the ownership dispute; Hochalpe emphasizes its high-altitude grazing land.

notes.label: Sanetsch-Tale
notes.text: the German form for the Sanetsch Valley on the linguistic and political borderlands above Savièse; Tal means ‘valley.’

notes.label: Savièser
notes.text: inhabitants of Savièse, used collectively for the community defending its pasture rights.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a high summer pasture and its pastoral holding, not simply an Alpine mountain; ownership of this grazing resource drives the conflict.

notes.label: Oberwallis
notes.text: Upper Valais, the upper and predominantly German-speaking part of the canton whose people reinforce Savièse in the legend.

notes.label: Lecktasche
notes.text: a shepherd's belt pouch, probably for carrying salt or other material given to livestock to lick; the precise local form is uncertain.

7a91fdaf1bec1d07e7fc8199d911ba39f281c2bc.summary: The Rabenschnabel, a rock formation by the Bannwalde above Altdorf, threatened during a terrible storm to fall upon the town.

notes.label: Bannwalde
notes.text: the source's historical inflected form of Bannwald, a protected forest maintained above Alpine settlements to guard them against rockfall, avalanches, and similar hazards; its protective role is essential to Altdorf's landscape.

3a0cc10fc997b1fe1c827eb74c7326a02528fe33.summary: 1. A fahrender Schüler said that a precious treasure was hidden in the Ochsenfad behind Göschenen.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a wandering scholar or student, a recurring folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; here he announces the conditions under which the Ochsenfad treasure will appear.

notes.label: Trychelgeiss
notes.text: a goat wearing a Trychel, the characteristic hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; one variant requires this treasure-revealing animal to be entirely white.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: Swiss German for the large cauldron used in Alpine cheesemaking; in the last two variants a golden Chessi or one filled with money serves as the treasure container.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: a goat boy or young goatherd, a recognizable role in Alpine pastoral life; the poor Geissbub is destined to find the golden Chessi.

notes.label: arigs
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German adjective meaning strange, uncanny, peculiar, or unusual; here it characterizes a fir tree that plays music while people try to fell it, and no single English adjective carries every shade.

notes.label: Tannli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Tanne, a fir tree; here the little fir stands beside an old dancing place and mysteriously produces music until it lies on the ground.

notes.label: Schlegelachs
notes.text: a heavy felling or striking axe, literally suggesting a mallet-like axe; here it succeeds in knocking the enchanted Tannli from its stump after the saw cannot make it fall.

c6a739e36e7c1c58c1e3643dc30931472d7cc11b.summary: Erdmännchen dwell in the Grossgruobis-Balm, and formerly they showed themselves very helpful to the inhabitants there.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like subterranean beings who can interact with human households; here one seeks skilled human help and offers an apparently worthless supernatural payment.

notes.label: Grossgruobis-Balm
notes.text: the named rock shelter or cave where the Erdmännchen live; Balm is an Alpine regional term for an overhang or shallow cavern, while the compound’s first element is a local place name.

notes.label: Talern
notes.text: the source’s dative plural of Taler, a historical large silver coin; the midwife imagines one or two bright coins but no mint, period, or value is specified.

notes.label: Wie meh dass zatterist
notes.text: dialect for ‘the more you scatter’; it refers both to the coals she throws away and to the supernatural wealth thereby lost.

notes.label: We minder dass hatterist.
notes.text: dialect for ‘the less you will have’; the rhyme completes the warning, although its grammar is intentionally preserved in the source’s regional form.

24e7748995b5aa3c659f5d7c54fe6b07cf800370.summary: Jost Gisler is a Senne, a chamois hunter, and also the village innkeeper of Unterschächen in Uri.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and often cheesemaking on a high pasture; Gisler combines this seasonal pastoral occupation with hunting, innkeeping, and guiding.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Wilden Mannli
notes.text: the source’s inflected dialect phrase for a “little wild man,” one of the Alpine wild or earth-dwelling folk; here he escorts the midwife into the rock, but the tale does not classify him more precisely.

notes.label: Herdwibli
notes.text: a dialect name for the little subterranean woman in childbirth, contextually close to Erdweibchen; the spelling and literal derivation are uncertain, so a more specific creature label would overstate the source.

notes.label: verzatterist
notes.text: a dialect verb meaning to scatter, spill, or squander; in the warning rhyme it predicts that the more leaves the midwife throws away, the less enchanted reward she will retain, while the exact shade between scattering and wasting is ambiguous.

notes.label: Erdweibchen
notes.text: literally a “little earth woman,” a subterranean or rock-dwelling female being in regional folklore; here she needs a human midwife, and the diminutive does not establish her exact size.

677be68ff58730af5c88dfe43adf95e5dceef0c0.summary: In the area of Sumiswald, Wasen, and Hornbach, people tell of a green rider on a snake.

notes.label: Maitschi
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German diminutive for girls or young women; here it refers familiarly to the farm's young washerwomen.

notes.label: Hülfterchen
notes.text: a diminutive regional word for a small saddle or riding harness; the green man first wears it around his own body and later puts it on the flood-serpent, so its precise construction is left unclear.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally a “little earth man,” a subterranean dwarf or earth spirit in German-speaking Swiss folklore; it should not be confused with the modern German use of Erdmännchen for a meerkat.

notes.label: Müschen
notes.text: a diminutive regional word for a small serving of soft mash or purée; here the enchanted peas make a nourishing pea mash that renews itself as long as two peas remain.

ea029086b9bf29c90f9327b4468275cb61708ddf.summary: The dwarf folk are otherwise distinguished by their diligent labor, but the females can also ‘fail.’

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal livestock pasture and its herding settlement, where the stray cow and dwarf woman are found.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fräuli
notes.text: Swiss diminutive for a little woman, here a silent wild female dwarf.

notes.label: Tschuppen
notes.text: a small fir or dense young conifer branched all the way to the ground, providing the being's shelter.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male workers on an Alp who tend livestock and perform dairying and farm labor.

notes.label: Weiblein
notes.text: an older diminutive for a little woman, used for the same idle dwarf as Fräuli.

notes.label: Amt
notes.text: the local authority or administrative office to which the herders intend to report their unwanted guest.

4add5d90eae24bc572030b4b2f9a669f048846e1.summary: Beyond the Schilz ravine from the village of Flums, in the Staudenrüsch on the Ruhstein, a godmother returning from a great Göttiwein left the child she had carried to baptism lying there.

notes.label: Göttiwein
notes.text: literally ‘godfather wine,’ a christening celebration or its festive drink provided by godparents; here it denotes the large baptismal feast from which the godmother was returning, though the precise local custom is not specified.

af99f5bced7d6981b04b6c9ddcc32f2298f95082.summary: In Klosters-Dörfli a man owned a house in which he had sitting a thoroughly curious, but still more exceedingly inconvenient, guest whom he was quite unable to remove and who, on top of that, was shameless enough to demand a bowl of milk every evening for his labor as a tormenting spirit.

notes.label: Klosters-Dörfli
notes.text: literally the “little village” section of Klosters, used here as the house’s location.

notes.label: Montafuner
notes.text: a person from the Montafon valley; this outsider advises moving the timber house.

notes.label: abzimmern
notes.text: to dismantle a timber structure piece by piece so that it can be rebuilt elsewhere.

notes.label: abgezimmert
notes.text: the past-participle form of abzimmern; the house has been dismantled down to its foundation when the spirit emerges.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally “little man,” the diminutive description of the small angry house spirit.

notes.label: Kellerbutz
notes.text: a cellar Butz—a goblin, bogey, or household spirit dwelling below the house.

notes.label: Urähni
notes.text: a Swiss German kinship term for a remote forebear, commonly a great-grandfather or great-grandparent; the story does not identify the ancestor more precisely.

notes.label: Butz
notes.text: a regional name for a goblin, bogey, or domestic spirit; this one is troublesome but also protects the owner’s property.

notes.label: pösselte
notes.text: an obscure regional verb for the spirit’s retaliatory activity in the house; context establishes noisy or troublesome haunting, but not its exact action.

11eb49386803084af2195b0a85b6f3ed4589e32a.summary: In 1531, most of the population of the Sarganserland converted to the new faith, as did Abbot Jakob of Pfäfers.

notes.label: About this telling

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ba689683c17d4c080a6a5126fb9f9315b8b1fc2f.summary: Filomena was a respectable seamstress. She had a sweetheart named Giovanni, a handsome young man who seemed to be a wealthy gentleman.

notes.label: About this telling

b6001fe108ed0cb45dc0bf47f710bfc1e014e2c2.summary: A carpenter from Grabs once walked home from Buchs late in the evening. He had been working there.

notes.label: Studner Brückli
notes.text: literally the ‘little bridge at Studen,’ using the Alemannic diminutive -li; it is the local crossing where the subterranean black figure offers its burning hand.

14395953d9304e85f58750a240f529e013fea3d9.summary: 1. At the house of Councilor Muheim in Flüelen, an old witch came begging for milk.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Fährlisau
notes.text: a regional term for a sow kept for bearing or nursing Fährli (piglets); here it is the household's breeding sow, which the family fears will die under the witch's curse, though the source does not say whether she currently has a litter.

notes.label: Angereesle
notes.text: the regional name and verb for this remembered courtship-divination ritual involving water scooped behind the back and a spoken charm; its full procedure was already forgotten by the narrator.

notes.label: Angerees
notes.text: the being, force, or ritual name invoked in the charm to help the speaker obtain a wife; the source does not explain its origin.

notes.label: Bettschgetbrätt
notes.text: a dialect compound apparently referring to a small bedstead board, bedside board, or footboard trodden during the charm; its exact physical form is uncertain.

cdf887a24f482e46487389fecaaed4e5318d0378.summary: On the Wildenberg Alp, an evil spirit once appeared in the middle of the night.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person working or staying on an Alp, especially an Alpine herder or dairy worker; the afflicted man belongs to the seasonal high-pasture community.

notes.label: Angetan
notes.text: literally ‘done to’ or ‘afflicted,’ a folk expression for harm imposed through bewitchment; the unexplained swollen leg is interpreted as supernatural injury rather than ordinary illness.

868831364f8f15356b69f4bfa5cb9514326f8e0b.summary: a) In Erpolingen and in the village of Altbüron stand two old farmhouses called Heidenhäuser.

notes.label: Heidenhäuser
notes.text: literally ‘heathen houses,’ a folk-archaeological name for farmhouses considered exceptionally old or attributed to unknown earlier inhabitants.

notes.label: Hochstud
notes.text: the tall central roof post or principal upright in a traditional timber farmhouse; the protective ox skulls were fixed to this structurally important point.

notes.label: Bresten
notes.text: an older Swiss term for disease, infirmity, or pestilence; here it denotes the threatening sickness against which the skulls were placed.

notes.label: Heidenturm
notes.text: literally ‘heathen tower,’ the traditional name of the old tower at Altishofen bearing the carved animal head.

27b58bf6e1ceeabf2b1595aa9bc6a0f21bbc7ab8.summary: Anna Vögtli, who had left her homeland of Bischofszell under evil suspicion, came in her wanderings to the Aargau parish village of Ettiswil.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

587d28d28d22e3d4f73c4f73ce7fbaf3776b7fde.summary: If one crossed the upper part of the Bärschner Alp some 60–70 years ago, one would unexpectedly come upon a dead spruce.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working landscape rather than simply a mountain; the Bärschner Alp is where herders encounter the named tree and apparition.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Annelis Grötzli
notes.text: the local name of the fallen tree associated with Anneli's haunting; Annelis means ‘Anneli's,’ while the source does not explain the precise dialect sense of Grötzli, so the complete name is retained.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman or senior herder responsible for livestock and cheese work on an Alp; his practical authority and refusal to fear the apparition drive the comic release scene.

notes.label: Anneli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Anna; here it names the dead woman both in human form and in the half-rotted stump that embodies her haunting.

6a7c3484a7c88d12f17fd91dabf8b5830e08118f.summary: Some acts of barbarity may well have been committed by individual crude and foolish peasants who knew no rules of war.

64341d3534da26dad766f0ab0201db3d98ffeb0e.summary: To the left of the road from Entlebuch to Wolhusen, an hour from the latter place, there once stood in a little wood a broad and proud old fir tree.

notes.label: heilig Tanne
notes.text: the local dialect form of ‘sacred fir tree,’ used as the particular tree’s traditional name; its perpetually clean ground and the tiny children disappearing beneath it mark it as a supernatural place.

18826021877447b170a9e374f48bf3f772fe05a5.summary: A farmer who wanted to milk his cow on the place known as the Höhe did not find her by the hut, but only after a long search, far away on a rock overgrown with alpine roses.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

337ba1e4e60add7a346ef0d66c9b94331d339449.summary: The late Antusuhans—the Hans belonging to Anton Anthanmatten—was a fine, upright man.

notes.label: Antusuhans
notes.text: a Valais Alemannic house-name meaning roughly ‘Anton’s Hans’; the parenthetical identifies him as Hans of Anton Anthanmatten, but the exact local naming convention is difficult to reproduce in English.

notes.label: Chilchuvogt
notes.text: Valais Alemannic for a church warden or parish custodian; Antusuhans holds this local church office and must attend the visiting bishop.

9078fbeb132c9681d6c1ddfdaba831d8e40ced9e.summary: a) A curious story of this kind once happened at Flüelen. There was a dance, and a pretty girl appeared there.

notes.label: Chunnsch m'r äu grad nachä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Are you coming right after me?’; in the first account the apparently casual dance-floor invitation acts as a witch’s coercive command.

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for a man’s or woman’s jacket, coat, or work smock; removing it transfers or breaks the supernatural compulsion in the first two accounts.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: the source’s historical German label for people represented as itinerant outsiders, often used pejoratively for Romani people; the account does not establish the individuals’ identity, so the charged original term is retained rather than silently treating it as a verified ethnicity.

notes.label: Chumm bald nachä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Come after us soon’; like the related title formula, it functions as a compelling command rather than an ordinary invitation.

notes.label: Mer wennt gah, chumm äu
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘We want to go; come too’; the third version presents the spoken formula as overcoming the girl’s will before she is found facing human violence.

c6c6fc85be09a1297bd8d7675cc902ffc14b6b15.summary: “Let us hear from ancient days of bold ancestors’ heroic frays, of spear-thrust and savage sword fight, of battle dust and hot blood’s mist.

notes.label: Sempacherlied
notes.text: the traditional Song of Sempach commemorating the battle and Winkelried; the source presents its opening verse but does not date that particular text.

notes.label: Sempachermarsch
notes.text: the Sempach March, a martial tune associated here with the Eidgenossen advancing into battle; the tale links it to the commemorative song without explaining their musical relationship.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades,’ the members of the developing Swiss Confederacy and their allied forces; ‘Confederates’ is the closest political sense, but the term also emphasizes sworn fellowship.

notes.label: Waldstätte
notes.text: the Forest Cantons or traditional central Swiss lands around Lake Lucerne; the four named here include Lucerne alongside Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden.

notes.label: Schultheiß
notes.text: a historical civic magistrate, often the chief official or mayor of a town; exact powers varied, and the tale applies the title at Sempach, Lucerne, and Zofingen.

notes.label: Eisenhag
notes.text: literally an ‘iron hedge,’ the densely projected wall of long spears confronting the Swiss wedge; it is a vivid battlefield image rather than a formally defined unit.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss spelling and form of Banner, a community’s or army’s battle standard whose loss carried military and civic significance.

notes.label: Retta Österreich, retta, retta!
notes.text: the source’s battle cry, approximately ‘Save Austria, save it, save it!’; its dialectal or multilingual form is preserved, and the wording is not further explained.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Bull of Uri,’ the large horn and its traditional sound associated with Uri’s forces; here its call leads the victors to Winkelried’s body.

notes.label: Walstätte
notes.text: an archaic word for the battlefield or field of the slain; despite its similar spelling, it is distinct in meaning from Waldstätte, the Forest Cantons.

10f6dd1146b9ecf2ab1a6ff5834b5cfc31f5b013.summary: In Zermatt, a mountain tract is called "Aroleid," which is said to mean sorrow caused by an Ari—a vulture or gray eagle.

notes.label: Ari
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for a large bird of prey, glossed by the source as vulture or gray eagle; the intended modern species is uncertain.

notes.label: Fäsche
notes.text: a long strip, band, or swaddling cloth hanging from the bird, signaling that it carries the infant; the exact textile item is uncertain.

6aa929f545b919128ad7af6c8b00c43c87e21d42.summary: A child of noble birth lost her parents at an early age. They left her nothing, however, except a will, which they gave to a good friend to keep until their daughter was grown, and a wonderfully beautiful dress.

notes.label: Aschengrübel
notes.text: literally an ash- or cinder-grubber, a demeaning household nickname for the soot-stained heroine and a regional name for the Cinderella figure; keeping it preserves the tale's local identity and the contrast with her noble dress.

notes.label: Rossbollen
notes.text: rounded pieces of horse dung; the coarse, dismissive word heightens the apparent worthlessness of the dwarf's gift before the remnants turn into gold.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally a “little earth man,” a dwarf-like subterranean or land-associated being in Swiss folklore; the title identifies the helpful little man with this tradition, not with the modern German word for a meerkat.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: chilte
notes.text: to spend the evening in a traditional courting visit, especially by a young man at a woman’s home; here it means lingering at such nighttime social activity on Christmas Eve.

notes.label: Kirchmeier
notes.text: a lay church administrator or treasurer responsible for parish property and accounts; the precise office varied regionally.

notes.label: Hornung
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic and German month name for February; the account is dated February 4.

notes.label: frau fastengält
notes.text: literally ‘Frau Fasten money,’ a dialect label for a seasonal payment to the schoolmaster; the account entry supplies evidence for the folk reinterpretation behind the demon’s name.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the quarterly Ember Days or Ember fasts of the church calendar; its sound was reinterpreted as Frau Fasten, giving the demon her later name.

notes.label: Zwölften
notes.text: the Twelve Days of the midwinter Christmas season, a liminal period rich in folk belief; exact regional boundaries can vary around Christmas and Epiphany.

notes.label: Kiltnacht
notes.text: a night associated with Kiltgang, the traditional practice of nighttime courting visits; here it is when Frau Fasten approaches the spinning room.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

0a177e8ee8dc2bbeb0238dab41e5f6516dd693f4.summary: Between Halbmil and Grünhag, where the great beech forest on an ancient landslide reaches down to the valley floor, an abundant spring, Saint Catherine’s Spring, rises a few steps from the country road.

notes.label: Rüfebach
notes.text: a mountain torrent and debris channel, literally a stream associated with a Rüfe; here it is the force that buried the former chapel and vineyards.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term that can denote a debris flow, the torrent carrying it, or the channel it cuts; here it is the event or flow that uncovered a bell.

fd326182c22d267db893a210d01d603f4b71a146.summary: At the Basatienwand near Sargans, one often hears calling, whimpering, and lamenting on moonlit nights.

notes.label: Basatienwand
notes.text: the locally named rock face near Sargans where the lovers fall and are heard haunting the cliffs; Wand means a steep wall or rock face, while the source does not explain Basatien’s derivation.

8d3813714c5d8a0a0b6898472915b6cd75a5df9f.summary: a) Beside the prison in Altdorf is a crossroads where the roads to Bürglen, Schattdorf, Attinghausen, and Altdorf intersect.

3268e2389cf027e2e625ff79b9fb90c6e75771cf.summary: Between the Samiklaus-Rütti and the Reesti at Bauen, on the lane to Seelisberg, people formerly saw a figure fairly often whose sex they could not tell.

notes.label: G'hirmistein
notes.text: the named stone on which the second apparition sits; G'hirmi can denote a stopping, resting, or sheltered place in regional usage, but the source does not establish the stone's exact practical function or the place-name's derivation.

notes.label: Gsangfescht
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘singing festival,’ here a district choral gathering in Madiswil.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: a dialect spelling of Galgenlölitier used in the festival verse; it means the uncanny animal-being associated with the little gallows wood.

notes.label: Galgenlölitier
notes.text: literally the ‘Galgenlöli animal,’ a demonic animal-shaped being linked with the dead, the earth, storms, and the Wild Huntsman tradition.

notes.label: Löl
notes.text: a proposed but rejected explanation of part of the creature’s name; the author says it is not the relevant word.

notes.label: Lo
notes.text: the regional word ‘forest,’ offered by the author as the root of Löli.

notes.label: Löli
notes.text: diminutive of Lo, meaning ‘little wood’ rather than a reference to the unrelated Löl.

notes.label: Galgenlöli
notes.text: literally ‘little gallows wood,’ the wooded place inhabited by the Galgenlölitier.

notes.label: Gragöri
notes.text: the proper name of the Wild Huntsman’s dog in a related local legend; no etymology is supplied.

notes.label: Zwölften
notes.text: the Twelve Days of Christmas, a liminal midwinter period often associated in Alpine tradition with returning spirits and the Wild Hunt.

dfeb33a8c44e96b5b5dbe26982ea4a8737c58b07.summary: One would never guess from the pleasant hills around Bassersdorf how haunted that region is.

notes.label: Heidenburg
notes.text: literally ‘heathen castle,’ the traditional name of the wooded hill near Bassersdorf; here it suggests an ancient pagan sacred site, although the narrator explicitly treats that history as uncertain.

notes.label: Steinmürli
notes.text: a local name meaning roughly ‘little stone wall,’ referring here to remains identified as Roman masonry and the haunted treasure site; the diminutive does not imply that the supernatural place is unimportant.

b757466b2e0fa345abf9322d0321f13d62418f6d.summary: Bad Buchen near Oberuzwil was once called ‘at the holy beeches.’ This name undoubtedly points back to a legend that has, however, been lost.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally ‘Lady Lent’ in Bernese Alemannic; the personified fasting season continues the household’s late-night weaving in the cellar.

96d22f069a529aa56f7e7c67a43338acfb4bcdbc.summary: At the Dreiangeli estate in Altdorf, perhaps some 30–40 years ago, a woman from the neighborhood often saw a priest walking back and forth at night from 11–12 o’clock with a book under his arm.

1f358e419ae2b9e0776ed5d61ca98cf1a44d3421.summary: Above the Schreia bridge, between Camperneis and Halbmil, before great floods one hears the brook being bailed out and sand being thrown at midnight, a consequence of old disputes over Schöpf-und Wuhrpflicht.

notes.label: Schöpf-und Wuhrpflicht
notes.text: the legally or customarily assigned duties to clear or bail a watercourse and to build and maintain its Wuhr, a weir, embankment, or flood defense; the haunting recalls old disputes over this shared water-management burden, whose exact allocation is not described.

e07fa5026b5984c21755657b7a9b3c87e59df65a.summary: At the Schutzenbirnbaum, between Rebstein and Balgach, a sinister black figure was also seen at night, driving the sweat of fear onto many a person's brow.

notes.label: Schutzenbirnbaum
notes.text: the traditional name of a pear tree or pear-tree site between Rebstein and Balgach; Birnbaum means ‘pear tree,’ but the local sense or origin of Schutzen is not explained by this brief account.

34cc430f6d8c903bcbed33abbdcc522c13a6f8a4.summary: It was never free of uncanny trouble at the Urnerloch. Those driving up from below very often found that the horses could not be made to go any farther there.

318bba7d7f710d22081cb584a70e0e291e27e26f.summary: From time to time in Graubünden, on the Furka between Ursern and Upper Valais, and in other places, one encounters patches of snow that look as red as though they had been soaked in red wine.

notes.label: Säumerseelen
notes.text: literally ‘muleteers’ souls,’ this name links red Alpine snow with the atoning spirits of wine carriers on pack routes; whether the color refers to a specific natural snow phenomenon is uncertain.

c13e737ea638ed50eec45b5b9462aeec01297854.summary: The Capuchins can banish spirits that become troublesome in inhabited places to a lonely spot.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Geissbachställeli
notes.text: literally ‘little Geissbach stable,’ with the Swiss German diminutive -li; here it is the remote shelter where travelers risk a night visit from the banished spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

f7b7d125cc26494e4dddda812639813943549244.summary: A young lady was banished into it and could be freed with three kisses. A farmer dared attempt it, but when after the second kiss the girl transformed into a dragon, the farmer wished to flee.

notes.label: Hügelimaidli
notes.text: literally ‘little hill maiden,’ an enchanted female figure from the cross-referenced legend; the diminutive regional form is retained because this text gives no further identification.

f06dfafcbd7c691859e6096ff10bdcd3983ef158.summary: When Conrad, Baron von Sellenbüren, once traveled with his people through the valley where Wolfenschiessen and Grafenort lie and climbed the Hennenberg, the region pleased him so well that he resolved to build a monastery for men there.

notes.label: Engelberg
notes.text: literally ‘angel mountain,’ the monastery and settlement whose name the legend explains through the heavenly singing heard by its founder.

ef671b603ff4d0a096ecade27f2ee136211cbaeb.summary: At Valendas Castle in 1452, the people sat in judgment upon Freiherr Jörg (Brun) von Räzüns.

notes.label: Freiherr
notes.text: a historical noble rank conventionally rendered as baron; the source’s title names Heinrich, while the historical narrative names Jörg (Brun), and both are preserved without silently reconciling them.

notes.label: Bund der Freiheit
notes.text: literally “League of Freedom,” the sworn alliance at Trons to which Jörg is said to have pledged himself.

notes.label: Rechberger-Fehde
notes.text: the Rechberg feud, an armed private or regional conflict through which the source says Jörg broke his vow.

notes.label: schwarzen Bundes
notes.text: the inflected form of “Black League,” described by the source as an alliance of nobles against popular freedom.

notes.label: Schamser-Fehde
notes.text: the Schams feud in which the peasants are victorious before marching through the Domleschg.

notes.label: talauswärts
notes.text: outward or down along the valley; the peasants drive the fleeing mercenaries ahead of them.

notes.label: Oberländer
notes.text: people from the Oberland or upper Rhine region of Graubünden who seize the Freiherr.

notes.label: Scharfrichter
notes.text: the public executioner charged with carrying out the death sentence.

notes.label: Blutgericht
notes.text: literally “blood court,” a court or judgment exercising capital jurisdiction; the intended execution gathering becomes a celebration.

50ce8a084edc1ae697752ad1fbccd58c3721d6d9.summary: This happened more than three hundred years ago. On an Alp in the Meien Valley called Aistner Alp, a certain Baschi Frech worked as a Senn for many years.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high seasonal pasture with its dairy buildings, here the Aistner Alp in the Meien Valley; its historical boundaries and ownership are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: a Senn is the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock, milk, butter, and cheese, Baschi’s summer occupation; his precise contractual status is uncertain.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Sennen is the plural of Senn, used for the condemned dairymen who repeat their work in winter; their identities and offenses are unspecified.

notes.label: Molken
notes.text: Molken can denote whey or, more broadly in older Alpine usage, dairy produce and cheesemaking work, neglected here by unjust Sennen; the intended scope is uncertain.

notes.label: Mithaften
notes.text: Mithaften are co-holders or partners sharing rights and produce from an Alp, among whom a dishonest Senn might distribute unequal portions; their legal arrangement is unspecified.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: Älpler are people who work seasonally on an Alp and preserve the prohibition against returning in winter; their individual roles and sources for the belief are unspecified.

notes.label: Gutsche
notes.text: Gutsche denotes the bunk, trough-like bed, or sleeping place in the Alpine hut where Baschi lies; its exact construction is uncertain.

notes.label: G'lieger
notes.text: G'lieger is the dialect term for Baschi’s bedding or accustomed sleeping arrangement within the Gutsche; its exact materials beyond old hay are uncertain.

notes.label: Kessi
notes.text: a Kessi is the large dairy cauldron in which Alpine milk is heated for cheesemaking, used here by the spectral crew; its material and capacity are unspecified.

notes.label: ankten
notes.text: ankten is the Swiss German verb for making butter—Anken—from cream, one of the ghosts’ rapid dairy tasks; their precise equipment is unspecified.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: Schotten is whey or a whey-based dairy liquid left from cheesemaking, appearing here in supernatural red, green, and yellow varieties; the cause and meaning of the colors are uncertain.

notes.label: Wintersennen
notes.text: Wintersennen are the spectral dairymen condemned to work the abandoned Alp in winter; whether the term reflects a broader local tradition or this tale alone is uncertain.

notes.label: Suffi
notes.text: Suffi is the ghosts’ name for the offered drink or batch of colored Schotten, from which Baschi wisely chooses green; its literal derivation and why green is safe are uncertain.

292f10d055d3ba25af403058d469f4b3b9511b29.summary: Three brothers, the children of poor people, went abroad to earn their bread.

notes.label: Veltliner
notes.text: a wine name used in Graubünden for wine associated with the neighboring Valtellina and its grapes; the source itself notes its antiquity and serving pairings, while the exact historic grape or style intended can vary.

da38393ed52f3c93c66a243c818585bb4f3ac1de.summary: When Beatus preached the Gospel in the Oberland, there were still little dwarfs, small ‘gesegnete Leutlein,’ or Bergmännchen, who lived in hidden rocky clefts.

notes.label: gesegnete Leutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little blessed people,’ a respectful euphemism for dwarfs or hidden folk; calling potentially uncanny beings blessed avoids insult and emphasizes their benevolence.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ cave-dwelling dwarf beings who help Beatus with pastoral and household work.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep rock faces, cliffs, or crags; the dwarfs bring chamois products down from this high terrain.

notes.label: Gemsmilch
notes.text: chamois milk, imagined as a rare Alpine food obtained by taming and milking wild chamois.

notes.label: Käslein
notes.text: literally ‘little cheeses,’ diminutive rounds prepared from the mountain milk and brought to Beatus.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Biberklee
notes.text: bogbean or buckbean, Menyanthes trifoliata, a bitter medicinal plant; despite Klee meaning clover, it is not an ordinary clover species.

ff14b5e6b4e63e4828f20b982aae00e176237ad7.summary: In ancient times, the people living around the Wendelsee dwelt apart from the world in paganism.

notes.label: Wendelsee
notes.text: an old or legendary name used here for Lake Thun, on whose northern shore the Beatus Caves and Sundlauenen are located.

notes.label: Bödeli
notes.text: the flat alluvial plain between Lakes Thun and Brienz around Interlaken; the diminutive regional name contrasts this low ground with the surrounding mountains.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a great serpent-like dragon of Germanic and Alpine tradition, often wingless or more snake-bodied than the familiar heraldic dragon.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German and Alpine term for a steep rock face, cliff, or exposed wall of stone; the dragon's outline is said to remain marked upon it.

7ece7fa2b260605c618cb72412a4fab696797c4b.summary: Beatus once traveled from his rock dwelling, before which he had built a chapel for the inhabitants' salvation, to the people in the Üchtland on the opposite shore of Lake Thun.

notes.label: Üchtland
notes.text: a historical German name for the region west of the Aare, especially the Fribourg area; the tale uses it broadly for the people across Lake Thun.

notes.label: Wundermantel
notes.text: literally ‘miracle cloak,’ the angel-woven garment on which Saint Beatus crosses Lake Thun; its failure functions as a moral judgment on even a small act of theft.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure based roughly on outstretched arms; its exact regional length varied, so the distance from shore is not given as a modern fixed measurement.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

ad844bf545cd2653a16deaf346bcb5087566049f.summary: a) In spring, when the cattle were let out onto the meadows for the first time, it was still customary in Unterwalden until quite recently to light several pieces of firewood in front of the stable, or at the place through which the animals had to pass, and then drive the cows over this fire—often…

notes.label: gallig und stössig
notes.text: a regional description of cattle as irritable or vicious and prone to butting; gallig literally suggests a bilious or angry disposition, while stössig emphasizes repeated thrusting with the head or horns.

notes.label: Frohnfasten
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Fronfasten, the Ember Days—quarterly periods of fasting and prayer in the Christian calendar; the belief marks calves born during these liminal observances as uncanny.

notes.label: Küchle
notes.text: small fried cakes or fritters; the form is a southern German and Swiss diminutive, and the exact local recipe is not specified.

notes.label: Chüeli
notes.text: Swiss German for little cows, using the characteristic -li diminutive; the affectionate form suits a children’s song.

notes.label: Laürz
notes.text: the dialect form used in the song for Lauerz in the canton of Schwyz.

notes.label: Flüeli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive related to Flue, a rock face, crag, or rocky rise; it may also function as a small local place-name here, so “little crag” is only an approximate sense.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

73bd8b84fbfc13edec35d7a48bd0de72b2a042f8.summary: Johann Jakob Scheuchzer writes in his natural history of Switzerland, published in the year 1746:

notes.label: Berg-Klinglen
notes.text: the source's historical spelling for ‘mountain ringing,’ a seasonal bell-like sound heard around Sax; some interpreted it supernaturally as underground music, while Scheuchzer proposed falling meltwater as its cause.

notes.label: Berg-Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings credited by some listeners with making the Berg-Klinglen as their hidden music.

2f45860891f8f08c72468dcbcfd5d9f0ca6ca9cc.summary: White-clad Bergmännli are said once to have lived among the rocks between Ganterschwil and Duferswil.

notes.label: Bergmännli
notes.text: this Alemannic diminutive means ‘little mountain men’ and denotes helpful subterranean beings associated here with a St. Gallen quarry; their precise relationship to dwarfs or mine spirits is uncertain.

8a572432ab18fbcb3a1cb850b0e743b680de256a.summary: A man from Silenen had paid interest in Erstfeld. On his way home, when he entered the Wyler Forest late in the evening, it suddenly seemed to him that he was walking between two high cliffs that towered up before and behind him.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

647513e0e05d14d3a53cda1fa56e06f9102a450d.summary: From 1610 to 1612 a terrible plague, the Beulentod, raged in Switzerland. Around Schwyz, houses containing infected people were ‘placed under ban and nailed shut.’ Food and everything necessary were passed to the unfortunate inhabitants from outside through an opening made for that purpose in the…

notes.label: Beulentod
notes.text: literally ‘boil-death’ or ‘bubonic death,’ the historical folk name used here for the plague identified by its swellings; it is not a separate modern diagnostic category.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Strenzen
notes.text: a plant or plant-based remedy named by the aerial voice as protection against plague; its precise botanical identity is not established by this source, so the term is retained rather than silently assigned to a modern species.

notes.label: Bibernellen
notes.text: an older plural name for burnet-saxifrage or related pimpinella herbs used in folk medicine; the source presents them as plague protection without specifying preparation or exact species.

07330c883395693640af415f601c7777ca7f066b.summary: The widow B ...... in Fläsch shared a stable with a neighbor whose wife was a witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Volksmagus
notes.text: literally a “folk magus” or popular magician, a practitioner reputed to heal, diagnose, or counteract witchcraft outside ordinary medicine; here the doctor uses herbs and ointments to cure the cow and break the spell.

notes.label: Emd
notes.text: second-cut or aftermath hay gathered after the first hay crop; the source says the cured cow eats it but does not specify how the fodder figures in the remedy.

975397e2f5f1d286baeb1c18ec78678f143f5205.summary: Bi de Spieler — Among the Card Players

notes.label: Bi de Spieler
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘among the players,’ with the context identifying them specifically as card players.

notes.label: heilige Obe
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for a ‘holy evening,’ probably the eve of a religious feast or another sacred evening on which ordinary amusements such as card-playing were taboo; the brief source does not name the exact feast.

notes.label: Frau Faschten
notes.text: literally suggestive of ‘Lady Fast’ or ‘Lady Lent,’ the regional supernatural woman who enforces sacred-season and nighttime taboos; traditions vary concerning her relationship to Lent, other fast days, and older female seasonal beings.

f9332be644949803f3d1b029cda4784036d68e7e.summary: Bi dr Altburg (By the Old Castle)

notes.label: Bi dr Altburg
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘by the old castle’; here Altburg is the haunted castle site from which finely dressed figures appear and change into black cats.

notes.label: Rächemacherüelk
notes.text: a Bernese dialect byname meaning approximately ‘rake-maker Üelk,’ with Üelk a familiar form of a man's name, probably Ulrich; here it identifies the woodcutter witness, although the source gives no formal name.

notes.label: Hösli
notes.text: diminutive Swiss German for short trousers or breeches; here both apparitions wear conspicuous white or velvet knee-breeches.

notes.label: Chüttel
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a coat or jacket; here the first uncanny man wears a red one.

notes.label: Tschöttelichappe
notes.text: a Bernese dialect term for a tasselled or tufted cap; here it is black, while the exact cut of the historical headwear is not described.

notes.label: Herli
notes.text: a Bernese dialect diminutive for a little gentleman or finely dressed young lord; here the elegant figure from the Altburg vanishes and is replaced by a black cat.

notes.label: Fäckechuttli
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a small coat with skirts, tails, or projecting flaps; here it is part of the second apparition's ornate clothing, although its precise historical cut is uncertain.

notes.label: Bi dr Thanbrügg
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘by the Than Bridge,’ the place where the nocturnal apparition occurs; Than is retained as the local name.

notes.label: Totebäumli
notes.text: literally ‘little death tree’ or ‘little dead-person tree,’ a dialect expression for a small coffin or bier-like object carried on the wagon; the exact object is not described.

notes.label: Bäumli
notes.text: literally ‘little tree,’ the shortened dialect reference back to the uncanny Totebäumli.

notes.label: Bi dr Wösch
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘at the washing’ or ‘while doing the laundry’; the title evokes communal washing rather than a modern washing machine.

notes.label: heilige Obe
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for a ‘holy evening,’ probably the eve of a religious feast or another sacred evening on which ordinary work such as washing was taboo.

notes.label: Bütti
notes.text: a large tub or vat, here a traditional wash tub; the dialect text says the unknown woman drives or strikes the people into it.

notes.label: Biberhoger
notes.text: a local hill name in which Hoger is Swiss German for a hill or knoll; the story associates this wooded rise with a former castle and a spectral procession.

notes.label: Chnübeli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a small bump, knob, or knoll; here it describes the little rise said to have held the castle.

notes.label: zwüsche de Wärchet
notes.text: a Bernese phrase meaning between the principal periods or rounds of farm work; it places the clearing job in a comparative lull in the agricultural schedule.

notes.label: d’Chappe lätz
notes.text: literally having one's cap askew or the wrong way around; idiomatically it means being in trouble or in a difficult fix, as the neglectful farmhand realizes he is.

notes.label: Schese
notes.text: a Swiss German form derived from French chaise for a carriage; here it is a grand, ghostly coach with four horses and mounted escorts.

notes.label: Bim Brunnstübli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘at/by the little fountain or spring house’; Brunnstübli is the local place-name, and the source does not specify whether it denotes a small building, chamber, or sheltered spring.

notes.label: Ärn
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the grain harvest; the boys are gleaning ears left in the fields during this seasonal work.

notes.label: Bureallmäng
notes.text: Bernese German for the farmers' common land, a communally used tract rather than one household's private field.

notes.label: Schlarpi
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect teasing or insulting word closest to ‘slouch,’ ‘slowpoke,’ or ‘clumsy fellow’; its precise force in the boys' speech is uncertain.

notes.label: Wingle
notes.text: Bernese dialect for swaddling cloths or infant linens; the supernatural little woman is seen washing them at the Brunnstübli.

notes.label: heilige Nacht
notes.text: literally ‘holy night,’ meaning Christmas Eve or Christmas night; regional folk belief credited a person born then with second sight, explaining why Hansueli sees what Seppli cannot.

notes.label: Bim Lölibrüggli
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “at the Lölibrüggli,” the little bridge where the spirit sneezes; Lölibrüggli is a local diminutive bridge-name whose first element is not explained.

notes.label: Lölibrüggli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive place-name meaning the “little Löli bridge”; it names the haunted crossing, while Löli’s literal or personal reference remains uncertain.

notes.label: Hälf dr es Ross
notes.text: Bernese dialect for “may a horse help you,” a deliberately wrong response to a sneeze; substituting Ross for Gott prevents the spirit’s release, though the source does not explain why the speaker uses it.

notes.label: Hälf dr Gott
notes.text: Bernese dialect for “may God help you,” the proper blessing after a sneeze that would have brought the spirit closer to rest and redemption; the formula reflects Christian protective speech in local oral tradition.

notes.label: Bim Schatzgrabe
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘while digging for treasure’ or ‘at the treasure-digging’; it names the ritual action whose required silence is broken at the decisive moment.

notes.label: Trögli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive of Trog, here a little chest or coffer that rises from the ground and is as heavy as lead.

notes.label: Hörli
notes.text: literally a little horn, corner, or projecting grip; the account means that the diggers nearly secured the Trögli by one such projection, but the precise part of the chest intended is uncertain.
Source note: the closing editorial paragraph refers to ‘the preceding two short legends,’ although this JSON source entry contains only the one treasure-digging account.

notes.label: Bim Weidgatter
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘at the pasture gate’; it names the place where the murdered person's spirit must serve out the remainder of his allotted lifetime.

notes.label: Ching dr Säligkeit
notes.text: literally a ‘child of blessedness’ or ‘child of salvation’; here it means that despite his temporary haunting, the murdered spirit is ultimately destined for salvation rather than damnation.

04cc286a14129c2c113e0a38c77996b19477800f.summary: Black Eichmann lives in an old oak tree that stands on the Wohlen road near the Upper Village; he sometimes climbs down from the tree to chase away a traveler or lead one far astray.

notes.label: About this telling

ddb0517eae0d5ee053085ac14cea9406ff3e8d23.summary: In the time of King Rudolf, Blatten Castle passed to the lords of Ramswag. In time, the once-proud knightly family became so impoverished that at last three brothers in the ancestral castle themselves served the wine they had grown nearby.

notes.label: About this telling

bc7f412d36a23943047fd45da24021a605688be0.summary: I have been told by a trustworthy person that once, unexpectedly in the night, a dead body stood upright before her—nothing but bones, in the form in which Death is painted.

notes.label: About this telling

16921db7cbb1def96983492317be8bfbf30da062.summary: A noble family of knights once lived at Steinach Castle, not far from the little town of Arbon.

notes.label: About this telling

42e501693cc9964ce84366b92148c8af54a09b7c.summary: At the time when the Vättnerberg was still inhabited, a house stood in the Spina; its foundation remains visible today.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a practitioner of the ‘black art,’ this denotes a sorcerer believed invulnerable to ordinary bullets; whether the label implies a witch, magician, or folk occultist more specifically is uncertain.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Dreifaltigkeitssalz
notes.text: literally ‘Trinity salt,’ this is a ritually charged salt mixed with gunpowder to make the silver bullet effective; its blessing and preparation are unspecified.

notes.label: Vättnerbergfeeden
notes.text: this obscure local terrain term names the place where the son’s body is found; its exact spelling, meaning, and location are uncertain.

8595b2cf211f1dca53f62eb1caf57cbb4df25336.summary: Many an Alp that was formerly full of flowers—a Blümelisalp—has preserved the memory of dreadful glaciation that broke over it suddenly.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Blüemlisalp
notes.text: literally ‘little-flower Alp’ or ‘flower Alp,’ the name of a once-blooming high pasture remembered as having been overwhelmed by glacier ice; the source also gives the spelling Blümelisalp.

9f553317bd9389ead525a23ed99677d8cf3e1f13.summary: It was during the Reformation in Bünden when, in a village in the Engadine, a little beggar man lay near his end.

notes.label: Bünden
notes.text: a historical shortened German name for Graubünden, recalling the region's leagues; it is the setting of the Reformation-era denominational joke.

3655f1276cc259d9e61fc342d0cfd1d135130441.summary: In the Grauholz, not far from the country road to Bern, two age-gray granite pillars stand on the mossy forest floor, with a mound dug over by treasure hunters rising between them.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: a Swiss German form for an apron, literally a cloth worn in front; Botti’s giant sister uses hers to carry the grave stones, though the garment’s precise local style is not specified.

fced19c4679611293013388b3d35be86f44c5560.summary: A farmer came to the Küsterli—the sexton—and complained that someone had stolen the hay from his meadow.

notes.label: Küsterli
notes.text: a diminutive regional form of Küster, meaning a church sexton or sacristan; the tale credits him with magically binding the thief.

notes.label: Fuder
notes.text: a wagonload or cartload, here a freshly gathered load of stolen hay.

2c0830c40c6ecff668ec3f1b89a1526061cf261f.summary: At a certain house near Uerkheim, a light becomes visible beside a field boundary on stormy nights, and at every turn of the year it becomes a fiery man carrying a shovel.

9fca662c80d55760d2f5845cd6ae7d60b32f586b.summary: When a beggar once spent the night in a Gaden, a ghost came in and said to him, ‘If you did not have a little piece of bread in your sack, I would tear you into rags and shreds.’ A ghost at Rynächt shouted the same thing to an insolent Obländner after he called to the ‘Chumuff,’ ‘Come down!’

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn bay, hay store, livestock shelter, or farm outbuilding in Alpine German usage; the beggar uses it as rough overnight lodging, while the exact room is not specified.

notes.label: Obländner
notes.text: a regional designation for a man from the upper country or uplands; the source does not specify the exact boundary of the district meant here.

notes.label: Chumuff
notes.text: the quoted local name or taunt addressed to the apparition at Rynächt; its literal derivation, the being’s appearance, and whether the name imitates ‘come up’ are uncertain.

notes.label: Vergältsgott
notes.text: this Alemannic devotional thanks means ‘may God repay you’ and is treated as a transferable spiritual reward for almsgiving; the exact theology of transferring it to the dead woman is uncertain.

5fb86b099f719acade372872173376ede9e2188a.summary: a) High inside the Bristenstock, a Vynediger revealed, there is a cave. Pure gold drips from its ceiling, and a Chochchessi has been placed beneath it; the kettle has long been full and is running over.

notes.label: Vynediger
notes.text: a regional form of ‘Venetian,’ used in Alpine legend for a foreign mineral seeker, treasure-knower, or magician credited with secret knowledge of mountain riches; the story does not distinguish those roles precisely.

notes.label: Chochchessi
notes.text: an Uri dialect compound for a cooking or boiling kettle; here it is set beneath the cave roof to catch dripping gold, but its size and material are unspecified.

notes.label: Rossgrind
notes.text: a rough Swiss German expression for a horse's head or skull; it gives the legendary gold lump's size without establishing whether the comparison means a living head or bare skull.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a wandering scholar or student, a recurring folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; here he reveals the golden supports beneath two mountains.

85a78a28d75b34bc6cdf6eed3298b3eeb09c5f9d.summary: Brunnenhans on the Giblour in the Canton of Fribourg

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the dairymen responsible for livestock and for producing butter and cheese on an Alpine or upland summer pasture.

notes.label: Tragref
notes.text: a regional back-carrying frame or pack support used to transport heavy loads up mountain paths; here it holds the flour and salt provisions.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: a tier, terrace, or distinct level of an Alpine pasture and its route or settlement; here the uppermost Staffel marks the high place where the disguised prankster confronts Brunnenhans.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

bccf4660466f1049d2d5669b64fe1bd30d8877d4.summary: The Vetaner once resolved to build a bridge across the Inn below their territory.

notes.label: Vetaner
notes.text: the people of Vetan, Jecklin’s historical German name for the Lower Engadine village now called Ftan; the tale makes them the targets of its village-fool humor.

70c9e62cf146a9cde09b8e6dc063ef8e1f4f3ff8.summary: The plague ruled fiercely here. It began and ended in the lowest house, which was so pestilential that a stick held through the window immediately turned black.

notes.label: Fuchsli
notes.text: literally a ‘little fox,’ a regional affectionate name for the small chestnut-colored horse drawing the corpse cart; the source immediately calls it a Rösslein, confirming that it is not an actual fox.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Burgfluh
notes.text: literally a ‘castle cliff’ or ‘castle crag,’ the named rocky site where the white-mounted knight appears; Fluh is a Swiss term for a steep rock face.

notes.label: hup-hup!
notes.text: the wild hunter’s repeated hunting cry; it imitates a call rather than carrying a clear lexical meaning.

notes.label: Scheiterbeige
notes.text: a neatly piled stack of split firewood; it serves as the landmark behind which the apparition vanishes.

notes.label: Sennhof
notes.text: literally a Senn’s farm or dairy holding and used here as a place name at Pfarsberg; the tale does not describe its historical connection to an Alpine dairyman.

d7fdd59f38e4ad89429fab20a930cff8236b223b.summary: People in Altdorf told of a woman who lived in the house formerly belonging to the Crivelli family, now the home of Fürsprech Karl Huber.

notes.label: Fürsprech
notes.text: an older Swiss title for an advocate or attorney; here it identifies Karl Huber as the later occupant of the former Crivelli house.

8924448694a8b1ca59ae85413dead9452cf67d11.summary: In the city of Baden there lived a wealthy grain merchant who knew how to force his wares upon poor people at high prices and, during times of famine, often sold them sacks of grain that were as much as half filled with Spreuer.

notes.label: Spreuer
notes.text: chaff, the dry husks and other light waste separated from grain; it is both the merchant's fraudulent filler and the fitting substance in which his rejected corpse must be buried.

notes.label: Totenbaum
notes.text: literally ‘death-tree’ or ‘dead person's tree,’ an older regional word for a coffin, reflecting the historical association of coffins with hollowed wooden trunks.

ccf6530d91548b18f97ab7a7ecb2681d9dddb968.summary: The parish of Beinwil, with a ruined castle site of the same name, formerly the property of the monastic foundation of Muri, lies near Meienberg in the Freie Ämter of Aargau.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

notes.label: Freie Ämter
notes.text: literally the ‘Free Bailiwicks,’ a historical subject territory in what is now Aargau; ‘free’ is part of the regional name and does not mean it lacked outside rule.

notes.label: Abgrube
notes.text: a waste, refuse, or privy pit; the exact kind of household pit is not specified, but it is the place into which the maids throw the informing bird.

c8c53221edc66ca37ec41ad6f5d63704a56c63ab.summary: a) On a pitch-dark night, a councilor was making his way home from Stans to Ennetbürgen.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little man, using the characteristic -li diminutive; here it names a small fiery spirit or revenant that can be compensated with a Mass.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Hoslen
notes.text: a local expression that the collector himself glosses as Ringen, meaning wrestling or grappling; the precise style of the tussle is not specified.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

8670f7bb416f7823e961b464428fa8cc3875598c.summary: On another occasion, a Sente of cattle at Mädems included a white cow whose wandering caused the Alpknechte much trouble, for almost every day she had to be fetched from a steep slope, a remote cleft, or even another Alp.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: a herd or organized group of cattle on an Alp; the troublesome white cow belongs to this mountain herd.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male workers on a seasonal Alp who assist with herding and dairy labor; they repeatedly retrieve the wandering cow.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture and its work areas, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior alpine dairyman who leads the hut and herd routine and makes the reckless exception in his prayer.

notes.label: B'hüt's Gott
notes.text: a dialect contraction meaning ‘may God protect it’; the prayer formula becomes dangerous when the Senn expressly excludes one animal.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: normally a gray or white horse, but here the herd's white cow is nicknamed Schimmel; the mismatch is retained because it is central to the source's wording.

notes.label: Molkendach
notes.text: literally the ‘whey roof,’ probably the roof of an Alpine dairy or whey-storage structure; the source does not identify the building more precisely.

notes.label: Brunnstübli
notes.text: literally a ‘little spring or fountain house,’ Brunnstübli names the small water structure in the Eichmatt beside the uncanny oak; its exact construction and purpose are uncertain.

notes.label: Allmäng
notes.text: Allmäng is the Bernese dialect form of Allmend, communally held village land crossed here by the old ditch; its historical boundaries and ownership arrangements are unspecified.

notes.label: Roone
notes.text: Roone appears to mean a log or tree trunk laid as a crossing over the brook; its exact dialect sense and whether it served as a footbridge or channel are uncertain.

notes.label: Liechtli
notes.text: literally ‘little lights’ in dialect, Liechtli are the moving luminous apparitions that separate, reunite, and leap above the ditch; their nature and interpretation are uncertain.

3af49a0f9bba3a1840ca2e59d36cf70e220ec659.summary: A spirit is said to have roamed from time to time near the ruins of Spillberg Castle.

notes.label: Bühl-Anneli
notes.text: the local name of the female spirit haunting Spillberg; Anneli is a Swiss German diminutive of Anna and Bühl means a hill or hill-site, so the closest sense is ‘little Anna of the hill,’ but the account does not identify her historical origin.

8373b330d15f72955fe8bec874ffe6848d002290.summary: It was late at night, and the moon illuminated the countryside, when the vigilant pastor of Isental, Peter Josef Egger (1848–1875), saw a man carrying a Handbräntli come out of the Gaden at Guetig and head toward the village.

notes.label: Handbräntli
notes.text: a small portable wooden dairy container fitted for carrying by hand; here it holds the milk stolen from the cows, though its exact size is not stated.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German term for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; here it is where the cows are milked, but the exact structure is not specified.

notes.label: b’stellä
notes.text: the infinitive Uri dialect form meaning to halt, bind, or call someone to account by authoritative command; in this tradition old priests could use it as a quasi-spiritual power.

notes.label: z’ruggtrybä
notes.text: Uri dialect for driving or compelling someone or something back; it is paired with b’stellä as a power attributed to older clergy.

notes.label: B’stellt
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of bestellt, here meaning that the priest authoritatively halted, fixed in place, or summoned the suspected thief through clerical command; the story treats this as an old spiritual ability, not merely an ordinary request.

cd5d49a81d7c6412ac1352204841b12e93f64d4c.summary: Two ‘Knaben’ went to the Sevelerberg for a Stubete. The two young women of the house were delighted by the visit and went to the kitchen to bake cakes.

notes.label: Knaben
notes.text: literally ‘boys’ or ‘young men’; the source places the word in quotation marks, and in this courtship setting it refers to the visiting unmarried young men rather than small children.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a sociable evening gathering traditionally held in a farmhouse parlor, often involving music, visiting, and courtship; here it provides the occasion for the young men's visit.

notes.label: Küchli
notes.text: small fried or baked cakes or pastries; the exact recipe is unstated, but the young men refuse them after seeing the witches obtain the cooking fat from a toad.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

ad8077b2c3f4a8b5ae6474f22c9c27a8f2bc934a.summary: On Oberprod, 100 years ago, there lived a man as strong as a tree, Bartholomäus Lutz.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night folk,’ a nocturnal spectral procession whose members include the dead and people soon to die; Barthli recognizes his own double at its end.

notes.label: Barthli
notes.text: an affectionate regional diminutive of Bartholomäus; its use makes the ominous self-address sound familiar and personal.

notes.label: Hosenstoss
notes.text: one leg or side of a pair of trousers; Barthli’s spectral double reproduces the half-dressed state in which he hurried to the window.

notes.label: bidinggli
notes.text: a dialect word meaning ominous, portentous, or deeply significant; seeing oneself without a mirror is treated as a death omen.

notes.label: gug-geisend
notes.text: an obscure dialect expression retained from the source, apparently describing two figures peering or staring inward; its exact construction and nuance are uncertain.

notes.label: Pfifter
notes.text: the difficult dialect or printed form used for the opening through which the two figures look, evidently the window in this context; the precise local spelling and derivation are uncertain.

c31c8fe13adf85b99963639a54fc71048cadefa1.summary: A rowdy company in an inn at Isental mocked religion and made jokes about it.

notes.label: und das stäng jetz nu dert, het der Isitaller gsäit, wo miër dass v'rzellt het
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘and it still stands there now, said the man from Isental who told me this’; the narrator preserves the informant’s claim that the cross remained visible evidence.

a5ddc95d97a39d51a396efcd26eefa5f20cffb8e.summary: One of the many hills called Homberg in the Aargau Jura lies toward Oberfrick, close to the part of the village called In der Gipf.

notes.label: In der Gipf
notes.text: the local name of a section of Oberfrick near the Homberg; it is a place-name rather than an instruction meaning ‘in the summit.’

notes.label: Freiung
notes.text: a privileged or exempt place, sometimes a sanctuary or legally immune ground; here it is an ownerless boundary plot where ordinary law is imagined to remain perpetually suspended.

notes.label: Schlossmusik
notes.text: literally ‘castle music,’ the supernatural martial music heard around the Thierstein ruin at the appointed holy times.

c32119375cc0e8194904b08574199ce6cbbd8905.summary: Above Botenwil, a village in the Uerkheim valley in the district of Zofingen, lie shrub-covered remains of walls on a hill, once the manor house of a violent Vogt.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff, steward, or local lord exercising delegated authority; here the violent Vogt is the former master of Botenstein and returns as its weather-bringing spirit.

957e4389d6138e9bc029125b5a955c7e4e6de9d5.summary: Shoemaker Zacharias Imholz found a large, coal-black cat highly suspicious when it blocked his way one evening behind Hergerig at Spiringen, beside a marker stone, and stared at him with grass-green, sparkling eyes.

notes.label: Diä mueß m'r etz hinecht nitt nu Stei heischä
notes.text: Uri dialect, literally ‘She need not ask me for stones tonight now’; the shoemaker decides against throwing a stone and chooses the protective sign of the cross instead, so the line carries dry, defiant irony.
notes.anchor: Diä mueß m'r etz hinecht nitt nu Stei heischä

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

60ad5a5b9327299522d011a6b9a1d98487c25cbc.summary: On the southeastern slope of the Gibloux, an extension of the Jorat range, lie the villages of Vuisternens-en-Ogoz, Villarslod, and Rueyres-Saint-Laurent, on the right of the road from Fribourg to Bulle.

notes.label: Bolosché
notes.text: the passage’s regional French-speaking name for the wild plums eaten during famine; the exact plum variety and modern spelling are uncertain.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herder who tends cattle and makes cheese on high pasture; the source also glosses him more broadly as a mountain worker.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or level with huts and livestock facilities; here the fountain stands beside it, and it is not an indoor shelf or stage.

notes.label: Schlossen
notes.text: regional German for large hailstones; the term emphasizes the damaging frozen lumps accompanying the storm.

notes.label: Catillon la Toascha
notes.text: the local Franco-Provençal or French-region name attached to the accused hunchbacked woman Catillon; Toascha’s exact literal sense is uncertain in the passage, so the full attested name is retained.

e4e15f47a564155183e33b8289b8245d2bfc9786.summary: a) The Arniloch. An old man related during his final illness: Beyond Wolfenschiessen, one leaves the Engelberg road and travels to the side across Alpine pasture to a steep rock wall into which the Arniloch opens.

notes.label: Arniloch
notes.text: literally the ‘Arni hole,’ a cave with a seasonal lake, hidden gold, and a lost mine entrance near the Arnialp.

notes.label: Wänd er au is Goldloch?
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Do you also want to go into the gold hole?’—the locals’ suspicious or knowing response to requests for directions.

notes.label: Enziloch
notes.text: a named cave or hole that mysteriously clears away anything scattered before it; the source does not explain Enzi.

notes.label: Mondmilchloch
notes.text: literally ‘moon-milk hole,’ the standard name for a cave on Pilatus; moonmilk is also a soft white cave deposit, though the story does not discuss the geology.

notes.label: Mahmilchloch
notes.text: the Obwalden regional form of Mondmilchloch, referring to the same cave and its legendary passage through the mountain.

832e5581fb640babe4a9bbef79630ab52c47c0f6.summary: High on the Schreckhorn, as in other Alpine regions, sounds like the report of a fired rifle can often be heard among the glaciers.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.
