8b860ef4f16ddef894ae6af2a6f92f641b99a704.summary: When Emperor Charlemagne was staying with his court in the old city of Zürich and living in the canons' house called zum Loch, he had a pillar with a bell erected at the place where Felix and Regula, the holy martyrs of the Theban Legion, had been beheaded.

notes.label: zum Loch
notes.text: the historic Zürich house-name, literally ‘at the hole’; it identifies the canons' residence in which Charlemagne is said to have stayed and is retained rather than treated as an ordinary direction.

notes.text: Bernese German for ‘cats are merry’; the title refers to the secret nocturnal gathering understood as a meeting of transformed witches.

notes.label: Maudi
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a tomcat; here it is also how the household cat is addressed when its nighttime activity is exposed.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the Betglocke is the evening prayer bell whose ringing begins the wild hunter’s nocturnal passage; the exact local ringing time is uncertain.

notes.label: Voralp
notes.text: a Voralp is a lower or intermediate seasonal pasture used before or after the highest summer grazing, here the hunter’s resting place; its exact location above Grandvillars is unspecified.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Sennen are Alpine dairymen responsible for herds and dairy production, here forced to remain silent during the spectral hunt; their number and identities are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: Stafel denotes a seasonal herding and dairying station, including its huts and stable, besieged here by the spectral hounds; the source’s exact distinction between the Stafel and Voralp is uncertain.

notes.label: Aelpler
notes.text: Aelpler is the source’s older spelling for a person working on an Alp, here the young cowherd struck by the hunter; his name and precise role are unspecified.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Chimpettere
notes.text: Bernese German for a woman in childbed or the postpartum period; here it specifically means a woman who dies while recently delivered and is feared to return bodily unless the associated customs are observed.

notes.label: Sinzel
notes.text: a rare Bernese word for a sill, ledge, or narrow household shelf; here the family leaves the dead woman’s missing shoes upon it so that she will stop returning.

notes.label: Chimpetti
notes.text: a Bernese term for childbed or the customary period of postpartum confinement; the first journey outside the house is expected to be to church.

notes.label: Totebaum
notes.text: literally ‘dead-person tree’ or ‘death-tree,’ a regional name for a wooden coffin; the vivid term carries more folkloric force than the plain English coffin.

notes.label: Käsgräbt
notes.text: literally a ‘cheese burial’ or ‘cheese funeral,’ the modest funeral meal of wine, bread, and cheese served by poorer households.

notes.label: Fleischgräbt
notes.text: literally a ‘meat burial’ or ‘meat funeral,’ a more substantial funeral meal contrasted with the poorer household’s Käsgräbt.

notes.label: Röselirot
notes.text: literally something like ‘little rose-red,’ an enigmatic traditional address in the children’s folk prayer; its exact referent is uncertain, and readers should understand it as a preserved prayer formula rather than ordinary prose.

2d3a89434e0444051cc393e1f12db74ff0d65a57.summary: A wandering scholar who had learned magic in Salamanca once came during his travels through the world, which he undertook with the Devil’s aid, to Lake Türlen.

notes.label: Vreneligärtli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little Vreni garden,’ here the local name for Saint Verena’s impossible garden on the ice-covered Glärnisch; ‘Saint Verena’s Garden’ conveys the identification but not the affectionate regional form.

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

7200e3b981d8bcd8f58f1102ab734ea2791f5c4c.summary: This lies on the Türlersee in the Canton of Zurich in the direction of Heferschwil.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Fuss
notes.text: a historical foot measure whose exact length varied by place and period; the source uses it to estimate the trench’s length without identifying a local standard.

notes.label: Vreneli's Gärtli
notes.text: literally ‘little Verena’s garden,’ the traditional name of a high place on the Glärnisch to which the storm carries Kriemhilt; Vreneli is an affectionate Swiss diminutive of Verena.

2fc33c57cf95228cd61f3f17d7a43f713ee086b4.summary: The Sennen and herds had returned home from the Alp when a man from Weisstannen had to go back up once more to fetch something left behind.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, denoting Alpine dairymen and herders who seasonally worked with livestock on high pastures; the supernatural visitors’ exact identity is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, an Alp is a high seasonal pasture with its associated huts and dairy work, here already vacated for the season; the particular Alp is not named.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Triel
notes.text: here Triel appears to denote a sleeping ledge or platform inside the Alpine hut; its exact construction and the term’s local range are uncertain.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: in this dairying context, Schotten is a whey-based food offered by the nocturnal Sennen; its exact preparation and consistency are uncertain.

622ecc82a27f9d9c8b693cdce9cfea571e52d34b.summary: In the Frick Valley and the Hauenstein Black Forest, people still believe that on Christnacht, and perhaps also on Andreasnacht, one can glimpse the future.

notes.label: Christnacht
notes.text: literally ‘Christ night,’ the night of Christmas Eve into Christmas Day; in central European folklore it is a liminal sacred night suited to divination and supernatural encounters.

notes.label: Andreasnacht
notes.text: Saint Andrew’s Night, the eve of Saint Andrew’s feast; it is traditionally associated with courtship and future-spouse divination, though this passage only says the rite may also be practiced then.

e4ff11c64e863aca7ceff13dcd618c189bc72dd8.summary: The two Regli brothers and other hardworking people in Meien set out together on the eve of the first Wilditag—that is, on the evening of August 10—for the upper Meiental, so that early in the morning they would be ready at their Wildheu plots.

notes.label: Wilditag
notes.text: literally a ‘wild-hay day,’ here the first locally recognized day of the dangerous high-slope hay harvest, explicitly dated to August 10.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: hay cut from steep, remote mountain grassland rather than an ordinary farm meadow; the workers travel into the upper valley to harvest their separate plots.

notes.label: Chumm flingg
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Come quickly’; the unexplained call from the heights is understood by Regli as a summons to his death.

notes.label: Wildheuer
notes.text: harvesters who cut and carry Wildheu on steep Alpine slopes; Regli and the people across the valley are identified by this seasonal work.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope wind characteristic of the Alps; here it rapidly dries the newly cut mountain hay.

notes.label: chittelet
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb explicitly glossed by the collector as gently shaking or stirring; it describes the Föhn moving the scrub and old windows.

notes.label: Droslen
notes.text: a regional name for Alpine scrub or a shrub species growing on the slopes; the source does not identify the plant securely enough for a modern botanical name.

notes.label: Planggen
notes.text: steep grassy mountain slopes or ledges used for Alpine haymaking; the term emphasizes terrain more hazardous than an ordinary meadow.

notes.label: Tristbett
notes.text: the prepared base or bed on which harvested hay is built into a Triste, an outdoor haystack; Regli carries the first load to it.

notes.label: Nossen
notes.text: a local rock feature or projecting overhang beside the narrow path; the source establishes that Regli must turn toward the wall to pass it but does not define its exact shape.

0f0cf0d43b244daf79077351eb6b73b66c0861de.summary: a) At Klariden in former times, a black Chüehli and a little black dog appeared from time to time upon the field of ice and rubble covering the vanished Klariden Alp.

notes.label: Chüehli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little cow, with -li as the diminutive; in Chüehli Brändi it forms part of the supernatural cow's traditional name, while the significance of Brändi beyond the cow's pitch-black teats is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, herds, and dairy operation, not merely a mountain; the legend explains the destruction of the Klariden and Blümlisalp pastoral landscapes.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle, milking, and cheese production; the cursed Senn is transformed into or represented by the black cow, although the variants do not explain that transformation consistently.

notes.label: Hirzechüeh
notes.text: literally a ‘deer-cow’ or hind, the dialect name given to the supernatural cow from Klariden; its precise animal form is uncertain because the account still describes it as being milked like a cow.

notes.label: Melchteren
notes.text: a regional dairying measure or vessel represented as being filled with milk; ‘milking-pails’ is the closest contextual sense, but its exact capacity and whether it counts vessels or full milkings are uncertain.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; here it is part of the Alp's extravagant dairy abundance and is used with cheeses to make a stairway or path.

notes.label: Handbräntli
notes.text: a small portable wooden dairy container fitted for carrying by hand; the mother asks that it be filled with Alp produce, but its exact size and construction are not stated.

notes.label: Bräntli
notes.text: a traditional lidded wooden carrying vessel used for milk or other Alpine dairy produce; here the same container has been deceitfully filled with cow dung.

notes.label: Wellchessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheese-making cauldron, apparently substantial enough for the couple to try using it as shelter; Well- may indicate its great size, but that nuance is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: Swiss German for the cauldron used to heat milk in Alpine cheese-making; here the couple holds it over their heads during the fatal storm.

notes.label: Milchlikraut
notes.text: literally ‘little milk herb,’ a pasture plant credited with making the Klariden cows extraordinarily productive; the source does not identify a botanical species.

notes.label: Landeshauptmann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or governor of Valais, historically a leading office of the republic; in the tale, election by lot opens the office to Hans.

notes.label: Hostie
notes.text: the consecrated Communion wafer; recovering and swallowing it heals the woman, implying that its improper presence with the frog caused or sustained the illness.

notes.label: Kronen
notes.text: plural of Krone, a crown-denominated coin or unit of money; the tale does not specify the exact regional currency standard.

notes.label: Louisdor
notes.text: gold coins modeled on or named for the French louis d'or and widely recognized in Swiss commerce; Hans asks for five and receives ten.

notes.label: Landesvorsteher
notes.text: literally ‘head of the country,’ used here for the elected Valais leader and apparently equivalent in the tale to Landeshauptmann rather than a separate lower office.

3efae876b9a1602fbca23be9ae2a45180f294f95.summary: At Eisten in the Visp valley stood a little hut inhabited by three people: father, mother, and son.

notes.label: Hanse
notes.text: an affectionate regional form of the name Hans; the parents use it for their son, and the story retains it as his personal name.

notes.label: Landeshauptmann
notes.text: literally “captain of the land,” the title of the chief magistrate or governor in historic Valais; the election of this official draws the travelers to Sitten.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical coin used in Switzerland and neighboring regions; Hanse's statement that he has not one Batzen means that he has no travel money at all.

notes.label: tschu, tschu
notes.text: a repeated herding call used here by Hanse as he drives the sheep home before joining the travelers.

notes.label: Kronen
notes.text: plural of Krone, a historical crown coin; Hanse modestly asks for three but receives five after the woman's cure.

notes.label: Louisdor
notes.text: the German form of louis d'or, a French gold coin that also circulated as a unit of value beyond France; Hanse asks for five and receives twice that amount.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff or territorial governor; Hanse's companions use the title mockingly when they imagine that he too expects to win high office.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Grünspecht
notes.text: literally a green woodpecker; the companions hurl it at Hanse as a dismissive insult implying a foolish or presumptuous young fellow.

notes.label: Landesvorsteher
notes.text: literally the head of the territory or country; the tale uses it for the office to which the authorities nominate Hanse, in the same election it otherwise calls that of the Landeshauptmann.

f1c859c7a902dfc0451fb8742f352c37a64569a0.summary: Once, in Peist in the Graubündnerland, many young fellows had gathered at an inn, where they amused themselves with games and feasting and knew how to make a very merry night of it.

notes.label: Graubündnerland
notes.text: the land or region of Graubünden, emphasizing the canton's distinct regional identity.

notes.label: der Grüne
notes.text: literally ‘the Green One,’ the stranger's color-based folkloric epithet before the revelers recognize him as the Devil.

notes.label: Peterli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Peter; the affectionate ‘little Peter’ proves clever enough to save the whole company.

notes.label: der Böse
notes.text: literally ‘the Evil One,’ a traditional euphemism for the Devil that avoids naming him directly.

3739b0ed4d3caac43dccc0e9c993ffebb0ac7430.summary: At the far end of the Safien Valley, a wildes Männlein tended the cows for several years, in return for which people gave him milk to drink.

notes.label: wildes Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘wild little man,’ a nonhuman mountain being who helps with Alpine herding; receiving human clothes makes him self-conscious and ends his service, a motif shared with household-spirit traditions.

f5f58ea07556814717371a4444c0aea611e3cee2.summary: In Dangstetten on the right bank of the Rhine, a poor widow lay wasting away with illness.

notes.label: Leseholz
notes.text: deadwood, fallen branches, or small wood legally gathered from the forest rather than timber felled from living trees; the daughter collects it as poor household fuel.

notes.label: Dreiröhrenhut
notes.text: literally a “three-tube hat,” an old regional hat form probably referring to a three-cornered or otherwise folded hat; the source emphasizes its unusual size but does not describe its construction precisely.

270f08bc101706ec0b02e33ad6ccdc7b16a4fdc2.summary: a) Joggelisepp of Hinterhohenegg, a strong, powerful man, was walking home in the evening from the Huttwil market.

notes.label: Joggelisepp
notes.text: a compounded Alemannic personal nickname, approximately ‘Jakob-Joseph’; it identifies the strong man from Hinterhohenegg in the first episode.

notes.label: Biberlitier
notes.text: literally ‘Biberli animal’ or ‘little beaver animal,’ though its form is not described; it is the local weather-linked apparition that grows gigantic when wrestled.

notes.label: Hürrligespenst
notes.text: the local name of the obstructing ghost on the Seitenberg road; Gespenst means ‘ghost,’ while the source does not explain Hürrli’s literal origin.

notes.label: Hürrli
notes.text: the shortened local name for the same unseen spirit, recognized chiefly through the impossible obstacles it places in travelers’ paths.

notes.label: Runde
notes.text: literally a round or circuit; here it likely means the young men’s nighttime social or courting rounds, though the source does not specify the activity precisely.

notes.label: Nachtbuebe
notes.text: literally ‘night boys,’ referring to young unmarried men who roam or return from nighttime social and courting activities, not to small children.
The first occurrence of Tafel appears to be a dialect or transcription error for Tüfel, ‘Devil,’ which the story uses later.

d815e6b7b90c7afe761ab882396f55378562d894.summary: Alois Infanger, a farmer from Bauen, communicated the following legend to me in writing:

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Ds Iddi tüet lyttä, i cha nyd üßrichtä.
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Little Idda is ringing; I can accomplish nothing’; Ds Iddi personifies St. Idda through the chapel bell whose protective ringing thwarts the witch.
notes.anchor: Ds Iddi tüet lyttä, i cha nyd üßrichtä.

notes.label: Brächä
notes.text: a local dialect name or noun for the broad landslide at the source of the Bawerbach; the precise lexical derivation is uncertain, while the story clearly associates it with the landslip.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture and its associated working landscape, not simply any mountain.

a2dd6e4f8334b928b5c936f2305a0ca2fa89d76a.summary: The maiden in the Geltenfluh near Engelberg had been condemned into the form of a dragon because she had disobeyed her father.

notes.label: heimgarten
notes.text: to take part in a Heimgarten, an evening social or courting visit in a household; the rescuer's never having participated marks the ritual purity demanded by this story.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face, crag, or cliff in Swiss usage; both the Geltenfluh place-name and the dragon's attacks depend upon this precipitous terrain.

2a2b9954e168c99be013b74d986f712e7fd8c978.summary: A belief formerly prevailed in this country that lightning, hail, and storms must very often be attributed to the art of witches.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

96298eb617abec774d82efeb3bf7ff775fc9367d.summary: The conjurer went to the place where the treasure was supposed to lie, drew the circle, and, kneeling, spoke his prayer: an invocation of the Most Holy Trinity to preserve him from evil, demonic influences.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

dbcde26720b200f02ff12dab1f883f22d891ba71.summary: Long ago, at the Hostet on the Vorder Mühlebach in the Schächen Valley, there lived three Meitli who could read extraordinarily well—even Latin.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a regional word for an orchard, homestead plot, or named farm property; here it functions as the locality on the Vorder Mühlebach, whose exact boundaries are not stated.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young unmarried women, using the characteristic -li diminutive; these three are literate enough to read Latin but their ages are not given.

notes.label: Küchengänterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small kitchen cupboard, wall cabinet, or shelf; the pastor takes the sack of rice from it, but its precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Hörnermann
notes.text: literally ‘horned man,’ a euphemistic or descriptive regional name for the Devil; the pastor uses it while ordering him to gather the rice.

da39b444a80c0e5e543e1577580b016b510f831e.summary: In May 1865, two Basen of the Paggi family went from Braggio to the market at Roveredo.

notes.label: Basen
notes.text: plural of an older kinship term that can mean female cousins or aunts; the story establishes that the two Paggi women are relatives but not their exact degree of kinship.

notes.label: salva venia
notes.text: Latin for “with your pardon” or “saving your permission,” used humorously as a polite disclaimer before mentioning a pig.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: the centime subdivision of the Swiss franc; one woman pays thirty more for her piglet.

notes.label: Oui, Oui-Schreier
notes.text: literally “oui, oui criers,” a comic imitation of the piglets’ squeals using the French word for yes.

notes.label: Friedensrichter
notes.text: a justice of the peace or local conciliating magistrate whose attempted mediation fails.

notes.label: Kreisgericht
notes.text: the court of the local Kreis or circuit before which the piglet dispute is first tried.

notes.label: Bezirksgericht
notes.text: the district court that hears the appeal as the second instance.

notes.label: Tessin
notes.text: the German name for the canton of Ticino, home of the advocates in the duck dispute.

notes.label: Qua, qua
notes.text: the written imitation of a duck’s call whose allegedly distinctive pronunciation supplies the story’s joke about expert evidence.

notes.label: Ligitanten
notes.text: the source’s historical or erroneous spelling for litigants, the parties who must share the court costs.

7fab48d6a1239961db19959cd4e8998b63c592ec.summary: Above Gähwil are found the ruins of old Toggenburg Castle. Popular tradition tells of a Count Heinrich who is said to have lived here in the 12th century.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a836ead3fd86c40f3bb3dc315215a7f0a1a00407.summary: Countess Margaretha of Gruyère shed tears in church over her childless marriage.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d1619d1f16c854344decd04902d6f434c785e9f4.summary: When the Sennen are up on the Alpen, it sometimes happens that at night a voice is heard like that of a Senn calling the cows, and the cows immediately follow that voice under the leadership of the Meisterkuh.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, Alpine herdsmen and dairymen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high seasonal pastures.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal livestock pastures and their farm settlements, not simply the Alpine mountain range.

notes.label: Meisterkuh
notes.text: literally ‘master cow,’ the leading or dominant cow that guides the herd when the mysterious voice calls.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and dairying settlement; the boy and cow return there after their unexplained three-day absence.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

5e7e8c5024ef9292fd172103645e568016808e3f.summary: At the Kilchberg near Andermatt, a strange howling and shouting could sometimes be heard, though no one knew who caused it.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7ff163bbccf68d3aed540a2b128f351af2c695fa.summary: When the cattle move out of a stable, a ghost sometimes moves into the deserted place.

notes.label: Bläste
notes.text: a regional word for blister-like eruptions, sores, or a rash around the mouth; the source links them to the poisonous breath of a haunted stable but does not identify a precise medical condition.

ea36d2266c7cd7b9344d7526170afcbb696d84b7.summary: High Rialt, you proud old castle,

notes.label: Domleschger-Tale
notes.text: the source’s inflected historical form for the Domleschg valley in which the castle rises.

notes.label: Hohenrätier
notes.text: literally the lord or man of High Raetia, Cuno’s threatening self-designation in the poem.

notes.label: Sassen
notes.text: resident dependents, tenants, or subjects settled under the castle lord’s power; the poem leaves their precise legal status unstated.

notes.label: Rappe
notes.text: a black horse; Cuno’s mount carries him and the abducted maiden toward the cliff.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive or tyrannical lord who holds others under oppressive power; after death Cuno must ride around the ruined castle.

notes.label: Hoch Rialt
notes.text: the high castle of Rialt, also invoked through the title Hohenrätier applied to its lord.

ec50a2ff004bcecc9f3a35118c93eef4ac2b689d.summary: At Haldi lived a man who treated his wife with dreadful harshness and cruelty.

notes.label: Ä, chum-mer doch nitt mit dynä Filänä!
notes.text: Uri dialect dismissing the pregnant wife’s appeal, approximately ‘Oh, do not come to me with your Filänä’; Filänä is an insulting or belittling word for her expected offspring, possibly associated with foals in light of the horse-headed punishment, but its exact literal derivation is uncertain.
notes.anchor: Ä, chum-mer doch nitt mit dynä Filänä!

notes.label: Rossgrind
notes.text: a rough Swiss German expression for a horse’s head or skull; each of the child’s two heads is compared to one.

notes.label: Ja, d'r Tyfel hesch byn-d'r!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Why, you have the Devil with you!’; the husband’s curse is made bodily when his wife gives birth to a snake.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Alemannic name for the oppressive night-being associated with nightmares, chest pressure, and sleep paralysis; this account explains it as a child transformed by a parent’s curse.

notes.label: Dü Cheibä Toggel!
notes.text: a forceful Uri insult meaning approximately ‘You damned Toggel!’; Toggel means a clumsy fool, oaf, or lout, while Cheibä intensifies it with the contemptuous force of carrion, rogue, or damned creature, and the insult magically creates the similarly named Toggeli.

3c44c2017b4d2cc0fcd523e96135e998e21bf190.summary: Old Gläusler used to work as a Senn at Gufären in the Maderan Valley, just below the hotel, and he had often talked himself into saying, “If I go up to the Alp just once more next year, the Devil may take me!” But that is how the Alpine herders are: even when they swear every year that they will…

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock, cheese making, and the seasonal pasture operation; Gläusler’s precise rank among the herders is not further described.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy work, not simply a mountain summit; the annual ascent and return structure the herders’ way of life.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: z'bättä riëffä
notes.text: Uri dialect for going out to call the Alpine household to prayer, an evening devotional custom; the hostile black figure specifically prevents Gläusler from performing it.

7f4f0b372825115fba75a4042158753327c99ce8.summary: When a traveler descends the north side of the Bernina Pass, about half an hour below the summit, at the mouth of Val Minore, a place is pointed out that is called Curtinatsch.

notes.label: Curtinatsch
notes.text: the local name of the vanished settlement and mining site below the Bernina Pass at the mouth of Val Minore; the source offers both a historical mining explanation and a punitive legend.

notes.label: Argentèra
notes.text: a regional place-name connected with silver, glossed by Jecklin as “silver slope”; it identifies the steep slope near surviving mine adits.

6f1f191bdea0e83c984e4223d0e29c0b94db9cc7.summary: There was a time when cows on the alpine pastures had to be milked three times each day because Cyprian, Baldrian und Bibernell were such milk-producing herbs.

notes.label: Cyprian, Baldrian und Bibernell
notes.text: the traditional three-herb formula blamed for the former abundance of Alpine milk; Baldrian is valerian and Bibernell commonly a burnet or pimpernel, while the precise plant meant by Cyprian is uncertain in this source.

3ed5b668d5aaa29b6e050ab3f612181ec4b00d96.summary: A rooster once said to his little hens, “Come quickly up into the room and peck together the bread crumbs on the table.

notes.label: Gse gse gse gse gse gse gsehstaber?
notes.text: a compressed Swiss German question roughly meaning ‘See, see, do you see now?’; its repeated gse also imitates the hens' clucking, so the joke depends on both meaning and animal sound.
notes.anchor: Gse gse gse gse gse gse gsehstaber?

notes.label: Ha ha han i's nit gwüßt?
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Ha, ha, didn't I know it?’; the repeated ha and han give the rooster's answer a crowing, laughing sound that answers the hens' wordplay.
notes.anchor: Ha ha han i's nit gwüßt?

notes.label: D Brösmeli uf em Tisch
notes.text: Aargau Swiss German for ‘the little crumbs on the table’; Brösmeli is an affectionate or small diminutive of crumbs, and the dialect title is retained beside its English meaning.

f43bf63b03fa7e155fa6418c01190fc05bf9f3ee.summary: Nothing more is heard of the Härdwîblenä. People are now very foul (malicious), and since they scattered ashes for them, they have not returned.

notes.label: Härdwîblenä
notes.text: dialect plural of Härdwîbli, ‘little earth-women.’

notes.label: Ifang
notes.text: the proper name of a tract of meadowland where seven houses stood; it can also denote enclosed or newly claimed land.

notes.label: Härdlüt
notes.text: dialect for ‘earth people,’ the wider group to which the Härdwîbli belong.

notes.label: Härdwîbli
notes.text: singular ‘little earth-woman,’ a helper who gives an inexhaustible flax bundle on condition of secrecy.

notes.label: rîstä
notes.text: a bundle or strick of prepared flax ready for spinning.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Strihä
notes.text: the dialect place-name for Strîchen, identified by the source as a Jura mountain containing the beings’ dwelling.

notes.label: Äschäbrünneli
notes.text: literally ‘little ash spring,’ said to run cloudy on the days when the earth-women wash inside the mountain.

notes.label: d'Härdwîbli am Strihä
notes.text: Aargau dialect for ‘the little earth-women at Strihä,’ naming diminutive subterranean helpers associated with a Jura mountain.

8b3c0b39e2d553713df229e917b0108940ebf53f.summary: Once a woman hired a little goat herd and told him that he should come at a proper time to eat breakfast, so that he could let the goats out before it grew so late.

notes.label: Nidlu
notes.text: Saas/Valais dialect for rich cream; the woman serves it as yet another nourishing inducement meant to get the boy out with the goats.

notes.label: Geisshirtji
notes.text: a Saas German diminutive for a little goat herder or goatherd boy; here it identifies the hired child whose appetite exceeds his willingness to herd.

notes.label: Gad nid gani!
notes.text: the compressed Saas-dialect punch line, closest to ‘I'm not going at all!’; retaining it preserves the sound and abrupt comic refusal on which the anecdote turns.

notes.label: D's ful Geisshirtji
notes.text: Saas German for ‘the lazy little goat herd’; Geisshirtji is a diminutive goatherd title, and the affectionate-sounding -ji sharpens the joke when the boy finally refuses to work.

51731326b85cfbed43d7c6872f950d048b446d63.summary: At Ryfel in Zermatt, near the Ryfelhorn, is a fairly spacious cave with a narrow entrance.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: D's Morisch Loch
notes.text: the dialect place-name of the cave near the Ryfelhorn, approximately ‘the Morisch Hole’; the meaning of Morisch, the cave's exact identification, and its connection to the shepherd are uncertain.

d4eb0cf4181780e1e9292ddbbc269ab990e0d4aa.summary: Once there was a good, upright farmer who never cursed the weather, whatever it might be.

notes.label: D's Wetter ist guot
notes.text: Valais German for ‘the weather is good,’ the farmer's unwavering formula that he rises from his deathbed to affirm even during the storm.

notes.label: Lich ufg'lägu
notes.text: Valais dialect for a corpse laid out for viewing before burial; the phrase describes the body from which the farmer sits up.

notes.label: Totuwächter
notes.text: Valais dialect for watchers of the dead, people keeping the traditional vigil beside the laid-out body before the funeral.

8b8b9763831f2a802fd061a080a8e913030af895.summary: 1. Platti-Liese, a Müetterli who died in 1890 at the great age of 100, related: Once, several men were working with timber in the Erstfeld Valley.

notes.label: Müetterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Mutter, literally ‘little mother’ or ‘old mother’; here it is a familiar designation for the centenarian Platti-Liese, not a claim of kinship.

notes.label: D'Stund isch da
notes.text: literally ‘the hour is here,’ an Uri-dialect death call announcing that the destined moment has arrived even before its victim; the title and repeated formula are retained because their exact wording binds the variants together.

notes.label: D'Stund isch noochä-n-
notes.text: approximately ‘the hour is near’ in Uri dialect; the voice’s altered formula again announces an imminent appointed death.

notes.label: Föhnengwächti
notes.text: a mass or drift of snow formed or destabilized by Föhn conditions; it breaks loose like a snow slab or small avalanche, but the source does not define its exact snow structure.

notes.label: Hyr miër, z' Jahr diër
notes.text: an Uri-dialect omen meaning approximately ‘this year me, next year you’; the maid’s ensuing one-year decline supplies the context, though the compressed formula leaves its speaker and addressee unstated.

50f14f118920311d5cc21924e3cc5e39006f5124.summary: Two hundred years ago, four cats danced together at the Geissweid near Zug.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: an Ammann was a local magistrate or chief official, whose wife is implicitly identified with the wounded cat; the officeholder, jurisdiction, and alleged transformation are unspecified.

4b8576217f863ddaa03132b4982b2f3507a65a25.summary: A man was advised that when the Toggeli came to torment him, he should quickly seize it and dance around the room with it three times.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for the nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; this account says that physically seizing it and completing three dance circuits reveals it as a young woman.

notes.label: Städeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Stadel for a small barn, granary, or farm outbuilding; the abandoned structure serves as the supposed site of the chain-rattling ghost.

c2ea692ed1ffae272b60bc9343c35b6ca3ea1b64.summary: In a remote, lonely little house on Seelisberg there was a haunting; everyone in the whole municipality knew it.

notes.label: hed üffg'g upfet
notes.text: the source’s irregularly spaced Uri dialect wording for the hidden man having lifted or jerked his head upward; the narrative establishes the motion, but the printed form may preserve a transcription or spacing artifact.

notes.label: Tot isch tot; wenn d'tot bisch, sä gupfisch nimmä!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Dead is dead; if you are dead, you do not raise your head again’; gupfisch describes the repeated upward jerk or lift.
notes.anchor: Tot isch tot; wenn d'tot bisch, sä gupfisch nimmä!

notes.label: Chlopfhammer
notes.text: literally a knocking or beating hammer, here the shoemaker’s cobbling hammer used to strike the supposed corpse; the exact historical tool form is not described.

notes.label: Jä, ich ha g'säit: tot isch tot; wenn d'nu einisch gupfisch, sä schlah-n-i mid-em Chlopfhammer dri!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Yes, I said: dead is dead; if you raise your head once more, I will strike with the Chlopfhammer’; the warning preserves the tale’s repeated formula.
notes.anchor: Jä, ich ha g'säit: tot isch tot; wenn d'nu einisch gupfisch, sä schlah-n-i mid-em Chlopfhammer dri!

notes.label: Schüehni
notes.text: an Uri nickname or occupational diminutive for the shoemaker, based on Schueh, ‘shoe’; it identifies the same wager-taker rather than a new character.

notes.label: Jetz bisch g'wiss tot
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Now you are certainly dead’; the shoemaker’s grim closing formula confirms that the prank has become a killing.

b6ab568b47a04bf5c3dbf049ca341bf919970bfe.summary: and the Teetälä are said once to have come as far as the Ortflüeh just before Stäg.

notes.label: Teetälä
notes.text: an obscure Uri dialect plural apparently denoting diminutive or personified figures of death; the fragment says they came as far as the Ortflüeh, but gives no physical description, so the precise sense remains uncertain.

notes.label: Näfel
notes.text: a dialect plant name most likely referring to carnations, pinks, or a related ‘little nail’ flower; a ring of them emerging from the ground precedes the plague, but the exact botanical species is uncertain.

b6aac243afd207fdbb4f7eca11d06d4bedb25ede.summary: Christina Zgraggen from the parish of Amsteg was playing Versteckis with other children near railway watchman's cottage no. 42.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Versteckis
notes.text: the Swiss German children's game of hide-and-seek; the unexplained drops fall while Christina is playing near the railway cottage.

notes.label: getschättert
notes.text: an onomatopoeic dialect verb suggesting loud clattering, pattering, or splattering rather than a single quiet drip; the exact unseen sound or quantity of liquid is not specified.

c75e3ca298a380a12e164670c6abe9756eb64b81.summary: The old Sigrist of Schattdorf, who had to walk through the cemetery late at night, found a human skull in his path.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German and southern German title for a church sexton or sacristan, whose duties could include tending the cemetery; his church office makes his contempt for the skull especially pointed.

notes.label: Channsch de morä züe-m'r chu ds Mittag ässä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Then you can come to me for midday dinner tomorrow’; the mocking invitation becomes binding when Death accepts it.
notes.anchor: Channsch de morä züe-m'r chu ds Mittag ässä

notes.label: Nur innä
notes.text: a dialect invitation meaning ‘Come in’ or ‘Just come inside’; the whole family unwittingly admits the skeletal guest.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

11d7dac219d5565480a2490d96d0190a5f4187b8.summary: It is a general popular belief that every person has an appointed hour of death.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

91439d9a56507d767151563cee5a9cc70b53546e.summary: One of the Seld-Trynelers was walking toward Lehn at nightfall, returning home from the market in Altdorf, when he suddenly heard splendid music behind his back.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: the diminutive of Gaden, an Alpine barn, storehouse, farm chamber, or outbuilding; the source identifies a small rural structure behind Trudelingen without specifying its exact use.

notes.label: Bödemli
notes.text: literally a ‘little piece of ground’ or small level patch; the horse rolls upon this named or topographic spot beside the road.

d24084344ca5e0460465635de6b65d6e7329115e.summary: People have also sometimes seen the likeness or spirit, as it is said, of persons still living walking in their houses or elsewhere several days before their death, while those people themselves were still hale and healthy; they died soon afterward.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

99a463273e9fd2f56dfbdd25e7ea8ca4a8e080df.summary: On one of the high plateaus between Brugg and Waldshut by the Black Forest, seven dwarfs lived together in a little house.

notes.label: Lumpenmaitschi
notes.text: a harsh Alemannic insult for a disreputable or ragged girl, with Maitschi meaning ‘girl’; in context the suspicious woman accuses the traveler of sexual impropriety, while the exact force ranges from ‘worthless girl’ to ‘slut.’

2583d2f2a7282a7ba07fe80fafb0fd929075f550.summary: In a house in Schattdorf, people often heard an inexplicable clatter among the wooden beams stored in the Laube.

notes.label: Laube
notes.text: here a covered gallery, porch, loft-like open space, or attached storage area in a traditional house; beams are stored there, but the architecture is not described precisely enough to choose one narrower English term.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: in Bernese folk belief, the Doggeli is a nightmare or pressure demon felt sitting on a sleeper’s chest; its independent identity versus a witch’s projected form is explicitly uncertain in the source.

notes.label: Bindbaumlätsch
notes.text: this dialect compound denotes a binding loop or knot used in the bedstead charm; its exact construction and literal relation to a Bindbaum are uncertain.

notes.label: Hälslig
notes.text: this appears to be a small collar-like loop or strap hung at the head of the bed; its precise material, shape, and dialect meaning are uncertain.

notes.label: Bundhoogge
notes.text: this dialect form denotes the binding hook placed in the loop as part of the charm; its exact hardware form is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here Alp does not mean a mountain pasture but the older Germanic nightmare being whose pressure is preserved in Alpdruck; its relationship to the locally named Doggeli is uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

b98392466290907f1a0bace562c724d940b7d60d.summary: A Jewish man who had fled Austria came with his five children to the race of giants at Kalkeisen and asked for protection.

notes.label: Judenhüttle
notes.text: literally ‘little Jews' hut,’ the historical local name assigned to the refugee family's dwelling outside the church; the diminutive -le is regional, while the label reflects the story's Christian outsider framing.

notes.label: Kratzere
notes.text: the local name of the rocks from which the crowned white snake arrives; it is preserved as a place-name.

notes.label: Schwefelkies
notes.text: literally ‘sulfur pyrite,’ the older German name for iron pyrite; its angular metallic crystals are explained as the melted snake crown's grains of gold.

Historical context: the closing commentary accurately translates the source's anti-Jewish stereotype as a historical claim and explicitly marks it as defamation; it should not be read as factual information about Jewish belief or practice.

d75541b6ea5bae933e091e52ee5132924d58da43.summary: Dem Ungfel wehre — Guarding Against Misfortune

notes.label: Dem Ungfel wehre
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘to ward off misfortune’ or ‘guard against bad luck’; the title is ironic because the prescribed remedy fails completely.

notes.label: ungfelig
notes.text: dialect for unlucky, ill-fated, or continually subject to mishaps; it describes the farmer's worsening condition.

notes.label: tromsigs
notes.text: dialect meaning approximately crookedly, contrary, or all wrong; the exact nuance is uncertain, but nothing proceeds properly for him.

notes.label: Wohrsägeri
notes.text: dialect for a female fortune-teller or soothsayer, literally a woman who ‘says what is true’; her advice is treated skeptically by the story's ending.

notes.label: schwarze Rache
notes.text: literally ‘black palate’ or dark roof of the mouth in this dialectal animal description, not ‘black revenge’; the dog is selected by an uncanny physical mark whose ritual significance is unexplained.

notes.label: Doppelspore
notes.text: double spurs, an unusual paired growth on a rooster's legs; the fortune-teller requires this rare animal trait for the failed counter-charm.

5f61c86b611cee0d2f534739f2447c041853dd45.summary: Once, on a most holy Trinity Sunday, my grandparents sawed down a Wiälesch—a rowan tree, Sorbus aucuparia.

notes.label: Wiälesch
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for the rowan or mountain ash, Sorbus aucuparia, as the source explicitly glosses it; the punishment follows from felling it on Trinity Sunday rather than from any stated property of the tree itself.

468b12e75219e70cd8ffa943999297ef315ed7bc.summary: For many years a decaying Heutuch hung above a cliff on Furner-Berg where no human foot could reach it.—It is said to have belonged to a Furner who was gathering Streue in the nearby forest on a Sunday.

notes.label: Heutuch
notes.text: a large cloth used to gather and carry hay or similar loose material; its unreachable remains become the enduring warning in the tale.

notes.label: Furner
notes.text: an inhabitant of Furna in Graubünden; the term identifies both the mountain and the person who violates Sunday rest.

notes.label: Streue
notes.text: forest litter such as leaves, needles, or cut vegetation gathered for animal bedding rather than food.

645de31c3118d28d80de3977a79d3553fc48d88e.summary: The lords of Strättlingen were kind, devout, and just; only a few formed a dishonorable exception.

notes.label: Höllmoos
notes.text: literally ‘Hell Moor,’ the place near the Thunersee to which evil spirits are ordered to carry Diebolt’s soul; the legend explicitly explains the continuing place-name through the soul’s cries there.

3ef7f442d3256f3b18dd252f01c2f2e07aa712d8.summary: Hunter Dietrich lived in Muridorf some sixty years ago and once lay in wait for a fox in the nearby Muriwald.

notes.label: Osterkohlen
notes.text: literally ‘Easter coals,’ these are blessed or ritually significant coals used here in protective ammunition against a bewitched animal; their exact source, blessing, and local ritual use are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

e11b272a9a4aa57532ab7a0f58e86a6952c3f75a.summary: At the time when the Faustrecht still prevailed, a knight named wicked Dietrich dwelt at Reifenstein.

notes.label: Faustrecht
notes.text: literally ‘fist-law,’ the medieval practice of pursuing private force or feud when effective public law did not restrain the powerful; it describes the violent order in which Dietrich rules.

notes.label: Schelmenloch
notes.text: literally ‘rogues’ hole,’ the local name of a notorious cave near Wasserfallen associated with its own robber legends; Loch here denotes a cave or hollow, not merely a small opening.

notes.label: Jahrzeitenmesse
notes.text: an endowed Catholic anniversary Mass, ordinarily commemorating the dead; Dietrich violates the sanctuary while the priest is celebrating this memorial observance.

623abf61c28209bbd5a48b6a8798853e4c968227.summary: On the high Alpine pastures, one should either pray and call others to prayer diligently from the very beginning, or else not pray at all.

notes.label: spitzen Nessli
notes.text: a quoted local place-name or terrain designation on the Fiseten cattle pasture; the story establishes only that it is naturally inaccessible to cattle, so its narrower topographic sense is left open.

ba7fd12d3ed22f363a03eae1ed4a1fab5235c78b.summary: With these words a reckless debtor in Isental used to console his creditors and dismiss anyone who tried to admonish him.

notes.label: Diä gross Gloggä zallt's de
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘The great bell will pay it then’; the debtor’s mocking promise imagines his funeral bell settling what he owes, and the bell’s refusal supplies the moral judgment.

f4f074fc6b342a3f8601f915469af9468334db92.summary: Whether Gespenster exist or not—basta—one must not mock! Riseler-Josti of Erstfeld learned that.

notes.label: Gespenster
notes.text: ghosts or spectral beings; the opening leaves their objective existence undecided while insisting that mockery remains dangerous.

notes.label: basta
notes.text: an Italian-derived interjection meaning ‘enough’ or ‘that settles it’; its use gives the narrator’s warning a clipped, emphatic finality.

notes.label: Boglikapuziner
notes.text: the local name of the Gespenst associated with the Bogliberg, literally suggesting a Bogli Capuchin; the source does not explain whether it appears as a friar.

notes.label: es sich nicht spöttlen lässt
notes.text: the dialect-inflected phrase means that the being will not tolerate being mocked; the diminutive-sounding verb sharpens the narrator’s admonition.

e698911ecd2aeb40911a4d0844291789938c9c1b.summary: At that time there lived three famous physicians: Doctor Tuet in Glarus, Doctor Kohler in Schwyz, and Doctor Füster in Uri.

notes.label: Füster
notes.text: the name of this Uri Faust-like wonder doctor, whose bargain with the Devil and refusal of a final chance at grace form the legend; the personal name is retained rather than anglicized.

notes.label: b'setzen
notes.text: Uri dialect for paving or laying out a surface; the Devil must cover the road with coins immediately before Füster’s horse and gather them immediately behind it.

notes.label: Fünfliber
notes.text: Swiss five-franc coins; Füster makes the Devil use them as paving stones, but only for the single horse-length currently beneath and ahead of him.

notes.label: Solang diese Kerze brinnt
notes.text: the first line of a rhymed Swiss-German promise meaning ‘So long as this candle burns, God has kindled grace for you’; the angel offers Füster time to repent while the flame lasts.

notes.label: Das hed alligs der Vatter verzellt; der hed äs Büech gha und hed vill dri gläsä.
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Father always told that story; he had a little book and read in it a great deal’; alligs means ‘always’ here, and the closing statement identifies family reading and oral retelling as the informant’s source.
notes.anchor: Das hed alligs der Vatter verzellt; der hed äs Büech gha und hed vill dri gläsä.

2f97768719400fefae36ab040ce53ceaa72d5f73.summary: 1. a) Within living memory, he lived in the canton of Glarus and practiced medicine by sympathetic magic.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

0a8dbabd6071c6bcbe23ef688028c8b7a739ab6c.summary: One Sunday in the haymaking month, I was visiting a neighboring house. I had not yet left it, and it was about seven in the evening, when I saw my father, dressed in his Sunday best with a snow-white shirt, freshly shaved and with newly cut hair, come down the steps of our house and walk toward the church.

notes.label: G'wychtä
notes.text: literally ‘the consecrated place,’ an Uri dialect name here encompassing the church and burial ground; the direction in which the double walks determines the omen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

17618512779b12818e1917a2c4e57532e0b139b2.summary: Merenschwand is a large, sprawling municipality whose main street is built along the country road where it curves toward the east.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” a regional folklore label for an uncanny creature attached to a particular settlement; here it is the pig called Dorfloos, not ordinary village livestock.

notes.label: Dorfloos
notes.text: Merenschwand’s local name for this shape-changing spectral pig and village haunt; Dorf suggests the community, but the intended historical sense of Loos is uncertain and should not be reduced to the modern English word “lot.”

cec72cee79aeda68ae98a1c1bac6a2450b5fe7e7.summary: At night a black dog comes out of a barn in Birr’s upper village and disappears into the cellar of the next house, while at the same time a black pig comes out of that cellar.

notes.label: Dorftiere
notes.text: literally “village animals,” regional folklore apparitions attached to particular settlements rather than ordinary livestock; here the plural covers the shape-linked dog, pig, and fiery horse of Birr.

notes.label: Breitmatter
notes.text: the local name of the sinister hunter and returning ghost associated with the Breitmatt; the form suggests a man belonging to that place, but the source does not give his personal name.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: the traditional practice of an itinerant craftsperson working temporarily in customers’ homes; here it explains why the tailor is traveling to the Breitmatt.

notes.label: Chilbi
notes.text: a Swiss parish fair or local festival, evoked by the temporary stalls and crowd gathered to watch the soldiers.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Brünnlig
notes.text: a local name for a small supernatural being; the source shows it riding on a shovel but does not explain the name or its class.

notes.label: Dr Brünnlig uf dr Schuﬂe
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the Brünnlig on the shovel,’ naming the little spirit carried home unknowingly.

notes.label: Schuﬂe
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘shovel,’ preserving the source’s typographic ligature.

notes.label: Fasnacht
notes.text: the Swiss carnival season before Lent, also a traditional time for frying festive pastries.

notes.label: Büri
notes.text: Bernese German for a farmer’s wife or female farmer.

notes.label: Was Tüfels hesch jetz du druffe?
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘What the devil have you got on there now?’; invoking the Devil makes the spirit disappear.
notes.anchor: Was Tüfels hesch jetz du druffe?

d64668a86597f10009437ccda5eb7195941b863f.summary: The Plague Documents from the plague years are completely lacking in our area.

notes.label: Chorgerichtsmanuale
notes.text: minutes or registers of Protestant consistorial courts, which can preserve local social and mortality evidence.

notes.label: Sterberödel
notes.text: death rolls or mortality registers, historical lists that may record epidemic deaths.

notes.label: Oberaargau
notes.text: the Upper Aargau, the northeastern Bernese region around towns such as Langenthal rather than the canton of Aargau itself.

notes.label: grosse Sterbet
notes.text: an older expression for the ‘great dying,’ the plague mortality remembered as a collective catastrophe.

notes.label: Schwinde
notes.text: literally a great wasting or disappearance, another personified name for the plague's mass mortality.

notes.label: Bur
notes.text: Bernese German for Bauer, a farmer; the dialect repeatedly identifies the man who vanishes with his team and crop.

notes.label: Dr Bur mit em Fueder Garbe
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the farmer with a load of sheaves,’ the title of the brief plague-landscape tradition.
notes.anchor: Dr Bur mit em Fueder Garbe

notes.label: Fueder Garbe
notes.text: a wagonload or cartload of grain sheaves rather than a single bundle.

notes.label: grosse Stärbet
notes.text: the Bernese dialect form of ‘great dying,’ introducing the localized account of the vanished grain field.

notes.label: Ofeplatte
notes.text: dialect for stove tiles or slabs, found underground when the road is made and treated as traces of the former settlement or farm.

notes.label: Dr Chilacher
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the church field,’ a burial ground associated with deaths during the plague.

notes.label: Chilacher
notes.text: Swiss German compound of Chile, church, and Acher, field.

notes.label: Stützli
notes.text: a small steep slope, rise, or supporting embankment near the Chilacher.

notes.label: Erniesse
notes.text: dialect infinitive for sneezing; the explanation says the Black Death came through sneezing.

notes.label: Hälf dr Gott
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘God help you,’ the blessing said after someone sneezes.

98315dd344f355025a1f4b7578c743a42e7b7810.summary: Dr Geischt im Sodloch — The Spirit in the Well Shaft

notes.label: Dr Geischt im Sodloch
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the spirit in the well shaft’; the title identifies the unseen occupant whose space the children violate.

notes.label: Sodloch
notes.text: a deep well hole or well shaft, related to the Swiss term Sodbrunnen; here it is an old opening by the Altburg, not merely a shallow puddle or pit.

notes.label: Zwieseli
notes.text: a small forked branch, twig, or similarly two-pronged object; the diminutive describes what the supernatural blow felt like, while the actual striker remains unseen.

b4c6e573770f1c45aa7a602f8192cc862f77cb5f.summary: Dr Geischt im Stal — The Spirit in the Stable

notes.label: Dr Geischt im Stal
notes.text: dialect for ‘the spirit in the stable’; the apparition is blamed for repeated livestock deaths, although its exact form is not described.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Chriesichratte
notes.text: a cherry-harvesting basket or pannier; carrying liquid milk in such a basket is presented as evidence of the Capuchin's extraordinary holiness or power.

notes.label: Chumm vüre, grüens Vögeli
notes.text: dialect for ‘Come forward, green little bird,’ the Capuchin's ritual-sounding summons; why he addresses the stable spirit as a green bird is not explained.

notes.label: tätscht
notes.text: dialect for making a smack, slap, or thumping sound; the spirit's final explanation is terse, and what produced or pleased it about the sound remains ambiguous.

74f39ad7091dc2b911492e41050fd1b9db9d3364.summary: Dr Giger im Schmiedwald — The Fiddler in the Schmiedwald

notes.label: Giger
notes.text: Swiss German for a fiddler or violin player; here it names the mysterious musician as well as his social role at the dance.

notes.label: Dr Giger im Schmiedwald
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the fiddler in the Schmiedwald’; the unknown musician's self-playing instrument marks him as an uncanny visitor at a secret woodland dance.

notes.label: im Verschleikte
notes.text: Bernese dialect for acting secretly, furtively, or out of sight; the clandestine character of the dancing helps give the crossroads gathering its dangerous folkloric setting.

notes.label: Gigli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a little fiddle; the instrument continues playing from the tree while its owner dances.

5a03cbf137854570c9b5a42861a6b3391ace33f9.summary: Dr grüen Jeger — The Green Hunter

notes.label: Dr grüen Jeger
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “the Green Hunter”; here he is a green-clad diabolical apparition with a black dog whose appearance immediately precedes a storm, though the passage does not equate him explicitly with the wider Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Dr guet Wätter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘good weather,’ the dead man’s byname based on his unchanging refrain.

notes.label: Es isch guet Wätter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘It is good weather,’ the man’s habitual claim even in terrible conditions.

notes.label: dr guet Wättter
notes.text: the source’s lowercase spelling of the man’s dialect byname, literally ‘the good weather [man].’

notes.label: Totebaum
notes.text: literally ‘dead-person tree,’ a dialect term for a coffin, originally associated with a hollowed tree trunk.

notes.label: Es isch guet Wetter
notes.text: the final, slightly normalized spelling of ‘It is good weather’ spoken from the coffin.

notes.label: Guetwätter
notes.text: the collector’s joined form of the dead man’s byname in the interpretive commentary.

6bd6e69ea8ff4573f670e9413a40f3642fa6bbe8.summary: Dr Has i dr Horschtert — The Hare in the Orchard

notes.label: Dr Has i dr Horschtert
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the hare in the orchard’; the title’s retained phrasing preserves the oral register in which the uncanny hunting account was recorded.

notes.label: Horschtert
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form for an orchard or fruit-tree enclosure; here it is the place where the hunter repeatedly encounters the same uncanny hare.

f2d01aaea2e780b94d26f5d935b9c40382d8a01d.summary: The Devil appears as a little green man and often as a distinguished gentleman; but the goat’s foot, recalling the satyrs and fauns of antiquity, frequently betrays his origin:

notes.label: Dr Her mit de Geissfüsse
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the gentleman with goat feet,’ the disguise through which the Devil’s animal nature is revealed.

notes.label: jasse
notes.text: to play Jass, the traditional Swiss trick-taking card game.

notes.label: Geissfüess
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘goat feet,’ the physical sign that exposes the gentleman as the Devil.

notes.label: Tüfel
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Devil.’

notes.label: Was gisch, was hesch
notes.text: an idiom meaning ‘as fast as he could’ or ‘in a flash’; literally its words are roughly ‘what you give, what you have.’

677b1db49df091fe204f1bd45528918ee055410a.summary: Dr Her uf em Ällmig — The Gentleman on the Common

notes.label: Dr Her uf em Ällmig
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the gentleman on the common’; the Her is a penitent spirit tied to land whose boundary he wrongfully moved.

notes.label: Ällmig
notes.text: a Bernese form of Allmend, land held or used in common by a village community; the shared-land setting makes the displaced boundary a communal wrong.

notes.label: nid sufer
notes.text: literally ‘not clean’ in Bernese dialect, but in this folkloric setting it means uncanny, troubled, or haunted rather than physically dirty.

notes.label: Hie har u dert har
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘this way and that way’; the spirit's repeated words express his uncertainty over where the stolen boundary belongs.

notes.label: Marche
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a boundary or boundary marker; moving one was a serious offense, and restoring the stake releases the guilty spirit.

notes.label: Lohhäwle
notes.text: the local place-name where the apparition was encountered; its exact location and the literal derivation of the dialect name are uncertain.

notes.label: Lohhäwlebock
notes.text: the buck-like or buck-named spirit of the Lohhäwle; the brief account defines it by its sudden leap onto people's backs rather than by a clear physical description.

notes.label: Bölima
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a bogeyman or frightening figure used to scare children; the Lohhäwlebock served this disciplinary storytelling role.

notes.label: Dr Lohhäwlebock
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the Lohhäwle buck,’ the named bogey-being that unexpectedly leaps onto a traveler's back; Bock literally means a male goat, but the apparition's form is not otherwise described.

notes.label: Dr Müller mit sine Töchtere
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the miller with his daughters,’ the title of this matchmaking farce.

notes.label: Schriss
notes.text: a dialect term for a sweetheart, suitor, or marriage prospect; the daughters have none, though the word's exact nuance is local.

notes.label: Obesitz
notes.text: an evening social gathering or visit, often a setting for courtship and communal conversation.

notes.label: Ätti, Mil älle
notes.text: the first daughter's childlike or defective dialect speech, approximately addressing ‘Father’ and reporting something about the milk being gone; the compressed wording is ambiguous.

notes.label: U, nüt dädä, nüt dädä
notes.text: the second daughter's equally childish speech, approximately ‘oh, don't say that, don't say that.’

notes.label: Död is, i nüt deit a. I de Ma ha!
notes.text: the third daughter's babbling, apparently insisting she did nothing and wants a husband; its deliberately mangled wording is part of the joke and cannot be mapped with certainty.
notes.anchor: Död is, i nüt deit a. I de Ma ha!

notes.label: Gwunger
notes.text: curiosity, appetite to know, or inquisitive desire; the daughters' speech gives the visiting lads all the answer they need.

cbf87720155f902130bb0e319524d21dda9ab045.summary: Dr Pfarer versumt d’Predig — The Priest Misses the Sermon

notes.label: Dr Pfarer versumt d’Predig
notes.text: dialect for ‘the priest misses the sermon’; the title frames the cleric's hunting absence and improvised biblical rebuke as a comic tale.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor, here the official who personally inspects whether the Friday preaching order is obeyed.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Sigerischt
notes.text: a Swiss German form of sacristan or church sexton responsible for ringing the bells; the priest's wife uses the prolonged peal to summon her husband home.

notes.label: Chanzelrock
notes.text: literally ‘pulpit coat,’ the clerical gown or preaching robe hurried out to the returning priest so he can enter the pulpit at once.

notes.label: Tägscht
notes.text: dialect for Text, the scriptural passage chosen as a sermon text; the priest pointedly selects the verse about a thief arriving unexpectedly.

5bd6269a8d862e5e34be7b61f68e50eb7d8e1edc.summary: Dr Schatz im Huttelwald — The Treasure in the Huttelwald

notes.label: Dr Schatz im Huttelwald
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “the treasure in the Huttelwald”; the retained title preserves the local storytelling voice, while Huttelwald is a place-name whose derivation is not explained.

notes.label: Isehafe
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for an iron pot or cauldron; buried treasure is imagined inside this durable household vessel, although its size and shape are not given.

notes.label: Chrott
notes.text: Swiss German for a toad, here the hideous black guardian that speaks from the treasure site; whether it is a transformed person, spirit, or simply a monstrous toad is left uncertain.

notes.label: Dr Schatz im Stallgang
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the treasure in the stable passage,’ where the farmer secretly buries his chest.

notes.label: Stallgang
notes.text: the passage running through a stable between stalls or feeding areas.

notes.label: Volleschüble
notes.text: a dialect name for the small wares the peddler sold; the precise object is uncertain in the printed form.

notes.label: Bidure
notes.text: compassion, pity, or fellow feeling, which moves the household to admit the traveler.

notes.label: Schuﬂe
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘shovel,’ preserving the source’s typographic ligature.

notes.label: Büri
notes.text: Bernese German for a farmer’s wife or female farmer.

notes.label: Geissbock
notes.text: Swiss German for a male goat or billy goat, ridden backward in the treasure-release ritual.

notes.label: Schmiedwald
notes.text: literally ‘smiths’ forest,’ the woodland name linked here first to the seven smithies of the burned town and then to the pasture that reverted to fir woods.

notes.label: Chloschterbrünnli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘little monastery spring,’ the surviving place-name at Frybech that the account uses as evidence for the vanished monastery.

notes.label: Gutschti
notes.text: a local livestock term for the cattle or young bovines whose tongues the boy cuts out; the source’s dialect form does not make their exact age or sex certain.

notes.label: Chutscheler
notes.text: the local name of the punished animal tormentor heard bellowing in the storm; its sound echoes the cry ‘Chutsch, chutsch, chutsch,’ and the commentary compares the apparition to the Wild Huntsman.

notes.label: Dr Spieler
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the gambler’ or ‘the card player’; Spieler can mean a player generally, but the story's warning and final rejection of cards make gambling the intended sense here.

notes.label: Tuben
notes.text: Bernese dialect for pigeons; the wording suggests that pigeons, like money, were being gambled for or used as stakes.

notes.label: grüens Manndli
notes.text: Bernese German for a ‘green little man’; the boy immediately recognizes the uncanny figure, but the source does not give it a more specific identity or appearance.

notes.label: Müetti
notes.text: an affectionate Bernese German form of ‘mother’ or ‘mama,’ used by the frightened boy as he begs to be admitted.

notes.label: Dürst
notes.text: a Swiss regional name for a terrifying Wild Hunt figure or storm-riding spirit; the collector compares the green little man's roaring departure with this being but does not say they are identical.

notes.label: Dr Stieregrlng
notes.text: the title's printed Bernese form for ‘the bull's head’; the unusual final spelling is retained exactly, while the body uses Stieregring and Gring.

notes.label: Seppsuhs
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Sepp's house,’ the familiar local name of the old farmhouse on the slope near the Tubeloch.

notes.label: Stieregring
notes.text: Bernese German for a bull's head or skull; hung from the lower roof ridge, it is feared as a spirit vessel and later discussed as an apotropaic animal offering.

notes.label: Gring
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘head,’ here the shortened name for the suspended bull's skull that the children fear.

notes.label: Unghür
notes.text: Bernese German for an uncanny monster, apparition, or dreadful being; the children's comparison conveys terror without identifying a specific creature.

notes.label: Schürwärch
notes.text: Bernese German for barn construction or structural barn work; the skull is removed when the farmer has this part of the farm building renewed.

notes.label: Alti Brüch
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘old customs,’ the title of another account to which the collector refers rather than an explanation supplied within this story.

ca90f7aa3af449523acf910b838f2cff6023f6d9.summary: Dr Strähl nid lo stoh — Do Not Leave the Strähl Standing

notes.label: Strähl
notes.text: a regional forestry term for an upright comb-like strip, snag, or remnant left during tree felling; the source says a witch can knot it, but does not describe its shape clearly enough for a more exact identification.

notes.label: Dr Strähl nid lo stoh
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘do not leave the Strähl standing’; the warning concerns a remnant left when felling a tree, though Strähl’s exact forestry sense is not defined.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Dökter
notes.text: dialect plural for doctors, used here especially for folk healers or wonder-working physicians whose knowledge extends beyond ordinary medicine; the source compares them through the period’s anthropological framework.

notes.label: Löchlidokter
notes.text: literally the ‘Löchli doctor,’ a named or bynamed wonder doctor believed able to send his soul from his body; Löchli’s place or household reference is not explained here.

notes.label: Dökter u Manne, wo meh hei chönne weder anger Lüt
