notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘doctors and men who could do more than other people’; the phrase marks unusual knowledge or magical ability rather than a credential.
notes.anchor: Dökter u Manne, wo meh hei chönne weder anger Lüt

notes.label: Wasendoktor
notes.text: literally the ‘turf doctor’ or doctor associated with Wasen, the byname of folk healer Ulrich Zürcher; the source does not explain whether Wasen is a place, household name, or method.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Dr Süidürscht
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for the Süidürscht, a storm-associated airborne being whose arrival sounds like swine and brings a violent downpour; the name’s literal derivation and the being’s form are not explained.

notes.label: Gchutt
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a clattering, crashing, or jumbled noise; here it is one part of the strange sound heard high in the air.

notes.label: Grochel
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a rough rumbling, rattling, or grunting sound; its distinction from the accompanying Gchutt is a matter of sound quality rather than a separately identified creature.

notes.label: More
notes.text: a regional word for a sow, used in the fishermen’s comparison for the airborne noise; no actual animal is seen.

notes.label: e Chuppele Färli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a bunch or litter of piglets; the phrase conveys the noisy imagined group, but gives no exact number.

notes.label: Totewage
notes.text: the dialect compound meaning ‘death wagon’ or ‘wagon of the dead’; the little tree carried upon it and the exact identity of its followers are left unexplained.

notes.label: schwarz Beck
notes.text: literally the ‘black baker,’ apparently a local nickname for the man who meets the wagon; whether schwarz describes his appearance, family name, or reputation is uncertain.

notes.label: Bördli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small bank, edge, or roadside embankment; the witness presses against it to let the supernatural procession pass.

notes.label: Dr Totewage
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the death wagon’; it is a horseless nocturnal funeral-like vehicle followed by a black-clad procession and associated with changing weather.

5f49d4aa741572c354b7fe90e4b518004bc69d5f.summary: The following story bears witness to a childlike, devout faith and may probably be regarded as the experience of a dream:

notes.label: Dr Tüfel isch gli parat
notes.text: Bernese dialect meaning ‘The Devil is soon at hand’; the title expresses the tale’s warning that despair and unbelief quickly invite a demonic presence.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Frau, ‘little woman’ or ‘wife’; here it affectionately designates the farmer’s long-suffering wife and does not mean a child.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a ‘little man’; here the tiny black, goat-footed figure is a manifestation of the Devil rather than an ordinary dwarf.

notes.label: Rauchchuchi
notes.text: literally ‘smoke kitchen,’ a traditional kitchen space blackened by open-hearth smoke; the comparison conveys the apparition’s smell of soot and scorching.

notes.label: Ofeblatte
notes.text: dialect for the stove plate or ledge of a room-heating stove; the little Devil dances on its corner, though the exact stove construction is not described.

notes.label: Vogeldürscht
notes.text: a local name for a noisy airborne Wild Hunt phenomenon; the elements suggest birds and rushing, but the precise etymology is uncertain.

notes.label: Dr Vogeldürscht ob em Schmiedwald
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the Vogeldürscht above the Schmiedwald,’ naming an airborne manifestation linked with the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a field, vineyard, or woodland watchman charged with guarding crops or property.

notes.label: Dr wild Jeger
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘the Wild Huntsman’; it names the spectral hunter whose noisy passage over local landmarks foretells a change in weather.

notes.label: Dr Willading
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the Willading,’ using Dr as the masculine definite article; here the form names both the historicalized tyrant and the demonic leader of the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Frondienst
notes.text: compulsory unpaid labor owed to a lord, closest to corvée service; here Willading forces local people to dig the drainage channel regardless of their fear or hardship.

notes.label: Chutt
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a sudden gust, rush, or squall; here the spectral hunt passes in an instant like a burst of wind, and the exact intensity is contextual.

notes.label: Wälschlang
notes.text: the source's Bernese dialect form of Welschland, the French-speaking lands to the west; here the storm and spectral hunt are said to come down from that direction.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Dürst
notes.text: a regional Swiss name for the demonic leader of the Wild Hunt; the accompanying commentary connects it with Middle High German Dürste, ‘giant,’ though the etymology is presented as interpretation rather than certainty.

notes.label: ’s Wuetis Heer
notes.text: literally ‘Wuoti's Host,’ a northern and eastern Swiss name for the Wild Hunt or army of souls; the source relates Wueti to Wodan, but wider scholarship does not make every regional tradition identical.

notes.label: Zischtig
notes.text: Swiss German for Tuesday; here the weekday name is cited as a linguistic survival of the old god Ziu, an etymological-cultural claim within the source's commentary.

notes.label: Wuotanes heri
notes.text: an Old High German phrase meaning ‘Wotan's army’ or ‘host of Wotan’; here it is offered as the linguistic basis of the raging spectral host, though it is a scholarly reconstruction rather than dialogue from the legend.

notes.label: Dr Wättermacher
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the weather-maker,’ a person credited with deliberately raising or stopping rain and hail through ritual actions.

notes.label: useme Rieme mälche
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘to milk from a strap’; the impossible milking is interpreted by the source as a surviving fertility charm.

notes.label: haslegi Rüetli
notes.text: little hazel rods or switches; rhythmically striking a matched pair imitates the sounds and movement of the desired storm.

notes.label: Riesel
notes.text: small hail, sleet-like grains, or graupel rather than a destructive fall of large hailstones; the visitor specifically asks for only a little.

notes.label: Sägetzen
notes.text: the source's dialect name for the saw blade or toothed piece set into the roof gutter as a counter-charm against hail.

notes.label: ’s Hauigen
notes.text: the toothed or cutting edge of the saw; the charm supposedly breaks the weather-maker's power when a hailstone damages one of its upward-facing teeth.

notes.label: Gespanen
notes.text: the source's comparative name for another ritual practitioner or companion figure; the immediate story does not identify that figure more precisely, so the inflected source form is retained in the editorial discussion.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

e6fb1a99b41b6e06599a308be21dcb4b9c1adce3.summary: Legends must not be treated as historical sources, or only with caution. Time passes; the memory of particular events fades; individual components are lost; foreign material intrudes.

notes.label: Du bin ig im Runzifal gsi
notes.text: Bernese German for approximately ‘Then I was in Runzifal,’ a saying the author links tentatively to Roland at Roncesvalles, though its living meaning had become obscure.
notes.anchor: Du bin ig im Runzifal gsi

notes.label: Jetz isch Murten uber.
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Now Murten is over,’ a dark proverbial memory probably associated with the Battle of Murten.

notes.label: Driluege wie Schybi
notes.text: approximately ‘to look in like Schybi,’ perhaps recalling Christian Schybi of the Swiss Peasants’ War; the author explicitly treats the connection as uncertain.

notes.label: Do si no dr Predig d’Lüt chuppelewis zsämegstange; uf em Chilehof si sie bliebe stoh u hei brichtet, jetz sig dr Präschten a de Härdöpfel; aber mi söll de luege u dra dänke, was sie sägi, es chöm de no a d’War u zletscht a d’Lüt; das fähl si nid.
notes.text: a Bernese German memory of people clustering after the sermon and saying the blight was now on the potatoes, warning that it would next reach goods and finally people; some dialect details permit alternate shades of meaning.
notes.anchor: Do si no dr Predig d’Lüt chuppelewis zsämegstange; uf em Chilehof si sie bliebe stoh u hei brichtet, jetz sig dr Präschten a de Härdöpfel; aber mi söll de luege u dra dänke, was sie sägi, es chöm de no a d’War u zletscht a d’Lüt; das fähl si nid.

notes.label: Zwingher
notes.text: a coercive or tyrannical lord who holds others in subjection.

notes.label: Dr Zwingher uf dr Altburg
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the tyrant at the Altburg,’ naming the oppressive legendary lord of the buried stronghold.

notes.label: Uflot
notes.text: a dialect insult for a thoroughly bad, disreputable, or filthy person; its precise force varies regionally.

notes.label: Bidure
notes.text: compassion, pity, or fellow feeling; the lord has none when the father pleads for his child.

notes.label: Sodloch
notes.text: a deep well shaft or pit; the legend imagines it extending down to the bed of the Langete.

94a3ae300cb06052e4e46dd1c35cef401ac5f04a.summary: Dr Zwingher uf ern Schlössli — The Tyrant at the Schlössli

notes.label: Zwingher
notes.text: the dialect form of Zwingherr, a coercive feudal lord or tyrant who compels labor and seizes property.

notes.label: Dr Zwingher uf ern Schlössli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the tyrant lord at the little castle’; the dialect title frames the lord through coercive power over the farmers.

notes.label: Schlössli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small castle, fortified manor, or manor house; here it is the tyrant's seat and the farmers' target.

notes.label: Säch
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect term for the cutting iron of a plow, closest to a coulter or plowshare; the farmer tears it free and uses it as the weapon against the lord.

b9b4b23265eb07973bfc187aa4f93c57e87c15d7.summary: The ‘Dokter Füst’ or ‘Dokter Füster’ (also Füstus) had the Evil One entirely in his power and tormented him without limit.

notes.label: Dokter Füst
notes.text: an Uri form of Doctor Faust’s name; the source also records Dokter Füster and Füstus, linking the local trickster-magician to the wider Faust tradition without making the forms separate characters.

notes.label: O, äs sind nu vill meh lääri Sackli g'sy as seeligi mid-ämä Cheeräli!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘Oh, there were simply many more empty little sacks than ones with a grain in them!’; the humor rests on the devil having prepared a separate sack for every grain.
notes.anchor: O, äs sind nu vill meh lääri Sackli g'sy as seeligi mid-ämä Cheeräli!

notes.label: Heig-em's doch bi Läck und bi Brosmä-n-üffg'frässä!
notes.text: an emphatic Uri dialect exclamation meaning that Füst ate the whole load, ‘down to lick and crumb’; it stresses total consumption rather than naming additional foods.
notes.anchor: Heig-em's doch bi Läck und bi Brosmä-n-üffg'frässä!

notes.label: Wenn ds Mül nu üfftüesch, sä friss d'r dy Büeb!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘If you open your mouth once more, I’ll eat your boy!’; the threat is answered by the equally terse formula Sä fris-ä, ‘Then eat him.’
notes.anchor: Wenn ds Mül nu üfftüesch, sä friss d'r dy Büeb!

notes.label: Vom Dr. Füstus hed alligs ds Furggälä-Vreni im Isitall vill verzellt. Äs hed äs ganzes Büech g'ha nur vo dem Dr. Füstus
notes.text: Uri dialect reporting that Furggälä-Vreni in Isental often told stories of Dr. Füstus and that there was a whole book about him; Furggälä-Vreni is a local byname whose exact derivation is not explained.
notes.anchor: Vom Dr. Füstus hed alligs ds Furggälä-Vreni im Isitall vill verzellt. Äs hed äs ganzes Büech g'ha nur vo dem Dr. Füstus

c641149d75a305ec5b2c1a631c5c23a521fa79a8.summary: At the beginning of August in the year 1696, Barth. Alegro of Ponte (Veltlin), who was tending cattle in the mountains on a pasture belonging to the municipality of Stuls near Bergün, met with a strange adventure.

notes.label: Veltlin
notes.text: the historical German name for the Valtellina valley in present-day northern Italy, given as Barth. Alegro’s place of origin.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a variable historical measure roughly comparable to a fathom or an adult arm-span; Jecklin says the first dragon was two Klafter long, but the exact local length is not specified.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Wurm
notes.text: an older Germanic folklore word for a great serpent or dragon, not an ordinary earthworm; it identifies the creature in the second account.

notes.label: Stulser-Gebirge
notes.text: the mountain region around Stuls near Bergün where the two dragon accounts are located; Gebirge denotes a mountain group or mountain country.

169d2b2f741f1a90792ca89e6e6d07d27140a16b.summary: In the great forest that spreads up the mountain from Kriens and Malters, dragons lived in former times.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Draguner
notes.text: dialect plural for dragoons, mounted soldiers who appear in an uncontrollable host.

notes.label: Draguner zum Heiterloch us!
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘dragoons out of the Heiterloch!’—soldiers magically emerge from a book or from the named hole.

869e53056f49f757f5e12e1ebd63c63e0d449b6d.summary: Drei Schritt ab Wäg—Three Steps Off the Road

notes.label: Drei Schritt ab Wäg
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘three steps off the road’; the warning tells a traveler exactly how far to move aside for the supernatural procession.

notes.label: Walkibrügg
notes.text: literally the ‘fulling-mill bridge,’ the locally named bridge above which the narrator's father hears the warning.

notes.label: Usem Wäg, usem Wäg! dass niemer bschänt wird
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘Out of the way, out of the way, so that no one is harmed’; it is the protective herald's cry before the Wild Host.
notes.anchor: Usem Wäg, usem Wäg! dass niemer bschänt wird

notes.label: Bernertracht
notes.text: traditional Bernese regional dress; the apparition's clothing marks her as a local countrywoman rather than identifying the older Wild Hunt motif.

notes.label: Drei Wünsch
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘three wishes’; Wünsch is the dialect plural used in the title and opening heading.

notes.label: Chilemüs
notes.text: literally ‘church mice’; the comparison ‘poor as Chilemüs’ is the Swiss German counterpart of the English idiom ‘poor as church mice.’

notes.label: grüens Manndli
notes.text: literally ‘little green man’ in Bernese Swiss German; the diminutive figure grants the wishes, and the commentary associates him with the Devil without making him explicitly identical to the Devil.

notes.label: Hoorsträhle
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German word for a hair comb; the object is a fashionable comb, not a strand or lock of hair.

0903e1544a1b4fc3f62ad882356e98ecc2ba7457.summary: There was no small amount of haunting in a Gaden at Schweinsberg in Attinghausen.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine barn bay, stable, storage building, or farm outbuilding; here it houses cattle, but the source does not specify its exact construction.

notes.label: Gwätte
notes.text: the fitted corner joint or interlocking timbers of a traditional wooden building; here the farmer jabs the fork into that part of the Gaden, though the precise local construction is not described.

notes.label: Palme
notes.text: in Swiss Catholic usage, blessed Palm Sunday greenery rather than necessarily a literal palm leaf; here it is used as protection against a haunting.

notes.label: Kreuzstreich
notes.text: literally a ‘cross-stroke,’ a protective crossing gesture made over the tangled chain in the three highest Names; the exact motion and spoken formula are not recorded.

notes.label: Haselzwick
notes.text: a blessed hazel twig or switch used to make the Kreuzstreich; the historical form and size of the implement are not specified.

notes.label: glockenpfennigganz
notes.text: an Uri/Glarus expression meaning completely intact despite appearing to fall apart; it literally invokes a Glockenpfennig or ‘bell penny,’ but the idiom's precise material image is uncertain.

003505e354c9fb8b99ac13097f4e3ed77901c861.summary: A hunter had wounded a little fox and stowed it securely in his rucksack. As he crossed a bridge over a ravine on his way home, a voice called from the nearby forest: “Dryaheegi, where are you?” And from his rucksack came the clear reply: “In Heinriki's rucksack!” At that, the hunter threw away his…

notes.label: Dryaheegi
notes.text: the unexplained Uri-dialect name called from the forest to the enchanted or uncanny fox; its exact derivation and literal sense are uncertain, so the name is retained rather than normalized into a specific creature type.

8f15a77f19c6e313e80cc98a9cfc42970c7c8235.summary: Every year in spring, the Wylerplangg avalanche thunders down into the valley from the heights of the Rienzenberg chain.

notes.label: Läuwitiär
notes.text: the same ‘avalanche beast’ without the dialect article Ds; Läuwi is an Alpine dialect form for avalanche and Tiär means animal or beast.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a historical local usher, beadle, or public officer; the source uses the title for the man at Stall-Eggen but does not specify his exact duties.

notes.label: Ds Läuwitiär
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘the avalanche beast’; the legend personifies the Wylerplangg avalanche as a powerful animal that the French soldier imagines he can confront and even fight.

9fd00e032892cb2682e65a4e462502faaccac82e.summary: 1. a) During a terrible flood several 100 years ago, a Rübi from the steep, torn stream valley threatened to destroy the old hamlet of Wytterschwanden in the Schächen Valley.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow or torrent carrying water, earth, and boulders down a slope; this one advances with the witches and stops when the chapel bell rings.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young unmarried woman, with the -li diminutive; here she is the quick-thinking witness who rings the protective chapel bell, while her exact age is not given.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a Swiss German orchard or tree-planted homestead ground; the witness sees the advancing debris flow and witches from this cultivated plot beside the hamlet.

notes.label: Santä-Toni-Sywli
notes.text: the shortened form used in the English prose for Saint Anthony’s chapel-bell nickname; the source records several dialect spellings, all referring to the same bell.

notes.label: Fährli
notes.text: a dialect word literally suggesting a piglet or young pig, offered as an alternate ending to the same bell nickname; it reinforces the animal wordplay but does not explain why the bell is so called.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for women or ‘little female persons,’ sometimes familiar or dismissive in tone; here it identifies the two climbing witches without securely describing their age or size.

notes.label: Ds Santä-Toni-Sywli
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Saint Anthony’s little Sywli,’ the full traditional title of the chapel bell; Sywli literally suggests a ‘little sow’ or ‘piglet,’ but here it is a bell whose ringing stops witches and a debris flow, and the reason for the animal nickname is unexplained.

f56b1932f74e2950b85c577816248464fba74f54.summary: Two witches amused themselves by trying to hurl the Vierschröt rock down upon Bürglen.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Ds St. Peters-Sywli
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Saint Peter’s little sow’; it is the witches’ mocking personification of the parish or chapel bell whose ringing defeats them, with Sywli a diminutive of sow.

notes.label: M'r chennet nymeh machä, ds St. Peters-Sywli gysset.
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘We can do no more; Saint Peter’s little sow is squealing’; the bell’s sound is cast as a pig’s cry while functioning as sacred protection.
notes.anchor: M'r chennet nymeh machä, ds St. Peters-Sywli gysset.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: St. Peters-Zug
notes.text: a local place-name at the foot of the Vierschröt associated with Saint Peter, patron of the parish church; Zug here is part of the proper name, not the city of Zug.

2da9408f17785e1ac91adf077326d3e3de7aacd3.summary: Only a generation ago, the friendly Erdmännchen were a universal topic of conversation in the mountain village of Oberflachs, in the district of Brugg.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally “little earth men,” subterranean or cave-dwelling dwarf-like beings in German-speaking Swiss folklore; here they help with farming and childcare and foretell storms, and they should not be confused with the modern German word for meerkats.

notes.label: Dünne
notes.text: a regional thin bread cake or tart, related in form to a Wähe; the source specifies cream and diced bacon here, but recipes and spellings vary by locality.

c7808650b851821ff82f6ef4de6284b3ae8a4268.summary: In the village of Remigen in the district of Brugg, the Erdmännchen used to visit a certain house.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean household helpers; here they visit through an underground passage and reward a morally ordered household.

notes.label: Herdmännliloch
notes.text: a local cave-name meaning approximately “little earth-men’s hole” or “dwarf hole”; its dialect form ties the site to the visiting Erdmännchen, but the source does not describe the passage’s physical extent.

notes.label: Bützbergköpfli
notes.text: a local diminutive place-name for the little summit or knoll of Bützberg; Köpfli literally suggests a small “head” or rounded height.

notes.label: Breneli, blib du hübsch deheimen, me suecht die guete Chüe im Stahl und nid uf em Märit
notes.text: an Alemannic admonition meaning “Breneli, stay nicely at home; people look for good cows in the stall, not at the market”; it expresses a historically gendered ideal of domestic modesty, while comparing prospective brides to cattle in a way modern readers may find demeaning.
notes.anchor: Breneli, blib du hübsch deheimen, me suecht die guete Chüe im Stahl und nid uf em Märit

notes.label: Dür d’Luft us!
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘away through the air!’ or ‘out through the air!’—the route by which the creature carries off crops.

notes.label: Galgelöli
notes.text: a dialect form of Galgenlöli, literally the ‘little gallows wood,’ where local people have fields.

notes.label: Heu
notes.text: hay, the first cutting of meadow grass.

notes.label: Ämd
notes.text: the later hay crop or aftermath cut after the first hay harvest.

notes.label: Gwächs
notes.text: dialect for crops, growth, or produce from the fields.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: a dialect form of Galgenlölitier, the uncanny animal-being of the little gallows wood that carries crops through the air.

notes.label: Müetti
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German term for mother.

notes.label: Steigerige
notes.text: an auction or bidding occasion; fear of the creature made these fields worth almost nothing when offered.

notes.label: dür ’s Tenn düre
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘through the threshing floor/barn,’ repeated within the account.

notes.label: Dür ’s Tenn düre!
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘through the threshing floor!’ or ‘right through the barn floor,’ the creature’s habitual route.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: a dialect form of Galgenlölitier, the uncanny animal-being associated with the little gallows wood.

notes.label: Töri
notes.text: a little door or gate, torn apart when it does not provide enough passage.

notes.label: Witi
notes.text: width or clearance; the creature enlarges the opening until it is wide enough.

notes.label: D‘Eierimariann
notes.text: the Bernese dialect name Eierimariann with its article, approximately ‘the egg Mariann’; the story associates her with magically stealing eggs, though it does not state whether that deed created the byname.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Hooggestäcke
notes.text: the dialect name for Mariann's ordinary-looking staff or walking stick with a hollow handle that whistles when blown; its exact construction and the first element's derivation are not explained.

notes.label: D’Bisighere
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic, approximately “the lords or spirits of the Bisig,” naming cloud-riding beings whose direction predicts weather; Here may mean “lords” but the beings’ exact identity as dead souls or weather spirits remains uncertain.

notes.label: Here
notes.text: Bernese dialect for “lords” or “gentlemen,” used here for the beings imagined riding with the clouds toward and away from the Bisig; the following commentary places them in a cycle about the dead in the wind, but does not define them individually.

notes.label: Galgenlölitier
notes.text: the name of a Madiswil supernatural animal, literally a Galgenlöli creature, grouped with legends of the dead in the wind; the passage does not explain Galgenlöli, the creature’s appearance, or how its tradition connects to the Bisighere.

6c47258398f0ece26f522389eec71daa9bab8226.summary: D’Därm us em Buch! — The Guts Out of Your Belly!

notes.label: D’Därm us em Buch!
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the guts out of the belly!’; the gruesome title names Frau Faschte’s threatened punishment for violating the customary limit on late work.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally ‘Lady Fast’ or ‘Lady Lent’ in Bernese Alemannic, a regional female bogey who enforces seasonal and nighttime work taboos; her relationship to Lent, Ember observances, and older supernatural women varies across traditions.

notes.label: Chiltobe
notes.text: a Bernese dialect evening gathering for spinning, other handwork, socializing, and courtship; here working too late at such a communal work-night exposes a person to Frau Faschte.

7a371dfa4060d1069e2c0dc73c60f3542eef380e.summary: D’Frau Faschte nimmt Lüt — Frau Faschte Takes People

notes.label: D’Frau Faschte
notes.text: the regional name of the female supernatural figure blamed for the sledders' disappearance on Holy Night; Faschte resembles the dialect word for fasting, but the brief source does not explain her origin or exact nature.

notes.label: D’Frau Faschte nimmt Lüt
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Frau Faschte takes people’; the title presents Frau Faschte as an uncanny female being who makes people disappear, not as an ordinary woman observing a fast.

7cef5db11bad9b1129780f6852e50c70e787948f.summary: D’Frau Faschte u d’Frau Vrene — Frau Faschte and Frau Vrene

notes.label: D’Frau Faschte u d’Frau Vrene
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Frau Faschte and Frau Vrene,’ two supernatural sisters associated with calendrical rules, household work, and frightening visits.

notes.label: Müetti
notes.text: an affectionate Bernese German form of ‘mother’ or ‘mama’; the account openly depends on the narrator's fading memory of her stories.

notes.label: Zilete
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a long series, abundance, or whole run of stories; the exact quantity is deliberately indefinite.

notes.label: Faschtezit
notes.text: Bernese German for the fasting season, especially Lent; Frau Faschte's name and visits are tied to this sacred calendar period.

notes.label: Füürobe
notes.text: Bernese German for Feierabend, the proper stopping time at the end of the workday; continuing to spin beyond it invites supernatural punishment.

notes.label: Chuder
notes.text: the coarse tow or tangled short fibers left from preparing flax or hemp; Frau Faschte ruins both this raw fiber and the spun yarn.

notes.label: wiegle
notes.text: Bernese dialect for rocking, especially rocking a cradle; the narrator is uncertain but thinks this was Frau Vrene's customary activity.

cce941069229fa4e92431227d8d2e1b033b8d2c2.summary: Alongside the hosts of spirits that rush over hills and valleys during the twelve nights, a solitary figure appears: Frau Fasten.

notes.label: D’Frau Faschte
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘Frau Fasten’ or approximately ‘Lady Fasting,’ a punitive female winter spirit remembered during the holy season; her name connects her with fasting, but the tale does not define a precise calendar feast.

notes.label: Löifterli
notes.text: a diminutive regional form for a small upper window, vent, or louver opening; Frau Faschte's ability to enter through it emphasizes that even a tiny aperture offers no protection.

notes.label: D’heilig Eich
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “the holy oak,” the remembered sacred tree on the Horbeweid; the source explicitly leaves open whether its holiness came from pre-Christian veneration, a saint’s image, or a later interpretation.

notes.label: Schärmtanne
notes.text: a Swiss German compound, approximately a sheltering, spreading, or shade-giving fir; here it denotes a notably large tree remembered by the grandmother, but its exact species and local technical sense are uncertain.

5c2084691a396dcf316ae744a2f6726fbccbe04a.summary: D’Häx, wo all Altjohrobe chunnt — The Witch Who Comes Every Altjohrobe

notes.label: Altjohrobe
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “Old Year’s Eve,” the evening of the old year before New Year’s Day; here it is the annual time when the supposed witch passes, though the precise span of the observance is not stated.

notes.label: D’Häx, wo all Altjohrobe chunnt
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “the witch who comes every Old Year’s Eve”; the title names a recurring midnight apparition, while the commentary identifies her with Frau Fasten.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: chilten
notes.text: the Swiss nighttime courtship custom of young people visiting and socializing, often after ordinary working hours; here the carpenter assumes the pair are keeping such a late visit, though the exact relationship is not stated.

notes.label: Unghüür
notes.text: Swiss German for an uncanny monster, apparition, or dreadful supernatural thing; here it describes only what the carpenter’s clattering sounds like, not an actual being.

notes.label: auf der Stör
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German expression for an artisan working temporarily in a customer’s household rather than in a permanent shop; here the tailor is lodging or working at the house, but the duration of his service is unstated.

notes.label: Chutteli
notes.text: a Bernese dialect diminutive for a small garment, likely a jacket, bodice, or smock; the tailor is finishing it, but the source does not make the garment’s exact cut certain.

notes.label: Frau Fasten
notes.text: literally “Lady Fast” or “Lady Lent,” the punitive female seasonal being who appears when people work beyond the permitted time; the commentary links her to the witch, while her derivation from fasting customs or older belief remains uncertain.

notes.label: Heuel
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a frightening drawn feature or grotesque face, possibly emphasizing an open mouth or howling expression; the source gives no fuller description, so the precise pictorial sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Ofenwüsch
notes.text: literally something like a “stove wisp” or “stove brush,” the form in which Frau Fasten was said to appear at Madiswil; its physical appearance and whether Wüsch means a bundle, brush, or shaggy figure are not clarified.

notes.label: D’Rottalhere
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the Rottalherren, or Lords of Rottal; in regional legend these uncanny lords are heard shooting, and their distant gunfire serves as an omen of approaching bad weather.

672ab1b82051f49668f10e8bc19b110116faeb21.summary: D’Sau i dr Langete — The Sow in the Langete

notes.label: D’Sau i dr Langete
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the sow in the Langete’; the title names an unseen nocturnal apparition identified only by the sound of a sow and piglets moving through the river.

notes.label: D’Schwindte bringe
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘bringing the wasting sickness’; the Schwindte is identified by the commentary as plague, carried invisibly in the demon's basket.

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: the haymaking season or hay harvest, usually in early or midsummer; here the plague-bringer encounters people working in the meadow.

notes.label: Wibervölchli
notes.text: a Bernese dialect diminutive for a little female person or woman; here it describes the strange, proudly dressed plague-bringer without initially marking her as supernatural.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little woman, with -li as the diminutive; here the scholarly commentary uses it for the outwardly ordinary female plague demon.

notes.label: D’Spielerlibuebe
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the little gambling/player lads’; despite the playful diminutive, the group practices forbidden magic, alchemy, and treasure digging.

notes.label: Spielerlibuebe
notes.text: the title term without its article, referring to the group of young gamblers or players who act as ritual treasure seekers.

notes.label: Schwarzchünschtler
notes.text: Bernese German for practitioners of the ‘black art,’ meaning magicians or occultists; their attempt to manufacture gold and dig treasure gives the term its sinister sense here.

notes.label: Tägscht
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘text,’ here a ritual text that must be read before sunrise in three churches for the treasure-working to succeed; the source does not say what the text contained or who read it.

a7363b5ab5c4762adf61ea1a01f40a9cf6f44d90.summary: D’Stummli u d’Schlange—The Mute Girl and the Snake

notes.label: Stummli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a mute or non-speaking girl; the name functions as her defining designation rather than a personal name.

notes.label: D’Stummli u d’Schlange
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the mute girl and the snake’; Stummli is a diminutive designation for the girl, while Schlange means snake.

notes.label: War
notes.text: the source's Bernese word for the group of livestock the girl takes to pasture; it means a herd or drove, though the animals are not specified.

notes.label: Seelentier
notes.text: literally ‘soul-animal,’ a folkloristic term for an animal form in which a person's soul leaves and later reenters the body; here the snake performs that role.

notes.label: D’Tube banne
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘binding or enchanting the pigeons,’ using banne for magical constraint or control.

notes.label: banne
notes.text: to bind, constrain, or control through a spell; the attempt to prevent flight instead kills or destroys the pigeons.

notes.label: Moosjoggi
notes.text: the man's local nickname or name, combining Moos with Joggi, a Swiss German form of Jakob; the source does not explain why he bears it.

notes.label: Tübeler
notes.text: a pigeon keeper or pigeon enthusiast, derived from the dialect word Tube for pigeon.

notes.label: schwarzgstieleti Tube
notes.text: black-stockinged or black-footed pigeons, describing the birds' dark lower-leg or foot markings.

notes.label: Schopfjoggine
notes.text: a dialectal, apparently dismissive name for pigeons that continually remain at home or around the loft; its literal formation and exact breed reference are uncertain.

notes.label: öppis cheibs mache
notes.text: dialect for doing something nasty, cursed, or devilish; the buyer fears the seller may use harmful magic to recover the birds.

notes.label: Firscht
notes.text: Swiss German for the ridge of a roof, where the pigeons perch briefly after being bound.

notes.label: Brünnlig
notes.text: a Bernese name for a fiery human-shaped apparition, closest in sense to a ‘little burning one’; here it appears life-sized, with flame flickering between its ribs.

7db140f88f50e5068db853490c6149c2214fe29f.summary: E bösi Fleuge — A Wicked Fly

notes.label: E bösi Fleuge
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a wicked fly’; the insect is understood as a person's spying magical form, not an ordinary troublesome fly.

notes.label: Landsassechammer
notes.text: the source's dialect name for a local chamber, body, or meeting associated with resident country people; its exact institutional function is not explained in the brief tale.

notes.label: meh chönne, weder Brot ässe
notes.text: Bernese German literally meaning ‘able to do more than eat bread,’ an idiom implying occult or extraordinary powers beyond ordinary human ability.

5a625ba83ad791cf64209e47726f56540f062012.summary: E Chrott unger eme Mischthufe — A Toad beneath a Manure Heap

notes.label: Chrott
notes.text: Swiss German for a toad, a form witches often assume in regional legend; here the toad is implicitly the witch injured at the same time as Meieli, although the identification is inferred rather than directly stated.

notes.label: E Chrott unger eme Mischthufe
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “a toad beneath a manure heap”; the dialect title states the witch’s animal disguise and the place where she intends to blight the field.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Charscht
notes.text: a Swiss German name for a heavy hoe, mattock, or similar pronged field tool; the farmhand strikes the toad with it, but the source does not specify the implement’s exact local form.

68e0a8c2081fc191b4133bcbf05d8d37351d3117.summary: E glichligi Hasegschicht — A Similar Hare Story

notes.label: E glichligi Hasegschicht
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘a similar hare story’; the wording presents the account as another example in an existing cycle of tales about elusive hares and animal-form witches.

notes.label: Rain
notes.text: a field edge, bank, or sloping boundary strip rather than rain from the sky; here it also identifies the house and woman associated with that landscape feature.

notes.label: Halbfränkli
notes.text: a colloquial diminutive for a half-franc coin; chopped coin fragments are loaded as magical ammunition believed capable of wounding a witch in animal form.

notes.label: Gschröt
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the ordinary shot or pellets loaded in a gun; the hunters place the half-franc fragments ahead of it in the barrel.

notes.label: wo meh heig chönne weder Brot ässe
notes.text: literally someone ‘who could do more than eat bread,’ a cautious folk euphemism for a person credited with witchcraft or supernatural powers.
notes.anchor: wo meh heig chönne weder Brot ässe

9fea325ca7ee0751f6460f4777cfecbd2a9b390c.summary: E graui Chatz — A Gray Cat

notes.label: E graui Chatz
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a gray cat’; the title identifies the animal form taken by the girl's wandering soul.

notes.label: schlofsturm
notes.text: Bernese dialect for being sleep-drunk, groggy, or dazed on waking; the boy has been asleep while the girl's soul is away.

notes.label: Seelentier
notes.text: literally ‘soul-animal,’ a folkloristic term for an animal form in which a person's soul leaves and later reenters the body.

notes.label: Seelentierchen
notes.text: diminutive plural of Seelentier, ‘little soul-animals’; the commentary applies it especially to small, quick creatures such as mice, flies, weasels, and birds.

notes.label: Gspane
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a companion, fellow traveler, or associate; this apparently supernatural road companion can summon rain and snow merely to demonstrate his power.

7b7d0c66af7f6244b2fbbe23be91a6886505b82e.summary: E Has u doch e ke Has — A Hare and Yet No Hare

notes.label: E Has u doch e ke Has
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a hare and yet no hare’; the title signals that the animal is understood as an uncanny death apparition rather than an ordinary hare.
notes.anchor: E Has u doch e ke Has

notes.label: Githung
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a miser or extremely stingy person; the narrator uses it to characterize the dying farmer, though the tale does not explicitly say that miserliness caused his fate.

notes.label: Sägetzen
notes.text: a Bernese regional form for a scythe or its cutting assembly; the narrator has just returned from cutting grass when the death-sign appears.

7023c2ee0b25272e2612005c42408d5fa0a24f5d.summary: E Herti i dr Sägetze — A Hardness in the Scythe

notes.label: Herti
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a hardness, resistance, or magically obstructed place; here it afflicts the mowing tool so that work becomes impossible until the scythe is beaten with white hazel.

notes.label: Sägetze
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for the scythe or its cutting assembly; the exact tool form is not described, but it is what Häulehans can no longer mow with and then ritually strikes.

b0081280a992ab3d463fe05128a36495915779af.summary: E Häxetanzplatz — A Witches’ Dance Place

notes.label: E Häxetanzplatz
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a witches’ dance place,’ a secluded clearing explained first through witch belief and then through competing theories of ritual or secret social dancing.

notes.label: Häxetanzplatz
notes.text: literally ‘witches’ dance place,’ the traditional name of the level clearing below the Hunzegütsch; the source debates rather than confirms its historical use.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Ofeziechli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for small oven implements, probably pokers, rakes, or similar tools imagined as witches’ flying mounts; the exact implement is not described.

notes.label: Gigli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for a little fiddle or violin; the Devil is said to hang his instrument on a fir branch while the witches dance.

notes.label: Bödeli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little level piece of ground, floor, or clearing; here it is the forest clearing whose earlier purpose is disputed.

notes.label: Chorgerichte
notes.text: Reformed church moral courts that supervised conduct and disciplined offenses such as forbidden dances; they were institutional authorities, not simply choirs or musical judges.

notes.label: Kilttänze
notes.text: dances associated with Kilt or Kiltgang, customary nighttime visiting and courtship among rural young people; church authorities viewed such gatherings as morally dangerous.

fc07ac0363849a67a4f254fdb6b6acb388543518.summary: E Lohersteiversetzer (A Mover of a Loherstei)

notes.label: E Lohersteiversetzer
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a mover of a Loherstei’; the title identifies a dead boundary-stone mover, while the body spells the stone Locherstei and the precise local element Loher or Locher remains uncertain.

notes.label: Loherstei
notes.text: a Bernese dialect term for the illicitly moved stone, evidently a boundary or landmark stone; Stei means ‘stone,’ while the precise local sense of Loher is not explained.

notes.label: Hüttegmein
notes.text: a communal gathering or meeting associated with an Alpine or farm hut; here several farmers remain sitting afterward until midnight, although the occasion's formal purpose is unstated.

notes.label: Locherstei
notes.text: the spelling used in the story's dialogue for the stone moved forward by the restless spirit; it is evidently a boundary marker, but whether Locher refers to a hole, boundary, or local name is unclear.

notes.label: Rüetli
notes.text: a little rod, switch, or twig, with -li as the diminutive; here it marks the original hole where the stone must be restored.

c7fa8ca2db908ae32ce6d3cdcad40ae78e9af18a.summary: E Ma wässeret — A Man Irrigates

notes.label: E Ma wässeret
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a man irrigates’; wässern refers to directing water through meadow channels, and the title identifies the recurring apparition by this work.

notes.label: unghüürig
notes.text: Bernese dialect for uncanny, haunted, or inhabited by something supernatural; the brief account does not identify the man or explain why he returns.

notes.label: wässeret de Gräbe
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘irrigates the ditches,’ describing the traditional management of meadow water channels; the layout and ownership of these Gräbe are not stated.

96f609da53cd438faf8030a655c154b5a4dff4aa.summary: E ruche Luft — A Raging Wind

notes.label: E ruche Luft
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a rough, raging wind’; Luft normally means ‘air,’ but here it denotes the violent wind that announces the death.

notes.label: Widli
notes.text: a small flexible withy or twisted twig used as a tie; the hanged man’s fir tree is said to have twisted into this binding shape.

notes.label: Wedele
notes.text: bundles of brushwood, twigs, or small firewood bound together for carrying or use; Widli served as the ties around such bundles.

80afcd7bdc1ca8ba0c63509807b309a909b809b7.summary: E schwarze Bock im Stall — A Black Billy Goat in the Stable

notes.label: E schwarze Bock im Stall
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘a black billy goat in the stable’; the animal functions as an unexplained protective presence that ends the livestock mishaps.

notes.label: Läheme
notes.text: the source's dialect designation for the affected man, probably a local family or house-name form; the brief account does not identify it securely enough to replace with a personal name.

notes.label: Hälslig
notes.text: a Bernese neck tether, collar, or stall fastening for cattle; finding two cows caught in one is the recurring sign that something is wrong in the stable.

notes.label: E schwarze Hung
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘a black dog’; the title preserves the local sound and identifies the spirit's animal form.

notes.label: Hung
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form of Hund, ‘dog’; the black animal is understood as a dead person's unresting spirit.

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a regional form related to Bannwart, a field, vineyard, or forest warden; the tale says the spectral dog had once been such a man.

6522d0c7574d19559b6a131bb9b30b89e67dcbea.summary: E schwäri Burdi — A Heavy Burden

notes.label: E schwäri Burdi
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a heavy burden’; it names both the literal half-foal carried repeatedly up the cliff and the moral burden of the brothers’ cruelty that must be atoned for.

notes.label: Füli
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for a foal; the diminutive identifies the young animal the brothers cruelly drive over the cliff and whose two halves become their corresponding burdens after death.

notes.label: E schöne Tänzer
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a fine’ or ‘handsome dancer’; the masculine Tänzer refers to the alluring young stranger, who is revealed as the devil.

notes.label: Heri
notes.text: a Bernese dialect diminutive or familiar form for a young gentleman or little lord; here it describes the green-clad dancer, and its polite appearance masks the devil.

notes.label: Giger
notes.text: Swiss German for fiddlers or string musicians, singular Giger; here they begin the last dance of the evening.

notes.label: Gade
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form for a barn, stable, or lower farm building; here it is the room below the parents where the stranger reveals himself, and the exact interior use is not specified.

notes.label: Trögli
notes.text: a diminutive of Trog, a small trough, chestlike bench, or similar low farm furnishing; here the stranger sits on it, but the tale does not specify its exact form.

notes.label: Geissfuess
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘goat's foot’; here the limb inside the dancer's boot exposes him as the devil.

8c1d7570e7c4e38da1a72f58e95edcd24f2888f4.summary: E verböhrte Geischt — A Spirit Bored into Wood

notes.label: E verböhrte Geischt
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a spirit bored or fastened into something’; it reflects the folklore idea that a banished spirit could be confined within a tree or other object.

notes.label: verböhrte Geischt
notes.text: a spirit confined as though bored into the stump; the form conveys magical binding rather than ordinary physical drilling.

notes.label: Brüsch
notes.text: Bernese dialect for brushwood or scrub; it is the uprooted vegetation the farmer burns before cultivating the pasture.

notes.label: Härdöpfel
notes.text: Swiss German, literally ‘earth apples,’ meaning potatoes.

9ff87ae144891a0ff31ad76274480bd13a0a56ec.summary: E wehlige Brüel — A Terrible Bellow

notes.label: E wehlige Brüel
notes.text: Bernese German for a dreadful, anguished bellow or roar; the context leaves deliberately uncertain whether it is the cry of the killer or the victim.

notes.label: E Wächseltaler
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a Wächseltaler,’ a magically obtained coin that draws other money away; the title's e is the indefinite article ‘a.’

notes.label: Wächseltaler
notes.text: literally a ‘changing’ or ‘exchange thaler,’ a magical coin acquired through a dangerous church-door rite and believed to steal or attract other money.

notes.label: Alerunen
notes.text: the source's dialect form for an Alraun, a magical mandrake root or familiar spirit obtainable as the ritual's alternative reward.

notes.label: Trögli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small trough, chest, or box; here it is the container in which Ueli keeps money.

notes.label: Schübeli
notes.text: a diminutive for a little bundle, stack, or compact pile; the story describes Ueli's stored money without specifying its exact arrangement.

notes.label: rübis u stübis
notes.text: a Bernese idiom meaning completely, utterly, or bag and baggage; Ueli finds all the stored money gone.

notes.label: Wechseltaler
notes.text: the High German form of Wächseltaler used in the commentary for the same magically mobile coin.

notes.label: Hecketaler
notes.text: an alternate folkloric name for a magical thaler that breeds, attracts, or carries off money; Hecke suggests supernatural propagation, but the story does not define the mechanism further.

notes.label: Alraun
notes.text: a mandrake root imagined as a magical household familiar or wealth-bringing object; the commentary links its tradition to that of the Wechseltaler.

notes.label: Chehrjoggi
notes.text: a local personal nickname in which Joggi is a Swiss German form of Jakob; the meaning of the first element Chehr and the person's precise identity are uncertain.

notes.label: Zilete
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a row or line of things; here it describes the silver coins beside the uncanny gentleman.

notes.label: Silbergäld
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘silver money’ or silver coins; its presence beside a black dog gives the brief scene the character of a guarded supernatural treasure.

notes.label: E Zilete Silbergäld
notes.text: Bernese dialect for approximately ‘a row of silver coins’ or ‘a line of silver money’; Zilete suggests an arranged row, but the exact extent or form of the hoard is not specified.

6c08821fcc50c7be37a11113b628495b65d7e178.summary: Ears of grain once grew straight from the ground without stalks, as tall as they now do together with their stalks.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

dacbafe4ea755c1c18ab8eebae3cadc3b3aeb9b4.summary: A farmer who died only in recent years at Grindelwald in the Bernese Oberland was called the miracle doctor by his neighbors because of all kinds of secret arts.

notes.label: Besegnungs-
notes.text: the combining form of Besegnung, ritual blessing or healing with sacred signs and formulas; the doctor mixes such folk-Christian practice with secret magic.

notes.label: Matte
notes.text: a meadow, especially a managed grass or hay meadow; the servant enters it to mow after tasting the snake foam.

notes.label: Mattenblümchen
notes.text: literally ‘little meadow flower,’ an affectionate diminutive; after the servant gains hidden perception, even the tiniest flowers bow to him.

8b7295abb3dd0add34ac318a70aa268af69830cf.summary: Near Köllikon, a village by Aarau, lies a woodland place called Jm Eber. Within it dwells a Schimmelreiter called Ebermann, who rides from Köllikon across the woodlands, the Ester, and the Egerten, up toward the village of Safenwil.

notes.label: Jm Eber
notes.text: the source's printed place-name form, likely an older typographic or transcription rendering of ‘Im Eber’ (‘in the boar’); it anchors the apparition and helps explain the name Ebermann.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally a rider on a white or gray horse; in German-language legend it is a compact apparition type, here the spectral rider ranging through the woods.

notes.label: Ebermann
notes.text: literally ‘boar-man,’ but here the proper name of the Schimmelreiter associated with the woodland printed as Jm Eber rather than a claim that he has a boar's body.

notes.label: Egerten
notes.text: a historical plural for fallow or temporarily uncultivated fields and also a landscape name; here it identifies terrain crossed by Ebermann.

notes.label: Garbebänger
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the bands or ties used to bind harvested sheaves; stolen from three households, they are made into the magical nest that draws away those households’ eggs.

0545d02f2c38e1e6140a5c1c84ec7fc906e27324.summary: Well, I certainly do not believe that absolutely none of it is real. A man from Gurtnellen once told me something that surely was supernatural.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Einä-n-ohni Chopf
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘one without a head’; it is a descriptive expression for the half-white, half-black apparition rather than a securely established class or proper name of spirit.

319a7dc0c6ef40b13d4393a6d612d02dc97729d4.summary: At Castelen Castle, a devout maid named Lisette served Landvogt Bucher. She soon had an opportunity to prove her purity.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a Landvogt was a territorial bailiff or governor in the historical Swiss Confederacy, here the maid’s master at Castelen; the tale does not specify Bucher’s dates or jurisdiction.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Züpfen
notes.text: this older regional plural denotes women’s braids in the taunting rhyme; its exact spelling, pronunciation, and symbolic implication are uncertain.

notes.label: Jüppen
notes.text: this older regional plural denotes long women’s skirts or dresses in the parallel taunt; the precise garment style and the rhyme’s social nuance are uncertain.

393a02b72fc7952e8f2646f008654e2732eac36f.summary: The little village of Zufikon, a quarter of an hour from the town of Bremgarten in the Reuss valley, borders the edge of a great fir forest called the Nüeschwandwald.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

ced23d9027be0a81a4627424d7d4fa469506624d.summary: ‘As was reported earlier, when Carolus Magnus built the foundation at the Grossmünster provostry, at that time he—Emperor Charles—was often in residence at Zurich.

notes.label: Glöggli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little bell’; Charles makes it an unusually direct summons through which anyone—even the snake—can seek imperial justice.

notes.label: Wurm
notes.text: an older German word for a serpent, dragon, or creeping creature; the source itself identifies this Wurm as a snake rather than a giant dragon.

notes.label: Rüschi
notes.text: a patch of reeds, rushes, brush, or waterside growth; the precise vegetation is uncertain, but it shelters the snake's eggs at the water's edge.

notes.label: Krott
notes.text: a regional form of Kröte, meaning toad; the emperor condemns it for occupying or threatening the snake's nest.

notes.label: Wasserkirche
notes.text: literally ‘Water Church,’ the historic Zurich church traditionally associated with the martyrdom of Felix and Regula; the account explains its name through the water surrounding the site.

notes.label: Alarune
notes.text: the local name for an occult familiar or spirit appearing as a black cat on the doctor's shoulder; it resembles Alraune, the mandrake familiar of German folklore, but the spelling and this animal form make the precise classification uncertain.

7ad1a57fa60a417c7d5f73bf8a7911d7e1efe4d4.summary: En alti Stadt — An Old Town

notes.label: En alti Stadt
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘an old town’; the legend explains present place-names as remnants of an ancient settlement.

notes.label: Rothus
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘town hall’ or ‘council house’; the tale uses it to explain the place-name Roth.

notes.label: Schmiedte
notes.text: a dialect form for the smithy; it is linked etiologically with the modern local name Schmiedige.

notes.label: Süimärit
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘pig market’; the story places it at Schweinbrunne as another trace of the vanished town.

7d14dfb43ff3e8b1252e8678d327c2ebd4f8c2e9.summary: En usälige Bur — An Unblessed Farmer

notes.label: En usälige Bur
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘an unblessed,’ wretched, or morally ill-fated farmer; the title condemns him without stating his hidden wrongdoing.

notes.label: nid ganz e sufere
notes.text: literally ‘not quite a clean one’ in Bernese German, an indirect judgment that can imply moral disreputability or uncanny impurity rather than physical dirt.

notes.label: Totebaum
notes.text: literally ‘dead-person tree,’ a regional name for a coffin, reflecting its wooden material and funerary purpose.

notes.label: Totehof
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the churchyard or cemetery, literally the ‘yard of the dead.’

notes.label: Chuppele Chräihe
notes.text: Bernese German for a cluster or flock of crows; their perching on the coffin marks the dead farmer as ominous or unblessed.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

5c8a35dd230671f683b5760468c1b231cabf9a2e.summary: One morning on Alp Wängi at the Kinzig Pass, two cows were found in the barn entangled in one and the same chain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its barns, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain; the chained cows are found in its livestock building.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

ec73c72055fb0b36aae65fc5bde0a1b40177e0d7.summary: a) The castle maiden on the ruins of Habsburg Castle in the little Rhine town of Gross-Laufenburg carries a Stauf filled with wine in her hand.

notes.label: Stauf
notes.text: an old drinking vessel, cup, or small beaker, here filled with wine and central to the ritual that can release the enchanted castle maiden.

notes.label: Finstergässschen
notes.text: literally ‘little dark lane,’ the local name for the forest path between Wallbach and Zeiningen where treasure omens appear.

notes.label: Thaler
notes.text: large historical silver coins; the sack promises one coin for every leaf rather than a modern fixed currency value.

notes.label: Hudikreuz
notes.text: the local name of the old cross near Leuggern where the costumed maiden appears; Kreuz means ‘cross,’ but the meaning of Hudi in this name is uncertain.

notes.label: Güggehü-Hütli
notes.text: the local name for the maiden's small traditional hat; Hütli is the Swiss German diminutive ‘little hat,’ while the precise form or derivation of Güggehü is uncertain.

notes.label: Jüppe
notes.text: a traditional women's skirt or dress in Alemannic and Swiss regional costume.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: literally a cloth worn in front, meaning an apron as part of the maiden's regional costume.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosed boundary line in Swiss and southern German usage; the maiden follows it across the field.

notes.label: Elendskreuz
notes.text: literally ‘misery cross’ or ‘cross of affliction,’ here the name of a boundary cross associated with an execution legend.

notes.label: Oeltrotte
notes.text: an oil press or the building containing one; Trotte is the regional term for a press installation, more often encountered with grapes.

notes.label: Rise
notes.text: a steep natural or constructed chute, slide, or gully down which water, timber, or debris descends a mountainside.

notes.label: Bruchmattmaidli
notes.text: literally the ‘little maiden of Bruchmatte,’ the local name for the white-clad guardian of the treasure chest; Maidli is Swiss German for a young girl.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, recurring seasonal days of fasting and prayer in the traditional Christian calendar; folklore often treats these liminal periods as times of heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Disli-Andres
notes.text: a local byname meaning ‘Andres of Disli’ or ‘Disli's Andres’; it identifies the witness from Gippingen rather than a supernatural figure.

notes.label: Karste
notes.text: a heavy hoe or mattock used to break and cultivate soil; striking the ground with it reveals the hollow sound beneath the site.

c1e4807344d2a314d32d7497d3af65fe5faddcb9.summary: Once there was a very poor family that lived in a rented little house. St.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the warm bench built beside or around a masonry stove, a customary resting place in a traditional house; Tarock lies there beside the hearth fire.

notes.label: Mooh
notes.text: a dialectal interjection retained exactly; in context it has a loose conversational force such as ‘well’ or ‘why,’ but the source does not establish a narrower local definition.

a289675d7e6b99fb0174fab61e65020c8a7217db.summary: In the Gstalden near Flawil, on the road toward Magdenau, there are said to be two holes in which Erdmannli formerly lived.

notes.label: Gstalden
notes.text: the local place-name near Flawil; it is related to Stalden, a sloping path or hillside, but the source uses it as a specific location.

notes.label: Erdmannli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for ‘little earth-men,’ underground dwarf-like beings associated with holes, caves, and hidden dwellings; -li marks the diminutive.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-men,’ the standard-German title form corresponding to dialect Erdmannli in the body; these are underground dwarf-like beings associated with holes, caves, and hidden dwellings.

c0c6e63656f1310311e8b4580649a2a70d1a16da.summary: a) The Erdmännchen had their little troubles too. A Härdmännchen lived near the Mangeli at Menzingen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-men,’ dwarf-like underground or mountain beings in German-speaking Swiss folklore; here it is the broad name for the helpful but weather-vulnerable little people.

notes.label: Härdmännchen
notes.text: a Swiss dialect form of Erdmännchen, literally ‘little earth-man’; here it names the helper living near the Mangeli, with Härd reflecting the regional pronunciation of Erde.

notes.label: Sprengmontag
notes.text: a regional carnival Monday observance, identified in the source with Güdismontag; here it is the occasion for the farmer's two days of dancing, and local customs attached to the name varied.

notes.label: Güdismontag
notes.text: the Lucerne-area Swiss German name for Carnival Monday; here it glosses Sprengmontag and explains why the farmer leaves to revel before Ash Wednesday.

notes.label: Härdmandli
notes.text: another dialect diminutive for ‘little earth-man,’ closely related to Härdmännchen; here it refers to the same helper defending his retreat from the wind, and the spelling records local speech.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope wind characteristic of the Alps; here it is imagined as lethally drying to the small folk even though human observers experience sunny warmth.

notes.label: Wilde
notes.text: literally ‘wild ones,’ a historical folklore label for marginal cave- or mountain-dwelling people; here it groups supernaturalized outsiders and should not be read as a neutral modern ethnographic category.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Heiden-Mandli
notes.text: literally ‘little pagan man,’ a dialect name for the helpful cave-dwelling neighbor; here it reflects the source's old folk classification and not a precise statement about religion or ethnicity.

notes.label: Boni
notes.text: a local Alpine farm term for a sheltering barn, storage space, or similar part of the mountain holding; here the Wilde hides there under a haystack, while the exact building type is not specified.

837db4f728a848c4ea952e6ce92e10d7a01232f1.summary: One evening while the cows were being milked at Salwiden above the Schlacht on the Sörenberg, an Alpine servant spilled an entire bucket of milk and began cursing over it in his coarse way.

notes.label: Erdleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ the collective name in the story for the dwarf-like beings who claim spilled, uncursed milk and make inexhaustible cheese from it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Walt Gott!
notes.text: an old blessing meaning approximately ‘May God rule’ or ‘May God watch over it’; the master speaks it over the Alp when the last cow departs, following local custom.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like beings associated with the land, farms, and Alpine dairy work; the story also calls the group Erdleutchen, ‘little earth people.’

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the dairyman responsible for livestock, milking, and cheesemaking on an Alp; the title uses this characteristic Alpine role even though the narrative also calls the men master, servant, and milker.

0d0ad4efc819c4f708197817387224e98289c66b.summary: Stiftshalde is the name of the state-owned woodland that stretches above the vineyards of the Fricktal village of Hornussen.

notes.label: Erdmändliloch
notes.text: the little earth men's hole or cave, the local name of their overnight dwelling.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally little earth men, a regional name for subterranean household-helping dwarfs; it is unrelated to the modern German name for meerkats.

notes.label: Pfannendotsch
notes.text: a regional pan-cooked egg cake or pancake; recipes and consistency vary locally.

notes.label: Krautwähen
notes.text: savory Swiss open tarts filled with cabbage or greens.

notes.label: Ramwähen
notes.text: Swiss open tarts made with cream; Ram is a regional form of Rahm.

notes.label: Zipärtlikuchen
notes.text: cakes made with Zipärtli, small local damson-like plums also called Cyper plums.

notes.label: Erbgrind
notes.text: a feared scalp affliction, literally hereditary scab; the precise historical diagnosis is uncertain.

c718622e33061098473c31b3be270731890a45bf.summary: On the left side of the confluence of the Aare and Rhine, where the Reuenthal and Fullerfeld meet, lies a low mountain into which three caves lead.

notes.label: Most
notes.text: fermented or unfermented fruit juice, commonly apple or pear cider in Swiss usage; the nearby winepress complicates the exact drink intended, which the source does not specify.

notes.label: Wähen
notes.text: Swiss flat cakes or tarts with a thin pastry base and sweet or savory topping; the source praises their thin dough but does not specify the topping.

notes.label: Höchli
notes.text: a diminutive for a small raised part or projection, here a part of the plow upon which the cake is laid; the exact component and plow design are not identified.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings associated with caves, hidden wealth, exchange with farmers, and altered time; the tale does not explain whether all its little folk form one community.

7381dedb3b0c89ebd41a7ddc898c9941a25a7abf.summary: A farmer once came to a learned chemist in the land of Schwyz and confidentially told him the following:

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like subterranean beings in Swiss folklore; here an Erdmännchen silently marks a rich metal vein, while uncanny noise punishes deceptive crystal seekers nearby.

aaaa9e7d34a9b52ee7bfdace64b0697996ac2790.summary: Ere Jumpfere erschint dr Meister—The Master Appears to a Maiden

notes.label: Jumpfere
notes.text: Bernese dialect for an unmarried young woman or maiden; she performs the marriage-divination rite and later becomes the farmer's wife.

notes.label: Ere Jumpfere erschint dr Meister
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the master appears to a maiden’; Meister denotes the male head of the farm household and, in retrospect, the maiden's future husband.

notes.label: Müetti
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive for mother, comparable to ‘Mama’; she is named as the narrator's source.

notes.label: angereesle
notes.text: the source's verb for performing the Angereesenacht divination ritual; its etymology and exact calendar date are not established here.

notes.label: Hemlistock
notes.text: the ritual implement used as a broom in the divination; Stock means stick, but the precise object indicated by Hemli is uncertain.

notes.label: Ghüder
notes.text: Swiss German for rubbish, sweepings, or refuse; the maiden must carry it out while walking backward.

notes.label: Angereesenacht
notes.text: the local name of a night used for marriage or death divination; the account does not securely identify its date.

notes.label: Büri
notes.text: a Bernese designation for the farmer's wife or female farmholder; here she is the current wife whose death the apparition foretells.

b3146de46c99cf81fe4f65f58d5d5f3f8378f630.summary: Es arigs Liecht — A Strange Light

notes.label: Es arigs Liecht
notes.text: dialect for ‘a strange,’ ‘peculiar,’ or ‘uncanny light’; arig also describes the innkeeper's dream, linking the roaming light with his detached dreaming soul.

notes.label: Zweuerli
notes.text: a diminutive name for a small serving or inexpensive measure of drink, likely wine; the exact volume or price intended in this Bernese setting is not stated.

notes.label: arig
notes.text: dialect for strange, peculiar, or uncanny; its emotional force lies between mere oddness and supernatural unease, so no single English adjective captures every occurrence.

notes.label: Es bös Heicho
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘an evil homecoming’; Heicho carries the sense of coming home, and the title points to the murderer's fatal return to the burial place.

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: the haymaking season and its work, a major communal labor period in rural Swiss life.

notes.label: Sägetze
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the long scythe used in haymaking; the bloody bone catches in its blade and exposes the crime.

notes.label: Bahrrecht
notes.text: literally ‘bier right,’ a historical ordeal-like belief that a murdered body would bleed anew in the murderer's presence; the source's commentary uses it to interpret the legend.

ade55ea5506954417fe8d2b056df667863694a38.summary: Es chlis Manndli winteret War — A Little Man Winters the Livestock

notes.label: es chlis Manndli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘a little man,’ a diminutive supernatural helper whose care succeeds only while the farmer respects the prohibition against looking.

notes.label: Es chlis Manndli winteret War
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘a little man winters the livestock’; winteret means tending or keeping animals through winter, not simply spending the season oneself.

notes.label: War
notes.text: a dialect collective for the farmer’s livestock or stock of animals; it does not mean the English word ‘war’ or merely commercial wares.

notes.label: Bühni
notes.text: the upper floor, loft, or hay-storage level of the farm building; the farmer first checks the remaining hay there before entering the stable.

notes.label: War bi Lib
notes.text: literally the livestock ‘in life’ or ‘alive’; the phrase confirms that every animal remains living and in good condition despite consuming remarkably little hay.

notes.label: Es chlis schwarzes Fraueli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘a little black woman,’ the small household or tree spirit displaced when the walnut is cut down.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive meaning ‘little woman’; here it names the black female spirit who claims a right to remain on the property.

notes.label: Heimet
notes.text: a home farm, farmstead, or hereditary rural holding rather than merely a house.

notes.label: heilige Zit
notes.text: Swiss German for the ‘holy season,’ usually the Christmas period, when the spirit's attacks on the goat are especially severe.

notes.label: Beijichorb
notes.text: dialect for a beehive basket or skep, used as the container in which the caught Fraueli is confined.

notes.label: Husfirscht
notes.text: Swiss German for the ridge or ridge-beam of the house's roof, beneath which the spirit's basket is placed.

a8cd20c3170ff492a8f2d684cc3ada33c2af9c2d.summary: Es Ei im Füür—An Egg in the Fire

notes.label: Es Ei im Füür
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘an egg in the fire’; the heated egg is part of a rite intended to expose a harmful witch.

notes.label: Chehr
notes.text: a round, circuit, or turn of one's customary route; the narrator is passing the farmhouse while making such a round, though the purpose is not specified.

notes.label: Chuchibode
