ac4861a2a9c1c6e932ee3997effec362688f1ff4.summary: In Rüti, a hamlet in the municipality of Meerenschwanden in the Freienamte, an old thatched house is well known because the Guetisee passes straight through it on every Fronfastennacht.

notes.label: Freienamte
notes.text: the historical inflected form used here for the Freiamt region of Aargau; it identifies a particular former bailiwick or district rather than a generic ‘free office.’

notes.label: Guetisee
notes.text: the local name for an uncanny nocturnal host that travels as a noisy herd of swine; the name may be related to regional Guetisheer or Wüetisheer traditions of the Wild Hunt, but the source does not establish the derivation.

notes.label: Fronfastennacht
notes.text: an Ember night associated with one of the quarterly fast periods in the Christian calendar; Swiss folklore often treats these calendrical nights as times when spirit processions are active.

notes.label: Mick - mick!
notes.text: the piglets’ imitative cry as the supernatural herd passes through the house; the spaced historical spelling is retained from the source.

notes.label: Gutisee
notes.text: the source’s variant spelling of Guetisee in the second paragraph; both forms denote the same unseen or swine-shaped supernatural host, though local spellings and possible etymologies vary.

58849ced34681449699e241a3603374faa6b0e5c.summary: On a height of the Lindenberg in the Freiamt called the Guggernollen lives the Guggernül-Anneli, whose plaintive song always announces a change in the weather.

notes.label: Guggernül-Anneli
notes.text: the familiar female name Anneli joined to a local variant of the Guggernollen place-name; she is a place-bound lamenting being whose song foretells changing weather.

notes.label: Gausserwibli
notes.text: literally a little wailing woman, named for a lamenting or howling voice associated with the Gausserhölzli forest; the body of the source uses the expanded standard-German form Gausserweiblein for the same being.

notes.label: Bernerbieter
notes.text: people from Bernese territory; the source explicitly identifies them here with the Reformed Protestants imagined as the Catholic district's opponents in a final confessional battle.

notes.label: Eisenhag
notes.text: literally an ‘iron fence’ or ‘iron enclosure’; the prophecy compares the line of sunlit bayonets surrounding the Lindenberg to a woven barrier of iron.

notes.label: Gugenrain-Babeli
notes.text: a local woodland spirit-name combining the Gugenrain place-name with Babeli, a Swiss German feminine diminutive commonly associated with Barbara; this feared-looking but generally harmless revenant appears to berry-picking children and foretells weather.

notes.label: Bachthal-Anneli
notes.text: a local spirit-name combining the Bachthal place-name with Anneli, a diminutive of Anna; the brief cross-reference places her among the same family of named female woodland and weather beings.

49661ff1db8f44df8486e27689d21ef64c9be67f.summary: Around Muri, the Gutis-Ee is held to be a long spectral procession, preceded by a man with a tall staff who cries, “Uß Weg!” Behind him rolls a great roller that takes up the entire width of the road.

notes.label: Gutis-Ee
notes.text: a Freiamt name for a roaming supernatural host related to regional Wild Hunt traditions; here it is a road-filling procession of animals and child spirits, while the precise meaning of Ee and its relationship to Guetisheer spellings are uncertain.

notes.label: Uß Weg!
notes.text: an Alemannic command meaning “Out of the way!”; the staff-bearing leader cries it before the supernatural procession arrives, and the spelling records dialect pronunciation rather than a different instruction.

notes.label: Schelleli-Buebe
notes.text: literally “little-bell boys,” the local name for the noisy child spirits in the procession; Schelleli suggests small livestock bells, but the source describes their sound only as screaming and rumbling.

notes.label: Frohnfastennächten
notes.text: an older spelling and inflected plural meaning the nights of the Fronfasten or quarterly Christian Ember fasts; these are liminal nights when the houses on the procession’s route must remain open.

notes.label: Zwölften
notes.text: literally “the Twelves,” the traditional twelve-night midwinter period around Christmas and Epiphany; supernatural visitations and household taboos cluster around it, while exact regional dates could vary.

ffa6adb64d35938ee64a2345de54d6a28cfe7518.summary: ‘Mä heig wellä ds Chloschter Einsidlä z'Geschänä büwä, aber mä heigs nit chennä wägä dä Bächä.’—‘They are said to have wanted to build the monastery of Einsiedeln at Göschenen, but they could not because of the streams.’

notes.label: Mä heig wellä ds Chloschter Einsidlä z'Geschänä büwä, aber mä heigs nit chennä wägä dä Bächä.
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘They are said to have wanted to build the monastery of Einsiedeln at Göschenen, but they could not because of the streams’; the statement presents local waterways as the reason the famous monastery was founded elsewhere.
notes.anchor: Mä heig wellä ds Chloschter Einsidlä z'Geschänä büwä, aber mä heigs nit chennä wägä dä Bächä.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Maria Hilf
notes.text: the Catholic devotional invocation ‘Mary, Help,’ used as the dedication of the chapel at Altref and understood as a protective title of the Virgin Mary.

notes.label: D'sant Nikläusä Chappäli z'Geschänä und ds Maria Hilf Chappäli z'Altref syget diä eltästä Gottshyser im Kanton Üri.
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘The Chapel of St. Nicholas at Göschenen and the Maria Hilf Chapel at Altref are said to be the oldest houses of worship in the canton of Uri’; Gottshyser literally means ‘God's houses.’
notes.anchor: D'sant Nikläusä Chappäli z'Geschänä und ds Maria Hilf Chappäli z'Altref syget diä eltästä Gottshyser im Kanton Üri.

001256b070f635eb6e4a882ab7d9c1e691718f25.summary: Long ago, Göscheneralp too belonged to the parish of Silenen. When people carried a body to the parish church for burial, on the first day they went with it as far as Wyler in Gurtnellen, placed it there overnight in St.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

0441d53a4916b647b5bdff02092f4fbe9294979c.summary: Long ago, G’steig Valley is said to have been a lake whose climate was so mild that grapevines flourished on its shores.

notes.label: Abesite
notes.text: literally the ‘evening side,’ the local dialect expression for the west-facing side of a valley.

notes.label: Uf der Morgesite z’hinderst im G’steig
notes.text: the source’s local orientation phrase, meaning approximately ‘at the far back of G’steig on the morning side,’ that is, the east or southeast side.
notes.anchor: Uf der Morgesite z’hinderst im G’steig

notes.label: Hubel
notes.text: a regional word for a rounded hill, knoll, or rocky rise; here it serves as the local name for the spur called Burg.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss topographic word for a cliff, crag, or exposed rock face; the exact landform varies by locality.

fae33c7d3452021bde99c9e579e3704b79ad13ad.summary: 1. On the Wyttenalp in the Etzlital, a hailstorm once drove an entire Sennten, together with the herder and Zuhirt, over a Fluh to their deaths.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: a full organized Alpine cattle herd or cattle-and-dairy unit under pastoral management, not merely an unstructured group of cows.

notes.label: Zuhirt
notes.text: the assistant herder working under or alongside the principal Hirt with an Alpine herd.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a sheer rock face, cliff, or crag; both versions send people and livestock over one.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, grazing rights, and dairy-working landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schellenkuh
notes.text: the leading or prominent cow wearing the large herd bell; stopping her is meant to stop the entire Sennten behind her.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine field or slope of loose rock, scree, or avalanche debris; the herd falls into the Gand above Urwängi.

notes.label: Babergerschoss
notes.text: the named steep chute or slope below the Fluh in the second variant; Schoss can designate a sharply descending terrain feature, while the precise local boundary is not supplied.

aa302e6546705a9721eb2c8769324ff5917d3ede.summary: In the little village of Rieden, young men threshing grain were discussing a suicide that had occurred in the town of Baden, a quarter-hour away.

notes.label: Selle
notes.text: the source's regional word for the upper rung of the climbing fixture, immediately glossed as Sprosse; the young man loops the enchanted straw around it.

779cd7671ea9305e1c7d6cee67c23ccb4b708643.summary: Throughout the region around Eckwyl, even in these recent years, a woman was shunned and avoided because she was considered a Hasenfrau.

notes.label: Hasenfrau
notes.text: literally a ‘hare-woman,’ a woman believed able to take hare form; the animal's appearance during Hannele's unexplained absence is offered as evidence for the accusation.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Besegnungen
notes.text: ritual blessings or healing formulas, here attempted by Capuchin friars after the child's injury; the word belongs to a Catholic folk-healing setting that can overlap with exorcistic practice.

b0cc99ba9da6e631c0dd187cdd48ab128dc53ebd.summary: Hans am Sand, a Siegrist at Hasle in the Bernese Oberland, did not want to become Reformed.

notes.label: Siegrist
notes.text: a church sacristan or sexton responsible for duties such as caring for the building and ringing its bells; the precise scope of Hans am Sand’s office at Hasle is not stated.

notes.label: Hasle Burä
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for the peasants or farmers of Hasle; the poem predicts that they will come to regret the religious change, but it does not identify particular people.

3a445f8f2630085b55e62d5984239161258ff0c9.summary: When Hans turned twenty, he packed his few belongings into a bundle, took one sack full of bread and a second full of onions, and set out into the world.

notes.label: Zoccoli
notes.text: the Italian and Ticinese name for wooden-soled clogs; Hans proposes changing from these everyday clogs into shoes before departing with Death.

06b2ac72596f54d1df0722ad6ee089bb124ef664.summary: In the land of Raetia there was a man who was poor, but no stronger or more handsome man could be found in all the mountains.

notes.label: gebig
notes.text: a regional adjective meaning giving, generous, or openhanded; the tale contrasts Hans’s compassionate generosity with Urschel’s refusal to share, and the quoted form preserves the narrator’s dialect coloring.

notes.label: häbig
notes.text: a regional adjective for holding tightly to possessions—thrifty or well-provided in some contexts, but emphatically close-fisted and miserly here; the source pairs it with geizig and contrasts it with gebig.

notes.label: Marend
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alpine term for a field-worker’s meal or substantial snack, often eaten around midday or later in the day; here the narrator immediately calls the meager food a midday meal.

194398548f912845b61f0d0e9a21816dc11b3b51.summary: Hans Binz is said to have lived five hundred years ago in Iberg behind Schwyz, on the farmstead called the "Hirsch." Like his two daughters, he possessed a giant’s strength.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

09664903d067f04b9df7a2bd939147ba1b5609c3.summary: A native of Säckingen, Hans Riss roamed about as a wandering scholar in his youth.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: ungefreute
notes.text: an archaic regional adjective for children who are afflicted, failing to thrive, or believed to be bewitched; the exact range of ailments is not specified.

notes.label: Fahrt
notes.text: literally a journey; here it is a prescribed ritual pilgrimage intended to redeem a wandering spirit, as the source’s own gloss Wallfahrt confirms.

notes.label: Apostützerei
notes.text: an obscure archaic legal or religious label for Riss’s forbidden conjuring and deception, possibly related to apostasy; its precise historical classification is uncertain.
The apparent OCR forms wad and ulmging are read contextually as ward and umging.

4d31eeb881708c5bd2abfec45b8c35a08826692c.summary: Hans von Bramberg was a harsh, misanthropic man, cold as the stone of his castle, cruel as the tiger, unfeeling as the grave, dark as night.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

9b1145fce8376df8ff647670d44d08e1728bd227.summary: Three times in succession, Hans Kuhschwanz on the Trichelegg at Grindelwald dreamed that he must go to the Sinnebrücke in Thun, where he would learn something that could help him to future good fortune.

notes.label: Kuhschwanz
notes.text: literally ‘cow tail,’ Hans's unflattering local surname or byname; becoming rich makes him eager to replace it with a name he considers more dignified.

notes.label: Pfiffikus
notes.text: a clever, shrewd fellow; the frail stranger uses it ironically because Hans has traveled to Thun merely on the strength of a dream.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: large historical coins named from the German Thaler; the source calls the treasure golden Taler, although the denomination was most commonly associated with silver and is not specified more precisely here.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the territorial bailiff or governor who represented higher authority in a district; in the tale he has power to grant Hans a more prestigious name.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

6ea674b490701c0c31f63c4e05fab43063a86954.summary: a) The so-called Helgenhüsli at the Twerenfallen outside Menzingen is said formerly to have been uncanny.

notes.label: Helgenhüsli
notes.text: literally a little saints' or holy-image house, a regional diminutive for a small chapel or wayside shrine; the text calls the same structure a chapel but gives no architectural detail.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical Swiss local magistrate or chief administrative official; Uhr is the officeholder's surname, while the office's precise powers varied by canton and period.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally the prayer bell, usually a church bell rung at a set devotional hour such as the Angelus; in both episodes its consecrated sound ends supernatural bewilderment.

notes.label: Bildstock
notes.text: a small freestanding wayside shrine or image pillar bearing a sacred image; this one displays Saint Apollonia and marks a former execution site.

notes.label: Mörderwäldli
notes.text: literally “little murder wood,” a dialect place-name suggesting a site associated with killing; the source lists it without recounting its particular legend.

notes.label: Hexenbächlein
notes.text: literally “little witches' brook,” a local watercourse name whose wording preserves its association with witch lore; no specific episode is supplied here.

notes.label: Mordshagel
notes.text: a quoted local name or sobriquet associated with the killing of a girl; although it literally resembles “murder-hail,” the excerpt does not identify the killer or explain how the name arose.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a girl or young woman; the possessive may imply the Mordshagel's sweetheart, but their exact relationship is not stated.

notes.label: Mordshagellied
notes.text: the local song about the Mordshagel killing; the compound means “Mordshagel song,” but neither its lyrics nor its genre is preserved in this excerpt.

f43a4bcc574508c20e28c83ef98a41a12ceda44d.summary: The ruin of the White Castle, also called Weisswasserstelz, lies near the little town of Kaiserstuhl on the right bank of the Rhine.

notes.label: Im Hornig sind d'Chatze zornig
notes.text: ‘In Hornig the cats are angry,’ a rhyming saying in which Hornig is a traditional name for February and Chatze is Swiss German for cats.

547dd4f139a3f3c7a3acbedf495f8a20dd19a1b5.summary: Heutier was the name given in Zurzach to that evil woman who, it was said, rode out through the chimney on every odd-numbered night to attend the Hexenrath and, upon returning, tormented sleepers in the form of the Schrätele.

notes.label: Heutier
notes.text: literally ‘hay animal,’ a Zurzach byname for the evil woman who rides to the witches’ assembly; why this particular name is used is uncertain.

notes.label: Hexenrath
notes.text: literally ‘witches’ council,’ the nocturnal gathering the woman attends through the chimney; the spelling preserves the historical source form.

notes.label: Schrätele
notes.text: an Alemannic name for a nightmare spirit or oppressive nocturnal being; here the returning witch assumes this form to torment sleepers, though regional descriptions of the creature vary.

c33c6ca46b482f8eac93702226d2a69a08f9e047.summary: At night near Ober-Siggingen, a farmer tries to catch a foal running loose and is thrown into a pool of manure, where he must struggle about until dawn.

notes.label: hopen
notes.text: the source's exact transcription of the dead carter's unexplained call on the Grepenbuck; its closest meaning is uncertain, and here the sound functions chiefly as evidence of his haunting.

notes.label: Rossheiri
notes.text: a Swiss German nickname combining Ross, ‘horse,’ with Heiri, a familiar form of Heinrich; here it names the hanged carter whose calling voice haunts the route.

50e7fb25127894ade0a8b14f4ae501f7b2003981.summary: It had always been said that things were not right in the hut on Alp Bärrlibutz in the Erstfeldertal.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, together with its huts and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Bärrlibutz is the named Alp whose hut is haunted.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

2ede7cbb9a1a32e407a44b2130162e2ebb4038cf.summary: 50 years ago a basket-maker’s family lived at Stockenweid and was badly tormented and harmed by evil spirits.

notes.label: Choge-Gschrei
notes.text: this St. Gallen dialect expression denotes an appalling or infernal racket in the haunting; its literal force and degree of offensiveness are uncertain.

notes.label: heilige Öbed
notes.text: this dialect phrase means ‘holy eves,’ likely the evenings before major feast days, when the apparition was especially active; which particular feast eves were intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a practitioner of the ‘black art,’ here an alleged sorcerer blamed for the haunting; whether the label means magician, witch, or folk occultist more specifically is uncertain.

4c7868147e7113b388fce3a131aa9bf205389048.summary: Many people kept a Hauswurz plant upon their roofs or garden fences. If it grew tall or even flowered, this was considered a sign that someone in the household would soon die.

notes.label: Hauswurz
notes.text: the houseleek, a hardy succulent of the genus Sempervivum traditionally grown upon roofs and walls; although widely regarded as protective, its unusual flowering is treated here as a household death omen.

53df03136428ce8ea9a7d7c7bfb5dabafab30747.summary: The same physician could also render boiling water harmless; he took a gold coin from it without burning his hands or arms.

notes.label: Dingstätten
notes.text: historical Germanic and medieval assembly or court sites where legal judgments could be rendered; the narrator connects the doctor’s feat to an older judicial ordeal, though the custom was broader than Switzerland alone.

a1824dd7f2ee82af4fc4fa8c478b26a7aab6d079.summary: In Bürglen a man known to have died at 90 years of age was seen gazing for a long time up at the roof of a house in which he had lived his whole life.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or unmarried woman, with the -li diminutive; the informant calls the teller an old Meitli, which may imply a lifelong unmarried woman rather than a child.

26b7dee8f8a2132b1f0fa7a631fe13ffb4d370f2.summary: Not far from Dagmersellen, a monastery is said to have stood in a forest, and many a person is said to have come to harm on the path that runs beside this place because it is haunted there.

notes.label: Fronfastennacht
notes.text: an Ember night, one of the nights associated with the quarterly Catholic fasts; in Swiss folklore, such times are especially open to spirits, visions, and supernatural ordeals.

f3e8a71655bcfd57ecc3a2b80a454d1fca257078.summary: In the present convent church on the Au near Steinen, one sees on the Gospel side a deep Sodbrunnen that sprang forth in the 14th century when the grave of a nun regarded as holy was opened.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a deep draw well or shaft well, here revered for healing water that sprang up at a holy nun’s grave.

34b7378abef5b0a889c43d20e0376744a1939826.summary: Many years ago, in the Valais village of Ernen, a seven-year-old little boy named Joseli lay dying.

notes.label: Großvaterli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘dear little grandfather’ or ‘granddaddy,’ with the affectionate diminutive -li; Joseli uses it while asking his grandfather for the forgiveness needed to enter heaven.

notes.label: Öle
notes.text: a Swiss regional term for an oil mill or oil press; it is the father’s workplace beside the pond, not simply ‘oil’ itself.

f9c78ab155e7a7e53c571b7395579a6a9ddb73e0.summary: In a pleasant plain, where magnificent meadows and woods alternate with thickets beside the gently flowing Muta and the Staubbach, while across the way wooded slopes with a mighty vertical rock wall and tiered pastures above broad Nossen meet the eye, three quarters of an hour from the church at…

notes.label: Nossen
notes.text: a regional topographic plural for broad projecting slopes, ledges, or mountain ‘noses’; here tiered pastures extend above them, but the compact landscape description does not define their exact landform.

7e667c1d608fc936961ae279bb452f5b5b5dbb49.summary: Opposite Amsteg, in Butzen, lived a girl. One day some Heiden came into the house and begged for this and that, and she gave them what they desired.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: historically ‘heathens’ or non-Christians, but in Alpine lore the word can also mark imagined ancient, foreign, uncanny, or magically knowledgeable people; the account does not establish a historical religion or ethnicity.

notes.label: Gufen
notes.text: an Alemannic word for a pin or large needle; the girl uses it to prick a vein so that she can write with her own blood, but its exact size is not specified.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: the inflected plural or collective form of Stubete, an evening social or courtship visit in a household; the informant’s youthful visits suggest personal familiarity with the woman rather than a formal interview.

05c8c6ef372ac5abc8013cf0edb647dce395fb02.summary: is the name of a gully that descends into the lake at the entrance to Isental, near the Fruttchäppäli.

notes.label: Heidenvolk
notes.text: literally ‘heathen folk’; the historical account pairs it with the othering label Zigeuner, a word often applied to Roma but also used indiscriminately for itinerant outsiders. The group's exact identity cannot be established from the tale, and the labels are retained to document the source, not to endorse them.

9614038bb933a895da7d0290cd87f2f8c8a52f18.summary: A treasure lies in the Heidenloch, deep inside the mountain in an iron chest.

notes.label: Heidenloch
notes.text: literally ‘heathen hole,’ the local name of the cave; in older German-speaking place-names, Heiden can suggest a pre-Christian, ancient, or mysterious site and need not identify any historically known people.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ dwarf-like beings of mountain and mining folklore who possess or guard underground treasure; the diminutive can sound endearing, but these beings are deadly in the tale.

e9d81fe4b8fbb6a22c7946825bb5a012b1c28e67.summary: Among Heine's acquaintances, it is generally believed that he understands Bannen extremely well.

notes.label: Bannen
notes.text: magically binding, immobilizing, or placing someone under a spell; Heine fixes the cherry thief to the tree until he chooses to release him.

notes.label: Steinebühl
notes.text: the named stony hill near Baden associated with Heine; Bühl is a regional word for a hill or rise.

d78cd77f9f4d06bfb38494f56492ebffdc7d4468.summary: Lord Heinrich of Strättlingen cared nothing for gold or property. The only gold capable of making his heart happy was the music he drew from the strings of his lute, the songs in which he praised the wonders of the world and the beauty of women.

notes.label: Minne
notes.text: the medieval German ideal and poetic practice of courtly love; in the story, Heinrich's sincere love contrasts with Wolfhart's coercive desire.

notes.label: Kienholz
notes.text: resin-rich pinewood used as a bright torch or splint; Heinrich swings the burning wood three times as a nighttime signal across the lake.

notes.label: Bächiholz
notes.text: literally the woodland at or by the Bächi brook, the lovers' meeting place beneath the beeches; Holz here means a small wood rather than timber.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: an oppressive territorial lord or petty tyrant, literally a lord who compels; the label characterizes Wolfhart's coercive power.

notes.label: Wurzgärtlein
notes.text: a diminutive herb, kitchen, or medicinal garden; Ita is first seen by Wolfhart within this modest household space.

notes.label: Schappel
notes.text: a maiden's ornamental headpiece, wreath, or chaplet; throwing Ita's into the lake is meant to suggest she drowned.

notes.label: Marmelstein
notes.text: a folk or dialectal form meaning marble stone; the paired memorial stones communicate first grief and then renewed hope.

notes.label: Mir tät für minen ganzen Lenzen
notes.text: the opening of an archaic verse meaning approximately ‘For all my life's springtime, one little flower shone enough for me; now Ita lies below, my violet, no spring shall ever again be mine’; Lenzen turns life into spring, while Veil is violet.
notes.anchor: Mir tät für minen ganzen Lenzen

notes.label: Veil
notes.text: an older poetic form of Veilchen, ‘violet,’ used both for Ita's emblem and as Heinrich's tender name for her; it does not mean an English face covering.

notes.label: Minnesänger
notes.text: a medieval German lyric poet and singer of courtly love; Heinrich's music, social role, and devotion to Ita frame him in that tradition.

cc94163eef957d8609a781b40b6a6981f5474dad.summary: The road that today leads from Cur to Mayenfeld followed a partly different course before the railway line was built.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical German spelling of Chur, the present capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Brücken-Butz
notes.text: a bridge-haunting Butz or bogey-spirit; here it seeks release by repeatedly sneezing beneath the bridge.

notes.label: Helf dir Gott!
notes.text: literally ‘God help you!,’ the traditional blessing addressed to someone who sneezes; in the tale it unexpectedly redeems the Brücken-Butz.

0ecf6b4a9ebd158d08d0967d6ee03af069e69193.summary: a) In former times, in some parts of central Switzerland, people also believed in a kind of friendly, helpful house spirit, generally called an "Unghür," whereas a "Gespenst" was understood to be a more malicious being.

notes.label: Unghür
notes.text: in this central Swiss usage, a familiar and often helpful household spirit, explicitly contrasted with the more malicious Gespenst; elsewhere the word can mean a monster or uncanny being.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Verbergis
notes.text: a regional children's hiding game, equivalent in context to hide-and-seek.

f8a37a9ee1a4aac242679d1a1cdf4cec0e04f6e0.summary: In Guarda, a man lived in discord with his wife. Once, when he was to load his hay in a mountain meadow in order to take it home, he had no one to help him, for his quarrelsome wife refused.

notes.label: Diale
notes.text: the singular local name in this Graubünden story for a female supernatural being with goats’ feet; she helps load the hay and is mistaken for the Devil.

notes.label: Fuder
notes.text: a full cartload or wagonload, especially of hay or another farm product; the Diale stands upon it while helping the man.

notes.label: Eug suess
notes.text: the Romansh words supplied by the source for “I myself”; the man uses them instead of his name, creating the story’s fatal wordplay.

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: plural of Diale, the host of related female beings who accept the dying Diale’s answer “I myself” and therefore do not pursue the man.

notes.label: Chi suess fà, suess giauda
notes.text: the Romansh proverb rendered by the source as “What one does oneself, one enjoys oneself”; in context it is a darkly ironic response to what the Dialen understand as self-inflicted harm.

0fb07cecbf86129e3bde2997c41b2a917b9ea915.summary: On the old country road that passes Forsteck Castle, hauling was very arduous in former times, and both driver and horses needed a great deal of patience.

notes.label: Hi, i Gotts Name
notes.text: a dialect driver's command meaning forward or gee, in God's name; the pious formula replaces cursing and restores the horses' ability to pull.

6dd63c8622746330499b45bfb4ee2b39d7c0b4b8.summary: In olden times the woods of the village of Tegerfelden extended almost down to the meadows of the town of Zurzach.

notes.label: Gemeindebann
notes.text: the legally and customarily bounded territory under a community’s authority and use rights; here its annual inspection protected the shared forest boundary, and Bann means jurisdictional bounds rather than a magical curse.

notes.label: Hie noche und hie nein müend ihr d’Marche setze!
notes.text: the bribed witness’s Alemannic boundary-setting cry, approximately ‘Here close by and here inward you must set the boundary’; Marche is the boundary line or marker, while the exact directional force of the paired dialect adverbs is locally dependent.
notes.anchor: Hie noche und hie nein müend ihr d’Marche setze!

notes.label: Juchart
notes.text: a historical Swiss unit of land area, originally associated with the amount one could plow in a day; its size varied by region, so the lost ‘hundred Juchart’ cannot be converted precisely without local evidence.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Bannbeschreitung
notes.text: the formal communal perambulation or walking inspection of territorial bounds and their markers; the custom publicly maintained legal memory of the forest boundary.

notes.label: Hie noh und hie nein!
notes.text: the shortened ghostly repetition of the earlier boundary-setting formula, roughly ‘Here nearby and here inward!’; its precise local spatial nuance remains uncertain, but it reenacts the fraudulent survey.

5ff25ea17b22b384da3051c678dafc4e383effa9.summary: A young man from Bürglen was going to a Stubete. As he left home, his worried Christian mother made the sign of the cross upon his forehead with holy water.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a sociable evening visit or farmhouse-parlor gathering, often associated with visiting, music, shared work, or courtship; the young man's mother gives him protective blessing before he leaves for one.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

94795e24d625e9d15eebf3a4acf8afcab7664782.summary: A man succeeded in catching the Schrättlig. In the morning, he filled a little bottle with the contents of his chamber pot and sealed it very tightly.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a Swiss form related to Schratt, here a nocturnal oppressive spirit or witch-being that can be magically trapped through the victim's urine; the discovery that it is the man's wife links the creature with witchcraft rather than defining a separate species.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a Swiss high-mountain summer pasture and its seasonal herding operation, the place to which the man carries the sealed bottle.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

6fba472f7823a62ab13c01096a1b79b516e80672.summary: When the Glarus goat herder tries to swim across the Oberblegisee, the Haggemann living in it bites off his head.

notes.label: Haggemann
notes.text: the name used here for the Oberblegisee water being that decapitates the swimmer, apparently a regional relative or form of the hooked Hakenmann.

notes.label: Hakenmann
notes.text: literally ‘hook man,’ the malicious Zurich and Glarus water ghost imagined with an enormous hook and associated with drowning victims.

notes.label: Tremmel
notes.text: a regional word for logs or tree trunks, used as a size comparison for the water spirit’s monstrous fish.

notes.label: Hoggema
notes.text: the title’s local form of the threatening hooked water spirit whose related names in the text are Haggemann and Hakenmann; the source does not explain whether the spelling marks a distinct Glarus being or only dialect variation.

c989cb6c4cc11e367b60475fe28ae5e6e6f990c9.summary: 1. Several men from the Amsteg area, whose names are still given, resolved to dig together for metals or Strahlen—in short, for valuables—in the ruined mine gallery by the ‘Höhe’ in the Ried at the foot of the Bristenstock.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: in central Swiss mineral culture, rock-crystal points or specimens sought in mountain fissures; the first account groups them with metals and other valuables rather than rays of light.

notes.label: strahlen
notes.text: the regional occupational verb for searching mountain fissures for rock crystal; in the final maxim it means prospecting together, not emitting light.

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: central Swiss crystal seekers who prospect mountain rock for valuable specimens, traditionally relying on specialized landscape knowledge; the plural here describes the men who find the monstrance-shaped crystal.

d51b97698733631638ddda915e8176d210cce142.summary: Kalktaren is the name of a wooded region between the Steinebühl and Ober-Endingen.

notes.label: Kalktaren
notes.text: the local name of the woodland between Steinebühl and Ober-Endingen where the violent farmer's ghost rides.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally ‘gray- or white-horse rider,’ the form taken by Hoppedihop after death.

notes.label: Hoppedihop
notes.text: the apparition's name, imitating his rhythmic call as he strides or rides through the forest.

notes.label: Reissbündel
notes.text: a bundle of brushwood or small cut branches whose supernatural weight prevents the horses from moving the wagon.

21d20f94e784833ef726b17f10ec4401ca067d76.summary: The devil has a horse's hoof. He impressed one as a mark upon a rock on the Trübseealp in Nidwalden.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: A mia duonna e al mulin
notes.text: the first line of the mill inscription in a regional Romance form, meaning “To my wife and to the mill”; it sets up a joking comparison between the two.
notes.anchor: A mia duonna e al mulin

notes.label: Mauncha saimper qualchosin.
notes.text: the second line of the mill inscription, meaning “Something is always lacking”; together the lines imply that both wife and mill continually need something.

notes.label: Mayenfeld
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Maienfeld in Graubünden, where these inscriptions were recorded.

notes.label: Prätigau
notes.text: Jecklin's historical spelling of Prättigau, the Graubünden valley where these moral, devotional, and humorous house inscriptions were recorded.

328c496778bf5dbe88559a173c4a4ab641685e1f.summary: Twice, a devastating plague raged among the cattle summering on the Alp of Ällgäu in the Canton of Bern: first in the summer of 1718 and then again in the summer of 1800 or 1801.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working dairy settlement, not simply a mountain; the plague strikes cattle summering on the Alps of Ällgäu and Bohl.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss fresh whey cheese, distinct from ordinary curd cheese; the annual charitable distribution includes both regular cheese and Zieger.

notes.label: Reckholder
notes.text: a regional Swiss word for juniper; its branches are burned with other brushwood so the curative smoke envelops the cattle.

notes.label: Twirrispeicher
notes.text: the named storehouse or granary where the unsalted cheese and Zieger are carried for distribution; the source establishes its ritual role but does not explain the first element of the place-name.

notes.label: Sankt Johannsen
notes.text: the local name for the annual Saint John's charitable cheese-making and distribution custom, observed here according to the old calendar.

notes.label: Sankt Johannser
notes.text: an alternative local name for Sankt Johannsen and, in context, for the Saint John's distribution observance itself rather than simply a person from a place called St. Johann.

a3da4171160ea8cd359d6d10a1d8b590ad199dfe.summary: On the Göschner Alp, there were very many toads and snakes. They entered the houses, went into people's milk and food, or whatever was being prepared.

notes.label: Göschner Alp
notes.text: the high summer-pasture community at Göschenen; Alp denotes both the mountain grazing land and its working settlement.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar,’ a wandering learned or magical practitioner in German-speaking legend who possesses occult arts; here he charms away snakes and toads for payment.

notes.label: Fahrige
notes.text: the source's shortened regional designation for the fahrender Schüler, emphasizing the itinerant stranger rather than an ordinary school pupil.

54628028c0662e17cfd8028f637eb685c2e643e0.summary: Like his late father before him, Gianni practiced the fisherman’s trade. To be sure, he had never had much luck at fishing, for he caught only a few fish each day.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally a ‘forest brother,’ an older regional name for a male religious hermit or lay recluse living apart from ordinary society; here he is one of the teacher’s hermit brothers, not merely a biological brother living in a forest.

931491b75efd7605a9247cbfab1f8d8cdf536249.summary: a) At the end of summer, when people were descending from an Alp in the canton of Uri, a milking stool had been left behind, and one of the Handknaben had to fetch it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture together with its seasonal herding and dairy operation, not simply the Alpine mountain range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Handknaben
notes.text: junior male helpers or hired boys attached to Alpine farm work; one is sent back for the forgotten milking stool.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: the hut serving a summer Alp, used for shelter and often for dairy work; the abandoned hut becomes the meeting place with the spectral Sennen.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or herdsmen responsible for cattle and milk processing on an Alp; the story contrasts the supernatural Sennen with the living Senn who comes from greed rather than need.

notes.label: Käsekessel
notes.text: the large cheese-making kettle suspended above the fire in an Alpine dairy hut.

notes.label: Suffi
notes.text: a regional term glossed by the source as Käsmilch, the liquid from cheese making closest to whey; its red, white, and black forms embody different moral uses of milk.

notes.label: Jauchzen
notes.text: an Alpine whoop, ringing call, or wordless vocal flourish related to yodeling; here it is treated as a learnable supernatural gift rather than ordinary shouting.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman in charge of cattle and milk work during the summer season.

notes.label: Waldhorn
notes.text: literally ‘forest horn,’ a horn instrument; in this source it is one of the musical skills the dwarfs offer, and the exact historical instrument is not specified.

d363f834df2256e1d2559941ce85a5ca4d936b3d.summary: Balthasar Jörgi, called Hunkeler, of Nebikon in the Amte Willisau, related this on the Thursday before Oswaldi in 1509.

notes.label: Amte Willisau
notes.text: an inflected older form for the historical Lucerne administrative district or bailiwick containing Nebikon and Willisau.

notes.label: Oswaldi
notes.text: St. Oswald's feast day used as a calendar marker; ‘Thursday before Oswaldi’ dates Jörgi's testimony in the older ecclesiastical manner.

notes.label: Kilchweg
notes.text: Swiss German for a church path, the route used to reach worship or burial and therefore a culturally liminal place for the nightly haunting.

notes.label: Sankt Jakob
notes.text: St. James and, in pilgrimage usage, Santiago de Compostela; Jörgi vows this long journey after recovering from the specter's attack.

notes.label: Schiesset
notes.text: a local shooting event or shooting festival held at Willisau, apparently alongside the fair; the exact program is not described.

notes.label: Kronen
notes.text: the inn called the Krone, or Crown, where Jörgi eats and becomes embroiled in the later dispute.

notes.label: Hudler
notes.text: a contemptuous regional insult for a shabby, disreputable, or good-for-nothing person; its breadth makes the innkeeper's precise accusation ambiguous.

5eaa9487258f6228757afc681cea1a77bab68f30.summary: Z’ wild Mandle het sis Wort g’halte.—The wild Männlein kept its word.

notes.label: Z’ wild Mandle het sis Wort g’halte.
notes.text: Bernese dialect meaning ‘The wild little man kept its word’; the wording introduces the tale in its regional voice, and Mandle is a diminutive supernatural designation rather than merely a small human man.
notes.anchor: Z’ wild Mandle het sis Wort g’halte.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ the text’s name for a wild, dwarf-like Alpine being; it borrows and returns a cow honorably, but the legend gives no more specific species or origin.

notes.label: Rudersberg-Fluh
notes.text: the local rock face or crag at Rudersberg; Fluh is an Alpine Swiss term for a steep exposed rock wall, more specific than the general English word ‘mountain.’

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a diminutive for the supernatural Alpine being that borrows the cow; ‘mountain dwarf’ is close, though the source does not explicitly classify it as a dwarf.

notes.label: Kühscheid
notes.text: literally the ‘cow separation,’ the customary autumn division and departure of cattle from the communal high pasture; it marks the Alpine seasonal handover, not an ordinary sorting of cows.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

dd380e3eebcda54b47369c66818ed21f79592e2a.summary: Kestenbaum is the name of a beautifully situated farmstead in the municipality of Horw on Lake Lucerne.

notes.label: Kestenbaum
notes.text: the local farmstead name interpreted as ‘chestnut tree,’ using Kesten, a regional form of Kastanien; the planting legend explains both the grove and place-name.

6dc8c34fecb9ec60e7969d7901414a026a92e289.summary: Once, while King Rudolf of Burgundy was resting at his castle at Strättlingen on Lake Thun, he had a dream and fell into a trance.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7bafdcb316e283c3e28abf531977e615496ae040.summary: During a Hochgemuter on the Alp, two Räfiser—men from Räfis—Baba-Hans and Long Badist, had taken refuge in a hut on the Buchserberg.

notes.label: Hochgemuter
notes.text: a local St. Gallen weather word for a violent mountain thunderstorm; the source's form is unusual, and its exact relation to standard Hochgewitter is uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Räfiser
notes.text: people from Räfis near Buchs in the St. Gallen Rhine Valley; the label identifies the two men's local origin.

notes.label: Wüetihö
notes.text: the dialect name given to the raging storm or storm-being passing over the hut; the wording personifies the weather, but the source does not clearly distinguish a supernatural creature from the tempest itself.

eb57979632276688ff0929cc3bb0810bf8e6b8b1.summary: A young man who tended cattle on the Vättnerberg did not come down into the valley for an entire week to fetch food.

notes.label: Wildbret
notes.text: game meat supplied by the dwarf father to the young couple.

notes.label: Ziegern
notes.text: the process of making Ziger, Swiss whey cheese, by heating and treating the whey remaining from cheese production.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey, the liquid remaining after curds form; the dwarf calls its recoverable value the true gold.

notes.label: Käskessi
notes.text: the large cheese-making kettle or cauldron in which milk and whey are heated in an Alpine dairy.

3a103b6f724f88c7ab89923f6da6494dc6c582e7.summary: When the first inhabitants of Sargans were at a loss as to what name they should give the place, they went to the nearby little River Saar and decided that the settlement should be named after the river and the first object that came floating downstream.

notes.label: About this telling

320095628adf6655e994ff1260e164d7daf45a37.summary: Listen, Toni: in olden times it was not always advisable to buy pigs. A man from Urswil near Hochdorf, where they had the famous Streggelen, once learned this.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: Streggelen are witchlike or Wild Hunt beings in central Swiss tradition, here invoked as a famous feature of Hochdorf; their exact connection to the enchanted straw-pigs is uncertain.

3186c6f365067b48d50cd400ccb1ff3bbe7e17ec.summary: a) In Göschenen there was a man of gigantic strength named Melch Tresch.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: here a Mass is a historical regional liquid measure and the bottle holding that quantity of wine; its exact local volume is uncertain because the measure varied by place and period.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: a Säumer is a pack-train carrier who transported goods with laden animals across Alpine routes; the Ticino man’s cargo and route are unspecified.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the Landammann is the chief magistrate of a Swiss rural canton or polity, here acting for Uri’s honor; the officeholder and exact period are unspecified.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: this Swiss German word means butter, apparently consumed from the cauldron in this test of strength; whether it was melted, clarified, or another dairy preparation is uncertain.

notes.label: Kessi
notes.text: this Alemannic form denotes the large cauldron from which the brothers drank; its size and specific dairy use are uncertain.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: here Viertel is a historical dry measure used for flour, not merely the abstract fraction ‘one quarter’; its exact local weight or volume is uncertain.

2cd09ea0be4dc97791aba6474d53256d5a8f0309.summary: How the Black Death Came to Huttwil

notes.label: About this telling

cb0040c137fa1528c225f46ebdaa454a5316b72f.summary: In former times, the charming little lake in the upper Kander valley looked different from today.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: the plural of Fluh, steep rock faces, cliffs, or crags; the boy falls while gathering high-mountain hay on this dangerous terrain.

notes.label: Seiltuch
notes.text: a strong rope-cloth, sling, or carrying sheet used to bundle and transport wild hay from steep slopes; the precise rigging is not described.

notes.label: Seelein
notes.text: literally ‘little lake,’ with the diminutive -lein; it affectionately names the hidden Blausee and should not be confused with Seele, ‘soul.’

46c785d687a2e0bbbb8a3570e31c51ad8592633f.summary: Lord Arnold of Strättlingen, mindful of how the Archangel Michael had always helped him and his people, resolved to build a church dedicated to the saint.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

b94e7aa76c77a6548c20a7d3dc924be483c06b1b.summary: What an experience a handsome young farmhand had on the Ragaz Alp Bardiel! He too saw the spirit women and had to choose one from three different Schottä.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Bardiel
notes.text: the named seasonal high pasture above Bad Ragaz where the farmhand encounters the spirit women.

notes.label: Schottä
notes.text: the source's St. Gallen dialect plural for distinct groups or companies; here the spirit women appear in three differently marked companies, one of them green, though the exact nature of the distinction is not explained.

notes.label: gjoulät
notes.text: the source's dialect form meaning yodeled or called out in a yodeling voice; its sound helps preserve the oral character of the account.

notes.label: Cheise
notes.text: Swiss German for cheese-making; the wished-for Kuhreihen is heard during the central dairying work of an Alp.

notes.label: Kuhreihen
notes.text: an Alpine herding call or melody, related to the French-Swiss ranz des vaches and often performed in a yodel-like manner; it is more specific than an ordinary song.

notes.label: Wie der Kuhreihen [Jodler] kam (Mundart)
notes.text: ‘how the Kuhreihen [yodel] came (dialect)’; the exact catalogue title is retained because Kuhreihen names a specifically Alpine vocal tradition and Mundart identifies the Swiss German telling.

42da53558f38ef5116435d26246c3ae14a289054.summary: In summer the whole company of little dwarfs often came down from the Flühen into the valley and joined the working people, either helping or merely watching, especially the Mäder during the Heuet.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: this Swiss plural denotes steep cliffs or rock faces from which the dwarfs descend; the exact formations in the Haslital are unspecified.

notes.label: Mäder
notes.text: Mäder are the men who mow hay, here observed or helped by the dwarfs; their exact work group and tools are unspecified.

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: this Alemannic term denotes the haymaking season and its communal labor; its precise timing is uncertain and varied with altitude and weather.

notes.label: Dürscht
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German folklore name for a roaring or crying aerial apparition, related in regional tradition to the Wild Hunt; here it is identified only by its owl-like but distinct call, so its exact form remains unspecified.

9f8c34a809f3358fe70b533929d2c8e2021a35b1.summary: The cartulary of Muri Abbey relates how, in the earliest times, free peasants lived in the villages of Buttwil, Geltwil, and Wallenschwil; how free men cultivated their land at Wohlen; and how Muri already had its own baptismal church before the year 1024.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: the singular regional name corresponding to Freie Ämter, today also used for an Aargau cultural and geographic region; although literally suggestive of a ‘free office,’ here it names the territory rather than making a claim about personal liberty.

notes.label: Im Eigen
notes.text: literally ‘in the owned property’ or ‘in one's own domain,’ a local territorial name at the confluence of the Aare and Reuss; the source treats it as a surviving place-name, and its exact historical jurisdiction is not explained.

notes.label: Freie Ämter
notes.text: literally ‘Free Offices’ and conventionally ‘Free Bailiwicks,’ the historical name of an Aargau region administered as common Swiss subject territories; the story pointedly contrasts the name's ‘free’ with the inhabitants' loss of rights, so a single smooth English rendering would lose the wordplay.

notes.label: Landgraf
notes.text: ‘landgrave,’ a territorial count of high rank in the medieval Empire; retaining the German title preserves the political setting in which Guntram intervenes as judge and lord.

notes.label: Morgengabe
notes.text: literally ‘morning gift,’ property traditionally given by a husband to his wife in connection with marriage; it is not simply her dowry, and the story uses Ratbot's gift of the Freiamt as proof of his presumptuous ownership.

notes.label: Bifang
notes.text: a medieval land-law term for an enclosed, bounded, or newly claimed tract, often an assart; here it denotes land drawn inside the monastery's domain, but the precise tenure implied by the chronicler's usage remains uncertain.

d5b7cc500fd0ff08e5ed69927f8588f8216be486.summary: The Hasler and Grindelwalder once quarreled over possession of a tract of land.

notes.label: Hasler
notes.text: people from the Haslital or Hasli region, one side in the pasture-boundary dispute with Grindelwald.

notes.label: Grindelwalder
notes.text: people of Grindelwald, who secure the disputed land through an oath made literally true by soil hidden in a man's shoes.

notes.label: Milchschöpfen
notes.text: a milk scoop or ladle worn on the swearer's head as part of the strangely worded oath; the source does not explain why it signifies being ‘at home.’

notes.label: Zwirgi
notes.text: the local pass or slope above Meiringen as far as which the perjurer's lamenting ride is seen.

notes.label: Mannsdenken
notes.text: literally ‘within a man's memory,’ meaning within living memory or the span remembered by the current generation.

notes.label: Scheideggalp
notes.text: the high seasonal pasture at Scheidegg whose ownership the deceptive oath is said to establish.

19a9b1016f901fb5dc26f425801a007b3f7150a9.summary: Once, when the Alp at Compadiels was being cleared out, a milking stool was forgotten, and the Handbub was sent up to fetch it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Handbub
notes.text: the junior male helper on an Alp, subordinate to the experienced dairymen; unlike the later Senn, the Handbub is sent there on legitimate business and receives the spirits’ gift.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen responsible for cattle and cheese-making during the summer grazing season; the three strangers resemble supernatural Sennen.

notes.label: Jauchzen
notes.text: loud, ringing Alpine whooping or calling, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; the Handbub chooses it as his supernatural art.

5f30a5e2e9faad62cb35c9a2ac847480cd2ebb13.summary: In the year of the Lord 811, Emperor Charlemagne undertook a campaign against the heathens in Spain.

notes.label: Harschhörner
notes.text: old Swiss military or field horns; the source immediately calls them Heerhörner and connects their ceremonial right of use with Roland, but the exact historical instrument is not described.

notes.label: Kreuzablösung
notes.text: an unusual historical expression apparently referring to the Deposition or Taking Down of Christ from the Cross as an emblem on Uri's banner; the source does not describe the image, so the precise heraldic sense remains uncertain.

df270537b7f5d88dbb23fd45445e1d55ed43e838.summary: Six hundred years ago, at Terenschatten in the lower Simmental, directly beside the Simme, there stood an old and famous house of God and little monastery occupied by several brothers of the Order of St.

notes.label: Brünnelein
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive meaning a little spring or fountain; here it is the warm medicinal source discovered in the gorge and later shared with all sufferers.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; here the healing water springs directly from it.

notes.label: Näpflein
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive for a small bowl, cup, or dish; here Gervasi draws one vesselful of the spring water for Küngold, and its exact shape is not specified.

5fbff46e6e0846ae821e61e99f2d2216f9fc69e7.summary: Not far from Lake Thun, behind the Ralligen vineyard, lies the place called Einöde.

notes.label: Zwerglein
notes.text: literally ‘little dwarf,’ the diminutive used for the persecuted but powerful mountain being; its ability to direct the landslide makes it more than an ordinary small person.

notes.label: Spitzi Fluh
notes.text: Bernese wording for the ‘pointed Fluh,’ a local sharp rock face or crag; Fluh is an Alpine Swiss terrain term more specific than a general hill.

notes.label: Männchen
notes.text: literally ‘little men,’ the dwarf-like mountain beings hammering the rock apart; the tale treats them collectively without defining a more precise supernatural class.

notes.label: Schlegel und Weggen
notes.text: dialect for ‘mallet and wedges,’ the stone-working tools said to have held or taken effect in splitting the Fluh; Weggen here means wedges, not bread rolls.

31bca1e53d560f3459a3d895d12c5dae6df109a8.summary: How the Löchlidokter Quickly Reaches New York

notes.label: Löchlidokter
notes.text: this Bernese byname means approximately ‘little-hole doctor’ and identifies a folk practitioner credited with clairvoyant or soul-travel powers; its exact origin and the historical person’s identity are uncertain.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: this Alemannic diminutive denotes a small private room or parlor into which the Löchlidokter withdraws; its exact use and furnishings are unspecified.

notes.label: Ruehbett
notes.text: this dialect compound means a rest bed or daybed upon which the practitioner lies during his trance; its precise form is uncertain.

notes.label: Burema
notes.text: this dialect form means a peasant or farmer-like man and describes the figure seen in New York; whether the husband recognized specific clothing or only a general rural appearance is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kilt- und Räbeltänze
notes.text: this source phrase names prohibited nocturnal courting and revel dances said to influence witch-flight traditions; the precise distinction between the two dance types and their local forms is uncertain.

98dc4fae75f59804081b776a8678b0aab0dfea86.summary: Buochs in Unterwalden, Canton of Nidwalden

notes.label: Unterwalden
notes.text: the historical Swiss territory comprising Obwalden and Nidwalden; the heading also specifies Nidwalden to locate Buochs more precisely.

notes.label: Buw-Ochs
notes.text: literally ‘building ox,’ the tale’s folk-etymological form for Buochs; it refers to the ox loaded with construction timber, not to a historically verified derivation of the place-name.

notes.label: Bu-Ochs
notes.text: the dialectal contraction of Bau-Ochs, ‘building ox,’ offered by the source as an intermediate form leading to Buochs; this is a traditional wordplay rather than modern linguistic evidence.

notes.label: Ufi cko!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘come up!’ or ‘come up here!’; the story treats the churchward summons as the origin of Uffikon, but presents a folk etymology, not a demonstrated historical one.

notes.label: wart m'r am See
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘wait for me at the lake’; its resemblance to Wartensee supplies another playful folk etymology rather than a reliable account of the name’s linguistic origin.

47407f445f61689fbcd86c4f6b4fef915e4517ca.summary: The people of Hasli tell a legend of how, when the migrating peoples divided the Alps among themselves, those of Grindelwald acquired the alp beyond the Donkey’s Back.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional local or territorial magistrate who presided over communal legal and administrative matters; ‘magistrate’ is the closest English role, but the office’s authority and rank varied across Swiss regions and periods.

89197a1d3ec5a2cf3bc622ec9011cef8e704d0f1.summary: In olden times the lower municipality of Wilägeri had taken out a loan from the municipality of the city of Zug, on condition that the borrowed sum be repaid on a specified day.

notes.label: Wilägeri
notes.text: a historical or dialectal name for Unterägeri, the ‘lower Ägeri’ community in the canton of Zug; the story contrasts its delegates with officials from the city of Zug.

notes.label: Ägerer
notes.text: people from the Ägeri valley or its communities, including Wilägeri; here it refers to the borrowers and their delegation.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally ‘prayer bell,’ a church bell marking a canonical prayer time and, in this tale, the contractual end of the day.

notes.label: Most
notes.text: fermented or fermenting fruit juice, usually apple or pear cider in Swiss usage; the hosts instead serve stronger, more prestigious wine to delay their guests.

notes.label: Betglockenzeit
notes.text: literally ‘prayer-bell time,’ the deadline defined by the ringing of the Betglocke rather than by a clock hour.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a high-elevation summer pasture and its associated grazing rights or holding, not simply a mountain peak; this is the property pledged for the loan.

notes.label: Sankt Michaelissigrist
notes.text: literally ‘St. Michael's sacristan’ or ‘St. Michael's sexton,’ the church attendant whom the Zug conspirator persuades to ring the bell early.

notes.label: Kreuzlitaler
notes.text: the name of a thaler-type coin, probably associated with a cross design; here the coins' jingling ominously echoes the prematurely rung bell.

notes.label: Alpeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Alp or Alpe, meaning a small Alpine pasture or upland holding; the diminutive does not make the loss economically trivial.

notes.label: Zugeralpeli
notes.text: literally ‘the people of Zug's little Alp,’ the place-name commemorating Zug's acquisition of the pledged upland pasture.

notes.label: Zugerli
notes.text: a shorter diminutive place-name for the same Zug-owned pasture; in this context it does not mean a person from Zug.

notes.label: March
notes.text: a regional Swiss word for a boundary, border line, or boundary marker; the tale closes by emphasizing the unusual boundary of the disputed land.

7f0bb54a9b06eb7bdf8562fddd7a7bb753423440.summary: The upper Rätzliberg in the farthest Simmental, from which the Landwasser rises in seven springs, was once a fertile Alp where Mutterne and Adelgras grew in abundance.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture used for livestock and dairying, not simply a mountain peak; the curse destroys an entire productive grazing landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.
