notes.label: Mutterne
notes.text: a historical Alpine plant name, generally associated with an aromatic, nutritious pasture herb; the source uses it as evidence of rich grazing but does not identify the species botanically.

notes.label: Adelgras
notes.text: literally ‘noble grass,’ an old laudatory name for high-quality Alpine forage; the exact modern plant intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd product distinct from ordinary aged cheese; the basket of fresh Ziger forms part of the pasture rent.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or dairyman responsible for cattle on an Alp; here he summers the herd and delivers the pastoral rent.

35369453cc07b4ebee62f85c23c75a2da2793013.summary: In olden times the Sennen are said not to have understood how to prepare “sweet” cheese.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: wild beings or wild people of Alpine folklore credited here with knowledge of rennet cheesemaking; the tradition's classification and portrayal vary by region.

notes.label: Maiensäss
notes.text: a mid-altitude seasonal farm or pasture, commonly occupied between the valley and the high summer Alp; the encounter occurs at the Schuders Maiensäss.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: a little male member of the Alpine Fänggen, presented as both the Senn's companion and the keeper of a valuable dairy secret.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd's milk and cheesemaking; the plural Sennen in the title frames the episode as an origin tale for local dairy knowledge.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gizimagen
notes.text: literally the stomach of a kid goat, used here as the rennet source that curdles milk without first souring it; the tale does not describe how the stomach was prepared or dosed.

2b87ce6889d2ea07f92a585c1cd9751d2904090c.summary: Where the village of Fischbach stands today, several hundred years ago only three brothers of the Seiler family had their permanent homes.

notes.label: Metzen
notes.text: a historical Central European dry measure whose capacity varied by locality; here it measures a mass of Zurich coins, so no single modern volume can be inferred safely.

notes.label: Angster
notes.text: a small historical Swiss silver coin, here a Zurich penny bearing the heads of Saints Felix and Regula; its value and the quantity contained in the stated measures are period-specific.

notes.label: Juchart
notes.text: a traditional Swiss measure of land area based broadly on what could be plowed in a day; its size varied considerably by canton and period, so an exact modern acreage is uncertain.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

a0a781907ebf4c88b09d53e5f986554412827c54.summary: It was in the year 1038 when Karl von Hohenbalken, hunter of the monastery, set out to hunt.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

0cc387328db92efc4ec57fab4ca8fb8025b18b5d.summary: A witch had suddenly made a child ill with her salve. Then she wanted to help again and did so in this way.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Güsel
notes.text: Swiss German for rubbish, refuse, or household sweepings; here it means debris gathered from behind the door for a folk-healing fumigation, though the exact material is not specified.

notes.label: Palmen
notes.text: in Swiss Catholic usage, blessed Palm Sunday greenery rather than necessarily literal palm leaves; the source calls for three kinds but does not identify the plants.

notes.label: Kernenmehl
notes.text: a regional term for flour made from grain kernels, often wheat or spelt in Swiss usage; the historical source does not identify the grain more narrowly.

2cb058d9a242a108d11a5f0fb22ca5007c76a639.summary: How They Dug for Treasure at the Altburg

notes.label: Christoffelgebet
notes.text: literally the ‘Christoffel prayer,’ a named body of powerful prayers and formulas used by regional treasure diggers for conjuration and protection; its precise wording and whether the name refers directly to Saint Christopher are not supplied here.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

c24775cef214df11a32689914c69c75c91fb8839.summary: If one has an opportunity to throw something after the Schrättlig, it must remain.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a Swiss German name for an oppressive night spirit, nightmare being, or goblin-like creature; here it can assume the form of a straw and then a woman, and the term does not establish one fixed anatomy or sex.

2251dfe973d13bc7733fcd0cbade5af67b2e1f27.summary: How to Ward Off the Doggeli

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a regional nocturnal pressure spirit associated with nightmares and the sensation of a being sitting on the sleeper's chest; this Bernese account describes it as small and green, able to enter through a keyhole, and repelled by placing a Bible beneath the head.

1bd9f0f78e499ede0035307eb26386f25decda24.summary: If someone carries in his pocket an egg laid by a black hen on the morning of Charfreitag—Good Friday—he can recognize which women in the community are witches.

notes.label: Charfreitag
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Karfreitag, Good Friday; the egg must be laid that morning and carried into church as the identifying charm.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Wissa Fada, schwarza Fada, wissa Fada, schwarza Fada
notes.text: an Alemannic formula meaning “White thread, black thread, white thread, black thread”; the accused women repeat it while turning their thumbs, though the tale does not explain the thread imagery further.
notes.anchor: Wissa Fada, schwarza Fada, wissa Fada, schwarza Fada

08baf9a26b6af8a394cae33d069e7a49cfa3d6ba.summary: In olden times, two old unmarried women suspected of witchcraft lived in the old Schwander house beside the rectory in Sisikon.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Napolitäner
notes.text: in nineteenth-century Swiss usage, a man associated with or formerly serving in Neapolitan military service, not necessarily a native of Naples; the contributor is identified by this old service nickname, but his exact unit or period is not given.

aac1460f1660bcc9cf24d254b5e0be8e89b365f3.summary: ‘Hujum! Wela chnunt und cheart mi um!’ is the challenge to single combat.

notes.label: Hujum! Wela chnunt und cheart mi um!
notes.text: an eastern-Swiss dialect challenge approximately meaning ‘Hujum! Who will come and turn me around?’; it invites a duel, though Hujum itself is an exclamatory cry without a secure literal equivalent.
notes.anchor: Hujum! Wela chnunt und cheart mi um!

notes.label: Stubeti-Buben
notes.text: young men attending a Stubete, an evening household gathering often connected with socializing or courting; here they conceal their identities on the road.

notes.label: Vordiele
notes.text: the front bay, floor, or loft section of a barn; the disguised challenger hides beneath it, but the source does not specify the exact barn construction.

17495b269287a217b72e507d319234fc4227c011.summary: 1. In the old wooden cottage beside the new schoolhouse in the Wyler at Gurtnellen once lived the wealthy farmer and hunter Sebastian Daxli.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’; in German-speaking Alpine legend this is an itinerant learned figure often credited with occult or magical knowledge, not merely an ordinary student. Here he reveals a lead vein that remains inaccessible to others, though the source does not explain his identity or powers.

notes.label: ghäcklet Plattä
notes.text: the quoted local name for a rock slab or stony feature crossed on the way into the Fellitobel; the dialect suggests a hacked, notched, or roughened slab, but its exact form and whether the phrase functioned as a fixed place-name are uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

61df8907cb1504b9e2e6eb95a9f81ae1253117d3.summary: On the right bank of the Aare, the hunting din begins in the Aarau Oberholz; one hears the cry “Aho” and the blowing of a horn.

notes.label: Todtengässlein
notes.text: literally ‘little lane of the dead,’ an older-spelling local path-name on the Wild Hunt’s route; whether it reflects a burial route or another origin is not explained.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Holzweibel
notes.text: literally a ‘wood or forest bailiff,’ here the named supernatural huntsman Landluegi; Weibel denotes an official or attendant, but the figure’s exact folkloric office is uncertain.

notes.label: Landluegi
notes.text: the Holzweibel’s name, suggestive in Swiss German of looking over or watching the land; the passage treats it as a proper supernatural name without explaining the derivation.

notes.label: W. Jagd
notes.text: the source’s abbreviation for Wilde Jagd, the Wild Hunt; the title maps the supernatural procession’s routes around Aarau rather than ordinary hunting grounds.

notes.label: Wiesberg-Joggeli
notes.text: a local diminutive name, approximately ‘little Jakob of Wiesberg,’ for one manifestation of the Wild Huntsman; the individual tradition behind the name is not supplied.

notes.label: Ewigjäger
notes.text: literally ‘eternal hunter,’ a regional name for the perpetually roaming Wild Huntsman.

notes.label: Walti, dede, hudada!
notes.text: the huntsman’s traditional cry to his dogs at Wölflinswil; Walti may be a dog’s name, while the remaining calls are sound-words whose exact lexical meaning is uncertain.

notes.label: Chum, wenn d’ öppis bisch!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘come if you are anything at all’; the drunken challenge provokes the Wild Hunt to attack.

5d456ab0f2a09f10342289a283d7539f185b1c20.summary: To go chamois hunting on a Muttergottestag is sacrilege and is certain to bring misfortune.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Muttergottestag
notes.text: literally a ‘Mother of God day,’ a feast of the Virgin Mary; the variants identify both mid-August, the Assumption on 15 August, and Herbstmonat, including 8 September, so it does not denote only one Marian feast.

notes.label: Grattier
notes.text: literally approximately a ‘ridge animal,’ a regional Alpine expression for chamois, especially game encountered high on mountain ridges.

notes.label: z'Mitte Augsten
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘at mid-August,’ here the Feast of the Assumption of Mary; the calendrical phrase is central to the hunters' offense.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; Gemsfeyer and Gornern are named Alps crossed or used by the hunters.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Skapulier
notes.text: a blessed Catholic scapular or small devotional token worn or carried for protection; thrown to the abducted hunter, it breaks the chamois's power over him.

notes.label: Herbstmonat
notes.text: the traditional German month-name for September; the source uses it when locating Marian feast days in the autumn month.

notes.label: Eidgenössischer Bettag
notes.text: the Swiss Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance, and Prayer; hunting on this nationally observed religious day is treated as feast-day desecration.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a cliff, steep rock face, or crag; after the third shot, the chamois thrusts the hunter over one to his death.

notes.label: uff d'Bäch
notes.text: Uri dialect literally meaning ‘up/on the Bäch’; it appears to be a local place expression on the hunters' route beyond Balmen, but the source does not identify its exact feature or modern boundary.

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: the plural of the regional ridge-animal term Grattier, meaning chamois hunted in the high Alpine terrain.

notes.label: Steinmanndli
notes.text: literally ‘little stone men,’ an Alpine name for humanlike stone figures or cairns; here the punished hunters are transformed into visible stone pillars on the highest peaks.

6281d18ffd72d3fdbb89e085e3d07ab3f7ed84b7.summary: Hälf dr Gott — May God Help You

notes.label: Hälf dr Gott
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘May God help you,’ used here as the customary blessing after a sneeze and, when spoken three times, as the formula that can release the supernatural woman; its power in the tale depends on invoking God rather than merely offering ordinary help.

notes.label: Hälf dr es Ross!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘May a horse help you!’; substituting a horse for God turns the expected blessing into a joke and breaks the exact release formula the woman needed to hear a third time.

d14a8f8c1f9e7e9c55423f852a42eb55e7cd8371.summary: The road from the village of Koblenz on the Aargau Rhine to the little town of Klingnau is wild and passes many uncanny places.

notes.label: Giritzmoos
notes.text: the local name of the pathless marsh below the Steingraben; Moos commonly means bog or marsh in Swiss place-names, while Giritz is left unexplained.

notes.label: Härdli-Geist
notes.text: literally the ‘Härdli spirit,’ a local revenant condemned to restore boundary stones he moved fraudulently while alive.

notes.label: Heiri
notes.text: a Swiss familiar form of Heinrich, here the alternative identity ‘Heiri of Zurich’ assigned to the Klingnau apparition.

notes.label: Engelwirths
notes.text: an older possessive form meaning the innkeeper of the Engel, or Angel Inn; the variant says Wengi mistook the spirit foal for that innkeeper's animal.

notes.label: Härdlimann
notes.text: a regional name for the haunting figure near Klingnau; it suggests a diminutive ‘little Härdli man,’ but the source does not securely explain Härdli or distinguish the name from the boundary-moving spirit.

notes.label: Geisterfüllen
notes.text: literally ‘spirit foal,’ the supernatural young horse that follows Wengi, grows to a monstrous size, and may take a woman's form.

notes.label: Häxebäse
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘witch's broom,’ a bewitched twig cluster or growth believed here to make a carried load dwindle.

notes.label: Häxebeeri
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘witch berry,’ an ominous berry or plant object with the same power to prevent a gathered load from increasing.

notes.label: Burdi
notes.text: a carried bundle or load, especially of gathered vegetation, brushwood, or fodder; the concealed witch object makes it shrink.

notes.label: Chrättli
notes.text: a small carrying or gathering basket; anything collected in it fails to accumulate when one of the witch objects is present.

fae0dbe3675afacc153e4912488a399d811fe41f.summary: Höch uf u nienen a! (Up High and Touch Nowhere!)

notes.label: Höch uf u nienen a!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for a broom-flight command approximately meaning ‘Up high and touch nowhere!’; nienen a conveys avoiding contact with anything, though the compact magical formula allows more than one idiomatic English rendering.

notes.label: Chutt
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word for a sudden gust, rush, or squall; here the enchanted broom takes off with the speed of a burst of wind.

notes.label: Wihalle
notes.text: a dialect form understood as a wine hall or large drinking hall; here it is the mysteriously merry destination of the witches' flight, although the source does not identify its real-world location.

640debbda943bcc06f642631718fc40f63e3f815.summary: Hölderli Jokeb is the burning man who appears in the Güllihau near Endingen, a forest in which he hanged himself.

notes.label: Hölderli Jokeb
notes.text: the local personal name of the burning-man apparition near Endingen; Jokeb appears to be a regional form of Jakob, while the source gives no secure explanation of Hölderli, so the full folkloric name is retained.

notes.label: Hü, i Gotts Name!
notes.text: Bernese dialect for approximately ‘Gee up, in God's name!’ and a traditional call for setting draft horses in motion; it fails here because the treasure instructions required invocation of the three holy names, meaning the Trinity, rather than this customary singular formula.

notes.label: Chnübeli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for a little knoll or rounded hill; the treasure wagon's shaft protrudes from it and finally pulls the farmer inside the mountain.

notes.label: Schümmle
notes.text: dialect diminutive plural of Schimmel, white or gray horses; the ritual requires four with not a single black hair.

2d0bd3ec44b921d9dbbb0361367f24861508f87d.summary: Hünemauch was a notorious thief from Klingnau. At last he was caught and imprisoned in the fortified part of Zurzach town hall called the Heichel, or Heinrich, and Gäucheln House.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

977e07c80a44b09dc0830bbbfe0b19ba57b58fcb.summary: At Attinghausen in Talacherli, perhaps about 100 years ago, N. Zgraggen once spent the night in the Untergaden of a half-ruined barn.

notes.label: Untergaden
notes.text: the lower level or livestock portion of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding beneath the Obergaden; Zgraggen sleeps there.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper hay-storage level of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding above the Untergaden; the uncanny noise begins there.

notes.label: Ich bi dunnä, und du bisch dobä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I am down below, and you are up above’; the title preserves Zgraggen’s defiant claim that the barn’s two levels will keep him safely apart from the ghost.

notes.label: Rumplä dü, wië d’witt; ich bi dunnä, und dü bisch dobä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Rumble as much as you like; I am down below, and you are up above’; the spirit immediately disproves the man’s confidence.
notes.anchor: Rumplä dü, wië d’witt; ich bi dunnä, und dü bisch dobä

notes.label: Rischi
notes.text: an interior feature of an Uri barn used for storing or moving hay, apparently a bay, chute, or passage between levels; the ghost descends through it like a load of hay, but its exact construction is not described.

025fe32727d2c65957a26610bf4d510408991a18.summary: The former inhabitants of the Lötschental are said to have been rather simple-minded people.

notes.label: Lötschental
notes.text: the Valais valley in which the tale is set; the narrator caricatures its former inhabitants as simple-minded.

notes.label: Langgletscher
notes.text: the glacier at the far end of the Lötschental near which Toni tends the sheep.

notes.label: tschu, tschu
notes.text: Toni's traditional-sounding call to gather or summon the missing sheep; the source does not define it further.

notes.label: Ziecht wieder
notes.text: dialect for “pull back” or “pull me back up”; its sound is misunderstood as a question about seeing a Widder, or ram.

notes.label: Siehst du Widder, siehst wohl auch Aue
notes.text: literally, “If you see rams, surely you see ewes”; the villagers' absurd reply depends on mishearing Toni's cry Ziecht wieder.
notes.anchor: Siehst du Widder, siehst wohl auch Aue

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: literally a holder or wielder of authority; here it is the village's mocking-grand title for its young president.

notes.label: Dorfpräsident
notes.text: the president or chief elected officer of the village community, lowered into the lake first in deference to office.

notes.label: Filzkragen
notes.text: literally “felt collar,” used here as a comic insult suggesting a grasping skinflint; its precise local force is not otherwise defined.

notes.label: Lötscher
notes.text: people from Lötschen or the Lötschental, collectively portrayed in this jest tale.

notes.label: pumpenregenvoll
notes.text: an emphatic regional or comic formation suggesting being utterly full or saturated; in context the villagers are thoroughly drunk after drinking white wine, while the word's exact literal formation remains uncertain.

notes.label: potz Wetter und Steinschlag
notes.text: a comic Alpine-flavored exclamation, approximately “by storm and rockfall,” uttered when the villagers find Toni alive.

notes.label: Lötschen
notes.text: the shorter valley-name used in the concluding statement that the community nearly died out.

83ce5066b3432ce4afe96c6bef88321f363ef1fb.summary: I dr Bisighohle — In the Bisig Cave

notes.label: I dr Bisighohle
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘in the Bisig cave’; the title names the treasure cave or pit where the golden wagon remains sealed.

notes.label: Diechsle
notes.text: a dialect word for a small lizard; its appearance from the mountain immediately precedes the discovery of the enchanted treasure wagon.

cfc8c86426e80d365878a171620ddd477d942f76.summary: I dr Chuchi — In the Kitchen

notes.label: I dr Chuchi
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘in the kitchen,’ the domestic space where Frau Faschte inspects order and punishes neglected utensils.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: the local punitive female winter spirit known in standard German as Frau Fasten; around the holy season, she enforces household order through threats.

notes.label: heilige 0be
notes.text: intended as dialect for ‘holy evening,’ probably heilige Obe, meaning Christmas Eve; the source prints a zero in 0be, so the exact form is retained as a likely typographical or transcription ambiguity.

notes.label: Füürobe
notes.text: Bernese dialect for Feierabend, the end of the working day or stopping work; the joke first says the household stops early, then says Frau Faschte will make the utensils ‘stop work’ by smashing them.

notes.label: Chelle
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ladles or large cooking spoons; hanging them in a straight row demonstrates the kitchen order Frau Faschte demands.

notes.label: sie schlöi alls z’Hudle u z’Fätze
notes.text: dialect for ‘she would smash everything into rags and pieces’; the violent idiom conveys the threatened punishment if the kitchen is not orderly.
notes.anchor: sie schlöi alls z’Hudle u z’Fätze

b4ce8eb56ce076ea460bcb0e3ef66738d96914e9.summary: I dr gueten alte Zit — In the Good Old Days

notes.label: I dr gueten alte Zit
notes.text: dialect for ‘in the good old days’; the nostalgic title becomes comic because the tale centers on trickery and stolen refreshments.

notes.label: Chuderjoggi
notes.text: the poor trickster's local nickname; Joggi is a familiar form of Jakob, while the force of Chuder in this personal byname is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Brönnts u Weggli
notes.text: literally ‘spirits and little rolls,’ meaning distilled liquor and bread rolls provided at the woodland dance; they become the food and drink Joggi steals.

notes.label: Unghüür
notes.text: an uncanny monster, horror, or grotesque thing; here it is the stuffed horned goatskin made to resemble the Devil.

notes.label: wildi Jagd
notes.text: dialect for ‘Wild Hunt,’ the supernatural rushing host whose wild scattering provides the comparison for the terrified dancers' flight.

notes.label: Räf
notes.text: a wooden carrying frame worn on the back for loads, baskets, or containers; Joggi loads the stolen bottle and roll basket onto it for his escape.

notes.label: I dr Lohäule
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘in the Lohäule,’ a local wooded place where the narrator hears signs associated with the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Wärchgschir
notes.text: Swiss German for work gear or tools, here the equipment the woodcutter gathers before setting out for home.

notes.label: Lisebethli
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive of Lisebeth or Elisabeth; the storyteller turns to her as a witness or listener.

notes.label: I dr Sant Angereesenacht
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘on St. Andrew’s Night’; this divinatory night, traditionally associated with discovering a future spouse, frames the mistress’s ritual.

notes.label: Hemlistock
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for the lower part or tail of a shift or shirt; she uses it as the ritual cloth, though the garment’s exact form is not specified.

notes.label: Gade
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a chamber or small room; here it is the private room she cleans before preparing the divination table.

b0edc11a7fe99376c9a61e46dab407483ba08ac3.summary: Through the walls of Iberg Castle, knights and noble maidens can still be seen wandering at night in long, flowing garments.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

88cf89b753eaba4acb9d795b8c7d82d2bb317c62.summary: The “Iceland moss,” an Alpine plant also used in pharmacies, has little tubes and leaves.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, an Alpine dairy herder or cheesemaker responsible for livestock and milk processing on a high pasture; the repeated milking drives the curse in this origin legend.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpleute
notes.text: literally ‘Alp people,’ meaning the herders and other workers living together on a high Alpine pasture during the summer season.

notes.label: Dürgras
notes.text: literally ‘dry grass,’ a regional folk name for Iceland moss in this legend, explained by the plant's suddenly withered appearance after the herder's curse.

notes.label: Chaschteler
notes.text: the local woodland name explained by the tale as deriving from Chaschtell, the dialect word used for the former castle; the exact grammatical force of the place-name is regional, so it is retained rather than forced into a standard English form.

notes.label: Im Chaser
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘in the Chaser,’ the local area behind Wyssbach where a castle is said to have stood; Chaser functions as a place-name, and the source does not establish a safe literal derivation.

notes.label: Heubeeristüdeli
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for little blueberry bushes or patches, with -li marking the diminutive; here the tired woodcutter lies among them before his disturbing vision.

notes.label: Bäseris
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the slender brush or twigs cut for making brooms; the precise plant material is not stated, though the men work in a young birch.

notes.label: Birchli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a small or young birch tree; the narrator climbs into it to cut the broom material.

notes.label: Füdlechlopferchutte
notes.text: a vividly comic dialect name for a long coat whose tails strike or ‘slap’ the backside as the wearer walks; it helps mark the apparition's old-fashioned dress.

notes.label: Büssichappen
notes.text: the source's dialect name for the apparition's cap; Chappen means a cap, but the precise material or sense of Büssi is not secure enough here for a narrower English equivalent.

notes.label: Pinte
notes.text: a small tavern or drinking house; after the frightening encounter and soaking rain, the two men head there for a drink.

notes.label: Zwöierli
notes.text: a small serving of wine or other drink identified by the dialect diminutive for ‘two’; the source assumes the familiar local measure or price without specifying it more precisely.

notes.label: Im Übergang
notes.text: literally ‘in the transition,’ a local way of naming the political and military upheaval surrounding the French occupation; the title does not specify a single formal regime change.

notes.label: Mäss
notes.text: a dry measure or measuring vessel for grain; the dispute is whether the French soldier receives a level or heaped measure of oats.

notes.label: Chnebel
notes.text: a stick, bar, or cudgel used here to strike the filled grain measure level; it immediately becomes suggestive of the farmer's physical resistance.

notes.label: zable u gable
notes.text: a dialect rhyming expression for agitated saber-brandishing, gesturing, or making a threatening commotion; the exact component meanings are uncertain.

notes.label: ghufets
notes.text: dialect for ‘heaped,’ meaning the grain should rise above the rim rather than be measured level.

notes.label: Bschüttloch
notes.text: a slurry, manure, or cesspit opening; putting the soldier there is both concealment and a deliberately degrading end.

1779b33403f0bc8d88bff85eae8516a150d20c9d.summary: Not only Tannhäuser but others as well have entered Frau Vrene’s Mountain, or Venus Mountain.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8abd498f2976e406827ebf25431cffd1bbff4fd8.summary: Every year a fahrender Schüler stopped at a farmer's house and spent the night there.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling student’; in German-speaking folklore this is an itinerant learned figure often credited with astrology, divination, or magic, as the stone-reading here indicates.

notes.label: Oberdiele
notes.text: the upper wooden floor, gallery, or loft space beneath the roof; its exposed roof beam creates the setting for the threatened hanging.

00e4206ec3a68318f6ceab1f6d1fc7ebb49faae4.summary: that sets the Rübenen in motion and rides down the valley on them.

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: Uri regional usage for destructive mountain torrents or debris-laden flood flows rushing down gullies; here they are personified as forces the Ribi-Vreni can start and ride.

notes.label: Ribi-Vreni
notes.text: the local female name for the being said to set destructive torrents in motion and ride them down Göscheneralp; Vreni is a familiar form of Verena, while the exact derivation of Ribi and the being's nature remain uncertain in this fragment.

751950982e0146563441afde43b97f76580d619d.summary: At Sargans, naturally, the castle simply has to be haunted, whether it wishes to be or not.

notes.label: Armsündersaal
notes.text: literally the ‘poor sinner's hall,’ a traditional room name at Sargans Castle associated in the tale with fearful solitary nights and rattling chains; poor sinner was a customary expression for a condemned prisoner.

notes.label: Statthalter
notes.text: a deputy, governor, or administrative officeholder; the title is retained because it belongs to the historical political world represented by the castle ghost.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the bailiff or governor who administered a subject territory for the ruling Swiss cantons; the ghost's old office explains his concern with the cantonal arms.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Ringmurtürli
notes.text: dialect for a little door in the castle's ring wall or encircling defensive wall; the diminutive makes it a specific local architectural feature.

notes.label: Urner-, Schwizer- oder Glarner-Woupä
notes.text: Sargans dialect for the coats of arms of Uri, Schwyz, or Glarus; these heraldic signs recall the cantons whose officials governed the territory.

notes.label: Beistampfli
notes.text: the title’s Bernese-dialect diminutive for a bone-stamping mill where bones were pounded into bone meal; the spelling reflects dialect and may omit the ‘n’ heard in standard German ‘Bein.’

notes.label: Beistampfi
notes.text: the corresponding non-diminutive dialect form for the bone-stamping mill itself.

notes.label: Dräck am Stäcke
notes.text: literally ‘dirt on the stick,’ a regional form of an idiom meaning to have wrongdoing, guilt, or disreputable secrets on one’s conscience.

notes.label: toll Sang
notes.text: an uncertain Bernese expression for the objectionable material the miller allegedly mixed into people’s bone meal, probably meaning foul, wild, or dreadful stuff; its exact literal sense is unclear.

2966949994b0829229a764dba1aa274362fe9bbc.summary: In the boulder-strewn Urbachtal, the alpine herders relate that in ancient times a herdboy could not find a single stone to throw after a disobedient little calf.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7d55124d4e22c447197a7cd7d117177c8e7325bd.summary: Here and there in the mountains, and especially in mines, there are mountain spirits and Bergmänner, small gray men with large felt hats hanging low.

notes.label: Bergmänner
notes.text: literally ‘mountain men,’ small gray mine spirits distinguished here by their large hanging felt hats; the term can also mean miners, but these beings are supernatural.

notes.label: Bergknappen
notes.text: historical ore miners working underground; the tale prescribes ritual behavior that protects them from the Bergmänner.

76df91aa24f6b5b56563a9bc8784decff6da79af.summary: In the Möttelischloss near Rorschach on Lake Constance, two girls appear in white dresses and red shoes, bound with chains.

notes.label: Möttelischloss
notes.text: the regional name of the castle near Rorschach where the chained maidens guard an unrecovered treasure; Schloss means castle, while the Mötteli element belongs to the site's proper name.

647f2ef04752702cca0ecd81b9ed9c75124b0992.summary: Somewhere, a priest wanted to banish a Gspängst that was inside a Gaden. But it bawled at him mightily and reproached him: did he no longer remember that, once at a farmer’s place, he had trodden the finest Choränähli into the Schüehneschtlä?

notes.label: Gspängst
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Gespenst, meaning a ghost or apparition; here it is the being the priest laboriously drives into confinement.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn bay, hay store, or farm outbuilding in Alpine German usage; the ghost begins inside it, though the exact internal arrangement is not described.

notes.label: Choränähli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive apparently meaning a tiny grain or kernel; the ghost’s reproach pairs it with Schüehneschtlä in an obscure phrase whose exact action and significance remain uncertain.

notes.label: Schüehneschtlä
notes.text: an Uri dialect form related to shoe-laces or shoe thongs; the ghost’s phrase about a Choränähli being trodden into them is preserved conservatively because its exact idiomatic meaning is uncertain.

notes.label: Rischi
notes.text: an interior feature of an Uri barn used for storing or moving hay, apparently a hay bay, chute, or passage between levels; the source does not define its exact construction.

notes.label: Schabelehn
notes.text: a local place-name retained from the Bernese German title; the source gives no derivation.

notes.label: Chiltnacht
notes.text: the evening or night of Kilt, a traditional period of visiting and courtship; here it marks the twilight when the apparition is seen, though the precise local calendar sense is unstated.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally something like ‘Lady Fast,’ the name of a frightening female figure used against disobedient children; whether Faschte refers to fasting season or another local name is uncertain.

notes.label: Ifahrt
notes.text: a local access lane, entrance, or driveway below which Frau Faschte stands; the exact terrain is not described.

notes.label: Gring
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘head,’ often with a coarse or emphatic tone; Frau Faschte’s is unnaturally long.

ef17b5c2ac37c021771f2468c3f393a93ca56856.summary: Great treasures lie hidden in the Strättlighubel by Lake Thun. The key to them hangs invisibly upon an elder bush.

notes.label: Strättlighubel
notes.text: the hill associated with Strättligen near Lake Thun; Hubel is a Swiss German word for a rounded hill, knoll, or mound.

88129e8774a5b941dcbb4b4a0d79035c2202b00e.summary: One man said that he would now go onto a high mountain and ‘Bylätod ga ds Fiddlä-n-anäha,’ that is, offer defiance to the bubonic plague.

notes.label: Bylätod ga ds Fiddlä-n-anäha
notes.text: a coarse Uri-dialect challenge meaning approximately ‘to go wag one’s backside at the bubonic plague’; the source itself glosses the gesture as offering defiance, and Bylätod is the dialect form of ‘bubonic death.’

f22c3c66c8daeb2b3cd5c2c1e397815b54e06802.summary: The Wittenholz is not a safe or wholesome place either. At night, a repulsive cry is often heard there.

notes.label: Wittenholz
notes.text: the local wood or woodland place-name where the uncanny nighttime cries are heard; Holz can mean a wood or stand of trees.

7fdf59e7745d79e06738880b23823aa663e0efd7.summary: Among country and mountain people, the belief is widespread that no one can escape an approaching destiny, an ordained fate. — Certainly, what God has determined and ordained for a person will not fail to occur.

notes.label: 6 Hornung 1749
notes.text: an older calendrical expression for February 6, 1749; Hornung is the traditional German month-name for February, preserved here because it anchors the fatal avalanche in local historical memory.

671d0b22bf8b827ba61f6ce2e2769260cf603191.summary: The Creator had sent out one of his angels to adorn the young earth with every kind of beauty.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

235b1c4be859d2748388df620919a3d667a32534.summary: The French had a commander who was proof against blades and bullets. For a long time, no one could overcome him.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fdc2b6c3ae61e40cd8cfd1534854691c41ac80b6.summary: In the 12th century, a powerful lord named Burkhard lived at Unspunnen Castle near Interlaken with his wife and their only daughter, the beautiful Ita.

notes.label: Unspunnen
notes.text: the castle name and, in this legend, the name attached to a recurring Alpine festival of reconciliation near Interlaken; readers should understand the narrative as a legendary origin story rather than a documentary account of the festival’s history.

notes.label: stillen Donnertag
notes.text: a regional historical expression for Maundy Thursday, the ‘quiet Thursday’ of Holy Week; the source uses the inflected lowercase phrase while dating the rebels’ defeat.

7cc440cf4d6faf981bbe996a7d0af708030f7985.summary: a) Another time, on Schmutziger Donnerstag, Jaggli Lander came along with a rooster.

notes.label: Schmutziger Donnerstag
notes.text: literally ‘Dirty Thursday,’ an Alemannic Carnival day before Ash Wednesday; the magician’s public illusion occurs amid this festive calendar setting.

notes.label: Trämel
notes.text: a heavy log or tree trunk; enchanted onlookers see the rooster or cricket dragging one, while the four-leaf-clover bearer sees only a stalk of hay.

notes.label: Heiwhahlä
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a stalk or wisp of hay; it is the tiny real object magnified by Jaggli Lander’s illusion into a whole log.

notes.label: Müheim
notes.text: a local name explicitly glossed by the source as a field cricket; the rarer variant assigns the impossible feat to this insect instead of a rooster.

notes.label: Vierklee
notes.text: literally ‘four-clover,’ a four-leaf clover believed to confer luck and the power to see through magical deception.

notes.label: Kumeedi
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of ‘comedy’ or theatrical performance; one variant places the rooster’s illusion in such an entertainment, without describing its staging.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Bländwärch
notes.text: literally ‘blinding-work,’ magical glamour or deception that makes people see what is not there; four-leaf clover is said to protect against it.

a1985e42e8af607c644a86120e3a93e3ff916659.summary: Jaggli Lander, the fahrender Schüler, once walked up through ‘Altefer-Dorf.’ His shoes were tied with Nielen and his trousers were torn, but he certainly knew how to make music!

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a folklore figure credited with occult knowledge and uncanny arts; Jaggli can reveal hidden wrongdoing and make impossible music, yet the closing proverb says such men could not help themselves.

notes.label: Nielen
notes.text: regional Swiss German for the long climbing stems or vines of wild clematis; using them as makeshift shoelaces emphasizes Jaggli’s poverty despite his powers.

notes.label: Holderknebel
notes.text: literally an ‘elderwood cudgel’ or stout billet of elder wood; here Jaggli impossibly uses the same object as a violin bow and then as a pipe or trumpet.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; the footnote identifies which members of the Brand family held it and when.

notes.label: Alpabfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial and practical autumn descent of cattle and herders from the high seasonal pasture, often accompanied by prominent livestock bells; Jaggli’s piping makes the herd behave as though that procession has begun.

dd362944c3c01860603729462c05d7d280aa5927.summary: It appears, however, that the Landammann took the musician’s frank speech to heart after all, for Jaggli Lander was banished from the country even though he promised the people of the Schächen Valley that, if he were allowed to remain, he would reopen the salt spring on the Vorder Mühlebach that an…

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; the account attributes Jaggli Lander’s banishment to this official.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

fd1c850605c162732b7540d42241e9801a184c07.summary: 1. Jaggli Lander[1] was a fahrender Schüler who could do and knew more than other people.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a folklore figure credited with occult learning, unusual powers, and knowledge of hidden treasure; Jaggli Lander is a named example rather than an ordinary student traveling for school.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss and south-German coin denomination; the tale deliberately leaves its modern value unspecified and stresses that exactly five coins replenish themselves.

notes.label: im Chnollen
notes.text: an Uri place-expression meaning approximately ‘in the knoll’ or ‘among the rounded heights’; it names the location at Surenen where Lander says the fir-sized gold bar lies, but the account does not identify a precise modern site.

97c6bf0a885d78e253385c94026731be2e05c001.summary: Two hunters had often hunted in the Schachen at Erstfeld. One evening, one of them took it into his head to frighten the other, whom he knew to be nearby.

notes.label: Wäuti
notes.text: an Uri name for an uncanny being, threatening apparition, or nocturnal bogey; here it turns a hunter’s prank back upon him, but the source does not identify its form more precisely.

081b28386c385ad64459ef7449242ea07263d0b3.summary: 1. On Bristen, a man from the Reuss valley met a strange little man with a large lump of gold, who said, “I have enough!” The man from the Reuss valley wondered where he had made the find.

notes.label: Jetz hesch-mi iberfragt
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘now you have asked me too much’ or ‘asked beyond what may be answered’; in both variants, the unnecessary question breaks the possibility of receiving hidden treasure knowledge.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’; in German-language folklore this is an itinerant learned man credited with secret or magical knowledge rather than an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; here the man is descending from the named Alp Sewen when he is shown hidden crystals.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

a61a285c1806d70c77f22851048764d20ec69088.summary: The largest canton in Switzerland is the canton of Graubünden, but it is sparsely populated.

notes.label: Arve
notes.text: the Swiss stone pine, a high-altitude Alpine tree especially associated with Graubünden and Engadine landscapes.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical title for a young or lesser nobleman; here it marks the arrogant lord of Fardün rather than simply meaning ‘young man.’

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: literally coercive or oppressive lords, a polemical Swiss historical term for castle-holding tyrants who denied local freedom.

notes.label: Mus
notes.text: a thick porridge or mash; the exact German word is retained because the insult, forced meal, and repeated command all turn this humble household food into the story's central symbol.

67248fb77097550af7bd8dda2111317c3f56135b.summary: According to the parish registers at Wassen, where a Johannes Ambort married in 1635, the Ambort family came from Valais.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Jahrzeit
notes.text: an endowed annual Catholic memorial observance, commonly including a Mass for the deceased; Ambort establishes substantial perpetual commemorations for himself and his wife.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man’; here it familiarly designates the mysterious traveler later identified as the fahrender Schüler and does not necessarily establish his physical size.

notes.label: G’liger
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a sleeping place, bed, or simple lodging; the stranger promises to accept the humblest arrangement, whose exact form is not described.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or ‘traveling student,’ a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; he is not merely an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Bleue
notes.text: a regional name for a pounding or fulling installation, probably a mill used to beat cloth; the source lists it among Ambort’s businesses but does not specify its machinery or product.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: in Swiss Alpine usage, going Strahlen means searching rock cavities for crystals; here the parenthetical source gloss explicitly identifies the sought objects as crystals.

2b1b90d4fc686037f1a74fc347f3bbcd378700ac.summary: In a village there was a house for rent. More than a hundred people had already lived in it.

notes.label: Ave Maria bell
notes.text: the traditional church bell marking the Angelus prayer, commonly rung at set times such as evening and morning; in the tale its ringing defines the nightly span of the haunting.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

0e77d451fe2da1d9862847330661339b90a3b049.summary: In former times, devastating epidemics prevailed among the Alpine cattle on the Allgäu Alp in the region of the Hohgant.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Zigerrumpf
notes.text: a large remaining piece, heel, or compact mass of Ziger broken into the communal dishes; its exact form is not specified.

notes.label: Johannisziger
notes.text: literally Saint John's Ziger, the name of this annual charitable dairy offering made after Saint John's Day; Ziger is a Swiss whey or curd cheese without one exact English equivalent.

b4793f185a30028fb4c44b364e82afb6a4b0d210.summary: A king had a young noble retainer called Junker Prahlhans because he always promised much and delivered little.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a title for a young nobleman or gentleman, historically below the highest ranks of titled nobility; here it marks Hans as a courtly retainer rather than part of his given name.

notes.label: Prahlhans
notes.text: literally ‘boasting Hans,’ a comic nickname for the retainer who promises impossible quantities; it is paired in the warning verses with the harsher nickname Hans Grossmaul.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a historical large silver coin promised for each of the hundred birds; exact values varied by place and period.

notes.label: Hans Grossmaul
notes.text: literally ‘Hans Bigmouth,’ the jester's mocking name for the boastful Junker; Grossmaul implies loud bragging rather than a physical description.

notes.label: Dukat
notes.text: a ducat, historically a high-value gold coin promised for each fish; the tale uses escalating coin names comically rather than defining an exchange rate.

notes.label: Dublone
notes.text: a doubloon, a gold coin promised for each hare; its precise value is immaterial to the story and not stated.

b52b7c11b5e02aa78f328c292ec8eac7962526b9.summary: Seven strong men from Ried went into the Fellital to make hay a few decades ago.

notes.label: spettlä
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to taunt, challenge, or recklessly provoke, especially by inviting an uncanny being to show itself; the warning carries a supernatural caution not fully captured by ordinary ‘teasing.’

notes.label: Beckli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small basin, bowl, or cup; here it is the drinking vessel from which Byni takes another serving of fortified coffee, while its material is unspecified.

fcb70ad27f1d34d48205d0dcde47249b038334d3.summary: The family name of strong Jörg of Praden is not known. For the construction of the church in his little village, his home community of Praden in the Schanfigg valley, he carried all the required sand uphill on his own shoulders from a considerable distance.

notes.label: Maltersack
notes.text: a large sack associated with the Malter, a variable historical dry measure; the tale uses it first for Jörg’s loads of sand and then for the two sacks of flour he carries together.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Bündner
notes.text: a person from Graubünden; the visiting strongman challenges the strongest local man, and Jörg defends Bündner honor.

notes.label: Hosen-Lupf
notes.text: literally a “trouser lift,” a Swiss wrestling bout in which opponents grip and throw one another by their clothing, closely associated with the tradition of Schwingen.

notes.label: Curer
notes.text: the people or civic authorities of Cur; they reward Jörg by letting him carry away as much flour as he can.

608915e01912488dac2e828d4a406a84371d1021.summary: A man from Schinznach had been at Kilt with the daughter of the Wildiküfer in Oberflachs (see No. 327).

notes.label: Kilt
notes.text: the customary evening courtship visit in Alemannic Switzerland; the man has been visiting a young woman, not attending a formal religious or civic event.

notes.label: Wildiküfer
notes.text: a local byname meaning approximately ‘the cooper of Wildi’ or ‘Wildi cooper’; it identifies the young woman’s father, while the precise place or family reference in Wildi is uncertain.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: a young man making a customary evening courtship visit; his late nighttime return places him in the path of the apparition.

notes.label: G’schaffigen
notes.text: dialect for a conspicuously busy or industrious fellow, used ironically for the black figure watering a meadow at midnight; the quotation marks signal the narrator’s mockery.

notes.label: Kaibenrain
notes.text: the local slope-name where the apparition vanishes; Kaib historically can carry senses connected with carrion or a dead animal and Rain means a bank or slope, but the legend does not establish a single etymology.

notes.label: Rössligrube
notes.text: literally ‘little-horse pit,’ the nearby place-name associated with buried horse bones; Rössl(i) is a Swiss diminutive for horse.

77fca60e19067bf3671acb2c8123225d9508e5e2.summary: Many, many years ago, there was once again war in the land of Valais, as was no rarity there.

notes.label: Furk
notes.text: the local name for the position south of the Schwarzsee where Karl stations his improvised defenders; Furk is an Alpine terrain and pass word, but the story treats this as a particular place.

notes.label: Hochegge
notes.text: literally a high ridge or high edge, the named terrain above Karl's position at the foot of the Theodul Pass.

notes.label: Karl unter den Weibern
notes.text: literally ‘Karl among the women,’ the story's enduring Valais expression for one man by himself in a company of women.

262347c24cbd8b5224baa934144d86466663ddbb.summary: Old Karl Vonmentlen of Seedorf used to tell this story: ‘We owned a gray cat that went away every Saturday evening.

notes.label: About this telling

e7228a4e5c30c3afdb3cc9421add47313c06ad67.summary: a) On the Hundsrügge, a long hill at the aforementioned place between the Rotsee and Buchrain, there once lived a wicked woman.

notes.label: Nachthuri
notes.text: a local name for a female night-bogey or wandering hag associated here with the murderous mother’s ghost; the exact derivation of Huri is uncertain.

notes.label: Bölimann
notes.text: a widespread regional sack-carrying bogey said to seize children; the collector explicitly states that the word’s origin is obscure.

notes.label: Butz
notes.text: a southern German and Swiss term that can mean a bogey, ghost, masked figure, or frightening apparition; here it denotes a supernatural child-snatcher rather than a human being.

notes.label: Bölibautsch
notes.text: the Unterwalden name given as a variant of Bölimann; it refers to the same sack-carrying children’s bogey, but the force of the added element -bautsch is not explained.

notes.label: Geuggel
notes.text: one of the regional bogey-names that can substitute for Bölimann; the source supplies no separate form or story and does not explain its etymology.

notes.label: ’s Bauggi
notes.text: a contracted dialect name for another substitute children’s bogey; the article ’s means “the,” while the origin and precise imagined appearance of Bauggi are not stated.

notes.label: Böggel
notes.text: a bogey-name related in this account to Bölimann; Rochholz proposed a derivation from Bock, “he-goat,” but the text presents that as a scholarly interpretation, not a settled fact.

notes.label: Nachtböggel
notes.text: literally a “night Böggel,” the Lungern form of the bogey whose practical role is to drive children home after dark.

notes.label: Mamuggi
notes.text: a Zug children’s bogey-name associated by the collector with muffled or half-stifled crying; its independent form and exact etymology remain unclear.

notes.label: Seemuggi
notes.text: another Zug bogey-name paired with Mamuggi; See ordinarily means “lake,” but the text only explicitly connects the names with muffled crying and gives no separate legend.

notes.label: Müggen
notes.text: the collector’s term for a half-suppressed cry, whimper, or muffled vocal sound; he uses it to explain the names Mamuggi and Seemuggi.

notes.label: Nachtheuel
notes.text: a night-bogey whose name people reinterpreted as an evil owl; the collector instead claims an older connection with Frau Holle, a conclusion he attributes to scholarship.

notes.label: Heuel
notes.text: one of the regional forms or imitative names evoking an owl in the popular explanation of Nachtheuel; its precise distribution is not given.

notes.label: Hüwel
notes.text: a second regional form or imitative owl-name listed in the popular explanation of Nachtheuel; its difference from Heuel is not specified.

notes.label: Hu
notes.text: a short regional or imitative owl-name in the collector’s list; it may echo the bird’s call, but the text does not establish an etymology.

notes.label: Hau
notes.text: another short regional or imitative owl-name in the collector’s list; its relationship to Hu and the other forms is not explained.

notes.label: Bogetegüggi
notes.text: the specifically local Rickenbach children’s bogey associated with the Bogetewald; its compound name is retained because the source gives no reliable literal derivation.

notes.label: aufhockt
notes.text: literally “hops” or “perches onto” someone’s back; in Alpine supernatural tales a being that aufhockt becomes a crushing burden the victim must carry.

notes.label: Sträggelennacht
notes.text: the “night of the Sträggelen,” invoking central Swiss female Wild Host or winter spirits as a threat to children; the passage does not specify its calendar date.

notes.label: Stüpfelenacht
notes.text: a local Obwalden fright-night name connected in the text with stüpfeln, to prod, prick, or torment; an evil witch is said to punish disobedient children then.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kinderpopanzen
notes.text: collective bogey figures invoked by adults to frighten children into obedience or away from dangerous places; Popanz can mean a bogey, scare-figure, or imaginary terror.

69c217bea4ef5ca621896e4039162bb8567d8849.summary: On the wooded height of the Hard between Siffelen and Laufenburg on the Rhine, one passes a high slope called Auf dem Kinz.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ the regional subterranean little folk who use the holes and caves beneath the Kinzhalde and once helped local farm workers; the word can overlap with dwarf traditions without fixing one precise supernatural species.

notes.label: Erdmännlisstube
notes.text: Alemannic for the ‘little earth men’s parlor’ or chamber, the named underground room near Wallbach; Stube suggests a domestic living room and makes the cave feel like the beings’ household space.

notes.label: Kinzhalden-Joggeli
notes.text: the local apparition’s place-based name, with Joggeli an Alemannic diminutive of Jakob comparable to ‘little Jack’; the story gives competing human identities for him, so whether it is a personal name or generic byname remains uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Malter
notes.text: a historical regional dry measure used here for grain; its size varied by locality and period, so ‘more than fifty Malter’ conveys a large repeated cartload without a reliable modern conversion.

notes.label: Long
notes.text: the dialect word explicitly glossed by the source as the axle pin or linchpin; removing it makes the cartwheel fail, which is the Joggeli’s characteristic attack on carters.

c3981772f6638222e004dc7dd0ac7512f0b46951.summary: A rich farmer from Kaisten in the Fricktal plowed away his field neighbors' boundary furrows, stole their stacked tithe sheaves at harvest time, and was, besides, a drunkard and a blasphemer.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Kinzhaldenjoggeli
notes.text: the local name for the punished man haunting Kinzhalde; Joggeli is an affectionate or belittling Swiss German form of Jakob, while the story says the man's actual surname was Winter.

notes.label: Long
notes.text: a regional word for the axle pin or linchpin that keeps a wagon wheel in place; here the spirit pulls it out and repeats the sabotage whenever the repairer curses.

notes.label: Untervogt
notes.text: a historical deputy bailiff or subordinate district official; here Winter holds Austrian authority over Eiken and abuses it for dispossession and forced recruitment.

notes.label: Täubi
notes.text: an Aargau dialect word for frenzy, raging madness, or violent agitation; here bewitched men leap into the water in that state, and the parenthetical source gloss is Tobsucht.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a traditional local forest or boundary warden charged with guarding regulated woodland; here a timber thief initially mistakes the roaring apparition for this very real official.

2b794da3ea5f86e5b29c2a5a9aae10d582d9cdf4.summary: Kirchmaier was both the richest and the most miserly farmer in the village.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

f5968166d3b916a4959710eae009b75d5a2f4e27.summary: Once, in the Visp valley, a knight appeared upon a proud black horse. He looked exceedingly noble, and no one knew him.

notes.label: Hackbrett
notes.text: a hammered dulcimer, a trapezoidal string instrument sounded with small beaters and strongly associated with Alpine folk music; the youngest sister plays it in the evening.

notes.label: Ritter Goldbart
notes.text: literally “Knight Goldbeard,” the tale's name for the murderous stranger whose beard appears woven from fine golden threads.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally “God's acre,” an older term for a consecrated burial ground or churchyard; the two murdered sisters are buried there.

78efd2ea10d11ffab864edba7973fe70c24dd006.summary: One Sunday, Knight Hans Jeuch stood at the window of a house he owned in the place called the Clus and looked up toward Schlapin.

notes.label: Montavoner
notes.text: men from the Montafon, called Montavon in the source; in this battle legend the word identifies the attacking force by its home valley.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or stream gorge; the attackers descend and retreat through this constricted terrain.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a gray horse, often pale enough to be described as white; Jeuch's mount is force-fed wine before the charge.

notes.label: Gelte
notes.text: a broad wooden vessel or tub; Jecklin specifies that this one held 8–10 Mass and was filled with wine for the horse.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical liquid measure whose exact volume varied by place and period; the source describes capacity in local units rather than modern liters.

notes.label: Closterser
notes.text: people of Closters, the historical spelling used here for present-day Klosters; they form Jeuch's defending force.

notes.label: zetteten
notes.text: a dialect verb that Jecklin himself explains as allowing none of the fallen to rise again; in the battle context it means the Closterser finished off those Jeuch struck down.

notes.label: Dörfli
notes.text: literally ‘little village,’ here used as the name of the place where the defenders rest on their return.

44f5d8908dcb03b168d24353e20be093184492bc.summary: Knight Jörg of Jörgenberg was a brave warrior, but at the same time the terror of the entire region.

b26cd185c1bf3e50a14fa750d17eb74a5bcb9aed.summary: Violanda, a daughter of Vespasian Salis, brought Salenegg Castle to Knight Anton Molina.

notes.label: Reissaus
notes.text: a colloquial expression meaning to run off, flee, or make a hurried escape; the second tradition imagines the Evil One making off with Molina’s soul.

c42b24799d8899add8c16d520a5a03044f9ab23e.summary: On the plain of the Seez valley lies the rocky hill called Tiergarten, covered with scrub oaks, hollies, and other bushes, where before the Reformation the territorial court often assembled.

notes.label: Tannhuser
notes.text: the dialectal and historical song-form of Tannhäuser, the legendary knight and minnesinger; the spelling is retained because the tale explicitly connects several regional forms of his name.

notes.label: Frau Vrenasberg
notes.text: literally ‘Frau Vrena's mountain,’ a local Sarganserland name equated in the story with Venusberg; Frau Vrena blends the regional Verena figure with the wider Venus-mountain tradition.

notes.label: Tiergätslied
notes.text: the local name for the Tannhuser song once sung around Tiergarten; its exact compound etymology is uncertain, but it identifies the regional ballad rather than a separate story type.

notes.label: Frau Vienus Berg
notes.text: the exact local song-form of ‘Lady Venus's mountain’; its spelling preserves the ballad's dialectal pronunciation and distinguishes this verse wording from Frau Vrenasberg elsewhere in the story.

notes.label: Chur-Rätier
notes.text: a historical-cultural designation for a person of Chur-Rhaetia; here Natsch speculates that Tannhäuser came from this regional Rhaetian milieu, a claim the editor presents only as conjecture.

notes.label: Nerz
notes.text: the exact word recorded in the Entlebuch song for the place or condition to which Tannhuser might return; its intended reading is uncertain and may reflect dialect, corruption, or transcription, so it is not silently emended.

notes.label: Frow Venusberg
notes.text: the dialectal song-form of Frau Venusberg, ‘Lady Venus's mountain’; here it names Tannhuser's enchanted destination and preserves the Entlebuch wording.

0b90f5946b0aeff8f56165e865d7df337dea8c85.summary: At the Leggistein estate near the village of Wassen, two devout siblings once lived together, a brother and a sister.
