111eda48befa03af50a07438f8a802aebc17d28b.summary: Long ago, when witches still practiced their malice upon the “dear livestock” and household goods, there was also a witch in St.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kuh-Lene
notes.text: literally “Cow Lene,” the local nickname of the old woman accused of witchcraft; Kuh identifies her folkloric association with harming and magically restoring cattle, while Lene is a familiar form of a woman's name.

notes.label: g'rodlet und g'rupft
notes.text: a dialect phrase for rattling and tugging at the stable door; the clipped forms convey the sounds announcing Kuh-Lene's arrival, but the source does not specify the exact motions.

notes.label: Stranga Stuppa
notes.text: a dialect expression for a strand of spun fiber, apparently flax or hemp fiber or tow; the precise grade of fiber is uncertain, while the charm clearly requires it to be spun by a seven-year-old girl and wound around the cow's horns.

notes.label: Landweibel
notes.text: a historical Swiss public officer serving judicial or cantonal authorities, broadly comparable here to a court constable; the judge disguises him as the Devil to frighten Lene into confessing.

notes.label: laid
notes.text: a Swiss German dialect form meaning ugly or hideous, not the English word “laid”; here the disguised Landweibel makes himself appear terrifying at the window.

4d141c8c2492b9d00c454acb676d0abcddcf2480.summary: Belief in the power of the Alpspruch had disappeared among many people, even among the Alpknechte of Ladils.

notes.label: Alpspruch
notes.text: a protective spoken prayer, blessing, or ritual call recited upon an Alp; omitting it allows the herd to wander down into the valley fields, though the source does not give its words.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired servants who tend livestock and perform dairy work on a seasonal high pasture; even these working herders have ceased believing in the protective formula.

notes.label: Satz
notes.text: a designated grazing section or pasture area within an Alp; the exact enclosure or land-management form intended at Ladils is not described.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or cattle-tender, especially within an Alpine pastoral setting; he was responsible for reciting the Alpspruch.

notes.label: Kuhstapfen
notes.text: literally ‘cow tracks’ or ‘cow footprints’; the tracks in the grain fields give the locality its enduring name.

06af93f7a94a37ae10eb0cc6ae56ad5916f37f38.summary: Above the silk factory behind the village of Küttigen near Aarau rises a crumbling wall of Jura rock.

notes.label: Küngstengut
notes.text: the local Aargau dialect name for the Königstein castle site or estate; ‘Küngsten’ reflects the dialect form of Königstein, while ‘Gut’ can mean an estate or property.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive feudal lord or tyrannical holder of local authority; ‘tyrant’ conveys the behavior but not the historical lordship embedded in the term.

notes.label: Twing
notes.text: the local jurisdictional district and body of seigneurial rights whose subject inhabitants owed labor to the lord; it is related to ‘Twing und Bann.’

notes.label: Schneeschmelzi
notes.text: literally a place where snow melts; the source glosses it as a mountain ridge, likely invoking the crest or watershed beyond which the snowmelt drains.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Cheibenstatt
notes.text: the local name of the burial spot; ‘Cheib’ can mean carrion, a carcass, or contemptuously a rogue, and ‘Statt’ a place, so the name carries both bodily and abusive overtones.

notes.label: Landjäger
notes.text: members of the historical cantonal rural police or gendarmerie, a more specific institution than generic ‘police officers.’

f1e4db4d85562ec499d82389cfb4577631bfd645.summary: Once there was a strong young fellow named La Ramée. He had enlisted as a Reisläufer and had already served for more than seven years without being promoted.

notes.label: Reisläufer
notes.text: a Swiss soldier who went abroad for paid military service, especially in foreign mercenary regiments.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a ringing cry of joy, related to the high, carrying calls and yodel-like exclamations heard in Alpine traditions.

notes.label: Nastüchlein
notes.text: an older or dialect diminutive for a small handkerchief, here embroidered with the princess's initials as a recognition token.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Schwartenhals
notes.text: literally something like ‘hide-neck’ or ‘thick-neck,’ the witch's contemptuous insult for the rough-looking soldier.

notes.label: Humpen
notes.text: a large drinking mug or tankard; the bewitched drink served in it causes La Ramée to forget the princess.

0d77a94f040bdf2ebaf38cecde02cb1e5b35f20c.summary: The great body of water that is said once to have extended from Gontenschwil far down through the Kulm Valley toward the Aare region is called Lake Gondeli.

6ec3f32d446a9e2484c9eb11574b490cddca14cf.summary: was formerly a beautiful meadow. One summer day, people were busy making hay there.

2f77ba62bd22e8a2471702634e6d19632dca1e60.summary: a) On the Sewli Alp high above Silenen, at the foot of the sheer, sky-high rock walls of the two Windgellen, Lake Sewli lies in a deep hollow.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the Sewli Alp is both the prosperous pastoral world that is destroyed and the landscape surrounding the lake afterward.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent Alpine downslope wind; the deeply set lake is sheltered from it even though Föhn can be stormy in the surrounding mountains.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Planggen
notes.text: steep Alpine grass slopes or hillside pasture patches that are difficult and dangerous to graze; the source contrasts them with the family's formerly easy, abundant pasture.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; using both cheese and Anken to build a bridge or road turns sacredly abundant dairy wealth into the instrument of sacrilege.

a78292542c8cc525d5e27ed281d504077690860a.summary: A narrow mountain valley descends from the Rote Horn to the Plessur. In this wild, confined valley, which sheep visit in summer, lies a small mountain lake.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an alpine herdsman's dairy hut where milk is processed during the pasture season; the legend places the drowned dwelling beneath the lake.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working farm landscape; the woman's curse destroys both the Senn and his Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and cheese-making on an Alp; here his refusal and malicious drink bring the catastrophe.

notes.label: Magen
notes.text: literally ‘stomach’; in this dairy context it means stomach-derived rennet or curdling material, maliciously added to the woman's milk, though the source does not specify its preparation.

notes.label: Urdensee
notes.text: the mountain lake-name whose origin the legend explains through the sinking of the Sennhütte; the story does not give a secure literal derivation of Urden.

d1f229b9bb712955e7e8c5a7b5b8bc18fcabd91c.summary: Above the farms of Hägelen, a quarter of an hour from the little town of Kaiserstuhl on the left bank of the Rhine, stand two very large rocks.

notes.label: Lampohrenfluh
notes.text: the local name of the cliff and dwarf cave; Fluh means a steep rock face or crag, while Lampohren refers in the tale to the beings’ great flopping ears.

notes.label: lampten
notes.text: the source’s regional verb for the dwarfs’ ears flopping or hanging out from beneath their caps; the tale itself uses the word to explain the place-name Lampohrenfluh.

ffb844ec7438cd1d7ac44d1237c04b287dcbf0db.summary: Many things are told about him. In his younger years, he made a journey to the underworld.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the presiding magistrate or chief elected official of a rural Swiss canton; Christen is remembered as both a public leader and a benevolent magician.

notes.label: Joch
notes.text: literally a yoke, and in Alpine geography a saddle-shaped mountain pass; the invaders approach and retreat across such a pass.

notes.label: Sagholz
notes.text: heavy timber prepared for or produced by sawing, likely a substantial beam or log in this tale; the rooster carrying it is an illusion of impossible strength.

70e676197c5db0a34ea926c6eefb30cc531bb7d2.summary: According to legend, Landesstatthalter Hans Kuon lived at Törelen in the municipality of Spiringen and built the beautiful house that still stands today on the rear Mühlebach above the road.

notes.label: Landesstatthalter
notes.text: a historical Swiss cantonal office, broadly a deputy or acting chief magistrate; its exact powers and rank varied by canton and period, so the Uri title is retained.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow, rockslide, or torrent carrying earth and stones down a slope; here it is both the disaster and the locality associated with it.

dd6b462cb06d945d3d8277fc65ca0ab606d018d8.summary: Lass ab vo dine Wärke! (Leave Off Your Works!)

notes.label: Lass ab vo dine Wärke!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘Leave off your works!’ or ‘Stop what you are doing!’; here a supernatural voice warns the treasure-seeker away, and Wärke gives the command an archaic, solemn tone.

notes.label: Charfriti
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for Good Friday, standard German Karfreitag; here the sacred day is the annual moment when the treasure-marking blackthorn appears.

notes.label: Mur
notes.text: a dialect word understood here as a sow or pig-like beast; the enormous animal bars the treasure-seeker's road, though the brief tale leaves its exact supernatural form ambiguous.

7bb57b4d636443438287047fe8597232e7829858.summary: Once, driven by the need to expand, the inhabitants of the plain at Interlaken sent a pair of scouts into the valleys to learn where grazing grounds might be found for their growing herds.

notes.label: Lauter Brunnen
notes.text: literally ‘nothing but springs’ or ‘clear springs,’ the phrase used in the tale as a folk-etymological explanation of the place-name Lauterbrunnen; the wordplay allows more than one literal nuance.

notes.label: einen Grindelwald
notes.text: the source's phrase for a Grindelwald, interpreted here as a forest associated with a Grindel, a barrier or enclosure; this is a folk etymology within the legend, not a definitive linguistic derivation.

03ec54d005964d210a99965243a51a99ddaeaee0.summary: A traveler arrived at an inn in the dark of night and demanded that Hans drive him through the forest without delay that very evening; the forest began directly behind the inn, and Hans served as both house servant and coachman.

notes.label: Potz Tausend
notes.text: an old regional oath of exasperation, roughly ‘zounds’ or ‘by the thousand’; its comic force marks the moment Lazy Hans finally warms to the fight.

7da383f63b7ad9884e3f1cba549e8be975597ae7.summary: At the Bieli in Ennetmoos lived a witch with two sons, Hansli and Seppli. Her husband was very devout.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Hansli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss diminutive of Hans; the form marks the witch's son as a familiar local boy rather than a grand folkloric magician.

notes.label: Seppli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive of Josef or Sepp; this son resists witchcraft and protects himself with holy water.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

13918510bb36a708789735be3259271815356e25.summary: Peter Schwarz, known in the Sarganserland as ‘Bartli Peter’ because of his Capuchin beard, often heard the same spirit—see ‘The Fiddler’—sometimes playing the fiddle and sometimes blowing the field fife.

notes.label: Bartli Peter
notes.text: a regional nickname for Peter Schwarz, formed from Bart, ‘beard,’ with a diminutive ending; the source connects it to his Capuchin-style beard.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

995f97d970fc21f789c5de68c1b574d167747f53.summary: At one time, the four present-day Oberschwandberge at Spiringen belonged to a single owner and were ‘free and clear’—free of mortgages.

notes.label: den Berg aufwerfen
notes.text: literally ‘throw up’ or ‘throw open the mountain’; in this regional landholding context it may mean abandoning, opening, or physically overturning the mountain property, but the terse source does not resolve which forceful sense the farmer intends.

b542ae0063dde5c05ee9a2861ffd71d8869274cb.summary: In the year 1264, Kyburg Castle, until then the ancestral seat of the counts of the same name, passed to the House of Habsburg.

9251fe057193e0f54e22b4a8d00319217f435f67.summary: Once there lived in Rome a noble and powerful man named Pontius Pilate. Despite his power and standing, however, the earthly judge's punishment overtook him for the many crimes he had committed.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘traveling student,’ a learned itinerant figure in German-speaking folklore often credited with magic, conjuration, or occult study.

notes.label: Rosenkreuzer
notes.text: a Rosicrucian, a supposed member of the esoteric Rosy Cross tradition; here the designation marks the student's power as a conjurer.

notes.label: Pilatussee
notes.text: literally ‘Pilatus lake,’ the legendary mountain lake said to contain Pilate's body and to release storms when disturbed.

notes.label: Karfreitag
notes.text: Good Friday, the solemn Christian day on which Pilate alone is allowed to rise and circle the lake.

notes.label: Pilatusberg
notes.text: the German name ‘Pilatus mountain’ for the massif near Lucerne, whose name the legend connects to Pontius Pilate.

e144cc71ea473c8f72edc43cd9931404c0ab9435.summary: On one of the islands in Lake Lauerz rises a ruined old tower, the last remnant of Schwanau Castle.

fa1346d42bb945a8537d873c00a603e0a81b9154.summary: Long, long ago, a Senn once lived on the Clariden-Alpen with a ‘frivolous wench’ whom he held in such high honor that he paved the muddy and otherwise dirty path from the dwelling or herdsman's hut to the Käsgaden with cheeses so that she would not soil her shoes and feet.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a high pasture; here he profanes his own cheese and mistreats his mother to indulge his lover.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the retained source plural denotes high seasonal pasture lands in the specific Swiss sense, not merely the mountain chain; the Clariden grazing grounds become barren under scree.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Käsgaden
notes.text: a small Alpine building or room for making, ripening, or storing cheese; here the Senn lays cheeses along the dirty route to it as stepping-stones.

notes.label: Suffy
notes.text: a regional dairy term, probably whey or a whey-based drink left from cheesemaking; here the hungry mother asks for it with milk, but the exact preparation is not specified.

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: the plural of Firn, old compacted mountain snow or firn fields that can feed glaciers; here the upper masses collapse with the rocks and bury the pasture.

943694093b9a24e4ba64804b745c8dc1b56b6ed2.summary: Long ago, there were beautiful pastures on the Schafselbsanft. Now nothing more can be seen of them because of the Fire, but the fact that the Fire came down was Balz's fault; he was the last Sänn.

notes.label: Schafselbsanft
notes.text: the local mountain or high-pasture name on which the lost grazing land lay; its exact literal formation is uncertain and is not supplied by the source.

notes.label: Fire
notes.text: the dialect form corresponding to standard German Firn, compacted old mountain snow or a permanent snowfield; in the tale it moves destructively like an avalanche or glacier mass.

notes.label: Sänn
notes.text: the dialect form of Senn, an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on a summer Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its seasonal herding operation, not merely the mountain range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sänte
notes.text: a dialect form related to Senntum, the Alpine herd and dairy operation managed by a Senn; Balz intends to drive it up to summer pasture.

notes.label: Pantebrugg
notes.text: the dialect form of Pantenbrücke, the bridge from which Balz sees the old woman below; the exact historical spelling is retained.

notes.label: Hock du nu da unde; worum bist abe
notes.text: the old woman's request is answered with this dialect taunt, closest to ‘just sit down there; why did you go below?’; Balz's refusal and laughter provoke the reversal at the end.
notes.anchor: Hock du nu da unde; worum bist abe

notes.label: Jez will ich lache
notes.text: dialect for ‘now I shall laugh’; the old woman repeats Balz's mockery back to him as she drives him over the edge with the moving Firn.

notes.label: Firn
notes.text: compacted old snow that survives a summer and can feed a glacier; here the standard-German version uses it for the destructive mass called Fire in the dialect version.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman in charge of the herd and dairy work during the summer season.

notes.label: Senntum
notes.text: the Alpine cattle herd and associated seasonal dairying unit under a Senn's management; Balz is taking the whole operation toward its pasture.

notes.label: Pantenbrücke
notes.text: the standard-German form of the bridge-name rendered Pantebrugg in dialect; it marks the point above the hollow where Balz refuses aid.

41d85a1e6e247e7697c8fa55a1dbb631fcebd3c5.summary: Not far from Moosburg and Friedrichshafen, on the bottom of Lake Constance, lie the ruins of a castle called the Wasserburg.

notes.label: Kornmäuslein
notes.text: literally ‘little grain mice,’ this is the barons’ cruel nickname for starving petitioners, answered by the supernatural arrival of real rodents; whether the wording derives from an older local formula is uncertain.

d65966fe4f03f125aa4562c05e96452ce1a89b9d.summary: In former times, a snow-white feathered dragon ruled Lake Seray in the Untern Ormundtale, the Lower Ormont Valley, near Mount Chavonnaz—a lake also called the ‘green lake’ because of its color.

notes.label: Untern Ormundtale
notes.text: the source's older German form for the Lower Ormont Valley in Vaud, the setting of Lake Seray.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, often made from the whey remaining after other cheese production; the dragon accepts the sweet variety from young women.

25aaaf88ada9ab435ed6cb656a60072d18125961.summary: In the middle of the Green Lake, on its bottom, lies a treasure of pearls and precious stones.

d5eb6873abdf5df1d88bf6ab50989703719d7ab8.summary: Between the rocks of the Rheinfall, the forms of white horses are often seen swaying back and forth.

notes.label: Rheinfall
notes.text: the Rhine Falls at Schaffhausen, whose rocks, whirlpools, and dangerous descent anchor the horse, wagon, and ghost-boat traditions.

notes.label: Allemannen
notes.text: an older spelling of Alemanni, the early Germanic people whom the account says sacrificed the white horses at the falls.

3783c2cc05d8d6495e96d3f4c0132ccf1b7713e5.summary: Linthbord-Anneli was a young girl from Uznach. From childhood, she was lame in both feet.

notes.label: Linthbord-Anneli
notes.text: the local affectionate name for Anna of the Linth riverbank, with Anneli as a Swiss German diminutive of Anna; the name ties the healed pilgrim to the site of the chapel and miracle.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

e75bb1d8170f6d80f004c52c2c51d721430210ef.summary: Every year the Venediger Mandli comes to the Kamor and places its little jug where pure gold drips out of the mountain.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: ‘Venetian,’ here the shortened name for the mysterious mineral-seeking little man rather than simply any inhabitant of Venice.

notes.label: Venediger Mandli
notes.text: literally ‘little Venetian man,’ a folklore figure associated with foreign prospectors—often Venetians—believed to know secret Alpine mineral deposits.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here not an alpine pasture but an old Germanic name for a nightmare or chest-pressing spirit, later connected in scholarship with dwarf and elf words; the term’s historical relationships are debated, and its modern Alpine geographic sense would be misleading in this context.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Nachtmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little night man,’ a regional name formerly used for a nightmare-pressure demon; the source treats it as related to later night-folk beliefs, but the exact being varied by locality.

notes.label: Nachtlütli
notes.text: literally ‘little night people’ in Swiss German, small nocturnal beings associated with fields, forests, and rocky caves; ‘night folk’ is close, but the source notes that their character does not fit neatly with the proposed nightmare-spirit origin.

484e6f96bede2a9b052767f1523acf2834b56026.summary: Haglestä is the name of a Jura mountain in the Fricktal near the village of Magden.

notes.label: Ramwähen
notes.text: a regional Swiss baked dish or pastry, probably a rich cream-topped Wähe, served here by the little mountain men; ‘cream tart’ is the closest sense, but the exact historical recipe and local form are uncertain.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

333117ee7ee0f64b785396f6115d940912f2c120.summary: One morning, Lord Kaspar of Strättlingen rode out from his castle. As was his custom, he had hung a rope from his belt.

notes.label: Schultheiss
notes.text: a historical civic and territorial office comparable to a chief magistrate, mayor, or bailiff depending on place and period; here the officeholder serves Lord Kaspar while plotting against him.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

46f965057b106d93cd72e2661ef779f85e859ec3.summary: A young man on Alp Hangbaum very often visited a girl in Seelisberg. It was a long journey of at least six hours, which took much time and exhausted him.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain; Hangbaum is the named Alp where the young man works before making the long journey to Seelisberg.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

bb3c00bac500a9f342ab837dcdbcd599f8472414.summary: Läng wie ne Bingbaum (Long as a Binding Pole)

notes.label: Läng wie ne Bingbaum
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘long as a binding pole’; the exact dialect title is retained, and the comparison emphasizes the apparition's dragon-like length.

notes.label: läng wie ne Bingbaum
notes.text: the title phrase repeated in the narrative, meaning ‘long as a binding pole.’

notes.label: Galgelöli
notes.text: the local place-name near the apparition's route; its relation to Galgen, gallows, contributes an ominous association, but the source does not explain the full name.

notes.label: Bisig
notes.text: the local destination or place-name toward which the fiery apparition flies.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: the dialect form of ‘Galgelöli animal,’ the mysterious creature named for the place from which it comes.

notes.label: Galgenlöliltier
notes.text: the source commentary's standard-Germanized spelling of Galgelölitier; it refers to the same local apparition rather than a separate species.

notes.label: Bindbaum
notes.text: a long pole used to bind or secure a load, especially hay on a wagon; it is the standard-German form used by the commentator to explain dialect Bingbaum.

notes.label: Lüt banne
notes.text: dialect for ‘binding people,’ magically fixing someone to a spot so that physical effort cannot carry the person away; the companions' call breaks or releases the binding.

notes.label: Hoschtert
notes.text: a dialect word for an orchard, especially the tree-planted ground around a farmstead; the boys are there taking apples when the binding occurs.

5243c64105d18fd73c5acb23b5bad58cbd88cf4d.summary: Magdenau Abbey was spared from the plague in the years 1611 and 1629, while the epidemic claimed many victims “not only in this county of Toggenburg, but also in places throughout Germany, Wälschland, and the Gidgnossschafft.” The nuns regarded this as a special grace from God.

notes.label: Wälschland
notes.text: Wälschland is an older German-speaking Swiss term for Romance-language lands, likely including French- or Italian-speaking regions here; the quotation’s precise geographic scope is uncertain.

notes.label: Gidgnossschafft
notes.text: Gidgnossschafft is the quotation’s historical spelling of Eidgenossenschaft, the Swiss Confederacy; the exact territories included by the diarist are unspecified.

5dcca7103f97a0d9d569e83ff59d1ebe409262a9.summary: One day, old Hans-Melki, who lived behind the parish church in Silenen, took up his scythe to mow the grass beneath the trees on his smallholding, for it had begun to scorch.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Steifass
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Steinfass, the narrow vessel a mower carries for the whetstone and its water; placing the root in it transfers the root's magic to the scythe, though the source does not describe the vessel's material.

044ff159b0e13f3d69783fe47aa51aa36e6c9386.summary: Near the little Solothurn town of Olten, on the cantonal border with Aargau, there is a so-called Maiden’s Field, which received its name as follows.

1256bf7a4bfb35dade2382a10a545ccda8493bf3.summary: It was nearly 100 years ago. At Schattdorf, the Fygstuehler family had “a whole great spread of hay” lying out in their meadow.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Heegerli
notes.text: a regional diminutive and potentially disparaging label for a hunchbacked woman; the source immediately glosses the hump and insists that the young woman was otherwise respectable, while the word's further nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Sympathie
notes.text: in this historical folk-belief context, not ordinary emotional sympathy but hidden correspondence or sympathetic magic through which one thing is thought to influence another; the informant distinguishes this supposedly sinless art from culpable witchcraft.

cdedb824e6407d337ef72ee172c6f35ac8ed37d1.summary: In the year 1388, on the 23rd of Christmonat, the Count of Savoy suffered a significant defeat at Visp; four thousand enemies of our freedom lost their lives there.

notes.label: Christmonat
notes.text: literally ‘Christ month,’ a traditional German name for December; the battle date is therefore 23 December 1388.

notes.label: Reisteisen
notes.text: a heavy iron levering, prying, or lifting tool used here to bar the barn door; the precise local implement is not described.

notes.label: Zehnden
notes.text: a historical Valais district or tithing, comparable to a territorial canton subdivision; here it means the district of Visp, not merely a religious tithe.

notes.label: Mannenmittwoche
notes.text: literally ‘men's Wednesday,’ the Wednesday before Christmas commemorating Visp's legendary victory; the name associates the feast with the men lost or involved, though the source does not give a narrower derivation.

3e7fe2c8920ce64130a8c5f7ca725a4953029bc7.summary: Long ago, in the Canton of Basel, a strong castle called the Fürstenstein stood high above the village of Ettlingen.

notes.label: Burgfrieden
notes.text: the legally protected precinct or peace-zone belonging to a castle, not merely a state of peacefulness; the mother and child leave the Fürstenstein's protected bounds to walk on the surrounding heights.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep rock face or cliff; here it is the sheer, partly concealed precipice over which the child falls.

notes.label: Maria Stein
notes.text: literally ‘Mary Stone’ and the name of the later monastery and pilgrimage place; the story connects the name and foundation with the Virgin Mary's rescue of the child from the rocky fall.

0b973653815d05da4d50d5254242f30edaeb4ee5.summary: Not many years ago, a Tyrolean was staying in the Veltlin who feared no one and claimed to be the strongest man in all Christendom.

notes.label: Veltlin
notes.text: the historical German name for Valtellina, the Alpine valley in present-day northern Italy; the people and wine of the valley are called Veltliner in the source.

notes.label: überhöhen
notes.text: a regional verb glossed by the source as “to master”; here it means to surpass or defeat the boastful strongman.

notes.label: Marty
notes.text: a familiar form of Martin; the source later calls the same man Hans Grass, an internal name inconsistency preserved in the translation.

notes.label: Roten
notes.text: literally “a red one,” an elliptical colloquial name for a glass of red wine, here genuine Veltliner wine.

notes.label: Spesen
notes.text: expenses or travel costs; Grass is enticed by the promise that he will incur none.

notes.label: stete Losung
notes.text: the source glosses this expression as night quarters; it means the Tyrolean’s regular lodging at the inn.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: a historical German expression for Romance- or Italian-speaking lands; here it refers to the Veltlin and is not the name of a modern country.

notes.label: caput
notes.text: the source’s colloquial, Latinized way of saying “broken” or “done for”; it describes the Tyrolean’s four injured ribs.

94d22615f5ae7f4b07776a7244fb7f678cd3fa76.summary: As long as the population of the Fricktal was smaller and its woods and pastures therefore more abundant than today, grazing livestock in all the mountain communities there was as customary as it still is in the Alps.

notes.label: Sennknecht
notes.text: an assistant working under a Senn in an Alpine dairy operation, helping with milking, butter, and cheese; Knecht indicates a hired male farm servant rather than a knight.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the dairyman responsible for livestock and for producing butter and cheese on an Alpine or upland summer pasture; the role combines herding and skilled dairy work.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Heidenweibchen
notes.text: literally “little heathen women,” benevolent female mountain beings in this local tradition; Heiden is a historical folkloric label and does not identify a known modern religious or ethnic community.

notes.label: Wähen
notes.text: Swiss flat baked cakes or tarts, made sweet or savory; here they are exceptionally rich cream cakes, not ordinary bread loaves.

notes.label: Zwehel
notes.text: a regional word for a clean cloth or towel; here it serves as a snow-white cloth on which fresh bread is laid.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: communal village land, comparable to a common; here it is shared grazing ground on which the helpful beings once left food.

notes.label: Hesch ab s’ Martis Brunnne g’soffe, dass d’ e so brüelisch
notes.text: a local Alemannic taunt meaning roughly “Have you drunk from the Martisbrunn, that you are bellowing so loudly?”; it jokes that the spring makes Wittnau people foolish or offensively loud.
notes.anchor: Hesch ab s’ Martis Brunnne g’soffe, dass d’ e so brüelisch

notes.label: Bannbeschreitung
notes.text: the ceremonial communal walking of a municipality’s boundaries, often in spring and with religious or legal significance; it renews knowledge of the boundary rather than merely providing a casual hike.

3c236ab27bdf830990274d50a1800ed9d3fc650e.summary: During the holy nights, an unknown pilgrim occasionally stops at the Döttingen winepress, which is also called Bachmann’s winepress after a more recent owner.

notes.label: Himiletzi
notes.text: an Aargau dialect term for the covering or canopy above a marriage bed, where protective Mary’s Milk is placed; ‘bed canopy’ is the closest sense, but the word’s literal formation and exact construction are not explained beyond the source’s own gloss.

c833e8c14bbe43273db9c3b21f286e640bf43cc4.summary: At the southernmost boundary of German-speaking land rises the Matterhorn, the western neighbor of Monte Rosa.

notes.label: der laufende Jud
notes.text: literally ‘the walking Jew,’ the source’s historical regional name for the Christian folklore figure more commonly called the Wandering Jew; it reflects an anti-Jewish legendary tradition and should not be read as a description of Jewish people generally.

notes.label: Matterjoch
notes.text: the high pass by the Matterhorn connecting the surrounding valleys; the legend uses repeated crossings to measure vast environmental change, without giving a literal chronology.

c24809b23d6a9ff140855f36e9445653d00fd83d.summary: Once, at 12 o'clock at night, a man from Burgerau was passing the ‘Stiegelen’ on his way home when he heard someone sneeze.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

9939fb3ada2438bdbb69b1495e3010d4394ae5ba.summary: In the Lötschental, close beside the bank of the swirling Lonza, rises a tower-high rock obelisk called the Längstein or “Ankenchübel” (butter churn).

notes.label: Ankenchübel
notes.text: the local name for the tower-high rock obelisk, glossed by the source itself as a Butterfass or butter churn; a later passage spells the same churn-name Ankenkübel.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal Alpine pasture and the working farm landscape associated with it, not merely a mountain peak; the fertile land here supports a chamois herd before the curse.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Meier
notes.text: the historical local office or title held by Waldis, rather than a first name; the tale says the valley community entrusted him with the Meieramt.

notes.label: Matten
notes.text: Alpine or valley meadowlands used for hay or grazing; the chamois descend into these cultivated meadows, which the curse later turns to scree.

notes.label: Talschaft
notes.text: the organized valley community that, according to Waldis, conferred his office and underlies his claim to the valley’s resources.

notes.label: Meieramt
notes.text: the office and authority of a Meier in the valley; the source does not define its precise legal powers, despite Waldis’s expansive claim.

notes.label: Ankenkübel
notes.text: the spelling used later in the tale for the enormous butter churn first called Ankenchübel; Anken is a Swiss German word for butter, while Kübel denotes a tub or vessel.

notes.label: Gemsbutter
notes.text: literally chamois butter, the supernatural butter made from the mountain spirit’s chamois milk; the story distinguishes it from ordinary dairy butter.

notes.label: Meier Waldis Klamm
notes.text: the tale’s name for the gorge where Waldis stalks the white buck and falls to his death; the source presents the name as still current but gives no narrower location.

notes.label: rote Lauine
notes.text: the local place-name onto which Waldis’s hat rolls; Lauine is a historical or regional spelling related to Lawine, avalanche, but the source does not establish whether the phrase names an avalanche path, slope, or other feature.

notes.label: Inhutine
notes.text: the local name the tale gives to the spot associated with Waldis’s fallen hat; its derivation and precise modern identification are not supplied.

101db1194871bef204856a7cd3a947ac2c65ec94.summary: At Göschenen there lived an immensely strong man named Melk Tresch.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical regional liquid measure and, here, the bottle holding that quantity of wine; the measure varied by locality and period, so its exact modern volume is uncertain.

1d98450cf0fd6b1656797a054e74d0fad3552d29.summary: Around the village of Wettingen, the saying about proud and violent people is, ‘One might think he was Metteli’—one could almost think he was a man like Metteli, the famous Vogt.

notes.label: Metteli
notes.text: a family name and legendary personal name with variants Mötteli, Mettelin, and Mattelin; here it refers at once to a reputedly rich historical patrician, a severe Vogt, a proverbial figure, and a supernatural rider, and the source itself argues without proving that these traditions share a mythic origin.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a bailiff, steward, or territorial official exercising delegated lordly authority; Metteli is remembered as a famous and overbearing Vogt, but the passage does not identify the precise jurisdiction or legal office he held.

notes.label: Bannholz
notes.text: literally a wood placed under a ban or communal protection, often subject to special rules of use; here it is both a landscape destination on Metteli’s fixed ghostly route and a historical woodland designation, without further legal detail.

notes.label: Auszüger
notes.text: a member of the select field contingent called out from a Swiss militia for active campaigning; here Metteli serves as an Auszüger in 1499, though his rank and unit are not specified.

notes.label: Landsknechte
notes.text: German mercenary infantrymen of the late medieval and early modern periods; here they are the troops who capture and ransom Metteli, while the poem’s compressed wording leaves parts of the second capture uncertain.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Müeda Mötteli
notes.text: an Appenzell dialect proverbial expression, literally something like ‘tiresome Mötteli,’ for an annoying or burdensome person; the source contrasts it with ‘rich Mötteli,’ but does not explain how the insulting sense arose.

notes.label: Glîchsaeree
notes.text: an archaic epithet cited from Reinhart Fuchs and used there as a contemptuous name; its closest sense may involve a flatterer, dissembler, or ingratiating person, but the source supplies only its function as an insult.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Muetisheer
notes.text: the spectral host or Wild Hunt associated by the author with a figure named Muet and said to pass through the Martisbauer’s cellars with hounds; the proposed linguistic and mythological connection is the author’s interpretation rather than an established identity.

notes.label: Guetisheer
notes.text: a regional name for a supernatural roaming host active around Christmas, compared here with the Thuringian Frau Motte; its spelling and exact relationship to the Wild Hunt, Muetisheer, and other named hosts remain uncertain.

notes.label: Mottisheer
notes.text: the Swabian name given here to the nocturnal tumult of the Wild Hunt and, figuratively in Burgdorf, to noisy children pouring from school; the author uses it as linguistic evidence for a link among Mötteli, Mutti, and Muet, a connection that remains speculative.

f510ee6dffafa0aa994a1776bae1862bea3ce252.summary: When the stern and resolute Lord Jost Ammann, a citizen of Fribourg in Üechtland, sat in the high rock castle at Ruw as Landvogt for his gracious lords and superiors, on March 1 in the year 1634 of Christian rebirth he had a woman from Ecublens called Mia Varmy, widow of Jakob Blanche, brought before him.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor exercising judicial authority under the old Swiss political order.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Schöppen
notes.text: older form of Schöffen, lay judges or assessors sitting with the presiding official.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a court or government usher, constable, or official messenger.

notes.label: Schetta
notes.text: the regional name supplied for a nocturnal witches’ dance or sabbath; its language and exact etymology are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Schetzéron
notes.text: the regional term glossed by context as crab apples or small wild apples used in the alleged poison mixture.

a705fe3170521687039d3785aa544e446d44c1f4.summary: A fertile little side valley toward the Necker is called the Äulein, where Michel lived long ago.

notes.label: Äulein
notes.text: the local diminutive valley-name near the Necker where Michel once lived; the account treats it as a proper place-name and does not establish a secure literal derivation.

38b1f36fe42e83c28d74fcb4068bf3f94e43788d.summary: Among the afflictions of Alpine husbandry on Mount Pilatus were snakes that sucked the milk from cows.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the working hut of a Senn, an Alpine herdsman and dairyman, on a seasonal high pasture; it is more specifically tied to cattle and cheese-making than an ordinary mountain cabin.

07a2c9d90634721e605a07e2bc9a530d9b1efd67.summary: People came into an inn in Altdorf and ordered coffee. Milk must be terribly scarce, they added by way of explanation, since none could be had anywhere.

notes.label: Geisshebamm
notes.text: literally ‘goat midwife’ in Swiss German, the landlady's comic or disparaging nickname; the source does not explain how she acquired it, although her magic involves drawing milk from a glove.

notes.label: Waldhäntschä
notes.text: an Uri term for a coarse protective glove worn by forestry workers; the source explicitly gives that use, and the witch treats the glove as a magically milkable animal.

notes.label: Dymlig
notes.text: the thumb or thumb-piece of the glove, corresponding to standard German Däumling; here it is pulled like a teat, while the diminutive coloring is difficult to reproduce in English.

notes.label: Böllen
notes.text: Swiss German for an onion; here the woman's impossible speed lets her fetch one from a distant Glarus garden to brown over the evening meal.

1af9ca2238724c73c0ae0db0aa165bc93fb34da5.summary: Our ancestors seem to have regarded millet as a finer food, one that the poor in particular did not receive every day.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

notes.label: Hirsmontag
notes.text: literally ‘Millet Monday,’ the first Monday after Ash Wednesday and, in this Zurich custom, a guild festival associated with millet and the carrying of a coal basket; a generic ‘festival Monday’ would lose the calendrical name.

notes.label: Jsengrind
notes.text: the dialect name of the figure or object carried in the Zurich butchers’ guild procession on Hirsmontag; its closest literal sense may be ‘iron head,’ but its precise form and ritual significance are not explained here.

notes.label: Mis Seelelämmeli
notes.text: Bernese dialect literally meaning ‘my little soul-lamb,’ an anguished endearment for the lost child or its soul; the compound blends Christian soul-language with the tenderness of calling a child a little lamb.

notes.label: Rohrbechbechli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for the little Rohrbach brook; the repeated bach/bech element may reflect the local name and generic ‘brook,’ so an exact non-redundant English place-name is uncertain.

notes.label: O, mis Seelelämmeli! O mis Seelelämmeli!
notes.text: the apparition's repeated lament, ‘Oh, my little soul-lamb! Oh, my little soul-lamb!’; repetition turns the affectionate name into an enduring confession of grief and guilt.
notes.anchor: O, mis Seelelämmeli! O mis Seelelämmeli!

notes.label: blutt
notes.text: in this regional usage, bare, barren, or stripped of growth rather than the English word blood.

notes.label: Tanngrozen
notes.text: small, stunted firs or scrubby conifer growth forming a ring around the barren place; the exact botanical form is folk description rather than a species name.

notes.label: Hexenbesen
notes.text: literally ‘witches’ brooms,’ dense broom-shaped clusters of branches; English botany also uses ‘witches’ broom’ for this abnormal growth.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Wunderfiz
notes.text: an urge of meddlesome curiosity or inquisitiveness; the person’s curiosity makes her pour out more than instructed.

notes.label: Alpdrücken
notes.text: the oppressive sensation historically attributed to an Alp spirit, broadly corresponding to nightmare or sleep paralysis but carrying a supernatural meaning here.

notes.label: Dreck vor d’ Ohre
notes.text: literally ‘dirt before the ears,’ a protective dialect formula said before speaking about witches so that they supposedly cannot overhear.

notes.label: Mönli
notes.text: an obscure dialect word for the red marks said to appear in a witch’s eyes; its precise shape or intended image is uncertain in this source.
Source uncertainty: the historical source itself breaks off after the capital letter ‘H’ in section c; no missing word or event has been inferred in this translation.

084600f6ba02c193e8e24b960bb898defbbfd6c6.summary: 1. On the old road from Seelisberg toward Emmetten, something often led nighttime travelers astray so that they marched all night without knowing where they were.

notes.label: drei Gädmer
notes.text: literally the ‘three barns’ or ‘three farm buildings,’ using a regional plural related to Gaden; the quoted phrase functions as a local place-name in Altdorf, and the buildings' exact uses are not given.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a Swiss German orchard or tree-planted homestead ground; here it is part of the named haunted area and the home location of Riedliger Thadees Mariä.

notes.label: Bsetzi
notes.text: a paved or cobbled yard, path, or standing area; here it is the hard-surfaced ground before Ratziger's farm building where the spell ends.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine barn, stable bay, storage building, or farm chamber; here it belongs to Ratziger, but the account does not identify its precise agricultural use.

cffec3c5338c649a087f9bb1d9f60e75495dd3e6.summary: In Naters stands a very ancient and uncanny Beihus, where a steep heap of Totuchöpf und Todugibei—skulls and bones of the dead—stands piled and stacked high.

notes.label: Beihus
notes.text: literally ‘bone house,’ a charnel house or ossuary where human remains displaced from graves are reverently stored.

notes.label: Totuchöpf und Todugibei
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘skulls and bones of the dead’; the repeated dead-related forms emphasize the ossuary's immense visible and imagined depth.

notes.label: Liechtji
notes.text: a Valais diminutive meaning ‘little light’ or devotional lamp; pious visitors keep it burning beside the bones while praying for departed souls.

notes.label: Armu-Seele
notes.text: dialect for ‘poor souls,’ the dead—especially souls understood in Catholic tradition to await release from Purgatory—who benefit from the living's prayers.

notes.label: Nachtbuob
notes.text: literally ‘night boy,’ a nocturnal mischief-maker or young lout; he attempts to frighten a woman engaged in prayer.

notes.label: Chlupf
notes.text: dialect for a sudden fright or shock; the boy's terror is so severe that it leads to illness and death.

notes.label: Das dem und dem nüt g'scheh ist, ist as g'fällig's Wunder! — dem heint d'Abg'storbnu gholfu! Schi lähnt nix u'vergoltu!
notes.text: the Valais saying means approximately ‘That nothing happened to so-and-so is a blessed wonder! The departed helped that person; they leave nothing unrepaid!’; it presents the dead as grateful and reciprocal protectors.
notes.anchor: Das dem und dem nüt g'scheh ist, ist as g'fällig's Wunder! — dem heint d'Abg'storbnu gholfu! Schi lähnt nix u'vergoltu!

notes.label: Mit de Totu ist nit z'g'spassu
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘the dead are not to be trifled with’; the title states the tale's rule that the grateful dead actively protect those who pray for them.

9e5b68790cc5b09ccd4db1ad17284181a37b3df8.summary: Young “Knaben” and girls from Luzein went on a sleigh ride one beautiful, moonlit winter evening.

notes.label: Knaben
notes.text: literally boys, but Jecklin glosses the word here as Jünglinge, indicating youths or young men rather than small children.

8d3d6c3a529fbb11ba3baf4dc033a54c73c88b1e.summary: Everyone in the Maderan Valley knew that a hut on the Stössi Alp was haunted.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; the haunted building is a work hut on the named Stössi Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schwimmlig
notes.text: an Uri dialect plural for mushrooms or fungi; their abundance over the hut floor provides the target of the skeptic’s mocking stone throw.

notes.label: Z' Spettlä tüet nië güet
notes.text: an Uri saying meaning approximately ‘mocking never does any good’; Spettlä covers derisive taunting or making sport of something, especially the uncanny, rather than harmless joking.

a087f2807c8753f2aed519437fc968a3a50a7eb7.summary: In Tägerfelden stands a ruined little manor with an adjoining meadow called the Schlossbreite.

notes.label: Schlossbreite
notes.text: literally the castle's broad field or meadow strip, the named ground belonging to the ruined manor where the sow appears.

notes.label: Betzeitglocke
notes.text: the prayer-time or Angelus bell; its Saturday ringing marks the sow's regular emergence.

notes.label: Moor Moritz
notes.text: the local name of the supernatural sow and, by extension, of the punished Moritz in animal form; the source does not explain Moor securely enough to translate it as an ordinary color or ethnic label.

notes.label: Chile-Rainli
notes.text: Swiss German for a small church or chapel slope; Chile means church, Rain a sloping boundary or bank, and -li is diminutive.

notes.label: Juchart
notes.text: a historical Swiss land measure based on the area that could be plowed in a day; its exact size varied by locality.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Stück
notes.text: literally ‘pieces’; in this historical grain-rent context it is an unspecified counted unit of oats, and the source equates ten Stück with one Mannwerk.

notes.label: Mannwerk
notes.text: literally a ‘man's work,’ a variable historical measure of land or agricultural labor; here the parenthesis equates it with the stated oat obligation.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss and southern German term for a church sexton or sacristan responsible for practical care of the chapel.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a young or lesser nobleman and landed gentleman; here it is Moritz's social title before his decline.

notes.label: Tauner
notes.text: an impoverished rural cottager or day laborer with little or no land of his own; Moritz's descent to this status marks the loss of his estate.

notes.label: Tagwerk
notes.text: literally a day's work and, historically, the amount of land associated with one day's labor; local values varied.

notes.label: Hochjagd
notes.text: the privileged hunt for large or high-status game, historically connected with seigneurial hunting rights.

notes.label: Betzeitläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the prayer or Angelus bell; the noun describes the recurring time and sound around which the apparition moves.

4020feb7c4f9cc25955ef4c5c532f690200db7ae.summary: a) One extraordinarily strong man from Ursern was Felix Renner of Realp, called gsturä Felix because he was considered somewhat mentally disturbed.

notes.label: gsturä Felix
notes.text: Felix Renner’s Uri byname, associated by the source with being mentally disturbed or confused; gstur can also carry shades such as stubborn or contrary, so the historical label’s exact tone is uncertain and potentially pejorative.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy work, not simply a mountain summit; several feats occur within that working landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a fresh Swiss whey cheese or curd made from proteins remaining after ordinary cheese making; the pigs foul it along with the regular cheese.

notes.label: Schwinget
notes.text: a bout of Swiss-style wrestling, especially associated with Schwingen; the invitation is friendly, but Felix rapidly turns it into a beating.

notes.label: Walserbatzen
notes.text: an opaque joking compound following Felix’s fight with men from Valais, evoking Walliser or Walser and Batzen, a coin or lump; the exact objects or battered remnants supposedly left to gather are not identified, so the punch line remains uncertain.

notes.label: Hiänä
notes.text: the local name for part of the suspension or support apparatus of an Alpine cheese cauldron; Felix gets his head and neck beneath it, but the source does not establish its exact form.

notes.label: Horner
notes.text: a traditional Swiss and south German calendar name for February; Antoni Bennet goes to vineyard work in Sion during the Horner and March.

notes.label: Frässmuttli
notes.text: a diminutive name for a feeding, eating, or food vessel; it provides a comic measure of the giant man’s enormous trouser legs, but its exact shape and size are not specified.

notes.label: Droslenstaude
notes.text: an Uri name for a green-alder shrub; the source’s own footnote identifies Drosle as green alder, Alnus viridis, while Staude indicates the bush or shrub Baumann imagines gripping against an avalanche.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a low, broad wooden vessel or trough used especially in Alpine dairying; Baumann boasts that he could lie on one over exploding powder, though the precise vessel in this stunt is not described.

665898d384916214620bb954e00ac4349e1636c7.summary: At Wattingen, about a quarter of an hour beyond the mountain village of Wassen, a stepmother and her daughter lived together harmoniously in a small house.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

5fcedda5525e6de0f71ce1508a7e62808bec5f35.summary: a) On Arniberg in Uri, a farmer had lost a cow and could not find it anywhere.

notes.label: Bergmandli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little mountain man,’ the Alpine helper that reports the lost cow’s location; ‘mountain dwarf’ is close, though the source does not define a species.

notes.label: Bilfluh
notes.text: the local Fluh under which the cow is found; Fluh means a steep Alpine rock face or crag, while the first element Bil remains a place-name.

notes.label: Trichelkuh
notes.text: a cow wearing a Trichel, a large sheet-metal livestock bell with a duller tone than a cast bell; here it identifies the farmer’s brown missing cow.

notes.label: Nutzen
notes.text: literally the ‘use’ or ‘yield’ from the cow, specified here as the cheese and butter produced while it was away; it means dairy returns, not an abstract benefit.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; it appears as part of the cow’s accumulated dairy yield.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth man,’ a helpful dwarf-like household or mountain being in Swiss tradition; the closest English label is ‘earth dwarf,’ but its regional role includes tending cattle and granting inexhaustible food.

notes.label: munzig
notes.text: Swiss German for very tiny or minute; it emphasizes the supernatural woman’s diminutive size, though the precise dialect spelling varies regionally.

notes.label: Lanzig
notes.text: a central Swiss seasonal word for spring or the springtime, when winter fodder would normally be running low; its agricultural timing drives the widow’s curiosity.

notes.label: Erdweiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth woman,’ the female counterpart to an Erdmännchen; here she tends the cow and multiplies its milk and hay, while the tale does not specify whether this is a distinct class of being.

a0947935d8208134248d7cfb0f40c85fb5afb221.summary: There are few valleys in Valais where, at one place or another, harmful mountain spirits have not demonstrated their destructive power through mud avalanches, landslides, rockfalls, falling stones, and Wieggisch.

notes.label: Wieggisch
notes.text: a Valais word for a destructive surge of mud, debris, or water comparable to a mud avalanche; the source lists it among the mountain spirits' characteristic disasters.

notes.label: Gufer
notes.text: a Valais term for a boulder field, scree, or rockfall deposit; in Fuchs-Gufer and Täschgufer it forms part of named hazardous landscapes.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Schlammwieggische
notes.text: plural mud-and-debris surges; the Illgraben's flows reach the Rhône and can back up its water.

notes.label: Hausset
notes.text: a regional name for a fiber crop grown for household spinning, probably flax or hemp in this context; the precise plant is genuinely uncertain from the source wording.

notes.label: Wubb
notes.text: a completed web or length of woven cloth in the local weaving economy; English ‘web’ can suggest other things, so the dialect term is retained.

notes.label: Muetter, spring!
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘Mother, run!’; the child reveals that the hunted hare is his own transformed or supernatural mother.

notes.label: Jeger
notes.text: dialect for Jäger, a hunter; the spelling reflects the tale's Bernese speech.

notes.label: Has
notes.text: dialect for Hase, a hare; the boy appears to offer game but warns the hare he calls Mother.

notes.label: Hüng
notes.text: dialect plural or collective for hunting dogs; despite the boy's condition, the hunter deceptively brings them.

e8d6a13e77fa43964d42242a3d9f9a68d0e7f893.summary: In former times, wild people lived on the Flums alps. They did not associate with the other inhabitants of the land and lived in quiet seclusion in the most remote forests and rock caves.

notes.label: Ruchrinde
notes.text: literally ‘rough bark,’ the wild girl’s personal name; it links her linguistically with forest life but may function simply as a folklore name.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Jochtrager
notes.text: literally ‘yoke carrier,’ the wild woman’s call to the man carrying a sled across his shoulders like a yoke.

notes.label: Muggisturz
notes.text: the personal name of the deceased wild man, identified in another local version as Ruchrinde’s father; the source gives no reliable etymology.

f83fc246ca7a21235de1cf2a595ab6f4e786638b.summary: Many years ago, a harsh and miserly, even unjust man administered the bishop’s estate of Mulinära below Trimmis.

notes.label: Mulinära
notes.text: the local name of the bishop’s estate below Trimmis administered by Hans; the source supplies no closer derivation or description of the property.

notes.label: Fürsten-Älpli
notes.text: the named little high pasture haunted by Hans; Älpli is a Swiss German diminutive of Alp, referring to a small seasonal grazing and dairy holding rather than simply a mountain.

notes.label: Mulinära-Hans
notes.text: the dead steward’s local ghost-name, combining the estate Mulinära with Hans, which the source explicitly identifies as his baptismal name.

notes.label: Fürsten-Alp
notes.text: the non-diminutive form used later for the same named high pasture as Fürsten-Älpli; an Alp is a seasonal livestock and dairy holding, not merely a summit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: z'Tal gefahren
notes.text: a regional phrase meaning that the herds, herders, and equipment had already been brought down from the Alp to the valley at the end of the grazing season.

notes.label: herumholtschen
notes.text: a regional verb for moving or shuffling heavily and noisily around a place; the source emphasizes the sound outside the hut, while its exact gait remains unspecified.

notes.label: Holtschen
notes.text: the noun used for the heavy shuffling or clumping sound made outside the hut, corresponding to the verb herumholtschen in the preceding clause.

notes.label: Loset
notes.text: a Swiss German plural imperative meaning “listen”; the hunter uses it to alert his companions that the sound is Mulinära-Hans.

notes.label: grusig leid
notes.text: a regional expression describing Hans’s dreadful, grim, or ghastly appearance; grusig conveys horror or revulsion, while leid adds a miserable or forbidding cast whose exact shade is ambiguous.

notes.label: Schüssla
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a bowl or dish; Hans’s invitation promises one filled with meat.

notes.label: Kanta
notes.text: a regional form for a jug or pitcher; Hans carries one filled with beer.

notes.label: Pritsche
notes.text: a plain wooden sleeping platform or bunk in the Alpine hut, beneath which the frightened dog hides.

notes.label: Mad
notes.text: the vanished village-name that the account connects with mown meadows; this is a local folk etymology rather than secure linguistic proof.

notes.label: Madmatten
notes.text: the meadow lands across the bridge where the woman tended livestock; Matte is a regional word for meadow, and the name preserves Mad's association with the buried settlement.

c2cebd1a885f4c7f5e123ef0f8f70d318845bf51.summary: The so-called Mutt-Schüerli at Chnubel near Gontenschwil, a house and barn, formerly stood above on the Homberg opposite.

notes.label: Mutt-Schüerli
notes.text: the dialect name of the relocated farmstead, with Schüerli meaning a little barn or shed; here the building's interrupted move establishes the Wild Huntsman's later route, while Mutt likely relates to the associated name Mutti.

notes.label: Mutti
notes.text: the huntsman's regional name, for which the source lists the senses strong, rich, stocky, and malicious; because several meanings coexist, no single English gloss captures the epithet.

notes.label: Muet
notes.text: a variant name-form cited for comparison with Mutti; it may overlap with words for spirit, disposition, or courage, but the source supplies no final etymology.

8c28d33a0fe0415555a1724509bb21694c5c556f.summary: An Unholde who lived in Gschwend near Menzingen taught her children Mäusemachen and similar arts.

notes.label: Unholde
notes.text: an older Germanic folklore label for a malign supernatural woman or witch; it is stronger and less humanizing than the neutral modern word woman.

notes.label: Mäusemachen
notes.text: literally ‘making mice,’ the source's name for an alleged witchcraft skill, likely the magical production or sending of mice; the exact mechanics are not explained in this episode.

notes.label: Krügli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small jug or pitcher; the man's emptying of the entire vessel turns the intended light shower into a cloudburst.

notes.label: Skapulir
notes.text: the source's Swiss spelling of scapular, a Catholic devotional garment or object; invoking Jesus while refusing to remove it breaks the witches' Sabbath illusion.

notes.label: Tobelbrückli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a little bridge over a Tobel, or steep ravine; here it is the small bridge over the Lorze on which the girl is left exposed.

4a03ecc4e357a02705776d78ca846f3161d4d99e.summary: Mühle-Seiler was a master who compelled spirits, from the district of Signau, where he lived at Mühleseilen, the place from which he probably also took his name.

notes.label: Nachtlütli
notes.text: Bernese German, literally ‘little night people’; these nocturnal supernatural beings dance in the meadow and leave visible rings behind.

notes.label: Chüehweid
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘cow pasture,’ used here as a local landscape name at one end of the route.

notes.label: obere Glasbech
notes.text: the printed Bernese place-name, closest to ‘Upper Glasbach/Glass Brook’; the exact modern identification is uncertain, so the source form is retained.

notes.label: Matte
notes.text: the Swiss German word for a meadow; here it is the grassland on which the Nachtlütli's dancing rings appear.

notes.label: Rossise
notes.text: Rossise is the Bernese dialect word for a horseshoe, appearing as treasure that would have turned to gold if taken; its exact pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Böhnli
notes.text: Böhnli is the dialect diminutive for little beans, here treasure in disguise that becomes gold when carried home; the bean variety and why some treasure disguises differ are uncertain.

notes.label: Chaserebärg
notes.text: Chaserebärg is the dialect place name of the hill where two nail-treasure episodes occur; its modern identification and spelling are uncertain.

notes.label: Scheubeli
notes.text: Scheubeli is the little child’s garment pocket, apron fold, or small container into which the nails are placed; its exact form and dialect meaning are uncertain.

8a93bab9668f6f58f0500258476e5e936a61b1a0.summary: In this collection of legends, several ‘stones’—that is, mostly exposed boulders or masses of broken rock—play a role.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, rights, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; several stone names are located on named Alps.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Jützsteine
notes.text: literally stones used for a Jutz or carrying Alpine call; the account identifies them as places from which people call down into the valley to signal.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or cry used to hail across distance or express joy, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; here it functions as a signal from a Jützstein.

notes.label: Stäflen
notes.text: stepped or terraced levels of an Alpine pasture or its successive grazing stations; the precise local extent of the Bristen Stäflen is not given.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.
