9e468549cb2f4ca9b7f2186e3ee1ef6bf56ba22e.summary: On the Alp Zuazo-dessus, many years ago, there once lived very peacefully, yet helpfully and obligingly, a mountain spirit called Napfhans, Jean de la Bolieta.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and dairying landscape; the spirit safely herds cattle on its most dangerous grazing places.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Napfhans
notes.text: literally ‘bowl Hans,’ the German name of the helpful mountain spirit; it refers to the bowl of cream left as his nightly payment and is paired with the French Jean de la Bolieta.

notes.label: Jean de la Bolieta
notes.text: the French regional name paired with Napfhans for the same mountain spirit, approximately ‘John of the little bowl’; the precise dialect spelling and etymology are retained from the source.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or senior cattle herders; they maintain the customary offering that the skeptical newcomer violates.

notes.label: Nidle
notes.text: Swiss German for rich fresh cream; the bowl placed on the roof is both payment and a sign of reciprocal respect toward the spirit.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or group of huts at a particular elevation; its roof is the customary place for Napfhans's offering.

notes.label: Schindanger
notes.text: a carrion ground or knacker's place where animal carcasses are disposed of; the ravine's name, paired with Le corzau, memorializes the seven flayed or torn cows.

b12ec31548248cb7a5c1bd028eed438d6982762f.summary: Near Brienz, a valley called Tiefital or Teufital is said in olden times to have had permanent inhabitants even during the winter; now, however, only the little place of Engi has a few winter dwellings here.

notes.label: Heidenhäuser
notes.text: literally ‘heathen houses,’ a traditional antiquarian name for structures believed by local people to be extremely old; it signals an imagined pre-Christian origin rather than proving who built them.

notes.label: Hasler
notes.text: inhabitants of the Hasli region around Meiringen; their local usage ‘an der Gossen’ links the vanished village-name to the wider landscape.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman's or herdsman's hut; its absence marks the legendary valley's change from a settled winter village into unproductive high ground.

2895258042df48ae1ff7a511fd9ae923bf7fc9ad.summary: At Oberkäsern in the Maderanertal, a frivolous Senn willfully neglected the nightly Betruf.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy production; his ritual duties here include making the nightly protective prayer call.

notes.label: Betruf
notes.text: a traditional Alpine prayer call, often sung or projected over the pasture to invoke divine protection for the people, animals, and Alp; deliberately omitting it exposes the herd to the spirit in this tale.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

755ca63e43dbf9f4eb512d248988de5d487a71ae.summary: Neutaler, härddick — New Thalers, Thick on the Ground

notes.label: Neutaler, härddick
notes.text: a Bernese expression describing new thaler coins lying or rolling in dense profusion; the title promises conjured wealth, but the coins cannot be picked up before the Devil arrives.

notes.label: härddick
notes.text: literally dense or thickly strewn; in the tale it describes the magical abundance of new coins covering the floor rather than the physical thickness of one coin.

notes.label: Obesitz
notes.text: an evening visit or social gathering in a neighbor's house, traditionally a time for shared work, talk, and storytelling.

notes.label: Allmäng
notes.text: a Bernese form of Allmend, common land; here it appears to function as the local name of the place or property where the gathering occurs.

notes.label: Ofetritt
notes.text: the step, platform, or low seat beside a masonry room stove; Stöckliheiri watches the escalating recitation from this characteristic place in the parlor.

notes.label: Christoffelgebätt
notes.text: a Saint Christopher prayer or folk charm; the source does not give its wording, but repeated recitation here serves as the ritual that summons coins and increasingly ominous signs.

notes.label: Agetsche
notes.text: Bernese dialect for magpies; their pecking at the windows is the first uncanny response to the charm.

notes.label: dr Grüen
notes.text: ‘the Green One,’ a color-based folk euphemism for the Devil; his offer to demonstrate the ritual's proper completion frightens the group into stopping.

406a56510928e43ef8d8156a6faa4951f3763d42.summary: Beneath the castle rock upon which the scant remains of Neu-Toggenburg can be found, a secret entrance was once constructed that led to the castle and also down the valley as far as the little town of Lichtensteig.

893b6689d0dab1e0e6a34f0fd4a2ed4483974c77.summary: It is also told of Nidberg Castle that the people could not overcome the Zwingherr who lived there until a Burgmagd was persuaded to give a signal when he was asleep.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: literally a ‘coercive lord,’ an oppressive castle ruler or tyrannical feudal lord in Swiss liberation legends.

notes.label: Burgmagd
notes.text: literally ‘castle maid,’ a female domestic servant in a castle household; her intimate access makes the assassination possible.

f89f5335f8d9cba97a960fced6cb4d2f75e97952.summary: Old Nidelgret on the Glatt, ‘known from the lake to Andermatt,’ made butter for herself through witchcraft.

notes.label: Nidelgret
notes.text: a local female name or byname combining Nidel, ‘cream,’ with Gret, a short form of Margret; here it identifies the witch whose butter-making spell the greedy Senn copies.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a high pasture; here he secretly learns Nidelgret's spell and magnifies it disastrously.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Hexengut
notes.text: literally ‘witches' due’ or ‘witch-property,’ the first name given to the two spoonfuls taken magically from each cow; the compact tale does not distinguish its function clearly from Hexenzoll.

notes.label: Hexenzoll
notes.text: literally ‘witches' toll,’ a magical levy of dairy produce from each cow; here Nidelgret asks only spoonfuls, while the Senn greedily asks for buckets.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick or rich cream; here its magically multiplied volume becomes a deadly flood.

notes.label: Ankenstock
notes.text: a Swiss German compound meaning a mass, block, or store of butter, with Anken meaning butter; here one remains petrified at the destroyed house, although its original shape is not specified.

d9a10ca49f93d645f9f6dfb8f8dc1a870304916f.summary: In the canton of Uri, not far from Andermatt, stands a white block of stone.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream; the old woman produces impossibly more from one cow than an entire herd yields.

notes.label: Sommerfahrt
notes.text: literally ‘summer journey,’ the seasonal drive of cattle up to high pasture; it marks the abundant milking period on the Alp.

notes.label: Nidelgret
notes.text: literally ‘Cream Gret,’ the byname of the old woman whose magically abundant cream leads to her imprisonment in stone.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cattle herder or cowherd, particularly one working with dairy cattle; curiosity and greed lead him to enlarge the stolen charm.

notes.label: Gebs
notes.text: a shallow wooden dairy vessel used to hold milk or cream; spellings and exact shapes vary regionally.

notes.label: Sennenzoll
notes.text: literally the ‘Senn's toll,’ a supposed portion owed from each cow; here it names the cream supernaturally taken from other herds.

notes.label: Hexengut und Sennenzoll, von jeder Kuh zwei Löffel voll!
notes.text: ‘Witches' goods and Alpine dairyman's toll, two spoonfuls from every cow!’; the charm disguises magical theft as a customary dairy due.
notes.anchor: Hexengut und Sennenzoll, von jeder Kuh zwei Löffel voll!

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kübel
notes.text: a large bucket, tub, or pail; replacing spoonfuls with bucketfuls turns the charm lethal.

notes.label: Hexengut und Sennenzoll, von jeder Kuh zwei Kübel voll!
notes.text: ‘Witches' goods and Alpine dairyman's toll, two bucketfuls from every cow!’; the Küher's greedy alteration multiplies the flow beyond control.
notes.anchor: Hexengut und Sennenzoll, von jeder Kuh zwei Kübel voll!

notes.label: Glatt
notes.text: the watercourse or local terrain over which the storm comes; although glatt normally means ‘smooth,’ it functions here as a place-name whose exact reference is uncertain.

d92f9c9e7de0e2297c10615cf15ba592fbc86780.summary: In Uri, there once lived a woman whom people considered a witch because she made as much Nidel, or cream, from one cow as others made from twenty cows.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick fresh cream; the source explicitly glosses it, and its impossible abundance becomes lethal.

notes.label: Hei, Astaroth! flink auf und hol'
notes.text: the opening of the charm meaning ‘Hey, Astaroth! Quickly go and bring two spoonfuls from every cow, as witches' goods and Sennenzoll’; it orders demonic collection of a small share from every herd.
notes.anchor: Hei, Astaroth! flink auf und hol'

notes.label: Sennenzoll
notes.text: literally the ‘Alpine dairyman's toll,’ the portion of milk or cream taken from each cow; in the charm, it disguises supernatural theft as a customary due.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cattle herder or cowherd, particularly one working with dairy cattle; he copies the charm but cannot control its result.

notes.label: Ankenstock
notes.text: literally ‘butter block,’ from Swiss German Anken, butter; the cream-filled house becomes a great white stone block imprisoning both figures.

notes.label: Nidelgret
notes.text: literally ‘Cream Gret,’ the byname of the witch whose magically abundant cream defines both her reputation and punishment.

68310fa5bf9b06ed7ff3dd314c3d3c1fc3730fb7.summary: Nidelgrethe was an old, strange witch. She owned only a single cow and yet always had more Nidel than fifty of the best cows would yield during the Sommerfahrt.

notes.label: Nidelgrethe
notes.text: the witch’s byname combines Nidel, ‘cream,’ with Grethe, a familiar form of Margarethe or Margaret; it characterizes her by the magically abundant cream she produces.

notes.label: Witch accusations

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for rich cream, especially the thick cream skimmed from milk; the term is retained because the charm and the witch’s name both depend upon its regional sense.

notes.label: Sommerfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal movement to, and working period upon, summer Alpine pasture; here it denotes the dairy yield over that summer-pasture season, although the precise local duration is unstated.

notes.label: Gwunder
notes.text: Swiss German for curiosity or an irresistible desire to know; it is personified here as something that seizes the cowherd.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cattle herder or cowherd, particularly one working with dairy cattle; here curiosity leads him to spy upon Nidelgrethe and greed leads him to enlarge her charm.

notes.label: Gebs
notes.text: a large traditional wooden dairy tub or vessel used in handling milk or cream; the source does not establish its exact size or construction.

notes.label: Herengut
notes.text: an opaque, archaic, or possibly corrupt word in the magical charm, apparently referring in context to goods or yield claimed by magic; its exact derivation and intended meaning are uncertain.

notes.label: Senuenzoll
notes.text: the first spelling in the source’s charm, probably a dialectal or corrupt form of Sennenzoll, literally a dairyman’s toll; the textual variation is preserved rather than silently normalized.

notes.label: Sennenzoll
notes.text: literally a ‘dairyman’s toll’ or ‘Alpine herdsman’s levy’; within the charm it names the magical portion taken from every cow rather than a documented civil tax.

notes.label: Kübel
notes.text: a large bucket, pail, or tub; asking for two Kübel instead of two spoonfuls from every cow turns the cream charm lethal, while the vessel’s exact capacity is unstated.

c428bcc4a51dfd40c1a25d5c3bf31e6ca700a09e.summary: In the great beech forest between Uezwil and Kallern in the Freienamte, at the summit where footpaths from perhaps five villages cross, there is a level, treeless spot with a long reddish-brown strip on which grass has never grown.

notes.label: Freienamte
notes.text: an inflected historical name for the Aargau Freiamt, the former ‘Free Bailiwicks’ region; here it locates the forest between Uezwil and Kallern rather than describing a generic free office.

notes.label: Fasnachtsfeuer
notes.text: bonfires kindled for Fasnacht, the Alemannic-Swiss carnival season before Lent; here the Tägerli has served since ancient times as a communal fire and games site.

64a1d6e14f069eda29f7538ad863b321d36e1f64.summary: No einisch will dr hälfe! — I’ll Help You One More Time!

notes.label: No einisch will dr hälfe!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘I’ll help you one more time!’; the warning figure grants a final rescue from the danger brought on by the boy’s magic book and makes clear that no further protection will follow.

d409cd19b070968d2602fcd7c1867770936ddaa2.summary: In olden times, throughout the entire Hallwiler-Seethale there was no church or churchyard except on Staufberg, several hours away.

notes.label: Hallwiler-Seethale
notes.text: older spelling for the Lake Hallwil valley, whose communities once shared the distant Staufberg church and cemetery.

notes.label: Ungebür
notes.text: an archaic word for gross impropriety or outrageous misconduct, here the drunken dropping of a lord's coffin that the procession must repeatedly expiate.

notes.label: Retterswiler Dörfli
notes.text: the ‘little village of Retterswil’; Dörfli is a Swiss diminutive that conveys the settlement's small scale.

notes.label: Galgli
notes.text: a diminutive place-name related to Galgen, ‘gallows,’ for the thicket where the spectral party rests and feeds its horses.

notes.label: Chilchthal
notes.text: Swiss spelling for ‘church valley,’ the named hollow through which the procession passes above Seon.

notes.label: Vogts Grosse
notes.text: the source's local designation for the female witness associated with the bailiff's household; whether Grosse is a surname, nickname, or household role is unclear.

notes.label: Reffenthal
notes.text: the named valley from which stormy weather approaches whenever the funeral procession travels.

notes.label: Schürberg-Pass
notes.text: the local pass over which the procession's accompanying storm is said to roar.

notes.label: Leichenrossen
notes.text: literally ‘corpse horses’ or funeral horses, the animals drawing or accompanying the bier and receiving the ritually significant oats.

notes.label: König Abel
notes.text: ‘King Abel,’ the Schleswig name cited for a local form of Wuotan who receives an overnight sack of seed oats.

notes.label: Gebund Haber
notes.text: an older expression for a bound sheaf of oats left at harvest for the supernatural rider's horse; Haber is a regional word for oats.

notes.label: Rößlibrod
notes.text: literally ‘little-horse bread,’ a shaped ritual loaf discussed as a survival of offerings connected with the sacred horse.

notes.label: Leichenconducts
notes.text: an older learned term for the funeral cortège or conducted procession whose horses and riders bear elaborate ornaments.

7fe654ea3a9673b94c665dad0847debcdeb81e1a.summary: A 75-year-old man from Silenen relates: I had an old chest in my room that was half filled with bedding, sheets, and covers.

notes.label: Braschlen
notes.text: an Uri dialect noun from a verb for persistent rustling, rattling, or rummaging noises; here the unexplained sound in the chest is understood as a death omen, and no single English sound-word captures it exactly.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: an Alpine German term for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; here the woodcutter falls from a high one.

7e2d4fde9cbecea29a5fd8a4dfb83a8a5300b584.summary: Nümmen umecho — Never Came Back Again

notes.label: Nümmen umecho
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘never came back again’; the title describes the permanent effect of the householder's impatient rebuke.

notes.label: Nachtlütlli
notes.text: literally ‘little night people,’ small nocturnal house-visiting beings; the source does not say whether they are dwarfs, spirits, or another class of visitor.

notes.label: Sinzel
notes.text: the dialect name for the raised interior ledge, shelf, or structural perch onto which the Nachtlütlli leap; its exact household form is uncertain.

notes.label: Nüt rede!
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Say nothing!’; the command expresses the ritual silence required while digging for enchanted treasure, where even a brief remark breaks the attempt and drives the seekers away.

notes.label: Tagwen
notes.text: an old eastern-Swiss term for a local communal district or body of citizens owing shared labor; here it introduces the community of Oblinden.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain pasture and its working territory; the Goldloch is located in the Alp of Kamm.

notes.label: Goldloch
notes.text: literally ‘gold hole,’ the ore-bearing cave from which the chronicle derives Goldingen's later name.

notes.label: Jenner
notes.text: an older regional form of Jänner, January; the cave pond was filled during the earthquake of January 1756.

notes.label: Schlipf
notes.text: a regional term for a landslip or sliding mass of earth; together with subsidence, it fills the underground pond.

968edf24182572a5aee35d4f7209ee3253859fed.summary: On an Alp high in the Ryßtal, a Senn, a herdsman, and a farmhand were together, as is customary.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, dairy work, and working community, not simply a mountain peak; the Senn and his companions spend the grazing season there.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd’s milk processing and cheesemaking and often for directing the seasonal hut; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Gliger
notes.text: a regional sleeping place or bedding in an Alpine hut, often a simple bunk, hay bed, or straw bed; the stranger agrees to accept whatever kind the workers have.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working on a seasonal high-mountain pasture; here the collective term covers the hut’s pastoral workers rather than merely mountain residents.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine scree slope or tract of loose rock and debris; the Senn finds the heavy glittering stones in one, but the story does not identify their mineral.

notes.label: Tschoopäsack
notes.text: literally the pocket of a Tschoopä, a regional jacket or work coat; one of the exceptionally heavy stones tears through it.

notes.label: Vinediger
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Venediger, literally ‘Venetian,’ but in Alpine treasure lore a mysterious foreign mineral seeker credited with recognizing valuable ores and stones and sometimes with magical travel; the story also links this figure directly with Venice.

9d9d26549adaa3948d8617a40f5d2b613dbda966.summary: In the Chuchi, near St. Leonard’s Chapel in Erstfeld, people were working at the hay.

notes.label: Chuchi
notes.text: literally ‘kitchen’ in Swiss German, here the name of a locality near St. Leonard’s Chapel in Erstfeld rather than an indoor room.

notes.label: Ä b'hiätis!
notes.text: an Uri dialect protective exclamation, approximately ‘May God preserve us!’; the narrator inserts it at the height of the supernatural storm.

d27e91d82cf7216f0f775638cbd9e973aeeffe06.summary: 1. A rich, grasping farmer envied his poorer neighbor, who owned a beautiful but completely debt-burdened farm.

notes.label: Fürsprech
notes.text: a historical Swiss term for an advocate, attorney, or legal representative who speaks for a party in court; the tale plays on his professional power of speech failing at divine judgment.

notes.label: Kei's Wort häint-s-mi lo redä
notes.text: the exact Uri-dialect verdict, ‘They did not let me say a single word’; its terseness completes the tale’s joke about lawyers being unable to argue in the next world.

79a36775fea9e8f259dcc28101cae25659d5f8d9.summary: a) About 60 years ago, an old woman in Schattdorf told her children:

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: an Uri regional, often disparaging name for a strange, disreputable, or uncanny female figure; her muttering walk precedes the localized hail, but the word itself does not define her powers.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Gampelen
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture toward which the Guschi walks; Alp denotes a pastoral landscape and working holding, not merely a peak.

notes.label: Häftli
notes.text: little fasteners, hooks, or clasps said to be found embedded in hailstones; the object’s exact form is not described, so the regional word remains visible.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Rossnägel
notes.text: horseshoe nails, which one informant says he found inside large hailstones and explains as debris whirled aloft by the wind.

notes.label: Schlossen
notes.text: a regional German word for large hailstones; here they are said to enclose hair and horseshoe nails.

notes.label: Wetterhexe
notes.text: literally ‘weather witch,’ an Alpine folklore figure blamed for making hail and storms; the variants connect one Guschi’s passage and strange objects inside hailstones with witches’ weather-working.

ae4a7e3b6ce004b46251151feb94cc224e3d17b8.summary: Heilig Eich. Beside the Unterskapf farm on the road from Hergiswil to Menzberg stood three gigantic oaks, one of which has now been felled.

notes.label: heilig Eich
notes.text: regional wording for ‘holy oak,’ using Eich rather than standard German Eiche; the tree becomes sacred through shelter, the hidden Marian image, and local prayer.

b6f0948e8aa09957b968d8a021726dca0f63b53e.summary: Our old Schalemee—now there was a gentleman! As long as he was our pastor, there was never any hail or great flood.

notes.label: Schalemee
notes.text: the dialect rendering of the Jesuit pastor's surname Chalomeille, transformed into the legendary name of a weather-worker and exorcist; it should not be confused with Schalmei, a shawm, without further evidence.

notes.label: Dublonen
notes.text: doubloons, historical gold coins imagined raining from the oak; the story gives no mint, date, or exchange value.

notes.label: Neutaler
notes.text: literally ‘new thalers,’ a historical coin-name whose exact issue and value are not identified in the tale.

notes.label: Fünfliber
notes.text: Swiss five-franc pieces, literally ‘five-livre’ coins in popular speech; the coin list deliberately evokes abundant money from different familiar denominations.

notes.label: Agatha-Segen
notes.text: a blessing associated with Saint Agatha, traditionally invoked for protection against fire; Schalemee circles the burning house three times while speaking it.

notes.label: Pfaffen
notes.text: a disparaging or familiar term for priests and clerics; the speaker contrasts modern clergy's supposed uselessness with the old pastor's legendary powers.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Ungergschlacht
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect name for a lower compartment or under-section of a storage chest; the precise construction of the compartment is not specified.

notes.label: Trögli
notes.text: a diminutive of ‘Trog,’ literally a little trough or chest; here it is a small household storage container, whose exact form may vary regionally.

notes.label: Gadeslaube
notes.text: a Bernese farmhouse term for a gallery or balcony associated with the barn or outbuilding; the exact architectural form is locally variable.

notes.label: Bammertjöggel
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name combining Bammert, a dialect form of Bannwart for a field, forest, or vineyard warden, with Jöggel, a familiar form of Jakob; here he is a local cunning man who controls animals and works thief-binding magic.

notes.label: Tschöttelichappen
notes.text: a dialect name for the Bammertjöggel's cap, which he places beneath his arm while summoning animals; Chappe means a cap or head covering, but the source does not make the first element or the cap's special character clear.

notes.label: drei höchschte Näme
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the ‘three highest names,’ probably an invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; its use places the destructive charm within Christianized folk magic, although the source does not spell the names out.

notes.label: Armesünderschmalz
notes.text: literally ‘poor sinner's grease’; this account explicitly identifies its ritual substance as earwax, so that local definition governs here.

notes.label: Schoreniggeli
notes.text: unripe or stunted cherries that fall before maturing; their appearance is the only fruit the bewitched tree manages before becoming bare.

notes.label: Tütschi
notes.text: a Bernese word for a wooden block or section of tree trunk; in the sympathetic magic described here, it serves as a material stand-in for the thief and receives the blows intended for him.

notes.label: Chehrumtürli
notes.text: an old Bernese expression for a turning point, coming around, or change of mind; the source says the beating brings the thief to this point, meaning that he is compelled to yield and return the stolen goods.

632174df34ed7c27e4343c2e9fba42928af8dad4.summary: In a large village lived a married couple so poor that the husband had to go abroad to earn his bread.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Bületod
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for death in a plague outbreak, formed from Büle, ‘swelling’ or ‘boil,’ and Tod, ‘death’; the name evokes the buboes of plague, while the whip-stroke makes the young witness remember the communal catastrophe.

9996696b85e9dc18d33e7ebf7f6c466fe91d95ac.summary: Thus the Toggeli once took charge of all a Senn's lean cows for the entire winter, upon his promise not to call any of them by name when they returned in spring.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a Swiss regional name for small supernatural beings; in this tale they are benevolent cattle keepers until a broken promise and a cruel prank drive them away, and they should not be confused automatically with every nightmare-spirit also called Toggeli elsewhere.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder responsible for livestock on a high pasture; his naming of the restored cow breaks the Toggeli's condition.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpauffahrt
notes.text: the seasonal spring ascent of livestock and herders to the high Alpine pastures; the cows return from winter care as this annual movement approaches.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face or cliff in Swiss landscape usage; the Toggeli drive the cattle along it, and the named cow then falls from the rocks.

notes.label: Hoho die Gäbel ist ämel alle z'weg!
notes.text: the dialect exclamation means approximately ‘Ho there, Gäbel certainly is in splendid shape!’; Gäbel is the cow's individual name, whose utterance violates the promise, while the idiom alle z'weg praises her excellent condition.
notes.anchor: Hoho die Gäbel ist ämel alle z'weg!

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ a widespread German and Swiss name for subterranean or mountain-dwelling little people; the title equates them here with the Toggeli.

b2786556454c455d11fab68091446f4d0ac07f03.summary: The upper, southern part of this Alp is today a stone wilderness—Gand—one to three hours long, interrupted by several patches of eternal snow.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its grazing rights, huts, livestock, dairy work, and community, not simply a mountain peak; this account contrasts Fellenen’s former pastoral fertility with its present stony upper ground.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine scree slope or tract of loose rock and debris; here it has expanded into a long stone wilderness broken only by permanent snow.

notes.label: Grätli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small ridge or crest; it names the upper limit of the former smooth pastureland.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: organized Alpine cattle herds and their complete pastoral or dairying units, not merely unstructured groups of cows; Uri and Graubünden herding communities once met with them on the high ground.

notes.label: Bündner
notes.text: people from the canton of Graubünden; the term marks the neighboring pastoral group meeting the herders from Uri.

6205b4f0fbc10043f060e1e1b5e861b3dda2af28.summary: A knight once rode out hunting. By chance an old man came toward him and asked the noble lord for a gift.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

309c226c416f15889ad0748c459614434bf93882.summary: A Swiss man from the Bernese Oberland was once traveling abroad, a considerable time ago, and one evening stopped at an isolated hut, where an old man received him hospitably.

notes.label: Gauliweiblein
notes.text: this diminutive means approximately ‘little Gauli woman’ and names the enchanted female being of the Gauli Glacier; her precise folkloric type and connection to that place are uncertain.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, denoting Alpine dairymen and herders working on high seasonal pastures; the account does not specify which workers saw the apparition.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Engstlenfräulein
notes.text: this name means ‘young lady of Engstlen’ and identifies the wandering daughter seen near the Engstlenalp; whether she belongs to a broader class of Alpine maidens is uncertain.

notes.label: Geissmaidlein
notes.text: this Alemannic compound means ‘little goat maiden’ and names the seductive Hasliberg figure revealed by her goat feet; whether she is imagined as demonic, enchanted, or partly animal is uncertain.

609abc39b189e91f84226fed0822ab1f79d9cdc6.summary: One fine morning, a rich miller awoke because the great millwheel had stopped.

notes.label: fürbass
notes.text: an old regional word meaning onward or farther ahead; the maiden continues steadily toward the castle without turning to the voices behind her.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

10c1fd626efbb3efdee0a89a0598c3672efd86f1.summary: Of this matter there would indeed be much to write and say. Some such fiery spirits have appeared to living people in such a way that one could distinctly see the human figure and shape of a dead, already withered and emaciated human body, some directly before their eyes.

notes.label: Zeine
notes.text: an old Alemannic word for a woven basket or wicker container; the image seems to be fire shining through an open weave, though the precise object is not identified.

notes.label: Rütti
notes.text: a clearing made by cutting and often burning woodland; the glowing spirit is compared to a charred stump left there.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: old plural for boundary markers or boundary lines, not the modern German word Märchen meaning folktales; moving them was a grave offense against one’s neighbors.

notes.label: Züsler
notes.text: a local name for flickering or sizzling fiery apparitions; the spelling varies as Züslern and Züsslern in the historical source.

notes.label: Hagmarch
notes.text: a boundary marked by a hedge; the tale links a displaced hedge boundary to the unrest of a dead soul.

notes.label: Rosen
notes.text: an unclear historical comparison for the fiery spirit’s curved flight; the wording may evoke a firework or another sweeping light, but the source does not resolve it.

notes.label: Büsser
notes.text: literally penitents or atoners; here they are dead souls undergoing punishment and appearing as fiery wandering men.

a5e6d24a6827a8e7362ad49de60badc7a115551e.summary: He was actually a man of Schwyz, but for many summers he stayed ennet der Märcht on the Urnerboden.

notes.label: ennet der Märcht
notes.text: a local phrase meaning ‘on the far side of the Märcht,’ probably a boundary or named boundary locality; the source does not specify which legal or geographic line is meant.

notes.label: Urnerboden
notes.text: the high valley and extensive seasonal pasture belonging to Uri beyond the Klausen Pass, despite its access from the Glarus side; it is a working pastoral region rather than merely a village street.

notes.label: Ries
notes.text: the challenger’s name, which also means ‘giant’ in German; the narrator explicitly exploits that coincidence by saying he was a literal giant in size and strength.

notes.label: Schwingen
notes.text: traditional Swiss wrestling in which opponents grip special breeches and try to throw each other; this legendary private match is made lethal and unregulated, unlike the modern festival sport.

90342d0b7fb6d23d42d6158fafd0e4d40187f598.summary: Because landholdings in the Werdenberg region are greatly subdivided, in autumn cattle usually cannot be grazed freely but only gestumpet.

notes.label: gestumpet
notes.text: tether-grazed by fastening each animal to a movable stake, a practice suited to highly subdivided parcels where free grazing is impossible.

notes.label: Hafte
notes.text: the rotating tether, two to three meters long, by which an animal is fastened to a stake while grazing.

notes.label: gibt man nach
notes.text: literally ‘one gives more’ or ‘lets out,’ here the local expression for moving the stake after the nearby grass has been eaten.

notes.label: Stümper
notes.text: the source's form for dishonest living tether-grazers who place stakes so their cattle trespass; it is not being used in the modern sense of an incompetent person.

notes.label: Stumper
notes.text: people or spirits who practice stumpen, grazing cattle while each animal is tethered to a movable stake; the title's plural identifies both the occupation and its punished dead.

notes.label: Studner-Riet
notes.text: the marsh or wet meadow associated with Studen; Riet denotes reed land, fen, or marshy ground.

notes.label: Stadtner-Riet
notes.text: the marsh or wet meadow associated with the local Stadtner area; like Studner-Riet, it is a place from which the punished spirits are heard.

notes.label: Marchenrücker
notes.text: literally ‘boundary-marker movers,’ the body text's regional spelling for people condemned after fraudulently shifting property boundaries.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: plural boundary markers or boundary lines, related to the Swiss regional word March; the dead repeatedly try and fail to restore them.

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: the title's spelling for people who move boundary markers, literally ‘boundary movers’; the body uses the variant Marchenrücker.

c4f2de9632a419a77f25c0818b754010b5b5174c.summary: it is said that in ancient times a Jewish man mined ore there, smelted it, and refined it.

notes.label: Häfen
notes.text: in this Alpine German context, large pots, cauldrons, or vessels rather than modern harbor basins; the treasure consists of three such containers filled with different metals.

notes.label: Schmelzi
notes.text: a regional diminutive or site-name for a small smelting works or smelting place; the charcoal is taken as evidence that ore was once processed there.

notes.label: Judsfad
notes.text: the historical local place-name used by the source in the Meiental, apparently formed from an older word for a Jewish person and a path or site-name element; the precise toponymic history is uncertain, and modern readers should recognize the period ethnic label rather than treat it as neutral current usage.

32777594f244b1de7d7964a2c921cded53440de8.summary: The following is told in the Simmental about the Türsten-Gjäg.

notes.label: Türsten-Gjäg
notes.text: a Simmental dialect name meaning approximately “Türst’s Hunt,” a regional form of the Wild Hunt or spectral host; Gjäg denotes the hunt, while the story does not describe Türst himself.

notes.label: Kiltgang
notes.text: a traditional nighttime courtship visit in rural German-speaking Switzerland, when a young man went to see a sweetheart; customs varied by region, and here it simply places the encounter on his way to her.

9d3264e8b5e09d2d601cf7ea0b73bf154016d4e7.summary: In the Untertal, the pre-glacial valley of the Schilz, beneath the great Gufel, wild people once lived.

notes.label: Gufel
notes.text: a cave, rock shelter, or large overhanging recess in Alpine usage; the wild people live beneath this prominent natural shelter.

notes.label: Grohbergerin
notes.text: a woman from Grohberg; the source later spells the same designation Grotzbergerin, and both historical forms are retained rather than silently harmonized.

notes.label: wildes Weiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little wild woman,’ the female member of the poor, harmless wild people who rewards the woman's kindness with leaves that become gold.

notes.label: Grotzbergerin
notes.text: the second spelling in the source for the woman earlier called Grohbergerin; it appears to denote the same person, but the textual variation is preserved.

notes.label: Bettlaub
notes.text: dry leaves gathered for filling bedding or serving as stable litter; the woman mistakes the supernatural gift for this ordinary low-value material.

c632d204e406329b275f6d51aeee29ec48ee8d6d.summary: 1. A great treasure is hidden on the Flüeli (Zwing-Uri) near Amsteg; if it were found, the whole canton of Uri would be rich enough.

notes.label: verlochet
notes.text: an Alpine German verb meaning concealed, stowed, or hidden away, especially underground; the source presents the treasure as deliberately cached during wartime.

notes.label: Franzosenzeit
notes.text: literally the ‘French period,’ the regional historical name for the era of French invasion, occupation, and political upheaval around 1798; the account does not date the treasure's burial more precisely.

notes.label: Reissack
notes.text: the source's spelling for the sack full of money; it may literally mean a rice sack or reflect another regional sack term, but its material and former contents are not specified.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: Swiss German for a goat boy, a young herder responsible for goats; the prophecy makes such a poor working child the treasure's eventual finder.

notes.label: Brawä
notes.text: an uncertain Uri dialect landscape term, probably a steep grassy bank, brow, or slope; it locates the three buried chests above the Stössialp.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: in central Swiss mineral culture, fine rock-crystal points or crystal specimens sought by Strahler; the word does not mean ordinary rays of light here.

notes.label: Z'Mitte August
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘in the middle of August’; the belief fixes the treasures' appearance to midday between 12 and 1.

945791f92d5ac7b666aee0513cb90b4f0ea96a49.summary: 1. Once, as a fahrender Schüler passed Abfrutt at Göschenen, he looked for a long time from the millstream up toward the forest.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally an ‘itinerant scholar’ or ‘traveling student,’ but in Alpine treasure legend a wandering learned practitioner able to perceive hidden wealth and occult properties of the land.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep exposed Alpine rock face, cliff, or crag; the roadlike mark beneath the Fluh is said to indicate buried leather money.

notes.label: Fahrende Schüler
notes.text: the plural of fahrender Schüler, the several wandering learned practitioners whose revelations about hidden treasure are collected under the title.

92dc6f46483373f27385e0ebecba20956499d322.summary: The hill on which the castle of the lords of Sellenbüren once stood is called the Ofengüpf by the farmers in the village of Sellenbüren near Zürich.

notes.label: Ofengüpf
notes.text: the local hill-name, literally something like ‘oven crest’ or ‘stove-shaped summit’; Güpf is a Swiss word for a peak or top, but the source does not explain why the castle hill bears this name.

4cc8433c6496573e876eb7af4abf74f431a5a2d7.summary: a) In the woods near Geezig above Seedorf, a hunter had shot a fox and put it in his rucksack.

notes.label: Handbräntli
notes.text: a small portable wooden dairy container fitted for carrying by hand; the shot fox turns into an old, battered one, while the exact size and construction are not specified.

notes.label: Bräntä
notes.text: a regional wooden vessel or carrying tub, often worn on the back for transporting milk, water, or other material; variant b grotesquely identifies the fox’s replacement as one used for manure.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fa8a04c74fe4e0d0ee1c1f639ac976a4cca31578.summary: According to an old legend of the people of Sargans, girls who through their own fault become old maids must assemble after death at the great marsh near Schaan in Liechtenstein.

notes.label: Grüsch
notes.text: Swiss German for bran or the coarse husks separated from milled grain; here the dead women receive the impossible penance of sorting it and tying its tiny heaps together.

116ea4e51b187642b7ed47249c3a7d8c21a569ab.summary: Few girls in the Bernese Oberland die as old maids. Almost every one soon finds her Uli or Heiri, with whom, as a tender and caring housewife and loving mother, she shares the joys and sorrows of this life.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

473a04f72727e5057fdbeab323e06918512f31a4.summary: That is, on a Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday in one of the Fronfasten weeks, people always said that one should not go out with a gun.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, traditional quarterly Catholic periods of fasting and prayer; the source specifies Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday of such weeks as the ‘old days’ on which one should not carry a gun.

notes.label: Hybi
notes.text: the source’s Uri plural for small caps or bonnets and its own gloss for what the shot foxes have become; the exact construction and material of these historical caps are not described.

notes.label: Hübä-n- und Chäppli
notes.text: the source’s Uri name for the old women’s headdress ensemble to which the Hybi belonged, approximately ‘hoods and little caps’; its precise historical arrangement is not described.

notes.label: Z'altä Tagg
notes.text: literally ‘on an old day,’ an Uri dialect expression for a Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday during a Fronfasten week; the quarterly Ember observances were treated as ritually charged times when ordinary activities such as hunting could become dangerous.

6a56c64aa966828fa1899655ddd1ecb0adfff1f4.summary: Hansli had a Fraueli named Bethli, and Bethli had a husband named Hansli. Hansli and Bethli were both thoroughly respectable people, and both could eat a thoroughly respectable amount of bread.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Frau, meaning a ‘little wife,’ ‘dear wife,’ or simply ‘woman’ in a familiar register; the source’s tone can be affectionate or gently comic rather than literally describing Bethli’s size.

notes.label: Rouft
notes.text: an Aargau dialect word for the hard outer crust or end portion of bread in this context; its exact regional loaf form is not specified.

notes.label: Mutsche
notes.text: the softer inner bread or crumb portion contrasted with the Rouft in this story; elsewhere related Swiss forms can name a small loaf, so the precise local form remains uncertain.

notes.label: Vergöustig
notes.text: an uncommon Aargau dialect expression for the fatal wasting or deprivation caused here by the couple’s stubborn contention over food; its finer historical nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: Gott bhüet is dervor
notes.text: ‘God preserve us from that,’ a Swiss German protective closing formula that turns the couple’s absurd fate into a warning for listeners.

notes.label: Brodässe
notes.text: Aargau Swiss German for ‘bread-eating’; the title announces a comic tale built around the two couples’ incompatible preferences for parts of a loaf.

c38fc853d9ea72ee31b342476e4453e2b801de04.summary: On Castle Hill near Rohrbach, before every thunderstorm one hears howling, cracking whips, and a rattling wagon at the very spot where the former lord of the castle wished to build an enormous bridge.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

62632ca42e420e1fd5cdc23d10c35fce4fce4bfe.summary: Fahrende Schüler looked through the Bergspiegel into the rock wall and discovered immeasurable treasures of gold and silver there, as they did at the higher Steienwand and in the Goldloch of nearby Alp Sennis.

notes.label: Fahrende Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘traveling scholars,’ a folkloric class of itinerant learned magicians credited with secret books, divination, and treasure-finding; they are not simply modern students on a journey.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a magical or divinatory viewing instrument said to reveal treasures inside mountains; the account does not describe its physical construction.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Sennis
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture of Sennis; Alp denotes an Alpine grazing landscape and settlement, not merely a summit.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians,’ the Alpine folkloric name for mysterious foreign mineral prospectors believed able to find and transform valuable ores; it may refer to legendary treasure seekers rather than ordinary residents of Venice.

notes.label: Beguinenkloster
notes.text: a Beguine religious house or convent-like community for lay religious women; it was not necessarily a formally vowed monastic order, so ‘nunnery’ would be imprecise.

c79bf87daa450e25351b28c7dd07f1d8fcbb9839.summary: In the year 1871, when during the months of June, July, and August I was assisting Herr Alex.

notes.label: sich künden
notes.text: literally to announce or make oneself known; here it names the belief that a dying person’s soul can signal or appear to someone emotionally close at a distance.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, where Herr Hauser receives the news that is relayed to the narrator.

d3c6c8147f1ef890f0518c1829c80b0a9f2a85e3.summary: in the Etzlital, something used to drive the livestock out with stones on the final evening before the Alpabfahrt.

notes.label: Alpabfahrt
notes.text: the practical and often ceremonial autumn descent of livestock and herders from the high summer pasture; the haunting occurs on the last evening before that departure.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its grazing rights, huts, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain peak; Culma is the named pasture in this fragment.

fab053652195ce60786c88b660c8927310c78554.summary: The first bells at Silenen—the great bell at Spiringen—were cast in the Streissrütti, on the Achern.

notes.label: About this telling

4f986da36aef139595f602d745f75364d48bfea9.summary: a) In Gibelflüh, people hung little red coats and cloaks on the door as gifts for the Erdmännchen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ Erdmännchen are subterranean household and farm helpers who withdraw when mocked, deceived, or given clothing; whether the episodes treat them as the same beings is uncertain.

notes.label: Ziberlisturm
notes.text: literally a ‘Ziberli mound or tower,’ Ziberlisturm is the porridge dish rewarded to the earth folk, apparently containing or leaving small stones; its ingredients and the meaning of Ziberli are uncertain.

notes.label: Erdleute
notes.text: literally ‘earth people,’ Erdleute is another collective name for the small supernatural helpers; the source does not specify a distinction from Erdmännchen or Erdleutchen.

notes.label: Erdleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ Erdleutchen names the male and female barn helpers associated with a cave; its relationship to the other two names is uncertain.

notes.label: Futtertenne
notes.text: the Futtertenne is the barn floor or bay where fodder is handled and where milk and bread are set as wages; its exact layout is unspecified.

notes.label: auf der Stör
notes.text: auf der Stör describes an artisan, here a tailor, working temporarily in the customer’s home rather than in a permanent shop; the duration and payment of this visit are unspecified.

d7e85527eae59ec7ffcbfd70d141719ddea93162.summary: Before the railway was built, livestock leased out for Sömmerung in the Glarus Alps was driven from Flums over the passes at Schönbühl and Wissmil.

notes.label: Sömmerung
notes.text: the seasonal summering of livestock on high pastures, including the grazing rights or arrangement by which outside cattle are taken onto an Alp.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial or practical seasonal drive of livestock up to an Alp; here two farmers plan the difficult cross-pass journey together.

notes.label: Wetterhut
notes.text: a broad protective weather hat worn against mountain rain or snow; on the dark figure, it also signals the storm about to arrive.

notes.label: Stollen
notes.text: the named slope, spur, or passage toward which the apparition drives the cattle; the source does not clarify whether it is a mine-like tunnel or merely the local terrain name.

notes.label: Irrkraut
notes.text: literally ‘straying herb,’ Irrkraut is a folkloric plant believed to cause disorientation or magical wandering, often identified here with fern; the exact species and mechanism are uncertain.

notes.label: Vom Irrchrut
notes.text: Vom Irrchrut is the dialect title of a related account, approximately ‘Of the Straying Herb,’ referenced but not reproduced here; its exact contents and relationship to this commentary are unspecified.

3bda2ce37f6b2f7d57c1d091dc6455383e11c0ec.summary: On the Oberplegi Alp at the Glärnisch, which is now covered by glacier ice, there once lived an alpine dairyman who had sinned with a maiden named Kathrin.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

5f9459cc481f2839588fe1961a068f19d10eff91.summary: A treasure is buried on the Schatzbödeli, or Burgli, in the Ysleren at Attinghausen.

notes.label: Schatzbödeli
notes.text: literally a ‘little treasure ground’ or small treasure plot, the local place-name in the Ysleren where the buried hoard is said to sink away when the diggers leave it.

83277e1049f9e96214564346261f7246a36e4356.summary: On the Surenen Alps between Engelberg and Uri, there is a curious tradition that attributes the mountain pasture's reversion to wilderness to a different sacrilege.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a traditional German-speaking folktale figure imagined as an itinerant student or cleric versed in occult knowledge and secret arts; here he supplies the ritual solution to the monster.

9fa15ab0ab317e7faf12094e26a1c0a2d1a81bfd.summary: In the municipality of Erstfeld, a subterranean lake is hidden beneath the Wanneli Alp, and if it ever breaks out, all of Ripshausen will perish.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Wanneli is the named Alp above the threatened settlement.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a German-language folklore figure credited with occult learning and secret knowledge; here he reveals the hidden lake and its future danger.

00252b2b184f72183a36717e4fdc600a8c6d7f68.summary: 1. Yes, yes, Father, you are already saying that clergymen were never capable of such a thing, but then you are a clergyman too.

notes.label: Zurücktreiben
notes.text: literally ‘driving back’; in Uri legend it is a coercive magical practice, often attributed to clergy or sorcerers, that compels a thief to return stolen property, sometimes under mortal supernatural threat if the owner fails to receive it.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; here he brings butter down for market, but his precise Alpine occupation is not stated.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: Swiss German for butter; here it is produced on the high pasture, carried in large loads, and sold at the dedicated market in Altdorf.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain summit; several episodes take place in this working pastoral landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Trinkel
notes.text: a regional name for a resonant livestock bell, especially a cowbell used on Alpine pastures; the exact local bell form is not specified here.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine farm building or compartment that may serve as a byre, barn bay, or storage room; here the closed door and the farmer's work suggest a livestock or farm outbuilding, but its exact internal use is unstated.

notes.label: Kilbi
notes.text: a Swiss parish fair or annual church-dedication feast, traditionally marked by communal festivity; the theft occurs on the eve of this local celebration.

notes.label: Gabelen
notes.text: a regional carrying frame worn on the back for transporting a load; here the frame is stolen together with its load of Anken, though its precise construction is not described.

notes.label: zähetusig Rittertag
notes.text: this Bernese dialect name means the feast day of the Ten Thousand Knights and marks the annual ghost procession; the precise local date and saints’ tradition intended are uncertain.

3f0cd1836a1411b2e1bea0895c2c2dd6fa539aa1.summary: The Villasurer—or people of Filisur—know very well what a fine thing dear sunshine is, ever since they discovered that, when the glories of the earth were divided, they had received rather too little of that splendid gift, sunlight.

notes.label: Villasurer
notes.text: the source’s local name for the people of Filisur, which it also supplies in parentheses; the humorous tale makes them ingenious fools.

notes.label: Holzteuchel
notes.text: bored wooden pipes or conduits traditionally used to carry water; the joke has the villagers pipe sunshine through them instead.

notes.label: Gulden
notes.text: a historical currency unit; the source specifies that the quoted price uses old Graubünden money.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: a small historical coin and subdivision used with the Gulden; the exact price of 6 Gulden and 48 Kreuzer is preserved.

bc9a27da66fb72eadf89391c1d860883604af1ee.summary: 1. Father Egger in Römerstalden was once walking home from Morschach late at night.

notes.label: Kemletzenkapelle
notes.text: the source-exact local chapel name near Römerstalden, literally the Kemletzen Chapel; the story places the death omen on the nearby road.

notes.label: bim verhyttä Stei
notes.text: the source's second local name for the place by the Seikberg footbridge, literally something like ‘by the accursed stone’; the precise force of verhyttä and the location's history are uncertain.

notes.label: Schlampihut
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for the apparition's drooping or slouching hat; its exact historical style and material are not specified.

notes.label: Häuri
notes.text: one of two uncertain Uri labels for the headless-looking apparition above the fir tree; the account describes its glowing forehead disk but does not establish the word's literal sense or the being's class.

notes.label: Wäuti
notes.text: an Uri name for an uncanny being or nocturnal bogey; here it is an alternative label for the indistinct, apparently headless apparition, whose exact nature remains unresolved.

notes.label: Aveläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the Ave or Angelus bell, here the morning church bell that marks the revelers' reunion rather than an ordinary secular summons.

notes.label: z'altä Wochen
notes.text: literally ‘in the old weeks,’ the local calendrical expression here explicitly identified with a Wednesday in one of the Fronfasten periods.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the traditional quarterly Ember Days or Ember fasts in the Catholic calendar; Swiss folklore often treats these observances as times of heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a sociable evening visit or farmhouse-parlor gathering, often associated with visiting, music, shared work, or courtship; this man is traveling to one at night.

311b5f98d58f621555df63d96125de705d13ff3e.summary: In the land of Unterwalden there is a mountain path that winds upward through a wildly broken wasteland of stone.

notes.label: Rissenen
notes.text: this Alpine terrain term appears to denote broken scree runs or erosion chutes crossed by avalanches; its exact distinction from the neighboring Runsen is uncertain.

notes.label: Runsen
notes.text: Runsen are steep gullies or channels down which water, debris, or avalanches descend; their precise form along this unnamed path is uncertain.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Marienfäden
notes.text: literally ‘Mary’s threads,’ this devotional folk-name denotes fine gossamer interpreted as the Virgin’s protective veil; the exact natural material observed is uncertain.

notes.label: Wildheuer
notes.text: Wildheuer are cutters of wild hay on steep, uncultivated Alpine slopes, a hazardous traditional occupation; the source does not specify which slopes they used here.

cc089d816474347580804394f30c157505e97833.summary: According to popular belief, it comes from the little monastery that is said to have stood in olden times in the ‘Nonnenbaumert,’ in the Balgach forest.

notes.label: Nonnenbaumert
notes.text: a local place-name approximately connected with a ‘nuns' orchard’ or tree enclosure; the former little monastery is located there, but the name's exact dialect components and land use are uncertain.

99153da201ed7ad1ea57470b3196a10db24b9f02.summary: In the 17th century, almost all the inhabitants of the little mountain village of Schuders died of a plague-like disease after a herdsman brought the affliction down from the Alpe.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working settlement; the herdsman sleeps there outdoors before carrying the illness down to the village.

061444c02c3cff478bf83e8718b42eb2e02c80ef.summary: At the Rinkenberg estate in the Weisstannental, a man had died, and the bailiff sent his servant there to fetch the finest cow from the stable.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Besthaupt
notes.text: a feudal death-duty entitling the lord or bailiff to the deceased tenant’s best head of livestock; both the animal and the customary legal claim are contained in the term.

d6d453813babfa4d36d72e14971e8c48239a332e.summary: Do you know the Paradise in Bündnerland?

notes.text: the land or country of the Bündner, meaning Graubünden; the poem addresses a ruined place within the canton that bears the ironic name Paradise.

85523a7407980a0fa2b7a5c44e911bf39d0d8192.summary: Dean Georg Salutz, at one time pastor in Cur, distinguished himself through his great learning and affable nature as well as through his gigantic strength.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, the capital of Graubünden and the place of Salutz’s ministry.

notes.label: lupfen
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German verb meaning to lift or raise; the source itself glosses it as lifting upward.

notes.label: Kaufmannsstück
notes.text: literally a “merchant’s piece,” here a very heavy commercial package or piece of merchandise; the source does not identify its contents.

notes.label: auflupfen
notes.text: a related Swiss verb meaning to lift something up or onto a higher surface; the carters challenge Salutz to raise the Kaufmannsstück onto the wagon.

notes.label: Mulinära
notes.text: the local place-name used for the location between it and Trimmis; the source provides no closer identification.

notes.label: abhaldig
notes.text: a regional adjective meaning sloping or on a descent; it explains why the stalled sawlog is difficult to move.

notes.label: Trämel
notes.text: a heavy log or timber intended for sawing, glossed by Jecklin as Sägenholz.

notes.label: ab Stätt
notes.text: a regional phrase meaning “from the spot” or “from where it stands,” as Jecklin’s own gloss explains.

notes.label: wättete
notes.text: a regional verb meaning that the farmer loosened or unhitched the ox from its harness; the source glosses the form as löste.

notes.label: Stadal
notes.text: an uncertain local term for the part or point to which Salutz attaches the yoke; Jecklin gives no gloss, so the physical detail is left unresolved.

notes.label: einwätten
notes.text: the corresponding regional verb for hitching or yoking the ox in again after Salutz has moved the log.

notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. 9d9a0cd03f73ff4813b451439f53c0fcd251b46d.summary: a) Southwest of the city of Lucerne, toward Unterwalden, Mount Pilatus, full of wild beauty, many-peaked and jagged as it is, raises its highest pinnacle to 6700 Zoll (= 2119 m); others stand beside it toward east and west, almost every one distinctive in form and legend.

notes.text: literally an historical inch measure, yet the source equates 6700 Zoll with 2119 m, which is dimensionally inconsistent and likely reflects a source or transcription problem; both the printed unit and supplied metric value are retained without silent correction.

notes.label: Risinen
notes.text: steep slopes or channels of loose rock debris in Swiss Alpine usage; the mountain path crosses them on its approach to the bare walls.

notes.label: Runsen
notes.text: erosion gullies or torrent channels cut down a mountainside; paired with Risinen, the term evokes unstable Pilatus terrain.

notes.label: Windsbraut
notes.text: literally ‘bride of the wind,’ a traditional personification of a violent whirlwind or storm; Cysat compares the rushing nocturnal spirits with it.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: detached barns, storehouses, or livestock buildings; people fear that the storm-host will carry these rural structures away with everything else.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the Alpine dairy hut where a Senn processes milk and where travelers can receive fresh pastoral food.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face or cliff in Swiss landscape usage; the Dominiloch opens in the face of one beneath the Widderfeld.

notes.label: Gemsmätteli
notes.text: literally a ‘little chamois meadow,’ the rocky Alpine place reached after crossing gullies and sheep pastures; the diminutive Mätteli denotes a small meadow.

notes.label: Gnepfstein
notes.text: the named rocking stone on the Mittagsgüpfi associated with the conjurer's struggle; its first element is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Schwungsteine
notes.text: literally ‘swinging’ or ‘rocking stones,’ large balanced stones that can be made to rock and sound with little effort but are difficult to dislodge.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a learned itinerant magician in Alpine legend who can exorcise and bind spirits; Schüler here does not mean an ordinary schoolchild.

notes.label: Pilat wirf us din Kath
notes.text: the provocative Swiss German call means approximately ‘Pilatus, throw out your filth/dung’; Kath is an old spelling for excrement or muck, and the taunt is said to provoke the lake spirit into storms and floods.

notes.label: Domini
notes.text: the name given to the apparently human stone figure guarding the cave; the source offers legends about it but no secure derivation of the name.

notes.label: Frostaffel
notes.text: the named Stafel or Alpine pasture station below the Dominiloch; the source does not explain the Fro- element or the site's exact pastoral level.

notes.label: unser Cornel
notes.text: literally ‘our Cornel,’ an alternative familiar local name for Domini's stone figure; Cornel is a personal name, but the source does not identify a historical person.
