c0062b11e94fc52715505e03661de30fa1cb9a78.summary: a) At the time when the bubonic plague prevailed in Uri, a wealthy young lady lived in the old stone house at Trudelingen and also owned property in Flüelen.

notes.label: Schellenkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Schellen, resonant livestock bells; counting nine such lead or bell cows as nine Sennten conveys the scale of whole herds inherited during the plague.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: plural of Senntum or Sennten, an Alpine dairy herd understood as a managed cattle collective; the equation with nine bell cows suggests nine separate herds rather than nine individual cattle.

notes.label: Nynänynzg
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘ninety-nine’ within the plague lament ‘Is that not a great (a bitter) lament, ninety-nine in one grave (77 maidens in one grave)’; the source preserves alternatives in parentheses and writes ninety-nine as a dialect number word but 77 as digits.

notes.label: Tohlä
notes.text: a regional architectural word for a small opening, chute, hatch, or passage through which isolated plague patients received food; the source does not specify its precise construction.

notes.label: Ähä, d'Bylä chunnt wider
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Aha, the boil is coming again’; Bylä names both the plague swelling and, mockingly, the little cloud believed to carry the disease.

notes.label: Pürli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little, poor, or humble farmer; it indicates modest rural status and does not establish the old person’s physical size or gender beyond the source’s grammar.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a girl or young woman; in these plague accounts it can also label an unmarried older woman, so the precise age must be taken from each context rather than from the word alone.

notes.label: versehnaagget
notes.text: an obscure Uri form describing the living woman’s unnoticed crawl or escape from the corpse collectors; the context establishes that she got away, but the word’s exact manner or etymology is uncertain.

notes.label: Trychelkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Trycheln, the deep-toned sheet-metal livestock bells used in Swiss pastoral culture; inheriting ten or nine such cows signals substantial plague-era property transfer.

notes.label: Trinkelkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Trinkel bells, generally smaller livestock bells; the distinct source spelling is retained rather than silently merged with Trychelkühe.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy work; here the Senn of Niederalp has just called the Alp household to prayer when the warning voice answers.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Enzen
notes.text: a plant or plant-based remedy named by the spirit as protection against plague, probably related to regional gentian names; the source does not securely identify a modern species.

notes.label: Strenzen
notes.text: a plant or plant-based remedy named by the spirit as protection against plague; its precise botanical identity is not established by this source.

notes.label: Bibernell
notes.text: a historical German plant name commonly associated with burnet or pimpernel species and medicinal use; this tale does not identify the exact plant or preparation intended.

457e28be4251719db00f5cdc1e560e5265623353.summary: In 1565, a grievous pestilence raged so cruelly that only 93 people remained in the village of Mosnang: 30 whom God had graciously spared from so terrible an evil; 33 who had been struck by the grievous plague but had risen again fresh and healthy; and 30 who were so weak that they could never be…

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

notes.label: Kirchweihe
notes.text: the anniversary feast of a church's dedication, often observed as a local festival; the account measures the plague period from St. Verena's Day in 1565 through this feast in 1569.

notes.label: Pfarrkinder
notes.text: literally ‘parish children,’ an older pastoral term for the members or parishioners of a parish rather than only young people.

notes.label: Mesner
notes.text: a parish sacristan or sexton responsible for church service and practical duties; here multiple Mesner assist amid the epidemic and themselves become ill.

notes.label: Totenbaum
notes.text: literally a ‘dead person's tree’ or ‘death tree,’ a historical term for a coffin, reflecting its wooden construction; one had already been prepared for a man mistakenly thought dead.

notes.label: Kreuzgänge
notes.text: religious processions, often penitential or supplicatory and associated with the cross; Mosnang vows three such communal observances along the village's four roads.

notes.label: Bitt- und Bußgänge
notes.text: supplicatory and penitential processions undertaken to ask divine aid and express repentance; the cited devotional booklet prescribes the three plague-vow observances.

d17c2e888cf968681ef941f5d5c55986d9930089.summary: In Jonschwil, 332 people died of the plague—that is, most of them in Oberuzwil, which at the time was still kirchgenössig to Jonschwil.

notes.label: kirchgenössig
notes.text: belonging to the same parish or ecclesiastical community; Oberuzwil was then served by and church-affiliated with Jonschwil rather than politically absorbed into it.

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard Swiss canton abbreviation for St. Gallen, included in the catalogue title to locate Jonschwil.

8439a0a35e395c023b6332d24da6df2d457f3536.summary: It is said that the Devil plays music for everyone who hangs himself. Indeed, a man cut down alive from the rope is said to have fiercely abused his rescuers, for never in his life had he heard such merry dance music.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

591446faa1ac3fb5b74c733cbb0edb6018454257.summary: On Hanig, the Alp belonging to Grächen, the Bozo is said often to have played its tricks on the Sennu and the herdsman even when the Senntum-Veeh were there.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for a bogey, haunting spirit, or frightening supernatural being; here it is the unseen poltergeist troubling an Alpine herd, and the word does not identify a more precise class of spirit.

notes.label: Sennu
notes.text: a Valais dialect form of Senn, the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and dairy work on a seasonal pasture; the source’s shifting grammatical forms leave the worker’s exact rank and number somewhat uncertain.

notes.label: Senntum-Veeh
notes.text: Valais dialect for the cattle belonging to a Senntum, an organized Alpine herd and dairying unit; “herd cattle” is the closest sense, but it does not convey the unit’s seasonal economic and social organization.

notes.label: Senntum-Chessi
notes.text: the large kettle used by a Senntum for Alpine dairy work, especially cheese making; here the spirit taps on it, and the vessel’s precise size and local construction are unstated.

notes.label: Hellblata
notes.text: Valais dialect, literally a “hell ledge” or “plate of hell,” used here for the lowest level or shelf of hell in a curse; it is a vivid local spatial image rather than a formally defined theological place.

573c5b05ea6352673c80b3ffde0ce28f7046ae33.summary: Such a Poltergeist formerly showed itself in a well-known house. During Advent and Fronfasten, its banging was often heard.

notes.label: Poltergeist
notes.text: literally a ‘banging spirit’ in German; although now familiar in English, the word here specifically describes a household spirit known through loud impacts and a visible stable apparition.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the traditional quarterly Ember fasts of the Western Christian calendar; pairing them with Advent places the haunting in ritually charged periods of fasting and seasonal transition.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ a folk-Catholic expression for a dead soul awaiting release from purgatorial suffering; it implies that the haunting seeks deliverance, not merely that the spirit is pitiable.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

1e5fce9d603649b6410b03d61c5cbd1448b17d55.summary: In Surava stands a house in which no fire burns at night. Anyone who wishes to spend the night in this house hears wood being split until morning in the chamber adjoining the room where he hopes to rest.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the bench built beside or around a masonry room stove, traditionally a warm resting place; the house’s spirits throw down anyone who tries to sleep upon it.

2056ad31bd59b8efe22b8bb379aea1c35e22a473.summary: A herdsman from Mels had a cow on the alp of Foo. It would not remain with the herd, and the Küher had to keep it constantly in view.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cowherd responsible for tending and milking cattle on a seasonal pasture; here the Küher’s negligent failure to guard one cow binds him after death to carry it back up, though his relation to the other herdsmen is not specified.

9439c6b847981e4f040a6156f0811415be70b3f0.summary: 1. In the Träs Valley beyond the boundary, a light was often seen at night moving some distance upward, first following the path and then entering the valley, where it vanished.

notes.label: Schloffen
notes.text: a local or dialect topographic term for passages, clefts, lanes, or narrow ways; the young man walks through them beneath the Zingel, but the account does not define the terrain more precisely.

9f96119e074401a890b90fc031be67b593f8c3c2.summary: In the year 1845, there were very many Erdäpfel, or potatoes; but a large portion of them were rotten or diseased.

notes.label: Erdäpfel
notes.text: literally ‘earth apples,’ a regional German word for potatoes; its use here preserves the St. Gallen wording and the period voice of the account of the 1845 crop disease.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

246f01ffdd94212408c7aab16f019156e6c47c0a.summary: The Sagenbach flows through the Sennis alpine pasture at Tscherlach. It leads upward into a rocky recess between the Sichli and the Gamsberg.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians’; in Alpine mining lore, mysterious foreign prospectors credited with recognizing and secretly removing valuable ores that local people overlooked.

49a422cc7b6a88a295c2084c47253e64253ff681.summary: At certain times, a dull thunder like cannon fire sounds out from the Rothorn and the Änziflue into the Lucerne countryside.

notes.label: About this telling

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

34d4a20835226c3a476f2885ad51764d7775840d.summary: Many tales circulate among the people about processions of the dead and midnight wanderings of spirits.

notes.label: Temper-(Quatember-) Kinder
notes.text: literally ‘Ember children,’ people born during the Church’s quarterly Ember periods and traditionally believed in parts of Switzerland to possess second sight; here they can foresee processions of the dead, though local beliefs about the term vary.

notes.label: Todesangstglöcklein
notes.text: literally ‘little death-agony bell’; at St. Theodul’s it is the bell rung when someone dies, reinforcing the church’s association with the nocturnal dead.

6eeb0a1267394e7931cfe667c26bbf5a24469363.summary: After a hailstorm, people went outside and inquisitively examined the hailstones.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

95999ce837c705e3017f1d0f898100a34d945128.summary: A girl in an Abendsitzstube, where spindles were turning busily and much was told about apparitions of the dead, Bozen, and goblins, boasted of her fearlessness.

notes.label: Abendsitzstube
notes.text: the room used for an Abendsitz, an evening gathering devoted to spinning, shared work, conversation, and storytelling; the girl's wager grows from this communal setting.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: regional bogey spirits, apparitions, or goblins used in frightening tales; the form is plural here, and its exact creature type can vary by locality.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

0c1628cdf32ce9698f2ea406e18205b48d19d537.summary: Purgatory is said to have once been on earth. The poor souls wandered about in human form with blue lights, and also as dogs, cats, etc.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

7beec6cfe173aa524259704636c99ce0159744d0.summary: In former times, the land from the Reuss as far as France was called Burgundy.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Kunkel
notes.text: a distaff, the staff on which unspun flax is held while thread is drawn and wound onto a spindle; Queen Bertha's portable spinning equipment symbolizes exemplary household industry.

notes.label: Wälschland
notes.text: a German-speaking Swiss term for French- or Romance-speaking country, often especially western Switzerland; here its exact geographic extent is not specified.

2187adfffeeaad73051bd9029524cf1b48eec992.summary: Already ninety years ago, people in Mels related that a young man had been severely pressed by a Schrättlig.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a St. Gallen night-pressing being akin to a nightmare demon; when trapped here it becomes first a bird and then a woman who marries its captor, leaving its gender, original form, and stated connection with Venice unresolved.

notes.label: Rabi Chrischtes Sackmässer
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Rabi Chrischte’s pocketknife,’ the object mysteriously left behind years before its owner arrives.

notes.label: Sackmässer
notes.text: Swiss German for a pocketknife.

notes.label: Allmäng
notes.text: dialect form of Allmend, communally held land or common pasture.

notes.label: Zähntschür
notes.text: literally ‘tithe barn,’ a barn used to store produce collected as tithes.

notes.label: E min Troscht
notes.text: an exclamation roughly ‘Oh, my consolation!’ expressing shock or astonishment.

notes.label: Ote
notes.text: dialect for breath; recognizing the impossible visitor takes the girl’s breath away.

notes.label: Gade
notes.text: a room, chamber, barn space, or small outbuilding; here it is the place where the soldier appeared at the table.

notes.label: Heriemersch
notes.text: an emphatic dialect exclamation of alarm or astonishment; its exact derivation and force are uncertain.

notes.label: z’Chile
notes.text: literally ‘to church,’ used here for going to church to marry.

notes.label: Eggs
notes.text: a dialect expression in the narrator’s figurative closing about household difficulty; its precise sense in this phrase is uncertain.

notes.label: Gredi
notes.text: an orderly course, groove, or proper track; the closing suggests that one demand follows another in family life.

7244ea9214c9c94dc9324dfe6c3e1bd99e7c64ce.summary: In the tenth century, Radbod founded a castle on his own estate in Aargau, called Habsburg (Hawk Castle, rocky nest), small but strong.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c90ffe92c7ddea36b23a82684945edd21b697252.summary: Above the vineyards of Hornussen in the Fricktal, at the height of the road, lies a place called Jn der Hand.

notes.label: Jn der Hand
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling of the local place name ‘In der Hand’; its literal meaning is ‘in the hand,’ but the tale does not explain the name’s origin.

notes.label: Rainhalden-Joggeli
notes.text: a diminutive byname meaning approximately ‘little Jakob of the Rainhalde,’ the resident ghost who appears as a crying bird or a green hunter; his human identity is not supplied.

notes.label: Finsterhölzli
notes.text: literally ‘little dark wood,’ a diminutive place name for the lower woodland where IHS is cut into beech trees as protection.

notes.label: Goldne Geisweg
notes.text: literally the ‘golden goat path,’ the local name of the route used by the supernatural golden goat; the source does not say whether goldne describes color, material, or treasure symbolism.

notes.label: goldnen Geisbrunnen
notes.text: literally the ‘golden goat spring’ or ‘golden goat fountain,’ the destination of the goat on the Geisweg; its physical form and location are not further described.

notes.label: Hudada!
notes.text: an imitated hunting cry associated with the spectral green hunter; its literal meaning is unclear, and mocking it provokes the pursuit.

notes.label: Hutte
notes.text: here a carrying frame, basket, or pack used by journeyman carpenters to haul their tools, not a dwelling hut; the exact regional design is unstated.

f2df20e12a419a1af492eaecf57a0b2e0d129bcc.summary: People in the countryside are often heard to say, “as rich as the Mötteli,” or “he has Möttelis Guet,” while knowing little of why.

notes.label: Möttelis Guet
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Mötteli’s property/wealth,’ a proverbial expression for exceptional riches.

notes.label: Rappestäh, genannt Mötteli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Rappenstein, called Mötteli,’ the imperial-style form connecting the family name with the castle.

notes.label: Möttelischloß
notes.text: literally ‘Mötteli castle,’ the later popular name of the castle formerly called Sulzberg.

notes.label: Güraschi
notes.text: a dialect borrowing from French courage, meaning nerve or bravery; no seeker has enough to confront the dog and kiss the maidens.

notes.label: Otier
notes.text: a dialect form of Untier, a monstrous or dreadful beast.

notes.label: Müttelis Geld
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Mötteli’s money,’ proverbial riches that can be discussed but not found.

eacd9433cd93319bc5b11217f0a0f3a18d0f6593.summary: Raubold was a loudmouthed rogue who had been forced to flee the Melchtal over worthless misdeeds.

notes.label: Beinschelle
notes.text: a large leg bell worn above the ankle; Raubold adds hanging chains to frighten people.

notes.label: Haslikind
notes.text: literally a ‘Hasli child,’ an affectionate regional name for the innocent girl from the Oberhasli.

notes.label: Felsenbalm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter or shallow overhang cave, both the girl's herb-gathering destination and Frau Ute's refuge.

notes.label: Drudin
notes.text: a female supernatural being associated with night pressure, witchcraft, or fate; here it is another designation for mysterious Frau Ute.

notes.label: Hilfjo
notes.text: a regional cry for help, heard by the girl as she approaches the attack.

notes.label: Mägdelein
notes.text: an older diminutive for a young maiden or girl, here the courageous Hasli rescuer.

notes.label: lötigen Kristallring
notes.text: a crystal ring described by the historical weight unit Lot; whether the adjective specifies its weight or quality is uncertain, but it transmits the matchmaking heat.

5f917e26b479dc35bd14942ad9fc619b424c2fe2.summary: When ravens, half starved and acting needy, come boldly into towns and villages, common people believe a time of high prices is at hand.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7021f4066a7327bcb21904853c2b387524de3ec8.summary: The old people sometimes said that the village of Realp had stood up on the Biel in ancient times.

notes.label: Allmeini
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for communally held land or common pasture, contrasted here with privately owned Eigä around the former village site.

notes.label: Frealp
notes.text: an older spoken form of the place-name Realp; the source’s footnote explains it as a redivision of the phrase uf Realp, while also recording the rarer form Ryalp.

7c108965f836b3b237f2886b02ce7752e6b05169.summary: In those unhappy days when, as elsewhere in the world, the Eidgenossen fought one another fiercely over religion, the old, many-towered city of Solothurn also divided into two religious parties.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘companions bound by oath,’ the historical confederates; the story stresses that religious enemies remain joined by their older covenant and friendships.

notes.label: Schultheiß
notes.text: the historical title of Solothurn's chief civic magistrate; Wengi's office combines responsibilities that modern English might divide between mayor and senior judge.

notes.label: 30. Weinmonat
notes.text: literally the ‘30th day of Wine Month,’ an older German name for October; the date therefore corresponds to October 30, 1533.

notes.label: Fünförtigen
notes.text: the people of the five Catholic cantons; the capitalized form treats the five-canton alliance as a collective group.

notes.label: fünförtigen Eidgenossen
notes.text: the confederates of the ‘five places’ or five Catholic cantons—Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, and Zug—acting together in the religious conflict.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: a German-speaking Swiss term for French- or Romance-speaking lands; here it refers broadly to the territories beyond the Gotthard where the men had fought together.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a low, broad wooden milk vessel; setting it astride the confessional border allows both sides to share the meal without formally yielding territory.

notes.label: Milchsuppe
notes.text: literally ‘milk soup,’ here the celebrated shared dish of Catholic milk and Reformed Zürich bread that symbolizes confederate fellowship across religious divisions.

notes.label: Friß uf dinem Erdrich!
notes.text: dialectal German for ‘Eat on your own soil!’; the mock rebuke turns a contested border into playful table etiquette rather than violence.

notes.label: Stadtmeister
notes.text: a historical senior city office, here held by Strasbourg's delegated mediator; ‘city master’ is literal, but the source does not define the exact constitutional rank.

8d7bc4e98c624e8e3ef1307d1c9a90b09858af7c.summary: All witches have watering eyes and red, inflamed eyelids. They inherited this from their mothers, who likewise practiced sorcery, and in the same way pass it on to their children.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Freienamte
notes.text: the source's historical dative form for the Aargau Freiamt, a regional and district name rather than the generic phrase ‘free office.’

notes.label: Weisen Weiber
notes.text: literally ‘wise women,’ an older label for women credited with occult or healing knowledge; the source connects their fiery gaze with the stigmatizing bodily traits it assigns to witches.

3f797d09f4c18fe096fd4da2628be6a4d8a4e568.summary: On the Rothenrain near Zeihen in the Fricktal, a farmer often encountered at night and in the early morning a white-clad maiden who wore a wreath in her hair and sang the line, “Joyfully to the choir of angels!” The farmer told his cleric and was advised that, as soon as the maiden returned and…
