2fbd8747a403465b65fdb2540068e81ace77416f.summary: The property of the Ortsgemeinde of Oberterzen extends far into that of Mols in the Weidtal.

notes.label: Ortsgemeinde
notes.text: in St. Gallen, an Ortsgemeinde is a local civic corporation historically holding communal property alongside the political municipality; its precise legal powers at the time of the dispute are uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

f51e4b57101604aa544ce42b3d3ee8ee879eb30a.summary: On the mountain road from Reigoldswyl toward Titterten stands the ruin of Reifenstein.

notes.label: Stillen-Freitag
notes.text: an older regional name in the source for Good Friday, literally the “silent Friday”; the apparition’s annual return is tied to this solemn Christian holy day.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: a diminutive spring or fountain; here it is the small water source in the meadow where the enchanted maiden washes each year.

notes.label: strählen
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic verb meaning to comb, groom, or dress hair; here the rescuer must comb the maiden’s hair despite the flames, not merely stroke it.

2c0e1e0c762b0e1115c7a8a4258b661b777b5667.summary: A poor, old, unsteady little man once visited the Malbun alp and imploringly asked the herders for a little buttermilk.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Cyprio
notes.text: the local plant name used in the curse for the reindeer lichen of this account; the story identifies the affected plant through its title, but the word’s literal origin and whether it once denoted a broader lichen or pasture plant are uncertain.

6b8107f862f410e0abc3fdea4272b00eaa4da40f.summary: St. Oswald’s Church is said to have been erected on the spot where a church built as early as the time of the plague is said to have stood.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical Swiss local magistrate or chief administrative official; here the Ammann travels together with Zug’s clerk to secure saints’ relics, though the office’s exact powers varied by canton and period.

59497a5cf2dd567c63482b9b960d4b459323f4fd.summary: Two men with tightly filled money belts came from the Lauis market and walked down through the dark Wassnerwald.

notes.label: Lauis
notes.text: an older German-language name for Lugano; the Lauis market was the market at Lugano, south of the Gotthard.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

f10836c669d5acf6828257b86e65f31154ff43e0.summary: Rentierflechte, together with Muttern and Ritz, was the best fodder of the Alps; the plants produced so much milk that the cows had to be milked three times daily.

notes.label: Rentierflechte
notes.text: reindeer lichen, the fodder lichen whose loss the curse explains; the source later gives the scientific spelling Cladonia ragniferina.

notes.label: Muttern
notes.text: a regional plural or collective name for alpine spignel, one of the highly milk-producing fodder plants restored by the counter-charm.

notes.label: Ritz
notes.text: a Graubünden German name for alpine plantain, Plantago alpina, and the other fodder plant restored by the counter-charm.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who work or pasture livestock on a high Alp, including herders and dairy workers rather than Alpine residents in general.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Cypro
notes.text: the name used for reindeer lichen in the first curse; the prose afterward uses Cyprian, and the word's origin is explicitly described as obscure.

notes.label: Cyprian
notes.text: the prose name for reindeer lichen in the legend; it corresponds to Cypro in the curse and was omitted from the restorative charm.

notes.label: Bünden
notes.text: an older German form of Graubünden, the Swiss canton where several of the plant-name variants are recorded.

notes.label: Fideri
notes.text: a Graubünden regional name for reindeer lichen.

notes.label: Massigge
notes.text: one Graubünden name given for Iceland moss, a lichen often confused with reindeer lichen.

notes.label: Masegga
notes.text: a variant Graubünden name given alongside Massigge for Iceland moss.

notes.label: Muttere
notes.text: a regional name for alpine spignel, identified in the source as Meum muttelina.

notes.label: Muttara
notes.text: a Romansh-derived regional form for alpine spignel, unrelated to German Mutter, ‘mother.’

notes.label: Alpenbärenwurz
notes.text: the German botanical name for alpine spignel, the aromatic alpine herb identified as Meum muttelina in the source.

notes.label: Mutteri
notes.text: another regional form in the alpine spignel name-family used across German-speaking Switzerland.

notes.label: Mutternen
notes.text: another regional form in the alpine spignel name-family used across German-speaking Switzerland.

notes.label: Rom-Blueme
notes.text: an Appenzell name for alpine spignel; Blueme means ‘flower,’ while Rom may reflect a regional or Romansh association.

notes.label: Rahm-Blume
notes.text: another Appenzell name for alpine spignel, literally ‘cream flower,’ evoking the plant's association with rich milk.

notes.label: Riz
notes.text: a variant of Ritz, the Graubünden German name for alpine plantain.

notes.label: Adelgras
notes.text: a Bernese Oberland name for alpine plantain, literally ‘noble grass.’

notes.label: Nadelgras
notes.text: another Bernese Oberland name for alpine plantain, literally ‘needle grass.’

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard abbreviation for the canton of St. Gallen, used in the parenthetical location attached to the title.

1ef51b3c91bc33a55ab01243ce213d870e09fcd8.summary: Resti Castle lies in the Hasli Valley not far from the village an der Gassen, now Meiringen.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form of Bannwart, a local field, forest, or boundary warden charged with protecting restricted communal land; ‘warden’ is close, but the exact office and jurisdiction varied locally.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Verdingbueb
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a boy placed with another household under a labor or foster contract, often as a cheap farm servant; ‘indentured boy’ is only approximate because the historic Verdingkinder system had distinctive Swiss legal and social conditions.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

0d6d69b95da39b4506ea8f683484c4b0e65f2df9.summary: In July 1566, when the Reuss was running high, it was reported in Bremgarten that a serpent as large as the load-pole of a hay wagon rose from the river and devoured the cattle grazing on the bank.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fe5ac34324c30c34269b3e5cb9d8a380e19fe935.summary: Many, many years ago, a merchant from Milan is said to have been murdered at an inn in the Sustu.

notes.label: Sustu
notes.text: a Valais dialect form referring to the Sust or Susten, a stopping place or settlement associated with a goods depot and travelers' lodging; the exact inn intended is not identified in the tale.

notes.label: Wölbi-Binnu
notes.text: a Valais dialect architectural term for a hollowed beam or timber in the vaulted structure of the house; the precise construction detail is uncertain, but it serves as the hiding place for the gold.

notes.label: Zellota
notes.text: a Valais dialect word for a narrated tale or story, related to German Erzählung; the collector notes that the same tale circulated on the Brigerberg.

a0bb013b2e0024e4fdbe5e48dc11a560ecc8a3b3.summary: The Alp Arpitetta lies in the farthest reaches of the Eivischtal and looks down upon the mighty tongue of the Durand Glacier.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal Alpine pasture together with its working farm landscape; Riborrey lives, farms, and keeps his herd on the Alp Arpitetta rather than merely visiting a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Eivischtal
notes.text: the historical German or local name used by the source for the valley containing the Alp Arpitetta; the tale does not supply a modern equivalent or exact boundary.

notes.label: Leealp
notes.text: the named Alp opposite Riborrey’s, whose owner provides the isolated household’s connection for baking bread; the source gives no derivation for Lee.

notes.label: Kuhfelsen
notes.text: literally “Cow Rock,” the place where Riborrey makes sacrifices instead of attending the valley church; the source does not specify the rite, recipient, or exact location.

notes.label: Anniviarden
notes.text: the source’s plural name for the people of the Val d’Anniviers; their astonishment marks Riborrey’s rare appearance in the valley church.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Moncerna
notes.text: the mountain place at whose foot permanent snow signals that Riborrey must leave the Alp Arpitetta; the source does not identify its exact modern location or boundaries.

notes.label: Anniviard
notes.text: the singular masculine form used for a man from the Val d’Anniviers; Riborrey insists that his daughter marry one, but no such suitor appears.

1fd397b875a7d1f419ed6339afe6799f8f6b77f7.summary: On this side of the village of Ober-Schupfart in the Frick Valley, the Rindelenmoor carries on its mischief in the Rindelen.

notes.label: Rindelenmoor
notes.text: the local name for a spectral pig haunting the Rindelen near Schupfart; Moor here names an uncanny being rather than a wetland, and the apparition can also be perceived as a dog by only one traveler.

notes.label: Rochelenmoor
notes.text: an alternate regional name for the Rindelenmoor, linked by the source to its ravenous grunting and rooting; the exact dialect derivation of Rochelen is uncertain, but it emphasizes the creature’s noisy, hungry behavior.

bd372d107b47c2267aa2fa71a55bc32f8df21a7d.summary: a) The Oedlisberg, also called the heaped-up hill, is a rounded height in the woods beside the mountain road leading from the village of Birmensdorf to Fislisbach.

notes.label: Oedlisberg
notes.text: the source's spelling of the local wooded hill-name on the Birmensdorf–Fislisbach road, where the armed spectral host appears.

notes.label: heiligen Nächten
notes.text: literally ‘holy nights,’ a calendrical period around Christmas and the turn of the year when supernatural processions are especially expected.

notes.label: Mattenland
notes.text: literally ‘meadow land,’ the named broad grassland shared by the Lengnau and Endingen area where the ghostly riders appear.

notes.label: Kloster
notes.text: literally ‘convent’ or ‘monastery,’ here the proper name of a thicket rather than a surviving religious building; it motivates the procession of spectral nuns.

7cfc01cc1d27389161ceeb5033e977919c581ab8.summary: Forsteck Castle lies between Salez and Sennwald. This castle formerly belonged to the Barons of Hohensax, who took their name from Hohensax Castle, built by the founder of their line.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

eb6bb13feacf39c5bc767c7096aff4914c3f06bc.summary: Almost every day before or after the hunt, a hare crossed the path of old hunter Roni, or Hieronymus.

notes.label: Roni
notes.text: a familiar regional form or nickname for Hieronymus, the old hunter who recognizes the hare as a transformed human.

notes.label: Gesegnetem
notes.text: literally ‘something blessed,’ meaning blessed ammunition or material loaded into the gun to wound a supernatural shapeshifter.

6c88c864f928088b36d531401d2ca5ee3d5d9d18.summary: In the small meadow belonging to the little Rudenz castle at Flüelen, three perfectly circular and completely bare patches could be seen, arranged in a triangle, upon which grass would never grow.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d6180bf080f3db1e4f3caf022b199373cb775ee4.summary: Rue is blessed nine Klafter deep into the earth. For when the Mother of God received her first ‘Monatsrose,’ she hid it beneath a rue plant.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure based on outstretched arms; ‘nine Klafter deep’ expresses the extraordinary depth of rue's blessing rather than a precise modern metric value.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Monatsrose
notes.text: literally ‘monthly rose,’ a euphemistic folk expression for menstruation; the account links Mary's first period with rue's protective blessing.

notes.label: Weihekräutern
notes.text: herbs gathered for church blessing, especially in Catholic seasonal customs; rue is said to belong in every such consecrated bundle.

8eb70a9dc1832278aa34130d507e4aa21f8df4f4.summary: a) According to legend, in a time of national distress the people of Schwyz ceded the beautiful Ruossalp to Uri for a Viertel of silver coins—an old man said a Viertel of rubles—but retained a right of redemption for a precisely fixed term.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: literally a ‘quarter,’ but also a historical measure or monetary quantity; the source does not identify the exact unit behind a Viertel of silver coins or rubles, so the term remains deliberately unspecific.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the powerful warm downslope wind of the Alps, personified here as Uri’s strongest champion who delays the Schwyz boat with violent lake waves.

notes.label: Seckelmeister
notes.text: the historical treasurer or keeper of the public purse; he refuses the late redemption payment on Uri’s behalf.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its buildings, grazing rights, herd, and working landscape; the legends explain how ownership of Ruossalp passed from Schwyz to Uri.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young unmarried woman; the old Meitli is portrayed as extraordinarily wealthy by the standards of a cash-poor age.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning the several high seasonal pastures on the mountain chain rather than the Alps as a whole.

867aa4c80080c555fc6cc52a7488b1356e6b1b79.summary: Ruten im Garte—Rue in the Garden

notes.label: Ruten
notes.text: the regional name here used for rue, an aromatic herb credited in folk belief with protection from witchcraft.

notes.label: Ruten im Garte
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘rue in the garden’; rue was treated as a protective plant whose presence supposedly kept witches away.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Rutesalbi
notes.text: literally ‘rue salve,’ a folk ointment made from rue and believed to heal harm caused by a witch.

357c676aa24a4c941d5fa96f865421237dfe2614.summary: Above Bronschhofen, on the height still called Burstel (Burgstall), a castle once stood.

notes.label: Burstel
notes.text: a local St. Gallen form glossed in the source as Burgstall, the site or remains of a vanished castle; here it names the height above Bronschhofen.

notes.label: Jahrzeit
notes.text: a Catholic anniversary observance, commonly an endowed annual Mass for the dead; Mathilde establishes one at Wil, though the source does not name its beneficiary.

notes.label: Tübrunnen
notes.text: the shortened popular form of Tiefenbrunnen or Tüwinbrunnen; the narrator contrasts this living local pronunciation with the written name Dreibrunnen.

notes.label: Ketnhof
notes.text: the source’s historical term for an estate or administrative manor of the Counts of Toggenburg; its exact institutional form is uncertain and may reflect a regional or textual variant.

notes.label: Turbengräber
notes.text: literally ‘peat digger,’ a regional form for the worker who cuts measured layers of peat; his practical labor symbolizes the loss of the ponds’ older poetic myth.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

79c170f0a4ccf23a35d7c45f479b29654e13d972.summary: Near the larger lake on the Curer Alp stand several “gestrickte” houses and stables, joined from smoothly hewn beams or logs.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its working farms, buildings, livestock, and dairy landscape, not simply a mountain peak; the houses stand beside a lake on the Curer Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: gestrickte
notes.text: literally suggesting something knitted or interlaced, but here Jecklin explicitly uses it for log construction made from smoothly hewn beams or trunks fitted together.

notes.label: Ehni-Alter
notes.text: a dialect expression that Jecklin glosses as many generations; it emphasizes the house's great age without supplying a count of years.

notes.label: Ung'fäll
notes.text: a mishap, accident, or misfortune; the house spirit first prevents every Ung'fäll, and occasional misfortune begins only after she leaves.

notes.label: Fräuli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive meaning a little lady or little woman; here the red Fräuli is a protective female house spirit, not merely a human girl.

notes.label: Capatüsli
notes.text: an unusually shaped women's head ornament or headdress; Jecklin associates it with the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries but does not identify a narrower costume type.

notes.label: Übernacht
notes.text: a request for overnight lodging or hospitality; the travelers seek shelter because the storm prevents them from continuing.

notes.label: Schnetz
notes.text: a regional cutting knife, likely a pocket or working knife; the source does not describe its exact form, so the object remains visible rather than being narrowed to a specific modern knife type.

notes.label: sich zu weiggen
notes.text: a dialect expression explicitly glossed by Jecklin as ‘to move’; it marks the moment the rigid guest begins to stir and regain consciousness.

notes.label: Dusla
notes.text: a dialect noun for a forceful punch or blow delivered with the fist; Jecklin's form ends in -a, while a Swiss German Dictionary discussion gives the headword as Dusle.

notes.label: Tablatt
notes.text: a wooden slab fixed to an upright post and used as a small table or shelf for food; this definition comes from Jecklin's own parenthetical gloss.

notes.label: Hiene
notes.text: the handle or handgrip by which the girl pulls the treasure-pail; Jecklin supplies the standard-German gloss Handhabe.

d9aaf2b1f364d39326f02f5e2d9f226a558bad5c.summary: Sachen umetriebe — Making Things Come Back

notes.label: Sachen umetriebe
notes.text: Bernese dialect for making stolen things ‘turn back’ or be returned through magic; the verb also suggests driving the thief restlessly until restitution.

notes.label: Friti
notes.text: dialect for Friday, a ritually charged day on which the farmer commissions magical nails.

notes.label: zsämeglütet
notes.text: dialect for the communal evening or prayer bells having rung together; the timing places the act after a recognized bell signal.

notes.label: Schmiedte
notes.text: an older or dialectal form for smithy, the workshop where the specially timed nails and hammer are made.

notes.label: Wengelbaum
notes.text: apparently the turning shaft or main arbor of the farmer's mill, later called Wendelbaum in the commentary; transferring the wheel's motion to the thief is the charm's logic.

notes.label: Stang
notes.text: probably a ritual rod, barrier, or fixed magical station required along the thief's route; the brief dialect account leaves its precise form unclear.

notes.label: Diebsbann
notes.text: literally ‘thief-binding,’ a charm intended to stop, torment, identify, or force restitution from a thief.

notes.label: Rossnägel
notes.text: horseshoe nails; their association with iron, the smithy, and exceptional ritual acquisition gives them magical force.

notes.label: Hämmerli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning ‘little hammer,’ specially made after the Good Friday nails for driving them into the magical image.

notes.label: Satorformel
notes.text: the SATOR AREPO word-square formula used as a protective or coercive charm; the manuscript preserves a corrupted version rather than reproducing it here.

notes.label: Höusch in einer schmietten zwei RossneggeI um Gotteswillen.
notes.text: dialect for approximately ‘Beg two horseshoe nails from a smithy, for God's sake’; RossneggeI appears to contain a transcriptional capital-I or spelling irregularity.
notes.anchor: Höusch in einer schmietten zwei RossneggeI um Gotteswillen.

notes.label: Kammrad
notes.text: a cogwheel or toothed gear, probably in a mill; fixing the written charm to its motion is intended to drive the thief restlessly.

notes.label: Wendelbaum
notes.text: the rotating mill shaft or axle whose ceaseless movement the charm transfers symbolically to the thief; it appears to be the standardized form of Wengelbaum above.

notes.label: Bammertjöggel
notes.text: literally ‘little Jakob the field-warden,’ a named folkloric practitioner associated with driving nails into a fruitful tree; the outside story explaining him is not included here.

notes.label: gefährliche Worte
notes.text: literally ‘dangerous words,’ the popular label for coercive magical formulas believed to bring spiritual and practical ruin.

f3972ad8961d920be3d3e690965da47a7b60d8ef.summary: a) An hour above Amsteg, where the wild Reuss descends into a broader valley, the small hamlets of Intschi and Graggertal lie on its left bank amid rubble and rocks, between which only scattered shrubs and fir trees grow poorly.

notes.label: Berglüt
notes.text: dialect for mining people or miners, literally ‘mountain people’; the men use the occupational identity in their blasphemous boast.

notes.label: Wir Berglüt bruchet ises Herrgott's Liecht nimme!
notes.text: the miners’ exact dialect boast, ‘We miners no longer need our Lord God’s light’; their mine collapse turns the words into the tale’s punishment formula.
notes.anchor: Wir Berglüt bruchet ises Herrgott's Liecht nimme!

notes.label: d'Schmelzi
notes.text: literally the local ‘smelting place’ or smeltery, a rocky site south of Amsteg associated with ore processing; the footnote preserves an alternate silver-ore tradition.

notes.label: In des obern Treschen
notes.text: the historical name or possessive description of the Amsteg establishment now identified as the Hotel zum Hirschen; its exact reference to a proprietor or building is not further explained.

notes.label: der Präzis
notes.text: Johann Tresch’s byname, literally ‘the precise one’ or ‘the exact one’; it may characterize his reputation as a narrator, but the source does not say why he bore it.

notes.label: Bleue
notes.text: a regional name for a pounding or fulling installation, probably a mill used to beat cloth; the source lists it among Ambort’s property without specifying its machinery or product.

notes.label: Beinstampfe
notes.text: literally a bone-stamping or bone-crushing mill; it is listed beside the Bleue as another installation owned with the inn.

notes.label: Schachli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive place-name from Schachen, generally low ground, scrub, or land beside water; the exact historical site is not described here.

notes.label: Intschialp
notes.text: the named seasonal high pasture above Intschi where the alternate footnote locates silver extraction at the Erzstock.

05656ec1165029d3201384335c2582fc88292e5a.summary: Saint Anne’s Chapel was originally supposed to be built near the Schwandsbrücke.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7da67e925faa1e427bf083d8863d4866b5bffe1d.summary: Saint Eloi is the patron of smiths. It is said that, to shoe horses more conveniently, he cut off their legs and then attached them again.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

04f413d7375433e1f9f16b3669f415205146a1bc.summary: In the most ancient times, an old Celtic people lived beside—or rather, in—Lake Zurich.

notes.label: Saint Maurice
notes.text: Saint Maurice is associated with the Theban Legion and with the abbey at Saint-Maurice in Valais. References to him belong to a regional tradition of Christian martyrdom and devotion; the particular miracle remains the collector’s telling.

source.label: Abbey of Saint-Maurice

f836e88b43ca3c7caa2401b6f88beb2ea2735abe.summary: Remüs has the most beautiful church in the Engadine; it is dedicated to Saint Florinus.

notes.label: Remüs
notes.text: the historical German name for Ramosch in the Lower Engadine; the legend presents it as Saint Florinus’s church, burial place, and former pilgrimage center.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Vintsgau
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling of Vinschgau, the Alpine valley containing Matsch where Florin’s parents settle after their pilgrimage.

notes.label: Gemeinde
notes.text: a word that can mean a community, municipality, or congregation; here it denotes the formal local assembly held at Remüs in 1530 to decide whether to accept the Reformation.

8776c8fa2d52c6a8002020d68f21f2a7588dcaf0.summary: After Gall recovered at Arbon through the grace of Christ, it soon became clear that divine Providence had preserved him for greater things in the German lands.

notes.label: Mühletobel
notes.text: literally the ‘mill ravine’; Tobel is a Swiss and southern German word for a steep, narrow wooded gorge, here formed by the falling Steinach.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Vita S. Galli
notes.text: Latin for ‘Life of Saint Gall,’ the hagiographic tradition cited as the source behind this account of the saint and the bear.

db811c40bd1bf9c2c778303eb9ed1b3597e6b136.summary: Having lost his way while returning from Rome, Knight Saint Martin is said to have reached the summit of the Ringelberg and looked from there into the dreadful depths of the Tamina riverbed.

notes.label: Höhe
notes.text: literally ‘the height,’ the locally named elevated spot on the Calfeisen path where the miraculous hoofprints are shown.

notes.label: Alpenbesitzer
notes.text: owners or rights-holders of Alpine pasture holdings, not owners of the Alps mountain range; they cut protective pieces from Martin's cloak for their livestock.

dbf06f5b180ec12db14f8a397c202d053f4da87e.summary: Outside Allenwinden, on the road to Ägeri, stands the St. Meinradskäpeli.

notes.label: St. Meinradskäpeli
notes.text: literally ‘Saint Meinrad's little chapel,’ the roadside shrine marking where the traveling saint rested.

notes.label: Vaterunser
notes.text: the Our Father or Lord's Prayer; pilgrims combine it with placing a leg in the saint's bodily imprint as a remedy for fatigue.

aed57a19664f51a7d6f8ce9aac50a5e133cb0eef.summary: Lord Berchtold and Lady Aureliana lived at Strättlingen. Their only child lay ill.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a37010bc1d74820913605e5ad00c158cb13a70f5.summary: In the time when dear God would sometimes descend to our wretched earth, there lived a very devout and humble man in quiet seclusion, almost like a forest hermit.

notes.label: Mohr
notes.text: an archaic German term historically applied to a Black person or a person imagined as coming from North Africa; it is now outdated and often offensive, and remains here only because it is the tale’s repeated historical byname.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ a Catholic folk-religious term for souls in Purgatory who may need prayer or protection; the little devils are roaming in search of them.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

dfd1789a981fdaf3ed65c5471bc63035cda27816.summary: a) On a journey, Jesus and Peter arrived at an inn where they had to sleep in one bed.

notes.label: Stande
notes.text: a regional word for a large wooden vat or tub, also glossed as Kufe by the collector; here it was intended to hold a slaughtered pig.

notes.label: Säuludi
notes.text: the folkloric name given here to a particular bone in a pig’s spine that was imagined to resemble a man in a vat; Säu refers to a pig or sow, while the exact force of Ludi in this anatomical name is uncertain.

808815a5a7aef2dea1b7e04850b7d1fea5dd34e6.summary: Close beside the lower Grindelwald Glacier there once stood a chapel dedicated to Saint Petronella, built into an overhanging Felsenbalm.

notes.label: Felsenbalm
notes.text: an Alpine rock shelter or shallow cave beneath an overhanging cliff; the regional terrain word describes how Petronella's chapel was tucked directly against the glacier.

a5f2c260c685abda742206e1b0a4c4637fc1312c.summary: At the beginning of the seventh century, St. Columbanus, abbot of the Irish monastery of Bangor, left his homeland to work as a missionary among the still-pagan peoples of the Continent.

notes.label: Desertina
notes.text: the historical Latin-derived name associated with the wilderness and later monastery settlement of Disentis; the source supplies it parenthetically and also uses it independently.

notes.label: Lukmanier
notes.text: the Alpine pass south of Disentis, now commonly called Lukmanier Pass or Passo del Lucomagno; Columbanus crosses it toward Italy.

notes.label: Toparcha
notes.text: a historical Greek and Latin title for a local territorial ruler or chief; the source applies it to Placidus as head of the valley.

notes.label: Curia
notes.text: the historical Latin form of Chur; Placidus meets Count Victor there.

8791b89439b055b57fb1e027969f3b1cd85332ca.summary: Where Saint Theodore's Chapel now invites travelers to rest in prayer beside the hermit's little house on the ascent from Hergiswil to Menzberg, only a Bildstock honoring the saint originally stood.

notes.label: Bildstock
notes.text: a small roadside or wayside religious shrine, often a pillar or niche holding a sacred image; Saint Theodore's image preceded the later chapel.

9a2f6e762574987259879f465e78c264cb24c02c.summary: From the village of Schleuis, a much-used footpath leads to the high-lying settlement of Ladir, winding past Löwenberg Castle and through meadow and forest. — About halfway along, in the woods, lies a block of stone 1 meter long, 2/3 wide, and 1/2 high, on whose upper surface two depressions can be…

notes.label: Ladurs 998
notes.text: the historical place-name and year supplied parenthetically for Ladir; it is preserved as source apparatus rather than read as part of the legend’s chronology.

notes.label: talein, talaus
notes.text: literally “into the valley, out of the valley,” an idiom meaning up and down or throughout the valley as Zeno travels to preach.

notes.label: Satanas
notes.text: a historical Latinizing form of Satan used by the source for the Evil Spirit.

notes.label: Luziferus
notes.text: a historical Latinizing form of Lucifer; the source alternates it with Satan and the Evil One.

7ca5b1bc9738bb2c3005e88a88b95c8542a97515.summary: Lucius, King of Britain, left scepter and crown and fatherland in order, following his inner impulse, to preach the Gospel to the pagans on the mainland.

notes.label: Luzien-Steig
notes.text: the historic steep passage and route at the northern approach to Graubünden, associated here by name with Saint Lucius.

notes.label: Majae-villa
notes.text: the Latin-form name used in the source for the former Roman station at present-day Mayenfeld, now Maienfeld.

notes.label: Bünden
notes.text: Jecklin’s shortened historical form of Graubünden, the Swiss canton in which the legend is set.

notes.label: Curia Raetorum
notes.text: the Latin name for ancient Chur, literally the chief settlement or court of the Raetians; the legend treats it as the destination of Lucius’s mission.

notes.label: St. Luzius Löchlein
notes.text: literally “Saint Lucius’s little hole,” the name of the small rocky grotto associated with his hermitage; the source prints Luzius with an internal spacing artifact.

notes.label: Trimons
notes.text: the historical name form given alongside modern Trimmis, the place of Emerita’s martyrdom in the legend.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

14c4f312352ca8e83acb4f1735262c62a29d2d5e.summary: It is also reported of the Scheibenfluh in Schangnau—called Schibegütsch from 1812 onward—where the Emme rises, that a great hole descends into the same mountain, and that if someone wantonly throws something into it, violent weather results.

notes.text: The source’s parenthetical attribution beginning with Hans Rudolf Grimm has no closing parenthesis; that incomplete punctuation has been retained rather than silently regularized.

12fb02f9189c1d509061181f042aefff38ef8c29.summary: The knight Hans von Wilberg rode out to the Battle of Näfels. His only daughter, Gutta, troubled by dark forebodings, begged him to remain apart from the bloody struggle this one time.

notes.text: The printed source appears to contain a corrupted word before the final sentence about wine growing above the ruins; the translation follows the clear contextual sense without adding further detail.

14a328921672b27a52b578f704a7c544d584d97e.summary: Satan does not like holy water. That is why it was—and still is—a devout custom, though admittedly not to more modern taste, to keep holy water in living rooms and diligently make the sign of the cross with it.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

30d833ce2e05efc8478a34f3d525706c4de57024.summary: In Peist, late one evening, Satan in the flesh once entered a house in which a company of young fellows had gathered.

notes.label: Peterli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Peter; the source later alternates the spelling Peterle for the same clever young man.

notes.label: Nu g’mach, döt isch mi Hinderma!
notes.text: the Alemannic line means approximately “Easy now, there is the man behind me!”; Peterli makes his shadow into the supposed final person for Satan to seize.
notes.anchor: Nu g’mach, döt isch mi Hinderma!

235fe63de4fb9d12def6698fa165144eeea43189.summary: In the Canton of Bern, not far from the capital, there lived a saddler called wicked Franz, or sometimes Sattler-Franz.

notes.label: Helle Platte
notes.text: the local name of a smooth, dangerous rock slab on the Grimsel route; the historical source glosses helle here as ‘slippery,’ so the place-name should not be read only in the modern sense ‘bright.’

493e36d2736cf979c40ae0eaea348a3d8d79ae81.summary: A Piedmontese packer brought a train of packhorses over the Grimsel in the Bernese Oberland and down through the Hasli valley.

notes.label: Lägel
notes.text: a traditional transport vessel or small cask used in Alpine pack trade, here carrying red wine on each horse; ‘wine cask’ is the closest sense, but its precise capacity and form varied regionally.

ef3acf309e48d4dc934481b8feffa33c17ea0bfd.summary: The so-called Schaflaufen is a recreational game known throughout German-speaking Valais for both younger and older youths.

notes.label: Schaflaufen
notes.text: literally ‘sheep-running,’ a vigorous springtime chasing and capture game played by Valais youths on dry meadows before the grass grows.

notes.label: Tuss!
notes.text: the final word of the traditional counting-out rhyme; the child on whom it falls becomes a catcher, while its literal sense in the rhyme is uncertain.

notes.label: Todeskreuze
notes.text: literally ‘death crosses,’ memorial crosses erected where sudden or violent deaths occurred, here beside the road below the playing field.

f85f799183bde8ac23485135c345d4eaed4053dc.summary: In a village in Aargau on the left bank of Lake Hallwil—no one can identify it more precisely now—there lived a young blacksmith named Peter Mangold.

notes.label: Fasnacht
notes.text: the Swiss and Alemannic Carnival season before Lent, marked by disguises, music, and dancing; here it is the one festive period that draws the dutiful blacksmith away from home.

notes.label: Hopser
notes.text: lively hopping dance tunes or dances related to the Hopser tradition; here Peter sings them while hammer and anvil supply an imagined accompaniment, and no precise choreography is specified.

notes.label: Schellen
notes.text: resonant bells, often small costume or animal bells; here Peter wears many on his carnival clothes, and their supernatural ringing later warns dancers.

notes.label: Wamms
notes.text: an older spelling of Wams, a close-fitting historical man's jacket or doublet; here it forms part of Peter's bell-covered disguise.

notes.label: Schellenpeter
notes.text: literally ‘Bell-Peter,’ the carnival nickname given to Peter Mangold because his costume is covered with small ringing bells; after death, the same sound announces his protective apparition.

8e094a140581ed22169e8391951b813a08b5f79f.summary: In the old castle—not the one in which all the walls and vaults still stand today; of the very oldest castle, only that square tower below the castle remains—there was once an evil, harsh Zwinghärr.

notes.label: Zwinghärr
notes.text: the local dialect form of Zwingherr, a coercive feudal lord or tyrant; the term defines him through abusive power over the farmers.

notes.label: Fraugärtli
notes.text: literally ‘women's/lady's little garden,’ the diminutive local name for the garden below the castle where the lord watches and punishes laborers.

notes.label: Vergelt'Z Gott
notes.text: the dialect thanksgiving formula, ‘May God reward you’; here it begins the apparition's thanks for finally being released when the tree is felled.

notes.label: Härd
notes.text: Swiss German for earth or soil; striking the haunted stump instead of the surrounding Härd is said to doom the treasure seeker.

notes.label: Schwizer-Dütsch
notes.text: Swiss German; Sutermeister's label identifies the linguistic form of the source account.

notes.label: Schloss Gräplang
notes.text: Gräplang Castle above Flums; Schloss is retained in the dialect title's proper-name form rather than treated as an unnamed generic castle.

notes.label: Mundart
notes.text: dialect; the label warns that the original story is printed in local Swiss German rather than standard German.

a108ff7cba307d67e0991708e371e1e77471f1c8.summary: There was once a very disobedient child at Rüezligen, between Wangen and Buttisholz.

notes.label: Schmutzli
notes.text: the dark-clad Swiss companion of Saint Nicholas who admonishes or frightens misbehaving children; in this cautionary legend, the role is dangerously taken by the Devil himself.

notes.label: schmelzen
notes.text: the source's quoted verb for what the disguised servant is supposed to do to frighten the child; it suggests rough handling or chastisement here, but the precise local sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Im Nienerlisgraben
notes.text: the opening of the child's dialect rhyme, ‘In Nienerli's ravine’; the following line says that the captive child must gnaw there, though the story does not explain what the child must gnaw.

f76ba39eb321ae2c2376ac478a3cee6f2128e38e.summary: A man named Schmutz, who preferred idleness to earning his daily bread through hard work with his hands, had become a burden upon the municipality of Zweisimmen.

notes.label: Schmützenried
notes.text: the place-name explained through the idle man Schmutz; Ried commonly denotes marshy or cleared land, though the exact historical derivation is not established by the tale.

85de55a477c0ed6ecdba624f303b3171066457b4.summary: a) Once a wealthy lord of Ursern rode over the Gotthard. He came to Milan and saw a garden beside a beautiful castle.

notes.label: Schneidergret
notes.text: a folkloric witch-name probably combining Schneider, ‘tailor’ or a surname, with Gret, a familiar form of Margareta; the exact historical or household reference is uncertain.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; here its brief melting time measures Schneidergret’s impossible journey to Milan and back.

notes.label: Gretli
notes.text: the affectionate or diminutive Swiss form of Gret, itself a familiar form of Margareta; in the execution account it refers to Schneidergret without implying that the crowd treats her kindly.

notes.label: Jeises
notes.text: an Uri dialect exclamation derived from the name Jesus, comparable to ‘Jesus!’ or ‘dear God!’; Schneidergret cries it while being seized.

notes.label: Brigitä, Brigitä Hagstäckä
notes.text: the repeated dialect incantation literally invokes Brigitä and ‘hedge stakes’; its ritual sense and the identity meant by Brigitä are not explained, so the formula is retained without resolving them.

notes.label: Nägeli
notes.text: a diminutive that can mean a little nail, clove, or carnation-like flower depending on context; in this repeated spell its intended referent is not recoverable, so the name is retained.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

1b10e7e06ddd204a7330f7996962ac616a85904d.summary: For a long time, this woman was considered extraordinarily pious in Ursern.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

12b71e3a1ceaae68ab0e9d37ac6b2cfeef87bffe.summary: In the Aletsch Valley, close to the glacier, there is said once to have stood a little wooden house, black with age, inhabited by a devout old widow.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Schoch
notes.text: a Valais dialect cry explained by the source as meaning that it is cold or that the speakers are freezing; it is repeated by the souls waiting outside.

notes.label: Altschmidja
notes.text: a Valais dialect name or byname for the old woman; it is approximately ‘old woman Smith’ or ‘the old smith-woman,’ but the source treats it as what she was called.

4da933bcc464dcc1d6d084143c1cc50702ec5f0b.summary: I lay in bed and was still awake when something came to the door lock, and an old little woman entered, a Mucherli.

notes.label: Mucherli
notes.text: a local diminutive for a small, old, possibly shriveled or witch-like woman; the precise nuance is uncertain, but it describes the form taken by the Schrättlig.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional St. Gallen night-pressing spirit associated with nightmare and the sensation of a being sitting upon the sleeper's chest; the experience closely resembles sleep paralysis.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Freienämter-Mundart
notes.text: Freienämter-Mundart identifies the Free Districts dialect of Aargau in which the framed oral tale is printed; the source does not specify the individual speaker’s village variety.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a Stubete is a sociable evening gathering in a household parlor, here the setting in which the children request the tale; the gathering’s guests and customary activities are unspecified.

notes.label: Stifeli
notes.text: Stifeli is the little monastery servant’s familiar nickname, possibly related to Stiefel or a personal name; its exact derivation and whether it was historical are uncertain.

notes.label: Schwarzwälder-Bläseli
notes.text: Schwarzwälder-Bläseli is the servant’s nickname, approximately ‘little Bläsi from the Black Forest,’ with Bläsi likely a familiar form of Blasius; his full historical identity is uncertain.

notes.label: Pater Schaffner
notes.text: a Pater Schaffner was the monastery father serving as steward or economic administrator, here assigning Stifeli’s successive jobs; the officeholder’s identity is unspecified.

notes.label: Schwebelpfîfli
notes.text: Schwebelpfîfli denotes the little fife or herding pipe whose whistle controls the sheep; its exact instrument type, spelling, and sound are uncertain.

notes.label: Gleck-chübel
notes.text: Gleck-chübel is a bucket or tub containing a tempting livestock lick or feed mixture, the only thing that wins the cows’ attention; its exact contents are uncertain.

notes.label: Meisterchnecht
notes.text: Meisterchnecht is the chief farm servant or foreman who orders and oversees other workers, Stifeli’s final promotion; the post’s exact place in Muri Abbey’s hierarchy is uncertain.

notes.label: Unterhömli
notes.text: literally ‘undershirt,’ Unterhömli is used figuratively for Stifeli as the steward’s intimate favorite or creature; the phrase’s precise tone and local idiom are uncertain.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Vitzlibutzli
notes.text: Vitzlibutzli is a comic or euphemistic name for a devil, goblin, or bogey, invoked as the height of partiality; the figure’s exact regional identity is uncertain.

notes.label: vor im Chopf de Springer, hintedrinn der Zwinger
notes.text: this dialect phrase is rendered approximately as ‘the jumper at the front of his head and the coercer behind,’ describing Stifeli’s duplicitous disposition or appearance; the metaphor’s exact referents are uncertain.
notes.anchor: vor im Chopf de Springer, hintedrinn der Zwinger

notes.label: Mir armi Seel
notes.text: literally ‘my poor soul’ in dialect, Mir armi Seel is Wilhelm’s exclamation upon discovering the holes in both hats; its precise emotional force and punctuation are uncertain.

67d4e51e3980653229603051173cb42c5694a10d.summary: By chance, a goat boy came to a cliff. There he heard a voice call: ‘Sesame, open!

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: a central Swiss dialect label for an uncanny, disreputable, or witch-like female figure; here an old Guschi announces the brothers’ fate, but the story gives no appearance or identity allowing a narrower classification.

636de2cc7686a9d3ff438c3a8c4902752396f761.summary: A road leads from the hamlet of Plattis to the village of Gretschins. Up to the right on a rocky headland there are still remains of walls, called ‘die brocha Burg’—the broken-down castle—in local speech.

notes.label: die brocha Burg
notes.text: local Swiss German for ‘the broken-down’ or ruined castle, used as the folk name for the surviving walls rather than as the formal name of a known stronghold.

c50895e8094ad48d8745e8b766300a3b944a9c3d.summary: Long ago there were only seven households in Sisikon. At that time there was no permanent Sigrist appointed to serve the church and priest; instead the people had to take turns performing the Sigerstendienst for one week each.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German and southern German title for a church sexton or sacristan who tends the building and assists its clergy; Sisikon did not yet have a permanent one.

notes.label: Sigerstendienst
notes.text: the local sexton's duty or period of service; each household performs it for one week in rotation.

notes.label: Sigersten
notes.text: a dialect plural of Sigrist, meaning church sextons or sacristans responsible for practical service to the church and priest; the title's seven are the seven householders rotating through the office.

04febd878685917612d727c32e4e394a99d2b741.summary: On the Lasa alpine pasture near Valens, there was once a reckless cowherd who was greatly vexed by a rather spirited cow.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Rüse
notes.text: a steep Alpine chute, gully, or run down which material can fall; the source does not make clear whether this one was natural or used as a working chute.

notes.label: Geistende
notes.text: literally someone who is ‘ghosting’ or haunting; here it names the dead cowherd returning as a penitent spirit, a nuance broader than simply ‘ghost.’

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a Swiss alpine pasture; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally ‘Lady Lent’ in Bernese Alemannic; a female personification of the fasting season who punishes the shoemaker for mocking her.

1da4790932cb66c0e95aae06da53e0a106e8f655.summary: 1. A chaplain at Bristen often went down to Amsteg.

notes.label: b'stellt
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for being magically stopped, bound, or immobilized; in these accounts reversing, removing, or carrying one's shoes breaks that restraint, while the rite's supposed mechanism is not explained.

4b97e77a8a38aaba1261a620d921d574e4f0bb86.summary: A shoemaker and a tailor once lived in the same house in a town. One day they said to each other: “We do not like it here any longer.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4b0f34f93d1b0cfa1551822499df614c69111dd8.summary: If a man has a witch for a wife, he notices it because at times a wasp or a bee flies from her mouth and, after a while, returns through her mouth into her body.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Fensterlädeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a little window shutter; the husband closes it to prevent the insect-shaped spirit from returning to the woman’s body.

fb0cd9bb865a5659a1a757a0e03a5685da862f3f.summary: An elderly man from the village of Reckingen in the district of Zurzach relates the following from the neighboring municipality of Böbikon, also in the district of Zurzach.

notes.label: Kreuzlibach
notes.text: the local stream-name, apparently combining Kreuzli, a diminutive connected with a little cross, and Bach, a brook; the tale gives no origin story for the name, so this reading remains tentative.

notes.label: Schlösslein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a small castle or fortified house; in the place-name Schlösslein Grünenfels it labels the supposed ruins, whose identification as masonry remains uncertain in the narrator’s own wording.

dc64bbf0a145a5c36faf07a3a3cc967956e28cb0.summary: Not far from the city of Bern lies the town of Burgdorf. Its founders were the brothers Sintram and Valtram, two powerful and courageous dukes of Lenzburg.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

65f9c5f7e66db6d9d906c55d39da62014caaa99f.summary: Late one midnight, the ferryman of Klein-Döttingen had to carry three people across the Aare.

notes.label: Schalte
notes.text: a regional ferryman’s implement, apparently the oar, paddle, or pole extended to receive payment; the source later calls the burned object a Ruder, so its exact form is not completely clear.

notes.label: Chilspeler
notes.text: a dialect form of Kirchspieler, meaning the people or parishioners belonging to a church parish; here it can also blur the living annual procession with the memory or spectral presence of those who drowned.

a795acd42c206bfaf09c89ce576a249664f179b8.summary: When the French were in the country—yes, then one could hide Meitli and money from them however one wished, and they still ‘g'schmeckt’—smelled out—everything, except what was concealed behind or beneath water.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young women; the saying groups them with money as things villagers tried to conceal from occupying French troops.

notes.label: g'schmeckt
notes.text: literally ‘smelled’ in dialect, used here for the French soldiers’ uncanny ability to detect what was hidden; the water exception is the tale’s central belief.

notes.label: Brawä
notes.text: the local place-name beside whose stream the smith hangs his money; the source does not define its exact modern location or terrain.

f9d527243ea23232832786806371fecd0a69b89d.summary: On Charfreitag, a woman from Bünzgen on the Rhine bank of the Black Forest wished to go to church in the village of Hochsol.

notes.label: Charfreitag
notes.text: an older regional spelling of Karfreitag, Good Friday; here the holy day is when ordinary snail shells become valuable coins.

notes.label: Kronenthaler
notes.text: large silver crown thalers used in the Austrian Netherlands and neighboring regions and familiar in Switzerland; here two magically replace the two collected shells, without the tale specifying their mint or date.

notes.label: Poppern
notes.text: a regional word for a faint knocking, tapping, or muffled popping sound; here it rises from beneath the sunken ground as the sign of a spirit's release.

b101d2d80a64d7a06d8b60c3b237221c08c4e7b8.summary: This occurred in Grossenteil at Giswil. In the uppermost houses of this district lived a poor widow with several children and a few livestock.

notes.label: auf der Stör
notes.text: a traditional arrangement in which an itinerant craftsperson worked for several days in the customer's home rather than in a permanent shop; here the shoemaker is lodging and working at the widow's house when he hears of the snake.

notes.label: Hagstecken
notes.text: literally a hedge or fence stake, a stout wooden pole used here as an improvised spear; the exact shape is described only as large, round, and sharpened.

notes.label: Ried
notes.text: wet meadow, marshland, or reedy ground; the official record places the snake's carcass on Giswil's Ried, but the passage does not specify the ground's exact drainage or use.

cc0d6fd775e73c800db588f3b897c21605c094ae.summary: People are still living who claim to have seen snakes that were not footless.

notes.label: Heggi
notes.text: a regional name for lizards, explicitly glossed by the collector; the belief that they are poisonous is reported rather than endorsed.

notes.label: Wättertätsch
notes.text: a regional name for the newt, explicitly glossed by the collector; its literal formation may evoke weather and splashing or striking, but the precise etymology is uncertain.

edfaea027b3edbd3f035cc22ccd8e9c267cb2c0c.summary: Late one autumn evening, a hunter stopped at the hut on Alp Tanzboden and lay down to rest after eating.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Tanzboden
notes.text: the named high alpine pasture where the hunter shelters; Alp denotes a mountain summer pasture and its associated farm buildings, not simply the mountain range.

3e729aaf513dc8aca861d2be41adf629da1594da.summary: The Totenbrunnen in the Intschialp, so called because legend says that someone drank himself to death at it; the seven Metzgerbrünnen on the eastern descent from the Surenen Pass, from which a butcher is said to have drunk himself to death in the heat; the Gretlibrunnen in Unterschächen; the…

notes.label: Helgenstöckli
notes.text: a diminutive wayside shrine, devotional pillar, or small structure holding a holy image; the source notes its place beside the valued Ottenbrunnen but does not describe its form or dedication.

a9b423789bf8f5cae212936c7f148db6726417d8.summary: At midnight on holy Christmas, the animals in the stable receive the power of speech, I suppose because the holy infant Jesus was able to warm himself with the breath of such animals.

notes.label: About this telling

5ec075051371f98a91d835822d15166cacf86c4b.summary: Several years ago, the Älpler in the Sennhütte on Blumalp above Stans noticed a small board set into the wall and suspected that something might be hidden behind it.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or pasturing livestock on a high Alpine pasture; here they are the seasonal occupants of the Sennhütte, not mountaineers in the modern recreational sense.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine dairy hut where herders live and make milk products during the summer grazing season; ‘herdsman’s hut’ misses its dairy-work function.

notes.label: Stutzerchen
notes.text: a diminutive of Stutzer, a short hunting gun or carbine; here the impossibly tiny weapon belongs to the uncanny packet, and its exact firearm type is not specified.

notes.label: G’lieger
notes.text: a dialect term for the hut’s sleeping platform or bedding place; the shaggy being comes onto it beside the sleeping man, but the precise construction is not described.

7e723fd9559eed1ea7c4b68d617b55519ce4da48.summary: Behind Gsteig in the Saanenland lies a barren place wildly strewn with countless boulders and called ‘in den grossen Steinen.’ Evil spirits formerly dwelt there.

notes.label: in den grossen Steinen
notes.text: literally ‘among the great stones,’ the local name of the boulder-strewn place behind Gsteig where the spirits dwell.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Geisterbannen
notes.text: the ritual art of binding, banishing, or confining spirits; the Capuchin is said to have learned it at Salamanca, a city often associated in European legend with occult study.

notes.label: Bannformeln
notes.text: spoken formulas of magical or religious binding and banishment; here they are combined with sacred words and signs, and only the strongest finally succeeds.

3c415a13799454ad3493e04780461e1428fb0f99.summary: The thunderstorms in the Entlebuch valley rise on the cliff heights at the Scheibengütsch behind Marbach and spread from there across the region.

d48d6a9e4d194ff2c147007a0a5971e6bf948368.summary: From the Lutherntale, which winds from Zell in the canton of Lucerne to the Napf—where Bern and Lucerne divide—along the Luthern in a north-south direction, a small side valley branches off behind the village of Luthern and leads to Nesslisboden or Scheidegg, where the Gewitterunholde mentioned earlier dwells.

notes.label: Lutherntale
notes.text: an older inflected spelling for the Luthern valley running toward the Napf in western Lucerne.

notes.label: Gewitterunholde
notes.text: literally ‘storm monster’ or malignant weather being, an apparition identified in an earlier linked account and placed near Scheidegg.

notes.label: Grauflue
notes.text: one spelling of the named gray rock face containing the spirits' swept-clean shelter; the source later writes Graufluh.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter or shallow cave beneath an overhang, common in Swiss place vocabulary.

notes.label: Senten
notes.text: a complete herd or drove of Alpine cattle; the cave is said to have room for an entire one.

notes.label: Lutherthal
notes.text: the source's alternate historical spelling of the Luthern valley, retained because both forms occur in the same account.

notes.label: Graufluh
notes.text: the alternate spelling for Grauflue, the rock shelter to which oppressive city gentlemen are said to be banished after death.

notes.label: Kratten
notes.text: the singular or variant form of the large carrying basket in which a conjurer transports one spirit.

notes.label: Milzjoggi
notes.text: a local nickname, literally suggesting ‘Spleen Joggeli/Jacob,’ for the bold man who challenges the cave spirits; the personal epithet's origin is not explained.

notes.label: Nüsse
notes.text: literally ‘nuts,’ used figuratively here for the lumps, bruises, or blows covering Milzjoggi's face after his challenge.

notes.label: Krätten
notes.text: plural of Kratte or Kratten, a large back-basket or carrying basket; the title emphasizes the incongruous transport of spirits in such containers.

245f13aa5e1be47065a4fb9009329bd624c7f7f9.summary: Spirits Like That Are Not to Be Joked With

notes.label: Gütterli
notes.text: a Bernese Alemannic diminutive for a small bottle or vial; here it serves as a sealed vessel in which a dangerous spirit has been confined.

notes.label: verpflöckt
notes.text: literally approximately ‘pegged away’ or ‘transferred by plugging’; a regional magical practice in which illness is displaced into a drilled hole and sealed there with a wooden plug.

notes.label: Bistel
notes.text: a dialectal name for a structural part of a traditional farmhouse that could retain plugged boreholes from this practice; the source does not define the member more precisely.

The dialect description of the afflicted woman literally says she became ‘backward’ after the bottle was opened; whether this means physically twisted, behaviorally altered, or generally deranged is not specified.

6c300db973bba2c509e578e73d4151904d4d914d.summary: a) Around the year 1336, a steward in Sarnen renounced the world and became a humble sacristan to atone for his sins.

580579d62b8d27ec859fa5512d5dbabb52ce6842.summary: Many people would not even have the courage to go up to the Spley-Chapili at midnight, when, on certain evenings, a goat or a black cat stands in one's way.

notes.label: Spley-Chapili
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for the little chapel at Splee or Spley; Chapili is an affectionate diminutive of ‘chapel,’ and the local spelling varies between the title and the dialect text.

notes.label: Friddhouf
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for Friedhof, a cemetery or churchyard; the passage humorously calls it safer than the chapel road because its dead are harmless.

notes.label: Toudnä
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for ‘the dead’; the final reassurance overturns the listener's fear by distinguishing buried people from the uncanny animals encountered on the road.

379d3435e53fc51279f0dad282419f08b3c070ab.summary: St. Georgen also took part in the assault upon the monastery at Rorschach.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally people bound together by oath; here it names the troops of the Swiss Confederacy who advanced on St. Gallen in 1490, not Swiss citizens in the modern general sense.

c7cbfa4ac96a6f368cfc234f3f770e36ae13d772.summary: 1. The Ronabrunnen in the Fellital is blessed by the Holy Father; it is more highly blessed than holy water, old Felli-Tresch claimed.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: männte
notes.text: the source's dialect verb for drawing or hauling something; the supposedly dead girl is being transported to the cemetery rather than walking in a procession.

notes.label: Hornschlitten
notes.text: a traditional Alpine horn sled with long curved runners or handles, used to haul hay, wood, goods, and here a body; the girl rises from it before burial.

notes.label: Capuchin friars

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Pater
notes.text: a Catholic title for a priest or religious father, especially a member of an order; the accounts use it for the clerics who bless the springs.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Sellenen is the named pasture containing one healing spring.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: g'heiliges
notes.text: Uri dialect for holy, hallowed, or endowed with sacred power; the spring water is treated not merely as clean but as spiritually efficacious.

notes.label: Eissen
notes.text: an uncertain regional illness term associated here with skin eruptions or bodily swellings; the source groups it with rashes and ‘impure blood’ but does not define a modern diagnosis.

notes.label: Riedbesen
notes.text: literally a broom or brush made from reeds or marsh growth; pilgrims cast one in as a votive object, though the source does not explain the offering's symbolism.

notes.label: Urbar
notes.text: a historical register of a church's or estate's lands, rents, rights, and notable entries; Isenmann's account is preserved in such a parish record rather than a modern medical source.

4fc827d78d59ccd0fb02ea20bfc091912fcad84a.summary: At the time when the new road to Tusis was being built, many Italian laborers were lodging in Räzüns Castle and slept on the ground floor.

notes.label: Spuck
notes.text: the title’s historical spelling or form for Spuk, meaning a haunting or ghostly disturbance; it is retained because it is Jecklin’s printed title word.

03dfa1031722e7272710af083032c961674145b5.summary: In olden times, a cruel bailiff lived in St. Anna Castle.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Blutbann
notes.text: a historical German-speaking legal term for a lord’s jurisdiction over capital crimes and punishments, often rendered ‘high justice’; the literal sense is ‘blood ban.’

4dcae8b2bac4177e8e8c12a64d9aa5c2c6cc6d06.summary: St. Burkhard, whose grave is still venerated in the Freiamt village of Beinwil, is also said to have lived in a hunter's house near Muri.

notes.label: Schuh
notes.text: a historical foot measure whose exact length varied by territory; the relic beam is described as one Schuh long, so this is not a modern standardized measurement.

dee38132699f4bc9d7406d25206ea8bf478d4de0.summary: The legend maintains that St. Francis of Assisi came in 1224 to visit the pious Countess Gutta at Schauensee near Kriens.

notes.label: Vrenelisgärtlein
notes.text: literally ‘little Vreneli's garden,’ the traditional Glarus name for the firn field on the Glärnisch massif; here it is imagined as the enclosed glacier home of Frau Vrene, and Vreneli is an affectionate diminutive of Verena.

39765a7a6f68387235b64f871e28f8243509c6d6.summary: Toward the end of the 4th or beginning of the 5th century, Gaudentius, Bishop of Novarra, came to the Rhaetian Alps while being persecuted by the Arians and sought protection from his pursuers in the valley of Bregallia, where, however, he found both pagans and Christian heretics.
