66af2169c6d770efad7467f83f46221b44f250aa.summary: After Saint Georgius, driven out and persecuted by the Arians around the middle of the fourth century, fled across the Alps, he is said to have found protection and welcome in ancient Raetia, lived for several years in our land, and been especially active in spreading Christianity. — Many…

notes.label: Val Tomiliasca
notes.text: the historical Romance name given for the Domleschg valley, the destination of Georgius’s missionary journey from Amides.

notes.label: Brühl-Wald
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical name for the dark forest through which the saint rides when his pursuers overtake him; Wald means forest, while the precise local scope of Brühl is not explained.

673df2c70ae621c3442777dc6352f31cd1044dbc.summary: The legend of St. Johann in Savien has the following meaning.

notes.label: Savien
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical German form of Safien, the Graubünden valley and community whose church venerates St. Johann.

notes.label: am Platze
notes.text: literally “at the Platz,” identifying the church at the principal settlement or village center traditionally called Platz within Savien.

notes.label: Savier
notes.text: the people of Savien or Safien; the legend notes that they retained the older patron saint despite the community’s Protestant confession.

notes.label: Carnusa
notes.text: the local valley and stream behind the church, imagined here as the abode of souls awaiting redemption.

1ee0388be43e0bf824b3061197d9a8135261fc09.summary: The lovely little village lies picturesquely above the Sitter. A small brook plunges down to the river in a bold leap.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a traditional Germanic dragon or great serpent, often imagined as wingless or low to the ground; here it is simply the dreadful monster of the Dragon’s Hole, and the brief account does not specify its anatomy.

563f2f37561040b27b2682721512286015e92d1e.summary: In the village of Brunnen, near the Geisssteg, a spring bears this name. Many, many years ago, a chapel of St.

notes.label: St. Kathrinenbrünneli
notes.text: literally ‘St. Catherine's little spring,’ an affectionate diminutive for the local healing springs and their vanished chapels.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep rock face or cliff; the second healing spring emerges from one near Hundsbühl.

notes.label: Glöcklein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning ‘little bell’; this miraculous chapel bell rings by itself at the foundational oath on the Rütli.

notes.label: Tellen
notes.text: a traditional plural formed from the name Tell, used here for the oath-taking Swiss freedom heroes associated with William Tell and the Rütli; it is not simply a family surname in this context.

1ffc24bb5753b4c2a51a8ca31ac7c42e2895c5ae.summary: In the ossuary beside the parish church in Naters, one finds a strange carved work representing a life-sized person nailed to a cross.

notes.label: St. Kümmernis
notes.text: the Valais name for the bearded crucified female saint also known as Wilgefortis, invoked especially in stories about resisting marriage and suffering; the account treats the carved image as able to leave Naters, while the saint’s legendary name and identity vary across regions.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss regional title for a church sexton or sacristan; ringing the church bells is the protective act that invokes St. Michael’s power.

notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘St. Michael has thwarted us’ or ‘stood against us’; the title repeats the supernatural voice’s explanation for the avalanche’s failure.

notes.label: Gaugraf
notes.text: a count exercising authority over a Gau, an early medieval territorial district; Hunfried's exact powers are not detailed, but the title places the chapel legend in the Carolingian political order.

629c0974ee9a75763752b003f74add00c279f767.summary: Victor, offered to God by his parents in his childhood, devoted his youth to piety and scholarly study and surpassed all his contemporaries in gifts of mind.

notes.label: Stiftsfrauen
notes.text: women belonging to a religious collegiate foundation or convent community; Victor’s sisters Aurora and Evalina hold this status at Cazis rather than being identified more narrowly by a monastic order.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

2233c109aa05e0de352f4a21ecf7434d0dfdd275.summary: The last tyrannical lord at Starkenstein Castle was visited by a close relative, and they decided to undertake a magnificent hunt on the Neuenalp opposite, where at that time chamois, roe deer, and red deer were plentiful.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Stoffel
notes.text: the source's local form for an Alpine cattle station or level of seasonal pasture, related to the more widespread Stafel; here Neuenalp Stoffel is a named place on the alp.

notes.label: Sennerin
notes.text: a woman who works at a seasonal Alpine dairy and tends the cattle and milk production; the role carries more specific Alpine associations than the general English ‘dairymaid.’

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Kuhreihen
notes.text: a traditional Swiss cattle-herding song or call, often associated with Alpine dairying and used to summon, soothe, or celebrate the herd; it is distinct from the alphorn playing mentioned beside it.

notes.label: Arten
notes.text: an uncertain recorded form in a list of improvised farm weapons; context indicates axes or similar chopping tools, but the exact local implement intended by the transcription is not secure.

29fee2ae6fd775a2a3514145fbcd7485163b507d.summary: A certain Staufer and his pupils Stadlin and Hoppo practiced strange sorceries long ago—perhaps four hundred years ago—in the Bern region and neighboring places.

notes.label: Stupa
notes.text: the historical source’s parenthetical form for a room or heated chamber, related to Stube; it may also be a learned gloss or wordplay tied to the account of Staufer’s death.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a local chief magistrate, administrator, or bailiff; Stiefelhans abuses the authority and social position associated with the office.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Stiefel
notes.text: literally ‘boot,’ the mountain height that gives the condemned ghost his byname or final place of banishment.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herder.

notes.label: Herdgeiter
notes.text: a regional wood-cutting knife or cleaver, glossed in the source as a Holzmesser.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Schwemm
notes.text: the name of an alp beneath the Kamor to which Stiefelhans is first banished; the source does not explain the place-name.

notes.label: zauerte
notes.text: performed a traditional Alpine herding call or song; the exact vocal practice intended is connected with Zauren.

notes.label: Zauren
notes.text: a traditional wordless or call-like Alpine vocal practice; answering it is said to place one’s livestock under the ghost’s power.

notes.label: Ave Mariarufen
notes.text: literally ‘calling the Ave Maria,’ a protective devotional call said to date from the danger posed by Stiefelhans.

cfcd8c5d5ca3e6c0fbf34d5badeaca89b907a57c.summary: During their nocturnal roaming, some young men from Unterschächen came upon a lonely Schlätterhüsli in which, contrary to every expectation, a little light gleamed.

notes.label: Schlätterhüsli
notes.text: an Uri diminutive for a small rustic hut or outbuilding; it serves as the cats’ dance house, but the exact building type intended by Schlätter is uncertain.

notes.label: Znyni
notes.text: an Uri spelling of Znüni, the customary midmorning meal or snack associated with the ninth hour; the supernatural feast occurs at night despite the meal-name.

notes.label: Kalazzen
notes.text: a local word explicitly identified by the source as the morning meal or breakfast; its wider regional distribution and etymology are uncertain.

notes.label: Stimperli
notes.text: the affectionate diminutive nickname given to the cat with the stump tail; the recognition exposes its identity as one of the nocturnal musicians and provokes its attack.

c29af6a25158094c3658e674bd8bd31b53282718.summary: One morning, a bell had disappeared from the church tower at Gretschins, and no trace of it could be found.

71e51c5551b3416fd51450ad6c47f741d4f252ae.summary: a) Near the Joch mountains by Engelberg, a glacier pushes its rubble down toward the Trübsee.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Salzröhrli
notes.text: the Engelberg regional name for the salt-filled barrel the immensely strong monastery brother carries in his fatal wager; the diminutive form does not imply that the load was small.

notes.label: Pfaffenhaufen
notes.text: literally ‘priest’s heap’ or ‘cleric’s mound,’ the burial place of the dead monastery brother and a local landmark tied to the glacier legend.

notes.label: Pfaffe
notes.text: an old, often irreverent word for a cleric; here it is the familiar name used when daring the dead monastery brother’s spirit to throw stones.

35bfc0b4111227ab24cc0c5c1bb6fb110680c0fb.summary: a) At the Burgfluh near Wölflinswil in the Fricktal, an isolated tower-shaped rock is called the Ankenkübel.

notes.label: Ankenkübel
notes.text: literally ‘butter tub’ in Swiss usage, a local name for the tower-shaped rock near Wölflinswil; its shape likely motivates the name, though the source does not say so explicitly.

notes.label: Kleinkindertrog
notes.text: literally ‘little-child trough’; in the local birth legend it is the place within the Ankenkübel from which the midwife retrieves infants.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: a Swiss regional plural or place-form related to Fluh, meaning a steep rock face or cliff; here it appears as an alternative name for the Fluchstein, and the exact relationship between the two names is uncertain.

notes.label: Kindlistein
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little-children stone,’ with the diminutive -li; the Roman-looking stone belongs to a wider Swiss tradition that infants are obtained from particular rocks.

3f811f9ee8ab0297b026e3c8027147ee2aea37eb.summary: The village of Merligen lies on Lake Thun between Saint Beatus’s Cave and Ralligen Castle.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Reiti
notes.text: here Reiti appears to denote the hayloft or an elevated resting place where the man sleeps; its precise local meaning and construction are uncertain.

notes.label: drei höchschte Nämen
notes.text: literally the ‘three highest Names,’ this protective formula likely invokes the Trinity and prevents the nocturnal being from strangling him; the exact wording of the prayer is unspecified.

197359d1f432bcc3be9b36a3b217c2df2acff532.summary: Christian Gall, a man from Bärschis, set out late one evening from the Malun alp on his way home.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

fb3de37e1c1a07d795d2eef8a56f447aaf8ec197.summary: One autumn day the carter Balz from Langwies came from Chur to Tschiertschen, and he intended to go home that very night.

notes.label: Ungfell
notes.text: an older Alemannic form of Unglück or Unfall, a mishap, accident, or misfortune likely to be deadly on the dark mountain road.

notes.label: Wildner
notes.text: a wild, fierce, or rugged man; it describes Balz’s fearlessness and rough temperament rather than a formal occupation.

notes.label: baschgen
notes.text: a regional verb meaning approximately to overpower, master, or get the better of someone; the source immediately parallels it with leading Balz onto the wrong path.

notes.label: letzen
notes.text: an Alemannic adjective meaning wrong, adverse, or left-hand; here it describes the false path onto which the Devil might divert him.

notes.label: Holzriese
notes.text: a steep timber chute or slide used to send felled wood downhill; this one descends into the ravine and becomes the wrestling ground.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided Alpine ravine or gorge, often containing a stream.

notes.label: Ries
notes.text: a steep chute or slide, here the shortened name for the Holzriese down which Balz and the Devil tumble.

notes.label: z'Tag glüt'
notes.text: a Graubünden dialect expression meaning that the bells rang to announce daybreak; their sacred morning sound ends the Devil’s hold.

notes.label: lugg
notes.text: a dialect word meaning slack, loose, or yielding; neither wrestler is willing to loosen his grip or let go.

notes.label: Balz-Ries
notes.text: the place-name given to the timber chute after Balz’s struggle with the Evil One; it memorializes the marks he carried on his neck.

6acdedda661b0be64b65ff3df51df21ffc1e60f0.summary: a) A Heidenweiblein once came to a mother in Erstfeld and sprinkled a powder into the roasted flour porridge she had prepared for her child.

notes.label: Heidenweiblein
notes.text: literally a ‘little heathen woman,’ a diminutive regional label often applied to an ancient, non-Christian, or otherworldly female being; here she gives the child supernatural strength, but the account does not further identify her people or nature.

notes.label: Gnärv
notes.text: an Uri dialect word related to sinew, bodily fiber, or strength; a ‘double Gnärv’ marks Karli’s extraordinary constitution, but the phrase is folkloric rather than a precise anatomical description.

444176fea2d5654157545c64957707d2c2955e50.summary: During the descent from a Mels Alp, a milking stool had been forgotten in the main hut.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high-elevation seasonal pasture and its associated dairy buildings, here abandoned after the livestock’s descent; the specific Mels pasture is not named.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Agathabrot
notes.text: Agathabrot is bread blessed in honor of Saint Agatha and carried as protection against fire, illness, or supernatural danger; the exact local blessing and use are uncertain.

notes.label: Zitgeiss
notes.text: Zitgeiss is the dialect term for the young goat staked in the wager; its exact age range and the source dialect’s pronunciation are uncertain.

b1a45caafff91d4e91d730695400634c768bfe2d.summary: Stephan Heinzmann of Visperterminen, who lived at the beginning of the previous century, was once delayed so greatly on business in Brig that he could not return home until night.

notes.label: Mux
notes.text: the slightest sound, movement, or sign of resistance, used in the threat that the captive attacker must not make a peep; the colloquial word intensifies Heinzmann's control of him.

984d520ab9996a979a6457be847295ccc197520c.summary: Three goat boys on the Giebelstöcke were overtaken by a thunderstorm. Two of them were afraid, made the sign of the cross, and prayed, ‘Jesus, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; b’hüet-is Gott und d’s heilig Chrytz.’ The third merely mocked, laughed, and boasted.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: b’hüet-is Gott und d’s heilig Chrytz
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘may God and the holy Cross protect us’; the boys append this protective formula to the names of Jesus and the four Evangelists during the storm.
notes.anchor: b’hüet-is Gott und d’s heilig Chrytz

notes.label: Krachen
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a deep cleft, ravine, or rocky chasm; here it is the seemingly bottomless lightning hole, not merely the sound of crashing.

da7bcbf0962f08667d97c8d39e98e13503ff2fa5.summary: Around Brunnen in the canton of Schwyz, on holy Epiphany Eve and during that night, people formerly made as much noise as possible.

notes.label: Treichlen
notes.text: large livestock bells made from hammered sheet metal; ringing them noisily in the procession is intended to influence or protect the coming fruit crop.

notes.label: Geisseln
notes.text: long whips cracked for loud ritual sound; together with bells, horns, and rattles, they confront the forest women.

notes.label: Strudeli
notes.text: one of the two named forest women addressed by the Epiphany noise rite; the diminutive name may evoke swirling or disorder, but her individual character is not explained.

notes.label: Strätteli
notes.text: the second named forest woman; the name may relate to a combing, dragging, or local personal form, but its precise derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: treichle
notes.text: the verb ‘to ring or sound Treichlen’; vigorous bell-ringing is believed necessary for an abundant fruit harvest.

e8f1b19382b77ff0404f2ba08fcb835e57d14ee8.summary: The late Doctor Jaggi, who many years ago lived in Gsteig, a lonely side valley of the Saanenland, understood the secret arts.

notes.label: gstellen
notes.text: dialect for magically stopping, fixing, or immobilizing a person or animal so an intended action cannot be completed.

notes.label: Strüdelbücher
notes.text: rare books said to teach Strüdel magic and other secret arts.

notes.label: Gsteigboden
notes.text: the lower ground or valley-floor locality at Gsteig where the cherry thieves are immobilized.

notes.label: Strüdeljaggi
notes.text: the magical Doctor Jaggi's nickname, combining Jaggi with Strüdel, a harmful magical entanglement or bewitching force.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night lads,’ young men roaming after dark for mischief, here to steal cherries.

notes.label: Alberholz
notes.text: wood from the Alber tree, likely whitebeam, poplar, or a related regionally named tree; its exact species is uncertain, but the staff breaks the spell.

notes.label: Bissen
notes.text: the local valley district where the miser lives and from which the Strüdeln disappear.

notes.label: verstrüdlet
notes.text: bewitched, tangled, or afflicted by Strüdel magic, here the supposed cause of the pigs' sickness.

notes.label: ferndrigen
notes.text: regional speech meaning ‘from last year,’ used of the miser's stored pork.

notes.label: Brosamlein
notes.text: a tiny crumb or morsel, the miser's minimizing description of the great quantity of meat he has hoarded.

notes.label: Strüdel
notes.text: the singular harmful magical force or agent blamed for the pigs' condition and symbolically attacked by rubbing the kettle.

notes.label: Hammen
notes.text: hams; seven of them emerge from the miser's smoke-cured stores.

notes.label: Strüdeln
notes.text: plural Strüdel forces or magical afflictions, declared gone after the doctor's ritual and redistribution of food.

notes.label: Wisch
notes.text: a wisp or bundled pad used to scour the copper kettle as part of the counter-magic.

c76c7bff221f6f247ec10e10444fb290891d36ac.summary: 1. A young man from Gurtnellen was walking home from Amsteg at night.

notes.label: äs Tanzspill
notes.text: Uri dialect for dance music or a tune played for dancing; it first alerts the traveler to the supernatural gathering.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge common in the Swiss Alpine landscape; the old pack road crosses the Fellitobel over the cats' illuminated dance site.

notes.label: Handorgelen
notes.text: a regional form for a hand organ or button accordion; the stumpy-tailed cat plays it above the brook.

notes.label: Stumper, spill is wider einä-n-üff!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Stumper, play us another one!’; the dancing cats address the musician by the nickname derived from its shortened tail.

notes.label: Kalatzen
notes.text: an Uri regional word for the morning meal or breakfast time; the context places the master's cat there the next morning, but the term's narrower household sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Soll-er-es firha?
notes.text: an Uri dialect question about whether the young man should bring up what he saw or confront the cat with it; the exact idiomatic force of firha is uncertain, but the following teasing speech makes the intent clear.

notes.label: So Stumper, wo bisch nächtig gsy?
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Well, Stumper, where were you last night?’; the teasing question exposes the cat's secret identity.
notes.anchor: So Stumper, wo bisch nächtig gsy?

notes.label: I ha miässä fort
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I had to go away’; the cat's brief human answer confirms its uncanny nature before the fuller accusation.

notes.label: Jä, dä hesch-di mein-i luschtig gmacht und bisch bim Tanz gsy und hesch üffg'spillt!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Well then, I think you enjoyed yourself, went to the dance, and played the music!’; being openly recognized causes the cat to vanish.
notes.anchor: Jä, dä hesch-di mein-i luschtig gmacht und bisch bim Tanz gsy und hesch üffg'spillt!

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young women; these four are locally reputed to be witches despite the narrator also calling them maidens.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: z'Gass
notes.text: a Swiss German expression for paying an evening social or courting visit; young men visit the four Meitli but are put off by their behavior.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: evening social gatherings held in a Stube, often involving company, music, courtship, or domestic work; the servant assumes the lit house is hosting another such gathering.

notes.label: Grind
notes.text: a blunt or familiar Swiss German word for the head; the cat wears a white nightcap on it, making the scene grotesquely domestic.

notes.label: Ich mag nimmä-n-orgälä, Stimper, tüe dü!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I cannot play anymore, Stimper; you do it!’; one cat hands the bone instrument to the familiar stumpy-tailed mouser.
notes.anchor: Ich mag nimmä-n-orgälä, Stimper, tüe dü!

notes.label: Mülorgäli
notes.text: literally a little mouth organ, here the uncanny bone used like a harmonica; the exact instrument is fanciful rather than a conventional manufactured mouth organ.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Stimper, mach üff!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Stimper, play up!’; in the shorter variant the dancing cats urge the musician to resume.

notes.label: Stumpäschwanz
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘stumpy tail,’ used as the cat's descriptive nickname in variant d; recognition by this name ends the apparition.

notes.label: Lüeg da! ysärä Stumpäschwanz!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Look there! Our Stumpäschwanz!’; the possessive identifies the supernatural musician as the speakers' household cat.

notes.text: the feminine designation tied to a Kastenvogt, a historical office or officeholder; the cited chronicle does not explain her exact legal status or duties.

58a47121b4ec05a1969a5d5cebf650b2781c2650.summary: a. Someone had just been hanged when three young men settled into an inn not far from the gallows and began drinking and playing cards.

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for a baptismal godfather or male sponsor; the dead godchildren repeatedly address their living godfathers by this kinship title while acting as their advocates in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Wesperli
notes.text: an Ursern name for a child believed to have died after baptism without tasting earthly food and therefore to have become one of the most beautiful little angels; the word’s derivation and any distinction from Wesperchind are not explained.

notes.label: Wesperchind
notes.text: an Ursern compound naming the same kind of newly baptized child who dies without earthly food and is believed to become an especially beautiful angel; the source does not explain how, if at all, it differs from Wesperli.

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: a regional jacket or coat; in this brief variant, an unidentified force draws the survivor’s garment tight over his head when the bells begin to ring, but the source does not identify the agent.

f6bdd02a1cab4721075163a7187751de7b9f17bf.summary: A sunken castle lies in the little lake of the village of Egolzwil, which belongs to the parish of Altishofen.

95e82b68dc85170fcf67a63aa1340ffd2c1e5110.summary: At midnight, people claim to hear a dreadful voice calling in the dark cellar vaults:

0f8f473938c155efc47174b1bc2eab6a120be22b.summary: 1. A man from Isental was walking home at night.

notes.label: Bätti
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive for a rosary or set of prayer beads; here the man swings it at the cats as both a physical and devotional defense, though the source does not describe its size or construction.

notes.label: Bättälyttä
notes.text: literally the ‘ringing for prayer,’ the prayer-bell or Angelus signal; here it marks the time after which old people warn against harming cats, though the story does not specify which daily ringing.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night lads,’ groups of unmarried young men who went out at night for courting, revelry, or rough customary pranks; here they roam Buchholz and provoke uncanny cats.

7b0998584867b8113621256572dc8ac1135dc68a.summary: That was the name of the B’hänki who lived all alone at Obriedli in Bürglen.

notes.label: B’hänki
notes.text: a dialect designation here for a feared woman believed able to work harmful weather magic; ‘witch’ is the closest contextual sense, but the word’s precise derivation and range are uncertain.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small barn, shed, simple farm building, or chamber; Susanneli lives in one before a house stands at Obriedli, but its exact use is not identified.

notes.label: Böllen
notes.text: Swiss German for an onion; Susanneli’s impossible speed lets her fetch one from Milan while the Anken warms.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for butter; it is left warming in the pan during Susanneli’s supernatural round trip to Milan.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: verhytt der heelig Chnodä
notes.text: the surviving dialect fragment of an Ursern saying about Susanneli after a fall; individual words suggest cursing or an ‘accursed’ condition and something holy, but the grammar and Chnodä are too uncertain to translate reliably without inventing a lost context.

6b2ccf436a8f6dfed845346029abcc43e7d93095.summary: On the Geilenbüel in Schattdorf lived three old, wanton girls who never went to church and mocked everything religious.

notes.label: Gugelfuhr
notes.text: the source’s name for irreverent foolery, rough horseplay, or a mocking game; the exact activity is not described, but performing it during worship marks the women’s offense.

b652ef37e89ee83da5eddbc2c14a2d22c9fead91.summary: A traveler on the Axenstrasse heard a voice call, ‘Take the key above the door and open all the doors!’ He looked around and saw a door in the rock wall and a golden key above it.

notes.label: Wybervolch
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic collective or dismissive expression for a woman or female person; here it first identifies the enchanted woman seated on the treasure chest, not a crowd.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: the diminutive form of Wybervolch, literally something like a ‘little female person’; it can sound familiar or dismissive, and here refers to the same enchanted woman awaiting release.

879252e88842e42ee3626eebcfa2bd0bb9cb052e.summary: In the mountain valley separating the municipality of Emd from St. Niklaus lies a high Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Augstkumme
notes.text: literally an ‘August hollow’ or ‘August basin,’ the name of a late-grazed pasture on the Belalp that the source compares with Augstbort.

notes.label: Goldbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘gold spring,’ the celebrated source beside the old Augstbort pass route; the account does not claim that it contains literal gold.

notes.label: Moosalpe
notes.text: the named high pasture route toward the district of Raron; Alpe here denotes the seasonal pasture landscape, not simply a peak.

notes.label: Alpleute
notes.text: people living or working seasonally on an Alp, including herders and dairy workers who witness the bewitched vessels and bells.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a grazing level, hut site, or seasonal station within an Alp; the vessels appear to roll from the roof down this working area.

notes.label: Alpvieh
notes.text: the livestock kept on a seasonal Alp, especially the cattle occupying its summer grazing grounds.

notes.label: Viehschälle
notes.text: a livestock bell, especially one carried by cattle; the phantom disturbance makes every bell seem to ring.

notes.label: Kalle
notes.text: the clapper inside a livestock bell; the return to silence is so complete that not one clapper strikes.

notes.label: Alpweib
notes.text: an older expression for a woman living and working on an Alp; here she tends the household and livestock, and the term should not be read as a modern neutral job title.

notes.label: Alpschwein
notes.text: a pig kept on an Alp, often fed with whey from dairy work; a maimed double of the woman's healthy pig appears beside the irrigation channel.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Augstbortalpe
notes.text: the high seasonal pasture at Augstbort; Alpe is a regional inflected form of Alp, and the landscape anchors the supernatural episodes.

notes.label: Abendsitz
notes.text: an evening social gathering for conversation and amusement; the rooster-footed stranger uses the invitation to lure the young women away.

537d7605e13b0265dec618aaae5a8f8a22cabfdb.summary: Jaggli Lander met a poor little farmer from Attinghausen on the Surenen-Egg, a man whom my informant’s father had still known, and the farmer lamented his need and misery to him.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ an itinerant learned figure often credited with occult or secret knowledge in German-speaking Alpine folklore; here he mysteriously offers to end the farmer’s poverty, and the label need not mean an ordinary student.

5e3e37d19213e4f0f5c24a45caf734adac8e230b.summary: In the village of Saas there once lived a man called Tamatterhans (Hans Anthanmatten).

notes.label: Tamatterhans
notes.text: the local byname for Hans Anthanmatten, formed from the Valais surname and the given name Hans; it identifies this remembered Saas character rather than a general folklore being.

notes.label: Geimer
notes.text: a Saas-dialect occupational or activity term connected here with handling and loading a firearm; its closest precise Standard German sense is uncertain, so the source form is retained rather than narrowed without evidence.

notes.label: G’leit
notes.text: a Saas-dialect word for the firearm or gun being loaded; the passage’s old technical wording is compressed, so the exact kind of weapon is not specified.

notes.label: Gimpilu
notes.text: a Saas-dialect place or occasion name in the shirt anecdote; its exact referent is uncertain from the passage, so it is retained as written.

784a81d9c1913eb3acec18461759c1519afdaa4f.summary: A boy was tending goats on the Tiergarten when he saw a door in a rock and opened it.

notes.label: Tiergarten
notes.text: a local landscape name for the hill or grazing area where the rock door and mysterious music are encountered, not a modern zoological garden.

notes.label: Zigeunerbanden
notes.text: a historical and now derogatory German label, literally ‘Gypsy bands,’ that older sources applied to Roma, Sinti, or other itinerant groups; it is retained only to make the source's prejudicial wording visible and should not be used as a neutral modern designation.

notes.label: Tannhuser
notes.text: the title's local form of the Tannhäuser name attached to the mysterious sleeper tradition; the body describes the ancient bearded men without identifying which one bears the name.

0d72b3fb59ad40bdd0afa54e275bb15b18a51748.summary: It was on a Sunday after Saint Othmar's Day. A man came walking down toward Altdorf from Bürglen, a little village at the entrance to the wild Schächen Valley, with the firm stride of a mountaineer.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the Habsburg territorial governor or bailiff; neither English title alone captures the office's political role in the Tell tradition.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Göller
notes.text: a close-fitting shoulder or neck garment; Tell tucks the second arrow into it rather than into a separate quiver.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the elected chief magistrate of a rural Swiss canton or district.

notes.label: Nauen
notes.text: a traditional broad, flat-bottomed lake vessel; here it is the Landvogt's roofed official boat.

notes.label: Maienlandsgemeinde
notes.text: the open-air cantonal popular assembly traditionally held in May; its crowd's grumbling supplies the storm simile.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, powerful downslope Alpine wind, culturally associated with sudden violent weather on Swiss lakes.

af0398c641a9af8d432323a54e8991ea441e5b1c.summary: A poor farmer from Seelisberg was working with timber on the Marcht. Discontented with God and the world, he cursed poverty and work, swore every imaginable curse, and wished for the Devil to come.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little man; it makes the seemingly friendly stranger appear unthreatening before his hoofprints reveal him.

notes.label: Teufelsbockbart
notes.text: literally ‘Devil’s billy-goat beard,’ the uncanny stranger’s mock personal or business name at a Zurich street address; whether it names the Devil himself, a demonic persona, or merely the beard is intentionally comic and uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, dairy work, and community, not simply a mountain peak; the forbidden book teaches how to harm such pastoral operations.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the farmer hides the book inside it.

notes.label: Dillbaum
notes.text: a regional building term for a heavy beam supporting or bordering the Dill, a barn’s boarded floor or hayloft; the exact structure of this Gaden is not described.

743992b245b8e70eb57c991bbb794c280a5e60df.summary: a) D'Tifelsbrugg und d'r Tifelsstei — The Devil's Bridge and the Devil's Stone (Altdorf dialect).

notes.label: D'Tifelsbrugg
notes.text: Altdorf dialect for ‘the Devil's Bridge,’ the bridge through the Schöllenen gorge; the apostrophe and Tifel spelling are retained from the source's dialect heading.

notes.label: d'r Tifelsstei
notes.text: Altdorf dialect for ‘the Devil's Stone,’ the huge rock the Devil means to use against the bridge; in the tale an old woman marks it with a cross and forces him to abandon it.

notes.label: Ürner
notes.text: dialect for the people of Uri; the term identifies the cantonal community that bargains with the Devil and collectively devises the goat trick.

notes.label: Landschriber
notes.text: dialect for the cantonal scribe or clerk who records an official agreement; invoking him humorously turns the bargain with the Devil into public business.

notes.label: Landsg'meind
notes.text: dialect for Landsgemeinde, the open assembly in which eligible citizens of a Swiss canton vote directly; here the people gather at Schattdorf to decide how to satisfy the bargain.

notes.label: Landamme
notes.text: the dialect form of Landammann, the presiding chief magistrate of Uri; he asks a councilor for advice during the Landsg'meind.

notes.label: Gitzibock
notes.text: a young billy goat; the people send it first across the bridge as a living but nonhuman payment to outwit the Devil.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Bull of Uri,’ a personification and martial emblem of the canton; the closing verse warns that this stronger defender, not another goat, would meet the Devil if he returned.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure whose exact length varied regionally; the stone's height and circumference are given in Klafter, so no single modern conversion is implied.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Teufelsbürde
notes.text: literally the ‘Devil's burden,’ the local name of the gneiss erratic near Wabern that Satan is said to have dropped while trying to destroy Bern.

9526dba694417f088fcac00a9280d404d7865a0f.summary: Not far from Bern, on the Gurten near Wabern, a granite boulder lay in the valley until not very long ago.

notes.label: Teufelsburde
notes.text: literally ‘the Devil's burden,’ the local name of the granite boulder said to have been thrown from the mountains; Burde emphasizes the immense load the Devil carried.

9f3904b7a32f386883eaedca625b0cafab7ae224.summary: The Kastenvögtin1 of Ursern often spent the night with Melchior Jauch’s family in Silenen during her journeys through the lowlands.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Chohli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive formed from the idea of coal-blackness, used here admiringly for the handsome black horse; the witch’s praise immediately precedes the animal’s fatal fall.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Schneidergret
notes.text: a folkloric witch-name probably combining Schneider, ‘tailor’ or a surname, with Gret, a familiar form of Margareta; the source identifies her as the witch actually intended but does not settle the name’s historical origin.

notes.label: Kastenvögtin
notes.text: the feminine designation tied to a Kastenvogt, a historical office or officeholder; the note says the narrator attached it to the wrong regional witch, while its exact origin as an office, household title, or byname remains uncertain.

59d33cbe73ae08566338ce6b87b30a38ea95cd2a.summary: This happened in winter, at the beginning of the eighties. The little boy of Councilman Rütti on Arni, named Vinzenz, was to fetch his mother a diaper that she had hung up not very far from the house.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

6608dc18a915d95e57ff0bbd299485040bcd6ca2.summary: On the Alp Greina there was a Senn who, on a rainy evening, went to the Zeitkühe upon the “Sattel” to give them the salt they needed.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Greina
notes.text: the high seasonal grazing area in the Greina region; Alp here denotes the managed pasture and its dairy operation.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and dairy work on the seasonal pasture.

notes.label: Zeitkühe
notes.text: a local class of cows kept apart at this stage or season of the pasture operation; the tale establishes that the Senn visits them to provide salt, but does not define the compound’s exact husbandry sense.

notes.label: Sattel
notes.text: literally a saddle, here the saddle-shaped mountain ridge or pass where the cows are kept and across which the spectral host travels.

notes.label: Nachtschaar
notes.text: literally a “night host” or “nightly company,” an old-spelling name for the supernatural procession whose route crosses the Sattel.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the other Alpine dairy workers who hear their missing companion’s voice and search for him.

57de073a8f3e9ebbc92e326b2d837b463fd74266.summary: Long ago, a Grundlawine plunged from the heights of the Brienz ridge, followed the Planalpgraben down across the Planalp holdings, and swept up earth, forest, stone, and a village standing on the Husstatt.

notes.label: Grundlawine
notes.text: a ground avalanche whose moving snow reaches or scrapes along the underlying terrain, often entraining earth, wood, and rock; the tale describes it carrying away an entire settlement.

notes.label: Fuss
notes.text: historical spelling of Fuß, ‘foot’; regional pre-metric values varied, so the stated 1000 Fuss conveys the great height of the descent rather than an exact modern measurement.

notes.label: Planalpfluh
notes.text: the named cliff or steep rock face below Planalp; Fluh is a Swiss and Alemannic word for a cliff, and the compound is retained as a local topographic name.

notes.label: ab Planalp
notes.text: literally ‘from Planalp,’ used in the legend as the survivor's byname and then joined into the surname Abplanalp; this is a traditional surname-origin story rather than verified genealogy.

08e94e38da5ddd31aae56dcc56e0388d7a36c2b3.summary: A legend once circulated in Törbel: whenever a municipal official was about to die, he announced himself during the night, from twelve o’clock until the morning Betenleuten, in the municipal hall through Brodzählen and noises, as though the municipal accounts were being settled.

notes.label: Betenleuten
notes.text: the ringing that calls people to morning prayer, probably a regional spelling of Betenläuten; it marks the customary dawn boundary of the apparition’s activity.

notes.label: Brodzählen
notes.text: literally suggests ‘counting bread,’ but its exact local or possibly corrupted sense is uncertain; in context it is an audible part of the ghostly reenactment of municipal accounting.

94bc0152efac3a13d39546e3ef57b0f12b7397fd.summary: In former times, the Gries behind Blindensee was a magnificent Alp. Three Stäfel stood there: Griesbalm, Lauchbalm, and Sandbalm.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, herd, grazing rights, and working landscape; the fertile pasture is transformed into glacier-covered Gries.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Stäfel
notes.text: seasonal stations, levels, or clusters of buildings within an Alp system; the three named Stäfel mark the former pasture’s extent and organization.

notes.label: Strichen
notes.text: regional wording for the cows’ teats; the curse gives them hornlike and thorny forms, but the account does not describe whether this is literal growth, injury, or disease.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live, work, or pasture livestock seasonally on an Alp; in the narrator’s present they are beginning to use the deglaciated Gries again.

e8eb759e9f8f8d36e61239984c487232b92fedd8.summary: In former times, Tscherlach had many cherry trees on its fertile soil and sunny slopes, their branches nearly breaking every summer beneath an overabundance of the finest fruit.

notes.label: Tscherlach
notes.text: the St. Gallen locality whose former abundance of cherries and later poor yield the stranger's curse explains.

77bba3a23c819ede4051e05ea860a529a9486ec7.summary: a) Klariden was once a magnificently beautiful Alp. The cows gave an outrageous Schapf of milk, so that they had to be milked three times a day.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain summit; the variants place the once-blessed fodder plant on several named Alps.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schapf
notes.text: a regional vessel or quantity measure for milk; the story uses one full Schapf to convey extraordinary yield but gives neither its exact form nor capacity.

notes.label: Milchkraut
notes.text: literally ‘milk herb,’ the white-sapped pasture plant said to have produced abundant milk before it was cursed; the collector records several competing botanical identifications.

notes.label: Milchlichrüt
notes.text: the Uri dialect form given parenthetically for Milchkraut, the legendary milk-rich herb; it is not a secure single botanical species across the variants.

notes.label: Muttern
notes.text: a valued aromatic Alpine pasture herb, generally identified with Alpine spignel or mutellina; cows are said to prefer the Milchkraut even to it.

notes.label: St. Joderstag
notes.text: the local feast day of St. Joder, a Swiss form of St. Theodore; here the Senn leaves for its Kilbi and dance, while the source does not state a calendar date.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese production on a high pasture; his absence leaves the resentful farmhand to milk alone.

notes.label: Kilbi
notes.text: a Swiss parish fair or church-dedication feast traditionally marked by communal festivity and dancing; here it draws the dairy workers away from their duties.

notes.label: Flüechächrüt
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘curse herb,’ one of the names given to the poisonous white-sapped plant after the farmhand’s curse.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for butter; the extravagant image of walkways made from cheese and Anken expresses the Blümlisalp’s former dairy abundance.

notes.label: Tyfelschrüt
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Devil’s herb,’ one of three names the Isental farmer gives to Potentilla Tormentilla as his version of the accursed plant.

notes.label: Tormäntschrüt
notes.text: a dialect plant name built from Tormentilla and ‘herb,’ used for the same Potentilla specimen; its spelling records local pronunciation rather than a different securely identified species.

notes.label: Tormäntillchrüt
notes.text: another dialect form meaning ‘Tormentilla herb,’ used by the same informant for the Potentilla he identifies as the accursed plant.

notes.label: Ciprion
notes.text: a Maderan Valley plant name used alongside spurge; the collector was shown reindeer lichen under this name, but the relationship between the name and a single botanical species remains uncertain.

37305afe5f09e85982bbdaf717dbc0a31a2f0345.summary: A man from Schattdorf had often encountered someone at night in a particular place who was pushing against a fence and whom he had to take for a spirit.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

65a8552aca287913c5634f8ddb2007c676064f6c.summary: The dwarfs went barefoot and often looked enviously at the shoes worn by other human children.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey left from cheese-making, named here in the belief that the captured being might reveal how to obtain gold from it; the word can have other meanings elsewhere, but the dairy context supports this sense.

notes.label: Gufer
notes.text: a regional Alpine word for a rocky outcrop, boulder pile, or stony place; the source specifically glosses it here as a rock head on a mountain farm, from which the Mannli calls its advice.

notes.label: wilden Mannli
notes.text: the exact inflected phrase quoted in the title, literally ‘little wild man’; the body uses Mannli, the local diminutive for a small nonhuman mountain being treated here as one of the dwarfs, whose seemingly comic advice warns that Alpine weather can change even when conditions are fair.

676c4823bf1f0cae63e3dc61eb1e5cae0ef097cd.summary: About 200 years ago, a peculiar kind of winged vermin, called simply “Muggen,” caused great damage to ripening grain in the Schanvigger-Tale.

notes.label: Muggen
notes.text: the tale’s collective name for a destructive kind of winged vermin that strips ears of grain; the exact insect species is not established, so it should not be narrowed automatically to modern mosquitoes or gnats.

notes.label: Schanvigger-Tale
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical form for the Schanfigg valley in Graubünden, whose ripening grain is attacked.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: the open-air assembly of eligible citizens used for communal and cantonal decision-making in parts of Switzerland; here it debates a lawsuit against the insects.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the presiding chief magistrate or leading elected official of the community or jurisdiction; he proposes the legal proceedings.

notes.label: Pradner
notes.text: belonging to Praden or its inhabitants; the insects are assigned territory under Praden’s land rights on the other side of the valley.

notes.label: Tschiertscher
notes.text: belonging to Tschiertschen or its inhabitants; the sentence alternatively locates the insects on land under that community’s rights.

notes.label: Muggen-Äuli
notes.text: the little riverside meadow or grove assigned to the Muggen; Äuli is a diminutive of Au, and the name commemorates the legendary legal banishment.

notes.label: Fug und Recht
notes.text: a legal formula meaning due authority and right; felling a tree restores the insects’ formally stated right to return each year.

ab4ac95405e20cba3d56e9f0ae26efe87d386ed2.summary: a) From Biberegg, the Aa flows through a deep Tobel past Steinen, which lies an hour from Schwyz.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge in Swiss and southern German usage; the Aa runs through one before reaching Steinen.

notes.label: Aha-Hudi
notes.text: the local name of a witch-like female flood rider on the Aa at Steinen; Hudi can be a disparaging term for a ragged woman, while the full name's derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Trämmel
notes.text: a regional diminutive or variant for a log or heavy piece of timber; the Aha-Hudi rides it through floodwater.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Trumm
notes.text: a large broken piece, especially a chunk or log of timber; the parallel Uri witch rides one downstream.

notes.label: Erb
notes.text: the Alp’s name is derived in the poem from Erbe and erben—an heir, inheritance, and inheriting—because seven successive heirs possess it within twelve hours during a night of repeated deaths.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

11d5460c861586c7b6bfa0a6156e4f049209ed1c.summary: At Seelegg in the Maderan Valley, two huts stood close together, one somewhat higher than the other.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy production, explicitly identified by the source as the group's head man; the specter counts him with the two challengers as a potential third victim.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture with its huts, livestock, and dairy work, not merely a mountain; the abandoned hut and its specter belong to that pastoral setting.

6d8ab1e8a48cdfdb042cfd9fd4f24ba87a28929a.summary: On an Uri Alp, they faced a terrible problem because no farmhand could remain there; all of them disappeared inexplicably a few days after the ascent to the Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, dairy work, and working territory, not simply a mountain or mountain range.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp; here the farmhand remains in the high pasture operation and lets the spirit accompany him back to the valley.

notes.label: Bresten
notes.text: a regional word for an affliction, disease, or wasting ailment; the wife’s long illness is supernaturally imposed, but its medical character is left unidentified.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

f3f249b10c222e83917219e679ffaeea9a33afdd.summary: A spirit dwelled on an alp called “Fellenen,” which extends alongside the Gotthard road toward the Oberalp near Urseren.

notes.label: alpen
notes.text: to pasture livestock and work seasonally on a high Alpine grazing ground.

notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an alp, especially a herder or dairy farmer.

notes.text: here the named high summer pasture contested by two communities, including grazing rights and possession rather than merely a mountain summit.

notes.label: Solatz
notes.text: the name of the beautiful Alp disputed by Untervatz and Haldenstein in the poem.

notes.label: Meister Urian
notes.text: literally “Master Urian,” a traditional euphemistic or humorous German name for the Devil, who teaches the farmer the deceptive oath.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: ordinarily “Creator,” but also a word for a scoop or ladle; the poem’s spoon-on-the-hat trick exploits that double sense in the oath, whose first version says “the head” and whose ghostly repetition says “my head.”

notes.label: Vatz
notes.text: the shortened historical form used in the poem for Untervatz, the community to which the disputed Alp is awarded.

11933f04022f0b9246b6e34ea3b5f7cde44b4588.summary: On the Tarnuz Alp belonging to Malans, in the Vättis Valley, there were very devout Sennen who every evening spoke a blessing over the livestock entrusted to them.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high mountain pasture with its associated grazing and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; here Tarnuz is the Alp belonging to Malans.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled dairymen and herders responsible for livestock and cheesemaking on an Alp; these Sennen perform the nightly blessing.

notes.label: Obersenn
notes.text: the head Senn or senior Alpine dairyman in charge of the operation; his special concern for one cow leads him to plan a separate blessing.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: normally the German word for a gray or white horse, but the source explicitly uses it here as the name or description of a white-gray cow; English readers should not picture a horse.

notes.label: Alp-Segnen
notes.text: literally “blessing the Alp,” the customary spoken blessing placed over livestock and the mountain pasture; in this legend, missing the individual blessing leaves one cow unprotected.

454cb6e3ba39dd3677e63ccfb3cc077b956158bc.summary: In former days, when spring wandered through mountain and valley with shawm and flower basket and the joyful Sennen had driven their herds back up to the Alp, the notes of two Alphorns could be heard from the Kaltbrunnenalp in the Hasli Valley almost every morning, exchanging call and answer in melodic conversation.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who take cattle to seasonal high pastures; their annual ascent marks the return of spring activity.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its dairy settlement rather than simply a mountain; Kaltbrunnenalp and Reichenbachalp are the lovers' separate summer workplaces.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: the Swiss plural of Fluh, meaning steep rock faces or cliffs; after the horns fall silent, the rocks and their echoes are said to sob and weep.

notes.label: Sennerin
notes.text: a woman who tends livestock and performs dairy work on a seasonal Alp; the young woman spends her summer on the Reichenbachalp and plays the answering horn.

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: old, compacted mountain snowfields or glacier surfaces that survive beyond a single season; the dawn light is described as gilding them.

notes.label: Alphorn
notes.text: the long, valveless wooden horn associated with Alpine herding and communication across great distances; the legend imagines the lovers using two Alphorns for musical dialogue between pastures.

notes.label: Jungsenn
notes.text: literally a ‘young Senn,’ a young Alpine herdsman or dairyman; it identifies the returning lover by his seasonal occupation.

notes.label: Lenzgruss
notes.text: a poetic ‘spring greeting,’ with Lenz an older literary word for spring; the hopeful melody is the young man's first call to his absent beloved.

960775af3ee009ffd434c64665023f89f76cb856.summary: A ruinous dispute long prevailed between the two worthy municipalities of Münster and Reckingen in Goms over the boundary marks that were to divide their districts.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high-elevation summer pasture and the associated seasonal farming place, not simply an Alpine mountain; the border Alp in this story was an economically valuable communal resource.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: auf Alpien
notes.text: literally ‘on Alpien,’ the locally named border Alp in Reckingen where the haunting occurred; Alpien is a place-name rather than the plural of Alps.

notes.label: Alpleute
notes.text: literally ‘Alp people,’ the herders and other workers who lived and worked seasonally on the high pasture; the term refers to a working community, not merely visitors to the Alps.

24b816a44864d5ccf83bafc80d5cba9ea59fdef4.summary: On an Alp—I do not know for certain whether it was Blüemlisalp—a hired hand once died who had cursed and quarreled terribly in life.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: erwellen
notes.text: an Uri Alpine dairying verb for heating or otherwise processing milk or whey during cheese-making; the scene clearly begins a dairy task, but the exact production stage is uncertain.

notes.label: Nidler
notes.text: a regional Alpine dairy term presented here as a destination or work station to which the spirit accompanies the hired hand; its precise referent or role is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a low, broad wooden vessel used for carrying or holding milk in Alpine dairying; the spirit carries one full of milk to the cauldron.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a distinctively Swiss whey cheese or curd made from whey left after ordinary cheese production; making it is one of the spirit's dairy tasks.

notes.label: Käsgaden
notes.text: literally a cheese storehouse or cheese outbuilding, a small Alpine room or structure where cheeses are made, salted, ripened, or kept; the exact mix of workroom and storage functions varies regionally.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy production; here the word identifies the prayerful worker whom the spirit assists.

efc2f98e9e8d82132938615dd4b8926fd6b47e05.summary: When in autumn the Sennen vacate the Alp and descend with the herd and dairy vessels, they cast one final glance back at the huts to see whether all the bolts have been thrown; and when everything is in order, they call, “Until next summer!” Silent mountain solitude descends over the Alp, and only…

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen who tend cattle and make cheese and butter during the high-pasture season; their autumn departure closes the huts for winter.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal Alpine pasture together with its huts, barns, pens, meadows, and dairy work, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope Alpine wind whose spring storm rapidly strips snow from the slopes and shakes the huts.

notes.label: Matten
notes.text: cultivated or managed Alpine meadowlands that green and flower as the seasonal snow retreats.

notes.label: Alpgenossenschaft
notes.text: the cooperative association whose members jointly manage the high pasture, inspect and repair its structures, and bear the loss of the stolen kettles.

notes.label: Meidenalp
notes.text: the named high pasture on which the repeated kettle theft and supernatural capture occur; the source gives no more precise boundary.

notes.label: Alpung
notes.text: the seasonal ascent of people and livestock to occupy and work the high pasture; the villagers discover the missing kettle when they climb up for it.

notes.label: Alpkessel
notes.text: the large copper dairy kettle used in the Alp hut for cheese-making; its expense and essential role make each theft a serious communal loss.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work on an Alp during the pasture season; here they collectively order the replacement kettle.

notes.label: Alpenvogt
notes.text: the officer or steward chosen by the Alpgenossenschaft to oversee the high pasture and protect its communal kettle; the source does not equate the post with a modern office.

notes.label: klafterhoch
notes.text: literally a Klafter high, using a historical fathom-scale unit to evoke the great depth of snow on the Alp; no exact measured depth is implied.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Schneereifen
notes.text: traditional snowshoes, literally snow frames or hoops, which spread the wearer’s weight over deep spring snow.

notes.label: Alpstaffel
notes.text: the principal hut or working station of an Alp complex; here its open door reveals the magically arrested thief, though the source does not detail the building’s layout.

4c48ed1994f5410ae4116730073038085a01438b.summary: In late autumn a hunter passed a hut on the Alpe Drusen in the Prätigau and heard a most peculiar noise and commotion inside, as though it were still midsummer and the Sennen were fully occupied. — Curiosity tempted the huntsman, and he went and peered through a knothole into the Alpine hut; inside…

notes.label: Alpe Drusen
notes.text: the managed Alpine pasture of Drusen in the Prätigau; Alpe denotes its high grazing ground, huts, and seasonal dairy work.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen responsible for livestock and cheese-making during the summer pasture season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpmuetter
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Alpmutter, literally “Alp mother”; she is the supernatural old woman presiding over the deserted pasture hut and its animal kitchen crew.

notes.label: Schmalz
notes.text: rendered or clarified cooking fat, often butterfat in an Alpine dairy context; the exact product is left broad because the tale only names Schmalz.

notes.label: Du Hanschäsperle, choz' mer Schmalz!
notes.text: Swiss German dialect meaning approximately “You little Hanschäsper, vomit up some Schmalz for me”; the following sentence confirms the deliberately grotesque sense of choz’ as disgorge or vomit.

dda12bada87bda12ca792396a2b95d89adc78760.summary: The Alpmutterli is the subject of an extensive cycle of legends. The figure has a teasing, maliciously gleeful character.

notes.label: Alpmutterli
notes.text: literally ‘little mother of the Alp,’ a female Alpine spirit in the Flums legend cycle; here she is teasing, weather-bringing, and able to consume hospitality without reducing the food.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person working or residing seasonally on an Alp, such as a herder or dairyman; here living pasture workers claim they have personally seen the Alpmutterli.

notes.label: Tusli
notes.text: a local diminutive for a small container, bowl, or carrying vessel; here it holds cream, but the exact material and shape are not specified.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick or rich cream; here the girls spill a vesselful when the Alpmutterli distracts them.

notes.label: fleugen
notes.text: the source's regional verb for swinging or swishing a garment; here the little woman moves her apron after the cream is spilled, and the parenthetical source gloss is schwenken.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here they tolerate the spirit to avoid worsening the bad weather it brings.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here the Flums Alp is where the spirit first appears and later forces an early departure.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the singular of Sennen, an Alpine dairy herdsman; here an inhospitable Senn rejects the Alpmutterli and is answered by a snowstorm.

notes.label: Bischen
notes.text: a regional word for a violent snow squall or snowstorm; here it arrives overnight after the Alpmutterli is refused hospitality.

03102b56db7fe4f5b7ee4c56a3c02620e84fb720.summary: In the Alpine regions of Switzerland, it was once a widespread custom to call out the Alpsegen into the gathering darkness at evening.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: literally Alp blessing, the evening protective call or sung prayer projected over Alpine cattle pastures; blessing alone does not convey the specifically Swiss herding rite or its regional formulas.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Volle
notes.text: a regional wooden calling funnel used to project the Alpsegen across the pastures; its precise shape and pronunciation vary locally.

notes.label: Buzen
notes.text: a regional plural for uncanny bogey beings or harmful spirits; here they are treacherous powers haunting remote Alpine pastures, while the word's forms and scope vary by dialect.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy work on a seasonal high pasture; herdsman or dairyman alone does not capture the full Swiss role.

notes.label: Nistern
notes.text: hay bedding, nests, or piled resting places within the wild hay; the exact physical form meant by this archaic regional plural is uncertain.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: an Alpine cattle herd understood as the Senn's managed, bell-bearing collective and sometimes the associated dairying unit; ordinary herd is the closest but narrower English sense.

notes.label: Alpbuzen
notes.text: a Buzen specifically associated with an Alp, here the treacherous spirit that steals the Sennten; it is a transparent regional compound but has no fixed English creature-name.

notes.label: loba, loba
notes.text: traditional cattle-calling syllables within the herding cry; they function as a vocal call rather than ordinary lexical prose and therefore remain untranslated.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: a seasonal level, station, or group of huts and pasture within an Alp; here it is the place into which the returning cows come, but the exact physical referent varies regionally.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high summer pasture and its working dairy unit, not simply a mountain summit; this pastoral sense shapes the blessing's setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

7c18336cdf6157882943dbbdcf2cc5c34018b02c.summary: A man of the Schächen Valley whose name is given, and who had risen from a poor, utterly penniless herdboy to a farmer rich in treasure, is said to have possessed an “Allarünä” or a “Gäldschyßer.” One hears all kinds of conjectures and opinions about it.

notes.label: Allarünä
notes.text: an Uri folk form related to Alraune, the magically wealth-producing mandrake or familiar; here it may be a toad, a root, or a tiny living figure.

notes.label: Gäldschyßer
notes.text: literally ‘money-shitter,’ the blunt Uri name for the wealth-producing familiar that doubles a coin placed beneath it; proverbial uses extend the name to any wished-for source of easy money.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.
