source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Wannelen
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture where some informants locate the familiar; Alp denotes the whole pastoral holding and its huts, not merely a summit.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small private room or parlor in the farmhouse; other informants locate the familiar there instead of on the Alp.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: the customary arrangement in which an itinerant craftsperson such as a shoemaker worked temporarily in a customer’s home rather than a fixed workshop.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man,’ using the characteristic -li diminutive; the accounts disagree whether the money familiar is a man-shaped root or a truly living tiny being.

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: the magical mandrake and, by extension, a root, animal, or little humanoid familiar believed to multiply money; this account deliberately preserves competing physical forms.

notes.label: Schächentaler
notes.text: a person from the Schächen Valley in Uri; the title identifies the wealthy owner by his valley rather than printing his locally known name.

notes.label: Allarünä
notes.text: an Uri folk form related to Alraune, the magically wealth-producing mandrake or familiar of wider German-language belief; in these accounts it appears as a grass-green frog-like being that produces money and requires dangerous ritual care.

notes.label: Alraunen
notes.text: the standard German plural of Alraune, historically a mandrake root or magically maintained familiar believed to bring wealth; the Uri stories deliberately describe living frog-like creatures rather than ordinary plants.

notes.label: aller Rünä
notes.text: a folk-etymological ritual phrase sounding like ‘of all Rünä’ and echoing Allarünä; it is spoken while digging beneath a white hazel for money, but the source supplies no fuller formula or explanation.

40163930721c3bc9fc87986ebad060a6ed2f688b.summary: The Alrune, a Capuchin of Rheinfelden told a poor tailor, is a strange animal that runs about at night with rolling eyes.

notes.label: Alrune
notes.text: this name refers here to a captured fortune-bringing familiar, related in name to the mandrake spirit; why the body calls it Alraun and gives it a doglike form is uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Hutte
notes.text: in this Aargau context, Hutte denotes a carrying basket or pannier used to capture and transport the creature; its exact construction is uncertain.

notes.label: Sparthaler
notes.text: literally a ‘saving thaler,’ this is the tailor’s single hoarded coin that seeds the magical multiplication; its denomination and origin are unspecified.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Rappen is a small-denomination Swiss coin, invoked here to emphasize that no money remained; the exact historical value intended is uncertain.

77609a8aaad2e7f50a47ba316d6be62ba7606126.summary: At Buckten in Basel-Landschaft lived a married couple who made passementerie only for appearance's sake, since they could live entirely from their invested capital.

notes.label: Alrune
notes.text: a wealth-bringing magical familiar whose name elsewhere belongs to mandrake and household-spirit traditions; this Basel account gives it the distinctive form of a green-and-gold bird that produces money and follows its owner.

notes.label: Thaler
notes.text: a large historical silver coin; the Alrune's promise of one coin every day explains the couple's otherwise mysterious investment income.

2f330d37ce205dfc86eee8eb208b3ea9c0ba9e0c.summary: ‘Someone in Flüelen had an Alrünäbiächli. All he had to do was read backward in it.

notes.label: Alrünäbiächli
notes.text: literally a ‘little mandrake book,’ an Uri dialect name for a small magical book or grimoire whose power is activated by reading it backward; the source does not describe its contents or relation to the mandrake beyond the name.

cdb7ff703aaa4d6f1f0977d8e555cda16d45f0bb.summary: Altels, a mountain in the Bernese Oberland, is said formerly to have ranked among the loveliest and most fertile cattle mountains.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

9fc6ad47629d1590509c7aa553a5ca0031b22880.summary: For years, a bitter dispute over the boundary at the Gulmen prevailed between the people of Amden and Stein.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a piercing alpine whoop or yodel-like cry; here the fraudulent runner uses it to announce victory, and his punishment is to repeat an uncanny version after death.

notes.label: Jauchzen
notes.text: the act or sound of giving a Jauchzer; in the final paragraph it names the supernatural cry still heard during storms.

notes.label: Beigeinsattelung
notes.text: the source's local name for the mountain saddle where the condemned cry is heard; Sattelung denotes a saddle-shaped pass, while the precise sense of Beigein is not established by the story.

595c715f8efd531d3fae9724844b9f12ff522b14.summary: In the village of Würenlingen, not far from Baden, there sat an Ammann whose long business experience repeatedly made him necessary to the community, although his usurious greed was equally well known and had long been universally despised.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional Swiss local chief magistrate or senior communal officer; the story’s officeholder combines civic authority with business influence, while the exact powers of the office varied by place and period.

notes.label: Aetti
notes.text: an affectionate or familiar Swiss German word for “father” or “dad”; the sons use it in a cruelly soothing rhyme, and the precise emotional register varies by dialect.

notes.label: Mättli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Matte, meaning a little meadow; in the sons’ rhyme its affectionate sound trivializes the wrong by praising the valuable field.

notes.label: Ammannsmatte
notes.text: literally “the Ammann’s meadow,” the local name joining the traditional magistrate’s title to Matte, a meadow; here it memorializes land obtained through his corrupt appraisal, though it may be a tale-name rather than a formal cadastral name.

e501643bea67da71e7096f484acae8fdad3c85e9.summary: Near Mettau in the Fricktal lies the extensive Amswald. A path leading through the woods is called the Amsbuck, and along it rides the W.

notes.label: W. Jäger
notes.text: the source’s abbreviation for Wilder Jäger, the ‘Wild Huntsman,’ leader or manifestation of the supernatural Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Amsupper
notes.text: the local name for the headless Wild Huntsman who rides the Amsbuck with two dogs and half a horse; the source gives no certain etymology.

1960c6a8307a4cc0c502c4522c67761975e77465.summary: Near Escholzmatt lived a wealthy married couple who had only one child. But the parents loved him so dearly that they literally possessed nothing dearer than their little boy.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

238b40c32e26bd6d03f2e93aa750a718793f300e.summary: Many, many years ago, Aletsch was not yet a sea of glaciers but only a wild Alp where a few herdsmen remained into the winter.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here a remote seasonal high pasture and herding landscape rather than simply a mountain; a few herdsmen remain at Aletsch even into winter.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Nachhirten
notes.text: literally ‘after-herdsmen,’ the local name for herders who remained on the remote Alp after the principal summer season and into winter.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Messfluo
notes.text: literally the ‘Mass cliff’ or ‘Mass rock,’ using the Valais and Swiss form Fluo or Fluh for a rock face; it names the rock where the angel is believed to have celebrated Mass.

f37451e90d3b8eaad164044e6733940dc7069528.summary: Every morning a good Geissbub drove the goats from Bürglen into the Riedertal.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally a ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd responsible for taking goats to pasture; his daily work brings him to the supernatural Mass.

notes.label: Büebli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little boy; here it emphasizes the herder’s youth and good conduct rather than a supernatural stature.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Jä, und d'Ängel, g'heered-er dië äu nitt?
notes.text: the boy’s exact dialect question, ‘And the angels—do you not hear them either?’ after learning that the priest cannot see the Mass.
notes.anchor: Jä, und d'Ängel, g'heered-er dië äu nitt?

notes.label: Schmerzhafte Mutter
notes.text: literally the ‘Sorrowful Mother,’ a devotional title for the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Sorrows; the discovered image leads to the chapel’s construction.

notes.label: So han-i's vo dr Müetter g'heert
notes.text: the elderly narrator’s exact dialect attribution, ‘That is how I heard it from Mother,’ preserving the maternal transmission of the legend.
notes.anchor: So han-i's vo dr Müetter g'heert

notes.label: Myttenstein
notes.text: a named stone in the Riedertal associated with another story the narrator could no longer remember; the source gives no literal derivation.

15c1f8212fe5983d3f311f09a4a91d13fd80bb36.summary: Once a family was working in a field. After everyone had worked very diligently, they suddenly saw a cloth spread upon the ground and silver vessels filled with food and drink.

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: female fairy-like beings of Graubünden and neighboring Romansh-speaking Alpine tradition who offer food and help but withdraw when people violate their conditions; related accounts sometimes describe them with goat feet.

notes.label: Iss und lass
notes.text: literally “eat and leave,” the Dialen’s formula permitting the workers to enjoy the meal while warning them to leave the valuable silver vessels untouched.

789549b7d62a1ac292ac0a7f0eb1f04171971bb7.summary: Six hours south of Fribourg lies the valley of Charmey, called Galmis or Gaimitz by the nearby German-speaking people.

notes.label: Galmis
notes.text: one of the historical German regional names given for French-speaking Charmey; the paired names reflect the valley's position at a language boundary.

notes.label: Gaimitz
notes.text: the source's alternate German name for Charmey, preserved beside Galmis because historical spellings and local usage varied.

notes.label: Hohmatt
notes.text: the mountain named by the source as the boundary between German- and French-speaking communities and the dangerous pasture watched by the spirit.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the skilled alpine dairyman responsible for the herd's milk and cheese work; he maintains reciprocity with the spirit by offering cream.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the alpine dairy hut where the Senn and helpers live and process milk during the grazing season; its roof serves as the spirit's offering place.

ed386455401ffd21a37cc196e9fe5717163180ee.summary: About 150 years ago, a young man from Obwalden was hanged as a thief in the Galgen-Mätteli.

notes.label: Galgen-Mätteli
notes.text: literally ‘little gallows meadow,’ the execution ground where the young man is hanged; the diminutive describes the plot, not the severity of the event.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for godfather; the priest addresses his dead godchild through their continuing ritual family bond.

notes.label: halb 2 Uhr
notes.text: literally ‘half [toward] 2 o'clock,’ meaning 1:30 in German and Swiss time-telling; the wording is retained to preserve the source's exact digit.

21a24963fb4b2405415e9bdf69c9961d41e2378c.summary: About a quarter of an hour below Glis, at the place called Breite Wege, there formerly stood a chapel.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Staffelgebet
notes.text: the prayers said at the steps or foot of the altar at the beginning of the older Roman Mass; the first dead man’s favorable sign occurs just before them, while the source does not identify the precise version of the rite.

4b268ab89f96b075c61b24f1c836a4f5e95e8447.summary: On the Fontanen Alp in the municipality of Giswil stands a little tower built of stone and called the ‘Heathen Tower.’ People claim that the ancient heathens erected it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tanngrotzen
notes.text: a rough young fir or fir-root club carried by the wild ‘heathen men’ as both walking staff and weapon; ‘fir club’ is the closest sense, but the word’s exact regional form and the object’s shape are uncertain.

d8bcb574a70322be54e1f2bb9e3479d63ec1b266.summary: a) Once a young man from Alplen, on the northern slope of the mountain range, walked through the Alpler Tor as far as the Achenberge at Bürglen—almost a day's journey—to go z'Stubeten.

notes.label: z'Stubeten
notes.text: Uri dialect for going on a social visit in someone's Stube, often with the sense of an evening courting visit; the long journey frames the young man's relationship with the girl.

notes.label: Chräpfli
notes.text: small pastries, commonly diminutive forms of Krapfen; the exact local shape or filling is not specified, and this variant substitutes them for the enchanted apples.

notes.label: Pintner
notes.text: a pig of a Graubünden breed, as the source's historical footnote explicitly states; after eating the enchanted apples, it is compelled to run to the girl's room.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape; the pigs kept there receive the strangely spotted apples in the second version.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

1a7f78dae3a0f454ac175bc93946fe43cbdbbcf0.summary: A man from the Oberland once returned to his mountain homeland after long military service abroad.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a325a44b2622ba04cdc6010af55ff0dd344d6aea.summary: A cunning Waldbruder named Haigeli, who had come from Swabia, sought in the previous century to exploit the religious veneration that the three Anglo-Saxons had enjoyed in the Freienämtern since ancient times—see No. 474.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally a ‘forest brother,’ a lay hermit or religious recluse living apart from a formal monastery.

notes.label: Freienämtern
notes.text: the source's historical plural-dative form for the Aargau Freie Ämter, the former ‘Free Bailiwicks’; it names a political region rather than generic free offices.

notes.label: Tagsatzung
notes.text: the historical federal diet of the Swiss Confederacy, an assembly of cantonal delegates; here it acts from Baden against the hermit.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a bailiff or territorial governor in the old Swiss political order, exercising administrative and judicial authority.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss and southern German term for a church sexton or sacristan responsible for the chapel's practical care.

3b6f3621f7e5cb8287fc6fc4f67017384c36dc80.summary: A man wanted to become a fahrender Schüler and said so to one who already was one.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar’; in German-speaking Alpine folklore this is an itinerant learned figure credited with occult or magical arts, not merely an ordinary student.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person’; here the figure appears in the likeness of, or is mistaken for, the apprentice’s own sister and beckons him from the protective circle.

ad116ee6bb09e3d0ad44c2a4c51cb5bbb5a78c2c.summary: The new Brünig road now leads many thousands of strangers past the foot of the named mountain in the dear, idyllic country of Obwalden.

notes.label: Geisbub
notes.text: literally a ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd; Geiss or Geis is the regional word for a goat, and the boy encounters the hidden army while tending the herd.

notes.label: Wunderfitz
notes.text: lively, sometimes nosy curiosity or an urge to investigate something strange; here it drives the Geisbub into the opening in the rock.

notes.label: Giswilerstocke
notes.text: the source’s inflected form of Giswilerstock, the mountain massif near Giswil in Obwalden; the hidden army occupies an enclosed realm within it.

4a9b61cdded656966bd53141250d9a80234e7884.summary: Around Escholzmatt, they call the so-called shooting of the weather Gurnigeln.

notes.label: Gurnigeln
notes.text: the local Escholzmatt name for thunderous ‘weather shooting’ believed to come from the Gurnigel or Schratten mountains; ‘cannonading’ approximates the sound, but the word also carries the regional supernatural-weather association.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

167dd9ff09791f593806fc3565d30eb41036b367.summary: On an Alp in the Prättigau, a Fänggenmannli once lived on very familiar terms with the Senn and received all manner of presents and gifts from him.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the Senn and Fänggenmannli share its cheesemaking workplace.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a male member of the wild forest or mountain beings called Fänggen in Alpine tradition; here it rewards the Senn's generosity by offering secret dairy knowledge.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd, milk processing, and cheesemaking on a seasonal pasture; his professional assumptions lead him to mock the supernatural second working of the whey.

daeb3c981a23b40ace3821428eaf83683b8a4911.summary: A housewife who was boiling eggs placed the empty eggshells on the Treche, or hearth.

notes.label: Treche
notes.text: a regional hearth or fireplace surface; the source explicitly glosses it as Feuerherd.

notes.label: Gottwerggi
notes.text: a Valais name for a household dwarf or little subterranean being, literally containing ‘dwarf’; the Got- element may be a dialectal or euphemistic formation rather than the word God.

notes.label: Häfilini
notes.text: a dialect diminutive meaning ‘little pots’; the Gottwerggi mistakes the empty eggshells for tiny vessels.

notes.label: Ja nu, ja nu! I bi do afu alts, i bsinnu mi, dasch scho drimal du Pfynwald abghauwu heint und wieder um uf gwagsu ist, aber so vil Häfilini ha ni do mi Lebtag no niemal gseh!
notes.text: the Valais dialect speech means approximately ‘Well now! I am already old; I remember the Pfynwald being cut down three times and growing back, but never have I seen so many little pots’; its immense age contrasts comically with ignorance of eggshells.
notes.anchor: Ja nu, ja nu! I bi do afu alts, i bsinnu mi, dasch scho drimal du Pfynwald abghauwu heint und wieder um uf gwagsu ist, aber so vil Häfilini ha ni do mi Lebtag no niemal gseh!

18b1b60c2b3556e47a4814bafcd7d29e6e64973a.summary: Few girls in the Bernese Oberland die as old maids. Nearly every one soon finds among the young men someone with whom she can share life’s joys and sorrows as a tender and attentive housewife and loving mother.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

dbfa1b6dc072b18527beda7cb7d94afe42867a9c.summary: An old man in Ruis in the Oberland related that his father had died when he—the boy—was still small, and that he once asked his mother what had actually been wrong with him.

notes.label: Oberland
notes.text: the upper country or upper Rhine region of Graubünden in which Ruis is located.

notes.label: Schichieu
notes.text: the local name of the estate where the father kept and fed his cattle.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, sturdy hunting rifle or carbine kept loaded as the father’s second weapon.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for a godfather, included among the baptismal gathering.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: Swiss German for a godmother, paired here with Götti.

b6af78ccd1593fdcea020327e2df15caf6483c37.summary: O mortal, mourn your sin in repentance,

notes.label: Prätigäu
notes.text: the Graubünden valley now commonly written Prättigau; Saas and the avalanche sites named in the poem lie within it.

notes.label: Jenner
notes.text: an older regional German name for January; the poem dates the disaster to the twenty-fifth day of that month.

notes.label: Pauli Bekehrung
notes.text: the traditional feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, observed on the twenty-fifth of January and used here to date the avalanche.

notes.label: Erdbidem
notes.text: an older regional form of Erdbeben, meaning an earthquake; the poem leaves uncertain whether earth movement or the morning sun’s heat triggered the snow.

notes.label: Schneebruch
notes.text: literally a breaking or collapse of snow, used throughout the poem for the destructive avalanche or snow slide.

notes.label: Galanda-Maiensäss
notes.text: the named seasonal pasture settlement at Galanda; a Maiensäss is the intermediate grazing station between the valley farm and the high summer Alp.

notes.label: Mäder
notes.text: regional plural for hay meadows or mown mountain grassland; here it appears both with Fendril and in the place-name Galanda-Mäder.

notes.label: Galanda-Grub
notes.text: the local hollow or gully at Galanda through which the second avalanche tore; Grub is an older shortened form related to Grube.

notes.label: Thole
notes.text: an old or regional terrain word paired with Galanda-Grub, evidently a hollow, gully, or ravine; Jecklin gives no more precise gloss.

f35636fc65df20c33b21705c6e3f05df1990af6f.summary: 1. The avalanche, or Rübi, came rushing down through the Rohr Valley.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a violent debris-laden mountain torrent or flow of snow, water, earth, and rock; the account equates it with the descending avalanche.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Stoss hinnä!
notes.text: the front witch’s exact dialect command, ‘Push from behind!’ addressed to her companion riding the avalanche.

notes.label: zich, zich!
notes.text: the rear witch’s repeated command, ‘pull, pull!’; the opposing positions and commands personify the avalanche as something they drive together.

notes.label: Galli
notes.text: a familiar diminutive of Gallus and here a personification of the great bell in the church dedicated to St. Gall; its protective ringing sounds like bawling to the witches.

notes.label: Vrenä
notes.text: a familiar Swiss form of Verena and here another personified name for the protective bell; the variant does not explain why the great bell bears her name.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a sacristan or sexton responsible for the chapel and its bell; his urgent ringing stops the avalanche.

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

notes.label: Vreni
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive of Verena and here the personified little bell of St. Verena; the voice says its ringing has stopped the riders.

00ee4bae01b394ab53fa46bdbd5c7dc50e2d6273.summary: On the Alpen of the Sarganserland, chiefly at their uppermost Sässen, the following Ave Maria is prayed.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: the plural pastoral use of Alp, meaning high seasonal cattle pastures and their working dairy units rather than the Alpine mountain range itself; this specific Swiss land-use sense shapes the prayer’s setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sässen
notes.text: seasonal stations or hut-and-grazing sites within the tiered Swiss Alpine pasture system; here the prayer is used chiefly at the highest stations, while the term can emphasize either the occupied site or its grazing level.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a serpentine dragon of Germanic and Alpine tradition, usually imagined as a great crawling monster; English lindworm is only an approximate borrowing, and its form varies across local lore.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: the hired male workers and herdsmen serving on an Alp; they are distinct from the lead Senn, and generic farmhands or herdsmen loses the seasonal Alpine organization.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a Swiss alpine pasture; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: the seasonal working hut on an Alp, typically combining shelter with dairy or cheesemaking functions; mountain hut is broader and may miss this pastoral role.

notes.label: Bhüt's Gott
notes.text: a recurring Alemannic protective formula, closest to may God protect it or may God preserve it; it structures the Alpine prayer’s successive invocations, while the protected object shifts with the following line.

notes.label: B'hüt Gott
notes.text: an orthographic and spoken variant of Bhüt's Gott in the same protective prayer, again invoking God’s protection; the omitted pronoun and apostrophe reflect dialect rather than a different ritual meaning.

notes.label: Bhüt' üs Gott
notes.text: the Alemannic first-person form meaning may God protect us; üs is us, and here the formula specifically asks protection from the dangerous hour and the animals named around it.

notes.label: bschissen
notes.text: a dialect form related to German bescheißen; in context its closest sense is to cheat, deceive, or possibly defile, but it can also carry the vulgar literal sense to shit on, making the precise force of this historical antisemitic line genuinely ambiguous.

acb3454809c0278c26e452c6a1bfec35603be545.summary: Several men were working high on the Valens mountain and also spent the night there.

notes.label: Bachgschrei
notes.text: literally ‘brook cry’ or ‘brook screaming,’ a regional uncanny sound or being associated with a stream ravine; the witness learns its nature but dies without revealing it.

notes.label: trotte
notes.text: the source’s quoted regional verb, probably meaning that the apparition trundled, waddled, or plodded along; its comparison to a sheep’s belly suggests a low, rounded movement, but the exact visual form remains ambiguous.

notes.label: Bergun
notes.text: a local name for a small mountain hay hut used to store fodder; the source itself glosses it as a Heuhüttchen, and the Bachgschrei vanishes inside.

be9a8f98446728d9a1cfc8f4d918a4031cf6e676.summary: The Hohle Gasse is the name given to that part of the road between the Jura villages of Auenstein and Veltheim where the Veltheim road opens toward Wildenstein Castle.

notes.label: Schachen
notes.text: a regional term for low, often brushy or wooded land beside a river; here it is the riparian ground along the Aare rather than an ordinary open meadow.

notes.label: Fergen
notes.text: the historical inflected form of Ferge, a ferryman; the parenthetical identifies the teller by his work on the Aare at Auenstein.

notes.label: Bachmaidli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning ‘little brook maiden’; here it names the returning spirit of a woman said to have killed her newborn child, though the name can blur the woman, the child, and the legendary figure.

notes.label: O hätt i numme das nit tho, So wär i jetzt i Himmel cho!
notes.text: Alemannic for approximately ‘Oh, if only I had not done that, then I would now have gone to heaven!’; the lament makes the apparition’s endless washing a penance for killing her child.
notes.anchor: O hätt i numme das nit tho, So wär i jetzt i Himmel cho!

2f5f1b93c6f9ff89492f68b22dfc76ed2cac070d.summary: When a woman in Seon once bore a child out of wedlock, she resolved to kill it and ran with it toward the nearest pond.

notes.label: Bachmaidli
notes.text: this Alemannic diminutive means ‘little brook maiden’ and names the child-killing mother’s returning spirit near Seon; whether the name refers to the woman, the dead child, or a fused legendary figure is uncertain.

notes.label: Bachthal-Anneli
notes.text: this dialect name means approximately ‘little Annie of the brook valley’ and is another name for the wailing spirit; its exact relationship to Bachmaidli and the historical spelling of the place are uncertain.

5eeab5be08599ca4c32653a0609cfebee4f7f2e1.summary: The Lengnau Dorftier usually comes running in the shape of a black poodle, splashes about in the stream at night, blocks the bridge, and plays all sorts of pranks on those crossing it.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally ‘village animal,’ a local supernatural animal associated with a particular community; here it is Lengnau’s shape-changing black poodle, not ordinary village livestock.

notes.label: Bachplätschi
notes.text: a regional name for a splashing stream specter, with Bach meaning ‘stream’ and plätschen suggesting splashing; the accounts identify it variously with a cursed general or Pilate, so its exact identity remains deliberately unstable.

notes.label: Nachtplätschi
notes.text: literally a ‘night splasher,’ an alternate local name for the Bachplätschi that emphasizes its nocturnal splashing and haunting rather than a distinct being.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: young men making customary evening courtship visits to women; here their noisy late return on Sunday night exposes them to the specter, and the custom is more specific than simply ‘suitor.’

06f01e58f84ed7e11997830562ea3ceba2464193.summary: In the Haushalden, the Solenbach runs between old oaks through mossy meadows into the Aare.

notes.label: Bachtier
notes.text: literally a ‘stream beast’ or ‘brook animal,’ the local name for this water-haunting bogey that misleads travelers and plunges into the Solenbach.

355df183d10c2af608505995860089dd9d0365f6.summary: Niklaus, a simple joker, was just cooking himself a bacon omelet as a special delicacy.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

e85a4bfeff9779af66ef5dd7494dc49d5d0d4cd4.summary: It is told in Savièse that a young fellow once wished to visit his sweetheart at night.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

2de5cc5c71c9b749bf5ed58a34428005d136e245.summary: In the Rachentobel, not far from the beautiful village of Appenzell, lived a small and needy farmer who sometimes also played the miller and ground his scant rye himself and baked it into bread.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c55b1eeb68059626b0a8c3770906dd2c4fd69707.summary: An old man related, on the authority of his mother-in-law, that when her parents still lived in Schwarzenbach, they baked for themselves, as most farming people did.

notes.label: Erdfräuli
notes.text: literally a ‘little earth woman,’ a diminutive name for a female subterranean household spirit or dwarf-like being; here she secretly prepares the family’s baking supplies.

notes.label: Ofenstänglein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little oven rod, rail, or bar on which the family hangs the garment; the source does not describe its precise position or construction.

notes.label: Sötti denn wo wäch (schön geputzt) sy, so wötti lieber nüme cho go bacha!
notes.text: Swiss German meaning approximately ‘If I am to be so finely dressed, I would rather never come to bake again’; the parenthetical gloss ‘finely dressed’ is supplied by the source, while the opening dialect wording is regionally idiomatic.
notes.anchor: Sötti denn wo wäch (schön geputzt) sy, so wötti lieber nüme cho go bacha!

b94ea62ad036cdc7edba66ddd59b150bdc2799dd.summary: Between Fiesch and Bellwald, at the edge of a slope, stands the pleasant hamlet of Bodmen, which offers a splendid view into the Fieschertal.

notes.label: Bala-Bach
notes.text: the named mountain stream running through the gorge near Bodmen; Bach means stream, while Bala is retained as the local name.

notes.label: Gratzug
notes.text: literally a ‘ridge procession,’ a Valais supernatural host that races ceaselessly across ridges, valleys, and countries; it overlaps with Wild Hunt and procession-of-the-dead traditions but has its own regional name.

notes.label: Englischen Grusse
notes.text: the source's inflected form of ‘angelic greeting,’ the traditional German name for the Ave Maria or Angelus salutation, not a greeting from England; Fortnaz's Marian prayer protects him.

dc7b0c69981ab011786ee5ec9d2b84f1a364a06d.summary: Once, several people from Riffenmatt were fortunate enough to catch two Erdleutli.

notes.label: Erdleutli
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ small subterranean or hidden folk who possess secret knowledge and magical skills.

notes.label: Salzbrunnen im Sortel
notes.text: literally the ‘salt spring in the Sortel,’ a secret resource whose location the captured Erdleutli are forbidden to disclose; Sortel is a local place-name of uncertain extent.

notes.label: Beikörnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little accompanying grain’ or secondary kernel found among oats; the hidden folk know a special use for it, but the story deliberately withholds that knowledge.

f746906c6844a7b75480583df76b5fe1eee52025.summary: At the home of the family[1] in the Lehmatt in the Schächental, ‘it’ came into the Hühnerkrummen every night.

notes.label: Hühnerkrummen
notes.text: a regional name for the enclosed chicken quarters or coop; the exact architectural form of Krummen is not further defined in the source.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine farm building or room used as a stable, barn, or storage space; here it houses the cattle.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Rübital
notes.text: a steep gully or little valley shaped by Rübi, destructive debris flows or torrents of rock and rubble; the fox-spirit is confined there.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: das syg der Herrgott 'tratzet, das tue Gott leid, tue den armen Seelen weh
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘that defies the Lord God; it pains God and hurts the poor souls’; it records the contrary belief that setting the knife is itself sacrilegious and injures souls in Purgatory.
notes.anchor: das syg der Herrgott 'tratzet, das tue Gott leid, tue den armen Seelen weh

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for departed souls undergoing purgatorial suffering and awaiting release through prayer.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

535373a524f4b035108fe1ad51a64339dd896725.summary: Samuel Schmid served as pastor in Sevelen from 1728–1771. His wife died.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman; here he leases hay and stays on the remote property where his dog detects the banished spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Futterhüsli
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘little fodder house’ or small feeding shelter, with the diminutive -li; it is the isolated building whose walls the dog barks at.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical regional unit used for stacked hay, wood, or spatial measure; here it prices hay, but the exact local quantity is not specified.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

ca7cdc40b61afd5926dc6d72f0619b9a1bfc5d9d.summary: It is certainly a somewhat peculiar phenomenon that no snakes are found at the two ends of the Visp Valley, Zermatt and Saas.

notes.label: Fahrende Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘itinerant scholars,’ folklore figures credited with learned magic or secret arts; the source unusually glosses them as experienced poor travelers living on charity, while hinting that people believed they knew more than ordinary survival.

notes.label: fahrende Schüler
notes.text: the singular, grammatically inflected form of Fahrende Schüler; the same unnamed traveler leads or summons the snakes, but the two valley versions describe different rites.

notes.label: Schlangengrube
notes.text: literally ‘snake pit,’ the stone-covered hole near the high footbridge into which the Zermatt snakes are said to have been led; the site is presented as a local landmark.

notes.label: Schlangenbanner
notes.text: a person able to banish, bind, or magically compel snakes; the Saas figure uses prayer and a dangerous ritual, but the source does not specify whether his power is religious, learned, or magical.

202f7ec3f7cf25c4546eec95872ca8b3cb16dfa3.summary: Journeymen are sitting in an inn. One of them declares that he can fasten any companion to the tavern bench with a Bann.

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: here a magical binding or prohibition that fixes a person to a bench, makes a body invulnerable, or traps someone in a tree; the word can also mean a legal ban or jurisdiction, but this tale consistently uses its spell-binding sense.

notes.label: Banner
notes.text: in this context the person who casts a Bann, closest to a spell-binder rather than a flag bearer; his exact magical procedure is unstated, and breaking the spell physically injures him.

notes.label: er het em derfür tho
notes.text: an Aargau dialect expression meaning that he has stopped the spell-worker’s trade or paid him back for it; the phrase accompanies the violent recoil of the broken Bann, and its literal construction has no neat English equivalent.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

fa8804b495362a984096cc594f084270c6ffa439.summary: In the middle Rossberg, the Bannhölzler-Flue rises starkly, and the following legend about it circulates among the country people:

notes.label: Bannhölzler
notes.text: the name of Walchwil's malicious mountain spirit, derived from Bann, a legal boundary or ban, and Holz, woodland; here it is the afterlife punishment of a false boundary witness, later magically confined or gebannt in the cliff.

notes.label: Bannhölzler-Flue
notes.text: literally the Bannhölzler's Flue, with Flue meaning a steep rock face or cliff; here its three colored-water holes imprison the spirit, horse, and dog.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally owned or collectively used village land, especially pasture; here competing claims to the Walchwiler-Allmend produce the lawsuit and define the spirit's territorial power.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Gottli
notes.text: Swiss German for a godchild, though in some regions closely related forms can denote a godparent; here the wealthy woman's gift is made to a person in Walchwil, and the brief wording leaves the relationship's direction somewhat ambiguous.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd; here he taunts the boundary spirit and escapes beneath the fence with the loss of one wooden shoe.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a hedge, fence, or enclosed boundary; here crossing beneath it takes the boy from common land beyond the Bannhölzler's power.

notes.label: Drackmünd
notes.text: a traditional name associated here with Mount Pilatus as the spirit's later place of confinement; the source gives it as an alternative location-name but does not explain its literal derivation.

notes.label: Gutsch-Chasper
notes.text: the local byname of a man from Aegeri who sees the spectral court on the Pfaffenboden; Chasper corresponds to Kaspar, while Gutsch is not explained.

notes.label: Zugerli
notes.text: a diminutive place-name meaning roughly ‘little Zug’ or ‘the little place toward Zug’; here it marks the direction in which the Bannhölzler runs, but the exact site is not described.

ca6655898f03ed3e9fd282c42047e855b4da26db.summary: In the “Zugerli” above Walchwil in the canton of Zug, the lower Rossberg is honeycombed with many grotto-like fissures.

notes.label: Zugerli
notes.text: a diminutive place name meaning approximately ‘little Zug place’ above Walchwil; the tale locates the fissured terrain there but does not define its boundaries.

notes.label: Bannhölzler
notes.text: a regional name for the banished, wood-associated spectral rider punished for fraudulently transferring communal land; its literal relation to Bannholz does not fully explain the figure’s identity.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land traditionally shared under local usage rights; wrongfully alienating the Walchwil Allmend is the official’s central offense.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Schöpfer und Richter
notes.text: literally ‘Creator and Judge,’ but the perjurer secretly applies the words to a Schöpfer, a ladle or spoon, and a Richter, a comb; the tale condemns this evasive wordplay as a false oath.

notes.label: Koli
notes.text: a name for a black or dark-haired horse derived from Kohle, ‘coal’; the source itself supplies this explanation, though why the call summons the Bannhölzler is unstated.

notes.label: Chilbitag
notes.text: a day of Chilbi, the local church-dedication fair or village festival, when games and social amusements are customary.

notes.label: Ries
notes.text: the set or formation of skittles knocked down by the thrown ball; the exact local game arrangement is not described.

075c53a1bd698084017196921f4d3fc01fe0564f.summary: Three masons, no one knew where, carried a cat up a church tower to baptize it there.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

281739008990d40f5cd2e54982f1fea74935355a.summary: The lord of Wartburg lived in the two castles now called the Sälischlösser, which lie in ruins on the two neighboring mountains past which the road from Olten to Aarburg runs.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the parish church’s sacristan or sexton, responsible here for ringing the baptismal bells; his stopping creates the omen that provokes the godmother’s curse.

368ccb5e473e77eee9fb5dcca26caa3bfc32c2a1.summary: Beyond the high mountain peak called Sureneneck, reached from Uri by crossing the Waldnacht Alp, lie the pasture-rich Surenen or Surner alps, where the following story is said to have occurred several hundred years ago.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person working or living on a high Alpine pasture, here the herdsman whose mock baptism creates the monster; ‘Alpine herder’ is the closest contextual sense.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘wandering scholar,’ a folkloric itinerant learned man often credited with magical knowledge; he prescribes how to raise the bull, though the source does not define his training.

notes.label: Stierengaden
notes.text: literally ‘bull shed’ or ‘bull stall,’ a named structure on the Waldnacht Alp traditionally identified as the place where the giant bull was raised.

3d57c7909fda25cf9630a00a87c6d2ece0e4a98e.summary: In the Säckenberg, a forest northwest of Frick that is discussed further in no. 186 a, a woman called the Barakenfrau can be seen in broad daylight.

notes.label: Barakenfrau
notes.text: the local name of a female forest apparition near Frick who misleads travelers; Frau means ‘woman,’ while Baraken may preserve a place-name or older designation, and the account does not explain its literal origin.

026de887dd9753190b8a70bf002f62ccafdc8cfe.summary: Long ago, a stranger of knightly bearing and mysterious character named Bareto came from far away.

notes.label: Stutz-Alpe
notes.text: the local name of the nearby Alpine pasture; Alpe here denotes a seasonal high-mountain grazing area rather than the Alps as an entire mountain chain.

notes.label: Bareto-Balma
notes.text: the local name of Bareto’s cave; Balma is a Romansh and Alpine regional word for a cave, rock shelter, or overhang, while the compound commemorates the tale’s exiled sorcerer.

d82d4eb3e145d292600705a39687ec8e5eae336e.summary: Amid steep rocks and overhanging mountain walls, below Zeneggen to the northeast, lies the almost deserted and little-tended spot called ‘im Eich.’ Few mortals have likely seen it, and still fewer have entered it because of its complete seclusion.

notes.label: im Eich
notes.text: literally ‘in the oak’ or ‘in the oak place,’ the secluded locality below Zeneggen; Eich functions here as a proper place-name, and the source does not confirm an actual oak grove.

notes.label: Hübschburg
notes.text: the named castle above Visp from which noblemen reportedly descended to church; despite modern hübsch meaning ‘pretty,’ the historical place-name may have another origin.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss German sacristan or church sexton responsible here for timing the bell according to the barons' arrival.

f8c07233be8b8751c44e3e95502760949266cd70.summary: A Baron of Brandis lies buried in the choir of the church at Lützelflüh. Legend says that whenever the Flühluft blows across the mountains and the snow threatens to melt, he is condemned to leave this resting place.

notes.label: Flühluft
notes.text: literally ‘cliff wind’ or ‘rock-face air,’ a local mountain wind associated here with rapid snowmelt and a rising Emme; it may behave like a warm föhn wind, but the source does not give a technical meteorological definition.

5b6b8205dd7b4e1f8a3da0e083e5da8268814101.summary: Around the year 1328, a Baron of Regensberg lived on Lake Zürich at Balb Castle, not far from the village of Küsnacht, whose ruins can still be seen today.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

cdbfd7e75455a51c8df70449cf61b7b37b5181ff.summary: The barons of Unspunnen-Rotenfluh had an evil reputation in the country. They squeezed the very marrow from their subjects and oppressed them in every way.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

72741fe3f77fb6e592e38c1c1665d3476703e7db.summary: Baron Johann of Weissenburg lived in a childless marriage at his ancestral castle on the Simme River.

notes.label: Talleuten
notes.text: the source's inflected plural for ‘valley people,’ the inhabitants of an Alpine valley regarded as a local community; here it denotes the baron's neighboring people, especially those affected by his bequest.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communal land held for shared local use, commonly including pasture; here the bequest is grazing common sufficient for 1400 cows, and the term carries a collective property sense not captured by merely ‘meadow.’

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Lecktasche
notes.text: literally a ‘licking bag,’ a herder's bag used to carry salt or similar material for cattle to lick; the dead baron uses it to distribute a supernatural reward or punishment through the salt.

bd043ebe119b22e931749b177e4ffaf082f72b9f.summary: The Baron of Weissenburg, who at his wife's instigation was stabbed during a hunt by an Austrian knight, had bequeathed one hundred white cows and a great Allmend for fourteen hundred cows to the poor.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held or used land, especially shared pasture; the bequest was intended to sustain the poor people's cattle rather than enrich private landowners.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Lecktasche
notes.text: literally a ‘licking bag,’ a pouch holding salt or a mineral mixture offered for livestock to lick; the dead baron uses it to reverse the theft of his charitable bequest.

837b58f1949bfbcd2398ecd6591b0643d0d3ae4a.summary: According to Basel legend, the basilisk, or Baselist, is the offspring of a cock mating with a snake.

notes.label: Baselist
notes.text: the Basel form of the name basilisk, the legendary cock-and-serpent monster closely associated with the city and used as its heraldic supporter.

e8fe2126646492cac88330e72807708520dd3563.summary: On the Thursday before Laurentii in the year 1474, on Basel's Kohliberg, where the Freileute lived and the Freiknaben sat in judgment, a rooster was burned together with an egg it had laid.

notes.label: Laurentii
notes.text: the feast day of Saint Lawrence used as a calendar marker; the execution occurs on the preceding Thursday.

notes.label: Freileute
notes.text: the ‘free people’ associated with Basel's Kohliberg and its special jurisdiction.

notes.label: Freiknaben
notes.text: officers or members of the same free jurisdiction who sit in judgment and order the rooster and eggs burned.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a great serpentine dragon of German-speaking folklore, used as the benchmark that even the tiny basilisk surpasses in terror.

notes.label: Gerberbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘tanners' spring or fountain,’ the site where the old chronicle says a basilisk was found.

notes.label: Leimentale
notes.text: an older inflected form of Leimental, the forested Basel valley where the Gerberbrunnen was located.

ac1920b971f4e23a5a87e4b548d95b0f7d0b45f3.summary: Because the Eidgenossen had always been a people ready for war, eager to fight, and enterprising, they were not content at home to herd and tend cattle on their Alpine pastures, stalk wolves and bears in the forests, till the fields in the valleys, or peacefully pursue trades and crafts in the towns and villages.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades,’ the historical members and fighting forces of the Swiss Confederacy; in this account it means the Swiss Confederates collectively, not modern Swiss citizens in general.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: a historical German-speaking Swiss name for Romance-language lands, here especially Italy; Welsch can be geographically flexible and can carry an outsider’s or othering perspective.

notes.label: Herbstmonat
notes.text: literally ‘autumn month,’ a historical regional name for September; the date 13. Herbstmonat therefore denotes September 13, but the source’s wording is retained.

notes.label: Stier von Uri
notes.text: literally ‘Bull of Uri,’ the great war horn whose bellow rallied the troops of Uri and the Confederates; it is a named battle instrument and symbol, not a living bull.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or presiding official of a Swiss canton or rural polity; the title combines political office with military leadership in this account.

notes.label: Welschen
notes.text: historical collective term for Romance-speaking people or foreign troops; in this battle narrative it refers principally to the French and Italian adversaries, and its exact reference shifts with context.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older spelling for a military banner or cantonal standard; preserving or recovering a Panner carried exceptional communal and military honor.

notes.label: Bündner
notes.text: a person from Graubünden, historically a member of the Three Leagues; the strong fighter called Samson is identified by this regional origin.

22f4f13b19ad5a28b47f3433681f42d7306f3992.summary: After the Eidgenossen of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden had sworn their league at Rütli and, with God's help, driven out and destroyed the evil Landvögte, the Austrian duke Leopold flew into a rage.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally people bound together by an oath; here it names the confederates of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, the founding communities of the early Swiss Confederacy, rather than Swiss citizens in the modern general sense.

notes.label: Landvögte
notes.text: plural of Landvogt, territorial bailiffs or governors who exercised a distant ruler's authority; in this patriotic legend they represent the Habsburg regime expelled by the confederates.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: the ‘Bull of Uri,’ the emblematic great war horn of Uri or its bellowing sound, used here to summon and hearten the confederate levy.

notes.label: Harsthörner
notes.text: war horns used to call or signal a Harst, an armed body or levy; the source associates these horns specifically with Unterwalden.

notes.label: Letzimauer
notes.text: a defensive wall or barrier built across a narrow valley approach as part of a Letzi frontier defense; the force initially waits behind the one near Arth.

notes.label: Milchtanslein
notes.text: an archaic diminutive expression involving a small milk vessel; the source uses ‘to know where the Milchtanslein runs’ idiomatically for grasping how matters stand or from which direction the danger will come, while its precise literal image is uncertain.

notes.label: Wintermonat
notes.text: an old German and Swiss calendar name for November; the battle date given here is 15 November 1315.

notes.label: Haarus
notes.text: the battle cry attributed here to the people of Schwyz, with a force roughly like ‘out’ or ‘at them’; retaining the cry preserves its sound and legendary identity, since a single exact English equivalent is uncertain.

a7bb3c6f297053f3896bb2d21ee04f6ab77f9239.summary: In the evil year 1444, when the Swiss Confederates were fighting a civil war against Zürich and its Austrian allies and therefore lay in the field around that city and its strongholds, a great French army suddenly advanced through Alsace toward Switzerland to wage war upon it.

notes.label: Armagnaken
notes.text: the German-Swiss name for the Armagnac mercenaries who invaded in 1444; in Swiss memory they became the overwhelming foreign enemy at St. Jakob.

notes.label: armen Gecken
notes.text: literally ‘poor fools,’ a mocking folk reinterpretation of Armagnaken based on similar sound rather than historical etymology.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Banner, a military or civic standard around which troops gathered; losing one carried communal as well as tactical significance.

notes.label: Siechenhaus
notes.text: a medieval or early-modern isolation house, especially for people with leprosy or chronic disease; its cemetery and chapel become the Swiss final position.

notes.label: Urner
notes.text: the people and soldiers of the canton of Uri; Arnold Schick is named as their captain in the story.

notes.label: Gewalthaufen
notes.text: the main mass or principal battle formation of a Swiss army, contrasted here with the comparatively small vanguard; Gewalt conveys concentrated force rather than lawless violence.

adce694fff2539763a097222edf7c2565ec7f01c.summary: On the Alpe of Luvis, a man with an axe under his arm came into the Sennhütte every day during Käsen and stood there for a long time without saying a word; then he went on his way again.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working settlement; the supernatural visitor appears on the Alpe of Luvis.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the hut on an alp used by the Senn and other workers for dairying and cheesemaking.

notes.label: Käsen
notes.text: the seasonal work of making cheese, especially the daily processing of milk on an alp.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: an Alpine pasture hut; the final sentence uses this broader term for the hut where the stranger had appeared.

notes.label: Lichbritter
notes.text: a local name for the upland plain beyond the Theodul Pass, explained in the tale as a popular corruption of German Leichgerippe, ‘corpses’ skeletons’; the etymology is folkloric and its linguistic history is uncertain.

cebc63da5ef868901553a932093068a4ece9f791.summary: When the people of Schuders dragged their first bell with immense effort up the steep road from Schiers to their mountain village, a number of Wild-Lütli came toward them just as they were about to cross the Schrau-Bach with their precious burden.

notes.label: Wild-Lütli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild people,’ a diminutive name for the Alpine wild folk; they oppose the church bell because such beings traditionally cannot bear bell-ringing or harmonious sound.

notes.label: Schrau-Bach
notes.text: the named stream on the steep route from Schiers to Schuders where the villagers and Wild-Lütli fight over the bell.

4321a9d375763bd547a7f5335392d76bd597b7a7.summary: A man at Ried had a son who was as healthy as a chamois and had cheeks as red as dry cherry leaves.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Schlossvögte
notes.text: plural of Schlossvogt, castle bailiffs or governors associated with privilege and authority; the father's saying contrasts their wine with the family's plain drink.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey or a whey-based dairy liquid left from cheesemaking; it forms part of the boy's strengthening Alpine diet.

notes.label: Glockenrock
notes.text: a gray, bell-shaped frock or smock worn here as a pre-trouser garment; the source does not describe its precise cut, but treats the grown youth's continued wearing of it as childish.

notes.label: Rockbub
notes.text: literally a “frock boy,” a teasing or descriptive name for the youth while he still wears the Glockenrock rather than trousers.

notes.label: Vater, warum erstandet er geng?
notes.text: the boy's dialect question meaning “Father, why do you keep resting?”; geng means continually or always, and erstandet here means stop or rest.

notes.label: Warum Ihr geng erstandet?
notes.text: the boy's repeated dialect question, again meaning “Why do you keep resting?”

notes.label: Mahde
notes.text: the mown swath or strip of grass laid down by a pass of the scythe; the boy's swath is twice as wide as his father's.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its pastoral operation, not merely a mountain summit; the father speaks of leaving it at the end of the grazing season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schuh
notes.text: a historical foot measure whose exact local length varied; the fir trees are said to be one Schuh in diameter at ground level.

notes.label: Riedbub
notes.text: literally the “Ried boy,” the tale's name for the extraordinarily strong youth from Ried even after he has grown into a young man.

notes.label: Bast
notes.text: the wooden pack saddle fitted to a horse or mule for carrying loads; when its girth breaks, the Riedbub carries both saddle and manure himself.

notes.label: Schwinger
notes.text: a Swiss-style wrestler, especially one who grips an opponent's clothing in the tradition of Schwingen; the word refers here to the giant champion.

notes.label: Mütt
notes.text: a historical Swiss dry measure for grain whose capacity varied by locality; the tale does not specify the local volume of the Riedbub's reward.

notes.label: Reisteisen
notes.text: a heavy iron levering or prying implement; here it is a long iron bar with which the burdened Riedbub pulls nuts from the branches, though the source does not define its exact tool form.

notes.label: baumstark
notes.text: literally “tree-strong,” an emphatic description of immense physical strength; it is retained in the title as part of the hero's traditional designation.

3cf9f3d9f8ff3dfb0d9ed415e0632b8dc12414a7.summary: On the Bemmernalp in the municipality of Schwarzenberg stands one of the many chapels called Schimmelkirchen.

notes.label: Schimmelkirchen
notes.text: literally ‘gray-horse churches,’ a regional name for lonely chapels linked to tales of a gray or white horse accidentally trapped inside; the label describes a folkloric chapel type, though the origin of each individual chapel’s story is uncertain.

65066f3e0092de620cdf484cf0c7beee8b497386.summary: A bear once lived in the Kiental and caused great losses among the herds. A courageous man named Peter Zahler went up the valley with an old halberd to confront the beast.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman working on a high pasture; in this story the term identifies the mountain worker whose familiarity and strength allow him to grapple with the bear on the narrow path.

1d239ba8542324baacb8c9a48c6fbb3d801660ea.summary: Once a merchant wished to go to market, and he asked his three daughters what he should bring home for them.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

625f895ce3a6be70120b674a4a9762e086d31553.summary: Once a farmer and his wife went into the field to gather hay. At the edge of the forest, the woman set down a little basket in which a healthy baby boy slept and went about her work.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

9d6d4c300522b0fa467fc0931734fe8fddade98a.summary: During the Milanese Wars, a Swiss soldier known as the graue Melser once stood guard before a palace in Milan.

notes.label: graue Melser
notes.text: literally ‘gray man of Mels,’ the soldier's local byname; gray may refer to his appearance, clothing, or reputation, but the brief source does not explain it.

notes.label: Gafarrabüel
notes.text: a local hill-name known both to the soldier from Mels and, uncannily, to the Milanese lady; Büel commonly means a hill or rise, while the Gafarra element is not explained.

a72155273f140ceff6aebc0e048da3cfc90e437f.summary: A group of young men traveling around midnight from the community of Klein-Ftan to Groß-Ftan saw, aided by the moonlight, a human body lying upon the ground in a meadow not far from the road.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

62b29ee0c7333e9a222dc53021a79420c84b4e88.summary: This forest stands on the Lindenberg in the municipality of Hohenrain. A scoffer at religion once fell from the beech tree.

notes.label: blutten
notes.text: a dialect form meaning ‘bare’ or ‘uncovered’; here it names the patches where no grass grew, and the quotation marks emphasize the narrator’s local wording rather than a separate supernatural being or place-name.

619e15f725eebcc592d395e964ce45e5a18c0813.summary: There lived an old Burgvogt who wished his son, the young count, to marry someday so that the right to the Burgvogt’s office would remain within the family.

notes.label: Burgvogt
notes.text: a castle bailiff, governor, or steward holding authority over a castle district; the precise office varied historically, and here it is a hereditary status the old officeholder wants kept in the family.

57863e5c48887df01f773cd758814432f7e9fff0.summary: A man from Uri served as a Senn on a Glarus Alp—he worked there as a dairyman; I believe he was from the Schächental.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle, milking, and cheesemaking on a seasonal high pasture; the source itself glosses the man’s work, while his exact rank beneath the master is not stated.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: Swiss German for the large cauldron used to heat milk in Alpine cheesemaking; here the milk will not set in it until the scapular expels the beggar.

notes.label: Turner
notes.text: the pivoting support or crane from which an Alpine dairy cauldron is hung and swung over the hearth; the Senn hangs the protective scapular on this specialized fixture.

notes.label: Schwychögä
notes.text: an opaque Uri dialect insult applied by the Protestant farmhands to the uncanny beggar after the scapular drives him out; ‘everlasting’ and ‘perjured’ establish its abusive force, but the word’s precise literal sense is genuinely uncertain.

456ef75ce5e8c55dcc8b1d2ca5e9b2d049aadda1.summary: An hour beyond the city of Aarau, the mountain village of Upper and Lower Erlinsbach lies in the Jura.

notes.label: Fuss
notes.text: a historical foot measure whose exact length varied by territory; the source's three thousand Fuss describes the surrounding elevation and should not be read as a modern survey measurement.

notes.label: Legföhren
notes.text: low-growing, often prostrate mountain pines adapted to exposed slopes; the source pictures an unreachable line of them along the outer rock pinnacles.

notes.label: Sennweide
notes.text: pasture used by Sennen and their cattle, especially within a seasonal Alpine dairy economy; its livestock bells carry down into the valley.

notes.label: Hühnerweih
notes.text: a regional or historical name for a bird of prey associated with hunting fowl; it is rendered as the source's local term because the exact modern species intended is uncertain.

notes.label: die Frau
notes.text: literally ‘the Woman’ or ‘the Lady,’ the reverential local name for the mysterious female guardian of the Lorenzo spring who survived Wil's destruction.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a traditional communal warden charged with watching protected woods, fields, or boundaries; the local Bannwart is the recent witness who encounters die Frau.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
