notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarfs or earth spirits; they inhabit the Ramsfluh caves, employ the midwife, and depart riding their birds.

notes.label: Wähen
notes.text: the historical inflected form here of Wähe, a Swiss flat tart or open pastry; villagers baking were expected to leave one at the window for the Erdmännchen.

notes.label: Alpenraben
notes.text: literally ‘Alpine ravens,’ large black mountain birds linked with the cave dwarfs as messengers and mounts; the source's folk name does not establish a precise modern species.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: a regional and historical word for an apron or front cloth; the woman tries to warm her numbed hands beneath it and accidentally loses much of her uncanny payment.

notes.label: Je minder as b'hebsch,
notes.text: the first line of an Aargau dialect couplet completed by Je minder as hesch, together meaning ‘The less you keep, the less you have’; the Erdmännchen repeats the warning each time part of the apparently worthless but enchanted payment falls away.

notes.label: fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep rock face or cliff; it survives here as the ending of the surrounding place-names Zwilfluh, Geisfluh, Ramsfluh, and Wasserfluh.

3a28fddcc25ba4414307f89c76872f06358ec704.summary: In some places, from time to time before bad weather or even after a great thunderstorm, one hears rockfalls or avalanches rolling through steep ravines, gullies, or avalanche tracks.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

518c4457f9a6cdfab44b1ba3bf9d464de0ae140c.summary: In the spring of 1887, an unknown beggar came to Spiringen and knocked at a farmhouse in Hellprächtig, asking for food and drink.

notes.label: About this telling

894cb7df89d54b8cf6376b46033eb7a0294e7752.summary: Once in autumn, a little white horse belonging to Landammann Megnet or Azarias Püntener of Altdorf remained behind on the Fiseten Alp and could no longer be found.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or presiding official of a Swiss canton or rural polity; the story is uncertain whether Megnet or Azarias Püntener held the horse.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, rights, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; Fiseten is the named pasture on which the horse is lost.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Märcht
notes.text: the local name used to locate the chapel ‘beyond the Märcht’; it is related to a boundary or boundary feature, but the story does not identify the precise landmark.

notes.label: Krontaler
notes.text: a large silver crown thaler familiar in Switzerland and neighboring regions; ‘leather Krontaler’ appears to describe a substitute or token made of leather, but its exact monetary status is uncertain.

notes.label: Hideltanne
notes.text: a local name for a particular kind or form of fir beneath which the mare and foal were found; the source gives no botanical description, so the exact sense of Hidel- is uncertain.

d5a482800358ed4ac2accf67d26daf17992e7927.summary: Near the St. Anna Chapel at Baden, a poor wooden cross formerly stood above the road, and this is told about its origin.

notes.label: Hausvater
notes.text: literally ‘house-father,’ the male head and provider of a household; the title stresses the condemned man's duty toward his soon-to-be-orphaned children.

notes.label: Bürgerspital
notes.text: the civic hospital or charitable institution for citizens that later occupied the former execution-site area in Baden.

8fdd921e79811cfc1a3e77fd3ddfe0ba380b2f94.summary: A folk tradition maintains that the great bell of Spiringen (of Schattdorf) was cast in Spiringen (Schattdorf) itself, on the Achern (on the Kilchenacher).

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally an ‘itinerant scholar’ or ‘traveling student,’ but in Alpine legend a wandering learned practitioner credited with occult knowledge; here his wide travels lend authority to his judgment of the bells.

9c4bc25a0875d9807f18b7a59bf039dbc9ebd1a7.summary: The great bell at Grossdietwil is called the Mother of God Bell. An even larger one is said formerly to have stood in its place.

65e1b87532e0aea3b4b2ec9c2651b976c0e7dc5a.summary: 1. A farmer complained to his farmhand about how terribly uncanny things were at his mountain holding.

notes.label: Fänz
notes.text: a substantial Alpine flour-and-butter porridge or paste; regional recipes and consistency vary, and the source only emphasizes that this serving is hearty and rich.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; the second account does not specify the man’s exact duties.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

027e5f2b86302d13e6edb0992e63f0d5732c12cc.summary: Among the spirits, those that dwell on alpine pastures form a group of their own.

notes.label: Lanzig
notes.text: an Obwalden seasonal word for spring, related in sense to the older German Lenz; here it marks the customary season when the alpine herds ascend, though the exact span of the season is not defined.

notes.label: Senten
notes.text: the closest sense is a cattle herd organized as an alpine dairy unit or its seasonal procession; in this account the Senten goes up and later departs, so the word may encompass more than the animals alone.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for work with the herd and milk on the high pasture; it is a culturally specific pastoral role rather than a generic dairyman, while the man’s exact rank and duties are not given.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Unghür
notes.text: an Alemannic form closest to an uncanny creature, specter, or monster; here it is a grieving alpine spirit that takes a man’s shape and joins the descent, leaving its exact supernatural nature ambiguous.

341df114c3d6cabb8cd89b92e497a07fd34f4b02.summary: In the Epsach field stands a large stone beneath which two dwarfs are said to have lived in former times.

4d42815226539d4ffd677602fb3643c25e68b40f.summary: Once, the dwarfs asked a midwife for her services. As payment, they filled her apron with coals.

notes.label: Bergleutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain people,’ dwarf-like supernatural inhabitants of the mountains; their apparently worthless payment becomes gold only after the midwife has left.

23512ada42176ad557bb4df5bddee784f68c0aa7.summary: Once a Fahrender Schüler came up to Bergli and entered a hut. He cannot have been a rich one—they can only make other people rich—so, for God's sake, he asked the Senn for something to eat.

notes.label: Fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’; in German-language folklore the name often denotes an itinerant learned man credited with magic, conjuration, or secret arts, as in his banishment of the snakes here.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman in charge of cattle and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; the role is more specific than a general shepherd.

notes.label: Chilbi
notes.text: the Swiss German church dedication fair or village fair; in the Senn's quoted dismissal ‘Chum mer ad Chilbi, du Strolch,’ the literal wording is retained because the source itself explains its contextual force as refusing to deal with beggars.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss fresh whey cheese, distinct from ordinary curd cheese; it is one of the dairy foods offered to the traveler.

notes.label: Fänz
notes.text: an Alpine flour-and-butter dish, explicitly glossed by the source; regional recipes and consistency can vary.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the assistant or subordinate Senn who helps with the herd and Alpine dairy work.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here not simply a mountain but a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its dairy settlement, the working landscape compared by the Sennen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Ateren
notes.text: the Kleintal dialect plural for adders or snakes, corresponding to standard German Nattern and preserved in the dialect title and final account.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: whey, the liquid remaining after milk has curdled in cheese-making; the dialect version uses this Alpine dairy term where the standard-language version says Molke.

notes.label: Tunstigsatere
notes.text: a Kleintal dialect name for the harmful adders that bite cattle and are believed to suck milk; the story secures the creature's role, but the compound's precise literal derivation is uncertain.

010f33353a0f91747f7e63f5abebc0e189cb5fa1.summary: In the Pfaffenloch, not far from Gutbrunnen and a quarter of an hour from Rümligen Castle, numerous Bergmännchen made their home in olden times.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally little mountain men, here supernatural dwarf-like beings who live in the Pfaffenloch and help neighboring households; elsewhere the word can also denote mine spirits, so ordinary little men or miners would be too narrow.

d9814c08534776d68aee5b56fe9d9001fb5e728c.summary: a) The side of the Stanserhorn facing Obwalden is called Branzhorn, and one of its slopes is called Steinberg.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ helpful dwarf-like Alpine beings living in rock caves and assisting with livestock and hay.

notes.label: Älper
notes.text: people working or staying on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; they host the Bergmännchen and rely upon its labor.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennhütten
notes.text: plural of Sennhütte, the Alpine dairy and herders' huts where milk is processed and seasonal workers lodge.

notes.label: Älplerspeisen
notes.text: the characteristic foods of Alpine herders, likely dairy-based fare from the Alp; the source does not list the exact dishes.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent Alpine downslope wind; the helpful being refuses responsibility for the livestock whenever this dangerous weather approaches.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man,’ a familiar designation for the Bergmännchen rather than necessarily a statement that it is child-sized.

notes.label: Haselzwicken
notes.text: paired forked hazel switches or rods; the being uses them as magical tools to drive the hay through the air.

notes.label: Emde
notes.text: the later cutting of grass or aftermath hay, often finer than the first hay crop; here it lies in the field with the ordinary hay.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn, hay building, or rural outbuilding; the source explicitly glosses it as Scheune.

notes.label: Schwemmen
notes.text: openings in the barn through which hay is pitched or blown inside; the exact local architectural form is not described.

aed5ffd78754194a3a0e7f3c78b6cd8f8671fb4a.summary: There once lived an old man in Ernen in Valais. On Eggel in the Hochfluh, he owned a small, secluded property with a stable and a little brown house.

notes.label: Ladsteinen
notes.text: heavy stones used to press freshly made cheese; their exact shape and the local pressing arrangement are not described.

notes.label: Butterstock
notes.text: the formed heap, block, or storage mass upon which freshly churned butter is placed; the precise dairy form and measure can vary regionally.

notes.label: Kupfergelten
notes.text: broad copper tubs, pans, or shallow vessels used in the milk cellar; setting milk in such vessels helped the cream rise.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: the Swiss German word for cream, especially the rich layer that rises on milk; the source itself glosses it with standard German Rahm.

notes.label: Vorbruchmilch
notes.text: a warm dairy drink associated with the stage before the curd is broken or cut during cheesemaking; its exact regional preparation is not specified here.

notes.label: Butterliere
notes.text: a regional name for a butter-working or churning implement heard operating in the room; the source does not describe its construction, so the exact device remains uncertain.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like Alpine helper associated with hidden mountain spaces and dairy work; clothing him ends his service, a motif also found in traditions of household spirits.

891e428a1fc22631641169b29c15a53693d41236.summary: In the nearly 600-meter-high rock face of the Gonzenhaupt lies an iron mine probably used as early as Roman times and called the Erzloch by the people of the Sargans region.

notes.label: Erzloch
notes.text: literally ‘ore hole,’ the local name for the old iron mine in the Gonzen rock face above the Sargans region.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ the German diminutive used in the narrative for the benevolent warning spirit known in the title as Bergmännli.

notes.label: Knappen
notes.text: historical miners, especially men working underground in an organized mining operation; the singular form is Knappe.

notes.label: Knappenhaus
notes.text: literally ‘miners' house,’ the building where the mine workers ate and gathered near the workings.

notes.label: Knappe
notes.text: the singular of Knappen, an old occupational word for a miner rather than a reference here to a knight's squire.

notes.label: Lehmgrube
notes.text: literally ‘clay pit,’ the named working area where the Hobi brothers were positioned above the shaft.

notes.label: Bergmännli
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a Swiss German diminutive for a mine spirit; it is the title's form of the being called Bergmännlein in the body.

e2195b159c9cb09a1cd3b65347efb603cdda653e.summary: One moonlit night in Birrwil, two brothers were guarding a pear tree whose ripening fruit had often been stolen from them.

notes.label: Bergschwarz
notes.text: the deceased neighbor's local surname or byname, literally analyzable as ‘mountain-black’; here it identifies the ghost who disturbs boundary stones, but the tale gives no reason for the name and does not present it as a creature type.

d2fe228ca7e1f06892aa24fafcb7e34f547da9d5.summary: 1. If one wants a Bergspiegel or Weltspiegel, one must dig a hole in the ground at a crossroads on Holy Night, bury a mirror in it with the glass turned downward, and remain standing on the pit from 12 to 1 o’clock.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally a ‘mountain mirror,’ a magically prepared mirror that sees through mountains and across great distances; the ritual risks the first viewer’s life.

notes.label: Weltspiegel
notes.text: literally a ‘world mirror,’ the alternate name for the same far-seeing magical object; the tale does not distinguish its powers from those of the Bergspiegel.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a German-language folklore figure credited with occult learning; he is not an ordinary schoolchild but the owner of a visionary mirror.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; two episodes concern people serving on or owning such working pastures.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Ja, ja, d'Glarner chennet ä so eppis, das hennt-si scho meh g'seit
notes.text: the exact dialect observation, ‘Yes, yes, the people of Glarus know such things; that has been said of them before,’ preserving the tale’s regional reputation for magical knowledge.
notes.anchor: Ja, ja, d'Glarner chennet ä so eppis, das hennt-si scho meh g'seit

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small Swiss coin and monetary unit; the phrase means that every last bit of the stolen money returned, not that the coins had a fixed modern purchasing value.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin and unit of money whose value varied by canton and period; it is named alongside Rappen to stress that the full purse was restored.

notes.label: Nachrichter
notes.text: a historical executioner or officer who carried out judicial punishments; such socially marginal specialists were also credited in folklore with magical and divinatory knowledge.

notes.label: b'stellen
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb here meaning to stop, constrain, or hold someone by magic; the source groups it with binding and driving thieves back, not ordinary ordering or appointing.

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: a magical or religious binding prohibition or spell; forgetting to lift it leaves the thief frozen beneath the hut door through the winter.

notes.label: Alpchessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheese-making cauldron used on a high seasonal pasture; the thief remains burdened with the very dairy vessel he was stealing.

notes.label: Türgricht
notes.text: an Uri word for the structural frame or opening of a doorway; the magically arrested thief stands upright beneath it, but the source does not specify its individual timbers.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a regional diminutive-derived word for a large dairy or cheese-making cauldron; here it is the shortened reference to the same stolen Alpchessi still on the thief’s back.

c924bd862e4a6a1e5d8e71a25697ebb2bc189543.summary: On certain nights one often hears a ghastly screaming, wailing, and groaning from the Egg and across the long ridge of the Grenchnerberg.

notes.label: Sennbuben
notes.text: boys or junior workers attached to neighboring Alpine cattle-and-dairy operations; their competitive calls provide the human comparison for the ghost’s cries.

notes.label: Dönnel
notes.text: a local diminutive or nickname related to Anton or Toni, used for the condemned former dairyman; the source varies the form as Tönni and Tönnel.

notes.label: der Beserîsz-Dönnel hünet!
notes.text: a dialect cry meaning approximately ‘the Beserîsz-Dönnel is howling!’; Beserîsz-Dönnel is a local form of the figure’s broom-cutter nickname, while the exact shade of hünet is uncertain beyond a loud uncanny cry.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the skilled Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd’s milk processing and cheesemaking, often directing the seasonal dairy household; the ghost’s betrayal consists specifically in abusing this trusted communal role.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schirmtanne
notes.text: literally a ‘sheltering fir,’ a broad-branched landmark tree beside the cliff; the ghost intends to slaughter a cow there and is said to have taken his own life there.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper loft or hay-storage level of a traditional barn or dairy building; here the servants sleep above the main room and retreat from its hatch when the haunting begins.

notes.label: Tönni
notes.text: another local diminutive form of Toni or Anton for the same condemned dairyman called Dönnel elsewhere in the tale.

notes.label: Kessitanz
notes.text: literally ‘kettle dance,’ the ghost’s violent performance on the cheesemaking equipment, which sets the entire dairy house and its contents in motion.

notes.label: Herdbakten
notes.text: the pivoting hearth arm or crane whose hook suspends the dairy cauldron over the fire; the precise regional construction is not otherwise described.

notes.label: Wellkessel
notes.text: the large copper dairy cauldron used to heat several pails of milk and make very heavy cheeses; the first element’s precise regional derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Kessischild
notes.text: a removable shield or guard associated with the dairy cauldron and hearth; the source names it but does not fully describe its material, shape, or exact protective function.

notes.label: Harischbletz
notes.text: a movable wire scouring mesh woven like armor or chain mail; Dönnel uses it to scrape the cauldron into a booming percussion instrument.

notes.label: Menzeug
notes.text: a collective regional name for the hanging dairy or stable gear, here including heavy chains and cattle and horse bells; its exact inventory could vary by farm.

notes.label: Ankendrehfaß
notes.text: a wheel-shaped rotary butter churn; Anken is the Swiss German word for butter, and the source carefully describes the vessel’s crank, inner paddles, bunghole, and outlet.

notes.label: Liren- oder Trüllbudertanz
notes.text: the local or jocular name for Dönnel’s ‘lyre- or whirling-churn dance’; the exact derivation is uncertain, but it denotes the combined kettle-and-churn performance that animates the house.

notes.label: Gönli
notes.text: one of the regional names in the source’s catalogue of small eating or dairy vessels; its exact shape and distinction from the neighboring bowls are uncertain.

notes.label: Schufen
notes.text: regional scoops or shovel-like utensils listed among the eating and dairy ware shaken from the wall.

notes.label: Bollen
notes.text: rounded bowls or vessels in the dairy-house inventory; the source does not specify their size or exact use.

notes.label: Eßgepsli
notes.text: small wooden eating bowls or dishes, a diminutive related to Gepse, the broad wooden vessels used in Alpine dairying.

notes.label: Freßmütteli
notes.text: small feeding tubs, bowls, or measures; the colloquial compound is more rustic and disparaging than an ordinary word for tableware.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese or curd made from the whey left after ordinary cheese production; it is listed separately from milk and Schotten.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey or a whey-based dairy liquid remaining from cheesemaking; the regional term can vary in meaning, but the surrounding dairy inventory supports that sense here.

notes.label: Zigertrimmen
notes.text: regional troughs, trays, or forms used in handling Ziger; their precise shape and function within the next morning’s cheesemaking are not specified.

notes.label: Melkteren
notes.text: regional milking vessels or measured milk containers; the exact vessel form and local capacity are uncertain.

notes.label: Taußlein
notes.text: small dairy tubs or vessels in the source’s regional equipment list; the passage does not distinguish their precise construction or use.

notes.label: Bennen
notes.text: wooden dairy or carrying vessels, possibly basket- or tub-like; their exact local form is not defined in the tale.

notes.label: Brenten
notes.text: plural of Brente, a tall wooden carrying vessel often used for milk or other liquids and sometimes fitted to be carried on the back in Alpine regions.

notes.label: Bückten
notes.text: regional back-carried or bucket-like dairy vessels, probably related to wooden Bütten; the source does not distinguish them precisely from Bennen and Brenten.

notes.label: Käsejarbe
notes.text: a movable wooden cheese hoop or mold that holds a fresh wheel while it takes shape and dries; in the haunting, every hoop bursts.

notes.label: Kühbube
notes.text: literally a ‘cow boy,’ the youngest junior cattle worker or servant in the dairy household, not the modern American sense of cowboy.

notes.label: Schnetzeldecke
notes.text: a rustic insulating cover or blanket associated with chopped plant filling or material; it keeps the Kühbube warm, but the source does not state its exact construction.

notes.label: Tönnel
notes.text: a further local diminutive form of Anton or Toni for the same former community Senn called Dönnel and Tönni elsewhere in the tale.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; it is one of the dairy products the dishonest Senn steals from the people of Grenchen.

notes.label: Besenreisser-Anton
notes.text: the tale’s compound nickname for Anton, approximately ‘Broom-Twig-Cutter Anton’; it associates the condemned dairyman with cutting or gathering brush for brooms, though the source does not give a separate account of that occupation.

6e8630cdf5e9228a8ada9dbf55d5888bc51b67b1.summary: The last wild Mannli on the Matschiels Alp once told the alpine herdsmen that they did not know how, after cheese was made, the very best thing still remained in the whey.

notes.label: wild Mannli
notes.text: literally ‘wild little man’ in Alemannic, a solitary Alpine little-folk figure who possesses secret knowledge of dairying; wild marks him as outside settled human society, not merely ill-behaved.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning ‘little man’; here it is the shortened name for the last wild Mannli of the Matschiels Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

e437de097b708dc44f46d1e2189fce88dc6c3d91.summary: It is told from many hundreds of years ago that a Senn lived at the Sonnenberg farm in Jberg.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible especially for making cheese on a mountain pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Sennkessi
notes.text: a Swiss German dairyman’s large cheese kettle or cauldron, here filled with boiling milk.

2c528eef99f1e856589266a33f7179454ad938aa.summary: About fifty or sixty years ago, a strange Bettelmandeli wandered through the Alps of the Brunnital begging for Anken.

notes.label: Bettelmandeli
notes.text: literally a ‘little beggar man,’ an Alemannic diminutive for the uncanny itinerant figure who gathers butter and retaliates with hail; the tale never classifies it more precisely as human, spirit, or weather-worker.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; its repeated use matters because the figure refuses other dairy products and somehow transports an impossible quantity of butter to Montefun.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a distinctively Swiss whey cheese or curd made from whey left after ordinary cheese production; the Bettelmandeli explicitly refuses it in favor of Anken.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy work, not simply a mountain; the Bettelmandeli visits these working pastures and retaliates against the people on the Laue Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Geschner
notes.text: an uncertain Uri comparison for the fir trees left stark and stripped by hail; the context suggests bare, ruined, or skeletal-looking forms, but the exact noun and image cannot be recovered securely.

7ed01438fa09aaed848df61c62d77d57df2ef82b.summary: In the ‘Betten,’ where a little stream separates the municipalities of Rebstein and Marbach, people formerly saw the Bettenhund with a tongue hanging far down, fiery eyes, and a long tail.

notes.label: Bettenhund
notes.text: literally the ‘Betten dog,’ the named local apparition attached to the stream boundary between Rebstein and Marbach; despite its frightening form, the source says it never harms anyone.

7346959539f5695c8dfa8b7c8939a14ce30adfa8.summary: A distinguished learned man once told of a hermit who lived in the Helvetian lands—though no one knows in which years—that the auxiliary bishop of Costnitz, today’s Constance, visited him to discover what might lie behind his reputation.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

notes.text: a dialect form meaning a beggar's bundle or sack; here it becomes the dead wanderer's recurring instrument for tripping people on the path, and Büntel corresponds to standard German Bündel.

234fd066ed6570f62c2f9625714058eb458126f3.summary: Many years ago, a shoemaker lived at Ruis in the Oberland. Half an hour from the village, he owned a smallholding called “Sereins,” from which he could support two cows.

notes.text: a hooked farm or stable implement associated with bindings or chains; the tale does not describe its exact construction, but the shoemaker uses it to strike the mysteriously tethered cow.

notes.label: Pardenner-Bödeli
notes.text: the small level patch or meadow associated with Pardenn behind Klosters where the fox is tied; Bödeli is a diminutive of Boden.

notes.text: literally “witches’ dance,” the supernatural gathering for which the lady says she arrived late.

87ba3f7caf4615bdbb167ae63ce618cf2f99f9b7.summary: a) A fallen Entlebuch Meitschi lived heedlessly for a time. All at once, however, she became afraid of people and gloomy and visibly approached death.

notes.label: Meitschi
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young woman; the source uses it while morally condemning the unmarried mother.

notes.label: Chreiehus
notes.text: literally the ‘crow house,’ the local house-name where the Mummeli occupies the stove before being driven to the attic.

notes.label: Mummeli
notes.text: a regional name for a frightening female apparition or bogey; here it is the unresting mother associated with the Bibern.

notes.label: Bekle und Kachele
notes.text: regional plurals for bowls or basins and earthenware pots or dishes; the Mummeli smashes the household crockery.

notes.label: Estrich
notes.text: Swiss German for an attic or roof space; banishing the Mummeli there moves it away from the household stove without expelling it entirely.

notes.label: Himmelseppel
notes.text: a local nickname, literally something like ‘Heaven's Seppel’; Seppel is a familiar form of Joseph, but the reason for this man's epithet is not given.

notes.label: Höll
notes.text: literally ‘Hell,’ here explicitly the name of a house where the late-night drinkers mock the Mummeli.

notes.label: Bibern-Mummeli
notes.text: the local name of the lamenting female revenant bound to the Bibern stream; Mummeli suggests a frightening female spirit or bogey figure.

0033faf4c2cb7fa5d9bcf0dc11c3182148cdcb4c.summary: The holy Father Gallus, now advanced in years, journeyed once more to the place from which he had set out, in order to strengthen through his ministry a center of Christian splendor.

notes.label: Bildstock
notes.text: closest in English to a wayside shrine, this is a small freestanding devotional monument bearing a sacred image or niche; here it marks the former chapel site near Kappel, while its exact architectural form is not specified.

08ac215bd09db12a16c91af27d85f7d355fe9ba1.summary: Once a man came to a rich household and spent the night in the stable. Around midnight someone came with a sack full of money, buried it, and said: ‘Now, Devil, guard it until they drive a white billy goat through the stable.’ The next morning the man went on his way.

775968191f0a31543fa3f6942cc000eb5af6ff1d.summary: The master wants to shake the Birnli, the Birnli will not fall: the master, he sends the Jockli out, he is to shake the Birnli: the Jockli does not shake the Birnli, the Birnli will not fall.

notes.label: Birnli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little pear; the diminutive -li gives the chain song its familiar sound and is therefore retained in every repetition.

notes.label: Jockli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Jock or Jakob, used here for the little lad or servant ordered to shake the pear.

notes.label: Hündli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little dog; its -li diminutive is part of the cumulative sound pattern.

notes.label: Prügeli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little stick or cudgel; it is sent to strike the Hündli in the expanding chain.

notes.label: Fürli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little fire; the source itself glosses it as Feuer, and its diminutive form is retained for the song.

notes.label: Wässerli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little water or small quantity of water; it is personified and sent to extinguish the Fürli.

notes.label: Kälbli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little calf; it is sent to lap up the Wässerli and continues the cumulative -li pattern.

89e871fd56d1db7526a3dc35ebe0975bca4cc06e.summary: Many an episode is still told from the time of the witch trials, and in different places the accounts agree so closely that there seems to be something more at work than merely the arbitrary inventions of talkative Märchenerzählerinnen.

419ed06e1a5b983f9d364f4b7963d8bde7fd5761.summary: Three men of the Gamma family[1] from Geissplatte in Göschenen had often observed a light at night gleaming high in a rock face above Wyggen.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter, overhang, or shallow cave in Swiss Alpine place vocabulary; Sandbalm is described as unusually large and spacious.

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: Swiss Alpine crystal seekers or mineral hunters who enter rock faces and cavities in search of valuable specimens; here the word also sharpens the irony of their rejecting daylight for a gleaming crystal.

cf9c3ee0db563ba7b29b310a0caedacaeb78ccae.summary: ‘Lament upon lament! Seventy-seven in one grave!’

notes.label: Obesitz
notes.text: literally an evening sitting, a communal gathering for conversation and storytelling; it overlaps with Stubete but can emphasize the evening visit itself.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a social gathering in a home or parlor, often involving shared work, music, or storytelling; here it is a traditional rural setting for oral legend-telling.

8e4020ab35f8a25084e99fc35308e5d980e2e0aa.summary: The epidemic raged terribly in our region in the year 1629. In the parish of Grabs it carried off 1109 people, in Buchs 230, in Sevelen 380, and in Wartau more than 700.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Leiterwagen
notes.text: literally ‘ladder wagon,’ an open farm wagon with ladder-like slatted sides; here it is repurposed as the community's daily corpse cart.

notes.label: Resslabühl
notes.text: a local hill or rise on the route into Werdenberg; Bühl means ‘hill,’ but the source does not explain the first element of the place-name.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical measure based on an arm span, used here for the height of a stack of linen; its exact standardized length varied by region and period.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Bibernelle
notes.text: the German folk plant-name commonly applied to burnet saxifrage or a related pimpinella; exact botanical identification can vary in traditional usage, and the plant appears here in a rhymed plague remedy.

ab9fec8ad459e7bf867d7fdc704b413be09a85e2.summary: The black figure in the post dwells at Klingnau, at the desolate site where the ancient ancestral castle of the lords of Klingen once stood.

notes.text: a regional word for a carrying basket, often woven and fitted with handles; here the supernatural hen fills it with eggs for market.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little man, with -li as the diminutive; here the small green figure attempts to bind the girl by having her enter her name in his book.

notes.label: Bädli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Bad, a small bathhouse, bathing place, or spa; here it is the local landmark behind which the black house stands.

6f5342a9522ffebb28436bc775cfe074a62e771c.summary: On the summer Alps, the “schwarze Bub,” or “the Black One,” plays an important role.

notes.label: schwarze Bub
notes.text: literally ‘black boy’ or ‘black lad’ in the Valais source, a supernatural cattle thief also called ‘the Black One’; the story signals an uncanny figure but supplies no human ethnicity, origin, or fixed appearance.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Steinhirt
notes.text: literally ‘stone herdsman,’ a local term here glossed as a stone man or Mellig, apparently a cairn or stone marker from which the herdsman calls; its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Mellig
notes.text: the local alternative name attached to the Steinhirt or stone man; the source offers no further gloss, so whether it is a place-specific cairn type or proper name remains uncertain.

211ccde87e0b405f092ddb56c71e42245dacddaa.summary: On an alp in the Oberhasli in former times, the Sennen had cows killed—always those that gave the most milk and were the finest.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Aelpler
notes.text: a person working or residing on an alp during the pasture season, closest to an Alpine herdsman or pasture worker; here several Aelpler try to break the haunting, but their individual jobs are not specified.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for milk processing and often cattle on a seasonal high pasture; the story uses the plural Sennen for the community and Senn for the successful herdsman, without defining his rank.

notes.label: Melchtern
notes.text: plural of a regional milk pail or milking vessel; the supernatural cow fills whole Melchtern, but the source gives neither their material nor capacity.

notes.label: Milchgaden
notes.text: literally a ‘milk room’ or dairy chamber in an Alpine hut, used for handling and storing milk; here the Senn carries the milk there before pouring it into Gebsen, while the room’s exact layout is unstated.

notes.label: Gebsen
notes.text: shallow wooden dairy vessels in which fresh milk was set so that cream could rise; the Senn pours the impossible cow’s milk into them, but their number and dimensions are not given.

83318e457461c0ab34f555f3310d021d112dc55b.summary: In former times, cows were killed on an Alp in the Oberhasli, always those that gave the most milk or were the most beautiful.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Melchtern
notes.text: plural of a regional word for large milk pails or milking vessels; drawing whole vessels full without emptying the enchanted cow's udder measures the difficulty of the redemption task.

55d567b9679f24967da3b69907d29eaecb39294c.summary: The Jüppe is a hamlet an hour from Leuggern, from which a servant was once sent across the Aare to Klingnau late at midnight.

notes.text: literally ‘sunken lane,’ retained here as the route’s local name.

notes.text: literally ‘black man in the riverside meadow,’ the local name of the wandering treasure guardian.

notes.label: Au
notes.text: a riverside meadow or floodplain.

53b150e41bc83118b42b01f19b58f1b05e7a265f.summary: Along the water conduit that runs from the Lägern mountain to Wettingen Abbey walks a black figure in a monk’s habit, called the Black Pfaff.

notes.label: Pfaff
notes.text: an old, often disparaging word for a cleric or priest; here the Black Pfaff is a monastic-looking ghost associated with the abbey’s water conduit, though his historical office was waterworks master.

c4fe0d8319c6a2f60ef0b8ff33584a912e838533.summary: A flowering pasture with a stately Alphütte once lay where the Bischoler-See now lies on the Heinzenberg. — This beautiful grazing ground belonged to a rich, avaricious Senn.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: a hut on a high summer pasture, used as the living and dairy-working base for the seasonal herd.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman or head herdsman responsible for cattle and milk production on an Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Lab
notes.text: rennet, the coagulating substance used in cheesemaking; the Senn maliciously gives the traveler milk over-soured or curdled with it.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the dairy hut in which a Senn lives and works on the high pasture; the poodle drags the offender out of it before the flood.

d6a7a5061fae94b458b6c6d198ff255a8ee05315.summary: A despairing man once hanged himself on the old bridge in the Erlenholz. From then on, a black poodle was often seen at night walking over the spot or sitting in the middle of the bridge.

notes.label: Vehschicklers
notes.text: an inflected regional form for a livestock dealer, drover, or person who dispatches cattle; the supposedly spectral dog belongs to such a known tradesman.

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard Swiss abbreviation for the canton of St. Gallen, locating Gaiserwald in the catalogue title.

3303ce532598e093b467ea3ad05800c791a9e762.summary: In September of the year 1868, at the time of the terrible flood, two farmers on the Vals Mayensäss called “au] dem Boden” in Peil saw the black Wassermann, who always brings dreadful downpours with him when he appears.

notes.label: Mayensäss
notes.text: a seasonal farmstead and pasture at an intermediate elevation, traditionally occupied between the valley farm and the high summer Alp; the Vals holding in Peil is threatened by the flood.

notes.label: Wassermann
notes.text: literally a “water man,” a male water spirit rather than an ordinary human; this black figure is believed to summon destructive rain and flooding unless greeted courteously.

notes.label: wüst
notes.text: in this quoted older regional use, fierce, hideous, or savage in appearance and conduct, not merely empty or desolate.

notes.label: Wuhrungen
notes.text: protective water-control works such as embankments, dikes, or reinforced barriers built against a stream or flood; the exact construction used at the hut is not described.

notes.label: Gudla
notes.text: muddy floodwater, sludge, or debris-laden slurry in which the apparition rolls; the precise local composition is not specified.

notes.label: Rüfen
notes.text: the plural of Rüfe, Alpine debris flows or landslide torrents carrying earth and stone down steep slopes.

notes.label: Erdschlipfe
notes.text: earth slips or landslides, especially masses of saturated ground sliding down a slope during heavy rain.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or stream gorge into which the landslides and debris flows descend.

notes.label: Wasser-Butz
notes.text: literally a water Butz, an uncanny water bogey or frightening spirit; Butz denotes a specter or bogey used to frighten people, not a zoological creature.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: an Alpine debris flow, landslide torrent, or the channel cut by such a flow; here one breaks loose beside the hut and enters the stream.

8ba6b7d9a28307e856dff7f90beacc8487428610.summary: In ancient times there lived in the upper Rhone Valley a capable blacksmith who enjoyed a large clientele and was known far and wide simply as the Blacksmith of Rumpelbach.

notes.label: Halben
notes.text: a historical half-measure or vessel for wine; the story does not establish its exact local volume.

notes.label: Muskateller
notes.text: Muscat wine, here described as golden and brought to the blacksmith while he works.

notes.label: Butzenscheiben
notes.text: small round panes of thick crown or bottle glass traditionally set into leaded windows; the wife peers through them from the house.

notes.label: Lehnstuhl
notes.text: an upholstered armchair; it is one of the blacksmith's three magically binding objects.

notes.label: Nagelsack
notes.text: literally a nail sack or pouch; whoever reaches into this second binding object cannot withdraw a hand without the blacksmith's help.

notes.label: Dreifuss
notes.text: a three-legged stand or trivet for a cooking vessel; the supposed repair lets the blacksmith send the Devil to the Nagelsack.

notes.label: Sonntagsgewand
notes.text: literally “Sunday clothes,” the respectable best clothing the blacksmith claims he must put on before leaving with the Devil.

notes.label: Teufelsewigkeit
notes.text: literally a “devil's eternity,” a comic intensification meaning forever in the blacksmith's threat.

notes.label: Höllentor
notes.text: literally “gate of hell,” where Death first takes the blacksmith and the inhabitants refuse him entry.

notes.label: Fegefeuer
notes.text: purgatory in Catholic tradition; its gatekeepers reject the blacksmith just as hell has done.

notes.label: Himmelspforte
notes.text: literally “gate of heaven,” the doorway guarded by Peter and named again in the closing dialect rhyme.

notes.label: Schurzfell
notes.text: the leather apron worn by a blacksmith; once he throws it through the heavenly gate and stands on it, he claims a place upon his own property.

notes.label: uf siner Sach
notes.text: Swiss German for “upon what is his own” or “on his own property”; the legalistic joke completes the blacksmith's rhyme and his trick for entering heaven.

2fc2cc797545bf9d9eff8f577e34bc976c28ae61.summary: Above Schönbrunnen, on the new country road from Ägeri toward Hinterburg between Bethlehem and the so-called Loch, lies a piece of land with a barn belonging to the Schönbrunnen farm and called the Bleiche.

notes.text: this is the local name of a wood between Bethlehem and Edlibach from which the apparition approaches; its literal meaning, historical spelling, and exact boundaries are uncertain.

notes.label: Bleiki-Muoterli
notes.text: this Alemannic name means approximately ‘little mother of the Bleiche’ and identifies the female apparition tied to that farm landscape; the name’s exact derivation and whether later sightings were disguises are uncertain.

455bee79882940e3220f46f171ca6a569f35b2a3.summary: An old woman once joined a goatherd boy on a high Alpine pasture and spoke to him most kindly and sympathetically.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

2ebfc6897e0813355cc1861fce8ec8d506aa766d.summary: In Val Castiel near Untervatz, on the rocky slope, stand two old, thick, tall-trunked beeches very close together.

notes.label: Tatsch
notes.text: a quoted regional descriptor for the toads’ feet, suggesting a broad, clumsy, or splayed form; the source does not define the exact dialect nuance, and the word has other meanings in other Swiss contexts.

notes.label: Uo, Us
notes.text: the written form of the enormous toads’ uncanny cry; it functions as a sound rather than a phrase with a secure independent translation.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German landscape word for a steep, narrow ravine or stream gorge; the charcoal-burning site lies toward such a ravine.

notes.label: Kohlen-Joggeli
notes.text: a local diminutive designation for the charcoal burner and his returning ghost; Joggeli is an affectionate or familiar form of Jakob, while Kohlen identifies him with charcoal.

3073dd25af9972fb7c5a8bf15df7c82d0cdcf1c0.summary: Count Eberhard of Kyburg had returned across the mountains to his city of Thun from the university at Bologna, where he had led a lively student life and spent a great deal of money that his miserly brother Hartmann begrudged him.

notes.label: Schneggen
notes.text: this older regional form, literally ‘snail,’ denotes the castle’s winding or spiral staircase; its exact architectural layout is uncertain.

notes.label: Blutströpflein
notes.text: literally ‘little drops of blood,’ this is the local flower-name linked by the legend to Hartmann’s death; the precise botanical species intended is uncertain.

3d43d8eec5a39e0bce88bf0c77bcc383168e6c45.summary: The name “Bläss-Ecke” for the Blasecken Pass in St. Antönien is said to derive from the following legend.

notes.label: Bläss
notes.text: a traditional animal name derived from the white blaze running from forehead to nose; the mare’s name drives the legend’s place-name explanation.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, not simply a mountain peak; the mare escapes from this summer grazing land.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.
