notes.label: Montafun
notes.text: the historical form used here for Montafon, the neighboring valley in present-day Vorarlberg, Austria.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal movement of livestock and herders to the high summer pasture; here it marks the springtime return to the Alp.

notes.label: Blässegg
notes.text: the pass name the story derives from the mare Bläss; this is a folkloric place-name explanation rather than linguistic proof.

b60b83527bbd5c05cd2b253d0bdbf71449f56514.summary: a) The Clariden legend is repeated with slight changes on Uri's Blümlisalp, a basin-shaped valley filled with snow and ice on the Uri-Rotstock.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy production on a seasonal high pasture; the legend makes his abuse of pastoral abundance and his mother central to the curse.

notes.label: Treichlenkuh
notes.text: a cow wearing a Treichel, a large hammered sheet-metal livestock bell, often a leading or especially prized animal; Bäbi is explicitly the Senn's finest cow.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its seasonal livestock-and-dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the curse destroys an entire productive pastoral world.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Firn
notes.text: compacted old snow that survives a summer and can feed a glacier; it replaces the flower-rich Alp and becomes the spirits' place of wandering.

notes.label: Melckschmutz
notes.text: a historical spelling for a milker's protective garment or apron; the exact article is uncertain, and it melts in the cow's supernatural heat.

notes.label: Melkschmutz
notes.text: the source's second spelling of the same uncertain milker's protective garment or apron; both spellings are preserved because both occur in the account.

notes.label: Handbräntli
notes.text: a small portable wooden dairy vessel designed to be carried by hand or on the back; the mother brings it when she comes asking for milk.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: a full organized Alpine cattle herd or cattle-and-dairy unit under pastoral management, not merely an unstructured group of cows; the cowherd is told to flee with it.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheese-making cauldron used to heat milk; the Senn and Kathry attempt to shelter or escape beneath it.

notes.label: Melchteren
notes.text: a regional dairying measure or vessel represented as a quantity of milk; ‘milking-pail’ is the closest contextual sense, but its exact capacity and whether it counts vessels or full milkings remain uncertain.

notes.label: abers Plätzli
notes.text: a dialect phrase for a small bare or snow-free patch, especially one exposed amid snow; the cow is said to be milkable there, though the patch's exact location is not given.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: the whey left after cheesemaking; serving the mother sour whey instead of milk belongs to the Senn's insulting treatment of her.

notes.label: Mürägsims
notes.text: the source's name for a degrading mixture of lime and assorted dirt scraped from a wall; its exact recipe is not fixed beyond the narrator's parenthetical gloss.

notes.label: Alpsennten
notes.text: the complete herd and dairy unit belonging to an Alp; it follows the departing mother except for Bliämi, making the loss broader than one cow.

notes.label: z'alten Mittwoch
notes.text: literally ‘on old Wednesday,’ a calendrical folk designation for a Wednesday in the old-days interval around year's end; the source does not further define which Wednesday is meant.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the Swiss and southern German word for butter; the dialect version depicts such abundance that people wade through cheese and Anken.

f94ad8e317b1da543d196fb0249f6a07aed6ed7f.summary: The broad snowfield behind the Dembachhorn was in ancient times a splendid, fertile Alp belonging to the richest farmer in the valley.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, buildings, dairy work, and grazing economy, not simply a mountain summit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennerei
notes.text: the Alpine dairy building or operation where milk is processed into cheese and related products; its steps have grotesquely been built from cheese wheels.

notes.label: Ziegerballen
notes.text: balls or rounded masses of Zieger, a whey-derived cheese or curd product; their use as paving displays the son's wasteful abundance.

notes.label: Zieger-stollen
notes.text: the source's hyphenated form for large bar-, slab-, or block-like pieces of Zieger; the tale says they stand as high as a man and are used to fence the livestock pen.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen responsible for livestock and cheese production on an Alp; here they waste butter by using it in a skittles game.

notes.label: Blümlisalp
notes.text: literally a “flower Alp,” the traditional name in the title for the fertile high pasture destroyed beneath the Dembachhorn; it evokes the lost flowering landscape rather than naming an ordinary garden.

3676651cee5bb5778a67b9daa1f0e6a6bdd8ef6d.summary: Where the Turtmanngletscher flashes and gleams on sunny days as though made of pure silver, there formerly stood the most beautiful and largest Alp in the high valley, the Blümlisalp.

notes.label: Turtmanngletscher
notes.text: the Turtmann Glacier whose ice is said to cover the lost pasture and imprison the guilty figures.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and dairy settlement, here the rich farm landscape destroyed by falling ice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Blümlisalp
notes.text: literally an Alp rich in flowers, the beautiful pasture buried beneath the Turtmann Glacier after the household's cruelty.

notes.label: Sennenpaar
notes.text: literally a pair or couple of Alpine dairy workers, the prosperous parents who originally inhabit the pasture.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker; here the daughter's husband who mistreats her blind father and favors Kathrin.

notes.label: Turtmännin
notes.text: the local name for the stream or torrent draining the Turtmann Valley and glacier, heard roaring in spring.

notes.label: Ryn
notes.text: the dialect form of the dog name Rein in the final supernatural lament; both forms are preserved.

notes.label: Buhl
notes.text: an older word for a lover or paramour, identifying Kathrin as the Senne's illicit beloved in the final lament.

notes.label: Blu"mlisalpen
notes.text: the source's typographic or OCR-corrupted inflected form of Blümlisalp in the dialect line; it is preserved exactly while the adjacent English gloss restores the place-name.

942e3b06e3a12b624101665345a27ed334aef5fc.summary: Above the rock wall of Valeis stood a pine whose branches projected over the yawning abyss.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work during the summer season.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high-mountain summer pasture and its seasonal herding operation in Swiss usage, not simply the mountain range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bockschinden
notes.text: literally ‘skinning the buck,’ the local name for the dangerous feat of hanging head-down by the knees from a branch; no actual goat is skinned in the episode.

notes.label: Zeitkuh
notes.text: a cow or heifer at the proper time in pregnancy or near calving; the source itself glosses the prize more broadly as a fine pregnant bovine.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ a lay hermit or holy man living in seclusion; his pious formula rescues the herdsman.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep Swiss ravine or gorge; the spectral dog repeatedly trots through it between the heights and open valley.

notes.label: Valeisenhund
notes.text: the spectral ‘Valeis dog’ into which the doomed Uli enters local legend; the formation marks association with Valeis rather than a distinct dog breed.

b997040dc23a14eb84ad1f8e7a7a27a2085e704c.summary: A dead man was once found on the road between the villages of Gontenschwil and Zetzwil, bearing every sign of a violent death.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the bailiff or governor who administered a subject territory on behalf of a Swiss city or canton; petitioners rang the castle bell to seek his justice or charity.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

52ec8196a02f59a3fb60aaf28dc781789b512441.summary: An old ferryman in the little town of Aarburg firmly maintains the truth of the following events, which he and his father claimed to have experienced.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a Weidling is a long, shallow riverboat traditionally rowed, poled, or steered on Swiss rivers, used here as the Aarburg ferry; its exact size and propulsion on this journey are unspecified.

notes.label: Fehr
notes.text: Fehr is an older or regional word for the ferryman, referring here to the father endangered by the storm; whether it was also a local occupational title is uncertain.

notes.label: Bornjungfrau
notes.text: literally ‘maiden of the Born,’ the Bornjungfrau is the treasure-bearing woman believed to leave the Bornberg once a century to bathe and seek release; her identity, origin, and relation to the ferry calls are uncertain.

dcd59467eb443d3ae25d852fdbe534e9f19b62cc.summary: On certain nights, the Botenhund is said to have run from the long trough near Schänis to the former Letze below Maseltrangen—a great, long dog with eyes like windowpanes and goat's feet.

notes.label: Botenhund
notes.text: literally ‘messenger dog,’ a long, goat-footed spectral hound traveling a fixed route; the story does not explain what message it carries.

notes.label: Letze
notes.text: a defensive barrier, boundary fortification, or narrow-pass earthwork; the dog's route ends at the former Letze below Maseltrangen.

notes.label: Kilt- oder Stubetengänger
notes.text: young people traveling to nighttime courtship visits or sociable farmhouse-parlor gatherings; the hound rarely challenges these customary evening travelers.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: das schwarze Marili
notes.text: literally ‘the little black Mary,’ the postilion's irreverent diminutive for the Black Madonna of Einsiedeln; the legend treats the nickname as mockery of a sacred image.

d80d832af4b50758a18360bf1ce135795504181f.summary: One night, some twenty years ago, a band of young people merrily walked home from the village of Habsburg through the forest.

notes.label: gebannt
notes.text: magically bound, confined, or banished by ritual authority; the troublesome dead man is imprisoned in a bottle and removed from his former home.

04500c02cfe5a4e40b25e445261b7de3f49c9dfc.summary: A few years ago, a farmer near Brugg dug an old walnut tree out of his field and found a sealed glass bottle beneath its stump.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

f7200cd9a630a2dcdda96829527ba7ed78e2dbd5.summary: In former times Landammann Brand lived on the Tal estate in Spiringen. He owned the Oberschwandberg, where things were very frequently stolen from him.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional title of a senior cantonal or communal magistrate in central Switzerland; it marks Brand as a leading public official.

notes.label: b'stellen
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of bestellen with the magical sense of stopping, fixing, or binding a culprit in place; the priest’s act leaves the thief unable to move until touched.

a74049ee1e1a4ef3830d71057feec5cd0d95f226.summary: At the time of the Reformation, when governments in many cantons became unfaithful to the Catholic Church and forced the people to abandon the old faith, Switzerland was filled with unrest, contention and quarrels, misery and distress.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Linien
notes.text: plural of Linie, a small historical unit of length called a ‘line’; its exact local value varied, and here it measures the slight raised imprint of the sandal.

notes.label: Pierre bénite
notes.text: French for ‘blessed stone,’ the bilingual Valais name given to the boundary rock marked by the Capuchin and Satan.

730c7e255287e44f4b763ab5935bf5a7bb782131.summary: More than fifty years ago in the Sagewald near Römerswil, young fellows were rolling balls in a game.

notes.label: Hohlen
notes.text: a local name for the jubilant call or whoop made by the winners of the ball-rolling game; the precise form of the vocal custom is not described, and the source places the word in quotation marks.

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for a baptismal godfather or male sponsor; the ghost's repeated address appears connected to a deceased baptismal sponsor, although the exact reciprocal use in the quoted exchange is ambiguous.

notes.label: armen Seele
notes.text: literally ‘poor soul,’ a Catholic folk designation for a suffering or unredeemed dead soul, often imagined as undergoing penance and needing help; here the wandering spirit seeks release by having a displaced boundary stone restored through a prescribed act.

eeb2a7c565b23f11a6133a5ce917863ef3452141.summary: If one neighbor cheats another out of his land, after death he appears every night as a fiery skeleton upon the dishonestly acquired field.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: an itinerant craft arrangement in which a tailor or other artisan worked temporarily in a customer's home, often receiving lodging and meals as part of the engagement.

cafccee0af57151d632b2be8cb4f2b040afd83a7.summary: Christelis Franz had been at the village inn and went home late at night, choosing the footpath across the Hub although he had often heard that it was not safe there.

notes.label: Markstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking land or property limits; moving one fraudulently was a serious violation of communal and property order and becomes the cause of the haunting.

notes.label: Der Markenrücker
notes.text: literally ‘the boundary-marker mover,’ a person condemned after death for shifting a property stone; the white cap signals that this particular spirit remains redeemable.

ba2c10a032bfe00a70704beffc162c6978f991ea.summary: The Gemeindebann of the two Fricktal communities of Wölflinswil and Wittnau had always bordered one another, but in many places the Bannmarken on both sides had long since disappeared.

notes.label: Gemeindebann
notes.text: a community's legally bounded territory or jurisdiction, including its fields and common land; it does not mean a magical ban here.

notes.label: Bannmarken
notes.text: boundary markers defining a Gemeindebann; their removal enables the official's land fraud.

notes.label: Bowäldler
notes.text: the enduring insulting nickname of Wittnau's fraudulent boundary official and later his ghost; the source does not securely explain its literal derivation, so it is retained rather than guessed at.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss and southern German title for a church sexton or sacristan, one of the Bowäldler's public offices.

notes.label: Gemeindeammann
notes.text: the presiding municipal official or mayor of a Swiss commune; as officeholder, the Bowäldler abuses public authority for Wittnau's benefit.

notes.label: Jucharten
notes.text: plural of Juchart, a variable historical Swiss land measure based on the area plowed in a day; the fraud costs Wölflinswil many such units.

notes.label: Augenschein
notes.text: a formal on-site judicial inspection of disputed land or evidence, not merely an informal look.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical administrative or judicial official; here it is the shortened title for the Gemeindeammann.

notes.label: Zeitstein
notes.text: literally ‘time stone,’ the dialectal name here associated with the church clock or its clock face; the taunt links it to the clock ropes from which the culprit hanged.

notes.label: Oerkensünder
notes.text: literally an ‘Oerken sinner,’ a reciprocal village insult derived from the falsely enclosed Oerkenhalde land.

notes.label: Balmerainsünder
notes.text: literally a ‘Balmenrain sinner,’ the parallel insult derived from another tract crossed by the fraudulent boundary.

c4a8d496606bfce9f8d0ed9889fba7eedb743b45.summary: The event occurred in the year 1837 on the Alp Stössi in the Maderanertal, and a reliable man, the former postmaster Kyd in Brunnen, related it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, grazing rights, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain peak; Stössi is the pastoral setting where the family summers its goats.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senntenbauer
notes.text: an owner or master of a substantial Alpine dairy herd and its seasonal operation; the boy's father works for such a wealthy pastoral employer on the Urnerboden.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the assistant to the Senn, helping manage livestock and dairy work on an Alp; it identifies the father's seasonal occupation rather than an ordinary farmhand's rank.

notes.label: Bänkli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a small bench; the grandfather sits on the one outside the hut while watching the children.

notes.label: Hansseppli niänä meh
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Hansseppli is nowhere anymore’; the children's compressed cry expresses that he has disappeared, not merely stepped out of sight.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Geissbuben
notes.text: Swiss German for goat boys, young herders responsible for goats; these two boys find Hansseppli beneath the fir.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: 14 Nothelfer
notes.text: the Fourteen Holy Helpers, a traditional Catholic group of saints invoked collectively in urgent danger and illness; the mother vows a Mass in their honor.

notes.label: Plangg
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a steep grassy slope, clearing, or mountainside strip; workers occupy it in the alternate account, but its exact boundaries are not stated.

notes.label: E nu, d'r Hansseppli isch da!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Well now, Hansseppli is here!’; the workers exclaim in astonishment when the missing child becomes visible by the stump.
notes.anchor: E nu, d'r Hansseppli isch da!

notes.label: Chräpfli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for small filled pastries, fritters, or dumpling-like morsels; the child says the otherworldly food was something like them but cannot say that he truly ate.

notes.label: Seelmesser
notes.text: a priest or chaplain endowed to celebrate Masses for the souls of the dead; the historical footnote uses it as Dittli's clerical office from 1863 to 1867.

notes.label: Muttergottespfründe
notes.text: a benefice or endowed chaplaincy dedicated to the Mother of God; the footnote names the Altdorf office Dittli held from 1867 until his death.

notes.label: Haglatte
notes.text: a long wooden fence rail or pole used in a traditional Hag fence; Dittli drags one over in an attempt to sound the river's depth.

016f608d2ce6ee995a19dc061987c6db6e2457ba.summary: The tenant farmer Brändli in the so-called Stampis-Baumgarten near Chur was sitting one evening in the living room with his wife and two of his boys, aged 6–8, when the two boys suddenly called to their parents, “Oh, just look!”

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

0598bb33b2dab88f958d761d708ef12d9ca1691b.summary: In olden times, it was an ugly, eerie little house. The Dorfwüör ran through the kitchen.

notes.label: Dorfwüör
notes.text: the village watercourse or artificial channel running through the settlement; in Valais such channels had practical local functions not conveyed by the generic word ‘stream.’

notes.label: Boze
notes.text: the dialect plural of ‘Boz,’ encompassing bogeys, specters, and frightening supernatural manifestations rather than one narrowly defined kind of ghost.

notes.label: piste und towwu
notes.text: an uncertain Valais dialect sound-pair describing the haunting activity in the room, apparently forceful stamping, thudding, bustling, or raging; the exact actions cannot be recovered with confidence.

notes.label: Eye
notes.text: a regional word for an alluvial riverside tract, island-like meadow, or wooded floodplain; the exact landscape meant in this Naters account is uncertain.

notes.label: Rottu
notes.text: the Valais German name for the Rhône River, culturally distinct from the standard German ‘Rhone’ and English ‘Rhône.’

notes.label: Bozuhiischi
notes.text: a Valais diminutive meaning the little house of the Boze or bogeys, the affectionate-looking diminutive contrasting with its terrifying reputation.

notes.label: Bozhaus
notes.text: a Valais dialect compound for a house haunted by a ‘Boz,’ a bogey, specter, or frightening supernatural presence; ‘haunted house’ does not preserve the local creature-name.

69ef324bdaf2d5b021677aa6d7fb03180cb2f16b.summary: Blattu-Schuz is uncanny too. As early as ten years ago, an Emd man saw the Bozo clearly there beneath the chapel in the morning, while it was still dark.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for a frightening, shape-changing local apparition or bogey; at Blattu-Schuz it appears as woolly balls, a lamb, a cat, or a person and misleads travelers, while the word does not identify one fixed form.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

01d904bfe20cb0425be156b7823606b85d9e18a4.summary: At Höhstegen in Saas, so people related at an Abendsitz, things were said to have once been very uncanny.

notes.label: Abendsitz
notes.text: literally an ‘evening sitting,’ a customary social gathering in a house or common room for visiting, talk, and amusement; here the gathering runs late and is morally linked with making sport of the dead, though the story does not specify its other activities.

notes.label: ho uf'gjuzot ha
notes.text: a Valais dialect phrase meaning roughly ‘to have whooped or yodeled high’; it describes the resonant Alpine cry answered by the traveler, while the wording does not distinguish sharply between a shout, whoop, and short yodel.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais dialect name closest to a bogey, haunting spirit, or frightening supernatural being; here it is the presence at Höhstegen that whistles and whoops and later manifests through a crushing goat, so the story does not resolve whether it is a ghost, demon, or more general bogey.

66b689b24c34f2acae8632e27769ba660ddbcee5.summary: The Biffigwald behind the village of St. Niklaus is also said to be very uncanny.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais regional name for a frightening supernatural presence or bogey; here it is not given one fixed body but manifests through malformed or misplaced animals, uncanny cries, and a wind confined to the forest.

593e0f5741df3364c420cee556db095ab0836ba9.summary: Once the Güggel said to his Hüendli, “Come quickly up into the sitting room and peck together the bread crumbs on the table; our mistress has gone out to pay a visit.” Then the Hüendli said, “No, no, we are not coming.

notes.label: Güggel
notes.text: Swiss German for a rooster or cock; here the dialect name helps carry the fable’s imitated bird cries, though spellings vary by region.

notes.label: Hüendli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive plural for little hens or chickens; here it names the cautious birds whose repeated cry is represented as speech, and the form can refer affectionately to chickens rather than a precise age.

9d64e5c1a8a0e0c745814fd927a7fd2fb7e7caed.summary: Once a man who wished to fell wood in the Steigwald found a young, beautiful fox tied to a beech with a rope.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

185624fd20d806e51638c275593b63964f4f1b73.summary: The marshy woodland called Breitsee was once a lake. Today the forest preserves of two Fricktal municipalities, Wallbach and Möhlin, meet at their boundary there.

notes.label: Schinnhut
notes.text: a regional historical hat worn in the Fricktal; the account identifies it as locally customary but gives too little detail to determine its exact material, shape, or a reliable English garment equivalent.

notes.label: Breitseemaidli
notes.text: an Aargau dialect name meaning ‘little maiden of the Breitsee,’ used for the silent local apparition who befriends herdboys; ‘maidli’ is an affectionate diminutive, and the figure’s identity remains uncertain.

4a2edc45951eb29286c58ef8c39a3abf38014b7c.summary: The ghostly brickmaker dwells in the great Grindel oak forest. His home is said to have been a brickworks at the end of the forest, where the road through the Suren valley crosses the Lucerne border.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Sprossen
notes.text: literally ‘rungs,’ ‘shoots,’ or projecting crosspieces; the poem applies the word unusually to the marble-like rock, so its exact local or poetic sense—possibly ribs, ledges, or projections—remains uncertain and is not silently replaced by a conjecture.

notes.label: Stürvis
notes.text: the name of the high mountain village in the poem; the source's spelling is retained rather than replaced by a conjectural modern form.

5080bbf54c875baac79795df7651b0c462b792b4.summary: A young man sat in a skiff upon a broad, rushing river and rowed toward the opposite bank, for there his bride stood waiting for him.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a Klafter is a historical fathom-like measure based on outstretched arms, used here for the apparition’s short distance from the boat; its exact regional length in this telling is uncertain.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

f2af86ae46c278809f45a1560225baf529227579.summary: An old folk legend in Ursern teaches that whoever ‘frevelte’ in the Briggwald—that is, felled wood there—had his right hand cut off.

notes.label: frevelte
notes.text: committed a forbidden or sacrilegious forest offense; the collector glosses it specifically as felling wood in the protected Briggwald, punished in legend by loss of the right hand.

7c307ae2e6fb55deffc82d72dfdef0f901b7e220.summary: A Senn once spent the summer on the Ammertenberg with his two boys. They led a merry life, reveled in abundance, whooped often, and ate and drank to their hearts' content; but they worked little.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a high pasture; the father's misuse of dairy food and tools is central to the tale's moral setting.

notes.label: Milchmelchterlein
notes.text: a diminutive regional word for a small milk pail or milking vessel; the family first profanes it by bathing their feet in it and later fatally forgets it during the descent.

notes.label: Britschen-Kübel
notes.text: the tub or vat holding the Britsche dairy mass; turning it over releases the material from which the little man is molded.

notes.label: Britsche
notes.text: the white dairy mass from which a small cheese could have been made; the source makes its cheesemaking use clear but does not securely identify its exact modern product or stage of curdling.

notes.label: Britsche-Manndli
notes.text: Bernese Alpine dialect for the ‘little Britsche man,’ a grotesque figure molded from a white dairy mass that comes alive; the precise dairy meaning of Britsche is uncertain, though the tale says it could have been made into cheese.

notes.label: Toggel
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a crude doll, goblin, or bogey-like figure; here it describes the silent dairy-mass effigy before it begins to move.

notes.label: Nydle
notes.text: Swiss German for cream; smearing it on the creature's nose is one of the herders' mocking acts of dairy-food waste.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Alpabfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal descent of people and livestock from the high Alp to the valley; the Capuchin's warning makes complete packing during this ritual move the condition for escape.

notes.label: Leilach
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a linen sheet or cloth used here to bundle the herders' equipment for the Alpabfahrt.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Leitkuh
notes.text: the lead cow of the descending herd, often an especially trusted or decorated animal; her call back toward the father marks his separation from the procession.

notes.label: Feuerplatte
notes.text: the hearth slab or stone by the fire; the boys find their father struggling there with the creature.

notes.label: Achar
notes.text: a regional word for a crowd, band, or troop; here it is the armed party that goes back up to the hut, while the exact size is unspecified.

notes.label: töpperlen
notes.text: a dialect verb for tapping or pattering repeatedly; it describes the creature's uncanny knocking on the windowpanes.

e0ebf81853c00fde9f6a8af676b6ff1b96002f3b.summary: In ancient times, a Küher lived at Stalden, a height in Bern's Saanenland. Nothing was right, good, or sacred to him or his friends, and they thought they had to mock everything.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or cattle herdsman, especially one working with dairy cattle on an Alpine pasture; here he creates the cheese figure with his mocking companions.

notes.label: Käsmilch
notes.text: literally ‘cheese milk,’ meaning the hot whey or liquid left from cheesemaking; here it is poured into the hollow cheese figure to warm it, though the source does not describe the precise stage of production.

notes.label: Britschenmännchen
notes.text: a standard-German diminutive variant of Britschen-Mandli, literally a ‘little Britschen man’; here it names the cheese creature after it becomes a nightly tormentor.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its buildings, not simply any mountain; here Stalden is abandoned as an Alp until the monster is defeated.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here they have been driven away from Stalden and are told how to raise the monster's opponent.

notes.label: Unterstafel
notes.text: the lower seasonal station or pasture tier of an Alp; here it is the farthest point to which the doctor says the men may accompany the bull.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the singular of Sennen, an Alpine dairy herdsman; here he obeys the doctor's instructions and watches the bull from a distance.

notes.label: Vorstafel
notes.text: a fore-station or early-season station within an Alp's sequence of pasture levels; here the narrator uses it for the place where the Senn releases the bull, apparently corresponding to or near the previously named Unterstafel.

notes.label: Britschen-Mandli
notes.text: the Saanenland name of the little figure made from leftover soft cheese that becomes a monster; Mandli means ‘little man,’ while the exact dialect derivation of Britschen is uncertain but is contextually associated with the cheese mass.

c37e6a3bd6b3a55fd063436004ba45b3dd466443.summary: 1. One evening two young men from Bürglen intended to go z'Stubäda gah—to pay an evening courting visit—together.

notes.label: z'Stubäda gah
notes.text: Uri dialect for going on an evening social or courting visit to a young woman's parlor; the two unmarried men are setting out together on such a visit, not merely entering an ordinary room.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge common in the Swiss Alpine landscape; here it is dangerous ground into which the men are supernaturally misled.

notes.label: G'hirmi
notes.text: an exact local place-word for the feature on the Höchi where the dog waits and rages; it may denote an enclosure, gate, or fenced passage, but the source does not define it closely enough to be certain.

notes.label: Tryni
notes.text: an affectionate Uri form of the woman's name, probably Katharina; it functions as her personal name in the story, and the source does not give a fuller form.

notes.label: g'mäntelet
notes.text: Uri dialect glossed by the source as niedergeschlagen, meaning downcast, dispirited, or weighed down; both newlyweds already appear conscious of the vow's consequences.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ a folk-Catholic expression for a dead soul awaiting release from purgatorial suffering; the alternate version says the men's vow was made to obtain such a soul's redemption.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

984299e97068c71a2ca50898f13a2fd125781073.summary: In the depths of the Tobel, not far from the bridge leading to the village of Jenisberg, an old castle or castle-like building is said once to have stood, and legend reports, from father to son, an immense treasure said to lie buried there.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully, often cut by a torrent.

notes.label: Brombrenzer
notes.text: the name given to the wealthy mine owner after Brombreis or Brombrenz; whether it began as a personal byname or simply meant the man of that place is not resolved by the story.

notes.label: Knappen
notes.text: miners or mine workers, historically also trained journeymen within a mining operation.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a “wandering scholar,” a folklore figure credited with learned or magical arts, here the ability to seek and conjure a buried treasure.

notes.label: Schüler
notes.text: literally “scholar” or “student”; in this paragraph it refers back to the magically knowledgeable fahrender Schüler, not an ordinary schoolchild.

notes.label: Geissbock
notes.text: Swiss German for a male goat or billy goat; the enormous black animal guards the chest.

95374b52b5dcf696f574e420aba13d1e30880663.summary: The brooks must not be polluted because in many places the inhabitants of entire sections of a village draw the water they need from such streams, known as Brunnenbäche.

notes.label: Brunnenbäche
notes.text: literally ‘fountain/spring brooks,’ small streams used as communal water supplies for parts of a village rather than merely ornamental watercourses.

notes.label: Unservater
notes.text: the regional plural of Unser Vater, or the Lord's Prayer; requiring three of them is a communal religious penalty for fouling the shared water.

8661e61bdd3dcd29fe4f1fd479df5d0f8df29a90.summary: The old fisherman who still lives near Klingnau related what once happened to him with a Brünnlig.

notes.label: Brünnlig
notes.text: an Aargau name for a wandering fiery apparition or burning man; prayer drives it from the riverbank in the first account.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a narrow, shallow riverboat traditionally used on Swiss rivers; here the fishermen turn it into the Aare's current to escape.

notes.label: Girizmoos
notes.text: the locally named marsh or moor toward which the fiery being travels; its precise modern location is not established by the source.

notes.label: Brünnling
notes.text: a variant name for the same fiery apparition called Brünnlig in the first account; in this version, a curse rather than prayer dispels it.

notes.label: Brünnigs Mannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little burning man,’ another regional form for the fiery being, emphasizing its small humanlike shape.

notes.label: Was Tüfels hesch du dô?
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘What the devil have you got there?’; accidentally naming the Devil breaks the apparition's hold.

35e6855898fba40db00b03ab7fff3e8a0d20574f.summary: A carter from Wohlen in the Freiamt, who traveled to Alsace every autumn to fetch wine, encountered a will-o’-the-wisp in the meadows outside his village and called to it: ‘Come here and light my way!’ The Brünnlige did so in return for the promise that a Mass would be read for it.

notes.label: Brünnlige
notes.text: an Aargau regional name, also appearing in the source as Brünnling, for the fiery will-o’-the-wisp that guides the carter; the name’s closest literal sense may suggest a small burning or glowing being, but its precise derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

1cabe55334f046f34c467a159fbd9bf71d25d7e1.summary: There once was a Zimbelma, a man who worked in the forest. His wife meant to bring him his midday meal there, but robbers seized the woman, dragged her into a cave, and forced her to cook and wash for them.

notes.label: Zimbelma
notes.text: the Aargau-dialect designation for the man whose work takes him into the forest; the immediate context suggests a timber or forest worker, but the source does not establish his exact trade, so the original term is retained.

notes.label: Bueb
notes.text: Alemannic Swiss German for a boy or young fellow; here it remains the hero’s tale-name from childhood through his accession as king.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight measure whose exact mass varied by jurisdiction and period; the impossible walking stick weighs ten of them, so no modern kilogram equivalent is imposed.

notes.label: Steihauer
notes.text: Aargau dialect for a stonecutter or stonemason; the name functions as the strong companion’s descriptive tale-name.

notes.label: Eichedräjer
notes.text: Aargau dialect for an ‘oak-twister,’ the companion introduced while twisting an oak to the ground by its branch; the source also gives the variant form Eichebrüjer once.

notes.label: Biswind
notes.text: the cold, often forceful Bise wind familiar on the Swiss Plateau; the source uses it here as a simile for the uncanny little man’s speed.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large kettle or cauldron in Swiss German, commonly associated with Alpine dairy work; here it serves as the vessel in which the Bueb and later the princesses are raised and lowered through the shaft.

notes.label: Butelli
notes.text: an Alemannic form derived from French bouteille, meaning bottles; the three groups of strengthening bottles stand before the successive dragon chambers.

notes.label: Pfifli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little whistle or pipe; blowing it summons the old little man whose help repays the Bueb’s mercy.

803583f27095ee8999d45855cb71ee9241a6b87c.summary: If one goes from Grandson toward the village of Montagny, on that broad plain one notices a not particularly high hill lying among the fields several hundred paces off the main road.

notes.label: Waatländer
notes.text: the source's historical German word for a person from Vaud, now more commonly Waadtländer; the farmer provides the legend's claimed local oral authority.

notes.label: Tuilerien
notes.text: the local French-derived name meaning ‘tileworks’; the collector identifies it with the site of a Roman amphitheater belonging to Aventicum.

notes.label: Wehrgehänge
notes.text: the sword belt, baldric, or harness carrying a warrior's weapon; unbuckling Charles's old equipment in silence is the central act of release.

notes.label: Tophet
notes.text: the local name of the rock on Lake Neuchâtel from which Johannes must throw the monstrous cat; the source associates it with a submerged ancient approach and pagan sacrifice.

notes.label: Heidenweg
notes.text: literally ‘heathen road,’ the alleged ancient pebble road by which pagan priests processed toward a lake-god temple; the label reflects the Christian antiquarian interpretation in the source.

notes.label: Bonnerre äe eünt!
notes.text: the source's dialectal or garbled French-like oath that pain almost makes Johannes utter; its exact original wording is uncertain, and speaking it would break the required silence.

notes.label: Ladre du eiel...
notes.text: another incomplete, garbled French-like curse that Johannes suppresses after the sword wounds him; the uncertain source spelling is retained because the self-restraint, not a precise translation, matters to the ordeal.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: large historical silver coins; Johannes fills only his handkerchief with golden Taler, showing restraint despite the open treasure.

14d0b88b624af529a2bf81df7e8d3629e17b3ce0.summary: The height on which Moosleerau lies is called the Stierengarten, or Bull Garden.

notes.label: d'Hell
notes.text: the dialectal local name of the fertile plot where the victims were buried; d' is the article ‘the,’ while the source does not clarify whether Hell has its ordinary sense or an older place-name sense.

notes.label: Hellrüter
notes.text: the local name for the last tyrant lord’s apparition associated with d'Hell; the second element is approximately ‘rider,’ but the spelling and nuance are dialectal.

notes.label: Sech
notes.text: a historical regional word for the plow’s coulter, the cutting blade that the farmer tears free and uses against the tyrant.

notes.label: Kornhübeli
notes.text: literally approximately ‘little grain hill’; the former name of the hill where the first crop in the pasture country was said to have been harvested.

notes.label: Chnübeli
notes.text: the locally shortened dialect name derived in the story from Kornhübeli; it is the hill’s later name.

5ce7c3b04829cc87ab91cadb80f5617821ac9cb1.summary: In the middle of the village rises a cone-shaped hill bearing traces of old masonry, with a deep ditch running halfway around it.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Burgmutter
notes.text: literally “castle mother,” the affectionate local name given to the bailiff’s worthy wife; the tale does not explain whether Mutter marks age, social protection, or later communal memory.

notes.label: Burgfrau
notes.text: literally “castle woman” or “lady of the castle,” the title’s local designation for the bailiff’s wife at Merenschwand; it names her through the Burg rather than giving a personal name.

notes.label: Burghündlein
notes.text: literally ‘little castle hounds,’ the local affectionate-sounding name for the spectral hunting dogs heard at Bischofsstein; despite the diminutive, they are frightening agents of the condemned castle lords’ endless Sunday hunt.

d0b7a6eb6e95ddc652f50a1c6d1f5821b44443f1.summary: When a change in the weather is due, and especially when the holy season approaches, people at the foot of Brunnegg hear a sustained din above at the castle.

notes.label: Burgvogt
notes.text: the bailiff, castellan, or administrative governor of a castle and its domain; this cruel official becomes the returning supernatural hunter.

notes.label: Choli
notes.text: a dialect name for a coal-black horse, glossed in the source as a Rappe or black horse; it is the Burgvogt's hunting mount.

notes.label: Hop-Hop!
notes.text: a traditional huntsman's urging or rallying call; its sudden silence marks the place where the murdered woodcutter died.

5f94615f302f1b8aaacce1e98b5e9ed4cd86a365.summary: The Hasli Valley is exposed to frequent destruction. In 1797, a mudflow of dissolved shale destroyed many houses and meadows at Schwanden.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

94d33ed72e75b52a26fc17d7a355c0c3d7f57e9e.summary: In the previous century, a Junker lived in the old mill at Seon. He made himself greatly hated by the people of the surrounding area because he forced them to have all their grain ground at his mill.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical German title for a young nobleman or member of the lesser landed nobility; here it marks the mill owner’s social rank, not simply a personal name.

dac9d89f6c3c88daf47a96c3922716d00b97b79a.summary: A devastating livestock epidemic twice prevailed on the Ällgäu mountain above Habkern in the district of Interlaken.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Sankt Johannisnacht
notes.text: Saint John's Night, the eve associated with the Nativity of John the Baptist; here the old-calendar observance is shifted to early July.

notes.label: Alps
notes.text: in Swiss pastoral usage, the high seasonal pasture holdings of Bohl and Ällgäu, including their herds and dairying operations, not the mountain range in general.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a whey cheese traditional in Switzerland; it is distributed with unsalted cheese as a ritual gift to the poor.

notes.label: Twirrispeicher
notes.text: the named storehouse or granary where the dairy alms are carried and distributed; the exact derivation of Twirri is uncertain.

notes.label: St. Johannsen
notes.text: the local name for the annual charitable dairy distribution performed on old-style St. John's Day.

notes.label: Brühlfritzli
notes.text: a diminutive byname meaning approximately ‘little Fritz of Brühl,’ the Oberland wonder-doctor credited in the alternate account with binding the plague into a tree.

52f7b580759514e1e241a95547e87f14422c147c.summary: A “Venediger” once came to the poor man Christen Casolf in Conters in the Prätigau and told him to come into the mountains with him.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine mining legends, a supposedly Venetian or foreign ore-seeker credited with secret knowledge of mineral deposits; he reveals the silver vein and protects the excavation with a circle.

notes.label: Casana-Alpe
notes.text: the Casana Alpine pasture where the hidden silver deposit is found; Alpe denotes the high seasonal grazing area.

notes.label: Silberkies
notes.text: literally “silver pyrites,” a historical mining term for silver-bearing or silver-colored ore; the exact mineral meant in this tale is uncertain, so the German term is retained.

4a170a6cc750116850af8a753cbc8bf76db60a10.summary: For many years on Alplen, Brunneler-Franzsepp of Unterschächen held the responsible office of herdsman.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gelti
notes.text: an Uri regional name for the goat disease described here as stopping milk production, causing blindness and wasting, and sometimes killing the animal; the historical account does not establish a modern veterinary diagnosis.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Gabälä
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for a load-carrying frame worn on the back, apparently used here to carry the bundle of firewood; its precise construction is not described and the closest literal association is with something forked.

notes.label: Volla
notes.text: a wooden milk funnel used in Alpine dairying; Franzsepp appears to use it here like a speaking trumpet while proclaiming the Gospel toward the four directions, although the source does not explicitly describe that acoustic function.

notes.label: Schinhuet
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for the large, broad hat worn by the unknown old woman suspected of witchcraft; the passage makes its conspicuous size clear but does not identify its exact historical type, material, or construction.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

475c6d8e36442205c3df8418a4d084bd58eee02f.summary: Near Zofingen, the meadows called the Brühlmatten are a haunted place for burning men.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Aufhock
notes.text: a regional name for a supernatural burden or spirit that jumps onto a traveler’s back and grows crushingly heavy; ‘back-rider’ or ‘pressing spirit’ is close, but the being’s form and the term’s exact local range are uncertain.

d4940a5aff0ae82f12586e38efcdd5aaf8c54f87.summary: A girl was returning home from the annual fair and expected her bridegroom to catch up with her on the way.

notes.label: Rüti
notes.text: a cleared or grubbed parcel of land, common in Swiss field- and place-names; the bridegroom secretly enlarged his plot at his neighbor's expense.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the warm bench built beside or around a masonry stove, a customary resting place in a traditional house.

notes.label: Marchsteine
notes.text: boundary stones marking neighboring parcels; moving them is both theft and a classic folkloric cause of posthumous punishment.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: boundary markers or boundary lines; the bridegroom confesses shifting them to take half his neighbor's clearing.

notes.label: Lebkuchen
notes.text: spiced honey cakes or gingerbread-like cakes, carried from house to house for sale by the woman who transmits the account.

0cb67657ef7e9c49f08e744a3fca70a41b458d98.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, the richest farmer by far in the land of Entlebuch was the lord and master of Kreienmoos near Escholzmatt.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

34e51ad57b02131289e27537e92365513becc88e.summary: a) When Rudolf of Habsburg purchased the city of Lucerne from the Abbot of Murbach in 1291, he placed Baron von Grünenberg over the people of Lucerne.

notes.label: About this telling

b447f3c0329057862c4ed547e2c70991f3b5332e.summary: Our grandparents relate that people formerly did not know today's Carnival masquerade, but that every village had a ‘Butzi’ who wore reddish-yellow men's clothing and a large painted wooden mask.

notes.label: Butzi
notes.text: a masked Carnival figure who disciplines, mocks, brushes, and gives bread to villagers; the name can denote various frightening or costumed beings regionally, but this story defines the specific local office and costume.

notes.label: Beniner
notes.text: people of the local Benken area, whose haunting traditions the collector connects with the Butzi; the exact dialect formation is retained because the passage does not explain it.

notes.label: Fastnacht
notes.text: the pre-Lenten Carnival season, when the masked Butzi publicly exposes wrongdoing; it carries communal ritual and disciplinary functions beyond a simple costume party.

notes.label: Schnitz
notes.text: dried slices or pieces of fruit, commonly apples or pears, stored as provisions; the source does not identify which fruit filled the miser's bins.

notes.label: Kreuztaler
notes.text: a historical thaler bearing a cross or known by that regional coin-name; the exact issuing authority and value are not specified.

notes.label: Fronfastentage
notes.text: the Ember Days, quarterly Catholic fast and ordination periods traditionally associated in folklore with heightened supernatural activity; the spirit rages chiefly during these days.

notes.label: Chriesikratten
notes.text: literally a ‘cherry basket,’ a carrying basket or pannier associated with harvesting cherries; Hieronymus uses this ordinary regional implement to capture the spirit.

notes.label: Gemeindsbutzi
notes.text: literally the ‘community Butzi,’ the officially recognized or customary village performer; his line's extinction is linked to the disappearance of the associated hauntings.

notes.label: Grubmannli
notes.text: literally ‘little man of the Grub,’ the haunting transferred with the rebuilt stable; the narrator also calls it a servitude, treating the spirit as a burden attached to the property.

notes.label: Tschuppismannli
notes.text: literally ‘little man of Tschuppis,’ the dead farmer's local apparition riding a dragon-like stallion whenever a happy couple arrives.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a hidden golden skittles or ninepins treasure; Ries may refer to the set or playing arrangement, but the precise regional object intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Glarnerklafter
notes.text: an old Glarus fathom, a regional length measure whose exact historical value could vary; the treasure is said to lie ten such units from the burial place.

53a73c93145e2498090406c53d34066736018b39.summary: It is said that a man, small in intellect but large and strong in body, once went to a high mountain pasture to feed his overwintering sheep.

notes.label: Bärenfaller
notes.text: literally ‘bear-feller’ or ‘one who causes a bear to fall’; it becomes the Valais family byname after the ancestor wrestles a bear downhill into an abyss, though ‘faller’ preserves a deliberate play on the fall.

73a2b08e30a0e03ad1f35dbcc5a8359294ff9322.summary: At the time of the Old Zürich War, which the enterprising people of Zürich waged against the people of Schwyz and their Eidgenossen over the inheritance of the Count of Toggenburg, a company also formed in the sorely pressed city that was a good defense and honor to it and a great vexation to the enemy.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades,’ the historical term for members of the Swiss Confederacy; here it refers especially to Zürich's confederate opponents from the mountain cantons during and after the Old Zürich War.

notes.label: Schildnern zum Schneggen
notes.text: the source's name for the Zürich association from which the Böcke formed, approximately the ‘shield companions at the Schneggen’; its precise institutional status is not explained in the tale, so the historical name is retained.

notes.label: Böcke
notes.text: literally ‘billy goats’ or ‘bucks,’ the defiant nickname of the young Zürich company; the account uses it as their collective proper name and repeatedly plays on their bold, vigorous character.

notes.label: Verkommnis
notes.text: an older word for a negotiated agreement or settlement; here it is the final peace accord from which the hostile confederates insist the Böcke be excluded.

notes.label: Becherlupf
notes.text: literally a ‘lifting of the cup,’ a convivial drinking bout or drinking contest; it is one of the pleasures that can no longer relieve the exiles' homesickness.

notes.label: Waldstätte
notes.text: literally ‘forest states,’ the traditional collective name for the central Swiss lake cantons around Lake Lucerne; the story uses it both in the lake's old name and for the mountain territories responding to Fries's capture.

notes.label: Nauen
notes.text: a large, heavy traditional transport boat used on Swiss lakes; it carries the Böcke from Brunnen to Flüelen across the Lake of the Four Waldstätte.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional title of the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity; Fries of Uri combines political authority, military experience, and the role of honored hostage in the story.

notes.label: Weidlinge
notes.text: plural of Weidling, a long, narrow, shallow-draft boat used on Swiss rivers and lakes; the armed Böcke use two fast Weidlinge to intercept the slower market boat.

a18a140810caac6de706169e267825c582b18ab5.summary: A separate part of the village of Wölfliswil in the Fricktal is called the Bödemli because of its level position.

notes.label: Bödemli
notes.text: the local diminutive name for the level part of Wölfliswil, related to Boden, ground or flat land.

notes.label: Bödelmergeist
notes.text: the prophetic ‘spirit of the Bödemli,’ appearing as a red fox to warn of destructive weather; the spelling shifts slightly from the place-name in the source.

c3f8da6d82c4a935e9c730e12279b1b4a8e4da53.summary: When bad weather is approaching, once the wind is already whistling over the ridges, catching in fissures and rocky clefts, and producing strange tones, the resting herders hear the ‘Faser’ (herder, cowherd) at night.

notes.label: Faser
notes.text: a herder or cowherd defined by the act of fasen, calling livestock together with prolonged cries; here the supernatural Faser is often the living herder's audible double.

notes.label: fasen
notes.text: to call, lure, and gather a herd over a broad high pasture with powerful extended sounds; here a herder hears his own double performing the call before snowfall.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here it is the open range across which the warning calls carry and which is snow-covered by morning.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Chüa, fé, fé! Hoi, joh! Büüsch, Büüsch!
notes.text: the source's exact sequence of regional livestock-gathering cries, beginning with Chüa, ‘cows’; their practical force and sound matter more than a literal word-for-word English rendering.
notes.anchor: Chüa, fé, fé! Hoi, joh! Büüsch, Büüsch!

notes.label: Büscheler
notes.text: a regional name for the calf herder, associated with the gathering call Büüsch; here his nighttime voice can be an uncanny warning that the herd must be collected before snow.

notes.label: Alpler
notes.text: a regional spelling for a person working or residing seasonally on an Alp; here the pasture workers ritually invoke protection against the ominous Wetterfasen.

notes.label: Wetterfasen
notes.text: literally ‘weather fasen,’ the uncanny pre-storm sounding of herd calls; here Alpine workers treat it as a warning or apparition and invoke protection against it.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: a local name for the herders' sleeping platform or resting place at Fursch; here the two men lie on it when they hear the supernatural call, while the exact construction is unspecified.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheese-making on a high pasture; here the experienced older Senn identifies the mysterious voice as the cowherd's own double.

954eb02d0c67485181a3e9895ff17fc4a40d89ca.summary: In the year 1564, a very severe plague raged along the Rhine and especially in the region of Basel.

notes.label: About this telling
