4b90148698e5fb338e0fab0e5d2bf33cfdea929e.summary: There was also a thoroughly capricious fellow of a Butz in the Ober-Säss at Schlapin.

notes.label: Butz
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German dialect word for a bogey, uncanny spirit, or masked fright-figure; this Alpbutz inhabits the high pasture and rewards generosity but punishes greed.

notes.label: Ober-Säss
notes.text: the upper Säss, or seasonal station of an Alpine pasture, at Schlapin; a Säss includes the huts and working area used while livestock graze at that level.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal movement of livestock and herders between the valley and the Alp; because this occurs in autumn, the passage refers to the descent or departure from the high pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Grosshirt
notes.text: literally “chief herdsman,” the senior man directing the pasture crew; Jecklin contrasts him with the subordinate Kleinhirt.

notes.label: Kleinhirt
notes.text: literally “little” or junior herdsman; here he is the young subordinate whom the Grosshirt sends back alone.

notes.label: Dajagmach
notes.text: Jecklin’s quoted local name for the Butz’s dwelling or haunt on the Nonnenalp; the precise dialect construction and referent are uncertain, so the form is preserved.

notes.label: Alpbutz
notes.text: literally an Alp Butz, a supernatural bogey or spirit attached to a high Alpine pasture; here it rewards the junior herdsman’s generosity and destroys the greedy chief herdsman.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: an Alpine-pasture station or its immediate hut-and-pen area; the animal and the resting herdsman are both within this working place.

notes.label: Marende
notes.text: a regional Alpine word for a snack or light meal carried for work or travel; sharing it wins the Kleinhirt the spirit’s favor.

notes.label: Schelmapfifli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for the little pipe or whistle given by the Butz; the source also shortens it to Pfifli, and its exact name carries a playful or roguish nuance.

notes.label: Pfifli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Pfeife, meaning a little pipe or whistle; it is the shorter form used for the Alpbutz’s musical gift.

dc5455741332c68d3610601998de889fba10b69a.summary: A man in Parpan caught a Fänggenmannli with the loop of a hay rope. It made the most comical leaps and desperate attempts to escape, but nothing helped; it could not free itself.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a male member of the wild mountain beings called Fänggen; human bloodletting is said to have enabled or prevented its capture.

notes.label: Hättest du schröpfen und z’Ader glan,
notes.text: the opening of a dialect verse meaning ‘Had you been cupped and bled like another man, you would not have caught me’; whether Tamerlan's unusual bodily condition gives him power or the creature identifies a missed protective custom remains ambiguous.
notes.anchor: Hättest du schröpfen und z’Ader glan,

ca4f1ea5e203eea49d18ffddc722a325650fed63.summary: During the plague years two brothers lived in Fanas. They bored a hole into a Tramen in their parlor and shut their share of the plague inside it, then drove a wooden peg into the hole and went abroad until the plague had passed and everything was peaceful again.

notes.label: Tramen
notes.text: a substantial timber or beam in the room's structure; the brothers bore into it to imprison their allotted portion of the personified plague.

a19d6eaf83f04bf20aa5897040ae21692b25b490.summary: A farmer had fed the livestock at the Maiensäss and then lay down upon the ‘Tril’ to sleep.

notes.label: Maiensäss
notes.text: a mid-altitude seasonal farm or pasture used between the valley holding and the high Alp, especially in spring and autumn.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: the source's quoted local word for the farmer's sleeping surface at the Maiensäss; its exact construction is not explained.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a Swiss German night spirit or oppressive goblin, related to the Schrat or nightmare being; here it enters in the shape of a black cat and can speak.

3f1780e16dafcd4e3416b0bf91c5ce426c9db4bc.summary: At Conters, a wild little man herded the goats. He never entered the village, but came only as far as a stable above it, to which the goats were driven for him.

notes.label: Röthi Nöthi
notes.text: this rhyming dialect address means approximately ‘red Nöthi’ and personifies the red wine the wild man distrusts; the name Nöthi and the phrase’s exact wordplay are uncertain.

notes.label: Tschöpen
notes.text: this Graubünden dialect plural denotes jackets or outer garments in the wild man’s weather advice; the exact garment style and the deliberately paradoxical advice are uncertain.

57f72a2085daedd355028325915d131a778077fa.summary: Although the wildes Männlein sometimes spent long periods in contact with other people, they nevertheless always kept some distance from them and made sure that the way behind them remained clear so that they could flee if necessary.

notes.label: wildes Männlein
notes.text: literally a ‘wild little man,’ a small, swift, unusually strong Alpine folklore being rather than an ordinary feral human; keeping an escape route behind itself is one of the tale's defining traits.

notes.label: Heuseil
notes.text: a heavy hay rope used to bind or move loads of hay; its agricultural strength explains how the captor can tether the otherwise powerful being.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

285e41945c4952f9b987946b62dd10976938e86f.summary: Their thirst for gold often led Venediger into the land of Unterwalden, especially to the Arniloch near Engelberg.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians’; in Alpine mining lore, mysterious foreign prospectors believed able to locate and remove mineral wealth hidden from local people.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirrors’; legendary prospecting instruments said to reveal the hidden interiors of mountains and rock masses.

29e1f4af67cfa8ff6030e7178dda0616e7afd9ec.summary: The following sad legend tells what a mother can dare and often generously risk for her child.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e3313746f91aba390dfa1466e739c2f06e8b8f35.summary: At Brigerberg above the Bleikinu, where the old road went over the Simplon mountain, a great treasure is also said to have existed in ancient times.

notes.label: Fräuli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a young lady or little woman, here the noble female spirit guarding the treasure; her human origin is not explained.

notes.label: ner Temperwuchu
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘an Ember Week,’ one of the traditional quarterly periods of fasting and observance in the Christian calendar; why birth during that week qualifies the rescuer is unstated.

notes.label: bis zum nintu Grad
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘to the ninth degree,’ used as a span of family fortune or misfortune and apparently meaning through nine degrees or generations of kinship; the exact genealogy is not defined.

notes.label: Geisterbrut
notes.text: the source’s dialectal or textual form for the spirit woman being carried, probably ‘spirit bride’ rather than literally ‘spirit brood’; the wording is uncertain, so it is preserved.

notes.label: schneewissi Tuba
notes.text: Valais dialect for a snow-white dove; the redeemed maiden assumes or resembles this form as she ascends to heaven.

64f4a143aa09dfca40a8f58db03a7ceaf45faba6.summary: For a time, unknown Italians in beggars’ clothing were seen roaming the Casanna-Alpe every year.

notes.label: Casanna-Alpe
notes.text: the Casanna Alpine pasture where the disguised Italian prospectors search among the grazing grounds; Alpe denotes the managed high pasture rather than only a peak.

notes.label: Venezianische
notes.text: literally “the Venetian [territory],” an older regional way of referring to the lands associated with Venice into which the herdsman drives cattle for market.

notes.label: gewixt
notes.text: Jecklin’s quoted colloquial verb, glossed in the source as geschlagen, meaning that the herdsman struck or beat the supposed beggar; its modern associations should not obscure that explicit historical gloss.

notes.label: vertattert
notes.text: a regional word for being thoroughly startled, frightened, or flustered; the source explicitly glosses it as erschrocken and ängstlich.

e1e1e2374607d34b7ee31503528812fb9594b12f.summary: The Hasliacker, also called Maienacher, now lies within the village jurisdiction of Schinznach.

notes.label: Castelerreiter
notes.text: literally ‘Castelen rider,’ the local apparition who rides from Castelen Castle to the cursed wet place at Hasliacker; the compound identifies him by his route, while the tale gives no personal name or history.

1de36e499bad6d5a0770b9f2f57256b99c77b0b0.summary: A maid who served at Gräplang Castle often heard violent sneezing near the castle but never saw a person.

notes.label: Helf dr Gott
notes.text: a dialect blessing after a sneeze, literally ‘may God help you’ and functionally close to ‘God bless you’; in this St. Gallen legend the spoken formula releases an unseen wandering spirit, giving the everyday courtesy explicit salvific power.

65d450ccde653bf43ca65b6a466f7bc0993aaffb.summary: When the young women of the Fricktal cross into neighboring Basel-Landschaft at harvest time to work as reapers, the young men who remain at home sometimes visit them there by night.

notes.label: Lebhag
notes.text: a living hedge made of planted, intertwined growth rather than a dead fence; its impossible overnight appearance and extension through the air help mark the procession’s road as supernatural.

94e3fdf7eccb81364a173dc69c96dfa4ce4fa358.summary: At night, at twelve o'clock, as the anniversary of the Battle of Sempach began, a weeping voice is formerly said to have been heard here at the castle ruins: “Konrad, Konrad,” whereupon the bright-toned answer came, “Hier Österreich!” (“Austria here!”) And behold: a black knightly figure with a…

notes.label: Hier Österreich!
notes.text: literally ‘Austria here!’ or ‘Here, Austria!’; the spectral response identifies the wounded knight with the Austrian side in the conflict around the Battle of Sempach.

92ca13413a0dfcf6d8c0ac7141f2e2e6705c64e6.summary: There are different accounts of how the defiant Wildenburg, enthroned in wild beauty upon a Bühl in the Tobel between the Lorze and the Schwarzenbach near Allenwinden in the canton of Zug, fell.

notes.label: Bühl
notes.text: a hill or rounded rise, here the elevated site upon which Wildenburg stands above the ravine.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, often wooded ravine or mountain gully, common in Swiss and southern German place vocabulary.

notes.label: Wildenburger
notes.text: the last lord or member of Wildenburg, used as a territorial designation for Werner Rycha.

notes.label: verbutzt
notes.text: disguised, masked, or bundled up so as to conceal identity; the exact historical form is uncommon, but the context makes the father's impersonation clear.

notes.label: Helparte
notes.text: a historical spelling of Hellebarde, a halberd or long-shafted polearm; Elsener displays the severed thigh upon it while rallying the citizens.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a local chief magistrate or administrative official who acts together with the council.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally ‘rider on a Schimmel,’ a mounted apparition upon a gray or white horse.

1b56545596e459efeaee0131af0e1d290137f7c6.summary: Even at the beginning of this century, the farming family that had occupied the rooms of the knightly residence was not their undisputed owner.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

17865ccd8cff4e516e1f6f90d4a43de0dd900ed1.summary: Great treasures lie hidden in the ruins of the two Mannenberg castles, which were burned down along with Laubegg in 1350 by forces from Bern, Thun, and Frutigen during their raid into the upper Simmental.

b023f7f139d0f553d7e9417f4adee52bfa4a701c.summary: a) We have already encountered the cat as a form assumed by witches.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, the skilled Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle, milk, and cheesemaking during the summer pasture season; English has no single equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its seasonal farm operation, not simply a mountain peak; livestock and dairy workers occupy it during the grazing season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

ccf9df5f1fd19e84a817188d5e30378249af6474.summary: Butzä-Fränzi, who tended his cattle in the Ochsengaden in the ‘Gründen’ at Silenen, would now and then observe a cat rolling back and forth in the grass near the stable (it ‘wallowed’ there); each time, one of his animals would soon perish.

notes.label: Dörfli
notes.text: literally ‘little village,’ the local name for the small settlement or quarter containing the chapel of the Fourteen Holy Helpers; it functions as a locality rather than merely expressing smallness.

notes.label: Gläck
notes.text: a regional livestock lick or feed mixture, often containing salt or flour; here it carries metal filings from a chapel bell, but the source does not specify the ordinary recipe.

notes.label: Geissgelti
notes.text: an Uri regional name for a disease of goats or livestock, elsewhere in this corpus associated with lost milk, wasting, blindness, or death; the historical belief gives no secure modern veterinary diagnosis.

10cde8ccd145aa2385b69650186c5177b3858358.summary: In a little house at Attinghausen, the meat they meant to cook for their midday meal was constantly stolen from the bronze pot.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow or torrent carrying earth, stones, and water down a slope; here it ruins two meadows, but the source does not specify the flow's precise material.

8d5735e0de43a188be70411d52b7a1733113fe64.summary: During an evening Heimgarten, several young men and women from the area around Stilli made a wager among themselves.

notes.label: Heimgarten
notes.text: an evening social visit or gathering in a home, especially among young people; the wager arises during this communal recreation.

notes.label: Besegnungsformel
notes.text: a spoken blessing, protective charm, or conjuration formula; the girl forgets it when the supernatural cat appears.

notes.label: E rock chunt mer wol für mis g‘lismets chamisol.
notes.text: Aargau dialect, closest to ‘A skirt will suit my knitted camisole well’; her nervous rhyme fixates on the promised garment instead of the protective formula.
notes.anchor: E rock chunt mer wol für mis g‘lismets chamisol.

notes.label: chatz oder chol, dir wird’s diner lebtag nümme wol.
notes.text: the cat's Aargau-dialect curse, closest to ‘Cat or coal, for all your life you will never again be well’; the rhyme foretells the girl's fatal illness.
notes.anchor: chatz oder chol, dir wird’s diner lebtag nümme wol.

652a83ec415e318c1c07ce5483dbdc2365ad717c.summary: A king's wife bore him a child, whose “planets were read” at once. The planets gave a sorrowful answer.

notes.label: böse Stund
notes.text: literally the “evil hour,” here a fatal moment fixed by astrological destiny rather than merely a difficult time; the protective invocation prevents the foretold death until that hour has passed.

27fbb4e52b6ab4369c7a23995945ae301e4a0a88.summary: Because a cat had often disturbed Saint Gregory at his studies with its cries, every year on the feast of this holy Doctor of the Church, the schoolboys of Rapperswil killed a cat.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

751f3946fb7fa5b5d25faf0eaeb40f5dba069807.summary: A woman from the town of Glarus, where I was employed for a long time, told me the following as certain truth: “When I was a young girl, a large black cat usually walked ahead of me on my outings, wearing a little bell around its neck.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

7e75b1f01988cc3c5293cd1e92252384e7f0d4b5.summary: Youthful high spirits may often have overstepped all bounds during the frequently wild amusements in the Tanzhaus at Schattdorf, and we need not be surprised when talkative Legend, the stern judge, warns us with a grave expression and threateningly raised forefinger that even today, on Saturday…

notes.label: Tanzhaus
notes.text: literally ‘dance house,’ a communal building or hall used for dancing and festivities; the tale remembers its excesses through lingering sounds and obstructive cats.

notes.label: tanzä, bödälä, träppälä, geuzä-n- und johlä
notes.text: an Uri dialect sound-list meaning approximately ‘dance, stamp the floor, trip or step about, give high calls, and holler’; the near-synonyms evoke a noisy revel rather than five precisely separable formal dances.
notes.anchor: tanzä, bödälä, träppälä, geuzä-n- und johlä

71b032d5abfd80886b422c285d2c237d11c11d6f.summary: 1. During a nocturnal journey near Attinghausen, my cousin passed an old, abandoned little house.

notes.label: Pattsch
notes.text: an Uri word used here for a huge, hulking cat-like creature; its insulting or monstrous force is clear, but its precise literal image is uncertain.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: groups of unmarried young men who roamed outdoors at night for courting, socializing, or pranks; here they are among those who hear the cats’ music.

notes.label: Betenläuten
notes.text: the ringing of a church bell that calls people to prayer, here the morning bell whose sound ends the cats’ nocturnal revelry.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine scree field or slope covered in loose rock; the nearby Gand shelters many feral cats after the supernatural company disperses.

691d8cbfd22856194d8c6f5ba8dd09ddac2010cf.summary: Once decent people are dead, they are free of every toil and task. But the herdsman who drove cattle in the field between Mörikon and Niederlenz cannot rest.

notes.label: Haho! Hüo!
notes.text: traditional Alemannic cattle-driving cries rather than lexical speech; here their repeated sound identifies the cruel herdsman’s ghost, and no more exact semantic distinction between the two calls is given.

notes.label: Nebelmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little fog man,’ a regional name for a small mist-associated supernatural being; it appears only in the source’s comparison to a related Graubünden tradition, whose details are not supplied here.

e942abd718aa6f907e928430aa437aeefa24b587.summary: The Oldenhorn forms the boundary between the cantons of Bern, Vaud, and Valais.

notes.label: Bergleute
notes.text: literally ‘mountain people,’ here wild supernatural inhabitants of the Oldenberg who guard cattle rather than human miners.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: thick fresh cream, used both as payment to the wild guardians and later as a charitable festival food.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, mixed with cream or curdled milk in offerings placed on roofs.

notes.label: Bödemli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning ‘little flat ground or terrace,’ the named place far below the dangerous Homades slopes.

notes.label: ergustet
notes.text: dried off or without milk, describing cows that return almost entirely depleted after the supernatural drive.

notes.label: Grangel
notes.text: bad, diseased, or decaying flesh found between the cows' toes after their ordeal.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Bergfest
notes.text: the annual mountain or Alp festival whose Sunday must be kept free of games and dancing.

notes.label: Saufsonntage
notes.text: literally ‘drinking Sunday,’ the popular name for the Bergfest day on which cream is distributed to the poor.

834937abf17921f41b0716f8b197c3c14928bcaf.summary: In the previous century, teasing and provocations of one kind or another often occurred between the Älpler and herdsmen on the Alps by the Sulzfluh and the Montavoner beyond the mountain range.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or living seasonally on an Alp; here it refers collectively to the Alpine herders among whom the source says these punishments were customary.

notes.label: Montavoner
notes.text: a person from the Montafon valley beyond the mountain range from Partnun; Jecklin uses the historical form Montavon rather than modern Montafon.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or cattle dairyman, more specifically tied to tending the milk cows than the general English word herdsman conveys.

notes.label: Partnun
notes.text: the high valley and Alp area by the Sulzfluh above St. Antönien, from which the Küher crosses the pass in this tale.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Handbube
notes.text: a junior Alpine hand or herdsman’s assistant; he is the first member of the crew to see the returning Montavoner.

notes.label: heisse Milch
notes.text: literally “hot milk”; the source names jumping into it as one of two Alpine punishments but does not specify its preparation beyond calling it hot.

notes.label: bürchlen
notes.text: to blow an alphorn as a signal; here the condemned Küher must continue until the exertion kills him, while using the calls to report the raid.

notes.label: Heer-Kuh
notes.text: the special herd designation given to the black-brown cow in the source; Jecklin does not define the precise rank or function of this cow.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here a high summer pasture together with its huts, herd, and seasonal work, rather than a single mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

2ffd7549fdfb8c01a3537a19239bdf14594a559d.summary: Before the Limmat flows into the Aare, it divides once more into two branches near Stroppel and forms the Limmat-Schachen, with an island belonging to the municipal territory of Gebenstorf.

notes.label: Limmat-Schachen
notes.text: Schachen denotes low, often wooded alluvial ground beside a river, here the island landscape where the Limmat meets the Aare; its historical boundaries and terrain are uncertain.

notes.label: Rostbauer
notes.text: this local designation means the farmer at the property called Rost and is used almost as a household name; the origin of the place-name Rost is uncertain.

notes.label: Gütterlig'schaner
notes.text: this is the source’s opaque local byname for the Birmensdorf fortune-teller consulted about the cellars; its etymology, spelling, and implied specialty are uncertain.

notes.label: Schaff
notes.text: here Schaff denotes an open tub or vat of water used for divination, not a cupboard; the vessel’s exact material and capacity are uncertain.

32071a6e351044a38c9eff0251582a9d02887214.summary: The “Länggass” near Ballwil, leading across the Höchi and Chrüzweid from Ballwil toward Eschenbach, was formerly enclosed on both sides by dense shrubbery.

notes.label: Länggass
notes.text: this local road-name means approximately ‘long lane’ and denotes the old hedge-lined route from Ballwil toward Eschenbach; its exact historical alignment is uncertain.

notes.label: Teufelsgass
notes.text: literally ‘Devil’s lane,’ this was the western of the older roads toward Eschenbach on which the monster also appeared; the name’s age and exact route are uncertain.

8b28a1ebbaad7a452e1f0ae9ef58344c8679c1d9.summary: The Bürgenberg, or Bürgenstock, on the Waldstättersee near Lucerne is split and is therefore bound together with a golden chain—or, according to others, held together by an iron rod.

notes.label: Bürgenberg
notes.text: the local or historical mountain name also given as Bürgenstock; Berg means ‘mountain,’ and the legend imagines the massif as physically split.

notes.label: Waldstättersee
notes.text: a historical shortened form related to Vierwaldstättersee, the German name for Lake Lucerne; it evokes the lake of the old Forest Cantons.

ae47bfb116cf8817e6b7ae0e45becc9ec884fb3b.summary: In return for the monthly delivery of one chamois, the hunting enthusiasts of Vättis were granted permission to pursue the noble Waidwerk.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Waidwerk
notes.text: the traditional art and practice of hunting, framed as a regulated and honorable pursuit rather than casual killing; here access depends on a monthly chamois payment.

notes.label: Bannen
notes.text: magical binding, compelling, or conjuring by words or ritual; the hunter unknowingly learns an illicit art that prevents the chamois from fleeing.

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a ‘black artist,’ a practitioner of black magic; the hunter becomes one unintentionally through the stranger’s instruction.

notes.label: Hosenlupf
notes.text: literally a ‘trouser lift,’ a Swiss wrestling bout in which opponents grip one another’s clothing; the monk uses it figuratively for a direct spiritual contest with the Devil.

e4f07eb4255251c4fab100569c45cf87cd5a9a69.summary: A poacher in the Kiental had a sweetheart whom he wished to marry. She would give him her hand, however, only if he gave up his reckless hunter’s life.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep Alpine rock faces or cliffs; the hunter’s shot among them provokes the fatal avalanche.

3fe6a5480df40c10f0c6e2e53c0ff5c194df8869.summary: Often, when a thunderstorm is approaching, a bang like the crack of a firearm is heard on the Schreckhorn, followed by a rushing and groaning not unlike a dying person’s death rattle.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Fuhrgeiss
notes.text: in this Alpine hunting context, Fuhrgeiss denotes the leading female chamois of the herd; her exact age and role are uncertain.

notes.label: Stutzen
notes.text: a Stutzen is a short hunting rifle associated with Alpine marksmen; the weapon’s exact type and caliber are unspecified.

notes.label: Fluhband
notes.text: this Swiss terrain term denotes a narrow ledge running across a cliff face; its size and location on the Schreckhorn are uncertain.

27e8110e2a1cff7d8f1a72b62c8855294d9239c4.summary: I have often heard it said that the chapel at Altdorf is a battle chapel; a battle was once fought there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

29210bf30cc897b708c5a864cd7af14f1474be98.summary: The chapel at Brunnen in the canton of Schwyz is said to be the church richest in grace between Rome and Einsiedeln.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

472953b236e0a60b86d65b4e64a61b19814ea5f8.summary: 1. Long ago, a chapel is said to have stood at Äsch.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a folkloric itinerant learned figure credited with magic, divination, treasure-finding, and secret knowledge; the title does not mean an ordinary modern student traveling between schools.

3b87a62ea448ccf4b5b13e9be9fb5bd3e32f13ba.summary: I no longer know exactly when it happened—it was certainly a very long time ago.

b41784553c6d2dd5238cc9b4534ab1500c6f87d2.summary: In the Turtmann valley, where people claim still to find traces of the old road that led over the Augstbort into the Visp valley and was often used in earlier times, ‘Meiden’ and ‘Gruben’ are said to have been villages.

notes.label: Alpstaffeln
notes.text: Alpine pasture stations or groups of seasonal herding and dairy buildings at a particular elevation; the ruined settlements have become seasonal rather than permanent habitation.

notes.label: Turtmänna
notes.text: the local name of the Turtmann stream or river running through the valley; the quotation marks identify the watercourse, not a female character.

notes.label: Alpengemeinwerker
notes.text: members performing communal work for an Alp or Alpine pasture association; the exact duties and legal organization are unstated, but their collective labor makes them the natural chapel builders.

96be72fbdaddd7494c70f49135cf73007de7d2a2.summary: The people of Trub in the Bernbiet had fallen away from the Catholic faith and cast out a beautiful image of St.

notes.label: Bernbiet
notes.text: the Bernese country or region, historically the lands associated with Bern; the word evokes a broader cultural territory rather than only the modern city or canton.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a sacristan or sexton, the church officer responsible for the building, bells, and practical preparations for worship.

notes.label: Aveläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the Ave or Angelus bell, here the morning church bell; it marks a devotional time of day rather than an ordinary summons.

9300000ac2a999afe2b425a06e4343167eaeea04.summary: About an hour above the parish village of Visperterminen, in the midst of a romantic forest, stands a prayer house called the Chapel of St.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

notes.label: Ziteigl
notes.text: the Graubünden pilgrimage-site name retained in the chapel title and account; the source identifies it as a high-mountain Marian sanctuary in the parish of Salux but gives no etymology for the name.

0a54055abe48f219f049e7955a1d1f08b92b4e41.summary: Landammann and Pannerherr Wolf Dietrich Reding, who owned the whole of Loterbach, Ebnet, Zimmerstalden, and many other properties around Jberg near Schwyz and was very rich, demanded certain rights from the members of the Jberg community concerning water, water conduits, and cart roads.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the old Swiss political order; its authority was broader than that of an ordinary mayor.

notes.label: Pannerherr
notes.text: literally the lord or custodian of the banner, a military-civic office associated with bearing and protecting the territorial standard; duties varied by polity.

notes.label: Bauernsame
notes.text: the local body of farmers acting collectively as a corporate rural community, especially in matters of common rights; it does not simply mean several individual farmers.

6b52c97a02afb5fc2ac7589d19d8ba08f0673ee0.summary: At this chapel, which lies beneath a high and threatening rock, a forest brother’s little house was once built, where a poor hermit dwelt.

notes.label: Fischel
notes.text: a small historical regional container or measure for dry goods, here peas; its exact capacity varied, and the point is the sudden sound of many peas cascading over the benches.

notes.label: Mi-ni mi! In Banji!
notes.text: the black rider’s opaque Valais-dialect reply; the source supplies no gloss, and whether Banji is a local destination, a formula, or a corrupted wording cannot be resolved responsibly from this story alone.

notes.label: z’en Hochflühen
notes.text: the Valais place-form in the chapel’s name, approximately ‘at the high rock faces’; it identifies the chapel beneath a threatening cliff, and the exact grammatical contraction belongs to the local dialect.

79821acf1b7f8a5513b866e47c6a4ee586fbe5f4.summary: A beggar spent the night in a house where the mother was near her confinement, and he prayed loudly and fervently: “Not in this hour, in the other; not in this hour, in the other!” After the child came into the world, they asked the beggar why he had prayed in that way.

notes.label: Hähli
notes.text: the Uri name for the chain from which a cooking or dairy kettle hangs over the hearth; the source immediately supplies this explanation.

notes.label: Turner
notes.text: the pivoting beam or crane from which the kettle and its chain hang and can be swung over the hearth; the cat sits upon this specialized fixture.

088f4a6db2193724a8e0a1fb4f9c9c1344042254.summary: In the Herrenholz, a strip of woodland above Erlisbach near Aarau, the crying of a child can sometimes be heard by an abandoned bog-iron mine.

notes.text: The apparent OCR form Baunm is read as Baum.

2fab8a7a53e07220e56d81d181dd33a9e57e528f.summary: 1. Once, as a little group of children played together outdoors, a band of Zigeuner came along the road.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a historical and now derogatory German exonym often applied to Roma and Sinti, but also used indiscriminately for itinerant outsiders; it is retained to expose the source's hostile classification, and the tale does not establish the band's identity or validate its accusation of child-stealing magic.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans,’ a historical othering label also applied loosely in Swiss legends to itinerant or supposedly ancient outsiders; its use here does not identify the travelers' actual religion or ethnicity.

notes.label: Tschöpli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a short jacket or little coat; the mother's removal of the touched garment breaks its power over the girl.

notes.label: Tschoopä
notes.text: a dialect variant for the same jacket or coat called Tschöpli just before; the discarded garment itself waddles after the travelers, but the exact difference in form or size between the two words is uncertain.

edcb8f454da6faefff79551b41f27764706a6a3b.summary: Not very long ago, a child from the village of Twann went missing. The child's parents set out with all their relatives and acquaintances to search for it, but for a long, long time, it could not be found.

notes.label: Schlossfluh
notes.text: literally ‘castle cliff,’ the steep rock and ruined stronghold above Twann where the child is supernaturally entertained; Fluh denotes a cliff or crag.

fc62deb7074d01f0583090950ecfcf7f40befb26.summary: On Wisoberg in Nidwalden lived a female monster who often let it be known that she went to Germany to kill children.

notes.label: About this telling

f3d24d76f9b1d1b06ebf651b41e8ce03dab01835.summary: Between the valley through which the little Frick river flows and the Hardwald, which extends for half an hour along the left bank of the Rhine below Laufenburg, rises a chain of hills called the Chinzhalde.

notes.label: Chinzhalde
notes.text: the local name of the wooded hill chain; the legend later interprets or reshapes it as Kindshalde through the murdered child.

notes.label: Kindshalde
notes.text: literally ‘child’s slope,’ the explanatory name said to derive from the father’s crime.

e3fe37f794c80f0a9f25f7f6251a9ca23ae56b36.summary: This can be attested. A female figure descends from Thun’s churchyard, which lies high above the town beside the mountain church with its world-famous view.

notes.label: Stadtlauben
notes.text: the covered street arcades characteristic of many Swiss towns; here the ghost passes beneath Thun’s arcaded walkways, not through garden bowers.

notes.label: Untergässli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive place-name meaning “little lower lane”; it identifies the alley of the Crown Inn rather than a generic underground passage.

a377ea4657b615adebf6c81bb04d50e335dd5cb5.summary: At Oberrickenbach in the canton of Obwalden, an Alp is called Sinsgäu. It was told that years ago a farmer led a young cow across this Alp into the Sulztal in Uri.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working landscape; Sinsgäu is the particular Alp crossed toward Uri.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sinsgäu
notes.text: the place-name used in the story body for the Alp called Sinsäu in the input title; the variation is preserved rather than silently regularized.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: the traditional game of skittles or ninepins; the small supernatural children block the narrow Alpine passage with their play.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.
