4439c26994e7d5b36117bfeccf4880c171e40198.summary: In the municipality of Oberkulm, a footpath leads westward uphill from the part of the village called Im Obersteg to a heap of rubble, the remains of an old dwelling.

notes.label: Seckelmeister
notes.text: literally “purse-master,” the historical treasurer or keeper of a community’s public funds; the tale identifies the murderer by this office but gives no details of his jurisdiction.

notes.label: chli Weidli
notes.text: Swiss German for “little pasture” or “little grazing plot,” the former local name of the secluded land later called Eichenrain; it functions as a place-name rather than a measurement of acreage.

notes.label: Weidgang
notes.text: communal grazing or the recognized right and practice of driving livestock onto shared pasture; here it had been abolished, but the source does not specify the local ownership arrangement.

b8b03f6a6b81fd7088d6b6ce99b8f910b8be73b4.summary: A quarter-hour below Klingnau, heading toward Koblenz, one comes to the Zurich road that leads into the Rütinen; from there, a path branches left into a forest called the Äpelöö.

notes.label: Rütinen
notes.text: cleared or grubbed woodland tracts, related to Swiss place-names in Rüti; here it names the terrain reached by the Zurich road.

notes.label: Waldbann
notes.text: a legally bounded forest district together with the community's rights and restrictions over it; the dispute concerns both acreage and jurisdiction, not a supernatural ban.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor administering a bailiwick; the parties bring their forest-boundary dispute before the Landvogt at Baden.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: boundary lines, markers, or stones delimiting municipal land; shifting them secretly allows Koblenz to appropriate the disputed forest.

notes.label: Anstand
notes.text: a hunter's fixed waiting place or the practice of standing in wait for game; the two hunters encounter the three-legged hare while posted there.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosed boundary line; the disembodied voice follows the men along this landscape division toward Klingnau.

notes.label: Käppeli
notes.text: literally ‘little chapel,’ with the Alemannic diminutive -li; it is the named roadside point where the pursuing voice finally stops.

notes.label: Choblezer
notes.text: a dialect form of Koblenzer, ‘man from Koblenz,’ used as the local name of the boundary-haunting apparition; the tale does not state whether it is the bribed official or a collective embodiment of the dispute.

ce42322f0d7bd9807a3444eb56c37abdff2814a5.summary: On Schwalmis, an Alp in Beckenried, there is a cave or Balm called the Chrezenchuchi.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter, overhang, or shallow cave; the Chrezenchuchi is identified as this kind of Alpine feature rather than a built room.

notes.label: Chrezenchuchi
notes.text: literally something like ‘basket kitchen’ or ‘carrying-basket kitchen,’ the local name of the treasure cave; Chuchi means kitchen, while the exact sense of Chrezen in this place-name is uncertain.

notes.label: Fronfastenmittwoche
notes.text: the Wednesday of an Ember-week fast, one of the traditional quarterly Catholic fasting periods; its eve is presented as a liminal time when hidden treasure becomes visible.

c2132da46c579215c36e776fe56c435dd27119e6.summary: 1. a) The Chriäsibüeb was once a sorcerer in Zürich who could do more than other people.

notes.label: Chriäsibüeb
notes.text: literally ‘cherry boy’ in Swiss German, the local nickname of the human trickster and magician; this story explains the name through his theft of cherries.

notes.label: Cheefi
notes.text: Uri dialect for a cage, lockup, or jail; the parenthetical dialect account emphasizes that the captive was shut away, but the exact prison structure is not described.

notes.label: Gumel
notes.text: an Alemannic word for potatoes; the clinging earth, rather than the food itself, supplies the Chriäsibüeb’s means of becoming invisible.

notes.label: D'Zürcher sind so schwarz wiä d'Rappä
notes.text: the opening of an Uri dialect taunt meaning ‘The Zürichers are as black as ravens'; its second line says they cannot catch the Chriäsibüeb, whose spelling varies within the verse.
notes.anchor: D'Zürcher sind so schwarz wiä d'Rappä

notes.label: D'Zircher sind witzig
notes.text: the opening of an Uri dialect verse saying that although the people of Zürich are clever, their towers pointed, and their eyes raven-like, they still cannot catch the Chriäsibüeb.

notes.label: Iähr Herä vo Ziri (Üri)
notes.text: the opening address of an Uri dialect taunt to the lords of Ziri or Üri; it says that despite their eyes they can catch the Chriäsibüeb nowhere, while the exact comparison Fili is uncertain and therefore remains untranslated in the verse.

notes.label: Kastenvögtin
notes.text: the local title or byname of a reputed witch from the Muotatal; the source parallels her magical flight with the Chriäsibüeb’s without explaining the name’s origin.

notes.label: Chlungeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small ball or skein of thread or yarn; the trickster uses its unrolled strand as the means of his aerial escape.

b4e40a1211450b4d1b756c53626b8289c88ab626.summary: Once again he was seized and was to be executed. But they were willing to spare his life if he would pray a single ‘Holy Mary, Mother of God!’ He refused, however, and said, ‘I prayed an Our Father ten years ago, and it is still burning low in my throat.’ The executioner was about to perform his…

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the older Swiss political order, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; even he cannot identify the true head.

notes.label: Urispiegel
notes.text: Uri's local cycle of comic trickster tales, named in analogy with the wider Till Eulenspiegel tradition; here it classifies other pranks told about the Chriäsibüeb.

notes.label: Chriäsibüeb
notes.text: literally ‘cherry boy’ in Swiss German, the local nickname of the trickster whose execution ends this cycle; the source does not explain how he acquired it.

3876e6e43fbfe0aac4afdc22ecc5a29f3d90a938.summary: At the weekly market in the little town of Brugg, a woman from Veltheim had bought some very fine Chuder for little money.

notes.label: Chuder
notes.text: Swiss German for tow, the coarse, tangled fibers left from processing flax or hemp; it was a market commodity, and the spirit's rhyme plays on the woman believing she bought only the fiber.

notes.label: Chudermandli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Chuder man,’ the dialect name for the small haunting spirit concealed in the woman's bundle of tow; Mandli is a Swiss German diminutive of ‘man.’

663aebda6cd433038006aa75afb40c7190fd195f.summary: According to an old tradition, a hermits’ chapel once stood in Mörschwil. In the year 1494, several human skeletons were found there at a site enclosed by ancient masonry.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2a40a91f8d580aab8b98054d850544ade989ad6b.summary: The church at Grabs is among the oldest in the country. It already existed in the year 614 but was probably built still earlier.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b972d2a73990145d0622c62e2053dbd776b802e1.summary: The first Christians who settled along the Kien and Kander wished to build a house of God.

notes.label: Gornerweiden
notes.text: literally ‘Gorner pastures,’ the selected meadowland in the Kiental where the first church was unsuccessfully begun.

notes.label: Blümlisalp
notes.text: the prominent Bernese Oberland mountain massif above the Kiental; despite Alp in the name, English readers should understand it as a proper mountain name.

notes.label: Postillon
notes.text: a mounted or coach-driving postal servant who handled the mail coach and its horses; the joke measures the church tower's unusual low height against his long whip.

e9c10f329184bdd208ceb779e226ea9ec4773ac2.summary: In the beautiful Tößtal, the good old church stands on a hill in the village of Wila.

notes.label: Tößtal
notes.text: the source's spelling of the Töss Valley, the Zurich landscape in which Wila and its church are situated.

notes.label: Feierabendglocke
notes.text: the bell marking the close of the working day, heard from Turbental as the kind lord tends his garden.

notes.label: Talleute
notes.text: literally ‘valley people,’ the rural inhabitants whose trust the younger Breitenlandenberg earns.

notes.label: kirchengenössig
notes.text: belonging to or served by the same parish community; before Wila's church was built, its people were ecclesiastically attached to Turbental.

notes.label: Wilaer
notes.text: the people or inhabitants of Wila, who carry out their lord's bequest.

notes.label: Frontage
notes.text: compulsory communal labor days or corvée service assigned for the church construction, not the English word ‘frontage.’

notes.label: Töß
notes.text: the source's spelling of the Töss River, personified as traveling vigorously and remaining ever awake through its rushing.

notes.label: Trämel
notes.text: heavy timbers, beams, or logs laboriously hauled to the intended building site.

notes.label: Nebelgeister
notes.text: literally ‘mist spirits,’ the spectral forms that grow from river mist and move the building materials.

notes.label: Nebelschürzen
notes.text: literally ‘mist aprons,’ the flowing vaporous folds in which the spirits carry huge stones and timbers as if they were tiny objects.

notes.label: himmelklar und föhnlauter
notes.text: a poetic compound phrase meaning ‘clear as Heaven and as lucid as a Föhn sky,’ expressing the villagers' sudden certainty about the dead lord's will.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a young nobleman or lord, here the affectionate social title the villagers use for the murdered Breitenlandenberg.

notes.label: Talschaft
notes.text: the valley community understood as both landscape and body of inhabitants, into which the finished church looks down.

notes.label: Kirchhof
notes.text: the churchyard surrounding the church, often also a burial ground; its roses perpetuate the fragrance of the lord's former garden.

69d7c5cb99718bba2db27caa09977a27637112bf.summary: The holy bishop Nicholas gave his name to the village and region where he is now venerated in a beautiful house of God; before that, the place may have been called “Gasen” (Chauson).

notes.label: D’s Glasi lat nit!
notes.text: Valais dialect meaning ‘Glasi will not allow it!’; Glasi is a local familiar form of Nikolaus, so the goblin acknowledges that St. Nicholas is preventing the mountain’s collapse.

91f8de0de7a8d9591699275e20c88b0220af44b3.summary: The little church of Blumenstein stands apart from the village. In olden times our mountains were inhabited, while the lower regions along the Gürbe as far as Seelhofen formed a lake.

notes.label: ewige Jud
notes.text: literally ‘eternal Jew,’ the historical German label for the Wandering Jew of Christian folklore; it carries an antisemitic tradition and should be understood as a legendary motif, not a claim about Jewish people.

notes.label: Winde
notes.text: the source's unusual word for the barren state into which the region is cursed, probably a waste or desolate tract; its exact regional sense or possible textual corruption is uncertain.

396f8d608e4c08f622d7aa23627047719a75eb7f.summary: The inhabitants of the municipality of Isérables are said to have been rather simple-minded people in earlier times, and amusing Schildbürgerstücklein are told about them.

notes.label: Schildbürgerstücklein
notes.text: short comic tales about proverbially foolish townspeople, comparable to wise-fool or Gotham stories in English tradition; here the label frames the people of Isérables as the butt of the joke.

notes.label: Kuhplatsch
notes.text: a colloquial word for a cow pat; the villagers treat the dung beside the church wall as a grave desecration.

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: a historical local officeholder or executive authority; the tale implies that Aloys's proposal makes him a likely candidate at the next election, but does not specify the office's exact powers.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a sexton or church caretaker; he brings the basin of holy water requested by the villagers.

notes.label: Sonnenkuchen
notes.text: literally a “sun cake,” the tale's comic euphemism for the cow pat after it has dried in the sun.

1e0a2085cd38fd01e838f67b8f84f9c47897580a.summary: It is related that the church tower of Naters is very old, that it was built by the pagans and only centuries later fitted out for Catholic worship.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight used here for bell weights; its exact mass varied by place and period, so the figures fifty and twenty Zentner are preserved rather than converted to a modern unit.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: the Swiss German word for a godmother; here Countess Blandra serves symbolically as godmother at the Catholic naming or ‘baptism’ of the bell, a ritual analogy rather than human baptism.

notes.label: geschworenes Metall
notes.text: literally ‘sworn’ or ‘vowed metal,’ apparently metal pledged or donated for the sacred bell casting; the account makes its ritual or legal status unclear, so the phrase is retained.

notes.label: d'Alta
notes.text: dialect for ‘the old one,’ the familiar name of Naters’s second large bell; it distinguishes this nearly five-hundred-year-old bell from Antonia, while the spelling preserves the local article and feminine form.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Christmonat
notes.text: literally ‘Christ month,’ a traditional German-speaking name for December; ‘the ninth day of Christmonat 1755’ therefore means 9 December 1755, and the original calendrical wording is retained for cultural context.

notes.label: Sant Kümmernis
notes.text: the local name for Saint Wilgefortis, represented as a crucified woman and invoked as an intercessor; the cult figure has several names and legendary identities, but this account equates Sant Kümmernis directly with Wilgefortis.

notes.label: Theodulspende
notes.text: literally the ‘Theodul distribution’ or charitable gift, a promised recurring offering at Blatten associated with Saint Theodul and protection from disaster; the story does not state what was distributed or to whom.

notes.label: Wieggisch
notes.text: the local name for a catastrophic flood, torrent, or debris flow said to have issued from the Bruchigraben and threatened Naters; the exact natural process and the origin of the name are not explained.

notes.label: Kastlan
notes.text: a Valais form of castellan, a judicial or administrative official connected with a castle district; here it survives in the house name Kastlan Gasser, though the text does not identify Gasser’s office or date.

7f5c36a99266bc09873452d1b6662716359c3a2b.summary: One day, a little boy strolled singing toward the cozy village of Sellenbüren.

notes.label: Versehglöcklein
notes.text: the small bell rung when a priest carried the sacraments to a dying person; its familiar ritual sound draws the boy toward the hidden churchyard.

notes.label: Firnfeld
notes.text: a field of old, compacted mountain snow or firn; the comparison makes the spirits' garments Alpine-white and brilliantly reflective.

notes.label: Sternenblumen
notes.text: literally ‘star flowers,’ the radiant flowers woven into the spirits' wreaths; the source does not identify a precise botanical species.

notes.label: Chüeiher
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for a cowherd or cattle drover; here it names an invisible supernatural herdsman heard driving cattle through the Chaltenegg.

notes.label: Unzit
notes.text: literally ‘untime,’ an uncanny or forbidden hour outside ordinary human activity, commonly associated with nocturnal supernatural encounters.

notes.label: Treichle
notes.text: large sheet-metal Swiss cattle bells with a deep, clanging sound; they make the invisible herd audible.

7a660f7b0dcd5806df38d9cb754d46de4c438f62.summary: According to the legend, on the site of the present Steigwaid above Mayenfeld there once stood the great city of Wolfsnest.

notes.label: Überrüfung
notes.text: a regional term for destructive burial or overrunning by a debris-laden flood or mass flow; the tale itself describes lake water mixed with stones and rubble, so this is more than ordinary inundation.

2d4f17f4145af7dadc0910c6a53cc0d60a87021a.summary: The Clariden in the land of Glarus and several Blüemlisalp pastures in the Bernese Oberland are principal homes of this legend.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

66adaeabec912f0182fb0db19127d3fe4cae5ad0.summary: In the municipality of Gurtnellen lived a man who knew and could do more than other people.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

116032c240ae3347dd0152fe3f1b21e000fb4c22.summary: The people of Lötschental also wanted a clerk. They sent delegates to Sion to bargain for one there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4c5ae4c6cf1976d7e87f151495f01dc597bcb2ad.summary: There was once a beggar in Scarl who lost his way in the forest and came to a cave.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8132671a4baab04fc5585d63e903f24ea6a62af5.summary: Once there was a beggar who lost his way in the forest and came to a cave. A giant lived there, and he was a man-eater.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

19c39d3db3d9aca3b42d4006a08938f3f25ff645.summary: A young king’s son sought a wife at the neighboring courts. At the very next court where he appeared, he liked the old king’s beautiful daughter so well that he asked for her hand.

notes.label: Schöpplein
notes.text: a diminutive of Schoppen, a traditional small serving or measure of wine; the exact volume varied by place and period, so here it means the patrons’ modest glass or measure at the new inn.

ce787cefb8da8363056cf868ecaa33b9354de359.summary: The people of Filisur in Graubünden could not understand why the Lord God had placed such a high mountain directly in front of their sun.

notes.label: Holzdünchel
notes.text: a hollowed wooden pipe or conduit traditionally used to carry water; the joke treats sunlight as though it could be piped downhill through one.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: The Kreuzer was a historical small-denomination coin used in parts of Switzerland and neighboring lands. Its value varied across monetary systems; in some Swiss systems it counted as one quarter of a Batzen. A named coin in a tale is therefore not a modern cent with a fixed national value.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Kreuzer

notes.label: Laublager
notes.text: literally a ‘leaf bed,’ a rustic sleeping place or mattress made with dried leaves; Barthli lies down on it before his planned early start.

notes.label: Schlegelsäge
notes.text: literally a ‘mallet saw,’ apparently a loud, rhythmically rasping saw or folk comparison for heavy snoring; the exact tool meant by this comic compound is uncertain.

notes.label: Unschlitt
notes.text: rendered animal tallow used for candles or lamps; Uschi prepares it with a wick to keep light while manually operating the clock all night.

notes.label: Perpendikel
notes.text: an older regional form of ‘pendulum’; by moving it herself, Uschi makes the stopped clock mark time but leaves no opportunity to prepare breakfast.

56288a00b34b6457755c3dba60fba41b86109fff.summary: Another Waldfängge near Conters once herded all the village goats for an entire summer.

notes.label: Waldfängge
notes.text: a wild forest being of the Alpine Fänggen tradition; here he acts as the village’s uncanny but dependable goatherd until the young men intoxicate and bind him.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: wild forest or mountain beings in Alpine folklore, credited here with secret knowledge for making gold or an elixir of life from spent whey; traditions about their nature vary by region.

notes.label: Tschôpa
notes.text: a regional form related to Tschoope, meaning a coat or jacket; it is retained because its dialect sound carries the closing rhymed weather maxim, whose joke is that the advice is uselessly obvious.

97a35d92276a2b8f0a9e7df49d86786a4b99fa19.summary: South of Wartau Castle, a path runs beneath the wall and around the castle hill.

notes.label: Dörre
notes.text: a drying place or installation, often a heated drying kiln used for grain, fruit, or other produce; here the woman asks whether wheat is being dried there, though the source does not describe its construction.

ea0d136a19c245c04a76ce1e79d8ca27b32bb33c.summary: It appears that the Erdmännchen were not skilled in every art and science but needed human help in certain matters.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like underground beings who need a human midwife and reward her with enchanted coals.

notes.label: weise Frau
notes.text: literally ‘wise woman,’ a traditional term for a knowledgeable midwife or female healer.

notes.label: Je mehr ass de zattest (zerstreust) je weniger de hattest!
notes.text: dialect for ‘the more you scatter, the less you have,’ warning that discarded coals are actually treasure.
notes.anchor: Je mehr ass de zattest (zerstreust) je weniger de hattest!

aa112cf329e5455f23e041d2517b85325374c62a.summary: A Fänggenmannli who lived at the far end of Savien on the Valätscher-Alpe in a ‘Balma’ once came by night to the Bühel farm.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a small male member of the wild forest or mountain beings called Fänggen in Alpine tradition; here he is husband and father, and English categories such as dwarf or goblin would narrow the source too much.

notes.label: Balma
notes.text: a Romansh and Alpine regional word for a cave, rock shelter, or overhang; quotation marks in the source mark the local term for the Fänggen family’s dwelling.

notes.label: Läufer
notes.text: here a passage, gallery, or exterior access-way at the house from which the woman looks out; the source does not describe its construction closely enough to choose one architectural equivalent.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little man; here it refers back to the wild Fänggenmannli rather than an ordinary child-sized human.

notes.label: Fänggenweiblein
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg woman,’ the Fänggenmannli’s wife in childbirth; the compound preserves her membership in the same wild-being tradition.

notes.label: Büchel-Frau
notes.text: the woman of the Bühel farm, identified by the household place-name rather than a personal surname; the spelling varies from Bühel in the preceding sentence.

notes.label: Je mehr zerzass't, je minder d'hast
notes.text: Graubünden dialect for ‘The more you scatter, the less you have’; the rhyming warning becomes literal when every dropped coal vanishes instead of turning into gold.
notes.anchor: Je mehr zerzass't, je minder d'hast

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy-working landscape, not merely a mountain peak; Valätscher-Alpe is the source-exact name at the far end of Savien.

1c3c0333ff8bfa6c23ea75757f3a0d2a26b79f7b.summary: My legend goes back a mere 1466 years and arrives at the year 398, when Pope Anastasius and Emperor Honorius requested and received help from the 3 Lands.

notes.label: Schneeberger
notes.text: literally ‘snow-mountain people,’ a legendary old designation here applied collectively to the people of the 3 Lands before their Roman campaign; the passage does not identify exactly which communities the name includes or establish it as a historical self-designation.

6eaa1733faee5398d66f21d2ff7369a719c1d5e5.summary: Around the year 1730, Jann Fausch, who lived on the Stutz near Seewis in the Prätigau, had a large, coal-black cock.

notes.label: trolte
notes.text: a dialect past tense meaning ‘rolled’; Jecklin supplies the standard-German gloss in parentheses, which the translation preserves.

notes.label: Bächt
notes.text: a regional word for refuse or sweepings; a Bächt shovel is the household shovel used to carry such waste, not a specialized ritual object.

bdbf8a5612d73ef065d895a1d194296f61c3ce60.summary: The red garb of the Wild. Hunter.

notes.label: Rotthaler
notes.text: a regional name for the Wild Hunter derived from the Rotthal, the glacial ‘red valley’ placed in Alpine legend between Bernese and Lucerne landscapes.

notes.label: Rothenburger
notes.text: another red-associated regional name for the Wild Hunter and for figures linked with Rothenburg; the essay connects it with Lucerne's historical battle cry.

notes.label: Strüdelenhexen
notes.text: witches associated with the wild Alpine region around the Rotthal; the precise Strüdelen element is not securely explained in the source.

notes.label: Aelpler
notes.text: the source's older spelling of Älpler, a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, whose pastoral viewpoint turns the spirit host into enchanted livestock.

notes.label: W. Heer
notes.text: the source's abbreviation for Wildes Heer, the ‘Wild Host,’ a supernatural nocturnal procession closely related to the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Wamms
notes.text: an older spelling of Wams, a close-fitting jacket or doublet; the Wild Hunter's is long and red.

notes.label: Leibchen
notes.text: a fitted bodice, vest, or short jacket worn on the upper body; here it is another red layer in the apparition's costume.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: an apron, literally a cloth worn in front; the spirit maiden's red apron participates in the color symbolism.

notes.label: Heidentschöpen
notes.text: a Black Forest name for red petticoats used around fever patients and women in childbirth; the source derives Schöpen from French jupon and associates the garment with ‘heathen’ custom.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal livestock pasture and dairying settlement, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: W. Jäger
notes.text: the source's abbreviation for Wilder Jäger, the Wild Hunter, leader of the supernatural nocturnal hunt.

notes.label: Rötheli
notes.text: a regional diminutive name for the robin, identified by the Latin rubecula and treated as sacred and protective against lightning.

notes.label: Buddlergräufle
notes.text: the source's Graubünden name for the lingonberry, cited as a red plant linked by antiquarian comparison to Wuotan's festival.

notes.label: Raffausle
notes.text: the source's Glarus name for the Alpine rose, another red plant drawn into the same comparative color tradition.

notes.label: Grauflete
notes.text: a traditional festival name from the Muotatal that the author associates with Wuotan; the precise historical derivation is antiquarian and not established by the story itself.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Grünhütler
notes.text: literally ‘green-hatted one,’ a Graubünden Alpine specter whose nocturnal knock foretells that snow will cover the Alp.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and cheese-making in the seasonal hut.

notes.label: Grünrock
notes.text: literally ‘green coat,’ an Aargau name for the Devil or, in gentler Wild Hunt traditions, the green-clad supernatural hunter.

notes.label: Glücksheer
notes.text: literally ‘host of good fortune,’ a melodious, comparatively benevolent form of the supernatural procession; the positive name may also be euphemistic.

notes.label: Rübeli
notes.text: a green half-velvet fabric or garment named in the source as the Wild Hunter's clothing; its exact textile construction is regionally specific.

notes.label: Breitsee-Maideli
notes.text: the ‘little maiden of Breitsee,’ a regional spirit figure whose green apron is cited as another example of spirit costume.

notes.label: W. Jagd
notes.text: the source's abbreviation for Wilde Jagd, the Wild Hunt, a supernatural procession of riders, hounds, and noise.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical Swiss administrative or judicial official; the comparative haunting official is distinguished by green slippers.

notes.label: Walfeld
notes.text: literally the field of the slain or battlefield, used in the author's mythological comparison of Frau Held with a fate-knowing Norn.

notes.label: elsternfarbig
notes.text: literally ‘magpie-colored,’ sharply divided between black and white; the author uses the color pairing for beings poised between life and death or opposing moral states.

58b25a1771f00b4616fd0938fa04270bc4a54aa9.summary: There once lived on the Reppisch, a border stream between Aargau and Zürich territory, a teacher whose home and name shall remain unmentioned here because legal proceedings concerning him and his present fate took place only recently.

notes.label: Sonntagskinder
notes.text: literally “Sunday children,” people born on a Sunday who in Swiss and wider German-speaking folklore were credited with unusual luck or second sight; here the term explains why the maid alone can see the ghost, although the precise local belief is not specified.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

79fe2017e7c3b1e3ad04cd2bd6ac73ff4a781b21.summary: In the Val d'Illiez lived a poor family that called nothing its own but a black, dilapidated hut through which the wind whistled and a patch of meadow in front of it where a small mountain cow and two goats found their scanty fodder.

notes.label: Der Grüne
notes.text: literally “the Green One,” a folkloric designation for the green-clad stranger who is revealed by the bargain to be the Devil; his color, pointed headgear, raven feather, and money sack mark his uncanny role.

notes.label: Giltsteinofen
notes.text: a masonry room stove made with Giltstein, a heat-retaining soapstone or potstone used in Alpine houses; the newborn child is lying behind it and is therefore the unintended object of the bargain.

notes.label: Gevatter
notes.text: a traditional term for a godparent or someone linked through baptismal sponsorship; the narrator uses it darkly and indirectly for the supernatural claimant attached to the boy from birth.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Stridel
notes.text: a Valais and Alpine folklore term for a male witch, sorcerer, or dangerous night-roaming supernatural man; traditions vary in the being's precise nature.

notes.label: fürbass
notes.text: an older regional adverb meaning onward or farther ahead; the boy continues resolutely after the first priest refuses him.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally a “forest brother,” an older regional name for a male religious hermit or lay recluse living outside a formal monastery; here the apparently devout hermit is contrasted with his murderous brother.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Wiriwäri
notes.text: the contemptuous and deliberately vague word used by the voice behind Hell's gate for the cross fixed there, approximately a troublesome thing, fuss, or obstruction; the story does not give it a more precise object meaning.

notes.label: Himmelsbrot
notes.text: literally “bread of heaven,” the miraculous daily bread delivered to the Waldbruder by a heavenly messenger; the tale does not identify it more specifically as ordinary bread, manna, or sacramental bread.

5e4ed485f9c6505488935a32654ad225d62477d1.summary: In the city of Lucerne there once lived a cooper who often wandered through the dense forests and clefts of Mount Pilatus in search of wood for making wine barrels.

notes.label: Wintermonat
notes.text: literally ‘winter month,’ a historical German name used here for November; the passage gives the confinement as beginning on its 6th day, while the regional naming convention is older than the modern calendar term.

a1e4ff9cfcd45178de6a30bf54883dad18ab0f3b.summary: There are people in the world who cannot live among their fellow human beings without dispute and quarrel and must forever argue with one person or another.

notes.label: Hotzdecke
notes.text: a coarse blanket pieced and woven from waste tow or flax fibers; its low material value contrasts with the fortune consumed by the lawsuit.

9c1784b3ee1de2a0dee4d9836c9784fcb02a03af.summary: a) Santaburg once stood upon a bright hill between Nebikon and Dagmersellen, where nothing but desolate woodland is now found.

notes.label: Nüsse
notes.text: the local name quoted by the source for the skin eruption, swelling, or ulcer suffered after the apparition; its exact medical diagnosis is not supplied.

a9d2171885cad8b6f6d31be8d76975fde2fdb5a3.summary: Folk tradition says that council meetings were held from time to time in Kaspar Gisler’s house in Schattdorf.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f6c23dbe08742e8fe5c7c048c2f3d789c274ece8.summary: In ancient times a road led from Milan to Brig, then across the Beichtgrat into the Lötschental, and from there across the Lötschen Pass—where paving stones can still be seen—to Kandersteg.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its pastoral working landscape, not merely a mountain peak; the tale says the present glacier fields were once rich grazing lands.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Niederlande
notes.text: literally “low lands,” an older geographic expression here for the wealthy country or countries down beyond the mountains; the story does not establish that it means the modern Netherlands specifically.

notes.label: Söller
notes.text: an architectural term for an elevated terrace, gallery, or balcony; the source does not describe the castle's precise design, but places its snow-white Söller at the water's edge.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: Alpine pack-train carriers who transported goods with laden horses or mules across mountain passes; they are part of the traffic on the old road.

notes.label: Alprosenblüten
notes.text: blossoms of the Alpenrose, an Alpine rhododendron; the comparison describes the countess's vivid red cheeks rather than cultivated roses.

notes.label: Venediker
notes.text: the tale's older regional form for a Venetian; Jegerlehner explicitly glosses this traveler as a nobleman from Venice.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen responsible for livestock and dairy work on high seasonal pastures; they later see the countess in snake form.

81217633f72e91e773857d4e26330aacfb66dd25.summary: High in the Naters Alp called Lusgen, on the boundary of the Aletsch Valley, one finds a deeply fissured rock that is partly split into large Blatten, or broad stone slabs.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Blatten
notes.text: an Alpine landscape word for broad, flat plates or slabs of rock; here their table-like surfaces give the haunted place its name.

notes.label: Z'en-Tischen
notes.text: the local Valais place-name, literally ‘at the tables,’ for the level rock slabs on the Naters Alp; the table image explains the name and anchors the countess's treasure apparition in the landscape.

cecf63fe3faba166561f87c52f48d0fb940c8c0a.summary: The Alp called Lusgen lies on the Gletscherbord of the upper Aletschgletscher.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its associated seasonal working landscape, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Lusgen
notes.text: the named high pasture on the margin of the upper Aletsch glacier where the tables of rock and their treasure lie.

notes.label: Gletscherbord
notes.text: the rocky bank, margin, or ledge beside a glacier; here it locates the Lusgen by the upper Aletsch glacier.

notes.label: Aletschgletscher
notes.text: the Aletsch glacier, whose upper reaches border the story's pasture and rock field.

notes.label: Alphütten
notes.text: huts belonging to a high Alpine pasture operation, occupied when the cattle are driven up for the season.

notes.label: Felsenmeer
notes.text: literally a “sea of rocks,” a field of weathered blocks and slabs rather than a body of water.

notes.label: zen Tischen
notes.text: the local name meaning approximately “at the tables,” given because many of the flat rock slabs resemble stone tables.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine herder and dairyman working on a high pasture; the poor Senne is the witness to the treasure apparition.

notes.label: Quatemberkind
notes.text: a child associated by birth with the Church's quarterly Ember Days and traditionally credited with perceiving hidden or supernatural things.

notes.label: Silberlinge
notes.text: silver coins or pieces of silver; they form one of the two heaps the Countess continually rearranges.

notes.label: schämig
notes.text: a regional or nonstandard adjective meaning shameful or embarrassing; the Senne tells himself that fleeing from a woman would be disgraceful.

notes.label: Eringertal
notes.text: the Valais valley where the Senne imagines buying the finest herd after becoming rich.

notes.label: Brigermarkt
notes.text: the market at Brig, which the Senne imagines attending at the major spring and autumn fairs with a heavy purse.

notes.label: haldab
notes.text: a Swiss regional direction meaning down the slope or downhill; the disappointed Senne uses that route back from the rock tables.

882e3db984a0c7bb7a9fabbbe626d900bbc94d9c.summary: Many years ago, during wartime, men from Valais raided the Alpen belonging to the people of Lenk in the upper Simmental and drove away a large number of stolen cattle.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: plural of Alp, the seasonally used high-mountain pastures, huts, and working landscapes from which the cattle are stolen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

f792fff8daa2246adc72f5ac3d00eafcec05f4f7.summary: Storms and sudden snowfall on Alpine pastures, the proximity of wild animals, or swarms of stinging insects sometimes make a herd of cows on an alp so confused and wild that it takes flight and, no longer heeding the herder’s calls, plunges over rock walls to its death.

notes.label: das Rücken der Kühe
notes.text: literally ‘the moving/departure of the cows,’ the traditional name for a herd’s sudden uncanny flight and disappearance.

notes.label: Volle
notes.text: a large milk funnel used as a resonator through which the herder sings the evening blessing across the high pastures.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen or herders greeted by the resonant blessing.

notes.label: Hirtenmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little herder-man,’ the mountain spirit that leads the missing cows away and later returns them.

notes.label: Melktern
notes.text: a regional measure or yield of milk from a milking; the exact quantity is not specified.

notes.label: Baren
notes.text: the feeding rack, manger, or stall place before which Oswald mimics milking his absent cows.

notes.label: Lecktäschlein
notes.text: literally ‘little licking bag,’ a small shoulder bag probably holding salt or another livestock lure; the exact contents are unstated.

notes.label: Melkzitzen
notes.text: milking teats; one is missing from the lead cow as the mild punishment for Oswald’s half-uttered curse.

f24d3eb39fabaecd81133330413fafbaa69d1897.summary: On the Wergistalalp and Bussalp in the Grindelwald valley, it happens that the cows rücken.

notes.label: rücken
notes.text: to move off or depart; here it names the cows’ mysterious collective disappearance rather than ordinary movement.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen or herders responsible for livestock and milk production on a high pasture.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herder, whose authentic call can counter the supernatural voice.

notes.label: Meisterkuh
notes.text: literally ‘master cow,’ the leading or dominant cow that guides the herd.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Das Rücken der Kühe
notes.text: literally ‘the moving/departure of the cows,’ a regional supernatural motif in which a herd follows an uncanny herder’s call and returns days later.

d9c1596b711ac776b3c699413ca08184edb2508e.summary: One day, when the mother at Klosterberg in Isental returned to the house from her fieldwork and meant to tend to the child in the cradle, the child had vanished.

notes.label: Barnen
notes.text: an interior level or hay-storage area in an Uri stable or barn; the mother finds the abducted infant there, though the building’s exact arrangement is not stated.

c7cfe9c00a25a2199701be8d57a40775ade696d3.summary: In St. Antönien a young man named Andreas loved a girl called Röseli.

notes.label: Jung-Volk
notes.text: literally the ‘young folk,’ the local body of unmarried or marriageable young people whose conduct and festival customs are governed collectively.

notes.label: Chilbi-Vorsteher
notes.text: the elected leader or overseer of the local Chilbi youth; he enforces propriety and receives the customary right to choose a festival dancing partner.

notes.label: Chilbi-Sonntag
notes.text: the Sunday of the Chilbi, the annual church-dedication feast or parish fair; Jecklin glosses the occasion as Kirchweih.

notes.label: Chilbi-Maidli
notes.text: literally the ‘Chilbi girl,’ the young woman selected as the Chilbi-Vorsteher's regular dance partner for the festival.

notes.label: eingesungen
notes.text: literally ‘sung in’; the unusual burial expression evokes the funeral singing that accompanies Andreas into his grave or ‘cool bed.’

notes.label: beim Kreuze
notes.text: literally ‘by the cross,’ the enduring local place-name attached to the spot where the rising cross finally fell and decayed.

9c81e4afa3f0e3cfa5fdf5e95b9b0acbb7a6de01.summary: On the summit of the Eccojalaz rises a steep rocky pinnacle called the little rock, le petit vanni.

notes.label: le petit vanni
notes.text: the French local name glossed by the source as ‘the little rock,’ a sheer pinnacle on the Eccojalaz; the exact regional sense or spelling of vanni is not further explained.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or senior cattle herders on high pastures; their ability to carry the cross up depends upon the hermit's sacred assurance.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: cowherds or Alpine cattlemen; later local Küher cannot repeat the ascent without the spiritual promise that aided the first men.

notes.label: Britschelade
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for the board or plank of a simple wooden platform or bed-like structure on which the crow perches; the closest literal sense is ‘pallet board,’ but the brief account does not make the object’s exact form or setting certain.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

4eaab2f144f48b52424de2f91c26b0a122505c19.summary: Every afternoon, a girl went behind her parents’ house with her little bowl of warm milk containing bread and would eat nowhere else.

13b28d7e06ad5bef7dcfb4b921f3d4ec00af7826.summary: Southwest of the village of Niederlenz, in the level grain fields, lies a charming hill richly overgrown with tall grass and planted with many cherry and apple trees.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

41699098cbec4f27de62c52a4cc003c15246dcb3.summary: Toward Sarmenstorf, in a forest, lie the last remains of Fahrwangen Castle.

notes.label: Maitau
notes.text: literally ‘May dew,’ this phrase contrasts spring freshness with the blood in which Agnes boasts of bathing; whether it quotes an older tradition or literary embellishment is uncertain.

notes.label: Agnesgeschrei
notes.text: literally ‘Agnes’s cry,’ this is the local name for the lamenting aerial sound believed to announce weather changes; its natural cause and historical spread are uncertain.

0920489a0594f44f99174686b1539b6488869bce.summary: The crystal cave at Kobelwies must have a hidden exit. A fox ran in through the front and later emerged again at Freienbach.

notes.label: About this telling

5066a19740d392a6bdf641ef3058d6b6707aa781.summary: Long ago, one evening, a herder on Alp Tschingelfeld at the Faulhorn was gathering his strayed goats far from the hut.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high seasonal pasture with its working landscape, here Tschingelfeld at the Faulhorn; the herder’s exact grazing area and hut are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: an Älpler is someone who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, here the herder tempted into the crystal cave; his name and precise duties are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpenstock
notes.text: an Alpenstock is a long mountain walking staff used for balance and probing, here struck against the crystal; its material and exact form are uncertain.

3849f135097fc3d774dbcdb60788b0879ddacc5e.summary: The most skillful crystal diggers were the Capuchin fathers. By magical arts, they once discovered a crystal vault on the Eigen near the Rotstock, many, many Klafter deep inside the mountain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure, commonly based on the span of outstretched arms but variable by place; the repeated phrase indicates that the crystal vault lay very deep inside the mountain rather than supplying a modern exact depth.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarfs or earth spirits in German-speaking folklore; they remove the crystals and should not be confused with the modern German use of the word for meerkats.

f5161d7d9eadcb885482435ad0e62267ed64128c.summary: Yes, foxes are cunning; they watch a person to see whether he is lotze—lying in wait for them.

notes.label: lotze
notes.text: an Uri hunting verb meaning to lie in wait, watch, or stalk; the fox is believed able to count or detect those waiting to shoot it.

notes.label: Heuburde
notes.text: a burden or bundled load of hay; one hunter hides inside it so the fox will count only the visible man.

notes.label: Zugaden
notes.text: a local type or name of hay-storage building or barn; the hunters use it as their concealed shooting position, while the source gives no fuller architectural description.

44859e1cd81cbc92be3e09a203fb4e2281e490a3.summary: In ancient times there lived a capable smith who enjoyed a large clientele.

notes.label: Sacki
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little sack or bag; here it is the smith’s nail bag, enchanted so that a thief’s hand remains trapped inside.

5c49e214fc1041eb9bd2406c0854fc7ed8a2d26d.summary: In the village of Tenna in Graubünden, where the remarkable Bluter live, there once lived the Geschworene Valentin Suter.

notes.label: Bluter
notes.text: literally “bleeders,” the historical name used here for people at Tenna known for an inherited bleeding condition; it is an old community label rather than a supernatural term, and the source does not discuss its medical cause.

notes.label: Geschworene
notes.text: a sworn communal officer or juror in older Swiss local government; Valentin Suter’s title marks civic standing, but the exact duties and authority varied by commune and period.

notes.label: Gemeindeweibel
notes.text: the communal beadle or official messenger who summons residents and carries out council orders; here he drums the voters together, while the office’s broader duties are unstated.

notes.label: Gemeindegenosse
notes.text: a member of the local commune with recognized communal and, here, voting rights; membership historically involved more than mere residence, though the tale treats the assembled men satirically.

notes.label: Wildmännlein
notes.text: literally a “little wild man,” a small supernatural mountain dweller associated with cattle, practical knowledge, and avoidance of humans; here one recognizes the mole and later another is tricked by villagers, but the two need not be the same being.

notes.label: Wildleutchen
notes.text: literally “little wild people,” diminutive supernatural folk of the Swiss mountains who tend animals, give shrewd counsel, and withdraw after human ingratitude; the term overlaps with dwarfs and wild people but does not define a single fixed species.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Röteli
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive meaning “little red one,” the Wildmännlein’s name for the red-wine trough; it identifies the visibly red drink, not necessarily the Swiss cherry liqueur that can bear the same name.

notes.label: wie d'witt
notes.text: Swiss dialect for “as you please” or “whatever you like”; it supplies the final rhyme of the Wildmännlein’s deliberately unhelpful weather advice, and its colloquial tone is part of the joke.

9887fae519f2e9cb6196bf1671dd36e7668b439c.summary: Two men lay in wait inside a small, two-man Tatschihüsli on the Göscheneralp.

notes.label: Tatschihüsli
notes.text: a small, rudimentary local hut or shelter, here explicitly sized for two hunters; Hüsli means ‘little house,’ but the source does not explain Tatschi or the hut’s construction.

notes.label: liämsch
notes.text: an Uri dialect adverb suggesting a sly, watchful, ingratiating, or oddly familiar look; the fox peers toward the hidden hunters, but the exact shade of manner is uncertain.

notes.label: Beize
notes.text: a hunting bait or baiting place set to lure an animal within range; here the fox repeatedly returns to it despite the shots.

784bce32826fdb9aac12fc586aa7497eb022c5ba.summary: On an Alp in Schanvigg, a little beggar man wrapped in ragged clothes once approached a woman who was just boiling butter.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock-and-dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; butter-making belongs to that working landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schanvigg
notes.text: Jecklin's historical spelling of Schanfigg, the Graubünden valley in which the tale is set.

notes.label: Auf-Gehen
notes.text: literally ‘going up’ or increasing, one side of the beggar's question about the butter's state during boiling; the source does not define a more exact technical stage.

notes.label: Ab-Gehen
notes.text: literally ‘going down’ or diminishing; Jecklin explicitly glosses it as the butter's growing less, and the beggar turns the ordinary process into a perpetual curse.

85896fac6098b56b996406382fe4b0cc71b027d8.summary: Once, a wrongdoer was whipped in Zug and driven out of the country with his back raw.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally owned and used land, often shared pasture or open ground belonging to a municipality; the wrongdoer's curse makes Zug's common land barren.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Reisepfenning
notes.text: literally a ‘travel penny,’ a small coin or allowance given to someone sent away so the person does not depart wholly destitute; withholding it is treated as part of the injustice that empowers the curse.

f382c32214cb0c0fa2da686606de04f840365f20.summary: It grows on the Blümlisalp in Uri and is cursed by God because of the sins of the Sennen.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen or herders; their sins are said to have transformed a milk-giving blessed plant into a cursed herb.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

e0101f0dddb0c24d2b4fb83e4d9f0c22d29e9ef2.summary: At the far end of the Calfeisen Valley lies Alp Zarduna, which provides summer pasture for more than 290 head of cattle.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its buildings, not simply any mountain; here Alp Zarduna is large enough to summer more than 290 cattle and contains the haunted dance ground.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: traditional Ember Days or Ember seasons, quarterly periods of fasting and prayer in the Western Church; here their nights are paradoxically occasions for the devil's gatherings.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally ‘prayer bell,’ the church bell calling the community to prayer; here its ringing in Vättis ends the nocturnal revel and makes everything disappear.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Patres
notes.text: the Latin-derived German plural for ordained religious fathers or priests; here many monastery priests are away preaching for the feast, while the precise order is not named.

notes.label: Vättner
notes.text: a person from Vättis; here it identifies the former chamois hunter, now the abbot, by his home village rather than by a personal name.

0063fea33e222968033f3b2f048e047a8ec1ce00.summary: I owe the following legend to an earlier and a later account, which did not entirely agree; I have tried to reconcile them as well as possible.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

8f2e4c04f3780fe61f71587a035ddb8b7695f09e.summary: The farmhands on the Bäschneralp had decided to have a merry day and for this purpose summoned two fiddlers and several young women from the village of Bärschis to the Alp.

notes.label: Bäschneralp
notes.text: the high summer pasture associated with Bärschis; Alp denotes both the pasture and its seasonal livestock operation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alplergesellschaft
notes.text: literally ‘company of Alp workers,’ the group of herders and farmhands socializing together on the high pasture.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term for a herd of cattle pastured together, sometimes implying the organized dairy herd and its seasonal unit.

notes.label: Tatsch
notes.text: a regional pan-cooked dish, broadly a thick pancake or broken pancake preparation; the source shows it cooking in butter but does not give a recipe.

notes.label: Kesseli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small kettle, cauldron, or deep pan used over the fire.

6c0c398acee49be78206b3c2ba58d41cf7b36c63.summary: At Portels on the Flumser Kleinberg, in the Harzloch, stands a house that, like many very old houses, has a large chamber or hall.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss German and Alpine term for a steep, narrow ravine or gorge; here it is the uncanny chasm through which the Schilz rushes below the natural bridge.

notes.label: Gwelb
notes.text: the local dialect form of Gewölbe, ‘vault’; in this story it is the proper local name for the upper natural rock bridge over the Tobel, not a built ceiling.

60259d69ea8230ccad2ebadf8efca909f62110ac.summary: Near the Giessbach lies an open promontory toward Lake Brienz, covered with splendid grass and called the Tanzplatz in local speech.

notes.label: Tanzplatz
notes.text: literally ‘dance place,’ the local name for the grassy promontory where Alpine workers gathered; it is a remembered communal site, not a formal ballroom.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: male Alpine dairy herders who tend cattle and make cheese on high summer pastures; ‘herdsmen’ alone misses the dairy occupation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennerinnen
notes.text: female Alpine dairy workers or herders, the feminine counterpart of Sennen; the term places the dancers within seasonal mountain-pasture life.

fad4b1199eafb60f7291b135de7cd843e2abb3af.summary: Tanzplatz and Spielplatz are local names frequently found in Aargau for woodland and pasture.

notes.label: Tanzplatz
notes.text: literally ‘dancing place,’ a recurring Aargau field- and woodland name associated with supernatural dances; here it names both communal pasture and a forest clearing.

notes.label: Spielplatz
notes.text: literally ‘play place,’ another recurring local landscape-name; here it identifies a wooded height linked with a witches' Sabbath, not a modern children's playground.

notes.label: Almend
notes.text: communally owned or collectively used village land, especially pasture; here the common land near Unterentfelden bears the name Tanzplatz.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Elfliwiese
notes.text: literally ‘little-elf meadow,’ the meadow beside the Seengen fir forest; the diminutive Elfli suggests small supernatural beings, though this passage gives no separate legend about them.

notes.label: Brunnenjungfern
notes.text: literally ‘well maidens’ or ‘spring maidens,’ female water spirits associated with wells and springs; here they are remembered as dancing with woodland beings.

notes.label: Waldmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little forest men,’ diminutive woodland spirits; here they dance with the Brunnenjungfern at named clearings and pastures.

notes.label: Hexentanz
notes.text: literally ‘witches' dance,’ the local explanation for dark rings in mountain-meadow grass; it overlaps with wider fairy-ring traditions but is explicitly attributed to witches here.

a5f8cb3fcff6f6de5e1c7095de85b408ae090cf7.summary: Yes, one has often heard it said that when a person goes hunting at night, not everything out there is clean unless one has something blessed along.

notes.label: Osterchohlä
notes.text: literally ‘Easter charcoal,’ charcoal from the blessed Easter fire carried here as a sacramental protection beneath the gunpowder; the practice reflects Catholic folk belief rather than an ordinary ingredient in ammunition.

notes.label: Fuxätüssi
notes.text: the Uri dialect name for the fox-hunting ambush or baiting place where the hunter lies in wait; its exact physical construction is not described.

notes.label: Steimittschä
notes.text: Uri dialect for a heap or pile of stones, explicitly glossed by the collector; it provides the hunter’s cover.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure, locally variable but roughly the span of outstretched arms; ‘several Klafter’ conveys a substantial fall without inventing a modern conversion.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Port
notes.text: the source’s Uri terrain word for the steep frozen slope or ground down which the hunter is thrown; the exact landform cannot be established from this passage.

notes.label: Jetz witt doch ga lüegä, ob's der Tyfel nid äu 'putzt heig!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘Now you had better go and see whether the devil has not got him too!’; the verb 'putzt is idiomatic and may imply seizing, striking, or doing away with the fox.
notes.anchor: Jetz witt doch ga lüegä, ob's der Tyfel nid äu 'putzt heig!

notes.label: Gspor
notes.text: Uri dialect for a trace, track, or sign; not even the least evidence of a real fox remains in daylight.

e68f5fe57683bd1f669b72907d91ff5074bc8cd0.summary: After the death of Duke Galeazzo Sforza of Milan in the year 1478, all sorts of disputes arose between the land of Uri and the rulers of Milan, until at last the Landammann of Uri and his councilors declared war on the duke and his wife.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity; here the officeholder of Uri directs war policy.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘confederates’ or ‘oath-comrades,’ the troops and members of the Old Swiss Confederacy.

notes.label: Lauine
notes.text: an older spelling of Lawine, an avalanche; it kills sixty Zurich troops during the Alpine crossing.

notes.label: Landespanner
notes.text: the cantonal banner and, by extension, the force mustered beneath it; Panner is an older Swiss spelling of Banner.

notes.label: Landsturm
notes.text: the general territorial militia levied for local defense rather than a standing professional force.

notes.label: Christmonats
notes.text: genitive of Christmonat, literally ‘Christ month,’ a traditional name for December; the date is therefore December 27.

notes.label: Fußeisen
notes.text: iron traction fittings, cleats, or crampon-like devices worn on the feet, giving the Swiss secure footing on the ice.

5466d05a5055edd1d2eeca2f4f6e132e518c7b44.summary: On the western slope of the Davoser-Schwarzhorn, a district bears, not without reason, the name “tote Alpe”; it is the most dreadful wasteland imaginable.

notes.label: Davoser-Schwarzhorn
notes.text: Jecklin’s compound name for the Schwarzhorn associated with Davos; the dead pasture lies on its western slope.

notes.label: tote Alpe
notes.text: literally “dead Alp,” the local name for the barren high-pasture district; Alpe denotes the grazing tract rather than only a mountain.

notes.label: todte Alpe
notes.text: the older spelling used later in the same source for tote Alpe, “dead Alp”; both printed forms are preserved.

notes.label: Molken
notes.text: in historical Alpine usage, a collective term for dairy produce and not necessarily only modern English “whey”; the tale emphasizes the pasture’s former dairy abundance.

bc8b35928b32b8b55c1713fd6c1b9384a076fc49.summary: A young knight, Kunz von Stein, once rode into the land of Glarus. He was a poor fighting man who possessed nothing but a humble, gloomy Burgstall that seemed to consist entirely of corners.

notes.label: Kunz von Stein
notes.text: the poor adventuring knight's name; Kunz is a traditional short form of Konrad, while von Stein marks his minor noble identity.

notes.label: Burgstall
notes.text: the site or remains of a castle and, by extension here, Kunz's poor castle dwelling; it need not imply a functioning grand fortress.

notes.label: Blustregen
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘blossom rain,’ the fragrant continual fall of linden blossoms into Windegg's abandoned courtyard.

notes.label: Burgfräulein
notes.text: a young noblewoman or maiden of a castle; Kunz assumes the silent reader is the wealthy daughter of the house.

notes.label: ewigen Lichtes
notes.text: the source's inflected form of ‘eternal light,’ the sanctuary lamp kept burning before the consecrated altar in a Catholic chapel; its dim glow illuminates the animated tombs.

notes.label: Berta von Windegg
notes.text: the last maiden of Windegg's line and Kunz's dead betrothed, whose hoped-for release fails when he cannot answer the marriage vow.

2a8e4d7dd2c75b36386571b57b6c744c7d69f0eb.summary: I have heard from old people that around the year of Our Lord 1526 there were two good fellows and drinking companions, one from the March in the canton of Schwyz and the other from Rapperswil.

notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or presiding official of a Swiss canton or rural polity; ‘governor’ is only approximate and misses the office’s specific confederal and cantonal setting.

3d4d275e25f302cabd80854ed709e3b4f92c63c6.summary: When he was a fourteen-year-old boy, a citizen of Schuders had for a time to help his father, who served as the Messmer, perform the Tagläuten because an injured hand kept the father from pulling the bell alone.

notes.label: Messmer
notes.text: a church sexton or sacristan responsible for practical duties including ringing the bells.

notes.label: Tagläuten
notes.text: the ringing of a church bell to announce daybreak; here it is performed before dawn on Christmas night.

notes.label: Christnacht
notes.text: literally ‘Christ night,’ the night of Christmas Eve into Christmas Day, a sacred and liminal time in Alpine folklore.

notes.label: wind und weh
notes.text: a regional expression for becoming faint, sick, and deeply distressed; the spectral murmuring and lament affect both witnesses physically.

665f7f658e3cdcd1910c5a125dd888b728498f75.summary: There are days in the year on which the Church and devout believers customarily perform special prayers, devotions, and good works for the comfort of the departed.

notes.label: Seelentage
notes.text: literally ‘souls’ days,’ special days of prayer and good works for the departed; folk belief also makes them moments when the dead or the spirits of those soon to die can be seen.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss regional title for a church sexton or sacristan, responsible here for ringing the burial bell; his church office places him in the role of both seer and final victim.

notes.label: Loser
notes.text: a dialect word for a listener or eavesdropper; the unseen voice uses it for the Sigrist who hears the dead being enrolled, thereby enrolling him as well.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for souls of the departed still needing prayer and release, often understood as souls in purgatory rather than harmful ghosts.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

notes.label: gesegneten Stein
notes.text: literally ‘blessed stone,’ paired by the source with French pierre bénit as a landmark on the Bernese border; its precise physical form and ritual history are not described.

notes.label: Hilari-Seelentag
notes.text: a local January souls’ day associated with Saint Hilary, when the departed are believed to leave the villages and return to the high snowfields; the source gives no precise calendar date.

notes.text: a Valais dialect form meaning uncanny, haunted, or inhabited by something supernatural; the chapel’s precise disturbance is the priest’s recurring appearance.

38bae8b749bd48638489ab8f7b69952f1ea028ae.summary: On August 8, 1375, Baron Anton vom Turm had the venerable Bishop of Sion, Witschard Tavelli, and his court chaplain thrown down from Seta Castle to die a violent death.

notes.label: Kreuzbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘Cross Spring’ in German, paired in the bilingual Valais name with French fontaine des croix; the many small wooden crosses planted by drinkers commemorate Bishop Tavelli's death there.

4d9b3e6c2cfc61f52b7e928974b401f57e987794.summary: In former times, there were very many judges with power over life and death.

notes.label: Freigerichte
notes.text: historical territorial courts or jurisdictions possessing authority to impose capital punishment; despite frei, ‘free,’ the term does not mean that defendants received judgment without cost or constraint.

notes.label: zer Metjen
notes.text: a local Valais place expression within Täsch identifying where Schallbetter lived; the source gives no explanation sufficient to resolve its exact modern form or literal meaning.

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally ‘God's acre,’ a traditional German term for a consecrated cemetery or churchyard; the severed head repeatedly returns there instead of remaining at the execution ground.

fa2ec8eb840583d0727743065c8db3bb2c1cb965.summary: Not far from the Bruderbalm on the Bürgenberg (Bürgenstock), a strange spring rises in the depths of the lake.

notes.label: Bruderbalm
notes.text: literally ‘brother's Balm,’ the named rock shelter near the Bürgenstock; Balm is a Swiss Alpine word for a shallow cave or overhang, while the identity of the ‘brother’ is not explained here.

ffae4fbcd8eaccd485023db4bc2f784b998eda5c.summary: The lords of Trostburg and Liebegg were jointly required to survey the valley's entire Bann and divide it anew among the local country people.

notes.text: a legally bounded district, jurisdiction, or body of common land rather than a magical ban in this context.

notes.label: Bannteile
notes.text: the allotted shares into which the land of the Bann was divided; making one share disappear is the lords' fraud.

notes.label: Hundsloch
notes.text: literally ‘dog hole,’ the named rock cleft where the punished lords' spectral coach and dog-associated apparition vanish.

notes.label: Bannteiler
notes.text: an official or landholder responsible for dividing land within a Bann; the title literally means ‘divider of the Bann.’

notes.text: normally a Swiss German kinship term associated with a baptismal sponsor, used here by the godmother when addressing the boy; whether the source uses it reciprocally for a godchild or as an affectionate form is uncertain.

notes.text: in Swiss usage, an Alp is a high seasonal pasture and its associated working landscape, here Findels; the precise bounds of this named Alp are unspecified.

2d9649c9b90d369f07e67a531bd032907859b34a.summary: A small, lovely mountain lake on the slope of the Bristenstock, separated from the abyss by only a narrow band of rock, will one day burst out and flood the region.
