notes.text: literally a wandering scholar or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning and secret knowledge of treasure; here the role is one possible identity of the stranger who knows what lies inside the Bristenstock.

notes.label: Vynediger
notes.text: a regional form of ‘Venetian,’ used in Alpine legend for a foreign mineral seeker, treasure-knower, or magician credited with secret knowledge of mountain riches; the story does not distinguish those roles precisely.

83e3d40ab64034c2dd26beba5ccc1f29fd921f9b.summary: At Lammerbach in the Brunni valley, where a broad Boden is now covered with debris and scree, there was once magnificent pastureland.

notes.label: Boden
notes.text: a broad, comparatively level tract of ground or valley floor in Alpine place-description; here it is the debris-covered area left by the collapse.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation; the title describes the loss of such grazing land, not the destruction of an entire mountain.

0c600dc4803a647f11f45839fc82e840938cc38a.summary: Thys Gruber of Bärswil in the upper Simmental was a fortunate man. He owned the finest alps far and wide, so that his neighbors could rightly call him Rich Thys.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.text: The difficult hour refers to childbirth; Lauigraben was retained as the local ravine name.

ec37b7d200dc07aad5bbdcd4c6229cfb6d4f583a.summary: Between the Furggengütsch (fork, branching pass) and the Steinige Matt on the Hohgant in the Bernese Oberland, the gorge of the Karrhohlen opens southeastward toward the Alpine pastures of Bösälgäu, its floor filled with fragments of rock.

notes.label: Furggengütsch
notes.text: a local topographic name built from Furgg or Furke, a fork or mountain pass, and Gütsch, a projecting hill, ridge, or elevated knoll.

notes.label: Karrhohlen
notes.text: the local gorge name; Karr may evoke carts, as the legend suggests, while Hohlen can mean a hollow way or ravine, but the tale itself treats the derivation as uncertain.

notes.label: Alpläger
notes.text: the resting or encampment ground on an Alp where livestock gathers and herders operate; here low earthworks around it are interpreted as former city walls.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ benevolent dwarf-like Alpine beings who protect the settlement until its inhabitants become corrupt.

notes.label: Furggefluh
notes.text: the dialect compound in the warning's first line, meaning the cliff or rock face at the Furgg; ‘D' Furggefluh ist g'spalten’ says that this rock face has split.

notes.label: Schlegel und Wegge erkalten
notes.text: a cryptic dialect warning literally saying that ‘mallet and wedge grow cold’; it evokes tools ceasing work or an appointed time running out, and its precise proverbial force is uncertain.

notes.label: wer fliehen will, der lauf
notes.text: the closing dialect command, ‘whoever wishes to flee, let them run,’ making the preceding omen an urgent warning of destruction.

89493ab077dde9050d185af085714f697bf20d17.summary: Folk legend has quite a different account of this event from what our historical narrative presently indicates.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: plural of Zwingherr, meaning oppressive castle rulers or tyrannical feudal lords in the vocabulary of Swiss popular liberation traditions.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: literally a ‘coercive lord,’ an oppressive castle ruler or tyrannical feudal lord against whom rural people rebel in the legend.

notes.label: Brüllen
notes.text: literally ‘bellowing’ or ‘roaring’; the legend explains the local place-name through the dying cries attributed to the lord and his men.

notes.label: Heimwesen
notes.text: a Swiss term for a rural homestead or landed farm holding, including its house and associated land rather than only the dwelling.

notes.label: Grossrath
notes.text: an older spelling of Grossrat, a member of a cantonal Grand Council; it identifies Zbinden's public office, not part of his surname.

notes.label: Schwefelbergbad
notes.text: literally ‘Sulfur Mountain spa,’ the name of a Bernese medicinal-bath establishment whose proprietor is identified in the source.

4a27705b947dfad60495fe5dfa7b2d4671057237.summary: Many, many years ago, according to a tale from Goms, Gross-Ernen was a stately village in the region near Fiesch.

3393bb13a86203bd44a0ba682311087417f3c1c2.summary: At Rinderbüel in the Maderan Valley, an entire Sennten lies buried beneath a mighty mass of stone debris.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: an organized Alpine herd or the whole cattle-and-dairy unit under a Senn, not merely an unstructured group of cows; the rockfall destroys the livestock and working community together.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the name Rinderbüel is attached to this pastoral place after the catastrophe.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd, milk work, and cheesemaking on a seasonal pasture; in both versions he recognizes the danger before the other workers do.

notes.label: Trychelchüehli
notes.text: a little cow wearing a Trychel, the characteristic hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; the diminutive marks the poor widow's sole cow, which alone survives with the herdsman.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter, overhang, or shallow cave used here to house the calf separately; the exact shape of the Rinderbüel shelter is not described.

0b67fae3abc78669baf00914b0e9a2b42fed700e.summary: Where Burglauinen [Burglauenen] now stands in the canton of Bern, there was once a beautiful village called Schillingsdorf.

4c06768ff57390de76e1ee0882735e98da245289.summary: Where the Turtmann Glacier now fills the head of the valley with its masses of ice, there once lay the flower-rich Blümlisalp, the most beautiful Alp in the entire valley.

6bd7a36804ef0e7c420747146e649e38e3465c98.summary: On the right bank of Lake Thun, not far from Ralligen Castle’s tower and the little village of Merligen, the city of Roll lies buried beneath rubble, according to a widespread legend.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like Alpine being associated with mountains and mines; here it is a hospitable stranger who alone foresees and warns of the rockslide.

notes.label: Schlegel und Wegge
notes.text: the warning rhyme’s dialect phrase, most closely ‘mallets and wedges’; it suggests rock-splitting tools standing ready, but the precise supernatural image and the historical form Wegge remain somewhat uncertain.

1f8b5c0228928076cdad885b023bc73828c00500.summary: The G'wüestboden in the Göscheneralp Valley, today a desolate field of rubble, was formerly called the Jäntelboden and was a flourishing meadow.

notes.label: G'wüestboden
notes.text: the present local name of the ruined ground in the Göscheneralp Valley, approximately ‘devastated ground’ or ‘waste ground’; the story contrasts it with the former fertile Jäntelboden.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its livestock-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; horses once grazed on the fertile ground before its destruction.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: hennt dri' g'niält
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the two women rummaged, stirred, or worked about in the spring; the exact physical action and purpose are not described.

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: the plural of an Uri regional word for destructive debris flows or mountain torrents carrying rock, mud, and water; they rush down with the streams and bury the meadow.

2680d34ed180d70b4d23cf82c569009d077fc6e9.summary: Toward Lenk, the valley broadens. The slopes are strewn with cozy little houses in which happiness, joy, and merry songs dwell.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or cry of joy, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; the boy’s cry sounds defiantly through the oppressive air.

eab3c6873d18883a5bd23644cdd5e3b9bb707558.summary: At the end of the 18th century, there were stern rulers and oppressed people not only in Switzerland but in every other country of Europe as well.

notes.label: Eidgenoß
notes.text: the historical singular form of Eidgenosse, literally an ‘oath-comrade’ or member of the Swiss Confederacy; in the poem it addresses a Swiss Guardsman through the Confederates' ideal of sworn loyalty.

08197399aeb5b92a98483fde8ab83ff54c8d6af7.summary: A fahrender Schüler prophesied that one day the “Hengst,” the rocky, steep slope of the “Spitze” below Alp Obsaum, would collapse and fill the narrow valley west of Unterschächen.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’; in German-language folklore this is an itinerant learned man credited with prophecy, magic, or occult knowledge rather than an ordinary school pupil.

b0dd408beb289faa8591e040ff0a697f2121b140.summary: Today there are two Alp holdings at Fellenen, Vorderwaldi and Hinterwaldi. In former times they formed a single magnificent mountain estate called Waldi and belonged to a rich farmer.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, dairy work, and grazing rights, not simply a mountain peak; Vorderwaldi and Hinterwaldi are two such working holdings formed from the earlier Waldi.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young women, using the characteristic -li diminutive; the three Waldi-Meitli are old enough to attend dances and later marry.

notes.label: Fastnacht
notes.text: the pre-Lenten carnival season in German-speaking Switzerland, marked here by community dancing rather than merely a single night.

notes.label: Senntenhütte
notes.text: the working hut of a Sennten, an organized Alpine cattle herd and dairying unit; the rock breaks loose above this central pastoral building.

notes.label: Viehsennten
notes.text: organized livestock herds together with their Alpine herding and dairy units, not merely scattered individual animals; the source says both people and these pastoral groups were buried.

ef84b989366971ef079a06bf83c830e25bfd5a44.summary: When the four-o'clock stroke sounds dull and solemn from the church tower at Schänis in the evening, a mysterious being on Petruns Alp above Rüttiberg, awakened by the holy sound, begins its activity.

notes.label: Petruns Alp
notes.text: the named high pasture above Rüttiberg where both bell and buried spirit are heard; Alp denotes a summer pasture and its associated farm buildings.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an alpine herdsman and dairyman; in the first account, his aggressive pursuit of the supernatural bell leaves him paralyzed.

notes.label: Dätsch
notes.text: the spelling used at the end of the second account for the same mysterious being called Detsch in the title.

notes.label: Detsch
notes.text: the title-name of the elusive buried apparition whose call shifts underground; the body gives the variant spelling Dätsch, and the name's literal sense is uncertain.

d97a7a6ea7a61ad02e1c82d81357b5b57c4b98c5.summary: One of the rises, or Knubel, of Mount Rigi is called Bärenzingel. Not far from it, the municipality of Weggis owned an Alp that bordered above upon another belonging to the people of Arth and was called Langen-Moos.

notes.label: Knubel
notes.text: a rounded rise, knoll, or hump in the landscape; Cysat uses it for one of Mount Rigi's elevations.

notes.label: Bärenzingel
notes.text: the local name of the Rigi rise haunted by the damaging specter; Bären suggests bears, while Zingel can denote a belt or enclosure, but the exact place-name history is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture with its livestock, rights, buildings, and boundaries; the threatened movement of the entire Alp is both a landslide and supernatural judgment.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Langen-Moos
notes.text: literally ‘long marsh’ or ‘long moss,’ the Weggis Alp into which the specter descends and whose ground begins to shift.

notes.label: Crützgang
notes.text: Cysat's early-modern spelling of Kreuzgang, a religious procession carrying a cross; it is one of two competing remedies used against the specter.

notes.label: Bettfart
notes.text: an early-modern form meaning a prayer pilgrimage or penitential procession; it joins communal worship to the Crützgang at the endangered site.

notes.label: Tüffelbeschwörer
notes.text: Swiss and early-modern spelling for ‘devil-conjurer,’ a ritual specialist believed able to command or banish the specter; Cysat condemns this remedy as forbidden magic.

d4706be6a3f4d9eb68109b5ef80f3949c3d6b03b.summary: On the sunny side of the Schrattenfluh in the Entlibuch lies a barren region almost without roots.

notes.label: Schrattenfluh
notes.text: the karst mountain ridge whose bare, furrowed limestone landscape the legend explains as the result of a curse.

notes.label: Entlibuch
notes.text: the source's historical spelling of Entlebuch, the Lucerne region containing the Schrattenfluh.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: plural of Alp, high seasonal livestock pastures and dairying settlements rather than the entire Alpine range.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman, here the sole owner of the once-fertile high pasture.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, often made from the whey left after other cheese production; the brothers replace it with dung in the blind man's milk.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its farmstead, the productive landscape destroyed together with the cruel brothers.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

805a576a2e781a44676c27b943be71c436b2a280.summary: D’s Macolvi was the cleverest little man in Lenk. But he was forfeit to the Devil, and whenever the Devil came from time to time to fetch him, they made a wager together.

notes.label: D’s Macolvi
notes.text: the Bernese dialect name, with a neuter article, for Lenk's proverbially clever little man; the unusual grammatical gender gives the figure a diminutive, folktale-like quality even though English uses he and him.

623907bdc492bb326c8c8b699b1bf3c1c445d834.summary: The beautiful auricula primrose—Linnaeus’s Primula Arioula—blooms on rocks in the Alps and Prealps and is therefore called Fluhblume in the Waldstätten.

notes.label: Fluhblume
notes.text: literally ‘rock-face flower,’ a central Swiss name for the auricula primrose growing on steep Alpine cliffs; its dangerous habitat makes it a traditional pledge of courageous love.

notes.label: Waldstätten
notes.text: the traditional collective name for the central Swiss forest cantons around Lake Lucerne; usage and canton membership vary historically, so it is more culturally specific than simply ‘forest regions.’

notes.label: Badönikli
notes.text: the Entlebuch regional name given for the auricula primrose; its literal derivation is uncertain, and the source records it chiefly as a local plant name.

notes.label: Händscheli
notes.text: the Zurich-area diminutive meaning ‘little glove,’ a local name for the auricula primrose inspired by its form or appearance.

notes.label: Bärenöhrli
notes.text: the Aargau diminutive meaning ‘little bear’s ear,’ a local name for the auricula primrose and close to the plant’s broader ‘bear’s ear’ naming tradition.

notes.label: Florblümli
notes.text: the Glarus diminutive meaning approximately ‘little Flor flower,’ a local auricula name whose first element’s exact sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Fräulischlössli
notes.text: the Graubünden name literally suggesting a ‘young lady’s little castle,’ used for the auricula primrose; the figurative basis is not explained in the passage.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: the plural of Fluh, steep exposed Alpine rock faces or crags; the terrain term explains both the flower’s name and the mortal danger of gathering it.

notes.label: Fluhblumen
notes.text: the plural of Fluhblume, the cliff-growing auriculas brought as bouquets and pledges of love; the regional plural is retained because it names the culturally significant flowers rather than generic blooms.

7af17a3b1b3c4c0de30a8ed1a1a889e79beb4988.summary: a) While threshing, a farmer's servants in Hergiswil talked about all kinds of ghostly things.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Wart
notes.text: the named high mountain pasture above Illgau; the tale gives Wart both as its established name and as the shouted command ‘wait,’ making the fatal delay an origin story for the place-name.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: the traditional open-air assembly at which eligible citizens of a Swiss canton vote directly; the source associates an old meeting place with the Alp's boundary landscape.

notes.label: Kuhdeischlig
notes.text: Schwyz dialect for cow droppings or a cowpat; the collector jokes that the dialect tale retains its native pastoral dress with this manure still attached.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a high pasture; the older Senn's religious admonition contrasts with the younger herders' reckless game.

notes.label: Avetüre
notes.text: the local Schwyz name for an adventurous feat, stunt, or gymnastic amusement; here it means a dangerous contest rather than a narrated adventure.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working seasonally on an Alp; here it refers to the herders who abandon the hanging man to chase the fox.

notes.label: Der Grüön
notes.text: Schwyz dialect for ‘the Green One,’ an indirect name for the Devil or an uncanny green figure; the source places him on the hut roof but does not explain his exact relation to the fox.

notes.label: Steischlinggäre
notes.text: a Schwyz dialect term for a stone-slinging implement; the source shows Werni intending to throw a stone upward with it, but its precise construction is not described.

ef937fede5cf481da162d182d010711ed4447aa0.summary: Two wayward brothers once lived in Merligen. During a bitter quarrel, each called upon the Devil to make the other's fields and meadows barren forever.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Basi
notes.text: in Valais dialect, Basi is a familiar term for a female cousin or aunt, used deceptively for the Devil’s female form; the exact kinship sense intended by the Senno is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, an Alp is a high seasonal pasture and its working settlement, here the setting for summer dairying; the particular Alp and its location are not identified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senno
notes.text: this Valais dialect form of Senn denotes the Alpine dairyman whose negligence and pact drive the tale; his exact rank within the hut’s work group is uncertain.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Wichwasser
notes.text: this dialect form means holy water and marks the herder’s protective devotional practice; the source does not specify its blessing or container beyond the later vessel.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Grimpol
notes.text: the Senno uses this apparently contemptuous dialect word for the blessed crucifix and holy-water vessel; its precise literal meaning, spelling, and degree of insult are uncertain.

notes.label: Nachtgschiwwata
notes.text: this Valais dialect image means approximately a nocturnal shadow or fleeting night apparition, describing the Basi’s secret arrival; its exact literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Summerig
notes.text: this dialect term denotes the Alpine summer season and its period of grazing and dairying before descent; the exact calendar dates are unspecified.

notes.label: Stubji
notes.text: this Valais diminutive denotes a small room or parlor inside the Alpine hut; its precise function and layout are uncertain.

7e1f41316558507a642d80f0bc12de14019a314f.summary: a) Alraune as a Child. People believed Alraunen could be found beneath a white hazel bush upon which mistletoe grew.

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: the magical mandrake and, by extension, a childlike, animal, or root-figure familiar believed to multiply money; these accounts deliberately vary its physical form, while repeatedly treating ownership as a pact with the devil.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, traditional quarterly Catholic periods of fasting and prayer; Swiss and Alpine folklore often treats these liminal observances as times when supernatural beings or hidden things become accessible.

notes.label: Hochgericht
notes.text: literally a “high court,” but historically also the authority and physical execution place associated with capital justice; here it means gallows or execution-ground sites rather than a modern appellate court.

notes.label: Ilgen
notes.text: an older regional plant word, usually referring to lilies or sometimes iris-like flowers; the exact species whose roots were carved into fraudulent Alraunen is not established by the source.

notes.label: Krone
notes.text: a crown-denominated coin rather than a royal crown; the account calls Zender's example false, implying counterfeit money used in cheating, but does not specify its issuing authority or value.

notes.label: Hausi
notes.text: a familiar Swiss German personal name or nickname, often related to Hans; the narrator says the man's family name could be supplied but was customarily withheld in favor of this name.

notes.label: Arun
notes.text: the dialect form of Alraune in the final oral account; there it is a toadlike dependent familiar passed from owner to owner, with the third possessor doomed to die alongside it.

2f65c3a965dfcb92397ea84ebd5352a285be1fc3.summary: As in many places, Menznau in the canton of Lucerne performed at its Resurrection celebration the Osterspiel scene in which devils raged inside the church during the procession.

notes.label: Osterspiel
notes.text: an Osterspiel is a traditional Easter or Resurrection drama, here staged as part of a Lucerne church procession; the source does not specify the script, date, or exact form of the local performance.

7a454f303ae7b78ff8225207048d93cd059d9316.summary: The holy Easter festival had come. For the afternoon sermon, Beatus also traveled across the Wendelsee to Einigen on his cloak.

notes.label: Wendelsee
notes.text: a historical regional name for Lake Thun, used in legends of Saint Beatus; readers should understand it as the same lake rather than a separate body of water.

37e3823a99a1e298b341544ef2bc57cc3a61c441.summary: a) During the building of the Rapperswil bridge, the cheated Devil kicked from behind the dog that leaped across first in place of a human being.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a ghostly huntsman or leader of a nocturnal wild hunt in Central Swiss tradition, accompanied by hounds; the permanently open house provides a passage for his night chase.

72d41465c7bd2733f3a0ddc0ca3ba65bc91c9d2f.summary: King Rudolf of Strättlingen once had a remarkable dream. This dream moved him to build twelve churches throughout the area from Frutigen down to Thierachern and to found a monastery at Amsoldingen.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

40f4a88b558b701719a3c4b4d67c07dd19e67c76.summary: While visiting a sick person, a priest saw someone reading a little book that caught his attention.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

e1aa25c24d2b50e04fcf2c43d0ff44ae312cdb21.summary: The Evil One himself once appeared in Grub and was naturally no welcome guest.

notes.label: Töbeli
notes.text: the Swiss German diminutive of Tobel, a steep, often wooded ravine; here it refers to the nearby Sacktobel as the devil's destination.

notes.label: Chöbeli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little Kübel—a tub, pail, or bucket; here it is the supernatural container in which the devil is transported and grows too heavy to move.

notes.label: Ins Töbeli im Chöbeli!
notes.text: a rhyming Swiss German exclamation meaning ‘Into the little ravine in the little tub!’; here the devil names both the place of his confinement and the vessel that will carry him there.

notes.label: Sacktobel
notes.text: the local name of the ravine where the devil is confined; Tobel means a steep ravine, while Sack suggests an enclosed or dead-end shape, although the tale does not explain the place-name.

33c14277777105acb9225ea635e16cc04e803ebe.summary: It appears that, in the ruinous works he intended to carry out in the Bündner-Oberland, the evil spirit chiefly set his mind upon using stones as the aids and tools of his dark, calamitous deeds: in Vals, in Ladir, and, according to the following legend, in Savien as well. —

notes.label: Bündner-Oberland
notes.text: the German regional name for the upper Graubünden country, broadly the Surselva and neighboring uplands; it identifies the setting of the related stone legends.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a grammatical or regional form of Alp, a high mountain pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation; Camana and Theuri are working grazing landscapes, not simply mountain peaks.

notes.label: melchsten
notes.text: a regional superlative associated with producing abundant milk; the source itself glosses the herbs as the most fragrant and productive.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp-Entladung
notes.text: the seasonal clearing of a high Alp when livestock, people, and equipment descend after the summer grazing period.

notes.label: Talfahrt
notes.text: literally the journey down into the valley, the seasonal descent of herds and Alpine workers at the end of high-pasture grazing.

notes.label: Johanni
notes.text: the feast of St. John the Baptist, traditionally observed on June 24; here the church bells rung for its patron interrupt Satanas’s work.

notes.label: schurig
notes.text: a regional form meaning horrible, eerie, or causing a shudder; the narrator reports it as a proposed folk etymology for Theuri and its variants.

d7f38715fe1f0fb9c7b4b23c258ec43e3dc46159.summary: Without realizing what he was doing, a man once read from a book of magic, and then—Gott b'hiätis darvor—the Devil entered the Stube in the shape of a large, black, shaggy dog and refused to leave.

notes.label: Gott b'hiätis darvor
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘God preserve us from it’; the protective aside accompanies the dangerous naming and arrival of the Devil.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of a German-speaking Alpine house; the conjured dog-shaped Devil enters it and refuses to leave.

notes.label: Agathamehl
notes.text: flour blessed in connection with Saint Agatha, whose sacramentals were traditionally associated with protection against fire and other danger; here the consecrated flour compels the Devil to depart.

notes.label: Da friss, Büdel, und darnah mach-di fort!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Here, eat, cur, and then be off!’; Büdel is a contemptuous address to the shaggy dog-shaped Devil.
notes.anchor: Da friss, Büdel, und darnah mach-di fort!

notes.label: baschta
notes.text: a dialect form of Italian basta, meaning enough, settled, or in any case; the storyteller uses it to close off doubt about the Devil being forced to swallow the flour.

547b4ec217f0504d351b3414079e4fc6d2f90f2d.summary: Between Schwyz and the Muota Valley, in the Häsingen region opposite Selgis, a great stone slab lies beside the country road.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fb27147d76b8575a17ffaa8b39d8f7c9cf16b08f.summary: a) The Unterhauser had exhausted every artifice in trying to sow discord between an honorable married couple.

notes.label: Unterhauser
notes.text: literally an “under-houser” or inhabitant of below, a regional euphemistic name for the Devil that avoids naming him directly.

notes.label: Räspi
notes.text: a small twig or little branch, explicitly glossed as Ästlein by the collector; the Devil keeps the stream between himself and the woman even while delivering her reward.

44e15666788686e37dc88654c72f23536635195a.summary: A reckless young man from Entlibuch met a sad end. He had once climbed the Kreuzfluh on the Hohgant.

notes.label: Potz Krüz
notes.text: this Alemannic euphemistic oath invokes the Cross, approximately ‘By the Cross,’ at the instant of the young man’s fall; its exact force and pronunciation are uncertain.

64afaaef73b22a3c90f684da19fdb1585a535b9a.summary: Saint Beatus was accustomed to preach at Aesch. Once, when he was somewhat delayed, his companion Saint Achatus had taken his place.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

1a67183cc338ae078829de86e2e3bcdbbe5c575c.summary: Once the Devil came to Strättlingen Castle dressed poorly as a pilgrim. Because it was very cold, Lord Wernhardt took pity on him and sent him his cloak to cover himself.

notes.label: About this telling

ec91358ae1503f8067f4f385ae57915334f1b7af.summary: Every evening, a bed must stand prepared in a secluded room in the tower at Wyl.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin and small unit of money whose value varied by canton and period; here several Batzen serve as the supernatural guest's lodging fee.

829ab80f58b5beedda3b92b97e27c023c6537a7d.summary: There once was a woman who led a wicked life. She met a gentleman and took him home.

notes.label: Geissfuss
notes.text: Swiss German spelling for ‘goat's foot’; the source's Appenzell dialect uses the plural Gässfüess, and the concealed goat feet reveal the apparently genteel stranger as the Devil.

ded6a603a4874ad538d38054bc185a64ce003f74.summary: One evening, several men sat together in the tavern at Pont-la-ville and discussed the need for a bridge over the Sarine, whose waves there foam and rage in a wild whirlpool between rocks and cliffs as nowhere else along its course.

notes.label: Wams
notes.text: a close-fitting historical man's jacket or doublet; here its green color first makes the disguised devil appear to be a hunter.

109c534623acfbc41e0affcf2bfe7420c0bf4ca4.summary: A poor farmer came home through driving snow and sat on the bench by the stove.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small Swiss coin denomination; its historical value varied, while here it emphasizes that the sum is exact to the last coin.

notes.label: Ellermutter
notes.text: an obscure traditional name for an old female figure accompanying the Devil, often understood as a devil's grandmother or elder mother; the source does not define her identity.

notes.label: Erbsmus
notes.text: a thick pea dish or pea purée; it is the culturally specific meal used in the trick, and its exact preparation varies regionally.

notes.label: Frauenfasten
notes.text: a regional calendrical observance or women's fast-night associated here with the gift of protective white peas; its precise local date and custom are not explained.

79923e83b19946270147291fc70348447956fc5e.summary: In the Bernese Oberland, on the wooded mountain ridge between the upper Simmental and the Diemtigtal, lies a beautiful Alp rich in grass that is used by the Sennen of the municipality of Zweisimmen; it is called the Gestelenalp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture with its working landscape and buildings, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled alpine dairymen responsible for herds and cheese production during the summer pasture season.

notes.label: Gestelenalp
notes.text: the named high pasture used by Zweisimmen's herders and the setting of the annual gathering and the footprint rock.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work on an Alp during the grazing season; here the word includes the regional alpine community attending the festival.

notes.label: Dorfet
notes.text: a communal social visit or gathering, here an annual Sunday mountain festival bringing together herders from the surrounding valleys.

notes.label: Sennerinnen
notes.text: female alpine dairy workers or herders; the wealthy young Sennerin at the center of the legend belongs to this working community.

notes.label: Gestelengrat
notes.text: the Gestelen ridge, which forms both the watershed and the boundary between the Simmental and Diemtigtal sides.

notes.label: Teufelstritt
notes.text: literally the ‘Devil's step’ or ‘Devil's footprint,’ the name given to the footprint-like hollows and, by extension, the rock that preserves the warning legend.

notes.label: Dorfsonntag
notes.text: the Sunday on which the annual Dorfet is held; the calendrical name makes the festival a recognized local occasion.

notes.label: Sennerin
notes.text: the singular of Sennerinnen, a woman who works seasonally as an alpine dairy worker or herder; here she is the wealthy young woman whose pride drives the legend.

notes.label: Älplerinnen
notes.text: the feminine plural of Älpler, meaning women who live or work seasonally on an Alp; here they are members of the regional alpine community attending the festival.

notes.label: Ländler
notes.text: a lively Alpine folk dance and its characteristic tune, commonly in triple meter; it opens the dancing whose first place the proud woman covets.

795a3088cb1e456861d628c12f74bfae58350a42.summary: A farmer was supposed to build a new house, but to finish it so quickly that the task was almost humanly impossible.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

29de51fa56742923956ec18f80420a99e4aed3f7.summary: In the fiercest snow squall, a poor farmer came home and sat down on a bench beside the warm stove.

notes.label: Rappe
notes.text: the source’s singular dialect form of Rappen, the small coin worth one hundredth of a Swiss franc; the Devil claims that not even the smallest part of the debt money is missing.

notes.label: Gvatter Schwarz
notes.text: literally ‘Godfather Black,’ a familiar and mocking Swiss German form of address for the Devil; the farmer uses it after trapping his hoof in the smith’s clamp.

notes.label: Chistli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a little chest or box; here it is the Devil’s magical wish-chest, summoned through a rhymed formula.

notes.label: Schlier
notes.text: the dialect name for the additional pieces of fuel the farmer lays beneath a debtor’s cauldron; their fire-feeding function is clear, but the source does not specify their exact size or form.

notes.label: Aetti
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German word for father or daddy; the children use it for the farmer while mourning his departure.

notes.label: Erbsmues
notes.text: an Aargau dialect name for a thick cooked pea dish or pea mash; the Devil orders it made from black peas, while the enchanted white pea turns the meal into a weapon.

notes.label: Fraufaste
notes.text: a regional name for one of the quarterly Ember-fast periods in the Christian calendar, associated in Swiss tradition with heightened supernatural activity; the account does not identify which season is meant.

notes.label: Nothpfenig
notes.text: an older expression for an emergency penny or reserve coin kept against hardship; the supernatural gift of white peas is figuratively presented as such a last resource.

6d480d0fc84ca4804e61b1435352e709a5c1bf16.summary: There is a little town in Switzerland named Schiltach that in the year 1533, on 10 April, suddenly burned completely to the ground.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

1946b9836bebd28b8833ea81622c6ed4b1227ee4.summary: The narrow rocky ridge on which Brunegg Castle stands on the Kestenberg has been cut through to a depth of about thirty feet and a width of fifteen feet.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4fbac8f2b077c22dac3b8dd82e8ab594421e3c47.summary: Near the city of Sion, on the western bank of the river that gave the city its name, there stood in ancient times, according to a legend, a pleasant little house amid beautiful vineyards, inhabited by a pious married couple.

notes.label: g'schafft und g'spukt
notes.text: this Valais dialect phrase says that uncanny activity and haunting continually occurred in the Devil’s House; the exact distinction between the two verbs and their pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: verwindet
notes.text: verwindet describes the harmful twisting, warping, or wind-like affliction suffered by anyone who stares at the witch; the precise symptoms and dialect derivation are uncertain.

2970c27f0b9da8bfc6baca292025a643300a6215.summary: The legend tells how Satan, leaving the Lötschental as a tourist — he may not have been treated especially well there — climbed somewhat crossly up the Risihorn.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

00fcc1479013e496ef4a53e6ac06cb55ccd12717.summary: A little farmer once lived on the Weissenburgberg. On a bitterly cold winter day, when stone and bone alike were frozen, the devil came to him in the guise of a young huntsman.

notes.label: Stubenofen
notes.text: the large masonry or tiled stove heating the main living room, often with a broad warm surface on which one could sit; parlor stove is only approximate, and that sit-able construction is essential to the wager.

a94be89993f00d79abec5654930c2b5a8862d959.summary: In Guarda, a man lived in discord with his wife. When he needed to load the hay in his mountain meadow to carry it home, he had no one to help him, for his quarrelsome wife refused.

notes.label: Diale
notes.text: the singular local name in this Graubünden story for a female supernatural being with goat feet; she helps with the hay and is mistaken for the Devil.

notes.label: Fuder
notes.text: a full cartload or wagonload, especially of hay or another farm product; the Diale stands upon it while helping the farmer.

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: plural of Diale, the host of related female beings who accept the dying Diale's answer ‘I myself’ and therefore do not pursue the man.

753ab65d6c75e22a2f13e0ae240efa0d448a249e.summary: In the Lower Engadin and the Münstertal, certain fairy-like female beings formerly appeared, just as legend in other valleys of Graubünden still tells of such beings under the name Waldfänken.

notes.label: Waldfänken
notes.text: a Graubünden name for fairy-like forest beings known from other valleys; the source compares them with the Dialen without saying the two traditions are identical.

notes.label: wilden Männlein und Weiblein
notes.text: literally ‘wild little men and little women,’ another class of Alpine wild beings from which the exclusively female Dialen are explicitly distinguished.

notes.label: Dialas
notes.text: the Romansh regional plural for these female beings in the Lower Engadin and Münstertal; Dialen is the Germanized form used by the source's title and narration.

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: a German plural used for the goat-footed female fairy beings of the Lower Engadin and Münstertal; they feed workers, guide the lost, and withdraw permanently when human beings violate their hospitality.

notes.label: Diale
notes.text: the singular form for one of the Dialen; in this account, one silently answers a pregnant woman's craving with a steaming loaf.

notes.label: iss und lass
notes.text: literally ‘eat and leave,’ the Dialen's rule of hospitality: guests may consume the offered food and drink but must leave the valuable silver vessels untouched.

9921c15ed0437b1e958d3219145ed13d8f1389a6.summary: In the Graubünden Prättigäu, the mountain men are called Geissler, Gaisser, Küher, Wilde Leute, and Waldfänken; in the Romansh-speaking Münsterthal they are called Dialen and are imagined as little men who wear scarlet garments adorned with gold and lace, which they customarily hang out in the sun and fresh air.

notes.label: Geissler
notes.text: one of several Graubünden names listed for mountain dwarfs; literally it can denote a goat herder, reflecting the beings' association with Alpine livestock, though the source does not distinguish this group from the other local names.

notes.label: Gaisser
notes.text: a regional variant alongside Geissler for the mountain dwarfs; its closest sense is likewise ‘goat herder,’ but here it names a supernatural little person rather than an ordinary herdsman.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: literally a cowherd or Alpine dairyman; in this Prättigäu list it is also a folk name for the mountain men, showing how supernatural beings were described through familiar pastoral occupations.

notes.label: Wilde Leute
notes.text: literally ‘wild people,’ a broad Alpine folklore name for humanlike beings living beyond settled society; here it is presented as another Prättigäu name for the mountain dwarfs.

notes.label: Waldfänken
notes.text: a Graubünden name for wild forest beings, here grouped with benevolent mountain dwarfs; the exact singular form and derivation are not explained in the source.

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: the Romansh-area name used in the Münsterthal for richly dressed, benevolent little mountain people associated with old mines, chamois, cheese, and miraculous food gifts; the source gives no literal derivation.

notes.label: Ofenberg
notes.text: literally ‘furnace mountain,’ the local mountain name connected in the story with dwarfs and the region's former smelting and mining activity.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Dialenlöcher
notes.text: literally ‘Dialen holes,’ the local name for openings or caves near the Cierfer-Alp that are identified as dwellings of the Dialen.

notes.label: las foras dal las Dialas
notes.text: the Romansh form printed by the source for the ‘holes of the Dialen’; its historical spelling is retained, including the repeated article.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Etschroggen
notes.text: rye brought from the Etsch or Adige region south of the Alpine watershed; in the isolated Münsterthal it supplied flour for the highly valued bread baked only about once a month.

50c7ddaf7e9fafa23d484e9769e630014dcc333e.summary: While its parents were making hay up in the mountain meadows, a five-year-old child went looking for strawberries and could no longer be found that evening.

notes.label: Dialen-Kind
notes.text: literally “Dialen child”; the Dialen are female supernatural beings of Graubünden mountain lore, and the wondrously dressed child who feeds and guides the lost five-year-old is understood to belong to them.

7f612ef8eca235c2072b286a7d3ac75499b09a49.summary: A beautiful golden-yellow cat, with its whiskers neatly swept back and its fur smoothly groomed, often came visiting a kitchen when the household sat together in a cozy circle.

notes.label: Treche
notes.text: a Valais regional word for the hearth or cooking place; the source itself supplies Herd as a gloss, and the warm ashes make it the visiting cat's favored seat.

b860d24e1d066ea1c598899df767a359eff4ddb8.summary: A little dwarf came to a farmer and hired itself out. But it imposed the condition that he must never look into the stable or up at the haystack, and strictly forbade him to enter.

notes.label: Dingzwerglein
notes.text: approximately ‘little hired dwarf,’ formed around dingen, to hire or engage for service; the being works under a secrecy taboo, but whether the name was a fixed regional creature-type is uncertain.

644ade6814e500909f740d9d6aee32eb7043b352.summary: At Bauen near Seelisberg, an Erdmännchen once said to a farmhand: ‘Chüetriber, säg dem Churre-Murri ’s Chussi-Mussi sei gstorben’—‘Cowherd, tell Churre-Murri that Chussi-Mussi has died.’ With that it vanished, and since then no more Erdmännchen have been seen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-men,’ a regional name for subterranean dwarf-like beings; the death announcement functions as the moment their kind withdraws permanently from human sight.

notes.label: Chüetriber
notes.text: Swiss German for a cowherd or cattle driver, the human intermediary addressed by the Erdmännchen.

notes.label: Churre-Murri
notes.text: the rhyming name of the being who is to receive the death announcement; its literal meaning and whether it names an individual or a class of beings are not explained by the source.

notes.label: Chussi-Mussi
notes.text: the rhyming name of the being reported dead; the source provides no secure literal meaning, but the announcement of this death explains why the Erdmännchen are never seen again.

769ec2fe125af471bfe29eff3990626fe1c3815b.summary: During the last French war—which every patriot of Upper Valais can recall only with a curse because of the atrocities committed in his homeland—the following two tragic events also occurred.

notes.label: Pfin
notes.text: an older German and Valais form associated with Pfyn in the Rhône valley; the fortification there belongs to the remembered landscape of the French fighting in Valais.

notes.label: Rittikapelle
notes.text: the locally named Ritti chapel near which the French soldiers rest; retaining the compound preserves the account's precise regional landmark.

7e4fa8516bcd5d86805aa5d3ecdcbfb92fe24e10.summary: A boy in Obersaxen used to visit his girl every day except Thursday, on which evening the young woman had forbidden him to visit.

notes.label: Schatz
notes.text: literally “treasure”; an affectionate German term for one’s sweetheart or beloved, used here for the boy’s girlfriend before he discovers her witchcraft.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

8fa6579cde68130c43cf17c29f53058c6a5255f6.summary: This healing water is said to have been discovered by a Geissbub. As he tended the goats in that area, he repeatedly saw a limping stag come to this spring and drink from it—or perhaps bathe or stand in it as well?

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally ‘goat boy,’ a boy who tends goats; Geiss is the regional word for a she-goat or goat generally, and Bub means boy.

notes.label: Schwendi Kaltbad
notes.text: literally ‘Schwendi cold bath,’ the local medicinal spring or cold-water bathing establishment whose healing reputation the legend explains.

c081fe84b5a03672b9615ac7a01afb309aac7e08.summary: In the sitting room of a low house on the ‘Höhe’ below Wassen, a woman’s body lay on a bench near the window, and the women keeping vigil had fallen asleep during their monotonous prayer.

notes.label: Weibervolk
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic collective or dismissive expression for a woman or female person; here it names the dead woman’s apparition and should not be read as a neutral modern label.

notes.label: Hättisch dü mich dobä-n-appägstitzt, sä hätt-ich Gwalt, dich hiä i ds Tobel appä z'stitzä!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘If you had pushed me down up there, I would have had the power to push you down here into the ravine’; the apparition states the unrealized reciprocal danger.
notes.anchor: Hättisch dü mich dobä-n-appägstitzt, sä hätt-ich Gwalt, dich hiä i ds Tobel appä z'stitzä!

8664ad5e08ca0d61e90fdb49934aeeb8c1f131d0.summary: Many years ago, a spirit inhabited a fir tree on Weesen's Oberbütz Alp and gave a jubilant cry whenever bad weather was about to arrive.

notes.label: Oberbütz
notes.text: the named Weesen Alp where the weather-warning spirit inhabits first a fir tree and later the dairy hut.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture with its huts and working landscape, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled alpine dairymen responsible for herds and milk work during the summer grazing season.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the seasonal Alpine dairy hut where the Sennen live and process milk and where the spirit resumes its disturbances.

1e7e98cec381398437a456935802c1a5e8c43a0c.summary: Between Niederuzwil and the Hub, a gigantic dog roams about at night. Whoever meets it loses the way, must wander about for almost the whole night, and comes home dripping with sweat after arduous travels.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

b674df264dd14ab126c93aeb3e680d2ca0856901.summary: A farmer had an Alrünli, an animal like a little frog; it had made him rich.

notes.label: Alrünli
notes.text: an Uri diminutive for a magical Alraune familiar, explicitly described here as an animal like a little frog; it brings wealth but imperils its owner's soul if he cannot dispose of it before death.

notes.label: Geldscheisser
notes.text: literally a ‘money-shitter,’ a blunt folk name for a magical familiar that produces wealth; the grotesque term emphasizes profit gained through a diabolical compact.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: the broader German name for the magical mandrake or money-bringing familiar; this local story treats it as the same little toadlike being called Alrünli rather than as a plant root.

135f3f951528f55c3d2fe6940eacfc595cb127a4.summary: In earlier, long-vanished times, remembered only by tradition with its powerful memory, the wild, high Alp Chammli at the head of the Schächen Valley extended much farther than it does today.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, herds, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the two versions describe the formerly larger Chammli and Blüemlisalp pastoral landscape before glaciation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kaiserspiel
notes.text: a traditional Swiss card game played with a 48-card pack; the legend makes the robber band equal in number to the deck and gives its members card-based names, though it does not map every nickname to a precise modern rank.

notes.label: Bsetzi
notes.text: a paved or cobbled yard or standing area; here the rescuers cover the stone surface before the barn so the departing cattle will make less noise.

notes.label: Schallä-Panggi
notes.text: the robber's card-based nickname, apparently connected with a bell-suited playing card whose pictured figure has a damaged or oddly posed right leg; the source does not identify the exact card or explain both name elements.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd, milk work, and cheesemaking on a seasonal pasture; both versions place this specialist worker in charge when the robbers attack.

notes.label: Erwellen
notes.text: a regional cheesemaking operation performed at the cauldron, involving the working or gathering of curd; the source names the stage without describing the exact technique.

notes.label: Pichel
notes.text: a regional Alpine horn or pastoral wind instrument whose signals carry down the valley; the Senn uses an agreed musical language to tell his sweetheart that the herd is being stolen.

notes.label: Betruf
notes.text: the traditional Alpine prayer-call spoken or sung by a herdsman to ask divine protection over an Alp, its people, and livestock; here it is normally delivered from the Sennen Slab.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Turner
notes.text: the pivoting support or crane from which an Alpine dairy cauldron hangs and can be swung over the hearth; the robbers bind or suspend the Senn from this specialized fixture above the fire.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: Swiss German for the large cauldron used to heat milk during Alpine cheesemaking; its retention also preserves the Uri counting rhyme's sound with Essi and Blessi.

notes.label: Trychelchüeh
notes.text: cows wearing Trycheln, large hammered sheet-metal livestock bells with a sound distinct from cast bells; the exact plural form is preserved in the counting rhyme and the later musical warning.

notes.label: Flüeh
notes.text: an Uri/Alemannic form of Fluh, a steep rock face or Alpine crag; it is retained to preserve the counting rhyme's sound with Trychelchüeh.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: the Alpine legendary name for wandering Venetian or foreign mineral seekers believed to know hidden ores and treasures; the comparison invokes this folklore cycle rather than merely any person from Venice.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: the full organized Alpine cattle herd or cattle-and-dairy unit managed by a Senn, a broader pastoral concept than an undifferentiated group of cows.

notes.label: Pintnerland
notes.text: the Senn's regional name in his horn message for the territory of the hostile people beyond the mountains, contextually Graubünden; the precise derivation and geographic limits of Pintner are uncertain.

notes.label: Hundsläufer
notes.text: literally a ‘dog-runner,’ a legendary swift and tireless runner said here to lack a spleen and to run obliquely like a dog; the tale treats this bodily explanation as folk belief.

notes.label: Pintä
notes.text: the shortened dialect destination in the second horn call for the same hostile Graubünden country or people called Pintnerland above; its exact grammatical and geographic sense is uncertain.

3d22f5c487c8e4306dc900edba2b7f85eab76950.summary: Since the most ancient times, a dog is said to have worked mischief on the Rotenbüel* and disturbed the livestock at rest.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a Bernese name for a nightmare or chest-pressing spirit, here imagined as a being that suckles from sleepers and can make even a boy develop milk-bearing breasts; its physical nature and exact literal origin remain uncertain.

a35d28449e52bb9c8071f0f1150850ac2b72b6e1.summary: One evening two young men went from Surrhein to Laus “z'hengert.” When they reached a stable, they saw other young men lying in wait for them, so they hid in the hay piled inside the stable and meant to wait until the others left.

notes.label: z'hengert
notes.text: a dialect expression for going out on an evening social visit, often with a courting implication; the source does not specify the young men's exact destination in Laus.

notes.label: Doggi
notes.text: a nocturnal pressure spirit associated with nightmares and the sensation of a crushing weight during sleep; in this story it escapes in the form of a white pig.

658abc8b57d2a06ed2e21d933c02acaa5acb1fe0.summary: Below the “Stafel” of the Alpe Drusen stands a great stone, and a dreadful legend is told of the Stafel and the stone:

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a grazing level or working station within an Alp, including its hut-and-pen area; both the pasture station and the nearby stone anchor the legend.

notes.label: Alpe Drusen
notes.text: the managed high pasture of Drusen where the Senn and farmhands live and work seasonally.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman responsible for the pasture’s dairy operation; here he leads and completes the mock baptism.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Blätzen
notes.text: scraps or patches left from worn-out clothing, used to construct the life-sized doll.

notes.label: Juppe
notes.text: a regional women’s skirt or petticoat; the source specifically glosses this garment as an Unter-Rock.

notes.label: Gstältli
notes.text: a short fitted bodice or little body-garment worn with the Juppe; the diminutive and exact construction are regional.

notes.label: Tschööpli
notes.text: the upper portion or jacket-like part of a regional woman’s dress, as the source’s own gloss explains.

notes.label: Züllii
notes.text: lacing cords used to fasten the Tschööpli; the unusual double-i spelling is preserved from Jecklin.

notes.label: Häftli
notes.text: small clothing hooks or clasps used to fasten the woman’s garment.

notes.label: Ringgen
notes.text: buckles on the doll’s pair of shoes; the source explicitly supplies this meaning.

notes.label: Flor-Bödeli
notes.text: the base or cap-like foundation of the woman’s headdress; Flor suggests a light or gauze-like fabric, but its precise regional construction is not fully described.

notes.label: Chrüseli
notes.text: the fringes, ruffles, or lace trimmings of the female headdress, as indicated by the source gloss.

notes.label: Muss
notes.text: Jecklin’s form of Mus, a soft porridge or mash; the farmhands smear it and cream upon the doll in their mock feeding.

notes.label: Plümpen
notes.text: the largest class of cowbells, rung here in sacrilegious imitation of church bells for the mock baptism.

notes.label: Gebse
notes.text: a broad, shallow wooden vessel used for milk in Alpine dairying; placed on a chopping block, it serves as the mock baptismal basin.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairy workers whom the parody assigns the role of baptismal sponsors.

notes.label: Götteti
notes.text: godparents or baptismal sponsors in Swiss German; the Sennen assume this role in the mock rite.

notes.label: Pfarrer
notes.text: the parish priest; the Senn assumes this role in the blasphemous imitation of baptism.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gorge; the fleeing farmhands must cross three before they are permitted to look back.

476dfa06def057221e42538de5483e5cac855a91.summary: On the Valésa Alp in Somvix, several mischievous herdsmen once made a doll from cheese curds and treated and pampered it like a living child.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the Senn’s assistant in a Swiss alpine dairying household; ‘assistant dairyman’ is close, though duties and rank varied by region and pasture.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the head dairyman responsible for milk and cheesemaking on a Swiss alp; ‘alpine dairyman’ is the closest English role, but it does not fully convey the Senn’s traditional authority within the seasonal pasture household.

f31a009b7e5c4c46a990150f066ae248218cdb7a.summary: Many years ago, at the foot of Pizocel mountain between Chur and Ems, stood a building called the Dolmetsche-Haus.

notes.label: Dolmetsche-Haus
notes.text: the preserved local name of the isolated inn between Chur and Ems; the source gives no derivation for Dolmetsche, so its literal sense remains uncertain.

aaf3cc0ca1abae2923d3a69472dc131fc990c9d5.summary: Once, when the emperor was hard pressed by the heathens, he summoned the people of Hasli in the Weissland and of the lordship of Brienz, which belonged to the empire, to come to his aid.

notes.label: Weissland
notes.text: the historical or legendary territory associated here with Hasli; literally ‘white land,’ but the account uses it as a regional name.

notes.label: Kriegsharst
notes.text: a compact war band, levy, or troop of fighting men; Harst is an older Swiss military term for an armed body rather than a modern unit size.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Banner, a military or civic standard; the painted donkey becomes the heraldic emblem of Brienz.

661f2d11922d607aed5a33000a0c6cfb17319ff9.summary: Wile is the name of a small settlement in the district of Wollerau, Canton of Schwyz.

notes.label: drei Teufels Namen
notes.text: literally ‘three devils’ names,’ preserved from the repeated ritual formula ‘in three devils’ names’; the tale reverses the burial rite by repeating its donkey, cloak, and circling in the opposite direction.

88cc7ba387293b964b3aca4d3f0eb97bb70a9776.summary: In the wooded high valley of Buffalora (in the Münstertal), benevolent fairies once lived, and a beautiful green Alpine valley spread out there.

notes.label: Buffalora
notes.text: the high valley and Alp landscape by the Ofenpass in Val Müstair, described here as the former home of benevolent fairies.

notes.label: Münstertal
notes.text: the German name for Val Müstair, the Graubünden valley in which Buffalora lies.

notes.label: Donna di Vanüglia
notes.text: Jecklin’s body-text variant of Donna di Valnüglia, the white female specter banished into the valley of Nüglia.

notes.label: Zernetz
notes.text: the historical German spelling used here for Zernez, the Engadine village where the apparition had served as a castle stewardess.

notes.label: Donna di Valnüglia
notes.text: the title form of the apparition’s name, meaning the “Lady of Val Nüglia”; the body of Jecklin’s text spells the name Vanüglia.

d473d65446af2a7f7a5e6440acdc1e54ac75c4c3.summary: In a certain house at Veltheim, the sitting-room door sometimes opens by day as well as by night.

notes.label: Kobold
notes.text: a household spirit or goblin whose disruptive visit opens the door and overturns the cradle but does not injure the child or mother.

notes.label: Frickthaler-Dorfe
notes.text: older inflected spelling meaning ‘Fricktal village’; it locates the parallel self-opening doors at Obermumpf in the Aargau Rhine region.

6f28ad53bbd19d00398262c4391ee7f45dd8ffc7.summary: The Hundskehre is, as already stated, an enclosed triangle with a path running all the way around it; on two sides, the path forms the church way, and on the third, the boundary with the upper village.

notes.label: Frohnfasten
notes.text: an older Swiss spelling of Fronfasten, the quarterly Christian Ember fasts; regional folklore treats these observances as liminal times for apparitions, and the source does not specify which seasonal fast is meant.

notes.label: Dorfhund
notes.text: literally “village dog,” a local supernatural animal attached to a community and its boundaries; here it is a calf-sized one-eyed apparition rather than an ordinary village dog.

d982cc4961139e28f460d6e301d83648491c4fe4.summary: The Dorfhund of Nesselnbach is the size of a calf, with short legs, a very long tail, and plate-shaped eyes that spray fire.

notes.label: Dorfhund
notes.text: literally “village dog,” a local spectral animal attached to a particular settlement rather than an ordinary communal dog; here it is calf-sized and fire-eyed.

notes.label: Schoppen
notes.text: a historical regional liquid measure and, by extension, a serving or glass of drink; its exact volume varied, so the farmer’s many Schoppen of schnapps should not be assigned one fixed modern quantity.

ea0e2b89d061f5e690d94e2bb8ac7292b724a2ab.summary: Reitnau’s three village lanes form a triangle. At its right angle stands a house in which the Dorfhund lives.

notes.label: Dorfhund
notes.text: literally “village dog,” a local spectral animal bound to a settlement and its calendrical weather lore; here it is a shaggy, calf-sized apparition whose sight causes illness.

notes.label: Kratzergässli
notes.text: a local lane-name; Gässli is the Swiss diminutive of Gasse, a narrow lane or alley, while the significance of Kratzer in this place-name is not explained.

abffc979ce78c3a18e1d23d80bb66486cd707865.summary: It makes its rounds only within the village. At first, it appears as a tiny little creature shaped almost like a hedgehog.

notes.label: Dorfthier
notes.text: historical spelling of ‘village beast,’ a settlement-bound apparition that changes from a hedgehog-sized creature into something as large as a hay wagon.

8e4692318806784ed43f361b96c3c3b5577c1d28.summary: A neighbor stood talking at the window of the Lütwil cobbler while their two little dogs played together in the meadow before them.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” a local name for a supernatural communal apparition that changes animal shape; here it grows from a kitten into a gigantic boar.

e7cd605e1490be66c5537ec52a4d8e72be4af391.summary: This Dorftier lives in the Brunnmatten there. It runs as far as the woods, then turns from the highway back into the village and disappears beside the church at the churchyard.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” a regional folklore name for a shape-changing apparition attached to a settlement; here it forms from a brushwood pile and pursues the brothers, rather than representing ordinary wildlife.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally “night lads,” village youths abroad after dark, sometimes associated with courtship or rowdy behavior; here they are specifically feared as quarrelsome attackers.

notes.label: Reiswellen
notes.text: tightly gathered bundles of brushwood, twigs, or small branches used as fuel or stored material; the brothers mistake the supernatural mass for such a pile when they pull out clubs.

notes.label: Holzbeige
notes.text: a carefully stacked woodpile or woodstack, often built against a structure; here it rises beneath the eaves and becomes the brothers’ refuge.

2a076dcd569b6f68d7900843ab52d8234817bfb0.summary: The Dorftier of Safenwil was about the size of a calf, with a long, very thickset body, short legs, and black coloring.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” a regional folklore label for an uncanny creature associated with a particular settlement; Safenwil’s plate-eyed black beast is usually harmless, but it is not ordinary livestock.

bf35604cdefec9c9c08c1ef5b222eb3f500d4a15.summary: At Lake Hallwil there is a young lord of Hallwil transformed into a toad. When encountered, this animal swells to the size of a winnowing basket and has eyes like pewter plates.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally ‘village animal,’ a local folklore label for a monstrous or uncanny creature associated with a particular settlement; here it is Seengen's wandering toad-shaped nobleman, not an ordinary village animal.

98e65eff200bddd1da0c85ea8d7bbc41a3c8fff0.summary: On nights during the holy seasons, the Dorftier goes from the town of Brugg through the villages of Umiken and Villnachern and, on its return, vanishes in the middle of Umiken.

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” the local name for a shape-changing communal apparition rather than an ordinary animal belonging to the village.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical local magistrate, administrator, or head of a municipality; the precise powers varied by place and period, so “mayor” would be too narrow here.

4fdefbe8659259ceeb32913a685aed1084a9f959.summary: A knight came to an abandoned castle and found in one chamber the finest foods and wine, which he enjoyed greatly.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7057f957b3d432b8731ff03d88725f9f8c463e96.summary: On the Greifensee, whose solitude and stillness are broken only by the wingbeat of a wild duck and the cry of the hawk circling above it, there stood during the Old Zurich War a humble little town, enclosed and watched over by a strong castle hard beside the lake.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘companions bound by oath,’ the historical Swiss confederates; in this account the term identifies Zurich’s besieging opponents rather than all people in the modern federation.

notes.label: Tummlern
notes.text: a historical siege engine named by the source among the attackers’ equipment; its exact construction is not described, so the term is retained rather than assigned to one modern weapon type.

notes.label: Katzenköpfen
notes.text: literally ‘cats’ heads,’ a historical name for a kind of siege implement or projectile; the source does not explain its precise form.

notes.label: Blyden
notes.text: historical stone-throwing siege engines, broadly comparable to large catapults or trebuchets; the spelling is retained from the source.

notes.label: Schirmen
notes.text: literally ‘screens’ or ‘shields,’ protective siege coverings used by attackers approaching fortifications; the source gives no construction details.

notes.label: Luginsland
notes.text: literally ‘look into the land,’ a traditional name for a high lookout point or tower from which the defenders watch for relief.

notes.label: Ilgen
notes.text: an older regional word for lilies or iris-like flowers; here they are golden-headed plants growing in the execution field, but the source does not establish an exact modern species.

7e87a0606ad37c24de9ce646c56453657696d943.summary: On the southern side of the Kuhmettler lies the Drachenloch, which leads so deep into the mountain that inside one can hear the bells of the Toggenburg cattle herds on the Rossalp.

notes.label: Drachenloch
notes.text: literally ‘dragon's hole,’ the local cave-name on the Kuhmettler; this brief account emphasizes its extraordinary depth and underground water rather than relating an encounter with a dragon.

a222d084c71e7a1d375255cdac4503248c3249fb.summary: In the land of Unterwalden beside Lake Lucerne, a terrible monster dwelled in time beyond memory.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a serpentine dragon of German-speaking legend, often wingless or only loosely defined in form; this account gives it scales, claws, flight, and fiery breath.

notes.label: Ödwyl
notes.text: the story's name for devastated Wyl, interpreted as ‘desolate Wyl’; it is a legendary place-name explanation rather than a linguistic proof.

notes.label: Milchtanslein
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for a small milk can or dairy vessel carried by the herdboy.

notes.label: Unterwaldner nid dem Wald
