notes.text: literally the people of Unterwalden ‘below the forest,’ the historical regional designation corresponding to Nidwalden.

notes.label: Drachenried
notes.text: literally a dragon marsh or wet meadow; the title attaches the dragon legend to a named landscape, although the body instead emphasizes Wyl and Ödwyl.

936d8ba888be9e471eec936b9d8e854cd3aaa33d.summary: Near the ruins of Eppenberg, ten minutes from Bichwil, is a pasture called Mettlen.

notes.label: Schlipf
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a landslip or sliding mass of earth; the dragon's passage is said to have caused one at Zuckenriet.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

7370fb19bdd94171be378aa5f93f067d2662bf8f.summary: High above the village of Vättis, in the yellow mountain at an elevation of 2100 meters, there is a grotto, surely one of the most interesting in Switzerland.

notes.label: Drachenloch
notes.text: literally ‘dragon's hole,’ the local name of the high grotto above Vättis; the legend explains the name by making the cave the dragon's former mountain dwelling before its fatal flight to the Calanda.

655579988c999273085fd58a786c2df492c64807.summary: A dragon lived near Azmoos, and it was said that as soon as it moved its tail, the village would be buried by the mountain.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a518c95fc05d8f874b3016039f1afbd89946fcb6.summary: Because the Rhine plain was often flooded in former times, the country road draws into the narrow pass between the Blosenberg and Blattenberg.

notes.label: Hirschensprung
notes.text: literally ‘stag's leap,’ the name of the Rhine-valley narrows explained first by a leaping stag and then associated with the petrified dragon.

notes.label: Blattenwand
notes.text: literally ‘Blatten wall,’ the local rock face above Oberriet in which the dragon's stony head and jaws are said to remain visible.

a9a1b4c83450942699ffa8df74eec4f9f0fa44d1.summary: In the Galtenfluh above Engelberg in Uri is a cave in which a dragon lived.

notes.label: Galtenfluh
notes.text: the named steep rock face above Engelberg where the dragon lives; Fluh is a Swiss word for a cliff or crag, while the source does not explain Galten securely.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and cheese-making on a high pasture; here the rich Senn is the father's preferred suitor.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: garten
notes.text: the source's verb for having made nighttime courting visits; prior participation disqualifies the wealthy suitor from the required chastity.

notes.label: Heimgarten
notes.text: an evening household visit, often with a social or courting sense; in this account it is equated with the Kiltgang.

notes.label: Kiltgang
notes.text: the traditional nighttime courting visit paid by a young man to a village girl; the story treats experience of it as proof the suitor is not chaste.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep exposed rock face or cliff in Swiss usage; the rescuer and dragon fall over it while wrestling.

8e1a43f526fc26025688a2d25327716394e2f654.summary: It was wintertime. Snow lay meters deep around the huts and weighed upon the forest's lowest branches.

notes.label: Jeizenen
notes.text: the local Valais place named as the farmer's home; the story does not further identify its boundaries or modern spelling.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its associated seasonal farmstead, not simply a mountain peak; the farmer goes up to it in winter for wood.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Klamm
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided gorge or chasm, here the inescapable cleft into which the sled falls.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a long, serpent-like dragon of Germanic and Alpine tradition; the cave dragon lies stretched along the wall in this form.

notes.label: Höhenfeuer
notes.text: literally a fire on the heights, such as a mountain beacon or bonfire; the dragon's jagged wings flare like one.

notes.label: Schweifringel
notes.text: a circular curl or ring in the dragon's tail; the farmer straddles one as though it were a saddle.

notes.label: Drachenkegel
notes.text: literally “dragon cones,” referring in context to the dragon's cone-shaped droppings or deposits, which prove to be pure gold.

notes.label: Tötzli
notes.text: small compact blocks or ingot-like rectangular lumps into which the remaining dragon gold is formed.

a98c7dbdef5c9111af61b951950de231e1068a40.summary: Joh. Branca of Guarda is said, with the aid of a conjurer, to have covered the little Alpiglia-See at the foot of Pic Mezdi—where a dreadful dragon lived—with leaves and branches, thereby forcing the monster to leave the place in the midst of a terrible storm.

notes.label: Alpiglia-See
notes.text: the small Alpine lake at the foot of Pic Mezdi where the dragon lives; See means lake, while the local Alpiglia name is retained.

notes.label: Innspruck
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for Innsbruck, where the dragon is finally killed.

ddde811958b54f75d3a06169107671f31ff6ad1d.summary: A dragon appears to a child and says: ‘Do not flee, but redeem me! Only do what I tell you, and you will become fortunate.’

notes.label: B'hüt mer Gott mis Chind!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘May God protect my child!’; here the father's spontaneous protective exclamation breaks the redemption trial and causes the dragon and key to vanish.

27b2ccb139d12d8a675ab40f25ab20ad81339b45.summary: On the eastern side of the church hill at Zernez lies Lavin’s Galtvieh-Alpe of Macun, where a dragon inhabits the largest of the small Alpine lakes.

notes.label: Galtvieh-Alpe
notes.text: an Alpine summer pasture for Galtvieh—cattle not currently giving milk, including young or dry animals; Macun belongs to Lavin for this grazing use.

802258ce32e239554b8242663d81e984233c5350.summary: Above Lake Thun lies the cave of the hermit Beat, who converted the inhabitants to Christianity.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

f3ba6d12616fa6cc14fa39214b6a5dea0c0e2f88.summary: Long ago, when the castle Castellum still stood at Castiel in Schanvigg, a dreadful Lindwurm dwelt nearby in the “deep Tobel.” It blocked the way through the ravine and could be appeased only by having a human being brought to it as a sacrifice every month from one of the three communities of…

notes.label: Schanvigg
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Schanfigg, the Graubünden valley containing Castiel and the three communities named in the legend.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a dragon-like great serpent of Germanic and Alpine legend; this creature has enormous wings, breathes fire, and demands human sacrifices.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided Alpine ravine or gorge, often containing a stream; the dragon blocks the path through this one.

notes.label: Allermannsharnisch-Wurzel
notes.text: literally an “everyman’s-armor root,” the protective Alpine plant root traditionally identified with Allium victorialis; here it helps expose or overcome the dragon, though the source does not explain the mechanism.

notes.label: Castieler-Tobel
notes.text: the named ravine at Castiel; Tobel is the regional word for a narrow, steep-sided Alpine gorge, often containing a stream.

ae45e917d074a42563bee9245738d26a44146a98.summary: A dragon once appeared to a child in the Simmental and said, “Do not flee, but redeem me.

notes.label: Bhüet mer Gott mys Chind!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘May God protect my child!’; the father’s protective invocation interrupts the dangerous act and causes the dragon—and the chance of redemption—to vanish.

a13075874b976fb44f25f246c9383f58aba7230a.summary: In a small high valley between Schafmatt, Feuerstein, and Weissguggel in the parish of Hasle in Entlebuch, an Älpler once killed a dragon, and the place where it was buried is still pointed out.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially an alpine herder or dairyman; here the Älpler kills the dragon but dies as a result.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Spilmösli
notes.text: the local name of the high-valley site where the dragon was buried; -mösli suggests a small marshy meadow or moor, but the source does not explain the full place-name securely.

483e7b7454278f1ace0f5b6a35fa8d763e602458.summary: A dragon, still in its youth, devastated the region around Meerenschwanden by tearing up all the field crops wherever it passed.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d1cc97297ecbdebd61f80baf9ca9818b6a104e46.summary: Above the now-vanished baths of Lüzelau near Weggis, on the rock face, there was a beautiful level tract with pleasant estates called Wylen.

notes.label: Wylen
notes.text: the local name for the level estates above Lüzelau where tradition placed an earlier settlement; the source does not explain the name's derivation.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar,’ a folkloric learned wanderer often credited with magical or occult powers rather than merely an itinerant student.

notes.label: grüwlich Gewässer
notes.text: older regional wording for a dreadful or horrifying flood of water driven down from the mountain when the dragon leaves.

notes.label: Tüffel
notes.text: Swiss German for Teufel, the Devil; the old quotation casts the dragon-removing scholar and his supernatural service as diabolical and ruinous.

1e5b81cb84396b5cf7c8874b6974d3c31ba9507f.summary: A farmer near Lucerne once saw a dragon flying from Mount Rigi toward Mount Pilatus while he was working in the field.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

9a7dd7b298d69d9616c3df7b1cd674f149ace1a0.summary: In the municipal forest of Rohrdorf stands a boulder the size of a washhouse.

notes.label: Wiesbaum
notes.text: a long, heavy pole used to secure hay or another load on a wagon; the dragon's length is compared with this familiar rural implement, whose dimensions were not standardized.

notes.label: Jauchenfaß
notes.text: a barrel or tank for liquid manure; the earthy farm comparison describes the dragon's extraordinary thickness.

notes.label: Hemmetschwyler-Trotte
notes.text: the historical local name of a winepress or press-house site near Bellikon; the story places the former Drachenstein there, while the exact building no longer survives in the account.

notes.label: Uristier an der Neuß
notes.text: the title of a parallel bull-and-dragon tradition cited by the collector; the historical spelling Neuß is retained, and the abbreviated reference does not explain the tale fully.

notes.label: Bachthier in Entfelden
notes.text: the historical title of the collector's cross-reference, literally ‘brook beast in Entfelden’; its old spelling is retained because this story supplies no further account of that creature.

d0b9da0959086acc51c32693321fb3a15cdea45f.summary: At first, the slopes along the valley floors were inhabited. Later, the settlements may have spread upward and downward almost simultaneously.

notes.label: Lindwürmer
notes.text: plural of Lindwurm, a serpent-like dragon of Germanic and Alpine legend, often imagined without the fully winged form of later heraldic dragons; the collector rationalizes such beings as memories of swamp creatures or vapors.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

e5b2d7f57765a3963e84d0e27f6b43571178a759.summary: During the Fassnacht days, the young men of Uri, masked and disguised, used to storm about the communities like madmen and sometimes clap their hands as they went.

notes.label: Fassnacht
notes.text: the Swiss carnival season before Lent, marked here by masked bands of young men moving noisily through Uri’s communities.

notes.label: Drapoling
notes.text: an Altdorf term for a masked carnival figure and, in this legend, the name of the irreverent reveler condemned to return as a ghost.

b1d190abbdd89ecee4d3fae18872da4de8c446f5.summary: It is said to have arisen when the three men swore the oath to liberate the country.

notes.label: Tellen
notes.text: the German plural formed from the name Tell, meaning the three Tell-like oath heroes in this version; it should not be read as three members of one family named Tellen.

notes.label: Rütli
notes.text: the lakeside meadow traditionally associated with the founding oath of the Swiss Confederacy; the story connects its national significance with the sleeping-hero belief.

notes.label: Dreibrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘three springs’ or ‘three fountains,’ the feature said to have arisen where the three oath-takers founded Swiss freedom; the compact place-name is retained because the source does not specify whether it refers to natural springs or built fountains.

565311608f144b48a295a42dce11f6aca509e267.summary: After the owner died, a rich and grasping Senn made an unjust claim to an Alp and forest.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and cheese work on a seasonal mountain pasture; here the wealthy Senn fraudulently claims land after its owner’s death.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its grazing and dairy operation, not simply any mountain; the disputed Alp is treated as inheritable property.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schwörfinger
notes.text: literally ‘oath fingers,’ the three fingers raised or used in a traditional German-speaking oath gesture; their miraculous impressions in the stone expose the perjury.

notes.label: ZH
notes.text: the standard Swiss canton abbreviation for Zürich; it distinguishes this Dreifingerstein tradition from similarly named traditions elsewhere.

notes.label: Dreifingerstein
notes.text: literally ‘three-finger stone,’ the named rock whose three hollows are explained by the false-oath legend; the German name is retained so readers can recognize the local landmark tradition.

f1f957dd13058a41220db708748440147f3041c6.summary: By the chapel, a beautiful clear spring flows out from beneath the rock. It is conducted into a wooden trough or basin beside the chapel.

notes.label: unser Lieben frowen Brunnen
notes.text: early New High German for ‘Our Dear Lady's Spring,’ a Marian name given to the water after its discovery.

notes.label: das kalte Bad
notes.text: literally ‘the cold bath,’ the common name for the intensely cold spring when used as a healing immersion.

notes.label: S. Jackobi des Merern Apostels tag
notes.text: the feast day of Saint James the Greater; the historical phrase dates the reported gathering of bathers.
notes.anchor: S. Jackobi des Merern Apostels tag

notes.label: Der schwösterbrunnen
notes.text: an early-form spelling of ‘the sisters' spring,’ another name explained by the tradition of the three sisters.

notes.label: Landvögten
notes.text: territorial bailiffs or governors appointed over subject lands; the inflected plural belongs to the account's historical German.

notes.label: Eydgenössische Chroniken
notes.text: ‘Confederate chronicles,’ histories of the Swiss oath-confederacy invoked as support for the political background.

notes.label: Landtvogt
notes.text: the account's historical spelling for a territorial bailiff or governor, here the Austrian official whose intended abduction drives the sisters into hiding.

notes.label: Herdlütten
notes.text: literally ‘little earth or hearth people,’ subterranean or mountain-dwelling helpers whom the account compares with ancient pygmies.

notes.label: Liechtstubeten
notes.text: evening communal gatherings for spinning, handwork, conversation, and courtship, traditionally held in a lit household room.

notes.label: Dreischwesternbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘Three Sisters' Spring,’ the Rigi healing spring whose name is linked to three sisters hiding from an Austrian bailiff.

7209bb380e5458d603af0ad2eda62884a2cd3781.summary: A father had a daughter named Seline, who was his whole delight. They owned a little house down in the valley and had little to eat.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Drächen
notes.text: a local kitchen word that the narrator explicitly equates with the Herd, meaning the stove or hearth beside which Seline is made to work.

notes.label: Drächengrudel
notes.text: the degrading household nickname given to Seline because she performs the lowest kitchen work beside the Drächen; the source establishes the connection but gives no independent literal derivation for Grudel.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Grudel
notes.text: the shortened form of Drächengrudel used by the cook and narrator for Seline in her kitchen-servant disguise; it carries the sense of a dirty, lowly drudge, though the source does not provide a separate gloss.

38964e2aafdc14a180d45c19e5febbcef525dbb0.summary: Meeting a vicious bull in an open field is no joke; neither taking up a position nor showing a clean pair of heels will help.

notes.label: Hochalpen
notes.text: high-elevation seasonal mountain pastures and their working landscapes, not merely the upper reaches of the Alpine range; the Hanigalp above Grächen is the setting here.

89edbb0334e8c1579c5346a25a85fecae5706a03.summary: In the castle at Cernez there was once a stewardess who enjoyed the complete confidence of the knightly household.

notes.label: Knochenmann
notes.text: literally “bone man,” a personification of death comparable to the Grim Reaper; here he comes for the stewardess without exception.

notes.label: Geisterbanner
notes.text: literally a person who bans or binds spirits; in Alpine folk belief such a specialist could compel a troublesome ghost to leave and confine it elsewhere.

notes.label: Schafalpe
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used for sheep, not merely a generic mountain; Nüglia is described as a small sheep alp belonging to Valcava.

notes.label: Duonna di Valnüglia
notes.text: the Romansh name by which the apparition is known, literally the woman or lady of Valnüglia; keeping it preserves the story’s local Engadine identity.

839648a86e6235907e5e473c74c442861f0d2e0b.summary: The Dusseli is a little dog that frequently appears in the Suren Valley during thunderstorms.

notes.label: Dusseli
notes.text: the local name used for the small doglike apparition that appears in storms and can swell into a black man; the source does not explain the name's derivation.

notes.label: Dusseli-du, dä!
notes.text: a dialect call roughly meaning ‘Dusseli, you there!’ addressed as one might call a familiar little dog, just before the creature reveals its supernatural form.

21ef6687569207998dc21d81abafce9b72a893fe.summary: Once, in a village, there lived a very poor family. The youngest child was as small as a dwarf and was therefore called Nanino.

notes.label: Polenta
notes.text: the Italian name, also customary in Ticino, for the maize porridge the robbers plan to cook from the stolen grain; it is a regional staple rather than a generic flour dish.

4067ea6b2770f1fca56544107f0c63d2974873e2.summary: At Bettelried in the Simmental there was once a Stampfe where people came to have their barley pounded into groats.

notes.label: Stampfe
notes.text: a Stampfe is a water-powered pounding mill used here to process barley into groats; its precise machinery and scale are uncertain.

notes.label: Stampfmüllerin
notes.text: this is the female proprietor or miller associated with the Stampfe, here the woman who clothes the dwarf; her exact occupational duties are unspecified.

notes.label: Fegmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little sweeping man,’ this names the hidden helper who pounds grain and cleans the mill; whether it is the same being as the first dwarf is uncertain.

4fc902a306f34df0b8ae09c14a4e180b0ee2b2c8.summary: A young man of Oberems married Türliwirli, the daughter of a dwarf. One day the woman asked him to promise never to call her by name, and he gave his word.

notes.label: Türliwirli
notes.text: Türliwirli is the personal or fairy name of the dwarf’s daughter whose husband is forbidden to speak it; its literal meaning, origin, and exact Valais pronunciation are uncertain.

notes.label: Alpwerk
notes.text: Alpwerk denotes the seasonal work carried out on an Alpine pasture, which takes the husband away from home in June; his particular task and pasture are unspecified.

35eddbebed3692912a47e20535ec22cf39be9494.summary: Behind Itramen near Grindelwald, a man was making hay. Just as he looked around to see what the weather might do, a little dwarf in a long shaggy cap stood beside him and asked for a handful of hay.

notes.label: Sennerei
notes.text: an Alpine dairying establishment or the herd and operation belonging to it; here its approaching bells announce the magically fattened cattle, though the word can carry several closely related senses.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman; at the end it refers to the farmer as he inspects the returned cow.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

0f90ede28c50e1fd65765f13250c932332e9e36a.summary: J. Martin Usteri of Zürich relates in his Dichtungen (edition by D.

notes.text: The phrase meide die Sprünge was rendered as avoid the drops in the mountain-path context; it could also echo the cheese's bounding leaps.

c77e647731f96ba8e81f3157e727d0207048dd99.summary: One day in the depths of winter, when Hans, an honorable man of Guttannen, went from his hut into the mountains to prepare his Losholz for the journey home, he suddenly heard a peculiar whimpering behind a rock along the way, as though a child were crying in pain.

notes.label: Losholz
notes.text: timber allotted by communal right or lot for a household to cut and take home; the exact local allocation practice at Guttannen is not described.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: an Alpine serpentine or dragon-like monster associated with rocky mountain terrain, related in folklore to the Tatzelwurm; this one coils around a dwarf, but its size and anatomy are not fully described.

notes.label: Wichtelmännlein
notes.text: a diminutive for a little goblin, dwarf, or household-spirit man; here it refers affectionately to the injured dwarf king, not a separately identified species.

notes.label: Enzenwasser
notes.text: a spirit or medicinal drink made from gentian root, used here as a reviving cordial; strength and preparation are unspecified.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope Alpine wind that can rapidly melt snow; its overnight arrival creates the wedding’s miraculous interval of spring.

notes.label: Schwiböglein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little arch or arched feature and used here as a named place in the Rätrichsboden; the source does not describe whether it is natural or built.

b60a8c4c8c063a59255ea0414e476dcf7516f150.summary: Where the Lütschine leaves the actual Grindelwald valley lies the village of Burglauenen, situated on a slope north of the Lütschine.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: an old fathom-like measure of length whose regional value varied; the torn rock face is described as several Klafter thick rather than given a modern metric measurement.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

e9608ddd63095b6dba7f168a48f7b577e730134d.summary: About 200 years ago, there were still many dwarfs in the region of Ins, living thereabouts in forest caves.

notes.label: Holzleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wood people,’ one name for the dwarfs based on their wooden kitchen utensils.

notes.label: Erdleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ the corresponding name when their utensils or association are understood as earthen.

notes.label: Holzmütterchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wood mother,’ the cave-dwelling dwarf woman renowned as a midwife.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: an apron, literally a cloth worn in front, used here as a carrying cloth for the apparent tile fragments that prove to be gold.

notes.label: Je mehr du zatterst, desto minder hast du
notes.text: ‘the more you scatter, the less you have,’ the dwarf midwife's warning that discarded pieces are valuable.
notes.anchor: Je mehr du zatterst, desto minder hast du

notes.label: zattern
notes.text: to scatter, drop, or let pieces fall one by one; the man stops doing it only after the warning.

24ab42ebe1b64a3cf00a3e11bdef773942da31a9.summary: On the eastern side of the Längenberg, west of the village of Kaufdorf, stands the Gutenbrunnenfluh, in which the so-called Pfaffenloch is located.

notes.label: Berg- oder Steinvölkchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain people or little stone people’; a regional folkloric name for dwarf-like beings credited with shaping the cave’s stone formations.

e4cc235233078e689db2920974a68eb8afd1ed4b.summary: Long ago, the Haslital was the favorite abode of the dwarfs, or Töggeli. They often came down from the Flühen in whole crowds.

notes.label: Töggeli
notes.text: a Bernese regional name for small dwarf-like supernatural beings; here they are benevolent Alpine helpers, healers, and providers of inexhaustible food.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep exposed rock faces or cliffs from which the Töggeli descend.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: plural of Firn, old compacted snowfields or glacier snow high in the mountains; the story imagines radiant halls within them.

5db42786b674444a4d2b8b355ebb7429b98578b9.summary: In olden times a Küher named Dietrich lived in the Great Riedera. He had been born on a Quatembernacht and therefore could see every dwarf, kobold, poltergeist, and mountain spirit.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cowherd or cattleman, often working within a seasonal dairy operation; here it identifies both Dietrich and the later livestock owner, though their exact rank relative to a Senn is not stated.

notes.label: Quatembernacht
notes.text: literally a “Quatember night,” one of the nights associated with the quarterly Catholic Ember Days; Swiss folklore often treats such times as granting second sight, but the story does not specify which seasonal observance marked Dietrich’s birth.

notes.label: Schrätteli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive for a Schrat or Schrätt, a small troublesome household or nature spirit akin to a kobold; here it helps, imitates, sulks, and harms cattle, so “dwarf” captures only part of its character.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal pasture; here he leaves a dairy offering for the unseen spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gebslein
notes.text: a diminutive of Gebse, a shallow wooden dairy bowl or tub used for milk or cream; the exact vessel size varies, and here it serves as the spirit’s offering dish.

notes.label: Sürbelen
notes.text: a regional dairy term glossed by the source as the whey remaining after Ziger has been removed; it is an inferior offering in the spirit’s eyes, though its exact preparation is not described.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd made from the whey left after ordinary cheese production; here its removal leaves the poorer Sürbelen offered to the spirit.

notes.label: Gaumen
notes.text: a regional verb or noun used here for feeding and tending the cows, as the source itself glosses it; its precise division between feeding, foddering, and general care is uncertain.

notes.label: Tenn
notes.text: the threshing floor or central working passage of a Swiss barn; Dietrich flees through it, though the barn’s exact layout is unstated.

56f5d666e416a4df74bba3775e10e166b8f31a3d.summary: When the reapers lie down for their midday rest in the heat of summer, Erdmännchen two Spannen tall creep out of a cleft in the rock.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like beings of German-speaking Alpine folklore who live in or beneath the earth; here they secretly feed resting farmworkers but withdraw permanently after a human steals their tableware.

notes.label: Spannen
notes.text: plural of Spanne, a historical handspan measured between the outstretched thumb and little finger; the exact length varied, so ‘two Spannen tall’ indicates extremely small stature rather than a precise modern measurement.

ba9c2f5a3a94a792079a93fb5e129c5d0503d85b.summary: Not far from Salez, on a rock with a broad view, lie the ruins of old Forsteck Castle, of which only one tower with tremendous masonry remains.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Zwerglein
notes.text: a German diminutive meaning ‘little dwarfs’; the miners are small bearded underground beings rather than merely short humans.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a deep draw-well or shaft well from which water is raised by bucket; the kitchen maid unknowingly hauls the baron up through it.

notes.label: Bergklingeln
notes.text: literally ‘mountain ringing’ or ‘mountain jingling,’ the local name for the unexplained bell-like sounds attributed to the underground dwarfs around Forsteck.

33a6ac6ae4ea4a047aa86cdac50c3bfaa0522448.summary: In the Bernese lowlands, where grain is also cultivated, the dwarfs help to harvest it.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f9fb2564b1c4eda9c563061a393e111da24f99da.summary: The Gonzen too had its little dwarfs, which is almost self-evident for such an ancient mountain so rich in ore.

notes.label: Erzbild
notes.text: a historical mining term for an exposed ore body, ore face, or visibly mineralized formation; here it marks the high location near the Gonzen dwarfs' underground dwellings, although the exact mine feature is not described.

5f7f784b812995228453449188f2b0f17bbefd16.summary: When one goes from the church village of Zimmerwald by way of Niedermuhlern toward the pleasant little village of Rümligen at the foot of the Längenberg, a narrow footpath, often cut through rock, descends a very steep, rocky slope covered with brush.

notes.label: Kindbettmahlzeit
notes.text: literally a ‘childbed meal,’ a celebratory meal connected with childbirth and the mother’s lying-in; it is a communal family occasion, not ordinary bedside food.

notes.label: Zwerglein
notes.text: literally ‘little dwarf,’ the affectionate diminutive used for the helpful cave being; the term’s tone is gentler than simply ‘monster’ or ‘spirit.’

notes.label: Gevatterleuten
notes.text: the godparental kin and guests connected through a child’s baptism; here they are the people to be served wine at the childbirth celebration, a relationship not captured fully by ‘friends.’

4d07a4d30a0c2a2d3855a14acdc0dd20db522f6d.summary: The Alpknechte of Bärschis once had an easy time of it: the little dwarfs herded, milked, and churned butter for them.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired hands or servants who tend livestock and perform dairy labor on a seasonal Alp; their gift of human clothing inadvertently ends the dwarfs' service.

notes.label: Fissler
notes.text: the local occupational name for the goatherd's assistant, as the source itself explains; its wider dialect range and derivation are uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its dairy settlement rather than simply a mountain; the dwarfs secretly perform the herders' work there.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tschöpli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a short jacket or little coat; together with the new hat, it inspires the dwarfs' human helpers to offer a complete outfit.

notes.label: Häsli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a little set of clothes or outfit, not a ‘little hare’ in this context; the gift drives the dwarf away.

notes.label: Betläuten
notes.text: the ringing that calls people to prayer, especially the evening Angelus bell; the gifts are returned just before this devotional signal.

notes.label: Zwergvölklein
notes.text: literally the ‘little dwarf folk,’ a collective diminutive for the community of dwarfs; after the rejected gift, the whole group disappears.

2100edf8f595ff12dfebb7afd03551e00ee5b859.summary: Near the miraculous little church of Einigen on Lake Thun, a dwarf lived in a forest very long ago.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c2e3ad76e621137c0107091f9c6130b4fd7271de.summary: High among the crags, the dwarf-mother was in labor. The dwarf hurried down into the valley to summon the midwife.

notes.label: Vergeltsgott
notes.text: a traditional expression of thanks meaning literally ‘may God repay it’; here the midwife politely blesses the dwarf for what appears to be a poor reward before discovering its supernatural value.

d5fa16bcddf9e0861cea61ea488d41de7537ae2b.summary: The Bornberg, which extends along the left bank of the Aare from the town of Aarburg to the town of Olten, has in its craggy crest a cave so large that it can be clearly distinguished from far away in the valley.

notes.label: Herenloch
notes.text: the local name of the large cave on the Bornberg where the little folk first live; the source does not securely explain the name’s derivation, so it is retained rather than normalized.

notes.label: Herdmännli
notes.text: a local Alemannic name for the dwarf-like little folk of the cave, probably related to Härdmannli, ‘little earth men’; the printed Herd- spelling should not be reduced to ordinary modern German for a herd.

notes.label: Sichellöse
notes.text: a harvest gathering or celebratory meal marking the completion of work with the sickle; inviting the little folk expresses customary reciprocity for their field labor.

notes.label: Flegelrecke
notes.text: a gathering or meal associated with the completion of threshing by flail; the exact local custom is not described, but it is paired with the Sichellöse as a reward for harvest work.

notes.label: Wunderfilz
notes.text: the source’s regional or transcriptional form for an overpowering itch of curiosity, related to Wunderfitz; it explains the girls’ compulsion to discover the little men’s hidden feet.

notes.label: Chrüsch
notes.text: Swiss German for bran, also glossed by the source with Italian crusca and German Kleie; the girls scatter it so the hidden feet will leave visible traces.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean or cave-dwelling dwarf-like beings in German-speaking Swiss folklore; the name should not be confused with the modern German word for meerkats.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Heidenküche
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ kitchen,’ a traditional folk name for a hollow rock or cave imagined as an ancient dwelling; here two successive caves bear the same name.

notes.label: Steckhof
notes.text: an isolated farmstead or outlying holding apart from a clustered village, sometimes with a distinct historical legal status; the Chraitel Steckhof consists of only two houses.

ff2c13808b908ab798c8bbed7e4af0d5eefd5ed5.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, the plague once raged in Grindelwald, and countless people died.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like Alpine being who reveals otherwise hidden knowledge, here a herbal remedy for plague.

notes.label: Astränzen
notes.text: the dialect name in the rhyme for Astrantia, or masterwort, an Alpine herb historically credited with medicinal powers.

notes.label: Bimpinäll
notes.text: the dialect name for Bibernelle or burnet-saxifrage, a medicinal herb; the rhyme advises using it together with Astrantia.

notes.label: Chranken
notes.text: the dialect spelling of Kranken, ‘the sick’; the two-line verse means, ‘Use Astrantia and burnet, so the sick will not die so quickly.’

8626ca87ce31618c0a87b069590172caee694e9b.summary: In a great city lived a poor married couple who remained childless for a long time.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a dragon-like serpent of Germanic and Alpine legend, often imagined as long-bodied and heavily scaled; its armor breaks the rescuer's sword.

e198aaa7d4fe09e86b0fe8fd42240b1882c5e6c4.summary: On a warm July day, a widow—I do not know from which village—climbed the mountain to make hay.

notes.label: Aquila
notes.text: the Latin and Italian word for ‘eagle,’ adopted here as the girl’s name in a Ticinese tale after the bird raises her.

49d7116eb6b1ea90dd7f4b840828c1f0a73666b9.summary: Behind the Ramsfluh and Wasserfluh in the Fricktal Jura lie two delicately rising wooded peaks, the two Strîchen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-man,’ a dwarf-like subterranean being of Swiss folk belief; here the Erdmännchen live beneath the Strîchen in a luminous settlement and seek a human godmother, but the term has no exact English equivalent.

c01dc0f141425526fe4c659c2f00169353109a16.summary: Below the Lauiberg by the small Lake Sihl on the Yberg Alpine pastures of the canton of Schwyz, there is a threefold echo.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick or whipped cream; here the moonlit snow looks as though a giant had poured whipped cream over the pastures.

notes.label: Sihlseeli
notes.text: the affectionate diminutive of Sihlsee, literally ‘little Sihl lake’; here it names the uncanny small mountain lake below Lauiberg rather than the larger modern reservoir.

notes.label: Lauine
notes.text: an older or regional spelling of Lawine, meaning avalanche; here it is a spent avalanche tongue projecting into the unfrozen lake.

notes.label: Karrenbödler
notes.text: a local demonym for a person from Karrenboden; here it identifies the young man by his home area, and no natural English equivalent exists.

a2a5bb0ecdc2dbc4f09c0e051c157ac295124395.summary: If one goes from Sennwald toward Forsteck, one encounters, on the right side of the road near the bathhouse, a swamp that is said once to have been a lake and is also called Eglensee.

notes.label: Egelsee
notes.text: the recurring name of several supposedly bottomless small lakes; literally it can suggest ‘leech lake,’ although the source emphasizes the shared name rather than proving its origin.

notes.label: Egelmoossee
notes.text: a related lake-name combining Egel with Moos, marsh or bog, and See, lake; it is cited as another name in the same bottomless-lake tradition.

c9f524d62dbd026a20e806c69dae4790cc44f1d7.summary: More than one body of standing water in Switzerland is known by the name Egelsee.

notes.label: Weinmonat
notes.text: an old German month name, literally ‘wine month,’ used here for October; the parenthetical modern month is supplied by the source.

notes.label: Bannholz
notes.text: a wood placed under legal, communal, or protective restriction, often managed to shield settlements or resources; here it is the named forest opposite the lake, but its specific ban is not described.

notes.label: Egelsee-Hüper
notes.text: literally the ‘Egelsee hopper’ or ‘Hüp-caller,’ the specter named from the rider’s repeated cry as he and his horse sink; the wordplay joins the place and sound.

notes.label: Bannholz-Hüper
notes.text: the corresponding name ‘Bannholz hopper’ or ‘Hüp-caller,’ locating the same specter in the nearby restricted forest.

notes.label: sah man vil gespenster in Ross und Küihgestalt schreiendt
notes.text: historical German meaning approximately ‘many spirits in the form of horses and cows were seen crying out’; its spelling is preserved as quoted evidence of the older haunting tradition.
notes.anchor: sah man vil gespenster in Ross und Küihgestalt schreiendt

137974c703bd0ed2bb160b077ce0d3f604279061.summary: Every time before the Emme swells, a green rider is said to be seen approaching on a gigantic green snake.

notes.label: Eggiwil-Fuhrmann
notes.text: literally ‘Eggiwil carter’ or ‘Eggiwil wagoner’; it is the local name for the green rider whose appearance foretells whether the Emme will flood destructively.

The source uses a preposition that literally reads ‘out of a gigantic green snake,’ although the image appears to be of a rider approaching on one; the translation follows that contextual reading while recording the ambiguity here.

a9b03fde8a42af6ac6ccd79dd5f0109826190d16.summary: Northeast of Hettiswil, in a forest called Eichhallen, a hunting-like clamor is heard from time to time.

notes.label: Eichhallenjäger
notes.text: literally the ‘Eichhallen hunter,’ the punished spectral huntsman whose renewed chase is heard in the named forest before rain.

notes.label: Eihorn
notes.text: the Bernese-dialect word for a squirrel; here the animal is implicitly an old woman in transformed shape, so the local creature-word is retained.

notes.label: Bosse Buebe
notes.text: Angerees’s dialect rebuke meaning bad, naughty, or mischievous boys; the narrator explicitly remembers ‘bosse’ as his characteristic word, making the exact form culturally significant.

2af6460266adc2b08d1b71848b95f2f83b2e0d3c.summary: In the depths of Lake Seelisberg lives a monster known to the inhabitants of the region by the name Elbst.

notes.label: Elbst
notes.text: the local Uri name for the shape-changing, dragon-like monster of Lake Seelisberg that lures people with floating forms and attacks alpine livestock; its literal derivation and relationship to other spirit names are uncertain.

c13a591da3a58cd9416319f2a63ad83543cd2f2a.summary: There is probably scarcely a high Alpine pasture believed to be free of ‘Bozen’ or haunting spirits.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: the plural of Boze, a Valais dialect name for bogeys, haunting spirits, or frightening supernatural beings; here it is a general class of spirits believed to inhabit high pastures.

notes.label: Trinkelriemen
notes.text: leather straps carrying Trinkeln, the broad sheet-metal bells worn by Alpine cattle; here grain ears and vine leaves caught on the straps prove the herd's impossible night journey.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here it is the supposedly haunted place where cattle remain late in the season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpenstafel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or cluster of seasonal herding buildings; here its unnatural emptiness invites imagined sights and sounds of spirits.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their working landscapes; here the term contrasts populated lowland settlements with the seasonally deserted uplands.

notes.label: feldern
notes.text: a Valais pastoral verb meaning to pasture or graze livestock on available fields; the source itself glosses it as weiden, and here the young man keeps his cattle on the Alp longer than others.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

7ffe4ff5db374e5c5a468e8f714d6ce63286e4cc.summary: In a lonely corner of the forest lived Schnetzer Jos with his wife and a son who had just reached adulthood.

notes.label: Schnetzer
notes.text: a local byname attached to Jos; although its form resembles words connected with cutting or carving, the story does not identify it securely as a trade, place-name derivative, family name, or tool, so it is not translated conjecturally.

notes.label: zu Lichte
notes.text: literally “to the light,” an older expression for an evening visit by lamplight, especially a courtship visit to a sweetheart; it describes the son's regular Saturday journey across the Rhône.

notes.label: Arbenwald
notes.text: the tale's proper name for the deadly forest; its pairing with Arvenholz in the enchanted palace associates the name with the Arve, or Swiss stone pine, without defining an exact real-world location.

notes.label: Stola
notes.text: an ecclesiastical stole, here treated as a blessed protective vestment; the condemned young man wears it into the forest and later uses it to bind and strike the demonic dog.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Arvenholz
notes.text: wood of the Arve, the Swiss stone pine characteristic of the Alps; the enchanted palace is built from this aromatic Alpine timber.

5e2901f826008e37514ec19866ff27c32fee2de4.summary: Centuries ago, a rich man made a sport of luring the poor into his house under the guise of generosity and delighting in the pains his cruelty had devised for them there.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ a traditional diminutive for a dwarf-like supernatural being; here the ancient, stooped beggar pronounces the rich man’s curse, but the story does not name a more specific class of spirit.

notes.label: Sonntagsbrod
notes.text: literally ‘Sunday bread,’ bread reserved for the special Sunday meal; it appears in an obscure curse formula about catching fish, and any ritual or proverbial force beyond that literal sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Irrwisch
notes.text: closest to ‘will-o’-the-wisp,’ a wandering marsh light that folklore can personify as a spirit; here it is the fiery man compelled to aid the carter, without resolving whether the light and the cursed man are distinct.

notes.label: Chillef
notes.text: Aargau dialect for Kirchhof, ‘churchyard’ or cemetery; in the verse it directs the carter to carry the wooden cross there, the act that releases the haunting.

notes.label: Feuermann
notes.text: literally ‘fire-man,’ a fiery wandering spirit rather than an ordinary firefighter; here the enchanted rich man appears as a marsh light, and the exact relationship between the person and the light is part of the legend’s ambiguity.

3905506ec39a6bbfbb570a6cde0a4d3bf560a3bf.summary: 1. Schnyderberg-Joos of Linthal was following the goats on the Kammeralp and asked for something to drink there.

notes.label: Erwellen
notes.text: a regional cheesemaking operation performed at the milk cauldron, involving the working or gathering of curd; the source identifies the stage at which the milk fails but does not describe the precise technique.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for milk work and cheesemaking on a seasonal pasture; each version centers on a Senn whose dairy process has been magically disrupted.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

ad14c164e8b48b7a8ca82e4cee9fbd5b276b15fc.summary: On the northern precipice of the Titlis, above the so-called Hochpfad, one can see a rock slab called the Jungfrauenhöhle, of which the following legend is told:

notes.label: Hochpfad
notes.text: literally ‘high path,’ the local name for the elevated route below the cave on the northern face of the Titlis; it functions as a named landmark, not merely any mountain trail.

notes.label: Jungfrauenhöhle
notes.text: literally ‘maiden’s cave,’ the named rock hollow where the enchanted herder’s daughter is confined.

notes.label: Engelberger
notes.text: a man from Engelberg; the local demonym identifies the would-be rescuers whose moral purity is tested by the dragon.

2a545be91c6448baff6164ef3e883a0d777f12cd.summary: A king and queen had a daughter who would not live as they wished. Her father became so angry that he put a curse upon her.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

536c87b20f62607eb883d9552f4326d8213ee32b.summary: If a pocketknife is folded shut and set spinning on a table or anywhere else, it soon disappears.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

40d35c0c4c24b83651578fe2968cf4f2de732fc4.summary: On a hill immediately before the Fricktal village of Oeschgen, remnants of walls and buried underground passages still point back to the castle that once stood there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

adc41e827afe4a38901c2d03afa10294184daa9c.summary: In the sealed subterranean vaults of Gerunda, a wonderfully beautiful maiden sits beside enormous treasures.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7f9a652be4b80abda77bc39a3a02857dbec6c0c4.summary: Neither tree nor grass thrives on the Scheibenfluh, but at its summit is a cave in which lives an enchanted maiden named Salina.

notes.label: Scheibenfluh
notes.text: the named Fluh, or steep rock face, where Salina's cave lies; the source does not explain the Scheiben element of the place-name.

2e423935739562f3d242f9f5dbc4010b28f42985.summary: The ruins of Ramstein Castle lie near the village of Bretzwil in the Basel countryside, between the Jura passes of Ober-Hauenstein and Passwang.

notes.label: Sennhütten
notes.text: plural of Sennhütte, seasonal Alpine dairy huts used by herders for shelter and milk work; the huts here were built partly from the ruins of Ramstein Castle.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; the recurring curse kills his finest cows.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Angriff
notes.text: literally ‘attack’; in this local account it is the name given to the unexplained cattle mortality that returns every ten years after the enchanted beam is mishandled.

notes.label: Sennhaus
notes.text: the house or working dairy building occupied by a Senn on an Alp; the haunted structure is ultimately dismantled to escape the recurrent cattle deaths.

441b4c7dcf6ab66a885f50da6b49e8fbd123525e.summary: In Obervaz, a wolf for a long time caused great harm among the sheep. It was often hunted, but no one ever succeeded in killing it.

notes.label: Tiroler-Schleifer
notes.text: this denotes an itinerant Tyrolean grinder or sharpener who provides the counter-magic; his name, trade route, and source of ritual knowledge are uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

7f441cdfb1325b17d07d80d74115745e709ab6b4.summary: Near Lausanne is an oak grove called Sauvabelin. In this grove lies an open place overlooking Lake Geneva.

notes.label: Nortzén
notes.text: the Vaud regional-language name for the female necromancers or enchantresses gathering in Sauvabelin; the source describes their rites in detail but does not supply a literal translation or secure etymology.

aac38630203ddfdd9f30d1356e7684e06db9b7f4.summary: About 5 years ago, three young men from Wassen attended a ski evening in Wyler.—And this is a true story!—Around midnight they set out for home.

notes.label: Äschäwald
notes.text: the local name of the forest where the encounter and immobilizing disturbance occur; Wald means forest, while the first element is retained as a place-name.

notes.label: b'stellte es ihn
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that an unseen force stopped, beset, or held him fast; the source describes his inability to move but not the mechanism.

a8e130cdc0a5fa3d1d5e0bc267a94448d6d5b52a.summary: The Schanzenberg rises gently from the Rhine valley at Kaiserstuhl, stretches for hours into Zurich’s Bachsee valley, and then falls steeply, forming the boundary between the lands of Aargau and Zurich.

notes.label: Gaugenossenschaft
notes.text: a historical territorial association whose members held common rights; here it is the community that jointly used the Schanzenberg as pasture, and it is related to but not identical in wording to the title’s Genosssame.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Twing
notes.text: a local manorial or village jurisdiction and the territory subject to it; the free farms once lay within the castle’s legal district.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally “little mountain men,” small supernatural beings associated with caves, hidden wealth, and helpful labor; here they are the benefactors of the old farming community.

notes.label: Erdmännchenhöhle
notes.text: literally “little earth-men’s cave,” the local name for the inaccessible cave traditionally regarded as the beings’ dwelling.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic term for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; here it is the Schanzenberg cliff containing the Erdmännchenhöhle.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean household helpers; in this story the term alternates with Bergmännchen.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: traditional evening social gatherings held in a household or communal room, often involving visiting, conversation, work, music, or courtship; here even the supernatural helpers attend and bring gifts to the children.

notes.label: Genosssame
notes.text: a historical association or corporate community of people holding and using common rights, especially pasture; here it joins the old farmsteads around the Schanzenberg and is more specific than a modern cooperative.

a6c8b5632031b9d05ee00dc8b94f8dd598e95ecd.summary: The last of the Counts of Froburg was Eberhard, a harsh man toward his subjects and an insatiable hunter.

notes.label: Stalden
notes.text: a Swiss German topographic word for a steeply sloping road or path; here it is the rise beside Olten's covered bridge where the old woman confronts the count.

notes.label: Sennhof
notes.text: an estate or farm associated by name with Alpine dairying and a Senn; in the story it is the later establishment occupying the ruined castle site.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face, crag, or cliff; it describes Froburg's fractured rocky foundation rather than an ordinary hill.

notes.label: Jammeili
notes.text: Jammeili is the poor woman’s familiar or dialect nickname, perhaps related to lamenting, who voices the end-time prophecy; her full name, life, and exact home beyond Toggenburg are uncertain.

af7207d6106f5c172815a465afcb013dd913f5e1.summary: This spring was famous among the Unterwalden Sennen. It begins to flow in spring when the cattle are driven to the Alpen and stops in autumn.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or herders responsible for cattle and cheesemaking during seasonal pasturing; the spring’s timetable follows their working year.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: plural of Alp, high-elevation summer pastures and their associated seasonal farming places, not merely mountain peaks.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Engstlenbrunnen
notes.text: the named Engstlen spring; Brunnen can mean a spring, well, or fountain, and here it is a natural seasonal water source with morally responsive behavior.

8e0abf116ad2498c3d1ece16d015c3485525f6ef.summary: From time to time, a magnificent, heavy chamois buck showed itself in the Etzli Valley.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Waldblacken
notes.text: regional wording for broad-leaved dock or a related large-leaved dock growing in woodland; the drops of blood appear on its leaves, but the historical account does not identify the plant more precisely.

ba4f91ee9a57e6a8532bd7e1266e069971bdd957.summary: As is well known, the Kalfeisental was formerly inhabited by free Walser. According to legend, a giant of tremendous strength and size once lived among them.

notes.label: Kalfeisental
notes.text: the high valley behind Vättis in the canton of St. Gallen, historically associated with Walser settlement.

notes.label: Walser
notes.text: members of the German-speaking Alpine communities descended from medieval migrations out of Upper Valais; ‘free Walser’ refers to their remembered legal privileges.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the bailiff or governor who administered a subject territory for a Swiss canton or allied lord; the giant is summoned to his court at Sargans.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

a915c4c4028e8f07aa5e66c80c56f95a35c8918e.summary: Tiny little people lived in stone caves upon the wooded heights of the Frickberg, into which they had quite prettily and orderly cut openings for daylight.

notes.label: Schober
notes.text: a field stack or shock of harvested grain or hay; the helpers prevent the farmer from leaving such harvest structures outside overnight.

notes.label: Mandel
notes.text: a traditional counted group or shock of sheaves; the exact regional count varied, so the historical term is retained alongside Schober.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: communal evening visits or household gatherings, often combining sociability with shared textile work.

notes.label: raiten
notes.text: the source's regional verb for processing hemp stalks in preparation for fiber work; the precise step—breaking, stripping, or combing—is not specified.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Erdbibberli
notes.text: the local diminutive name for the tiny cave-dwelling helpers of Frick; Erd means earth, while the precise derivation of bibberli is not securely explained by the account.

473318cc4dbd88afddea87ddfdc4849e62972fd6.summary: a) The foremost home of the Erdmännchen and Wildleutchen was the legend-rich Mount Pilatus, where they were called Berglütli or Härdmannli.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ small underground or mountain beings associated with hidden places, livestock, aid, and treasure; the term covers varied regional beings whose exact nature shifts across these accounts.

notes.label: Wildleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wild people,’ small beings of uncultivated mountain country related here to the Erdmännchen; ‘little wild folk’ is close, but their relationship to other Alpine wild people remains uncertain.

notes.label: Berglütli
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain people’ in Swiss German, a Pilatus-region name for the small beings otherwise called Erdmännchen or Härdmannli; the accounts do not establish whether every name denotes exactly the same class.

notes.label: Härdmannli
notes.text: literally ‘little earth or ground man’ in Swiss German, a small Pilatus-region guardian of mountain animals; the form varies in the source, and its precise distinction from related dwarf and spirit names is uncertain.

notes.label: Herdmännlin
notes.text: an archaic written variant of Härdmannli, meaning approximately ‘little earth or ground men’; the quoted account uses it for male and female mountain spirits, and its spelling should not be confused with modern Herd, ‘hearth.’

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled herders and dairy workers who tend livestock and make cheese on seasonal Alpine pastures.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Liechtstubeten
notes.text: evening social gatherings held by lamplight in a home, often for spinning and other work along with conversation; translating it only as ‘spinning rooms’ would hide the communal custom.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or presiding official of a Swiss canton or rural polity; ‘chief magistrate’ is approximate and misses the office’s specific confederal and cantonal setting.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: the traditional spoken or sung alpine blessing calling divine protection over people, livestock, and pasture; its exact wording and ritual form varied regionally and are not supplied here.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: ergaltet
notes.text: a dialect pastoral term meaning that an animal has ceased giving milk or become dried up; here it describes cattle returned supernaturally thin and unproductive, while the exact degree of illness is uncertain.

notes.label: Doggelistein
notes.text: literally the ‘Doggeli stone,’ the local boulder beneath which the helpful beings live; Stein means stone, while the name Doggeli can refer to quite different night spirits in other Swiss traditions.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Doggelistube
notes.text: the ‘Doggeli room’ or chamber, the hollow beneath the Doggelistein imagined as the little beings’ dwelling.

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: the local name here for tiny benevolent household helpers living beneath a boulder, although related Swiss Doggeli traditions can denote very different night spirits; the name’s literal origin and the beings’ exact class are uncertain.

notes.label: Fusthansli
notes.text: literally ‘fist Hansli,’ a local name for a clever little being only as large as a fist; Hansli is a diminutive of Hans, but the figure’s broader folkloric identity is not explained.

notes.label: Ditteblakenblatt
notes.text: a dialect name for a large broad dock or similar broad leaf used as the Fusthansli’s shelter; exact regional plant naming can vary.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical Swiss and Central European measure based on the span of outstretched arms, used here for distance inside a cave; the closest English sense is ‘fathom,’ but its exact length varied locally.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Herdmanndliloch
notes.text: literally the ‘little earth-man hole,’ the name of a cave or opening at Barburg associated with the mountain beings.

notes.label: Älplerchilbi
notes.text: a Swiss alpine herders’ fair or parish festival marking the pastoral community and often the season’s end; ‘alpine fair’ is close, but the procession customs and timing varied by locality.

d10e80df3ebc8fa2b56e0fb445039afe27c849cb.summary: Late one autumn, when all the livestock were already back in the valley, a little farmer from Guggisberg took the shortest route over the mountains with a cow he had bought in the Simmental.

notes.label: Küherlager
notes.text: literally a ‘cow-herder's bed,’ the rustic sleeping place used by an Alpine cattle herder in the seasonal hut.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like subterranean beings; their nighttime feast seems to slaughter the cow yet leaves it alive except for the portion accepted by the farmer.

notes.label: Käskessi
notes.text: Swiss German for a cheese cauldron, the large vessel normally used to heat milk for cheesemaking; the Erdmännchen use it instead to cook the cow's flesh.

notes.label: Barren
notes.text: the cattle manger, feeding rack, or stall barrier where the restored cow stands; exact stable fittings varied by region.

e98acc60cfd9f272e0bf7ff6737b8af1d4c8eb30.summary: The Erdmännchen are not all of one kind. There are also evil ones who cause more harm than good.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like cave beings who can be helpful cattle keepers or dangerous abductors.

notes.label: Furrenfluh
notes.text: the named rock face near Guttannen where the hostile Erdmännchen live; Fluh is a cliff or crag.

notes.label: Selbhan
notes.text: a local proverb or taunt probably related to ‘self-done, self-had,’ meaning that the being brought its beating upon itself; the source does not spell out the derivation.

notes.label: Prinz Selbhan
notes.text: ‘Prince Selbhan,’ the mocking name permanently attached to the beaten Erdmännchen.

16abf31b1fe24e822b0cce310478ed41438e9aaf.summary: In the Gutbrünnenfluh near Gutbrunnen is a cave known as the Pfaffenloch. The entrance to this cave is very narrow, but its interior is extremely spacious.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ a German-speaking Alpine folkloric class of subterranean dwarf-like beings who may help nearby people or keep their own hidden households; ‘gnomes’ is close but would erase the tradition’s specific name and variable character.

f50dfadfb8eb5f27add6c15fa9ff83e9cf768ac1.summary: Up on Frickberg, an Aargau state forest near the village of Wegenstetten in the Fricktal, lies a cave of little height or width.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ a regional name for dwarf-like underground or cave-dwelling beings; this 1858 account locates them on Frickberg and attributes birdlike bodies to them.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and dairy work on a seasonal mountain pasture; the Erdmännchen idle near him during the long summer days.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: the Swiss German haymaking season or hay harvest; the dwarfs bring wine to the Büttihalde people during each Heuet, distinct from the later grain harvest.

notes.label: Hozzli
notes.text: a regional carrying basket or back-basket, glossed in the source as a Tragkratte; here it holds wine, omelets, and coffee packed for the farm people.

notes.label: Welschhuhn
notes.text: an older regional word for a turkey, literally a ‘foreign hen’; the source compares the dwarfs’ cloaked bodies to a tailless one.

notes.label: Hünggi, üf!
notes.text: a dialect command meaning ‘Little hens, fly up!’; the Erdmännchen cry it as they reveal their ability to fly rather than leave footprints in the ash.

notes.label: Kitt
notes.text: a regional collective noun for a brood, covey, or flock of wild fowl; the exact species is unstated, and the comparison emphasizes the group’s whirring flight.

notes.label: Schratt
