notes.text: an old regional name for a dwarf, goblin, or wild spirit; the historical footnote connects it with Alpine karst fields, but that collected explanation is preserved as folklore rather than asserted as modern etymology.

notes.label: Schrätteli
notes.text: the dialect diminutive of Schratt, meaning a little dwarf, goblin, or spirit; it appears in the footnote’s historical vocabulary comparison.

notes.label: Schrattenfluhen
notes.text: plural for rugged Alpine limestone or karst formations associated with a Schrattenfluh; the footnote describes them figuratively as seas of stone.

notes.label: Schrattenfelder
notes.text: plural for fields of fissured limestone pavement or karst terrain; the historical author treats them as dwarf habitat and links their name to Schratt.

notes.label: Schlaarzla
notes.text: the collected Sonneberg name for little field and house spirits in the comparative footnote; its precise dialect derivation and relationship to Swiss Schrätteli are not established by the story.

notes.label: Mohren
notes.text: the source’s historical plural for ‘Moors,’ used here as an outdated racial label for Africans; it is retained to mark the wording of the 1858 comparative note and is not current neutral terminology.

e267e56cd215a84684a1a5ae131484cfcc18e4e8.summary: In former times, small wild men, Erdmännchen, lived everywhere in the caves of Pilatus.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like wild or subterranean beings associated here with Pilatus caves, helpful farm work, healing knowledge, and dangerous retaliation.

notes.label: schwarze Astrenzen
notes.text: black Astrenzen, probably a regional plant name related to Astrantia or masterwort and recommended against plague; the exact species and preparation are not stated.

notes.label: Bibernellen
notes.text: burnet-saxifrage or a similarly named medicinal plant used in traditional remedies; the source gives no recipe or botanical identification precise enough to exclude regional variants.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Geissen
notes.text: Swiss and southern German plural for goats; the wild beings treat chamois as their own domestic herd.

notes.label: Wildmannen
notes.text: plural of Wildmann, ‘wild men,’ the cave-dwelling beings also introduced as Erdmännchen; whether the two names mark exactly the same folklore category is not explained.

notes.label: Gemskäs
notes.text: literally ‘chamois cheese,’ an inexhaustible cheese made from the milk of the Wildmannen’s chamois; its production and ordinary culinary equivalent are supernatural and unstated.

725436596e233a5acb83afda51fcb0f261330040.summary: Half an hour outside Lucerne, at the tower called Seeburg, an underground passage leads down to the foot of the hill on which the tower stands.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth man,’ a diminutive name for a subterranean dwarf-like being in Swiss folklore; here it is a small, white-bearded treasure guardian living in Seeburg's underground passage.

notes.label: Hundstagen
notes.text: the source's inflected form of ‘Dog Days,’ the traditionally hottest period of summer; the legend makes this the Erdmännlein's annual season of appearance rather than supplying an exact calendar date.

notes.label: Schuh
notes.text: a historical foot-length measure whose exact size varied by locality; here 2 Schuh conveys that the Erdmännlein is extremely short, but the source does not establish a single modern conversion.

23ca439d993fcf52a69c1761bde77de529c3fd8d.summary: Beneath Seeburg Tower, not far from Lucerne, there is an underground passage.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little earth man,’ a subterranean dwarf or earth spirit in German-speaking folklore; it should not be confused with the modern German use of Erdmännchen for a meerkat.

8ebff253dc4d3517d1fca2db73ce19e6ef26463d.summary: Near Leuggern, a village close to where the Aare flows into the Rhine, there is a round cave in a mountain wall in the woods between Fehrenthal and the Mooshalde.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ diminutive subterranean beings comparable to dwarfs or earth spirits but described here with their own local appearance and domestic-helping customs.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally ‘prayer bell,’ the evening church bell that marks the beings' permitted arrival and structures the community's day.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan, the attendant responsible here for ringing the bell.

e8ae1d211e2f5892ba7064e00792fc0044a0c151.summary: The Stolten is a quarry near the village of Kirchleerau. Its late owner was in league with the Erdmännchen who had their dwelling there.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: another diminutive form meaning ‘little earth men,’ referring to the same beings at the Stolten.

notes.label: Nimm numme es Tötzi Spinnhoppe und stoss sie is Loch.
notes.text: Swiss German for approximately ‘Just take a little wad of cobwebs and push it into the hole’; the supernatural blasting advice uses a dialect word for a small tuft or bundle and Spinnhoppe for cobwebs.
notes.anchor: Nimm numme es Tötzi Spinnhoppe und stoss sie is Loch.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ diminutive subterranean or dwarf-like beings who advise and serve the quarry owner but resist being displayed.

3fbb383b617acd7a27ba9f6cd9cc58de8be3d863.summary: 1. One day the family at Restig in Spiringen looked through their telescope at the opposite side of the valley.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person’; here it denotes a female apparition whose precise age, identity, and bodily nature are not given.

notes.label: Fürscheibe
notes.text: an Uri term for an apron-like front cloth or garment panel; the teller is unsure whether the apparition wore this red article or a red skirt.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small barn, shed, farm outbuilding, or chamber; the apparition enters it briefly, but the source does not identify its exact use.

notes.label: Erdschlipf
notes.text: a regional word for a landslip or sliding mass of earth; the apparition’s route foretells where the first slide will break loose.

notes.label: Brächä
notes.text: an Uri terrain word for the unstable, eroding landslide scar or broken ground left by earth movement; it continues to widen, but its exact geomorphological boundary is not defined.

cf0d9cd5787a51e9e67a1d989d2569f98c634cb0.summary: When one walks from the Fricktal village of Zeihen toward the sawmill, there is a beautiful fir forest on the left and vineyards on the right.

notes.label: Jmberger-Wag
notes.text: the recorded local name of the waterfall and the beings' final refuge; Wag commonly denotes moving or pooled water, but the first element and exact topographic sense are uncertain.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ a hermit or lay religious recluse living in the woods; the holy man's former presence adds Christian sanctity to the uncanny landscape.

notes.label: Erdweibchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth women,’ subterranean or cave-dwelling female beings who help poor villagers but have partly animal bodies; the diminutive does not necessarily imply child size.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little spring’ or ‘little fountain,’ the diminutive for the water source bubbling inside the Erdweibchen's cave-household.

notes.label: Reisswelle
notes.text: a tied bundle or faggot of brushwood and small branches gathered for fuel; helping assemble one is practical woodland labor.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

455d45a4f5265078fd8fe6274a51b8dcd2ad964b.summary: The Hufenfluh lies on the Aare's right bank in the Zurzach district. It is a rock face containing a large, deep cave.

notes.label: Hufenfluh
notes.text: the local name of the cave-bearing rock face beside the Aare; Fluh is a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep cliff or wall of rock, while the source does not explain Hufen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarfs or earth spirits in German-speaking folklore; they should not be confused with the modern German word for meerkats.

notes.label: Erdweibchen
notes.text: literally a ‘little earth woman,’ the female counterpart of an Erdmännchen; here one lives successfully as a tiny, industrious mill servant until recalled underground.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: a regional and historical word for an apron or cloth worn in front of the body; her failure even to change it emphasizes how suddenly she leaves her human service.

2ca1e5ad9965be52fc228d9e82884224b42dc988.summary: Count Rudolf von Erlach had been the Swiss commander in the great battles that the country won against foreign enemies.

notes.label: Oerkentier
notes.text: literally the ‘Oerken animal,’ the local name for a valley spirit believed to inhabit the stream called the Oerken; the account does not define its form or clarify whether ‘animal’ is literal, so the folkloric name is retained.

1269b142e5a69cbea9668545d260e0e6023d0b49.summary: In the form of a loaded hay wagon, it rolls by itself into the meadow stream called the Wütherich, which runs from the village into the Aare; whenever anyone encounters it, however, it immediately shrinks into a dog and is then called the Dorfpudel.

notes.label: Dorfpudel
notes.text: literally ‘village poodle’; here it is the local name for the enormous black dog-form of Erlisbach’s supernatural village beast.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: an old regional measure of liquid; here it denotes the daily allotment of milk given to each woman in childbed, and the exact modern volume is not specified.

notes.label: woddeln
notes.text: a quoted regional verb for the beast’s ominous, rushing activity or noise in the village stream; the source does not define its action more precisely.

f8a2283702153c4b133158e06d29818d79650a2b.summary: The Chapel of Our Lady in the Ernerwald, a much-visited pilgrimage site, was built in the years 1683 to 1709.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

5be139a2fe6ec6df81993f4c12bfc441be757017.summary: A wooded mountain in the municipality of Bassersdorf is called the Heidenburg, and its lower spur the Engelrain.

notes.label: weiße Frau
notes.text: literally a “white woman” or “White Lady,” a widespread German-speaking type of female apparition often bound to a place, treasure, or need for redemption; here it names Frau Escher, though her history and moral status remain uncertain.

notes.label: Escherfräulein
notes.text: literally the “young Lady Escher” or “Escher maiden,” the spectral treasure guardian associated with the Heidenburg; Fräulein marks an unmarried young woman, but whether Escher is a family name, local label, or both is not explained.

a4beb8790a36b97a4d0f50053c3af860fd7a99fb.summary: In Schneisingen's Oberholz there is a round, masonry-lined hole in the ground that appears to be the remnant of an old tower.

notes.label: Oberholz
notes.text: literally ‘upper wood,’ the local forest name at Schneisingen where the masonry-lined pit and the Etelmutter's dwelling are located.

notes.label: Etelmutter
notes.text: the local name of the red-skirted female guardian of Schneisingen's forest and buried heathen treasure; its exact derivation is uncertain, so the name is not flattened into a generic ‘witch’ or ‘forest mother.’

notes.label: Muttergottesli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive meaning a little image of the Mother of God, specifically the inexpensive fired-clay Marian figures pilgrims bought at Einsiedeln; it functions here as protection.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: The Kreuzer was a historical small-denomination coin used in parts of Switzerland and neighboring lands. Its value varied across monetary systems; in some Swiss systems it counted as one quarter of a Batzen. A named coin in a tale is therefore not a modern cent with a fixed national value.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Kreuzer

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

498359e8d2ab9929353f081e43210e75046a20e7.summary: At Gsteig in the Bernese Oberland, a deceased pastor preaches an eternal sermon to the dead of his congregation.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

69a3ade9e07c6a5aa0d353e8dca94e38aa261fb7.summary: The clergyman of Flums went to Gräplang Castle to read a mass there for a former lord of the castle who had died.

notes.label: Johrzit
notes.text: Swiss Alemannic for Jahrzeit, the Catholic anniversary mass or memorial observance for a dead person; here the priest is on his way to perform that rite for the former castle lord.

d6445281f791e7165045a62841e06d3f99503aad.summary: From the idyllic mountain village of Krinau, a somewhat rough road leads over the Egg to the beautifully situated hamlets of Altschwil, Schaufelberg, and Rotenfluh.

notes.label: Egg
notes.text: a common Swiss topographic word for a ridge or narrow height, here the road crossing above Krinau rather than an egg-shaped object.

notes.label: Weidgatter
notes.text: a pasture gate controlling livestock movement between adjoining farm properties.

notes.label: Schein- oder Leuchtholz
notes.text: literally ‘shining or luminous wood,’ decayed wood whose biological glow provides the tale's natural explanation.

notes.label: Hallimasch-Lagerfäden
notes.text: honey-fungus rhizomorphs or cordlike fungal threads running through the rotting wood and associated with its glow.

55f2aaf6a7cc546e6600c1d01b5ad1e5bd3c84d9.summary: One winter, a man from Peist wanted to slaughter a head of cattle and had prepared everything needed except the “Aufzug,” from which slaughtered animals are hung—he had forgotten it in the Mayensäss in spring, when he had been obliged to butcher an animal there.

notes.label: Aufzug
notes.text: the lifting tackle, gambrel, or similar hanging apparatus used here when butchering livestock; the source defines it by its function rather than its exact construction.

notes.label: Mayensäss
notes.text: an intermediate seasonal pasture settlement, with meadow and hut, used between the valley farm and the high summer Alp.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: plural of Fängg or Fänggin, powerful and dangerous wild beings of Graubünden forest and mountain lore; these two pursue the man but are stopped by a church bell.

notes.label: I schmeck Menschenfleisch
notes.text: Swiss German dialect meaning “I smell human flesh,” the first Fängg’s recognition that a man is nearby.

notes.label: und i Christeblut
notes.text: Swiss German dialect meaning “And I smell Christian blood,” completing the pair’s threatening exchange.

notes.label: Gstüpp
notes.text: a regional word for light debris such as dust, chaff, or fine fragments seen or scattered in sunlight; the threat imagines tearing the man apart just as completely.

notes.label: Hätt's nit grad' glüt, hätten mer di zerrissen, wie d's Gstüpp an der Sunn.
notes.text: Swiss German meaning “Had the bell not rung just then, we would have torn you apart like Gstüpp in the sun”; the ringing forces the Fänggen to stop.
notes.anchor: Hätt's nit grad' glüt, hätten mer di zerrissen, wie d's Gstüpp an der Sunn.

7decea5fcca8308071d52bcdd93329efff5bfa64.summary: At Summerigsrod in the Weggital, or Wägital, there is a square place called the Gevierte and enclosed with stones, which according to popular belief no one can enter without punishment.

notes.label: Gevierte
notes.text: literally ‘the quadrangle’ or ‘four-sided place,’ a stone-enclosed taboo area at Summerigsrod; the source does not explain why entering it is fatal or who sanctified it.

notes.label: Geissbuben
notes.text: goat-herding boys; their quarrel takes place while tending animals in the Alpine landscape.

notes.label: Gitzerli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a young goat or kid; the affectionate small-animal form sharpens the cruelty of throwing it into the forbidden square.

7befa1c22bf73435a35a93e088f7fb570c9a7f78.summary: From Saint Wolfgang in the Zug region, the road to Hünenberg passes the Lohwald, a small wood.

notes.label: Lohmännlein
notes.text: literally the ‘little Loh man,’ the local goblin or woodland being attached to the Lohwald near Hünenberg; Loh is an old woodland place-element, and the source gives no personal name for the creature.

notes.label: Weinrebenkapelle
notes.text: literally the ‘grapevine chapel,’ the chapel whose construction in the former vineyard is credited with ending the Lohmännlein's hauntings; the source does not provide another dedication name.

69bb8e888088d1873bdb8909d99272af7a226158.summary: At Gräplang Castle there once lived an evil lord who in his wickedness demanded the impossible from the peasants.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

0ebeb35a99ae320e881128aff691e1219c1d9f63.summary: Old Dorothea Hofmänner once heard something rustling outside the window before she fell asleep and saw a poodle slip in through a broken pane and sit upon her chest.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b20cdc5575c1be7df4fe0de5b848d6f4dee701e5.summary: At the outbreak of the Sonderbundskrieg, a prudent citizen of Wassen, in the presence of an innocent girl, hid a fine little hoard of cash in a pile of sand that was not especially large.

notes.label: Sonderbundskrieg
notes.text: the German and Swiss name for the brief Swiss civil war of 1847 between the federal forces and the Catholic conservative Sonderbund cantons; the story uses its outbreak only to explain why the money was hidden.

notes.label: um keinen Gugger
notes.text: a dialect idiom of emphatic impossibility, literally invoking ‘no cuckoo’ but meaning ‘not for anything in the world’ or ‘by no means’; it does not identify an actual bird in the search.

notes.label: Bees
notes.text: Uri dialect for the Böse, the Evil One or Devil; the belief is that buried money passes under demonic power unless innocence, personal guarding, or a blessed object protects it.

8d837fcc953469c3b79765e7ceae384d5699a3e0.summary: Whoever climbs to the Kulm of the Moléson on the evening before St. John's Day and chooses a bare place there where neither bells nor speech can be heard and where neither stalk nor fern grows will see the Prince of Darkness appear and hand over a bag filled with gold coins.

notes.label: Kulm
notes.text: a summit or highest crest, especially in Swiss mountain usage; the ritual must be attempted at the top of the Moléson.

3450daf71bcd430b0d5eb0e4471ee822c34e68d5.summary: In former times a great double-edged sword was displayed in Zurich; it had been welded together close beneath the hilt.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c484eb20aa8fa297e473be7ea1ec5b9f19fe6585.summary: The Fahl at Altsäss is a very steep slope broken by rocky outcrops, reaching down to the stream that separates the Alps of Altsäss and Maltschül.

notes.label: Fahl
notes.text: the local name for the steep, rocky slope at Altsäss; the source explains its terrain but not the name’s origin.

notes.label: Fahlwegli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning the little path across the Fahl; it is the narrow, treacherous livestock route on which the cow is made to fall.

notes.label: fällig
notes.text: literally related to ‘falling’ or ‘liable to fall,’ used locally and in quotation marks for the dangerous stretch where livestock may lose their footing; its exact dialect nuance is not further defined.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cowherd and dairy worker who tends cattle on a seasonal high pasture; here he is responsible for the herd, though the source does not describe his dairying duties.

notes.label: Vitz
notes.text: a regional word for a sharp blow, switch, or flick delivered to the cow’s ear; the precise implement or motion is not specified.

notes.label: Grozen
notes.text: a regional term for a fir tree or fir sapling; the parenthetical ‘fir’ is supplied by the source, but the tree’s size and exact species are not stated.

notes.label: Fahlmann
notes.text: the supernatural ‘man of the Fahl,’ condemned to reenact the cow’s fall; Fahl is the local name of the dangerous slope, so a generic translation such as ‘pale man’ would be misleading.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working livestock landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Altsäss and Maltschül are neighboring named Alps divided by a stream.

9b7b6b8f0ba7294461de277d857a09515712f162.summary: Near Serneus stands an old, ruined house called the “Gmür” (masonry). A Geisshirte named Flury once lived there.

notes.label: Gmür
notes.text: a regional form related to Gemäuer, meaning masonry or ruins; it has become the ruined house’s local name.

notes.label: Geisshirte
notes.text: a goat herder; Geiss is Swiss German for goat.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: legendary itinerant Venetians or southern mineral seekers believed in Alpine folklore to recognize hidden ores and treasures by secret arts.

notes.label: Los-Tobel
notes.text: the named ravine where Flury tends the goats; Tobel denotes a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully.

notes.label: fahrende Schüler
notes.text: in the singular title, literally a “wandering scholar,” a folklore figure associated with learned or magical knowledge; the title links this tradition with the Venediger who visit Flury.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape; Casana is the alp named in the title.

9080126276cef3af14543a194866f626e50e4996.summary: Just as the Venediger, or fahrende Schüler, roamed through most Alpine regions and by means of their art found and gathered treasures unknown to the inhabitants of the land, they also discovered in the mountains above Trimmis a spring of liquid gold.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: legendary itinerant Venetians or southern mineral seekers believed in Alpine folklore to recognize hidden ores and treasures by secret arts.

notes.label: fahrende Schüler
notes.text: literally “wandering scholars,” folklore figures associated here with the Venediger and with learned or magical knowledge used to find treasure.

notes.label: Quartkanne
notes.text: a traditional measuring jug or can; this one is described as holding two measures and is buried to collect drops of liquid gold.

notes.label: Pa d'aur
notes.text: the local place-name of the mountain cone, glossed by the historical source as “the Gold-Producing One”; the retained wording preserves that source explanation.

7a330416b9830dc534780dbd4fad743361d5e7f4.summary: The fahrenden Schüler were recognized by the fact that, when they walked along the road, they constantly twirled their hooked staffs in circles before them with their right hands.

notes.label: fahrenden Schüler
notes.text: the source’s inflected plural form of fahrende Schüler, literally wandering scholars or students; in German-speaking folklore they are itinerant learned magicians credited with secret study and wish-granting, not ordinary schoolchildren.

11e1c60df42f66eebc6d53fe0a970ba60b8e4bc9.summary: Farmer S. of .... near Eggersriet wished to conjure the Devil with several like-minded men.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

285b98aae786bf8720c406475c136740ba9bb2e8.summary: At a spring on Pilatus, a fairy appears every spring leading two goats by a bridle.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

52d6ef6621e5d2980e207e4e62d2ebe1a04db95f.summary: In ancient times, there were many enchanted women in Switzerland who meant very well by the people and often helped them in costly and evil times.

notes.label: Futterschwinge
notes.text: a Futterschwinge is a broad winnowing basket or agricultural tray, from which Queen Bertha scatters seed across the land; its exact form and whether the source intends grain or fodder are uncertain.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Nidel is Swiss German for rich cream, served here whipped and associated with the Dent de Vaulion; its precise preparation and provenance are unspecified.

notes.label: Eisbeerblätter
notes.text: Eisbeerblätter are leaves of the tree or shrub called Eisbeere, possibly a service tree or rowan relative, replacing the fairy gold; the exact plant species intended by the source is uncertain.

788757f67981b9c5ee02fc79ca83a75d8697a134.summary: On the front rock face of the well-known Flimser-Stein, above the ruins of Belmont Castle, a stripe of calcareous tufa colored with iron oxide runs down, almost blood-red.

notes.label: Flimser-Stein
notes.text: the prominent rock mass and cliff above Flims; Stein here names a major landscape feature rather than a single loose stone.

notes.label: Oberland
notes.text: the traditional ‘upper country’ of Graubünden along the upper Rhine, now also known as the Surselva; it is a regional designation, not a separate state.

de942ad894f47d521c759d938012c09e073b99f4.summary: In former times, the people of Uri had a stubborn dispute with their neighbors from Glarus over the territorial boundary.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or residing seasonally on an Alp, such as herders or dairymen; here workers from Uri and Glarus dispute use of neighboring high pastures.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here both cantons drive their livestock up to graze.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: plural of Senntum, a managed Alpine dairy herd or the pastoral unit traveling with it; here the Uri and Glarus groups bring their cattle onto the disputed grazing land.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their working landscapes; here they lie below the Clariden glaciers between the two valleys.

notes.label: Standesläufer
notes.text: an official runner or messenger representing a Swiss canton, with Stand referring to a member-state of the Confederation; here the two runners physically determine the Uri-Glarus boundary.

555d2590ae446086cce99e6900726e41b9eacacf.summary: On the Badiels alp at Vättis there was a Küher. Every night a cow went to a dangerous place where she could easily have plunged down and fallen to her death.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a Swiss cowherd responsible for cattle on an alp; his deliberate failure of care condemns him to perform the night watch forever as a spirit.

ecb92cf598cf0ffed8d9c8b3a05f2a489e1701bf.summary: At Bild stands a Torkel where a black dog appears at night. It is a Torkelmeister who failed to keep his oath and administered his office dishonestly.

notes.label: Torkel
notes.text: a wine or grape press, and by extension the press-house containing it, in Alemannic-speaking wine regions.

notes.label: Torkelmeister
notes.text: the official or master responsible for operating and administering a Torkel; the black dog is understood as the punished spirit of one who violated that entrusted office.

c9b8f55ad5c7929e1cc8cf6360b68d56b26e3985.summary: The Mandliserberg in Uri, together with one of its ridges, the Jakober, forms the southern boundary of the wild Leutschach Valley, whose upper end, formerly a beautiful Alptrift, is now covered with immense granite boulders.

notes.label: Alptrift
notes.text: a high seasonal grazing pasture or tract used for moving and feeding livestock; the former productive landscape is contrasted with the later boulder field.

notes.label: Hinnech chumeni dä!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Tonight I am coming!’ or ‘This night, then, I come’; the mountain’s personified warning precedes the fatal collapse.

notes.label: z'Furt
notes.text: the local place name explained by the repeated warning fort, ‘away’; the tale presents a folk etymology rather than an independently verified origin.

640732b5499d458644d7f6d548d5e07c51d39dd7.summary: In a castle called Gilgenberg there once lived a Landvogt who got along quite well with the farmers.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor exercising delegated authority; in this comic tale he is the castle-based representative of the ‘gracious authorities,’ so the historical title is retained rather than flattened to a modern office.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

7dd823ba455a96310d8f57de555c760c52754ebb.summary: Late one night, a farmer passed the ruined Ruchenberg Castle in Graubünden.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

6a42c3b67dd1f4fd10727470cc9ac94893101a98.summary: In Aargau it is the farmer of Hornussen who felled a fir tree on Sunday. On his way home he met our Lord God, who let him choose his punishment: either to sweat eternally in the sun or to freeze in the moon.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: d’War
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect or possibly corrupted source form paired with people as objects of the farmer’s healing; context most likely means livestock or domestic animals, but goods, stock, or another dialect form cannot be ruled out with certainty.

notes.label: fählber
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect form describing the farmer as he senses death approaching; its closest contextual senses are frail, failing, infirm, or mortal, but the exact shade is uncertain.

097462ab397f4dc62693ddf37a111502aed5020e.summary: A farmer in Trons owned a Mayensäss called “la Cavrida,” situated in the middle of the forest.

notes.label: Mayensäss
notes.text: a seasonal intermediate mountain holding, with pasture and buildings used between the valley farm and the high summer Alp; here la Cavrida lies in the forest above Trons.

notes.label: Fenile
notes.text: a local, Romance-derived word for a hay barn or hayloft; the tale identifies it only as the place from which the cat leaps.

99704fae72c6db6cd3f6c211524e585e4668a4f0.summary: A man had lost a head of cattle on the Alpe Vereina, but soon found it again.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working settlement; Vereina is the alp where the animal disappears, is restored, and later returns.

notes.label: Closterser
notes.text: a person from Closters, the historical spelling used here for present-day Klosters; the term identifies the animal’s owner by his home community.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: the shorter form of Alpe, again meaning the worked seasonal high pasture rather than merely a mountain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

383decec2c95212c6e2196b389dad9f2069d413c.summary: For three nights in succession, Niggi Eggel in Weingarten dreamed that he would find his fortune on the Rhône bridge near Sitten.

notes.label: Niggi
notes.text: a Swiss German familiar form of the name Niklaus or Nikolaus; it is retained as Niggi Eggel's personal name throughout the story.

notes.label: Stutt
notes.text: a regional word for a structural support or post; the stranger's dream locates the buried treasure beside this support in the cellar.

notes.label: fürbass
notes.text: an older regional adverb meaning onward or farther ahead; Niggi says nothing and continues on his way while pondering the stranger's dream.

notes.label: Handwanne
notes.text: a hand-carried tub or trough used here as an improvised litter in which the gravely injured Niggi is borne home; the source does not describe its exact form.

70687b80400399096b0c8ab6fd34ce890e71e9c0.summary: A farmer in Fäsch received money from his brother in America with which to support their old father.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally ‘poor soul,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for a departed soul unable to rest until a wrong is repaired or prayers are supplied; it does not imply that the father was financially poor.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

447cc8d98f90a5d76d954fa2ac7b779f5d6cca11.summary: After the descent from the Alp, a Senn sent his boy back up to fetch a forgotten milking stool.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high-elevation seasonal pasture with its dairy buildings, here deserted after the seasonal descent; the specific pasture is not named.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: a Senn is the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese production, appearing here both as the boy’s employer and among the spectral dairy crew; whether they are the same figure is uncertain.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: the Tril is a sleeping platform, loft, or raised resting place in an Alpine dairy hut on which the boy lies; its exact construction and local meaning are uncertain.

notes.label: Milchmuttlen
notes.text: Milchmuttlen are broad vessels or tubs used to hold milk in Alpine dairying; their exact size and form in this hut are uncertain.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Nidel is Swiss German for rich cream skimmed from milk, here removed by the Senn before cheesemaking; its precise fat content is unspecified.

notes.label: Kessi
notes.text: a Kessi is the large dairy cauldron in which Alpine milk is heated and made into cheese; its material and capacity are unspecified.

notes.label: Zusennen
notes.text: Zusennen are assistant Alpine dairymen working under or alongside the Senn, here operating the butter vessel; their precise rank and duties are uncertain and varied regionally.

notes.label: Ankenkübel
notes.text: an Ankenkübel is a large butter-making tub or churn—Anken being Swiss German for butter—worked here by two assistants; its exact mechanism is uncertain.

f6b92ff5a65ad789676912bb9a2035b4997b1620.summary: A vigorous Sumvixer who lived near an Alp once resolved to go to an Alpine pasture that otherwise had a very bad reputation.

notes.label: Sumvixer
notes.text: a man from Sumvitg, historically German Sumvix, in Graubünden; the regional demonym identifies the fearless protagonist.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, grazing rights, and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the senior Alpine dairymen or herders responsible for livestock and cheese making on a seasonal Alp.

notes.label: Handbub
notes.text: the junior male hand or boy performing subordinate work on an Alp; the story emphasizes that not even the lowest-ranking worker can be seen.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of a German-speaking Alpine house or hut, where meals and household life center.

notes.label: umgehen
notes.text: literally to go about or walk around; in a legend it means to haunt a place or return after death as a restless spirit.

notes.label: Zusennen
notes.text: plural of Zusenn, assistant Alpine dairymen working beneath or alongside the senior Senn in the organized pasture household.

34bde0d29c0ae0c00c7f40e477b2bda8a2524fcf.summary: A king had been ill for many years. No physician knew of a remedy that could cure him.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

6549bd7c923d5391b2ef67f03554444cedce39ec.summary: From time immemorial the people of the three Waldstätten—Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden—lived in peace and quiet around their many-armed mountain lake.

notes.label: Waldstätten
notes.text: literally ‘forest states,’ the historical collective name for Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, the three central Swiss lands around which this founding legend is organized.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: literally ‘alp blessing,’ an evening protective prayer or call traditionally sounded from a high pasture across the mountain hollows; its mournful change reflects the communities’ oppression.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, often powerful downslope wind of the Alps; here it roars into the valleys and threatens the houses while church bells provide reassurance.

notes.label: Tätschhäuschen
notes.text: a local diminutive for small, low or squat-roofed houses; the exact architectural form is not described, but the word emphasizes the modest dwellings battered by the Föhn.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor exercising delegated rule; the Austrian-appointed Landvögte in this national legend turn imperial protection into oppressive lordship.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or valley polity; Stauffacher and Fürst hold this native office in contrast to the imposed Landvögte.

notes.label: Nauen
notes.text: a large traditional lake or river boat; the heavy Nauen carries the Schwyz delegation across the Urnersee to and from the oath meeting.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Bull of Uri,’ the great horned war horn and, by extension here, the emblematic horn carried with the Uri delegation; it is an object and symbol rather than a living bull.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: the traditional open-air assembly in which eligible citizens vote publicly; the conspirators’ open vote is compared to this Swiss institution.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally companions bound by oath, the historical term for the Swiss confederates; here it identifies the men standing in the newly sworn covenant, not simply citizens of a modern federation.

7e36a139f1e467916483bd7f47a766fcc82ebc0d.summary: Where the merry whoops of the Wildheuer ring out from the grassy ledges of the Federi on sunny August days, the rich grass was formerly grazed by a cheerful little cattle herd under the supervision of a Senn.

notes.label: Wildheuer
notes.text: Alpine laborers who cut wild hay on steep, uncultivated mountain ledges; their whoops locate the legend in a hazardous working landscape.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder on a high pasture; his duty of care for the herd makes the loss through negligence blameworthy.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: wandeln
notes.text: literally ‘to wander’ or ‘walk,’ used in Swiss ghost lore for being condemned to roam after death rather than resting.

notes.label: Federi-Mannli
notes.text: literally the ‘little Federi man,’ the punished herdsman's local spirit-name derived from the Federi mountain area; the title's diminutive does not imply that he was physically small.

93e56a8f3c2f0d656d148549f1c8b39db65051d1.summary: Halfway between Aarau and the bridge at the village of Rohr, on the side of the road that drops steeply into the marshes of the Rohrer-Schachen, stands a moss-covered tree stump.

notes.label: Rohrer-Schachen
notes.text: the riverside Schachen belonging to Rohr; Schachen is a Swiss regional word for low alluvial ground, often wooded or marshy, beside a river.

notes.label: Fehrenlinde
notes.text: literally the ‘ferry linden,’ using the older regional form Fehre for Fähre, or ferry; the tree marked the former boarding place on the Aare.

notes.label: Wuhr
notes.text: a regional term for a constructed river barrier, weir, or protective embankment; Felsberg borrows money for such flood-control work.

notes.label: Gulden
notes.text: historical guilders or florins used as a unit of money; both occurrences of 300 identify the principal of the disputed loan.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Quatember-Abend
notes.text: the evening associated with one of the Ember periods in the Christian calendar, recurring four times a year and often treated as an uncanny time in Alpine tradition.

notes.label: Comilitonen
notes.text: Jecklin’s learned historical word for comrades or associates; here they are the men who knew of the treasurer’s fraud and share his posthumous boundary-setting punishment.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking the legal division between municipalities; the ghostly company must repeatedly reset one at the former Felsberg–Tamins boundary.

f3880e31a5cc50762664e89f8656c8ddaab99a1a.summary: Two maidens of good family from the region of Escholzmatt fled the valley bailiff’s lustful desires into a cave on the Scheibengütsch.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

2df9a7bf604bcf66c1667cd35f31062cf886484d.summary: On the Lasa Alp, near the Ragaz hut, a spirit well known in that region played his fiddle at night on the Stofel.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its associated pastoral operation, not simply any mountain; Lasa Alp is the named pasture setting of the story.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Stofel
notes.text: an Alpine pastoral term for a level, station, or group of buildings on a seasonal pasture; here it names the place on the alp where the ghostly fiddler plays, and ‘pasture’ alone loses that specific layout.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled herders and dairy workers who tend livestock and make cheese on a seasonal Alpine pasture.

notes.label: Alpruf
notes.text: the traditional Alpine herder’s call or sung prayer made on the alp, often invoking divine protection over people, animals, and pasture; its exact local words are not given in this story.

7cea2cd26561c442965d4ec461e4e7e89d911aa7.summary: A farmer who was very devoted to drink and was also a fiddler demanded another Mas of wine from the innkeeper, who was his Gevattermann.

notes.label: Mas
notes.text: a historical regional measure for liquids, here wine; its exact volume varied by place and period, so the source does not imply one modern standardized quantity.

notes.label: Gevattermann
notes.text: a man joined to another household through baptismal sponsorship, broadly a godfather or co-godparent relation; the kin-like bond helps explain the innkeeper's personal bargain with the fiddler.

db6fb04c8eb9e4b1e4569bccd89abe23cf5d5d18.summary: A Zusenn had taken to Fursch his fiddle, which he passionately loved and played beautifully; there, he liked to sit on the Stollen to play.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: an assistant Alpine dairyman subordinate to the chief Senn; he remains at Fursch after the herd descends.

notes.label: Stollen
notes.text: the named slope, spur, or ledge where the Zusenn plays; the source does not clarify whether it has any tunnel-like form.

notes.label: aussennen
notes.text: to finish out the Alpine dairy season after the main herd or other workers have departed; the Zusenn remains alone for this final work.

notes.label: Greller Jöri
notes.text: a local personal byname, approximately ‘Jöri of Grell’ or ‘shrill Jöri’; the source gives no secure explanation of Greller.

notes.label: Sufetuse
notes.text: the local name for the Molken-Tanse, a back-carried vessel used in collecting dairy alms; the term's literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Molken-Tanse
notes.text: a tall wooden carrying vessel for whey or other Alpine dairy produce, commonly transported on the back.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: the high seasonal pasture and dairy holding; the invisible music warns that snow will abruptly close it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

ef88b567eaa9025882e3e622ef4e0b8dc6669199.summary: A fiddler from Sargans called Giger Hans Jöri crossed the Rhine late one evening into Liechtenstein, where he was to play the next morning.

notes.label: Giger Hans Jöri
notes.text: dialect for ‘Fiddler Hans Jöri,’ with Jöri a regional familiar form of Georg; the byname identifies him by his occupation.

notes.label: Gsundheit Hans!
notes.text: dialect for ‘Health to you, Hans!’ and the opening of his habitual self-toast, whose pious blessing breaks the supernatural feast's spell.

bb04b1f17aefe6acade7ed4dd02f74a4ba4f1982.summary: In another Tobel, people claim to have heard a fiddler playing his tunes at night.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow wooded ravine or gorge, a common Swiss landscape term more specific than an ordinary valley.

8f19fb32f0c7f9858fb3df8f054ea08a5804518d.summary: Giger Hans-Jöri was crossing the Rhine late one evening into Liechtenstein, where he was to play.

notes.label: Giger Hans-Jöri
notes.text: ‘Fiddler Hans-Jöri,’ with Giger meaning a violin or fiddle player and Hans-Jöri a regional form of Hans-Georg; it functions as the musician's descriptive name.

notes.label: Gsundheit Hans! Gseg' ders Gott, Hans! Furcht der nüt, so gschieht der nüt.
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Health, Hans! God bless you, Hans! Fear nothing, and nothing will happen to you’; the self-directed protective saying violates the supernatural host's ban on drinking a health.
notes.anchor: Gsundheit Hans! Gseg' ders Gott, Hans! Furcht der nüt, so gschieht der nüt.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Riet
notes.text: a reed-filled marsh, fen, or wet meadow; here it is the local landscape where folk belief places witches' dances.

dc9a2bfa732498b9caeb78c7f8f783a1643d4f0b.summary: A young man from Fidris once went abroad. In the course of his travels he also came to Paris and bought cherries from a woman in the marketplace.

notes.label: Schwein-Boden
notes.text: literally “pig ground,” the locally named place above Fidris where the woman says she danced.

notes.label: Fidriser-Hexe
notes.text: literally the “Fidris witch,” a woman encountered in Paris who claims to have danced above Fidris the previous night.

0e330764bff520d06a9e1d303be75158c3645704.summary: Where it stands, a horse dealer and a string—that is, six—horses were once held fast by a spell.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

dded01773eced5ea607423de428f02feb2626a08.summary: It is sad and very discouraging for a cultivator when the crops do not stand safely in the field.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

7cac0d780f0b27f1765518375ed1f0559e65d82c.summary: A road once led from Eberseck Monastery—remains of it can still be found—along the Rickenbach, across the Altbürer Allmend, behind Bohnern, and through the Grosswald toward Saint Urban. — Old people related that during the Fronfastenwochen they commonly saw a fiery coach drawn by fiery horses…

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held local land, often used for pasture or shared resources; the old road crosses the Altbürer community's common land.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Fronfastenwochen
notes.text: the quarterly Ember weeks of fasting and prayer in the traditional Christian calendar; Swiss folklore often treats these liminal periods as times of heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Betglockenzeit
notes.text: literally ‘prayer-bell time,’ the morning hour marked by the church bell calling the community to prayer; the source gives no exact clock time.

6239d316820f1ca7d05f0a7c2671212772f28d2b.summary: A fiery dragon dwells beneath the red slab on Alp Maltschül. It appears only before a flood.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Maltschül
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture at Maltschül; Alp denotes an Alpine grazing area and its working landscape, not simply a single mountain summit.

43bcf8a19da5919efde054cf13a72666dfa13218.summary: On the Kreuzweide or Kreuzmatt near the village of Muri, a fiery goat in particular is seen in the water meadows alongside many a fiery man.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Dorftier
notes.text: literally “village animal,” a regional folklore label for an uncanny creature attached to a particular settlement; in Oberhofen it is the gigantic Geiss, not ordinary livestock.

notes.label: Geiss
notes.text: Swiss German for a female goat; here it names both the fiery apparition in the title and Oberhofen’s immense snow-white shaggy village beast.

notes.label: Nachtbube
notes.text: literally “night lad,” a young man who roams after dark for courting, watchfulness, or mischief; this narrator says only that he and his companions were lying in wait, so his exact nighttime purpose remains unstated.

16636568255098099deb42dda3fc334c2e67e64b.summary: My uncle was walking through a dense forest at night when he suddenly saw a fiery man standing some distance ahead.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

cf1cc9a0d0e2aaaef615a28df51f79905f2b24f1.summary: Below Klingnau, one must turn onto the footpath directly by the Bildstöckli to reach the Machnau and cross the Aare there.

notes.label: Bildstöckli
notes.text: a diminutive roadside devotional shrine, image pillar, or wayside religious marker; it serves as the landmark for the path into the Machnau.

notes.label: Fehren
notes.text: an older regional plural for ferrymen; the two Klingnau boatmen must carry the fiery revenant across and back on Christmas Eve.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a long, narrow, flat-bottomed riverboat traditionally used on Swiss rivers and propelled by oars, poles, or paddles; it is vulnerable enough that the boatmen fear their passenger will burn through it.

notes.label: Hardwald
notes.text: a woodland on firm or wooded communal ground, often preserved in place-names; Leuggern Hardwald is where the fiery man disappears, though the source spells the locality adjectivally.

notes.label: Schwibele
notes.text: the two-handed shaft or handle of the boat implement called a Schalte; the collector glosses its grip but not the word's wider technical range.

notes.label: Schalte
notes.text: a steering or propulsion implement used in the Weidling, likely a broad oar or boat pole; its exact local construction is uncertain, but its long handle safely receives the spirit's touch.

notes.label: Giriz
notes.text: a local name for a desolate wetland, scrub, or waste area toward which the fiery man flickers; the precise landscape and name derivation are uncertain.

notes.label: Brünnlig
notes.text: a local name for the burning or fiery spirit, related to brennen, ‘to burn’; its blackened finger marks remain visible on the Schwibele.

f887134a2ac5a9c44496a2568bd19721e3d8d35a.summary: A courageous man was walking outside Lengnau through the grain field beside the Surb known as G'wandle.

notes.label: G'wandle
notes.text: the local name of the grain field beside the Surb near Lengnau; its apostrophized dialect form is retained because the brief source does not securely establish a literal derivation.

e006d1296b035fbea01fe63ecaa8215bf5afed3c.summary: At the beginning of this century, the brickmaker of Rekingen was driving a wagonload of lime from the brickworks.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

c51820e021e7934fedf9a2ecb0228427f23c3edd.summary: Once an old ferryman at Hauenstein sat in his fishing boat, and as it grew ever darker, he fell asleep.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a traditional flat-bottomed riverboat of Switzerland and the Upper Rhine, commonly propelled by oars or poles; here it is the Machenau ferrymen’s craft.

notes.label: Zündler
notes.text: literally something or someone that kindles or burns, used here as a name for the fiery supernatural passenger; it does not identify his origin or exact kind of spirit.

notes.label: Schalte
notes.text: a regional boating term for an oar, paddle, pole, or related steering implement; the source specifies a double-gripped shaft but does not make the implement’s exact form clear.

696a1484a9b4d21458dad74a4610c4b8aba35ae7.summary: An old mouse catcher from Littau still remembered very well that in his youth he had often seen a hideous specter in Thorberg Castle, which has now been restored.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss German and Alpine term for a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge; here it is the landscape below Thorberg Castle into which the apparition is banished.

82c5f555c6ea3544f1c37ab90bda168e532e99f2.summary: Mount Prabé in Savièse, visible from Sitten, is believed to be filled with much uncanny haunting.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

409a4133cef3710e400b435bf24d884486d75a9b.summary: Long ago there was a king who had an exceedingly beautiful daughter named Bianca.

notes.label: Sbranaferro
notes.text: the Ticinese Italian name of the knight’s first supernatural dog; the source itself glosses it in German as Eisenfresser, ‘Iron-Eater,’ emphasizing the dog’s power against the giant.

94aed375de071eb5d44e1a4c04833920e48812c2.summary: The women once won a war; that is why they are now permitted to lead the prayers and go first in the offertory procession.

notes.label: About this telling

f8edd1b7d4f2e66e6b7058276a8d59201a234fb3.summary: It was in gray antiquity, when green Alp pastures stretched where glacier avalanches now thunder, and in the remotest reaches of the high Alpine valleys there still stood villages and hamlets where fine fruit flourished, vines grew green, and yielded a delicious wine.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, buildings, and working landscape, not simply a mountain summit; the vanished villages are replaced by such pastures.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpkraut
notes.text: the grasses, herbs, and other forage plants growing on an Alp; the herds graze this high-pasture vegetation during the best summer months.

notes.label: Pfaffenholz
notes.text: the local name of the woodland where the corrupt presidents buried the money and later haunt; literally it suggests a “priests' wood,” but the story does not explain the name or precise site.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for livestock and dairy work on a high seasonal pasture; this Senne is traveling back to the Meidenalp.

notes.label: Runse
notes.text: a steep erosion gully, ravine, or water channel down which a small stream flows; the Senne bends to drink there.

notes.label: Dreispitz
notes.text: literally a “three-point,” the three-cornered hat or tricorne associated with older dress; it helps mark the president's ghost as belonging to the past.

notes.label: Vollenbrücke
notes.text: the named bridge where the Senne must withstand three apparitions at midnight; the source does not explain the place-name's derivation.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: here the plural name for black horses, not the Swiss coin also called a Rappen; on the second night bears ride these supernatural horses.

notes.label: Talschaft
notes.text: a valley community or valley-wide territorial district whose settlements share a regional identity and institutions; the Senne imagines becoming its richest man.

188dfe3a8d1da7a42c4b5dcd233a170f40d968be.summary: In former times, so the story goes, two houses stood some distance apart in Kalpetran, a hamlet on the valley floor between Stalden and St.
