ede462e6f21a89c0fba503f8b492eca6fc1ddb79.summary: The skill and goodwill of the Erdleutchen were not slight. A herdsman on Seelisberg lived on the best of terms with the Herdmännchen.

notes.label: Erdleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ subterranean household and farm helpers whose favor rewards generous human neighbors.

notes.label: Herdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little hearth men,’ a local name here for the small otherworldly helpers who tend the herdsman's farm.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent downslope wind of the Alps; in the story it traps the farmer across the lake and keeps the little folk hidden.

notes.label: Giebeli
notes.text: the individual name or pet-name of the goat whose stomach supplies what is needed for cheesemaking; the exact nuance of the name is uncertain.

notes.label: Lup
notes.text: rennet, the coagulating substance traditionally prepared from a young ruminant's stomach and used to turn milk into curds.

cf7a2f27dd0473c2886afefcf5f23573b169af5a.summary: In the most ancient times, when there were still more pagans than Christians in the country and the latter, who lived in Schwyz and Unterwalden, had only one priest, the faithful from Ennetmoos in Unterwalden had to travel many hours over lake and land to Iberg in the present canton of Schwyz for…

notes.label: Kirchgang
notes.text: literally a ‘church-going’ or church procession; here it denotes Iberg's parish procession as a corporate body entitled to ceremonial precedence.

notes.label: Kreuzfahrt
notes.text: literally ‘cross journey,’ a religious procession or pilgrimage led by a cross; in this context, it does not mean a modern sea cruise.

notes.label: Fluhblumen
notes.text: literally ‘cliff flowers,’ Alpine flowers gathered from rocky heights; their wreath commemorates the parish's origin among high mountains and remote Alps.

notes.label: Saumweg
notes.text: a pack trail for laden animals, especially mules, crossing terrain unsuitable for wagons; the old route links Einsiedeln, the Silalp, and the Klöntal.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Silalp
notes.text: the Sil high pasture or Alpine tract on the old pack route; Alp denotes a seasonal pastoral landscape, not only a mountain summit.

notes.label: Föhnenberg
notes.text: the named mountain near Gersau; although the name resembles Föhn, the story gives no weather explanation for it.

notes.label: Stande
notes.text: a cooper-made wooden tub or vat adapted here as a small boat for crossing Lake Lucerne; the exact design of this improvised craft is not specified.

notes.label: Waldstätten
notes.text: literally ‘forest states,’ the historical collective name for the central Swiss cantons around Lake Lucerne, especially Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, with Lucerne often included.

d4d382c3b25ebfb870e25dbe803dda3f0fcd4cbe.summary: Römerstalden, a secluded little mountain village in the district of Schwyz that now has barely 123 inhabitants, is said once to have been much more populous and blessed with a far milder climate than at present.

notes.label: Römerstalden
notes.text: the secluded Schwyz mountain settlement whose depopulation the tale attributes humorously to the first appearance of freezing water.

notes.label: Hier können wir nicht mehr weilen, das Wasser ist uns dick geworden
notes.text: ‘We can no longer remain here; the water has become thick on us,’ the villagers' literal-minded description of ice and their reason for leaving.
notes.anchor: Hier können wir nicht mehr weilen, das Wasser ist uns dick geworden

111706a78ef180d56f53f396fcc448447991efa4.summary: Kunigunde, the cupbearer's daughter of Landegg, was betrothed to the knight Ulrich Muntprat, but the knight faithlessly abandoned her.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

4f14ee91611940d468b90140877f9ea7b54fd4d1.summary: Among the many visitors to the Visp valley, there can be few for whom Kipfen—which one must pass through after Kalpetran, within Stalden, and before St.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: a diminutive of Brunnen, meaning a little spring or fountain; here it forms part of the traditional place-name “Fluonazen's Brünnlein.”

notes.label: Meiertum
notes.text: the territory, jurisdiction, or office governed by a Meier; calling it free presents Kipfen as a self-governing local district, although the tale does not define its formal powers.

notes.label: Meier
notes.text: a historical estate or community administrator who could also exercise judicial authority; it does not map cleanly to the modern English word mayor.

05c90f7011924eb3cb1761c4bc691de268509050.summary: When one approaches the small village of Mägenweil on the road between the towns of Lenzburg and Baden, one sees large granite blocks lying in abundance on both sides of the road and extending far into the fields.

notes.label: Weisstein
notes.text: retained because the source’s intended historical function is uncertain; context suggests a conspicuous guide, marker, or pointing stone left beside the Roman road.

notes.label: Fischbank
notes.text: literally ‘fish bench,’ the local name of the great boulder linked here to a legendary pagan-era fish market.

notes.label: Fraufasten
notes.text: apparently a regional or source variant connected with a traditional fasting season, possibly ‘Fronfasten’ or the Ember fasts; its exact calendrical meaning here is uncertain.

notes.label: Wär’ doch ämel au das Donners-Füdli-Schlîfe verbî
notes.text: an Aargau dialect outburst meaning approximately ‘If only this damned thunder-butt grinding were finally over’; ‘Füdli’ is a diminutive for the backside, ‘Donners’ an oath-like intensifier, and speaking the phrase ruins the treasure ritual.
notes.anchor: Wär’ doch ämel au das Donners-Füdli-Schlîfe verbî

2942350197cd9634c40c99352478f0e6a5b8b99b.summary: When the fishermen of Schattdorf and Attinghausen engaged at night in forbidden fishing at Rynächt, in the Giessen that flow past there—one of which springs from the rock—and feimten fish, something would sometimes throw little stones down upon them from the sheer cliff.

notes.label: Giessen
notes.text: a regional plural for rushing or spring-fed streams, channels, or cascades; the passage describes several local watercourses at Rynächt and says that one emerges directly from the rock.

notes.label: feimten
notes.text: an uncertain regional verb for an illicit method of taking fish; the context establishes poaching but does not securely identify whether the technique involved stunning, poisoning, netting, or another practice.

b920d3ab48a97821891d1d5d8765f0eafc9a89e0.summary: Above Küsnacht on blue Lake Zurich, the hamlet of Itschnach lies on a small plateau.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow, often wooded ravine or stream gorge common in Swiss terrain vocabulary; the dragon cave lies within such a thorny ravine.

notes.label: Fledermausstein
notes.text: literally ‘bat stone,’ the hidden cave's local name; despite the name, the legend concerns a dragon and does not say that bats inhabit it.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a great serpentine dragon of Germanic legend, often wingless or long-bodied; the story also calls it a dragon, but never gives a complete anatomical description.

notes.label: Schloff
notes.text: a narrow crawl, slot, or constricted rock passage through which a person must squeeze; its wet, cold tightness nearly traps and suffocates the knight.

notes.label: Bärtschen
notes.text: an uncommon sound-word paired with snorting for the noise of what seems like a pasture full of bulls; it suggests bellowing, grunting, or harsh roaring, but its exact acoustic sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Dole
notes.text: a narrow tube, drain-like channel, or rock passage; here it is the tight conduit opening into the dragon's broad grotto.

notes.label: Drachenschloff
notes.text: literally ‘dragon crawl’ or ‘dragon passage,’ the suffocatingly narrow approach to the lair; it combines the creature with the regional word Schloff rather than naming a separate being.

6ed9227901fe7ac4bc34d4c155ee94c9b8fa9469.summary: In earlier times one heard much from old people about fiery, flying dragons that traveled from one mountain to another.

notes.label: Chnubul oder Chnollo
notes.text: Valais dialect for a dark knot, clump, or rounded mass seen at the head of the fiery apparition; the paired words describe its shape rather than identify a separate creature, and their exact nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: Vuivra
notes.text: the Francophone Alpine form related to French vouivre, a flying dragon- or wyvern-like being; here it is crowned, fire-winged, and feeds on gold sand in the mountain lakes.

notes.label: Fassnacht
notes.text: the Carnival season before Lent; the expression ‘lean Fassnacht’ evokes meager fare after the ice has kept the hungry Vuivra trapped too long.

notes.label: Cavalier
notes.text: the French label ‘horseman/rider’ inserted by the source for the wild spectral rider of the Francophone Eringertal; it does not identify a titled nobleman here.

5088d229dc5e242356bf0ea6105a299328a990d9.summary: In the small green mountain lakes of Lona, Larduzan, and Esserce in the canton of Valais lives a dragon called La Vuivra.

notes.label: La Vuivra
notes.text: La Vuivra is the French or Franco-Provençal name for the winged, jewel-bearing serpent or dragon of Alpine folklore, here associated with the Valais mountain lakes; the name’s local pronunciation and whether the lake dragon and Vouvry viper are the same being are uncertain.

dd1fbc5099107f5f2df02485e20b945855b496a3.summary: At the time when the Eidgenossen were at war with Duke Leopold of Austria and defeated him so powerfully at Sempach, an entire line of castles belonging to Austrian nobles stood around lovely little Lake Baldegg.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘confederates bound by oath,’ the forces of the early Swiss Confederacy; the word carries a historical political identity more specific than generic ‘Swiss soldiers.’

notes.label: Harsthörner
notes.text: war horns used to signal or rally a Harst, an armed body or battle formation; their feared roar never reaches the fog-hidden castle.

notes.label: Mau
notes.text: the local name of the upper terrain where the disoriented Eidgenossen finally recover their bearings; the source does not explain its derivation.

notes.label: Procul estote profani!
notes.text: Latin for ‘Keep far away, you profane!’ or ‘Let the profane stand afar’; the chapel inscription warns irreverent intruders away and memorializes divine protection.

9517c082dfb8fcddf1401ef3246d63545d264ab1.summary: From the back of the Gerstenhorn, an arched mountain ridge extends westward as far as the Schwabtor.

notes.label: Bettenalp
notes.text: the named summer Alp below the Faulhorn where the father and son manage the cattle.

notes.label: Folle
notes.text: the local name for the funnel-shaped hollow whose narrow outlet opens above the abyss; the word is retained because it functions as a specific landscape name.

notes.label: Lugistein
notes.text: the local name of the large square, split stone opposite the Folle; Lugi may suggest looking or watching, but the source offers no etymology.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or herdsmen responsible for the cattle and milk work of a summer Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss word for a steep rock face, crag, or cliff; the Folle's outlet lies at its edge above the abyss.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially Alpine herders and dairy workers; the son's desperate method is described as their custom.

notes.label: Gemsjäger
notes.text: chamois hunters; together with the Älpler, they hear the spectral herd in the high country.

notes.label: Sennerei
notes.text: an Alpine dairy operation or the place and working unit in which a Senn processes the herd's milk; its bells continue to sound supernaturally.

notes.label: sçä, sçä, sçä!
notes.text: the source's exact printed cattle call, used by the herdboy to coax or direct the animals; its pronunciation and narrower local meaning are not explained.

notes.label: Follenküher
notes.text: the cowherd associated with the Folle; Küher is an Alpine cowherd, while the title may refer to either the vanished father or the dead son and does not resolve that ambiguity.

74e83bca9bfb69af5ef5becdfdf9f5828b587dd2.summary: Robbers roamed the dense spruce forest between Brig and Turtmann, plundering, stealing, and terrifying the village communities.

notes.label: Freiherr
notes.text: a German noble title conventionally rendered as baron; the story retains it as part of Stockalper's public rank and reputation in Brig.

notes.label: Bratenwender
notes.text: literally a “roast turner,” the kitchen servant responsible for turning meat on a spit before the fire; the disguised Stockalper uses the job to observe the robbers' cave.

notes.label: Es geht nicht immer so, sondern auch so!
notes.text: literally “It does not always go this way, but sometimes that way”; Stockalper makes it seem like foolish talk about changing the direction in which he stirs, then repeats it at judgment as a joke about the reversal of fortune.
notes.anchor: Es geht nicht immer so, sondern auch so!

e5827616fcebec2922c303097b7d6a14acda8caf.summary: Once there was a foolish lad. He was poor and no longer had either father or mother.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a historical large silver coin-name whose value varied by place and period; the fool offers one to the road mender after finding the robbers’ money.

5a19b1d41918d93f0975cdb169585c72db3755de.summary: In ancient times, when dwarfs still ran through the forests like ants, there were also mighty giants who possessed a dreadful strength.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: a Swiss plural for steep rock faces, cliffs, or crags; here their fourfold echo magnifies the giants’ voices, while the exact landform is not specified.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a hard Alpine conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones can resemble nail heads; it is characteristic of parts of the Swiss Prealps, and here its hardness makes the giants’ contest extraordinary.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight measure used in German-speaking Europe, conventionally around 50 kilograms in later metric usage but variable by place and period; the tale uses it loosely to convey enormous weight.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese, traditionally made from the whey left after ordinary cheese production; its moist, crushable texture lets the tailor counterfeit a stone, although the exact local recipe is unstated.

notes.label: Morgengabe
notes.text: literally a “morning gift,” the traditional gift associated with marriage and historically given by a husband to his bride; the tale humorously reverses or broadens the custom by making the kingdom the tailor’s wedding gift.

7d96f469fd10fbd400cb6e88c214491c8f61e578.summary: Only a few years ago, a man from the mountains of Mörel encountered a stranger standing by the road at night near Nussbaum, a small estate between Mörel and the Nussbaum bridge.

c6f74c5cb39b2669366b2eb536d06296b5d76a54.summary: Above the fertile meadows and fields of the Savièse mountain spreads a great forest upon Mount Prabé.

notes.label: Wasserleite
notes.text: a mountainside irrigation channel, especially the Valais watercourses also known as Suonen or bisses; this dangerous channel conveys Morge water through cliffs to the meadows.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

notes.label: Wasserfuhr
notes.text: literally a ‘water conveyance,’ another term here for the labor-intensive irrigation work or channel system; its distinction from Wasserleite is not made precise.

notes.label: torrent neuf
notes.text: French for ‘new torrent’ or ‘new channel,’ the local name given to the dangerous Wasserleite; despite torrent, the context describes a constructed irrigation watercourse.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

notes.label: Plan dy danses
notes.text: a local French or Franco-Provençal place name meaning approximately ‘dance ground’ or ‘plain of dances’; it names the clearing used for secret dances, but the source does not standardize the spelling.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: a raised loft, platform, or gallery inside an Alpine hut, here reached by a small ladder and used as the hay-sleeping place; the dialect word does not reveal the structure’s exact layout.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheese-making cauldron, normally hung over the fire to heat milk; the uncanny men use one despite there being no milk in the cellar, and its material and size are unstated.

notes.label: Muttlä
notes.text: a dialect name for a bowl, tub, or shallow dairy vessel placed on the table; here it is filled with Schottä, but the vessel’s exact form is uncertain.

notes.label: Schottä
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for whey, the liquid left after curds form during cheesemaking; it is the supernatural meal offered to Christa after the impossible nighttime cheese-making.

793d335643407163a46d389732c03aa558cd9e3c.summary: According to an old legend, in the days when the Romans began to spread through our country and had already settled in ancient Helikon, a nobleman of that people became separated from his retinue while hunting, in the heated pursuit of a magnificent red deer through the gorges of the Sense.

notes.label: Sense
notes.text: the German name of the river called the Singine in French; its gorges and bilingual setting shape the Grasburg landscape.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a dragon-like serpent of Germanic legend, often wingless or long-bodied; killing it makes the rock safe for the hunter's castle.

notes.label: Aventikum
notes.text: the source's Germanized form of Aventicum, the Roman city at modern Avenches from which the commander supplies workers.

notes.label: Crassusburg
notes.text: the legendary original name of Grasburg, said to derive from its Roman founder Crassus; the tale offers this as an origin story rather than documented etymology.

notes.label: welschen Raubritter
notes.text: an older German expression for a Romance-speaking robber knight; welsch marks linguistic and cultural otherness from the German-speaking narrator's perspective and can carry a disparaging tone.

30019b66932106312678225d62fd01fc866f29f9.summary: Once there was a distinguished nobleman. He was very often bored, for he was old and could no longer shine in tournaments, among the ladies, or at any other knightly pastime.

notes.label: Fischenz
notes.text: a Fischenz is a legally defined fishing right or fishery, not merely a favorite fishing spot; the source does not specify the privilege’s exact boundaries or feudal terms.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the Föhn is the warm, often forceful Alpine downslope wind used here as the measure of the dream’s roar; the actual weather conditions remain uncertain because this occurs within a dream.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Nixen
notes.text: Nixen are German-speaking water spirits, often imagined as dangerous female beings, here blamed for trying to pull travelers into the Rhine’s depths; their precise form in this local tradition is uncertain.

00e794a5e1c779b1c1402a77f72e82ca975cea83.summary: It was around the year 1200. Where the lovely City of Roses stands today, there were then only a few fishermen’s huts.

notes.text: a historical German-speaking office translated only approximately as bailiff, steward, or governor; here Count Rudolf’s Vogt is a trusted seigneurial official who advises him, while the office’s exact powers varied by territory and period.

21cd194658f2a808f798d730ded712fb1bd92c6b.summary: “Selber han, ist über Vater und Mutter,” says an old proverb. Whoever has something of their own is their own master and therefore need not depend upon the favor and caprice of others.

notes.text: literally ‘having one's own is above father and mother’; the proverb praises material and institutional independence rather than dependence even upon close family, and frames the communities' determination to support their own parishes.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

notes.text: literally a ‘church meadow,’ here the named meadow endowed to the priest at St. Niklaus so that its fodder could support a horse for pastoral travel.

notes.label: O weh, wir kommen zu spät! — Der Gauch geht schon mit Kappe und Stücke um die Kirche herum.
notes.text: approximately ‘Alas, we are too late—the fool is already going around the church with cap and staff’; Gauch is a contemptuous ‘fool’ or ‘cuckoo,’ while Kappe und Stücke appears to mock the bishop's ceremonial dress and staff during the consecration procession.

notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture together with its huts, herd, and dairy operation, not merely a mountain peak or the Alpine range.

notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working seasonally on an Alp, especially its herders and dairy workers; here the Capuchin addresses the whole pasture community.

notes.text: the Italian word for a master or proprietor, natural in the Ticino setting; here it refers to the man in authority who shoots at the fox.

notes.text: an Alpine cheese room, storehouse, or small dairy outbuilding where cheeses are made, tended, or kept; the exact division of work and storage space is not stated.

9f990d708a2a1df8b962f0c64ae421d9ae518483.summary: Enough has already been heard about brinnige Manä, or fiery men, about the Schrättlig and the Grääggi.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional diminutive related to Schrat or Schrätteli, names that can denote a troublesome spirit, nightmare-being, or uncanny creature; this brief allusion does not identify which local sense is intended.

notes.label: Grääggi
notes.text: the dialect name of another locally familiar supernatural being; the collector assumes the audience knows it, and this passage gives neither a literal derivation nor enough traits for a secure English identification.
