notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Swiss centime coin and a traditional byword for a very small amount of money; the landlady refuses any payment because the hunter once spared her fox form.

8ec8c2ee95477b02a7c4a9c69dbc084aebfeda9b.summary: One evening Martin Schnider of Mädris was lying in wait as a hunter on his mountain holding at Pasatti.

notes.label: das Tenn
notes.text: a regional neuter form for the barn's threshing floor or central work floor, where the hunter throws the apparent foxes.

notes.label: Tenne
notes.text: the more general German form for the threshing or work floor of a barn; it denotes the same space called das Tenn in the preceding paragraph.

notes.label: Ofensäule
notes.text: literally ‘stove pillar,’ a structural column or support associated with the large masonry stove in a traditional heated room; the fox is hung from it overnight.

notes.label: Anstand
notes.text: a concealed or stationary waiting position used by hunters watching for game, here taken up inside the stable rather than a modern sense of propriety.

89dbef307255e08545a5915ed0f525f2c2a31f0f.summary: Something uncanny once happened to two councilors down at Rynächt. Late one evening they had come from the council in Altdorf and wanted to go home to Erstfeld and Silenen.

notes.label: Bleegi
notes.text: a strip, flap, or piece from the hem or lower part of a woman’s skirt; the exact cut of the historical garment is uncertain, but the transformation exposes the fox tail as a piece of women’s clothing.

df59f051160fa405a72e3dc13cbd5c625dcc0283.summary: Once, the noble Count Wilhelm lived at Wartau Castle, gentle toward his subjects and kind to his own people.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f50dceba6104c7fe68a2926ccebaad01288c867b.summary: 1. a) At Gurtnellen, on the Grossprächtigen estate beside the Reuss, lived a councilor whose wife had come across Lake Lucerne with two sisters, each of whom married a councilor.

notes.label: Grossprächtiger
notes.text: the local designation for the man associated with the Grossprächtigen estate; the source uses it like a house-name or place-derived byname and does not explain its origin.

notes.label: Berggut
notes.text: a privately held mountain farm or pasture property, often with buildings and seasonal agricultural use; it is more specific than a generic mountain.

notes.label: jaiken
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to chase, hunt, or drive away; the fearless farmhands use it for pursuing the specter.

notes.label: Russdiele
notes.text: literally the soot loft or soot platform above the hearth or chimney, where soot collected and where the cats or specters are found.

notes.label: Frau Ratsherrin
notes.text: an older title for a councilor’s wife rather than necessarily a woman holding the council office herself; the bilingual title preserves the source’s social designation.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman or herder responsible for livestock and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; it is Hans Zurfluh’s former occupation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: ds Melkä Bärg
notes.text: the dialect place-name of the Arni mountain holding, approximately ‘the milking mountain’; the story identifies it as the modern name without further derivation.

notes.label: tohlete
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to endure, thrive, or last in a place; no hired man survives or remains long on the haunted holding.

notes.label: staiken
notes.text: a regional variant of jaiken, meaning to chase or drive away; the story explicitly records both forms.

notes.label: manschen
notes.text: a playful dialect verb for eating, used in the proverbial exchange about whether to chase the specter or eat first.

notes.label: gebeindelt
notes.text: literally furnished with legs; the condemned witch says her barrel of fleas was not yet given legs, grotesquely presenting the vermin as unfinished weapons intended for Uri.

notes.label: Böllen
notes.text: the Swiss German word for onions; the Göschenen witch fetches them impossibly from Milan while boiling down butter.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; Ankeneinsieden is the process of boiling or rendering it down.

notes.label: Chämi üff und drüß und fort und niänä-n-a!
notes.text: an Uri witch-flight formula meaning approximately ‘Up the chimney and out and away, touching nowhere’; it commands an unobstructed supernatural departure on the broomstick.
notes.anchor: Chämi üff und drüß und fort und niänä-n-a!

notes.label: Chessli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Kessel, a small cooking pot or kettle; here it is the copper vessel holding the rice porridge.

notes.label: Aschischi, nuschischi! wem-mer-sch z'erscht jäikischi uder wem-mer z'erscht manschischi!
notes.text: a playful, strongly rhymed Uri formula whose final question means ‘Shall we chase it first, or eat first?’; the opaque opening words are retained because the source does not establish a secure literal meaning, though it separately records äschischi as a variant of manschischi.
notes.anchor: Aschischi, nuschischi! wem-mer-sch z'erscht jäikischi uder wem-mer z'erscht manschischi!

notes.label: Z'erscht wem-mersch jäikischi, de chenne-mer nachhär mit Rüehwä manschischi!
notes.text: the answering formula means ‘First we shall chase it; then afterward we can eat in peace’; its comic rhyme helped make the exchange proverbial.
notes.anchor: Z'erscht wem-mersch jäikischi, de chenne-mer nachhär mit Rüehwä manschischi!

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: the small, warm living room or parlor of a Swiss house; the councilor confronts his wife there.

notes.label: Schweizebrühe
notes.text: the name of a regional broth or cooked dish in this variant; the source does not identify its ingredients securely, so the exact food-name is retained.

notes.label: Breitbiäl
notes.text: Uri dialect for a broad axe or broad-bladed hatchet, one of several weapons assigned to the farmhand in alternate tellings.

notes.label: Gertel
notes.text: a regional heavy knife or billhook used for cutting brush and wood; some variants substitute it for the sword.

notes.label: Asisi, nusisi, wem-mers z'erscht jäikä uder wem-mer z'erscht ässä?
notes.text: a later proverbial form of the playful, partly opaque question, meaning ‘Asisi, nusisi, shall we chase it first or eat first?’; people repeated it jokingly before meals.
notes.anchor: Asisi, nusisi, wem-mers z'erscht jäikä uder wem-mer z'erscht ässä?

notes.label: Äs müess also doch eppis a der Sach sy!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘There must therefore be something to the story after all’; narrators treat the survival of the proverb as evidence for the legend.
notes.anchor: Äs müess also doch eppis a der Sach sy!

a8c28d7115510a6ea0898ad38d2fdaff934d8575.summary: A man in the Solothurn region was likewise a Fraufastenkind. Once, when he intended to go to Solothurn, he encountered a woman carrying a child upon her arm and a glowing rod in her hand.

notes.label: Fraufastenkind
notes.text: a person born during the Fraufasten or quarterly Ember-fast period and therefore believed able to perceive spirits; the exact calendar observance varied in popular usage.

35fadd409e70f9c82dbf66e0512b9b7b9ff45b50.summary: It is said that all those born at the midnight hour around Fraufasten can see spirits.

notes.label: Fraufasten
notes.text: a Swiss Catholic name associated with the quarterly Ember fasts; regional timing and beliefs varied, and the source specifies only birth around this period at midnight.

notes.label: Fraufastenkind
notes.text: literally a ‘Fraufasten child,’ someone born during the seasonal Fraufasten period and believed to possess second sight; here the girl can see dangerous spirits but is protected by keeping silent for twenty-four hours.
The source title mentions ‘hare’s paws,’ but no hare or paws appear in the surviving story text; the title has been translated without inventing a missing episode.

99788aedcce4f6325f3c8c6a416381e9ecfdfebd.summary: The Free Walser very probably also possessed several settlements in Weisstannen, including the Alps of Laui and Valtona.

notes.label: Walser
notes.text: Walser were German-speaking Alpine settlers whose communities often held distinctive medieval rights and freedoms; here the expression ‘Free Walser’ links old settlements around Weisstannen with local families and institutions, though the tale speaks only probabilistically of their presence.

notes.label: Heidenstöfeli
notes.text: a local diminutive place-name, approximately ‘little heathen rise/spot,’ for remains on the Plattenboden or Stierenlager; Heiden in Swiss antiquarian usage often marks ruins believed to be very ancient, not a securely identified pagan site.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional local magistrate or administrative head; the claim that Valtona had its own Ammann presents it as a self-governing community.

notes.label: Walserweide
notes.text: literally ‘Walser pasture,’ a surviving place-name cited as evidence of former Walser presence near the Weisstannen Klosteralp.

37b4027fc2f0224bbf5dc53377bc7a9aa018a268.summary: On the rocky shelf of the Aare's bank, where Aarau's town hall and church now stand, a strong tower called Rore rose in the earliest times.

notes.label: Freihof
notes.text: literally a ‘free court’ or privileged holding; here it is the fortified sanctuary at Aarau where people seeking protection from oppressors could claim refuge.

notes.label: Adelbändli
notes.text: the surviving local name for the short lane and lodging area beside the castle approach, with the diminutive Bändli suggesting a small strip or band and Adel referring to the noble retainers who stopped there.

e0256c3b4ac72f84869a1dfe4d32c264703de462.summary: The final days of May 1799 were very sorrowful days for the good people of Upper Valais.

notes.label: Landbrücke
notes.text: literally ‘land bridge,’ the local name used here for the bridge at Visp where the people of Upper Valais renewed their resistance; it is a proper place-name, not a general reference to a land bridge.

notes.label: Hölelen
notes.text: the quoted local place-name where Zeneggen's council and priest meet the French; it resembles a dialect diminutive related to a hollow or small hollow, but the source does not establish a precise derivation.

notes.label: Brachmonat
notes.text: an old German month-name, literally the ‘fallow month,’ normally meaning June; thus the 11th of Brachmonat is June 11, though the historical wording is retained.

e018efdb6c938591415b05f619d8f3f7b5f3aad6.summary: As everyone knows, nothing was safe from the hands of the French. They even knew how to find money buried in the ground.

notes.label: Futterfass
notes.text: literally a ‘fodder barrel’ or ‘feed cask,’ a storage vessel here hung on the door as the only hiding place protected from the French soldiers' enchanted treasure-finding balls; the tale does not explain why it is immune.

a0e061fe46d94911b9db78386df80ddb4e2ad50c.summary: 1. During the Franzosenzeit, a Frenchman was shot or beaten to death near St.

notes.label: Franzosenzeit
notes.text: literally the ‘French period,’ the era of French invasion, occupation, and warfare in Switzerland around the turn of the nineteenth century; the story does not identify the dead soldier or exact engagement.

notes.label: Skapulier
notes.text: a blessed Catholic scapular or small devotional token worn or carried for protection; placing one on the exposed bone, with repeated prayers, gives the restless remains ritual aid.

fc2e61149916c7de5814848e227a7d446a59f1a4.summary: At the southern foot of the Bürgenberg (Bürgenstock) in the canton of Unterwalden (Nidwalden), several hundred paces upward from the lake near Saint Anthony's Chapel, a small cave formed of fissured limestone lies in a sloping meadow.

notes.label: Föhnwind
notes.text: the warm, dry downslope föhn wind of the Alps; here it accelerates snowmelt that feeds the intermittent spring.

notes.label: Friedhöfler
notes.text: the local short name for the periodic spring and brook; it resembles a word for someone or something connected with a cemetery, but the source explicitly says the reason for the name cannot be guessed.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German name for the French-speaking lands to the west, especially Romandy; here it marks the old woman's place of origin rather than a foreign country in the modern sense.

notes.label: Maibrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘May spring’ or ‘May well,’ another name used here for the remarkable periodic source; the account does not say whether Mai refers to the month, seasonal flow, or a local name.

notes.label: Tropf! Tropf! Tropf!
notes.text: German for ‘Drip! Drip! Drip!’; one interpretation hears the periodic cave water in the dead woman's voice.

notes.label: Kopf! Kopf! Kopf!
notes.text: German for ‘Head! Head! Head!’; the competing interpretation makes the ghost repeat the price she rashly offered in her challenge.

notes.label: Friedhöflerbach
notes.text: the stream-name formed from Friedhöfler and Bach, ‘brook’; the narrator notes the irony that this violently intermittent water shows none of the calm suggested by Friedhof, ‘cemetery.’

352e3306b6b2c1ef3d53d6982d65b33c3ffb5674.summary: On bright summer nights, when the sound of herd bells on all the surrounding alps and the yodels of the Sennen had faded against the cliffs of the Ammertenhorn, and no sound dared disturb the holiness of the night except the young Simme winding down into the valley from its confined bed of foam in…

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, Alpine herdsmen and dairymen on high summer pastures; their yodeling helps establish the tale’s Bernese mountain setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

50aba5f9e402e2c093e5b45fb40e5ee842ba1b02.summary: In the Bernese Oberland is a region called the Saanenland where the nights are anything but safe.

notes.label: Laubbett
notes.text: a Laubbett is a bed or mattress filled with dried leaves, presented here as a safe place during the nocturnal procession; its exact construction and seasonal use are uncertain.

notes.label: Guckauskämmerchen
notes.text: literally a ‘little look-out chamber,’ Guckauskämmerchen denotes a small upper or projecting room where the resident sleeps; its exact architectural form in the Saanenland is uncertain.

notes.label: Friesenvolk
notes.text: literally ‘Frisian people,’ Friesenvolk names the legendary settlers and their dead nocturnal host that follows the same route between the Saanenland and North Sea; the tradition’s historical relationship to real Frisian migration is uncertain.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high seasonal pasture and its associated buildings, here crossed by the spectral Friesenweg; the particular pasture is not named.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: a Senn is the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy work, here careful to keep the spirit route open; his identity is unspecified.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: Älpler are people who work seasonally on an Alp, here lying fearfully in the hay while the procession passes; their exact number and duties are unspecified.

notes.label: Traggabel
notes.text: a Traggabel is a forked carrying frame worn on the back for transporting Alpine produce, here supporting a butter sack; its exact construction is uncertain.

notes.label: Buttersack
notes.text: a Buttersack is a bag used to carry butter from the Alp into the valley, loaded here onto the carrying frame; its material and capacity are unspecified.

notes.label: Meisterknecht
notes.text: a Meisterknecht is the chief farm servant or foreman left in charge during the Senn’s absence; the post’s exact authority and the man’s identity are unspecified.

notes.label: Wildheulager
notes.text: a Wildheulager is bedding made from wild hay cut on remote or steep ground, here the farmhands’ loft bed; its depth and arrangement are uncertain.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: Gaden is a regional term for a barn, stable, or enclosed building section, through whose cracks the farmhands see the stars; its exact architectural scope here is uncertain.

notes.label: Friesenvolch
notes.text: Friesenvolch is the dialect form of Friesenvolk used in the host’s demand to pass through the stable; the source’s exact Saanenland pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: Wildheu is hay harvested from uncultivated, often steep mountain grassland, from which the foreman climbs down; the source does not specify where it was cut.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

d6a56dea191f69b2c38d78b09f3e950700de21c3.summary: When children in and around Sargans are naughty, or when they still roam the streets and make noise in the evening after the Betläuten, the Froshas comes for them.

notes.label: Betläuten
notes.text: the evening prayer-bell ringing, after which children are expected to be home and quiet.

notes.label: Froshas
notes.text: a Sargans-area bogey who carries disobedient children into the Valeistobel; the name's literal derivation is unclear in the source.

notes.label: Valeistobel
notes.text: the steep Valeis ravine or gorge into which the Froshas carries children.

notes.label: Valeishund
notes.text: the feared ‘Valeis dog’ said to inhabit the church-tower-deep hole in the ravine.

notes.label: Hüllafrau
notes.text: a female bogey invoked against children who resist washing and combing; Hülle may suggest a cave, hollow, or frightening covering, but the source does not define her form.

notes.label: Baubau
notes.text: a nursery bogey name comparable to ‘bogeyman,’ used as a general threat when children do not behave.

notes.label: Traubenmännli
notes.text: literally ‘little grape man,’ the vineyard guardian who chases grape thieves with a pruning knife.

f06127f46e75a21152b05478dceec30a62861c3f.summary: 1. a) Two unmarried men from Schattdorf were returning home from a pleasant Stubeten.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: an evening household gathering or courting visit in Alpine custom; the first pair are returning from one when they discover the witches.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night lads,’ young men who go out after dark for social visits, courting, or revelry; their customary curiosity drives them to the window.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: a diminutive of Stube, a small heated parlor or living room; the witches’ magic rebounds when its vessel is moved inside.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young unmarried women, using the characteristic -li diminutive; the variants also use the inflected plural Meitlenen for the alleged witches.

notes.label: Häfelein
notes.text: a diminutive of Hafen, an older regional word for a pot or earthenware vessel; it contains the weather-working liquid or ointment.

notes.label: pfitzerten
notes.text: the collector’s dialect word for giggling; the witches laugh while preparing harm for the blossoming fruit trees.

notes.label: wem-mer de das vor ds Pfeischter üsästellet, vercheemet's de bi Zittä dirr's Obst hyr, d'Lytt
notes.text: the witch’s dialect description of setting the vessel outside so the local people’s fruit will be blighted; the intended destruction is clear, while the verb’s narrow shade between withering and freezing is uncertain.
notes.anchor: wem-mer de das vor ds Pfeischter üsästellet, vercheemet's de bi Zittä dirr's Obst hyr, d'Lytt

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: bim schwärä Tirrli
notes.text: literally ‘by the heavy little gate or door,’ a dialect locality label at Obrieden; the source does not identify the structure more precisely.

notes.label: Susanneli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Susanne or Susanna; it is the local familiar name assigned to one of the alleged witches.

notes.label: Gang doch uff ds Ofäbänkli ga liggä!
notes.text: the exact dialect invitation ‘Go and lie down on the little stove bench’; the Ofäbänkli is the warm bench built beside or around a room stove.
notes.anchor: Gang doch uff ds Ofäbänkli ga liggä!

notes.label: Was wem-mer hinecht g'schändä?
notes.text: the witches’ exact dialect question, ‘What shall we harm tonight?’; they choose the region’s nut crop.

560dc298b3c2a842b31cde7ef96123e0680553fa.summary: In the ruins of Schwarzenstein Castle at Obersaxen, a black figure of a man is said to rise from his crypt at midnight with a little chest beneath his arm.

notes.label: Fräulein
notes.text: literally a young unmarried woman or maiden; in castle legends the word often identifies a supernatural castle maiden bound to hidden treasure and awaiting release.

9b6f7c4284f182308d3bb32154384ba10fa9065c.summary: At Rosenburg there lived a grim, hardhearted knight with his angelic daughter.

notes.label: Alpenhorn
notes.text: the long wooden Alpine horn used by herders for music and signaling across mountain distances.

notes.label: Fräulein
notes.text: historically an unmarried young woman and, in this castle setting, the knight’s young noble daughter; the retained title carries a more specific social tone than simply “girl.”

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully, often cut by a torrent.

notes.label: Frohnfasten
notes.text: a regional historical term for the Ember fasts, the recurring church fast periods associated with the quarterly Ember Days; the knight’s annual ride occurs during this sacred season.

cdb0ac51b2d734d8261d4058452a18ae251951b0.summary: The pious and charitable wife of Cuno, Knight of Ruchenberg, had assisted the queen of the elves, who reigned within the mountain, during childbirth.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: the traditional game of skittles or ninepins and, by extension, its complete set of pins and balls; this golden elven set can summon mountain spirits and becomes the promised treasure.

notes.label: Fräulein
notes.text: historically a title for an unmarried young woman or maiden, here the pious daughter haunting her ancestral castle rather than a modern form of address.

f1b0bf58cfff1af367752b53eb7036024ca13c80.summary: There was once a soldier. He had served as a volunteer for two years, and when his time was over, he wished to return home.

notes.label: Backtrog
notes.text: a large traditional wooden kneading or dough trough used in breadmaking; this one is big enough for the woman’s visitor to hide inside among the fresh dough.

a726ffdecb074bfc85cdb11176a504c32a530de2.summary: A young man in Savièse, it is told, was very fond of hunting and spent many a fine day in the high mountains.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Lerchen
notes.text: literally ‘larches’ or ‘larks’ in standard German, but neither sense fits the battlefield action securely; the context suggests a possible historical misprint or transcription for Leichen, ‘corpses,’ so the source form and uncertainty are retained.

c6ff401be3e13858e0bd6479130b59a418095658.summary: In the Burgerwald above Muschels there once lived a tiny race of people called the gray dwarfs, who were sometimes visible and sometimes invisible.

notes.label: Hans Aeby, sag dem Appele, Appela sei tot.
notes.text: Alemannic-inflected German meaning ‘Hans Aeby, tell Appele that Appela is dead’; Appele and Appela appear to be paired personal names or diminutive bynames, but the source identifies only Appela as Aeby’s mother-in-law.
notes.anchor: Hans Aeby, sag dem Appele, Appela sei tot.

notes.label: Hans Aeby, sag dem Appele, d'Appela sei tot!
notes.text: the repeated regional call meaning ‘Hans Aeby, tell Appele that Appela is dead’; d’ is the contracted feminine article, while Appele’s identity remains unstated.
notes.anchor: Hans Aeby, sag dem Appele, d'Appela sei tot!

382ebb42ec037fe232ab3f2db2c9c86b243bf547.summary: Just as many legends tell of ancient landslides, prophecies also live in the speech of the people that hold out the sorrowful prospect of great lakes forming over beautiful fields and inhabited villages when high mountains break away and plunge down.

notes.label: Schuh
notes.text: a historical foot measure whose exact length varied by territory; the source reports roughly one and a half Schuh of ground subsidence, so it should not be read as a modern standardized unit.

9e134e43582c217ba72131e96b2b7b2145a5deb4.summary: The Fährenthal near Leuggern was formerly a single farm whose landed property extended from Mandach and Hettenschwil to Leuggern and from there along the road to Böttstein.

notes.label: Fehren
notes.text: the source's historical regional word for ferrymen who lived by the former Aare crossing; their occupation supplies the folk explanation of the name Fährenthal.

notes.label: Hinterbänkli
notes.text: literally a ‘little rear bench,’ the local place-name for the spot near which the murdered brother was buried; the source does not describe the feature behind the name.

858afb41e4c9ceb8bb534632799623947bd5226a.summary: Before one reaches Gretschins from Oberschan by way of Malierfi, one comes to the Kropfenbrünneli.

notes.label: Kropfenbrünneli
notes.text: the local name of the notorious little spring on the way to Gretschins; literally it suggests a ‘little goiter spring,’ but the account does not explain the name or connect it directly with the swine apparition.

notes.label: Fährlisau
notes.text: a sow with piglets, from the regional word Fährli for a young pig; the apparition swells to ox-size while her litter multiplies beyond counting.

notes.label: Fährli
notes.text: the regional plural or collective form for young pigs or piglets; in the apparition, their impossible increase overwhelms the passerby.

feb2e148672f8106df11404bb9dc7dca7c7e9649.summary: In Maladers, a Fänggenmannli tended a farmer’s cows for a long time and also took care of the stable work during the farmer’s absence.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: a diminutive male Fängge, one of the wild forest or mountain beings of Graubünden tradition; this one quietly tends cattle and performs stable work.

notes.label: Gepse
notes.text: a broad, round wooden dairy vessel used for milk or cream in Alpine households and cheesemaking.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Mann, “man”; here it refers back to the small Fänggenmannli.

fb3775aac1a3a958b74d468b621df8a729c40fd4.summary: A Fänggenmannli in Savien behaved in a manner similar to the Kühjer at Conters and Monbiel.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: a little male Fängge, one of the shaggy or wild beings of Graubünden and neighboring Alpine tradition; here it acts as a supernatural cattle-herder.

notes.label: Savien
notes.text: the historical place-name spelling used in the source for the Safien valley in Graubünden; the source form is retained rather than silently modernized.

notes.label: Kühjer
notes.text: an older regional plural for cowherds or Alpine cattle tenders; the opening compares the Savien being with helpers known at Conters and Monbiel.

notes.label: Fängge
notes.text: the shortened name for the wild Alpine being; receiving human clothes causes it to admire itself, abandon its staff, and leave service.

955dce24d8d6cef93a534c826388e949a32e4199.summary: Once a forest Fänggenweiblein watched curiously as a man split laths in a wood near Churwalden.

notes.label: Fänggenweiblein
notes.text: a diminutive female Fängge, one of the wild forest beings of Graubünden and neighboring Alpine traditions; Weiblein means “little woman,” but the compound names a distinct folklore figure.

de9b1c33a181de9b04bffb8f2648ca16bc734f19.summary: The following legend shows how the strong wild maidens did not dislike seeking the company of handsome young Sennen on the Alpen and tending their herds.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the senior Alpine dairymen or cheesemakers whose company the wild maidens seek.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, seasonal high-mountain pastures and their working settlements.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape, where the son winters with the cattle.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennerei
notes.text: the Alpine dairy workspace or operation in which milk is processed into butter and cheese.

notes.label: Madrisa
notes.text: the wild maiden’s name and the name borne by the rocky peaks to which she returns.

notes.label: Habe
notes.text: the household’s livestock or herd, not possessions in general in this context.

notes.label: Molken
notes.text: dairy yield or milk products; the wording can also denote whey, but here the context broadly emphasizes the abundant production of the well-fed cattle.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an inflected form of Senn, the young Alpine dairyman who later calls Madrisa’s name toward the peaks.

notes.label: Fänggin
notes.text: a female Fängge, one of the strong wild beings of Graubünden and neighboring Alpine traditions.

2d985e19919fc01f91c29c05cd891a3587c2b12a.summary: In Luzein there still stands today a stable whose massive wooden beams the present owner’s Urähni, with the help of his maid, a Waldfänggenmädchen, dragged into place and fitted together. — This Fänggin is said to have been very well liked in her master’s family, and their distress over her was…

notes.label: Urähni
notes.text: a regional kinship word for a remote male ancestor, broadly a great-grandfather or still earlier forefather; the exact generation is not stated here.

notes.label: Waldfänggenmädchen
notes.text: literally a “forest-Fängg girl,” identifying the maid as a young female wild being of the forest rather than an ordinary servant.

notes.label: Fänggin
notes.text: the feminine form of Fängg, a wild forest or mountain being in Alpine folklore; here she lives as a household maid but retains supernatural kinship and disappears after learning of her father’s death.

notes.label: Ruchrinden
notes.text: the Fänggin’s byname, literally suggesting “rough bark”; the tale does not explain whether it describes her appearance, forest nature, or family identity.

notes.label: Gicki Gäcki uf Hurgerhorn
notes.text: the supernatural figure and place phrase reported by the mysterious voice; uf means “on” or “at” in Alemannic speech, while the source gives no further explanation of Gicki Gäcki or Hurgerhorn.

9c72c5f6b4c0b22d14941c4c15882abd61edc3a4.summary: On Alp Tschuggen above Langwies, a man was splitting laths for a fence. As he worked so diligently, he was suddenly addressed by an uncanny-looking figure.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Tschuggen is the named Alp above Langwies.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Hinter-Ehni
notes.text: a great-grandfather or more distant male ancestor; Jecklin supplies Ur-Grossvater, ‘great-grandfather,’ as the gloss here.

notes.label: Pfiff
notes.text: literally a whistle, but here explicitly glossed as a clever ruse or trick—the only means by which the man can escape the forest being.

notes.label: Wald-Fänggin
notes.text: a female Fängg associated with the forest, one of Graubünden's powerful and dangerous Alpine wild folk.

notes.label: Fänggin
notes.text: the feminine singular of Fängg, a wild Alpine being; she is also called a Wald-Mutter in this story.

notes.label: Wald-Mutter
notes.text: literally ‘Forest Mother,’ an alternative name in the source for a female forest-dwelling Fängg or wild woman.

notes.label: Selbthan
notes.text: an archaic-looking name meaning approximately ‘self-done’; by giving this false name, the trapped Fänggin makes her cries sound as though she did the harm to herself.

notes.label: Wegge
notes.text: a dialect word for the wedge that holds the split lath apart; removing it clamps the Fänggin in the wood.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: the plural of Fängg, the band of wild beings who answer the trapped Fänggin's cries and pursue the man.

notes.label: z'Huderen
notes.text: a dialect expression glossed by Jecklin as Fetzen, ‘rags’ or ‘shreds’; it describes being torn violently to pieces.

13415e40175161809e21181b7ef3b4dcbf65f3f8.summary: Near the Gafarra alpine pasture in Rhaetia stands a hill called the Gafarrabüel, a gathering place for witches.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gafarrabüel
notes.text: the local hill name combines Gafarra with Alemannic Büel, ‘hill’ or ‘knoll’; here it names the witches’ gathering place by the Gafarra alpine pasture.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

004d08488050304882be089d36b238382f4cf2b6.summary: An elderly man from Felsberg once went into the woods to gather wood. He also came to the area of the “Goldene Sonne” gold mine, high on the Galanda.

notes.label: Goldene Sonne
notes.text: literally “Golden Sun,” the proper name of the gold mine high on the Galanda; the tale associates its vicinity with gold that appears and vanishes, but does not establish the mine’s historical output.

b57202c43d95fd948cb49877c0253e60628d0df8.summary: In Gutenburg, municipality of Lotzwil, district of Aarwangen, there was in olden times a tyrant-lords' castle whose ruins can still be seen.

notes.label: Galgenlölitier
notes.text: the local name of a brown four-footed flying apparition identified with the returning tyrant lords; Galgen means ‘gallows’ and Tier means ‘animal,’ but the middle element Löli and therefore the full literal sense remain uncertain.

580cbb55ea544e6b0aedfb2698866ce97fe68728.summary: Saint Gall once passed through our district while wandering across the Rhine lands.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little spring or well; here it emphasizes the modest natural source that becomes a sacred local landmark.

notes.label: Gallenbrunnen
notes.text: ‘Gall's spring’ or ‘Saint Gall's well,’ combining the saint's name with Brunnen, which can denote a spring, well, or fountain; the legend explains the name through Saint Gall's blessing.

2a1fde2c45a954ed5e180084d9e92cec0c4903ad.summary: During his journey through the Arbon forest, Gallus also came to a spring. He refreshed himself there and blessed it in return.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

52a9ca5c8c2169e77be50791ccb14ba56705d449.summary: There once were several young men who played cards together every day, even on Sunday.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7a2a102ea296d014b43abc0d62b50bf45b72f288.summary: In an old meadow hut at Bödem on the Grossberg near Flums, several young men frequently and passionately gambled through half and whole nights.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

107f01949d7c3cabeac19c0ae41677643fb44396.summary: In former times, while its owners were still alive, such a cheerful and merry life prevailed in this castle that it continues even after their deaths.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d686f8b6c5bbc8e24a77069fcf8d575f79fb97b7.summary: 1. a) Whenever the Gangbach plunged down destructively near Schattdorf, a witch was repeatedly seen riding downstream on a Trähm[1].

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Trähm
notes.text: a regional word for a heavy log, beam, or timber on which the Gangbach witch rides; the historical footnote explicitly corrects Lütolf's spelling Trumm to Trähm.

notes.label: Holztitschi
notes.text: an uncertain Uri diminutive for a small chunk, billet, or roughly shaped piece of wood used as the witch's flood-borne mount.

notes.label: z'fahrädä chu
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning to come riding or driving down; it emphasizes the witch's active descent with the dangerous stream.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person’; here it marks the uncanny flood-rider rather than an ordinary woman.

notes.label: Gatzä
notes.text: a regional word for a ladle, dipper, or scoop; the Schächen witch uses it to throw brook water upward and intensify the weather.

a080d753246796c9e1a582ef299dc8227891a754.summary: A footpath leads from Vättis to Untervaz across the Alps of Owaggis and Salatz.

notes.label: Oute Garmina
notes.text: the source's local place-name for the witches' dwelling beside the alpine path; its exact literal sense is not explained.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its associated working landscape, not merely the Alps as a mountain range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Dreifaltigkeitssalz
notes.text: literally ‘Trinity salt,’ salt blessed or ritually associated with the Holy Trinity; mixed with powder here, it helps a consecrated silver bullet strike the witches.

notes.label: Garmina-Hexen
notes.text: literally the ‘Garmina witches,’ three shapeshifting sisters attached to the local Garmina landscape above Vättis.

64802553ae4a54fc7fa3932d99f85c6f3b98236f.summary: From the earliest times, an unusual regional custom known as the Gassengericht has existed in Uri.

notes.label: Gassengericht
notes.text: literally ‘street court,’ an emergency Uri tribunal assembled on the spot from the first suitable citizens encountered; its judgment is described as fully binding despite the improvised selection of judges.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or head of government in a Swiss canton or rural polity; here the Landammann decides whether urgency exists, recruits the judges, and presents the case.

cc2a6d08d53644b50845e48224ae0b1da1f9cf95.summary: Where the mighty Gauli Glacier now fills the broad valley floor, in former times lay the beautiful Blüemlisalp, the property of a wealthy Sennerin.

notes.label: Blüemlisalp
notes.text: literally ‘little-flower Alp’ or ‘flowery high pasture,’ the fertile former estate said to lie buried beneath the glacier; Alp denotes the whole seasonal pastoral holding, not just a peak.

notes.label: Sennerin
notes.text: a female Alpine dairyman or senior dairy worker; the cursed owner is defined by her pastoral occupation and responsibility for the herd.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine herding and dairy hut; timber emerging from the glacier is treated as physical evidence of the buried pasture settlement.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gauliweibchen
notes.text: literally ‘little Gauli woman,’ the regional name of the condemned Sennerin's apparition; the diminutive need not imply that she is child-sized.

notes.label: Gauliwibli
notes.text: the Alemannic equivalent of Gauliweibchen, again meaning the ‘little Gauli woman’; the source records both forms without distinguishing different beings.

notes.label: I und min Kathrin und mini Küh brün und min Hund Rhin müssen immer und ewig auf Blüemlisalp sin.
notes.text: the dialect lament means ‘I and my Kathrin, and my brown cows, and my dog Rhin must remain upon Blüemlisalp forever and ever’; whether Kathrin is a person or another named member of the pastoral household is not explained.
notes.anchor: I und min Kathrin und mini Küh brün und min Hund Rhin müssen immer und ewig auf Blüemlisalp sin.

35afa6add05823701955365862edc3dd4ae79773.summary: The Oberfelder family up on the Schattdorf mountains were just churning butter when the Geezigerli[1] from Attinghausen entered—a small, peculiar, poor old woman—and demanded some fresh Nidel.

notes.label: Geezigerli
notes.text: the diminutive nickname of the poor old woman, derived according to the source's footnote from the farmstead Geezig; its exact social tone beyond the diminutive is uncertain.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for rich fresh cream; the Geezigerli demands it before churning and supernaturally spills the cream when offered buttermilk instead.

3c582c254d8ea8e287bd1e2543e593d463c19444.summary: At the witching hour, the Geissbachzopfi rides a white horse past the Majenpfüsis and down across the Schreja.

notes.label: Geissbachzopfi
notes.text: the local name for a mounted night spirit associated with the Geissbach area; Geissbach is a place-name and Zopfi is a dialect diminutive related to a braid or tuft, but the account does not explain the figure’s appearance or the name’s exact origin.

bd6a1bf5197327aa219ec187df26f2dfb4d505c6.summary: The Vonöischi, or Illgraben as it is also called, is a rock basin of wild grandeur, with reddish walls washed by rain that rise bare and sheer like the crater walls of an extinct volcano.

notes.label: Vonöischi
notes.text: the local name for the wild rock basin that the story explicitly identifies also as the Illgraben.

notes.label: Illgraben
notes.text: the steep Valais erosion ravine or rock basin beside which the boy grazes the goats; tradition makes it a place of banished spirits.

notes.label: Pfynwald
notes.text: the great forest on the Illgraben's alluvial delta through which the boy travels between the ravine and the Rhone.

notes.label: Zytgeissli
notes.text: the story's local term for a fully grown goat that has not yet borne a kid; this is the missing animal.

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: a holder of local communal authority; the missing goat belongs to him, and the boy fears losing his herding post.

notes.label: Zi-i-irbi
notes.text: the boy's long-drawn herding call for the missing goat; the source provides no separate literal meaning.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Gank
notes.text: the source's unusual printed form for the long passage inside the mountain, likely related to German Gang, but retained without silently correcting it.

notes.label: Laubsack
notes.text: a sack or mattress stuffed with dried leaves and used as simple bedding; the ending contrasts it ironically with the dangerous featherbeds.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally a goat boy, a young herder responsible for tending goats; his search leads him into the mountain's supernatural halls.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a historical local court or community officer, usher, or messenger; the story does not specify the rich cousin's exact jurisdiction.

notes.label: Quatemberkind
notes.text: a child associated by birth with the Church's quarterly Ember Days and credited in Alpine folklore with perceiving spirits or hidden supernatural things.

notes.label: Zirbi
notes.text: the shortened call or familiar name used for the missing goat after the earlier cry Zi-i-irbi; the source does not define it further.

56e9de1b5e1fbe2508e433ed6eabdb7a106efa69.summary: A Geisshirt returned merrily to the Sennhütte every evening. The Älpler said, “Goat's milk cannot make him so merry.” They spied upon him and saw him lie upon his stomach at the upper edge of the forest and press d's Mul an's Haltji.

notes.label: Geisshirt
notes.text: a goatherd, from Swiss German Geiss, ‘goat,’ and Hirt, ‘herdsman’; his unexplained merriment leads the other Alpine workers to spy on him.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the working hut of Alpine herders and dairymen upon a seasonal high pasture; it is more specific than an ordinary mountain cabin.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally upon an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; they are the Geisshirt's suspicious companions.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: d's Mul an's Haltji
notes.text: Valais dialect for pressing ‘the mouth against the little slope or bank’; the phrase describes how the hidden barrel is tapped at ground level, while Haltji's exact physical form is not explained.

4b30e90f9da215bf44b3941cca6b0b42ed4c70d8.summary: The last village in the Prättigau in Grisons is Klosters. Anyone wishing to go from there to the high valley of Davos by the old road will notice, not far from the village, a boulder of unusual shape.

notes.label: Geissler
notes.text: a goat herder or goatherd, from Geiss, the Swiss German word for goat; the occupational name also gives the Geisslerstein, literally the goatherd's stone, its name.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a fresh Swiss whey cheese made from proteins left in the whey after ordinary cheesemaking; it is distinct from the regular cheese that accompanies it as the wild herder's payment.

0cc490ab0f4ff7375c306dd5dd0ec0789f94872e.summary: On a late-autumn day, a hunter was pursuing game in the territory of the Valpun Alp, which belongs to the municipality of Luzein.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp-Entladung
notes.text: the seasonal clearing of a high Alp when livestock, people, and equipment descend after the summer grazing period.

notes.label: Säss
notes.text: an Alpine dairy-hut site or small seasonal settlement on a high pasture; here it identifies the Valpun station.

notes.label: Pritsche
notes.text: a simple sleeping platform or bunk used by Alpine herders in dairy huts, as the source itself explains.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the skilled dairyman and herder in charge of cheesemaking on an Alp; the tale says the apparition had held this role in life.

notes.label: Geistersenne
notes.text: literally “spectral Alpine dairyman”; a Senn is the skilled herder and cheesemaker responsible for a high-pasture dairy, while this one returns as a punished spirit.

9fc58fce4200eb256e9794de54f4cdd517a4c987.summary: From Thierstein mountain, a little brook descends through the meadows of Oberfrick and Wittnau and joins the Wölfliswil stream not far from the road that leads from Frick over Benkenberg to Aarau.

notes.label: Geistwegli
notes.text: literally ‘little ghost path,’ with the Swiss German diminutive -li; it is the haunted meadow footpath where the miller challenges the spirit and later follows it.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Maria Einsiedeln
notes.text: the traditional name for the Marian shrine and pilgrimage at Einsiedeln Abbey; the vow is a pilgrimage honoring Mary at Einsiedeln, not a journey to a separate person or settlement named Maria.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Geistmüller
notes.text: literally ‘ghost miller’ or ‘spirit miller,’ the local sobriquet given to the miller after his encounter and sudden white hair; it associates him with the redeemed spirit rather than saying that the miller himself is a ghost.

ef279613662ed677df0d421c094bacad82dba9b2.summary: A man from the Schächen Valley would have liked to possess a Geldscheisser.

notes.label: Geldscheisser
notes.text: literally a ‘money-shitter,’ a deliberately coarse folk name for a magical familiar or animal expected to produce wealth; here it appears as a red-bellied newt suspected to be the Devil.

notes.label: Martini
notes.text: St. Martin’s Day on November 11, a traditional seasonal marker in Alpine rural life; the late date makes the newt’s appearance especially unnatural.

36f5ff566a2ae70e4c8460bff169853867eb7e8c.summary: In former times the communities of Upper Valais were much richer and better off than they are today.

notes.label: Gemeingeld
notes.text: literally ‘community money,’ the collectively owned municipal treasury kept under several keyholders; the Valais examples lament both its theft and the decline of older communal stewardship.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Dechili-Josi
notes.text: a Valais nickname meaning approximately ‘little-blanket Joseph,’ from Dechili, a diminutive of ‘cover’ or ‘blanket’; it identifies the foreign weaver by the bedcovers he made.

007d0e1980f99089e17653f05bb081b5007e2165.summary: A Fänggenmannli lived in the Trockenhöhle above Camana in Savien, where he had set up a very fine chamois dairy.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a “little Fängg man,” a male wild forest or mountain being in Alpine tradition; here he keeps a supernatural chamois dairy and guards its cheesemaking secret.

notes.label: Trockenhöhle
notes.text: literally “dry cave,” the named cave above Camana in Savien where the Fänggenmannli keeps his dairy; the source gives no further geological description.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally “ridge animals,” a regional Alpine expression for chamois that emphasizes their high rocky habitat; the source immediately treats them as the animals milked in the cave.

notes.label: Gemskäslein
notes.text: a shortened spelling within the story for the title’s Gemsenkäslein, literally “little chamois cheeses”; the variation belongs to the source wording rather than indicating a different food.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alemannic diminutive meaning “little man”; here it is the shortened name for the Fänggenmannli, not an ordinary child-sized human.

notes.label: Gebsen
notes.text: shallow wooden dairy vessels used for holding or setting milk; here the small fir-wood vessels contain chamois milk, but their exact dimensions are not given.

notes.label: Gemsenkäslein
notes.text: literally “little chamois cheeses,” the title’s diminutive name for the sweet cheeses made from tame chamois milk; their supernatural production is the secret at the center of the tale.

7c895acab576e9b8667bcb53fac9d3e665423bc5.summary: A famous Gemsjäger once lived in the Guttannen valley. He had already shot so many Grattiere that the people had burned the number into a beam at the village inn with a hot iron.

notes.label: Gemsjäger
notes.text: a chamois hunter; in Alpine culture the role implies expert movement through dangerous high terrain, while the tale condemns this hunter's excessive bloodlust.

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally ‘ridge animals,’ a Bernese Alpine term for chamois; the source alternates this local name with Gemse.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like subterranean or mountain beings in Swiss folklore; here they regulate the taking of chamois and punish the broken bargain.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short hunting rifle associated with Alpine marksmen; reaching for it signals the hunter's return to prohibited killing.

57300504012629d46585e41c5d3c511f76946bdc.summary: A Fänggenmannli lived in the dry cave above Camana in Savien, where he had set up a quite fine chamois dairy.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a male wild forest or mountain being in Alpine tradition; here he keeps a supernatural chamois dairy and guards its cheesemaking secret.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally ‘ridge animals,’ a regional Alpine expression for chamois that emphasizes their high rocky habitat; the source immediately treats them as the chamois milked in the cave.

notes.label: Gemskäslein
notes.text: literally ‘little chamois cheese,’ the sweet miniature cheeses made from the tame chamois’ milk; their supernatural method of production is the secret the brother tries to steal.

notes.label: Gebsen
notes.text: shallow wooden dairy vessels used for holding or setting milk; here the little fir-wood vessels contain chamois milk, but their exact dimensions are not given.

e0f5ccb699041ffe148e9716b5e565f2807b73a4.summary: In the communal cellar of Törbel lies an old wine barrel whose hoops and staves can no longer be distinguished.

notes.label: Kellerstutt
notes.text: a local word for a structural post or support in the communal cellar; the round speaking stone stands beside it, but the source does not describe its precise form.

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: the historical Törbel municipal office held by Baschi; the officeholder addresses the council, manages its cellar meeting, and leads the officials before the full assembly, but the source does not equate the role with one modern office.

notes.label: Marjosi
notes.text: a local name for a wine jug holding a Doppelmass, or double measure, handed to a councilor at the end of the cellar session; its exact modern capacity is not supplied.

notes.label: Doppelgrosskanne
notes.text: a named local wine jug or serving measure used in the council’s procession; its compound suggests a doubled capacity, but the source gives no exact modern volume.

notes.label: Doppelkanne
notes.text: the double jug or measure holding the leftover wine that Baschi takes and that his son must later restore; its exact capacity is not stated.

notes.label: Gräbt
notes.text: a regional term for the funeral, burial, or graveside observance at which the dead Gewalthaber’s virtues are praised; the source does not describe the ceremony further.

notes.label: Wässerwasser
notes.text: water allocated or carried for irrigating cultivated meadowland; its timing makes every minute precious to the irrigator.

notes.label: Wasserfuhr
notes.text: the irrigation channel, watercourse, or run by which the Wässerwasser is conducted toward the meadows; the source does not specify its construction.

notes.label: Matten
notes.text: cultivated meadowlands requiring irrigation for their grass or other vegetation, rather than simply any open fields.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

631403cdcf0ca495c08cea7d07e5174beddfac01.summary: In the cellar of the municipality of Törbel stands an old wine vat. In the middle of the vat is a somewhat suspicious bung-hole—one might say, well suited to secretly drawing off wine.

notes.label: Gewaltshaber
notes.text: a historical Valais communal office; in this account he presides over the municipal council and addresses the assembly, so ‘communal chairman’ is the closest contextual gloss, though the title’s powers may have varied locally.

notes.label: Grossen Vergeb
notes.text: the local name for Corpus Christi Day; its literal derivation is uncertain, and the observance is associated here with the municipality’s traditional communal drink.

notes.label: B’scheide
notes.text: the source glosses these as wooden cupfuls; they function as customary measured servings of communal wine, and the dialect plural is retained because it names the local drinking practice rather than merely any cup.

notes.label: Marjosi
notes.text: the local name for a large double jug used to carry a full measure of wine from the cellar meeting into the larger assembly; the source gives no further etymology or exact modern capacity.

notes.label: Ponten
notes.text: the regional word for the large bung or stopper in the wine vat, contrasted with the suspicious smaller side opening used for quietly drawing wine.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

notes.label: Kreuzmittwoche
notes.text: literally ‘Cross Wednesday,’ a local religious calendar designation associated here with the parish procession to Glis; the source does not specify its wider liturgical equivalence.

618a1d76a7348edae0367ea30af20b3ad528c11c.summary: In the Toggenburg and Appenzell regions, some people still believe that there are men who can gfören themselves—that is, make their bodies entirely insensible to every blow, even blows from a crowbar, except for one small spot on the body, usually beneath the nose or under the armpit.

notes.label: gfören
notes.text: the verb for magically making oneself insensitive or invulnerable to blows; the text treats the practice as a folk belief and also notes that some men may merely have concealed pain.

notes.label: Krummbachhämmel
notes.text: the feared brawler’s byname, combining the place or stream name Krummbach with Hämmel, ‘wether’; its precise insulting or identifying force is uncertain.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Sidelenbein
notes.text: the name of the bone or bone-like club carried by the brawler; its exact anatomical source and regional word formation are uncertain from the account.

notes.label: Gfrörni
notes.text: a dialect noun for the protective invulnerability produced by gfören; here it fails to protect the brawler from the fall.

notes.label: Gfröre
notes.text: the regional name for a supposed magical state of bodily invulnerability to blows, except at one hidden vulnerable spot; it is not ordinary freezing despite its resemblance to the German word for frozen conditions.

notes.label: Ledigen

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Besenreiterinnen
notes.text: literally ‘broom riders,’ a vivid name for witches imagined as flying to nocturnal gatherings; here they meet at the Gönhard's stone table with other demonic women.

858cce8109fb2384f8f4681ccba26db11056d752.summary: a) In the Totenbodenwald near Altbüron, close to the stone cross, a spirit is said to be bound within a circle of three Schwieren, or posts.

notes.label: Schwieren
notes.text: the source's regional word for posts or stakes; three of them define the spirit's binding circle, though they hide themselves from anyone who intentionally searches for them.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Bresten
notes.text: a regional term for an affliction, epidemic, or wasting disease among livestock; in these accounts it is the harmful form or effect through which a spirit ravages the herd.

9dde9335a011a3250555d11c5e0df6a98b012026.summary: One night an old man rode through the “Züge” between Wiesen and the Hoffnungsau smelting works.

notes.label: Züge
notes.text: the quoted local name for the route section between Wiesen and the Hoffnungsau works; the source does not define whether it refers to gullies, avalanche tracks, or a narrower named district.

notes.label: bock-still
notes.text: a regional intensifier meaning utterly or stock-still; the horse is supernaturally unable to move despite whip and spurs.

notes.label: weiggte
notes.text: a dialect past-tense form explicitly glossed by Jecklin as bewegte, ‘moved.’

notes.label: Dreimaster
notes.text: literally ‘three-master,’ an older colloquial German name for a tricorne or three-cornered hat, not a sailing ship in this context.

06bbe89b6705d0a8b62cb03f04129a5c67461902.summary: The Ilmibodenalp belongs to the municipality of Escholzmatt in the Entlebuch.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: historically a young nobleman, country squire, or untitled member of the landed elite; the social rank is more specific than simply ‘old man.’

notes.label: Fronfastennächte
notes.text: the nights associated with the quarterly Ember fasts, regarded here as especially ‘dark’ and dangerous times when the spirit gains lethal power.

82d1b01f1aa26ca61c063e5f065d70f66fbd2d6e.summary: Türä-Teeni of Wassen was coming from Geschenen on a winter night when snow lay on the ground.

notes.label: wiëtig
notes.text: a quoted Uri intensifier conveying something immense, formidable, or fearsome; it heightens the unprecedented size of the ghost’s Finken rather than specifying their material or style.

notes.label: Finken
notes.text: Swiss German for soft house shoes, slippers, or light low shoes; the apparition wears impossibly enormous ones outdoors in the snow.

211d9738c1ef6f4bbfccea2bfd29ae7ce2fa4d56.summary: A hardworking grown daughter who lived in the so-called little Caviezl house in the Lürlibad above Lochers-Gässli near Cur once set out for home late in the evening after eating supper at the farm where she had worked.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, the nearby city in Graubünden.

notes.label: Zunachten
notes.text: a regional expression meaning at nightfall or as evening closes in, the time when the freed apparition most often appears.

10b4c04a63c80867bd4c5e8b452702d9bfe3c19a.summary: Stables—Stadel or Gaden—are generally taken over by monsters when uninhabited.

notes.label: Stadel
notes.text: a detached farm storage building or barn, especially for hay or grain; regional forms and uses overlap with Gaden.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a regional barn, stall, or small farm outbuilding; its exact function varies by locality.

notes.label: Heiterloch
notes.text: the small hayloft or ventilation opening through which the creature looks; the precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Bettelmummeli
notes.text: a diminutive regional name for a disguised or bundled-up begging woman, used here for the boys' mistaken identification of the apparition.

notes.label: Nüessi
notes.text: bumps, knocks, or minor injuries received from the encounter; the exact bodily effect of this dialect plural is uncertain.

c048ddb94c9c529cddd6be28b76d59ae4588d6f8.summary: Formerly the path from Bristen to Frentschenberg as far as the Frutt lay lower than it does today.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a natural rock shelter, overhang, or shallow cave in Swiss Alpine place vocabulary; here the small recess beside the old path is called the ‘cold hole.’

notes.label: kalte Loch
notes.text: literally the ‘cold hole,’ the source-exact local name of the small Balm beside the former path; the missing article reflects the name as printed.

5f340f6042a1d0e42ed782e627c76a5136b56561.summary: The courageous son of the Sigrist in the village of Kulm was a childhood playmate of men of the Kulm Valley who are now elderly.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan, responsible here for the church tower and clock; the office may combine practical and liturgical duties.

notes.label: Schmalzküchlein
notes.text: small cakes or fritters fried in rendered fat; the exact regional recipe is not specified, but their domestic frying continues comically amid the falling body parts.

notes.label: Schurzfell
notes.text: a craftsman’s protective leather apron; the tailor places his own apron on the spectral gold because the legend requires a personal possession to secure a ghost treasure.

175f7bbbae4d7a473b9c3fa0525e94cdfb988c72.summary: Years ago, fierce boundary disputes prevailed between the neighboring municipalities of Süs and Lavin.

notes.label: Süs
notes.text: the historical German name used here for present-day Susch in the Lower Engadin; the tale concerns its municipal boundary with Lavin.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: a marked boundary stone establishing the limit between jurisdictions or properties; moving it turns the Lavin claim into both a legal fraud and a spiritual offense.

notes.label: inu’ il dess eu metter?
notes.text: a Romansh question meaning “Where shall I put it?”; the boundary-stone mover repeats it after death until someone tells him to return the stone to its former place.

notes.label: Grund und Grat
notes.text: literally “ground and ridge,” a formula expressing that the adjudicated boundary should endure as long as the land and mountain crest themselves remain.

notes.label: Freund Hain
notes.text: Jecklin’s form of Freund Hein, a traditional German personification and euphemistic name for Death, who comes to take the dishonest stone-mover away.

notes.label: O pover disfortüna! metta’l, nel nom del segner, inua tü hast tut.
notes.text: the carter’s Romansh-influenced reply, meaning “O poor unfortunate one, in God’s name, put it where you took it from”; the instruction releases the ghost.
notes.anchor: O pover disfortüna! metta’l, nel nom del segner, inua tü hast tut.

8e0dcb37516eaf65040416af70dc5ec0420c23dd.summary: Between Cernez and Cierfs, in the middle of the Ofen-Passe, one encounters an old inn that is said to have stood there for several centuries.

notes.text: the source’s inflected historical spelling of the Alpine pass now often called Ofenpass or Pass dal Fuorn, linking the Engadine side with the Münstertal.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of an Alpine or German-speaking house or inn, traditionally the room where household members and guests gathered.

c48b486a86b9b6756200532e2ec9ac5f075e687a.summary: On a lonely meadow on the slope of the Bürgenberg (Bürgenstock) beside the Waldstättersee, two souls, father and daughter, lived in a quiet cottage.

79553f44907a22f529d05ddfefebcf67c9442c04.summary: Jos. Maria Simmen of Realp knows this tale: One summer, a Realp farmer named Balz Regli is said to have had ten or eleven cows on the Bort in Isenmann’s Alp, with a farmhand and one of his boys there as well.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture with its livestock, huts, and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; the cows and workers stay on Isenmann’s Alp for the summer.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese production on a high pasture; here the farmhand provocatively leaves a dairy drink for the ghost.

notes.label: Süffi
notes.text: an Uri dairying term for a thin whey or whey-like liquid produced during cheesemaking; the exact processing stage and consistency meant here are not specified.

notes.label: Sattor
notes.text: a contemptuous regional label here applied to an unruly, ill-disciplined fellow; the modifier meisterlosig supports that sense, but the word’s exact local etymology and social shade remain uncertain.

b8c5896290344ea06a62d44d346ac3d7651fbf6c.summary: On the Alp ‘Altsäss,’ whenever the Sennen took a milking stool down to the Untersäss, it returned to them on the Obersäss.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its herding and dairy establishment; Altsäss contains distinct upper and lower stations.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or senior cattle herders; the singular Senn owns the promised goat and dishonestly refuses the boy's reward.

notes.label: Untersäss
notes.text: the lower seasonal pasture station or settlement within an Alp; the boy carries the recovered stool down toward it.

notes.label: Obersäss
notes.text: the corresponding upper pasture station or settlement; the stool supernaturally returns there, where the giant uses it.

notes.label: Glockengeiss
notes.text: literally ‘bell goat,’ a female goat distinguished by its bell and promised as the boy's reward; the giant insists twice in the verse that it rightfully belongs to him.

notes.label: Die Hitz und der Witz
notes.text: literally ‘the heat and the wit,’ followed by Und die Beiss, ‘and the bite’; the giant's unexplained list names what enabled the boy's success, but the source gives no earlier objects matching all three, so their exact referents remain ambiguous.

ad98b4877c7014e66151645f04f11fe58aad7a96.summary: About 60 years ago, the Bernese brought a tremendous giant on a chain up through the land of Glarus as far as Linthal and challenged the people of Glarus to a Schwinget.

notes.label: Schwinget
notes.text: a contest or festival of Schwingen, the traditional Swiss style of wrestling in which opponents grip special breeches and try to throw one another onto the back; this challenge is therefore a public test of regional honor, not an ordinary brawl.

notes.label: Raben
notes.text: literally ‘Raven,’ apparently the house or inn name where the Bernese party lodged in Linthal; the source does not further identify the establishment.

notes.label: Glarner Mandli
notes.text: Glarner means a person of the canton of Glarus, while Mandli is the Swiss German diminutive ‘little man’; here it contrasts Fridli’s small, aging body with his extraordinary strength rather than belittling him.

d07f64211701ed812c610cff872519f75f1a88a0.summary: In the Thur valley lived a giant named Eishexe, meaning ‘terrible.’ He needed no bridge across the Thur, no matter how greatly it swelled or how fiercely even his enormous horse resisted the current.

notes.label: Eishexe
notes.text: the giant's local name, which the source itself glosses as ‘terrible’; although modern German can parse Eishexe as ‘ice witch,’ that literal reading does not fit the collector's explanation or the male giant.

7f1a11ef54f600e5e0efc880aa3ca85d11252f50.summary: Before Saint Donatus, Archbishop of Besançon, converted the Gruyère region to Christianity, an enormous giant had made his home there whom the people of that region, in their pagan blindness, revered and worshiped as an idol.
