notes.label: Centner
notes.text: the source’s historical hundredweight unit; its exact local weight could vary, so the original measure is retained rather than converted.

notes.label: Kohlermus
notes.text: literally ‘charcoal-burner’s mush,’ a substantial flour-based Alpine dish; here its enormous portion demonstrates Rotzer’s giant appetite, though the precise historical recipe is not specified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

41d20a645fede84a809100869202ff87682d1264.summary: In the Gadmental there is a footbridge from rock to rock called the Heidenweg.

notes.label: Heidenweg
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ path,’ this is the local name of the fragile rock bridge in the Gadmental; its age, construction, and association with pre-Christian beings are uncertain.

dcf7db50ff35510bb88b1d33dd1545577ade71b5.summary: The Geissberg near the village of Villigen extends eastward into a cone-shaped projection.

notes.label: Burgfräulein
notes.text: literally ‘castle maiden,’ here a giant woman ruling the ruined Burg rather than an ordinary young noblewoman.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Wirtel
notes.text: the spindle whorl, a weighted disk that steadies a hand spindle; its gigantic stone form is said to remain in the Aare.

d22f14a86e643ae29361f310fca3ce62169060a2.summary: Near the Bründlenalp lies the Dominikhöhle. Before its entrance sits a gigantic stone figure to which nature has given human form.

notes.label: Bründlenalp
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture near the cave; Alp denotes a pastoral landscape and settlement rather than only a mountain peak.

notes.label: Dominikhöhle
notes.text: the locally named Dominic Cave before which the naturally human-shaped stone giant sits.

notes.label: der Riese des Berges
notes.text: literally ‘the Giant of the Mountain,’ the people's name for the petrified defender who could fight outsiders but was overcome by horror at Swiss civil conflict.

17e52b16dd42a0070ca7dcfc04c394898e6a59d7.summary: There in the canton of Schwyz lived two giant siblings, a brother and a sister.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Mäss
notes.text: a historical Swiss dry measure whose volume varied by locality and commodity; here it quantifies the salt carried by the giantess, but the source does not permit one exact modern conversion.

040c17531f84dbd6b955c0a9490cc8521be499fc.summary: A father and son were plowing. The son stood in front beside the animals, which were moving forward in harmony.

notes.label: Giesischmied
notes.text: the local Aargau name of the club-bearing apparition in this tale; ‘Schmied’ means ‘smith,’ while the sense or origin of ‘Giesi’ is uncertain, so the full supernatural name is retained.

8cf420a48828e5825c9a280b219b77677359741d.summary: The Buzen are thoroughly uncanny, malicious night goblins who wish human beings no good.

notes.label: Buzen
notes.text: a regional form used here for malicious nocturnal bogey spirits, and in the singular for one such spirit; they mislead travelers and endanger livestock rather than functioning as harmless sprites.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially an alpine herder or dairyman.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: the traditional spoken or sung blessing over an Alp, its people, and livestock; together with holy water and a good conscience, it protects against the Buzen.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Betglocken
notes.text: prayer bells, commonly the evening Angelus bells; their falling silent marks the hour when the Gifibuzen begins to range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: steep alpine ravines or gullies; driving cattle into them makes the spirit materially dangerous.

notes.label: Gifibuzen
notes.text: the particular Buzen attached to the Gifi above Münster; its name combines that local mountain place with the goblin type.

notes.label: Jauchzen
notes.text: a loud alpine whoop or cry; here the normally human mountain call becomes a terrifying supernatural shriek.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face, crag, or cliff in Swiss usage; the misled traveler risks being tripped over its edge.

notes.label: Fastnachtszeit
notes.text: the Carnival or pre-Lenten season, a calendrical period traditionally associated with festivity and, in stories, loosened boundaries.

notes.label: Fastnachtsmontag
notes.text: Carnival Monday; the young herder descends expecting a festive evening but is detained all night by the spirit.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the singular prayer or Angelus bell whose ringing marks the young man's departure.

notes.label: Söller
notes.text: a raised gallery, landing, or porch-like platform at the stable; at dawn the youth discovers he has been circling without leaving it.

abe05897d2ab9b2b77c4a3a08fca19a2acd798f5.summary: As Gerig Heiri of Spiringen traveled home from military service, one evening he accompanied a young, pretty, and, as he thought, respectable girl along the open country road.

notes.label: Firstkämmerchen
notes.text: literally the little chamber at the roof ridge, a small attic or loft room directly beneath the ridge; the cat enters it through a small window opening.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

8763fb55b1653c74729cc0acc2c4859335db04b8.summary: Poor people lived in Oberried. The father was at work, and the mother told her eight-year-old daughter to fetch the midwife.

notes.label: Je mehr du zatterst, Wie minder du hattest
notes.text: a dialectal rhyming warning whose closest contextual sense is ‘the more you scatter, the less you would have had’; zatterst may also suggest fumbling or agitated spilling, and the invisible hand prevents the frightened girl from losing her gift.
notes.anchor: Je mehr du zatterst, Wie minder du hattest

8d3295203c0e413b01564b1daaad94a4572e9ebc.summary: In the little village of Tracht, whose windows look so pleasantly upon the waves of Lake Brienz, all the young men went up to the Alps to fetch Flühblumen and then, early on the first morning of May, set them before their girls' doors.

notes.label: Flühblumen
notes.text: literally flowers from the Flühe, or high rocky alpine slopes; the young men gather them as May Day courtship gifts to place before their sweethearts' doors.

notes.label: St. Johannestag
notes.text: St. John's Day, the feast of John the Baptist; in this local legend it becomes the anniversary on which Lake Brienz is believed to demand a victim.

f14bf8e67268f272f8df7eda81178a71934fbe0b.summary: When the valley at the foot of the Schratten was still inhabited by Heiden, a beautiful girl lived in the region.

notes.label: Schratten
notes.text: the rugged limestone and karst ridge now associated with the Schrattenfluh; the title's ab der Schratten means ‘from the Schratten.’

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: historically ‘heathens’ or non-Christians; in Swiss legend it often marks imagined ancient, pre-Christian inhabitants rather than a securely identified people.

72cc1aad657b888f81a491e9a9ef5cd8473db7d6.summary: Just as the Blüemlisalp, according to the legends of the people of Frutigen, was once fertile, so too the glacier-covered Rätzliberg was once a fruitful Alp on which Mutteren and Adelgras blossomed in abundance.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture used seasonally for livestock, not simply a mountain peak; here it is the once-fertile grazing land later covered by glacier ice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Mutteren
notes.text: a historical Alpine plant name, generally associated with an aromatic, nutritious mountain-pasture herb; the source pairs it with Adelgras as evidence of rich grazing, but does not identify the species botanically.

notes.label: Adelgras
notes.text: literally ‘noble grass,’ an old laudatory name for high-quality Alpine forage; here its abundance marks the lost fertility of the Rätzliberg pasture, while the exact plant intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd product distinct from ordinary aged cheese; the basket of fresh Ziger forms part of the herdsman's yearly payment from the Alp.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; the rich Anken is part of the annual pastoral rent, and the reduced amount after the hailstorm provokes the owner's curse.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or dairyman responsible for cattle on an Alp; in this context the role includes summering the herd and delivering dairy produce to the landholder.

fcfc28eea5a3712feff352264ea5385e111f1a48.summary: Between Valais and the southwestern Bernese Oberland lies the Saanetsch Glacier, from which the Saane flows.

notes.label: Saanetsch
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Sanetsch, the high pass and glacier region between Valais and the Bernese Oberland.

notes.label: verlorene Berg
notes.text: literally ‘lost mountain,’ the barren Valais slope whose destruction the legend explains; the source's lower-case form is retained.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: a level or stage of an alpine pasture, often including a seasonal herding station or its buildings.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high summer pasture and its pastoral farmstead, not simply a mountain in the Alps.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Triften
notes.text: grazing grounds or stock-driving pasturelands; the plural here names the rich pastures buried by rock and ice.

47da9c14070bc94edca03c3a886bbf190f433463.summary: Above Flims in Graubünden lay a green alp belonging to a widow. Beside it were the properties of a rich man.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

c83fb4bd0fa5784a3f886bdf67ca79dcbd65b327.summary: In the Bremgarten forest, which belongs to the city of Bern and forms a large peninsula in the Aare, lies the Glasbrunnen, much visited by walkers for its spring water.

notes.label: Glasbrunnen
notes.text: the established local name of the spring in Bern’s Bremgarten forest, literally “glass spring” or “glass fountain”; the tale connects it with clear water, ruins, and treasure but does not explain the name.

notes.label: Jagdschlössli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive meaning a small hunting lodge or hunting castle; here it is an antiquarian interpretation of exposed foundations, not a historically verified identification.

notes.label: Wilde Jagd
notes.text: the Wild Hunt, a supernatural nocturnal procession of hunters, hounds, or the dead known across German-speaking folklore; here it passes at Easter and Christmas with a three-legged pack and a huntsman distributing money.

bf547f72355a26fe33a92b66868341a986536272.summary: In a castle lived a maiden who was so beautiful that nothing lovelier could be seen anywhere in the world.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

5c6ae6d7e1183b688163b26c67a5b27bd5d68dc6.summary: Above the Fricktal village of Maisprach, a path through the Jura forest leads to a little-known spa.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a Swiss communal forest or land warden charged with watching protected resources and boundaries; here he encounters the cave dwellers, though his exact legal powers are not specified.

notes.label: Landjäger
notes.text: an older Swiss and German-speaking term for rural or cantonal police officers, literally “country hunters”; here they are the authorities the borderland cave dwellers evade.

notes.label: Gleichaufshöhle
notes.text: literally the “Gleichauf cave,” named for the dishonest administrator and his repeated claim that everything came out Gleichauf; the cave name preserves both his nickname and the pun.

notes.label: Klosterschaffner
notes.text: an abbey’s secular steward or estate administrator, responsible for property and revenues; here he abuses that position in a boundary dispute, though the office’s exact jurisdiction is unstated.

notes.label: Gleichauf
notes.text: literally “even,” “level,” or “coming out equal,” the corrupt Klosterschaffner’s cynical phrase and resulting nickname; the joke is that his supposed balance transfers the farmers’ loss to the abbey’s gain.

f05e6f9d2ddf3e20b158f0cb9c4931191904b51a.summary: For some time, a farmer in Bristen had been unable to make any Anken at all.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; the farmer’s inability to make or obtain it is attributed to witchcraft.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine dairy cauldron or kettle, traditionally used for heating milk and making cheese; the sympathetic-magic act makes the witch appear dead within it.

f050113f4c2923e43054e296b1407afa111f67cd.summary: Above the village of Waltenschwil in the Freiamt is a bathing place called the Hexengumpen.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: a historical region of Aargau whose name recalls the former ‘free bailiwicks,’ not a modern municipal office.

notes.label: Hexengumpen
notes.text: literally ‘witch pool,’ a deep bathing hole or hollow in a stream believed to house the dangerous being.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Chlungge
notes.text: the body-text name for the red-haired female water spirit who pulls bathers down and torments children.

notes.label: Glunggeri
notes.text: the title-name for the female water-haunting being; it appears related to the body-text form Chlungge, but its exact derivation is uncertain.

c532dafe7e6e91ef71a960aea6c197decd6cf09a.summary: The Glärnisch has a cube-shaped, snow-covered eastern summit called Vrenelis Gärtli.

notes.label: Vrenelis Gärtli
notes.text: literally ‘Vreneli’s little garden,’ the traditional name of the snow-covered eastern summit of the Glärnisch; the legend interprets it as the garden imposed upon a banished magician.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally an ‘itinerant scholar,’ a folklore figure often credited with learned magic or forbidden arts rather than merely a traveling student; the source does not state his school or specific powers.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

aa64d4ca241e8718f261865e1d304768eb0e03b4.summary: When the Wild Host rides from the Froburg across into the Fricktal, it comes to rest on the mountains near Ormalingen, at the place where the city of Malhausen is said to have perished.

notes.label: Wütigs Heer
notes.text: a regional name for the raging or Wild Host, a noisy supernatural procession related to Wild Hunt traditions; its ominous or beneficial meaning changes with the season in this account.

notes.label: Gutigs Heer
notes.text: literally the ‘good host,’ a favorable or euphemistic name for the same supernatural procession; the form is preserved because it contrasts with Wütigs Heer.

notes.label: Glücksheer
notes.text: literally the ‘host of good fortune’ or ‘lucky host,’ the auspicious name for the procession when its Christmas marches are taken as a promise of a plentiful harvest.

52ce877036a106274c47be1d8875ca789c00e727.summary: To the left of the road leading from Zweisimmen to the health spring at Lenk lies the village of Bettelried.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: Flühe is the plural of Fluh, steep rock faces, cliffs, or crags onto which the village goats climb; the precise grazing route is unspecified.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: a Geissbub is a boy who tends goats, here the poorly paid village herder; his name and age are unspecified.

notes.label: Gemskäslein
notes.text: literally ‘little chamois cheese,’ Gemskäslein is the dwarf’s self-renewing food for the hungry goatherd; its ingredients, size, and connection to chamois are uncertain.

notes.label: Geisshirt
notes.text: Geisshirt is a goatherd responsible for the village’s goats, used here for the boy after he receives the cheese; any distinction from Geissbub is uncertain and not specified by the source.

b17f46c7ce6bd36e9669ae18a1c54166f057b569.summary: On the Clariden Alps, a Senn is said in former times to have kept a wanton woman and held her in such honor that, from the dwelling or Sennhütte to the Käsgaden, he covered the otherwise muddy path with cheeses so that she would not soil her shoes.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder responsible for cheese production; the son's abuse of dairy food reverses the hospitality and stewardship expected of that role.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the seasonal dwelling and working hut of Alpine dairy herders; the cheese-paved path begins at this residence.

notes.label: Käsgaden
notes.text: literally ‘cheese storehouse’ or ‘cheese outbuilding,’ a small structure where dairy products are made or kept; regional usage can vary between a workroom and storage building.

notes.label: Suffi
notes.text: a regional whey-based food or drink, explicitly described here as whey mixed with Ziger; its precise consistency and recipe are not specified.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese, generally made from the albumin-rich whey left after ordinary cheesemaking; the source identifies it as the ingredient mixed into the Suffi.

4e18c2508ad7eb321d4af2211465df2df2e311ad.summary: As everywhere else, many stories are still told in Naters about the Godwerdjini, or dwarfs.

notes.label: Godwerdjini
notes.text: Godwerdjini is the local Valais plural for small supernatural mountain beings or dwarfs, shown dancing, working, and withdrawing when offended or clothed; the name’s derivation and exact dialect pronunciation are uncertain.

notes.label: Godwerdji
notes.text: Godwerdji is the singular form of Godwerdjini, used for the individual dwarf who feeds livestock, serves at the mill, or visits the spinner; whether every episode concerns the same being is uncertain.

notes.label: Schafessen
notes.text: literally ‘sheep eating’ or ‘sheep feast,’ Schafessen names a mountain communal meal said here to have been learned at dwarf dances; its historical menu and relationship to actual Valais custom are uncertain.

notes.label: Werch-Hechel
notes.text: a Werch-Hechel is a sharp-toothed hackle used to comb flax or hemp fibers, concealed here as a cruel seat at the dance; the implement’s exact local form and the dialect verse’s wording are uncertain.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

4c8e04873012107802f763de3485c9c1785e3ee1.summary: A man from Zermatt is said once to have fallen in love with a Godwerji girl and chosen her as his life companion.

notes.label: Godwerji
notes.text: a Valais name for the small, dwarf-like wild or earth people of local tradition; a Godwerji woman may marry a human under a prohibition whose violation makes her return to her own world.

notes.label: Holzmuoterli
notes.text: literally something like ‘little wood mother’ in Alemannic dialect; here it is a forbidden insult directed at the Godwerji wife, though the precise connotations that made it offensive are no longer explained.

7a6a609ecf7be65f79ca53b047021b872fa9b54e.summary: About 100 years ago, a Venedigermannli came to the house of a farmer, Jakob Eberle, on the Kleinberg.

notes.label: Venedigermannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Venetian man,’ a diminutive Alpine folklore figure associated with foreign prospectors who secretly recognize mineral wealth; the story treats it as uncanny, but does not say whether it is human, dwarfish, or supernatural.

644ca9e93d3801f8d9bb1769b9b8fc5bb8655063.summary: Near the Zurich village of Jachenhausen on the Pfäffikersee, the well-preserved earthworks of a Roman fort can be seen.

notes.label: Potz Dünner-Hagel, e goldige Chetti!
notes.text: a Swiss German exclamation approximately meaning ‘By thunder and hail, a golden chain!’; the excited outcry breaks the silence expected in many treasure legends and immediately precedes the chain’s escape.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a heavy pronged grubbing hoe or mattock used to break soil; its tine catches the final link, so it should not be understood here as the limestone landscape term also spelled karst.

3b87c0471d1c25545c9822d39c51a7a702aa49f7.summary: In former times, a simply dressed man in a light smock and broad-brimmed hat came to Vermol every year and lodged there with the farmer L.

notes.label: Dreiböhri
notes.text: the regional name for a three-cornered hat, literally something like a ‘three-peaked’ hat; the source itself glosses the shape, but the exact local construction and origin of the name are uncertain.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine legend, a name for supposedly Venetian or southern prospectors credited with secret knowledge of mountain ores and often treated as magicians; ‘Venetian’ gives the geographic association but not this regionally specific folkloric role, whose historical basis is uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

37b00b568f29527ccd29e8c4b975c8582800414b.summary: A gold-maker once lived in Lenk. He led a strange and mysterious life, always sought solitude, and was often seen crossing the mountains at night into neighboring valleys.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

724ca6b33cf038013a23683bdd9409246301c1d7.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, the Vineder came to the Schnebelhorn to search for gold.

notes.label: Vineder
notes.text: a regional form meaning people from Venice; Swiss Alpine mining legends often cast such outsiders as secretive prospectors able to recognize and remove hidden ore, and here they are imagined as little men. The term may describe legendary Venetians rather than a historically identifiable group.

notes.label: Vineder-Manuli
notes.text: a dialect compound meaning approximately ‘little Venetian men’; in this account it combines the legendary Venetian gold prospector with a diminutive, dwarf-like figure. The spelling is source-specific and its exact dialect formation is somewhat uncertain.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive meaning ‘little men’; here it is the shortened name for the vanished Vineder-Manuli rather than an ordinary description of their height.

notes.label: Goldloch
notes.text: literally ‘gold hole,’ the local name for the mine opening on the Schnebelhorn; the tale treats the visible shaft as the surviving entrance to the legendary Vineder workings.

0156d97a73003a068398a09d6afc26d38a86984f.summary: A man from Mezza-Selva named Lemm, who had a wife from Fonday, once intended to travel to his wife’s home region.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term for a debris flow, the torrent carrying it, or the channel it cuts; here Lemm finds metal in the blue clay of the channel.

notes.label: Philippstaler
notes.text: a historical thaler coin associated with rulers named Philip; the source gives Lemm’s payment as sixteen such coins but does not identify the precise issue or modern value.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its associated grazing ground or settlement; in the title it refers to the Casana Alp, not to the entire Alps mountain range.

b0efaa2e1815bc899cee793968f81523b7b2a752.summary: In former times, the Wertemati family of Plurs successfully operated a gold and silver mine at the Parpaner Rothorn. — According to an old legend, one Mass of pure gold flowed daily from the mountain’s veins; every morning the vessel was changed, the day’s yield was piled into great barrels, and…

notes.label: Plurs
notes.text: the historical German name used in the source for the town now commonly called Piuro; the mine’s wealth is carried there.

notes.label: Parpaner Rothorn
notes.text: the mountain identified with Parpan whose veins yield the legendary daily flow of precious metal.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical measure whose exact local quantity could vary; the tale claims that this amount of pure gold flowed each day.

323e16f823c2794e7445517dcbd494df1088725d.summary: In the Küpfen above Langwies, a poor man of Langwies owned a mountain meadow and wanted to build a house there.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: in German-language legend, a wandering scholar or student often credited with occult or secret knowledge; the source does not specify whether this visitor is a literal student, cleric, or magical practitioner.

notes.label: aaber
notes.text: a regional form meaning free of snow or snow-free, as the source itself explains; the warmth over the gold vein makes this spot emerge first in spring.

acf115fdb872ab4a64dd76c8a66fc41da3da9241.summary: In the Kalten-Wässern above the Simplon road, where a realm of glaciers now lies, a vein of gold is said to have flowed from a rock many years ago.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a magical seeing instrument used to reveal hidden treasure at a distance; it is not an ordinary reflective landscape feature.

notes.label: Wünschelrute
notes.text: a divining rod used to locate hidden water, minerals, or treasure; its changing direction guides the seekers but does not protect them from the treasure guardian.

notes.label: Hafen
notes.text: a regional and older word for a pot or earthen vessel, not the modern German word for a harbor; the golden spring drips into this container until it is nearly full.

notes.label: verwachet
notes.text: an older or regional form meaning ‘watches over’ or ‘guards’; the source places it in quotation marks, suggesting marked local usage, while the gray little man’s precise powers remain unstated.

7382647e46faa83a8e634e32a9c3f060cea191dd.summary: On the Vilteser Alp, almost high up by the Wildsee, at a fearsome precipice, a red slab—although no others like it are found there—is said to stand all by itself against the rock face like a door.

notes.label: Vilteser Alp
notes.text: the source's dialect form for the high pasture associated with Vilters; Alp means a seasonally used mountain pasture rather than merely a mountain, and the red stone doorway is located high within it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Goldbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘gold spring’ or ‘gold well,’ a hidden supernatural source behind the upright red slab; the name may indicate either a spring whose water is golden or one that yields magical gold-bearing water.

notes.label: fahrende Schüeler
notes.text: dialect for a ‘wandering scholar,’ a learned itinerant figure credited in Alpine folklore with secret or magical knowledge; here he alone repeatedly finds the hidden spring, and the source does not explain whether he is literally a student.

notes.label: Goldwasser
notes.text: literally ‘gold-water,’ the substance secretly drawn from the Goldbrunnen; the brief account does not say whether this means liquid gold, gold-bearing water, or magically valuable water.

c27b29542674c02c7b2a2023b1c08f7109248e1c.summary: There was a time when all those rigid rocks, glaciers, and seas of ice were sunny pastures on which the richest grass and juiciest clover flourished.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their pastoral landscapes rather than the Alpine mountain chain as a whole; the legend imagines today's glaciers as once-fertile grazing land.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here they preserve the tale and promise an annual cheese offering.

63259a1fdbe1295e372860a0d22c434a68af6c56.summary: On the slope of the high ridge of the Suleck in the Bernese Oberland lie several alpine pastures, which an old song characterizes thus:

d0c733bef91e0d5a30c53a1fc9e7c7f97c216117.summary: Between the villages of Endingen and Oberlengnau, above the so-called Mûrstege, one comes to a spring.

notes.label: Mûrstege
notes.text: the recorded local name of the crossing or path feature below the spring, perhaps literally a ‘wall footbridge’; the circumflex and exact place-name derivation are retained from the source.

notes.label: Boddemaidschi
notes.text: local Alemannic for approximately ‘little Boden maiden’ or ‘maiden of Bodde,’ the white-clad golden treasure guardian; Bodde appears to be the locality's name, while the exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Boddebächlijumpfere
notes.text: literally ‘young lady of the little Bodde brook,’ an alternate title for the Boddemaidschi that ties her directly to the spring's streamlet.

notes.label: Boddebächli
notes.text: the ‘little Bodde brook,’ with the Swiss diminutive -li; it is the stream where the maiden appears, combs her hair, and guards treasure.

notes.label: Boddeschloss
notes.text: literally ‘Bodde Castle,’ the vanished stronghold said to have stood by the spring; the legend links its unknown former owners to the site's treasure.

c753a3fb1e09f694ccea582f98558b008e4124df.summary: There was once a farmer at Irgenhausen, a hamlet beside the Pfäffikersee. He owned a small Heimwesen that reached to the silent blue lake.

notes.label: Heimwesen
notes.text: a farmstead or small landed holding that combines home, land, and livelihood; the farmer first owns a marginal one beside the lake and later buys a more productive property.

notes.label: Tanse
notes.text: a tall container carried on the back for transporting milk, water, or other liquid; the source does not state what this farmer’s Tanse contains.

notes.label: Laubsack
notes.text: a sack or mattress stuffed with dried leaves and used as simple bedding; it reflects the farmer’s modest household rather than an ordinary bag of fresh foliage.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a digging implement such as a mattock, hoe, or pick; its tine catches the chain, but the precise tool form is not described.

notes.label: Potztausend
notes.text: a mild, old-fashioned exclamation of astonishment, approximately ‘good heavens’ or ‘by the thousand’; it intensifies the farmer’s excitement without adding literal numerical information.

notes.label: Apfelblust
notes.text: Swiss German for apple blossom, especially the mass of blossoms in spring; the closing image evokes the orchard landscape around the Pfäffikersee.

da90ce24bb9cb4ab3f4a64812a2ead22f68ee093.summary: Near Dinhard is a forest in which wandering is joyful. It is also inviting to lie about there, and one begins to feel as though inside a fairy tale.

notes.label: elbisches Wesen
notes.text: an elf-like or otherworldly being; elbisch here evokes older Germanic hidden folk rather than Tolkien's later invented Elvish language.

notes.label: wirblig
notes.text: dialect for dizzy, whirling, or mentally disoriented; it describes the bodily effect of crossing the forbidden forest boundary.

notes.label: Weidmann
notes.text: a traditional term for a hunter, especially one understood through the customs and identity of the hunt; Hans's passion makes him ignore warnings.

notes.label: Blustherrlichkeit
notes.text: literally ‘blossom splendor,’ with Swiss Blust meaning fruit-tree blossom; the unnaturally magnificent flowering tree frames the deceptive maiden and dwarf.

f64253b8fadafd20a46b088b92e7dff964e2a488.summary: The old miller near the little town of Zofingen in the canton of Aargau had lost an elderly cousin.

notes.label: Bernerwägelein
notes.text: a small Bernese-style wagon or light carriage prepared for the miller’s journey.

notes.label: Laubbett
notes.text: literally ‘leaf bed,’ a mattress or bed filled with dried leaves.

notes.label: Hausmatte
notes.text: the meadow immediately belonging to and lying around a farmhouse.

notes.label: Guckauskämmerlein
notes.text: literally a ‘lookout little chamber,’ a small upper room or dormer-like chamber with a view outside.

notes.label: Herdkunst
notes.text: the masonry stove or hearth structure in the kitchen, found covered with gold ducats.

36d0885d7734b7ba36e788ae174521b0edcaa48e.summary: In Bern’s Simme Valley, where the cleanest and prettiest little wooden houses in the world stand, there once lived a young farm lad.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; the hidden keyhole appears beside its overhang on the alp.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop of joy, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; the lad gives one after taking the golden bell.

notes.label: Runskölbchen
notes.text: the source’s diminutive name for a fragrant plant part or flower spike tucked behind the ear; the exact botanical identification is uncertain, so the regional word is retained.

notes.label: Leitkuh
notes.text: literally ‘lead cow,’ the leading animal of an Alpine herd, often distinguished by a prominent bell; the lad imagines his golden bell adorning Lieseli’s lead cow.

e1791bf08e1258ebe827211d80fa59126464080a.summary: Below the parish village of Kloten is a marshy meadow called the Lachenwiese, with a small pond bearing the name güldenes Tor or güldenes Brünnlein.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Lachenwiese
notes.text: literally something like ‘pool meadow’ or ‘puddle meadow,’ the marshy meadow below Kloten containing the treasure pond; here it is a proper place-name rather than a generic wetland label.

notes.label: güldenes Tor
notes.text: archaic German for ‘golden gate,’ one of the pond's local names and also the great treasure-object said to rise from it; the tale deliberately blurs whether the name denotes the water, the submerged gate, or both.

notes.label: güldenes Brünnlein
notes.text: archaic diminutive for ‘little golden spring’ or ‘little golden fountain,’ another local name for the pond; Brünnlein may refer to a spring-fed pool rather than a built fountain.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: literally ‘Ember-season children,’ people born during the Church's quarterly Fronfasten periods and traditionally credited with second sight; here only they can see and report the rising treasure and golden gate.

f3610b67fadb977792542d3f9e1712dcdcc383ef.summary: In Graubünden there is a castle ruin called Ruchenberg, lying between the beautiful settlements of Trimmis and Zizers.

notes.label: lötigem Gold
notes.text: refined, assay-worthy, or pure gold; the adjective historically relates to measured fineness rather than molten metal alone.

notes.label: Heidi
notes.text: an exuberant regional exclamation, roughly ‘hey!’ or ‘away it goes!,’ accompanying the spectacular throw.

notes.label: pauz pardauz
notes.text: imitative exclamations for crashing and tumbling, like ‘bang, crash!’ as the ball strikes the pins.

f4bc69c800d99cead09d3ad30bc4d831d27be9e6.summary: A golden game of ninepins is said to lie near the Martinsbrücke. Many have already gone to fetch it but never returned.

notes.label: Martinsbrücke
notes.text: literally ‘St. Martin’s Bridge,’ the local landmark beside the guarded treasure cave.

21cffbdf0d567ace349ae2b3499282b061bb3c8a.summary: A servant named Friedrich fell in love with the daughter of the lord of the castle.

07b70390f0ba9e5e99ad0ff598b6e2cd211be061.summary: In ancient times, a castle containing unbelievable riches stood on Gasterholz hill.

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a complete set of skittles or ninepins, often appearing as a golden treasure in Swiss legend; the term denotes the whole playing set, not a single pin.

9f4bfd5fd9e6d46b551b48f75af634d7d908ac68.summary: 1. A cowherd once found it, no one knows how.

notes.label: Lahli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive for a foolish or simple fellow; the narrator’s judgment emphasizes that the cowherd abandons the treasure for an ordinary task.

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a complete set of skittles or ninepins, often appearing as a golden treasure in Swiss legend; it denotes the whole playing set rather than a single pin.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a recurring German-language folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; he is not an ordinary schoolchild here.

notes.label: Trychelgeiss
notes.text: a goat wearing a Trychel, the characteristic deep-toned hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; this treasure-revealing animal must also remain the same and entirely white across the variant span of years.

669585ec9b07cfdf8e7a5d2fc9cce2e3d07feae6.summary: a) The Rosstock, easily climbed from the Schächen, Muota, and Riemenstal valleys, is distinguished by an extensive and picturesque panoramic view.

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a complete set of skittles or ninepins, often appearing as a golden treasure in Swiss legend; the source distinguishes the set from its two golden balls and sometimes shortens the name to Ries.

notes.label: Schlärp
notes.text: an Uri dialect word apparently denoting an old, worn shoe or slipper; placing one on the treasure would claim or hold it in place, though the source does not explain the custom.

notes.label: Flüehblüemli
notes.text: literally a ‘little cliff flower,’ a dialect diminutive for a flower growing upon a Fluh or steep rock face; the species is not identified.

80f7725740a56ba0d5c3c761fe20e8b0b731fcf0.summary: An hour from Winterthur stands the old Mörsburg with its mighty walls. A quarter of an hour away, near the little village of Sulz, another castle, called Sulz, is said to have stood.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: a traditional skittle or ninepins set, comprising the pins and balls used in the game; in Alpine treasure legends, a precious golden Kegelspiel is often the supernatural treasure or reward.

b3d1b9a77ca0c3aa8ab15b6f9b8a84cec0116040.summary: In Sax too, people tell of a golden Kegelspiel said to be buried near the ruins of Hohen-Sax.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: a game of skittles or ninepins, and by extension the complete set of pins and balls; the treasure consists of a golden set, so neither modern ten-pin bowling nor the board game called ‘bowling’ is an exact equivalent.

ca442216a9f66e9f1a9cec0940e25c83569654b6.summary: A golden Kegelspiel is also said to lie buried in the ruins of Nieder-Juvalt Castle outside Rothenbrunnen.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: the traditional game of skittles or ninepins and, by extension, its complete set of pins and balls; golden sets recur as supernatural treasures in Alpine castle legends.

918c8f115f52d8f41eb393f62d1c58758a517685.summary: By the clouds, by the dark ones,

notes.label: Kegel
notes.text: the pins used in Kegelspiel; the German form is retained throughout the verse to preserve the repeated central image.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: the traditional German-speaking game of skittles or ninepins, played by rolling or throwing a ball at upright pins; this supernatural set is made of gold.

eea95026cbcb1040ac7561e6ea7f8fea7c14d182.summary: A Viertelstunde from the village of Obervaz lies the old ruin of the Freiherren von Vaz called “Nivaigl,” with its mighty walls.

notes.label: Viertelstunde
notes.text: an old travel-distance measure based on a quarter of an hour’s walk rather than a precisely surveyed length.

notes.label: Freiherren
notes.text: plural of Freiherr, a historical noble rank conventionally rendered as barons; the castles belong to the lords of Vaz.

notes.label: Nivaigl
notes.text: the local name of the ruined Vaz castle near Obervaz.

notes.label: Lunat
notes.text: the local name of the second castle above Lain, said to be linked underground with Nivaigl.

notes.label: Fräulein
notes.text: historically an unmarried young woman and, in this castle setting, a young noble maiden under enchantment.

notes.label: Kegelspiel
notes.text: the traditional game of skittles or ninepins; the maiden’s supernatural set and its balls are made of gold.

notes.label: reiner
notes.text: the source’s quoted word meaning pure, innocent, or morally undefiled; only such a young man may pass the dog.

notes.label: drei
notes.text: the source places “three” in quotation marks to emphasize the required number of kisses.

0859eec4e540b87ac9598b1fffe1854b2f3e5938.summary: The ‘Meggermeili,’ very well known in the city of Lucerne in her day, sometimes passed by on certain days early in the morning or at twilight in the evening, or traveled in a boat from Burgweidli to Angelfluh.

notes.label: Meggermeili
notes.text: a dialect sobriquet meaning roughly ‘little woman or girl from Meggen’; it identifies a locally familiar female figure, with a diminutive nuance that an ordinary personal name would lose.

130ffe4234185b2fa5a065c4457e77a12b57b8f4.summary: It is said of the Ofengüpfe, an ancient burial mound on the Breite in the canton of Zurich, that a golden plow lies within it.

da628dacaed3f6820cfdf702a569dfeded1609bd.summary: 1. Two men from the Riedmatt were working with wood beside their house when a strange Mandli came along the pack trail.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a man or ‘little man’; here it describes the unfamiliar wandering figure without securely indicating his stature or supernatural nature.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; he is not an ordinary schoolchild.

1a6b0cb84d3030ed22530a1b541a5bb077a06070.summary: a) Anyone who wants a golden wagon can recover one on the Ämmehorn, a mountain height beside the road from Hergiswil near Willisau to Luthern.

bc41d8425c1b0efcfb360c206f5ffea0d6909465.summary: Legend tells that Italian miners—naturally Venetians—worked the mine and, almost every Saturday, traveled homeward by secret paths, as unseen and unnoticed as possible, carrying little bundles of grains of gold.

notes.label: Goldloch
notes.text: literally ‘gold hole,’ the local name for the mine workings on the Dägelsberg; the accounts combine treasure legend with measured physical remains.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: a regional legendary name for mysterious Venetian or Italian mineral prospectors believed to know hidden ores and treasures; they are often treated as magicians rather than ordinary miners.

notes.label: S.A.C.
notes.text: the source's abbreviation for the Swiss Alpine Club, whose Bachtel Section stabilized the historic mine entrance.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a coarse Alpine conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones resemble nail heads; the inspected mine contains this rock and no visible gold.

c397eb2a559bb23bf1c50a3cb24dbcbd32ac059b.summary: On the ‘mighty Gamsberg,’ as the geologist Mösch calls the rugged summit above the Tscherlach Alp of Sennis, one can reach the Goldloch on the southeast side from an ‘eternal’ patch of snow—the remnant of a once-substantial glacier, judging by its beautifully formed moraines—by crossing a broad but…

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here Sennis and Castelun are named pastoral stations where the treasure-seekers lodge.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gufel
notes.text: a regional word for a sheltered rock overhang, recess, or shallow cave; here it describes the pine-ringed entrance from which the muddy Goldloch passage climbs into Gamsberg.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a ‘Venetian,’ but in Alpine folklore a mysterious foreign mineral seeker believed able to recognize and remove hidden ores or treasure; here he returns annually from Venice and guards the Goldloch's secret.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person working or residing seasonally on an Alp, such as a herder or dairyman; here the Venediger rewards his host, and the exact job within the pasture operation is not stated.

notes.label: Alpler
notes.text: the source's unaccented spelling variant of Älpler for an Alpine pasture worker; here curiosity drives this man to spy on the Venediger, and the distinct spelling is retained as recorded.

notes.label: Speltive
notes.text: a Swiss dialect form for a telescope or spyglass, glossed as Fernrohr in the source; here the herdsman borrows it to track the stranger from a distance.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Fickler
notes.text: a regional term for a sleeping platform, bunk, or bed-frame space in an Alpine hut; here the herdsman hides his sack beneath its bedding straw, though the exact furniture form can vary.

notes.label: Herbstalpfahrt
notes.text: the autumnal descent of people and livestock from the high pasture at the close of the Alpine season; here the herdsman carries the supposed ore down to the valley during that movement.

d5df7572cd155f036e7137dfe4d264fa2a5e858f.summary: One part of the forested Jura heights at the Schafmatt pass is called Rotholz.

notes.label: Goldloch
notes.text: literally “gold hole,” the local name of an abandoned mine working on the Schafmatt; in the legend it opens toward a vein and spring of inexhaustible gold.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep rock face or crag, present here in the place-name Ramsfluh; it signals the rocky dwelling-place of the Erdmännchen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean helpers; here they live in the Ramsfluh and abandon human houses after an insulting warning.

notes.label: Wähen
notes.text: Swiss flat baked cakes or tarts, made sweet or savory; here they are prepared after the bread baking, but the source does not specify their filling.

faca390527aba4370b852c82b1261076329e6c0a.summary: Near Twann on Lake Biel, a rocky crag called the Schlossfluh rises and bears the ruins of a castle whose name no one knows.

notes.label: Schlossfluh
notes.text: literally ‘castle cliff,’ the rocky crag near Twann bearing an unnamed castle ruin; Fluh is a Swiss word for a steep rock face or crag.

notes.label: Fronfastenkind
notes.text: literally an ‘Ember-season child,’ someone born during one of the Church's quarterly Fronfasten periods and traditionally credited with second sight; here such a person can see the elusive treasure.

notes.label: Goldsonnen
notes.text: a rare nominal form meaning approximately the gold's ‘sunning’ or shining in sunlight; here it names the vision of treasure displayed on a white cloth, while the exact local grammatical formation is archaic.

cefe312eabb43d93e2e52b841812062d22c71c47.summary: A Venedigermannli suddenly appeared above Valens on the Graue Hörner, where it placed a Stitze beneath a spring dripping gold and collected it full the following year.

notes.label: Venedigermannli
notes.text: literally ‘little Venetian man,’ one of the mysterious Venetian mineral seekers of Alpine legend who know otherwise inaccessible sources of precious metal.

notes.label: Stitze
notes.text: a regional small tub, pail, or handled dairy vessel; its exact shape is unstated, but the Venedigermannli sets it beneath the spring to collect gold over a year.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man,’ referring here to the Venedigermannli; the diminutive marks the folkloric figure without necessarily specifying childlike size.

notes.label: Goldstitze
notes.text: literally a ‘gold Stitze,’ the vessel filled from the gold-dripping spring; the title fuses the treasure with its characteristically regional container.

0c277917a1b4317f3a86225a7d2cbf18a71aa493.summary: A bull that has been sold to a butcher is led from the village of Gontenschwil to the nearest inn to meet its buyer.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4ecccd9ad3a301e27033e341ff2b065e03b18b5b.summary: During Lent, a man was walking from Terzen to Quarten between 11 and 12 o’clock at night.

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: literally a ‘boundary-marker mover,’ a Markenrücker is the condemned spirit of someone who shifted a property boundary and must restore the post; the person’s identity and the exact disputed boundary are unspecified.

77d9f434a173ca671cae1945105db587aa8381b9.summary: Between Schuoppis and Vögeliberg, a castle stood in ancient times; now only sparse remains, ramparts, walls, and hollows can be found.

notes.label: Furrenen
notes.text: the source's quoted local field word for the ridges, furrows, or worked strips upon which the silent dwarfs set the farmers' meal; its exact agricultural form is not described.

notes.label: sonnen
notes.text: literally to sun or air something outdoors; in treasure lore, hidden beings periodically expose treasure to the sun, creating the rare moment when mortals may see or take it.

notes.label: Schatzsonnen
notes.text: literally the ‘sunning of treasure,’ a Swiss and German folk-belief motif in which concealed wealth is aired in the open and may appear under a deceptive form, here as colored shards.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: Swiss German for a godmother; the hunter discovers that his own baptismal sponsor is the woman believed to have appeared as the fox.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: passen
notes.text: the hunter’s quoted regional expression for waiting in ambush or lying in wait for foxes attracted to bait.

notes.label: Gmach
notes.text: a regional form of Gemach, meaning the small room or chamber from whose window the hunter watches the bait outside his stable.

notes.label: Pfiff
notes.text: literally a whistle but idiomatically a clever trick, ruse, or special device; the hunter’s counter-magic is to load bread crumbs beneath the shot.

notes.label: Brodbros'men
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical dialect spelling for bread crumbs; placed in the gun barrel, they act as counter-magic that makes the witch-animal vulnerable.

d4237996eea8010fe435d8f8c222f3f568ea0938.summary: A numerous dwarf-folk called the Gottwergini had settled in the dense fir and pine forest of Oberems, and both good and bad things were told of them.

notes.label: Gottwergini
notes.text: a Valais regional plural name for the community of dwarfs around Oberems; the precise origin of the Got- element is uncertain.

notes.label: Oberems
notes.text: the upper Valais settlement whose forest, farms, and seasonal pasture work connect these dwarf traditions.

notes.label: Fasnachtszeit
notes.text: the Carnival or Shrovetide season before Lent, traditionally a time for communal celebration and dancing.

notes.label: Jungmannschaft
notes.text: the village's organized cohort or association of young men, which holds the Carnival dance.

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: a holder of local communal authority; the dwarfs steal and eat the pig he intended to slaughter.

notes.label: Monifang, wo hat der Darm sin Anfang?
notes.text: the dwarf's rhyming dialect question, “Monifang, where does the gut begin?”; Monifang itself remains unexplained in the source.
notes.anchor: Monifang, wo hat der Darm sin Anfang?

notes.label: Magen, Magen
notes.text: literally “stomach, stomach,” the companions' rhyming answer and signal before the three dwarfs vanish with the stolen pig.

notes.label: Kräuterfrau
notes.text: a woman knowledgeable in medicinal herbs and household healing, called to tend the dwarf's sick wife.

notes.label: Wie mehr du zatt (streust), Je weniger du hatt!
notes.text: a dialect rhyme meaning “The more you scatter, the less you have”; the source itself glosses zatt as streust, “scatter.”
notes.anchor: Wie mehr du zatt (streust), Je weniger du hatt!

notes.label: Filz
notes.text: literally felt, but used here as an insult for a miser or skinflint when the Kräuterfrau dismisses the dwarf's warning.

notes.label: Emserwald
notes.text: the forest by Ems beyond which the farmer's hut stands at the foot of the cliffs.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: the plural of Fluh, meaning steep exposed rock faces, cliffs, or crags.

notes.label: Barre
notes.text: a feeding trough or manger for livestock; the dwarf tells the family to fill it before their winter sleep.

notes.label: Heustock
notes.text: the stored mass or stack of hay, large enough here for the family and later the dwarf to hollow out a shelter inside it.

notes.label: Spätjahr
notes.text: literally the late part of the year, here late autumn when the family begins its winter-long sleep.

notes.label: Voralpen
notes.text: lower or intermediate Alpine pasture stations where stored hay is fed to cattle during winter.

notes.label: Sass
notes.text: a seasonal pasture station, hut, or livestock outpost where the dwarf tends the farmer's cattle; the source does not specify its exact buildings.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry Alpine downslope wind, which rapidly consumes snow and, the dwarf says, dangerously dries his body.

notes.label: Alles Wätter wäre zähm, Wenn der Wind nit chäm!
notes.text: the dwarf's dialect rhyme, “All weather would be tame, if only the wind never came,” explaining why the Föhn counts as bad weather for him.
notes.anchor: Alles Wätter wäre zähm, Wenn der Wind nit chäm!

notes.label: Gottwerg
notes.text: the singular form used for a member of the Gottwergini dwarf-folk, here the diligent worker at the rye mill.

notes.label: Klapperwerk
notes.text: the mill's clattering mechanism or machinery, which the Gottwerg rises even at night to inspect.

notes.label: Jetzt bin ich ein schöner Mann, Dass ich nicht mehr mahlen kann!
notes.text: the dwarf's rhyme, “Now I am a handsome man, so I can mill no more,” after his new clothes change his attitude toward dusty labor.
notes.anchor: Jetzt bin ich ein schöner Mann, Dass ich nicht mehr mahlen kann!

notes.label: Türliwirli
notes.text: the personal or fairy name of the dwarf's daughter, which her husband promises never to speak; its literal meaning remains uncertain.

notes.label: Alpwerk
notes.text: seasonal work carried out on an Alpine pasture, which takes Türliwirli's husband away from home in June.

bf90c5bb94cdf0b5131af8156ee78d2a9f1f4385.summary: In Valais, Gotwergi is the name given to small, hairy people who formerly lived in the forests and mountains and were highly skilled in magic.

notes.label: Gotwergi
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for small, hairy, magically skilled mountain or forest people, closest to dwarfs; the form is culturally specific and does not necessarily match the modern fantasy idea of a dwarf.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Nordwird
notes.text: the source's regional or variant form for the upper wind identified parenthetically as the north wind; here it is the violent weather that prevents the Gotwergi from tending the cattle, and the exact dialect spelling is retained.

1435c3a564b24017afdd80d2f37b217fedfdbe49.summary: There was once a woman who, when hired by people, said prayers at the graves of the dead in the cemetery and had a reputation for piety.

notes.label: Grabbeterin
notes.text: literally a female ‘grave-prayer,’ a woman hired to recite prayers at a deceased person's grave; the role reflects a local devotional service and the tale satirizes the supposed piety of one practitioner.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

368d535e1b13c07425410ee8b5a034a5a95142c6.summary: The fields on both sides of the country road between Sevelen and Räsis are called ‘the long ditch.’ Over a stretch of more than half an hour’s walk, no building stood here thirty years ago except an old barn, the Grabenstall.

notes.label: Grabengröll
notes.text: a local St. Gallen name for the uncanny nocturnal uproar along the ‘long ditch’; Graben means ‘ditch,’ while Gröll suggests rumbling or clattering, but no single English word captures the named phenomenon.

79c4e89dbc9cba7ba8f49a9818607718946dbca6.summary: In the langer Graben, an uncanny dog known as the Grabenhund appears at night and accompanies passersby for part of their way.

notes.label: langer Graben
notes.text: literally the ‘long ditch’ or ‘long ravine,’ the locally named route where the spectral dog appears.

notes.label: Grabenhund
notes.text: literally the ‘ditch dog’ or ‘ravine dog,’ a place-bound uncanny canine that follows night travelers without the brief source describing an attack.

03cdddb3e0a51454d67f0acbf0346ca40b553bd2.summary: In earlier times, when people were still devout and pious, two lovely childlike figures, a boy and a girl, could often be seen in the canton of Aargau when the grain in the fields came into bloom.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f456be8e19df6238fa4a3182ec68e2e062106ded.summary: A farmer walked through the meadowland behind the village toward the hill on which the grain field lay.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b869f893d244d8e77021b35b550efc0f5556ffd7.summary: One unjust Heller devours ten just ones; so runs an old proverb. That this is so can be observed often enough in the world.

notes.label: Heller
notes.text: a small historical coin and, proverbially, a tiny sum of money; the saying means that one dishonestly acquired coin consumes ten honestly earned ones, not that a fixed exchange rate applies.

notes.label: Brente
notes.text: a tall wooden grape-harvest tub, commonly carried on the back in Swiss wine regions; the stolen bunches are mixed into it before the stranger removes double the amount.

5db6142993d51aa3c9d2cea232dfc9207178a002.summary: The grateful dead have attracted particular attention in legend research. It repeatedly happens that the arme Seelen repay someone who did them good through prayer or other means and, in times of need, visibly come to that person’s aid in numbers superior to the enemy.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally “poor souls,” the souls of the dead—especially those in purgatory—who need prayers and may repay the living; here they appear as grateful supernatural protectors, though the passage also notes mythic elements beyond formal doctrine.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: a young man making a Kiltgang, the traditional Swiss nighttime courtship visit to a young woman; his route across the cemetery links an ordinary social custom with prayer for the dead.

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally “God’s acre,” a traditional German-speaking name for a consecrated cemetery; here it emphasizes the sacred burial ground the Kiltgänger crosses.

notes.label: schamrote Seelen
notes.text: literally “shame-red souls,” explained here as the souls of executed people; their red neck stripes and carried heads mark the manner of death, while the reason for the adjective schamrot is not fully explained.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss term for a church sacristan or sexton who cares for the church and assists the clergy; here he is also assigned to keep order near the cemetery.

c67f962178c62fa581913e83151600cea9df1f3a.summary: Councilman Karl Infanger's grandparents in the lower Baumgarten at Bauen once allowed an unfamiliar married couple who had found no shelter to spend the night in the Gaden.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the hospitable couple provides it as emergency lodging and allows the family to remain there after the birth.

be4d982c65b41b6d3ac91cbb2bb010fbf9e68f01.summary: On the Feuscha, a mountain farm at the front of the roughly 500-meter-high Krachenwand, in the middle of which lies a large inaccessible cave, there once lived a married couple frequently visited by the wilden Mannli who inhabited the cave just mentioned.

notes.label: Feuscha
notes.text: the named mountain farm at the Krachenwand where the human couple lives.

notes.label: Krachenwand
notes.text: literally ‘crashing wall,’ the high rock face containing the inaccessible cave of the wild people.

notes.label: wilden Mannli
notes.text: the plural cave-dwelling ‘little wild men’; Mannli is a Swiss diminutive, and the beings are a folkloric people rather than merely uncivilized humans.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: the shortened Swiss German form ‘little man,’ referring to the same cave spirit as he warns the woman about her discarded reward.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: wildes Mannli
notes.text: singular ‘little wild man,’ the husband who seeks help for his wife and rewards the human visitor with apparent coal.

notes.label: wilden Mannlis
notes.text: the source's inflected plural of wildes Mannli, Swiss German ‘little wild men,’ cave-dwelling Alpine beings whose gifts reward human aid but punish contempt.

499a4331c2b147f1a7763c7bb4966f05d7b1436a.summary: At the end of the last century, an innkeeper named Tschümperli lived in Steg.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e8ea90ade4eb6395bf47d0c84c6a6a3782cf653d.summary: When the forest torrent called the Lombach, which flows through the wild and narrow valley of Habkern and in summer, once the snow has completely run down into the valley, forms little more than a dry

notes.label: Lombachzaun
notes.text: literally ‘Lombach fence,’ a named bank, barrier, or settlement place along the torrent where residents gather to reinforce the channel; the exact local feature is not described.

notes.label: Lombachzwerg
notes.text: literally ‘Lombach dwarf,’ the gray riverbed spirit who warns where the spring flood will tear away the banks.

155c87dc9bbce09ff84a9b3b740f384f3ea0b07c.summary: After a battle once fought on the Breitfeld (Straubenzell, St. Gallen), several iron rods and a little green tree are said to have been buried in the ground there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a7b19c09ba549d63681aaddb942d32b78bfe453d.summary: The great bell in the church tower at Sarn formerly belonged to the municipality of Tschappina, and that municipality sold it to the citizens of Purtein.

notes.label: Schleife
notes.text: a simple drag-sled or runnerless sledge used to haul a heavy load over the ground; the men place the stolen bell upon one.

notes.label: Purteiner-Tobel
notes.text: the ravine associated with Purtein where the fiery-red cat confronts the bell thieves; Tobel denotes a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

b6b5884d3b55f983df0c48600c2254b2584fe0ac.summary: Once, Death is said to have raged terribly in the mountains of Naters. It is told that a shepherd in Aletsch picked up and ate a nut that a great bird had carried over the mountains in its beak and dropped before him.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture where the shepherd is the epidemic's first victim in the Saas version; it is a worked grazing landscape, not simply a mountain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: beigeten
notes.text: a dialect or regional past-tense form meaning ‘heaped’ or ‘piled up,’ which the source itself glosses; the cloth piles visualize the gravediggers' immense death toll and payment.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: an old fathom-like measure whose exact regional value varied; each gravedigger's accumulated linen is said to form a pile one Klafter high.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Trinkelkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Trinkel bells, generally smaller livestock bells; the twelve inherited animals signal how radically the plague has redistributed property.

notes.label: Bibinella
notes.text: the name of a medicinal plant gathered in the Massa-Kinn, probably related to Pimpinella or burnet-saxifrage traditions; the spelling and exact botanical species remain uncertain.

notes.label: gebaht's Brod
notes.text: dialect for ‘blessed bread,’ bread consecrated or prayed over and used as a protective remedy; the source does not identify a particular saint's blessing.

notes.label: gähen Tod
notes.text: literally ‘sudden death,’ here both the swift plague and the danger against which the herb and blessed bread protect.

notes.label: Massa-Kinn
notes.text: a local deep terrain feature associated with the Massa where Bibinella is found; Kinn may describe a narrow cleft or channel, but the exact landform is not defined.

7e405fbd7524263989c95ff80e4c4edb8782bdaf.summary: At the Chapel of Saint Justus by the Seez, the Seezchappeli, a large black dog passes during the Geisterstunde and goes up along the Spinnereigraben; it vanishes without a trace at the church path beneath the Steinbrückli.

notes.label: Seezchappeli
notes.text: Swiss German for the ‘little Seez chapel,’ the familiar local name of the Saint Justus chapel beside the river.

notes.label: Geisterstunde
notes.text: literally the ‘ghost hour,’ the liminal nighttime hour—often understood as midnight—when apparitions are expected; this source gives no exact clock time.

notes.label: Steinbrückli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a ‘little stone bridge,’ the precise landmark beneath which the spectral dog disappears.

ab8e98926c318fc9c8dc7f61f243709c4aa4c6ec.summary: Oberriet too had its witches and consequently its witch trials. Old court records relate how one of these poor beings confessed that she had made a terrible hailstorm above on the Fähnern and intended to draw it across the valley.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

a9978ada6c6b01054ede75bc401d00fed4d151df.summary: One day, the Lord’s disciples felt very hungry. They went into a house to buy a loaf for five Soldi.

notes.label: Soldi
notes.text: the plural of soldo, a small historical Italian coin also familiar in Italian-speaking Ticino; the disciples offer five, but no modern value is imposed.

5259348331797da204daae8b67a0ce12271ce719.summary: Yes, in the past they told all kinds of things, but half of it is not true.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d79aca667f46b86fd2a3e151b94024b27e0d53c0.summary: The great Sexer is a beautifully situated rocky summit in the broad Flums Alp of Fursch, rich in water and flowers, near a wonderfully lovely Seelein.

notes.label: Sexer
notes.text: the local name of the rocky summit and its treasure cavern in the Fursch Alp; despite its modern appearance in English, the source provides no sexual meaning or certain derivation.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Seelein
notes.text: literally ‘little lake,’ an affectionate diminutive for the small Alpine lake near the Sexer; it should not be confused with Seele, ‘soul.’

notes.label: Sexerloch
notes.text: literally ‘Sexer hole,’ the cave or rock opening associated with the summit's hidden treasure.

notes.label: Furschhütten
notes.text: the Alpine huts at Fursch used by herders and dairy workers; the plural names the small seasonal settlement.

notes.label: Geissler
notes.text: a goat herder or goatherd, from Geiss, the Swiss German word for goat; a poor one is destined to receive the treasure.

notes.label: Allermannsharnischwurz
notes.text: literally ‘everyman's-armor root,’ the folk name for Allium victorialis; its layered bulb covering and reputed protective powers connect it with armor.

notes.label: Augustheiligtag
