notes.text: literally ‘August holy day,’ the Assumption of Mary on 15 August, traditionally associated with blessing medicinal herbs; the ritual timing empowers the root.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or staying on an Alp, especially Alpine herders and dairy workers; they witness the dead debtor hurry toward the treasure site.

notes.label: Schwizerböden
notes.text: literally ‘Schwyz grounds’ or terraces, a named stretch of Alpine terrain crossed by the doomed man's apparition; the precise local boundary is unstated.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: cattle herders, especially men tending dairy cows on an Alp; they pursue the weather-portending woman with the umbrella.

3d7b500c03dfb06c4655b42f9714d7144b30c148.summary: The Great Snake in the Schmiedwald

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form of Bannwart, a local field, forest, or boundary warden charged with protecting restricted communal land; ‘warden’ is close, but the exact office and jurisdiction varied locally.

f778739c51c29265ec4e4f5217d9274716eec9ac.summary: In the oak forest on St. Peter’s Island in Lake Biel, toward which a pebble causeway called the Heidenweg extends through the lakebed from Ligerz, a gentleman dressed in green from head to foot is often seen walking back and forth among the trees and bushes.

notes.label: Heidenweg
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ way,’ the prehistoric or legendary gravel causeway connecting the shore near Ligerz with St. Peter’s Island.

notes.label: der Grüne
notes.text: German for ‘the Green Man,’ the local name of the green-clad Devil who presages a stormy nocturnal revel.

d77fd1d2abf31e88e59a7e685a09ad422c6d246d.summary: Between Bundalp and Dündenalp, a gray, barren strip extends across Griesalp on the mountain.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder who knows the protective conduct required when crossing the cursed strip.

notes.label: b`segnet
notes.text: dialect for blessing oneself, normally making the sign of the cross; the unusual grave accent is retained from the source transcription.

notes.label: Ausgestellt
notes.text: literally something like ‘stand aside’ or ‘set out,’ the warning cry announcing the Mattenwirt; the source gives no exact grammatical explanation, but the herder responds by moving to the right.

notes.label: Mattenwirt
notes.text: literally ‘meadow innkeeper,’ the cursed proprietor of the inn at the Green Meadow; his title becomes the apparition's name.

notes.label: Blümlisalp
notes.text: literally ‘little-flower Alp’ or ‘flowery high pasture,’ imagined here before glaciation as part of a fertile route toward Valais.

notes.label: Gamchi
notes.text: the local name for the high basin or passage near the Blümlisalp route; its exact dialect derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: pack-animal drivers and transporters who carried goods over Alpine routes; their traffic enriches the innkeeper before he begins murdering them.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its pastoral landscape; divine fire leaves this once-fertile ground barren.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

a744207136374223a058b5704e96252aa3b15070.summary: Throughout the region of Sumiswald, Wasen, and Hornbach, the legend of the green rider upon the snake is commonly told.

notes.label: Meitschi
notes.text: a Swiss German word for girls, familiar and diminutive in tone; the young women mock the weather spirit's warning before the flood arrives.

notes.label: Hülfterchen
notes.text: a diminutive regional word for a small saddle; the green man first wears it around his body and later saddles the flood-serpent with it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working landscape; here the flood devastates the Hinterried Alp and its cattle.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

c7979a8acb499a37571e058d61267a07242ca460.summary: Where one travels from Bützberg toward Wangen and Solothurn, a fairly broad and deep ditch lies in the middle of a forest.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor who administered a district on behalf of a ruling authority; powers varied, and this tale emphasizes Wiladnig’s coercive local rule.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Landvögte
notes.text: plural of Landvogt, the territorial bailiffs or governors who historically ruled the district; the source does not give the institutional dates.

notes.label: Oberamt
notes.text: a higher administrative district or bailiwick; Aarwangen is the Bernese district governed by the Landvogt in the tale.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: a rider mounted on a Schimmel, a white or gray horse; ‘green’ describes the rider’s clothing, not the horse, and the apparition is the punished official.

dc6b7da1dde7e3c5c743e94b57236ee177d575b9.summary: At the former wooden, covered red bridge near Bürglen—which was destroyed by fire in 1885 and replaced by a stone bridge—an old French grenadier was sometimes seen at night.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

13e24f3d846fd7136bc5efc6890a5ef71e29b8ce.summary: Once there was a king. I no longer know when he reigned or what his name was.

notes.label: Chratte
notes.text: a Swiss German hand basket; each brother carries the apples—or their magically transformed substitutes—in one.

notes.label: Wäidlig
notes.text: a Swiss German name for a small boat or skiff, glossed in the source as a Nachen; Hans must make one that travels faster on dry land than on water.

notes.label: Chelle
notes.text: a regional word for a wooden implement, often a ladle or scoop; the source itself gives only the broad gloss ‘wooden implement,’ so its exact form is left open.

notes.label: Haasepfäffer
notes.text: Swiss German for a richly seasoned hare dish, approximately peppered or jugged hare; Hans says the king can serve it to his visitors the following day.

The dialect source first says the princess carries the hare in a small apron and then uses a different diminutive for the fold or container from which it escapes; the translation preserves the action without forcing a more exact garment identification.

99035ba46db670790889cad91d423896f0732df7.summary: The Gräggi is a little creature the size of a pumpkin that sometimes flies and sometimes merely hops, runs, and tumbles, crying strangely and uncannily in all manner of voices.

notes.label: Gräggi
notes.text: elsewhere glossed in the source tradition as ‘the screamer,’ a shape-changing nocturnal creature or uncanny noise; here it flies, hops, runs, tumbles, and cries in many voices across both mountain and valley.

notes.label: Wüetihöh
notes.text: a regional name or imitative cry for an uncanny apparition or airborne wailing; one assumes the shape of a dung heap that runs away, while the other is heard but not seen, so the accounts do not establish a single fixed form or secure etymology.

94ecd6ccfe8c3c27c3cca1192c2a2322d78f815d.summary: In the Sargans region, the “Bachgeschrei,” but above all the “Gräggi,” takes Wodan's place.

notes.label: Bachgeschrei
notes.text: literally ‘brook cry’ or ‘brook screaming,’ a local uncanny sound or being compared with the Gräggi; the source gives it no separate description.

notes.label: Gräggi
notes.text: glossed by the source as ‘the screamer,’ a shape-changing nocturnal being or noise associated here with the local role of Wodan and the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Rebenstickel
notes.text: a regional word for a vineyard stake supporting grapevines; the Gräggi's passage sounds violent enough to break every one, though no damage remains by morning.

notes.label: Fronfastenkindern
notes.text: children born during the Fronfasten, the quarterly Ember Days of the Christian calendar; regional folklore credited such children with unusual perception or relations with supernatural beings.

notes.label: Stumpen
notes.text: the source's local name for the tethering stake moved after the horses graze a circle bare; elsewhere Stumpen can mean a stump or short thick object.

108bf23f62cdc2ac4566c16d167b54f44f51b965.summary: The Grääggi is a specter that appears in many different forms, but especially as a stuffed sack of leaves, a Kratten, an animal, and so forth, and it ventures out only at night.

notes.label: Grääggi
notes.text: an eastern Swiss name for a noisy, shape-changing nocturnal apparition; the tale treats it as a local form of the Wild Hunter or Wild Hunt tradition, while also recording a skeptical owl explanation.

notes.label: Kratten
notes.text: a large regional carrying basket, often worn on the back; the apparition imitates this familiar bulky object before tumbling away through the woods.

notes.label: Bachgschrei
notes.text: literally ‘stream-cry,’ the Ragaz and Pfäfers name for the Grääggi where it haunts the Fluppabach.

notes.label: Bachgrääggi
notes.text: the Vilters compound name for the apparition, combining Bach, ‘stream,’ with Grääggi.

notes.label: Gwääggi
notes.text: a Walensee-area name for the same apparition; its precise nuance is uncertain, but the related sound pattern suggests the creature's crying or noisy character.

notes.label: Borzi
notes.text: an alternative Walensee-area name for the apparition; the source gives no separate definition, so it should be understood as a regional supernatural name rather than a distinct creature here.

notes.label: Wüetihöö
notes.text: the Rhine Valley name for the apparition, evocative of the furious or ‘wild’ hunt; exact local associations may vary.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: the Entlebuch name for a Wild Hunt figure or leader whose passage is heard at night; the text explicitly treats the Grääggi as a corresponding local being.

notes.label: Stubeti
notes.text: a traditional evening social visit or gathering, often involving conversation, music, or courtship; here it simply explains why the shoemaker is returning late at night.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a local official or warden charged with guarding regulated communal land such as forest or vineyard; this role explains why C. J. suspects illicit timber cutting.

notes.label: Du utaufte Kogä, mach as fortchunst!
notes.text: a taunt in eastern Swiss dialect, approximately ‘You unbaptized wretch, be off with you!’; Kogä is a forceful insult and the spelling reflects the recorded dialect.
notes.anchor: Du utaufte Kogä, mach as fortchunst!

notes.label: I bin besser tauft as du; i heissä Matlin, Matlin!
notes.text: the apparition's dialect reply, ‘I am better baptized than you; my name is Matlin, Matlin!’; Matlin is identified parenthetically as Magdalena, making the answer a comic reversal of the man's taunt.
notes.anchor: I bin besser tauft as du; i heissä Matlin, Matlin!

notes.label: grüene Manndli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘little green man,’ a named uncanny being that punishes cruelty, judges supposedly worthless children, and abducts a young reveler; the three fragments do not clarify whether it is a dwarf, nature spirit, demon, or several beings sharing one folk name.

15e15fda0c9ae869851d20f69fa32689685da66f.summary: In the Chur valley, several small hills rise above the meadowland. On one of them, a quarter-hour’s walk from the city of Chur, stands an old cottage in whose cellar a golden set of skittles lay hidden for a long time.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ae93a16191a942cf748bfc07b024540298d97068.summary: On Alp Lavetz at the Stäzer Horn, a Berg-Butz tended the cattle for many years and protected them from harm, especially during foggy weather or at night.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape; Lavetz is the pasture protected by the spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Berg-Butz
notes.text: literally a mountain Butz, a local goblin or spirit who can both protect and punish; here he guards the herd until the offering is dishonestly changed.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an inflected form of Senn, the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal alp.

notes.label: Rahm
notes.text: cream, especially the rich sweet cream offered to the spirit rather than sour milk.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the hut on an alp used by the Senn and other workers for dairying and cheesemaking.

e53ff02bf2b0546732aa3ba4fc92d7351fa3767a.summary: At night between the towns of Baden and Mellingen, the Guenisheer passes. It comes over the Oedlisberg to Neunbrunnen in the Schönhard forest, crosses the Reuss there, and moves through Mellingen toward Brunneck Castle and Lenzburg.

notes.label: Guenisheer
notes.text: the local name of a nocturnal supernatural host traveling through Aargau, comparable to traditions of the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Verbind mer's, verbind mer's!
notes.text: Swiss German for approximately ‘Tie it up for me, tie it up for me!’—a dangerous supernatural request to secure the rattling wagon’s load.

notes.label: Gekessel
notes.text: literally a clattering like kettles, used here for the procession’s loud metallic din.

notes.label: Fraufastenabend
notes.text: the eve of a traditional Marian fast or Ember observance; it marks a spiritually charged night, though the exact feast intended is not identified.

notes.label: so halt au, du Donners-Chetzer, wenn i der's verbinde soll!
notes.text: Swiss German meaning roughly ‘Then stop, you thunderous brute, if I’m supposed to tie it for you!’; Donners-Chetzer is an abusive dialect epithet whose exact nuance is uncertain.
notes.anchor: so halt au, du Donners-Chetzer, wenn i der's verbinde soll!

notes.label: Guenis-Heerwagen
notes.text: the ghostly army wagon associated with the Guenisheer; Heerwagen means an army or host’s wagon, while Guenis is left unexplained.

6fae64c5b4cad224451c3c4282597b7f74106a30.summary: Pasturing livestock in the Aarau Jura had already disappeared in the previous century; only in the neighboring Solothurn Jura was it still practiced in part according to the old custom.

notes.label: 's guetigs G'heer
notes.text: the contracted dialect form used for the same supernatural music in the Aarau and Fricktal Jura; G’heer suggests hearing or sound, but the exact historical wordplay is uncertain.

notes.label: Guenishirt
notes.text: the named leader or herdsman of the musical host; the source assigns the role but gives no physical description or secure etymology.

notes.label: Glücksheer
notes.text: literally ‘host of fortune’ or ‘lucky host,’ the Küttigen name for the procession when understood as a sign of a blessed year.

notes.label: Guetisheer
notes.text: a spelling variant used both for the supernatural music and in a comparison for poor, unharmonious music, an ironic contrast the source explicitly records.

notes.label: Guetigsg'heer
notes.text: a local Aargau name for the airborne musical host heard around Aarau’s Homberg; the source connects it with good harvest omens but also records a Küttigen phrase using the name ironically for bad singing, so its literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Fasnacht
notes.text: the Swiss carnival season before Lent; the host may travel during this calendrical period as well as during the summer dog days.

notes.label: Alten Fasnacht
notes.text: literally ‘Old Fasnacht,’ the older-calendar carnival date used in the farmers’ rule that links its stars to the number of harvest reapers.

notes.label: Guetis- und Guenischheer
notes.text: a paired regional name for the same beautifully singing host around Lütwil, where its appearance foretells a fruitful year.

notes.label: Gunisheer
notes.text: the Birmensdorf-on-the-Reuss spelling of the supernatural host’s name; the source treats it as a regional variant rather than a different apparition.

notes.label: Guetis-Ee
notes.text: the Freiamt name for the Wild Hunt or Wild Host heard rushing through the air; the source supplies this identification, but the exact meaning of Ee in the compound is uncertain.

f67a0dd1fb173db0077f6f180741911ee75fac3e.summary: The Gugger, cuckoo, holds a foremost place in the bird world, which is partly “unghürigen” and partly prophetic of fate.

notes.label: Gugger
notes.text: Swiss German for cuckoo, a bird treated as both uncanny and prophetic.

notes.label: unghürigen
notes.text: uncanny, monstrous, or supernatural; the inflected source form characterizes one side of the bird world.

notes.label: Holl di d'r Gugger
notes.text: Swiss German curse, literally ‘may the cuckoo fetch you,’ with Gugger serving euphemistically as the Devil.

notes.label: Im Gugger
notes.text: literally ‘in the Gugger,’ a recurring place-name for sites often reputed to be haunted.

notes.label: Guggehu
notes.text: the name of an immortal nocturnal cuckoo- or owl-like bird around Iberg; the exact species and etymology are uncertain.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep exposed rock faces or cliffs.

ee80e1c3402654a6a2dbf72cd8acf05991420d18.summary: An old folk song from Aargau.

notes.label: Baderliedeli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive meaning ‘little Bader song,’ the seductive three-part song the rider promises to teach Anneli; its relation to the title-name is retained rather than normalized.

notes.label: Sternewirths
notes.text: literally ‘at the Star innkeeper's,’ meaning the inn named for the Star where Anneli's brother hears her distant cry.

notes.label: Rüdeli
notes.text: a diminutive personal name, likely ‘little Rudolf,’ used for the murderous rider in the climactic confrontation.

notes.label: Höppelidanz
notes.text: literally a ‘little hopping dance,’ a grimly comic name here for the rider's punishment while hanging from the horse's tail.

notes.label: Guggibaderlied
notes.text: the source's title for this Aargau narrative folk song; Guggibad appears to be a place or traditional song-name, while Lied means ‘song.’

693393e3bdfb06296f72fe5e7ac4ba7fe11fa96c.summary: Outside Muri the procession of the Gundisheer begins. Like a loudly grunting and rooting herd of pigs, it passes across the monastery field through the outer village and up the mountain toward Buttwil.

notes.label: Gundisheer
notes.text: a regional Aargau name for a roaring supernatural host or Wild Hunt-like procession; here it takes the form of a ghostly swine herd, while the name’s exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Hagöhrli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive glossed by the source as ‘little boar’s ear’; it is the affectionate or identifying call addressed to the captured supernatural piglet.

notes.label: Heiniguggeli
notes.text: an opaque dialect nickname used by the piglet for the youth carrying the sack; the source gives no literal explanation, so its comic or mocking nuance remains uncertain.

fd24d62517d9e2adfb182bae917682bad7ebc5eb.summary: In the little village of Freienwil, three quarters of an hour from the town of Baden, there lived a simple, pious farmer.

notes.label: Guet Wetter, gar guet Wetter.
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘good weather, very good weather,’ the habitual saying that gives the farmer his nickname.

notes.label: Gutwetter
notes.text: the unhyphenated body-text form of the farmer's nickname, preserved alongside the title variant.

notes.label: Todtenwacht
notes.text: historical spelling for the wake or vigil kept beside a dead person, traditionally accompanied by nighttime prayer.

notes.label: Gut-Wetter
notes.text: literally ‘good weather,’ the title's hyphenated form of the farmer's nickname, derived from his unfailingly optimistic answer.

8d24c413befeeeebab175ef2fd6e79a8b624d1aa.summary: The usual route between Grossberg and Kleinberg, which are separated by the deep Schilztobel, formerly crossed the rear natural bridge called the Gwelb.

notes.label: Schilztobel
notes.text: the deep ravine of the Schilz separating Grossberg and Kleinberg; Tobel is the Swiss term for a steep gully or gorge.

notes.label: Gwelb
notes.text: the local name for the rear natural bridge, related to Gewölbe, a vault or arch; it is both a route and the uncanny encounter site.

notes.label: Stubetegänge
notes.text: nighttime visits to a Stubete, a household social gathering associated with work, music, and courtship; unmarried young people used this path for them.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a traditional evening gathering in a farmhouse room, often combining communal work, sociability, music, and courtship.

notes.label: Betläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the prayer or Angelus bell; its morning sound marks the man's return to consciousness.

notes.label: Stegenbrückli
notes.text: a diminutive local bridge-name, meaning a little footbridge or plank bridge; the man wakes there without knowing how he arrived.

6a719ab34ce0311a35a8138b15f0938a50bc6c6d.summary: At the end of the village of Döttingen one reaches the Risi. At the steepest slope it drops far down to the Aare, which flows past below; on the other side, beyond a narrow strip of arable land, dense woodland begins.

notes.label: Risi
notes.text: a Swiss German landscape term for a steep scree, slide, or rubble slope; here it is the dangerous drop above the Aare and the apparition’s named haunt.

notes.label: Gîgelispanner
notes.text: a local Aargau byname for the spectral fiddler associated with the Risi and, in another tradition, Klingnau; Gîgeli suggests a little fiddle or fiddling, but the full compound’s literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Schlemperlied
notes.text: an old term for the sort of plaintive or disreputable tune the robber fiddles while posing as a beggar; its exact musical genre is not specified in the story.

notes.label: Unheilskreuze
notes.text: literally ‘misfortune crosses,’ wayside crosses marking sites associated with fatal violence or disaster; here they preserve memory of the Gîgelispanner’s victims.

notes.label: Grien
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for gravel or a shingle bank and here also the named riverside spot where the second Gîgelispanner drowned.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a local official or warden charged with enforcing restrictions in forest, field, or common land; the timber thieves fear his authority while stealing oaks.

a44f0e5f25916dd0875c5bf05a3275c07dd7a21a.summary: The thatched roof of a Tegerfelden farmhouse reaches almost to the church wall opposite it and runs in the same direction.

notes.label: Usmenni
notes.text: an Aargau term for a communal drove-way or strip used to move livestock; because it is ownerless boundary land, the farmer cannot simply drain it.

notes.label: Güggel
notes.text: Swiss German for a rooster or cock; only its head appears as the old householder's ghost.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Schoppengütterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small bottle of roughly Schoppen size; the Capuchins use it as a spirit bottle, and the precise vessel type is regionally colored.

notes.label: Güggelkopf
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘rooster's head’; the title names the apparition that repeatedly shoots from the drainage ditch.

notes.label: Rinngraben
notes.text: literally a runnel or drainage ditch; here it is the permanently muddy channel squeezed between farmhouse and church.

b91db02c307c7298351831746672844963d19ad6.summary: In the suburb of Brugg, down by the brickworks, there is a small house at the back of a courtyard belonging to a foreign family living abroad.

notes.label: Günnä
notes.text: the local name of the gray-hatted immigrant's house-bound apparition and weather sign; the source provides no secure literal derivation or fuller identity.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: small historical Swiss coins whose value varied by canton and period; the spirit leaves three each morning as payment for the maid's service.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

f230453c46e7a5f155c99ce1c40490dfda3605cc.summary: On a hot summer day, a poor old soldier walked along the highway, carrying a Habersack on his back and his entire fortune of six kreuzers in his pocket: three for brandy and three for bread.

notes.label: Habersack
notes.text: literally an ‘oat sack,’ also a soldier’s provision bag or knapsack; the magical wish turns this ordinary pack into a trap for spirits and a means of entering Heaven.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: The Kreuzer was a historical small-denomination coin used in parts of Switzerland and neighboring lands. Its value varied across monetary systems; in some Swiss systems it counted as one quarter of a Batzen. A named coin in a tale is therefore not a modern cent with a fixed national value.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Kreuzer

5feb420e4ef3e6c7e1aefe6c08d189dce0bb80c5.summary: Many, many years ago, a citizen of Oberendingen had a garden close beside his house that enjoyed a special reputation.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a heavy, pronged hoe or mattock used for breaking and cultivating soil; it is a traditional hand tool, not the limestone landscape meant by English geological ‘karst.’

notes.label: En Karst oder e Haue!
notes.text: Alemannic dialect for ‘a Karst or a hoe’; it is the spirit’s repeated request for a digging implement.

notes.label: Hackengeist
notes.text: literally a ‘hoeing’ or ‘mattock spirit,’ the unseen night worker that asks for a tool and digs the garden; the compound names its action rather than specifying whether it is a ghost, dwarf, or other being.

42b48c181b510c605bd7f8a4244e51891d5be3e0.summary: A man once hanged himself in the Schachen. As a suicide, he found no eternal rest.

notes.label: Hafnerli
notes.text: this is the local personal or household name attached to the helpful returning suicide; its derivation, identity, and possible connection to the potter’s trade are uncertain.

3272229b80fdaf29002983921c24b9e00ec9e6eb.summary: Once upon a time, a king was out hunting. He came to a hollow tree that the dogs refused to pass.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c929686267f16aabb9163a19fe86acae6444bb14.summary: Der Haarige — The Hairy One. Once there was a king out hunting.

notes.label: Der Haarige
notes.text: literally ‘the Hairy One,’ the name given to the magically altered prince; it marks both his appearance and superhuman forest strength until the second potion reverses them.

notes.label: Schuh
notes.text: literally a ‘shoe’ but historically also a foot-like unit of length whose exact value varied by place; the claim that the child grows one Schuh daily is fabulous rather than a precise modern measurement.

03c4756f8235574919dc53db1ed73354715f3fca.summary: On certain evenings, the people of Vättis claim to have heard a cry very near the village, on the hillside, called the Haldengeschrei.

notes.label: Haldengeschrei
notes.text: literally a ‘hillside cry’ or ‘cry from the slope’; here it is the local name for a death-omen heard near Vättis, a specificity that a generic English rendering would lose.

fb8c895efed3eb2f6785856b150f9bf3a0ecc1fe.summary: At the back of Oberried, where the Lord of the World created his most beautiful little spot on earth, the poor human heart often grows timid and oppressed.

notes.label: Haldensau
notes.text: literally ‘slope sow,’ the transformed mother condemned to race through the Haldenwald with her piglet-children; Halde means a hillside or slope, while Sau is a sow.

aba4c1c4496848100b3de81eb5cbfcf7b178c011.summary: The oldest part of Aarau rises as a narrow mountain road from the riverbed to the church.

notes.label: Halde
notes.text: the steep old quarter of Aarau rising from the river toward the church; the ordinary word can mean slope or hillside.

notes.label: Hokenmann
notes.text: a companion bogey used to frighten children indoors at evening; the source does not describe its appearance or establish the name's derivation.

notes.label: Neufranken
notes.text: literally ‘New Franks,’ a historical Swiss designation here for the approaching revolutionary-era French forces.

notes.label: Haldenthier
notes.text: the source's historical spelling of Haldentier, the same Aarau apparition associated with the church rock, weather, executions, and danger.

notes.label: Rollenloch
notes.text: literally a named ‘rolling hole’ or cave, the great rock vault beneath the Aarau church where unborn children are imagined to wait.

notes.label: Haldenbrunnen
notes.text: the spring or fountain below the Halde whose drainage is linked with the disappearance and possible return of the Haldenthier.

notes.label: hoolte
notes.text: the source's regional verb, glossed there as ‘called’ or ‘lured’; the beast voices an unusually moving warning cry while approaching the executioner's house.

notes.label: Haldentier
notes.text: the modernized spelling of Aarau's ‘slope beast,’ a gigantic shape-changing warning apparition associated with the old quarter called the Halde.

ef5cce9b3f03750a6b3810303ab2d8820d715d0c.summary: A butcher lived in Aarau a hundred years ago who had never cared to learn his trade properly.

notes.label: Katzengraben
notes.text: literally “cat ditch,” the historical local name of the blind alley where the Haldentier stays by day; the tale does not explain the name’s origin.

notes.label: Haldentor
notes.text: the former town gate at Aarau’s Halde; Tor means gate, and the ghost’s nightly admission makes the vanished fortification central to the legend.

notes.label: Haldentier
notes.text: literally “Halde animal,” the local spectral beast associated with Aarau’s Halde slope and former Haldentor; it is the punished butcher in dog form, not an ordinary animal of the hillside.

b1b7733466a5a31e51ea980471070f6a167c80fe.summary: In the Langental, Geschnitt Binn in Goms, stands the Chapel of the Holy Cross, a pilgrimage site much visited from near and far.

notes.label: Geschnitt
notes.text: an older Valais territorial or parish subdivision; here Geschnitt Binn locates the Langental within Goms, but the passage does not define its exact administrative status.

notes.label: Halseisen
notes.text: literally ‘neck iron,’ an iron collar or neck shackle; the freed prisoner's discarded restraint becomes a votive object displayed at the chapel.

a3918ed149e01fb8b8758880906a5668f736e756.summary: A young man from Gurtnellen was courting a woman from Bristen. A good friend warned him against this person: he did not like her; there was something peculiar about her, he said.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

9d8631c0c290b0cffcd27b3c9d473563ff5bd821.summary: For a long time, a hand projected from a grave in the cemetery at Spiringen.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

b43905a808e7921b5d4b80e4e0f81ce6cdf09d53.summary: Countess Bertha of Thierstein, who was abbess of Olsberg monastery, had a steward or Kastenvogt who was harsh and uncharitable toward poor people.

notes.label: Kastenvogt
notes.text: a lay steward, administrator, or protective bailiff of an ecclesiastical house and its property; the paired title Hofmeister suggests estate management, but the precise balance of judicial and financial authority is not stated.

e2d836d039710c3eda86dcc3a489072a1973f5bd.summary: For several evenings already, whenever the honorable Sigrist of Sisikon went to the church to ring the Betglocke, he had seen a child's hand protruding from a grave.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan, responsible for practical church duties; here he rings the evening prayer bell and tends the graveyard apparition.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally the ‘prayer bell,’ a church bell rung to call or mark communal prayer; its evening ringing brings the Sigrist repeatedly past the grave.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

fde2640f28af3d9fbfc5c19f633c8041290f6493.summary: A farmer from Meerenschwanden mocked a burning man whom he met at night in a meadow of fodder grass and repeatedly called to him, ‘Take me, Brünnliger, take me!’ When the figure promptly marched toward him, the farmer fled into the house and bolted the door behind him.

notes.label: Tennsthor
notes.text: the large door or gate of the Tenn, the barn's threshing floor; the story preserves an older spelling of standard German Tennentor.

notes.label: Brünnling
notes.text: a burning revenant or fiery supernatural man; the name derives from the dialect verb for burning, and the variants Brünnliger and brünnlige Ma in the tale refer to the same being.

5d645a81392231fa7d69a0eb473e92fe98988029.summary: Not long ago, two sisters, one from Bellikon and the other from Spreitenbach, went to visit their third sister in Baldingen.

notes.label: Galgenvögel
notes.text: literally “gallows birds,” an ominous folk name applied here to the crying magpies that foretell misfortune; the term can be used for carrion or ill-omened birds more broadly.

notes.label: Weidgang
notes.text: communal pasture or the recognized right and area for driving livestock to graze; here it names the Remetschwil grazing ground, while the exact ownership arrangement is unstated.

notes.label: Kreuzwegli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little crossroads or crossing path; crossroads carry supernatural danger in European folklore, and here the hare turns the woman around there, though the tale does not explain the place’s history.

e0eaba920dddd1b88ab1666036d0423d489290cf.summary: A woman in Zofingen from a noble family that immigrated to Switzerland from southern France steals meat from the town butcher shop while transformed into a cat, and fruit from the fields while transformed into a hare.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

39b0346a1772dd0a2116c565abf5a0dfe79f4b35.summary: The Harnischwibli dwells in the Harnischtöbeli, and the Leutschenbock makes a commotion in the nearby little wood toward Uznach.

notes.label: Harnischwibli
notes.text: the local name for a female spirit inhabiting the Harnischtöbeli; its closest literal sense is ‘little armored woman,’ but the name may instead derive from the ravine’s place-name, and the brief account leaves her form and origin uncertain.

notes.label: Leutschenbock
notes.text: the local name for a goat-like or goat-named spirit that haunts a wood toward Uznach; Bock means ‘billy goat,’ while Leutschen appears tied to the locality, and the being’s precise form and origin are not explained.

ddb9c4cb89cdac4a17568fe9bc319a339c7f8c65.summary: At St. Niklaus, on the Bort at the southern bank of the Riedbach, it is said that a judge once lived alone with his two daughters, whom he wished to see well provided for and well married.

notes.label: Vorschos
notes.text: a Valais pastoral measure meaning an armful, bundle, or carried portion of fodder; here the starving woman takes that amount of hay, but the term does not define a standardized weight.

683d7e54708f393c9b8b30d891147f90f394d838.summary: Between Zuzwil and Linggenwil, right beside the main road, lies a small wood called the Hasenholz, inhabited by a ghostly musician known as the Hasenholzgeiger.

notes.label: Hasenholzgeiger
notes.text: literally the Hasenholz fiddler, the invisible and place-bound ghost musician of this wood; his beautiful music both marks sacred seasons and entices travelers into enchantment.

notes.label: Fronfastentage
notes.text: the German and Swiss name for Ember Days, the quarterly sets of Christian fasting and prayer days; folklore often treats these sacred calendar periods as times of heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Torfmoos
notes.text: the local peat bog or moor beside the Hasenholz; Moos in Swiss place language can mean marshy ground and should not be understood here merely as botanical moss.

notes.label: Angelusläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the Angelus prayer bell; in this account the morning bell marks sacred time and breaks the fiddler's enchantment.

47d056b789cdcde5942c1dcf59efc5e1fed55941.summary: In a suburb of Basel stands a large old house that may well be many hundreds of years old.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

60f8597030581f951f6cfd4838f067682d2813da.summary: On the Riederalp or Mörjeralpe, which tourists pass on the journey between the Eggishorn and Belalp, there is an old three-story house by the chapel whose lowest dwelling is very uncanny.

notes.label: Mörjeralpe
notes.text: the Alpine pasture associated with Mörel, also called Riederalp in the passage; Alpe here denotes a high seasonal pasture and settlement, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: nisten und gummern
notes.text: a Valais sound-expression for the rustling, rummaging, or muttering heard in the haunted room; the exact verbs are dialectal, and the narrator likens them to parchments being handled.

notes.label: lahmen Tag
notes.text: literally something like a ‘lame day,’ a local expression for acquiring lasting lameness or the fateful occasion that causes it; both men are said to have suffered such harm in the house.

notes.label: Bozenstube
notes.text: literally the ‘Bozen room,’ the haunted lower room assigned to the chaplain; Bozen is a Valais plural or related form for bogey-like spirits, not the South Tyrolean city.

notes.label: Troggenspiel
notes.text: a traditional card game, likely a regional form related to Troccas or tarot play; the exact rules used by the chaplains are not given.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: a Valais name for bogeys, ghosts, or frightening supernatural beings; the priest initially rejects belief in them, while the story never provides a visible form for his attacker.

6d663744548e4bc8c1203ef1001c07a11c2dcc18.summary: a) It has always been claimed that the area by the Helgennussbaum on the road between Brügg and Trudelingen—which has now been replaced by a young linden tree—and also the whole stretch as far as the little chapel near Trudelingen were haunted.

notes.label: Steinriesel
notes.text: a regional word for a stony runnel, scree channel, or narrow rock-strewn slope; the title connects it to the unexplained rustling along the road, but the source does not map the feature precisely.

55c44b5c037e1ad24790d46bff8669cdb76afc19.summary: People in Hägglingen in the Freiamt had learned from a sorcerer what means could be used to reach a treasure whose existence had long been spoken of in that village.

notes.label: Hol ä’Säge
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘fetch a saw,’ retained because speaking the phrase breaks the required silence.

notes.label: Katzenstelleli
notes.text: the local field-name of the treasure site, literally a diminutive ‘cat place.’

ca7c93dac997532c5d33cd5bd4083aa4ddad791d.summary: Brunnenwiesler is the name of the black cat that meets people in Ober-Endingen on the footpath by the local Brunnenwiese and tries to lure them into the Surb flowing past.

notes.label: Brunnenwiesler
notes.text: a local byname meaning approximately ‘one from the spring meadow,’ given to the black cat and former meadow owner; the exact personal identity is lost.

notes.label: Wässerungsrecht
notes.text: a legally recognized right to take, channel, or use water for irrigation; the tale treats the owner’s improperly obtained new right as the cause of his animal punishment, without describing the lawsuit.

05861154293c50c3318ffe41a80ca92a9dfaedc7.summary: A housewife in Schwyz never wanted to go to bed before midnight. She explained to her husband, who disliked her spinning so long by lamplight, that she did not lie down earlier because otherwise a black cat would ride her as though mountain and valley lay upon her.

notes.label: Schnellkappe
notes.text: a large regional women’s cap or headdress; the precise style intended here is uncertain, but its size lets the husband impersonate his wife at the spinning.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

9b17180c81aefd41385f225ec77941b611f42b26.summary: Midway between Wettingen Monastery and the village of the same name, a quarter-hour away, stood two great stone posts constructed with a barred gate behind which the monks customarily closed the road through the monastery lands to farmers' wagons.

notes.label: beim schweren Gatter
notes.text: literally ‘by the heavy gate,’ the surviving local name for the site of the monastery's former barred road gate; the haunting begins after the structure is demolished.

652e1f0ee160c7e7ad1a9028e8adf5171b878b42.summary: On the Kleine Steig near Brugg there is a place where a witch in the shape of a black cat guards a treasure.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

f469bffeaa4075277a6e74fde6fe7995202422b1.summary: A rather elderly farmer from Battänia went to the market in Cur and set out for home again at night.

notes.label: Veltliner-Wein
notes.text: the historical German name here for wine from the Valtellina south of Graubünden; readers should not assume that it means the modern Grüner Veltliner grape variety.

486e3ad5f83e7795603f8f789d8358c21f3f667b.summary: Gitschenberg above Seedorf was very heavily haunted.

notes.label: erwellen
notes.text: an Uri Alpine dairying verb for heating or otherwise processing milk or whey during cheesemaking; the kitchen noise suggests this work, but the exact production stage is uncertain.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; here the next year’s first butter must be brought to the Capuchins as part of the ghost’s condition for redemption.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

245fde07e197c2b0929c831966914fafd5f9eac4.summary: Near St. Wendel, on the far side of the Linth, there once stood a chapel of which scarcely even ruins can now be seen.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

31e6d068b17ec7c6470dfed9e81331407ad94fca.summary: When an avalanche buried the Grimsel hospice several years ago, the servant who guarded the house alone through the winter heard the Hauri.

notes.label: Hauri
notes.text: the Hauri is a Juchliberg spirit whose cry warns the winter caretaker and whose action opens his escape; its appearance, name origin, and relationship to other Alpine warning spirits are uncertain.

notes.label: Kobolde
notes.text: the plural Kobolde denotes mischievous or hostile German-speaking place spirits, here imagined celebrating on the glacier; their precise connection to the avalanche and to the Hauri is uncertain.

9d1aae0c0fb2cf578aab2f84551bf07cd19b6f89.summary: In Serfrangen near Klosters, a Hausbutz called “Stutzli” still displayed all the good-natured and trusting character of a house spirit.

notes.label: Hausbutz
notes.text: a domestic spirit or house sprite; unlike a merely frightening bogey, Stutzli is gentle, helpful, and capable of redemption.

notes.label: Stutzli
notes.text: the personal diminutive name of the Hausbutz; the -li ending conveys smallness or familiarity in Swiss German.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the bench built beside or around a masonry stove, a warm focal place in a traditional household and Stutzli's favored seat.

3e39b22c16c4511919f315b2a318231540033a6f.summary: People still tell many things from our forefathers’ glorious struggles for liberty that the historians did not record.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a25640cbef313dd3e312cc33cd3ad33fe4bfa1c6.summary: Things are thoroughly ‘unghür’ upon the Riet between Werdenberg and Haag, especially near the gallows.

notes.label: unghür
notes.text: Swiss German for uncanny, haunted, or dangerously supernatural; the quoted word characterizes the whole marsh and gallows area.

notes.label: Riet
notes.text: a regional form of Ried, meaning marshy meadow, reed land, or wet ground; it names the landscape between Werdenberg and Haag.

b0962b517b85c8188e9309776c5489549df86be5.summary: The footpath leading upward from Pélier to St. Germain in Savièse was always believed to be somewhat uncanny.

notes.label: klafterlangen
notes.text: literally ‘a Klafter long,’ referring to the field warden’s exceptionally long official staff; a Klafter is a historical fathom-like measure whose exact length varied regionally.

9f3ef1fe6ec9e2ea794296d4158af5f34217de6d.summary: ‘Whenever they were haymaking at Oberkäsern in the Maderanertal,’ my mother often related, ‘it happened not infrequently that toward 9 o’clock in the morning a large man came up from the Kuhkähle to Oberkäsern, marched above Oberkäsern and across the Büel, and from there went down again toward the Brunni.

notes.label: Handbräntli
notes.text: a small portable wooden dairy container designed to be carried by hand or on the back; the headless weather spirit carries one, but its contents are not stated.

f51f2dc2e8a1e1eab6f328ee9e82d052562191c3.summary: Already a hundred years ago, a man from Altendorf was tending his livestock in the Feldrietle.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

de75405fc30185c54cf0a25c89c11dd2fd47d0f1.summary: Where the Niesen tousles the sea of clouds, there stood in ancient times a little house in which an honest married couple lived.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

169cd15cdef6efea0f3b5cc394ba217cd53e0d8e.summary: The married couple at the mill in Lengnau had an only son. One hears him called now Seppi, now Erni, for it was long ago that he lived; but he was regarded as the finest man in the country, and he was so strong that he had no one else to fear.

notes.label: Heidewîbli
notes.text: an Aargau dialect diminutive meaning approximately ‘little heath woman’ or ‘little heathen woman’; here it names the enchanted female being who aids Bartli, and the spelling preserves the source’s regional pronunciation and ambiguity between heath-dweller and pagan figure.

notes.label: Saum
notes.text: a historical Swiss measure of liquid or pack-load volume, often used for wine; its quantity varied significantly by region and period, so the seven Saum cannot be converted to one exact modern volume from this text alone.

84d012dcf9ba2932c38c835cc18580c32b2cf1bb.summary: In summer, one sometimes finds a finely curled, angelically beautiful child lying naked upon snow-white swaddling cloths in a flowering clover field.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like beings associated with subterranean places and the land; the heavy child is believed either to belong to them or to have been stolen by them from humans.

notes.label: Chrügeli
notes.text: an Aargau word for a small, healthy child; the narrator connects it with the uncanny infant and with the similarly named rock passages.

notes.label: Chrügelnägeli
notes.text: the Aargau name for mysterious narrow holes or passages in Jura rock whose interiors are unknown and which are implicitly linked with dwarf beings.

notes.label: Zwerlimatte
notes.text: literally ‘little-dwarfs' meadow,’ a local place-name beside the Chrügelnägeli on the Gislifluh that reinforces the site's association with subterranean little people.

75ff328bc9b0bf41307ab2e18464496b5ea7ee8a.summary: 1. One year after the chaplain of Meien had banished those two fiery dogs and brought peace to the valley’s livestock, the people of Meien carried the corpse of a valley man to Wassen, there to commit it to consecrated ground beside their parish church.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Lychkirmi
notes.text: a traditional stopping or resting place on a funeral route where coffin bearers set down their burden; here it is located on the Schanz and associated with an inherited prayer custom.

notes.label: Fyfi
notes.text: the name of the prayer observance performed at the funeral-route rest; the form suggests a set of five prayers, but this source does not identify the precise texts or ritual sequence.

b2c1d2a533e2c97b7435f1e9b40ffc3b64d263ba.summary: It was in the year 1193 that Cardinal Cintius, a papal envoy, and his retinue wished to travel back from Denmark to Rome.

notes.label: Heckenfischer
notes.text: the robber’s byname, literally something like “hedge fisher”; the source identifies Andreas von Marmels as a waylayer of travelers but does not explain the compound more precisely.

notes.label: Fahrhabe
notes.text: movable personal property or goods carried with a traveler, as distinct from land and buildings.

notes.label: Freiher
notes.text: the source’s historical or typographically shortened spelling of Freiherr, a noble rank conventionally rendered as baron.

notes.label: Fehde
notes.text: a formally pursued private feud or armed conflict under medieval custom, not merely a personal disagreement.

1ee3252348a48baf947c1503f1d050a16b879868.summary: In the gray age of paganism there was a salt spring in Ryken, between the Zofingen Boowald and the Aare; the location is not described more precisely.

notes.label: Heidemanndli
notes.text: literally ‘little heathen men,’ an Aargau name for helpful dwarfs associated with an ancient salt spring, farming signs, nocturnal labor, and magical replenishment; the label may imply pre-Christian antiquity rather than describing their religion, and the source varies its spelling.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Erdmannli
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ another Swiss name for subterranean or dwarf-like household helpers; here it refers to the same visitors as Heidemanndli, though the change of name may emphasize their earth-dwelling nature.

799095b132f2a74a93784a0683607cfe7d709e0c.summary: Years ago, complete strangers often came to remote farms and helped the inhabitants with their work.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans,’ a broad historical folk label for mysterious predecessors or religious outsiders; the source's final comment suggests that people in Flums may have used it for remnants of the earlier Romansh population.

notes.label: Heidenbau
notes.text: literally a ‘heathen building,’ a folk-archaeological label for a structure believed so old or technically mysterious that it was attributed to pre-Christian or unknown earlier inhabitants.

b632704f19c657d6b1a2e1d049fa03ea23d878d3.summary: On the northern slope of the Stockhorn range lies a solitary place surrounded on every side by forest.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans,’ a folklore label often applied to imagined ancient inhabitants or uncanny pre-Christian builders; here the two figures command weather and construct fire-protecting stone houses, not merely members of a known historical religion.

notes.label: Stockhorner
notes.text: literally ‘the one from the Stockhorn,’ the local name for the threatening storm or weather-being announced by the raised flag; whether it denotes the storm itself or a personified force is left ambiguous.

3ec0cbdc7b316a8d4fc9f563671943aac4dd324a.summary: Near the Alp of Fontanen by Giswil is the Heidenbrunnen, so called because the Heiden who once lived at Fontanen drew their water there.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working landscape rather than simply a mountain; Fontanen is the named Alp near the treasure spring.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Heidenbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘Heathens' Spring’; Heiden in such legends usually means imagined ancient, non-Christian inhabitants rather than a securely identified historical people.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans’; in Swiss place and treasure legends, the word often denotes vaguely remembered pre-Christian or otherwise ancient former inhabitants, whose precise identity is uncertain.

473535eb9b689d58f75d78996b71bfc02e1051ca.summary: Heidenhäuslein is the name given to a Zelge in the countryside of the Fricktal village of Zuzgen.

notes.label: Heidenhäuslein
notes.text: the diminutive form, literally “little heathen house,” used here as the local name of the cultivated plot; its association with Erdmännchen and excavated graves combines folklore with nineteenth-century antiquarian interpretation.

notes.label: Zelge
notes.text: a large crop section within a traditional common-field or three-field farming system; here it is the named area where the little folk helped farmers and graves were later plowed up, while its exact tenure is unstated.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally “little earth men,” subterranean or land-associated dwarf-like beings in German-speaking Swiss folklore; these helpers provide food and agricultural blessing until a farmer keeps their knife.

notes.label: Heidenhaus
notes.text: literally “heathen house,” a folk-archaeological name for a place believed ancient, pre-Christian, or connected with mysterious earlier inhabitants; the title preserves the traditional label rather than asserting the occupants’ actual religion.

4ef429c753ec0586118734256a8422475e41beb7.summary: An Alp of Giswil named Fontanen, which serves the farmers of Kleinteil as summer wilderness pasture and lies directly behind the so-called Giswilerstock, is said to have been the dwelling place of wild people or heathens in ancient times.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: an Alp is a high seasonal pasture and its associated working landscape, here Fontanen behind the Giswilerstock; its historical boundary and the phrase translated as wilderness pasture are uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: Älpler are the people who work or pasture livestock on an Alp, here said to have found old implements and interpreted the rock hollows; the finders’ identities and dates are unspecified.

notes.label: Heidenkilchli
notes.text: literally ‘little heathen church’ in Swiss German, Heidenkilchli is the local name for the isolated carved rock believed to have been a pre-Christian worship site; its archaeology and actual use are uncertain.

notes.label: Dusen
notes.text: Dusen is the source’s name for the rock’s strange grooves or hollows, some resembling footprints or body-sized cavities; the word’s exact dialect sense and whether the marks are natural or worked are uncertain.

notes.label: Heidenplatz
notes.text: literally ‘heathen place,’ Heidenplatz is one name for the ground surrounding the Heidenkilchli where dances and ruins were reported; its exact extent is uncertain.

notes.label: Heidenboden
notes.text: literally ‘heathen ground,’ Heidenboden is an alternate local name for the same surrounding area; whether it designated precisely the same tract as Heidenplatz is uncertain.

d27d89a1c48cb4c51fcc8592431923703abd2308.summary: In the Heidloch lies a treasure, deep inside the mountain in a great iron chest.

notes.label: Heidloch
notes.text: the dialect-shortened form of Heidenloch used inside the tale for the cave holding the iron treasure chest.

notes.label: Hündli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little dog; the small black guardian's bark summons the mountain beings.

notes.label: Bergzwerglene
notes.text: a dialect diminutive plural meaning little mountain dwarfs, the hidden owners or custodians of the treasure.

notes.label: Bergmännli
notes.text: Swiss German for little mountain men; they answer the Hündli's bark and prevent treasure seekers from leaving the cave.

notes.label: Heidenloch
notes.text: literally ‘heathen hole,’ the catalogue title for the treasure cave; Heiden names often attach pre-Christian or mysterious associations without proving an actual pagan origin.

5b37ca86c49dd08e45e20c61a061077769bdc464.summary: A band called Heidenvolk was passing Pfaffensprung. An old Heidenmüetterli lag a little behind.

notes.label: Heidenvolk
notes.text: literally ‘heathen folk,’ a historical Christian outsider-label used by the source for the traveling group; it does not establish their actual religion, ethnicity, or historical identity.

notes.label: Heidenmüetterli
notes.text: literally a ‘little heathen mother’ or old woman of the Heidenvolk; the diminutive is regional, while the account does not establish whether she is human, legendary, or supernatural.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source's regional name for the old woman's conspicuously large hat; its exact historical style, material, and the first element's derivation are uncertain.

dc0362ce56f0806594636ce2fb7203e5dd10a0b4.summary: About half an hour north of the hamlet of Zmutt, at the so-called Hubelwängen, a flat stone slab of considerable size can still be seen.

notes.label: Hubelwängen
notes.text: the named slopes near Zmutt where the slab lies; Hubel suggests a hill or knoll and Wängen slopes or meadows, but the exact local form is uncertain.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: historically ‘heathens’ or non-Christians, but in Alpine place-lore it can also mean ancient, pre-Christian, foreign, or vanished people; the tale's ‘wild’ figures are legendary rather than a reliable historical population.

notes.label: Heidenplatte
notes.text: literally ‘heathens' slab,’ the marked rock explained as an ancient assembly place whose hollows were made by heel-walking people.

ccf54f318f75fb4a53ca07ebe8211dc744e74cd2.summary: In the village of Klein-Döttingen, on the left bank of the Aare, stands an old house that has often been repaired and is now occupied by the Kalt family; it bears the name Heidenhaus.

notes.label: Heidenhaus
notes.text: literally ‘heathen house,’ the Klein-Döttingen home named for the visiting Heidenzwerge and later spared during the bombardment.

notes.label: Heidenzwerge
notes.text: literally ‘heathen dwarfs,’ the household-helping water dwarfs whose fire-binding arts supposedly gave them the label; the collector explicitly says that no one knows whether Heiden means they were actually non-Christian.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: historically ‘heathens’ or non-Christians, but in Alpine and Swiss folk vocabulary the word can also mark something ancient, uncanny, foreign, or attributed to a vanished people; the story itself questions the literal religious sense.

notes.label: Nuster
notes.text: a regional form of Noster, meaning a Paternoster or rosary; its discovery under the ridge tile offers a Christian protective explanation for the house's survival.

notes.label: Zigeunerkunst
notes.text: part of the old collector's label ‘Heiden- oder Zigeunerkunst,’ meaning ‘heathen or Gypsy art’ for supposedly magical fire-control; Zigeuner is now recognized as an offensive historical exonym for Roma and Sinti, and the phrase reflects period prejudice rather than a reliable description of those peoples.

eb24ed401e68b284629a9cb92880338ff3d42b92.summary: On the Kreuzhubel near Dagmersellen, in whose district in the Lutherthal a little image of Jesus was found, a widely visible cross stands at the forest edge.

notes.label: Kreuzhubel
notes.text: literally ‘cross hillock,’ the rise near Dagmersellen where the roadside cross and sacred tree stood.

notes.label: Lutherthal
notes.text: the source's historical spelling of the Luthern valley.

notes.label: heilig Tannen
notes.text: dialectal ‘holy fir,’ the tree shrine containing a Marian image and votive body-part offerings.

notes.label: versprechen
notes.text: here to make a healing or pilgrimage vow to a sacred place, not simply to make a verbal promise.

notes.label: ungefreute
notes.text: literally ‘unrejoiced’ children, explained by the source as infants who died before baptism and therefore lacked the full ritual welcome of Christian community.

6f43226995529fd4f16847be53340bcbbf385f4c.summary: A little girl had lost her father and mother and had cried bitterly because of it.

notes.label: Kathrindli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Katharina or Katherine; it marks the girl as a small child and is retained as her name.

notes.label: Sant Peter
notes.text: the dialect form of Saint Peter, portrayed in his traditional folkloric role as the gatekeeper of Heaven.

notes.label: Hellhafe
notes.text: an Aargau dialect compound meaning ‘hell-pot’ or ‘hell-cauldron’; the title points to the cauldron of boiling water in which the girl sees her mother.

4968fea8c2315f1cb82257ba526b016137e37b52.summary: Once, when Chählä-Jaggli of Gurtnellen was returning to Gornernalp after attending Sunday worship, he gave a Jauchzer as he entered the Alpine pasture.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or cry, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; Jaggli’s call is answered from the cottage and begins his relationship with the invisible helper.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Umghyr
notes.text: the narrator’s Uri name for the invisible uncanny being or haunting that assists Jaggli, follows him home, and warns of bad weather; its form, origin, and exact folkloric identity remain unspecified.

e206b6200b798e2f5b1acbe13796aab3816fbde5.summary: Once, a great Celtic people lived in Switzerland: the Helvetii. Their towns and villages stood chiefly in the central and western parts of the Swiss country.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ae1b3f6b0fe07911ee620d25e6abf45171d68ada.summary: A little boy and a girl who had gone out to pick strawberries lost their way in the forest.

notes.label: Waldfänkin
notes.text: a female forest giant or Wild Woman in Graubünden tradition; Fänkin is the feminine of a regional term for a giant-like wild being, and she saves the children through deception despite first confining them.

notes.label: Wilden Frau
notes.text: the source’s grammatically inflected phrase literally means ‘Wild Woman,’ a female wilderness being rather than simply an unruly human woman; here it is another designation for the Waldfänkin.

notes.label: Hennenkrippe
notes.text: literally a ‘hens’ manger’ or chicken feeding trough, here a confined part of the henhouse large enough to imprison the children; the source does not describe its precise construction.

notes.label: Wilde Mann
notes.text: literally ‘Wild Man,’ the Waldfänkin’s giant-like husband, whose appetite for human flesh makes him dangerous to the children.

notes.label: I schmeck, i schmeck Menschenfleisch
notes.text: regional speech for ‘I smell, I smell human flesh’; the repeated formula signals the Wilde Mann’s recognition of hidden children.

notes.label: Hennadreck
notes.text: regional form of ‘hen dirt’ or chicken droppings; the Waldfänkin uses the poultry smell as a plausible deception to save the children.

e9fa958e0f2031bb4f74bc68953c13365c2b1dd6.summary: A St. Antönier once saw the Hennenteufel.

notes.label: St. Antönier
notes.text: a person from St. Antönien; Barthli is identified by his home community.

notes.label: Hennenteufel
notes.text: literally “hen devil,” the spirit appearing as a second moving ball that torments the chickens.

notes.label: Montafuner
notes.text: a person from the Montafon valley; this visitor knows how to confront the Hennenteufel.

notes.label: Mayerhof
notes.text: the historical spelling of the local Meierhof or principal farm settlement where Barthli lives.

notes.label: Barthli
notes.text: the familiar diminutive form of Bartholomäus used for Barthli Flütsch.

notes.label: Montavoner
notes.text: the source’s alternate form for Montafuner, again identifying the visitor from Montafon.

notes.label: Hennenchrômen
notes.text: a place or fitting within the henhouse, probably a feeding trough or enclosure; the source does not define it more precisely.

notes.label: putschte
notes.text: a regional verb for butting, bumping, or violently knocking the other ball from corner to corner.

notes.label: heer
notes.text: an obscure regional verb meaning to master, overcome, or get the better of; the Hennenteufel cannot defeat the harder lead ball.

notes.label: Jagdstücklein
notes.text: literally “little hunting pieces,” meaning curious hunting exploits, feats, or tales recounted by the visitor.

f48de8375814d66675d78fa061dfa8e51bfc1212.summary: For many summers in succession, a Venediger came to Glarus, went up to a high alp, ate and slept with the herders, and spent the days gathering especially brilliant stones.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: ‘Venetian,’ used in Alpine folklore for Italian crystal and gold seekers credited with supernatural knowledge or powers.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Venedigerleute
notes.text: literally ‘Venediger people,’ the prosperous descendants’ local family byname derived from their ancestor’s supernatural benefactor.

notes.label: Venediger Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little Venetian man,’ a folklore figure associated with foreign prospectors believed to know secret Alpine mineral wealth.

43a0de496ea8858e30a5f06174800a96ba645e2f.summary: On the slope of the Sulegg above Wilderswil in the Bödeli lie some of the richest Alps in the region.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here Alp refers to a high seasonal pasture complex with its dairying landscape, not a mountain peak alone; the historical boundary and working arrangements of Suls are uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Treichel
notes.text: a Treichel is a large Swiss livestock bell, generally beaten from sheet metal rather than cast; the golden bell’s exact form and magical properties are unspecified.

d1138309dd3b0744d2b51db422b4bd0e71c311d5.summary: Once, the cows were of enormous size and had such an abundance of milk that they had to be milked into excavated ponds, which were very quickly filled.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7ffef238fedbbc0a00431df3684076eca5ed779a.summary: In the thickets and rock holes of the Walchwil Allmend, especially toward the Gnippenflue, dwelt the ‘Bergmandli,’ protective or tormenting spirits of the mountain inhabitants according to whether people deserved their goodwill or hatred.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held local land, often used for pasture, woodland, and shared resources; the Walchwil Allmend forms the beings' human-adjacent habitat.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Gnippenflue
notes.text: the local Fluh, or steep rock face, toward which the Bergmandli are especially said to live; the place-name's Gnippen element is not explained.

notes.label: Bergmandli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little mountain men,’ ambivalent beings who protect and enrich respectful households but torment those who earn their hatred.

notes.label: Herdmandli
notes.text: the title's regional name for little earth or mountain beings around Walchwil; the body calls them Bergmandli, and the source treats the names as referring to the same community of spirits.

072417b9bdc06f8ac1fc3d1e75a1b420e2243404.summary: There are as many little stories about the Herdmanndli on Pilatus as there are people who tell of them.

notes.label: Herdmanndli
notes.text: literally little earth or ground men in Alemannic usage, dwarf-like beings of Pilatus associated here with chamois, cattle, household help, and subterranean treasure; the modern English word ‘herd’ would suggest a misleading etymology.

notes.label: Berglütlenen
notes.text: Cysat’s archaic diminutive for little mountain folk, another name for the Pilatus beings; its historical spelling and precise local nuance do not have a single English equivalent.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the old Swiss political order; its authority was broader than that of an ordinary mayor.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Wildi
notes.text: an archaic regional noun for wild game or the pursuit of it; in this quotation it means the hunt from which the injured under-bailiff had to abstain.

notes.label: gaum
notes.text: to mind, watch, or guard; here it says the injured man had to remain at home and look after the house, with a housebound nuance not captured by ‘guard’ alone.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Lecktäschli
notes.text: a small herdsman’s pouch for cattle lick-salt, part of Alpine livestock care rather than an ordinary personal bag.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: a sung or recited protective blessing over the Alpine herd and pasture; in this tradition it can recall cattle from supernatural danger and is more than a generic prayer.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
