notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Abendruf
notes.text: the formal evening call projected across the alp, combining herd protection, prayer, and vocal ritual; local wording and performance customs vary.

notes.label: Volle
notes.text: the milk funnel through which the dairyman projects the evening blessing; the source itself identifies the implement, whose ritual use matters here more than its ordinary dairy function.

notes.label: Rufkäse
notes.text: the cheese specifically allotted by the community or pasture owner in return for performing the Abendruf, reflecting the communal economy of the alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

42dc847e823a2b3bd401ba98816e829abf3a38b9.summary: At the time when the County of Baden was still governed by three places—Bern, Zurich, and Glarus—a Junker from the land of Uri lived in the little village of Mellikon, near the Rhine in the Zurzach district.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: here Junker denotes a minor nobleman or landed gentleman from Uri, not a modern pejorative; his precise title and identity are uncertain.

notes.label: Grosshans
notes.text: this appears to be the name of a gambling game or high-stakes style of play that drives the steward to theft; its rules and exact meaning are uncertain.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: here Viertel is a historical dry measure for grain rather than merely the fraction ‘one quarter’; its local volume is uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Herdmännli
notes.text: literally ‘little herd man,’ this is the local name of the steward’s bound and mocking spirit; the name’s relation to livestock or the household is uncertain.

c6b40c89823553f512db2f9961f850cf4306acf6.summary: I. There are various isolated boulders in the land from beneath which the people living nearest have their supply of small children brought out.

notes.label: Kleinkinderstein
notes.text: literally a ‘small-children stone,’ a boulder beneath which folklore says newborn children are obtained; the tale treats the midwife’s retrieval as a traditional explanation rather than a physical account.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: here a digging tool such as a mattock, hoe, or pick used with the golden key to open the baby-stone; it does not mean the limestone landscape term in this sentence, and the implement’s exact form is unspecified.

notes.label: Herdmännlistein
notes.text: the source’s title and early name for the boulder formation associated with little earth folk and the folklore of fetching babies; the initial Herd- may reflect a local form or textual variant, and the later spellings differ.

notes.label: Erdmännli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings associated with the rock formation; the source alternates this name with standard German descriptions and variant spellings.

notes.label: Erdmännlistein
notes.text: literally the ‘little-earth-men stone,’ the spelling used when the nuns’ future excursions cease; it is a variant of the Herdmännlistein place name in the same account.

notes.label: Erdmannlistein
notes.text: another spelling of the ‘little-earth-men stone,’ used as the heading name in the second account; the source gives no reason for dropping the diminutive umlaut form.

notes.label: Freitisch
notes.text: a permanent right to free meals or board at an institution; the convent grants it to the small man as a reward, but the arrangement’s frequency and conditions are not stated.

c98193ba42ee85a5e06fe438dc1b445711eabc13.summary: On the Sulsalp, a herdsman once found a golden key and at the same time saw in the opposite rock wall a great black door that he had never noticed there before.

notes.label: Sulsalp
notes.text: the named seasonal high-mountain pasture where the herdsman finds the door; the -alp element denotes a working livestock and dairy landscape rather than merely a peak.

notes.label: Kuhschelle
notes.text: a cattle bell, especially the resonant bell associated with Swiss Alpine herds; its gold makes it a treasure, but choosing it instead of the maiden prevents her release.

8f0ef587b5fc46624a9edc7ee1f577f6823480ce.summary: A herdsman driving his flock came to a stream in a forest gorge. He wished that the devil would build him a bridge.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

3443723f08a243bebdc906ea5403a7cd23d13365.summary: Once the cows were of enormous size and had such an abundance of milk that they had to be milked into excavated ponds, which were very quickly filled.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

8ff06f8273cc65e34c65d0d252e99f4da6ccf4c9.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, this hermit inhabited the woods of the Grauholz, not far from the country road to Bern.

notes.label: Fuss
notes.text: the historical foot as a measure of length; its exact value varied by locality and period, while the claim of more than twelve Fuss marks Botti as a giant.

notes.label: Hünengräber
notes.text: literally ‘giants' graves,’ a traditional name for ancient burial mounds or megalithic graves whose monumental remains were popularly attributed to giants.

1af5da4d75e505d6a3133b81a2874bd5c4609ddf.summary: At a time when much internal turmoil and bloody strife raged in Valais between the people of Valais and the barons of Raron, who were very wealthy and had many friends, an enemy force crossed the Grimsel Pass into Goms in 1419 to begin subjugating the Valaisans at the very source of the Rhône.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

499199a2e26c6600c74748a052cdf43e4f210cd8.summary: West of the Rechberg near Wittnau lies the Buschberg. A path climbs diagonally across a steep slope to its summit, where a castle is said once to have stood, and leads to a pilgrimage cross.

notes.label: Herrenkutsche
notes.text: literally the “lords’ coach,” a spectral carriage associated here with the former castle lords; Herren marks people of rank or lordship, not merely a coach carrying any group of men.

f3a40f292fb1e18abdda0e979148b704dcbda208.summary: From the Rhine bank near the Aargau village of Koblenz down toward the Baden town of Waldshut, a conifer-covered height runs along the left side of the river; the newly built Rhine road follows its foot.

notes.label: Fullhalde
notes.text: the wooded slope by Full; Halde means hillside or embankment, while Full is the nearby village name.

notes.label: Herrmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little gentlemen,’ a respectful regional name for the dwarf-like helpers of the Fullhalde.

d00796c7171ed51026ab0e2b12e4fc29e3db702c.summary: On the Isenbühl, a steep slope northwest of the village of Niederwil, a monastery was swallowed by the earth.

notes.label: Isenbühl
notes.text: the local hill-name; Bühl is an older Alemannic word for a hill or rounded rise, while the intended sense of Isen in this name is not established by the tale.

notes.label: Riedmatte
notes.text: a regional compound for a wet or marshy meadow; here it names the specific meadow beneath which the monastery is said to have sunk.

notes.label: Heumüeterli
notes.text: literally a dialect diminutive “little hay mother,” the local name of the ancient female apparition near Niederwil; the tale does not say whether she is the spirit of the swallowed monastery, a field spirit, or another kind of being.

4d5250ae4eb79b526a6f91b98583ae071a55ccc8.summary: Only one tower remains of the ancient stronghold of Gösgen. High in this tower is a square opening called the Hexenloch.

notes.label: Hexenloch
notes.text: literally ‘witches' hole,’ the square opening high in Gösgen's surviving tower; its nocturnal light, revelry, and burst of wingbeats imply a witches' gathering without directly showing the participants.

d375dbd7c639e0f819238cc6f46ca432598083ee.summary: A young beggar came to a farmhouse and asked for a midday meal. The farmer turned him away, saying that he had no time just then because much hay still had to be brought into the barn.

notes.label: Wisch
notes.text: a wisp, bundle, or armful of hay; every portion the farmer grasps is immediately scattered by the magically directed wind.

notes.label: Hexenmeister
notes.text: literally ‘master of witches,’ a male witch or sorcerer; the tale treats his unworthy reception of Communion as the source or proof of his harmful power.

ab78981318f6b0e2c71c9cbd005e858f7d7b0c14.summary: On the Alp of Bäschnaten, belonging to the local municipality of Dorf, the terrain toward the Kuhmeltler forms a fairly steep slope that probably owes its origin to a great Erdschlipf that once descended from the upper reaches.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working territory; Bäschnaten is the named Alp containing the slope.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Erdschlipf
notes.text: a regional term for a landslip or sliding mass of earth; the witch rides such a slide until the chapel bell stops it.

notes.label: Hexenplatte
notes.text: literally ‘witches' slab,’ both the black sandstone block ridden by the witch and the local place-name derived from the legend.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Das Rufner Hündli fängt an zu bellen!
notes.text: ‘The little dog of Ruft is beginning to bark!’; the witch contemptuously likens the chapel's protective bell to a small barking dog.
notes.anchor: Das Rufner Hündli fängt an zu bellen!

aa77dac59674862d96977a612972900d35250b47.summary: In Nidwalden lived a musician who was greatly liked among the people as a cheerful dance fiddler and could be absent from no festivity.

notes.label: Kilbe
notes.text: a Swiss parish fair or church-dedication festival, typically combining worship, market, food, music, and dancing.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Hexentanz
notes.text: literally ‘witches' dance,’ both the supernatural event and the local name of the red-soil circle where the fiddler awakens.

notes.label: Alpboden
notes.text: the ground or meadowland of an Alp, a high-mountain summer pasture; the red circle contrasts with its surrounding green turf.

notes.label: Walburgisnacht
notes.text: Walpurgis Night, the eve of Saint Walpurga's feast and, in folklore, a night of especially active witches; the spelling is the source's form.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

872cbbe4472e5883e5b6688e27caea9535198cc5.summary: In the days when witches still existed, one of them attempted to leap from the Gunzen across the Seez Valley to the Alpnägelikopf.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Tapp
notes.text: a regional word for a tread, step, or footprint; here it is the mark left on the rock slab beneath the Alpnägelikopf.

notes.label: Pfarrersköchin
notes.text: literally a ‘parish priest's cook’; older folklore sometimes treated a woman serving long in a clerical household with suspicion.

notes.label: Pfaffenkellnerin
notes.text: a disparaging folk label for a clergyman's female servant or housekeeper condemned to wander after death; it reflects the source's anticlerical and gendered stereotype.

notes.label: Hexentapp
notes.text: literally a ‘witch's tread’ or ‘witch's footprint,’ the hoof-shaped impression attributed to the witch's failed leap.

e383b175f25223ea0397d19d438414495911216a.summary: a) Verena Spul from the Zug region is told by the Evil One to make a hailstorm.

notes.label: Gülle
notes.text: Swiss German and Swiss Standard German for liquid manure or farm slurry; Güllen is the inflected historical form in the source, and the spell requires striking it with a rod.

notes.label: Austagen
notes.text: an obscure historical calendrical expression, apparently naming a seasonal period, perhaps days in late summer; its precise dates cannot be established from this text alone.

notes.label: nordiger Hosen
notes.text: a quoted historical name for a type or material of breeches; the exact textile or cut intended by nordig is uncertain, so the phrase is retained rather than modernized speculatively.

notes.label: Zwilchtschoppen
notes.text: a short jacket or smock made of Zwilch, a strong coarse twilled linen or canvas; the clothing marks the apparition as an ordinary rural man.

notes.label: Cüeni
notes.text: a Swiss familiar or diminutive personal name, usually associated with Konrad; here it is the alias used by the demonic figure.

notes.label: Bisswetter
notes.text: a violent, driving spell of bad weather or squall; the exact historical nuance of Biss is uncertain, but the comparison emphasizes rapid, storm-borne flight.

notes.label: Holderzweig
notes.text: an elder branch or twig; Holder is the regional form of Holunder, and elder wood carried protective as well as magical associations in folk practice.

notes.label: Haberturm
notes.text: literally “Oat Tower,” the Lucerne tower named in the record as the customary prison for accused witches; the passage does not describe its architecture or administrative history.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Wannen
notes.text: literally “tubs,” “baskets,” or “winnowing baskets,” but here part of a quoted formula describing coercive examination; the precise torture procedure meant by the historical legal wording is uncertain.

notes.label: versegnet
notes.text: healed or treated through a spoken blessing, charm, or ritual act rather than ordinary medicine; in this case it accompanies lead-casting and repeated Christian prayers.

notes.label: Tschoss
notes.text: the local name for a leg ailment or injury; the historical record gives no symptoms precise enough for a modern diagnosis.

notes.label: Gligg
notes.text: a repeated charm syllable addressed to the wind; its literal meaning, if it had one, is unclear, and its sound and repetition are part of the spell.

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: the haymaking season or hay harvest, an important rural labor period whose exact timing varied with altitude and weather.

notes.label: Hexenvergichten
notes.text: an older legal-historical expression for witches’ confessions or depositions; the accounts summarized here come from prosecutions in which statements could be elicited under torture, as section f explicitly records.

b94118459ef5da5a459f4134a0fe8d788fd6788e.summary: In the Pilatus range, on a straight line between Sarnen and Flühli, stands the Feuerstein like a border guard between Lucerne and Obwalden.

notes.label: Feuerstein
notes.text: literally ‘firestone’ or flint, here the proper name of a mountain in the Pilatus range on the Lucerne–Obwalden boundary.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal livestock pasture, not simply a mountain peak; the household in the tale works on such an upland pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and cheese-making on an Alp.

notes.label: Alpschimmel
notes.text: literally ‘Alpine gray horse,’ the type of horse whose gallop the transformed man is forced to imitate through the air.

notes.label: Hexenzaum
notes.text: literally ‘witch bridle,’ a magical bridle that turns the person wearing it into a horse and transfers control to the witch; the term names both the object and the widespread transformation motif.

notes.label: Hexensabbat
notes.text: the witch-sabbath gathering imagined in early modern demonological folklore; the source presents the Alpine wife flying there with an international company of witches.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Notstall
notes.text: a restraint frame or emergency shoeing stall used to hold a difficult animal while a farrier works; here it contains the transformed witch only until she removes the bridle.

2559e38b3d4125cedbeedc1d2401776f16026ff2.summary: Between the Käserruck and the Gamserruck, the stony Hinterlist rests against the lower slopes at their foot; it is an Obersäss.

notes.label: Obersäss
notes.text: the upper seasonal level of an Alpine grazing settlement, occupied above the lower pasture during part of the summer transhumance.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Hinterrisi-Mandli
notes.text: a dialect spelling variant of Hinterrisi-Männli in the second source passage; it names the same scarlet-coated, fiddle-playing weather spirit.

notes.label: Hinterrisi-Männli
notes.text: literally ‘little man of the Hinterrisi’; the local weather spirit whose cries presage snow on the alpine pastures.

The first source passage calls the stony upper pasture Hinterlist, while the title and second passage use Hinterrisi; both forms are preserved because the source does not explain whether Hinterlist is a variant name or a transcription error.

34f9b4074cbfbaf9095b3afa46d68fed4bb42656.summary: A little dwarf once knocked at a farmer’s door and wanted to hire a cow. But because he smiled so roguishly and gazed out at the world with such blue eyes, the farmer did not entirely trust him.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

5f80e308deea0be5f9db8d0c384e36fe22e0f042.summary: From Naters one sees a high, strongly projecting mountain called Hochgebirg.

notes.label: Brigerzehnden
notes.text: the historical Brig district or Zehnden of Valais, a territorial division broadly comparable to a tithing or district; it is a regional political-geographic term rather than merely the town of Brig.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: zunderobschi
notes.text: Valais dialect meaning upside down or head downward; it specifies the murdered man’s position in the cleft.

notes.label: Abendsitz
notes.text: a customary evening social visit or gathering, often involving household company and courtship; here the murderers spend hours with the young woman before returning, more specific than simply ‘evening.’

notes.label: Hochgebirgsbozo
notes.text: literally the ‘high-mountain Bozo,’ the named haunting associated with the Hochgebirg cleft; Bozo is a Valais word closest to a bogey or frightening spirit, but the story leaves whether the apparition is victim, murderers, or a more general haunting unresolved.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais dialect name closest to a bogey, haunting spirit, or frightening supernatural being; in this title its precise manifestation is ambiguous because the tale describes cries and a flayed-cow apparition without identifying a single form.

e0a924c7a1c9142023a9ad099cb960c89a18cc63.summary: On the Nack, a hilltop near the village of Kirchleerau, traces of a former castle can still be seen.

notes.label: Hoden-Schüerli
notes.text: a hyphenated spelling of Hodenschüerli, the high path and omen-site between the Leerau and Rueder valleys; Schüerli resembles a diminutive of Schür, ‘shed’ or ‘barn,’ but the full place-name is not safely explained by ordinary modern German.

notes.label: Hode-Schüerli
notes.text: another spelling in the source for the Hodenschüerli site; here it lies on the route of the spectral carriage, and the dropped n may reflect dialect pronunciation rather than a different place.

notes.label: Hodenschüerli
notes.text: the traditional name of the high cultivated site near Leerau, used in the title; the source also prints Hoden-Schüerli and Hode-Schüerli, and the name's literal derivation is uncertain.

4cec9c21fedfe2b143afffb2c5a3451673affd62.summary: Near the area called the Bernerland by the village of Tegerfelden stands a farmhouse before which a woman appeared every night and awakened the inhabitants.

notes.label: Haue gä, go ge hacke!
notes.text: Aargau dialect meaning approximately ‘Give me a hoe, to go hoeing!’; the compressed request is nearly all the ghost can say.

notes.label: Wiederbring
notes.text: a shortened dialect promise meaning ‘bring back’ or ‘I will bring it back’; the hoe is indeed returned before morning.

notes.label: Hackengespenst
notes.text: literally the ‘hoeing ghost’ or ‘hoe ghost,’ named for the apparition's nightly request to borrow the farm tool.

e66cf0e9a361b36cc58df734a68b7bb64d58249f.summary: Waltersholz, a height near Kulm, is said once to have been the site of a chapel.

notes.label: Hoggebori
notes.text: the local name given to the chapel-building girl because of her pronounced hump; Hogge appears connected with a humped or bent form, but the precise sense of Bori and the full name’s historical derivation remain uncertain.

f373e0f3775b7b839c0bd097c7edef6caa9d5de4.summary: The “Spinnerin in Hohbach” is on everyone’s lips in Reckingen, Goms. — When children behave badly, the nursemaid is sure to have the evil spinner roam through the village and enter the house, either to prod the wicked, screaming, disobedient little ones with her long Kunkel or even to carry them…

notes.label: Kunkel
notes.text: a distaff, the staff that holds unspun flax or wool while spinning; the frightening woman also uses hers to strike children.

notes.label: Guggermilch
notes.text: literally ‘cuckoo milk,’ a fanciful or regional substance given to abducted children; its actual identity is not explained.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Hohbachspinnerin
notes.text: literally ‘Hohbach spinner woman,’ both the apparition’s name and a mocking label for someone slow to finish spinning or other work.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gellert
notes.text: part of the woman’s old-fashioned bodice or breast garment; the exact regional item is uncertain.

notes.label: Vorpletz
notes.text: a front bodice panel or stomacher forming part of the woman’s old-fashioned dress.

notes.label: Egge
notes.text: a ridge, corner, or projecting part of the Alpine terrain; the precise local landform is not specified.

85c5103622da250dfb3ea0b2238b6baf4ae9f4bf.summary: Anton Biner of Zermatt is also said to have heard the Hohlichtboze. When he was still a boy and drove the cows to pasture on the Mamad Alp one Sunday, he heard the spirit's voice on the opposite mountain, Hohlicht.

notes.label: Hohlichtboze
notes.text: the local name for the lamenting bogey or haunting spirit associated with Mount Hohlicht above Zermatt; the inflected form Hohlichtbozen also appears in the source, and the being can take the shape of a gray ram.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Salz-Riesche
notes.text: a local salt-feeding rack, trough, or chute where livestock lick salt; the ram-shaped spirit is said to descend as far as Z'mut and lick there.

notes.label: Hitzen
notes.text: the sheep's practice of gathering or sheltering in a shaded place during the heat; the wool thief constructs a one-way stone trap at such a place so the animals cannot climb back out.

2a06f6a031d4c547272cd953180c4955ad3bd167.summary: A much-used pack trail once ran through the Hohl. In a little house lived a packhorse driver who, being miserly and hardhearted, withheld well-earned fodder from the horses and also tormented them inhumanely.

notes.label: Hohlross
notes.text: literally the ‘Hohl horse,’ the local name for the punished packhorse driver who haunts the route through the place called the Hohl in equine form; translating it merely as ‘hollow horse’ would mistake the place-name.

acaafb65c8de94d3b4e3d56403bceadf02ff92c3.summary: Between the Wasserfluh and the Egg, two neighboring mountain ridges in the Aarau Jura, one encounters great fissures and clefts in the earth whose depth is immeasurable; they all lead into the underworld.

notes.label: Fünfbätzler
notes.text: a coin valued at five Batzen; denominations and purchasing power varied by polity and period, and the counterfeiter is said to have continued striking these coins in hiding.

notes.label: Schellenwerk
notes.text: a historical place or condition of penal confinement involving chains and compulsory labor; the reference suggests the counterfeiter was returned to the punishment from which he had escaped.

notes.label: Hubel
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a rounded hill, knoll, or raised part of a mountain; here it identifies the upper mass of the Wasserfluh rather than only its visible tip.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face, cliff, or rocky mountain slope in Swiss place-language; the cat reappears at a spring at its foot.

dc7a04452d026c0352f48a6c9711dd0e5e80ad89.summary: A tree is said to have stood in the middle of the village of Menzingen that, when the wind blew, made all the houses beside and near it tremble, for its roots extended that far.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain man,’ a dwarf-like helper whose size allows it to work safely on the dangerous hollow tree before vanishing inside it.

4915c1be39e1c8fdf775234c75bf1fc831457789.summary: Everyone young and old who lives in and around Lucerne knows the ‘heilig Buch,’ or Holy Beech, also called the Cross Beech, on the Meggen road not far from Seeburg.

notes.label: heilig Buch
notes.text: a Lucerne dialect form meaning ‘holy beech,’ the local name of the venerated Cross Beech sheltering a Marian image near Meggen; Buch here means ‘beech,’ not ‘book,’ and the tree’s present form succeeds an older beech.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

07141cdf6369c8c930782aa9c09fee6161e75448.summary: In the church at Kirchberg, a cross is displayed that is said to have floated through the entire church during the service on December 16, 1685.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

086f8618a7d624dec9be27b45047e8fddf93c512.summary: In ancient times there lived a Roman of royal lineage named Ptolemy. One day he went hunting and found a handsome, great stag, which he pursued furiously.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e37fe8d1e7b1beadd14d1dc8ba3559001aaa25bd.summary: In ancient times, so it is told in Vesch (Vex), three holy men came into the land of Valais: Germanus, Romanus, and Sylvius.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

0e33fadd5255951d6780681e9f0ff22f23322c6d.summary: Many, many years ago, things were not wholesome in the little woods at Winkensteig and Pfì, near Muolen.

notes.label: Holz-Nann
notes.text: literally Wood-Nan or Forest-Nan, the regional name of a feared woodland witch who becomes a haunting spirit after death.

notes.label: Steiwörfer
notes.text: literally stone throwers, unseen or supernatural beings that pelt travelers in the forest without hitting them.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Spinnmuggefade
notes.text: literally a spider thread or strand of cobweb; the saying emphasizes a witch's supernatural ability to hang from something impossibly slight.

60f5e9f0cc0e35ca4246e0af2c0d5c18a6e1b9d6.summary: On the shortest route from Lupfig to Wildegg, one comes in the middle of the forest between them to a quarry where a Holzbirnbaum formerly stood and about which many things are still told.

notes.label: Holzbirnbaum
notes.text: literally ‘wood pear tree,’ a wild or hard-wooded pear tree that serves as the haunting’s fixed landmark; the precise botanical variety is not specified.

notes.label: Spinnstuben
notes.text: communal spinning rooms or evening spinning gatherings where work, sociability, and storytelling were combined; they are a traditional transmission setting for such legends.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Felseli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little rock’ or ‘small rocky place’; here it is a local feature from which the hunter descends.

notes.label: Hoperli
notes.text: the local name or byname for the crooked spectral hunter; it is connected in the tale with his cry ‘hop’ and the verb hopen, but a more exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Fluderhosen
notes.text: very broad, loose, billowing trousers; the historical regional garment helps mark Hoperli’s old-fashioned and uncanny appearance.

notes.label: Nebelspalter
notes.text: literally ‘fog-splitter,’ a humorous regional name for a tall or pointed hat; the exact hat style in this account is not further described.

notes.label: hopen
notes.text: the local verb for uttering Hoperli’s characteristic ‘ho, hop’ hunting cry; it means more than ordinary hopping in this ghost-hunt context.

33c1e032fb0ff1d8b589d629afa40a8ce6b3de28.summary: Between Basel-Landschaft and the Aargau Fricktal, the crest of the Homberg runs on for hours.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Hooggema
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect form of ‘Hook Man,’ the water-side bogey said to reach from a stream and drag children in; the story explains his later child-frightening role, while his older supernatural status and precise appearance remain uncertain.

e92c6f62c5cd6b6ec40eb5d2b2aa3ef00283d5f7.summary: A poor family once lived by the Horelauenen.

notes.label: Horelauenen
notes.text: the named avalanche gullies or avalanche-prone slopes near Lenk where the poor family lives.

notes.label: Hofschaft
notes.text: the farm holding and its household economy, which the father neglects for the tavern.

notes.label: Burgbühlhubel
notes.text: a local hillock name combining Burg, ‘castle,’ Bühl, ‘hill,’ and Hubel, ‘knoll,’ where the Devil-like gentleman appears.

notes.label: Ich habe eine, und du hast zwon;
notes.text: dialectal rhyme meaning ‘I have one, and you have two’; zwon is an old masculine form of ‘two,’ and the grim arithmetic contrasts the stolen wife with the father's remaining children.
notes.anchor: Ich habe eine, und du hast zwon;

notes.label: Horelauenenbauer
notes.text: the farmer associated with the Horelauenen; the compound makes his locality part of his identifying name.

8ef171c80aa7933b1a886187a73b9ca45e96fd21.summary: When the two municipalities of Erschmatt and Bratsch wished to build a shared church, a fierce dispute arose between them over where it should be erected.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8e991a295dd49a1810b5655f2afe263674d3c606.summary: On the Bristen, a cowherd came upon the body of a dead horse. He cut off one ear, took it with him, and showed it to the Senn.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; the cowherd brings the golden ear to him.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for a man’s jacket, coat, or work smock; the source lists it as personal property that could have fixed the treasure apparition in place.

c0380403f0d9034539313d4644fed3700d86cddb.summary: Opposite the Swiss village of Wallbach on the Aargau bank of the Rhine lies a Baden village of the same name.

notes.label: Stechehörnlisee
notes.text: a local diminutive lake-name also applied to the area's pointed belemnite fossils; here both the water and the supposedly diabolical fossils share the name, whose literal dialect components are uncertain.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Chrüzischrezis
notes.text: a mocking dialect expression for making the sign of the cross, here including the wife's protective sprinkling with holy water; its playful or distorted form carries ridicule that a plain English ‘blessing’ would lose.

136015ce41790dd9efe46c2783a0ae03f688091f.summary: Near Charmey, between the hamlet of La Tzintre and the stone bridge Iou pon daou vanni (Ie pont du Vanni), lie the marsh meadows called Lé-Bourliandé.

notes.label: Zavudschaou
notes.text: the regional name for this horse-shaped marsh spirit near Charmey; the source gives no secure literal meaning, so the name is retained without conjecture.

16b7190bc0619a1dbff1fc733977f36ba03aa944.summary: a) This is told in the Wigger valley near the Napf. Across the way, in the Bernese village of Trub, they still have a cross on the top of the church tower from the good old Catholic days.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

ccac962f60803658c84bee706881850b2a0406b3.summary: Half an hour above the parish village in Visperterminen, in the charming solitude of the forest, stands a beautiful and much-visited pilgrimage chapel.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: a hut and working building on a high seasonal pasture; the archaeological traces found while preparing its site are offered as evidence for the vanished village.

3a368ed7a11a39ccc810244ae3dd7fcc10ba9b98.summary: Anyone who walks above the Grossstein, about half an hour northeast uphill from Naters toward the wooded heights, will be greatly surprised, upon emerging from the brush, to find himself suddenly at the edge of a yawning abyss.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fa58ddb7c21e9e8f69347f418c9a19f492be4487.summary: This house stands not far below the ruins of Supersaxo's castle. It belonged to the Landeshauptmann and noble knight who became embroiled in such a stubborn war with Cardinal Schinner, disastrous for the country.

notes.label: Landeshauptmann
notes.text: the historical title of the chief secular magistrate and military-political leader of Valais; here it identifies Georg Supersaxo's office and is more specific than an ordinary army captain.

1febddfe186fa9d6a278bf18877133e8f75a4f6f.summary: On an Emmental Bergheimat, a servant girl was milking her master’s cows one evening when a large snake with a golden crown upon its head came in through the open stable door.

notes.label: Bergheimat
notes.text: an Emmental mountain farm or upland home holding, combining the dwelling, agricultural land, and household economy; here it is the isolated setting for cattle and dairy work, though its exact tenure and elevation are not given.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker working with cattle and milk on seasonal pastures; the master suspects a neighboring Senn is visiting the girl, but the role’s exact local duties are not described.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

83607d110512fe85d06933fd1b335bbe43496db4.summary: In Tägerig, not far from Mellingen, a thatched house burned down. A man from the surrounding area bought the firewood from the demolished building to cart it home.

notes.label: Landwied
notes.text: a longitudinal wagon beam or long pole associated with securing and carrying the load; the dialect reply spells it Landwidd and reveals that the house spirit has taken its place at the rear of the fully loaded wagon.

notes.label: Jo, fahret numme zue, i sitze scho ûf der Landwidd hinde.
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Yes, just drive on; I am already sitting at the back of the Landwied,’ the unseen house spirit's dry confirmation that the greedy buyer has carried it away too.
notes.anchor: Jo, fahret numme zue, i sitze scho ûf der Landwidd hinde.

f1343c50c43b68bfad766eacbec0c1c7c6680ef8.summary: A certain Mönli of Davos, formerly a surgeon in the Sprecher Regiment in Austria, lived with his family in Cleven, but came to St.

notes.label: Cleven
notes.text: the historical German name used here for Chiavenna, the town south of Graubünden where Mönli lived with his family; the source gives no further detail about their residence there.

notes.label: Feldscheer
notes.text: an older term for a barber-surgeon or practical military surgeon; in St. Moritz, Mönli earns money by practicing in that capacity.

notes.label: Dochtlicht
notes.text: literally a wick light, an older simple lamp or light whose flame could go out; the source contrasts Mönli’s natural explanation with the uncanny impression that someone blew it out.

notes.label: Guttern
notes.text: a regional word that the source itself glosses as bottles; their exact size and shape are not specified, but their clinking makes the disturbance sound physical.

notes.label: Trucken
notes.text: a regional form for boxes, chests, or similar storage containers; the earlier parallel wording calls them boxes, and the source does not specify their precise construction.

f6e8039302f847d57c5ae788c7f0f9be65e4a8d3.summary: In the Siebenthal, today’s Simmental, there once lived a good, simple man named Jörg.

notes.label: Stampfmühle
notes.text: a water-powered pounding mill used to hull or crush oats, barley, and other material with vertical stampers.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge, often cut by a stream.

notes.label: Estrich
notes.text: in Swiss usage an attic or upper floor space beneath the roof.

notes.label: Fegemännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little sweeping man,’ the diminutive house spirit that cleans and operates the mill.

notes.label: Erdvölklein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth folk,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings to which the mill helper belongs.

notes.label: Hui
notes.text: an exclamation marking sudden, swift movement, like ‘whoosh!’

notes.label: Ig nit meh Gerste stampfe ma (mag);
notes.text: dialect for ‘I no longer want to pound barley,’ the clothed spirit’s declaration that its service has ended.
notes.anchor: Ig nit meh Gerste stampfe ma (mag);

notes.label: ig schön Chleideli ha (habe)
notes.text: dialect for ‘I have pretty little clothes.’

notes.label: ig jitz tanze ga!
notes.text: dialect for ‘now I’m going dancing!’

25856ec8bb39fe7816873be79bcbff47ede8432c.summary: An old craftsman from Schüpfheim in the Entlebuch often worked on the Stör in my parents’ house at Wettingen, and on one occasion he told the following story from his own family:

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: itinerant paid work performed by a craftsperson in the customer’s home rather than in a permanent workshop; the old craftsman visits the family in this capacity.

notes.label: Schorgrube
notes.text: a regional name for the farmyard manure or refuse pit; the grandfather considers making it the place of the goblin’s banishment.

notes.label: Heuete
notes.text: the Swiss German haymaking season or hay harvest; the goblin’s hat signs guide the mowers through its changing weather.

notes.label: Rosskummet
notes.text: a padded horse collar or the harness centered on it; the goblin hides in the old equipment and makes its attached bells clatter.

3d863023a58344bee7bfd28936ee7a0beb553372.summary: A rich farmer had died at Hornussen, and the people had accused him of all manner of evil.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: The Kreuzer was a historical small-denomination coin used in parts of Switzerland and neighboring lands. Its value varied across monetary systems; in some Swiss systems it counted as one quarter of a Batzen. A named coin in a tale is therefore not a modern cent with a fixed national value.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Kreuzer

889f970eba10345b0caef47283c05a985eff6348.summary: Nikodemiten was the name given to members of an Anabaptist sect in Arth. It arose during the stormy period of the Zurich Reformation and was suppressed, yet seems to have continued in secret, for in the year 1655 it again caused considerable unrest.

notes.label: Nikodemiten
notes.text: a polemical historical name for a secretive Anabaptist group in Arth, linked by the source to the biblical Nicodemus's nighttime visit to Jesus.

notes.label: Hummel
notes.text: literally a ‘bumblebee,’ but the precise object supposedly received in the group's Communion is unclear; the account belongs to hostile folk rumor about a persecuted religious minority and should not be treated as reliable ritual history.

notes.label: Hummelhof
notes.text: literally the ‘Hummel farm’ or ‘Hummel homestead,’ the surviving place-name associated with the alleged nighttime meetings.

aa96dc21038687efa7ca7fe9f50cf5e4568ac246.summary: In the forest below Casella, on the Grossberg at Flums, an unfathomably deep passage begins among the red rocks and runs westward toward the Tobel.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge in Swiss and southern German usage; the subterranean passage runs toward it.

notes.label: Hundloch
notes.text: literally ‘dog hole,’ the local cave or passage where a fiery dog guards treasure; Loch can mean a hole, cave, or confined opening.

b0a5b6ccab4c311d9d538ff82f95f6d4abe9001d.summary: In the Hagenau near Ganterschwil there was a so-called Hungerbrünneli that ordinarily stood dry and carried water only when a time of dearth was approaching.

notes.label: Hungerbrünneli
notes.text: literally ‘little hunger spring,’ a diminutive name for an intermittent spring believed to foretell dearth or famine; the commentary offers wet years and glacier-fed periodic flow as a natural explanation.

notes.label: Hungerbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘hunger spring’ or ‘famine well,’ the non-diminutive name used for the corresponding site at Rickenbach.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: plural of Alp, the high-elevation summer pastures and mountain-farming areas where glacier-fed periodic springs were observed.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Hungsdürscht
notes.text: a local name probably related to a rushing host or pack of hounds in the Wild Hunt; the exact etymology is uncertain.

notes.label: Vom Hungsdürscht und vom Vogeldürscht
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of the Hungsdürscht and the Vogeldürscht,’ two named nocturnal Wild Hunt phenomena.

notes.label: Vogeldürscht
notes.text: a local name for a bird-associated or airborne Wild Hunt manifestation, heard here as joyful massed birdsong.

notes.label: Chaserebärg
notes.text: literally ‘cheese-dairy mountain’ or a mountain associated with a Chasere, a cheese dairy; it is the local route toward the Altburg.

2052e608e3855188f537cad08f8577a26c04f403.summary: The Lirihanst is a tract of vineyard and woodland situated below Birmenstorf on the Brugg road.

notes.label: Störe
notes.text: the traditional itinerant work arrangement in which a craftsperson traveled to a household or farm to perform work on site, often receiving board as part of the engagement; the parents are returning from such work at Reuss, though the trade involved is not identified.

cee48c6a92f6e94b2b75b511e05975e2a44200a3.summary: In front of Ramstein Castle in Basel-Landschaft stands a Sennenhaus; thirty years ago, an older one stood there, but it was demolished and its rotten timbers used for burning lime.

notes.label: Sennenhaus
notes.text: a house or working dwelling for a Senn, an Alpine dairyman or cattle herder; the cursed timber is reused in the replacement building.

notes.label: Alle guten Geister!
notes.text: literally ‘all good spirits,’ an abbreviated protective exclamation invoking benevolent spirits or God's protection; here the prayer rejects the apparitions' request and drives them back into the beam.

notes.label: Angriff
notes.text: literally ‘attack,’ the local name given to the sudden livestock epidemic; the five-finger marks make the disease seem like a supernatural assault.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

d044fefa072e8ae9d7818efe8b9d35d2a2461feb.summary: ‘My sister-in-law's grandmother,’ relates a man from Fricktal, ‘was harvesting in the fields between Münchwilen and Eiken and was supposed to fetch water for the reapers from the Bruchmattbrunnen in the Bulsteltal.

notes.label: Bruchmattbrunnen
notes.text: literally the ‘Bruchmatte spring’ or fountain, a named rural water source from which the girl fetches water; Bruch and Matte may refer to marshy meadowland, but the exact place-name history is uncertain.

notes.label: Bulsteltal
notes.text: the recorded name of the valley containing the Bruchmattbrunnen; its precise dialect derivation is not explained in the source.

02a7675d9517fad0dc76b2f579cc3c36158123e4.summary: The Zwingherren who formerly inhabited Trostburg Castle in the Kulm Valley had built a separate huntsman’s lodge in the castle moat, and it still stands today.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: literally ‘coercive lords’ and closest here to the castle’s feudal lords; in Swiss legendary usage the word can emphasize oppressive seigneurial power, though this passage does not say whether it is a formal title or a hostile characterization.

821ab8678e3be81e1ac7f4dda0a312eb20ab0be4.summary: A hunter, J. M. of Klosters, had the habit of frequently using the expression “I! dass dich die Hexen ritten!” in conversation.

notes.label: I! dass dich die Hexen ritten!
notes.text: a regional exclamation and curse, roughly “Ah! May the witches ride you!”; the hunter uses it habitually without expecting the words to turn against him.
notes.anchor: I! dass dich die Hexen ritten!

notes.label: Ii, dass dich die Hexen ritten!
notes.text: the foxes’ lengthened echo of the hunter’s habitual curse, again meaning approximately “Ah! May the witches ride you!”
notes.anchor: Ii, dass dich die Hexen ritten!

949fe07b0f6442982a81985de29ad6f4565d98d4.summary: A hunter frequently roamed the Salbytenalp, and almost every time he met a spirit: an old man with a silver-white beard flowing to the ground, seated upon a rock slab.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its working landscape, not merely a mountain; Salbytenalp is the named place where the hunter repeatedly meets the penitent spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

5c30597cff7f782f5b76f97d178390abc489e765.summary: The highest mountain in the Fricktal is the Schaumberg. A hunter can often be seen on this mountain, though always only at night at twelve or one o’clock.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

0ae408ef091bbc9a4fb806a564701fe503b2c47d.summary: A man from Kulm was tying bundles of brushwood below the village near the forest.

notes.text: The source leaves Blas du mir.......! deliberately incomplete; it appears to begin a coarse or contemptuous dismissal, and the ellipsis is preserved.

fcdadb5eac6a305860633db79f8c894565edf257.summary: At Steg in St. Niklaus, it is said, there lived in the previous century a widow named Maria Biner who crossed the Vispenbrücke by the Junghöhe every morning to tend her livestock.

notes.label: Vispenbrücke
notes.text: the bridge over the Vispa watercourse near St. Niklaus; Brücke means ‘bridge,’ while Vispe is the local river name.

notes.label: Junghöhe
notes.text: the local height or rise beside the bridge on Maria Biner's daily route; Höhe means ‘height’ or ‘upland.’

notes.label: Lerchj an Jungen
notes.text: the local field or place-name where Jost Blatter dies; its exact modern identification and literal dialect sense are uncertain.

149e4e7ca7bb4e78a970aa77fd59443a6eb0d47f.summary: The Härdlifuhrmann roams through the Siggental at night and cracks his whip.

notes.label: Härdlifuhrmann
notes.text: the local name of this nocturnal carter spirit; Fuhrmann means ‘carter’ or ‘wagoner,’ while the source does not explain the precise local sense of Härdli.

ed0f40745716becf2446c49fbb63f2b13adf337a.summary: Below the Gipf, a quarter of the village in the municipality of Frick, lives the Hölenthier, where it obstructs many people wishing to cross the Ebnat field.

notes.label: Hölenthier
notes.text: the older spelling of ‘Höle animal,’ a spectral creature haunting the sunken road below Gipf; it appears as a giant-eyed dog, tall man, burden-spirit, or priest.

notes.label: Höle
notes.text: the local name of the hollow or sunken cart road; the source explicitly explains it as a Hohlweg.

notes.label: Morgenläuten
notes.text: the morning ringing of church bells; crossing the haunted hollow before this protective daily signal is dangerous.

notes.label: Fraufastenkind
notes.text: a person born during the Ember Days and therefore believed to possess second sight; Hegel's daughter can repeatedly see the spectral dog.

notes.label: Helgenstöckli
notes.text: a diminutive wayside holy-image shrine or devotional cross; from this landmark, the spirit rides upon travelers' backs.

9bc063dd90713bbbe06e124d404f05f748f0a94b.summary: In the year 1156, a Lord Diebold ruled at Strättlingen. His wife was Lady Anna, who bore him three sons named Richard, Otto, and Marquard.

notes.label: Kilchherr
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Kirchherr, the parish priest or cleric responsible for a church; he warns Diebold about violating the church's rights.

notes.label: Bannacker
notes.text: literally a ‘ban field,’ the named tract associated with protected, restricted, or jurisdictional land; the source identifies it as the place of Diebold's death but does not explain the exact legal ban.

notes.label: Höllenmoos
notes.text: literally ‘hell marsh,’ the wetland said to receive Diebold's visible departing soul and thereafter be haunted by his spirit.

notes.label: Bruderhaus
notes.text: literally ‘brothers' house,’ a small religious dwelling or hermitage; the Pope orders one erected by the haunted marsh as a perpetual memorial, though the source does not specify its community.

50c4a8b7ecbc79a10df9d728f5d7fb3bd0166224.summary: Old people still remember that the imposing Hüfi Glacier at the head of the Maderanertal filled the ground known as Gries, which extends westward at its foot for about half an hour’s walk.

notes.label: Bruderklausenweissagung
notes.text: literally ‘Brother Klaus prophecy,’ a Swiss prophetic tradition associated with Niklaus von Flüe, the 15th-century hermit and patron saint known as Brother Klaus; the story does not state which particular prophecy is intended.

bc3fe9efe351028ad51f25ffa38af040c697621b.summary: A pretty wooded hill between Holziken and Schöftland is called the Hügeli on the side where it meets the Surenbach.

notes.label: Hügeli
notes.text: literally ‘little hill,’ the local name of the wooded rise between Holziken and Schöftland.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a coarse Alpine conglomerate whose embedded rounded stones resemble nail heads; its boulders are interpreted as the castle's shattered foundations.

notes.label: Hügeligrotte
notes.text: the named Hügeli grotto, a low cave among Nagelfluh blocks where the maiden, dog, and treasure are said to dwell.

notes.label: Schlossbann
notes.text: the castle's dependent jurisdiction or estate territory; the phrase means Schöftland once fell under the castle's authority, not under a magical spell.

notes.label: Taufpathin
notes.text: the source's historical spelling of Taufpatin, a female baptismal sponsor or godmother expected to accompany the child to church.

notes.label: Bändler-Kirchweg
notes.text: the named church path used by local worshipers; it crosses the Hügeligraben where the maiden appears.

notes.label: Hügeligraben
notes.text: the Hügeli ravine or drainage channel crossed by the church-path footbridge.

notes.label: Maddänneli
notes.text: a local diminutive plant-name for the red primrose or cowslip that blooms beside the treasure only once in a century.

notes.label: Hügelimaidli
notes.text: Swiss German for the ‘little Hügeli maiden,’ the cursed noblewoman attached to the hill and cave at Holziken; Maidli is a diminutive for a girl or maiden.

bf1e5255c7b0353aed68b6726b50314eaba7a510.summary: More than fifty years ago, during haymaking season, a man from Böbikon in the district of Zurzach went into the forest to fetch wood.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-men,’ the underground dwarf-like beings of German-speaking Swiss folklore; here the hidden mine and metallic treasure make the weaver fear their domain, while the term does not specify a single fixed creature type.

b024aa31027f893ad4ee2300067362c4f24a8386.summary: An old little mother had a beautiful daughter. Because the mother’s weary limbs no longer allowed her to sit at the distaff and spin thread, she told her daughter to do it.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Spinnermann
notes.text: literally ‘spinning man,’ the mysterious itinerant spinner’s repeated self-description in his street call and fire-side song; he is ultimately revealed as Beelzebub.

notes.label: Krampf
notes.text: an unclear source word paired with Hanf for rhyme in the Spinnermann’s call; it may suggest toil, trouble, or strain, but no narrower unsupported meaning is imposed.

notes.label: Scheckenhäuser
notes.text: the source form for the empty shells the woman ties to her back, contextually snail shells, likely related to standard German Schneckenhäuser; the unusual spelling is preserved because its exact status as dialect or print error is uncertain.

3d5b36ea6775590bf50279738839bddeab51e162.summary: At the time of the Reformation, the iconoclasm also swept across our region.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Heiligenhüsli
notes.text: literally ‘little saints’ house’ in Swiss German, a small wayside shrine or devotional shelter for a sacred image; ‘wayside shrine’ is close, but its precise regional form and size could vary.

69923c3d7b22a612ce9d4cd4d52065d41256d74b.summary: When the knights of Reinach had their tower shot down, they moved from the mountain into the village and built themselves a house that differed from the other farmhouses only in having a squat spiral-stair tower.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f8e7c636eaffb417cc5f8a77efba5d42f1f85172.summary: At the much-visited pilgrimage chapel in Chandolin-Savièse above Sion, observers are surprised by the view into the long, wildly beautiful Sanetsch Valley.

notes.label: Herbstmonat
notes.text: an old German and Swiss month-name, literally ‘autumn month,’ normally meaning September; here it dates Joseph Bridy's fatal fall to September 17, 1869.

notes.label: Bildhäuslein
notes.text: literally a ‘little image house,’ a small wayside shrine or devotional niche; here it stands at the dangerous bridge in accordance with an Upper Valais custom.

notes.label: Neue-Brücke
notes.text: German for ‘new bridge,’ paired here with the French Pont Neuf as the old bridge's enduring proper name; the narrator jokes that its age makes the name inaccurate.

notes.label: Kabiskopf
notes.text: Swiss German for a head of cabbage; here it counts as the first ‘head’ sent across the devil's bridge in a trick based on the bargain's wording.

notes.label: Geiss
notes.text: Swiss German for a female goat; here the hungry animal follows the cabbage and becomes the second head crossing the bridge.

f82e1e7ce0dc266be883dc6403db92dc2a181315.summary: At the foot of the Simplon mountain, on a wild alp where the old pack road formerly passed through the Ganter valley, there stood many years ago an inn called “zur Tavernen.” Perhaps it too wished to grow rich too quickly; therefore a fate similar to that of many an inn today befell it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: zur Tavernen
notes.text: the inn’s name, approximately ‘at the tavern,’ retaining an older regional form.

notes.label: Tempertagen
notes.text: Ember Days, quarterly fast and prayer days in the church calendar that folklore often treats as spiritually charged.

notes.label: Johannili
notes.text: the diminutive personal name ‘little Johanna’ in the four-line Valais German cry, which says approximately, ‘I am called little Johanna; I was hostess at the tavern, gave out water for wine, and now must be in the cold waters’; the first line’s final fi is obscure in the printed dialect.

ce6bb80fe55cde76d47eea4c90db85b09d93f781.summary: In Boscha, a hamlet belonging to Steinsberg but situated nearer Guarda, there stood a little inn where members of a band of robbers often gathered for consultations and devised their sinful plans.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the bench built beside or around a masonry stove, a warm place for sitting or sleeping in a traditional household; the unrecognized son pretends to sleep there.

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for present-day Klosters in Graubünden.

notes.label: Schnaps
notes.text: a strong distilled spirit; the traveler has brought some and expects to eat bread with it.

notes.label: Trucke
notes.text: a regional word for a drawer or box-like compartment; the source explicitly identifies it as the table drawer where bread was customarily kept.

fe14d91017ac17af38940bf146b0cebb5f256baa.summary: At the end of the previous century, several farmers from the upper Fricktal conceived the notion that the highest Jura mountain in their area, the Strichen near Oberhof, must contain gold at its core.

notes.label: Bergknappe
notes.text: a trained mine worker or miner; in the tale the unfamiliar Bergknappe possesses uncannily exact knowledge of the mountain's hidden structure.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings associated with mines, buried wealth, and the dangers beneath Alpine and Jura landscapes.

24079bde2735e657eb4d9136fe6053ce885bd29f.summary: In the Bernese district of Oberhasli, between Meiringen and Guttannen, rises a sheer, steep rock called the Zuben.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: an Alpine pack-animal driver and carrier who transported goods across mountain routes, usually with mules; the condemned driver's invisible caravan preserves the sounds of a historical pack train.

20084be511d9db987075d47a736ff8bc2459dee3.summary: Another man heard his name called three times and stepped outside the hut. There he heard the same call, but from a great distance.

notes.label: Gott gsegn' es
notes.text: a dialect table blessing meaning ‘may God bless it,’ spoken over food before eating; here the hunter’s ordinary Christian formula breaks the supernatural feast and makes the entire company vanish.

notes.label: Irrchrut
notes.text: literally ‘wandering herb’ or ‘straying weed’ in Swiss German, a folkloric plant that makes anyone who steps on it lose the path and walk in circles; the story leaves its botanical identity wholly uncertain.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

5eb6d0b0de3e05a4379e0f66b037f91b1bf454c6.summary: North of the hamlet of Wintersberg lies a large forest that yields a rich harvest of berries of every kind in summer.

notes.label: Irrkraut
notes.text: literally ‘straying herb’ or ‘bewildering plant,’ a folkloric plant that makes anyone who steps on it lose the way; its botanical identity is deliberately unknown in the account.

95a7b297822eaee944c1245b29803f9c99559382.summary: In the Burghalde, an old hillside suburb of Lenzburg, there stood until a few years ago an old wagon shed used jointly by several people.

notes.label: Irrlicht
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering/deceiving light,’ ordinarily a will-o'-the-wisp or ghost light; this local account gives it the bodily form of a fiery man who punishes the boy.

800fdcdb31c821da292bdc809f3564d2797d01bb.summary: One evening, a woman had fetched flour from the mill at Erlinsbach and had to return to her house on the mountain by way of the Lorenzobad.

notes.label: Alle guten Geister loben rc
notes.text: the protective invocation printed in abbreviated form, approximately ‘All good spirits praise the King of Heaven’; the source itself explains rc as Latin Regem caeli, while the exact full traditional formula is not supplied.

notes.label: Irrlicht
notes.text: a will-o'-the-wisp understood in folklore as a wandering fiery spirit rather than only a natural marsh light; this one burdens and sickens the traveler.

cc3724d34871471b9679399b1a9ac4e7eea43b68.summary: The Jauchzerbotzen is said often to have been heard in the mountains of Naters.

notes.label: Jauchzerbotzen
notes.text: the inflected or compounded form used in the prose for the same Jauchzer-Botze; the ending marks grammatical usage, not a second creature.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: a hut on a high seasonal pasture, used by herders, workers, or hunters; the first victim answers the spirit from such a mountain shelter.

notes.label: Gevattermann
notes.text: a man connected through godparenthood or a close ritual-familial bond, extended here to the hunter's trusted companion; ordinary ‘friend’ would lose that relationship.

notes.label: Bächalpe
notes.text: the Bäch Alpine pasture, where the hunters arrange to meet; Alpe denotes a seasonal pastoral estate rather than merely a mountain.

notes.label: Kessiturn
notes.text: the pivot or crane used to swing a cauldron over a hearth, here a surviving fixture in the old rock hut; the exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Laggers Balme
notes.text: ‘Lagger's rock shelter,’ from Balm, an overhang, cave, or shallow rock recess; the old hunting shelter bears Martin Lagger's name.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Furge
notes.text: a high pass, saddle, or notch in the mountains; the uncanny call comes from that terrain beyond the Aletsch Glacier.

notes.label: Vorsteher
notes.text: a local head, overseer, or community official; the spirit identifies itself by this civic office but does not specify its exact jurisdiction.

notes.label: Kühschafe
notes.text: literally ‘cow sheep,’ household sheep grazed with the cows rather than kept in a separate flock; the source itself explains the practice and condemns the property damage they caused.

notes.label: Jauchzer-Botze
notes.text: literally a ‘jubilant-call bogey’ or ‘whooping spirit,’ named for its nighttime Jauchzer; answering its call is the dangerous breach of mountain custom.

5efbfa5003987302dc8fbea3944e9a2b9bba8507.summary: On the Naters mountain, below the beautiful Saint Anthony’s Forest, is a hamlet called Im Hasli.

notes.label: g’juzot
notes.text: Valais dialect for having given a high jubilant whoop or yodel-like cry; the source supplies it as the local wording for the apparition’s call.

notes.label: Chi
notes.text: a local Valais terrain term or place designation into which the apparition returns; its precise topographical sense is uncertain from this passage.

notes.label: Quatembertage
notes.text: the Ember Days, quarterly sets of fasting and prayer days in the Christian calendar; in Alpine folklore they are also liminal times when apparitions may be encountered.

notes.label: Jauchzerin
notes.text: literally a female whooper or yodel-like caller; here it names the white-clad apparition heard giving high calls on prescribed nights, not an ordinary singer.

1b0debb86ce64b036143a83d29ecc10743e7ca37.summary: At night, the Jonentier comes up from the Canton of Zurich, following the Jonenbach into the Freienamt.

notes.label: Jonentier
notes.text: literally the “Jonen animal,” a local monstrous apparition named for the Jonenbach; Tier here means a supernatural beast rather than an ordinary animal.

notes.label: Freienamt
notes.text: the historical and regional name for an area of Aargau formerly organized as the Free Bailiwicks; it is a place-name and does not simply mean a modern “free office.”

83b4c790a13cddb2f2e56e3eb925bc101f49cd57.summary: Many years ago there lived on Schattenhalb a Kesselflicker who, despite his best efforts, could no longer keep his family going because there was no work.

notes.label: Schattenhalb
notes.text: literally the shaded half or side, a local expression for the less sunlit side of the Valais valley where the tinker lives.

notes.label: Kesselflicker
notes.text: an itinerant mender of kettles, pots, and other metal vessels whose wares and tools form his heavy burden.

notes.label: Schattseite
notes.text: literally “shaded side,” the valley side where the Kesselflicker has already peddled through every village.

notes.label: Sonnseite
notes.text: literally “sunny side,” the opposite valley slope to which he crosses over the Rhone.

notes.label: Männchen
notes.text: literally “little man,” here the ancient, uncanny sole survivor who reveals the road to paradise.

notes.label: Klimpergeschirr
notes.text: literally clinking or jangling vessels, the old man's dismissive name for the tinker's metal wares.

notes.label: Kessler
notes.text: a shortened occupational form for the kettle-mender or tinker, used interchangeably with Kesselflicker in the story.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; the old man leads the Kessler onto a pointed one above the valley.

notes.label: Geschirrstecken
notes.text: the staff or carrying stick associated with the tinker's bundle of vessels, later used to keep his balance on the aerial path.

notes.label: Bergschritt
notes.text: the long, deliberate stride of someone accustomed to mountain travel.

notes.label: fürbass
notes.text: an archaic word meaning onward or farther ahead; the tinker keeps moving toward the light despite the abyss.

notes.label: Dom der ewigen Freude
notes.text: literally “Cathedral of Eternal Joy,” the inscription above the portal of the heavenly church.

notes.label: SZ (Sit Zion)
notes.text: the unexplained letters and parenthetical Latin-looking expansion printed on the heavenly guards' golden collars; both are retained without emendation.

notes.label: Werkzeugräf
notes.text: a framed carrying pack or back-rack for the tinker's tools and metalware, which he must take inside with him.

notes.label: Seligen
notes.text: the blessed souls in heaven who sing and offer praise in the choir.

notes.label: Vaterunser
