notes.text: the Lord's Prayer; the Kessler prays it so devoutly that he forgets to request his eternal dwelling.

48fe0b60f99b17ff346eed04e0088b327b7979b1.summary: Beyond the Gotthard Mountains, close to the tunnel, lies the little village of Eriels, or Airolo, the first village in Switzerland’s Leventina valley where Italian is spoken.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

46c3d0bdf86419dcf45930ece8f96e118b189360.summary: On the small vineyard hill called Klosterreben, a few minutes from the little Gnadenthal convent, stands a watchman’s hut used by the field guards in autumn.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c179ec7acf63aba95bc028e1638696ed2e80b198.summary: In the long wood near Langrüti at Hünenberg, canton of Zug, a clear, cold water called the Maiden's Spring wells up.

notes.label: Jungfernbrünnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little maidens' spring,’ an affectionate diminutive for the local spring at Hünenberg; here its water memorializes young women killed by a tyrant, giving ‘maiden’ both a descriptive and commemorative force.

8067dffb22934ff63bcfc87da15c4eb7e03a31df.summary: The Kahlofen Bauer is the fiery man who appears between Endingen and Würelingen upon a piece of land called Kahlofen.

notes.label: Kahlofen Bauer
notes.text: literally the ‘Kahlofen farmer,’ the local name for the fiery boundary-haunting spirit tied to the plot called Kahlofen; Bauer identifies his rural human role, while his punishment confines him to the land whose markers he moved.

924439c3bae35fd30271f9230586005dc4eb1fb0.summary: Only a few years ago, in the so-called Kapellentobel, a Pfaffenkellnerin wearing iron shoes is said to have been compelled to wander from the Kalktaren up to the Bühlbrücke.

notes.label: Kapellentobel
notes.text: literally ‘chapel ravine,’ the local gorge or steep gully through which the condemned figure wanders.

notes.label: Pfaffenkellnerin
notes.text: literally a ‘cleric's or priest's cellar-woman,’ apparently a female servant associated with a priestly household; the source gives no reason for her punishment or fuller account of her role.

notes.label: Kalktaren
notes.text: the local place-name for the area containing the lime kiln; its exact derivation is not explained.

notes.label: Kalkofen
notes.text: a lime kiln in which limestone is burned to produce quicklime; entering it destroys the facility but releases the wandering figure.

notes.label: Kalkbrenner
notes.text: the lime burner or kiln worker responsible for firing and operating the Kalkofen.

71d3e67d00c0fbffa2d4f1c5c91cc841664d8327.summary: Once, many centuries ago, there was a very evil time. In those unhappy days of religious wars, the Eidgenossen had become completely divided.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘companions bound by oath,’ the historic Swiss confederates; the word’s sense of personal covenant makes the fighters’ rediscovered friendship central to the story.

notes.label: fünf Orte
notes.text: literally the ‘five places,’ the Catholic cantons Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, and Zug acting together in the conflict.

notes.label: Hirthemd
notes.text: literally ‘herdsman’s shirt,’ the traditional work shirt worn here by the sturdy men from the mountain lands.

notes.label: Blechhut
notes.text: literally ‘sheet-metal hat,’ a simple metal helmet worn by the herders as soldiers; the source contrasts martial equipment with the domestic meal that follows.

notes.label: Milchmutte
notes.text: a large regional milk vessel placed directly on the border so both sides can eat from it without formally crossing into enemy territory.

notes.label: Schnappsäcke
notes.text: food or provision bags carried by the Zurich men; despite the modern association of Schnaps with liquor, the context here is the bread they bring to the meal.

notes.label: Eigenbrot
notes.text: substantial home-produced bread, literally ‘own bread,’ cut by the Zurich men into the Catholics’ milk.

notes.label: Milchgumpe
notes.text: a regional term for the deep pool or bowlful of milk in the Mutte, covered here by a golden layer of cream; the exact vessel distinction from Milchmutte is not fully explained.

notes.label: Blyb uf dym Erdrych!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Stay on your own soil!’; shouted while rapping spoons that cross the border, it turns territorial conflict into playful table discipline.

notes.label: Kappeler Milchsuppe
notes.text: literally ‘Kappel milk soup,’ the shared border meal of milk from the Catholic mountain cantons and bread from Reformed Zurich that symbolizes enduring confederate fellowship during religious conflict.

e32ce3d77f2f56647781c7caa510ad345d52c80d.summary: At the old wayside shrine near Saint Sebastian’s chapel, a ghostly dog appears at night and makes horses shy or prevents them from going farther.

notes.label: Kalbeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small or young calf; despite the diminutive, the comparison emphasizes the ghost dog’s unusually large size.

notes.label: Kappelihund
notes.text: literally ‘little-chapel dog,’ the spectral dog associated with the wayside shrine and nearby chapel; the source does not say whether Kap(p)eli names one specific structure or a type.

8b483b8e90bf1fd97bb356da63ed9419d1f3c540.summary: The Kastläne were once the foremost dignitaries in a community and, through old habit, therefore still enjoy considerable—if not the greatest—esteem among the people as public officials, although under newer law they have been overtaken by the “president” and no longer even belong to the municipal council.

notes.label: Kastläne
notes.text: the German plural of Kastlan, historical Valais castellans or chief local magistrates; the plural is retained in the institutional introduction.

notes.label: Landshauptmann
notes.text: literally ‘captain of the land,’ a senior territorial or cantonal military-civic office; it belongs to the source's list of older titles that sounded more distinctive than president.

notes.label: Rottenmeister
notes.text: the leader of a Rotte, historically a local territorial, work, or militia division; the precise duties varied, so the title is retained rather than forced into one modern office.

notes.label: Bannerherr
notes.text: literally ‘banner lord,’ a military-civic dignitary entrusted with a community's banner and the authority associated with it.

notes.label: Grosskastlan
notes.text: ‘grand castellan,’ a senior castellan or district judicial officer above an ordinary Kastlan in older Valais administration.

notes.label: Meier
notes.text: a historical estate or community administrator who could also exercise judicial authority; it does not map cleanly to the modern English word mayor.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional Swiss local chief magistrate or community head; its powers differed by place and period.

notes.label: Seckelmeister
notes.text: literally ‘purse-master,’ the community treasurer responsible for public funds.

notes.label: Gewaltshaber
notes.text: an authorized representative or procurator exercising delegated civic or legal authority; its exact local portfolio could vary.

notes.label: Kirchmeier
notes.text: a churchwarden or parish-property administrator responsible for the church's temporal affairs.

notes.label: Armenvater
notes.text: literally ‘father of the poor,’ an official overseeing communal poor relief.

notes.label: Alpenvogt
notes.text: an officer supervising a community's Alp, meaning its shared high-mountain pasture and associated rights.

notes.label: Schottenteiler
notes.text: literally ‘whey-divider’; a local alpine-dairy official who apportioned whey or other dairy shares among rights holders, though the exact Valais duties are not specified here.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a local court or community officer and public messenger; here he formally announces that the family council is canceled.

notes.label: Kastlan
notes.text: a historical Valais castellan or chief local magistrate, formerly the community's leading judicial and civic dignitary; the story contrasts the office's lingering prestige with the newer municipal president.

notes.label: Herr Kastlan
notes.text: the honorific ‘Mr. Kastlan,’ emphasizing that the night robber was the prestigious magistrate himself.

c9a54d227e1ebb81a045c9ebd4b7d9acb0d43669.summary: On the left bank of the valley stream, between Helikon and Zuzgen, rises the Häutig, a mountain whose upper height is a fine field of crops.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, often associated with caves, hidden households, and helpful work; here they harvest, plow, and lend tableware, but the term does not establish their literal size.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a historical municipal or communal warden, especially a keeper of woodland or other land under a local Bann; here he functions as a forest warden who hears Katharina underground.

notes.label: Buchhalde
notes.text: the local slope-name meaning approximately “beech-covered hillside”; it identifies the wooded place of the cave rather than a separate supernatural being.

abd1066497cb91b44f09d4366029e41f64558b21.summary: On a summer evening, a knight rode through a forest. In its deepest thicket, he dismounted to rest beside a rushing spring.

notes.label: Zauberwurzel
notes.text: literally ‘magic root,’ the plant growing beneath the middle of three golden crosses that reverses the court's enchantment; the story does not identify a botanical species.

notes.label: Katzenschloss
notes.text: literally ‘cat castle,’ the enchanted palace whose prince, princess, and court have all been transformed into cats.

328989e600b8cc7db95291935b2fc1603119e970.summary: Jaggli Lander, the fahrender Schüler, revealed that a golden Kegelries with two golden balls was hidden in the ruins of Attinghausen Castle.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a wandering scholar or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning, treasure knowledge, and magic; here Jaggli Lander knows where the guarded treasure lies.

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a regional name for a complete set or arrangement of skittles or ninepins; this supernatural treasure is made of gold and accompanied by two golden balls, though the source does not specify the set's exact form or number of pins.

f2935c8b91af36344fb7b066fccceaf66fb6061f.summary: above Sisikon is said in ancient times to have been the parish church for Römerstalden, Morschach, and Sisikon; according to others, however, it was founded in fulfillment of a vow, around the 18th–19th century, by a man from Schwyz who had served as a mercenary in France.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

3932d9970d0d75133bb88ee41e47e2783d16a7c2.summary: The Ketteler, a ghost with a clanking cow chain, travels from the Fäsch along the old alpine-pasture road over the Crappa, straight through the stable in the Dirsch, through the woodshed between the house and barn at Fadella, through the Pfaffenacker, over Muttli, Brünisberg, Zusli, Bülz, and…

notes.label: Ketteler
notes.text: the regional name of a chain-rattling cattle ghost condemned to roam the old alpine route; it is related to Kette, ‘chain,’ but functions as a specific local folkloric identity, and the account does not clarify whether the name predates the cattle thief’s punishment.

bb34f80ecd058537ebb914a7cd8501b0d983bb14.summary: Once there was a journeyman shoemaker whom the whole village called an eccentric.

notes.label: Vesperglocke
notes.text: the evening prayer or vespers bell; its regular ringing marks the journeyman's departure for his solitary walks.

notes.label: Mit Vergunst
notes.text: an old deferential formula meaning roughly ‘with your permission’ or ‘begging your pardon,’ used before the journeyman answers the crowned maiden.

notes.label: im Geding
notes.text: in a contracted hiring or service arrangement; the journeyman says he is employed by the village cobbler rather than established on his own.

notes.label: Stöckchen
notes.text: literally ‘little posts,’ the raised heels of the maiden's shoes, here specified in red.

notes.label: Laschen
notes.text: the shoe tongues, flaps, or tabs over the instep, also to be made red.

notes.label: Vorgeschühe
notes.text: the front or forepart of the shoes; the maiden first requires it to remain unpolished and later summons him back to polish it.

notes.label: Drangeld
notes.text: earnest money or a deposit paid to bind an agreement, here the first gold coin given for the work.

notes.label: Rötelbürste
notes.text: a shoemaker's brush associated with red coloring or red chalk, brought to finish the red-accented shoes.

notes.label: Amtmann
notes.text: an administrative and judicial official or bailiff; he enforces the journeyman's debts and imprisonment.

notes.label: setzte ihn an den Schatten
notes.text: literally ‘put him in the shade,’ a regional or older euphemism for putting someone under confinement or in prison.

d46fcd08deec14c79452994dcd61758817e45229.summary: Above Untervaz, in the gorge of the Cosenz stream, lie the ruins of Rappenstein Castle.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alpine term for a steep, narrow ravine or stream gorge, more specific than an ordinary valley.

notes.label: Fährli-Müetter
notes.text: a dialect compound for a mother sow; the pregnant pig is presented as an animal form of the female treasure guardian.

notes.label: i der Schnorra
notes.text: a dialect expression meaning ‘in the snout’; the sow carries the treasure guardian's large bunch of keys in her mouth or snout.

notes.label: was gisch, was häsch
notes.text: a dialect idiom for leaving with extreme speed or urgency; Jecklin explicitly glosses it as ‘in the greatest haste.’

8fd62cc53a8b2c421d46850b15ebe937f523f37f.summary: Captain Kienberg went to Venice and rendered the lagoon city excellent service in the war against the Turks.

notes.label: Wiler
notes.text: people or citizens of Wil in the canton of St. Gallen; here the demonym marks communal pride in Captain Kienberg.

notes.label: Kienberger-Kette
notes.text: literally ‘Kienberg chain,’ the golden military honor associated with Captain Kienberg and later given to the church for its monstrance.

45e8624a917a590b6884d62968862d3d27042476.summary: Several hundred years ago, the little village of Kienholz between Brienz and Meiringen was destroyed by a landslide and partly swept into Lake Brienz.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ffd3592d64d5d96249c87dbab53abdc97365d9c7.summary: Two Erdmännchen once came to a woman reputed to be an experienced Kindsmutter and urgently begged her to accompany them, for one of their females lay at home in labor.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings who dwell inside the mountain and reward human help with treasure.

notes.label: Kindsmutter
notes.text: an experienced midwife or birth attendant; literally ‘child-mother,’ it is an older regional occupational term rather than a reference to the woman's own motherhood.

notes.label: Kindsbetterin
notes.text: a woman in childbed—one giving birth or recovering immediately after delivery; here it is the female dwarf assisted by the Kindsmutter.

d3ee3c50ba2e8cfa08e23f2ab7fc44f5825adf08.summary: Once, within the walls of the good city of Zurich, there lived two king's daughters named Hildegard and Berta.

notes.label: Kirschenblust
notes.text: Swiss German for cherry blossom or the season's first cherry bloom, carried up from the lakeside villages with their bells.

notes.label: Burgstein
notes.text: literally ‘castle stone,’ used poetically for the sisters' secure stone stronghold at Baldern rather than for a single rock.

notes.label: Burgstall
notes.text: an older word for a castle site or fortified dwelling; here it refers to the high Baldern residence in which the sisters can no longer find peace.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Karlsturm
notes.text: the named Karl, or Charlemagne, tower of Zurich's Grossmünster; the story locates the new church directly opposite it.

notes.label: Fraumünster
notes.text: literally ‘women's minster,’ Zurich's historic convent church; the legend presents Hildegard and Berta as its first and second abbesses and explains its stag emblem.

d7ebf9ed69da40491bb213a25bb7f25e9978fca0.summary: From the so-called Pfaffen-Ställe, which lie approximately in the middle of the Castiel fields, one often sees a white-clad figure wearing a black apron ascend toward the church.

notes.label: Pfaffen-Ställe
notes.text: literally “priests’ stables,” the locally named stables in the Castiel fields from which the apparition is often seen.

notes.label: Kirchenjungfrau
notes.text: the unhyphenated form used in the narrative for the same church maiden.

notes.label: Hengert
notes.text: an evening social gathering or company; the source specifies here that it is a Gesellschaft der Ledigen, a gathering of unmarried people.

notes.label: Beinhaus
notes.text: an ossuary or charnel house where bones from the churchyard were kept.

notes.label: Messmerin
notes.text: a female church sexton or sacristan, responsible here for the early bell.

notes.label: z'Tag lüten
notes.text: Swiss German for ringing in or announcing the day with the church bell.

notes.label: Kilcha-Wibli
notes.text: Swiss German for “little church woman,” an alternate local name for the Kirchenjungfrau.

notes.label: Kirchen-Jungfrau
notes.text: literally “church maiden,” the white-clad apparition associated with Castiel’s church and its path.

aa35a97da96ff024061961e1b779324e712e8fb0.summary: 1. In volume II, pp. 83 ff., of his Naturgeschichte des Schweizerlandes (Zurich, 1746), the scholar Johann Jakob Scheuchzer tells the following legend, which he heard in August 1705 on his fourth mountain journey.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle, milk processing, and cheesemaking on a seasonal Alp; the role is central to both the older account and the later variants.

notes.label: Käsgaden
notes.text: literally a cheese storehouse or dairy outbuilding where cheeses are made or kept; paving the muddy working route to it with cheese dramatizes the Senn’s sacrilegious waste.

notes.label: Suffy
notes.text: a regional dairy term for whey or a whey-based drink left from cheesemaking; the older account does not specify its exact preparation.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, herds, dairy work, and working landscape, not merely a mountain; the legend explains how the productive Klariden pasture was buried beneath snow and ice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Buebli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a little boy; here it initially emphasizes the long-awaited child before the narrator condemns his spoiled upbringing.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey, the liquid remaining after Alpine cheesemaking; the parents’ use of whole milk instead is presented as extreme waste.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; the cheese-and-Anken path represents valuable dairy produce squandered underfoot.

notes.label: Süffi
notes.text: an Uri dairying term for a thin whey or whey-like liquid produced during cheesemaking; the exact processing stage and consistency meant here are not specified.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a fresh Swiss whey cheese or curd made from proteins left after ordinary cheese production; removing even the Zieger makes the mother’s meal poorer still.

notes.label: Rossbollen
notes.text: rounded pieces of horse dung; substituting them for the Zieger is a deliberately degrading abuse of the mother.

notes.label: Trychelkuh
notes.text: a cow wearing a Trychel, a large hammered sheet-metal livestock bell whose tone differs from that of a cast bell; Brändi’s mock baptism deepens the tale’s charge of sacrilege.

notes.label: Ich und Hüer Kathry und Trychelchüeh Brändi und Hund Parysi Miänt immer und ewig i Klarydä sy
notes.text: the first Uri-dialect Good Friday cry, naming the Senn, Kathry, the bell cow, and dog as eternally confined in Klariden; Hüer is a coarse form meaning ‘whore.’
notes.anchor: Ich und Hüer Kathry und Trychelchüeh Brändi und Hund Parysi Miänt immer und ewig i Klarydä sy

notes.label: Ich und my liäbi Kathry miänt ewig i Klarydä sy
notes.text: the shorter Uri-dialect variant, ‘I and my dear Kathry must remain in Klariden forever.’
notes.anchor: Ich und my liäbi Kathry miänt ewig i Klarydä sy

notes.label: Ich Sänn Hans, Chüeh Brändi, Hund Parysi und Hüer Kathry Miänt ewig i Klarydä sy
notes.text: an Uri-dialect variant naming Senn Hans, Brändi the cow, Parysi the dog, and Kathry as eternally confined.
notes.anchor: Ich Sänn Hans, Chüeh Brändi, Hund Parysi und Hüer Kathry Miänt ewig i Klarydä sy

notes.label: Sänn Mathys, Hund Parys, Trychelchüeh Brändi und Hüer Kathry Miänt immer und ewig i Klarydä verbannt sy
notes.text: an Uri-dialect variant naming Senn Mathys and the companions and saying they must remain banished in Klariden forever and ever.
notes.anchor: Sänn Mathys, Hund Parys, Trychelchüeh Brändi und Hüer Kathry Miänt immer und ewig i Klarydä verbannt sy

e77c630d7a2a5eb8d97095479b0fee479bf91abd.summary: a) To reach the banks of the Reuss in the little land of Uri from the Linth valley of Glarus, the traveler must follow one of the most beautiful Alpine paths over the Marchalp, where the border dispute took place, and the wild Klausen Pass with the picturesque Stäubibach.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible especially for making cheese on a high pasture.

notes.label: Nidelgret
notes.text: a byname for Kathri; Nidel means cream and Gret is a form of Margret, suggesting ‘Cream-Gret,’ though the narrative gives no explicit reason.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the seasonal Alpine dairy hut where a Senn lives and makes milk products.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or level with huts and livestock facilities, here belonging to the Senn.

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: plural of Firn, old compacted snowfields or glacier snow that cover the cursed alp.

notes.label: Dornenzizzen
notes.text: literally ‘thorn teats,’ the cow’s magically painful, thorn-covered teats that test a would-be redeemer.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Treichlenkuh
notes.text: a cow wearing a Treichel, a large hammered sheet-metal livestock bell, often a leading or especially prized animal.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: schwarz zäggeti
notes.text: Swiss German for black, curdled, clotted, or stringy milk; its abnormal texture and color mark the cow’s enchantment.

notes.label: Melkschmutz
notes.text: a milker’s protective garment or apron; the exact historical item is uncertain, but it melts in the supernatural heat.

notes.label: zäggät
notes.text: dialect for curdled, clotted, or stringy in texture, describing the enchanted milk.

notes.label: Milchkraut
notes.text: literally ‘milk herb,’ a white-sapped plant said to have been blessed before the alp was cursed; the botanical species is not given.

notes.label: verfluchte Kraut
notes.text: literally ‘cursed herb,’ the alternative name for Milchkraut after the inhabitants’ sin brought divine punishment.

notes.label: Ich und d'Kuoh Brändi und d'r Hund Ringgi und 's huore Kathri miend immer und ewig uf Blümlisalp si.
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘I, the cow Brändi, the dog Ringgi, and the whore Kathri must remain forever and ever on the Blümlisalp’; the harsh sexual insult is retained because it belongs to the condemned servant’s cry.
notes.anchor: Ich und d'Kuoh Brändi und d'r Hund Ringgi und 's huore Kathri miend immer und ewig uf Blümlisalp si.

544b4f089c93416499d6c516e650fb54d73c9e48.summary: A quarter of an hour west of the village of Eggersriet lies the hamlet of Egg.

notes.label: Kleebhund
notes.text: literally ‘Kleeb dog,’ named for the wooded locality called Kleeb near Eggersriet; this oppressive spectral dog rides late travelers’ backs, but the place-name’s deeper meaning is uncertain.

385aa2e14b516e130b8919605e0cda5cb9cd96b7.summary: The Walser pasture was once disputed. A false witness sprinkled earth into his shoes, put a ladle into his hat, and swore that he stood upon his own soil as surely as he had the Schöpfer above him.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: the German word can mean both the divine ‘Creator’ and a ladle or scoop; the false witness hides a ladle above his head so that his apparently sacred oath is literally true while intended to deceive.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working dairy landscape; the disputed Walser pasture is assigned to the Alp of Lax.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Klostergritt
notes.text: the local name for the convent-associated ghostly ride or procession heard with rattling and hoofbeats; Kloster means monastery or convent, while the exact dialect sense and derivation of Gritt are uncertain.

be3cc378b5e80a80bdd1dfdc069ab4df64baefa9.summary: 1. Within living memory, people in the Reusstal still spoke a great deal about a woman from above Golzer in the Maderanertal and considered her an old witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Nastuch
notes.text: a regional form of Nasentuch, historically a kerchief or square cloth that could be worn on the head; here the red cloth marks the Golzneri’s old-fashioned dress rather than serving as a modern pocket handkerchief.

notes.label: Golzneri
notes.text: the feminine local byname for the woman from Golzer blamed for the hay-whirlwinds; the suffix identifies her by place, while the source gives no personal name.

notes.label: Chunnd ächt eppä d'Golzneri?
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Could the Golzneri perhaps be coming?’; the question recognizes the strange wind as the reputed witch’s approach.

notes.label: Schwarbe
notes.text: an Uri haymaking word for a swath, windrow, or gathered strip of hay; the exact size and shape into which the knife is thrown are not specified.

notes.label: Gänterli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small cupboard or wall cabinet; the innkeeper opens it to take out a drinking glass.

notes.label: Sympathie
notes.text: in this historical folk-belief context, a learned magical art based on hidden correspondences and action at a distance, not ordinary emotional sympathy; the stories attribute the hay-whirlwinds to its practitioners.

notes.label: Der het da nitt fast g'jützet und isch bald einisch wider g'gangä!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘He did not linger there to shout for joy and soon went on his way again’; the ironic formula conveys the guest’s alarm and hasty departure.
notes.anchor: Der het da nitt fast g'jützet und isch bald einisch wider g'gangä!

21051868842f0b9098e17c78c4c2d2c14e5e9344.summary: An unbeliever stood beside the road during a procession and gave offense to the devout worshipers with his mockery.

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: a magical binding or spell that fixes the mocker in place and keeps the knife lodged in his knee; prayer during the next procession breaks it, while the account does not describe who casts the Bann or by what rite.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally the ‘night folk,’ a Vorarlberg supernatural company that dances after dark and punishes onlookers; here it supplies an older parallel to the Christian procession story, but its members and relation to the Wild Hunt are not specified.

notes.label: Schnetzer
notes.text: a regional word for a cutting knife, perhaps a large clasp knife or working blade; the Nachtvolk’s last dancer lodges it in the lintel and simultaneously in the observer’s knee, but its exact form is not described.

dde4a9f58586ebe12ad3e2968eb8b53d1facc62c.summary: In the fertile land of Vaud, between Lakes Geneva and Neuchâtel, there once stood a small castle inhabited by the Knight of Lasarraz.

notes.label: Morgengabe
notes.text: the traditional ‘morning gift’ made by a husband to his bride in connection with marriage; here the count demands a castle and cattle as the condition for his daughter's wedding.

notes.label: Wams
notes.text: a close-fitting historical man's jacket or doublet; here the knight uses it to conceal the punishing toads attached to his back.

8f87f7965eea91fd75639f2ed76b83871d8821cb.summary: In the ancient mountain fortress of Mitternholz, which rises not far from the wondrous Blausee upon a seemingly inaccessible rock and is therefore also called the Felsenburg, Knight Anton Imturn lived hundreds of years ago.

notes.label: Felsenburg
notes.text: literally ‘rock castle,’ the descriptive alternate name for the seemingly inaccessible fortress of Mitternholz.

notes.label: Landleute
notes.text: literally ‘country people’ or ‘people of the land,’ the local rural inhabitants acting as a political community rather than merely people outdoors.

notes.label: Rosskarren
notes.text: literally ‘horse cart,’ an agricultural cart drawn by a horse; the knight hides beneath its loose hay and straw.

e52d4ef03da0a3ad12e540306ee82cce07179fd2.summary: A legend circulates among hunters and herders that, at certain times in the summer months, when they pass through the Val Urschai at the still midnight hour, they see first a saddled horse as white as snow and then a knight as black as coal appear on the summit and see the knight vault onto the horse.

notes.label: Val Urschai
notes.text: the Romansh regional place-name for the Alpine valley where the spectral boundary rider appears; Val means valley.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

dd9d1884e87eefa51d8d328c56eecaf585020e8b.summary: Not long ago, while excavating at La Sarraz, a statue was discovered of a knight from the fourteenth century with two toads upon his cheeks and another such pair upon his back.

notes.label: Burgstall
notes.text: a historical term for a castle site, fortified residence, or the estate belonging to one; here it forms part of the bride's demanded marriage gift, and the story does not specify whether an intact castle or its holding is meant.

notes.label: Morgengabe
notes.text: the traditional ‘morning gift’ made by a husband to his bride in connection with marriage; here the demanded cattle and Burgstall consume all the groom's parents own.

notes.label: Maß
notes.text: a historical regional measure for liquids, often roughly a liter but varying by place and period; here it denotes the knight's large serving of strong beer rather than an exact modern volume.

2e62be434588d2cd43f098b33594de18dd483e18.summary: Many knights drowned in Lake Ägeri, in the Canton of Zug, during the Battle of Morgarten.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

faecbaf7c5cedcc36e06e3ff72a28a7d25986883.summary: In her pride, the knight’s daughter of Castelen in Aargau rejected a whole host of suitors and at last gave herself to a servant of low birth.

notes.label: Bapperlabab
notes.text: a deliberately garbled or nonsensical ending placed inside the opening of the Lord’s Prayer; it conveys the ghost’s broken prayer and moral conflict, but the source gives the sound no independent lexical meaning.

fd6927a74189681d0e1dd26001ffbcbf92afd7a9.summary: There are not so many Bozna in Saas, if one does not count the living. — Once, Weibelschhanschjobschannumarji’s husband (Weibelschjobschhanschannumarji was my late mother) encountered and took note of something strange.

notes.label: Bozna
notes.text: a Saas German plural for frightening apparitions, bogeys, or ghosts; the opening joke counts troublesome living people among them.

notes.label: Bozu
notes.text: the corresponding Saas German singular for a frightening apparition, bogey, or ghost; the frightened carrier assumes one is chasing him before the mundane cause is discovered.

notes.label: Triegelti
notes.text: a small dangling toggle, peg, or fastening attached to the carrying basket; its exact form is not described, but its swinging impact—not a ghost—causes the knocking.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Saaser Mundart
notes.text: the German label for the distinctive Alemannic dialect of the Saas Valley in Valais; the long chained personal names and much of the tale’s humor depend on that local speech.

notes.label: Der Chlopfer uf um Rigg
notes.text: Saas German for ‘the knocker on one’s back’; the title makes a supposed pursuing spirit out of the ordinary tapping sound behind the carrier.

e070a4827b8ad847246903eec242124ab5e9edaa.summary: A household spirit had lived for a long time in the house of the former Alt-Ammann of Kirchleerau; no one confused him with a ghost or a poor soul, however.

notes.label: Alt-Ammann
notes.text: a former or retired Ammann, the chief local magistrate or municipal official; here the title identifies the head of the Kirchleerau household rather than a personal name.

notes.label: Milchbrocken
notes.text: bread broken or crumbled into milk, a simple milk-and-bread dish; here a small bowlful is the household spirit's daily payment.

notes.label: Zwilchkleid
notes.text: a garment made of Zwilch, a strong coarse twill or drill traditionally woven from linen and later other fibers; here the Beckli receives a boy-sized suit each New Year.

notes.label: Beckli
notes.text: the local name of Kirchleerau's small household spirit; the diminutive ending -li marks something little, but the story does not establish the rest of the name's derivation.

e3ffc707e5027d6183c57232a333156347648110.summary: At Renens in the Romanel district, a Kobold haunts the place known as the Blancherie and is notorious for the wicked tricks it plays.

notes.label: Kobold
notes.text: a German-speaking household or place spirit, ranging from mischievous to dangerous; this one polices the working hours of washerwomen.

notes.label: Tçauce-villha
notes.text: a Vaudois regional name glossed by the source as ‘witch-mother,’ an old mounted female specter who suffocates victims; spelling and exact etymology are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Kouairon
notes.text: the proper regional name of an imagined dreadful house used to frighten misbehaving children; the source does not explain its etymology.

2f683314139d7472739c0e4ad6c3628a83319e69.summary: Between Allières and Cerniat stands a solitary house called Les Cerniettes.

notes.label: Kobold
notes.text: a Kobold is a German-speaking household or place spirit whose behavior may range from helpful to malicious, here an emphatically hostile haunting being; the tale leaves its exact nature and origin uncertain.

eafb1cd530cc63c54bf3129409f40d0d65d88468.summary: In a valley hollow of the Oberägeri-Allmend near the Schwyz border, at the foot of Sankt Jostenberg, the ruins of a forest hut are still shown where, in the previous century, a notorious Schwarzkünstler called the Kohler lived.

notes.label: Oberägeri-Allmend
notes.text: the common land or communal pasture belonging to Oberägeri, where the sorcerer's hut stood.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a practitioner of the ‘black art,’ a magician or sorcerer presumed to use forbidden magic.

notes.label: Kohler
notes.text: a charcoal burner; the occupational name identifies the forest-dwelling sorcerer.

notes.label: Teufelsbündner
notes.text: someone bound by a pact with the Devil, the charge attached to Kohler's sorcery.

notes.label: Gewild
notes.text: an older collective term for wild game animals, which appear to the hunters but cannot be shot.

d1a927b64359fa955a3671d61d0e391faf135827.summary: Between the municipalities of Peist and Langwies lies a long strip of forest called the ‘Mattenwald,’ which many years ago belonged to Peist.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning ‘little man’; here it names the condemned shape-shifting haunter, who can also appear as a giant or cow.

notes.label: Krachen
notes.text: the name of a particular rock in the Mattenwald to which the spirit lures the herdsman; although Krachen can also denote a cleft or ravine, the source explicitly calls this feature a rock.

notes.label: Krachenmannli
notes.text: the local name ‘little man of the Krachen,’ joining the named Mattenwald rock with the Alemannic diminutive Mannli; the false swearer’s changing size makes ‘little’ a being-name rather than a fixed measurement.

be82342c8bd70ebc9d5fdd58794ab6e1cdb5d152.summary: In Lucerne's Entlibuch, at the Risetenfluh, a Senn named Lustenberger had an Alp where his boy tended the goats.

notes.label: Entlibuch
notes.text: the source's spelling of Entlebuch, the Lucerne Alpine and pre-Alpine region with a strong pastoral and wrestling identity.

notes.label: Risetenfluh
notes.text: the named cliff or crag where Lustenberger's Alp lies; Fluh is Swiss German for a steep rock face.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and cheese-making in the seasonal hut.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal livestock pasture and dairying settlement, not simply a mountain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fahrender Schüler
notes.text: a wandering student-magician or occult adept in German-language folklore, not an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep rock faces or crags where the wandering scholar searches for stones and herbs.

notes.label: Fahrenden Schüler
notes.text: the source's inflected form of Fahrender Schüler, the traveling adept rewarded for his entertaining company and hospitality received.

notes.label: Geißbub
notes.text: a boy who herds goats; the humble pastoral role contrasts with the supernatural strength and wrestling fame he gains.

notes.label: Schwingen
notes.text: traditional Swiss belt wrestling, fought in sawdust or on turf by gripping special breeches; it is a major rural festival sport.

notes.label: Schwinger
notes.text: a competitor in Schwingen, especially an accomplished Swiss wrestler.

notes.label: Schwingerkönig
notes.text: literally ‘king of the wrestlers,’ the champion or preeminent Schwingen competitor of a region or festival.

notes.label: Älplerkirchweih
notes.text: a festive church fair or annual celebration for Alpine pastoral people, here including a major Schwingen contest.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the powerful Alpine herdsmen from the Bernese Oberland who enter the wrestling contest.

notes.label: gebodigt
notes.text: a wrestling term meaning thrown or brought flat to the ground, especially onto the back.

notes.label: Hosenlupf
notes.text: literally ‘breeches lift,’ a colloquial Swiss name for Schwingen based on the grip taken on the opponent's wrestling trousers.

notes.label: Kraftwurzel
notes.text: literally ‘strength root,’ the magical root that grants a full day of enormous power when bitten three times before sunrise.

8616950da650ed9b53cc801e9948d8ef43124cad.summary: In the municipality of Entlebuch, a man named Lustenberger owned an Alp at the Risetenfluh.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture with its hut and work areas, not simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a folk figure associated with itinerant learning, occult knowledge, and magic rather than an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the skilled alpine dairyman who oversees the seasonal hut, herd routine, and milk work; here he hospitably shelters the stranger.

notes.label: Neesen
notes.text: the source's parenthetical regional name for gambling or gaming; the precise game is not identified, but the offered gift would make its bearer win every time.

notes.label: Kraftwurzel
notes.text: literally a ‘strength root,’ a small magical root whose bite grants extraordinary bodily power until the day ends.

notes.label: Schwinger
notes.text: competitors in Schwingen, traditional Swiss belt wrestling; the root's power lets the small youth defeat renowned wrestlers.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally a ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd; the Entlebuch men use the humble role to conceal how formidable Lustenberger's son has become.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

92f72fe4fac3318223467884c488efb9482973a5.summary: The Burgschaft of Visp—Vispach—Fischbach is often mentioned in the old and more recent history of Valais and occupies a not insignificant place in it: sometimes because of its manly struggles for liberty, the Landräte held there, and the agreements concluded there; sometimes because of the rank and…

notes.label: Burgschaft
notes.text: a historical Swiss term for a burgh settlement or its civic community; here it distinguishes the lower settlement of Visp and its older political importance.

notes.label: Fischbach
notes.text: literally ‘fish brook,’ the name the wandering figure says the settlement bears on his second visit.

notes.label: Landräte
notes.text: plural of Landrat, historical territorial or cantonal councils; their meetings at Visp are cited as evidence of the settlement's public importance.

notes.label: Hübschburg
notes.text: the local castle or manor name above Visp associated with influential families; its literal formation is unclear from the story and is therefore retained.

notes.label: Überbühl
notes.text: the inn's place-name, closest to ‘over/beyond the hill’; the story invokes that literal sense to explain that the building once stood on raised ground.

notes.label: ewige Jude
notes.text: literally ‘eternal Jew,’ the source's historical Christian-legend label for the figure now commonly called the Wandering Jew; readers should understand that this is a traditional antisemitic figure condemned to wander without rest, not a neutral description of Jewish people.

notes.label: Schönbach
notes.text: literally ‘beautiful brook,’ the first name in the legend's sequence of folk etymologies for Visp.

notes.label: Leidbach
notes.text: literally ‘sorrow brook,’ the predicted third name, retrospectively connected with earthquake and flood.

notes.label: Martinsturm
notes.text: the local ‘Martin's Tower,’ whose elaborate stone crown and iron cross were damaged by the earthquake.

notes.label: Kreuzazfstecker
notes.text: the title's exact historical spelling for the worker who sets or mounts a cross, closest to ‘cross-installer’; the unusual azf sequence may reflect dialect or a printing error, but it is not silently normalized.

notes.label: Vispensand
notes.text: the local sandy ground or floodplain of the Vispe at Visp; it is where the falling cross-setter lands and dies.

f51c5371065db25add20d43d6a5552ac9de225e0.summary: a) At the Hohgant in the canton of Bern, the evil end of a man from Entlebuch is used to explain the name Kreuzfluh, between the Furgengütsch and Gäbelisfluh.

notes.label: Kreuzfluh
notes.text: literally ‘cross cliff,’ a steep rock face bearing a cross-shaped natural or miraculous marking.

notes.label: Potz Chrüz!
notes.text: a Swiss oath or exclamation, roughly ‘by the Cross!’; in the legend the cry physically creates the cross upon the cliff.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep exposed rock face or cliff.

notes.label: Bernbiet
notes.text: the Bernese territory or countryside, here contrasted confessionally with Entlebuch.

f2f206ca6107ed9bf5443147f6206febeefd10c2.summary: At the time when Leuk still lay on the shady side, there was between Agaren and Pfyn, where an endless forest now extends, a level tract overgrown with beautiful, great fruit trees, so that squirrels could hop from one tree to another along the entire distance.

notes.label: Mäschlerweiden
notes.text: the named pasture area forming one boundary of the surviving little plain; the source gives no modern identification or derivation.

notes.label: Meretschigraben
notes.text: the named ravine or drainage cut forming the plain’s other boundary; Graben denotes a ditch, gully, or ravine, but the source does not specify its exact form.

notes.label: Edlerboden
notes.text: the earlier name of Carus Edler’s level farm tract and later the setting of the supernatural judgment; Boden here denotes a level piece of ground or valley floor.

notes.label: Kreuzstein
notes.text: literally “cross-stone,” the inherited cross-shaped block bound in family dreams to the house’s fortune and misfortune; it proves to be an immense gemstone.

notes.label: Burgschaft Leuk
notes.text: the historical borough or castle settlement of Leuk where the herbalist lives; the term marks a civic settlement form rather than naming a separate person or castle in the tale.

notes.label: Himmelssprache
notes.text: literally “language of heaven,” a mysterious knowledge attributed to the herbalist; the source does not explain whether it means astrology, sacred learning, magical diagnosis, or something else.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a historical large silver coin or money unit; Carus has lived outside a money economy and does not recognize either the ten-Taler price or a gold coin.

notes.label: Schewi
notes.text: the individual name of Carus’s last black goat, whom he calls lazy because she remains near him; the source does not give an independent derivation for the name.

notes.label: Evolenerrasse
notes.text: the Evolène cattle breed demanded for the doctor’s second pair of cows; the judge insists that the animals also be among the finest.

notes.label: Vonöischi
notes.text: the named route or locality toward which the doctor travels to disguise his destination; the source does not identify its exact modern course.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Lämmerboden
notes.text: literally “Lambs’ Plain,” the later name given to the formerly named Edlerboden after the vision of the white lamb and two black dragons.

b82877bda64bcf41c2eec0d443eb7c831313e950.summary: A quarter-hour from Russwil, on a height in the Schächenbühlwald, stands a great and luxuriant fir tree with a sacred image of the cross upon it.

notes.label: Männchen
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ used in the expression for an animal sitting or standing upright on its hind legs; the hare's posture appears deliberately mocking rather than proving it becomes human.

notes.label: Kreuztanne
notes.text: literally ‘cross fir,’ the named tree bearing a sacred crucifix image; the nearby supernatural hare makes the otherwise devotional site uncanny.

5b8e4bdef5d0cad428787471deeb3a2ef500900d.summary: A quarter of an hour above the village of Steinen, close to the main road, flows a little spring almost completely covered by bushes.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Kropfbrunnen
notes.text: literally “goiter spring” or “goiter well,” the local name of a spring believed to give drinkers a goiter; the legend attributes the power to the goitered pilgrim who uncovered it, not to a medical explanation.

763615d0724de2621adf91631d5c9a1c2c39c882.summary: On the way from Oberhof to Wölfliswil, one enters the Hohle Gasse; the footpath beside it is called the Alte Kirchweg.

notes.label: Stegli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a little footbridge, stile, or narrow crossing; here it is the traditional place-name at the mountain spring where the maiden appears.

notes.label: Kränzleinjungfer
notes.text: literally a ‘little-wreath maiden,’ the local name for this friendly but unredeemed female spirit; her beaded and gold-cord crown recalls historical festive headwear of unmarried Fricktal women.

3eff2c14ed1d762ecd922a241282a4c08863e50e.summary: A young woman of Veltheim found a whole heap of thalers beside a drainage ditch.

notes.label: Krötenthaler
notes.text: this coined title combines Kröten, ‘toads,’ with Thaler, the coins that transform into them; whether it was a local nickname or Rochholz’s wordplay is uncertain.

1fff180401036e579b58e18a4e98f5ce30d58dcb.summary: The Rost is the name of a level tract of land in the municipality of Siggingen and is said to have been the northwestern end of the ancient Roman city of Vindonissa.

notes.label: Krümbihund
notes.text: the local name for a great fire-eyed spectral dog or monster haunting the Rost near Siggingen; Hund means dog, but the dialect element Krümbi and the creature’s precise form or connection with the Roman ruins are not explained.

0767a3d8bc043cb66c14e507eeaf89181efca13d.summary: The Krümmlihund haunts Obernußbaumen, a village in the Siggental. In the cattle lane at night, an animal with luminous, rolling eyes tumbles toward people; because of its rolling and contortions, it is called the Krümmlihund.

notes.label: Krümmlihund
notes.text: literally a regional diminutive name for a “crooked” or “contorted little dog”; here it is a shape-changing treasure ghost named for its rolling and twisting movements, although the source does not prescribe one fixed English creature type.

c4a52ffe443f8c2d6756e15bab5e133daa88418a.summary: Something similar (see: Christen Chüng of Weisstannen) happened to a young Älpler from Ragaz on the local Alp of Pardiel.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; the young man’s precise role is not stated.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its associated livestock and dairy operation, not simply a peak; Pardiel is the named pasture where the encounter occurs.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: a dairying term that can denote whey or a whey-derived curd; the tale presents three differently colored portions or forms, but does not explain their physical state or supernatural purpose.

notes.label: Gstüpp
notes.text: a regional word for light debris such as dust, chaff, or fine fragments visible or scattered in sunlight; the comparison threatens complete destruction, but the exact material intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Kuhreigen
notes.text: a traditional Alpine herding song or cattle call, related to the Ranz des Vaches; the legend explains the first such song in the Oberland as a supernatural gift.

bbc2fe708efde745323db162531fa476211773ef.summary: ‘Du, Hans,’ the Senn of the Alp Altsäss said to his Handbuben one evening, ‘der Trappli het si kündt; dia Chüa henn gruggt, un dia Nacht schneit's; morn fahran mir vu Alp; richt dia Schleipf her’—the Trappli has announced itself; the cows have rushed together, and tonight it will snow; tomorrow we…

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine herdsman or dairyman in charge of the cattle and milk work.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Altsäss
notes.text: the named seasonal high pasture where the Trappli is believed to frighten the herd; Säss refers to an Alpine pasture station.

notes.label: Handbuben
notes.text: the source's inflected form of Handbub, a young Alpine helper or herdsman's assistant who performs practical tasks.

notes.label: Trappli
notes.text: the local name of an unseen Alpine spirit believed to panic the cattle before a snowstorm.

notes.label: Schleipf
notes.text: a simple Alpine drag-sled or sledge used to bring loads down steep ground, here carrying the dairy produce during the emergency descent.

notes.label: der Trappli het si kündt; dia Chüa henn gruggt, un dia Nacht schneit's; morn fahran mir vu Alp; richt dia Schleipf her
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect announcing that the Trappli has made itself known, the cows have rushed together, snow will fall, and the helper must prepare for descent.
notes.anchor: der Trappli het si kündt; dia Chüa henn gruggt, un dia Nacht schneit's; morn fahran mir vu Alp; richt dia Schleipf her

notes.label: Molken
notes.text: dairy produce collectively, or in narrower use whey; here it means the milk-derived goods and supplies brought down from the Alp.

notes.label: Kuhrücken
notes.text: literally the cows' rushing or sudden mass movement, a herd behavior treated as a warning that snow and bad weather are coming.

1480e4f7c385767100dc9f69a7167f54ce855838.summary: It was Kilbi or alte Fasnacht, and a woman in the Fontanen near Menzberg was frying Küchli.

notes.label: Kilbi
notes.text: a Swiss parish fair or annual church-dedication feast, traditionally marked by communal food and festivities.

notes.label: alte Fasnacht
notes.text: literally ‘Old Carnival’; the regional observance of Carnival according to the older calendar or on a later traditional date.

notes.label: Küchli
notes.text: small Swiss fried cakes or pastries; their disappearance is the central act of theft in the legend.

notes.label: Küchligabel
notes.text: literally ‘Küchli fork’; the utensil used to handle the fried cakes, here employed as a countermagical weapon.

16971c26090d1ba63a643ed93984776e9f0feb54.summary: An owner of the castle estate above Jenins had a brutish servant, just as he himself was a harsh, miserly, hardhearted master over his own family and his subordinates.

notes.label: bürchelte
notes.text: a local verb explicitly glossed by Jecklin as blowing into a horn; here the neighboring servant uses the horn together with yodeling after the cattle are fed.

notes.label: Kuh-Reihen
notes.text: a traditional Swiss herdsman’s cattle song or call, related to the Kuhreihen or Ranz des vaches used around Alpine herds.

notes.label: Maysässen
notes.text: plural of Maiensäss, seasonal mountain-pasture holdings and buildings used between the valley farms and the higher summer Alps.

notes.label: Einfangen
notes.text: enclosed or fenced agricultural parcels; the local land-use nuance is retained because the source distinguishes them from Alps, Maysässen, and village stables.

notes.label: Panx-Gatter
notes.text: the named gate to which the ghost is finally confined; Jecklin gives neither a secure modern location nor an etymology for Panx.

notes.label: Küh-Joli
notes.text: the local name of the cattle-tormenting servant and later ghost; Küh associates him with cows or cattle, while the exact origin of Joli is not explained in the tale.

955c9cad1f3de971dbe44e3d1da273cb3c5a2e65.summary: A poor widow's only cow was also in a Sente at Fursch. This cow was the Küher's burden.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: an Alpine herd and associated dairying unit, related to Senntum; the widow's single cow belongs to this larger managed herd.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cowherd; the title and repeated name identify the punished herdsman through his responsibility for the cattle.

notes.label: Zöchtgras
notes.text: the source's quoted local term for tempting grass growing in dangerous terrain; it may imply especially choice or luxuriant fodder, but the precise dialect sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Stollen
notes.text: here a ledge, shelf, or narrow piece of ground above the rock face where the herdsman lays the bark; the word has other mining and structural senses not intended here.

notes.label: erfällte
notes.text: the source's marked term for the cow deliberately caused to fall to its death; it is closer to ‘felled by a fall’ than to an accidental fallen animal.

notes.label: Heller
notes.text: a very small historical coin and unit of value; atoning only one Heller per repetition emphasizes the immense duration of the herdsman's penance.

1c6fffb9e80c737a75f6c83b873c4fdfc11af064.summary: At Ganterisch there was once a young Küher who never grew impatient, scolded, or cursed when a cow spilled the milk during milking, even though this happened often.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: literally a cowherd, but in the Bernese Alpine setting it denotes a man who tends and milks cattle in the seasonal pasture economy; the role overlaps with that of a Senn, though the text distinguishes the words without defining their exact division of duties.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for milk and dairy work on the high pasture; here the dwarfs perform his Senn work and the watch is of a kind associated with the role, whose precise local duties may also include herding.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

330025a3a12447b6e637c4c179c053a917eaeff8.summary: On the Alp of Lasa above Valens, the Sennen often heard the loud call of a Küher in the evening, coming down from above between Vasana and the Laufböden: “Hoi, hoi!” It sounded as though an entire Sente were being driven through the air.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its dairy settlement; the uncanny call is heard over the Alp of Lasa rather than merely upon a mountain summit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who live and work seasonally with the cattle on a high pasture.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cattleman responsible for cows and dairy work; the invisible caller sounds as though he is driving a whole herd through the air.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: a Swiss term for an organized herd of cattle on an Alp, often including the animals under one dairy operation; here the whole ghostly herd is heard but not seen.

a565546929d9a06b9e39e70fe4af7d45450703f5.summary: Above Les-Arses, a hamlet not far from the mountain village of Charmey, one sees a great mass of rock called ‘la Pierre de la Beaume.’ Even at the end of the previous century, some masonry could still be seen upon it, the remains of a castle belonging to the La-Beaume family.

notes.label: la Pierre de la Beaume
notes.text: French for ‘the Stone of La Beaume,’ the large rock above Les-Arses that preserves traces of the family's supposed castle.

notes.label: Schultheiss
notes.text: the historical title of a city's chief magistrate, often rendered mayor; here the Schultheiss and council are Fribourg's governing authorities, not feudal servants.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

b605f4aa26e309f34087dd7337cab7616c5263bf.summary: A young man named Joseph Imboden, it is told from the previous century, lived alone at Sparren, a mountain hamlet in St.

notes.label: Heumonat
notes.text: literally ‘hay month,’ a traditional month-name usually referring to July, when haymaking dominates rural work; local seasonal timing could vary.

notes.label: Furgwängen
notes.text: the plural terrain or place-name revealed in the dream, apparently a known locality in the Jung valley; its exact landform and literal derivation are not explained by the source.

notes.label: Furgwäng
notes.text: the singular or uninflected local form used by the relative for the same Furgwängen location; the spelling variation is retained because it belongs to the recognition that solves the dream.

1d4493f7e622215fe070673c67e91b0cfcc7e199.summary: The Fritzefrieder of Gelterkinden in Baselland was as rich as he was envious.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss and south-German coin denomination whose value varied by canton and period; here the miser sends only half a Batzen, and no precise modern conversion is supported.

notes.label: Landhund
notes.text: literally a “country” or “district dog,” the local name here for the father’s nocturnal shaggy-dog apparition; whether Land identifies the countryside, a territory, or simply forms a traditional ghost-name is uncertain.

aab3ff2658c8b14737eae2e458945e9ba1ea1c15.summary: After it had rained heavily for several days in succession, senseless deforestation having deprived the soil of its support, part of the wooded ground above Montbiel (Closters) slid down at two o’clock in the afternoon on 6 June (Sunday) of the year 1770 and buried 11 houses occupied by 13…

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for present-day Klosters in Graubünden.

notes.label: Platz
notes.text: the central village settlement of Closters, distinguished here from outlying Montbiel; it is where people attend the sermon and where the victims are buried.

notes.label: eingemauert
notes.text: literally “walled in”; the source glosses the local usage as enclosed on every side by the landslide’s mud.

notes.label: Dublonen
notes.text: doubloons, high-value historical gold coins; Jeuch places twenty of them in the collection dish for those left without property or shelter.

notes.label: Miltigkeit
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling for generosity or liberality; the quotation says the donors’ generosity later brought abundant blessing.

108f541a3ae1e7090295bbb54ff6ba10b28f76b3.summary: The entire settlement of Untervaz is said to lie upon a mass of debris beneath which are the houses of a village buried many centuries ago.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a regional Alpine word for a debris flow or destructive torrent and, by extension, its channel; here it carries rock and mud from the Cosenz-Bach into the village.

notes.label: Raine
notes.text: the local name of the place where the priest is said to have been buried; it is related to Rain, a bank, slope, or field boundary, but the source does not establish a more exact landform.

e378a1b39eb783f13d0b2654a0534745e8f7a3f2.summary: A farmer once encountered, near the Holy Cross chapel at midnight, a large wagon loaded with a slurry barrel.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor under the old Swiss Confederacy; here he is punished for abusing fiscal authority in the Sarganserland.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Spiessgesellen
notes.text: literally ‘spear companions,’ an older term for comrades-in-arms or close associates; the story leaves their precise relation to the condemned Landvogt unclear.

d1692cd98fc571c28efcaa99c11f0081709db6bb.summary: In Husen a few years ago, on the eve of All Saints' Day, a young man went by moonlight to the field to bring home his white turnips before the frost set in.

notes.label: Plätze
notes.text: literally ‘places’ or ‘plots,’ used here as the local field-name crossed beneath the Langstielerbaum; its exact cadastral sense is not specified.

notes.label: Langstielerbaum
notes.text: literally ‘long-stem tree,’ the locally named pear tree associated with the uncanny All Saints' Eve noise; the source identifies Langstieler as a coarse pear variety.

dfd1e5824171318574a51f7eb4ac341e0b319b1f.summary: Animals too have a language that human beings would understand if they possessed a certain herb.

3a658fbca2b8477bb140dde9cbcaac4b389fcc56.summary: A farmer lived in Iffigen and had three small boys. Their mother was ill.

f756f266646caffeaefd7bf75e12954b3720f0f2.summary: The last dwarfs of Lenk lived in the Staldenschöpfen. They were two gray-haired companions.

notes.label: Staldenschöpfen
notes.text: the local place-name of the dwarfs’ final dwelling; its components suggest slopes or steps and sheds, but the precise terrain is not explained.

notes.label: Sie möge mit dr fürnäh, was sie wei,
notes.text: Bernese German for approximately ‘They may do with you whatever they wish,’ the escaping dwarf’s warning to the captive.
notes.anchor: Sie möge mit dr fürnäh, was sie wei,

notes.label: Verrat nit, was d'Reckholderstude z'bedüte hei!
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Do not reveal what the juniper bushes mean!’—the bushes conceal the entrances to their homes.
notes.anchor: Verrat nit, was d'Reckholderstude z'bedüte hei!

notes.label: Wachholderstauden
notes.text: juniper bushes, later identified as the vegetation hiding the dwarfs’ cave entrances.

8768957e56db3aa51d06465ed484310b7cf1d739.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, the last of his line lived in Bernegg Castle: a brutal, hard-hearted knight who practiced his malice upon everyone obliged to pass that way.

notes.label: Bernhardiner-Mönch
notes.text: a monk identified by Jecklin with Saint Bernard or a Bernardine house; the source does not specify his exact monastery or order.

notes.label: Tiefe-Tobel
notes.text: literally the “deep ravine,” the dangerous wooded gorge between Bernegg and Castiel in which the knight abandons the monk.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for a steep, narrow ravine or gorge, used in the second paragraph for the same route.

notes.label: Lanquart
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling of the Landquart, the river whose wild flood runs between the two rock faces beneath Fracstein.

2c45af8fcdff95e2fb8cf04b0766aa3931802171.summary: In Rätigau stands a wall of rock,

notes.label: Rätigau
notes.text: the historical regional form used throughout the poem for the surrounding area; it is retained exactly rather than silently normalized to a modern place-name form.

notes.label: Solavers
notes.text: the proper name of the fortress and ruin in this legend; the source gives no etymology, so the name is retained rather than translated.

5f190a45ec4cb6fb0bb0681c2dbfb5c491866394.summary: The last episcopal Landvogt at Pedenale was a man of great harshness and arbitrariness; he respected neither divine nor human law, and many an innocent person languished in the castle dungeon.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor exercising delegated secular authority; this last episcopal Landvogt rules from Pedenale and abuses judicial and fiscal power.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

57f4f3e575c0516b47fe8a229bec7cae4b2c7da2.summary: On the so-called “Toma-Caste” in Ems near Cur stood Amides Castle at the time when Christianity gained acceptance in Raetia.

notes.label: Toma-Caste
notes.text: the local name printed by Jecklin for the hill in Ems on which the tale places Amides Castle; the form is preserved because the source does not explain its precise linguistic construction.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, used here to locate Ems nearby.

notes.label: Zugnagel
notes.text: the stout pin belonging to an ox team’s hitching or draft gear; the farmer uses this implement as the weapon against the castle lord.

notes.label: Marchsteine
notes.text: boundary stones marking legal divisions of land; secretly moving them is the lord’s repeated injustice in life and part of his haunting after death.

801dc60ecb6ca7c865d5665220784656315b81ab.summary: The lords who lived in the castles near Süs thought nothing of stopping and plundering travelers, or of oppressing and tormenting the peaceful country folk nearby and then squandering what they had stolen in riot and revelry.

notes.label: Süs
notes.text: the historical German name used by Jecklin for Susch, a village in the Lower Engadine.

notes.label: Unter-Engadin
notes.text: the German regional name for the Lower Engadine, the lower section of the Inn valley in Graubünden.

notes.label: Crap Sasslatsch
notes.text: a Romansh place-name for the rock or rocky site near which the lord and his followers are ambushed; the source does not identify a more precise modern location.

e31613314f5ef4cea8655360be872c52e831a11f.summary: Several hundred years ago, a wicked Raubritter lived at Greifenstein Castle who attacked and plundered unsuspecting travelers on the road.

notes.label: Raubritter
notes.text: literally “robber knight,” a noble who uses his fortified position to waylay, imprison, and ransom travelers.

notes.label: Freiherr
notes.text: a historical noble rank conventionally rendered as baron; the Ehrenfels father and son bear it.

notes.label: Buschklepper
notes.text: a contemptuous term for a highway robber or brigand who lurks in cover; it is applied to the Greifenstein lord.

notes.label: Lämmergeier
notes.text: the bearded vulture, a large Alpine bird seen circling its cliff nest while the hidden murderer remains unseen.

0c2874ac5911e65c98993b51256dce7216dd7556.summary: Do you see the tower in the evening ray,

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff, governor, or lord’s official; in the poem it is used broadly for an oppressive ruler or authority, not in the modern sense of a legal guardian.

701b1bd9e083e64854f0ff0ea51277f1097cfa4d.summary: The swineherd of Untervaz was once grazing his bristly animals near Neuenburg Castle.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: an oppressive feudal lord or tyrannical ruler who holds people under coercive power; it is a moral description of lordship rather than a modern official title.

ec3ddfa0f0e8ecb92432e138a6b795e0ca21e0d3.summary: When one travels from Arbon along Lake Constance toward Rorschach, one sees on the right, at the edge of the ridge that slopes down toward the lake, a good half-hour above Steinach, a gray tower with a broad superstructure sitting like a giant's hat upon the massive masonry below.

notes.label: About this telling
