50cb93cf6e02263d5711650e8d7f97307cc3f1cc.summary: Midway between Facklastein and Marschlins Castle lie many fine estates, including a meadow in which a continuous row of depressions in the ground runs in the direction from one castle to the other and is said to indicate the existence of a secret passage between the two castles.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: coercive or oppressive feudal lords; Jecklin immediately characterizes the two last lords of Facklastein as tyrants, and the term emphasizes their domination over the peasants.

8b78243069795ee9e9d1e3b6dc47c3f66ab4eecb.summary: Long, long ago, a young and stately baron lived at the castle. His wife was a daughter of the lord of the old tower in Zuz.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: a lord's jurisdiction, legal power, or territory under that power; Caldar is the Vogt's boldest opponent within it.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: an oppressive feudal lord or tyrannical ruler who holds people under coercive power; the poem uses it as the moral name for the fallen castle lord.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff, governor, or castle lord exercising delegated territorial authority; the poem portrays Bärenburg's final Vogt as a tyrant.

efa1794fb219b52b0a5358942b1c62ea4cc9b9fb.summary: The most beautiful girl in the valley lived at Campovasto. She was the daughter of Adam, a very elderly Landmann, and the episcopal Vogt at neighboring Guardavall Castle had cast his lustful eyes upon her. — When he commanded, no contradiction counted; anyone he hated he could ruin through rent or…

notes.label: Landmann
notes.text: a man of the land or countryman; here Adam is an elderly freeholder rather than a dependent tenant.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: an appointed bailiff, governor, or lordly administrator wielding judicial and fiscal power over a territory.

notes.label: Zinsmann
notes.text: a rent-paying or tribute-paying dependent whose family is vulnerable to the Vogt’s demands.

notes.label: Burgvogt
notes.text: the castle bailiff or governor; it is the Vogt’s office viewed specifically in relation to Guardavall Castle.

notes.label: Zwingburg
notes.text: a coercive lord’s fortress used to dominate the surrounding population, not merely any defensive castle.

notes.label: Zwingherrschaft
notes.text: oppressive lordship or rule maintained through coercion; the uprising frees the region from it.

69b8fbbfb252db07d347444f8047d74b5bd29047.summary: Of all the men who, in the name of the bishop of Cur, served as Vogt at Aspermont Castle above the Mulinära, the last surpassed his predecessors in cruelty.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical German spelling of Chur, the episcopal city and present capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff, governor, or lord's official exercising delegated authority; the office varied by territory and period and is not the modern English sense of a legal guardian.

notes.label: Bödeli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little level piece of ground or clearing, especially noticeable within steep Alpine terrain.

notes.label: Schützenbödeli
notes.text: literally the ‘marksman's little level ground’; the place-name commemorates the spot from which the fatal crossbow shot was fired.

f068ff8e1f34ead8d1fffe29e74e22d76be159a0.summary: One day the Zwingherr of Ruchenberg sent one of his servants to the village of Trimons with instructions to demand a pair of oxen from the peasant living at Gadruffi.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive or tyrannical lord who rules through force and exactions.

notes.label: Gadruffi
notes.text: the local settlement or farmstead where the peasant resisting the demand for oxen lives.

notes.label: Burgvogt
notes.text: the castle bailiff or governing lord; the term emphasizes the official power behind his demand.

notes.label: Tenne
notes.text: the barn’s threshing floor where the harvested grain is beaten out and lies in abundance.

notes.label: lupfte
notes.text: a regional past-tense form meaning lifted or raised; the peasant takes the flail from its nail before striking.

0bc9b8b7ad6e147fd0d15045ab79429f150e5836.summary: Even today, the Rhine boatmen in Laufenburg tell one another what their fathers and grandfathers already told them about the Fire Man there.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a traditional narrow, flat-bottomed Swiss river boat commonly propelled by oars or poles; it places the crossing specifically in Rhine boat culture.

5f51bf3fd5685688f0f23a8c3ff669c7cfaabd0c.summary: Between Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn lies a mighty glacier called the Augsttalgletscher, or Theodul Pass.

notes.label: Augsttalgletscher
notes.text: the local glacier name used for the Theodul Pass area between Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn; its precise historical mapping may differ from modern glacier names.

notes.label: laufund Jud
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘wandering Jew,’ the period legend’s name for the eternally traveling Jewish figure who punishes refused hospitality; it belongs to a longstanding Christian folkloric stereotype and is not a neutral description of Jewish people.

notes.label: Winter-Gugfa
notes.text: a Valais dialect term for fierce winter gusts or storm winds; the exact meteorological nuance is uncertain, but here it denotes the roaring winter weather over the glacier.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

c08d59df76df6aa6149e4149252664cd8449d9d1.summary: 1. From his little hut by the forest in the Maderanertal, my father took aim and shot at a fox that was eating at the bait.

notes.label: Kilchweg
notes.text: Swiss German for a church path, a customary route to worship or burial; here its sacred or liminal status makes shooting across it dangerous except at an unspecified height.

867cc9c32b447799dca939a386830a5c9e08385a.summary: Treacherous spirits and Bozen are also said once to have existed in our Valais.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: a Valais plural for troublesome goblins, bogeys, or house spirits credited with frightening livestock and disrupting households; the exact nature varies by tale.

notes.label: Staffeln
notes.text: plural of Staffel, the successive grazing levels, hut sites, or seasonal stations of an Alp through which herds are moved.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: plural of Alp, seasonally used high-mountain pastures with their huts and work areas, not merely mountain peaks.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Natisserberg
notes.text: the source's historical form for the mountain area associated with Naters, where the carding-noise spirit inhabits a house.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: the singular form corresponding to Bozen, a troublesome goblin or house spirit; here it makes a sound like wool being carded.

notes.label: Fäsche
notes.text: a long swaddling or wrapping band used to bind an infant; the spirit grotesquely uses one on the mocking hunter.

notes.label: fäschte
notes.text: the Valais dialect verb meaning to bind or swaddle with a Fäsche; the source itself supplies the gloss.

notes.label: Aschenpappe
notes.text: a thick ash paste or ash-based pap; it is what witnesses find packed into the dead mocker's mouth, though the recipe is not described.

85b703ee18645d7e377d7bd4257c96b61645adbb.summary: Reindeer lichen was once the herb richest in milk upon our Alps. Its stems, which have now become hollow, were then entirely filled with milk; for that reason, the cows had to be milked three times each day.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd, milking, and cheesemaking on an Alp; this Senn's unwillingness to milk three times a day deprives later generations of the miraculous fodder.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Cyprio
notes.text: the local plant-name used in the dialect curse for the milk-rich reindeer lichen; it is closely related in name and motif to Zyprion traditions in which a valuable Alpine fodder plant is cursed and withers.

notes.label: Dass me dreimol muess go melche goh!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘that makes us go milk three times!’—the lazy dairyman's complaint about the extra work caused by the herb's abundance.
notes.anchor: Dass me dreimol muess go melche goh!

8f84ebb59f022c46b4dd3a052727448b943189eb.summary: On the Gotthard road, where it crosses the Gornernbach above a fine bridge protected by railings to the left bank of the Reuss, lies the Pfaffensprung.

notes.label: Pfaffensprung
notes.text: literally ‘priest's leap,’ the place-name for the gorge crossing where the cleric is said to have jumped; Pfaffe is an old and sometimes disparaging word for a cleric.

notes.label: Gottesurteil
notes.text: literally ‘judgment of God,’ an ordeal whose outcome is treated as divine proof of guilt or innocence rather than an ordinary trial.

3a09f705d4fe9f3026b51ac64086a92b89f18cb7.summary: Beneath the gloomy Giswiler Stock in the land of Unterwalden lies a beautiful farmstead called the Iwi.

notes.label: Vorsäß
notes.text: a lower or intermediate seasonal alpine pasture and its farm buildings, occupied before or after the herd moves to the high alp; ‘lower pasture’ is close, but the term denotes a specific stage in the Swiss transhumance cycle, whose local timing varies.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Thio und liog
notes.text: a deliberately retained Swiss German command meaning approximately ‘Do it, and see’ or ‘Do it, and then you will know’; the little man uses it to challenge the farmer to follow the cheese’s rule, while the archaic wording and precise dialect nuance are uncertain.

26656d4e7fde3d056312feb79b4319fd57353a48.summary: In former times, the Zwingherren tower in the village of Silenen and the tower on the Flüeli near Amsteg are said to have been connected by a leather bridge.

notes.label: Sägi
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Sage, meaning a legend or orally transmitted tale; the collectors preserve the local word while distinguishing it from testimony attributed simply to old people.

72ace180baf4c2328be44d37bfa44e6c0342b696.summary: A little below the Alpliger Lücke, the pass between the Gescheneralp and Realp, a man had hidden a stolen roll of leather in a Gand.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine scree field, stony waste, or slope covered in loose rock; the thief hides the leather there and is heard working it after death.

2f42271f2db313cc6af3d12d9a9b4be08c7b1553.summary: Above the beautifully situated city of Lucerne on Lake Lucerne stands a mighty, jagged mountain formerly called Frakmunt.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, denoting specialist Alpine dairymen and herders who worked on high seasonal pastures; their individual duties in the tale are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: in German-language legend, a fahrender Schüler is a wandering scholar often credited with occult learning, here specifically linked to Salamanca; whether the figure is meant as a student, cleric, or professional conjurer is uncertain.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: gnappe
notes.text: this dialect word in the Lucerne weather rhyme means approximately ‘waver’ or ‘turn unstable’ and is retained for the rhyme; its exact local shade of meaning and pronunciation are uncertain.

290ae5eeba9ae166c5cce14408c21a848bfb1a4b.summary: In the tenth century, a queen named Bertha ruled the Kingdom of Burgundy, which at that time also included the land of Vaud.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

0fed31ea53c701e67052301a5c1f6ad531b0265e.summary: Beside the church path that leads from Titterten to Reigoldswil, the ruins of Reifenstein Castle rise on a jagged, almost freestanding rock where a side valley opens into the broad and beautiful Reigoldswil valley.

notes.label: Christofelgebet
notes.text: a ritual prayer associated with Saint Christopher and used in treasure-seeking lore as a powerful formula for compelling spirits, hell, and the devil; here its interruption causes the conjuration to fail.

notes.label: Potz Hagel! Da hämmert's!
notes.text: an excited dialect oath and exclamation meaning approximately ‘By thunder! Something is hammering there!’; speaking during the ritual breaks its required silence.

notes.label: Nei, du Kaib! Jetzt hämmert's nüd!
notes.text: the conjurer's dialect rebuke, approximately ‘No, you wretch! Now it isn't hammering!’; Kaib is a strong regional insult whose force varies by period and locality.
notes.anchor: Nei, du Kaib! Jetzt hämmert's nüd!

de6b343c533271934d7b730c4a0e08263de61dbf.summary: A series of legends relates the destruction of the most beautiful Alpen of the Oberland.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their pastoral landscapes rather than the Alpine mountain chain as a whole; the legends explain their destruction by glaciers.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here the mother's curse transforms the grazing land into glacier.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

f8c5370a8c74b0f12990375b4cb5f44ff1707fb5.summary: On the Glärnisch, there was once a magnificent Alp. The whole region between the rugged Glärnisch and the Bächistock was a single pasture.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here the splendid pasture on the Glärnisch is destroyed by ice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sänn
notes.text: a Glarus dialect spelling of Senn, an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking; here the impious son works his own high pasture.

notes.label: Stubäti
notes.text: a traditional evening social visit or gathering in a farmhouse room or Alpine hut, often associated with courtship; here the young man invites only his sweetheart, and the exact planned entertainment is unstated.

notes.label: Fähri
notes.text: a rare Glarus dialect word used here for the dirty, cattle-trodden stretch around the huts through which the herdsman lays cheeses as stepping-stones; the exact physical sense may be mire, manure, or the fouled passage rather than a formal pasture division.

notes.label: Firä
notes.text: the Glarus dialect form used here for the glacier or mass of old snow and ice that descends over the Alp; it is related to standard German Firn but functions in the tale as the engulfing glacial mass.

notes.label: Jöristag
notes.text: a Glarus dialect form of Jahrstag, the yearly anniversary of an event or death; here it is the day when the condemned herdsman must emerge and call from the Glärnisch.

dd49d97930a992b7bebf1888ca888ff77b4d4e7c.summary: a) In the ‘hohlä Gässli’ at Lucerne—or, according to others, at Brunnen—a shoemaker lived in a tiny Tatschihüsäli.

notes.label: hohlä Gässli
notes.text: the exact dialect place-name ‘hollow little lane,’ located inconsistently at Lucerne or Brunnen in the variants.

notes.label: Tatschihüsäli
notes.text: an Uri diminutive for a tiny, humble, low, or squat little house; the shoemaker’s dwelling is described by the form, but its precise architecture is not established.

notes.label: Burdi
notes.text: an Uri dialect body term explicitly glossed by the collector as the womb or uterus; the sorcerer is accused of piercing it in cows.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning; here he identifies the supernatural tracking dog.

notes.label: Leithund
notes.text: literally a leading, tracking, or guiding dog; this magically gifted animal follows a sorcerer across water, and the tale’s two breeding rules do not correspond to a modern breed standard.

notes.label: Butig
notes.text: a regional word for a workshop, workroom, or small shop; the shoemaker is sitting in his when the Leithund attacks.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning ‘little man’; here it explicitly describes the sorcerer’s small stature without identifying him as a wild being.

notes.label: bürgen
notes.text: the German verb to stand surety or guarantee; the tale uses its sound resemblance to Bürglen as a legendary place-name explanation rather than a demonstrated etymology.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Gleitshund
notes.text: one variant spelling of the magically gifted tracking dog; the source alternates Leithund, Gleitshund, and Gleithund without explaining whether the initial consonant changes the creature’s kind.

notes.label: Gleithund
notes.text: another recorded variant spelling of the Leithund name; in this account it is recognized by its humanlike eating and is born under a different nine-pup rule.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working seasonally with livestock on an Alp; here they pursue the dog and recognize the hide buyer as the alleged sorcerer.

c776b17996d225ccd8d599ad8b279403085058f8.summary: Long ago, when a man was to be hanged or executed by the sword and a maiden came forward and offered to marry him, his life was spared provided that he consented to the marriage.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young woman; here the diminutive identifies the prospective bride in the tale's bluntly comic and historically sexist judgment.

notes.label: Rots Haar, spitzi Nasä
notes.text: the opening of an Uri dialect rhyme meaning ‘Red hair, pointed nose’; the full verse tells the hangman to strike because one execution is better than a hundred quarrels, expressing the condemned man's historically sexist judgment.

3219acd6a0d82d09193f2ec5a262120b38ae5fca.summary: When the Landvögte of the three lands of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden learned of Gessler’s death at the hands of the marksman Tell, they took fright.

notes.label: Landvögte
notes.text: Landvögte were territorial bailiffs or governors in the historical Swiss lands and are cast here as the agents of foreign tyranny; the historical accuracy of the tale’s blended offices and events is uncertain.

notes.label: Untervogt
notes.text: an Untervogt was a subordinate bailiff serving beneath a territorial governor, here attached to the castles of Schwanau and Rotzberg; the exact authority of each officeholder is uncertain.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Burgstall
notes.text: Burgstall denotes a castle site or the remains of a small fortification rather than necessarily an intact castle; the precise site called Perfiden is uncertain.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘bull of Uri,’ the Uristier is the canton’s great war horn and a symbol of its martial identity; the instrument meant in this telling and its historical date are uncertain.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Wämser
notes.text: the plural of Wams, denoting fitted jackets or doublets beneath which the herders concealed spearheads; the garments’ exact cut and period are unspecified.

notes.label: Kuh von Unterwalden
notes.text: literally the ‘cow of Unterwalden,’ this is the name given to the signal or war horn used in the castle ruse; the particular instrument’s history is uncertain.

notes.label: nid dem Wald
notes.text: literally ‘below the forest,’ this historical geographic expression underlies the name Nidwalden and locates Rotzberg; the intended forest boundary is unspecified.

95338069e589e3578d55df630b8bb8945e2ab718.summary: Northwest of the village of Oberfrick, the Homberg and the Thiersteinberg face one another.

notes.label: Sesseln
notes.text: the local name of the privileged farmland on the narrow valley floor below the Homburg; the source derives its exemptions from the countess's miraculous slide but gives no secure linguistic etymology.

notes.label: Rollbette
notes.text: the source's historical form for a bed capable of rolling or sliding; it carries the countess and infant safely down the slope, though its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep ravine or gorge in Swiss usage; the alternate version has the countess fall into one below Pfeffingen Castle.

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for a godfather; here the Bishop of Basel holds that ritual relationship to the rescued child.

notes.label: Junkernholz
notes.text: literally ‘Junkers' wood,’ the Frickthal forest named for the gathering of knights and their retainers.

notes.label: Freiung
notes.text: a place of legal immunity, refuge, or sanctuary; because three cantonal borders meet there, the tale imagines it as ground beyond any one rural police force's authority.

6906ae590f8ccd017c5384ae06746014fe58def9.summary: A man from Haldenstein was once standing watch while serving in the Dutch forces, and a powerful longing for his dear homeland came over him.

notes.label: S'isch Zit
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘it is time’; the witches repeat it as the ritual cue for each airborne departure.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Lichtensteiner-Bödeli
notes.text: a diminutive place-name meaning the little level ground or clearing at Lichtenstein; Bödeli evokes a small flat patch in mountainous terrain, not a broad plain.

02a9ccbdf6f438e2f25a3b966bb0d58ddc4e2722.summary: Two men who could not get along down in the valley could not do so up on the alpine pasture either, where one day they unexpectedly met.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Ilgen
notes.text: a St. Gallen dialect plant name closest to lilies, with the source itself identifying them as Berglilien or mountain lilies; the exact botanical species is uncertain, and in this tale the flower serves as the supernatural sign that exposes the murderer.

cb041c40f8dc40d8b558960439aea8550f2f3c98.summary: Whenever an Emmental Senn left his Alp in autumn and wished to go home, he had to leave a Kostkuh standing up in the stable; otherwise, he could never reach the valley safely.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder responsible for cheesemaking; the master leaves the cow while his subordinate, the Sennknecht, returns for her.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, and dairy economy; it is the abandoned autumn landscape through which the Black One pursues them.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kostkuh
notes.text: literally ‘provision cow,’ the one cow from the herd assigned to provide the Senn's own daily milk while he makes cheese; abandoning this intimate animal is presented as a required seasonal offering.

notes.label: Baren
notes.text: a regional or historical form for the cattle manger, feeding rack, or stall barrier beside which the abandoned cow's skeleton stands; the exact stable fitting is not further described.

notes.label: Sennknecht
notes.text: the Senn's subordinate herding and dairy servant; his attachment to Blumi leads him to challenge the supernatural rule.

notes.label: Kienfackel
notes.text: a torch made from resin-rich pinewood, valued for a strong flame; its light, together with bread and the dog, forms part of the servant's protection.

notes.label: Gaster
notes.text: a small sleeping chamber or loft-space in the Alpine hut; the source itself glosses it as Kammer, but exact hut layouts varied.

notes.label: Wellkessel
notes.text: the large dairy cauldron used to heat milk for cheesemaking; the first element's precise regional derivation is uncertain, while the vessel's use is clear from context.

notes.label: Turner
notes.text: the pivoting horizontal beam or crane from which the cauldron hangs and can be swung over the hearth; it is a specialized Alpine dairy installation.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture stage, station, or boundary at a particular elevation; the collector identifies this first Staffel specifically as the uppermost pasture fence.

354ecb522f4a6ecf5bdae7ba6e58b9829d94cfce.summary: Anyone going from the little town of Brugg to Zurzach encounters an old linden tree at the crossroads on the broad Ruckfeld, with benches built around its trunk.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin of varying value; the narrator uses it for the fiddler’s carefully saved earnings and later as the smallest unit of his cleared debt, so no fixed modern conversion is implied.

notes.label: Schöppchen
notes.text: a diminutive of Schoppen, meaning a small local measure or serving of wine; the exact historical volume varied, and here it emphasizes the innkeeper’s watered portions.

notes.label: Heulüecher
notes.text: literally a ‘hay-hole tool,’ glossed by the source as an iron hay hook; the innkeeper invokes it in dialect as a cruel means of dragging sleepy servants from bed.

notes.label: Lindegiger
notes.text: Aargau Swiss German for ‘linden-tree fiddler’; it is the dead innkeeper’s byname and later the name of his fiddling spirit in the Ruckfeld linden.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional Swiss local chief magistrate or senior communal officer; the innkeeper’s promotion gives him the authority he abuses, though the office’s precise powers varied by place and period.

notes.label: Schöppli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive for small servings or measures of wine; the ghost counts three of them in his boast about diluting wine, but the exact volume is uncertain.

notes.label: Schoppe
notes.text: the dialect form of Schoppen, a local liquid measure or serving; here one measure of water is mixed into the ghost’s fraudulent wine, with no reliable modern volume specified.

notes.label: Môss
notes.text: the dialect form of Mass, a larger liquid measure; in the cellar cry, smaller portions of wine and water are combined into one saleable measure, and its historical capacity could vary regionally.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night lads,’ young men who roamed after dark engaging in noisy customary pranks; the priest mistakes supernatural mockery for this once-common village mischief.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

5b5d24e2cf989c265a1493f9586693e439413241.summary: One of the largest and oldest trees in Aargau is the linden on the Bötzberg, which gave the nearby little village of Linn its name.

notes.label: Ruedels hûs
notes.text: Aargau dialect for “Ruedel’s house,” with Ruedel a familiar form of Rudolf; in the saying it means the Habsburg ruin associated with Rudolf of Habsburg, and the archaic spelling is retained for the rhyme and local voice.

e8e0be7724ead73ce4d919945935f23a1849ab96.summary: In former times, a mighty tall linden tree stood by the front mill at Hergiswil.

notes.label: Heilighäuschen
notes.text: literally ‘little holy house,’ a small roadside shrine or wayside chapel built here in reparation for felling the prayer tree.

notes.label: Mühlerain
notes.text: literally ‘mill slope’ or ‘mill embankment,’ the local site where the shrine stands.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

d2082f1e909656f73d516d389720eb2d50f8a156.summary: On the Grabser Alpen there once lived a terrible Lindwurm. It was as large as a tree trunk, dark red in color, and extraordinarily vicious by nature, for it devoured people and animals.

notes.label: Grabser Alpen
notes.text: the high seasonal pastures belonging to the Grabs area in St. Gallen, not a general reference to the whole Alpine range.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a great serpentine dragon of German-speaking folklore; this dark-red man-eater is killed by a specially raised bull rather than by a conventional hero.

fb46a2351d85c5a13654a63040fcfe11366e3ed9.summary: Between the villages of Ober-Siggingen and Unter-Siggingen, on the slope of the Siggingerberg, lies the little wood called Lirenhölzli, surrounded on the east and west by vineyards.

notes.label: Lirenhölzli
notes.text: the diminutive name of the small wood beside the Liren fields; Hölzli means a little wood or grove in Swiss usage.

notes.label: Liren
notes.text: the local field-name explained by the source from Latin lirare, the third turning or plowing of soil; the legend ties the cultivated ground to the murdered child’s cry, though the etymology is reported rather than independently proven.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: young men participating in Kiltgang, the traditional nighttime courtship visit to a sweetheart; here their late journeys take them past the haunted vineyard, not on an ordinary evening walk.

notes.label: Lirenkindli
notes.text: literally “little child of the Liren,” the local name for the murdered infant’s crying spirit; the diminutive carries both regional speech and the child’s smallness.

754b82b1e4f03f513068e824e34a6466656935dc.summary: A maiden was once clearing a piece of ground at Tödigerhütte on the Flumser Grossberg in order to plant potatoes.

notes.label: Allmende
notes.text: village land held or used in common, here the shared pasture on which the cattle graze.

notes.label: Blutanstossen oder Blutstocken
notes.text: historical regional names for the fatal blood-related or congestive ailment said to strike the cow after it hauled wood by its tail; the source gives no diagnosis precise enough for a modern veterinary equivalent.

notes.label: Maiensässe
notes.text: plural of Maiensäss, the intermediate spring and autumn pasture settlements between the valley farm and the high Alp; their inclusion makes the woman's wandering span the full seasonal landscape.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture and its working buildings, not simply a mountain; the ghost's punishment is tied to these human-shaped pastoral zones.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alptriften
notes.text: the open grazing grounds or pasture stretches of the Alp across which the apparition moves with supernatural speed.

notes.label: Das Alpmutterli
notes.text: literally ‘the little mother of the Alp,’ the local name for this cursed female alpine wanderer; the diminutive sounds familiar, but her endless circuit is a penitential haunting.

06702fc9fe3990b79b7f66b893041b6d8f405206.summary: In one place, a Rübi rushed down the valley and caused damage. The sacristan rang the bells against the storm with all his strength, but in vain; the priest prayed and blessed, but nothing helped.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri regional name for a violent debris-laden mountain torrent or flood surge; the account treats it as part of the storm and says that a funeral bell for children can halt its destructive course.

0381891b514baa052bc19fc030e7ca6d96fc9346.summary: Not far from a large city lived a broom maker who could barely manage to feed his wife and two boys.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8b869dc983b9546066854bf777fbe5890309c757.summary: Between Vernamiége and Mâse, in a ravine bounded by the two crossed ridges Charchilly and Terreyssy, it is said to be haunted and uncanny even today, from the Borgne up to the crest.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c04449f1a0e19507c14ed4fd5ce58087aa480a01.summary: Many years ago, on the Sandalp, which extends into the farthest corner of the Linth valley at the foot of the highest Glarus mountains, an evil man from Linthal had his Alpine dairy hut and, like the other herdsmen, spent the summer there with his cattle.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheese-making on a high pasture; here the title denotes the cruel master whose work includes boiling and separating milk.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

70b98c82e6038e9de25d9eacd3f8fdf94e6a0c32.summary: The Wiedereck is a mountain covered with vines from foot to crown, beside the village of Effingen in the Fricktal.

notes.label: Most
notes.text: freshly pressed and often still-fermenting fruit juice, here grape must produced by the vineyard harvest; it is not necessarily finished wine and can denote cider in other Swiss settings.

notes.label: Bruderhäuschen
notes.text: literally “little brother’s hut,” a local name for the cave associated with a Waldbruder, or forest hermit; Bruder here has a religious-hermit sense rather than indicating a sibling’s house.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling male beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean helpers; here they guide travelers, aid workers, and rescue distressed farmers.

notes.label: Erdweibchen
notes.text: the female counterparts of the Erdmännchen, little earth-dwelling women who finish work and nurse the sick; Weibchen is a folkloric diminutive, not a neutral modern label for women.

notes.label: z'Nüni und z'Abed
notes.text: an Alemannic phrase meaning “at the nine-o’clock break and in the evening”; z'Nüni is the Swiss midmorning meal or snack, so the line means the helpers brought bread at customary workday eating times.

notes.label: Wunderfitz
notes.text: a nosy, excessively curious person, often with a mildly mocking tone; here it labels the man whose prying drives the helpful beings away.

1ca53a024b89f7ff8090e675738b31a3178995c6.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, the Pestleutchen once brought the Great Death from foreign lands into the mountains of Valais.

notes.label: Pestleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little plague people,’ mysterious personified carriers said to bring the plague from place to place; the Valais account distinguishes them from the invisible Great Death itself, but never explains whether they are spirits, demons, or uncanny humanlike beings.

notes.label: Landeshauptmann
notes.text: literally ‘captain of the land,’ a senior political and military office in historic Valais, closest here to the chief magistrate or governor; the tale uses the title for Michel Tschampen without defining his exact powers.

notes.label: Rippbeimännlein
notes.text: literally the ‘little man of Rippbei,’ the cat’s diminutive and ominously familiar name for Michel Tschampen in his hiding place; it marks him as the final person demanded by the Great Death, while its tone may be mocking, intimate, or merely dialectal.

cd7d24730dbbcc4dab3ebcf1bd940b4055b767a5.summary: In Graubünden, above Camana in the middle of the Safien valley, there once lived a wild Fänggenmännlein.

notes.label: Fänggenmännlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a male member of the wild, often hairy mountain beings called Fänggen in Alpine lore; here he is benevolent until his cheesemaking secret is spied upon.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally ‘ridge animals,’ a regional poetic name for chamois that emphasizes their habitat on high rocky crests.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: the plural or attributive form of Fängg, a wild Alpine being; in ‘Fänggen cave’ it marks the cave as belonging to the Fänggenmännlein rather than naming a separate creature.

notes.label: Gepsen
notes.text: shallow wooden milk vessels used in Alpine dairying so cream can rise; the source glosses them as milk containers, and their exact shape could vary regionally.

9bc65cbf7463c7c2f02842055b5f1feb61981f2b.summary: In the Voralpe of Rouaz in the Sanetsch Valley, so it is told, a merry nighttime dance was once arranged.

notes.label: Voralpe
notes.text: a lower or intermediate seasonal pasture used before or after the highest summer Alp; the two Voralpen frame the young people's nighttime route through the forest.

notes.label: Voralpen
notes.text: the plural of Voralpe, lower or intermediate Alpine grazing stations; the forest between them becomes the place of the uncanny encounter.

notes.label: Morse
notes.text: the local name for a grinding or scouring place to which the spectral company threatens to drag the dancers; the imagery suggests a water-worn rock mill or gorge, but the source does not identify its precise landform.

ab0242f9652a48ec5ec3677bbaa3e0789e12055f.summary: Many dwarfs once lived at Fontanix on the Wangs mountain. One day, soft sighing and moaning were heard beside the road there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d6a6a3eade7a19c58ad4823cdc35d66b19b7b55d.summary: Behind the Aerlisbacher-Egg, between the little village of Hard and the old Lawrence Kapällele, there stands all alone in a valley a terribly overgrown Flue called the Ramsflue.

notes.label: Kapällele
notes.text: a strongly diminutive dialect form meaning ‘little chapel,’ here the old St. Lawrence chapel near Hard.

notes.label: Flue
notes.text: a Swiss topographic word for a cliff, rock face, or crag; the Ramsflue is hollow and contains the beings' cave.

notes.label: Ramsflue
notes.text: the named crag behind the Aerlisbacher-Egg where the little earth men originally live.

notes.label: Mändle
notes.text: dialect diminutive for ‘little man,’ used in several singular forms for one of the cave beings.

notes.label: Mändlene
notes.text: dialect plural for the little men, especially as they bathe and flee together.

notes.label: Tüble
notes.text: little doves; the bathing beings are compared to small birds splashing in the stream.

notes.label: Hardpûr
notes.text: the farmer from Hard; Pûr is the local dialect form of Bauer, ‘farmer.’

notes.label: Füederli
notes.text: a diminutive load or little wagonload, here of brushwood bundles.

notes.label: Rîswälle
notes.text: bundled brushwood, sticks, or fascines loaded for transport; the exact construction of the bundles is regional.

notes.label: Riese
notes.text: a steep timber or hauling chute down which the little man hops from the rock face.

notes.label: Bindbaum
notes.text: the long binding pole placed atop a wagonload to secure it.

notes.label: Bindchneble
notes.text: the binding toggle or lever used with the rope to tighten the wagonload beneath the Bindbaum.

notes.label: abba, das macht nüt: sälben tho, sälben gha!
notes.text: dialect for approximately ‘never mind; what one does oneself, one bears oneself,’ the little man's refusal to blame the farmer for its own mistake.
notes.anchor: abba, das macht nüt: sälben tho, sälben gha!

notes.label: Chrütli
notes.text: a little herb; the injured being chews it into a healing poultice that instantly removes the wound.

notes.label: Härdmandle
notes.text: a plural or collective dialect variant for the little earth men when they help farmers save crops from weather.

notes.label: Schärme
notes.text: shelter or protected cover, especially a roofed farm area into which hay and grain can be moved before rain.

notes.label: Tenn
notes.text: the threshing floor or central working bay of a barn, where the beings carry exposed crops at night.

notes.label: Ofe
notes.text: Swiss German for the masonry stove, whose warm top or bench the little men use as a winter sleeping place.

notes.label: Mäntele
notes.text: diminutive plural for little cloaks; the beings' scarlet garments conceal their feet from neck to ground.

notes.label: Maitle
notes.text: dialect plural for girls, among the curious village children who scatter ashes to reveal footprints.

notes.label: Buebe
notes.text: Swiss German plural for boys, the other curious children responsible for driving the beings away.

notes.label: Härdmändle
notes.text: another dialect plural form for the earth men, used when the ash prints reveal their duck and goat feet.

notes.label: Geissflue
notes.text: literally ‘goat crag,’ the deeper rock into whose crevices the offended beings withdraw.

notes.label: Härdmändlene
notes.text: Aargau dialect diminutive plural for ‘little earth men,’ helpful cave beings driven away by human curiosity.

57cac5c4b2287f18cc2b2849c0707eb6b85f33e6.summary: a) A poor wretch with a large brood of children was in great need. Once, as he walked sadly and pensively through a forest, he met a strange little man who spoke kindly to him and asked the reason for his dejection.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: a magical mandrake familiar believed to multiply money but to be dangerously difficult to discard; this Uri account gives it the bodily form of a frog or toad, rather than the anthropomorphic root figure familiar from other traditions.

4ed35c3af415b2f208e30e8ec3f327a4be2b416e.summary: One evening, a little man came to a farmer in the canton of Bern who fed his hay to livestock at a remote place and offered his services as a feed hand.

notes.label: Zwillich
notes.text: Zwillich is a sturdy two-thread twill or ticking used for work clothes, here the gift that ends the little being’s service; the fabric’s exact weight, color, and regional cut are uncertain.

4860918f45bcff073e2ed874ef33e1813076a69f.summary: An innkeeper’s son was hunting foxes. A beautiful little fox presented itself, and he took aim, but the animal darted away.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

571ffe13d65ffc9fec16195198d043f0f445d7eb.summary: A fox stole the finest lambs and kids from the owner of the Ebnet at Sisikon.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small barn, stable, storage building, or farm outbuilding; here it has a hay door and serves as the hunter’s hiding place, but its exact construction is not specified.

notes.label: Napolitäner
notes.text: in nineteenth-century Swiss usage, a man associated with or formerly serving in Neapolitan military service, not necessarily a native of Naples; the contributor is identified by this old service nickname, but his exact unit or period is not given.

386e9ca9a4ad2e8e83125a1a68d8fe0b3d39e9d6.summary: a) Two men from Uri, one married and the other a handsome bachelor, went hunting on the Glattalp in the canton of Schwyz.

notes.label: Teeltschi
notes.text: a small side valley, hollow, or gully on the Glattalp through which the hunters look uphill; the precise landform meant by this highly local diminutive is uncertain.

notes.label: Niälen
notes.text: a pliable wild vine or creeper, probably wild clematis, used here as a cord to tie the fox to a stone; the exact plant species intended by the dialect plural or collective form is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

fd62921e4d6267e53c6b17a0b3d1bcbbd04549bd.summary: Once there was a poor, hunchbacked woman who was always ailing. She had no one but a son who would gladly have gone to school.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: fôles
notes.text: a Jurassian patois label for traditional fantastic tales; Rossat’s French title describes these as dialect stories collected in the Bernese Jura, and the term should not be mistaken for the modern French word folles.

6775750fb2d208168cd6a6384b92764810478cc9.summary: A quarter of an hour outside Sculms rises a high rock wall. In the middle of this wall, an old mine adit has been cut, though it can no longer be reached today.

notes.label: Bergmannli
notes.text: Alemannic for a ‘little mountain man,’ here the diminutive name of the mine-dwelling mountain spirit who controls a supernatural source of liquid gold; it is not an ordinary human miner.

364dc22dcd538715eef06da65de61fd33b54eaf6.summary: An alp in Goms is said often to have been very uncanny. Suddenly at night the cattle would leap from their resting places and scatter bellowing in every direction, so that the Alpine herdsmen had the greatest difficulty driving them together again.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: a regional plural for frightening supernatural beings, roughly ‘bogeys’ or ‘goblins’; the herders contrast them with wild animals as a possible cause of the cattle’s panic, but the category is imprecise.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman; here the Senn confronts the gray spirit and assists its redemption.

notes.label: Betenläuten
notes.text: literally ‘prayer ringing,’ the ringing of a church bell calling people to prayer; the spirit’s confession lasts until this morning signal, though the precise local hour is not specified.

184a529f380d52065328c2c8daedeb5d705fa06e.summary: Once every year, a man from Bürglen drove cattle “across into the Italian-speaking country” to the Italian autumn markets.

notes.label: Allarünä
notes.text: an Uri folk name apparently related to Alraune, the magically wealth-producing mandrake or familiar of wider German-language belief; here it takes the form of a little green frog that doubles money but endangers its owner's soul.

notes.label: Allrünäli
notes.text: the diminutive regional variant of Allarünä, literally marking the creature as little; it names the same money-producing frog familiar, whose rules of ownership and care the tale describes.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

0367816f4e473561673e89af1434d60687f97e57.summary: Near the Riset barn, about half an hour below Guttet, a green man is said to have been seen often, and he played many a wicked trick on passersby.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

1271e1d194059f769e59a514cf3d3b14b7098ab2.summary: After wisdom was no longer lacking in any other community up and down the land, only the Senter (Sinser) still lacked it.

notes.label: Senter
notes.text: the inhabitants of Sent, with Sinser supplied by the source as an alternate form; the first episode makes them the last community still lacking wisdom.

notes.label: mo guarda
notes.text: the source glosses this local Romance or Romansh phrase as “just look”; the joke treats the exclamation as the origin of the village-name Guarda, though it is folklore rather than linguistic evidence.

notes.label: kommlich
notes.text: a regional word meaning convenient or comfortable, as the source itself glosses it; the people of Furna imagine how useful a single needle would be.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical Swiss local magistrate or chief community official; here the Gemeinde-Ammann claims to hold every municipal office and leads the absurd needle-seed expedition and punishment.

notes.label: ferggen
notes.text: a regional verb meaning to fetch, procure, or arrange transport, as the source glosses it; the Ammann travels personally into Tyrol for the supposed needle-seed.

notes.label: rübis und stübis
notes.text: a Swiss German expression meaning completely, root and branch, or without leaving anything behind; it emphasizes that the donkey consumes the entire green needle-crop.

e51d4540fb0cb945a2579b52b666f3726cb09b11.summary: Long ago, before the old trade road to and from the Zurzach fair passed through Tegerfelden, a wondrous married couple lived in this village.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Fronfastenkind
notes.text: a child born during an Ember fast, traditionally believed to possess second sight and power to see or address spirits.

notes.label: Gülle
notes.text: Swiss German for liquid manure or slurry collected at a farm; the little man accepts it as his new dwelling, provided his small dung heap remains untouched.

notes.label: Quatemberzeiten
notes.text: the four Ember seasons of the church year, quarterly fast periods that folklore treats as spiritually charged times.

notes.label: zwischen Feuer und Licht
notes.text: literally ‘between fire and light,’ a traditional expression for twilight, when indoor firelight begins to replace daylight.

notes.label: Wahrspruch
notes.text: an inscribed maxim or saying presented as carrying truth or wisdom; the source does not give its wording.

02e84af4068ab59f4b99828a0f501b66002c14b3.summary: Whenever the forest stream called the Lombach, which flows through the wild and narrow valley of Habkern, threatens to fill with water and overflow, a little man comes striding along its bed before the waters surge.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d875765a78c0c9956e37968d9f8ba0d267907b19.summary: The clock on the tower of the Mels church struck eleven. The priest, Dean Fils, lay in his first sleep.

notes.label: Mesner
notes.text: a sacristan or church sexton, here accompanying the priest at night with the lantern and assisting the sacramental visit.

notes.label: Vater-Unser
notes.text: the Our Father or Lord's Prayer; the editor explains daily recitation to Saint Joseph as protection against dying without spiritual preparation.

notes.label: jähen Todes
notes.text: literally ‘sudden death,’ preserved in the source's grammatically inflected quotation; it means death arriving before confession, Communion, or other preparation rather than necessarily a violent death.

c675ef10e19af27aa19ef499f65aaabcc79b82ef.summary: When the religious house of Interlaken stood at the height of its power and clever provosts had managed to extend its possessions far beyond the gates of Bern and concentrate the finest Alp holdings all around in their own hands—when abundance and luxury had become the watchword of its monks—the…

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its economically valuable livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the monastery’s control of such holdings illustrates its wealth.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss geographical term for a steep rock face, crag, or cliff; here it is the sheer drop over which the pursued girl leaps.

notes.label: Das Hardermannli
notes.text: literally ‘the little man of the Harder,’ the human-like stone face on the Harder above Interlaken; the legend identifies it with a condemned monk rather than a separate dwarf-like being.

03e75954452689070e83cab9d0cb71a3e0bfc3f1.summary: The Little Man on the Withered Branch

notes.label: Charer
notes.text: a Bernese-dialect occupational word, most likely a carter, cart driver, or carrier working among the villages; the exact scope of the job is uncertain.

notes.label: Jümpferli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive of ‘Jungfer,’ referring here to the farmer’s young unmarried maidservant; depending on context it can mean a young maiden, girl, or serving maid.

b8b6600c32dbdb74100486aaf4726b753719a5f9.summary: There were also Erdleutle in Uri's Jsenthal. One lived in a rocky cave from which it emerged to receive milk, Sufi, and similar foods from the nearby Senn.

notes.label: Erdleutle
notes.text: literally ‘little earth people,’ subterranean or cave-dwelling beings related to dwarf traditions; the plural names the class present in Isenthal.

notes.label: Sufi
notes.text: a regional whey-based dairy food or drink, elsewhere spelled Suffi; recipes varied, and this story does not state whether Ziger or another ingredient was mixed into it.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder; the cave being receives characteristic dairy foods from him.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Leutle
notes.text: literally ‘little person’ or ‘little being,’ an affectionate or minimizing regional form used for the Erdleutle; it need not imply a human child.

63e42f37d12eb3ad584c3bbc6c8206e5e44d6a42.summary: Once a poor, pious Bürli died and came to the gate of heaven. At the same time, a very rich gentleman was also there and wanted to enter heaven.

notes.label: Bürli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Bauer, meaning a little or humble peasant farmer; its social contrast with the rare rich gentleman is the point of the heavenly joke.

967d74b2183fc32a7484ff97eb171907ffbf338e.summary: In the fourteenth century there was a great Sterbet in the Bernese country.

notes.label: Sterbet
notes.text: a regional historical expression for a great mortality or time of epidemic dying; in this context it refers to the plague rather than to one individual death.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little man’; the strange figure and his wife carry the scythe and broom that symbolize mowing people down and sweeping the valley clear.

notes.label: Helf dir Gott!
notes.text: literally ‘May God help you!’ or ‘God help you!’; the tale gives the plague as the origin of this protective response to a sneeze, which resembles the English custom of saying ‘bless you.’

notes.label: Brotstein
notes.text: literally ‘bread stone,’ the level landmark where the corpse-bearers or drivers stopped to take bread and wine during the relay to the churchyard.

notes.label: Bäuerten
notes.text: traditional local communal and farming subdivisions, especially associated with Bernese Alpine valleys; they are more than ordinary neighborhoods and could organize shared land and local obligations.

notes.label: Zeitglockenstein
notes.text: literally ‘time-bell stone,’ the popular name of the second relay stone; the story links it specifically with the death bell announcing the corpses’ final journey, although the name can also evoke a bell marking time.

notes.label: Pestleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little plague people,’ the uncanny pair personifying or carrying the epidemic; Leutchen is diminutive, but the figures are agents or omens of mass death.

3e4added6501677e38ccd13e0c5ba32fa957a27a.summary: At the outlet of the beautiful and great Lake Geneva, in which the snow-covered mountains of Savoy are reflected, lies the proud Swiss city of Geneva, which even today likes to call itself the Republic of Geneva.

notes.label: Escalade
notes.text: the French Genevan name, literally ‘scaling,’ for the civic festival commemorating the nocturnal Savoyard attempt to climb the city walls; ‘the scaling’ gives the literal action but not the event’s enduring local identity, and this account does not supply its date.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

ce1af143b95b2e07b80579980359f11d02b1ced3.summary: In olden times, very strange, dark-haired people from the Welschland often climbed up onto the Swiss Alps.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: the Romance-language lands as viewed from German-speaking Switzerland, here the southern world from which the Venetian prospectors come; its boundaries are contextual rather than a single country.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians,’ but in Alpine legend, mysterious foreign mineral seekers credited with finding gold and knowing magic; the tale links them specifically to Venice while preserving their folkloric type.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or staying on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; they host, tease, and observe the visiting Venediger.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on the high seasonal pastures.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a whey cheese traditional in Switzerland, especially associated with Glarus; it differs from ordinary rennet cheese and is part of the shared Alpine meal.

notes.label: Wildheulager
notes.text: a bed or sleeping place made from wild hay cut on steep mountain ground; it locates the visitor within the Sennen's austere seasonal lodging.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: giltmirgleich
notes.text: literally ‘it's all the same to me,’ compressed into an adverb meaning indifferently or without concern; the playful narrative voice describes how the herders initially watch the stranger.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine dairy and herders' hut where milk is processed and the seasonal workers lodge.

notes.label: lötig
notes.text: of legally or reliably assayed purity or weight, especially for precious metal; the promised ‘lötig silver’ is sound, full-value silver rather than mere silver-colored material.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: herds or complete seasonal cattle-and-dairy units descending from the high Alps; the form is related to Senn but refers here to the pastoral groups, not simply individual herders.

notes.label: Marmelstein
notes.text: a folk or dialectal form meaning marble; the shining Venetian house signals the Venediger's wealth and foreign magnificence.

notes.label: Tätschhäuschen
notes.text: a small, low-roofed house, probably with a broad or flattened roof profile; Tätsch suggests something squat or flat, but the exact local construction is not specified.

notes.label: Laubbett
notes.text: literally a ‘leaf bed,’ a rustic bed or mattress filled or layered with dried leaves; both the miraculous return and the heavy silver are discovered in this humble domestic sleeping place.

notes.label: Venedigerleute
notes.text: literally ‘Venediger people,’ the prosperous descendants named for their ancestor's friendship with the legendary Venetian; it functions as a family byname rather than saying they themselves came from Venice.

15653614ddb7913f5ad3b3f61007548aec0ba604.summary: Among the rent-paying properties of the village of Koblenz, the 1664 rent roll of the Klingnau provostry lists, on page 192b, the Söthenzelge field section, whose boundary on the reed meadow is marked by the Little-Child Pear Tree.

notes.label: About this telling
