source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

29bb6b2b6c2c4d979a493cabf16b3eb19e712257.summary: On the road from the village of Leerau to Staffelbach lies the Grossstein to the west and, to the east, a basin-shaped depression in the valley called the Lochluege.

notes.label: Lochluegenjäger
notes.text: the local Aargau name of the former castle lord’s roaming spirit at the Lochluege; ‘Jäger’ means ‘hunter,’ while Lochluege is the place-name and the story leaves the figure’s exact historical identity uncertain.

1a6cd29c1fb1876374def708afb66aab4789d567.summary: What a plague of locusts is — or rather, what damage these tiny creatures can cause — is now, unfortunately, known from experience in the Upper Valais, especially around Visp.

notes.label: Straffeln
notes.text: the Upper Valais folk name for the destructive locusts described here; its closest English equivalent is simply ‘locusts,’ but retaining the dialect word preserves the name whose earlier reports local people had doubted, and its literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

6cd08ceaf09f871bb0037b994e357a25688de7d5.summary: Not far from Magdenau Abbey, Allenschwanden Castle stood on a Gütsch; and across the valley, likewise on a mountain ridge, stood another castle.

notes.label: Gütsch
notes.text: a Swiss German landscape term for a small projecting hill, ridge, or elevated spur; here it is the rise on which Allenschwanden Castle stood, and the precise landform depends on local usage.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

5a42ec941cf67751c57263a01946f575c977edf1.summary: Two hours above Brig, where the Rhone foams like a mountain torrent through its narrow bed of rock, lies the little village of Moerel.

notes.label: Moerel
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Mörel, the Valais village above Brig and below the Riederalp; the tale offers a legendary origin for its bull-head arms.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical title for a young nobleman or member of the lesser landed nobility; here it identifies both the ruling lords of Moerel collectively and the particular lord who confronts Baschi, rather than serving as a personal name.

notes.label: Goms
notes.text: the upper Rhone valley district whose villages and high pastures Baschi searches; its farmers later assemble to attack Mangipani from above.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schleife
notes.text: here an inclined timber chute or ramp built to roll logs and boulders down against the castle, not the drag-sled sense the word can carry in other Alpine accounts.

notes.label: Oberwalliser Völklein
notes.text: literally the “little people of Upper Valais,” an affectionate or folksy collective for the Upper Valais populace; the diminutive need not imply that the fighters were physically small.

5a50e9f533aecc65d0d348a3731dc82e861db04c.summary: On the southwest side of the Jungfrau, high above its foot, lies a fearsomely glaciated valley, the Rotental or Rottal.

notes.label: Alps
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their associated livestock grounds rather than the mountain range as a whole; the tale remembers a fertile pasture lost beneath ice.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: plural of Firn, old compacted high-mountain snow that survives a summer and can feed glaciers; here the trembling Firnen form part of the supernatural destruction, though the word may also evoke the snowy heights more broadly.

notes.label: Talherren
notes.text: literally “valley lords,” the oppressive rulers condemned to wander as weather-portending spirits; “the gray Talherren” is the local omen phrase, and it is unclear whether gray describes their appearance, the weather, or both.

8aebaf7376eaecf78715f17159ce30739ee8b661.summary: The first people to set foot in the Kiental were two brothers. When they saw the beautiful pastureland spreading through two valleys, they asked themselves how they should divide it between them.

notes.label: Kiental
notes.text: the Kien valley in the Bernese Oberland; Tal means ‘valley,’ and the name refers both to the valley and its settlement.

notes.label: Losplatte
notes.text: literally ‘lot slab’ or ‘casting-lots stone,’ the large flat stone upon which the brothers draw lots to divide the valley's pastureland; the place-name preserves the story of that division.

99bd216c7e6efcc90d386481ce19e9e7df3263b9.summary: On one of the branches of the Jura above the village of Ettingen lie the remains of Fürstenstein Castle, once the fortified residence of the Lords of Rothberg.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f17821fcfec1d1430b68064ddf5883881c72706b.summary: A farmer named Oswald at Itramen in the Grindelwald Valley had 7 magnificent cows.

notes.label: Lecktäschlein
notes.text: literally ‘little licking pouch,’ a shepherd's small bag for salt given to livestock, as the source itself explains.

notes.label: nach Sennenart
notes.text: ‘in the manner of alpine herdsmen,’ describing the dwarf's traditional herding yodel to the cows.

notes.label: Trift
notes.text: open grazing ground or a stock-driving pasture route, here the barren terrain where Oswald searches.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain men,’ dwarf-like alpine beings who tend animals but punish careless or irreverent speech.

notes.label: Dillen
notes.text: a regional word for teats; the missing fourth teat is the visible punishment for Oswald's muttered curse.

b4c1ecd8259b364d01720185e556e0ab9320c7cf.summary: In former times mining was also attempted at several places in the Stürviser-Tal, but without substantial success.

notes.label: Stürviser-Tal
notes.text: the valley district in which the unsuccessful mines and the Venediger’s hidden workings are located.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the senior Alpine dairymen or cheesemakers who preserve the local account.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: a legendary itinerant Venetian or southern mineral seeker believed in Alpine folklore to recognize hidden ores and treasures by secret arts.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker who once lodged the Venediger and is later told the mine’s secret.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

f68374dc5fa2b43110baa7cc10473f4c343e6ff4.summary: In the foothills of the Sanetsch valley, between Garey and Malonnaz, loose stone rubble shows the traces of an ancient landslide.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: a little spring or fountain, whose water the poor travelers share beside the rich man’s house.

notes.label: Voralpe
notes.text: a lower or intermediate Alpine pasture used before or after the livestock’s stay on the highest summer alp.

06764089fa0953feaf8606c3529f89ca6e99b8fc.summary: A hunter had lost his beloved Zytgeissli, as young goats are called in Valais, and this grieved him deeply.

notes.label: Zytgeissli
notes.text: the source's Valais name for a young goat; the diminutive also conveys the hunter's affection for the animal.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working settlement whose huts are deserted once the grazing season ends.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schirmtanne
notes.text: literally a “shelter fir,” a broad protective fir beneath which an animal can bed down among dry needles.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the hut of an Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker, used here by the hunter as an overnight refuge.

notes.label: Männchen
notes.text: literally “little man,” the diminutive supernatural figure who slaughters, eats, and then restores the goat.

notes.label: Wilt auch
notes.text: dialect for “want some too?”; the Männchen repeatedly offers the hunter meat from his own missing goat.

notes.label: hinet
notes.text: dialect for heute Nacht, “tonight,” as the source itself explains in parentheses.

notes.label: Fürheissli
notes.text: the spirit's dialect nickname for the hunter's rifle, glossed by the source as die Büchse; literally it evokes a little fire-hot object.

notes.label: Hund Beissli
notes.text: literally “dog little-biter,” the spirit's rhyming name for the hunter's protective dog.

notes.label: Zytgeisslil
notes.text: the source's final dialectal or irregular variant of Zytgeissli in the spirit's threat; it again refers to the lost young goat.

9eb7239edac80fb2572d2f43d874c891d355a03e.summary: An Austrian knight was captured by the Swiss in war and confined in the tower at Wallenstadt.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c1f712a984a41e178fcc86d8ba563ad8c3d98f54.summary: Years ago there lived in Ruis a very skillful hunter who, during the chamois-hunting season, brought home a chamois every day.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Ruiser-Alpe
notes.text: the high pasture belonging to Ruis through which the two hunters pass; Jecklin uses the historical place-name Ruis, now generally Rueun.

notes.label: Ruscheiner-Alpe
notes.text: the neighboring high pasture toward which the unseen chamois appear to flee, associated with Ruschein.

notes.label: Grattier
notes.text: literally approximately a “ridge animal,” a regional Alpine expression for a chamois or similar high-mountain game animal.

notes.label: Freigewehr
notes.text: literally a “free rifle,” an enchanted hunting gun whose shooter can strike otherwise unseen or supernaturally protected game; the source does not explain how the hunter obtained it.

bfa130033fe4fb167f696104793db5c813908b27.summary: The high pasture of Lusgen lies at Aletschbort and belongs to Belalp. The legend tells of the countess ‘z'en Tischen’ and her rich treasure.

notes.label: Boze
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for a bogey, haunting spirit, or frightening supernatural being; here the Lusgen Boze polters in an Alpine hut and demands an empty manger, but the term does not define its exact nature.

4cf8cfe35228c2056ea88260e70bf0fff9c5cf68.summary: More than a generation ago, a very poor man lived in Tägerig among the last houses on the country road toward Mellingen.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Geldschisser
notes.text: literally and coarsely a ‘money-shitter,’ a supernatural household creature that multiplies a seed coin overnight under strict rules; the grotesque name underscores the pact's debased wealth.

notes.label: Pfund
notes.text: a historical pound measure whose weight varied by territory and period; the prescribed ten Pfund of butter should not be treated as ten modern standardized pounds.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: Swiss German for butter; the absurd cure requires an entire market tub of it every day, though the source does not say whether it was eaten in any special preparation.

notes.label: Ständler
notes.text: the source's local label for members or associates of the suspicious Zofingen group; whether it denotes a particular religious tendency, an association, or merely a polemical nickname is uncertain.

notes.label: Lädeligugger-Xaveri
notes.text: the variant form of Lädeligugger-Faveri used in the body of the tale, with Xaveri making the underlying personal name clearer; both forms refer to the same man.

notes.label: Lädeligugger-Faveri
notes.text: a local nickname for the doomed man; Lädeligugger suggests someone who peers into little shops or display windows, while Faveri is a dialect form related to the name Xaveri, but the nickname's full local implication is uncertain.

3c91b4ace5710156fec180c4b96ca4e25838c019.summary: Humorous narratives travel up and down the country as ‘little samples’ or ‘little pieces.’ Almost every village in our region bears a nickname hung upon it by the teasing of friendly neighbors, but none stands out in particular.

notes.label: Läheme
notes.text: the local nickname for an inhabitant of the community mocked in this humorous tale; the closest sense is a village demonym, but the source does not identify its literal derivation or exact place-name, and the joke depends on retaining the label.

68fd3a9be5bdea8d2dace21ebec8e8f3d5175060.summary: At the time when the Swedes were besieging the town of Rheinfelden, they bribed a rich and violent citizen inside with a large sum of money to deliver the fortress into their hands.

notes.label: Drî-Iuege wie d’Chueh im Schwedekrieg
notes.text: a Rheinfelden dialect saying meaning roughly ‘to look as the cow did in the Swedish War,’ used for an extremely gaunt or wretched appearance; its cultural force comes from the story’s famine-starved cow, and the historical spelling is retained.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Saum
notes.text: a historical Swiss and south-German liquid measure, here used for the quantity of oil in Gast’s cauldron; its exact volume varied by place and period, so the source’s measure is left unconverted.

notes.label: Betzeitläuten
notes.text: the ringing that announced the customary time of prayer, an important marker in Catholic Swiss daily life; here it also marks the hour after which Gast’s apparition becomes dangerous.

notes.label: Lälle
notes.text: an Alemannic word associated here with a tongue thrust out in mockery and, by extension, the local name of Gast’s demonic apparition; the story itself explicitly derives the name from that gesture, though its wider dialect shades are not specified.

notes.label: Malter
notes.text: a historical regional dry measure whose size varied considerably; in this simile it conveys the monstrous swelling of a victim’s head rather than a precise modern volume.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

6369302b609e8c9223c3b3902bdd61a3343b8998.summary: On the side facing the village of Wegenstetten, high in the cliffs of the Fricktal Jura mountain called Homberg—or, to distinguish it from others of the same name, Thiersteinberg—lies a cave with a stone bench and baking trough hewn out on both sides.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-man,’ a regional diminutive for one of the helpful subterranean dwarf-like folk; here Lämmli inhabits a cave and secretly leaves baked food for farmers.

notes.label: Wähen
notes.text: Swiss flat tarts or open-faced baked pastries, which may be sweet or savory; the source does not specify the filling of those left by Lämmli.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

f508b90728a107a8368062b8de332c2121721425.summary: Two Geissbuben in Isental, who preferred stretching out in the cool shade to running after the goats, were seized by a farmer by their hair and ears because the goats had grazed the tastiest herbs from his land.

notes.label: Geissbuben
notes.text: literally ‘goat boys,’ young herders responsible for taking goats to pasture; their reluctance to pursue the animals causes the farmer’s assault and their magical revenge.

notes.label: Jung Büeba und jung Hind sell mä niä räupfä, sy vergässet's nitt
notes.text: the exact Uri proverb, ‘One should never roughly pull young boys or young dogs; they do not forget it’; räupfä evokes pulling, plucking, or rough handling.
notes.anchor: Jung Büeba und jung Hind sell mä niä räupfä, sy vergässet's nitt

notes.label: Ruossdiele
notes.text: an Uri house term for a soot-darkened upper wooden floor or loft space; the book is found there at home, though the source does not specify the house's precise internal arrangement.

notes.label: Geistliche Schild
notes.text: literally ‘Spiritual Shield,’ the title of a protective and magical religious book tradition; the boys use its backward-read passage for harmful sympathetic magic.

notes.label: G'sätzli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive of Satz, here a short passage, formula, or ‘little saying’ in the magic book that enables the revenge.

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: a regional jacket, coat, or work smock; blows struck upon the garment are transferred magically to the absent farmer.

notes.label: Hinki-Michi
notes.text: Michael Imhof’s local byname; Michi is a familiar form of Michael, while Hinki’s literal reason or reference is not explained.

404e02af855e6d606241b3ca3f6aff61cec04c3b.summary: 1. Perhaps half a century has passed since a man from the Bernese Oberland distilled Enzenschnaps at Leweren in the Meien Valley.

notes.label: Enzenschnaps
notes.text: an Alpine spirit distilled from gentian root; it is the valuable liquor repeatedly stolen from the distiller, but the source gives no strength or recipe.

notes.label: Haspel
notes.text: a hand-turned reel or winding frame; in these accounts, turning it magically compels a thief to run back with the stolen goods, although the source does not explain the device’s construction or spell.

notes.label: Enzenwasser
notes.text: literally ‘gentian water,’ another regional name here for the remaining gentian spirit that the magically compelled woman returns.

notes.label: Golzner Loch
notes.text: a harsh local nickname applied to the accused woman from Golzer; Loch literally means ‘hole’ and can be a misogynistic insult, but its precise force and the identities behind her sons’ nicknames ‘Devil’ and ‘Satan’ are not established.

0faaae2fa41dacf33fcd277224457ec838067799.summary: Feld-Baschi's family in Gurtnellen had “a fine row” of smoked meat hanging in the chimney when a Romani woman entered the house, looked at it, and praised it.

notes.label: About this telling

ff0b3aab0d2c528175a33457e64f32fc0a155158.summary: An Oberländer was serving as a sentry before the royal palace in Paris. He paced back and forth and thought of his family at home and of the church-dedication feast (perdonanza) in his native place that was being celebrated on that very day.

notes.label: Oberländer
notes.text: a man from an upland or upper-country district; in this Graubünden tale the precise home valley is not named.

notes.label: perdonanza
notes.text: the local Romance-language name supplied for the home community’s church-dedication feast, a communal religious festival with food, drink, and dancing.

49b1ff80432c377f0a666ec29bfc7a4de9a766c8.summary: Three hours above Spitzegg, a bare head of rock rises from the brown of the Alpwiesen.

notes.label: Alpwiesen
notes.text: meadowland belonging to high seasonal Alpine pastures; the term describes a working grazing landscape rather than simply any mountain meadow.

notes.label: Klammsprung
notes.text: the local name of the bare limestone rock that opens at midnight on Christmas; although Klamm and Sprung can suggest a gorge and a split or leap, the source gives no authoritative derivation.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Runsen
notes.text: plural of Runse, steep erosion gullies or channels down which water, snow, or debris can descend; the uncanny white flowers grow in these cuts and in the rock’s crevices.

notes.label: Alpenrose
notes.text: literally “Alpine rose,” the German name for an Alpine rhododendron; this legend gives the enchanted rock an ominous, rare white form that no one dares pick.

notes.label: Goldvögelchen
notes.text: literally “little gold birds,” the source’s name for the small gold objects Klaus stuffs into his pockets; the context treats them as treasure pieces but does not say whether they are coins or bird-shaped ornaments.

85f6ac50238de314414984df38db767c091ede7a.summary: a) Among the apparatus belonging to Hans Blattmann of Ägeri, who had to answer charges of sorcery in Lucerne around 1597, were the following objects: a fire mirror, keys, a Krampfring, a silver sign, small consecrated wax candles, Marsamen, a little book of blessings, and finally…

notes.label: Krampfring
notes.text: a charm-ring intended to ward off cramps, seizures, or similar bodily afflictions; such rings were sometimes made from metal associated with an execution site.

notes.label: Marsamen
notes.text: an obscure seed named in this historical magical inventory; the source gives neither the plant nor its intended use, so the exact identification remains uncertain.

notes.label: Jungfrauenperment
notes.text: literally ‘virgin parchment’; the source explains it as parchment made from a lamb and credited with protection against blows and stabbing.

notes.label: Hochgericht
notes.text: the place or apparatus of capital punishment, especially the public gallows; objects taken from it were believed to possess dangerous magical power.

notes.label: Grien
notes.text: an old or regional disease term in this remedy list; its precise ailment is uncertain from the source and should not be read as a modern diagnosis.

ebdcfa2b5b0d64fd8db71dc9bcab8b80dd3c8d2c.summary: Once, the citizens of the good city of Lucerne had a bitter dispute with the country people of the valleys of Unterwalden nid dem Kernwald over a right on the lofty Bürgenberg.

notes.label: Unterwalden nid dem Kernwald
notes.text: the historical designation ‘Unterwalden below the Kernwald,’ meaning Nidwalden, the lower division of the old Swiss canton of Unterwalden.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades’ or confederates; in Swiss historical usage it means members of the Swiss Confederacy and emphasizes their sworn mutual loyalty.

notes.label: Alpenglühen
notes.text: the reddish afterglow seen on Alpine peaks around sunset, known in English as alpenglow; the herdsmen initially mistake the firelit sky for this natural effect.

notes.label: Nauen
notes.text: broad, sturdy traditional boats used for transport on Swiss lakes; here the Nidwaldners cross Lake Lucerne in them.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the presiding magistrate or chief elected official of a rural Swiss canton, not simply a military commander.

7003552f9dae435c8184484f3f4078295c86eb06.summary: When magpies repeatedly chatter around a person, that person must pray, for each time something bad lies ahead.

notes.label: Schnorren
notes.text: a regional livestock term glossed by the source as the Vorderkopf, the front part of the bulls’ heads or muzzles; the crutch-blow there stops them at the critical instant.

ddb92aab5cb7a977c11212f784202b2ffc2e33e7.summary: In former times, a white maiden was often seen near the rectory at Birr in the Birrfeld, standing beside a cauldron full of gold.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2a92dc3b2eb15f012cbc8de8bf01e3e2bd698c4b.summary: Late one evening, a man from the Hohlenweg near Reinach was gathering brushwood in the forest in the region where the so-called fire pond lies.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

23f1400d4291726d854570c552753ff0a202d09e.summary: In earlier times, the young people gathered on Sunday afternoons at a level place above the little village of Portels to dance and play.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, usually steep and wooded ravine or gorge, common in Swiss German place-names; Schilztobel is both the apparition's home and the site of her attempted redemption.

9bdee78473a6e246f6408c43c6bbcb941160561e.summary: In the castle forest near Forsteck, a woman was gathering leaves. Suddenly a beautiful maiden stood before her and said: ‘I am under an enchantment here.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

9a35de23f146b674d12fa7888aeedc50860747a5.summary: Between the jagged masses of ice of the Pers and Morteratsch glaciers rises a solitary fairy island called Isla persa, the lost island.

notes.label: Isla persa
notes.text: Romansh for ‘lost island,’ the meadowed rocky island between the Pers and Morteratsch glaciers that survives after the old pastures are covered by ice.

notes.label: Arvengruppen
notes.text: groups of Arven, the Swiss stone pines characteristic of high Alpine forests; their presence emphasizes the woodland said to have been buried by the glacier.

notes.label: Morteratschfirn
notes.text: the old compacted snow or firn field of the Morteratsch glacier; the compound situates the trees directly beside the glacier's accumulation landscape.

notes.label: Munt pers
notes.text: Romansh for ‘lost mountain,’ the name given to the mountain after the glacier covers the Alp and its side valley.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and dairying estate, not merely a mountain peak; the tale explains the destruction of one formerly rich Alp beneath the glacier.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior herder responsible for cattle, milk, and cheese on an Alp; both Aratsch and the later keepers occupy this socially important pastoral role.

notes.label: Sennentum
notes.text: the Alpine dairy operation and its collective pastoral yield; measuring each cow's milk determines how the season's production is divided among livestock owners.

notes.label: Totenbaum
notes.text: literally ‘dead-person tree,’ a regional name for a wooden coffin; Annetta is laid out in it beneath the mirror according to local custom.

notes.label: Gebse
notes.text: a broad, shallow wooden dairy vessel used for setting milk and collecting cream; the returning maiden moves from one Gebse to another to inspect the dairy work.

notes.label: Mort Aratsch
notes.text: the lament is understood as ‘Aratsch is dead’ or ‘dead Aratsch’; its repeated sound supplies the story's folk explanation of the name Morteratsch, though it is not a strict modern Romansh etymology.

notes.label: Barba Gian
notes.text: Romansh for ‘Uncle Gian’ or ‘Uncle John,’ a respectful familiar name for the elderly Senn who accepts the maiden's nightly care.

notes.label: Schmaladida saja quaist' alp e sia pas-chüra!
notes.text: the historical Romansh curse printed by the source, meaning approximately ‘Cursed be this Alp together with its pastures!’; it transforms the helpful maiden into the agent of the pasture's ruin after her expulsion.
notes.anchor: Schmaladida saja quaist' alp e sia pas-chüra!

notes.label: Signura da Morteratsch
notes.text: Romansh for ‘Lady of Morteratsch,’ the enduring local title of Annetta's wandering spirit and guardian of the lost Alp.

97062b54571f1331da3d1511d08e4cc71cce6c1e.summary: The Laubsberg lies north of the village of Seon in the Hallwil lake valley.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Swiss coin and monetary unit, historically of low value; asking for only a few Rappen emphasizes the poor man’s modest request, but the source does not specify the coins’ precise contemporary purchasing power.

217f2afa4496a3b1ec89005a064402f051a6b93d.summary: On the high Russein Alp, a Senn worked vigorously with his assistants. One beautiful summer morning, the door suddenly opened and a figure entered, strange yet inspiring trust.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its livestock-and-dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; Russein is the working landscape where the Senn and his assistants encounter the maiden.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock, milk, and cheese work on a seasonal high pasture; the source also calls the workers herders, and their precise hierarchy is not described.

ace368a507fcd65953185d601d43c96d6adcbca9.summary: In a little house outside the village there once lived a desperately poor married couple who could scarcely feed themselves and their only little daughter.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

882cae524cff3c6d23bed4c28837b206c50e8b92.summary: A little more than half a century ago, a cooper named Dietrich lived in the Grosse Riedera.

notes.label: Quatembernacht
notes.text: an Ember night, one of the nights associated with the Church's quarterly Ember Days; folk belief credited people born then with second sight.

notes.label: Schrätteli
notes.text: a small household, nightmare, or goblin spirit in Alemannic folklore; this ragged red-capped one alternates between companionship and malice.

notes.label: Gaumen
notes.text: the source's regional term for feeding and tending cattle; it explicitly supplies this contextual gloss.

notes.label: Tenn
notes.text: the threshing floor or central working passage of a barn; Dietrich crosses it while fleeing the thrown pitchfork.

0f3a8ac70a7d23dc7a2eeee2d4cc9665ea2b309d.summary: Above Erlenbach in the Simmental, there once lived a miserly man. His miserliness was so great that he begrudged even the feed for his cow, which he had named Vreneli.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Schlittlen
notes.text: Swiss German for recreational sledding; here it denotes the communal winter pastime and the slope on which the fatal ride occurs.

3774152572a8d3d872f97b7a37de975b1d3f8bb8.summary: “One day,” relates a sixty-year-old man from Schattdorf, “I was sitting behind our little table in the room when, all at once, through the open door I saw a man in shirtsleeves standing at the hearth in the kitchen.

d4dbedd3f56e4a08879ef16d3386fef5784c4a9b.summary: A man still living heard it from the son of the person to whom this happened.

notes.label: z' Licht
notes.text: literally ‘to the light,’ a Swiss custom of evening visiting or courting during the hours when households gathered by lamplight.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: the lower barn room, stall, or storage level beneath the hay where the nocturnal company assembles.

notes.label: Eh lueget, die alt Gret chunt au!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Hey, look, old Gret is coming too!’ announcing the witch who prepares the flying ointment.
notes.anchor: Eh lueget, die alt Gret chunt au!

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Häfeli
notes.text: Swiss diminutive for a little pot or small cooking vessel in which Gret stirs the ointment.

notes.label: Wunderfitz
notes.text: lively or nosy curiosity; Niderist repeats the charm because he cannot resist finding out what it will do.

notes.label: Oben us und niene a,
notes.text: the first line of the flying charm, approximately ‘out above and touching nowhere’; its second line wishes the speaker to Vienna ‘bis Dunggis Ma,’ a final personal reference that remains obscure.

notes.label: fremdi Stadt
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘foreign or unfamiliar city,’ Niderist's first perception of Vienna after the magical flight.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source's name for Niderist's yellow-sulfur-colored hat; its exact historical hat type is uncertain.

notes.label: Wams
notes.text: a fitted jacket or doublet, here bright red and reaching to Niderist's loins.

notes.label: Wiener-Niderist
notes.text: ‘Vienna Niderist,’ the lifelong nickname earned from his involuntary magical journey and much-repeated story.

f7ad57abe4078998cd25c2e96f01676ce4a381e9.summary: Once an extraordinarily strong man from Schwyz came into the little canton of Uri, flaunted his strength there, and challenged every Urner to a contest.

notes.label: Urner
notes.text: a person from the canton of Uri; the visitor from Schwyz challenges the canton’s local strongmen collectively.

notes.label: Bergli
notes.text: literally a little mountain, but here a small upland farm or mountain holding where the family lives.

notes.label: tiäg grad abnyddlä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘was just skimming the cream’; Nidel or Nydle is cream, and the cellar task explains the full milk vessels he carries upstairs.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a large regional milk vessel, tub, or shallow vat; the younger son carries one completely full upon each open palm.

notes.label: Schächentaler
notes.text: a person from the Schächental in Uri; the local valley identity is central to the strongman contest.

notes.label: Schwinget
notes.text: an organized bout or gathering of Schwingen, traditional Swiss wrestling; the challenger withdraws after the handshake demonstrates his opponent’s strength.

42971d63ce8e0995ca3de96f5c93111235cac93c.summary: A Senn on the Waltensburg Alp was once asked by a poor woman for a drink of milk.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; refusing milk makes his punishment especially pointed.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the source locates the Senn on the Waltensburg Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

4b80c9d87e028c1ec204e791e73eb1204fb70335.summary: In a forest called Muntclü, between the municipalities of Scuol and Ftan, a man appears at the witching hour.

notes.label: About this telling

3730841ae6c34c99b37163ab069fa5b8d70c8d41.summary: One day up in the Lammatt at Flüelen, my mother saw an old Grittschimanndeli—that is, a poorly dressed, old, shriveled man.

notes.label: Grittschimanndeli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for the poorly dressed, shriveled old man whom the source itself glosses; the precise derivation of Grittschi and whether the figure is a human visitor or weather spirit remain uncertain.

notes.label: Wetterhut
notes.text: a broad protective weather hat, here old and gray with its brim hanging over the man's face; in context it helps mark the uncanny scythe-peener as a portent of the evening storm.

daa4ef60c5006499b1bbbddd653a61b79259065a.summary: In former times, a powerful lord named Montacuay lived in a castle in Valais.

notes.label: Tochtermann
notes.text: literally ‘daughter's man,’ an older word for son-in-law; Michel jokingly releases Montacuay from that relationship when ordered away.

notes.label: Käterli
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive of Katharina, approximately ‘little Käti’; Michel uses it tenderly for his wife while promising to return.

notes.label: Höllenbraten
notes.text: literally a ‘Hell roast,’ a damned person or soul whom the Devil goes to fetch as prey; it is macabre comic language rather than an ordinary cooked meal.

notes.label: Hostie
notes.text: the consecrated Communion wafer; the girl's illness persists because she unknowingly profaned it by stepping on it and carrying it on her shoe.

1ac4c4a74e1f858dfc83221c5341ca892f4fbf8e.summary: Below Villnachern, on a low rise, are the remains of a castle that vague legend calls Lichtenau.

notes.label: Mandlene
notes.text: an Aargau local name for the black, long-haired wild man who roams beside the Aare carrying willow bundles; the closest contextual sense is a named wild-man figure, while the word’s literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Mandlehenjäger
notes.text: an alternate local name for the same wild man near Villnachern; ‘Jäger’ means ‘hunter,’ but the force and origin of ‘Mandlehen’ are uncertain, so translating the full name would create a false precision.

659572ede5025e8757d0824dce55a718ebb017bd.summary: An 80-year-old Älpler from Gurtnellen, who had worked as a Senn for more than 50 years on the Alp Gornern, draws from the well of his memories: It was the 8th of Herbstmonat, late in the evening, when I sat together in the hut at Rosti, a Stafel of the Alp just named, with Waldi-Peter and a man…

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; here the narrator’s specific work as a Senn is also stated.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for a herd’s milk processing and cheesemaking on a seasonal high pasture; the narrator says he performed this work at Gornern for more than 50 years.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; Gornern is the named working landscape of the encounter.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Herbstmonat
notes.text: an old German and Swiss month-name, literally ‘autumn month,’ normally meaning September; here the encounter is dated to its 8th day.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a grazing level, station, or cluster of herding and dairying buildings within an Alp; Rosti is identified as one such station.

notes.label: erwellt
notes.text: the inflected form of Erwellen, a regional cheesemaking operation involving the heating or working of milk, whey, or curd; the narrator glosses it here as having completed the cheese and Zieger, but does not specify the exact procedure.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a distinctively Swiss whey cheese or curd made from whey left after ordinary cheese production; it is named separately from cheese in the narrator’s explanation.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Tschoope
notes.text: an Alemannic word for a jacket, coat, or smock; the figure’s is grayish, but its cut and material are not described.

notes.label: aber
notes.text: an Uri dialect adjective meaning open or free of snow; here it says the Alp remained snow-covered for three days after the omen.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man,’ here the uncanny headless wanderer whose passage foretells heavy snow; the diminutive does not necessarily establish his physical size.

39d418a2ead6e147b60e9c72683ef727bea63f24.summary: When they went up to Alp Hinterfeld in the Meien Valley, it happened now and then that a little Manndli wearing a pointed, broad-brimmed Wetterhut and carrying a stick was seen on the Alp, although it never came near the hut.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain; the people are making their seasonal ascent to Hinterfeld when the omen appears.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: literally a little man, here an uncanny Alpine figure whose appearance foretells snow; the source does not say whether it is understood as a spirit, wild being, or human-shaped weather omen.

notes.label: Wetterhut
notes.text: a broad-brimmed hat worn for protection from the weather; this Manndli's pointed version visually marks the apparition that warns of approaching snow.

9dc82148f001530615a3096ee212bcbe414afbb1.summary: It was in the famine year 1816 when my husband’s grandmother, then 16 years old, and her 11-year-old sister went with their mother on pilgrimage to the Schmärzächäppäli at Emmetten.

notes.label: March
notes.text: a regional word for a territorial or property boundary, its line, or a boundary marker; the three apparitions and their books are interpreted as evidence of a fraudulent boundary settlement.

f8149c65579a48b4feedf5ce8a619e80f15fb849.summary: On the Laueli Berggut adjoining the Alp of Bolgen, two farmhands were occupied in erecting the Hag.

notes.label: Berggut
notes.text: a privately held mountain farm or pasture property, often with buildings and seasonal agricultural use.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, grazing rights, and dairy-working landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosed property boundary; its supernatural displacement exposes an earlier encroachment.

notes.label: Marchbriefe
notes.text: written boundary charters or deeds recording the legally established property lines; they settle where the fence belongs.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land whose members possess shared use rights; part of it had unlawfully been fenced into the private holding.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: hagen
notes.text: to build, set, or repair a Hag fence or boundary; once the men fence along the lawful line, their work is no longer undone.

notes.label: March
notes.text: a property boundary or boundary line, not a fairy tale; the title names the rightful boundary of the Laueli holding.

ef30b30d14e9e2d52dc660730d917c29e26bd503.summary: One evening a man walked from Closters to Montbiel to feed the cattle. There beside the road, at the place called Bündelti, he noticed a stranger tampering with a Marchstein.

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for present-day Klosters in Graubünden.

notes.label: Bündelti
notes.text: the local place-name beside the road where the stranger tampers with the boundary stone.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking the legal division between parcels or jurisdictions.

notes.label: Montbieler
notes.text: a person from Montbiel; the term identifies the witness by his home settlement.

notes.label: Marchen-Setzer
notes.text: a setter or mover of property boundaries; Marchen here concerns boundary markers, not Märchen meaning fairy tales.

05c73ea633ef17418588beb63a8c74cbca7e288a.summary: In former times, a black man carrying a fiery piece of hewn timber is said to have been seen at night in many places, pacing up and down across open meadows.

notes.label: Marchen-Verfälscher
notes.text: a falsifier or fraudulent mover of ‘Marchen,’ the local land boundaries or boundary markers; the title identifies a punished boundary-cheat, not someone who falsifies fairy tales.

38393f70f8f83600c4eafd14f1fee8684cf7edfb.summary: A shoemaker from Putz once took the footpath toward Buchen. He met a tall man dressed half in black and half in white, with a shovel upon his shoulder.

notes.label: Marchenrücker
notes.text: literally a mover of boundary markers; such a figure is condemned for fraudulently shifting a property boundary, and here he gains release only after an honest person helps him restore the stone.

cdf04d020626fe6d4eae25b220fb82b85101fb43.summary: In the previous century, the municipality of Cernez is said to have appropriated the beautiful Alp of Buffalora from the municipality of Cierfs in a highly dubious manner.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, buildings, and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: boundary markers or the legally recognized boundary itself; the Cierfs representatives refuse to accept them until shown a sealed document.

notes.label: chavalgiaint da Buffalora
notes.text: a Romansh expression meaning the ‘rider of Buffalora,’ the local name for the mounted boundary ghost.

notes.label: schwarze Brand
notes.text: literally ‘black blight’ or ‘black burning,’ glossed only as a cattle disease by Jecklin; the source does not establish a precise modern veterinary diagnosis.

notes.label: sömmern
notes.text: to keep livestock on high pasture through the summer grazing season; the verb belongs to the Alpine pastoral cycle.

notes.label: Marchstein-Geist
notes.text: literally a ‘boundary-stone spirit,’ a ghost condemned to retrace the disputed municipal boundary created by the alleged fraud.

6786b2f7899333a71e516c839ef9e024563ebfce.summary: At Hutt-Egg in Bauen, something had often torn the Marchsteine from beneath the woods at night and carried them some distance farther down into the private property.

notes.label: Marchsteine
notes.text: boundary stones marking neighboring parcels; secretly moving them is a property offense and a classic folkloric cause of supernatural correction or posthumous punishment.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land traditionally shared under local usage rights, often as pasture or woodland; the ancestor’s offense was converting part of it into private property.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

b9a0c53603848d837bf8afe3af76cde445837465.summary: Once, up by the castle at Reinach, a farmhand was driving a plow in the field with his master.

notes.label: Marchsteine
notes.text: Swiss German for boundary stones marking the division between fields, properties, or jurisdictions.

notes.label: Hoggene
notes.text: the source's Basel-area dialect plural for heavy hoes or mattocks; the ghosts strike with them so violently that sparks fly.

notes.label: Marchversetzer
notes.text: literally ‘boundary-marker movers,’ people condemned in folklore for fraudulently shifting property or communal boundaries; the headless figures reenact their offense.

efcb5e65ab7ea9badfe1ecdb81f6f518437f626a.summary: On the holy night, people from Schwarzenbach crossed the bridge by the Töbeli and saw two headless men who looked like Fenersäulen; a large black dog with a fiery eye was there too.

notes.label: Töbeli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for a small ravine or narrow wooded gully, used here as the bridge's local landmark.

notes.label: Fenersäulen
notes.text: probably ‘columns of fire’ or flame-like pillars, describing the luminous appearance of the headless revenants; the exact dialect form is uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: literally ‘boundary-marker movers,’ people condemned after death for fraudulently shifting property markers to steal land.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard abbreviation for the canton of St. Gallen, used in the parenthetical location attached to the title.

e926e55e6fbf060682cf6c635b22d1798ad5ad09.summary: During his lifetime, he was a respected man. In that capacity, he was guardian over a widow's property.

notes.label: Marksteine
notes.text: boundary stones defining the widow's property, moved to conceal theft of land or timber rights.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: people born during the Ember Days who are traditionally believed able to perceive spirits and other supernatural activity.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the prayer bell, commonly the evening Angelus, whose ringing releases travelers immobilized by the haunting.

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: literally a ‘boundary-marker mover,’ a dishonest guardian condemned to haunt the land he stole from a widow.

6d785037b387f75586a4b2c5de781f223d7d159d.summary: A man in the Kreuzgässli near Oberschan was awakened in the middle of the night by loud knocking, as though someone wished to stop for shelter.

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: literally a ‘boundary-marker mover,’ the folkloric name for a person condemned after death to revisit or correct a fraudulently shifted property boundary; here the ghost finally finds rest after moving the stone.

55820a4cb5f4d7d104e40f9fa12577d2a594d5fe.summary: In the forest by the so-called Weihwasserplatte on the road from Pfäfers to Vättis, a fiery man is said sometimes to have appeared at night and shot glowing bullets at those passing after 12 o’clock.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7ceafc127002ddbca3396d5ecd6e256a7220a29a.summary: In ancient times, the marmots in the Saaseralpen belonged to the Blandrati counts in Visp, who possessed them not as public authorities but as Alpeigentümer.

notes.label: Saaseralpen
notes.text: the high Alpine pastures belonging to the Saas communities, not simply all mountain peaks near Saas; the story treats their marmots as a managed communal resource.

notes.label: Alpeigentümer
notes.text: owners of an Alp or high seasonal pasture; the counts' claimed marmot rights are presented as an incident of landownership rather than governmental sovereignty.

notes.label: Ständern
notes.text: the source's name for marmot winter resting places or den sites where selective stone traps were set; the precise local construction is not described.

notes.label: Gletscheralpe
notes.text: literally ‘glacier Alp,’ the enclosed high pasture at Fee where the marmot population dies out; Alp means a seasonal grazing area, not merely a mountain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Murmeltiervater
notes.text: literally ‘marmot father,’ an affectionate local title for Johann Baptist Ruppen as caretaker and restorer of the colony.

notes.label: Jägerpatent
notes.text: a government-issued hunting license; the narrator's dismissive ‘scrap of paper’ emphasizes conflict between new cantonal law and older communal conservation rights.

notes.label: Talgemeinden
notes.text: the valley municipalities or self-governing local communities of Saas; they collectively administer the marmots and defend the customary arrangement.

e126d3e611c90b4d800ddf728601e7cd73c3d729.summary: In the high rock wall of the nearer Eiger is a large opening. This opening bears the name Heiterloch but is also called the Martisloch.

notes.label: Heiterloch
notes.text: literally ‘clear-weather’ or ‘bright hole,’ another name for the opening through the Eiger; here the same feature is also called the Martisloch.

notes.label: Martisloch
notes.text: literally ‘Martin's hole,’ a local name for the opening through the Eiger associated with Saint Martin; related tellings use the variant Martinsloch.

notes.label: Martinsdruck
notes.text: literally ‘Martin's imprint,’ the human-shaped hollow opposite the Eiger's opening; local legend interprets it as the mark left when the gigantic Saint Martin braced his body against the mountain.

0aeeeed613f51d98f7e0b0f2166b7e7511e517bc.summary: Until recently there lived in Lungern a man—God rest his soul—who wanted to be capable of more than eating bread.

notes.label: Feldspiegeln
notes.text: literally ‘field mirrors,’ magical seeing devices said to reveal distant and underground things; their physical form and the reason for ‘field’ in the name are not explained.

notes.label: Rechner
notes.text: literally a reckoner or calculator, but here a practitioner who discovers hidden facts through supernatural calculation; ‘mathematician’ would miss the divinatory role.
The oath beim tausend is translated literally as ‘by a thousand’; what is implicitly counted is left unstated in the source.

720d4d7ee7e09e93d70191b2d93018c42efc1157.summary: A wonder-working doctor once lived by the Devil’s Bridge near Einsiedeln in the Canton of Schwyz.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Tagsatzungsherren
notes.text: the gentlemen or delegates of the Tagsatzung, the historical federal diet of the Swiss Confederacy; the flying minstrel is magically dropped into the midst of their formal meeting at Baden.

notes.label: Raster
notes.text: the local Einsiedeln farmers’ nickname for Paracelsus in this legend; the source supplies no secure derivation, so it is retained as a distinct folk name.

21702e8eefcdcb30a761c586a4398ef8f438950e.summary: On Christmas Eve, a young stray kitten lay down before the window of a house in Reinach whose inhabitants were called the Matthise.

notes.label: Matthisethier
notes.text: literally the ‘Matthise animal,’ the household’s name for the malicious cat linked to the family called Matthise; the tale ultimately identifies it with a human informer accused as a witch, but leaves the mechanism of transformation or doubling unexplained.

notes.label: Sittengericht
notes.text: literally a ‘morals court,’ a local disciplinary body enforcing religious and communal standards of conduct; here it fines the housewife for washing during sacred time, though the court’s institutional composition and jurisdiction are not stated.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor administering an Old Swiss subject district; here the Bernese Landvogt at Lenzburg judges and executes the accused witch, but the tale does not name him or define the legal procedure.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt
