389e7d6b5f0883eded03ed14ee85dbb7521a7b2b.summary: When the Swedes besieged the little Rhine towns of Laufenburg and Rheinfelden, they devastated all the surrounding country in the neighboring Jura and behaved with particular inhumanity in the valleys of Mandach and Hottwil.

notes.label: Kirchspiel
notes.text: an older term for a parish and the territory belonging to it; here it is also the local name for the open countryside beyond Hettenschwil.

notes.label: VIII Alte Orte
notes.text: literally the ‘Eight Old Cantons,’ the eight members of the Swiss Confederacy before its later medieval expansion; their shields are credited with deterring the Swedish troops.

notes.label: Sennenloch
notes.text: the local name of a wooded valley near Hettenschwil, literally a ‘Senn's hollow’ or ‘herdsman's hollow’; it marks the limit beyond which the Swedes supposedly would not advance.

notes.label: Schwedenholz
notes.text: literally ‘Swedes' wood’ or ‘Swedish forest,’ the local name preserving the memory of the troops' woodland position and entrenchments.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally people joined by oath; here it refers to the members and collective authority of the historical Swiss Confederacy, whose name was believed to provide protection.

notes.label: Schwedenloch
notes.text: literally ‘Swedes' hole,’ the local name for the mountain cave where unprotected Fricktal farmers were said to have hidden from Swedish troops.

notes.label: Schwetti
notes.text: the local name of the spectral riders' watering place; it is associated in the story with taking horses to water, but its precise dialect derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Mattisee
notes.text: the local name for the hundred-voiced cries, banging, and rattling of the spectral Swedish riders in rainy weather; despite ending in See, ‘lake,’ it names the uncanny uproar here, and its exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Schwedenhaus
notes.text: literally ‘Swedes' house,’ a building traditionally associated with the occupying troops and said to have been moved from the Schwedenholz into Hettenschwil.

notes.label: Hohle Gasse
notes.text: literally ‘hollow lane,’ the local forest place-name for the site of the vanished castle and its buried treasure.

notes.label: Kreuztaler
notes.text: a historical thaler coin identified by a cross design; the four coins appear to serve as ritual or practical supports beneath the treasure trough, though the source does not explain the custom.

d52c74f2848cf9606bbd78d52332fec93da6556d.summary: When the grain all around is still green in July, on the Mauerhubel it can already be seen standing in completely yellow strips as wide as a Heerstrasse.

notes.label: Mauerhubel
notes.text: literally ‘wall hillock,’ the low rise where crop marks and Roman-looking debris suggest a buried road and treasure.

notes.label: Heerstrasse
notes.text: an old military or major through-road; the prematurely yellow grain forms bands as wide as such a road.

notes.label: Haselstöcke
notes.text: hazel rods or staffs, plants traditionally used in divination and treasure-finding rites.

notes.label: Wolffriedli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive or familiar form of the name Wolfried/Wolfgang, identifying the digger whose encouraging shout breaks the required silence.

notes.label: nu chäch, no einist früsch i d'händ g'speuzt!
notes.text: Swiss German encouragement meaning approximately ‘come on, boldly—spit freshly into your hands once more,’ whose utterance makes the treasure sink.
notes.anchor: nu chäch, no einist früsch i d'händ g'speuzt!

63e6f0524fad1dd09a0e90c699fefa116615fce8.summary: The night ghost of the Freiamt village of Meerenschwanden is a pig that is indeed called the Dorfloos, but is just as often generally called the Dorfhund, because the latter name is the customary regional term for any familiar local ghost.

notes.label: Dorfloos
notes.text: the local name of Meerenschwanden’s familiar village ghost, appearing here as a pig; Loos is retained because the source treats it as a specific regional ghost-name and does not give a secure literal derivation.

notes.label: Dorfhund
notes.text: literally ‘village dog,’ but the source says it was the customary regional name for any well-known local ghost, even when—as here—the apparition took the form of a pig.

b0d3e1fd969375a5a87b5089ac9565d94d0d2e22.summary: At Wintersberg there still stands a little house where three men wished to win a treasure.

notes.label: Meerfräulein
notes.text: literally ‘sea maidens,’ supernatural female water beings rather than ordinary young women; the inland setting and closing joke about a seaport make the name deliberately incongruous, while their exact form is not described.

notes.label: Spinni
notes.text: a regional word for a communal spinning gathering or its associated room; here the source says that the Meerfräulein had reached the Spinni, but it does not explain the precise space or arrangement within the house.

49f6df8b47b4840bcec96bddcb59412e6d1d24b9.summary: A boy from Bonaduz, having returned from Swabia, told his parents, among other things, that he could dance on a thread. — Everyone laughed at him.

notes.label: Meistersfrau
notes.text: literally the master’s wife; in the historical craft-apprenticeship setting she is the wife of the boy’s master and a member of the household in which he learned his trade, while the tale casts her as his teacher in witchcraft.

notes.label: in der Ordnung
notes.text: literally “in order”; here the quoted phrase means that the boy had been put right or restored after clerical intervention.

notes.label: Bonaduzer
notes.text: a person from Bonaduz in Graubünden; the clergyman’s prohibition applies specifically to anyone from that community.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

727661673c5ccf1eed020ef796e403c633195beb.summary: Where the great Ferpekle Glacier now lies, there were once beautiful meadows and villages.

notes.label: Melkfassalpe
notes.text: the local Alpine-pasture name in the title, literally suggesting a ‘milking-vat Alp’; the surviving text instead centers on the lost country beneath the Ferpekle Glacier, so the precise relationship between the name and the story remains unexplained.

a402a1eb9c5781b7be6f5df093776f85c4d7740d.summary: In Naters I heard it told that once, up on the Belalp, a Chinig lived with his young daughter.

notes.label: Belalp
notes.text: the high Alpine terrace above Naters in Valais; the tale imagines a king looking down from this real mountain landscape.

notes.label: Chinig
notes.text: Valais dialect for König, ‘king’; retaining it preserves the tale's strongly regional voice.

notes.label: Hubul
notes.text: Valais dialect for a small hillock or knoll used here as the girl's lookout point.

notes.label: Vorschuss
notes.text: a regional word for the front of an apron or apron gathered up as a carrying pouch; the girl scoops the tiny workers into it.

notes.label: Der barmherzig Chinig
notes.text: Valais Swiss German for ‘the merciful king’; the exact dialect title is retained while the English gloss makes its meaning clear.

e6d267d1815cc744bd7b756f28d3e25a51db24bf.summary: With the Merzenstein, an exposed boulder on a mountain terrace at Wyssig above Bauen, a witch intended to destroy the church of Bauen.

notes.label: Merzenstein
notes.text: the local name of the exposed boulder on the mountain terrace at Wyssig; the legend says a witch meant to use it against Bauen’s church, but the source gives no derivation for the name.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

905c81b734107504f73da5409f91bfbf845255ce.summary: The parish priest down in the valley had long noticed that the Sennenfamilie of the Hungerlialp never appeared at Mass.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Sennenfamilie
notes.text: the household of an Alpine herder or dairyman living and working at the high pasture.

notes.label: Hungerlialp
notes.text: the named high pasture and seasonal farmstead where the family lives; Alp here denotes the pasture complex, not merely a peak.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its associated huts or seasonal farmstead.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Mariä Himmelfahrt
notes.text: the Catholic Feast of the Assumption of Mary, traditionally observed on August fifteenth; it is distinct from Christ's Ascension.

notes.label: Heidenvolk
notes.text: literally “heathen folk,” the priest's rebuke for a family he wrongly assumes is living without Christian worship.

notes.label: Hochwürden
notes.text: a traditional German form of address for a priest, approximately “Your Reverence.”

notes.label: Messamt
notes.text: a celebration or service of the Mass; the family's miraculous open-air observance is the story's central religious practice.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine herder and dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese-making on a high pasture.

notes.label: Lärchen
notes.text: larch trees, one of the characteristic Alpine trees surrounding the sacred meadow.

notes.label: Arven
notes.text: Swiss stone pines, the other Alpine trees named around the sacred meadow.

notes.label: Himmelsglocke
notes.text: literally the “bell of heaven,” a poetic image for the blue sky arching like a bell or dome above the meadow.

notes.label: Himmelswasser
notes.text: literally “heaven-water,” the family's name for the water held in the stone basin and used like holy water.

notes.label: Weihwasser
notes.text: holy water in Catholic practice; the Senne uses it as the priest's conventional name for Himmelswasser.

notes.label: Blumenvolk
notes.text: literally “flower folk,” a poetic collective for the many brightly colored wildflowers around the stone.

notes.label: Turtmanntal
notes.text: the Valais mountain valley to which the priest withdraws to live as a hermit.

notes.label: Klause
notes.text: a hermit's secluded cell or dwelling, where the men later find the priest dead.

2d6242f622c69615259cb31807d7089eeb8f2989.summary: The old and original "Felliser Josi" of Brig, a true child of temperament, was known as a seer of spirits.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c2a775549ab84c51e9ef7c949ac7cc131dacfd25.summary: On the right bank of Lake Brienz are two places almost two hours apart, one above Ringgenberg and the other below Brienz.

notes.label: Milchisbach-Hund
notes.text: literally ‘Milchisbach dog,’ the local name for the enormous spectral dog haunting the shore of Lake Brienz; Milchisbach is treated as a place-name, and the story offers no secure derivation for it.

3d5850b90a7c5848b463200f252d8c4235aafc16.summary: North of Unterseen lies the Habkern valley. From its head, at the Lombach Alp, flows the Lombach, which often still becomes terrible through flooding.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Volle
notes.text: a regional name for a wooden funnel used in alpine dairying to pour milk, here employed as a warning horn; ‘milk funnel’ describes the implement, but the term’s exact local shape and derivation are uncertain.

7e445c8711acfdd90563d696cd23575175d6ca24.summary: The Geissler ‘Köbi,’ Jakob, and ‘Seppen-Lihert,’ Joseph's Leonhard, tended goats together on the Langwiese.

notes.label: Geissler
notes.text: a goat herder; the occupational title identifies Köbi's everyday pastoral work before the tale reveals his magical milking ability.

notes.label: Köbi
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss diminutive of Jakob, used as the goat herder's familiar name.

notes.label: Seppen-Lihert
notes.text: the local byname meaning ‘Sepp's Leonhard’ or ‘Joseph's Leonhard,’ distinguishing the second herder through family association.

notes.label: Hirtenstock
notes.text: a herdsman's staff; Köbi uses it as a magical conduit to draw milk from a cow more than half an hour away.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Geschirrlumpen
notes.text: a dishcloth or kitchen rag; in the folk belief summarized here, witches and sorcerers use such a cloth as the magical medium for remotely milking another person's livestock, though the source does not describe the procedure.

29b7971263182db57ea7b1d0fac21417b069b74e.summary: In ancient times, a woman lived at Hasle im Grund of whom the people said that she could draw milk from a strap.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e097a8baf275b78124b63f233e27b9ff8e416159.summary: Many stories are also told in Zermatt about the Godverjinen—dwarfs—little earth men.

notes.label: Godverjinen
notes.text: a Valais dialect name for dwarfs or cave-dwelling ‘little earth men’ around Zermatt; the source itself gives those comparisons and later varies the spelling as Godwerjini.

notes.label: Godwerjini
notes.text: a spelling variant of Godverjinen, the local dwarfs or earth folk said to have been displaced into mountain caves; the form can be singular or plural only through context in this account.

notes.label: Hochalpe
notes.text: a high-elevation seasonal Alpine pasture and its working area; here a mountain farmer keeps a milk cellar there, rather than the word denoting the Alps as a whole.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick or rich cream; here the Godwerjini steal and feast on it in the mountain milk cellar.

notes.label: Handwanne
notes.text: a portable shallow farm tub, tray, or winnowing vessel; here it is large enough for the farmer to hide beneath, although the source does not specify its material or exact normal use.

notes.label: Lass du d'Wanderle nur rüsten und schlapps du brav!
notes.text: Valais dialect meaning approximately ‘Just let the little tub make its racket, and you keep gulping away!’; the old dwarf recognizes the farmer's attempted scare and tells the younger one to continue eating, while Wanderle is a diminutive vessel-name and the exact nuance of rüsten is contextual.
notes.anchor: Lass du d'Wanderle nur rüsten und schlapps du brav!

6d10753811da9744417e9cf390bc1092d6734435.summary: Hans Sager wished to go home to Willisau in the depths of night—this happened 300 years ago.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night people,’ a central-Swiss collective name for uncanny processions or companies of the dead who wander after dark; here they enter a sleeping household to consume milk and punish a living guest who will not continue with them.

d20e0b74b84aa335e729172b2162afd05757927d.summary: In the municipality of Oberwil in the Simmental, a mill once stood in the Alchbachgraben.

notes.label: Alchbachgraben
notes.text: the ravine or gully of the Alchbach in Oberwil where the doomed mill stands; Graben conveys both a watercourse cut and a steep-sided channel.

notes.label: Mahlknecht
notes.text: a hired mill hand, literally a servant engaged in grinding grain; here he seduces or otherwise ruins one of the widow's daughters.

notes.label: Talleute
notes.text: literally ‘valley people,’ the inhabitants of the Simmental whom the final miller oppresses until they curse the mill.

680d8920bd0d814de519e024a6177ae28f282d02.summary: A miller is long plagued by a wife who has given herself over to witchcraft, but he cannot prove it against her.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Müllihau
notes.text: a regional miller's tool name, apparently referring here to a pick or hammer used while working or dressing the millstone; the exact historical tool form is not explained in the source.

notes.label: Breithammer
notes.text: literally a broad hammer or broad-faced hammer; the miller uses it to sever the cat's paw, producing the identifying wound on his wife.

2ba2173aac927067a57549ea0efd8fe7ea5b963f.summary: At the mill in Brisecken, one mill hand after another mysteriously disappeared at night, so that the position acquired a bad reputation and no one wished to take it.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

7d2f5640517345c44eafb207547fe61516a3ecd5.summary: Some time ago, a pious and learned man wrote to Lavater that in the Graubünden mountains there was a silver mine upon which the head of that place, Landammann Peter Buol, had spent great sums in recent years but from which he had gathered no small wealth.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional title of the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity; Peter Buol's office combines political authority with ownership or leadership of the mine.

notes.label: Bergteufel
notes.text: literally ‘mine’ or ‘mountain devil,’ the capricious underground spirit that moves ore and violently punishes a miner's curses.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Bergknappen
notes.text: here the accusative singular of Bergknappe, a historical ore miner working underground; the plural has the same form, but this sentence refers to the single miner whom the spirit punishes.

87c4999507767d5fb4c99e23c8fe4a49fd12b5bd.summary: The gold veins on the Knapperkopf were discovered and secretly exploited by two brothers.

notes.label: Knapperkopf
notes.text: the named mining mountain above Vättis; Knapp is related to Knappe, a miner, and the place anchors both the mine and its legends.

notes.label: Knapperhütte
notes.text: the miners' hut at the Knapperkopf, used for lodging and ore storage; only a half-ruined structure remained when the account was written.

notes.label: Knappen
notes.text: historical miners who work the shafts and ore veins; the term can also mean squires elsewhere, but mining is the clear sense here.

notes.label: Mariengerichte
notes.text: the source's name for assemblies or courts held at Freudenberg Castle, apparently associated with a Marian observance; its exact legal and calendrical character is not explained.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a historical and now derogatory German label, literally ‘Gypsies,’ applied to Roma, Sinti, and other itinerant people; it is retained only to expose the source's persecution narrative and is not a neutral modern designation.

notes.label: vogelfrei
notes.text: literally ‘free as a bird,’ but historically meaning outlawed and denied ordinary legal protection; the tale presents this status as enabling murderous mob violence.

notes.label: Zigeunerin
notes.text: the feminine singular of the same historical derogatory label; here it denotes the wounded woman whose warning later saves the miners' families.

notes.label: St. Johanni-Tag
notes.text: Saint John's Day, the feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist; the men deliberately begin forbidden midnight work on this charged date.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

53f69d06627288ff5db6547ba86e72fedf9f5d02.summary: Near Grindelwald lived a little man known to the valley people only as the miracle doctor because of his arts.

notes.label: Matt
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a meadow, especially one cut for hay; after tasting the snake-foam, the servant goes there to mow and perceives every plant bowing to him.

4525bf90f629cf4c5fa1b4ccf9771030f5e34f98.summary: The servant rides behind, the knight ahead,

notes.label: Gelte
notes.text: a broad wooden tub, vat, or basin used in Alpine households and dairying; the promised abundance leaves every milk vessel wet.

2e7b6c995b294356661d01777f1320c2afd8ccd1.summary: Among the many votive tokens left by the faithful, one can see a ring hanging from a chain on the left in the center of the Maria Sonnenberg chapel on Seelisberg.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, often strong and gusty downslope wind of the Alps; here it makes travel on the lake unsafe and forces the pilgrims to approach Seelisberg overland.

52935a5e4a421a7747143f62284b0dc9c3cbe89b.summary: In Valais, people are also said once to have held it true that on Christmas night, while the clock strikes twelve and for as long as it continues striking, all livestock can speak human language.

notes.label: Tschuggen
notes.text: Tschuggen is an Alpine place-word for a rocky knoll, crag, or projecting outcrop, here the site above Zenschwidern where treasure appears; the exact landform and location are uncertain.

692ab039d98b674a09ee5c0a887428ebd18ab873.summary: High among the ice fields of the Bernese Oberland, in the middle of a glacier, there is a wondrous vault of ice that perfectly resembles the interior of a church.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

81d40b1758e3b176d3951a3923988c122186d9ae.summary: A magnificent painting depicting the Savior upon the cross once hung in the church at Unterseen and greatly adorned that house of God.

notes.label: Bödeli
notes.text: the low plain around Interlaken, between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz; here it names the local district through which the Reformation spread.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin of modest value; selling the sacred picture for only a few Batzen emphasizes how cheaply it was discarded before the abbey recognized it.

da3206d11866be0e4f47e9a6a9b23f0461b7a4ed.summary: Around 1430, a strange event occurred in Hildisrieden. When the foundation for the chaplain's house was dug, a lily, or Gilgenstock, appeared in the depths, sprouting directly from the heart of a corpse lying there.

notes.label: Gilgenstock
notes.text: an older regional word for a lily plant or lily stalk; its growth from the corpse's heart makes it a preserved sacred marvel.

cc8f17678b1c70ce93c188139823dac16529bb34.summary: Old Fluri Manhart in the Fäsch at Flums was a widely renowned ‘doctor’ whose Kundsame extended across the Rhine as far as Tyrol.

notes.label: Kundsame
notes.text: an older regional collective for a practitioner's clientele or circle of patients; it indicates that Fluri's reputation reached across the Rhine into Tyrol.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a traveling student associated in German-language lore with secret, magical, or forbidden learning; whether this guest is a literal student or an occult adept remains ambiguous.

31a61d0e3198c742fa5fb94b6fe7c97cc8009023.summary: It is told of a priest in Törbel that he stole the church treasure. When he was in danger of being discovered, he fled to Italy, where robbers attacked him in the open countryside.

notes.label: Landjäger
notes.text: Landjäger were rural mounted police or gendarmes whose imagined approach frightens the robbers; whether the miraculous sound imitated a particular regional force is uncertain.

45be78f020a1fea97ddf9ab297684cd2923beb38.summary: The people of Adelboden first settled at Boden, beyond the present village.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b8a79e6f0627f183127a487ca83382d3a9a87510.summary: In the depths of Lake Lucerne near the Bruderbalm, there is said to be a spring with the property that, if it is called three times in succession, it visibly surges from the bottom above the lake water with great commotion, and with such force that one must flee from it in haste.

notes.label: Bruderbalm
notes.text: a local name incorporating Balm, a rock shelter, overhang, or cave; the underwater spring lies near this landmark, but the identity of the ‘brother’ in the name is not explained.

242b7ef4816b74261850ec2b051896fd39d1c8b5.summary: In the mountain chain that separates the two Visp valleys, between the Balfrin and Monte Rosa, lies the mighty three-pronged range, 14,040 ft above sea level.

notes.label: Mischabel
notes.text: the traditional Valais name of the three-peaked massif now dominated in official usage by the summit name Dom; the source offers competing folk etymologies and treats the name’s true meaning as unknown.

notes.label: Schaub
notes.text: a regional word for a sheaf or bundled mass of straw; the climber carries one to make a visible signal fire on the summit.

fbab0a4f420d4db79e40e7de649f93eec3102598.summary: In the Prättigau, there was once a Fänggenmannli that had no fixed home but instead continually wandered up and down the valley.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: a little male Fängg, one of the wild forest or mountain beings of Alpine tradition; here the wandering figure rewards girls who care for its moss baskets and mocks those who neglect them.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little man, with -li as the diminutive; here it is the shorter name used for the Fänggenmannli.

f0e059ca996f1d9bf808ac325f2f2d7d152fb62e.summary: Not far from Ettiswil in the canton of Lucerne lie the ruins of Castelen Castle.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

53d51ab8e9b06ddc71df651d4175e7869ba1d55c.summary: Once an old, devout woman from Arosa also crossed the mountains to perform her devotions in the church at Obervaz.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman; the miserly Senn abuses his control of milk and rennet, and his recurring punishment becomes the lake’s weather omen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

e3cdacb141b7f5f8424356512725cdec3f312b5b.summary: A prosperous farmer followed the pious custom of giving a good portion to the poor whenever he baked bread.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Bozenkammer
notes.text: literally a ‘bogey-room’ or chamber assigned to a frightening spirit; the household confines the woman’s poltergeist there, and the exact local category of Bozen is not specified.

ac3d73e4fd1c2970c4c39255130ba83134cdd20d.summary: In Arbon, the old little church still stands beside the large new one. Beside the portal, a small niche can be seen in the wall, and within it is a stone bearing a large, elongated oval hollow.

notes.label: About this telling

0fcf10111d0aeac0cdcb2f68b3876c97be921387.summary: God the Lord had long since created the world and everything upon it. All parts of the world were already populated here and there with people, but for perfection they still lacked language, and the Creator resolved, by giving them language, to make them like his own image.

947daf142031b59af88ff18f03c12ec612da81cd.summary: One of the loveliest valleys in the canton of Zürich is the Tößtal. It is highly varied, and wherever one chooses to look, one always sees something appealing: now a cozy niche in the valley, now a pretty and distinctive village scene, and everywhere forests and hills of a cheerfully pleasing character.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer-pasture landscape and its herding world, which the upper Tößtal is said suddenly to resemble.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Runsen
notes.text: plural of Runse, steep erosion channels or gullies cut by water and debris on a mountain slope.

notes.label: Riesenen
notes.text: regional plural for scree runs or slopes of loose fallen rock; paired with Runsen, it makes the upper valley resemble a high-Alpine wilderness.

notes.label: Wildleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wild people,’ diminutive mountain beings imagined as former inhabitants of remote caves and forest hollows.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss word for a steep rock face, crag, or cliff; the farmer expects a Wildleutchen to peer down from one.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: the plural of Fluh, the rock faces that twilight makes resemble primeval giants and monsters.

notes.label: Armsünderglöcklein
notes.text: literally the ‘poor sinner's little bell,’ traditionally rung for a condemned person going to execution; the farmer's earlier gloomy face is contrasted with his joy at hearing of treasure.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a Venetian, but in Swiss and Alpine treasure lore a foreign seeker believed to possess secret knowledge of minerals and hidden riches; here his Bergspiegel guides him to the cave.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a divining or magical viewing instrument said to reveal hidden places and treasure; its workings are not described.

notes.label: Mo-Milch-Gubel
notes.text: the local name of the overhanging treasure rock; Gubel is a Swiss word for a crag, overhang, or rocky height, while the Mo-Milch element is unexplained in the story and may allude to cave ‘moonmilk,’ but that identification is uncertain.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep wooded ravine or gorge in Swiss usage; the men must force their way through it to the treasure rock.

notes.label: Turben
notes.text: Swiss regional plural for cut peat sods or turves; the darkness is fancifully said to be thick enough to cut like peat from a moor.

notes.label: lötiges Gold
notes.text: gold described by the historical fineness measure Lot, meaning assayed or high-fineness gold; the precise purity intended here is not stated.

notes.label: Schnitztruhe
notes.text: a chest holding dried fruit slices or Schnitz, into which children might eagerly reach; the simile describes the Venediger plunging both hands into the coins.

0c5bd19ca42205be0274cc6c7cc469ffbd266a54.summary: On the Heitmenegg Alp in the Schächental, one of the Alpine herdsmen was a terrible mocker.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high-elevation seasonal pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; Heitmenegg is where the herdsmen live and work during the grazing season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bräntä
notes.text: a regional wooden vessel or carrying tub worn on the back for transporting water, milk, or other liquid; here the herdsman takes it to the spring for water.

52c457899e41a24867065a7613a13da97e639eb8.summary: A king had a son. One day the son went hunting far away.

notes.label: Mohrenkönigin
notes.text: literally ‘Moorish queen’; Mohr is a historically common but now dated and potentially offensive German label for a dark-skinned or African person, while this tale gives no specific ethnicity or geography for the ruler of the mythical Green Land.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a measure or unit of measure; here it gives the barge’s length and width, but the source names no specific unit or modern equivalent, and it should not be assumed to have the liquid capacity found in other historical uses of Mass.

notes.label: Sieben Stangen
notes.text: literally ‘Seven Rods’ or ‘Seven Pole-Lengths,’ the name of the queen’s field; Stange can denote a pole or a traditional measure, but the tale does not establish the field’s exact dimensions.

a4d8ca59a2a9aa205b79352377bf15b6e3d06fd8.summary: A monastery is said to have stood at Nernetçan in former times. In the year 1849, the owner of part of the land was working to make it arable.

notes.label: Nernetçan
notes.text: the source's local Vaud place-name for the site of the lost monastery; its cedilla and spelling are preserved because the precise modern identification is uncertain.

95b44dac02f37df8427e99c4872b97c5e3eb88eb.summary: From the village of Frick across the Kaistenberg and the Kinzhalde as far as the town of Laufenburg, Erdmännchen lived in the caves of the Jura and the holes in the rocks along the Rhine bank.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean helpers; here they can assume bird form and assist with harvest work.

notes.label: Biberli
notes.text: a child-language name in the source for partridges or guinea fowl; it provides Rochholz’s stated explanation for the beings’ name and should not be confused automatically with the modern Swiss gingerbread called Biberli.

notes.label: Erdbiberli
notes.text: the local name for the bird-shaped Erdmännchen, formed from Erd, “earth,” and the child-language bird-name Biberli; here it does not literally mean small beavers.

notes.label: Biberzelten
notes.text: historical Swiss spiced gingerbread cakes or flat loaves; in this tale their name is connected folklorically to the Erdbiberli who bake them, while modern etymological explanations may differ.

f318a3e8a26ee1343151bbf75ecd5dc8b4d90ba8.summary: A young goatherd once peered through a wide crack in the tower wall and caught sight of the baron’s money chest.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land or common pasture, contrasted here with privately owned ground.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Stutz
notes.text: a steep slope, rise, or hillside in Swiss place-language, here the site near Ragaz where the pear tree grows.

fd2b331b6697a7b4ab4edc27bcbfcdcf37f335ee.summary: Underground passages are said to have led from one of the towers to Wartenstein Castle and beneath the Rhine to Brandis Castle in Maienfeld.

notes.label: Ochsenbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘ox spring’ or ‘ox fountain,’ the landmark reached within the legendary underground passage.

notes.label: Freiherr
notes.text: a German noble rank conventionally equivalent to baron, here the lord of Freudenberg.

notes.label: Spitzäckern
notes.text: the local field-name where the farmer plows; literally it suggests pointed or tapering fields.

ba48ae4c73a6d4b9d78b5f793306c3e57a96de95.summary: In the year 1792, Judge Anrig, father of Cashier Anrig in the Töbeli at Sargans, had a farmhand who tended the cattle on his Atschen estate, which lies close to the Hochwand on the Schollberg.

notes.label: Töbeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a small ravine or hollow and used here as a local place-name at Sargans.

notes.label: Tanse
notes.text: a back-carried Alpine container for transporting milk or other liquids, usually fitted with shoulder straps; the farmhand needs it emptied before returning for the treasure.

notes.label: Girenbüchel
notes.text: the local name of the small hill by the old Schollberg road where the treasure appears; Büchel is a diminutive of hill, while Giren is left as the place-name element.

notes.label: Büchel
notes.text: a small hill or mound; in the account it shortens the full place-name Girenbüchel.

fadd0285b726b11606544e8698a4059fd0f05d13.summary: Some mischievous herdsmen once took it into their heads to baptize a sheep.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on high pastures; here later workers try to deceive the monster about its nightly cream offering.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: a regional dairy term for whey, particularly the liquid remaining after curds or cheese are removed; here it is hidden beneath a thin layer of cream in a fatal attempt to cheat the monster.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working buildings, not simply any mountain; here it is abandoned until the monster and bull destroy one another.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

3bea2c1baf8ffca415d41edb8585894d1ae11e2f.summary: Below Laufenburg, where the stream named after the village of Kaisten flows into the Rhine, a bridge leads into the broad Hardwald.

b73f05dce7901bb6cf80da721915c9a23df911cd.summary: A farmer from Ueken possessed a great fortune in landed property. But he also sought to increase it by stealing his neighbors' fruit and wegmarchte—moving the boundary to take away—half of their Pünten and orchards.

notes.label: wegmarchte
notes.text: an older regional verb for moving or manipulating a property boundary so as to appropriate land; it is related to March, a boundary or boundary marker, not to military marching.

notes.label: Pünten
notes.text: fenced or specially cultivated garden and field plots, often near a settlement; the farmer annexes half of his neighbors' productive parcels.

notes.label: Hagstöcke
notes.text: hedge or fence stakes driven into the ground; the dead boundary thief's repeated fencing work predicts rain.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally ‘prayer bell,’ a church bell rung at set devotional times, often the Angelus; its evening sound sends the apparition out onto the road.

8697cd4a90aaebd7ebcace705acb5a05bf6057b8.summary: In a small valley on the Heinzenberg ridge lies the little Alpine lake Lüsch; it is surrounded by hills wreathed in heather and alpine roses.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often powerful downslope wind of the Alps; here its rising whistle and the terrain’s echo warn of an approaching storm.

notes.label: Heinzenberger
notes.text: inhabitants of the Heinzenberg region in Graubünden, on whose ridge the lake lies.

notes.label: Savier
notes.text: people of the neighboring Safien valley; Jecklin’s form reflects the regional German name used in the source.

notes.label: Lüschersee
notes.text: the unhyphenated body-text form of Lüscher-See, the small Alpine lake said to bellow before storms and release the monster.

notes.label: Domleschger
notes.text: people from the Domleschg valley; in the legend the word identifies the castle lords returning from an ibex hunt.

notes.label: Butatsch
notes.text: Romansh for a belly or paunch, used as the shortened name of the eye-covered lake monster.

notes.label: Butatsch cun ilgs
notes.text: the Romansh name given to the monster, literally “belly with eyes”; its body is imagined as a huge cow’s belly covered with staring eyes.

notes.label: Nolla
notes.text: the local name of the destructive mountain torrent below the Heinzenberg; the legend attributes the carving of its deep channel to the Butatsch.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for a steep, narrow ravine or gully cut by a mountain stream.

notes.label: starmentusa Notg
notes.text: a Romansh phrase meaning a terrible or terrifying night, used for the remembered night of storm and devastation.

notes.label: Lüscher-See
notes.text: the hyphenated title form of the lake-name; the body of the source calls the same small lake Lüsch and Lüschersee.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

notes.label: About this telling

37c44059144965563eb1e32a87a7ea89db786899.summary: According to the booklet of the Sennenbruderschaft of Gersau, it was during the night of the Feast of Saint James in 1593 when sixty head of cattle suddenly died in a single Alpine hut in the upper Gschwänd on Mount Rigi, with twenty-four more dying suddenly in other huts.

notes.label: Sennenbruderschaft
notes.text: a religious confraternity of Sennen, the Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who work on seasonal high pastures; the Gersau brotherhood preserves the memory of the cattle disaster and organizes the annual observance.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle on a seasonal high pasture; he carries news of the mass cattle deaths down to Gersau.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its dairy settlement rather than simply a mountain; the giants appear beside the huts on the Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn; the herders respond to the disaster by founding a confraternity and maintaining a day of penance and prayer.

notes.label: Moore
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a sow; this unaccountable sow appears outside the secured pig enclosure as an omen of severe weather.

notes.label: Fasnecht
notes.text: Swiss German for Carnival, a customary season for festive foods such as the fried cakes being prepared here.

notes.label: Sichlete
notes.text: a Bernese harvest-completion feast or gathering, another festive occasion paired here with Fasnecht.

notes.label: Juhe
notes.text: a bottled drink passed around at the celebration; the exact beverage denoted by this local word is not identified in the source.

notes.label: Rüchi
notes.text: a regional expression for a spell of rough, stormy weather; the mysterious animal’s visit foretells one.

70d248047306013e9ef720923190ff9038735dd6.summary: In Bern’s Kandertal, the farmers believe that whenever a white mass of storm cloud rises in the sky and announces a change in the weather, a Moore and her seven young can be seen within it. (Student Mäder of Baden.)

notes.label: Moore
notes.text: a historical regional animal-name that the passage treats as a sow-like storm-cloud being with seven young; the exact dialect derivation is uncertain, so the source form is retained rather than replaced with a more specific zoological term.

6d761ad7d1f21fe0620694e9e5f9e0efe91d9ab0.summary: One part of the little village of Attelwil, in the district of Zofingen, is called the Moos-Ester.

notes.label: Mooshündli
notes.text: the Swiss German diminutive of Mooshund, literally a “little Moos dog”; despite the affectionate ending, the unseen creature makes horses vanish and is linked to an illusory house fire.

notes.label: Mooshund
notes.text: literally “Moos dog,” the title’s local name for Attelwil’s barking spectral dog; Moos may mean marshy ground or refer specifically to the named Moos-Ester and Moosweg, so “marsh dog” would be too definite.

d30ed4560dcbc78f79e03b0b8a7da398204033f8.summary: A younger man from the Langenthal area gave the following oral explanation about this.

notes.label: Moosmann
notes.text: literally ‘bog man,’ an alternative form in which local people describe the same uncertain Erlenmoos haunting.

notes.label: Moospferd
notes.text: literally ‘bog horse’; Moos means marsh or bog here, and the apparition is linked to a real horse abandoned in dangerous wetland.

notes.label: Erlenmoos
notes.text: literally ‘alder bog,’ the named marsh where the horse vanished and the bellowing apparition is later sought.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night lads,’ young men out at night for mischief; here they are the pranksters who abandon the horse and cart in the bog.

notes.label: Leiterwagen
notes.text: a traditional farm wagon with ladder-like slatted sides, to which the spectral horse is grotesquely harnessed backward.

8c471277e64f022fe2195ada5ed3ff2c629cbb92.summary: In former times, on the Alp where the colossal Morteratsch Glacier now lies behind Pontresina, a young Senn named Aratsch summered the village cows.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its dairy operation, not simply the mountain range; the glacier ultimately covers this worked landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk processing during the summer season on an Alp.

notes.label: Barba Gian
notes.text: a Romansh form of respectful familiarity meaning ‘Uncle Gian’; Barba can address an older man even when he is not a literal uncle.

notes.label: Gebse
notes.text: a broad wooden dairy vessel or tub used in alpine milk handling; the spirit inspects the milk from one Gebse to the next.

notes.label: Mort Aratsch
notes.text: the lament understood in the story as ‘Aratsch is dead’; repeated aloud, it supplies the legendary folk etymology of Morteratsch.

notes.label: Senntum
notes.text: an Alpine dairy and herding unit or seasonal enterprise, including its herd and operation; here Gian retires from managing it when he grows old.

notes.label: Milchgebsen
notes.text: broad wooden dairy vessels or tubs for holding milk; the spirit inspects these containers to ensure the dairy work is in order.

notes.label: »Mort Aratsch«-Jungfer
notes.text: the maiden who cries ‘Mort Aratsch’; the source's printed compound makes the story's name explanation explicit.

notes.label: Schmaladia saja qua ist alp e sia paschüra!
notes.text: the printed Romansh curse, closest to ‘Cursed be this Alp and its pasture!’; its curse explains the glacier's destructive advance, though the source's historical spelling is retained.
notes.anchor: Schmaladia saja qua ist alp e sia paschüra!

notes.label: Alp Nova
notes.text: Romansh/Italianate for ‘new Alp,’ the later pasture at the limit of the glacier's advance.

notes.label: Isla Persa
notes.text: Romansh for ‘Lost Island,’ a rock island amid the Morteratsch ice and snow that preserves the memory of the former pasture.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Morteratsch Jungfer
notes.text: the ‘Morteratsch maiden,’ Annetta's restless spirit; Jungfer is an older word for an unmarried young woman, while the legend derives Morteratsch from her cry for the dead Aratsch.

24ccde9c57519baf332c627db77c6332d79f0755.summary: Not long ago in Täsch, an invisible hand lit a candle in the room of a sick girl, first on the table and then on the stove bench.

notes.label: Kuhtricheln
notes.text: large Swiss cowbells with a duller clanging tone than cast bells; their unexplained ringing inside the locked house marks the haunting.

notes.label: Totengang
notes.text: literally ‘going of the dead’; a regional term for a dead person’s uncanny return, passage, or ghostly visitation, whose exact form is not further described here.

81e40173a8a0f0675678286dad1a683255c3dea4.summary: In Puschlav, a father and his son once drove their sheep out to pasture. This pasture lay at the edge of a dense forest.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the historical German name for Val Poschiavo, the Italian-speaking valley in southern Graubünden where the tale is set.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: spektakulierte
notes.text: Jecklin’s regional verb here means that the father argued, made a noisy dispute, or remonstrated with the boy; its exact shade is colloquial.

notes.label: Knebel
notes.text: glossed in the source as a Knüttel, meaning a cudgel or stout club; here it is the weapon with which the father beats his wife.

0b3cea528ab528b707cfef99b6e4648e1d1e5b5c.summary: In their arrogance, the French took the statue of the Mother of God from the church and drove it headfirst into the peat soil at the Streichmähder.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.text: The source does not identify the ‘holy season’ more precisely, so it is not narrowed to a particular feast in English.

d2fb9b24f7727b7314981e3242e9c4b3bab48c59.summary: When people scorned the precious gift of the Erdäpfel and declared them fit only for pigs, God intended to make them grow in such a way that they truly would have been good only as pig feed.

notes.label: Erdäpfel
notes.text: literally ‘earth apples,’ a traditional Swiss and southern German word for potatoes; the legend explains why they remain suitable for people rather than only pigs.

notes.label: Räben
notes.text: a regional plural for turnips, probably field or fodder turnips; the source lists them separately from Rüben, so the exact botanical distinction is uncertain.

notes.label: Amte Willisau
notes.text: an inflected older form meaning the historical administrative district or bailiwick of Willisau, where the related grain tradition was reported.

d90b578d3f9e684ffc04431aef3e4aced40bcaf2.summary: In the year 1475, on the 13th of Wintermonat, the city of Sion was relieved by the Upper Valaisans from the siege of the Duke of Savoy.

notes.label: Wintermonat
notes.text: literally ‘winter month,’ a traditional name for November; the commemorated date is 13 November 1475.

notes.label: Planta
notes.text: the open square or field at Sion used here as the Savoyard army's position; it survives as a local place-name rather than meaning an ordinary plant.

notes.label: Leukerporte
notes.text: the Leuk gate of Sion, named for the direction toward Leuk; the Upper Valais troops arrive there before being redirected.

notes.label: Savièseporte
notes.text: the Savièse gate, the city gate facing Savièse; the relief force passes toward it to attack the besiegers' flank.

notes.label: englischen Gruss
notes.text: literally the ‘angelic greeting,’ the Ave Maria or Hail Mary recalling Gabriel's greeting to Mary; it is not an English-language greeting.

notes.label: Windelwäscherin
notes.text: literally ‘diaper washer,’ the besiegers' contemptuous name for Mary as the mother who washed the infant Jesus's swaddling cloths; their insult turns into recognition of her decisive protection.

notes.label: Gundisporte
notes.text: the Gundis gate of old Sion, where the commemorative Marian image remained until the gate disappeared; the name's exact derivation is unstated.

9d66ee5ccfbb7ec24e398a423564631f56141d9a.summary: Below Täsch, the Räti rises high above St. Niklaus with a sheer rock wall facing the valley.

11bd556b9b49757fff63e42ff9a7fb5f42667162.summary: The miller's wife of Wohlen fed her piglets white bread and gave them milk to drink but sent the poor away from the mill hungry.

notes.label: Malter
notes.text: a historical regional dry measure for grain; its volume varied substantially by place and period.

notes.label: Folge
notes.text: the named thirty-night period of church prayer for a departed person in this account; its exact relationship to other Catholic mourning observances is locally specific.

5c952acca5a9cc1b0d5a398efe73d5d049202341.summary: A father went with his son into the beech forest above the village of Räzüns to fetch wood. — Now, because it was very hot, the son became thirsty, and the father went with him to a spring he knew, where the son drank to his heart’s content.

notes.label: Haselstecklein
notes.text: a little hazel stick or wand; the diminutive emphasizes the simple twig with which the boy draws magical signs in the spring water.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

54bd22936dc490c9f391a52a38c89e207faa54ab.summary: In the mountain chain between the Saas Valley and Simplon, the two mighty Fletschhorn peaks (12,390 feet above sea level) tower toward the sky.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

8a9115c52216571a6504fca12e7b5a66ed5abae7.summary: At midnight the Muettiseel comes down along the Nässibach. It has the shape of a sack stuffed full of leaves.

notes.label: Muettiseel
notes.text: the local name of this unresting soul or apparition; Seel corresponds to ‘soul,’ while Muetti may suggest Swiss German ‘mother,’ but the source does not explain the name, so its precise derivation remains uncertain.

notes.label: Nässibach
notes.text: the local stream name along which the apparition descends; Bach means ‘brook’ or ‘stream,’ while the first element is a place-name and is left untranslated.

12bdbc7bdba03d19985e22ba61beb3c59d68d6b6.summary: If one walks uphill from the right bank of Lake Hallwil toward the heights of Fahrwangen, one passes the place where the castle of the barons of Fahrwangen once stood.

notes.label: Mumeli
notes.text: the local name of the lonely, fir-ringed place near Fahrwangen where the murdered knights were buried; its literal derivation is not explained in the source.

notes.label: wehweln
notes.text: a regional verb for one form of the spirit’s plaintive crying; its sound suggests lamentation, but the source does not distinguish it precisely from wehvern.

notes.label: wehvern
notes.text: a regional verb for the spirit’s mournful calling; the exact distinction from wehweln is not supplied.

notes.label: Mumelimann
notes.text: literally the man associated with the Mumeli; it is a local name for the restless dead man who runs to the burial place and cries around Lake Hallwil.

notes.label: Runelimâ
notes.text: an Alemannic alternate name for the Mumelimann; Mâ means ‘man,’ while the precise sense of Runeli is uncertain in this source.

notes.label: Schellenpeter
notes.text: literally ‘Bell Peter’; the local name on the opposite lakeshore for the weather-warning apparition heard as the jingling of sleigh horses.

19d1dd99c6d7c47eade2aeb06e253fc74a87f1e0.summary: Two hours into the mountains that lie west of Naters, above the village of Mund, stands a great black, almost round crag or rock; a cross stands upon it.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8ae81a7f67452f8ab271ea46f17efa1c02955cfb.summary: On the Oberrieterberg, the Wild Hunt is called the Muoltahee, also Multahee.

notes.label: Muoltahee
notes.text: the local Oberriet name for the Wild Hunt, a terrifying supernatural nighttime procession; the source records the name but does not establish its precise etymology.

notes.label: Multahee
notes.text: an alternate local form of Muoltahee for the same Wild Hunt procession.

notes.label: Du tust wie's Multahee
notes.text: literally ‘you carry on like the Multahee,’ a local comparison for someone behaving noisily, wildly, or uncontrollably.

notes.label: Wildfang
notes.text: literally a ‘wild-caught one,’ an unruly, impetuous, or boisterous person; here it is the kind of person compared to the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Norder Knorra
notes.text: a local name for the height from which the procession descends; Knorra likely evokes a knoll or rocky protuberance, but the exact local topographic sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Wüetihö
notes.text: the local name of a separate noisy, animal-like nighttime apparition near Büchel; its form resembles regional Wild Hunt names, but the source does not explain whether the beings are considered identical.

828c38d7760e289da5564578440d6655afd21218.summary: Wodan's raging host is called the Muotiseel here. Restless children are scolded:

notes.label: Muotiseel
notes.text: the St. Gallenkappel name for Wodan's raging host, a local form of the Wild Hunt; by extension, the saying compares a noisy, restless child to that tumultuous supernatural company.

notes.label: Du tuest wie-n-es Muotiseel!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘You're acting like a Muotiseel!’—a rebuke for a child behaving wildly or restlessly.

53d8491bfb9bcf133d604863ff99b1241b807e6e.summary: In olden times, a Zigeuner band once traveled down from the Bernina toward the Puschlav.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a dated and now derogatory German exonym historically applied to Roma and Sinti people; it is retained only to identify and contextualize Jecklin’s 1874 wording, not as a modern characterization.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the German name for Val Poschiavo in Graubünden, the valley toward which the travelers descend from the Bernina.

notes.label: Alpe Cavaglia
notes.text: the high seasonal settlement and grazing area of Cavaglia; the tale notes that its substantial houses make it resemble a small mountain village.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Zigeuner-Mutter
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical compound for the group’s eldest woman, using the same dated and derogatory exonym; the passage defines her as extremely old, frail, and blind.

notes.label: Muetterli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning “little mother” or “dear old mother”; the killers use it in a cruelly ironic farewell.

677011ee43587592492ff185f7024050f98bfc34.summary: Those rocks that rise so quietly and proudly above the waters of the Albula, ten minutes below Bergün, are called the “Bergüner-Stein.” Hundreds of travelers pass through the thoroughly Alpine valley of the Albula largely for the sole purpose of seeing this Bergüner-Stein, whose natural beauty can…

notes.label: Bergüner-Stein
notes.text: literally the “Bergün Stone,” the dramatic rock formation above the Albula below Bergün; Stein identifies the named rocky site rather than a small loose stone.

4686e36124c5fc8028718d0f878263b3cab22c36.summary: Between the villages of Schiltwald and Gontenschwil lies a gorge past which, in former times, the road through the wild forest to Beromünster is said to have run, connecting the Wyna and Suhr valleys there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4be660058cbef6181a8bddd299042a565231251d.summary: Where the magnificent mountain meadows of the beautiful Alpe Stavelchod spread out at the Ofen-Pass, the traveler journeying from Cernetz toward the Münsterhalde notices old, ruined masonry on the hill, to which the following legend is attached:

notes.label: Alpe Stavelchod
notes.text: the high summer pasture named Stavelchod near the Ofen Pass; Alpe denotes the managed grazing area and its seasonal workings.

notes.label: Ofen-Pass
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical hyphenated form of Ofenpass, the Alpine pass now also known as Pass dal Fuorn linking the Engadin with Val Müstair.

notes.label: Cernetz
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of present-day Zernez in the Lower Engadin.

notes.label: Münsterhalde
notes.text: the destination form printed by Jecklin in this passage; it appears to designate the route toward the Münster or Müstair valley, but the unusual historical wording is preserved rather than silently corrected.

e6aafbb43d42f8775557ba80348f715482ad7c21.summary: On the royal highway leading to the Simplon Pass, the traveler at Paino, not far from the Valais border, sees a collapsed church a short distance above the road.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

79f2b8c1d0c9e9c84069347459bbae1d87126a9f.summary: At Treib, opposite Brunnen on the Waldstättersee, a wedding was being held.

notes.label: Waldstättersee
notes.text: the historical German name for Lake Lucerne, literally the ‘Lake of the Forest Cantons’; it emphasizes the central Swiss cantons surrounding the lake rather than the modern city-based English name.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep rock face or crag; here it is the landmark near Gersau associated with the child's red shoe.

notes.label: Kindleinsmord
notes.text: literally ‘murder of the little child,’ the traditional name attached to the nearby commemorative chapel as well as to the legend; the archaic diminutive gives the term a devotional and memorial tone.

8adbe1739df1e5bee581999f2e4341f4b2c55d69.summary: The Senn struck the shepherd boy dead,

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for livestock and milk work on a seasonal alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face or cliff; the murderer throws the boy over it.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully, often cut by a torrent.

notes.label: Mess
notes.text: a quoted local name for an Alpine measuring or accounting gathering; the exact procedure is not specified, but the farmers assemble on the alp for it.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working settlement; the farmers go up to it together.

notes.label: Schierser-Alpe
notes.text: the high seasonal pasture associated with Schiers; Alpe here denotes a worked Alpine grazing and dairying site rather than simply a mountain.

370d3509a2ffef9fe5f0192cf5c93256d6ed8e38.summary: On the Stafelalp in the Saas Valley, at the elevation where tree growth ends, a stone lies in ground covered with rich pasture.

notes.label: Seelenwägen
notes.text: literally ‘weighing souls,’ a children’s knife-tossing game whose holes map the world, paradise, heaven, purgatory, and hell; the source also shortens the name to Seelenwäge, and exact local rules may have varied.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Geiselstock
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a whip handle or whipstock; children claim its broken remnant remains beneath the Murder Stone, though the adult narrator later finds no evidence.

784a056a9b2f92b35251d0f0d345c6b5bdc71f9b.summary: At Stalden on the Bözberg, a maid served in an inn. She accepted the courting visits of a young man from Linn until at last she had to press him urgently to marry her soon.

notes.label: Gadenfenster
notes.text: the window of a Gaden, a chamber, loft, or farm-building room; its use for nighttime courting access is central to how the murderer enters unnoticed.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Schwarze Mutter Gottes
notes.text: literally the ‘Black Mother of God,’ the revered Black Madonna of Einsiedeln whose shrine drew annual pilgrims across the Bözberg.

notes.label: aufs Rad geflochten
notes.text: literally ‘woven onto the wheel,’ the old execution formula for a body broken and displayed upon the punishment wheel; the murderer's restless ghost remains associated with both that violent sentence and the bloodstained spring.

9049c507db209301a79a0b563ff06db029fa1ea7.summary: Scarcely three minutes from the Kropfbrunnen at Steinen, the traveler enters a wood of beech and conifer.

notes.label: Kropfbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘goiter spring’ or ‘goiter fountain,’ the local landmark near Steinen; the source gives no explanation for the name.

notes.label: Aa
notes.text: a common Swiss regional water-name meaning a stream or river; here it is the rushing watercourse used by the murderer, not the letter sequence ‘AA.’

2db6f33833dbc58a72b9b24d1a14fd8e92041691.summary: A Handknab and a Senn were both in love with the same beautiful girl. One summer, the jealous Senn killed his rival during a night of thunderstorms and threw the body into the rushing Alpine stream.

notes.label: Handknab
notes.text: a junior male Alpine worker or dairyman's assistant serving below the Senn; the murdered young man occupies this subordinate role, though his exact duties are not described.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy production; the title marks the murderer's higher role within the same seasonal Alpine work community.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kilbi
notes.text: a Swiss German village fair traditionally associated with a church-dedication anniversary; here it is a communal autumn celebration with dancing, while the source does not describe any religious observance.

999e99aaab81879239c5cb8b87d49f74e09e995b.summary: A citizen of Niedergampel, whose wife lay deathly ill in bed, rode to the wonder doctor in Siders to fetch medicine.

notes.label: Siders
notes.text: the historical German name for Sierre in Valais; the citizen visits a healer there and later tells Peter that he has fetched medicine from the town.

notes.label: Mörderstein
notes.text: literally “Murderer’s Stone,” the tale’s name for the split rock against which the wandering child was killed; the source says the name remains in use.

notes.label: vogelfrei
notes.text: a historical German legal and social term for someone declared outside the law’s protection and liable to be hunted or killed; here it describes the murderer Peter’s outlawed condition.

notes.label: Kienspahn
notes.text: an older spelling of Kienspan, a resin-rich pine splint burned as a simple torch or lamp; Peter lights one inside his cave.

notes.label: Fuder
notes.text: a historical large-load measure, often approximately a cartload or wagonload; the tale uses the plural for several great quantities of bleached linen without specifying an exact modern measure.

a2e0714f06f2373e6c567c5658f22e0d095d648e.summary: In the great forest between Siders and Leuk, on the southern side of the Rhône valley, called the Pfynwald, stands a split Fluh known as the ‘Murderer's Stone.’ It is said to owe its name to the following dreadful legend.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep exposed rock face or crag in Swiss usage; here the split Fluh itself becomes the physical memorial called the Murderer's Stone.

290656e35be9a419ddaa9fb8428c047ef7ab2ab8.summary: In the year 17.., the wife of Nepomuk Landis of Menzingen went on pilgrimage to Maria Einsiedeln with her child, a twelve-year-old girl.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

7c4f509dd1c6243b69958b1b830761004ac5e30f.summary: High in the Zürich Oberland, with a broad view across the beautiful Swiss country, lies the little village of Sternenberg.

notes.label: Mutheseel
notes.text: the local name of an invisible, rattling monster said to descend Sternenberg at new moon and shred whatever blocks its way; the source does not explain the name's literal derivation or the being's appearance.

notes.label: Berggass
notes.text: Swiss German for the steep ‘mountain lane’ through Sternenberg down which the Mutheseel travels.

notes.label: Häcksel
notes.text: chopped straw or fodder prepared for livestock; the legend threatens that the Mutheseel reduces a person to this material, not merely to generic pieces.

notes.label: Brunnendünchel
notes.text: a hollow wooden conduit or bored log used in an old water system; its dark interior supplies the tale's intensely local comparison for the night.

notes.label: Drei Furchen aus dem Weg!
notes.text: literally ‘three furrows out of the road,’ the Mutheseel's command for an unusually wide clearance; the precise width of a furrow is not fixed.

notes.label: Gemeingut
notes.text: property held or understood as common to the community; the farmer invokes the road's shared status to resist being ordered aside.

notes.label: Knienicker
notes.text: a dialectal name for a crippling blow or condition that makes the knees buckle; the farmer's threat is vivid, but the exact ailment intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Rollenhegel
notes.text: the source's name for an old-fashioned folding pocketknife; the comparison depicts the terrified farmer doubled tightly upon himself.

eb62e9e8de8f082976a72438d9c8fda8d063e2df.summary: In former times, beside the abbey at Engelberg there was also a convent for women.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

898845fd8e6500bc3426d692c506e8f4351c12a3.summary: One day, a strange, unknown beggar came to Andermatt. The weather was so vile that no one would have driven a dog out of the house, and the uncanny night crept through the narrow lanes and corners of the quiet mountain village with its brown little houses.

notes.label: Ofenbänkli
notes.text: the diminutive name for a bench built beside or around a room’s masonry stove, traditionally a warm household seat; because both beds are occupied, the poor family offers it to the beggar as a sleeping place.

notes.label: zweimänniges
notes.text: literally ‘two-man’ or ‘two-household’ in this description of a divided house; the source makes clear that it had two halves but does not explain the building or ownership arrangement more precisely.

03752520b8ed5ce4fc4d3d3820a2ec88bf6c2f97.summary: A man from Klosters had a mysterious book with whose help he became versed in the black arts.—Once, while he was in church, some boys came upon this book and read the magic formulas.

notes.label: About this telling
