notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

53089fbf7bb8842e76dc09c10335f79f5554768e.summary: The older people of St. Carlo in the Puschlav tell of the following strange apparition, which they claim to have observed repeatedly.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the German name for Val Poschiavo, the Italian-speaking valley of Graubünden in which St. Carlo and Curvera lie.

318dd5eef77c7fcee7252616e6c0e8fb4e6dbac8.summary: For several summers, an Italian named Sander had set up his peddler’s table in the corridor of the bathhouse.

notes.label: Trinklaube
notes.text: at this spa, the Trinklaube was a covered drinking pavilion or gallery associated with taking the mineral waters; its exact architecture and position beside the bridge are uncertain.

45b1cdf84e9b5201c2246ae06aa4509c15d3f12e.summary: The schoolmaster of Wassen once spent the night in a house in Altdorf. Before he fell asleep, a woman with a rag tied around her head climbed into bed with him and lay down fully clothed, so close that she could not have come any closer.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7f8b59d1b87de9765eb56ff299433df7f6eb4849.summary: Here the Möttelin had their family vault because this wealthy family had made rich endowments to the church.

notes.label: Möttelin
notes.text: the byname of the wealthy Rappenstein family whose burial vault and stone arms were attached to the church; it is a proper family name, not a generic supernatural being.

notes.label: Herren Fasnacht
notes.text: literally ‘the lords' Fasnacht,’ a historical local carnival date used to identify the Monday after it; the source does not convert the observance to a modern calendar date.

e1e53e5a1384d0cd8273ca6940fb54f3d575524c.summary: The Mühlibach rises on the Geisboden and flows through a wild forest ravine and over rocky slopes toward Oberwil, where it empties into Lake Zug.

notes.label: Mühlibach-Dame
notes.text: literally ‘lady of the Mühlibach,’ the local name for the child-killing servant's elegant ghost; Dame emphasizes her refined appearance despite her peasant origin and crime.

notes.label: Mühlibachdame, chum, wenn's neumis mit d'r ischt!
notes.text: Swiss German meaning approximately ‘Mühlibach-Dame, come if you are anything at all!’; the taunt challenges the ghost to prove her power, and neumis mit d'r ischt carries the idiomatic sense of having substance, courage, or force.
notes.anchor: Mühlibachdame, chum, wenn's neumis mit d'r ischt!

d32e5b2b9d619d6e5ffefab3a12f392122e67499.summary: The upper part of the Maiengrün wood, between Hägglingen and Megenwil, is called Ofeholz.

notes.label: Müserifraueli
notes.text: the local diminutive name of the female being at the woodland spring, roughly “little Müseri woman”; the tale equates her with the Moosweib but does not explain Müseri securely.

notes.label: Moosweib
notes.text: literally “moss woman” or “marsh woman,” a female nature or place spirit; here it is another name for the Müserifraueli who owns the meadow and washes at the spring.

notes.label: Kuhblumen
notes.text: literally “cow-flowers,” a regional plant-name often applied to conspicuous pasture flowers such as dandelions; the source does not identify the species precisely enough to replace the term with one certain botanical name.

notes.label: Moosfräueli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive form meaning “little moss maiden/lady,” another name in the tale for the Müserifraueli; Fräueli marks a small or familiar female being rather than a modern form of address.

notes.label: Stifelirüter
notes.text: the local name of the mounted supernatural guardian of the Maiengrün wood; Rüter suggests a rider, while the meaning of Stifeli in the name remains uncertain.

notes.label: Freienamt
notes.text: the historical Freiamt region of Aargau; the source’s inflected form Freienamt refers to a territorial district, not simply an “open office” or unrestricted post.

1c2429236ded55d6c39bfed0e5ab3c907ac76309.summary: Just as Muri Abbey and the municipality of Bütikon once went to law over the Bannholz, so the city of Baden and the village of Gebistorf disputed the Müseren, a substantial forest above Gebistorf and Birmenstorf.

notes.label: Bannholz
notes.text: literally ‘banned’ or protected woodland, here a forest whose ownership and controlled use were matters of communal law; the passage compares it with the disputed Müseren forest but does not state the particular restrictions attached to this Bannholz.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor who represented the ruling authority in an Old Swiss subject district; here he presides over the decisive oath, while the text does not define the office’s exact jurisdiction.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Schultheiß
notes.text: a historical municipal chief magistrate, closest here to the presiding official or mayor of Baden; the office combined civic and judicial authority in ways that varied by place and period.

notes.label: Hüscht umme!
notes.text: a dialect driving cry addressed to the white horse, closest in sense to ‘go around!’ or ‘on, turn about!’; its force is that of a local horse command, but the precise maneuver intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Guttern
notes.text: an Alemannic word for large glass bottles or demijohn-like vessels carried by a glassware seller; here they are green and form his whole load, though their exact size and shape are not specified.

notes.label: Müserngeist
notes.text: literally the ‘Müseren spirit,’ the local name for the oath-breaking official’s haunting presence in the disputed Müseren forest near Gebistorf; it functions as a place-bound ghost name, although the account gives the apparition several different forms and actions.

fe1d911ac1bdea9a3b1923ad69d69f48d5973203.summary: In the municipality of Ober-Siggental, between the settlements of Obernussbaumen, Kirchdorf, and Tronsberg, lies a wood called the Tobelhölzli.

notes.label: Tobelhölzli
notes.text: a Swiss place-name meaning a little wood by or in a Tobel, a narrow ravine or wooded gully; the diminutive Hölzli indicates a small grove or wood.

notes.label: Nachmittaglamm
notes.text: literally “afternoon lamb,” the local name of the uncanny lamb in the Tobelhölzli; the source does not explain why it is associated with the afternoon or classify it more precisely as a ghost, omen, or enchanted animal.

aaaa2ff911d13404ea9c0ca37569b914f10b595a.summary: Before 1582, a Nachrichter lived in the region of Mainz and had a person from Lucerne in his service.

notes.label: Nachrichter
notes.text: a historical executioner or officer who carried out judicial punishments; such figures were also credited with illicit medical and magical knowledge.

notes.label: Totenbaum
notes.text: literally a ‘dead person's tree’ or ‘death tree,’ here a source of churchyard wood used for magical sight; the account does not identify the tree species or its exact ritual status.

7f28c0eac2d44db92cc64dac4a904de578dbe592.summary: The Nachtfräulein in Näfels was enchantingly beautiful. At night it stationed itself in every lane and on every path where a young man had to pass while going to visit his sweetheart at night or returning from her.

notes.label: Nachtfräulein
notes.text: literally a “little lady of the night,” the local name for this beautiful, elusive nocturnal female apparition; Fräulein here marks a maiden-like being rather than a modern form of address.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: young men taking part in Kiltgang, the traditional nighttime courtship visit to a sweetheart; the term refers to the suitors as a group, not ordinary nighttime pedestrians.

ff21a3af05652da6a2550c35e4662d6df40c409d.summary: In Mels, people knew—and still know—the Nachtfüllen that wanders upward from Plons as far as the shooting house.

notes.label: Nachtfüllen
notes.text: literally a ‘night foal,’ a supernatural nocturnal horse that reverses the rider's role by mounting and exhausting travelers or carries human riders away at uncanny speed.

notes.label: Riet
notes.text: marshy meadowland or reed country; here it means the low wet ground extending from Mels toward the Rhine.

notes.label: lüterlete
notes.text: a dialect verb referring to the sounding of early bells or the approach of daybreak; the riders discover where they are as the night ends.

notes.label: Stubeti
notes.text: an evening household gathering for visiting, courtship, conversation, or shared work, especially in Swiss rural life.

notes.label: Nachtrossen
notes.text: literally ‘night steeds,’ uncanny horses encountered as a group; Ross is an older or regional word for a horse.

dee7fad1481f9c45e8ba68642bf34fb3284728c9.summary: Among the inhabitants of Langnau in the Emmental circulates the legend of the Nachtgejäge.

notes.label: Nachtgejäge
notes.text: literally ‘night hunt,’ the Emmental name for a roaming spectral hunt heard with shots, dogs, and cries; here it follows a fixed route and intensifies before rain and at Christmas.

d349b8ab8098cab14401db597d013e146bd0d66c.summary: On the Hundsrücken, which extends northeast from the Rotsee near Lucerne to Buchrain, there once lived a wicked woman who was so unbearable that her husband left her, went to war, and soon met the death there that he had wished for.

notes.label: Hundsrücken
notes.text: literally ‘dog's back,’ the local ridge running from the Rotsee toward Buchrain where the woman's story is placed.

notes.label: Reisig
notes.text: brushwood, twigs, and small branches gathered as household fuel; the poor children collecting it echo the vulnerability of the abandoned daughters.

notes.label: Nachthuri
notes.text: the Lucerne name of the raging nocturnal female apparition created by the murderous mother's madness and death; Nacht means ‘night,’ while the regional Huri element suggests a frenzied, rushing, or shrewish woman but is not precisely defined here.

180cbf1addbe36c93403a16becce65996f1133ff.summary: The Nachtlütli Flee into the Forest

notes.label: Nachtlütli
notes.text: literally ‘little night people’ in Swiss German, the local name for diminutive folkloric beings associated with nighttime and the countryside; this brief account does not specify their nature beyond their flight from humans.

76c31f9878767045412851661a655899bd7b3cf7.summary: During Lent at Tiefencastel, two young men went one evening to a farmhouse to dance there with several girls, despite the commandment to fast.

notes.label: Nachtschaar
notes.text: literally the ‘night host’ or ‘night company,’ a supernatural procession of the dead or other uncanny beings in Alpine tradition; recognizing members makes the vision especially ominous.

120a09dbad3ecf527b1333a7e29e4a806afe303b.summary: Between the villages of Alvaneu and Schmitten lies a rugged, densely wooded Tobel through which a road also leads to the Alvaneu Baths.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge; here it names the feared forested passage between Alvaneu and Schmitten.

notes.label: Nachtschaar
notes.text: literally a “night host” or “nightly company,” an old-spelling name for the supernatural procession that compels the young man to wander and stand within its dance.

87cb71b4396a81442e2db6e5bc4a07cade05871e.summary: When the afterglow fades from the Urirotstock and night begins to overshadow the green mountain lake of Lake Lucerne, the lake country grows uncanny.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent downslope wind of the Alps; around Lake Lucerne it can raise dangerous waves and rapidly spread fire.

notes.label: Rütli
notes.text: the meadow above Lake Uri associated with the legendary oath that founded the Swiss Confederacy; the tale places the symbolic Bull of Uri there.

notes.label: Nachtspinnerin
notes.text: literally the ‘night spinner,’ a female supernatural guardian of industrious spinning who punishes lazy young women at midnight.

notes.label: Leewasserbrücke
notes.text: the locally named bridge at Brunnen where the Nachtspinnerin appears; the name refers to the Leewasser watercourse.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: young men or lads who go out at night for courting, revelry, or mischief; their distant jubilant calls intensify the mother's uncertainty.

notes.label: Mythen
notes.text: the pair of prominent mountains above Schwyz, the Grosser and Kleiner Mythen; despite the spelling, the name is not the German plural of ‘myth.’

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for a hedge or enclosure; the girl sleeps all day behind it.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Firn
notes.text: old, compacted perennial snow that feeds a glacier; the shining Firn high on the Urirotstock is part of the sight the blinded girl loses.

1186d08d5374bbe2528799407495c66eafbd7340.summary: This is one of the strangest ghost stories. Once, toward midnight, the schoolmaster at Flums heard a peculiar murmuring down in the street, like the prayer of a mighty host of people.

notes.label: Pfisterläuferli
notes.text: a small regional neck garment or shirt-collar worn by the hastily dressed sacristan; the precise historical clothing item is uncertain.

notes.label: Nachtvolch
notes.text: literally night folk, a spectral nocturnal procession containing the dead and people marked to die; regional traditions overlap with the night host and death procession.

da31a702aabbaa49bc9c50d1934c5a87178d9dfa.summary: At certain times, Fronfastenkinder see the Nachtvolk.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: people born during the Ember Days who are believed to possess second sight, especially the ability to see death processions and future victims.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night people,’ a spectral procession of the dead and those soon to die; seeing one's own double in it foretells death.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Mesner
notes.text: a sacristan or church sexton; the most recently deceased Mesner follows the priest at the head of the supernatural church procession.

notes.label: Sterbet
notes.text: a regional noun for a deadly epidemic or period of mass dying; here it names the plague foretold by the Nachtvolk.

b804412a3cfb1704e263b4c8b9e3026324d9ea51.summary: In Peist, where in former times the Totenvolk went about in great strength, the Nachtvolk likewise had much business.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” the regional name for a collective procession or company of the dead; the opening distinguishes it from, while associating it with, the Nachtvolk.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally “night folk,” a supernatural nocturnal company with which Brunold is compelled to travel until his friend pulls him across a protective boundary.

notes.label: G'spiel
notes.text: a regional word for a companion of the same age or a friend from one’s youth, as Jecklin’s own gloss explains.

notes.label: geprofetet
notes.text: a regionalized form meaning “prophesied”; Brunold says his supernatural obligation was foretold while he was still in the cradle.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: Swiss German for a godmother or female baptismal sponsor; Brunold attributes unusual knowledge and power to his Gotte.

notes.label: gähen
notes.text: an older regional adjective meaning sudden or abrupt, explicitly glossed by Jecklin in the threatened choice of deaths.

notes.label: Dachtrauf
notes.text: the roof eaves or drip line; in this tale it forms a supernatural boundary, since crossing it affects whether a person can see or act against spirits.

a051bc8d06c2e0d7ab6ff5402a2e3a00e22bc704.summary: A man from Castiel who kept his livestock at Calfreisen and fed it there each day was walking toward Calfreisen, as usual, in the first hours of the morning.

notes.label: reiben
notes.text: literally to rub; in this quoted rural context it refers to communal processing of hemp, though Jecklin does not specify the exact tool or stage.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally the ‘night folk,’ a supernatural nocturnal procession whose passing can physically batter a human observer.

notes.label: Castieler-Tobel
notes.text: the steep ravine associated with Castiel through which the Nachtvolk passes.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alpine term for a steep, narrow ravine or stream gorge, more specific than an ordinary valley.

9255037b194437dfd929e4eb348546d53ee16cae.summary: In the Prättigau, the Nachtvolk, or “fliegende Heer,” was first seen on the Steifer-Berg above Schiers by a Senn.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally “night people,” a supernatural nocturnal host in Alpine tradition, here equated with the airborne spectral procession.

notes.label: fliegende Heer
notes.text: literally “flying host” or “flying army,” a regional form of the Wild Hunt whose passage foretells communal disaster.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for livestock and milk work on a seasonal alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schlafgaden
notes.text: a sleeping chamber or small sleeping structure attached to an Alpine farm building; Gaden can denote a separate room or outbuilding.

notes.label: Töbel
notes.text: the plural of Tobel, steep and narrow Alpine ravines or gullies often cut by torrents.

a869aa1cecc88960bcdd2461e675c25c0aafb33b.summary: Late one night a peasant passed the ruined stable whose surroundings are called “Sand,” half an hour from the Meierhof.

notes.label: Sand
notes.text: the local name of the area around the ruined stable, not merely a description of its soil.

notes.label: Meierhof
notes.text: historically the principal farm or estate center administered by a Meier; here it serves as the reference settlement for the half-hour distance.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally “night people,” a supernatural nocturnal company in Alpine tradition; here they make music, dance, and handle golden balls before driving the witness away.

fb998ab682d19aae93288598c3ce678818716ad2.summary: On Rahl, a Gadenstatt above Fanas, a man from Schiers kept his cattle in the stable for feeding.

notes.label: Gadenstatt
notes.text: a mountain holding or seasonal farmstead characterized by its barns and stalls; the source itself glosses it as a Berggut, or mountain farm.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally “night folk,” a regional name for an uncanny nocturnal company or procession; this brief account reveals it only through many instruments sounding in the air and does not identify its members.

848ea7e7902cae6fecfcab5584252ce430c483dd.summary: After the Alpentladung, a man once came across the Jeninser Alp with a cow and spent the night in a hut.

notes.label: Alpentladung
notes.text: the seasonal clearing or unloading of an Alp when the herd and equipment are brought down at the end of summer grazing; the incident occurs afterward.

notes.label: Jeninser Alp
notes.text: the high summer pasture associated with Jenins in Graubünden, across which the man travels after the seasonal descent.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally “night folk,” a supernatural nocturnal company that feasts in the hut and magically takes flesh from the still-living cow.

notes.label: Nachtgesindel
notes.text: literally “night rabble” or “nightly crew,” a more disparaging label used in the second paragraph for the same supernatural company.

1cb99ef5fa7d31a87cc1514e28f1a56496481e7c.summary: In gray antiquity, a little village stood at the southwestern foot of the Gruonberg.

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: the plural of an Uri regional word for destructive debris flows or mountain torrents carrying rock, mud, and water; together with rockfalls they destroy the earliest village, and no individual event is dated.

notes.label: Friärächäppäli
notes.text: the local dialect name of the former round chapel in the Kreuzmatte; Chäppäli means ‘little chapel,’ while the meaning of the first element and the building's exact origin are not explained.

31dbc5071c00864f65f19281ac7c360804ff1803.summary: Long ago, before the handsome village of Flüelen existed at the southern end of Lake Uri, a cluster of houses stood beside the Gruonbach in a very fertile, blessed district—today called Winkel and Gruonmättli, then called Blumenau or Blumenfeld, while documents called the district Gronon.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri term for a destructive, debris-laden mountain torrent or flow; the witch releases one that dams the Gruonbach and later overwhelms the settlement.

notes.label: Wildmandli
notes.text: a little wild or mountain being in Alpine folklore; here it lives above the valley and gives the villagers three supernatural warnings.

notes.label: Flüeli
notes.text: a diminutive related to Flue or Fluh, meaning a small crag or rock face and also naming the local landmark behind which the survivors settle; its sound supports the tale's folk explanation of the name Flüelen.

notes.label: Ringgäribi
notes.text: the local name for the ring-associated Rübi unleashed after the witch loses her ring; the tale makes it central to Flüelen's origin, but the exact dialect formation of the compound is uncertain.

notes.label: dä Fliälänä
notes.text: the Uri dialect place-expression quoted in the source for the cliffs or rocky features below which Flüelen stands; it is retained because its sound forms part of the folk etymology, while its precise grammatical number is uncertain.

a7ae37002dee2c108b5fa4d3f0df5e37604478b5.summary: It is a small cave in the rock in which, immeasurable years ago, a dreadful dragon or Natter lived.

notes.label: Natter
notes.text: ordinarily an adder or snake in German, but the story uses it interchangeably with a man-eating, poison-breathing dragon.

notes.label: Natterloch
notes.text: literally ‘Natter hole,’ the dragon cave from which the legend derives the name Naters; this is a folk etymology, not proof of the place-name's linguistic origin.

051ac3b795ea8ee603d484e4af60a2797d625e8c.summary: On the Stutzalp in Graubünden, every Senn takes care that each cow receives its share of salt, for they always remember the wondrous Nebelmännlein who often appears there.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a Swiss alpine pasture; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Nebelmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little fog man,’ the diminutive local name for this mist-associated alpine apparition and penitent former herdsman.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working settlement, where the cattle graze and the mist figure wanders.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an inflected form of Senn, the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker responsible for cattle and milk work on a seasonal alp.

notes.label: Nebelmännlein
notes.text: literally “little mist man,” a diminutive supernatural herdsman who appears in cloud and snow and seeks to repair his unjust treatment of cattle.

notes.label: Tracht
notes.text: the traditional regional dress of the country; the apparition’s old-fashioned clothing marks it as belonging to an earlier local world.

notes.label: Triften
notes.text: open grazing grounds or pasture runs across which livestock are driven; here they are the meadows of the apparition’s penance.

notes.label: Stutz-Alpe
notes.text: the named seasonal high pasture of the poem; Alpe denotes a worked Alpine grazing and dairying site rather than simply a mountain.

9114c115e153dd466a4e01f0177b7a7f676af5db.summary: It is told that for many years an old house on the great mountain in the parish of St.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: schwifer
notes.text: a regional description of a place as haunted, restlessly uncanny, or full of ghostly disturbance; the exact nuance is uncommon and context-dependent.

notes.label: Boze
notes.text: a bogey, household spirit, or frightening supernatural being; here it behaves more like a persistent prankster than a destructive demon.

notes.label: Fensterläufer
notes.text: literally ‘window runner,’ the sliding or moving part of the traditional window mechanism with which the spirit traps someone looking out.

notes.label: Stubendiele
notes.text: the wooden floorboards or floor of the Stube, the principal heated living room in a traditional house.

notes.label: Neckerboze
notes.text: literally a ‘teasing Boze,’ the title's name for a mischievous household bogey that annoys residents without causing lasting harm.

5b806b613ade3e00f281a27f8aa130e9b150fd34.summary: In the year 1277, a Schwarzkünstler in the land of Uri was about to begin his conjurations for money with several farmers just as a terrible hailstorm was laying waste to the valley.

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a “black artist,” a historical German-speaking name for a sorcerer or practitioner of black magic; here the man offers paid conjurations, but the story does not explicitly say that he caused the hail.

notes.label: Negromant
notes.text: a historical German term for a practitioner of necromancy or forbidden learned magic, broader in popular usage than someone who only raises the dead; here it titles the itinerant conjurer, whose exact rites are unstated.

4a1002f4584ce59c551f38de3f7b3b720748ea99.summary: A fahrender Schüler passing through the Reuss Valley said, ‘If people knew what nettle roots were good for, they would be rich enough.’ The people of Wassen offered him 200 francs if he would reveal the secret, even in only two words, but they could not persuade him.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a folkloric itinerant learned figure credited with magic, divination, treasure-finding, and secret knowledge; here his hidden knowledge of nettle roots is supposed to confer wealth.

ee6a8c9e3ad5c693fa428115cc9211c34182ef5c.summary: The uppermost farmstead in the Rueder Valley is called Neulig. A hunter once lived there who was called the Neuliger.

notes.label: Neuliger
notes.text: the farm-name-derived byname of the hunter from Neulig, a farmstead at the head of the Rueder Valley.

notes.label: Festbannen
notes.text: magically binding or fixing game in place so it cannot escape the hunter; the tale treats it as an illicit hunting enchantment.

5806e1ae50ab1242a63ac38891a48edc35c2bfe8.summary: This is the Sieglauch, or Allermannsharnisch. In popular belief in Unterwalden, this root possessed special, virtually supernatural power.

notes.label: Sieglauch
notes.text: literally ‘victory leek,’ a traditional name for Allium victorialis, also known in English as victory onion or Alpine leek; the plant was credited with protective and medicinal powers.

notes.label: Allermannsharnisch
notes.text: literally ‘everyman's armor,’ another traditional name for Allium victorialis; ‘armor’ reflects its reputation as a defense against illness, magic, and witchcraft.

notes.label: Gichter
notes.text: an older folk-medical term for convulsions or seizure-like fits, especially in children; it should not be read as a precise modern diagnosis.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Neunhämmli-Wurzel
notes.text: a local folk name for the magically protective root identified in the text as Sieglauch or Allermannsharnisch; the name is retained because a literal rendering such as ‘nine-little-hammers root’ would not explain its cultural use.

724b77ad124e8866c9bda1e3fd359ea7c3deaf27.summary: On the road from the mountain village of Hettenschwil to Leuggern, where the Aare approaches its confluence with the Rhine, one must pass through the woods of Mooshalde and the spring-rich grove of Stubenbrünnli.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings in regional folklore; here they live beneath Steigfeld and secretly help with farm work.

notes.label: Nachtwerk
notes.text: literally ‘night-work’; the villagers’ name for the field labor the Erdmännchen complete unseen after the evening bell.

notes.label: Abendbetzeit
notes.text: the customary evening-prayer time announced by a church bell; the laborers bribe the sacristan to ring it early and summon the little men before dark.

notes.label: Neunuhrbrot
notes.text: literally ‘nine-o’clock bread,’ a midmorning farm laborer’s meal or snack; in this tale it is a large savory cake brought into the field.

notes.label: Waijen
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a flat baked tart or cake, often savory; this one is described as a brown-baked bacon cake.

notes.label: Hegel
notes.text: the source’s local name for a very small, inexpensive knife like a child’s knife, used by the little men to divide the Waijen.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: a small historical coin used in many Central European territories; the tale says one Hegel costs a single Kreuzer, but its exact local value is not converted.

notes.label: Krappenstecher
notes.text: the plowboy’s mocking local name for the little men’s poor cutting knives; the exact derivation and narrower tool sense are uncertain, so the source word remains.

notes.label: Bilmessschnitt
notes.text: a folklore term for an unnaturally straight, discolored swath through grass or grain, traditionally attributed to a supernatural cut or influence; Rochholz links it here to the dwarf’s underground forge fire.

notes.label: mohrischer Gesichtsfarbe
notes.text: an antiquated racialized phrase literally meaning ‘of Moorish complexion,’ used in the historical comparative note for dark skin; it is outdated and potentially offensive, and is retained only to make the source’s wording transparent.

ece898b58b2d75427c2bbb381f4fd04b275f2edb.summary: At the time of the Crusades, when many knights and men-at-arms had journeyed to the Holy Land to wrest Christ's Holy Sepulcher from the unbelievers, a knight from the city of Schaffhausen, where the beautiful Erkerstraße stands, had also traveled across the sea with them.

notes.label: Erkerstraße
notes.text: literally ‘oriel-window street,’ a Schaffhausen street distinguished by projecting bay windows and invoked as a mark of the knight's beautiful home city.

notes.label: Prügelwegen
notes.text: rough roads made from logs, poles, or corduroy-like timber; their poor condition limits the returning knight's speed.

notes.label: Reisigen
notes.text: mounted armed retainers or men-at-arms traveling with a knight; all but one drown while following him through the storm.

notes.label: Burgkatze
notes.text: literally ‘castle cat,’ an old name for a large fortress cannon; it could have signaled the castle's location through darkness and storm.

notes.label: Wendelstein
notes.text: a spiral-stair tower or winding tower structure in the castle; the memorial bell is hung high within it.

notes.label: Burgglöcklein
notes.text: literally ‘little castle bell,’ the affectionate narrative name for the same silver Neunuhrglöcklein when its sound guides lost travelers.

notes.label: Neunuhrglöcklein
notes.text: literally ‘little nine-o'clock bell,’ the nightly memorial bell whose sound guides travelers after the knight drowns at nine.

b38049d4f8a8eb5611fee6b53f775cd328dcc6d9.summary: The genial inhabitants of the city of Sion are very fond of beautiful Mayenberg and in summer go up in crowds with wives and children to enjoy the fresher air of field and forest.

notes.label: Mayen
notes.text: a Valais seasonal pasture or settlement at an intermediate elevation, occupied especially in spring or summer between the valley and higher Alp; the plural-looking local reference here describes the residents' beloved seasonal landscape rather than the month of May alone.

notes.label: Hofstatt
notes.text: a house-site, homestead ground, or settled plot; the founders deliberate there, although the passage does not specify whether a building already stood on it.

notes.label: Maria zum guten Rat
notes.text: ‘Mary of Good Counsel,’ the chapel's devotional title; retaining the German title preserves the locally recorded dedication, while 1776 is the stated completion or naming year.

044b9ceaa4562dddf840188d3dca738c3d90367f.summary: It was wintertime, and the courtroom in the courthouse in Lucerne was to be heated.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

befad82a8f1289843aa8e18271cee2c8c3d2bea3.summary: Many years ago, an honest Valais herdsman had taken his cattle up to the alpine pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Hackbrett
notes.text: literally a ‘chopping board,’ the Swiss hammered dulcimer whose strings are struck with small beaters; here its racing hammers drive the supernatural dance, and the name should not be confused with an ordinary board.

notes.label: Getjen
notes.text: a Valais regional topographic plural for steep slopes or rocky mountain ground; here it names the opposite terrain that throws the dancers' cries back, and its exact local nuance is difficult to reproduce in English.

notes.label: Bissaga
notes.text: a Valais dialect word for a large sack used to gather or carry leaves; the story itself glosses it as Laubsack, and the fiery procession is imagined plunging downward in that bulky, tumbling shape.

4bd5f7d6d54b138bc6e2052e19bc3eb67d8ab43e.summary: The Night Folk consisted of a great multitude of black figures. In their midst walked a white man who towered above them all and wore a large floppy hat—Wodan!

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

de629cbbb5afb142506532280cbe0417ba76364b.summary: In former times, a horrible night ghost haunted the streets and side roads around Plaffeien, but chiefly the place itself.

notes.label: Gassentätscher
notes.text: a regional name for Plaffeien's shape-changing night ghost, literally suggesting something that pads, slaps, or blunders through the lanes; here it appears as a dog, ox, and gigantic figure, so no single creature gloss is sufficient.

672b62e6eae76fc9da3772be7d9d4fc9d935856c.summary: In ancient times there were all manner of monsters in mountain and valley. Thus, in the Valais town of Sion, people often saw a three-legged horse galloping through the streets on moonlit nights.

notes.label: Üchtland
notes.text: a historical German regional name for the country around Fribourg; English readers may also encounter Fribourg itself styled Freiburg im Üechtland.

notes.label: Zawudschawu
notes.text: the regional proper name of a supernatural night horse in the Gruyère and Fribourg tradition; it carries frail travelers home but plays dangerous tricks on others, and the source does not explain the name's precise etymology.

notes.label: Buriander
notes.text: the source's name for the moorland route crossed by elderly travelers; its exact modern location and spelling are uncertain, so the name is retained rather than silently identified with another place.

notes.label: Saane
notes.text: the German name of the river called the Sarine in French; both names matter in bilingual Fribourg, so the English text gives Saane (Sarine).

1efbb0241e1f87f5f6efe6be1cb20e1433a26df9.summary: On dark nights in Eggerberg, lights are often said to have been seen: sometimes only one large light that dissolved into many smaller ones, and sometimes a considerable number of them wandering about at regular intervals.

notes.label: Vorlaube
notes.text: a covered outer gallery, porch, or passage along the front or upper story of a traditional house; here it is the open-air part of the old chaplaincy from which Mooser watches the lights, though the building’s exact form is not described.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

5cfd236801db07bd833e9cc667681c2fa6d79323.summary: Kaspar—the story takes place in the 1840s of the preceding century—a young unmarried man from Holzerberg in Bürglen, had paid an evening visit to his sweetheart at the very high mountain farm of Schindleren and was on his way home.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2e06bec4e77afa51b0daee27fe863bad83d7e935.summary: When the Alpine glow fades on the Urirotstock and night begins to overshadow the green mountain lake of the Vierwaldstättersee, the region around the lake grows uncanny.

notes.label: Urirotstock
notes.text: a mountain summit in the canton of Uri above Lake Lucerne; its high snowfields frame both the opening and the blinded girl's final loss of sight.

notes.label: Vierwaldstättersee
notes.text: the German name for Lake Lucerne, literally the “Lake of the Four Forest Cantons”; the source uses the inflected form Vierwaldstättersees, while the English text retains the standard place-name form.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry Alpine downslope wind that can blow violently around Lake Lucerne; in the tale it drives the waves and creates a grave danger of fire.

notes.label: Stier von Uri
notes.text: literally the “Bull of Uri,” a traditional name associated with Uri's great battle horn and its horn-blower, not merely an ordinary bull; the tale imagines its blast sounding across the lake.

notes.label: Rütli
notes.text: the lakeside meadow traditionally associated with the founding oath of the Swiss Confederation; it lies in Uri above an arm of Lake Lucerne.

notes.label: Nachtspinnerin
notes.text: literally the “Night Spinner,” the supernatural woman who spins on the bridge at midnight and punishes girls who have been idle at their spinning by day.

notes.label: Leewasserbrücke
notes.text: the locally named bridge at Brunnen where the Nachtspinnerin appears; the source treats it as an uncanny place but does not further explain the bridge-name.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Spinnlein
notes.text: an affectionate or diminutive form meaning “little spider”; the mother's lesson depends on the spider's spinning as an example for her idle daughter.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: groups of young men who roam together at night, sometimes making noise or playing pranks; here their jubilant calls sound beside the lake as the mother begins her search.

notes.label: Mythen
notes.text: the two prominent peaks near Schwyz, commonly understood here as the Grosser Mythen and Kleiner Mythen; the name is a place-name and does not mean “myths” in this context.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a Swiss German and older regional word for a hedge, fence, or enclosure; the girl says she slept behind it all day and half the night.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Rocken
notes.text: a distaff, the staff or support that holds unspun flax beside a spinning wheel; the blinding flash comes from the golden flax hanging upon it.

notes.label: Firn
notes.text: old, compacted snow that survives successive seasons high on a mountain or glacier; the girl can never again see it shining on the Urirotstock.

f02c4bf32f7e4c5461c028dbe800cbf1f36c17ff.summary: Near Brunnen, a white female figure appears on the Leewasserbrücke every night from twelve until one o'clock.

notes.label: Leewasserbrücke
notes.text: the bridge over the Leewasser near Brunnen where the supernatural spinner appears; Brücke means ‘bridge,’ while Leewasser is the local watercourse name.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

ba20dbee398db053247232991334b7175354a9bd.summary: Below Malans, where a road toward the village crosses the millstream winding through the meadows, uncanny things happen on dark and stormy nights:

notes.label: Han' Wasser geschüttet in den Win
notes.text: dialect for “I poured water into the wine”; Win is the local form of Wein, or wine, and the confession names the carter’s fraud.
notes.anchor: Han' Wasser geschüttet in den Win

notes.label: Muss immer und ewig verloren sin!
notes.text: dialect for “I must be lost forever and ever”; sin is the local infinitive form corresponding to standard German sein, “to be.”
notes.anchor: Muss immer und ewig verloren sin!

notes.label: taufte
notes.text: literally “baptized”; the ironic traditional expression means diluting wine with water, the same fraud for which the apparition is punished.

6568cc8bc501183f642dbdea5949fede682771be.summary: A man from the Engadin once related the following: My grandfather had a servant.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

bed275faafbd2eb23062c3559ac5b38d0095d8c2.summary: In the little village of Hütten, high above Lake Zurich and close to a small hill lake, there once lived a young man.

notes.label: Nesteln
notes.text: decorative laces, ties, or points used to fasten clothing or shoes; golden ones would signal conspicuous finery.

notes.label: Kirchweih
notes.text: a church-dedication fair or annual village festival, commonly featuring music, dancing, food, and courtship.

notes.label: Nixe
notes.text: a female water spirit who may entice humans into her lake; the German term can suggest both a beautiful water maiden and a dangerous supernatural being.

notes.label: Hüttnerseelein
notes.text: literally ‘little Hütten lake,’ the diminutive name of the small lake near Hütten above Lake Zurich.

notes.label: Einbaum
notes.text: a dugout canoe made from a single tree trunk; the young man fashions his from oak.

notes.label: Blust
notes.text: Swiss German for blossom or full bloom; here it describes the lake's luminous covering of white water lilies.

f21baa1c3870f9e33efacc925da0b480e3351f40.summary: In ancient times, as several older and younger local people told me—including a 90-year-old man, a person from Middle Planzern, and one from Rütteli—a very noble lady, a countess, lived at Rütteli directly below Planzern.

notes.label: Wysiglocke
notes.text: the locally named church bell donated to Altdorf by the countess; the source records its name but does not explain its literal derivation or ringing function more narrowly.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held or used land belonging to a local community rather than a private owner; this particular donated meadow is paradoxically called the ‘enclosed Allmend.’

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a debris-laden mountain torrent or its channel; here it also functions as a named feature on the countess’s route.

notes.label: Chappäli
notes.text: an Uri diminutive for a little chapel; the reported ruin may have been a small masonry prayer niche rather than a full church building.

notes.label: G'hirmistein
notes.text: the named stone beside the chapel remains; G'hirmi is a local terrain or structure-word whose exact literal sense is not established here.

fda1aa8d1fd8bb8bc883dd2ac4e8fe45449ec4da.summary: In Wil near Mettau, people point out a house before which a bull appears every night and thrusts its horns into the walls with pitiful bellowing.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

cb43583ec5e49f4323128c0035e8491c12ceeff1.summary: Some twenty years ago, whenever prolonged rain was coming, a nocturnal call could be heard in the Mühlimatte like the one customarily used to lure cows, and the regularly repeated words could be distinguished with complete clarity: ‘se se se!

notes.label: se se se! Chom, se se se!
notes.text: a regional cattle call meaning approximately ‘come, come’ rather than a full grammatical sentence; its repeated sound is both the boy's working call and his posthumous cry for help.
notes.anchor: se se se! Chom, se se se!

notes.label: Galgenhubel
notes.text: literally ‘gallows hill’ or ‘gallows knoll,’ the execution-associated rise where the priests imprison the spirit in a bottle.

notes.label: Fasnachtfeuer
notes.text: fires lit for Fasnacht, the pre-Lenten Carnival season; their continued use connects communal seasonal ritual with the older gallows and spirit-binding site.

1eae5ecf158b5cb911d6795e489bef0c03046a34.summary: 1. A councilor lived opposite the town hall in Altdorf.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

54d74711464080e2f8bf2c8d6e7f87d198880e2c.summary: In the forest below the hamlet of Acker, a cry for help is said often to be heard at night.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

5ff5db6ff05c1d1fc23115ba501724c70f9af4ff.summary: A legend similar to this one can be found in H. Colshorn’s book of fairy tales.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan; here he tends the church and first witnesses the nocturnal game.

notes.label: Tempertage
notes.text: a regional shortened form of Quatembertage, the Ember Days or quarterly fast days of the Christian calendar; the spirits are compelled to carry the coffin at these liminal sacred times.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

e5a3591f4fbc9803289ef5e91a8f04c211a000e9.summary: At the foot of the hill on which old Ruchenberg Castle stands, a stony Tobel passes by.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gorge cut by a stream; it appears both as a landscape term and within Scaläratobel.

notes.label: Alaräunchen
notes.text: a small uncanny being associated with the dark forest, probably related to the mandrake spirit called Alraun; the diminutive form and exact local nature are not explained.

notes.label: Scalära
notes.text: the local name of the ravine haunted by Chur’s dead civic officials; the source emphasizes its fearful associations but gives no etymology.

d936fa4a649ec47d780a49c48dce3046f85450bd.summary: High above, through the mountain holdings, ran the old Roman road. Nocturnal riders still appear upon it during the heiligen Zeiten.

notes.label: heiligen Zeiten
notes.text: literally ‘holy times,’ the sacred days or seasons of the Christian calendar—often Christmas and its surrounding nights—when supernatural processions are especially expected; this brief source does not specify the exact feast.

cc617e3064ab43f058b0eeb0a55590d712881af9.summary: At the foot of the Jura, not far from the village of Berolles in the canton of Vaud and a short distance from the so-called Roman road, there is an isolated, round hill of considerable size.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Nernetçan
notes.text: one recorded local name for the haunted hilltop or its central field near Berolles; the source also gives Nernier-Feld, and the name's precise derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Nernier-Feld
notes.text: literally ‘Nernier field,’ an alternate name for the hill's central ground where the supernatural banquet appears; Nernier may preserve a local place or family name whose exact reference is not explained.

3702b7bb340e36d4ba57fbd8623de1432afb4cb9.summary: A shepherd was tending his flock in Küeh-Vereina and one evening found that several sheep were missing.

notes.label: Küeh-Vereina
notes.text: the local name of the high-pasture area and hut where the shepherd spends the night; the source provides no etymology or modern boundary description.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a distinctively Swiss fresh whey cheese or curd made from proteins remaining after ordinary cheese production; the beings offer it separately from their regular cheese.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, an Alpine dairy worker responsible for livestock and cheese-making on a high pasture; the traditional occupational label is retained even though the two spectral beings in this tale are female.

c98867331a8557e16cf3946d722b9269c679bb03.summary: Two ‘Missionheerä’—Jesuit mission priests—once came to Flüelen and had someone show them the field path to Erstfeld.

notes.label: Missionheerä
notes.text: literally ‘mission gentlemen,’ the dialect designation here for two Jesuit priests conducting a Catholic popular mission; it does not mean overseas missionaries in this context.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: a historical quarter-unit used for varying dry measures; here it means a substantial measured quantity of nuts, not merely one quarter of a single nut, but the local capacity is not specified.

notes.label: Unholde
notes.text: the historical singular for a malign female supernatural being, witch, or demon; the saying imagines giving each such inhabitant half a nut.

notes.label: Unholden
notes.text: a historical plural for malign female supernatural beings, witches, or demons; the priest's exaggeration says they are so numerous along the unsettled Reuss that even half a nut apiece would exhaust his measure.

8ad3f6a539f02b220f3bd3ce60949e1a3d119202.summary: At the Stalden near Flüelen stands a Markstein like a specter from ancient times.

notes.label: Markstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking a legal or territorial division; its position at a three-way boundary supplies the stone's magical association with the number three.

notes.label: Ämter
notes.text: plural of Amt, historical administrative or jurisdictional districts; here the three named territories meet at the stone.

ff4ff4e1fbe58df95dbd9771b19ab0268aee01f9.summary: Near Ebersoll stands a little bridge beneath which a teasing nymph sits. She lets no traveler pass undisturbed, but she means no harm.

notes.label: Neis
notes.text: a regional word for a fresh flower, sprig, or small floral token worn on the cap; its exact botanical meaning here is uncertain, but it is intended as a gift for the young man's bride.

notes.label: Giessen
notes.text: a regional name for a rushing stream, cascade, or waterfall; here it is the watercourse emerging from the forest at Brunnadern.

notes.label: Nixchen
notes.text: a diminutive water spirit or little water nymph, related to Nixe; the being is playful and prophetic rather than overtly hostile.

notes.label: Nixe
notes.text: a female water spirit of German-speaking folklore, dwelling in a brook, river, or lake.

notes.label: Wasserfräulein
notes.text: literally ‘little water lady’ or ‘water maiden,’ another affectionate regional designation for the same nymph-like spirit.

b0bcf93b1e26fcc11c89cf20323e73d20c84cd56.summary: The village of Merligen lies pleasantly beside Lake Thun, and many merry stories are told throughout the Bernese country about its inhabitants.

notes.label: Heitere
notes.text: a regional word for brightness, clearness, or light; the apothecary exploits the delegation’s literal request by selling them a buzzing bumblebee in a box.

notes.label: Trucklein
notes.text: an older diminutive for a little box or chest, comparable to Swiss German Trückli; it is the carefully sealed container supposedly holding Heitere.

notes.label: räss
notes.text: sharp, biting, acrid, or strongly flavored in Swiss usage; the nettles’ sting convinces the villagers that their supposed salt crop is already potent.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: the local chief magistrate or community official; his leading position becomes literal when he heads the human chain reaching toward the lake.

notes.label: trüelen
notes.text: a regional verb for pressing grapes or operating a winepress; the source itself glosses it with standard German keltern.

notes.label: Trotten
notes.text: winepresses or the buildings containing them; the joke imagines hard grapes shooting from the presses across Lake Thun like bullets.

notes.label: Leuen
notes.text: an older regional form of Löwen, ‘lion,’ used in the name and sign of the Lion inn; the faded animal on the sign drives the riddle’s confusion with a monkey.

notes.label: Rahm
notes.text: cream, here absurdly used as a sweet whitewash for a blackened church, thereby attracting insects.

notes.label: Talgenosse
notes.text: a recognized member of a valley community who shared its obligations and rights; each one is required to contribute a bucket of Rahm.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Oberländer Schildbürger
notes.text: literally ‘Oberland Schildbürger,’ the imagined wise fools of the Bernese Oberland; Schildbürger stories assign absurdly literal reasoning to a particular town, but the jokes circulate among neighboring communities and do not describe historical intelligence.

5dc5ac08fc16114d1bcbcd092e9a0e7c40e47045.summary: In St. Niklaus, people tell of an old woman who lived in Riedacher in the commune of Gasenried, where she owned several fine meadows.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

1fc435743ed2a6a0d8a4f966fa203c6c2f61734c.summary: In the time of the parish priest Mâret, whose portrait can still be seen in the rectory at Savièse, it is related that a countless number of obstinate and malicious spirits called Mâlins lived in Mount Chamoréta in the Sanetsch Valley.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Mâlins
notes.text: a French-influenced Valais name for malicious, restless spirits, closest to ‘wicked ones’ or ‘cunning demons’; here they are rock-damaging beings who must always be given impossible work, but their precise supernatural class is not stated.

notes.label: Rebstichel
notes.text: a vineyard implement or support taken up by the tired priest, closest to a vine stake or pointed vineyard tool used as a walking aid; because the object is not described, its exact form and normal use remain uncertain.

39edce357a1405b03138aad8db69fabbee5dddc2.summary: When one goes from Frick through the Jura valley toward the Benken, an older mountain pass to Aarau—the newer pass being the Staffelegg—the first feature encountered below in the fairly broad valley is the so-called Alteberg, whose oaks have only in recent years been cut into railway sleepers.

notes.label: Oerkentier
notes.text: the local shape-changing stream and mountain spirit named for the Oerkenbach; the tale understands it as a murdered Swedish soldier’s ghost appearing as a wild man or several animals.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a coarse Alpine conglomerate whose embedded rounded stones can resemble nail heads; the cave’s former entrance block was a large mass of this characteristic Swiss foreland rock.

notes.label: Kreuzwoche
notes.text: Rogation Week, the period of processions and prayers before Ascension traditionally associated with blessing fields and seeking favorable weather; it is not simply any week marked by a cross.

notes.label: Waldhammer
notes.text: a municipal ax or hammer entrusted by the Ammann to someone traveling on community business; its exact administrative symbolism is not specified, but it is more than the farmer’s private tool.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a historical local magistrate, administrator, or head of a municipality; the precise powers varied by place and period.

notes.label: Maßflasche
notes.text: a bottle or flask sized to hold a Maß, a historical local liquid measure; both the container and the measure could vary by jurisdiction.

notes.label: Orko
notes.text: the Tyrolean name cited by Rochholz for a benevolent forest or wild-water spirit that he compares with the Oerkentier; the historical comparison does not establish that every regional figure was identical.

notes.label: Schrättel
notes.text: an older German name for a goblin-like, oppressive night, house, or woodland spirit; Rochholz cites it only as a comparative being in the medieval poem, so its exact relation to the Oerkentier remains uncertain.

notes.label: Orken
notes.text: the historical inflected form in Bintler’s verse for beings Rochholz relates to the Tyrolean Orko and the Oerkentier; it should not be read automatically as the modern fantasy creature called an orc.

notes.label: Elben
notes.text: an older German plural for elf-like spirits; the cited medieval verse pairs them with the Orken but gives no further description of their form or behavior.

c2c5a13f4524d63cc7849b391932b3a1fbc0ba32.summary: The skulls stacked in the charnel house at Andermatt seem to be rather sensitive.

notes.label: ä b'hiët-is nei!
notes.text: an emphatic Uri invocation meaning approximately ‘God preserve us, no!’; it strongly denies that Wolleb was drunk rather than naming an additional action.

notes.label: Tschiddlä
notes.text: a disparaging Uri dialect name addressed to the skulls in the charnel house, perhaps evoking bare, grinning, or toothless heads; its exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: So, so! iëhr altä Tschiddlä-n-iëhr, hinecht tüe-n-ich au einisch bi eich ubernachtä; werdet wohl nyt d'rgeget hä? Wennd's eich eppä nit passet, sä cheemet nur appä, i flrchte-n-eich nitt
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that Wolleb will spend the night with the old Tschiddlä and challenges them to come down if they object; the taunt provokes his aerial punishment.
notes.anchor: So, so! iëhr altä Tschiddlä-n-iëhr, hinecht tüe-n-ich au einisch bi eich ubernachtä; werdet wohl nyt d'rgeget hä? Wennd's eich eppä nit passet, sä cheemet nur appä, i flrchte-n-eich nitt

71290390714b9ebee3fd0de215e0b205e8bf93c5.summary: Battista had emigrated from Ticino to distant lands and made a great deal of money there, but after returning, he worried about where to hide it, for his wife was a true chatterbox who could keep no secret to herself.

notes.label: Goldvögel
notes.text: literally ‘gold birds,’ a regional or folkloric figurative name for gold pieces; the narrative immediately clarifies that Battista is hiding coins, but their precise denomination is unstated.

notes.label: Gevatterinnen
notes.text: plural of Gevatterin, traditionally a female godparent or woman joined to a family through ritual kinship, and more broadly a familiar female family friend; the exact relationship among the village gossips is not specified.

notes.label: Gevatterin
notes.text: singular form of Gevatterinnen; it can mean a godmother, female co-godparent, or familiar woman linked through ritual kinship, while this tale chiefly emphasizes her place in the gossip chain.

9354e802cab2284e0496460f07dbb262ae95cb2b.summary: On the hill nearest the village of Gontenschwil, a Sodbrunnen is still pointed out in the undergrowth as the last remnant of the old castle that once stood there.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a deep, usually stone-lined draw-well or well shaft; here it is the old castle's last visible remnant rather than a modern fountain.

notes.label: Oberholz
notes.text: literally ‘upper wood,’ the local woodland reached by the fleeing witness; whether it is a formal place-name or simply the upper part of the forest is unclear.

896466527a05cdf4c82a86229553dba6cce7719e.summary: The Waldhausen farm lies close to the village of Fisibach on a small hill crossed by the cantonal boundary between Aargau and Zurich.

notes.label: Burgstal
notes.text: the site or ground of a former castle, often recognizable only through ruins, foundations, or a traditional place-name; here it is the collapsed robber castle's location.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: literally ‘boundary stone,’ a marked stone defining a territorial or property border; its placement is especially apt on this hill at a cantonal boundary.

notes.label: Betzeit
notes.text: literally ‘prayer time,’ a time of day announced by church bells; in this tale its morning ringing marks the supernatural deadline for getting the treasure under cover.

301bfeb7a7d7fe568496d86c1474bdd07d63303c.summary: Not long before the last council held in Basel, there lived in the city a man suspected of sorcery.

notes.label: Belesen
notes.text: Belesen here denotes a clerical healing or exorcistic rite performed by reading sacred formulas over the afflicted person; the exact prayers, authorization, and ritual procedure are uncertain.

ec423e996ab5eac5180a7befa27456fa5c4941a2.summary: Only a few years ago, in old Curia Raetorum, “ins Gemein” people ended the working day earlier than we do in the year of salvation 1878. — Thus before dusk the Gebet-Glocke, the so-called Mittags-Glocke, sounded as the signal ending the workday for those laboring outdoors, and one hour later came…

notes.label: Curia Raetorum
notes.text: the historical Latin name for Chur, literally the curia or city of the Raetians.

notes.label: ins Gemein
notes.text: a historical expression meaning generally or as a common rule; the source places it in quotation marks.

notes.label: Gebet-Glocke
notes.text: literally “prayer bell,” here also the signal ending outdoor labor for the day.

notes.label: Mittags-Glocke
notes.text: literally “midday bell,” the alternate local name given for the Gebet-Glocke despite its seasonal evening use.

notes.label: Stübi
notes.text: the local name for the second evening ringing, whose bell is also associated with burials.

notes.label: Stübi-Glocke
notes.text: the second bell after the Gebet-Glocke, also identified as the Scaletta or burial bell.

notes.label: Andreas-Markt
notes.text: the St. Andrew’s seasonal market; the source dates it from 12 to 20 December and notes that the customary bells were suspended then.

notes.label: ins Gebet
notes.text: literally “into prayer,” the expression for ringing the community to the evening prayer observance.

notes.label: Lehrer-Seminar
notes.text: the teacher-training seminary that, at the source’s stated time, occupied the former cantonal-school role.
the source extraction's compact form for four and a half, or half past four; the raw digits are preserved so readers can trace the historical source.
the source extraction's compact form for five and a half, or half past five.
the source extraction's compact form for six and a half, or half past six.

notes.label: Stübi-Läuten
notes.text: the ringing of the Stübi-Glocke, after which the night watchman began his duty one hour later.

notes.label: Reichsstadt
notes.text: a Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire; the source recalls Cur’s former status.
the source extraction preserves historical German half-five notation in this order; it denotes half past four, not one twenty-fifth of an hour.
the source extraction preserves historical German half-six notation in this order; it denotes half past five.
the source extraction preserves historical German half-seven notation in this order; it denotes half past six.

notes.label: ruckweise
notes.text: in discrete steps or jumps; the bell times shifted by half-hour increments as daylight changed.

notes.label: antrat
notes.text: the source’s quoted verb for the watchman beginning or reporting for his duty.

notes.label: Abendwacht
notes.text: the evening watch and the opening set of verses called by the watchman.

notes.label: Zeit-Abrufen
notes.text: the hour-by-hour calling out of the time during the night watch.

notes.label: Tag-Anrufen
notes.text: the call announcing the coming day, delivered after midnight when dawn approached.

notes.label: Curer
notes.text: a person or thing associated with Cur, the historical form used here for Chur.

9e52940b5f672fa7e4a023dbb3a0aa5041c9983a.summary: In the Catholic Alps, it was and for the most part still is customary for a herder to call the Abendsegen aloud at a certain place every evening so that evil powers or accidents will not harm the herd.

notes.label: Abendsegen
notes.text: literally ‘evening blessing,’ an Alpine protective call sung or spoken over the herd; calls answering from Alp to Alp combine Catholic prayer with the practical ritual life of herders.

notes.label: Bhüet Gott Alls
notes.text: the opening of an Alemannic blessing meaning ‘May God protect all’; the following lines ask protection from the wolf's tooth, raven's beak, and lynx's bite, and the prayer's force depends upon the inclusive word Alls, ‘everything.’

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and dairying estate; the evening calls carry between separate Alps across the landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Rufkäse
notes.text: literally ‘call cheese,’ the special cheese given to the herder who performs the Abendsegen as payment for this communal protective duty.

notes.label: Bhüet Gott Alls, as der alt Schimmel nit.
notes.text: the careless dialect addition means ‘May God protect everything except the old gray horse’; excluding one animal from the blessing exposes it to the violent supernatural consequence.
notes.anchor: Bhüet Gott Alls, as der alt Schimmel nit.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or senior cattle herders; they witness the punished horse and learn the seriousness of the customary blessing.

523cb729ddc7f8abfa5767cfdc5129081a3db60f.summary: When the French invaded Switzerland and plundered the Freiamt, a nun from Fahr Abbey fled to her cousin in Sarmenstorf, a man called old Joggeli.

notes.label: Joggeli
notes.text: Joggeli is a Swiss German familiar form of Jakob and the dishonest cousin’s nickname, later applied to his ghost; his full historical identity is uncertain.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Estrichwinkel
notes.text: an Estrichwinkel is a corner of the attic or roof space into which the Capuchin binds the ghost; its exact position and the binding rite are unspecified.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

d16ae71f8c0afed0c8fd70b489842933a8774037.summary: A former Neapolitäner soldier lived on the Bristenberg. He is said to have been in Naples for a long time.

notes.label: Neapolitäner
notes.text: a historical Swiss name for a soldier who had served in Naples or the Neapolitan forces; the man may be Swiss rather than ethnically Neapolitan, and his foreign service explains the powers credited to him.

notes.label: Donnderchlapf
notes.text: the exact name of a place beneath the Hirrenbiechli, literally suggesting a ‘thunderclap’; the source does not identify the terrain feature or explain the name.

82e3eadd0bc68c61763bceba85cb51c2891cebdf.summary: Palfries was once inhabited by free Walser people. At the entrance to the Alp, “Kammjos” had his farmstead.

notes.label: Walser
notes.text: members of German-speaking Alpine communities descended from medieval migrants from the Upper Valais; their high-elevation settlements and later departures are central to this Palfries tradition.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: gnidlet
notes.text: the source's dialect verb for water forming a thin skin or crust of ice, an unfamiliar sign that warns the old high-mountain settlers of worsening years.

notes.label: Lägel
notes.text: a small cask, keg, or handled wine container used for carrying liquid; the woman's carrying one all the way up to Palfries demonstrates legendary strength.

notes.label: Hauptträml
notes.text: the principal heavy timber or main floor beam of a traditional building; its stated length and Benedikt's carrying it alone measure his extraordinary strength.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

74c00039f7b4a071228b528775fe3368baaac9e0.summary: Even now, a legend persists among the citizens of Wil that their town once stood and extended from the present Wasenmeisterswiese to Thuraustrasse; even now, several properties there are called ‘in the old town.’ Chronicles from the year 1650 record the legend above as already current in their time…

notes.label: Wasenmeisterswiese
notes.text: literally the ‘knacker's meadow,’ a local place name preserving Wasenmeister, the historical official or tradesman responsible for removing and processing animal carcasses; the name marks the meadow's former social use as well as its location.

notes.label: Leichengasse
notes.text: literally ‘corpse lane’ or ‘funeral lane,’ an old path name that may suggest a route used for carrying the dead, although the source supplies no further explanation.

notes.label: Reckholderhügel
