notes.text: a local name meaning the juniper hill, using Reckholder as a regional word for juniper; the account identifies it as the rise onto which Wil was supposedly moved.

5e5aaf59bcd4afa1eb6b346ff7aa855273208111.summary: Immediately after the Feierabend-Läuten, the watchman began his duty, and

notes.label: Feierabend-Läuten
notes.text: the ringing that announced the close of the working day and the beginning of evening, after which the night watchman took up his duty.

notes.label: Stunden-Spruch
notes.text: literally an “hour saying,” the distinct moral or devotional verse associated with each announced hour.

notes.label: Stundenruf
notes.text: literally the “hour call,” the watchman’s public formula announcing the bell stroke before the hour-specific verse.

notes.label: Tusner
notes.text: a person from Thusis in Graubünden; the title identifies this as the traditional night-watchman’s call of that community.

8e128576dc6780f13ab75458ecca206c1afb71c4.summary: In the vicinity of Iseltwald on the shore of Lake Brienz, one often hears a ghostly sound that rings now high, now low, like an Aeolian harp.

notes.label: Waldhorn
notes.text: literally ‘forest horn,’ a natural hunting or signaling horn and an ancestor of the orchestral French horn; here it is both the hunter's instrument and the source of the posthumous music.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on a high Alpine pasture; the joyful call evokes the vocal cries used across mountain valleys.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Grünrock
notes.text: literally ‘green coat,’ a traditional descriptive nickname for a hunter, based on hunting dress rather than the man's personal name.

notes.label: Jesusring
notes.text: literally ‘Jesus ring,’ apparently a devotional or symbolically Christian ring given by the hunter's bride; the source does not describe its design, so its precise form is uncertain.

notes.label: Stelzfuss
notes.text: literally ‘stilt-foot,’ a historical and potentially disparaging epithet for the crutch-using beggar who becomes the hunter's heir and buries him.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairy herders or cheesemakers who tend livestock and process milk on high summer pastures.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schalmei
notes.text: a traditional reed instrument, broadly a shawm or rustic pipe; the exact instrument intended can vary regionally, but here its melody is echoed by the supernatural horn.

notes.label: Wunderhorn
notes.text: literally ‘wonder horn’ or ‘miraculous horn,’ the tale's name for the buried Waldhorn once its supernatural moral and protective powers are revealed.

1496ead7829f5bca6bcbd672c045add5f8fe5b4b.summary: Near Räfis, by the Saar Bridge, a late traveler encounters a large black dog with only one eye.

notes.label: Butzenscheibe
notes.text: a small round bull’s-eye pane of old crown glass, commonly seen in historic windows; the comparison makes the dog’s single eye conspicuously large and circular.

4f4c24f8263a107f3cac43ee9004df37cbfc1fad.summary: In a mountain village of German-speaking Valais, the story goes, the village goat herd was entrusted for the summer to a young but rather alert shepherd boy.

notes.label: Gemeingeissstall
notes.text: literally ‘communal goat stable,’ the Gemeingeissstall is the shared overnight shelter for a village herd; its ownership, staffing, and exact local rules are unspecified.

notes.label: Geissstall
notes.text: Geissstall is Swiss German for a goat stable, placed here under a special village official’s policing authority; the building’s relation to the longer-named Gemeingeissstall is not specified.

notes.label: Geisshirt
notes.text: a Geisshirt is a goatherd responsible for the communal animals, here subordinate to the stable official; the office’s formal duties and compensation are uncertain.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally ‘goat boy,’ the Geissbub is the young communal herder accused of drinking milk directly from the goats; his name and age are unspecified.

notes.label: Geissstallvogt
notes.text: literally ‘goat-stable bailiff,’ the Geissstallvogt is the local official to whom the council delegates the embarrassing inquiry; whether this was a formal historical title or comic exaggeration is uncertain.

b3524da096c96f15dd35e6c3ddbb27d6167d2957.summary: A small Solothurn village close to the Aargau border of the Jura tells of one of its parish priests that he stole a golden chalice from the sacristy and, for this, was bound by a monk from Olten inside the Opferstock of Stüsslingen church until the present day.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Opferstock
notes.text: a locked church offering or alms box, usually with a narrow metal slot; the guilty priest is supernaturally confined within the very container associated with sacred donations.

6f7999dff9104a9cc36cbc6ea47e7afe7847e5ec.summary: On one of the wildest alpine pastures in the Schilzbach valley, two inhabitants of the region who had long borne grudges against one another once met unexpectedly.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Bahrprobe
notes.text: literally the ‘bier test,’ a medieval and early-modern ordeal in which a murder victim’s body was believed to bleed or otherwise react when touched by the killer; the account presents it as divine judgment, not reliable forensic evidence.

notes.label: Bahrrecht
notes.text: literally ‘bier law’ or ‘right of the bier,’ another name in the source for the formal custom surrounding the Bahrprobe before a public court.

2e57f4d57ab899702e62f77ad3243a75582a6c97.summary: Once, the citizens of the town of Brugg resolved to plant an oak forest within the communal territory.

notes.label: Mütt
notes.text: a historical Swiss dry measure used especially for grain and seed; its exact volume varied by locality, so the source's twelve Mütt indicates a large communal quantity rather than one universally fixed modern volume.

notes.label: Weinmonat
notes.text: an old calendar name for October, literally the ‘wine month’; the planting procession is dated 20 October 1532.

notes.label: Ruthenzug
notes.text: the name of Brugg's annual youth procession or festival, literally a ‘switch’ or ‘branch procession’; the story explains it through children carrying oak branches home after the commemorative forest circuit.

505ee6d5b17dd8a6cdb52cc386ed43df9d802a25.summary: Lake Türlen lies on the southern side of the Albis. Its waters are not said always to have washed the foot of the Albis.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f23f9e28bade6330f86362fd191c9bb4ec20bd1c.summary: Elsi was the most beautiful girl in the village of Sigriswil—beautiful beyond all measure.

notes.label: Flühblumen
notes.text: literally ‘cliff flowers,’ flowers growing on dangerous rock faces; here they are the Alpenrose blossoms Elsi demands.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep exposed rock face or cliff, especially in Alpine place-language.

notes.label: Alpenrose
notes.text: literally ‘Alpine rose,’ the German name for the rhododendron whose red or purple flowers grow in the Alps; the legend explains it as arising from Hans’s blood.

cb7181ef3e3edd74496873b06cfc91b0768ab2ad.summary: When God banished the fallen spirits to Hell, he set them a deadline by which they were all to have arrived there.

notes.label: Erdleutle
notes.text: the regional plural form corresponding to Erdleutchen; this etiological account makes these earth-folk fallen spirits caught at the earth rather than devils in Hell.

notes.label: Erdleutchen
notes.text: literally “little earth people,” a name for dwarf-like or subterranean beings in Alpine folklore; the title uses this Standard German diminutive form.

69ba2d197e67c74e5aa0fad45f25aa1ee3e323eb.summary: When the people of Unterwalden went to the pope’s aid in former times, among them was an exceedingly strong and vigorous man, full of zeal for the Holy Father’s cause and longing ardently to face the enemy.

notes.label: Hör Ma!
notes.text: the command means ‘Stop, man!’ or ‘Listen, man!’ in the story’s folk etymology; spoken aloud it forms Hermann, so the dialect wordplay supplies the legendary family name even though it is not a historical derivation.

bf0b29f3440acafa1e2ce993af7ed9760f2601a1.summary: This family is found in the canton of Schwyz, especially in Arth. Its origin is said to be as follows: In Mettlen in Wolfenschiessen, canton of Nidwalden, there lived a recognized and widely renowned cattle doctor.

notes.label: Almigrecht
notes.text: a historical Swiss communal-land right, related to Allmend or common pasture rights; here the newcomer receives both the lower and upper local rights, whose precise legal scope is not stated.

e859cc445131bbe40373e68e700fbb5184c0973d.summary: Long ago, a great rise in prices occurred in the land of the Swedes in the cold north, and from it arose a dreadful famine, so that the people were in a very bad way.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: an open-air assembly in which eligible citizens decide public matters directly, historically central to several rural Swiss cantons.

notes.label: Gaue
notes.text: plural of Gau, an old territorial district or region rather than a modern administrative unit.

notes.label: Salveglöcklein
notes.text: literally ‘little Salve bell,’ a devotional bell associated here with Our Lady of Einsiedeln and probably the singing or prayer of the Salve Regina.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Mythen
notes.text: the paired mountain peaks above Schwyz; despite their spelling, the local name is not simply the German plural of ‘myth.’

notes.label: Schwyzer
notes.text: people of the canton and historical land of Schwyz; the legend uses their name to explain the later name of Switzerland.

7b34a3a3ad8c4366c6936c59093e8219c03e072f.summary: In earlier times, the Balmen of the highest cliffs were inhabited by enchantresses and fairies.

notes.label: Balmen
notes.text: the plural of Balm, an Alpine and Swiss place-word for shallow caves, rock shelters, or overhanging cliff recesses; here they contain the fairies' richly adorned grotto homes.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Käsebrecher
notes.text: literally a ‘cheese breaker,’ the dairying implement used to cut or stir curd during Alpine cheesemaking; the goatherd's attempt to use this work tool as a weapon drives the fairies away.

b54cf5c83c2f78958fb26a9a1bbadcc25c511e13.summary: The wife of a councillor in Ennetbürgen near Stans was also one of those who loved the Black One more than her wedded husband.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: an old fathom-like measure that could be used for stacked firewood as well as length; exact regional volumes varied, and the story specifies two Klafter.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: auf die Stör
notes.text: a traditional arrangement in which an itinerant craftsperson worked at the customer's home; calling the shoemaker for only one pair provides the husband's pretext for sending his wife away.

notes.label: Finken
notes.text: Swiss German for soft slippers or house shoes; unlike ordinary outdoor shoes, they leave the witch without protective contact with the ground while she is tied atop the wood.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

9425265f743499fc885068fa06af4b162db636e2.summary: A spectral animal everywhere, the owl is no exception to the rule in our region.

notes.label: Schlierehüwel
notes.text: the uncanny Hüwel associated with the Schliera stream above Alpnach; the compound functions as the apparition's local name.

notes.label: Hüwel
notes.text: an Obwalden and regional name for a nocturnal owl or owlet, especially a bird treated in folklore as uncanny; the source does not fix a modern species.

notes.label: Hauri
notes.text: one regional name listed for the same night owl or owlet called Hüwel; its precise geographic range and species are not specified.

notes.label: Huri
notes.text: the Bernese-dialect variant listed for Hauri, again naming the uncanny night owl without identifying a precise modern species.

notes.label: Malefitzpulver
notes.text: literally ‘maleficence powder,’ a supposedly magically potent powder mixed into ammunition against an enchanted being; the source does not explain its composition or blessing.

f7030f03db6e91640cd4951c054cea655f407695.summary: At Darsier, on the sunny slope between Schiers and Fanas, there once stood a large stable belonging to a man named Padrutt.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Prätigau
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Prättigau, the Graubünden valley containing Schiers, Fanas, and Darsier.

notes.label: uf'm Bödeli vor's Padrutten-Stall
notes.text: Swiss German for “on the little level ground in front of Padrutt’s stable”; the woman in Holland identifies this as the witches’ dance site at Darsier.

notes.label: Holländer
notes.text: literally “Dutchman” or “Dutch,” the Prätigau folk name given here for the medicinal herb sage; the tale explains the name through witches from Holland rather than through botany.

notes.label: Padrutten-Bödeli
notes.text: the local name for the little level ground by Padrutt’s stable at Darsier; Bödeli is a Swiss German diminutive for a small flat piece of ground or clearing.

b78c41b62daacb480615f6f64bfe352facfe5427.summary: In very early times, the old Eidgenossen of the lands of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden once crossed the snow-covered Gotthard mountains to aid the pope.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades,’ the members of the Swiss Confederacy; in this historical legend, it names soldiers from the allied cantons rather than all modern Swiss citizens.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Banner, meaning a cantonal or military battle standard and the community embodied by it; the Zug Panner is both a cloth object and the honor defended across generations of standard-bearers.

notes.label: welsch
notes.text: Romance-speaking, Italian, or broadly non-German from a German-Swiss viewpoint; here it describes both the Livinen valley and the Milanese enemy, with a culturally distancing tone.

notes.label: Welschen
notes.text: the plural noun corresponding to welsch, here the Italian-speaking Milanese forces; the historical narrator uses the broad regional label rather than a precise ethnic category.

notes.label: Pannerherr
notes.text: the officer or standard-bearer charged with carrying and defending a Panner; Ammann Peter Kolin holds this perilous honor for Zug.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a traditional local magistrate or chief administrative officer; Peter Kolin's civic title accompanies his battlefield role as Pannerherr.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Uri bull,’ Uri's great war horn, whose animal voice represents the canton and rallies the arriving Confederates.

notes.label: Harsthörner
notes.text: military company or host horns of Unterwalden; Harst denotes an armed troop or battle formation, though the exact construction of the horns is not described.

notes.label: Rolandshörner
notes.text: Lucerne's named war horns associated with the heroic Roland tradition; they join the Uristier and Harsthörner in signaling relief.

e99a21f07da1d5fbed1fa39db6d2768a58b7ab56.summary: High above on the Matterberg lies a place that no one, or at least scarcely anyone, can find.

notes.label: Matterberg
notes.text: an older regional name for the Matterhorn or its mountain massif, on which the hidden animal paradise is placed.

notes.label: laufende Jud
notes.text: literally ‘wandering Jew,’ a historically anti-Jewish Christian folklore figure condemned to wander and curse; the note preserves the source's wording while identifying its prejudicial tradition.

notes.label: Alpgletscher
notes.text: the Alpine glacier beneath which the Vispe later becomes visible, contrasted with the warm hidden source-land above.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Zirbelnüsse
notes.text: edible seeds of the Swiss stone pine, sweet kernels that visitors may take provided they harm no animal.

notes.label: Plantanenstämme
notes.text: the source's unusual spelling for trunks of ancient plane-like trees; because the same passage otherwise names pines and maples, the intended species is uncertain.

279b05d5197084d549f43af0d4d4be3e5ccdbfde.summary: It is said of this mountain spirit: as long as he tended the cows, he always followed the same route with them, which is still called the Path of Napfhans, le chemin de Jean Bolieta.

notes.label: Napfhans
notes.text: the German regional name of the helpful mountain spirit also called Jean Bolieta; his former cattle path remains supernaturally free of stones.

notes.label: Herbstmonat
notes.text: literally ‘autumn month,’ a traditional regional name for September; without Napfhans, the herders must leave the upper pasture at its beginning.

084057fdcb61de9c58f72c4e60d9f5fcfa174e34.summary: Near the village of Einsiedeln lived the forest hermit Johannes. For more than 20 years he led a most devout life in his wilderness, and on account of the high degree of virtue he had attained, heavenly food was miraculously brought to him.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.text: The apparent source forms Mal and wildrs are read contextually as Einmal and wildes.

98279a8944317891b43f2cb0653064f7ae305272.summary: A young man of noble birth made an illicit proposition to an innocent and noble castle maiden of equal rank.

notes.label: Sankt Jakob
notes.text: literally ‘Saint James,’ a traditional shorthand for pilgrimage to a shrine of St. James, commonly Santiago de Compostela; the source does not explicitly name the destination, so that identification remains contextual rather than certain.

notes.label: Nägeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive related to Nelke and Nägelein, which can denote a clove or a carnation-like flower; the comparison concerns the miraculous flower’s exquisite spicy-floral fragrance, but the precise botanical sense is ambiguous.

8bf3219d6767ea9aefe411757b305c968c66ae1c.summary: The inhabitants of Oberwald explain the terrible thunder and cracking often heard in the nearby Rhône Glacier as follows.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ec3363b859c1c0be843b563e2803759e3fe0313c.summary: Once a merry group of children from Sumvix was playing near the wall of ruined Hohenbalken Castle.

notes.label: Hohenbalken
notes.text: the ruined castle above Sumvix where the armored apparition attempts to return the money.

c3d9bc2e3f97f2c08097a8e90f89b225bc0a009f.summary: The “Juden-Wegli” below Maladers is well enough known, especially because things are often not right there.

notes.label: Juden-Wegli
notes.text: literally “Jews’ little path,” the historical path-name printed by Jecklin below Maladers; the source gives no explanation connecting the name with Jewish people, so none is inferred here.

notes.label: Färli
notes.text: Swiss German plural for piglets, explicitly glossed as Ferkel by Jecklin.

notes.label: Färli-Müetter
notes.text: Swiss German for a mother sow with piglets; the hyphenated form first names the animal and later the condemned woman’s supernatural shape.

notes.label: Müetter
notes.text: Swiss German for “mother”; in this livestock context it refers to the sow after her piglets have grown.

notes.label: Färlimüetter
notes.text: the closed spelling used in the source for the same mother sow as Färli-Müetter.

notes.label: Ledige
notes.text: literally an unmarried woman; the historical term marks the mother’s marital status and is used repeatedly rather than naming her.

notes.label: Strich
notes.text: literally a line, stretch, or route; here it is the habitual track the sow and later the transformed penitent must walk.

8a511ad13d75bd96c3e85532ab66e9305b1713ed.summary: Gundoldingen, a hamlet in the Lucerne parish of Rain, is said to have been burned down by the Austrians during the Sempacherkrieg.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Sempacherkrieg
notes.text: the War of Sempach, the conflict associated especially with the Swiss victory over Habsburg Austria at Sempach in 1386; the tale places the hamlet's destruction within that wartime memory.

Textual note: the source title spells the inhabitants' name ‘Grundoldinger,’ while the narrative consistently gives the hamlet and its people as ‘Gundoldingen’ and ‘Gundoldinger’; both forms have been preserved in their respective fields.

54da42680ef4659d144047f1a24c9034c915c680.summary: Folk plays were formerly staged very often, and the farmers loved them greatly.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin of varying value; the debt collector’s public mockery invokes Batzen accounts as a symbol of burdensome petty debts, with no fixed modern conversion implied.

notes.label: Vorschosen
notes.text: a Valais form for front aprons, from Vorschürzen; the fool ridicules the daughters’ newly narrow fashion until communal satire makes them widen the garments again.

notes.label: Knüttelversen
notes.text: deliberately rough, old-fashioned rhyming doggerel used for the entire folk play; the closest English sense is ‘jolting verse,’ but the historic German theatrical term is retained.

4028a0bb8c112270f409c671811847421e4115b1.summary: In Grossdietwil there is said to have been a man who saw ghosts. But if he went outside after the Betglocken, the prayer bells, on a Fronfastennacht, the ghosts drove him away over hill and dale, usually across the Näbetsbergwald.

notes.label: Betglocken
notes.text: literally the prayer bells, this denotes the evening bell signal after which the spirits pursue the seer; the exact local ringing time is uncertain.

notes.label: Fronfastennacht
notes.text: this is a night associated with one of the quarterly Christian Ember fasts and treated here as a dangerous time for spirit-seeing; which Ember season is intended is unspecified.

08f0df23dcc9a4056ae08d09fcc817060edbb63b.summary: At the time of the plague in Graubünden, two small, old, spectral beings—a little man and a little woman—crept through the Felsenbach (Clus) and into the Prätigau.

notes.label: Ich schufla aba, du fägst zärnma
notes.text: an Alemannic dialect sentence meaning approximately “I shovel down; you sweep together”; it describes the pair’s division of labor in dispersing the plague.
notes.anchor: Ich schufla aba, du fägst zärnma

notes.label: Würgengel
notes.text: literally “strangling angel,” a traditional personification of death or plague that goes from house to house.

notes.label: Pest-Leutchen
notes.text: literally “little plague people,” a supernatural pair who personify and spread the plague with a shovel and broom; the diminutive does not make them harmless.

08705b4122c7f1718ed6c745d58815dd7467e20a.summary: When Lord Burkard resided at Strättlingen, a great pestilence prevailed in the German lands.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

63aac2fb875e00f0837388f60ea4b52ed48777f0.summary: In the year 1506, many credible people in the land of Schwyz, between Arth and Kilchgasse, saw the figure of a woman.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: the shorter form of Alpe, likewise denoting the worked high pasture rather than merely a mountain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schuldbrief
notes.text: a written debt bond or mortgage instrument; the rich man produces the allegedly forged document as proof that the widow’s husband pledged the pasture.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape; the widow’s only property is transformed into a mass of ice.

052f11be217d61156272cc01a1070d9f39403dc6.summary: Near Bürgeln by Lungern, to the left of the new Brünig road, there is a Fluh.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss topographic word for a cliff, crag, or exposed rock face; the exact landform varies by locality.

15a26bb8159f482411149cf2bcb408cd56358ba5.summary: Once there lived a wicked knight named Hans von Waldenburg. He had a strong castle that stood above the little town of Waldenburg in the Basel region.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

06eb0980151f00b9acc0d2842422152c07789cf6.summary: A beautiful walking path leads from Sevelen over the Heuberg and the Selva to the "brochnen Burg," and onward to Gretschins.

notes.label: Pfaffenchelleri
notes.text: the local name of the female apparition and, by extension, the streamside place where she washes children’s linen; ‘Pfaffen-’ suggests an association with a priest, while the precise sense of ‘-chelleri’ is uncertain.

e4a2b3ea998bcafa87fb6ffa5983634aea15cab1.summary: In the “Chratz” and the “Stumpenebnet,” there are said to be underground passages in which wrongfully acquired money lies hidden.

notes.label: Pfaffenchellerin
notes.text: the local name of the wandering treasure-guardian in the title; it may combine Pfaffe, an old word for a cleric, with a regional place or byname, but the source gives no derivation.

notes.label: Stüklewib
notes.text: a regional name meaning roughly ‘Stükle woman’ or ‘woman of Stükle’; Wib means woman, while the first element and whether this is the same apparition as the Pfaffenchellerin remain unexplained.

b3769706a8e56146816b572e3cfa8855fb59ead3.summary: Between the years 1740 and 1750, a general commotion arose in the village of Suhr over the claim that an old passage led from the parsonage beneath the church into a treasure vault in the Kirchberg, where the Heidenpfaffen were said to have hidden, among other valuables and jewels, the golden calf…

notes.label: Heidenpfaffen
notes.text: a polemical compound meaning ‘pagan priests’; the villagers imagine them bringing the biblical golden calf from Arabia, not a historically identified priesthood.

notes.label: Keichen
notes.text: an older regional word for cramped prisons, cells, or dungeons; here it refers to the Bernese detention spaces cut into the sandstone, but the exact form of each chamber is not described.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Pfaffenhöhle
notes.text: literally ‘priests' cave’ or, more disparagingly, ‘parsons' cave,’ the legendary underground passage associated with clergy and hidden treasure; Pfaffe can carry an anticlerical tone that neutral ‘priest’ does not fully convey.

7a25fdb402eaa44838e0cf97f61cc12fc8284a18.summary: a) Whenever Türst and Streggelen hunt near Horw and Kriens, with a pack of small dogs barking or yapping as they follow a large, one-eyed dog, the Pfaffenkellerin is always among them; she has a terrifying appearance, glowing eyes, and shaggy fur.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a central Swiss name for a leader or manifestation of the Wild Hunt, heard in stormy nocturnal pursuit; here Türst hunts together with the Streggelen.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: regional female or collective Wild Hunt beings, often imagined as rushing through the night with dogs; the source uses the name without describing their individual forms.

notes.label: Pfaffenkellerin
notes.text: literally something like ‘priest's cellaress’ or ‘priest's cellar-woman,’ the regional name of this shaggy, glowing-eyed female Wild Hunt being; the source records her behavior and place-name associations but does not explain the name's origin.

notes.label: Palmkäppeli
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘little Palm chapel,’ the local chapel used as the starting point of the Pfaffenkellerin's prodigious leap; the source locates it at the Bürgen.

notes.label: Geissfuss
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘goat's foot’; its alleged stone imprint marks the Pfaffenkellerin as an uncanny, possibly demonic being rather than an ordinary woman.

247a018cb26710a5cce31841ff132c685a9a1a28.summary: It is well known how, at the beginning of the 15th century, people in Swiss cities agitated against the housekeepers of clergymen, the Pfaffenkellerinnen, who were probably not driven away without cause and, if they reappeared, were put into the towers without mercy.

notes.label: Pfaffenkellerin
notes.text: a historical, disparaging regional label for a clergyman’s female housekeeper, often implying an illicit partner; the legend presents ten years in that role as placing her soul in danger.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tapp
notes.text: a dialect word for a step, tread, or footprint; here it names the impression her failed supernatural leap left in the rock.

e5dff481add6dabe3bd94e55bcacca65ac90375a.summary: In the mist-gray primeval past, when nearly all of Switzerland was still covered by ancient forests, a very ancient people clad only in skins lived in the Zürichgau.

notes.label: Zürichgau
notes.text: the historical region or county around Zurich; Gau is an older territorial designation rather than a modern canton.

notes.label: Pfahlbauer
notes.text: literally ‘pile builders,’ the name given to the imagined prehistoric inhabitants of Swiss lake pile dwellings; the narrative reflects the romantic archaeological understanding of its era.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: a warm, dry, often powerful downslope wind on the northern side of the Alps, here whipping up the lake waves.

notes.label: Einbäumen
notes.text: plural of Einbaum, dugout canoes hollowed from single tree trunks.

733b0fd7971029e9fe6fc5185cbe5112f28e1f33.summary: In the households of the little village of Tecknau, people used to set out a bowl of milk for the Bergmännchen and Erdfräulein who lived in the rock caves of the Eital between the two mountain ridges of the Oedenburg and the Scheideck; sometimes they even prepared butter and honey for them.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally “little mountain men,” dwarf-like beings associated with mountains, caves, or underground places; here they help Tecknau households and fieldworkers, and the term does not imply ordinary miners.

notes.label: Erdfräulein
notes.text: literally “little earth maidens,” female subterranean or cave-dwelling beings paired here with the Bergmännchen; “fairies” or “dwarfs” would each impose a narrower creature type than the source supplies.

notes.label: Pflugsbrot
notes.text: literally “plow bread,” the title’s name for the supernatural field meal left at the end of a furrow; the food may be a pancake or onion cake rather than a loaf, so the traditional compound is retained.

e787fe583f36bb2f3760766651c9c7d1d8fa9acd.summary: At Oberuzwil, a farmer had a sow whose young always died whenever they were a few months old.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

1cf5f28d49a1262f0b269e96414d08f586dbefe2.summary: a) In Ennetmoos near the so-called Mehlbach, an apparition in the form of a grunting pig is said to have been seen frequently.

notes.label: Pfaffenkellerin
notes.text: literally a ‘priest’s cellar-woman’ or female keeper of a cleric’s household stores, but in Central Swiss legend it names an uncanny female figure able to appear as a pig; this brief reference does not establish whether she is a ghost, witch, demon, or remembered servant.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a named Central Swiss supernatural hunter or Wild Hunt figure whose manifestations can include animals; here the Türst appears as a pig, but the passage gives no further detail about whether the name denotes an individual being or a spectral procession.

notes.label: Elbst
notes.text: a local Seelisberg name for an uncanny being or apparition, linguistically suggestive of an elf-like spirit; here it manifests as an entire herd of pigs, while its identity and the exact sense of the regional name remain uncertain.

14eb1234917f7a1021807dfe548e3f55bc1efc87.summary: At the ruins of Thierstein Castle in the Fricktal, a man once encountered several herdsmen and asked them to help him carry a large iron chest out of a dark place there.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

6c6517d401e0b01566f657ca9b34c7948a2fd7a9.summary: It is probably close to sixty years now since several young men from the village of Wittnau—some of whom still live there—climbed, at the urging and in the company of an older man, a spur of the Homberg called Weingarten.

notes.label: Sennenkelle
notes.text: the large wooden ladle used by a Senn in Alpine dairy work, especially for stirring or handling milk, whey, or curds; its comic use here turns the pig’s cauldron-shaped back into a dairy vessel.

dbc47989f2ef119eb0ab3b057e983843d487810d.summary: Through prudent thrift, Peter Wicki of Lucerne became a prosperous man and bought a little property in the wilderness of Theel, which he made his home.

notes.label: Theel
notes.text: the wilderness locality near Lenk where Peter Wicki settles and the pilgrimage chapel is founded; the exact place-name derivation is unstated.

notes.label: Bethäuslein
notes.text: literally ‘little prayer house,’ a diminutive devotional chapel or oratory; Wicki first imagines and then vows to build one.

notes.label: Hirschhörnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little stag horn,’ a small piece of antler bearing an image resembling Saint Barbara; whether it was a devotional object, handle, or carved amulet is uncertain.

ce8dfd42999bbcd45f50eac0688eb404b6d0aabd.summary: A good half hour south of Willisau, on a mountain ridge, lies the Bösegg farmstead.

notes.label: Güggelchen
notes.text: a diminutive Swiss German form for a little rooster or cockerel; it is the third roasted bird that revives as proof the hanged son still lives.

notes.label: Pimpernüsschenbaum
notes.text: a diminutive form of Pimpernussbaum, approximately ‘little bladdernut tree’; the pilgrim's cut staff takes root at Bösegg.

notes.label: Grimmen
notes.text: griping abdominal pains or intestinal cramps; the tree's fruits are credited with a folk-medicinal use against them.

notes.label: Pimpernussbaum
notes.text: the European bladdernut tree, Staphylea pinnata, whose inflated seed capsules contain hard rattling seeds; the Bösegg specimen is linked to the miraculous pilgrimage.

3ae870d738a75ec0b8aed1a40f8baecf76029805.summary: In former times, a pious and upright farmer lived in the Lötschental. But he was also an eccentric and did not behave as other people did.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

d6a0902619face7aa8d594573022b5ada0e861f9.summary: Anyone who believes that everything ghostly belongs to dear olden times and that all the Bozen have already died is mistaken.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: regional bogeys, frightening spirits, or goblin-like beings; the author uses the plural broadly for supposedly vanished supernatural creatures.

notes.label: Plaggeister
notes.text: literally ‘plaguing spirits,’ troublesome ghosts that progressively occupy and harass an inhabited house.

fc2ce201f34c860e03e7af7a2c9ef87c3bc779e0.summary: In late summer, a Senne wished to descend from Alp Malbun into the valley; there he no longer found his friends and relatives.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: a variant singular of Senn, an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking; here he returns from Alp Malbun to find the valley devastated by plague.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its buildings, not simply any mountain; here it first seems a refuge from plague but proves no protection.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male workers or farmhands serving on an Alp beneath or alongside the chief dairy herdsman; here they nurse their disfigured companion with butter and herbs.

b304ff740a8741999928279c9014eb2c15a4927c.summary: The plague first broke out in Toggenburg at Gupfen, then a single house in the municipality of Henau.

notes.label: Fräuli
notes.text: literally ‘little woman’ or ‘little lady,’ with the Alemannic diminutive -li; here it is a white female plague apparition whose sweeping announces infection, not an ordinary young woman.

bb22cf93654d0d2b6c4356b54bfe597cf779d0e1.summary: Very many people died here during the plague. Entire wagonloads of bodies were carried to the cemetery.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

580b604c05e46795b241d94415348b5c259698f2.summary: In 1611, fourteen people died in Wattwil in a single day. Because no gravediggers could be found for individual graves, the many bodies were laid in large common graves, whose mounds could still be seen behind the church 100 years ago.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

93ab1a668a927b5f9b28a988fb02a92262e7653f.summary: The Great Mortality was raging in the Grindelwald valley. One day, the people of Lauterbrunnen, who had long been spared the furious death, saw a little white cloud fly over the Wengernalp and settle in the Schiltwald.

notes.label: Wengernalp
notes.text: the named high pasture and pass area above Lauterbrunnen and Wengen; the plague cloud crosses it to enter the valley.

notes.label: Mehlbaum
notes.text: literally ‘meal/flour tree,’ the local landmark halfway down the valley from which the messenger calls the death toll; the source does not explain the name.

notes.label: Totenschauer
notes.text: officials or appointed witnesses who viewed and certified the dead; during the plague they pass from dwelling to dwelling performing this communal duty.

e3fad00d6c6226ccd96a4f8c47e1df6b2d5e8bc9.summary: 1. At that time they were building the rectory at Spiringen.

notes.label: Dubelloch
notes.text: an Uri building term related to a Dübel, a dowel or peg, for a drilled or mortised hole in timber; the source does not describe the precise joint, but the workers use the cavity to seal away the infected finger.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan; the brief reference assumes a vision described elsewhere in the source collection rather than retelling it here.

94f0ff10e7b5f259c9dc0052d3cffe1871d6f18c.summary: According to legend, at the time of the bubonic plague a single member of the entire council in Uri remained alive: Landammann Sebastian Heinrich Trösch (died 1637).

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or head of government of a Swiss canton or rural polity; the title identifies Sebastian Heinrich Trösch as the council’s leading public officer.

cacc264f48b0ee90c5eb307a24bf143a5a598bc1.summary: In Stalden, people also tell of a great plague during which there were so many dead that they were thrown uncoffined into open pits.

notes.label: Gribier
notes.text: a regional name for the gravedigger, likely influenced by neighboring Romance speech; he is paid in linen cloths but ultimately dies of the same plague.

notes.label: Törbier-Oschikehri
notes.text: a local Valais place name marking the gravedigger’s stone barn; its literal components and modern location are not explained by the source.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Kehrt um den Roten — den Toten;
notes.text: the source’s first enigmatic prescription line, approximately ‘turn around the red one—the dead’; the red/dead wordplay and intended action remain uncertain.
notes.anchor: Kehrt um den Roten — den Toten;

notes.label: Iss Bibinella — Pumpernella — und gebahts Brod,
notes.text: an obscure regional line instructing people to eat Bibinella, Pumpernella, and baked bread; the first two may be plant or food names, but the source does not identify them securely.
notes.anchor: Iss Bibinella — Pumpernella — und gebahts Brod,

notes.label: So hört uf der gähe Tod!
notes.text: dialect for ‘then sudden death will cease’; gähe conveys sudden or abrupt, and the line promises an end to the plague.
notes.anchor: So hört uf der gähe Tod!

1645199dd737874c9b6225a72aa583cb7217f110.summary: a) When the plague carried off many human lives in the land of Uri in 1629, an old maid in Gurtnellen—at Ryttigen—is said to have inherited nine—or twelve—Trinkelkühe in one week—or one night.

notes.label: Trinkelkühe
notes.text: cows bearing Trinkel bells, generally smaller livestock bells; inheriting nine or twelve within a week or night shows how radically plague deaths redistributed property, while the source preserves both numbers and both time variants.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Strenzen
notes.text: a plant or plant-based remedy named by the aerial voice as protection against plague; its precise botanical identity is not established by this source, so it is retained rather than assigned silently to a modern species.

notes.label: Beulentod
notes.text: literally ‘boil-death’ or ‘bubonic death,’ a historical folk name for plague identified by its swellings; these variants use it for the epidemic but do not establish a separate modern diagnostic category.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese production on a seasonal high pasture; here the role identifies the girl's sweetheart returning from Fellenen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Tötin
notes.text: the feminine counterpart to Tod (‘Death’), here explicitly personified as Death's wife and an independent bringer of plague; English has no matching gendered noun, and the tale does not say whether she is a broader named figure or a personification specific to these variants.

0d532bb5a30e2cbff79db5c31600423cc6215073.summary: In a single night, a Heuschrote passed by inheritance through nine hands.—A Zusenn went through the village of Weisstannen with his packhorse and spoke through a window with a young woman.

notes.label: Heuschrote
notes.text: a regional hay-related implement or structure passed from heir to heir; its precise form is uncertain here, while the nine inheritances in one night signify successive plague deaths.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: an assistant alpine dairyman or subordinate herdsman working under the principal Senn.

78df22165f7c11b306fe26a0ce51694e310c08e6.summary: Many legends are still told in Zermatt of great plague-like diseases that raged terribly among the population.

notes.label: Pfinkrieg
notes.text: the Valais name for the fighting associated with Pfyn during the French invasion period; it anchors the first outbreak account in regional wartime memory.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure based on outstretched arms and roughly comparable to a person's height; a Klafter-high stack emphasizes the extraordinary quantity of burial linen paid to the gravedigger.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Augstalberg
notes.text: the mountain route by which the young man leaves the affected region; the historical place-name is retained because its exact modern route is not identified in the source.

87263bd8134ef3f1ab8bc6eba07b22e7fb1d5994.summary: Of all the inhabitants of the Hölzliberg, only one remained alive and thus became the mountain's sole owner.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2b64dab45ad9f5c58ad8d7cba0c39671ddc4d3f3.summary: This year, a great mortality appeared in every place and quarter. First, on Saint Lawrence’s Day, a child of the tailor Melchior Grob, called Strub, died of the plague, "and was the first person." By November 13, 133 people had died, the last being master builder Seth Büelmann.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

3eded8ee320daf1bae5b5f80a29bc32fed6c41b4.summary: Once, when plague ravaged the Adelboden Valley, the people of Lenk established a plague cordon upon the heights of Hahnenmoos.

notes.label: Diktament
notes.text: a historical or dialect plant name in a plague remedy, probably related to Diktam or Diptam, ‘dittany,’ a herb credited with medicinal powers; the exact plant or preparation intended by this Bernese source is uncertain.

aa4b84417a4bc1b4fec62724d2acec4cc5c6ec70.summary: Gretschins also knows the little saying:

notes.label: Sieben Hansen in einem Grab
notes.text: ‘seven men named Hans in one grave,’ a compact plague rhyme emphasizing both mass burial and the commonness of the name Hans in the community.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

261fbaa0d68a7d4cd0b0ac2a952c0304f25ab963.summary: The Sevelen carpenter S. G. once went to Oberschan ‘zur Spinni.’ As he returned home through the Sevelen wood early in the morning—it was not yet daylight—he saw a little woman in the beech forest near the path and asked in surprise what she was doing there so early.

notes.label: Spinni
notes.text: a regional communal spinning gathering, often also an occasion for evening sociability; the carpenter is returning from one before dawn.

notes.label: Plattenwibli
notes.text: literally approximately ‘little woman of the slab’ or ‘hearthstone little woman’; the local byname is linked in the story to her double sitting on the kitchen hearthstone.

c78ec2f344716e2718c0d0cba5993a0741a324b4.summary: Toward the end of the previous century, near Glis, a man from Visperterminen was approached by a stranger who seemed to be in great haste and asked to perform a great service—it was around ten o’clock at night.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a grammatical or regional form of Alp, a seasonal high-mountain pasture and livestock operation; the dead man’s negligence occurred there, though his role and ownership of the animal are unstated.

notes.label: Erledigung
notes.text: here a formal or moral release from the unresolved claim arising from the lost cow, closer to discharge or forgiveness than ordinary task completion; the tale does not specify any civil or church procedure.

14ce3ab36590ee390520346cfdc35c9498a18630.summary: In olden times, two castles stood near Wolhusen. Not far from one of them, a farmer was earnestly plowing the field with two very fine oxen.

notes.label: Sech
notes.text: a historical regional word for the plow’s coulter, the vertical cutting blade ahead of the plowshare; the farmer removes it and uses it as a weapon.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

586e991c4e2b0fbb211bd66733a6c6e507bca7fb.summary: A widow once lived in Rüti who was very miserly and quick-tempered. She had one child, a girl of six.

notes.label: Plöhli
notes.text: the named mountain meadow north of Rüti where the child is killed, buried, and later haunted; the diminutive place-name becomes part of the apparition's identity.

notes.label: Plöhligeiss
notes.text: literally the ‘Plöhli goat,’ from Swiss German Geiss, ‘goat’; the white goat is the dead mother's penitent form, and its bleating or bell-ringing also functions as a local storm and flood omen.

71b3f042a44af98d49cf424bbbaa99182655e3a7.summary: Not far above the little town of Mayenfeld lies a fairly large estate called the “Pola.” It is enclosed by a wall.

notes.label: Pola
notes.text: the local name of the walled estate above Mayenfeld where the apparition rides; it is treated as a proper place-name rather than translated conjecturally.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a gray horse, often light enough to be described as white in English-language folklore; the word does not imply a supernatural breed.

notes.label: Pola-Reiter
notes.text: literally the ‘Pola rider,’ the conventional name of the mounted ghost attached to the Pola estate.

f2991c563729a5df4e3209643dd3ed0376c9c7bb.summary: On the boundary between the upper Freiamt and the old district of Rotenburg, behind Giebelflüh, lies the farm called “Tossolehn.” A few steps from the boundary stone stood the old farmhouse, which was demolished only about 20 years ago.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: a historical Swiss district whose name means ‘free bailiwick’; it is a regional designation rather than simply any free administrative office.

notes.label: Tossolehn
notes.text: the local farm name on the former boundary near Giebelflüh; Lehn can denote a holding or fief, while Tosso is unexplained.

notes.label: Kilbenen
notes.text: plural or dialect form of Kilbi, local church-dedication fairs or annual village festivals often accompanied by eating, drinking, and dancing.

notes.label: Feiämtlern
notes.text: dialect for people from the Freiamt, contrasted here with people of Lucerne in inn brawls.

notes.label: Sellen
notes.text: structural sleepers, sills, or heavy timbers from the demolished house; the exact building members intended by this regional form are uncertain.

notes.label: Gürtlerhans
notes.text: a byname meaning ‘Hans the girdler,’ identifying the artisan’s son through the family trade.

ee56236c969cc5bfd2ef6f5f73a337f510c56b75.summary: In olden times, a pious priest who was a professor once went walking with his young pupils in the Aletsch Valley to see its great glacier.

notes.label: Aletschgletscher
notes.text: the Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland's great Alpine glacier; local legend imagines its blue crevasses crowded with souls undergoing purification.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ usually a hermit or solitary holy man; here he appears in a traditional evasive explanation of where babies come from.

31aa3fba4f8566b9741103f2f18e6bd072affbc7.summary: On the Thursday before the Advent Fronfasten, the Posterlijagd was formerly performed in Entlebuch.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: Fronfasten denotes one of the quarterly Ember fasts in the Christian calendar, here the Advent observance; the precise local timing and liturgical framing are uncertain.

notes.label: Posterlijagd
notes.text: literally the ‘Posterli hunt,’ this was an Entlebuch masquerade procession held before the Advent Ember fast; the custom’s origin, route, and relationship to Wild Hunt traditions are uncertain.

notes.label: Posterli
notes.text: Posterli is the witchlike or animal-disguised figure pursued or represented during the local procession; the name’s etymology and the being’s exact folkloric identity are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

57f81a032e4d28d017b44c940d84228409baaebf.summary: “Why, nobody need come and tell me that none of all those things Pastor Miller had printed in the weekly paper are true,” the Postli of the Maderanertal declares heatedly (1913).

notes.label: Postli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a postman, post carrier, or local postal messenger; here it is the familiar occupational name of the Maderanertal narrator.

notes.label: Zeintli
notes.text: a diminutive of the regional Zeine, a handled carrying basket often made of wicker; the narrator’s sweat streams as water would through such a basket, though the exact vessel behind his comparison is not specified.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

dc59cc7d5238eaff9cc999d4f0c2fa63de115bfe.summary: An occurrence that took place in recent years shows how imagination can have an effect.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally “little man,” the diminutive figure said to haunt the stable and pelt travelers with stones.

9db016d3529b4bcb4a24bc479354d4944b8787ce.summary: 1. On the Nidwalden Alp of Niederbawen, out of laziness—or God knows why—they neglected to call the prayer for several evenings in succession.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Niederbawen and the other named sites are working Alps.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working seasonally with livestock on an Alp; the word can include herders and dairy workers without assigning each person a precise job.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy production; in these variants he is also the man who calls the protective Betruf.

notes.label: Folla
notes.text: the local milk funnel through which the Senn projects the Betruf across the Alp, as the source footnote explicitly explains; its exact material and shape are not stated.

notes.label: Betruf
notes.text: the traditional Alpine prayer-call projected over a high pasture to invoke divine protection for its people, animals, and land; the variants show the danger of omitting the call or spitefully excluding one animal from it.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: z'Stubeten
notes.text: an Alemannic expression for going on an evening household or courtship visit in the Stube; the two boys leave the livestock unattended for this social custom.

notes.label: Chüehli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little or young cow, using the diminutive -li; one variant substitutes this red animal for the dead bull.

5ef4a0d8dbb172007259e001a79d420acc65f5de.summary: 1. Three sinister women lived on a lonely, remote little mountain farm in Attinghausen.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper part or loft of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding, here filled with dry hay and used as the stranger's sleeping place; exact building arrangements varied.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Untergaden
notes.text: the lower part of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding beneath the Obergaden; in the second version, the Devil and witches gather there.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a diminutive regional form of Gaden, meaning a small barn, hay building, or simple farm outbuilding; the three hunters use the isolated structure as overnight shelter.

dc9842fbae7524a3d5551908196757608480329f.summary: A fourteen-year-old girl from Koblenz had been sent from her village on the Aargau Rhine to the little town of Klingnau on the Aare to buy bread.

notes.label: Jm Engel
notes.text: the historical spelling of the slope-name now read as Im Engel, ‘in the angel’; the source treats it purely as a locality.

notes.label: Appelöh
notes.text: the local name of the rock wall and cave inhabited by the Erdmännlein; its precise dialect derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf beings remembered through the cave's stone furniture and enormous cakes.

notes.label: Dünnen
notes.text: regional thin cakes, tarts, or flat baked goods, often comparable to Wähe; the exact topping is unstated, while their legendary size matches the stone table.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ a hermit or lay religious recluse formerly associated with the same landscape.

notes.label: Pro me, pro me!
notes.text: Latin for ‘for me, for me!’; with folded hands, the little man appears to ask the girl to pray on his behalf, though the object of the plea is not explicitly stated.

1d45318a278336eb0f6df8a422a26e3ecc95296b.summary: Soon after the time of Saint Sigisbert, a monk preached there, above the Reuss toward the mountain, and was later buried by the river.

notes.label: About this telling

8ccb8f20352f0ad5b4e32c3a72c74c630bfeb422.summary: In the center of their eyeball, dragons have a stone that glows like an ember and is of great worth and precious substance, like the stone from a dragon's head.

fba35a8d866740494a9a7c6d0afb0dac6f849066.summary: A large stone on the Göscheneralp is called the ‘pretty stone.’ It displays the carved family or house marks of the Göscheneralp, several initials, and dates.

notes.label: Bittgang
notes.text: a communal religious supplication procession, often made through fields or toward a threatened place to seek divine protection; here it halts the advancing glacier.

b85c90d937230e015b212a6332bee93a68bd003d.summary: One married man and one bachelor went together one evening to visit a widow and her pretty daughter in the neighborhood for amusement.

notes.label: Üff und drüß und fort!
notes.text: a dialect flight formula meaning approximately ‘up and out and away!’; the women recite it after anointing their sticks, and its exact wording is part of the magic.

notes.label: Wybervölcher
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic plural for female persons or ‘little women,’ often dismissive in tone; here it labels the widow and daughter whom the men suspect of witchcraft.

notes.label: Taapen
notes.text: a dialect word for an animal's paw; the cat's severed Taapen appears the next morning as the neighbor woman's ringed hand.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

128f9d95f184a1da6bf72008b7690430b84f5b15.summary: Today the venerable Capuchin fathers work beneficently as spiritual shepherds of the alert little people at the Matt in Urseren.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Urschner
notes.text: a regional demonym for the people of Urseren; the story contrasts them with invaders coming over the Oberalp, but its legendary chronology and group labels vary by version.

notes.label: Pintner
notes.text: the legend's dialect label for the opponents from Graubünden or beyond the Oberalp; ‘people of Graubünden’ is the closest contextual sense, while the word's exact geographic derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Valzauser
notes.text: the warning cry's uncertain name for the attackers; the source footnote tentatively suggests Valzasker, people from Val Verzasca in Ticino, but does not establish that identification.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Kurwalder
notes.text: the alternate warning cry's form for people associated with Churwalden or the Chur region; it belongs to a variant that changes the attackers' designation, and its exact historical reference is uncertain.

212c49d5531ba2293138ecccf033289003b20e69.summary: A large, freestanding boulder in the rear Etzliboden is called the Kreuzstein because for a long time it bore a wooden cross in memory of a fatal accident.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

fd167deed002227a339ed04411eec0442e074044.summary: Evo, the Klostervorsteher, once felt a great desire to go for a walk after the midday meal.

notes.label: Klostervorsteher
notes.text: the head or superior of a monastery; the story immediately identifies Evo's specific office as prior.

notes.label: Käpplein
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little cap; Evo puts it on before his walk, but the source does not specify the cap's exact clerical style or material.

3f84213f310260015157d839b4b37272c48f12ff.summary: A general legend of the procession of the dead, also often called the Gratzug or Symphonie, has remained in the mouths of the Valais people, especially in the mountains and valleys, down to our time.

notes.label: Gratzug
notes.text: this Valais name denotes a nocturnal procession of the dead whose route and sounds foretell death or cause illness; its etymology and relationship to the Wild Hunt remain uncertain.

notes.label: Symphonie
notes.text: in this Valais folk usage, Symphonie is another name for the audible procession of the dead, emphasizing its mixed music and noise; the term’s local origin and breadth are uncertain.

notes.label: d'Winda cho
notes.text: this dialect phrase means approximately ‘to come into the winds’ and describes being struck ill after entering the spirit procession; the exact medical and supernatural distinction is uncertain.

notes.label: Temperzeit
notes.text: this denotes one of the quarterly Ember seasons in the Christian calendar, treated as an uncanny time in the account; which Ember season is intended is unspecified.

notes.label: Schleif
notes.text: this is the named or descriptive upland place where felled wood blocked the procession’s route; its exact location and whether the word denotes a dragging track are uncertain.

09b9f505ae31ac14aa466565a333204cc900b996.summary: Twice a year, though not at any fixed time, the gates of Gottlieben Castle open at the dark hour of midnight, when not a single little star sends its light down through the gloomy clouds and the dreadful silence is broken only by the croaking of night birds and the mysterious whispering of the…

4246278cfc8edfe1818194a15a52e56eecbb0e88.summary: On a Good Friday, while the Passion was being sung in the church, a man from Seedorf walked through the little lane above Apro Castle.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

051af50b17146ab9702fe0ab4094422c70b1c9d6.summary: Two young men from Widnau promised each other that whichever of them died first must appear to the other on the threshing floor of the barn and bring definite news about the hereafter.

notes.label: About this telling
