b819395781dfc599c2e1a37ce12a1360085a8cae.summary: For many years, a peculiar Manndli lived all alone in Hohfuhr-Michel's ancient house in the Getschwyler.

notes.label: Manndli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a ‘little man,’ used familiarly for the solitary, eccentric resident; after his death the same name also refers to the ghost the boys provoke.

86671496fc8aa7bb9323a3560c380024d29467e6.summary: The poor little house on the Lauwi estate at Seelisberg, toward the Emmetten border, had long been haunted.

notes.label: Lauwi
notes.text: an Alemannic form related to Lawine, an avalanche or avalanche track; here it is the established name of the Seelisberg estate, and the story does not say whether a specific avalanche gave it that name.

notes.label: Gerümpelgänterli
notes.text: an Uri compound for a little cupboard, cabinet, or enclosed storage nook holding clutter; the ghostly banging comes from within it, but its precise built-in form is not described.

notes.label: G’rimpel
notes.text: an Uri dialect sound-word for a violent clatter, crashing, or rumbling commotion; the supernatural noise arises among the kitchen firewood.

notes.label: Miselen
notes.text: a regional word for small split pieces, chips, scraps, or kindling mixed with the larger firewood; the exact size intended is uncertain, but they fly from the doorway with the logs.

notes.label: Beige
notes.text: Swiss German for a neatly arranged stack or pile, especially of firewood; despite the apparent barrage, the whole woodpile is found intact and orderly the next day.

498ecb6cc0dbe03141578fb27cdffe27328fe958.summary: Across a terrace on the slope of the ‘Spitze’ stretch the green pastures of Alp Obsaum.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; here Obsaum is the named Alp whose abandoned hut remains haunted.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schweignapf
notes.text: a regional name for a bowl or basin used in Alpine dairying; the avalanche carries this vessel across the valley, but the source does not identify its material, size, or precise dairy function.

d81597e60cd0c353063e7a7645cc262ec246accf.summary: An hour above Amsteg, where the Reuss enters a broad valley, one sees between the little villages of Intschi and Drachental, on both sides of the river, mountain slopes entirely covered with debris of rocks and stones, from which only isolated trees and shrubs emerge meagerly.

notes.label: Wir Berglüt bruchet unsers Herrgotts Licht niememe!
notes.text: dialect for ‘We miners no longer need the light of our Lord God!’; Berglüt are mining people, and the boast about artificial candlelight becomes literal when the collapse buries them forever.
notes.anchor: Wir Berglüt bruchet unsers Herrgotts Licht niememe!

1f998fba7bde60f64996af4adbfdec3ecf3e3ed0.summary: Near Vallorbe in former times there stood a miracle-working image of the Mother of God, to which devout worshipers, travelers to holy places, and pilgrims streamed from near and far to implore healing and blessing.

notes.label: Heller
notes.text: a small historical coin used here as the fixed bridge toll collected by Romainmôtier Abbey; its value varied by period and currency system, so the denomination is retained rather than converted.

765622796d23b66b6eece6af4b068408b37497ee.summary: The following legend was told by the elderly Mr. P.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a historical Swiss title for a local civic or court official, usher, or official messenger; the source identifies P. Jos. Karlen by the office but does not specify its exact scope in Törbel.

notes.label: Visperzehnen
notes.text: the historical Visp Zehnten, one of the territorial districts of the old Valais polity; the source's spelling preserves the region's former political organization rather than merely naming the modern Visp district.

notes.label: Tanzlohn
notes.text: literally the ‘dance wages’ or payment earned by dancing; the Devil twists a festive expression into the missing dancer's infernal punishment.

998595746021c189d45cd915d5e97a4bcd518c73.summary: In the autumn of 1841, the municipality of Unterkulm assigned the firewood that it distributes annually to its citizens on the heights of those cliffs that border the high forest above.

b5164c0b72a87abcd9de64c99de0ddf3a3298b9c.summary: When Landammann Chr. Pallet was still working as a Fuhrmann, he once reached the foot of the Bergüner-Stein with his load at about midnight and found himself on the level ground not far from the bridge over the Albula.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or presiding official of a canton, district, or historical jurisdiction; the precise office varied by place and period.

notes.label: Fuhrmann
notes.text: a wagoner or carter who transports loads with a horse-drawn vehicle.

notes.label: Bergüner-Stein
notes.text: the named rocky route or landmark at whose foot Pallet encounters the disturbance.

notes.label: Fuhrmannsbrauch
notes.text: the customary manner attributed to wagoners or carters; here it specifically refers to cursing when the vehicle fails.

notes.label: Pökler
notes.text: the title’s local name for the unseen poltering or obstructing presence; the narrative describes its wheel-removing trick but does not define the being more precisely.

notes.label: Bergüner Steine
notes.text: the title’s inflected form for the Bergüner-Stein, the steep rocky passage or landmark near Bergün where the wagon is stopped.

1061650fc79bc47299ae4f8697fd04837604c163.summary: One summer, five herders grazed the herd on the Stäzer Alp, which belongs to Curwalden.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high mountain pasture, not simply a mountain peak; here the Stäzer Alp belongs to Curwalden and supports a summer herd.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled dairymen and herders who work on an Alp; here the neighboring Sennen come from Obervaz.

350fa248ba5f029519f9180cb71cb6ef07610284.summary: This story took place on an alp in the Wägital region of Schwyz and is related to the preceding one.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman responsible for livestock on a high summer pasture; here it refers to the newly hired Tyrolean servant.

notes.label: Holderknebel
notes.text: literally an ‘elderwood cudgel’ or short billet of elder wood; the servant boils these sticks and uses one against the cat-queen, though the source does not explain the ritual significance.

notes.label: Kessi
notes.text: Swiss German for a large kettle or cauldron; here it holds the boiling Holderknebel used to defeat the supernatural cats.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

e2ea13be27b9db259c24a181bf111ce3f3a6030c.summary: At the foot of the majestic Calanda mountain above the village of Haldenstein stands the ruin of the castle of the same name.

notes.label: Quelljungfer
notes.text: literally ‘spring maiden,’ the female personification or soul of a healing fountain; her disappearance coincides with the apparent loss of the water’s power, but the tale gives no cause.

fcffa81adeaf4a208b6cb0583c7881f4bc4c355f.summary: Once, the people of Zürich lived in bitter feud with their Eidgenossen. They had fallen out completely with them, especially with the people of Schwyz, over a great inheritance.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-confederates,’ the historical self-designation for members of the Swiss Confederacy, with a stronger sense of sworn political fellowship than simply ‘Swiss.’

notes.label: Bergstände
notes.text: the mountain cantons or their political communities, characterized here through their pastoral population.

notes.label: Gelten
notes.text: open tubs or pails used here to carry wine from the city to the troops.

notes.label: Weintansen
notes.text: large back-carried or transport vessels for wine; Tanse denotes a regional carrying vat or tub.

notes.label: Grünhag
notes.text: literally ‘green hedge,’ the named or descriptive hedge through which the attackers burst.

notes.label: Haarus!
notes.text: the battle cry attributed to the men of Schwyz and Glarus; its exact literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Sihlsteg
notes.text: the footbridge across the Sihl used by the fleeing Zürichers; Steg denotes a narrow bridge or walkway.

notes.label: Rennwegtor
notes.text: the city gate at the Rennweg approach into Zürich, the defenders' destination during the retreat.

notes.label: Grobschmied
notes.text: literally a ‘heavy’ or ‘rough smith,’ especially a blacksmith doing large ironwork; the comparison turns Stüssi's blows into hammer-strikes on anvils.

notes.label: Gewalthaufen
notes.text: the main mass or large body of troops, here the Zürich force able to escape while Stüssi holds the bridge.

notes.label: Fallgatter
notes.text: a heavy portcullis that drops vertically to close a fortified gateway.

notes.label: Landschreiber
notes.text: a territorial or cantonal clerk and senior public official; Küng of Glarus dies after saving the captured banner.

2033e9d72c1673622bb7362911891fd55ab85f1f.summary: A woman from Asp, a mountain village in the Aargau Jura, quarreled with her husband over their child.

notes.label: Quäcki
notes.text: the onomatopoetic local name of the groaning female apparition at Asp, derived in the tale from her lamenting voice; she is linked to a murdered child’s remains and weather change, but the narrative leaves her identity as mother, child, or composite haunting unclear.

notes.label: Quiggeli
notes.text: a diminutive, sound-imitating name in the children’s rhyme related to Quäcki; it evokes a whining or squeaking creature, though it is unclear whether the rhyme treats it as exactly the same apparition.

notes.label: Quäggli
notes.text: a second diminutive rhyme-name related to Quäcki and paired with Quiggeli; its function is chiefly onomatopoetic and teasing, with no separate being described.

notes.label: quägglet
notes.text: a dialect verb for whining, wailing, or making the Quäcki’s characteristic sound; the rhyme applies it both to the apparition on the stones and metaphorically to fretful children.

41d418f17300d2c99280a38dfbc79d7c57be4d38.summary: The Raging Host is called Mutterseel or Mutterseelen here. It fills the air with a repulsive cry, rolls ahead of the traveler in the form of a sack of leaves, and disappears as it came.

notes.label: Mutterseelen
notes.text: this St. Gallen name, literally suggestive of ‘mother souls,’ denotes the Raging Host appearing as a rolling leaf-sack; its singular variant Mutterseel and exact etymology are uncertain.

313b52b455c94fd24b18cef46fcc13c301f744f1.summary: There was a time when the people on either side of the Brienz ridge and the Brünig feuded with one another.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: Älpler are people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, here the Planalp community attacked by the raiders; their exact roles beyond the separately named Sennen are uncertain.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: the plural of Senn, denoting the Alpine dairymen responsible for livestock and cheesemaking; the number killed and their individual duties are unspecified.

notes.label: Follentrichter
notes.text: this appears to be a speaking funnel or horn used to project the evening Alpine blessing from one Alp to another; its exact construction, name origin, and sound are uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Mordstyen
notes.text: this local name is associated both with the ambush site and, in the source, with old weapons unearthed there; its literal meaning, spelling, and whether the second use is a textual corruption are uncertain.

4757aa3e0fb58c3dab11f986ffdff71f091c110e.summary: On the roof of an ancient Zurich country house, one notices a raised tile. Folk legend says that each successive owner of the house must never set this tile properly in place because a spirit descends through this opening in the roof into a connected room.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d7e090ced61b524896968fd6df680b84cad09bed.summary: Knight Heinrich Walther of Ramswag went to war with King Rudolf of Habsburg against the Bohemian king Ottokar and saved his lord's life at the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278.

notes.label: Burgstall
notes.text: the site or remains of a former castle, often a ruin or earthwork rather than an intact stronghold; Ramswag's spectral game continues in its underground rooms.

1c9ef2b2dedf7868db40da65acc25b0ad79b8599.summary: At Gurtnellen, on the Grossprachtigen estate by the Reuss, there lived a Ratsherr whose wife had come across Lake Lucerne with two sisters, each of whom married a Ratsherr.

notes.label: Ratsherr
notes.text: literally a ‘council lord,’ a male member of a governing council in a Swiss community; the historical office could carry municipal or cantonal authority, and the passage does not specify which council these men served.

notes.label: Maiensäss
notes.text: a seasonally used Alpine holding, generally at an intermediate elevation between the home farm and the high summer pasture; here it is the property called Berg, though the account does not detail its buildings or precise seasonal use.

notes.label: Russdiele
notes.text: literally a ‘soot loft’ or soot-darkened board platform in the upper part of a traditional house near the chimney; here it provides the passage and opening through which the apparition is driven, but the source leaves the exact architecture unclear.

notes.label: Ratsherrin
notes.text: the feminine form associated with Ratsherr; in this story it means the Ratsherr’s wife rather than a woman independently holding council office, a distinction the English title ‘councilwoman’ would obscure.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

eab8269b62543ef495cc9dfe541e66df643aa7c3.summary: Nearby on the Selimatt lies the Rauchloch, an opening in the earth similar to the Wetterloch of the Kamor in the upper Rhine valley.

notes.label: Rauchloch
notes.text: literally ‘smoke hole,’ the deep earth opening whose rising vapors are believed to foretell or bring rain.

notes.label: Wetterloch
notes.text: literally ‘weather hole,’ a comparable opening on the Kamor associated with atmospheric signs.

e89a117dc1debf916232af61a1b836e50ccee368.summary: Once there was a count of very ancient lineage but very modest means. One day he walked through the forest, pondering the future of his only lovely little daughter.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

11b56198c0c483f663de4c2b9a8eb2b22ac99cf9.summary: The Lords of Corbières bore a raven in their coat of arms. The family legend about it held that whenever a little son was about to be born to the house, it most courteously and gracefully dropped a silver ring from its beak, but whenever the birth of a little daughter approached, it dropped a gold finger-ring.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a0c1425d2bdde4b58cb3d51e3525ac695f39018a.summary: 1. Ravens never hatch soon enough except on Holy Saturday.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture with its herding and dairy-working landscape, not merely a mountain peak; the second raven nest is found by herders working on one in the Schächen Valley.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives and works seasonally with livestock on an Alp; this worker is lowered down the cliff by his companions to search the raven nest.

notes.label: Rappästei
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘raven stone,’ a folkloric stone hidden in a raven’s nest and believed here to make its bearer and any container holding it invisible; the account offers no natural identification for the object.

cba116d1cc2d9c413922a7562d45392d6e25275b.summary: After the time when Saint Gallus, Saint Fridolin, and Saint Columbanus had converted pagan Switzerland to Christianity with hardship and toil and churches and monasteries were being built everywhere, a God-fearing hermit lived on the Etzel mountain, where the Alps of central Switzerland begin.

notes.label: Finstern Wald
notes.text: literally ‘Dark Forest,’ the traditional wilderness around Meinrad's hermitage and the later site of Einsiedeln; it functions as a named region as well as a description of remoteness.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry Alpine downslope wind, often sudden and powerful; its nighttime arrival intensifies the forest's threatening sounds around the hermit.

notes.label: Maria Einsiedeln
notes.text: the Marian monastery and pilgrimage shrine at Einsiedeln that develops at Meinrad's burial place; Maria identifies its dedication to Mary rather than a separate person in the story.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Fähnlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little banner,’ and historically also a small military company under such a flag; here the ravens survive heraldically on the banner of Einsiedeln's Schwyz forest people, while the exact civic or military unit is unstated.

91dd3e11978e8b7ffefbddf1fae9ccc2e7377583.summary: Once, in our Swiss fatherland, the two highly respected, battle-tested captains Zurkinden of Zurich and Arnold Winkelried of Nidwalden—a descendant of the eternally unforgettable hero of Sempach—gravely insulted one another.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath comrades,’ members of the Swiss Confederacy joined by sworn alliance; the story repeatedly appeals to their loyalty above personal feud.

notes.label: Schwabenkrieg
notes.text: the Swabian War, the conflict in which the tale places the two captains' reconciliation.

notes.label: Landesbanner
notes.text: the territorial or cantonal banners under which regional contingents assembled, by extension also evoking the forces belonging to each banner.

notes.label: Grimmbärte
notes.text: literally ‘fierce beards,’ a vivid collective nickname for the two grim, hostile veteran captains.

notes.label: Gauen
notes.text: plural of Gau, historical territorial districts or regions from which the Confederate forces came.

notes.label: Landammänner
notes.text: plural of Landammann, the chief elected magistrate of a rural Swiss canton or polity, here participating in the army council.

notes.label: Landeshauptmänner
notes.text: chief territorial captains or senior military leaders before whom the two men make their pledge.

notes.label: Schweizerschwert
notes.text: literally ‘Swiss sword,’ here a double-edged sword wielded by Winkelried in close combat.

notes.label: Tross
notes.text: a body of followers, troops, or military retinue accompanying a leader; here it is the group with which Zurkinden rides to the rescue.

notes.label: Blechhüte
notes.text: literally ‘sheet-metal hats,’ helmets worn by the imperial cavalry, described hyperbolically as raining down together with heads.

notes.label: Kriegsknecht
notes.text: literally ‘war servant,’ an ordinary soldier or military retainer whose horse Zurkinden rides after losing his own.

a23ccb7ad90cea8a42161b6ae8cf072ef5bad342.summary: The parish village of Buch lies upon the Irchel ridge. On the road to this village, a red beech stands at the Stammberg.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

a2377d87824508d2b06250146e7f9c907cccc39a.summary: One evening, an elderly woman from the Solothurn village of Eppenberg still had to make a trip to Aarau.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a regional name for the leader or embodiment of the nocturnal Wild Hunt, here a spectral hunter who travels with black hounds; traditions about his exact identity and form vary across central Switzerland.

notes.label: Drei Schritt aus Weg!
notes.text: an archaic warning formula meaning approximately ‘three steps out of the way!’; the Türst shouts it to clear a path for his supernatural hunt.

notes.label: Güggel
notes.text: Swiss German for a rooster or cock; the old Dielsdorf bylaw makes the distance of the innkeeper’s rooster’s protected grazing depend on how far a sickle can be thrown from the roof ridge.

cc59e3dba4ca3693ca87fddf7b784aa24cc68181.summary: One evening, as is told in Savièse, a young fellow wanted to return alone to Rhumaz from the village of Drôna, where he had been at an evening gathering.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ccf2fcaac0dcad50cb1c829a09457dce7db42b97.summary: East of the city of Sion, two hills rise toward the sky, Tourbillon and Valeria.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a35feb09065215a82a1a58b5746a6bddb789b43a.summary: On every Quartember evening, as soon as the Betglocke has rung, a terrible ghost begins to make a disturbance in one of the barred chambers of Schloss Pigritz, continuing until nearly midnight.

notes.label: Quartember
notes.text: the Ember fast or quarterly fast days in the Christian calendar; the apparition returns on the evening associated with each observance.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the prayer or Angelus bell; its ringing opens the ghost's recurring period of haunting.

notes.label: Schloss Pigritz
notes.text: Pigritz Castle; Schloss is retained as part of the source's named site rather than reducing it to an unnamed generic castle.

dcfa33e5dd0ae1fd891f5b1a6efb13c443c6a68a.summary: The owner of an Alp in Entlebuch always leased it out, but no Lehenmann remained there long; all died of fear and horror because of the spirit that walked there.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture holding with livestock, buildings, and grazing rights; the spirit's presence makes the whole working property unusable.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Lehenmann
notes.text: a tenant or leaseholder who works property granted under a lease or older tenure arrangement; repeated tenants die before one endures the haunting.

notes.label: Gatter
notes.text: a livestock gate or barred enclosure entrance; opening it makes the spirit appear helpful rather than immediately hostile.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder who gradually overcomes fear and thereby redeems the spirit.

notes.label: weissen
notes.text: used verbally to mean ‘become white’ or whiten; the spirit's change from black to white visibly marks purification before it becomes a dove.

c4b28ba4d6d43795ea605fa2d3890cc1602b2b03.summary: In Ruis above Ilanz there once lived a rich man, A. C.

notes.label: Doggi
notes.text: a regional name related to Doggeli for a nocturnal tormenting or nightmare-like being; this brief tale does not describe its form or manner of attack.

notes.label: Doggiberufe
notes.text: literally the calling, vocation, or condition of being a Doggi; the girl says the man’s ritual has released her from that compelled supernatural role.

9b80f7dfabe8d405edc6473653cbfb9ac5a3935d.summary: Pasture boys near Vilmergen were tending their goats on the meadow slope toward the edge of a forest when they encountered a black figure beside a boundary stone and at once ran away in fright.

notes.label: Götti
notes.text: Swiss German for a godfather; the boy recognizes the dead man through this baptismal kinship, which also makes him the appropriate person to help the spirit make amends.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a heavy hoe or mattock-like digging tool; together with the shovel it lets the dead man move the boundary stone he had presumably set dishonestly in life.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: the reciprocal kinship word used by the dead Götti for his godchild in this source; elsewhere Swiss German Gotte commonly means ‘godmother,’ so the masculine boy in context makes this historical usage potentially confusing.

0b5a5c736cf1735a1b0c8e1b361d84a5f0721c95.summary: A regiment could go no farther on its march. At last it was noticed that the cause might be a hare that kept leaping back and forth in front of it.

notes.label: Marienthaler
notes.text: a silver thaler bearing Marian imagery; here its metal is recast as a magically effective projectile against a shape-changing witch, while the exact coin type is not specified.

be91b6e2649835201e5cde67490f450890f6411d.summary: In Leerau, a fiery dog and a spectral Gizzi often appear. Both are one and the same village animal, which runs here from Reinach by way of Gontenschwil and Rued.

notes.label: Gizzi
notes.text: a Swiss German kid goat; the village spirit alternates between this spectral form and a fiery dog.

notes.label: Sichellöse
notes.text: a harvest gathering or celebratory meal marking the end of sickle work; the reaper is returning from this customary occasion.

notes.label: Küchlein
notes.text: small cakes, pastries, or fried treats given to the reaper by the farmer's wife; offering them makes the supernatural dog grow.

f5ab745db43ec4478d7bc95ccade613f293f18f7.summary: The Reizibielbock dwells below St. Jost am Bürgen in Nidwalden.

notes.label: Reizibielbock
notes.text: the local name of a one-eyed spectral buck near St. Jost; Bock means male goat, while Reizibiel appears to be a place or byname whose derivation is unstated.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: young men out at night, especially returning from social or courtship visits.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a traditional evening social gathering in a farmhouse parlor, often involving music, courtship, or communal work.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn, storage building, room, or small outbuilding in Alpine usage; here it houses the monster.

notes.label: Nachtböckel
notes.text: literally ‘little night buck,’ a related child-frightening bogey in Unterwalden.

27bad0578d2b827e6987411bd56ab79865233527.summary: From his house, a man in Attelwil often saw a will-o’-the-wisp roaming back and forth at night over a nearby plot of land.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fdf70cb537e12fab8a4b56d21261e9bb50854feb.summary: The following is told of Johannes Brantschen in Zermatt: he dreamed that he would find his fortune in Sitten.

notes.label: Sitten
notes.text: the German name for the bilingual Valais city known in French and commonly in English as Sion; the German form is retained because it is the destination named in the source.

be9b8284eee7d0aa13cc6b18d1290e2c6df04245.summary: ‘I too want to tell a little story like the ones they have had printed in this book, but this one is no Märlein.—I was a boy of about thirteen when I served as a Geissbub for Blättäli-Seebi at Blättäli in Erstfeld.

notes.label: Märlein
notes.text: a diminutive of Märchen, meaning a little tale or fairy tale; the narrator uses it to deny that his account is mere fiction.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: Swiss German for a boy who herds goats; it describes the narrator’s farm work rather than a family name.

notes.label: Blättäli-Seebi
notes.text: the local byname of the man at Blättäli for whom the narrator herded goats; Seebi likely represents a personal-name form, but the source does not establish its full derivation.

notes.label: Feckerweib
notes.text: a historical, often disparaging Swiss label for an itinerant or socially marginalized woman, here represented as a palm reader; retaining it records the source’s prejudice rather than endorsing the term.

a32d4e2dc8acac3ba0b992ea6a0e401db828b02a.summary: Another herder fared less well after once cursing his unruly livestock and wishing that the Devil would take it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working farm landscape; the Devil throws livestock over its cliff-like edge.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: ich war im Fehlen
notes.text: literally ‘I was in error’ or ‘I was at fault’; the repentant formula also supplies the legendary explanation for the Alp's name Im Fehlen.

notes.label: Im Fehlen
notes.text: the Alp's name, understood by the story through the herder's confession ‘ich war im Fehlen’; the phrase therefore functions as both place-name and moral wordplay.

9b80657e3784b2268ce47a2187155bb2962a5d56.summary: When, on holy Easter Day in the year 1642, the village of Schwyz stood in bright flames and every building was consumed by the terrible element, a chapel above the parish church of Schwyz, called the Holy Cross, was likewise exposed to danger.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

06749b5b3ee14712ddd8591e0c27b14ed7c93444.summary: Around 1212, men from Unterwalden are said to have made a military incursion into Valais, roaming through the Rote Kumme—also called Jäginen—at the head of the Lötschental and through the Baldschiedertal.

notes.label: Rottmeister
notes.text: leaders or captains of local militia divisions called ‘Rotten’; the precise organization varied by region and period.

notes.label: Schotten
notes.text: whey, the liquid remaining from Alpine cheesemaking; the term carries the dairy setting in which the herdsman is killed.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist herdsman and dairyman responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on a Swiss alpine pasture; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Kessi
notes.text: the large Alpine dairy cauldron used to heat milk for cheesemaking; ‘kettle’ alone understates its scale and cultural setting.

notes.label: Untersenn
notes.text: the subordinate or assistant Senn in an Alpine dairy operation, with duties below those of the principal Senn.

notes.label: Hohpen, O Blessi
notes.text: the opening of the horn-call, apparently addressing or calling to a cow named Blessi; the exact sense of ‘Hohpen’ is uncertain.

notes.label: Trichelkue
notes.text: a bell cow wearing a ‘Treichel,’ a distinctive hammered sheet-metal livestock bell rather than a cast bell.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive for a girl or young woman; here it is the young woman washing greens who first understands the horn-call.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the Alpine hut that houses the Senn’s dairy work and often the herders, not merely a generic mountain cabin.

notes.label: Treichel
notes.text: a traditional hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; its timbre and construction differ from a cast cowbell.

34d02340e58d71970c5b67b172d44a590c6277bc.summary: The Reuss bridge at Sins will collapse when the Sins annual fair, which is held on it, once again falls on the first Sunday in May, bringing together more people than ever before.

notes.label: About this telling

40cbf184a88738552ce687ce11962adefd1335b6.summary: From the Aargau village of Mühlau, a ferry crosses the Reuss into the territory of Zug.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: terminiert
notes.text: for Capuchins, this means traveling an assigned district to solicit alms and provisions, not ending an appointment; the precise limits and rules of this round are uncertain.

notes.label: Patres
notes.text: this clerical plural means the Fathers, here the two Capuchin priests confronting the water spirit; their names and rank are unspecified.

7167d61218a31463954c5db8c29e1d0a474c7ded.summary: Long ago in St. Antönien there lived an old woman who was universally reputed and recognized to be a witch.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Hexen-Platz
notes.text: literally a ‘witches' place,’ a site associated with nocturnal witch gatherings; the darker rings of grass serve as visible folkloric evidence.

notes.label: besegneten
notes.text: literally blessed themselves; here it most likely means making a protective religious gesture such as the sign of the cross before passing the feared house.

notes.label: Knaben
notes.text: literally boys, but Jecklin immediately glosses the word as Burschen, indicating unmarried young men rather than small children.

notes.label: Zeit-Geis
notes.text: the dialect name for the goat staked in the wager; the source's prose gloss identifies it simply as a Geis (goat) and says it would be costly, but the compound's more precise husbandry sense is uncertain.

notes.label: stichdunkel
notes.text: a dialect intensifier meaning pitch-dark or completely dark.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Muass-Ratza
notes.text: a dialect compound for a very young child still eating mush; in the charm, the child's innocence protects the visitor.

notes.label: Hahna-Chratza
notes.text: the charm's dialect and rhyme-shaped name for the cock; Jecklin's own prose gloss identifies the protective animal simply as a Hahn, or cock.

notes.label: Fürli
notes.text: a diminutive of fire; here it refers to the little burning light of the candle lantern, the third protection against the witch.

4542037556574bd8a50e1f4c949db61f4fef9a00.summary: The little village of Büblikon, situated on a rise between Mellingen and Wohlenschwil, has suffered no further affliction since the Swiss Peasants’ War, which chose this very place as its battlefield.

notes.label: Zwilch
notes.text: a strong, coarse linen or hempen fabric, related to ticking or twill and traditionally used for durable work clothing; the gift is practical winter clothing rather than fine dress.

a863d1195ebea9851c0d342be673ca75c9af6011.summary: Anyone who knows the wildly steep mountain slopes of the Visp valleys, lined with high rock walls that are now solid and now fearfully fissured, will not be surprised that many a person seeking to exploit these dangerous regions for timber or pasture must die a violent death.

notes.label: Gradtier
notes.text: literally a ‘ridge animal,’ a hunters' term for a chamois found along a mountain crest; the grateful dead man promises it as a reward.

notes.label: Ausstich
notes.text: a regional hunting term, glossed by the source as a position from which a hunter can shoot at chamois; the exact terrain form is not otherwise specified.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

c5ec657045b8d4e10091ba3edadea9b7f4ba509f.summary: “What do I still lack for happiness?

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or head herdsman responsible for cattle and milk production; the poor Senn shares his food and receives the stranger’s blessing.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: here the rich woman’s high summer pasture and dairy estate, whose fertile grassland is burned and left covered with rocks after she refuses charity.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

739cdafcc4e378c9fded3e622ae93a4cdf6f90e2.summary: In the Hardwald between Böttstein and Leuggern, a man appears near a wooden wayside cross wearing a gray sash and white gloves, through which finger rings can be seen gleaming even at night.

notes.label: Brugg-Joggeli
notes.text: a local diminutive name meaning approximately ‘little Jakob of the bridge’; it identifies the particular spirit dwelling by the footbridge and old oak, but the account does not explain who he was or why he haunts the site.

notes.label: Hexenringe
notes.text: literally ‘witches' rings,’ dark circles of grass interpreted here as the dancing place of wicked women; the term gives a supernatural explanation for ring-shaped growth around the oak.

0bd42672ecbaac793ff5e7ff16ebbbc4e3f211c9.summary: At night, a man on a white horse is sometimes seen near Forsteck Castle. He rides from the castle, past the red stable, toward the farm.

fa40bb2f5f1906641e13bbbc6f24602b6da01ad5.summary: Anyone who turns southwest from the little village of Linn on the Bözberg toward the rising heights reaches a forest with a cheerful meadow precisely at its center.

notes.label: Hegel und Wetzer
notes.text: traditional mocking bynames for the people of Thalheim, literally suggesting choppers and sharpeners; here the names pun on their unauthorized cutting of wood, though the wider origin of the nicknames is not stated.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Landtag
notes.text: here a public territorial court or assembly at which the bailiff adjudicates the forest dispute, not a modern cantonal or national parliament.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: standard German for ‘judge,’ but in the oath trick it is also presented as the local name of a comb hidden under the bailiff's hat; the wordplay lets him falsely claim that his judge is above him.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: standard German for ‘Creator,’ but also a regional word for a dipper or serving ladle hidden above the bailiff's head; the double meaning enables the perjured oath.

notes.label: Hohop
notes.text: the wild, repeated call attributed to the spectral mounted bailiff; it resembles a driving or hunting cry, but the source does not give a literal meaning.

notes.label: Alongenperücke
notes.text: an allonge wig, the long, curled formal wig worn by officials in the early modern period; here it conceals the comb and ladle used in the oath trick.

notes.label: Im Gättibuch isch nid gar schön
notes.text: the opening Swiss German line of a joking local verse, ‘In Gättibuch it is not very fair’; it frames the forest as dark and unpleasant rather than making a precise aesthetic judgment.
notes.anchor: Im Gättibuch isch nid gar schön

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little man or husband, with -li as the diminutive; here a wife familiarly addresses her man before he goes to the tavern.

notes.label: Rüeschli
notes.text: a diminutive related to Rausch, intoxication or a drunken state; here the wife warns her husband not to bring drunkenness home, and the playful -li keeps the warning in the tone of a teasing rhyme.

ad43ef8c281ed3cf735fcb647b2faae4a8514d93.summary: At night, a man from Altendorf saw a rider on a white horse ascending through Stafanell on the Alp Farnboden near Sevelen.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high-elevation summer pasture and its associated seasonal farming place, not simply an Alpine mountain; Farnboden is the named Alp through which the dead rider travels.

e687c4042556973b17b4b1bcbaef53f133859fa2.summary: In the Simmental, not too far from the village of Erlenbach, rich in livestock and pastures, ruined masonry lies hidden on a mountainside among thorns and brush.

notes.label: Hauri
notes.text: a local name for an animal or spirit whose lament is treated as a warning of the riders; the source does not identify it more precisely.

notes.label: Tschinggenreiter
notes.text: the local name for the supernatural riders of Gafertschinken; Reiter means riders, while Tschinggen is unexplained and may reflect a place or regional byname.

notes.label: Marchsteine
notes.text: boundary stones; their flight through the storm evokes both violent weather and the disturbance of territorial order.

notes.label: Trabanten
notes.text: attendants, guards, or followers accompanying the riders, not celestial satellites in this context.

2b31811943cb6e1412178c42af3d99d6b79f4254.summary: To travel from Aristorf to the neighboring Fricktal, one passes by the cheese hut called Sennweid and reaches a tremendous stone said to mark the boundary between the cantons of Aargau and Basel.

6906cf7d5756f485911611d6c43caaccc3cff9c4.summary: In the Riedligger meadow at Wohlen, across which some of the local factory girls had to walk on their way home, there was a Brünnling in whose existence several high-spirited girls refused to believe.

notes.label: Brünnling
notes.text: a local Alemannic name for a burning or fiery male apparition; in this Aargau story he radiates enough heat to threaten shutters and demands a devout rosary, while the term’s precise wider classification is left open.

notes.label: Chum, brünniger Ma, zünd is!
notes.text: the girls’ Alemannic challenge, literally ‘Come, burning man, set us alight!’; retaining it preserves the taunting dialect speech that provokes the fiery being.

b141ad8a1ce1032891c2f2f5cb280a22f3ee9ebb.summary: It was often seen at night galloping and snorting across the Ried at Ennetmoos.

notes.label: Ried
notes.text: wet meadow, marshland, or reedy ground; here it is the terrain at Ennetmoos across which the supernatural horse gallops in every season.

notes.label: Riedross
notes.text: literally a ‘Ried steed’ or ‘marsh horse,’ the local name for the snorting nocturnal apparition; Ried can mean wet meadow, marsh, or reedy ground, so ‘marsh horse’ is only the closest compact gloss.

20974397439ecc3a3af1014fbedd2a483cec725a.summary: In the previous century, the Rigelitomme lived at the Fontanen, at the foot of the Menzberg, and his actual name was Thomas Wandeler.

notes.label: Rigelitomme
notes.text: the popular Lucerne nickname of the prophet Thomas Wandeler of the Fontanen; Tomme is a form of Thomas, while the origin and meaning of Rigeli are not explained, and the name attaches both local prophecies and an uncanny private ‘church’ to him.

notes.label: Bruder Klausen Weissagung
notes.text: literally the ‘Brother Klaus prophecy,’ a circulating body of predictions associated with the Swiss hermit-saint Nicholas of Flüe; this text says the prophecy is also attributed to Rigelitomme but does not quote it or determine its authorship.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

079244feb4fbc29246fb0d03e89b716b6e4f59bb.summary: In earlier times, the Nachtbuben of Erstfeld and Silenen fought terrible battles with one another.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: groups of unmarried young men who went out at night for courting, socializing, or pranks and could act as rival village bands; here the Erstfeld and Silenen groups engage in violent fights.

notes.label: Chlappertihli
notes.text: the quoted local name for a wooden hall beside the Silenen cemetery where meetings were sometimes held; the source itself supplies that function, but not the name's derivation.

55e3d8982673467bc3dc5af406497eaaea0a0fa1.summary: The old nobleman of Hallwil had one son. His name was Walther, but he had called himself Johannes after Christ's disciple ever since he and other nobles vowed to take up the cross and make a pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulcher.

notes.label: Großkellner
notes.text: the senior cellarer or provisioning officer of a monastery, an important administrative office rather than an ordinary dining-room waiter; the frightened porter summons him first.

notes.label: Gottesurteil
notes.text: literally a ‘judgment of God,’ a trial by ordeal believed to let divine justice reveal the rightful party; here the judicial duel decides the inheritance claim.

notes.label: Schirmvogt
notes.text: a secular protector and legal or military advocate of an ecclesiastical institution; the knight of Rüßegg fights on the monastery's behalf.

09dcf500145e81089a7729cf748bc20658597579.summary: On the mountain behind the Heidenburg (cf. no. 168: ‘The Spider at the Heidenburg’), a ring of pure gold lies stretched underground around the roots of an oak.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a local warden responsible for protected or bounded communal land, often forest; duties varied by canton and period, so ‘forest warden’ would be too narrow in every context.

c4d76bb89a614be4ea1b82e764226b7a85370559.summary: Half an hour from Bremgarten, the Buholdern forest begins on the left bank of the Reuss.

notes.label: Ringgenberger-Schlosskröte
notes.text: literally the ‘Ringgenberg castle toad,’ the supernatural treasure guardian associated with the supposed castle moat; the compound identifies its location and role but not its origin.

7036c6e88257b9c14b1d0a37d47786f91de8ceda.summary: In the mountain massif branching between the Lenzerheide and Arosa, the highest summit is the Rothorn, the red horn.

notes.label: Bündner Säumer
notes.text: a pack-horse driver from Graubünden who transported goods across Alpine routes; his occupational attention to the lead horse’s repeated flight is what saves him from the destruction of Plurs.

306af712431e3636589c301fa6e3213c018095f6.summary: a) The road dog is a great black animal with large shining eyes and a fiery maw, a white collar around its neck, and cuffs around its paws.

notes.label: Schultheis
notes.text: a Schultheis was a historical civic magistrate or chief local official, here accused of manipulating forest ownership; the office’s precise authority in the period imagined by the legend is uncertain.

notes.label: Fronfastennächten
notes.text: these are the nights associated with the quarterly Ember fasts in the Christian calendar and were often considered especially uncanny in Alpine folklore; the source does not specify which quarter’s nights are meant.

notes.label: Metzgschaal
notes.text: this Lucerne-area civic term appears to denote the covered meat market or butchers’ hall beneath which the beast passes; its exact building form and historical location are uncertain.

c42d53276a433602087edd7f604f0fce6eadcb18.summary: The road from Flims to the land of Glarus passes to the left of the Flimserstein and crosses the Segnes Pass.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its working landscape, not simply any mountain; here the once-fertile pasture beyond the Segnes Pass becomes permanently glaciated through the widow's curse.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: abere
notes.text: a regional Alpine verb meaning to become bare or free of snow as it melts; here the widow wishes that the falsely claimed pasture may never thaw and turn green again.

0b762daad3246d21b572d64841ce4a8dfe3deb52.summary: ‘In earlier times, people had to climb up ladders to get into Isental; that is why the people of Isental have the ladder in their coat of arms,’ a folk tradition reports.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar’; in German-speaking folklore this is an itinerant learned figure often credited with occult knowledge or magic, not merely an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: g'fahred Schüeler
notes.text: the Uri dialect form of fahrender Schüler, a wandering scholar or student-magician; the story implies uncanny knowledge of the road's future safety but does not explicitly call his statement a spell.

20ce639ebec02deb7c7d3c81e8021409d9b10d77.summary: On the Anarosa Alp in the Schams region, one finds a lake so small that a stone can be thrown across it from every side, yet it has an unfathomable depth and apparently an inflow but no outflow.

notes.label: Lai da Calandari
notes.text: the Romansh name of the small, bottomless ‘Lake of Calandari’ on the Anarosa Alp; the tale also calls it simply the lake, while preserving the local name connects its roaring, attraction, and hidden drainage to the Graubünden landscape.

d174839f2da0eb14cbb9fd29796b97f2b88e14ff.summary: 1. The Gotthard road was not always safe to travel.

notes.label: Kaiserspielries
notes.text: a Ries, or complete set of cards, for the traditional Swiss Kaiser game; the footnote explains that the count may be 48 in the version used here or 56 in an older form.

notes.label: Güetligaden
notes.text: the named Gaden beside the Gotthard road, a barn, hay store, livestock shelter, or farm outbuilding; its lower and upper levels structure both escape variants.

notes.label: Schallä-Joos
notes.text: a card-name used as a robber’s byname, referring to the Joos or jack-like figure of the Bells suit; the story explains his broken leg through the card image.

notes.label: Blass
notes.text: one of the robbers’ card-based names; the brief list does not establish which historical Kaiser-game card or nickname this form designates.

notes.label: Schiltä-Sü
notes.text: a card-name using Schilten, the Shields suit, and Sü, a traditional rank-name often associated with an ace or sow; exact rank terminology could vary by game and period.

notes.label: Mugg
notes.text: one of the robbers’ card-based names; the account gives no rank, suit, or etymology by which to identify it more narrowly.

notes.label: Gunten
notes.text: a deep pool or scour-hole in a river or stream; the robbers throw bodies into one in the roaring Reuss, where recovery would be difficult.

notes.label: Untergaden
notes.text: the lower or livestock level of a traditional Gaden; Hansli hides his horse there and later muffles its steps with coats and blankets.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper hay-storage level of a traditional Gaden; Hansli and Jost conceal themselves there beneath a plank or door.

notes.label: Schallä-Nyni
notes.text: the Nine of Bells in Swiss-German card terminology, offered as a variant of Schallä-Sü in Hansli’s deceptive answer.

notes.label: D'Schallä-Sü (ds Schallä-Nyni) müess üff ga tschodärä
notes.text: the exact Uri-dialect password-like excuse, ‘The Schallä-Sü (the Schallä-Nyni) has to get up to urinate’; Hansli exploits the robbers’ card names to pass as one of them.
notes.anchor: D'Schallä-Sü (ds Schallä-Nyni) müess üff ga tschodärä

notes.label: Bsetzi
notes.text: a paved or cobbled surface, here the hard yard or roadway across which Hansli lays cloth to silence his horse’s hooves.

notes.label: Der Hansli Metzger midem grossä Gäldgurt isch da, wenn-er eppis vonem wennt!
notes.text: Hansli’s exact Uri-dialect taunt, ‘Hansli Metzger with the great money belt is here, if you want anything from him’; he announces himself only as he escapes with the money.
notes.anchor: Der Hansli Metzger midem grossä Gäldgurt isch da, wenn-er eppis vonem wennt!

notes.label: Syg nu ä ganzä Stuck nachäg'hilpet
notes.text: the narrator’s dialect aside meaning that the injured Schallä-Joos still limped after the others for a considerable distance.
notes.anchor: Syg nu ä ganzä Stuck nachäg'hilpet

notes.label: Trämel
notes.text: a regional word for a log, beam, or heavy timber lying across the road; it trips Schiltä-Joos after Hansli cuts away the captured horse’s tail.

notes.label: Schiltä-Joos
notes.text: a card-name for a Joos or jack-like figure of the Shields suit; the legend explains the tail shown in the figure’s mouth as the horse’s severed tail.

notes.label: Ries
notes.text: a complete set or pack of cards and, by the tale’s extended wordplay, the entire robber band named after those cards.

notes.label: Ober
notes.text: a traditional Swiss-German playing-card court rank, comparable to an over or upper officer; one of the four Ober is to receive the captive girl as his wife.

notes.label: Krüsch
notes.text: chaff, bran, or fine milling refuse used here, like the alternate sawdust, to leave a visible trail to the hidden cave; the exact material is not specified more narrowly.

notes.label: Wellchessi
notes.text: a large rounded Alpine cheese-making cauldron; the cave entrance is compared to its circular shape, not identified as an actual dairy vessel.

notes.label: Fiddlä
notes.text: literally a dialect plural for backsides or buttocks, used idiomatically here for nerve or courage and explicitly glossed that way in the source.

notes.label: So jetz, wenn-er Fiddlä (d.h. Mut) hennt, sä cheemet!
notes.text: the besiegers’ exact dialect challenge, ‘Now then, if you have Fiddlä—that is, courage—come out’; Fiddlä literally evokes backsides but is explicitly glossed as nerve or courage.
notes.anchor: So jetz, wenn-er Fiddlä (d.h. Mut) hennt, sä cheemet!

notes.label: Ursner
notes.text: the regional demonym for people of the Ursern Valley; the story preserves a hostile old claim about their descent rather than establishing genealogy.

notes.label: Är heig nit mutz und nit cheus 'ta
notes.text: an obscure Uri-dialect formula saying Jost made neither movement nor sound—roughly, he did not make a peep—while hiding beneath the door.
notes.anchor: Är heig nit mutz und nit cheus 'ta

notes.label: D'Schallä-Sü müess üff ga brunzä
notes.text: Jost’s dialect version of the card-name excuse, ‘The Schallä-Sü has to get up to urinate,’ used to slip past the robbers.

notes.label: Schalläjos
notes.text: the unhyphenated verse form of Schallä-Joos, the card-name associated with the Bells suit and a jack-like figure.

notes.label: Schiltäsu
notes.text: the verse spelling of Schiltä-Sü, a Shields-suit card-name whose Sü rank is traditionally associated with an ace or sow.

notes.label: Eichläkeiser
notes.text: a card-name meaning the Kaiser of Acorns, one of the robbers called during the roll in Dr. Lusser’s verse.

notes.label: Rosäking
notes.text: a hybrid dialect card-name meaning the King of Roses, one of the robbers in the verse roll call.

notes.label: Schallädry
notes.text: the Three of Bells in Swiss-German card terminology, listed as a robber’s name in the verse.

notes.label: Schiltäjos
notes.text: the unhyphenated verse form of Schiltä-Joos, the Joos or jack-like figure of the Shields suit.

notes.label: Schellenjos
notes.text: a more standard-German spelling of the Bells Joos used in the verse’s escape cry, ‘Schellenjos rides on.’

6c1f22a1e92e358bc99871815328ad76b94d51e5.summary: On the bank of the Rhine below Rietheim stand the ruins of a mighty round tower from heathen times.

notes.label: Stüdler
notes.text: the name of Zurzach’s old, privileged guild of Rhine boatmen, responsible in the story for guiding freight through dangerous local rapids; it denotes a specific occupational body rather than boatmen in general.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a traditional shallow, flat-bottomed boat used on Swiss rivers, especially the Rhine; here the two spectral passengers step into the boatman’s working craft.

28e32d5a842bf6608f5badb4bc03986893db45ee.summary: In Grindelwald and elsewhere in the mountains of the Bernese Oberland, a ghostly mother sow often rages and makes a din at night.

notes.label: Rochelmoore
notes.text: the Bernese Oberland name used here for a noisy spectral mother sow or the porcine wild host associated with her; the creature's behavior is clear in context, but the name's exact dialect derivation is uncertain.

Content note: this 1910 source transmits an antisemitic Christian legend that collectively casts Jews as Christ-mockers and animalizes their children. The historical wording is translated for documentation and requires context if published; it is not endorsed here.

75291fb405defe54ef37f4015847c13f5521c634.summary: A man from the Bernese Oberland had set his sights on his Lieseli much too soon.

notes.label: Lieseli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive and familiar form of Elisabeth; its affectionate everyday tone contrasts with the remote enchanted rock maiden whom the young man fails to choose.

notes.label: untere Staffel
notes.text: the lower Staffel, one level or station within a tiered alpine grazing system; the spring there marks the young man's passage from ordinary pasture into the enchanted mountain.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: a stage, level, or pasture station within the vertical organization of an Alp; ringing the bell on every Staffel emphasizes the extent of his fruitless search.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial and practical seasonal movement of cattle and herders up to the high pastures; a decorated bell is an important part of that Alpine procession.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture and its working settlement, not merely a peak; the young man wanders through this pastoral landscape seeking the sealed rock.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

75860d2d1cde714570f2da6b85bafaa3ef5c1098.summary: At Gruobacher on Golzer in the Maderan Valley, a boy grew up wearing a Rock until he was 20 years old.

notes.label: Rock
notes.text: here a skirt-like garment worn by the boy rather than the English garment called a frock coat; its precise cut is not described.

notes.label: Trägi
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for one carried load or carrying trip, here a back-load of manure during farm work; the exact customary load size is not given.

notes.label: Grisskorb
notes.text: a large regional carrying basket used here for manure; the source establishes its function but not its material or exact capacity.

notes.label: Rockbub
notes.text: literally a ‘skirt boy,’ the tale’s name for a boy kept in a Rock, a skirt-like child’s garment, until the unusually late age of 20; the source does not explain the household custom behind the clothing.

71e9c48800d96048061bc24d25fe6f89b5ce6dba.summary: Up on Spissen above the Engstligental, a man stole a Tuehete, a rope-net bundle, of hay.

notes.label: Tuehete
notes.text: a Bernese Alpine rope net or netted bundle used to carry hay on steep ground; the source itself glosses it as a Seilnetz, and the stolen load becomes the thief’s identifying burden.

a300057af5ebaaf2a4f7f4f80e6dafb0b7790f5b.summary: The Rollibock is probably one of the oldest legends of Naters. It is said to have been a dreadful and powerful Bozo.

notes.label: Rollibock
notes.text: the horned, ice-covered monster of Naters whose rushing and ringing embody a catastrophic glacial flood; Bock means billy goat, while Rolli evokes its rumbling or rolling movement and sound.

notes.label: Bozo
notes.text: a Valais term for a frightening supernatural bogey, spirit, or monster; here it classifies the Rollibock as a dangerous being rather than an ordinary animal.

notes.label: Mörjelen-See
notes.text: the glacial lake at the Aletsch Glacier whose periodic drainage the commentary interprets through the Rollibock image.

notes.label: Massa-Chins
notes.text: the source's name for a fearsome constricted section or chasm in the Massa's glacial drainage route; the precise literal sense of Chins is not explained.

40e3a9679cb3b8b7af4ee56844d9757db04834f3.summary: An old man in Sax told me many years ago: “On a stormy, rainy day, a group of Roma asked me for shelter in my barn, which I granted out of compassion for the children.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

3c9e14dbd2a2d0fd942aaf1629ef7aa6487e050c.summary: a) Where the field is now called Neunthürmen, the amphitheater of Augusta, the great city of the Rauraci, stood in Roman times.

notes.label: About this telling
