91c5ca2da82b9388e7ebf8e57143d79700558c4e.summary: North of the present church in Wolfenschiessen, on the Plätzetürty and near the foot of the mountain, the place is still called Humligen.

notes.label: Plätzetürty
notes.text: a local field or district name at Wolfenschiessen; the source does not explain its component meanings.

notes.label: Humligen
notes.text: the traditional name of the buried settlement site north of the church.

notes.label: Hummligenbach
notes.text: the stream descending from the mountain at the site, preserving a slightly different spelling of the Humligen place-name; Bach means ‘brook’ or ‘stream.’

328361ccd2924cf10dbc9e3aab4bb0e7f84a9e91.summary: Hau is the name of the strip of woods on the right side of the road leading from Hägglingen to Wohlenschwil.

notes.label: Rosenkranzjungfer
notes.text: literally “Rosary maiden” or “Rosary virgin,” a female member of a Catholic lay devotional association; here the title becomes the name of a hypocritically pious woman’s ghost, and it does not mean a nun.

216bc7935260ec7e728384acab1ae465272687aa.summary: In Catholic regions, among other private church associations, there is also one of the Rosenkranzjungfern.

notes.label: Rosenkranzjungfern
notes.text: literally ‘Rosary virgins’ or ‘Rosary maidens,’ a Catholic lay association of fifteen village girls who process in special dress with candles representing Mary’s fifteen mysteries and undertake particular prayers; the source does not give the group’s formal statutes.

notes.label: Rosenkranztochter
notes.text: literally ‘Rosary daughter,’ the local name transferred from the girls’ association to a female spirit near Nesselnbach; her clothing suggests a maiden member, while the measuring rod implies an unatoned commercial fraud, and the link between those identities is only conjectured.

notes.label: Fraufastenmittwochen
notes.text: literally the Wednesdays of a women’s or Marian fast, the nights on which the spirit appears; the exact regional observance and its position in the liturgical calendar are not explained.

notes.label: Spenzer
notes.text: a fitted short jacket or bodice belonging to regional women’s dress; the apparition appears without one, but the source does not describe the normal garment’s cut or material.

notes.label: Schäppeli
notes.text: a small ceremonial maiden’s or bridal headpiece decorated here with movable gold and silver spangles; it marks local festive status, although its exact construction is not specified.

notes.label: Ellenstecken
notes.text: an ell measuring stick used by cloth dealers, based on the locally variable ell; the spirit’s rod suggests she cheated customers with a short measure, but no one has asked her and the accusation remains a supposition.

eafd707c3c7366d045e81cc0be7b8b046e8594ed.summary: The Rossheiri once dwelled on the so-called Siggenberg opposite the Geissberg.

notes.label: Rossheiri
notes.text: the local name of the spectral carter; Ross means horse and Heiri is a Swiss familiar form of Heinrich, roughly “Horse-Heiri,” but the tale treats the compound as a proper name rather than identifying a known historical person.

notes.label: Geisterstein
notes.text: literally “spirits’ stone” or “ghost stone,” the local boulder where the Rossheiri’s noise is strongest and the region’s spirits assemble.

0dfe7ef0b991c4f93889344dbd0eef011a13830b.summary: On sultry autumn days, and likewise in the middle of winter, a sudden roar of cannon fire sometimes arises, and in perfectly still air the sound is carried as far as our peaceable town of Aarau.

notes.label: Sonderbund War
notes.text: Switzerland’s short civil war of 1847 between the federal forces and the Catholic cantons of the Sonderbund; the English name retains Sonderbund because it was the alliance’s historical name.

notes.label: Rothenburger Geschütz
notes.text: literally the “Rothenburg artillery” or “Rothenburg gun,” the regional name for mysterious cannon-like sounds in the air; in the story it foretells war or prolonged bad weather rather than referring to a physical cannon.

fd16bbdc583db890a4f3586e4e75c298169c2976.summary: A fugitive from distant lands came to Thalheim in the Jura and bought Castelen Castle behind the Gislifluh, where he lived in complete seclusion with only a manservant and a maid.

notes.label: Gislifluh
notes.text: the prominent Jura ridge behind which Castelen lies; Fluh denotes a steep rock face or crag.

notes.label: De näm' i ned ewegg!
notes.text: Aargau dialect meaning ‘I would not take that away!’ or ‘I won't carry that off,’ the farmer's contemptuous refusal of the uncanny cloth.

notes.label: Tüchlein
notes.text: a diminutive for a small cloth or handkerchief; its repetition emphasizes the object's deceptively harmless appearance.

notes.label: Rothes Tüchlein
notes.text: historical spelling for ‘red little cloth,’ the repeatedly appearing handkerchief associated with the dead murderer's haunting.

24b874274f97572321570eebf983dc6e5a10f4ca.summary: Not far from Gersau lies a piece of rock that, because of its shape and color, is called ‘Rotschuo,’ the red shoe, by the local people.

notes.label: Rotschuo
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘red shoe’; the local Gersau name of the red, shoe-shaped rock understood in the legend as a petrified murder relic.

e8fabbdb03957fe41ff9aefa9eb0aad8b8880883.summary: In the lower Vorderland beyond the mountains of the Oberland, the air commonly resounds with strange roaring and cracking in high summer and harvest time.

notes.label: Rottalherren
notes.text: literally ‘lords of the Rottal,’ the cursed tyrants whose drilling, drumming, and howling are heard as unexplained clear-sky noises.

notes.label: Murtengeschütz
notes.text: literally ‘Murten artillery,’ the Bernese Seeland name for the same distant booming in clear weather.

notes.label: Blümlisalp
notes.text: literally a ‘flower Alp,’ here describing the Rottal's former beauty before rock and ice transformed it; it also echoes the regional mountain name Blüemlisalp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and pastoral landscape, where the supernatural goat defends the shepherd girl.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Firnen
notes.text: old compacted snowfields or firn ice on high mountains, imagined trembling when the valley is destroyed.

notes.label: ungetreue Boden
notes.text: literally ‘the faithless ground,’ the blood-reddened place-name memorializing the younger brother's treacherous murder.

2fd1e25c8ef16f320062b1444f46641b203fe40e.summary: Arx Dominorum de saxo, in French le château du rocher, commonly called Supersaxo because it was built upon rock—from which the Supersaxo family, formerly Michlig, took its name—was once the summer residence of the bishops of Valais.

notes.label: Flue
notes.text: this Swiss form denotes a cliff or prominent rock and here belongs to the castle’s local name in Naters; the exact rock feature intended by the historical name is uncertain.

ef8738728811da20c550337832319ef1ceb1c032.summary: The part of the forest nearest Bendel is called Runggel. The Runggelfräuli once lived there.

notes.label: Runggelfräuli
notes.text: literally ‘little woman of Runggel,’ the diminutive place-based name for the spectral washerwoman haunting the nearby forest.

notes.label: Sechtlein
notes.text: a small piece or batch of laundry that the thieving washerwoman must repeatedly wash as penance; the precise textile meant is uncertain.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally ‘Sunday child,’ a person born on Sunday and traditionally believed able to perceive spirits or hidden supernatural things.

5a4aa445be2e1efd9b90de8d110eb80c4ec24869.summary: In a valley of the Bernese Oberland stands a tall old tree whose crown, on beautiful moonlit nights when not a breath of air stirs around it, begins to sound and rustle as though a violent storm were passing through its branches.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; here the jealous killer is identified by this Alpine livelihood, but his exact job is not stated.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kiltgang
notes.text: the traditional Swiss nighttime courtship visit in which a young man went to see a young woman, often under locally regulated customs; here the rival is killed while returning from such a visit, though the tale gives no details of the local practice.

08aec60659046bd0d44928e4a5df6f3aecb8ebae.summary: On a lush green alpine pasture, a Senn once eked out a living with his family.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman who tends cattle and traditionally makes cheese on a high summer pasture; the role combines herdsman, milker, and cheesemaker, so no single English job title is exact.

f2db24387d754b2c27a33d83545c3f528f2e312a.summary: The owners of the Mädems Alp once had a boundary dispute with the people of Flums.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Ziel und March
notes.text: literally ‘boundary and boundary-mark,’ a traditional legal formula for the correct territorial limit.

notes.label: Wagenlochhund
notes.text: literally ‘Wagenloch dog,’ the fiery-eyed black canine apparition associated with an abandoned unbaptized child.

notes.label: Röllsutt
notes.text: a local name for the dark rocky woodland stretch by the Röll through which the uncanny host passes; Sutt may suggest wet or hollow ground, but its exact local sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Gräggi
notes.text: the local name of a noisy supernatural procession identified by the collector with Wotan’s Wild Hunt; the etymology is not supplied.

415197e2e022fc4a7f9fae6b6d89f6af76edb7c9.summary: a) Behind the chapel at Fernigen in the Meien Valley, which is dedicated to Saint John of Nepomuk, a Rübi once came roaring and rushing down.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a violent debris-laden mountain torrent or flow; here it is a personified destructive force ridden and driven by witches whose power is stopped by chapel bells, while the exact mixture of water, earth, and rock is not specified.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Luisä zich!
notes.text: the rear witch’s Uri dialect command, rendered approximately as ‘Luisa, pull!’; zich is an imperative of pulling or drawing, while the exact identity and spelling of the addressed name remain regional.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

052ca2b72f0e454ee7fe1649bfd1a8bb60ec7608.summary: A Rübi had shattered the parish church at Schattdorf. The people now wanted to build it farther down, in Bommatters Matte (or on the Spillmatt), but each night their work was miraculously undone, and every morning the tools, wood, and stones were found back at the old site.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri regional name for a violent debris-laden mountain torrent or flood surge; here it is a personified destructive force whose course can be halted by church bells.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Rübizug
notes.text: the gully or established track down which a Rübi rushes; the compound describes the hazard's channel rather than another supernatural being.

notes.label: Vreni
notes.text: a familiar Swiss form of Verena; the voice appears to use it for the one whose bell-ringing ‘screamed’ and stopped the torrent, but the brief account does not establish whether Vreni names a person, a bell, or a personified sound.

7217409ff39912e6f513be1564ba0fda2d6aaed3.summary: A mighty Rübi rolled down through the Wylertal opposite Silenen and threatened the surrounding region with destruction.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow or torrent carrying earth, stones, and water down a slope; its motion is magically linked here to the witches’ spinning and winding.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Vrenäli
notes.text: the affectionate diminutive name given here to Silenen’s weather bell, whose ‘crying’ stops the witches; the source does not explain whether the name formally refers to Saint Verena.

06f981bd2e7047da5d5aeaa2dd8a93fdcf85320c.summary: When one travels over the high Bernina mountain pass toward Puschlav, one comes, on the southern slope of the mountain not far above Pischiadello, to a place where in ancient times—a time of which no chronicle gives any account—there stood a little village named Zarera.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a mountain debris flow, the torrent carrying it, or the channel it cuts; here the word is also the place name for the site of Zarera, so its landform and disaster senses overlap.

056ecbc4ec1bdd3cd60afbfe03bc48d7028f16ad.summary: More than a hundred years ago, the village of Lenz was buried by a Rüfe. At the same time, high above the village in the mountains where the Rüfe broke loose, there lived a witch—a Tobel-Ungeheuer, or Rüfe-Butz.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term for a debris flow, the torrent carrying it, or the channel it cuts; the tale personifies the destructive flow as something the witch can berate and persuade.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge; here the plural landscape features echo with the witch’s quarrel.

notes.label: Tobel-Ungeheuer
notes.text: literally a “ravine monster”; Tobel is a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge, and the parenthetical uses this compound as one classification of the Rüfe Witch.

notes.label: Rüfe-Butz
notes.text: literally a “Rüfe bogey” or frightening spirit of a debris flow; the source offers it as another name for the witchlike ravine being, without distinguishing the forms more precisely.

125d4a62025560dceace4dc3ba2d34b579abc6a9.summary: From the wild Sulzbach at Spiringen to the forest-rich Brunni Valley in Unterschächen, an unbroken and magnificent fir forest once extended.

notes.label: Rüttinossen
notes.text: the local name for the crumbling rock spur, mountainside, or mass that collapses during the forest dispute; the narrative identifies a major rockfall but does not define the landform closely enough to choose one exact English geomorphological term.

c26f645fee4205edab0afb9c04d4a2cad93935e2.summary: Many years ago there lived in Ems a rich farmer who could not call a single virtue that otherwise adorns a person his own.

notes.label: Maisäss
notes.text: a seasonal pasture holding and its buildings between the valley farm and the high summer Alp; the farmer’s woodland holding is at Piz-Okul.

notes.label: mo, il giavel vul nuot saver da mei, el po buca tier
notes.text: the Romansh defiance that Jecklin translates as “the Devil wants nothing from me; he cannot come near me”; the original spelling is preserved.
notes.anchor: mo, il giavel vul nuot saver da mei, el po buca tier

notes.label: Maysässe
notes.text: the historical and inflected spelling used later for the same kind of seasonal pasture holding called Maisäss in the preceding paragraph.

163044a69735c532fe7abc63c49982bbf578804e.summary: On the footpath from Wegenstetten to Wittnau, two villages in the Fricktal, there once stood a solitary old pine high on the mountain.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: a historical small-denomination coin used in German-speaking Central Europe, including Swiss territories; its value varied by period and place, so no single modern English coin is equivalent.

notes.label: Heidenschopen
notes.text: a regional garment name for the long red upper garment formerly worn by older Black Forest women in this account; ‘heathen smock’ or ‘heathen jacket’ is the nearest literal rendering, but the precise cut and the force of the name are uncertain.

307aa6b9d346ed2bf02546ecef4cb83b535f3c03.summary: There are often parents who do not agree with their children when the latter wish to marry.

notes.label: Heumonat
notes.text: literally ‘hay month,’ this traditional German and Swiss month-name denotes July in the dated Valais account; calendar usage could vary historically, though July is the likely meaning here.

2aea812131cb2f257aa4f13a220dc2023195df1e.summary: Once, in the small Valais capital of Sion, a saintly bishop named Saint Jodern, or Theodor, lived in his lofty Tourbillon Castle.

8ccfd740b17c2e49c6bc106b3b28a6f2ce9f54da.summary: The uppermost valley of the Siebne, or Simme, was still a sparsely settled forest valley.

notes.label: Siebne
notes.text: an older local name for the Simme river and its valley; the source gives both forms to locate the future village of St. Stephan.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘pagans’ or ‘heathens,’ the Christian source's retrospective label for the valley's pre-Christian inhabitants; it should not be read as a neutral ethnic name.

072bbece60a804258c6fac41aa712af50f606901.summary: Flühli and Sörenberg once belonged to a lord who had people dig for gold and treasure on this estate of his.

notes.label: Deichel
notes.text: a hollowed wooden conduit pipe used to carry water, imagined here as being made of gold and protected from hostile magic; spellings and construction traditions vary regionally.

notes.label: Dünkel
notes.text: a regional variant name for the same kind of wooden water pipe; the source places it in quotation marks as the popular term, and its form varies across Alemannic dialects.

ebf0c44cf1d0f7fabe06125a39c144ba5468580b.summary: Good-natured dwarfs had revealed a salt spring to the Küher at Sortel, with the instruction never to draw more than one day's supply at a time.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or dairyman responsible for cattle on an Alpine pasture; the occupation includes the seasonal mountain-dairy setting implied by the tale.

notes.label: Sortelküher
notes.text: the compound ‘Sortel cowherd,’ identifying the Küher attached to the Sortel pasture or holding rather than a surname.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who tend cattle and make dairy products during the mountain-pasture season.

229ca3244a8340ead3817bdd1aa2859a6ce5d5e6.summary: Kindly dwarfs had revealed a salt spring to the Küher in the Sortel, an alp in the Stockhorn range, with the instruction that he should never draw more than one day's supply at a time.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: an Alpine cattleman responsible for cows and dairy work on a seasonal alp; the role is more specific than a general cowherd and is central to the economy described in the tale.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who live and work on seasonal high pastures; the first Küher shares the salt spring with these neighboring workers.

883afc4083ffcc5bc2828844580590ebf0b8bf3b.summary: At the foot of the Mutterschwandenberg in the Eichi, half an hour from Alpnach, a salt spring is said once to have flowed.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f95cb9df39bcaad2cfb19ae3175e069cfd094f14.summary: The Salwidenbad in the Entlebuch, between Sörenberg and Schibegütsch, had the following origin.

notes.label: Salwidenbad
notes.text: the name of a healing-spring bath in the Entlebuch; Bad here denotes a spa or bathing place rather than an ordinary bathroom, while the tale explains the spring's rediscovery.

f7298b07865336c5fbb10bf61bfeec26399ef385.summary: Strange things had long been happening on a certain Alp. Whenever the Senn began to erwellen, an invisible being entered the hut and helped him kindle the fire, pour milk into the Chessi, separate the curds, lift out the cheese, and zigern—make Ziger.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, huts, grazing rights, and dairy-working landscape.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or herder responsible for livestock, milk work, and cheese making on a seasonal Alp.

notes.label: erwellen
notes.text: a regional dairying verb for beginning or carrying forward a stage of Alpine cheese making; the source’s following task list supplies the practical context but not a single exact modern process equivalent.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a Swiss German form of Kessel, the large cauldron in which Alpine milk is heated for cheese making.

notes.label: zigern
notes.text: to make Ziger, the traditional Swiss whey cheese produced from whey left after ordinary cheese making.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male workers on a seasonal Alp who assist with livestock and dairy work beneath the senior Senn.

notes.label: Meisterknecht
notes.text: the senior or master farmhand entrusted with leading the work while remaining a hired servant.

notes.label: Alpgeist
notes.text: literally the spirit of the Alp, a supernatural being bound to a seasonal pasture through wrongdoing or unfinished obligations.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: property boundary marks or boundary lines, not fairy tales; moving them unlawfully creates a debt that binds the dead owner to the Alp.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land whose members possess shared use rights; the dead owner stole from it by shifting his private boundaries outward.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

ae42eb3654bf6b54e91047eafc1b04b20eec8c60.summary: At the sand pit on the western slope of the Frickberg, in the days when cattle were still driven out to pasture, a man appeared who resembled a cattle dealer, for he carried a whip slung over his shoulder and drove the cattle away.

notes.label: Weidbuben
notes.text: pasture boys or young herders charged with watching grazing livestock; they are the witnesses who describe the spirit’s transformation into a gigantic horse.

e251fc3cdea2b9213b146bbef4139fdd8da078b2.summary: When boys go to gather firewood among the bushes along the Rhine and one happens to step on a thorn, he says that the Sandheri pricked him, and the injured boy leaves the place.

notes.label: Sandheri
notes.text: the local name of a restless male spirit in the Rhine floodplain who is blamed when a thorn pricks a boy; Sand suggests the riverbank terrain and Heri can denote a little gentleman or man, but the name's precise formation is uncertain.

59a3caa07fca245fcac82d325232c29b91d2fa3f.summary: Where the Sardona Glacier now spreads its enormous masses of ice, the finest Alp for miles around once bloomed and grew green.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its dairying and livestock use, not simply any Alpine mountain; the tale explains the loss of the once-fertile pasture beneath the glacier.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and dairy production on a seasonal Alp; here the office also identifies the widow’s son by his livelihood.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the Alpine hut that houses dairy work and often the Senn and other herders, not merely a generic mountain cabin; the new hut symbolizes the son’s prosperity.

notes.label: Hundli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning “little dog” or “dear dog”; here it affectionately names Parvi in the rhymed cry, although Parvi’s identity beyond being the Senn’s dog is unstated.

notes.label: Schätzli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning “sweetheart” or “little treasure”; here it names Kathri affectionately in the ghostly rhyme, despite the narrator’s moral condemnation of her.

2ec862564b840923a400c7134f776a66047a649d.summary: 1. a) Several people from Schattdorf went to the house in the lower Hof to play for a bowl of cream.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: an Uri regional, often disparaging name for an old woman or uncanny female figure; the two Halbenstein accounts do not determine whether she is human, witch-like, or a ghost.

notes.label: Rystätunggeli
notes.text: the local name assigned to the Halbenstein ghost in one version; Tunggeli is a diminutive spirit-name, but the derivation of Rystät and the apparition's precise class are uncertain.

notes.label: Wäuti
notes.text: an Uri name for an uncanny being or nocturnal bogey; it wrestles with the bread-carrier, but the narrator cannot even determine whether its form is male or female.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent Alpine downslope wind; communities historically kept special fire watches during Föhn conditions because fire could spread rapidly, and the narrator is serving such a watch.

e62be3dce94e2cd271abc36d7e35234deea73671.summary: Wolf von Ringgenberg, whom his subjects called the Wehrwolf, was a cruel and merciless territorial lord.

notes.label: Wehrwolf
notes.text: the subjects’ punning or ominous byname for Wolf von Ringgenberg; it resembles Werwolf, ‘werewolf,’ while Wehr can suggest arms or defense, and the text does not claim a literal transformation.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive or tyrannical lord who subjugates others; it describes Wolf’s oppressive rule.

notes.label: Schadenburg
notes.text: literally ‘harm castle’ or ‘castle of damage,’ the cruel lord’s proposed boastful name for his new fortress.

notes.label: Freiburg
notes.text: literally ‘free castle,’ the avenging fisherman’s counter-name, contrasting freedom with Schadenburg and the Zwingherr’s oppression.

1e37c9361924cd3374f68a6b6a6f502c382a4a1d.summary: Not long ago, Castelen Castle in the Aargau Jura was still a state estate productive in grain and wine.

notes.label: Schaffner
notes.text: here the manager or steward responsible for administering a large agricultural and wine-producing estate, not a modern railway conductor; the tale blames successive Schaffner for the domain’s decline but does not specify their financial or labor duties.

notes.label: Thier in den Nüschelen
notes.text: literally the ‘beast in the Nüschelen,’ a locally familiar creature or apparition whose cries people mistake for the dying Schaffner’s; the passage assumes the name is known and gives no description of either the beast or the place-name Nüschelen.

97fbdf2c5345362930e898b015e940c41f03ad5d.summary: The legend tells us remarkable things about the former size and ancient power of this glacier.

notes.label: Gletscherrüfen
notes.text: glacier-associated Rüfen—steep gullies, debris channels, or scars left by torrents and mass movement; the word points to visible evidence of the glacier’s former reach, but the source does not distinguish each landform geologically.

notes.label: After-Sant-Jodrutag
notes.text: a locally named observance associated with the day following or after-feast of Saint Jodru or Jodern; the source says it was to be kept like the saint’s holy day but gives neither a calendar date nor a fuller explanation of After.

notes.label: verwahrte Person
notes.text: literally a ‘protected’ or ‘properly safeguarded person,’ probably someone ritually or spiritually prepared to represent each household in the fasting procession; the source does not state what sacrament, blessing, or qualification made the person verwahrt.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Abbüssung
notes.text: the serving or working off of expiatory penance; the glacier is imagined as a purgatorial space where poor souls atone, rather than merely as a place of earthly punishment.

notes.label: Temperkinder
notes.text: children or people believed to have been born during Ember times and therefore able to perceive spirits and hidden phenomena; the associated birth dates and visionary gifts vary regionally.

bc5f56cb57fe33b68d869e64c2e6bafcde30ab99.summary: Near the Fidriser-Au, beside the footpath to the village of Jenatz, stands a small house where, for many years, a gigantic maiden was seen at night, silently floating about in a white dress, with a pale face and loose dark hair.

notes.label: Schanänna-Jungfrau
notes.text: the local name of the gigantic white-clad maiden haunting the Fidriser-Au and Strahlegg; Jungfrau means ‘maiden,’ while the source gives no secure derivation for Schanänna.

notes.label: Sonntagskinder
notes.text: literally ‘Sunday children,’ people born on a Sunday who in German-speaking folk belief possess second sight or can perceive supernatural beings hidden from ordinary people; the term does not merely mean fortunate children.

notes.label: Schanänn-Jungfrau
notes.text: the title’s exact local spelling of the maiden’s name; the narrative uses the closely related form Schanänna-Jungfrau, and the source does not explain the variation.

5a2040f358c4c4054e2264281c8a94a717140885.summary: In Romoos in the Entlebuch, an old man told it to his sons, and I have it from one of them.

notes.label: Enzefluh
notes.text: the local rock face or crag in which the daughter is banished, with Fluh meaning a steep cliff; its first element and exact location within Romooser-Enzi are not explained.

notes.label: Schrattenjungfrau
notes.text: literally the “Schratten maiden,” a supernatural cave maiden associated here with Saturday appearances and changing weather; whether she is the same being as the Schatzjungfrau or a parallel local figure remains ambiguous.

notes.label: Schatzjungfrau
notes.text: literally “treasure maiden,” a supernatural young woman banished into a mountain or cave to guard wealth and often awaiting release; here she also produces storms, while the tale does not say how she might be redeemed.

84a2ae279692babc7173c1668e5dc395be40fbdd.summary: According to the legend, whenever a stone was thrown into the Scheibenloch on the Hirswängiberg or the Schrattenfluh, a thunderstorm arose.

notes.label: Scheibenloch
notes.text: the local name of the mountain hole or opening on the Hirswängiberg or Schrattenfluh; disturbing it with a thrown stone is believed to call up a thunderstorm.

c20b47ebc2372f9056c9ae5d632b79920e554e76.summary: In the Hard behind Birsfelden, on the chain of hills extending behind the two Gundeldingen and Binningen toward Bruderholz, and in Bruderholz itself, a man is often seen riding about on a large white horse, which is why he is called the Schimmelreiter.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally ‘rider on a white or gray horse,’ the local name for this spectral horseman around Basel; Schimmel means the horse's color here, not mold, and accounts differ on whether the rider is headless.

7346c0597199d0321fe35acfa33c6b44b868eda4.summary: Between Rickenbach and Ellikon lies a small wood through which a road runs.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a German horse-color term for a gray horse whose coat often appears white; the source redundantly calls it a ‘white Schimmel,’ emphasizing the uncanny mount's pale appearance.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally a ‘Schimmel rider,’ a rider mounted on a gray or white horse; here it names the headless mounted apparition haunting the road between Rickenbach and Ellikon.

caadf42998d431c4422a71b8fed8a39ebbe19b12.summary: It now also comes to mind how once several men had gathered and gone to dig for money out by the Salibrunnä.

notes.label: Salibrunnä
notes.text: the Oberhofen dialect form of Salibrunnen, the named mountain spring associated with treasure and Erdmännlein; the name’s first element is not explained.

notes.label: schûflä
notes.text: Oberhofen dialect plural for shovels; these treasure-digging tools fall back underground with the trough.

notes.label: chärst
notes.text: Oberhofen dialect plural or collective form for Karst digging tools, such as mattocks, hoes, or picks; their exact form is not specified.

notes.label: zipperlî
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for gout or painful gout-like trouble in the feet; it explains why the priest commonly rides instead of walking.

notes.label: I will's halb, i will's halb!
notes.text: dialect for ‘I want half, I want half!’; the unexplained rider’s demand leads a digger to break the required silence.
notes.anchor: I will's halb, i will's halb!

notes.label: de sakermentspaff
notes.text: a strongly insulting dialect expression for ‘the damned priest’ or ‘sacrament priest’; the blasphemous outburst is part of the speech that ruins the treasure recovery.

notes.label: drei schuehnä
notes.text: dialect for three Schuh, historical foot-like units whose exact local length varied; the deceased informant supposedly could locate the treasure within that distance.

notes.label: Erdmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ subterranean dwarf-like beings regarded as owners of the Salibrunnen and its disappearing pewter vessels; their role in the buried trough episode is implied rather than shown.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: a rider upon a Schimmel, a white or gray horse; the diggers mistake the approaching figure for the priest, and the tale later establishes that neither priest nor horse was physically there.

6ba740463555edcc6eb5054c183b2e83c027dbf3.summary: A butcher in Bern was named Henzi. Because he treated animals not as a slaughterer but as a knacker, he was given the name Schlachthäusi (Henzi).

notes.label: Schlachthäusi
notes.text: the cruel Bern butcher’s punning byname, blending the sound of Schlachthaus, “slaughterhouse,” with a personal-name form related here to Henzi; its exact historical nickname formation is uncertain.

notes.label: Metzgtier
notes.text: literally “slaughtering” or “butchery animal,” a regional name for a monstrous revenant associated with a cruel butcher; in Zurzach it is mentioned as a parallel creature without further description.

984506b67ef3de5183db9bdaa5968c6e3d751bb8.summary: From the village of Dottikon in the Freienamte, on the right side of the road leading to Othmarsingen and this side of the Steinhof, lies the so-called Hendschiker vineyard hill.

notes.label: Freienamte
notes.text: the historical inflected form used here for the Freiamt region of Aargau; Freiamt means ‘free bailiwick’ or ‘free district’ and identifies a particular Swiss region rather than a generic free office.

notes.label: Jucharten
notes.text: plural of Juchart, a traditional Swiss measure of land based on the area that could be plowed in a day; its exact size varied by region and period.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: communal land held or used collectively by a village community, comparable to a common; its cultivation and access were governed by local rights rather than ordinary individual ownership.

notes.label: Hungerbühl
notes.text: literally ‘hunger hill,’ the local name of the poor, formerly wooded tract; Hunger suggests its meager productivity, while Bühl is an older word for a hill.

notes.label: Schlangenbanner
notes.text: literally a ‘snake binder’ or one who magically commands snakes, a practitioner able to summon, banish, or render serpents harmless; Banner here comes from bannen, ‘to bind or exorcise,’ not from the English word banner.

494b7b8f4e8981a2c538eaf1cdae4ff03febd7c9.summary: On the south side of the Madriserhorn, the Saas Alp spreads out with its beautiful pastures.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the Saas Alp’s productivity and danger are central to the story.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Prätigau
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Prättigau, the Graubünden valley containing Saas and its Alp.

notes.label: Bündnerland
notes.text: a historical German name for the lands of Graubünden.

notes.label: Savien
notes.text: the historical spelling used by the source for Safien; Camana is named as the sole Graubünden Alp comparable to Saas.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: in German-language legend, a wandering scholar credited with learned or occult powers; here he performs the snake-binding ritual.

notes.label: fünfe
notes.text: literally ‘five’; being able to count beyond five is an ironic idiom for unusual cleverness or secret knowledge.

notes.label: Heer-Kuh
notes.text: the source’s name for the best or leading cow on an Alp, not a military animal; its death prompts the villagers to accept the stranger’s help.

notes.label: Schreier-Bach
notes.text: literally ‘Screamer Brook,’ the place-name the legend derives from the Schlangenbanner’s fatal cries.

notes.label: Schlangenbanner
notes.text: a person believed able to banish, bind, or magically compel snakes; here the wandering scholar performs the rite but is killed by the crowned white snakes.

1db542542742e13ebc3ad625bbd0fc7987edcaa3.summary: Opposite the mill in Rued, on the other side of the road, stands the noble family’s granary.

notes.label: Kernenmesser
notes.text: literally a ‘grain measurer,’ an appointed servant who measured grain received and issued from a granary; here Niggeli cheats by using unequal measures, though the formal status of his post is not described.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: literally a ‘quarter,’ here a regional dry measure for grain rather than simply one fourth in the abstract; the story contrasts a large receiving Viertel with a small issuing Viertel but gives no standardized capacity.

notes.label: Metzenkübel
notes.text: a large tub or bucket used as a grain measure, combining Metzen, a variable historical dry measure, with Kübel, a tub; its exact local volume is unspecified.

notes.label: Viertelsstreicher
notes.text: the straightedge used to strike grain level across the top of a Viertel measure; its rattling belongs to the ghost’s reenactment of his dishonest trade, though the object’s precise form is not given.

notes.label: Schloss-Niggel
notes.text: literally ‘castle Niggel,’ the local haunting name attached to the Rued granary and its former servant or lord; the tale alternates between Niggeli and Niggel and ultimately notes that Niggel is also a regional horse name, leaving the spirit’s identity deliberately unsettled.

f83793df541f4b572fbc1de6ea526cceb8a77833.summary: Gösgen is a Solothurn village on the left bank of the Aare, an hour upstream from Aarau.

notes.label: Steckhof
notes.text: an isolated outlying farmstead apart from the clustered village, sometimes carrying a distinct historical legal status; the Hagnau Steckhof lies across the Aare from the castle ruin.

notes.label: Schlossgrün
notes.text: literally something like ‘castle-green,’ the local name of Hagnau’s spectral castle lord; the legend links the name to his entirely green clothing rather than supplying an ordinary English creature category.

notes.label: Eicher-Almende
notes.text: the common land associated with Eich; Almende is an older form of Allmend, communally held village land rather than private property.

notes.label: Kornmetzen
notes.text: a grain measure or vessel based on the historical Metze dry measure, whose volume varied by locality; the comparison describes the witness’s grotesquely swollen head without fixing a modern size.

notes.label: Grundruhr
notes.text: a local riparian salvage claim, explained in the tale through the Strandrecht—the asserted right to take objects washed ashore by the river; the precise historical legal scope is not established here.

notes.label: Schachen
notes.text: low, often brushy or wooded land beside a river; here it identifies the raftsmen’s settlement area along the Aare.

d5e29b16f860fd66d3bee026b6ae6e9eb061853f.summary: On the right bank of the stream in the village of Wölflinswil in the upper Fricktal stands a narrow three-story stone house built against the mountainside, with a steep roof and stepped gables like an old bailiff's house.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: a young man making a traditional nighttime courtship visit, often climbing to or visiting a woman's window or household.

notes.label: Nachtbube
notes.text: literally ‘night lad,’ a young man roaming after dark for mischief rather than courtship.

notes.label: Schloßjungfrau
notes.text: the older-spelling variant ‘castle maiden’ used in the body for the same revenant called Schlossjungferin in the title.

notes.label: nit, nit! die zwo Schlange bißet!
notes.text: regional speech meaning ‘no, no, the two snakes are biting!’; the frightened father mistakes the maiden's long braids for serpents and ruins the rescue.
notes.anchor: nit, nit! die zwo Schlange bißet!

notes.label: Sägbaum
notes.text: a tree trunk grown thick enough to be useful as saw timber; only when the cherry reaches that size can it become the destined cradle.

notes.label: Schlossjungferin
notes.text: literally ‘castle maiden,’ the title's regional form for the proud dead daughter whose release depends on a human carrying ritual.

a6b666634b14d34cc95630c0c0017cd475d40077.summary: Wirlingen Castle on the Baden Upper Rhine has long since fallen into ruin, and forest trees grow upon its rubble.

notes.label: Schlosstanne
notes.text: literally ‘castle fir,’ the particular fir tree at the Wirlingen ruin to which the white maiden's fate was bound and whose wood became the child's cradle.

fdb4b43071f08e21a7f889ca7c1df0dbec763f0f.summary: A height at the southwestern end of the little village of Sulz in the Fricktal, on Aargau’s bank of the Rhine, is called the Schlössli.

notes.label: Schlössli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive meaning a small castle, manor, or castle-like house; here it names both the height and the successive houses built there, without proving that either was literally fortified.

notes.label: Schlösslibauer
notes.text: literally the “farmer of the Schlössli,” the local name or designation of the sorcerous landholder; Bauer identifies him as a farmer, while Schlössli ties him to the named house and hill.

notes.label: Banner
notes.text: in this folkloric context, a practitioner who binds, bans, or drives off supernatural powers by formulas; it does not mean a flag-bearer, and its exact distinction from the tale’s broader “sorcerer” is not defined.

5c2731ee758e77633de032eb3b9bad82d44a0d41.summary: According to legend, an old castle woman dwells among the remains of the old castle at Mayenfeld, which formerly belonged to the Barons of Brandis.

notes.label: Mayenfeld
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Maienfeld in Graubünden, the location of the ruined castle.

notes.label: Schlüsselfrau
notes.text: literally “key woman,” the supernatural castle woman whose many rattling keys secure hidden treasures; her frightening underground presence contrasts with her enchanting midnight song.

83d31fbe6361334973c3619c886beb321a294fa7.summary: Once, a shepherd boy lived below the castle ruin that stands high above the village of Tegerfelden and looks far out over the valleys of Aargau.

notes.label: Maienbutter
notes.text: literally ‘May butter,’ fresh spring butter that melts readily in the sun; the rural comparison means that the farmer's trout sell extremely quickly.

notes.label: Pfaffenkäppchenbaum
notes.text: literally ‘little priest's-cap tree,’ a traditional name for the spindle tree, whose cap-shaped fruit suggests the name; its ritually cut and seasoned wood is supposed to make the redeemer's cradle.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a ‘Sunday child,’ someone born on a Sunday and traditionally believed to possess special luck, second sight, or power to encounter and redeem supernatural beings.

notes.label: Berchtoldstag
notes.text: Berchtold's Day, a Swiss New Year holiday observed on January second; the public dancing and merriment provide the setting in which the outsider seeks a supernatural dance partner.

notes.label: Wäldler
notes.text: here a dismissive name for a person from the Black Forest, marking the miller's servant as a poor outsider whom the local girls refuse to dance with.

notes.label: Schwegelpfeifchen
notes.text: a little Schwegel or simple end-blown flute or pipe; the maiden's silver instrument enchants the listener and summons the animals of field and forest.

notes.label: Erlenhonig
notes.text: literally ‘alder honey,’ the sweet or sticky honeydew-like substance gathered from alder branches; the maiden uses it as a dressing upon the crown of her golden hair.

notes.label: O Erli, liebi Erli!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘O little alder, dear little alder!’ and the opening of the maiden's song; her hair must grow for another hundred years before she can rest, while the alder will then go to the stove as firewood.

notes.label: Schlüsseljungfrau
notes.text: literally ‘key maiden,’ an enchanted castle or treasure maiden identified by the bundle of keys she carries; she needs a courageous human helper to complete the trials that will release her and the dead under her care.

559b0c9f7bfd5b427502e4a638be75b30cf49f35.summary: The road from the Aargau village of Tegerfelden to the neighboring market town of Zurzach on the Swiss bank of the Rhine crosses wooded foothills of the Jura and passes an isolated rocky height from which the ruins of the knights’ castle of Tegerfelden look down.

notes.label: Cheibengraben
notes.text: the local name of the old ditch or marshy moat beside Tegerfelden Castle.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: Swiss German for steep rock faces or cliffs.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: the hard conglomerate rock common in the Swiss Alpine foreland, literally ‘nail rock.’

notes.label: Heimgarten
notes.text: a traditional evening household or neighborhood gathering for conversation and storytelling.

notes.label: Schlüsseljungfrau
notes.text: literally ‘key maiden,’ the supernatural castle maiden who carries the keys.

notes.label: Maienrieschen
notes.text: a local historical plant or gathering term retained because its precise referent is uncertain.

notes.label: Gertel
notes.text: a Swiss billhook or heavy hooked knife used for cutting brush and wood.

notes.label: Reissholz
notes.text: gathered brushwood or twig wood.

notes.label: Stümplein
notes.text: small quarter-sacks used to carry grain to the mill.

notes.label: Halbmütt
notes.text: half a Mütt, a regional dry measure used here for beans.

notes.label: Brabänterthaler
notes.text: Brabant thalers, large historical silver coins.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Heimatlose
notes.text: the historical Swiss legal and social category of people without recognized municipal citizenship or domicile.

notes.label: Körber
notes.text: basket makers, here the rural name given to itinerant families associated with that craft.

notes.label: Rockfäckde
notes.text: a dialect word for the tail or corner of a coat.

notes.label: Kuchenblümlein
notes.text: a regional name for the pasque flower, identified in the source as Anemona pulsatilla.

notes.label: Engelsüssstöckchen
notes.text: little stems of Engelsüss, or common polypody, whose sweet root was used as travel food.

notes.label: Kleinkindertrog
notes.text: literally ‘little-children’s trough,’ the legendary receptacle holding unborn infants.

notes.label: Lägel
notes.text: a regional word for a small wooden vessel or tub, used here to hold fish.

notes.label: Vatterunser
notes.text: Swiss German for the Our Father prayer, retained in quoted speech and translated inline.

notes.label: Wuhre
notes.text: a dialect form referring to a weir or the place around one.

notes.label: Burgsten
notes.text: a Tegerfelden field-name connected in the tale with the former castle stables.

notes.label: Tegerfeldisch
notes.text: the local dialect of Tegerfelden; the quoted speech is retained and glossed inline.

notes.label: Stöckchen
notes.text: the small raised heels requested for the maiden’s shoes.

notes.label: Jumpfere
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘maiden’ or ‘young woman,’ retained in quoted speech and translated inline.

notes.label: Stöckchenschuhe
notes.text: shoes fitted with the small heels called Stöckchen.

notes.label: Wiesbaum
notes.text: a long, strong pole traditionally used with hay loads and employed here as a lifting lever.

notes.label: Lupf
notes.text: the Swiss German imperative ‘lift’ or ‘heave,’ retained in the brother’s exclamation and translated inline.

notes.label: Zeine
notes.text: a shallow market basket carried on the head.

notes.label: Spill- or Spindelbäume
notes.text: regional names for spindle trees.

notes.label: Pfaffenkäppchen
notes.text: literally ‘little priest’s caps,’ a folk name for spindle trees based on their fruit.

notes.label: Chäppelibäumli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive folk name for the spindle tree tied to the maiden’s redemption.

notes.label: aufgestückt
notes.text: pruned or cut back so that a tree dries gradually before felling.

notes.label: Dorschkröte
notes.text: the source’s regional or folkloric name for the monstrous toad; the precise zoological referent is uncertain.

notes.label: Bechtelisgesellschaft
notes.text: the young people’s association that organizes the local Berchtold’s Day festivities.

notes.label: Rebleute
notes.text: vineyard workers or winegrowers.

notes.label: Stitzenträger
notes.text: bearers of the ceremonial wine vessels called Stitzen.

notes.label: Stitzen
notes.text: ceremonial vessels filled with wine during the Bechtelis round.

notes.label: Eierring
notes.text: a large, ring-shaped egg bread presented to the municipal council.

notes.label: Saum
notes.text: a historical Swiss liquid measure, used here for communal wine.

notes.label: Bechtelis
notes.text: the local name used for the Berchtold’s Day celebration and its evening dance.

notes.label: Wälder
notes.text: a person from the Black Forest, used here as an outsider label.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: a Sunday-born child traditionally believed to possess special luck or protection from spirits.

notes.label: Fürtuch
notes.text: a regional word for the apron or front cloth from which the maiden takes her flute.

notes.label: Schwegelpfeifchen
notes.text: a small Schwegel pipe, a simple traditional flute.

notes.label: Erlennhonig
notes.text: literally ‘alder honey,’ the local name for the substance gathered from alder branches in the tale.

notes.label: Erli
notes.text: an affectionate dialect name for the alder tree addressed in the song.

notes.label: Chrûselhôr
notes.text: dialect for the maiden’s curly hair.

notes.label: Oefelî
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little oven.’

notes.label: hungen
notes.text: a dialect verb for tree buds swelling but failing to open because of drought, as the source footnote explains.

notes.label: Brunnenbube
notes.text: literally a ‘well boy,’ a young worker associated with wells or waterwork.

notes.label: Stöckleinschuhe
notes.text: a variant form in the source for the maiden’s small-heeled shoes.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

660213646bfd8c53c0a6b40069aa300861513f47.summary: A large old thatched house in Mörikon, with an equally spacious Schopf built onto it, is regarded as the dwelling of the ghostly Schopftier.

notes.label: Schopf
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for a shed, lean-to, or covered farm outbuilding; here it is the spacious annex that gives the Schopftier its name, though the source does not specify its exact construction.

notes.label: Schopftier
notes.text: literally the “Schopf animal,” a local spectral beast associated with the farm outbuilding where the cruel miser’s stable stood; Schopf can mean a shed, lean-to, or covered farm annex, so no single English building term captures every nuance.

1e9a3f1c409a35493c88e8899ec4495a6420b8a5.summary: The Schratten is a mountain massif southwest of the village of Flühli, in the back of the Entlebuch.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schrattenjungfrau
notes.text: literally the ‘maiden of the Schratten,’ the proud daughter condemned to live beneath the Schibegütsch guarding treasure; the compound makes her a place-bound legendary figure, though the tale does not say whether she becomes a ghost, demon, or enchanted human.

93ea16b086d58bf88603482c0a04dc7b60db64b1.summary: The proud daughter of a wealthy Junker considered an upright young man who courted her beneath her because he was not of noble birth.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical title for a young nobleman or member of the lesser nobility; the maiden's father belongs to the rank she values above her suitor.

notes.label: Schrattenhöhle
notes.text: the ‘Schratten cave’ in the fissured limestone landscape of the Schratten; it is the maiden's treasure chamber and place of enchantment.

notes.label: hohen Donnerstag
notes.text: literally ‘High Thursday,’ a regional Catholic name for Maundy Thursday; the final Gloria bells before their Holy Week silence mark the one hour when the maiden appears.

notes.label: Schrattenmeitli
notes.text: literally ‘little maiden of the Schratten,’ combining the local limestone landscape name with the Swiss diminutive Meitli for a girl; it names the enchanted treasure guardian.

ebbd7f95069ab4ecbf7f8d16b273f6b3016365c3.summary: Late one night, a young man accompanied his beloved home from a dance. At the corner of a house, she told him that she still had something to do there and that he should wait for her a little while.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a Swiss German nightmare or oppressive night-spirit, related to the wider Alpine Schratt tradition; here it is a person compelled by a birth curse to take animal form and harm people or livestock.

567a7a892edf904cddace73b467f27ea37213354.summary: At night, the Schrättlig often entered our house and tormented first one family member, then another.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional St. Gallen night-pressing or tormenting spirit akin to a nightmare demon; when trapped, it becomes a straw whose injuries are transferred to a known woman, implying she assumed or projected the spirit's form.

20f97effde367c22a6ad4e4d143f771b9dd8c407.summary: A girl from Grabs was a maid in Rans. She grew visibly pale and wasted away.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a St. Gallen name, also spelled Schrattlig in the text, for a night-pressing being akin to a nightmare demon; here the attacker proves bodily linked to the girl’s father, leaving ambiguous whether he consciously transforms, sends a double, or is exposed as the creature.

a87f01ce0e48a2b7eb8fbb856c77f30eb8a000c7.summary: A girl was tormented by the Schrättlig. She placed a Karzine—an instrument used to comb wool finely—upon her chest.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a Swiss German night spirit or oppressive nightmare-being, related to the Schrat; this account identifies the attacker with a witch whose head presses upon the sleeper's chest.

notes.label: Karzine
notes.text: a wool-carding or fine-combing implement, as the source itself explains; its teeth prick the attacking witch's forehead when placed on the girl's chest.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

2cdab0f981f296582f63d45b8686eba87ff49126.summary: The Schrättlig entered a smithy, and when it was bound by magic, a piece of straw lay on the room’s floor.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional St. Gallen name for a night-spirit or witch-like oppressive being, here magically identified with a straw and trapped in a vise; its precise relationship to nightmare spirits called Schrätteli varies by locality.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

28c92ebb4cc7dcdad30bdc35984336cd0357e82d.summary: An old man from Sevelen told me the following:

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional night-pressing spirit associated with sleep paralysis and the feeling of a being sitting on the chest; in this Sevelen account it departs in the form of a black cat after an inverted, devil-invoking dismissal.

27d88fde7ec1fc7109d6c8b81ed8e0ffd33ebf49.summary: In Rans, a young man was tormented so horribly by a Schrättlig that he became ill, ever paler, and ever weaker.

notes.label: Schrättlig
notes.text: a regional nightmare spirit or witch-being believed to press and torment sleepers; the protective flax hackle wounds the human woman who assumed this role.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

84b775b0bfaaad8566f5c97c858e5593439eb8a1.summary: About 60–70 years ago, an old woman lived in the municipality of Menzingen.

notes.label: Schwabenhudi
notes.text: a pejorative nickname combining Schwaben, ‘Swabian woman,’ with Hudi, a dialect insult suggesting a disreputable, ragged, or witchlike woman; the legend turns the marginalized itinerant spinner into a practitioner of black magic.

notes.label: Scapulir
notes.text: the source's form of scapular, a Catholic devotional garment or small paired holy image worn on the body; Ammili's refusal to remove it breaks the glamour and makes the supernatural company vanish.

be5357d1022010388c615c88d4b108c3921e9c47.summary: Once, in a far, far country close beside the sea, there lived a wealthy merchant who had one son.

notes.label: Schwanenjungfrauen
notes.text: plural of Schwanenjungfrau, the three supernatural swan maidens living on the distant island.

notes.label: Schwanenkleider
notes.text: plural of Schwanenkleid, the magical ‘swan garments’ whose removal reveals the maidens' human forms and whose possession gives the hero leverage over one of them.

notes.label: Schwanenjungfrau
notes.text: literally ‘swan maiden,’ a supernatural woman who alternates between bird and human form through a removable feather garment; taking that garment binds her to the finder in this tale type.

79b2fd61837cf401fa6564361fd21b43b48db289.summary: Long ago, when the Swedes came from their cold lands into Germany to wage war against the German princes, they advanced across the Swiss border on the Upper Rhine.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: the elected or appointed local magistrate and community head; his authority and wealth make him the trader's customer and the village's central householder.

notes.label: Witterswyler
notes.text: the source's demonym for people of Witterswyl, modern Witterswil; retaining it keeps the community's collective role in the legend visible.

notes.label: Zelge
notes.text: one large crop section within a traditional common-field or three-field farming system; the supernatural horse plows nearly the entire communal section with impossible speed.

notes.label: Siegrist
notes.text: the church sacristan or sexton responsible for the building and bells; left alone, he rings the bells that help convince the Swedish commander that the empty village conceals an ambush.

notes.label: Schwedenroß
notes.text: literally the ‘Swedish horse,’ the village's name for the uncanny stallion they imagine came from the nearby Swedish force; it saves the inhabitants by drawing everyone away before the soldiers arrive.

7d8c8a6ae30752668e0cc1b6fe04e2266236f820.summary: A village blacksmith, a master highly skilled in his craft, knew how to make exceptionally good sword blades and received so many orders for them that he had to employ several journeymen.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: a little earth-dwelling being of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to a dwarf or subterranean household helper; here it is a tiny supernatural smith, and the term does not simply mean an ordinary little man.

notes.label: Twinggrenze
notes.text: the boundary of a Twing, a local manorial or village jurisdiction; here the stream marks the legal-territorial line between Schinznach and Veltheim, not merely an informal property edge.

notes.label: Schwertfeger
notes.text: a historical sword craftsman, especially a finisher, polisher, or cutler of blades; the tale’s title uses the old occupational name even though its protagonist is described broadly as a village blacksmith.

c747327433487dedd28f56ba719b0909fd224bc7.summary: In ancient times, when few but prosperous and strong people still lived at Grächen, a stranger once came to this mountain and claimed to be a great Schwinger.

notes.label: Schwinger
notes.text: a competitor in Schwingen, traditional Swiss belt wrestling; the visiting strongman’s challenge makes this culturally specific role more precise than a generic wrestler.

notes.label: Schwungkampf
notes.text: a wrestling bout in the Schwingen tradition; the source emphasizes strength and gripping but does not describe formal rules or whether this deadly contest followed customary sport practice.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for butter; here it is boiled or melted in a kettle and serves as a grotesque measure of the brothers’ capacity and strength.

notes.label: Ringkuh
notes.text: a dominant cow that tests or contests strength within a herd, especially in Alpine cattle culture; the proverb applies her meeting a superior opponent to the defeated wrestler.

87a7c5dd724d0be5e77b8854cd2d3cdcdf4223e2.summary: The nocturnal Schwirrenschlagen was often heard in former times and is still heard today.

notes.label: Schwirrenschlagen
notes.text: literally the driving or hammering of Schwirren; the unexplained nighttime sound is punishment for corrupt boundary and stream-bank practices.

notes.label: Schwirren
notes.text: wooden stakes used as property-boundary markers or as protection along a stream bank.

notes.label: Markenrücker
notes.text: literally ‘boundary-marker movers,’ people who fraudulently shift property limits and must restore them after death.

notes.label: Leidwerker
notes.text: people who maliciously damage protective stream works so flooding or erosion is diverted onto someone else's property; the exact historical legal scope varies.

notes.label: March rucken
notes.text: literally to shift a boundary; March is a Swiss term for a property boundary, and the dead farmer reenacts his offense along the route.

notes.label: Der Schwirrama ist wieder umganga
notes.text: local dialect for ‘the Schwirren man is wandering again’; Schwirrama is the community's name for the revenant heard driving stakes.

1e605c2f3078a8a84f1eaea8b6f884667e8330ec.summary: In ancient times, on the eastern slope of the Oberlaubhorn, there stood a little brown hut in which a poor family lived.

notes.label: gaumen
notes.text: a dialect verb closest to tending, watching over, or caring for someone; here the mother no longer wishes to gaumen the crying infant, with a possible additional shade of tolerating or attending to him that has no single exact English equivalent.

1bd2e6ab48dc973f09a692e3654d4e78e95229ed.summary: 1. a) A terrible storm threatened Unterschächen. As the first drops fell, an elderly man, whose name old people can still give, seized a scythe and laid it on the roof with its blade turned upward.

notes.label: Brinzlä jetz nur, dü Häx!
notes.text: Uri dialect for approximately ‘Just drizzle now, you witch!’; the man taunts the weather witch as the storm begins, while brinzlä suggests light rain or drizzling and its exact force is regional.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: I ha 'tänkt, sy miäß nu ds Hinder verhäuwä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘I thought she would have to cut up her backside now’; the blood on the upward-facing scythe is understood as the witch injuring herself, and the coarse comic wording is preserved.
notes.anchor: I ha 'tänkt, sy miäß nu ds Hinder verhäuwä

notes.label: D'Häx cha de noch mid-em Hinder drüber appäryttä!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘The witch can still ride over it with her backside!’; it mocks the witch's presumed attempt to pass over the upward blade, while the precise motion implied by appäryttä is regional.
notes.anchor: D'Häx cha de noch mid-em Hinder drüber appäryttä!

4f9b3107203cab968b392529d027983f12c9d28d.summary: On the mountain road leading to Naters Mountain, on the Fluh above the Schratt, a barn and stable have been built among rugged rocks.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: Fluh is an Alpine topographic term for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag, here the site above the Schratt where the barn stands; the exact feature and modern spelling are uncertain.

5dc053e73d63a7154f50df08e9dfc77b7fe39849.summary: From time to time the Black Death raged in the Simmental and sometimes carried off more than half the people of the valley.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

3ced13e4e88e34f0f33046feec6bd66daea0a595.summary: The poor souls for whom heaven remained closed because of sinful deeds on earth all slipped away to the Seefluh, where they made their nests in a hidden corner.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

bf6ef015d4de4564368932287ee7920488f3d68a.summary: a) Where the Seeli is now, there was once land. Two wicked men there fell into a quarrel.

notes.label: Seeli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive of See, literally a ‘little lake’; here it is the small lake at Seelisberg whose legendary origin the three variants explain.

notes.label: So hennt's alligs d'Schüelchind verzellt
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘That is how the schoolchildren always told it’; the formula identifies the first account as a children’s local tradition.

2375832ba06073f5961bc2b694956e338bd7ab9b.summary: A striking example of how the people often transfer ancient traditions to much later names appears in the Obwalden legends about the Jesuit Father Dr.

notes.label: Seminariherr
notes.text: the popular Obwalden title given to Jesuit Father Johann Baptist Dillier because he founded Sarnen's college; literally it suggests the ‘seminary master’ or gentleman of the seminary, but in the tale it functions as his legendary byname.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working dairy settlement, not simply a mountain; several named Alps form the setting for Dillier's magical interventions.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fahrigen
notes.text: an older regional label for itinerant people credited in folklore with feats of magic like binding streams and expelling vermin; its exact social scope is not securely defined by this account.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; here they must carry out the Seminariherr's ritual instructions.

notes.label: Arvenstock
notes.text: a trunk or substantial piece of Swiss stone pine, called Arve in Switzerland; the consecrated buried wood protects the Alp only as long as it remains unrotted.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: literally an ‘Alp blessing,’ a protective Christian prayer or ritual formula recited over the high pasture, its people, and livestock; the text supplies the full formula prescribed by Dillier.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Landesvater Bruder Niklaus
notes.text: ‘father of the country, Brother Nicholas,’ meaning the Swiss hermit and patron Nicholas of Flüe; the Alpsegen invokes him alongside other saints as a protector of the Alp.

notes.label: Alpenruf
notes.text: an Alpine prayer-call sung here in a plainchant tone through a funnel so that it carries across the high pastures; in this account it is the voiced performance of the Alpsegen and is said to be uniform throughout Obwalden.

35c27905e7890449f51e7e98268aee26a21461ed.summary: That entire mountain basin in the Solothurn Jura behind the knightly castle of Neu-Falkenstein, whose circular, funnel-shaped form catches the traveler’s eye, was once filled by a lake.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the dairyman responsible for livestock and for producing butter and cheese on an Alpine or upland summer pasture; here he is also the wealthy proprietor of the entire Lobisey operation.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight whose exact mass varied by jurisdiction and period; the source uses it to emphasize the extraordinary size of each cheese rather than a single universally fixed modern weight.

notes.label: Heinzen
notes.text: open wooden hay-drying racks on which cut grass was spread when it could not be brought directly into the barns; they kept hay raised and exposed to air.

notes.label: Tristenstöcke
notes.text: upright central poles around which hay was stacked outdoors in Tristen, conical or rounded haystacks; here they supplement the farm’s insufficient storage.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Neufranken
notes.text: literally “New Franks,” a historical local label here for the invading revolutionary-era French; it reflects the source’s period language rather than a separate modern nationality.

notes.label: Sennengeist
notes.text: the ghost of a Senn or Alpine dairyman; here it is the murdered and unquiet Lobisey proprietor resisting every attempted banishment.

notes.label: Lobisey-Teufel
notes.text: literally the “Lobisey Devil,” the later local name for the murderous Senn’s haunting spirit; Teufel conveys its dreaded demonic reputation, not proof that it is the Christian Devil himself.

9db06ecc5bbe6c761b286654af6890643695a0c7.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, on the Horenvällialp near Göschenen, arrogant and malicious Alpknechte made themselves a doll from rags, or ‘Blätzen,’ and throughout the whole summer first engaged in Gugelfuhr with it and afterward in outright cruelty.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male laborers working on a high seasonal pasture; their sustained mockery and abuse of the doll bring the punishment upon their own pastoral group.

notes.label: Blätzen
notes.text: Swiss German for patches or rags; the parenthetical source gloss identifies the scraps from which the doll is made.

notes.label: Gugelfuhr
