notes.text: the source's name for the rough foolery first practiced with the rag doll; it implies mocking horseplay, but the exact game or ritual is not described.

notes.label: Tunschili
notes.text: an Alpine name for an artificial doll or effigy that becomes a living punitive being after herders feed and abuse it; the diminutive form contrasts with its eventual violence.

notes.label: Mus
notes.text: soft porridge or mash, a staple food; smearing it into the doll's mouth ritually treats the effigy as alive before it truly begins to eat.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senne-Tunschili
notes.text: the title's compound for a Tunschili made by Alpine dairy hands or herders; Senne links the created being specifically with life on the high pasture.

b4c63b4f8a0614bf33957b1da12828dace48548a.summary: The great pasture above Muri in the Freienamte was formerly still worked by Sennen.

notes.label: Freienamte
notes.text: an inflected historical form of Freiamt, the Aargau region once known as the Freie Ämter or Free Bailiwicks; it names the territory, not a claim that every inhabitant was free.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairymen or senior cattle herders; their specialized work and clothing provide the pattern for the dwarf's service and gifts.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: the name of a dairy implement stored with the funnel, probably a strainer, settling vessel, or related milk-handling tool; the exact regional implement is not securely identifiable from the context.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Wamms
notes.text: a close-fitting jacket, jerkin, or doublet; the farmwife commissions it with trousers to clothe the naked helper in a respectable male outfit.

notes.label: Sennenzwerg
notes.text: literally ‘Alpine-dairyman dwarf,’ the small supernatural helper who performs the Sennen's barn and dairy work; the name combines his being-type with the occupation he imitates.

cab137eb1dcd3cd10c7509379d701ec5366f9960.summary: In former times, beneath a Felsschopf on the Schmützenriedfluh above Zweisimmen lived a great black serpent that wore a jeweled crown upon its head.

notes.label: Felsschopf
notes.text: a projecting rock head, overhang, or rocky shelter; it shades the goatherd and conceals the crowned serpent, but its precise geology is not described.

notes.label: zur Schwarzen Schlange
notes.text: the German inn name ‘At the Black Serpent,’ commemorating the creature whose crown supplied the owner’s wealth; the building later disappears in the first village fire.

720a67587fe61d429cee43296a540c8a6e75418f.summary: In very ancient times, a magnificent city stretched from the present little town of Werdenberg into the long hollow toward Sevelen.

notes.label: Gunten
notes.text: deep holes, pools, or underwater depressions in a lake; the submerged church-tower tips are said to be visible in these depths.

5987dc2f83b97dcc96797592448dfcfe15ff962d.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, a rich Senn lived in the Bernese Oberland and had an only daughter.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman and cattle worker responsible for livestock and milk production on a seasonal high pasture; here both the wealthy father and the poor suitor bear the occupational title, whose exact rank can vary.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a serpentine dragon of Germanic and Alpine tradition, usually imagined as a huge crawling monster rather than a winged dragon; its exact form varies in local lore, and here the sick creature is linked to the Serpent Queen.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical German-speaking measure roughly comparable to a fathom, commonly around 1.8 meters but varying by place and period; the tale uses three Klafter to convey the monster’s great length, not a modern standardized measurement.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated livestock and dairy operation, not merely a mountain; the neighboring Alp is the suitor’s place of work.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person who lives or works seasonally on an Alp, especially with livestock and dairy work; here it refers to the poor herdsman, while his precise role within the Alpine operation is not specified.

ea3282ad4ac4a0eb5aedeec242fa5228659857a5.summary: Long ago there lived an abbot who ate, drank, slept, and always went walking with his head held high, without thinking about anything.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

58e7d8c3acd0ac2e74b2d4252ca64fb386277bfd.summary: “One night, my grandfather sat in a tree and lay in wait for foxes. Before long, by God, seven foxes came along at once and arranged themselves neatly in a circle around the tree, and all seven turned their backsides toward Grandfather.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

02bc5bceb19b4eb6b5f0fa41433b753fde5c1e64.summary: The little brook that flows through the Malefizgraben into the Reppisch near Urdorf also forms the old boundary separating Aargau's Kelleramt from Zürich territory.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fc4abf3e5735c969a1c2458bd10f1c400c69354d.summary: A farmer was terribly tormented by the Toggeli. It came every night and pressed him.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Alemannic name for the oppressive night-being associated with nightmares, chest pressure, and sleep paralysis; this account identifies it with the farmer’s wife in cat form.

notes.label: Gertel
notes.text: a regional heavy knife or billhook used for cutting brush and wood; the source itself glosses it as a Haumesser, a chopping knife.

notes.label: drei höchsten Namen
notes.text: literally the ‘three highest names,’ a protective Christian formula likely invoking the divine persons or sacred names; the source does not spell the names out, so they are not invented here.

notes.label: Vagant
notes.text: an older social label for an itinerant or wandering person, sometimes carrying a marginal or disparaging sense; it describes informant Gottlieb Herger alongside his trade as a broom maker.

b8d0add42aaabaafe3cc9f0e2d0e3a3392abe655.summary: Above the village of Hausen, where the side road to Lupfig branches from the highway from Brugg to Lenzburg, stands an old signpost called the Stud.

notes.label: Stud
notes.text: the local name for the old roadside signpost above Hausen; the tale identifies its function but does not establish the name’s precise dialectal derivation.

notes.label: Ellenmaß
notes.text: a measuring rule based on the historical ell, a cloth measure whose exact length varied by region; the tailor grips it as a makeshift weapon.

notes.label: Ellenstab
notes.text: the tailor’s ell-rod or measuring stick, here the same occupational implement he swings at the apparition; it should not be understood as a modern meter rule.

bb5055f29ca029efe67488778a753e9cc103b731.summary: Nowhere in the higher regions of Switzerland have remains of fortifications, graves, and dwellings from a long-vanished and forgotten ancient world been seen at a greater elevation than by the little village of Ellisried in the Bernese Oberland, not far from Grasburg and Schwarzenburg.

notes.label: Helisee
notes.text: literally ‘holy lake,’ the vanished consecrated lake and ancient city near Ellisried; the tale builds the name into Helva's forgotten cult and subterranean realm.

notes.label: Ried
notes.text: wet meadow, marsh, or fen ground; the place-names Ellisried, Gazenried, and Kumried preserve the landscape left after the lake disappeared.

notes.label: Erni
notes.text: a Swiss familiar form of Ernst used for the young shepherd whom the otherworldly Helva draws below the mountains.

notes.label: Mungg
notes.text: Helva's brother and lord of high-mountain animals; Mungg is also a Swiss German name for a marmot, giving the spirit a specifically Alpine association.

notes.label: Eiger
notes.text: Helva's brother and teacher of minerals and natural forces; the name also evokes the great Bernese Oberland mountain, though the story treats him as a personified being.

notes.label: Alpenkönigin
notes.text: literally ‘queen of the Alps,’ Helva's title as ruler of the mountain spirits and the subterranean natural world.

notes.label: Huldinnen
notes.text: poetic German for gracious female spirits or beneficent maidens; it describes Helva's tiny, radiant attendants rather than ordinary girls.

notes.label: Pratina
notes.text: the source's older mineralogical form related to Platina, platinum; it appears among the metallic ore veins in the crystal caves.

notes.label: Jol
notes.text: the tale's name for Helva's cosmic father, called the mover of all and eternal light; it belongs to Zschokke's mythic construction and is not a standard Christian name for God.

notes.label: Hunger- und Maibrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘hunger and May springs,’ names for intermittent or seasonal springs whose changing flow was traditionally read as a sign of scarcity or seasonal abundance.

notes.label: Schratten
notes.text: Alpine supernatural beings, often rough, wild, or subterranean spirits; here the term broadly groups nature spirits who share both underworld and upper mountain life with the elves.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

3193377cb2211e632420643ace230d11720ebd20.summary: In ancient times the beautiful Lampertsch-Alp in Zervreila belonged to the people of Vals, but now it lies in the territory of Blegno.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its seasonal livestock operation, not simply a mountain peak; Lampertsch and Tomül are valuable grazing properties whose ownership is disputed.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bellenz
notes.text: the historical German name for Bellinzona in Ticino; the source’s period form is retained.

notes.label: Marche
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a boundary, boundary line, or boundary marker; here it denotes the stone cross whose removal undermines Vals’s claim.

notes.label: Marchstein
notes.text: literally a boundary stone, a marked stone defining a territorial or property border; moving the marker enables the territorial fraud and brings the culprit a posthumous punishment that this tale never says he escapes.

251b393acc6077015d992446d653f7b59ba46094.summary: In former times there was once a king who had a little daughter. She became gravely ill, and no one knew what ailed her.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its grazing land, livestock, huts, and working life, not simply a mountain peak; the messengers pause at a hut on such a pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Potztausend
notes.text: an old, mild German exclamation of surprise or emphasis, roughly ‘good heavens’ or ‘by thunder’; the happy shepherd uses it when revealing that he owns no shirt.

notes.label: Wams
notes.text: a close-fitting historical jacket or doublet worn over the upper body; opening it reveals that the shepherd has trousers and a tunic but no shirt underneath.

b2abac4b80b065d88d22eaa7fcd363c926653b60.summary: It was still in that time when people with warm-beating hearts lived in Niederdorf.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Nydle
notes.text: a Swiss German word for rich cream; the bewitched churn produces it without ordinary butter-making, and the stolen charm makes it flow from the shoemaker's pocket instead.

notes.label: Siebensachen
notes.text: literally ‘seven things,’ a fixed idiom for all one's few belongings or personal effects rather than a precise inventory of seven objects; the disgraced shoemaker gathers them before leaving.

8ef0394438e6150cd11f52b6699e154a2080da08.summary: When the people of Bern and their Eidgenossen charged King Ludwig's proud army near Laupen in the year 1339, with their Sichelwagen alongside them, a number of their men fled back into the safety of the forest.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath comrades,’ members of the Swiss Confederacy bound by sworn alliance; here they are Bern's allied forces at Laupen.

notes.label: Sichelwagen
notes.text: literally ‘scythe wagons,’ war wagons associated in the tale with projecting cutting blades or scythes; the source does not describe their exact construction.

notes.label: Armbruster
notes.text: a crossbowman, named for the Armbrust or crossbow; the term identifies the skilled Bernese shooter who answers Jordan's taunt.

notes.label: Hürsten
notes.text: plural of an older regional word related to Hurst or Horst, probably wooded rises, thickets, or rough ground; the mocking verse's exact local image is uncertain, but it places the defeated lords and helpers out in such terrain.

846b13c073796963e354540bb91e700c8d796e8d.summary: A poor shepherd girl once found a sick Stollenwurm in the hayloft of her hut.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: an Alpine dragon- or serpent-like creature, related in folklore to the Tatzelwurm and often imagined as short-legged and cave-dwelling; this one wears a tiny golden crown and rewards compassion.

notes.label: Schlangenkönigin
notes.text: literally ‘snake queen’; the source describes the Stollenwurm transforming its crown into this female magical being or object and says that special healing or beneficent powers belong to her, without explaining her form further.

9bee363c9a5ad0a807385d5a7cf48dc487f971a2.summary: After Baron Anton von Turm had Bishop Tavelli thrown down from Seta Castle in 1375, the people of Upper Valais, who remained loyal to their bishop, rose against him and besieged his castle at Niedergesteln.

notes.label: Zehnden
notes.text: the historical territorial districts or ‘tithings’ of Valais, each with political and judicial importance; making Lötschen subject to the upper Zehnden imposed regional subordination rather than a literal religious tithe.

6add169a65dcf7a57d4f2c0b273855ee282fee03.summary: At precisely 4 o’clock in the morning, the Sigrist of Silenen customarily rang the Ave.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a sacristan or church caretaker whose duties traditionally include ringing the bells and caring for the church; the Silenen Sigrist’s unfailing four-o’clock bell makes his absence ominous.

notes.label: Ave
notes.text: the church bell rung for the Ave Maria or Angelus devotion; here it is sounded at four in the morning as a regular call to prayer, though the source does not describe the complete local ringing custom.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

aa564d59ec3238a3ab9fe0bb37d56c4fc4221f55.summary: When the Sigrist of Silenen came home one evening after the Betenläuten, he said, ‘Now seven people in the parish will die one after another.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss regional title for a church sexton or sacristan; his duties here include the evening prayer-bell service, and he becomes both seer and seventh victim.

notes.label: Betenläuten
notes.text: the ringing of a church bell that calls people to prayer, commonly at a set time of day; the exact local office or bell sequence is not specified.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Nervenfieber
notes.text: literally ‘nervous fever,’ a historical disease label often used for typhoid or other severe febrile illness; the source does not provide enough evidence for a modern diagnosis.

435c8e09c9ce90d9ade9bbe7fb4ef1cb9cd9f68f.summary: In the little town of Bremgarten, children still tell of a woman called the old Sigristin who understood all kinds of magic.

notes.label: Sigristin
notes.text: the feminine of Sigrist, this denotes a female sacristan or church caretaker, here also feared as a witch; her actual ecclesiastical duties are unspecified.

notes.label: Brodwähen
notes.text: Brodwähen are savory flat breads or tarts, here topped with onions and made from leftover dough; their exact Bremgarten recipe is uncertain.

notes.label: Scharrete
notes.text: the source glosses Scharrete as dough remnants scraped from the kneading trough; their texture and use in the Brodwähen are otherwise unspecified.

bf2e3445dd6c2ec568d9ccaaa41303c49a5ca6cc.summary: Near the village of Seengen on Lake Hallwil, people know a so-called Silberbrünnlein, from which people are said to have nourished themselves in years of famine.

notes.label: Silberbrünnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little silver spring,’ an affectionate diminutive used here as the local name of a famine-sustaining spring near Seengen; ‘silver’ may evoke either its clear water or supernatural value, and the story does not decide between them.

9f7bdfb5e5c73ecaa0f54bc5c214ae03c0a5989f.summary: At Allenschwanden near Magdenau there was a violent castle bailiff. He took his own life in the nearby Sennhütte.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an Alpine dairy or herdsman's hut; the bailiff's suicide there attaches his later apparition to the surrounding pasture landscape.

notes.label: Silberhütler
notes.text: literally the ‘little silver-hatted one’ or ‘silver hatter,’ the local name of the restless former bailiff recognized by his silver-trimmed hat.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Guggenloche
notes.text: the inflected historical form of Guggenloch, a local ‘hole’ or hollow where the Silberhütler seizes Krumm; the source does not describe its exact terrain.

2eef25a3efa04c1c3fc60d2a54777527d32a916c.summary: On bright nights, when one looks from the Pfalz in Basel down upon the Rhine flowing past below, after doing so for a long while one sees a brightly gleaming point in the riverbed.

notes.label: Pfalz
notes.text: in Basel, the Pfalz is the elevated terrace beside the cathedral overlooking the Rhine, not a palace in the ordinary sense; the legend does not specify the observer’s exact position on it.

7a1fad41945f099821eee5d2fbf88e55d192db81.summary: Two children were once tending their father's sheep near Rünenberg, at the foot of the mountain that bears the ruins of old Scheidegg Castle.

notes.label: Rappenstücke
notes.text: coins denominated in Rappen, the small monetary unit traditionally used in Switzerland; the story calls them silver, and no exact historical denomination or modern value is supplied.

c94aa44025aa8b599f33b34c78de31d68c3ae782.summary: A count from Valais is said once to have appeared frequently at the court in the city of Turin to pay his most devoted respects to the Duke of Savoy.

notes.label: Trilch
notes.text: a sturdy, plain woven cloth such as ticking or drill, associated here with domestically spun rural clothing; the source does not specify fiber or weave beyond its brown color.

notes.label: Hofschranzen
notes.text: a contemptuous word for fawning, status-conscious courtiers or palace sycophants; their scorn and sudden deference drive the tale’s social satire.

78e0b3db5078586eeb356b7e8db58e82e63fba97.summary: The cows had been milked, supper eaten, and the rosary completed according to the Alpsitte of the time when the Senn rose to listen, before going to sleep, for where the herd might have settled.

notes.label: Alpsitte
notes.text: an Alp custom, here the established practice of completing the rosary before the herders settled for the night.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior alpine dairyman who directs the seasonal hut, dairy work, and herd routine and who receives the stranger's silver.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the assistant Senn, a subordinate alpine dairy worker who helps with milk and cheese production.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: the cowherd responsible for tending and moving the cattle between the Alp's grazing sectors.

notes.label: Baschi
notes.text: a Swiss familiar form of the name Sebastian; here it names a junior member of the alpine hut crew, identified in related St. Gallen material as a Küherbub or cowherd boy.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: the sleeping place or communal sleeping platform inside the alpine hut; the exact construction assumed by this St. Gallen source is not described.

notes.label: Butz
notes.text: the locally named daytime grazing sector toward which the herd would normally be driven; the warning distinguishes it from a safe lower corner.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: the seasonally occupied high-mountain pasture together with its work areas and buildings, not simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Käsgadenboden
notes.text: literally the ground or flat by the cheese-storage Gaden; it identifies the lower safe area where the stranger tells the herders to keep the cattle.

notes.label: Hinterbutz
notes.text: the rear or upper portion of the named Butz pasture where the foretold storm breaks with greatest violence.

notes.label: Hagelschlossen
notes.text: large, compact masses or lumps of hail; the word conveys a more destructive fall than ordinary small hail.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a Venetian, but in Alpine legend a mysterious foreign mineral seeker or treasure expert credited with finding hidden ores by secret knowledge.

notes.label: Runs
notes.text: a steep runoff gully, erosion channel, or debris-flow ravine; the storm-created channel becomes part of the place called the Silver Mine.

notes.label: Silbergrube
notes.text: literally the ‘silver mine,’ the enduring local name for the cleft and gully associated with the Venediger's supernatural extraction of silver.

51a033027c328fc57ea47a2c506bf163466f1351.summary: In the Freiamt village of Buttwil and the neighboring communities of the Lindenberg, it is still said that when the Neufranken advanced against Switzerland at the end of the previous century, the lords of Muri Abbey had a silver sow buried at the Chillholz farm, which then still belonged to Muri…

notes.label: Neufranken
notes.text: literally ‘New Franks,’ Neufranken is the source’s name for the French revolutionary forces advancing against Switzerland; the tale does not specify the precise campaign or unit.

notes.label: Gausermatten-Wibli
notes.text: literally the ‘little woman of Gausermatten,’ Gausermatten-Wibli is a female apparition whose cry warns of war danger; her identity and exact location on the Lindenberg are uncertain.

notes.label: Heidenbad
notes.text: literally ‘heathen bath,’ Heidenbad is an alternate name for the Bath of the Eleven Thousand Virgins on the Lindenberg; its physical nature, age, and legendary connection are uncertain.

notes.label: Odli
notes.text: Odli is glossed as ‘little Adam,’ the Buttwil farmer who supposedly profited from the silver sow; his full name, method, and historical identity are uncertain.

6409b1c9de05907b13e2773c8606b108f66da72e.summary: High on the Steienwand, which drops vertically into terrifying depths toward the valley floor between Bärschis and Tscherlach, a little water at times seeps from a fissure on its western side and traces a wet band visible from far away.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine treasure lore, a supposedly Venetian itinerant prospector credited with secret knowledge of minerals and hidden riches; the label need not mean that this particular figure’s historical origin can be verified.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a divinatory or prospecting instrument attributed in Alpine legend to Venediger treasure seekers and used here to inspect what lies behind the rock face; the source does not describe its construction.

b3613df604ba316f7f6fdf6c00767ba5e45bcf7b.summary: Formerly, people knew nothing of ice. One cold winter morning, the trough, or fountain, began to freeze over.

notes.label: Isch
notes.text: Valais dialect for Eis, ‘ice’; the girl's unfamiliarity with ice motivates her poetic description of the freezing water as silvering over.

notes.label: Jez hein mer Zit danna z'gann, z'Wasser fahd an z'ubersilbern.
notes.text: the Valais dialect sentence means ‘Now it is time for us to leave here; the water is beginning to silver over’; z'ubersilbern describes the new ice as a silver coating, not literal metal.
notes.anchor: Jez hein mer Zit danna z'gann, z'Wasser fahd an z'ubersilbern.

94185b881a884700235fede77c938915b5f3a5eb.summary: Three traveling companions agreed that they would share everything in common: food and drink, benefit and harm.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

27b7ccc7b368965a0f15de783f7637c23fe1c669.summary: The mountain beings can sing especially beautifully. They often sit on a steep, inaccessible rocky summit and sing down from their airy height so beautifully that the people below in the valley are utterly enchanted and believe they hear the angels of heaven.

notes.label: Melcher
notes.text: a farm servant responsible especially for milking and dairy cattle; his kindness to animals makes him acceptable to the Bergleutlein.

notes.label: Herdknecht
notes.text: a servant responsible for tending the herd; in contrast to the Melcher, this herdsman is skilled at singing but cruel and profane.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bergleutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain people’; small Alpine supernatural beings renowned here for music that sounds like heavenly song.

8a164704cbe992c38e5270300f318d735542cd3c.summary: In the days when Switzerland still had especially skillful woodcarvers, one such man lived in the Valais village of Reckingen, and he could carve exceedingly fine things.

notes.label: Ave
notes.text: the bell ringing associated with the Ave Maria or Angelus prayer; its recurring sacred time links the tree's song with the later image of the Virgin Mary.

notes.label: Talgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘valley fellows,’ the members or inhabitants of the local valley community, with a stronger sense of communal belonging than the generic word ‘neighbors.’

notes.label: Reistgeleit
notes.text: a prepared timber-sliding or skidding course used to move a felled trunk down a steep mountainside; the precise construction denoted by this regional historical word can vary by locality.

0a9f6de87bb2f0692c668f6f47d4866acd606b68.summary: a) The people of Iberg (canton of Schwyz) wanted to build their church entirely on the level floor of their valley.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

ade9bc4c96001e2756a7301c26d9d69a60f4cdbc.summary: The mountain on whose slope the village of Reitnau lies, in the Zofingen district, forms three successive tiers, each separated from the next by a small high valley.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a feudal lord exercising coercive local jurisdiction, often remembered in legend as an oppressive petty ruler; it carries a harsher sense than the neutral English “castle lord.”

notes.label: Fastnachtfeuer
notes.text: a Carnival or Shrovetide bonfire lit as part of the seasonal Fastnacht customs; it is a communal calendrical fire, not merely any nighttime brush fire.

c647c162324efa70be78dbe8abea4ff41522c922.summary: An Abendsitz was being held in the house of the Gewalthaber at Wyler in the Lötschental.

notes.label: Abendsitz
notes.text: a communal evening gathering at which household work, conversation, and storytelling take place; here the women spin while the elders tell tales.

notes.label: Gewalthaber
notes.text: a holder of local communal authority in whose house the evening gathering is held.

notes.label: Wyler
notes.text: the locality in the Lötschental where the Gewalthaber's house and the Abendsitz are situated.

notes.label: Lötschental
notes.text: the Valais valley containing Wyler and Kippel, the story's neighboring settlements.

notes.label: Schnurren
notes.text: comic anecdotes, yarns, or tall tales told aloud for entertainment at the evening gathering.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: uncanny beings, bogeys, or ghosts in regional usage; the source groups stories about them with stories about witches.

notes.label: Beinhaus
notes.text: an ossuary or charnel house where bones and skulls removed from graves are kept; the young man steals his uncle's skull from the one at Kippel.

notes.label: Kippeler Riedbord
notes.text: the named bank or slope near Kippel where the stolen skull has become almost too heavy to carry.

notes.label: Lärchen
notes.text: a locality on the young man's route here, not the ordinary German plural for larch trees.

notes.label: du Aff
notes.text: literally “you ape,” used by the skull as an insult meaning roughly “you fool” or “you idiot.”

c048301f74d8075a2a3e3a95a432b942299ecb58.summary: The dwarfs took a beautiful calf from a farmer who owned a stable full of cattle and slaughtered it.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

114d4fc2cc924bf7138366d18739760f3f1e3ca0.summary: Everyone knows the joy and delight of boys who, in winter, take merry rides on little sleds down sloping hillsides or steeper roads over hard snow.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Muolte
notes.text: a large regional wooden basin or trough repurposed here as a sled; its exact form and normal household use vary locally.

2e4280d72bc649b758f3a77c7375b69c86150bba.summary: The bellows pants, the forge sprays sparks,

notes.label: Welsch
notes.text: a historical German and Swiss term for Romance-speaking lands or people; here it contrasts those lands with German-speaking ones, and it does not mean Welsh.

a0f49b4d4b90cb9848cd47c38402af2cdf7187ca.summary: Not far from Surava in Graubünden stand the walls of a house. Inside, they have been stripped of all paneling and beams; the wind passes through the open window cavities, and above, the sky looks in.

notes.label: gahrt
notes.text: the source's historical verb for the bellows working, heaving, or roaring; retaining it preserves the repeated forge formula, whose exact sound-image is broader than a single English verb.

notes.label: Rabenstein
notes.text: literally ‘Raven Stone,’ a traditional German name for the public execution place or gallows site; the priest urges judicial atonement there rather than suicide.

9cadf745d82895baa4ca9c69394ad9366b0aa467.summary: At the foot of the church hill near the village of Brittnau, in the district of Zofingen, the municipality had to fell a walnut tree on the Almende in the year 1812.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: the historical spelling of Allmend, communally held village land used for shared pasture, woodland, and other resources; the dangerous walnut tree belongs to this civic landscape.

notes.label: Fuß
notes.text: a historical foot measure; its exact regional length varied, so the snake's stated 10 Fuß should not be read as a precisely converted modern measurement.

notes.label: Untervogt
notes.text: a subordinate local bailiff or judicial officer; his harsh enforcement duties and greed make his supernatural punishment morally pointed.

notes.label: Vergantungen
notes.text: compulsory public auctions, often of seized property, in Swiss legal usage; the Untervogt performs them as part of debt enforcement.

notes.label: Auffallskosten
notes.text: fees or attendance costs added when the officer appeared to conduct an enforcement action; the source says his ostentatious mounted arrival deliberately increased them, though it does not itemize the charge.

notes.label: Freikäse
notes.text: cheese received as a customary due, perquisite, or payment in kind; the Untervogt weighs what he has brought from his official business, but the source does not define the entitlement precisely.

notes.label: Schlangenkari
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Snake Kari,’ with Kari a familiar form of Karl; he is a locally known snake handler or specialist able to remove the creature from the scales.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

2766a77190709c92e05ba924ce46901f6347af46.summary: Last summer, when bread in the Aargau village of Menziken cost several Rappen more than at the neighboring Wyna mill in the canton of Lucerne, a poor household in that village regularly sent its boy to the mill on the Lucerne border for bread.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small-denomination Swiss coin, one hundredth of a franc; even a difference of several Rappen matters to the poor household.

notes.label: Wiesbaum
notes.text: a long wooden beam used to secure a load of hay on a wagon; the comparison makes the treasure snake strikingly long and upright.

3e843173a6898ec85b65f025e3279146db3c364e.summary: Many years ago, among the Lord of Grasburg's many servants was an excellent marksman.

notes.label: Lampe
notes.text: a traditional hunters' and storytellers' name for a hare, comparable to giving the animal a stock personal name; the cowherd did not have to surrender every illegally taken hare to the castle kitchen.

notes.label: Schermtanne
notes.text: a regional or historical name for a dense, sheltering fir used as cover; the cowherd hides behind it while spying and later ambushing the crowned snake, although the source does not identify the tree more precisely.

05a4dfa093ac99c912f292acf113c98771ddf7fa.summary: At the head of the Fieschertal lies a beautiful plain called Unterberg. Many hundreds of years ago, numerous snakes lived there and spared no living soul.

notes.text: OCR/source uncertainty: ‘am Banner den Tod gegessen’ was rendered contextually as ‘ate themselves to death on the man’; ‘Banner’ appears likely to be a corruption of ‘Manne,’ but the source wording is not conclusive.

bc9449aeb22256c838f8b46b7db6d1758f3efdea.summary: On the Bürgenberg, 1/2 hour from Stans, loud sneezing was often said to have been heard although no one could be seen.

notes.label: Hälf d'r Gott od'r d'r Diefel
notes.text: dialect for ‘may God help you—or the Devil’; the deliberately complete response to an unseen sneeze releases the spirit when an ordinary blessing apparently would not.
notes.anchor: Hälf d'r Gott od'r d'r Diefel

ba9d0b07b29f727a95086cb8fb843179193cfb90.summary: A rich farmer once lived in the little land of Appenzell. He had a strong and handsome but ill-natured son.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its dairying settlement, not simply a mountain; the Grünalp is both the son's wealth and the site of punishment.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and cheese production during the grazing season.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial seasonal movement of cattle and herders between valley and Alp; the tale uses it for the pastoral migration and its festive display.

notes.label: Senntenschelle
notes.text: the large ceremonial bell of an Alpine cattle herd, especially associated with the leading cow and the decorated procession.

notes.label: Treichle
notes.text: a large Swiss cowbell made from hammered sheet metal, producing a duller, clanging tone than a cast bell.

notes.label: Leitkuh
notes.text: the lead cow of the herd, decorated and fitted with the prominent bell for the Alpfahrt.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: the full Alpine dairy herd and its organized herding unit, not merely an individual group of cows.

notes.label: Loben
notes.text: the source's Appenzell pastoral name for cows, used affectionately and as part of the region's herding vocabulary.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream; geschwungene Nidel is whipped cream among the rich dairy foods offered to the sweetheart.

notes.label: Fenz
notes.text: a rich Alpine dish or soft porridge, commonly made with dairy fat and flour; recipes vary locally, so the regional name is retained.

notes.label: Tanse
notes.text: a back-carried Alpine vessel for transporting milk, whey, or other liquids, normally fitted with shoulder straps.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: whey, the liquid remaining after milk has curdled during cheese-making.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a fresh whey cheese characteristic of Swiss Alpine dairying, made from the proteins remaining in whey.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine herdsmen whose autumn descent is announced by echoing yodels.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, Swiss German for steep rock faces, crags, or cliffs; their echoes and thunder frame the mountain setting.

notes.label: Senntentreichle
notes.text: the herd's large Treichle carried by the lead cow, combining the pastoral terms Sennten and Treichle.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp; here it refers to the young herdsman at the end of the season.

notes.label: Firnschnee
notes.text: old, granular snow that has survived a melting season and begun compacting toward glacial ice.

notes.label: Gemsjäger
notes.text: a chamois hunter in the high Alps; only such a hunter is likely to stray into the remote snowbound valley.

notes.label: Bell
notes.text: the source's deliberately clipped sound-word for the dog's bark.

notes.label: Blaas
notes.text: the source's Appenzell sound-word for the bell cow's bawling or lowing beneath the snow.

notes.label: Breul
notes.text: the source's sound-word for the bull's bellow.

notes.label: Zaur
notes.text: an Appenzell term for a herdsman's song or wordless natural yodel, especially the Zäuerli tradition.

notes.label: Blängg
notes.text: the source's sound-word for the sweetheart's cry or wail.

notes.label: Glang
notes.text: the source's sound-word for the Senntenschelle's clang, completing the enchanted herd's chorus.

49f508d89192131ee737265085eff9e53eca5727.summary: At the very back of the Frutigen valley floor, between Oeschinen and the Breithorn, rises the Woman, more than eleven thousand feet high, her summits covered with a mantle of eternal snow.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

40ee9dc8a7629ff65aecb5633ab6c614b3b3a25a.summary: Once there was a shepherd boy who had to tend goats and sheep on the mountain every day.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Ätti
notes.text: this Alemannic family term means father or dad and is used when the newly invisible father is called; its precise regional pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a Sodbrunnen is a deep, dug well or shaft well into which the magical stone is thrown; its exact depth and construction are unspecified.

2774309322ebd181dde47b0285a4c1d11843ceba.summary: Near the village of Sennwald in the canton of St. Gallen, on a wooded rock from which one can survey a beautiful stretch of forest, lie the ruins of old Forsteck Castle.

notes.label: Irrwurzel
notes.text: literally ‘straying root’; a folkloric root that causes anyone who steps on it to become disoriented and wander repeatedly in circles.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a Swiss German name for a deep, vertically dug draw well; the baron’s underground journey ends when its bucket carries him into his own castle courtyard.

notes.label: Heumonat
notes.text: literally ‘hay month,’ a traditional regional name for July; the mysterious ringing is especially heard from its end through the end of August.

notes.label: Bergklingeln
notes.text: literally ‘mountain ringing’; the local name for the unexplained subterranean bell-like sound attributed to the dwarfs’ work or festivities.

377d5e196e6d125436203163aeddf9f6b65c201c.summary: From the village of Dürrenäsch, the road crosses the mountain saddle to the village of Lütwil on the shore of Lake Hallwil.

notes.label: Nachtbube
notes.text: literally ‘night lad,’ a young man associated with nocturnal mischief or disorder; Barthli-Sepp’s reputation makes his descent into the forbidden well especially reckless.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a Swiss regional compound for a draw well or shaft well; here it names both the feared old well and the center from which the sunken-city and Wild Hunt legends spread.

notes.label: Gufenstädtli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive meaning roughly ‘little town of Gufen’; the people of Lütwil use it for the legendary vast Roman city, but the name’s deeper derivation and its connection to Goffisberg are uncertain.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical title for a young or lesser nobleman; in the dialect weather saying, Junker Oberherr is the lord who readies and releases the Wild Hunt.

notes.label: Sodbaschi
notes.text: a local nickname for Sebastian of the Sodhof, with Baschi a Swiss short form of Sebastian; it names the Wild Huntsman who rides the regional forest circuit.

notes.label: Fraufastenzeit
notes.text: the time of the seasonal Fraufasten or Ember fast; Sodbaschi may be heard then, although the source does not specify which quarterly observance.

notes.label: Fils
notes.text: the source’s regional plant-name for coarse vegetation growing with sour grass at Tüfels Tanzplatz; its exact botanical identification is uncertain.

notes.label: Fronfastenkind
notes.text: a regional variant of Fraufastenkind, literally a child born during the Ember fast; such people were credited with second sight or supernatural ability, and here one could raise the guarded treasure.

191f041231d4ae1c5e5f999b9f0c7ce635b98330.summary: Tired from the hunt and overtaken by night, a hunter carrying a slain chamois sought shelter in the hut on the Alp of Ober-Novai from the dreadful approaching storm.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Pritsche
notes.text: a plain wooden sleeping platform or bunk in the Alpine hut, not an upholstered bed.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short-barreled rifle, especially a hunting or target rifle; the hunter lays it beside his bunk.

notes.label: Böden-Schuhe
notes.text: Jecklin’s term, explicitly glossed as wooden shoes, for the heavy footwear worn by the three spectral Alpine men.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk” or “people of the dead,” a spectral company whose procession is heard through its repeated psalm; the source’s title uses the older spelling Todtenvolk.

b5d6033deea9f0911461df482d98e32b1544c0c0.summary: In the Oberland it is told of the old “Zigeuner” that he could transform himself at will into a wolf or a bear.

notes.label: Oberland
notes.text: the upper country or upper Rhine region of Graubünden in which this account is told.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a historical German label now widely recognized as pejorative, conventionally associated with Roma or itinerant people; the source does not establish the man’s identity beyond applying this term.

notes.label: stiva bialla
notes.text: the Romansh expression supplied for the dance room, literally a beautiful or fine room used here for dancing.

notes.label: Brodessen
notes.text: literally “bread-eating” in the old spelling; the closing idiom says he knew more than ordinary everyday matters, implying occult skill.

9023fdf9fa13aa16ceed8c0efa189ddd01dcc3a0.summary: 1. At Getschwyler in Spiringen, the Heuer set about raking and bringing in the dried fodder.

notes.label: Heuer
notes.text: a haymaker engaged in the urgent seasonal work of cutting, drying, and gathering fodder; the several accounts contrast ordinary communal labor with magical efficiency.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper hay-storage level or loft of a Gaden; workers wait there to spread the hay as it flies inside.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Alemannic for a ‘little man’ or little fellow; here wild describes an uncanny or unruly farmhand, but the account does not classify him as a particular supernatural species.

notes.label: Gwätti
notes.text: timber joints, seams, or openings in an Alpine farm building; the hay forces its way through all of them, though the precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn, hay store, farm chamber, or outbuilding in Alpine German usage; here it receives the magically gathered hay.

notes.label: verchalberet
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of verkalben, to lose a calf, miscarry, or calve unsuccessfully; the wording makes all the cows suffer a bad reproductive outcome but does not distinguish stillbirth from other failed calving.

notes.label: Heidenmüetterli
notes.text: literally a ‘little heathen mother’ or old heathen woman, a female folkloric being offered as a variant identity for the magical worker; the source gives no more exact species.

notes.label: Jakobä-Tonis
notes.text: the household or family known by the combined house-name Jakobä-Toni; the plural refers to its members rather than several people each bearing that personal name.

notes.label: Gux
notes.text: an obscure Uri comparison for a sudden gust, rush, or flying mass; the context makes the hay surge into the barn, but the word’s exact image is uncertain.

notes.label: z'schnyädä
notes.text: an obscure dialect comparison for the hay’s flight, likely evoking snowing, cutting, or something similarly dispersed; the context establishes that every stalk enters the barn, but not the comparison’s exact image.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally an ‘itinerant scholar’ or ‘traveling student,’ but in Alpine legend a wandering learned practitioner able to command hidden forces and foretell weather.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss cream, especially thick or whipped cream; the stranger stirs the hay as one beats or whips cream.

545cb070f309c43a6a1cd3d4c6e20e525242a3e9.summary: On one holy Christmas Eve, a number of boys and girls from Obervaz took advantage of the fine sledding track and rode several times down through the village and farther on across the snow-covered fields and slopes.

notes.label: wysen
notes.text: Jecklin’s quoted dialect word, glossed in the source as lenken, meaning to steer or guide the sleigh.

notes.label: Val Pardatsch
notes.text: the local valley or ravine toward which the demonic driver carries the sleigh before it plunges into the Albula.

notes.label: im Rosenkranze
notes.text: literally “in the rosary”; the tale treats this state or inclusion in rosary devotion as the reason the two boys were cast off and saved, though the precise local devotional practice is not specified.

notes.label: Pardatsch-Tobel
notes.text: the steep ravine associated with Val Pardatsch; Tobel is a Swiss German word for a narrow, deeply cut ravine or gorge.

9926b1274707bcf2841103a6a39e9300eeaa0e67.summary: The fishing village of Koblenz lies at the mouth of the Aare where it enters the Rhine.

notes.label: Naue
notes.text: a traditional broad ferryboat or river craft used on Swiss and Upper Rhine waters; here it carries the spectral sow across from the opposite bank, while the precise construction of the Koblenz boat is not described.

a8063e4af77391cad56131ad9cb98c4eefa1e1d0.summary: In the city of Basel, a spectral creature often roams at night. It carries on its activity only from the place where the Spalenberg begins up to the Spalentor, and the creature is therefore called the Spalentier.

notes.label: Spalentier
notes.text: literally the ‘Spalen beast,’ Basel's route-bound night apparition named for the Spalenberg and Spalentor; its physical form is deliberately uncertain.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a serpentine dragon of German-speaking legend; the account lists it as only one possible form of the unseen Spalentier.

5dba2ecda9c7e74e960bc0a4fefd5eb6cb9ad457.summary: a) In the Laueli at Seelisberg, near the boundary with Emmetten, a man from Seelisberg lay in wait for foxes.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Swiss centime, one hundredth of a franc; the innkeeper refuses even the smallest coin in gratitude for having been spared.

eb65708030e8120358995f01c85e438749fab36d.summary: A headless man often appeared on the old bridge below Henau. Once my father came from Thurgau and crossed that bridge at eleven o'clock at night.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard Swiss abbreviation for the canton of St. Gallen, locating Henau in the catalogue title.

999e26756d9cf01bb38542b36053a2563649325c.summary: High above the summer hamlet of Selden in the Gasterental, where an old road leads over the Lötschberg to Goppenstein in Valais, beautiful summer pastures called Gfällalp lie behind the glacier queen Blüemlisalp.

notes.label: Gfällalp
notes.text: the named high seasonal pasture where the brothers' hut and herds stand; Alp denotes a pastoral estate and grazing area, not simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Austage
notes.text: the source's name for spring-warm days at the end of which the herds move into their mountain home; the precise calendrical or husbandry sense is not explained.

notes.label: Treichelglocke
notes.text: a large Swiss cattle bell made from hammered sheet metal rather than cast like a traditional Glocke; the lead cow wears it to keep the herd together.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Felsbalm
notes.text: a shallow natural shelter beneath an overhanging rock face; excluded from the hut, Uli spends the cold night in this exposed Alpine refuge.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: in Swiss Alpine mineral lore, crystals or crystal points found in rock or near glaciers; the three colors are used as divinatory lots for dividing the pasture, though the source does not identify every mineral.

notes.label: Rosenstein
notes.text: literally ‘rose stone,’ the reddish crystal Uli interprets as the token for Gfäll and its alpine roses; it may suggest rose quartz, but the source does not identify it mineralogically.

notes.label: Hansnarr
notes.text: literally ‘Hans-fool,’ a mocking compound used by the elder brothers to call Uli a simpleton rather than a personal name.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure based on the span of outstretched arms; regional values varied, so snow many Klafter high means an immense depth rather than one exact modern measurement.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Älplern
notes.text: the dative plural of Älpler, people who live or work seasonally on an Alp; the monk's binding of the spirits restores safety to this pastoral community.

9e261dbaea1866e41e11a3d9ce50b8db67e2b36a.summary: At Turnhalden near Escholzmatt—it is an eternity since then—three robber knights committed their evil deeds.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a deep, usually stone-lined draw well or shaft; the worst robber knight is condemned to dwell and strike the hour in its depths.

9ec33bc177a2ece5c650922c9641a1cf477abc36.summary: For a long time, belief in the so-called Schaaltier has prevailed in Bern. About 50 or more years ago, a butcher lived in the city who first tortured the animals he slaughtered in the cruelest manner.

notes.label: Schaaltier
notes.text: the Bernese name for the terrifying nocturnal animal apparition identified with the cruel butcher's restless soul; the source describes its all-surrounding cry but does not explain the name's literal derivation.

11732f5dfd83a719ff1c50b01355019459a92167.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, a monstrous knight lived at Drackenaug and was greatly feared for his misdeeds.

notes.label: Drackenaug
notes.text: the local castle-name used throughout the tale; its closing explanation connects the name with the fiery eyes of the knight's dragon form, though the source does not provide a formal etymology.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a “Sunday child,” someone born on a Sunday and traditionally believed to possess special luck or supernatural perception; here only such a shepherd discovers the knight's transformation.

46003df971d76d2710e2b419d0e6e4d1d1d20b55.summary: The area where the mill and sawmill stand in Räzüns today (1878) is called Giu Morè—down by the Gottesacker.

notes.label: Giu Morè
notes.text: the local place-name in Räzüns, glossed by the source as ‘down by the cemetery’; the legend associates it with plague burials and the spectral swine.

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally ‘God’s acre,’ a traditional German term for a cemetery or churchyard.

notes.label: Messmer
notes.text: a church sexton or sacristan responsible for practical duties including ringing the bells.

notes.label: Tagläuten
notes.text: the ringing of a church bell to announce daybreak; its sound ends Rosa Maron’s supernatural ordeal.

4669480f8ffc0f674162750aac56822940a97df5.summary: A young lad in Attinghausen once read from a spellbook. Suddenly, the door opened, and in stepped—God preserve us from him!—the living devil.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c76dcd7bdb21d3e69262ea6900096be9dea39968.summary: Old Councilman Baldriger, two other men from Unterschächen, and a certain Vögeli from the Auen at Linthal had visited the market in Altdorf.

notes.label: Ja, ja, chemet nur! mer heind Geld
notes.text: Uri and Glarus-area dialect for ‘Yes, yes, just come! We have money’; Vögeli boldly invites the ambush because he knows how to bind the robbers magically.
notes.anchor: Ja, ja, chemet nur! mer heind Geld

notes.label: So jetz, g'schauwet-s' nur!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Now then, just go and look at them!’; the exact verb can shade from looking at the immobilized men to dealing with them, but his companions are too frightened to approach.

notes.label: I ha-s' b'stellt
notes.text: Uri dialect literally suggesting ‘I placed, fixed, or ordered them’; in context Vögeli has magically bound the robbers to stand in place until he releases them.

notes.label: Jä nu, sä lach-s' dü jetz la gah
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Well then, let them go now’; the frightened companions ask Vögeli to lift the Bann rather than punish the robbers.
notes.anchor: Jä nu, sä lach-s' dü jetz la gah

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: a magical binding, prohibition, or spell that fixes a person in place; Vögeli deliberately releases it only once his companions are safe.

60c48174a0df6b8e3dc41c400061523b50d583dd.summary: Every hundred years, on Charfreitag and Maundy Thursday, a headless white woman goes down from the Heidenburg to the Aabach and washes.

notes.label: Charfreitag
notes.text: an older spelling of Karfreitag, Good Friday; the white woman’s hundred-year appearance is tied to this sacred day and Maundy Thursday.

notes.label: Wässermatten
notes.text: irrigated meadows managed by channeling water across them; inspecting them is a specific agricultural task rather than merely looking at wet fields.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a local communal warden responsible for a bounded forest, field, or other protected district; here he finds the injured farmer by the stream, while the exact scope of his office is not stated.

46119a71e0e6a036b63cba936b5391f537290a9d.summary: To the left of the Käsenberg, or Cousimbert, near Gruyères lies the deep Plassel gorge.

notes.label: Spielmannli
notes.text: literally ‘little minstrel’ or ‘little fiddler’ in Swiss German, the local name for this small supernatural musician who visits alpine workers; the diminutive conveys his size and folkloric identity, while his origin and foreign language remain unexplained.

bf31cdd302651e489452155bb9ce741ef45d4753.summary: Below and to the left of the Käsenberg, which the Welschen call Cousinber, lies the deep Plasselb gorge; to the right rise the Schweinberge.

notes.label: Welschen
notes.text: a traditional German-Swiss designation for French- or Romance-language neighbors; here it means the French-speaking people who use the name Cousinber, and its social tone can vary by context.

notes.label: Tarokenspiel
notes.text: a game played with tarot-family cards, literally ‘tarock game’; here it is ordinary evening recreation among mountain workers, not fortune-telling.

notes.label: Spielmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little music-man’ or ‘little minstrel,’ the uncanny fiddler's local descriptive name; the diminutive suggests his small stature without fixing whether he is a dwarf, spirit, or another being.

notes.label: Kiltgang
notes.text: a traditional nighttime courtship visit in rural German-speaking Switzerland, when a young man went to see a young woman; here it is recalled as an occasion for dancing, though customs varied by region.

notes.label: Kilbe
notes.text: the regional Swiss form of Kirchweih, a parish church dedication fair or village festival; here it supplies another familiar setting for dancing with one's sweetheart.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here they are the men whom the supernatural fiddler distracts from their duties.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Stafeln
notes.text: plural of Stafel, an Alpine pasture station or cluster of seasonal herding buildings; here the word refers to the neighboring mountain settlements where neglected duties lead to quarrels.

60b1245d821e362cfe4a562e96a8b5001db248af.summary: Anyone approaching the lovely place of Spiez from the lake will see the prow of a boat projecting from the front wall of the parsonage, which rises directly from the water.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

0118e644ec915d428bf988845a6af43790fe6bef.summary: At times, loud music can be heard resounding here. Nor does anything left at the site remain in place.

d7c8201c8bf0854b36be2d123f3606c45ea4a356.summary: One of the longest and most magnificent glaciers in the entire Alpine world is the Aletsch Glacier.

notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

notes.label: Käsräf
notes.text: a regional back-frame or pack-frame used for carrying cheese or other Alpine dairy loads; the relative is returning with it empty when he brings the widow firewood.

notes.label: Altschmidja
notes.text: the widow’s earlier local name or nickname, retained by the spirits in their chants; the source gives no authoritative derivation for it.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Giltsteinofen
notes.text: a traditional Valais heat-retaining stove built from Giltstein, or soapstone, and commonly fired from the adjoining kitchen; the glacier souls crowd around its stored warmth.

notes.label: Schoch
notes.text: the spirits’ dialect cry, explicitly glossed by the source as “we are freezing”; its repetition gives their nighttime chant its rhythm.

notes.label: Traggabel
notes.text: a carrying fork or frame used to bear a load on the back; the boy uses one to bring a fresh stack of wood up to the dying widow.

1e1ae30b036776ea1d075ce8972673101666d9df.summary: Above Uzmoos, in the Lafadarsch Forest, the turning of a spinning wheel can be heard without interruption on autumn nights.

notes.text: literally a ‘little light for the poor souls,’ a devotional lamp associated with souls awaiting redemption; here the spinner works by it after Saturday has passed into Sunday, though the source does not describe the lamp's form or ritual use.

notes.label: Wäuti
notes.text: an Uri name for the uncanny being that appears at the window to challenge late-night spinners; it behaves as a threatening nocturnal bogey or spirit, but the source does not identify its form or broader class.

21c3c23efb0b0b09632bb6f6977ce2e44c619896.summary: In earlier times much spinning was done in our region, and the women gathered together at Spinnstubeten as they did elsewhere.

notes.label: Spinnstubeten
notes.text: communal evening spinning gatherings where women worked and socialized together; this St. Gallen account treats attendance during Advent and Lent as a violation of inherited custom, though it does not state the full rules or religious rationale.

notes.label: Spinnfrauli
notes.text: literally the ‘little spinning woman,’ the local name for the vanished spinner’s warning apparition during Advent and Lent; the diminutive can sound familiar or belittling, but the tale presents her fate as violent and cautionary.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: itinerant craft work performed by a tradesperson in customers’ homes or farms rather than a fixed workshop; here a tailor returns from such an engagement, although the household and work are not specified.

4f243f4557e93c16dfa6c412ccb1e5a8daa79f7e.summary: In the woods near Ermenswil, at the Kühlenstich, scant remains of a ruined Sennhütte can still be seen.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: a Sennhütte is an Alpine dairyman’s hut used for seasonal milk and cheese work, here ruined in the forest; the hut’s age and former pasture are unspecified.

notes.label: Spinnfräuli
notes.text: literally ‘little spinning lady’ in Swiss German, the Spinnfräuli is the small nocturnal spinner who mounts the challenger’s head; her identity and relationship to the ruined hut are uncertain.

There lived an upright, industrious farmwife who loved and honored her husband and also raised her children well. — On many winter evenings, two beautiful girls came to Vulpèra from the little valley below the high Pic Pisoc.

97b84e9c2223b5c695e2a97ae4a19bb63e737d9e.summary: Below Werdenberg, by the Mädlibrücke, a black man may be seen; hunchbacked, he walks up and down behind the Felben and oaks along the old road.

notes.label: Felben
notes.text: a regional and older German name for willow trees, often pollarded willows in a rural landscape; the precise willow species and form are not specified here.

7089d99e51e598b1c34f808bd359e537ade1026b.summary: The Sagliaints stream forms the Grenzmarche between Lavin and Süss. The popular legend relates that this Grenzmarche was once advanced as far as the rocky projection of Crap Sasslatsch for the benefit of the people of Lavin: a man moved the boundary stone he had dug up at Sagliaints to that place,…

notes.label: Grenzmarche
notes.text: a boundary line or demarcation; Marche is a Swiss and southern German term for a boundary or boundary marker.

notes.label: Süss
notes.text: the historical German name used here for the Engadine village now officially called Susch.

notes.label: Crap Sasslatsch
notes.text: a Romansh place-name for the rocky projection in the tale; crap means rock or crag, while the full established name is retained rather than freely translated.

8ce8a3bd8ee12b2183bf2ae32469635206ccb27d.summary: At the Schwarzenbachhof near Allenwinden in the canton of Zug, the ghostly figure of a woman floats by at midnight, gazes into the fountain for a while each time, and vanishes again.

ed08fa596698de4dadb9e07f0dc99053dc23ae1e.summary: In the Port below the house in the lower orchard at Bauen, a good, strong spring once flowed.

notes.label: Port
notes.text: a local Uri terrain or property word naming the ground below the house in Bauen; elsewhere the word can denote a slope or barrier, but this brief account does not establish its exact landform here.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young unmarried woman, using the characteristic -li diminutive; the old figure is called either this or Müetterli despite the differing age implications.

notes.label: Müetterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning a little or old motherly woman; paired with Meitli here, it conveys a familiar local label rather than a certain family role.

notes.label: Fürscheibe
notes.text: an Uri term for an apron-like front cloth or garment panel; this apparition wears a red one with her old-fashioned costume.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source’s regional name for a conspicuously large old-fashioned hat; its exact historical style, material, and literal derivation are uncertain.

80499efe48b2598a012da3efad17a2400368b8dd.summary: In former times, a spirit in the shape of a burning man haunted the vicinity of Zuzwil.

notes.label: Chum bald noh
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘come soon after’ or ‘follow soon’; the redeemed fiery spirit's thanks also ominously foretells that the woman will soon follow it in death.

b9183eb61046643f2801279b21a2f65da5a28669.summary: At certain times, even before nightfall, one sees an elderly gentleman coming from the direction of the Bodmer and taking a walk, chiefly pacing up and down by the Türle-Garten and not infrequently passing people.

notes.label: Türle-Garten
notes.text: the hyphenated name of the garden or locality in Cur where the apparition chiefly walks; the next paragraph uses the closed form Türlegarten.

notes.label: Türlegarten
notes.text: the unhyphenated body-text variant of Türle-Garten, referring to the same garden and its washhouse.

notes.label: füri
notes.text: a Swiss German adverb meaning forward or out; here Jecklin glosses the phrase as the woman showing herself or coming out as usual.

notes.label: Kartone
notes.text: Jecklin equates this with a Quartane, a measure used to convey the extraordinary size of the swelling; the precise unit and comparison remain uncertain.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

9ea9e4c3fb01bdefe57ddad93bdaf4ce9646c434.summary: At Abfrutt an old man was often seen sitting by a wall, with a white beard flowing all the way to the ground.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small-denomination Swiss coin, one hundredth of a franc in the modern system; its exact historical purchasing value is not fixed here, and one coin per year emphasizes the immense length of the spirit’s penance.

2ce52b1a0316a284a5585e6f08612d086de12920.summary: Landskron Castle in the Leimental near Mariastein Abbey has lain in ruins since the revolutionary year 1798.

5d888a1e77295d3da3775e768755eb89e95c57c7.summary: Once, out of mischief or curiosity about what would happen, some Waidbuben drove seven Waidpferde into Calendari-See.

notes.label: Waidbuben
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical form for the boys associated with the grazing animals; context supports herding or pasture boys, but the exact occupational nuance is not specified.

notes.label: Waidpferde
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical form for the grazing or pasture horses driven into the lake; it is retained to avoid silently regularizing the source spelling.

notes.label: Calendari-See
notes.text: the named Alpine lake whose uncanny drawing power removes the horseshoes; the source title attributes a spirit to it but does not describe the being directly.

b4290309a55f76f2db27434128cfd90ab9005bc5.summary: Let no late traveler through the Münstertali feel tempted to jauchzen when he must pass the area of Aval sura.

notes.label: Münstertali
notes.text: a diminutive regional form for the Münstertal, literally suggesting the “little Münster valley.”

notes.label: jauchzen
notes.text: to give a loud, carrying Alpine shout or whoop; calling repeatedly summons the burden-bearing spirit closer.

notes.label: Aval sura
notes.text: the local place-name at which the burden-spirit disappears; the source presents it in several related spellings.

notes.label: jauchzt
notes.text: the source’s inflected verb for giving an Alpine shout or whoop, here the traveler’s first call into the night.

notes.label: l'hom dell' Aual sura
notes.text: the local name of the monster, approximately “the man of the upper stream or ravine”; the source securely links the name to Aval sura but varies its spelling.

notes.label: l‘Aval sura
notes.text: the apostrophized spelling used for the place opposite which the fiery-eyed Capuchin spirit appears.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: I' Anal sura
notes.text: the title’s historical or corrupted spelling of the local name that appears in the body as Aval sura, Aual sura, and l‘Aval sura; the variants are preserved because the source does not resolve them.

b57e54fc67c7ed4ca743f36673e97ebf0954ffbd.summary: On Alp Pardenn in particular, the “Rucken” of the cattle is sometimes observed.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working landscape; Pardenn is where the supernatural cattle panic occurs.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.
