notes.label: Rucken
notes.text: the local name for the cattle’s sudden supernatural agitation or stampede after the mysterious calls are heard.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the senior Alpine dairymen or cheesemakers who may be milking when the disturbance begins.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an inflected singular form of Senn; a dairyman caught milking is advised to abandon both pail and milk.

notes.label: ruckt
notes.text: the source’s verb for the herd entering the state called Rucken; its exact physical nuance is conveyed by the ensuing frantic running.

a6df56fa86441261df85780a8fd88cf6ca518716.summary: In Quadars, a man is said to have taken the leading role in a boundary settlement.

notes.label: Quadars
notes.text: the local place-name given to the wasteland created after the disputed forest burned; the perjurer’s spirit remains bound to it.

55a2cf01a8b93219f032cee19806f97d658df402.summary: Close to the woods above Chäschermatten, on the Riedberg, there stands on a completely secluded little Güetji a small black wooden hut where, a few years ago, things were also said to be uncanny.

notes.label: Güetji
notes.text: a Valais dialect diminutive for a small property or plot of land.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Teilholzji
notes.text: a small wooden sluice or divider used to direct irrigation water.

notes.label: Erbji
notes.text: the local field or place-name retained from the Valais dialect.

46b77f7d29f2b76f578874e73db3858c7d8abd02.summary: At the edge of the Glassauer Forest toward St. Peter, a black man haunts the area and is sometimes seen by people passing late through the woods.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided Alpine ravine or gorge, often containing a stream; both the mill and its surviving ruins stand in the Glassauer Tobel.

notes.label: ab Stett
notes.text: a dialect expression glossed by the source as ‘from the spot’; although the pair keep walking, the haunting prevents them from making any progress.

notes.label: z'Tag g'lüt
notes.text: Swiss German for the daybreak bell having been rung; at 4 o’clock its sound releases the miller from the apparition.

notes.label: z'rechten Zügen
notes.text: a regional expression glossed by the source as ‘without hindrance’; after the bell rings, the miller can finally continue normally.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on a high pasture; in the poem the cruel Senn is condemned to repeat his milking beside the lake.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated dairying ground, not simply any alpine mountain; here Intschialp is the named pasture belonging to Intschi, while the extent of the historic holding is not specified.

notes.label: Samiklausen
notes.text: the local dialect form given alongside St. Niklausen, the chapel and settlement name in the Geschenertal; it is not a separate location in this account.

notes.label: Waldbrüder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brothers,’ an older regional plural for religious hermits or lay recluses living apart from ordinary settlements; their precise ecclesiastical status is not stated.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

notes.label: Lochstafel
notes.text: the proper name of a Stafel, an Alpine grazing station or pasture level with associated huts and work areas; the source does not describe the exact boundaries of this named station.

notes.label: Pater
notes.text: a Catholic title for a priest or religious father; the boy’s word suggests that the mysterious celebrant is understood as a monk or member of a religious order.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ the singular regional term for the hermit whose body—or, in another interpretation, whose consecrated Host—is associated with the holy site.

notes.label: ganz Hosä-n-a'ha'
notes.text: Uri dialect, literally to ‘have whole trousers on’; the wording requires the treasure seeker to be wearing the trousers, not taking them off, but the source does not explain what makes the trousers ‘whole’ or why that condition matters.

993e6cae48d5f5b0d0059d0261cea3590d35e54e.summary: In the Lerchj at Jungen, in St. Niklaus, so it is told, a young man once lived alone in his house.

notes.label: Stubenofen
notes.text: the large masonry stove heating the main living room of an Alpine house; its warm top and built-in bench were usable household spaces, which explains why both family members and the spirit sit there.

notes.label: Boze
notes.text: a Valais regional name for a bogey, specter, or haunting spirit; here it denotes the dead dancer's familiar but touchy household apparition, whose precise visible form remains uncertain.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: the German word can mean both ‘soup ladle’ and ‘Creator’; the headman hides a ladle above his head so that his oath sounds like an appeal to God while remaining literally true, a pun with no clean English equivalent.

2f9bd29e4f74581fb2dd43d1db088c9e4e0a9e86.summary: Leidikon is a small village belonging to the Fricktal municipality of Sulz.

notes.label: Mühlenkennel
notes.text: this regional mill term denotes the wooden channel or flume carrying water to the mill machinery; its precise construction at the Leidikon mill is uncertain.

notes.label: Banner
notes.text: here a Banner is a clerical specialist who binds or banishes spirits, not a flag-bearer; the source does not specify his formal ecclesiastical authority or ritual.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Hahnenschritt
notes.text: literally a ‘cock’s step,’ this is the deliberately tiny annual distance by which the bound spirit may approach the mill; the legend gives no exact measure.

notes.label: Schoppenglas
notes.text: a Schoppenglas is a drinking glass holding a regional Schoppen measure, used here as the spirit’s magical container; the vessel’s exact capacity is uncertain because the measure varied by place and period.

notes.label: öppis chaist
notes.text: this Alemannic phrase means ‘can do anything’ within the young man’s challenge to the spirit; the exact dialect pronunciation and force of the taunt are uncertain.

6d7496a69b12a7eca87eef14b4a5ba9fecd115f1.summary: The farmstead of Brün, high up on the mountain, belongs to the municipality of Valendas, and this farmstead is divided into Vorder-Brün and Hinter-Brün.

notes.label: Marche
notes.text: a boundary or boundary marker in Swiss and southern German usage; the source leaves open whether the killing arose over the marker itself or the boundary dispute it represented.

notes.label: Carrèra-Tobel
notes.text: the local name of the steep stream ravine into which the hidden coffin is carried.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or stream gorge; the term is more specific than an ordinary valley.

e954b5acdfb46f9575b98e8b9c08c9389c0646b6.summary: Many years ago, one evening a Goldkrämer came into the village of Molinis and asked how much farther he had to go to Langwies.

notes.label: Goldkrämer
notes.text: an itinerant dealer or peddler in gold goods, jewelry, or precious smallwares.

notes.label: Rütteli
notes.text: the locally named place below Peist where the Goldkrämer is murdered and the haunting remains.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: a packer or packhorse driver who transports goods over mountain routes.

notes.label: Betzeit-Läuten
notes.text: the bell rung at the customary prayer time, generally toward evening; afterward the Säumer refuses to use the haunted road.

3063e385fa965c259717108d385e070a246dc24a.summary: In the portion of the Endingen Bünte that extends into the village, a poor sinner must haunt because he moved the boundary stones there.

notes.label: Bünte
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a Bünte is an enclosed field, meadow, or garden plot close to a settlement; the exact historical extent and land use of the Endingen Bünte are uncertain.

d13102a2a8319802785e22120e660c24b2efd20a.summary: The footpath leading from Ueken to Hornussen crosses a low mountain on whose summit many people have already seen an entire host of spirits.

notes.label: Betzeit
notes.text: literally ‘prayer time,’ the evening hour marked by church bells for communal prayer; traveling after it places the old man on the Eck at a ritually significant, dangerous time.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

746b8bbca0d86e55f5dc66f9ac752bf5d46a3107.summary: In the Brunneren pasture on the Katzenstrick near Einsiedeln stands a stable in which a spirit has taken up quarters.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

93438dd3ee5b503c9953e3aff00ed6bdb3b76ee6.summary: It was around the time of the Andreas-Markt (12–20 December), about 50 years ago, that J. v.

notes.label: Andreas-Markt
notes.text: the St. Andrew’s seasonal market; the source dates its local market period from 12 to 20 December.

notes.label: Geis
notes.text: Swiss German for a goat; Marmels cannot see the creature and identifies it only tentatively by its footsteps.

notes.label: Stein
notes.text: literally “stone,” but here a locally named point on the road associated with the laborer’s death and haunting.

notes.label: Täsche
notes.text: a regional word for a smack, blow, or slap; the source itself supplies “Schlag” as its gloss.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully, often cut by a torrent.

notes.label: Pech
notes.text: a quoted local expression meaning that he fled or took to his heels; this is not the ordinary German sense of pitch or bad luck.

cba134936ac554cbc8592ab91c110a0c78f671dc.summary: In another house in the same locality, a man once addressed a spirit and, when they parted, held out a roof shingle instead of his hand.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e4e2b4ea82dbafebb387f70664d3de038fb5eaad.summary: The so-called Ehrlenmauer extended from the eastern foot of the Stanserhorn toward the Engelberger Aa, across the common pasture of Oberdorf.

notes.label: Ehrlenmauer
notes.text: the local name of a former wall or embankment near the Engelberger Aa; Mauer means wall, while the first element may refer to alders or a place-name.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Helgenstöcklein
notes.text: a small roadside devotional shrine, literally a little structure for a holy image; travelers pray there for protection and direction.

notes.label: weheliches
notes.text: an older or dialect adjective meaning woeful, lamenting, or painful-sounding; it describes the cries attributed to condemned wood thieves.

007ef055df8287796b322bb296bf3eb87cf2822c.summary: Whoever will not believe in ghosts

notes.label: Sealära
notes.text: the spelling used for the place in the poem’s opening stanza, while its title has Scalära; both source forms are preserved because the text does not establish whether this is a historical variant or a transcription error.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge; in this satirical poem it is both the spirits’ place of punishment and a point of civic pride.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Loth
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling of Lot, a small unit of weight whose exact value varied by period and region; the baker is punished by finding his bread perpetually one Loth underweight.

notes.label: Mittnernach
notes.text: a regional form meaning midnight; it marks the hour when the ghostly company assembles for its ride to the Rhine.

notes.label: Beisäss
notes.text: a resident without the full civic standing or inherited rights of a Bürger, or citizen; the closing stanzas satirize local status prejudice by denying such residents even a place in Chur’s own purgatory.

notes.label: G'meingut
notes.text: a contracted regional form of Gemeingut, meaning communal or common property; the narrator jokingly treats the Tobel as the common property of Chur’s spirits.

notes.label: Scalära-Tobel
notes.text: the local name of the ravine associated with Chur’s folkloric purgatory; Tobel is a Swiss and Alemannic word for a steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge, while the source gives no derivation for Scalära.

ad4430802b3425430b1bdefa1c3a5aa722c6caa5.summary: When the caretaker of the town hall in Andermatt entered the council chamber early one morning, behold!

notes.label: Barmäloch
notes.text: an unexplained local compound naming the opening through which the councilors’ spirits must pass; Loch means ‘hole’ or ‘opening,’ but the first element and the object’s exact cultural reference are uncertain.

notes.label: Dur dass Barmäloch durä miënt all!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘They must all pass through the Barmäloch!’; the source neither defines Barmäloch nor explains whether it is a named opening, an object in the council chamber, or a figurative passage of judgment, so that central image remains uncertain.
notes.anchor: Dur dass Barmäloch durä miënt all!

8d5bf19e5bda0d65beff7da8220450d2fcd9478e.summary: In the so-called Old Zürich War in the year 1444, the little town of Greifensee succumbed to a siege by the Seven Cantons of the Swiss Confederacy.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

13b3463e76863fba42a2e142c4f40f18a49cfbef.summary: Behind Gsteig in the Saanenland lies a desolate place strewn chaotically with countless boulders and called ‘among the great stones.’ Evil spirits once dwelled there.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

aa429ba02359951f48a75767ebb81f75b17854d5.summary: When the Alpen lie buried beneath the weight of winter snow, people and livestock have descended into the valley, and, in the snowbound huts, the men carve wooden wares by the flickering Kienspan while the women work at the old-fashioned spindle, the dominion of the mountain spirits begins.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, the high-mountain summer pastures and working landscapes abandoned during winter, not simply the Alps as a mountain chain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kienspan
notes.text: a resin-rich pinewood splint burned as a small household light before modern lamps.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow ravine or gorge in Swiss and southern German usage; the mountain spirits gather in such rocky clefts.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine crystal seeker or mineral hunter who enters rock cavities in search of specimens.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: literally ‘rays,’ a traditional Alpine term for rock crystals; the story treats them as the mountain spirits' finest adornment.

45a6c5238a7c61ec9d7d3eb2098c6c7d02bf9931.summary: A sacristan had a son who was so wild and unruly that the father considered how he might curb the boy’s recklessness.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

31995130b9167af3cb9b03106dc34fc5ce565ce8.summary: Three brothers from the region went to war, each in a different direction. When they parted, they vowed to build a little chapel at the place where they met again in their homeland after the war.

notes.label: Spisschappeli
notes.text: the local name for the little chapel between Spiss and Bittleten; Chappeli is a Swiss German diminutive of chapel, and the name ties the brothers' votive building to its exact landscape location.

5984064fbcdf9cffbf518cb836b88a6c82b260c7.summary: Legend tells many remarkable things about Baron Kaspar von Stockalper. Because of his fine natural gifts, talents, command of languages, learning, and great prudence in business, he is said to have stood in high favor with the kings of France, Spain, and England, and especially with the Duke of Savoy.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

7dd787062ccf8449ce1de9ff98fd72e062b3484a.summary: In Schalb, two older children once had to watch a small child during Mass on a Sunday.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: g'fleckote Hund
notes.text: Valais German for a ‘spotted dog’; the impossible entrance and disappearance make it uncanny, but the source does not identify it as a devil, guardian, or other named being.

22b03091b007db22997e76abd0055fbf8986c776.summary: With a Sprengwurzel, one can open every lock. There was a man in Altishofen who knew how to do it.

notes.label: Sprengwurzel
notes.text: literally a ‘bursting root,’ a legendary plant or magical root said to spring locks and open anything closed; the tale gives a traditional woodpecker method for obtaining it but does not identify it with a secure botanical species.

bd48db7b994952807e2d2ee9ec4094d7def53216.summary: Near Haldenstein Castle, a maiden haunted a spring for many years. She often rose from it in a snow-white dress and warmed herself in the golden beam of the midday sun.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4545683ea29154ac420e07157b21d97d0d24c64a.summary: Close beside the road near Remüs stand the ruins of an old building called the Castle of St.

notes.label: Remüs
notes.text: the historical German name for Ramosch in the Lower Engadine; it was associated with the cult and pilgrimage site of St. Florin.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Serra plana
notes.text: the local field-name near Remüs where St. Florin’s reapers are working.

notes.label: La fantana da St. Florin
notes.text: Romansh for ‘the spring of St. Florin,’ the first line of the closing local couplet.

notes.label: Inua l'aua s'müdet in vin
notes.text: Romansh for ‘where the water changes into wine,’ completing the couplet and summarizing the miracle.

b453a24bae11a5c1e3c4f1a2aff3aba25d686471.summary: The Urden-Alpe belonged at one time to the Freiherren von Vaz, and concerning this Alpe the following legend is told of Donat, the last of them:

notes.label: Urden-Alpe
notes.text: the seasonal high pasture at Urden, jointly owned in the tale by Cavraisen, Castiel, and Lüen.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working settlement, not simply a mountain.

notes.label: Freiherren
notes.text: plural of Freiherr, a historical noble rank conventionally rendered as barons; the pasture once belongs to the lords of Vaz.

notes.label: Freiherr
notes.text: a historical noble rank conventionally rendered as baron; Donat’s extravagant demands and rides are tied to that social role.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: male laborers or herdsmen working on an Alp; the communities replace their old and defective hut.

notes.label: Spuck
notes.text: the source’s spelling for Spuk, a haunting or spectral disturbance; here it is Donat’s repeated supernatural ride.

9c82b7abd3e1c3b9ea05424e5c9e86dca1e4509e.summary: In the village of Schänis stands the old Heidenturm; the church belonging to it burned down in 1824.

notes.label: Heidenturm
notes.text: literally ‘heathen tower,’ a traditional antiquarian name for the old tower at Schänis; it labels the structure as ancient without proving a specific pagan origin.

notes.label: St. Gall-Weibchen
notes.text: literally the ‘little St. Gall woman,’ the female apparition seen in the old churchyard during the Ember season; the source does not explain her identity or connection with Saint Gall.

notes.label: Fronfastenzeit
notes.text: the season of the Fronfasten or Ember Days, quarterly Christian fasting periods marked in Swiss folk belief as liminal times; it is not the ordinary pre-Lenten carnival fast.

notes.label: Kratten
notes.text: a regional word for a basket, pannier, or open carrying container; this one holds the horseshoe nails that can become treasure.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: large historical coins named from the German Thaler; the two transformed horseshoe nails become valuable money, though the metal and denomination are not specified further.

ecd5cb43651d31630959fc651c92a15a51b21329.summary: It is also told of the same Bishop Saint Jodern that it was once revealed to him that the pope in Rome was in danger and should be warned.

notes.label: Planta
notes.text: the open square or field at Sion where Satan reaches the city with his double burden; it is a local place-name, not an ordinary plant.

notes.label: Dona! Dona! lit
notes.text: a dialect command approximately meaning ‘Sound! Sound! Ring!’; the exact word forms are uncertain, but the bishop's call draws the buried bell ringing from the ground.

notes.label: St. Jodern-Glocke
notes.text: literally ‘Saint Jodern's bell,’ the storm-protecting bell won through the bishop's wager with Satan; Jodern is the Valais form associated with Saint Theodulus.

15060c3f454b75bc9988761d0725b0fcc3cafd35.summary: Once, in the land of Valais, there was a very holy bishop named St. Jodern—Theodul-Theodor.

notes.label: Kufe
notes.text: a large wooden vat or cask, here the inexhaustible wine vessel blessed by St. Jodern; the compound St. Jodern-Kufe became a local expression for an unexpectedly abundant supply of wine.

9887d6bbf30dc750f13239249ece0275f5a70bd1.summary: About half an hour from the village of Ernetschwil stands the St. Johanner farmstead.

notes.label: verpfründeten
notes.text: entered a historical maintenance arrangement in which people transferred property to a monastery or institution in return for lodging and lifelong support; it was a legal and economic provision for old age, not simply a charitable stay.

fc080b90bd012809480e625a2541675121590b38.summary: Above the Haldenwald stood a half-ruined, soot-blackened Staffel that the Sennen passed only reluctantly.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or tier with its hut and working buildings, occupied at a particular stage of seasonal grazing; here the word refers to the half-ruined haunted structure itself.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheesemaking on high pastures; here generations of them warn one another away from the deadly Staffel.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: poppern
notes.text: a regional verb for making a muffled knocking, tapping, or popping sound; here it is one element in the monster's approaching clatter.

notes.label: Staffelungeheuer
notes.text: literally ‘Staffel monster,’ the being haunting the ruined Alpine station above the Haldenwald; its challenge tests whether a visitor will claim responsibility for doors he did not close.

2b8fe6cf3f28283f78a981d65468147c3f08b2ae.summary: A hunter from Beromünster in the canton of Lucerne hunted through the entire region as far down as the Ramholz forest near the Aargau village of Gontenschwil.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d71b869f6fe9137e004c29676cbd16b86a94791d.summary: It is an ancient tradition that an unknown hunter from distant lands pursued a stag as far as the place where the pilgrimage chapel in the Jagdmatt near Erstfeld in the canton of Uri is now much visited.

notes.label: Jagdmatt
notes.text: literally ‘hunting meadow,’ the Erstfeld pilgrimage site whose name the legend explains through the hunter's pursuit and conversion.

notes.label: Schweisstuch
notes.text: literally ‘sweat cloth,’ a devotional image of Christ's face associated with the veil of Veronica; it appears between the stag's antlers rather than referring merely to an ordinary handkerchief.

746b9610619e93db90b592be57550c12bba50994.summary: Every year around the holy days, a splendidly appointed coach drives through the village of Endingen at night.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a German horse-color term for gray horses whose coats often appear white; the silent spectral stagecoach is drawn by four of these pale horses.

5422bc7c0f41a47fe82d65eb738b37f9a37f2bb1.summary: Joggeli—little Jakob—who lived on the Geiswiese behind the village of Wettingen, was widely known as a sorcerer.

notes.label: Joggeli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive of Jakob, ‘little Jakob’; both the man and his helping household spirit share the name, creating the ambiguity behind his reputation as a sorcerer.

notes.label: Heubrüggi
notes.text: literally ‘little hay bridge,’ a Swiss term for the raised access or platform leading to stored hay; Joggeli need not climb it because the spirit sends fodder down.

notes.label: Stalljoggeli
notes.text: literally ‘stable Joggeli,’ the name of the household spirit who supplies fodder; Joggeli is a Swiss diminutive of Jakob, and the title distinguishes the spirit by its stable role.

606b74330b24b87bd2d745ee932c9a20f051ea07.summary: A king had it proclaimed that anyone who still had a light burning after the workday was over must be put to death.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Burgvogt
notes.text: a castle bailiff, castellan, or administrative steward responsible for a castle and its domain; here he hires the two boys, while the tale does not define the office’s precise jurisdiction.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

3d021538258851c305a68429286bd0fc89660164.summary: In the church at Tusis, which was dedicated to the Mother of God, there stood until the Reformation in that community, in the year 1526, a miracle-working statue of the Virgin Mary.

notes.label: Tusis
notes.text: the historical spelling used by the source for Thusis, a municipality in Graubünden; the legend connects its Reformation with the destructive torrent.

notes.label: Nolla
notes.text: the mountain torrent beside Thusis, notorious for carrying debris; the tale personifies it as punishing the removal of the Marian statue.

912bae0bbfa3cd71684151f6145eb8c11fe1e1d6.summary: The Staudentorkel stood at the southwestern end of the village on the country road leading to Maibach.

notes.label: Staudentorkel
notes.text: the local name of an old wine-press building; Torkel denotes a grape press or the structure housing it, while Stauden is the place-name element.

notes.label: Standen
notes.text: large upright tubs or vats used in handling grapes, must, or wine within the press building.

notes.label: Torkeln
notes.text: plural of Torkel, traditional grape presses or the broad, dark buildings containing them, which readily become haunted settings in local storytelling.

notes.label: Torkelbaum
notes.text: the great wooden press beam of a traditional wine press, whose creaking under pressure is imagined as ghostly groaning.

notes.label: geladen
notes.text: literally ‘loaded,’ the technical and figurative description of the press beam when the press is charged and under working pressure.

52bae817c95f752c783c1288b02f8171796543aa.summary: The house servant of a respected burgher family had noticed that his mistress and her daughter occasionally went out at night on Saturday and did not return home until toward morning.

notes.label: Häfeli
notes.text: Häfeli is the Swiss German diminutive for a small pot or crock, here holding the flying salve above the parlor door; its material, size, and contents are uncertain.

notes.label: Oben us und nienen a!
notes.text: this dialect flight formula means approximately ‘out above and touch nowhere,’ allowing the broomstick to leave cleanly; its exact grammar, pronunciation, and magical tradition are uncertain.

notes.label: Oben us und überall a!
notes.text: this mistaken version means approximately ‘out above and strike everywhere,’ causing the servant to be battered in the chimney; its translation depends on the dialect wordplay and is somewhat uncertain.

notes.label: Tüfel
notes.text: Tüfel is the Swiss German form of ‘Devil,’ whom the servant identifies instead of renouncing Christ; its exact dialect pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Steckenfahrt
notes.text: literally a ‘stick ride,’ Steckenfahrt is the magical nocturnal journey made astride an anointed broomstick; the destination and the salve’s ingredients are unspecified.

c6c900a8d5656942c979c4e9db7250779d26ac40.summary: In the Urschai-Tale, a saddled white horse stands upon a height. At night a coal-black rider must mount it and leap over an old wall on its back; the wall also forms the boundary between the respective Alpweiden of Vetan and Steinsberg.

notes.label: Urschai-Tale
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical compound for the Urschai valley, the setting of the rider’s apparition and the disputed boundary.

notes.label: Alpweiden
notes.text: high-pasture grazing lands belonging to Alpine communities; the wall separates those of Vetan and Steinsberg.

notes.label: Vetan
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical German name for the Lower Engadine village now called Ftan.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally a rider on a Schimmel, a white or gray horse; the coal-black rider’s repeated boundary ride is his punishment for a false judgment.

036c73062f75273a449a0bf7e6e7b4f92fc8cc82.summary: There once lived in St. Gallen a merry minstrel known as the Steucheler, and he himself related what happened to him with Doctor Theophrastus Paracelsus, whom he had often seen and knew very well.

notes.label: Steucheler
notes.text: the St. Gallen minstrel's regional personal byname; the source gives no secure literal derivation, so translating it as an occupation or character trait would be speculative.

notes.label: Tagsatzung
notes.text: the assembly of delegates of the Old Swiss Confederacy, here meeting at Baden; Federal Diet is the closest English label but can suggest a more centralized modern parliament.

notes.label: zugewandte Orte
notes.text: literally associated or allied places, the Confederacy's formally allied territories without the same status as the Thirteen Cantons; their exact rights and relationships varied.

notes.label: Schwegel
notes.text: a traditional small pipe or flute; its construction varies, and this tale also describes the minstrel's instrument as a transverse flute.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small Swiss coin denomination used here in the idiom that Theophrastus would not wager even one on Steucheler's neck; its historical value varied by place and period.

4ca53be2175ac426182fedec5b7dc15d6a50a224.summary: In the part of Hallwyl Castle called the old section because its rampart and moat have fallen into ruin, the spirit of an unfaithful steward can be heard groaning.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a traditional communal warden responsible for protected woods, fields, or boundaries; this Bannwart knew the story of the lords' acquisition of the Schlattholz and witnessed the steward's ghost.

notes.label: Sichelfeder
notes.text: literally a ‘sickle feather,’ a long curved plume worn behind the ear; it identifies the wandering steward, although the source does not explain whether it marked an office, fashion, or local costume.

4db4269eef8a8f6881862d93c674ef273ac63cfa.summary: In the upper village of Spiringen, we see a stately, well-proportioned farmhouse bearing the year 1577.

notes.label: Stickihaus
notes.text: the house at the locality called Sticki in Spiringen; Haus means ‘house,’ but Sticki functions here as a local name whose derivation is not explained.

notes.label: Twär-Äx
notes.text: an Uri dialect form meaning a transverse or crosswise axe, probably a broad-bladed woodworking axe; the challenge and source footnote preserve the name, but the precise historical tool form is not specified.

2b750a07c4c966b65e3d7b12b75c0ab5414d0b82.summary: The Stiefelireiter of Muri was not merely a malicious and hot-tempered little man; he also mocked religion and perverted justice.

notes.label: Stiefelireiter
notes.text: the regional name of this corrupt, boot-associated rider who becomes a mounted countryside specter; the closest literal sense is ‘little boot rider,’ but the name functions as a folkloric identity and its origin is not explained.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: the German word means both ‘Creator’ and ‘ladle’; Stiefeli hides a ladle above his head so his oath invokes God to listeners while remaining literally true, a pun without a clean English equivalent.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: ordinarily ‘judge,’ but here also a regional or punning name for the comb hidden above Stiefeli’s head, presumably something that ‘sets straight’; the exact implement-name usage is uncertain and is essential to his deceptive oath.

2bd9877b810457e4e3de8f47267b310001c23260.summary: The Maiengrün is the southern side of a long mountain ridge. On its southwestern slope lie the great quarries of Othmarsingen and Mägenwil, where Geisberg stone is quarried, and to the northwest the ridge extends along the left bank of the Reuss through the entire Freiamt.

notes.label: Stiefelireiter
notes.text: the regional name of the booted rider who haunts several sites in Aargau and is linked to a perjuring bailiff of Muri; the closest literal sense is ‘little boot rider,’ but the name functions as a specific folkloric identity.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: the German word means both ‘Creator’ and ‘ladle’; the bailiff hides a ladle above him to make his oath sound sacred while remaining literally true, a pun without a clean English equivalent.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: ordinarily ‘judge,’ but here also a regional or punning name for the large round comb hidden in the bailiff’s hair, likely through the idea of setting something straight; the exact implement-name usage is uncertain.

notes.label: Juchart
notes.text: a traditional Swiss measure of land area, broadly related to what could be plowed in a day; its size varied by canton and period, so the extent of the Klosterholz cannot be converted exactly from this account.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

ee8c1395e49b2f1313c264d039e3abbb6e36ef25.summary: The Stiefelireuter rides his white horse across the Müsswangerhöhe. As Vogt of Muri Abbey, he once deprived a poor widow of her little holding here by means of a false oath.

notes.label: Stiefelireuter
notes.text: literally ‘little-boot rider’ or ‘booted rider,’ the condemned spectral horseman associated with a fraudulent abbey official; the source body also gives variant spellings.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a bailiff, steward, or territorial administrator exercising authority for a lord or monastery; here the office connects the rider to Muri Abbey.

notes.label: Änzifluh
notes.text: a local cliff or crag near Hergiswil associated with sightings of the rider; Fluh denotes a steep rock face.

875f217d4c8c1d7dd70f3916c47e4a4af45cbb58.summary: Whenever people from the communities surrounding Muri Abbey had to perform compulsory labor for the monastery, a man in tremendously high boots regularly appeared among them and cruelly lashed the exhausted Tauner with a whip.

notes.label: Tauner
notes.text: land-poor rural day laborers or cottagers who depended on hired work; here they are exhausted under compulsory service to Muri Abbey.

notes.label: Stiefelirüter
notes.text: literally the ‘boot rider,’ the punitive revenant name derived from the estate manager's enormous boots and mounted appearances.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a gray or white horse; riding one gives the revenant his alternate name Schimmelrüter.

notes.label: Schimmelrüter
notes.text: literally ‘gray-horse rider’ or ‘white-horse rider,’ one regional name for the same wandering former estate manager.

notes.label: Markstaller
notes.text: a local name for the revenant around Hägglingen, probably connected with a boundary, stable, or office title; the source does not explain the exact derivation.

notes.label: Hopelirüter
notes.text: a local name for the rider in the Rohrdorf moor, derived by the source from his repeated cries or calling out.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

f162ed3e5292690892d402c125aa0247eb3f8a23.summary: In olden times, while Muri Abbey was occupied with enlarging its possessions in the Freien Amte through purchase, contract, inheritance, and lawsuit, it also laid claim to the Bärholz forest belonging to the municipality of Bütikon.

notes.label: Freien Amte
notes.text: the historical Free Bailiwicks, territories that included the area around Muri before the modern canton of Aargau.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: the territorial bailiff or governor who exercised judicial and administrative authority over the district.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Klosterschaffner
notes.text: the monastery's estate steward or financial administrator, responsible for managing lands and revenues.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: alpine herdsmen and dairymen, here credited with calling a milk ladle by a name that enables the false oath's wordplay.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: both ‘creator’ and ‘ladle’ in German; hiding the dairy ladle above his head lets the steward speak a technically literal but fraudulent oath.

notes.label: Holzfrevler
notes.text: people who violate forest rights by cutting or stealing wood unlawfully; the spectral rider drives them from the woods.

notes.label: Enziloch
notes.text: the notorious cave or chasm in Entlebuch to which dangerous spirits are said to be banished.

notes.label: Sentiloch
notes.text: a variant name in this account for the Enziloch, the cavern near the Blumalpe containing a supernaturally suspended rock.

notes.label: Blumalpe
notes.text: the named alpine pasture near the Enziloch; Alpe denotes a high summer pasture and pastoral holding.

notes.label: englischen Gruß
notes.text: the ‘Angelic Salutation,’ meaning the Ave Maria; the Sennen call it toward the cave as a protective prayer.

notes.label: Stiefelischreiber
notes.text: literally a ‘little-boot scribe’ or ‘boot clerk,’ the local name for the perjuring monastery steward whose trick depends on earth hidden in his boots.

bb5e9c45df8a819458d5c5525aea01a0b17b5e72.summary: On stormy spring nights, the wild Reuss rushes more violently through the Freie Amt in Aargau, for then the river carries the snowmelt of Lake Lucerne toward the Aare.

notes.label: Freie Amt
notes.text: the source's singular historical form of Freiamt, the Aargau region around Muri; literally ‘free office,’ it is a territorial name rather than a generic administrative agency.

notes.label: Stiefelreiter
notes.text: literally ‘boot rider,’ the corrupt monastic bailiff condemned to ride after death in the same towering boots that made him a feared figure in life.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a bailiff, governor, or estate administrator; this Vogt manages Muri Abbey's holdings and abuses his delegated authority.

notes.label: Stulpstiefel
notes.text: high cuffed boots with turned or extended tops, here reaching far above the rider's knees and providing a hiding place for earth.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: ordinarily ‘Creator’ in the oath but also a word for a spoon or ladle; the hidden utensil lets the rider construct a deceptive double meaning.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: ordinarily ‘judge’ but used here in a dialect pun for a comb; hiding it above his head supplies the oath's second false equivocation.

notes.label: Maiteli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little girl; the affectionate form contrasts with the frightening threat.

notes.label: Stiefelreiter, komm und hol mein böses Maiteli!
notes.text: Swiss-inflected German for ‘Boot Rider, come and fetch my naughty little girl!’; grandmothers use the revenant as a child-frightening threat.
notes.anchor: Stiefelreiter, komm und hol mein böses Maiteli!

notes.label: Ofenloch
notes.text: the warm recess, space, or nook associated with the large tiled stove in a traditional farmhouse room, where frightened children hide.

ba9f36afc8a27116d8a2b3b4e3717dfb91ef3e60.summary: Around Muri Abbey and throughout the so-called Freiamt in the canton of Aargau, the people tell of the Stiefeli- Rüter, or booted rider.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: the historical and modern regional name for the Aargau district around Muri; literally ‘free office,’ it is a proper territorial name rather than a generic free agency.

notes.label: Stiefeli- Rüter
notes.text: the source's spaced variant of the name, literally ‘little-boot rider’ or ‘booted rider,’ based on the apparition's conspicuous large boots.

notes.label: Wart, de Stifelirüter chunt!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘wait, the booted rider is coming!’ a threat used to frighten children into obedience.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a bailiff, governor, or seigneurial administrator; the title conveys the authority the rider abused over his subjects.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: ordinarily ‘creator’ in the oath but also a regional word for a ladle; hiding a ladle above his head lets the official swear deceptively.

notes.label: Richter
notes.text: ordinarily ‘judge’ but, according to the source's dialect pun, also a comb; the hidden object enables the second part of the fraudulent oath.

notes.label: Stifeli-Rüter
notes.text: the catalogue title's dialect spelling of ‘booted rider,’ the corrupt official condemned to ride after death; the body also prints the variant Stiefeli-Rüter.

7407cfff2516003b8f8500be0ebb09cffca7adc9.summary: The Stiftsdamen of Schanis also attended the witches' dances on the Gafarra-Bühl in the Weisstannen valley; the abbess rode at their head.

notes.label: Stiftsdamen
notes.text: women belonging to a religious collegiate foundation, often noble canonesses rather than cloistered nuns; the legend provocatively places the ladies of Schanis and their abbess among a witches' gathering.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

fd03a1713ac1951eaf1291a7d5d157ee713e26d3.summary: Schoren am Sattel in the canton of Schwyz is said formerly to have belonged to Aegeri in the canton of Zug.

notes.label: Markstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking property or jurisdiction; the perjurer's ghost leaps from marker to marker along the disputed border.

notes.label: Püpen, Hüpen
notes.text: regional words for whooping, exultant calling, or hopping; the paired forms describe the Stockpüper's noisy manifestations.

notes.label: Stockpüper
notes.text: the boundary-haunting ghost associated with the mountain called Stock; its second element refers to his whooping or leaping cries.

db2702eb020b009f215f6900216dc537254731cd.summary: At Ladils, the Molken were stored in a chamber a short distance from the actual Alpine hut.

notes.label: Molken
notes.text: dairy produce collectively, especially cheese, butter, whey products, or the season's processed milk goods; here it is locked in a separate storehouse.

notes.label: Käsgaden
notes.text: literally ‘cheese storehouse’ or ‘cheese barn,’ the separate chamber where Ladils's dairy goods are kept.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman responsible for cheesemaking and the stores; in this story, he conspires with the thief.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: schlarping
notes.text: an English verbal rendering of the dialect daher-schlarpete, meaning to shuffle, slap, or drag one's feet noisily; the sound defines the apparition.

notes.label: Stofel
notes.text: a regional form of Staffel, an Alpine pasture stage, station, or terrace at a particular elevation; the wooden-shod thief crosses it at night.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, traditional quarterly Catholic periods of fasting and prayer; the monk deliberately investigates during this spiritually charged time.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Schlarpi
notes.text: a shuffler or slouching, noisy-footed figure; first the living thief and later his condemned spirit bear the label.

notes.label: Alpsäss
notes.text: the Alpine holding, pasture station, or settlement area around the huts; the exposed thief flees across it toward the valley.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen who protect themselves from the ghost with a blessing.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: the Alpine blessing, a spoken or sung protective prayer traditionally recited over the pasture, people, and livestock; here it prevents the Schlarpi from causing harm.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

notes.label: Stofel-Schlarpi
notes.text: the shuffling or slouching figure of the Stofel; its name imitates the slap-drag sound of wooden shoes and becomes the dead thief's ghost-name.

0f2d383b6c28fc26a013e32ab74320580332e9c9.summary: Where the Guggernüll massif rises between Splügen and Nuvenen beside the young Hinterrhein, where the vulture nests or the raven croaks high above in the dreadful clefts, but no human foot ever dares ascend—there now dwell the spirits of the old Stoffler family.

notes.label: Stoffler
notes.text: a family name used collectively for the family’s cursed ancestral spirits, who cannot rest because of their wrongdoing in life.

notes.label: durband
notes.text: a dialect word glossed by the source as “throughout” or “without exception”; it says that every member of the family led a wicked life.

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally “God’s acre,” a traditional German name for a churchyard or cemetery.

notes.label: Rumor
notes.text: an older regional use meaning noisy disturbance, commotion, or uproar rather than an unverified report.

notes.label: Geisterbanner
notes.text: a folk specialist believed able to banish, bind, or conjure away spirits; the descendants hire one to stop the haunting.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Banner
notes.text: the shortened form here of Geisterbanner, the spirit-banisher standing in the doorway; it does not mean a flag bearer.

notes.label: Nu, nu wird's schö Wetter
notes.text: an Alemannic dialect cry meaning approximately “Now, now the weather will be fine”; the spirits repeat it as they gleefully undo their work when a storm begins.

6ccdb33e091b6dbcefd7dd9086a06e8855308f58.summary: a) On an Erstfeld Alp, they had endless trouble over the Alpchessi. It was stolen from them every winter, and they could find no trace of the thief.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpchessi
notes.text: an Alpine cheese-making cauldron used on a high seasonal pasture; the compound joins Alp, the pasture and dairy workplace, with Chessi, a cauldron.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine dairy cauldron, normally used to heat milk for cheese; the story alternates this general Uri form with the fuller Alpchessi and Wellchessi.

notes.label: Wellchessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheese-making cauldron used to heat and work milk; the source does not specify the vessel’s capacity or the additional nuance of Well-.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp; here the term includes the pastoral workers responsible for the huts and cauldron.

notes.label: Diebensegen
notes.text: literally a ‘thief’s blessing,’ a protective or binding formula placed in the cauldron so that its thief cannot escape; its wording and ritual preparation are not given.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

bbf5575a2b85b58732ff3b007b82dda2063dd431.summary: A Nachtbub in Isental had stolen a fence post. After his death he had to wander, and he was often seen running helplessly to and fro with his post, asking loudly and plaintively: ‘Wo müesä-n-äu hitüe?’—‘Where am I supposed to put it?’ Once a drunk snapped at him: ‘Dü Limel, tüe-n-ä wo-n-ä gnu…

notes.label: Nachtbub
notes.text: literally a ‘night boy,’ an Alemannic label for a young man out roaming at night, often for courting or mischief; here it identifies the fence-post thief rather than a child of a stated age.

notes.label: Wo müesä-n-äu hitüe?
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Where am I supposed to put it?’; the wandering dead man cannot make restitution until someone tells him where the stolen post belongs.

notes.label: Dü Limel, tüe-n-ä wo-n-ä gnu hesch!
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘You fool, put it where you took it!’; the blunt command supplies the customary release formula.
notes.anchor: Dü Limel, tüe-n-ä wo-n-ä gnu hesch!

notes.label: Gottlob, jetz bin-i erleest
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Thank God, now I am redeemed’; erleest expresses release or salvation from the dead man’s compelled wandering.

5865e29585640af87c7b2446c678d5d1b5dfcc45.summary: In olden times, the Lauibach flowed from the Bahlisalp in the Haslital, below the Alpwald and through the so-called Bärengraben toward Unterfluh, into its present channel.

notes.label: Gynlauine
notes.text: the local name of the watercourse or torrent whose course Stollenhans is persuaded to alter; its exact modern topographic identification is not supplied by the source.

notes.label: Port
notes.text: the prepared source's word for the bank or barrier that protected the village from the Lauibach; the form may reflect dialect or imperfect transcription, but its protective function is explicit in the sentence.

notes.label: Stollen-Hauri
notes.text: the warning spirit heard near the Stollen before dangerous floods; the tale links it to the vanished and remorseful Stollenhans, turning the man who diverted the water into a guardian who calls children to safety.

notes.label: Bueben
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘boys’; the warning call asks whether every mother's boys have made it safely home.

f6cae80fee2b401d5793c96923243ab6a6f77b35.summary: A legend preserved down to our time in several valleys of the Bernese Oberland and the Solothurn and Aargau Jura tells of a black-gray kind of snake and lizard said to be three to six feet long, proportionately very thick, and furnished with two pointed ears and two short front feet.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: literally a ‘stump-footed worm,’ a cryptid described as a thick snake- or lizard-like creature with pointed ears and short forelegs; Wurm historically includes serpents.

notes.label: Wurm
notes.text: an older broad word for a creeping creature or serpent, explicitly glossed by the source as snake.

notes.label: Stollen
notes.text: a short, thick foot or stump-like limb, offered by the source as the second element of Stollenwurm.

notes.label: Stollwürmern
notes.text: inflected plural of Stollenwurm, referring to multiple such creatures.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Drak
notes.text: an older or regional form of Drache, ‘dragon,’ cited in the bibliography’s discussion of Alpine herders’ creature categories.

0610bdaed8bac1624a8171ee89e4fba4e1aa02f7.summary: A herdsman in the Gadmertal related the following: there are two kinds of Stollenwürmer—white ones with little crowns on their heads, and black ones, which are more ordinary and more common.

notes.label: Stollenwürmer
notes.text: the plural form of ‘Stollenwurm,’ retained because the tale distinguishes white crowned specimens from more common black ones.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: the local name for a short, thick, wormlike or reptilian Alpine monster, related in tradition to the Tatzelwurm; ‘tunnel worm’ would be misleadingly literal.

74bc2a95ee33dc6f0ad521db62c5bda67c04194f.summary: The little daughter of a farming family from Oberhof, a mountain farm in the Fricktal Jura near Aarau, had been charged with cutting bean poles in the Saal mountain woods and was just setting to work on the trunk of a young pine.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: a legendary Alpine crawling creature described here as short-bodied, cat-thick, gray, two-legged, and strikingly bright-eyed; the source also prints Stollemwurm once in the first paragraph, an apparent spelling variant retained in this note rather than treated as a different being.

notes.label: Nädlein
notes.text: the source's diminutive object in the comparison ‘round as Nädlein’; context requires something small and round, but the precise regional referent is uncertain, so it is not silently normalized to an assumed standard-German object.

notes.label: Neutaler
notes.text: literally ‘new thalers,’ bright silver coins used here as the comparison for the creature's unusually luminous eyes; the term conveys coin-like brightness and roundness rather than a supernatural currency.

aab983950123ecd09e19ad4732fcf09e27f49b36.summary: Many years ago, a herdboy lived in Sagens and went into the mountains day after day with the village goats.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

22060ef3581160bf2f4e9d3a1f9125e89be4dfea.summary: Whoever harms the holy storks and Rauchspiren does not live long and will one day come to the very bottom of the Rollhafen.

notes.label: Rauchspiren
notes.text: a historical regional bird-name generally associated with the barn swallow, while related Spire names were also used for swifts; the source groups these protected, house-associated birds with storks, and modern species boundaries should not be imposed too confidently on the term.

notes.label: Rollhafen
notes.text: in regional folk belief, the lowest and worst place in hell; the image is connected with a pot or vessel suspended over fire by a chain running on a pulley, making ‘the bottom of the Rollhafen’ a threat of ultimate punishment.

notes.label: Petri Stuhlfeier
notes.text: the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, used here as the traditional calendar date for the storks' return to Veltheim.

notes.label: Petri Stuehlfiertag
notes.text: the poem's Aargau-dialect form of Petri Stuhlfeier, the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter; it anchors the stork's arrival in the local ritual calendar.

notes.label: Spier
notes.text: a historical Swiss bird-name commonly used for the swift, though Spire names could overlap with swallow terminology; the poem lists it beside swallows and larks as a separate herald of spring.

notes.label: G’wundersma
notes.text: literally a ‘curious man’ or inquisitive fellow; in the returning couplet, ‘Ei ei, du G’wundersma, in Ostindia / Uf eme Schuehmachershus!’, the stork teasingly answers that it wintered ‘in East India, on a shoemaker's house,’ reflecting fanciful popular geography rather than a precise migration record.

notes.label: welschen
notes.text: the source's own context-specific verb for the storks' extremely loud bill-clattering during their assembly; it should not be confused here with the more familiar Swiss use of welsch for French- or Romance-speaking people.

notes.label: Gelüng
notes.text: a collective regional term for edible slaughter offal, especially organs from the chest such as lungs, heart, and liver; here it describes the alternative to a pound of liver in the stork's daily endowed ration.

9c16b8733a52ee823672d1975816baff5203edc6.summary: On January 11, 1828, old Moser was buried at Mayenfeld—the “Eichhölzler,” as he was commonly called.

notes.label: Eichhölzler
notes.text: the locally formed nickname of old Moser, derived from the Eichholz estate between Mayenfeld and Jenins; it identifies origin or association rather than an occupation.

notes.label: Hinter-Ehni
notes.text: a great-grandfather or more distant male ancestor; Jecklin's opening identifies Johannes Maser specifically as the narrator's great-grandfather.

notes.label: Ehni
notes.text: a grandfather or male ancestor in Swiss German; throughout the framed narrative it is the shortened kinship name for the same Hinter-Ehni.

notes.label: Geiger-Hans
notes.text: literally ‘Fiddler Hans,’ Johannes Maser's byname, earned because no one from Ilanz to Davos was said to play as beautifully.

notes.label: Podagra
notes.text: an older medical term for gout affecting the foot; it explains both the knight's incapacity and his former habit of being turned in bed.

notes.label: gut tot
notes.text: literally ‘good and dead’; the quoted expression emphasizes that the corpse is thoroughly, unmistakably dead despite the whistle.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a young nobleman or lord, here Hector Molina after inheriting his father's estate; the title carries social rank rather than the modern English sense of discarded material.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a local magistrate or chief administrative officer; Hector calls for this authority when the dispute becomes heated.

notes.label: Weibel
notes.text: a court, municipal, or administrative officer who served summonses and enforced official orders; the office's exact local powers varied.

notes.label: Baldiron
notes.text: a historical military name remembered ominously in Graubünden; calling him the ‘new Holofernes’ compares him to the tyrannical biblical general.

notes.label: Gerichtswelbal
notes.text: Jecklin's unusual historical spelling for a court officer associated with Tusis; the precise rank is uncertain, so the source title remains visible.

notes.label: Teufelsranzen
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's paunch’ or ‘Devil's belly,’ the court officer's hostile and grotesque popular nickname.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical German spelling of Chur, the present capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: zwischen Cur und Mayenfeld
notes.text: the German title or opening words of the tune Molina orders Geiger-Hans to play, meaning ‘Between Cur and Mayenfeld.’

notes.label: Katzenwinkel
notes.text: literally ‘cats' corner,’ the traditional name for the inaccessible uppermost compartment of the tower where the ape hid the money.

notes.label: Turm-Estrich
notes.text: the tower attic or loft from which the ladder rose to the Katzenwinkel; Estrich has a regional upper-floor or attic sense here, not the modern flooring-material sense.

notes.label: verrobet
notes.text: an archaic or dialectal participle meaning robbed or stolen; Jecklin places it in quotation marks when revealing that Tristram took the purse.

notes.label: Halbe
notes.text: a half-measure of alcoholic drink; the precise vessel or local volume is not specified, but the phrase depicts the fiddler's former habit of heavy drinking.

notes.label: Dökterler
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive or colloquial formation from Doktor, closest here to a folk healer or lay practitioner; Dani’s association with conjuration gives the role a magical coloring, but the word can also carry a dismissive sense such as ‘little doctor’ or ‘quack.’

notes.label: Bossen
notes.text: a Bernese dialect exclamation used twice as Dani’s emphatic verbal tic, closest in force to ‘by heavens’ or ‘well then’; its literal derivation and precise strength are uncertain from the story alone.

9295bfc4fc03ee2a2777ee06da2944661fa518c4.summary: Seven boys had become lost in the forest and in the evening saw a little light, toward which they walked.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of a traditional German-speaking house, centered here on the great stove.

notes.label: Lavetschstein
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alpine term for soapstone used to build heat-retaining stoves; the exact stone tradition is locally associated with carved household ovens.

notes.label: Menschenfresser
notes.text: literally ‘human-eater’ or ‘man-eater,’ the tale's term for its cannibalistic giant, corresponding broadly to an ogre without replacing the source's name.

d4a280f5bd162634d3aa9c29979e13289edd4720.summary: Once there was a father who had thirteen sons. He was poor and therefore had the greatest difficulty feeding them all.

notes.label: Tredicino
notes.text: a Ticinese Italianate name formed from tredici, ‘thirteen’; it marks the hero as the thirteenth and youngest son.

notes.label: Soldo
notes.text: a historical small Italian coin also familiar in Ticino; ‘and one Soldo besides’ humorously means that Tredicino is worth a little more than all twelve brothers together.

618e95ca115f9a094be833428e0aa24f774c9ac7.summary: Once a good woman was married to a Stridel. She did not know it and therefore always acted in good faith.

notes.label: Stridel
notes.text: a Valais and Alpine term for a male witch or shape-changing sorcerer, related to regional words such as Strudel or Striga; here the husband takes wolf form, but the word’s precise relationship to vampire- or nightmare-like beings varies by tradition.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

40c0ff84eeb6dc24b8541b5ebc2c60d296bc8eb4.summary: Anyone who travels from Stalden along a poorly maintained footpath toward Esch in Zeneggen finds above the little village of “zer neuen Brücke,” amid carelessly cleared brush at the edge of an open wood, a poorly maintained barn and stable beside the road.

notes.label: trieschen
notes.text: this Valais term imitates or names the lowing call a cow directs toward her calf; its exact sound and distinction from trintschen are uncertain.

notes.label: trintschen
notes.text: this is the source’s alternate term for the cow’s calf-call that summons the snake; its precise dialect range and difference from trieschen are uncertain.

notes.label: Dillen
notes.text: the source glosses Dillen as the cow’s teats or milk ducts from which the snake drinks; the word’s exact anatomical nuance is uncertain.

a02836eee4e5f5931f8b5194a53fb874343d565c.summary: A man from Mezzaselva named Xander (Alexander) Florin went with his brother to Alp Pardenn to lie in wait for foxes.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Pardenn is the named Alp where the foxes gather.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Pardenner-Boden
notes.text: the level ground or meadow associated with Pardenn; Boden identifies a particular piece of terrain here, not an indoor floor.

notes.label: Prätigau
notes.text: the German name of the Graubünden valley from which Xander comes; it is retained as the established regional name.

notes.label: himmelerden-angst
notes.text: an emphatic compound built from Himmel and Erde, ‘heaven and earth,’ meaning overwhelmingly or immeasurably afraid.

329c2783fbfd743095fb67cbe7d07fd7147e4f92.summary: While the others had frightened the child half to death and the people, as so often happens, were talking the matter over among themselves, a hunter said that he too had once heard the following story.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Gemschtier
notes.text: a Valais dialect compound meaning a chamois-creature or chamois-animal; here it is specifically a young woman magically transformed into chamois form until three hunters have aimed at her.

Source-language note: this tale is printed in highly compressed historical Valais dialect. The transformation, the three hunters, and the Milan recognition are clear, but parts of the woman's final explanation are syntactically uncertain and have been rendered conservatively rather than silently embellished.

ab7dc706958ab84c79dbb20b54a890c8c4332596.summary: A father had many children. Then another little son was born to him.

notes.label: Gevatter
notes.text: a traditional term for a godparent or a person linked to the parents through baptismal sponsorship; the mysterious man first promises to be the child’s sponsor.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a historical large silver coin-name with values that varied by jurisdiction and period; the tale first describes sacks of silver Taler.

notes.label: Scheffel
notes.text: a historical dry-capacity measure whose size varied regionally; the silver and gold are measured by quarter-Scheffel amounts rather than by a fixed modern volume.

notes.label: Marengo-Taler
notes.text: the tale’s name for gleaming gold Marengo coins, associated with nineteenth-century gold pieces named after the Battle of Marengo; no exact monetary conversion is assumed.

70ea8867aa008e3e1ef30e2b62ce02506ca7ea91.summary: When the late Bishop von Preux was still parish priest in Siders, he was summoned one night to Noës—a little village below Siders between the highway and the railway—to attend a gravely ill man.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

b123c7f4a6a34df92aa73fd5023c5567e59420a9.summary: A Maskaradengesellschaft was roaming exuberantly around Closters-Platz. Not far from the church, it met a strangely dressed man with Geissfüssen, playing a »Hand«-Orgel (accordion).

notes.label: Maskaradengesellschaft
notes.text: a costumed masquerade or carnival company moving together through the village.

notes.label: Closters-Platz
notes.text: the central settlement of Closters, the historical spelling used here for present-day Klosters.

notes.label: Geissfüssen
notes.text: goat feet; Geiss is Swiss German for goat, and the musician’s feet mark his supernatural nature.

notes.label: »Hand«-Orgel
notes.text: literally a “hand organ”; the source parenthetically identifies the portable instrument as a Harmonika or accordion.

notes.label: aufmachen
notes.text: a quoted regional expression meaning to play music for an occasion; the source explicitly supplies “Musik spielen” as its gloss.

notes.label: klepfte
notes.text: a regional past-tense form for making a sharp cracking or explosive sound when the musician stamps.

5faaa812feb754f98c9b576f23085de5b5c4551c.summary: When the Jesuits were still in Brig, I heard a professor tell his students during a walk of a strange event said to have befallen a pious brother of their society.

notes.label: Triesten
notes.text: a local field-name or agricultural area near Brig where the Jesuit brother is working; the plural form’s exact topographical referent is uncertain from the passage.

befa2c4648ef11adbc58faf6dc43362bbf2d1199.summary: Many legends tell how people were saved from death by strange signs and warnings.

notes.label: Doppelgänger
notes.text: literally a ‘double-goer,’ an uncanny living double or apparition of oneself; here it acts as a warning by entering the doomed room ahead of the traveler.

notes.label: Gornergletscher
notes.text: the Gorner Glacier near Zermatt, a vast high-Alpine glacier where the disembodied warning saves Anton Biner from a moving boulder.
