94ffefa3d3b90eed71c51912d9f26cb7401a55d4.summary: About 90–100 years ago, for many years every spring a Wybervölchli came up through Wassen and Geschehen, saying that she was from Unterwalden.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person’; the recurring traveler may be human, witch, apparition, or seasonal omen, and the account deliberately does not settle her nature.

notes.label: Gstältli
notes.text: a small fitted bodice, strapped upper section, or supporting part of a traditional woman’s dress; the source identifies it as old-fashioned but does not describe its cut precisely.

notes.label: Dach
notes.text: literally a ‘roof’ or cover, here an old-fashioned striped umbrella covering, canopy, or shoulder-carried weather cloth associated with the separate umbrella stick; its exact construction is unclear.

notes.label: Lehkühe
notes.text: cows sought on temporary loan or lease, commonly under a seasonal pastoral arrangement; the woman asks for them but never visibly takes any away.

notes.label: Lanxi
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for spring; the timing of the traveler’s passage over the Gotthard is believed to foretell an early or late spring.

notes.label: Güetligaden
notes.text: the named Gaden in the Wassen forest; Gaden can mean a barn, storehouse, stable bay, or farm outbuilding, and this one functions as the traveler’s mysterious vanishing place.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

ee8a94f1851ee18da5f4619792b79f545ca0cefd.summary: There is hardly a village where this species has not been seen lying, standing, or walking along certain paths, especially at crossroads.

notes.label: Pfister
notes.text: an older southern German and Swiss occupational word for a baker; here it identifies Nuodi by his trade.

notes.label: Feldmattkäppeli
notes.text: the name of the small chapel or wayside devotional building at Feldmatt; the ending -käppeli is the Swiss diminutive of Kapelle and also appears in Lichttägelkäppeli later in the story.

notes.label: Helgenstöcklein
notes.text: small wayside devotional posts or shrines bearing a holy image; Helgen refers to saints or sacred images, while Stöcklein describes the small pillar-like form.

notes.label: Strassenhund
notes.text: literally “road dog,” the regional folkloric name for a supernatural black dog that haunts roads and crossroads; it is not an ordinary stray dog in these accounts.

notes.label: ewig Hund
notes.text: the dialectal local name meaning “eternal dog”; the nonstandard adjective ending is retained as part of the creature’s traditional name.

notes.label: Stellgässlihund
notes.text: the dog associated with the Stellgässli, a named little lane; -gässli is the Swiss diminutive of Gasse, and -hund means dog.

notes.label: Eischlebachhund
notes.text: the supernatural dog of the Eischlebach; the compound ties the guardian directly to its stream and the entrance to the Melchtal.

notes.label: Tanzlaubenhund
notes.text: the supernatural dog attached to the Tanzlaube at Sachseln, whose name literally means “dancing-pavilion dog.”

notes.label: Tanzlaube
notes.text: an open or partly open communal dancing pavilion or platform that could also host meetings and drill; Laube here is an architectural gathering space, not a modern domestic arbor.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

e8a78664221965ba001943481347df58f4e853b6.summary: Belief holds that a broad stretch of marshy meadowland near Lütwil is inhabited by all sorts of Moosgeistern and enchanted apparitions.

notes.label: Moosgeistern
notes.text: spirits of marshy or mossy ground; Moos in regional place-language can denote a bog or wetland rather than only moss.

notes.label: Eiet
notes.text: a local wetland place-name, also given as Ei, between which and the Gugge-Rain the spirit bottle is found.

dedd783779309242f93b6966db630e28c643bd23.summary: When one walks from the Domleschg valley toward Reichenau, where the two young branches of the Rhine unite, and looks across to the mountain chain forming the dividing wall between Graubünden and the cantons of Glarus and St.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning high seasonal mountain pastures and their pastoral landscapes rather than the Alpine mountain chain; three such grazing operations lie atop the Flimserstein.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpsennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen working on high pastures; here they are attacked by raiders from Glarus, and the compound stresses their pasture setting.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making; here one of them sacrifices his life sounding the alarm.

notes.label: Alphorn
notes.text: the long wooden Alpine horn traditionally used for signaling across mountain pastures as well as music; here its carrying sound summons help from the valley.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the singular of Sennen, an Alpine dairy herdsman; here the faithful Senn's blood permanently marks the rock.

notes.label: Heerkuh
notes.text: literally ‘herd cow,’ the lead or bell cow of a cattle herd; here all the stolen animals' bells are hung on this one cow to deceive the raiders.

0d270258ffc011eb20abff501fa5361c3082e4ff.summary: Along the road between Suhr and Entfelden, two villages near Aarau, lie several gravel pits filled with groundwater.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

71ffb05662261951217381d3390300707e0c885c.summary: In the great grainfields near Windisch, Emperor Albrecht was murdered by his nephew Johann and Johann’s fellow conspirators.

notes.label: Waldbrüder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brothers,’ religious hermits living outside a formal urban monastery; here two of them guard the first chapel and pray for the slain emperor.

notes.label: Fronaltar
notes.text: the principal or high altar associated with solemn worship; Agnes has the ground leveled for it when Strebel delivers his prophecy.

notes.label: Berchtoldenstaude
notes.text: the traditional name of Berchtold Strebel’s hazel shrub, whose life is said to determine how long the Königsfelden foundation will endure.

notes.label: zu nütti
notes.text: an older Swiss form meaning ‘to nothing’ or ‘of no effect’; Bullinger’s quoted wording declares the foundation had come to nothing when it was dissolved.

7f1219f01485f4a507d6571930854563b1773259.summary: Several Nachtbuben wanted to join in the customary local amusement of making the nighttime din raised with whips, chains, and bells around the houses of well-known families, in which grown girls in particular are rudely awakened from sleep by masked suitors.

notes.label: Nachtbuben
notes.text: literally ‘night boys,’ groups of unmarried young men who carried out nocturnal courting, masking, and rough customary pranks.

notes.label: Streggelenjagen
notes.text: the Freiamt and Lucerne name for the whip-, chain-, and bell-filled nighttime custom directed especially at households with marriageable young women.

notes.label: Fraufastenmittwochs
notes.text: the Wednesday of the pre-Easter Fronfasten, or Ember fast; Swiss dialect Fraufasten reflects a reinterpretation of Fronfasten and does not mean a special fast for women.

notes.label: Lebhag
notes.text: a living hedge forming a property boundary; its open gap becomes the supposed place where the hunted being can be caught.

notes.label: Jörri
notes.text: an Aargau diminutive or dialect form of Georg; his companions select him as the innocent target of their prank.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: the female Wild Hunt or bogey-like being supposedly driven into the sack; the captured cat's monstrous expansion turns the customary fiction into a supernatural punishment.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Streggelenjagd
notes.text: literally the ‘Streggelen hunt,’ the noisy masked custom of pursuing an imagined female Wild Hunt being; the title uses Jagd while the text also gives the verbal noun Streggelenjagen.

0a8d66c7effc4b45a3ac14e322ba83e1daabf780.summary: There are countless legends that mention the extraordinary physical strength of individual people in the distant past. — Some have already been cited.

notes.text: The source form Fürstbaum is understood contextually as a regional or archaic form of Firstbaum, the ridge beam of the barn.

893bb0f71a4bdc4d13f7aad4b1d66d96bd8fd43d.summary: A small, unassuming Berner Mandli often wandered about Wassen and Meien. One day in a butcher’s shop in Wassen, he saw an ox weighing nine hundredweight hanging up.

notes.label: Berner Mandli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Bernese man’ in Alemannic speech, an affectionate or belittling description of the small wandering strongman; the diminutive contrasts deliberately with his extraordinary strength.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

4ac51c157448976e3af65fbcdb17c01c54cd5186.summary: a) An older man had an extraordinarily strong son who one day happily reported that he had wrestled with many opponents during his Stubeten but had not yet found anyone who equaled him in strength.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: evening household visits or social gatherings in a Stube, often involving courtship, conversation, music, or communal work; here they also provide occasions for the son’s wrestling contests.

notes.label: Chilwi
notes.text: a regional Swiss German form of Chilbi, the church-dedication fair or village festival; the strong young man customarily visits young women there for festive food.

notes.label: Chrapfen
notes.text: an Uri dialect spelling of Krapfen, fried or baked pastries associated with festive occasions; the source does not specify their shape, dough, or filling.

345f17b5b67da6e70678d441c13a5672dd89ebd3.summary: The “great Mettier,” father of the “strong Mettiers,” had his dwelling below Platz-Langwies, in the so-called “Müller-Hause,” and owned land in the Tiejen—that is, on the Alp—where he fed his livestock in early winter.

notes.label: Tiejen
notes.text: the local name of an Alp, or seasonal high pasture, above Langwies; the source supplies no further etymology.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its seasonal livestock operation, not simply a mountain peak; the source itself uses Alp to explain the Tiejen.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: hehl
notes.text: a regional word for smooth glare ice; the source explicitly supplies Glatt-Eis as its explanation.

notes.label: Schnetze
notes.text: an unusually large open pocketknife used here to trim the branches from a young fir tree; the source defines its form but not a more precise modern knife type.

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure based on outstretched arms; here it measures loads of hay, but local historical values varied, so the fractions should not be treated as precise modern conversions.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

notes.label: Buob
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a boy or son; here it explicitly refers to Mettier’s youngest son.

notes.label: wie isch g'gange?
notes.text: the dialect question means “How did it go?”; the father asks how his son managed the downhill hay load.

notes.label: Dann kannst Du noch ein Mann werden, ich hatte g'nug, bin aber au schu a alt's, schwach's Mannli.
notes.text: the dialect means approximately “Then you may yet become a man; I had enough to do, but I am already an old, weak little man”; the father unknowingly carried the strain of both loads and understates his own strength.
notes.anchor: Dann kannst Du noch ein Mann werden, ich hatte g'nug, bin aber au schu a alt's, schwach's Mannli.

notes.label: Gebse
notes.text: a broad wooden dairy vessel or tub used for carrying or holding milk in Alpine households; Mettier carries one full vessel in each hand.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical German-speaking Swiss capacity measure whose exact volume varied by place and period; the source says each Gebse held 8-10 Mass, so no single modern conversion is secure.

notes.label: Ja, i bin nüt meh, aalt schwach's Mannli, aber doben in da Berga, da sind die rechta Manna, gönd nu ufa.
notes.text: the dialect means approximately “Yes, I am nothing anymore, an old, weak little man; but up there in the mountains are the real men—just go on up”; his comic understatement frightens the French away.
notes.anchor: Ja, i bin nüt meh, aalt schwach's Mannli, aber doben in da Berga, da sind die rechta Manna, gönd nu ufa.

notes.label: First
notes.text: the roof ridge beam being positioned upon the new stable; the source glosses it as Firstbalken, and it overlaps in this account with the longer timber called the Tramen.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: in German-language legend, a wandering scholar or student often credited with unusual learning or powers; here the traveler demonstrates extraordinary strength rather than explicit magic.

notes.label: Tramen
notes.text: the long ridge timber extending the full length of the building, into which the axe is driven as a handle for turning the First.

notes.label: Trotz dem Bündner, der das tut.
notes.text: the challenge means approximately “I defy any Bündner to do that,” or “Let a man of Graubünden do the same”; the wandering scholar boasts after turning the beam with two hands.
notes.anchor: Trotz dem Bündner, der das tut.

notes.label: Trotz dem Welschen, der das tut.
notes.text: Mettier’s answering challenge means approximately “I defy any Welsch man to do that”; Welsch denotes a Romance-speaking outsider here and does not mean Welsh.
notes.anchor: Trotz dem Welschen, der das tut.

703e9c70fa10830f99dfa218a6ea4f57e918a771.summary: There once lived a small family that scraped through life with great difficulty, although it consisted of only three people: a father, a mother, and a son about twenty-five years old.

notes.label: Napoleon
notes.text: a historical French gold coin denomination that circulated widely in Switzerland and neighboring regions, commonly a twenty-franc coin; the tale states only that the lad’s monthly wage is six such gold pieces and does not identify their exact issue.

77db2aab9d53df17210fea12c2091c8aec85feea.summary: Once a giant came in from outside to Altdorf or Bürglen and boastfully challenged the people to single combat.

notes.label: Schwingen
notes.text: traditional Swiss jacket wrestling, in which opponents try to throw one another; the tale treats the challenge as a lethal feat rather than a regulated modern bout.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine dairy cauldron normally used to heat milk for cheesemaking; here it is improbably filled with boiled Anken as a test of strength and capacity.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for butter; all four siblings drink the boiled or melted butter to reveal who can consume the most.

notes.label: Lunzi
notes.text: an Uri vessel-name here glossed by the source as a Doppelliter, a two-liter bottle or measure of wine; its exact historical shape is not described.

notes.label: Muotataler
notes.text: a person from the Muota Valley in Canton Schwyz; the title makes his valley identity central to the strongman legend.

notes.label: äs Läckli Salz
notes.text: literally ‘a little lick of salt,’ the strongman’s jokingly modest request for an enormous load; Läckli remains deliberately diminutive even when it later means seven Zentner.

notes.label: Röhrli
notes.text: a diminutive regional name for the salt container or barrel given to the strongman; the diminutive is comic, since its contents weigh seven Zentner.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight unit whose exact local weight could vary; the source specifies seven of them, so the unit is retained rather than silently converted.

notes.label: äs Seilti
notes.text: literally ‘a little rope,’ another humorous diminutive for the rope needed to carry the seven-Zentner salt load.

ecee151eb3d921b0238d1ed82d9bd5c2541efaf3.summary: Once, on his travels, a little tailor came hungry and half fainting to a Sennhof and asked for something to eat at midday.

notes.label: Sennhof
notes.text: a farm or dairy holding associated with a Senn and Alpine milk processing; here the traveling tailor receives a meal there, although the source does not define the establishment’s exact scale.

notes.label: Zigermilch
notes.text: the liquid dairy food associated with making or serving Ziger, broadly whey or a whey-based milk preparation; the tale does not specify its exact consistency, and the remaining solid is called Ziger.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese or curd product made from whey left after ordinary cheesemaking; the tailor wraps the remainder for his journey and later kills flies settled upon it.

notes.label: Hüslischnägg
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘little house-snail,’ meaning a snail carrying its shell; its retractable feelers provide the tailor’s supposed horn-blowing feat.

notes.label: Husthier
notes.text: the source’s dialectal ‘house animal’ or domestic animal; paired with Hüslischnägg, it supports the comic wordplay by treating the shell-bearing snail as an animal with a house.

notes.label: Malchis
notes.text: an unexplained name or dialect label suddenly applied to the first giant when the tailor beheads him; because the source does not introduce or define it earlier, the exact form is retained without assigning a firmer identity.

Source note: The title translates Schnitter literally as ‘Reaper,’ while the body consistently calls the protagonist Schniderli or Schnider, a little tailor or tailor; the source’s title-body contradiction is preserved rather than silently harmonized.

05077bdd5d5151256519105bebfacd88db9fcca1.summary: Toward western Switzerland, where the French-speaking and German-speaking Confederates can scarcely tell one another apart anymore and are able to speak both languages, lies beautiful Lake Biel with the large, green St.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive feudal lord or tyrannical holder of local authority; ‘tyrant’ conveys the behavior but not the historical lordship embedded in the term.

notes.label: Bosnickel
notes.text: a regional insult for a malicious rogue, brute, or scoundrel; its comic-vicious flavor is stronger and more culturally specific than any single English equivalent.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight measure whose exact mass varied by place and period; retaining it preserves the source’s quantity without imposing a potentially false conversion.

notes.label: Hüsten und Hotten
notes.text: a paired expression for traditional carters’ calls used to urge or direct draft animals, roughly comparable to ‘gee and haw’; the exact calls and directional associations vary regionally.

496324e947c0cb0cf78a4cf332ba58e3c8080577.summary: Once again—the year I do not know—the Italians intended to attack the pope.

notes.label: About this telling

c3a9f936917d940e87ce8f211ab17680ca1f141b.summary: They once brought a giant in chains to Wassen, people in Isental say. As he went up through the village, he tore stones from the paving and crushed them between his paws.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical German-speaking Swiss liquid measure, here a large serving or bottle-measure of wine; its exact capacity varied by place and period, so the source does not support a precise modern conversion.

notes.label: I will-ä wenigstens ga g'schäuwä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘At least I will go and have a look at him’; the strongman's understated remark contrasts comically with the violence of the encounter.

notes.label: Wassner
notes.text: the local demonym for a man from Wassen; the title makes the village's unnamed strongman its champion against the foreign giant.

d2f4a6a245b64267fb70dd11456e7d26397997e1.summary: Old people still know many things to tell about strong Zahner, who lived on the old road to Gauen.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine herdsmen and dairymen; the two visiting men from Toggenburg expect their pastoral strength to match Zahner's.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gasterländer
notes.text: a person from the historical Gaster region of St. Gallen, here strong Zahner's regional identity.

notes.label: fürbass
notes.text: an archaic word meaning onward or farther away; the challengers depart subdued after seeing Zahner lift the plow one-handed.

notes.label: Heudiele
notes.text: the hayloft floor or upper hay platform where Zahner mischievously places his neighbor's full-grown horse.

notes.label: Ellenreiter
notes.text: a mocking name for a tailor, literally an ‘ell-rider,’ referring to the measuring stick or ell used in the trade.

1a6741cc0b1145b2d6fdd8adebc59325904fc8d6.summary: Once there was a beautiful castle maiden who loved venison more dearly than any other food.

notes.label: Sträggele
notes.text: a central Swiss name for the female figure of this Wild Hunt pair; its associations include nocturnal, stormy, or witch-like beings, but the story gives no secure literal derivation and identifies her only as the condemned castle maiden.

notes.label: Dürst
notes.text: a central Swiss folkloric name for the male leader or figure of a nocturnal Wild Hunt; its closest contextual sense is the doomed hunter, while its literal origin and relation to other regional forms remain uncertain.

0be8370896ff6df22e285c8bfca3aa8be2c0ba0a.summary: Two girls who had a reputation for witchcraft lived on the Murgerberg. Nevertheless, a young lad often visited them, though he was never welcome.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Stubetiknabe
notes.text: a young man who attended a Stubete, an evening household gathering for spinning, sociability, and courtship; courting lad conveys the role but not the regional institution.

ec320e7a8d8bccf235215df056766130119c719a.summary: Not far from the Alp Fontanen lies the Stäfeliloch. Treasures are said to be hidden in it, but they are guarded by a dragon and therefore cannot easily be raised.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated grazing grounds or buildings, not merely a mountain peak; Fontanen is the named Alp here.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Stäfeliloch
notes.text: the local name of the treasure cave or hollow; Loch means a hole, den, or cave, while Stäfeli is a diminutive place-name element whose exact local reference is uncertain.

notes.label: Golddrachen
notes.text: literally ‘gold dragons,’ treasure-associated dragons believed to dwell where precious metal lies in Alpine rocks or caves.

4164c5a951846f63a11b8683ff517e9479ca2dfe.summary: The district of Unterseen, extending along the right side of Lake Thun toward the Nase, is said in earlier times to have stood under Austrian rule.

notes.label: Stäudlein
notes.text: this diminutive means a little shrub or sapling and names the ageless willow boundary marker of Austrian rule; its species, survival, and historical boundary role are uncertain.

2c60b0e0deaa2fe77feacd6f9c75d9463ecf7492.summary: Between Lütisburg and Mosnang still lies the hamlet of Lang-Aufeld. In the gray mists of antiquity, a proud and pleasure-loving girl lived there.

notes.label: Stöckli
notes.text: the regional name used here for the girl’s exceptionally high, narrow shoe heels; the ordinary modern sense is ‘high heels,’ but the story makes these particular heels the instrument of her posthumous penance.

notes.label: Stöckli-Meitli
notes.text: literally ‘little Stöckli girl’ in Swiss German, the local nickname of the fashion-loving dancer condemned to wear through iron high-heeled shoes; ‘girl in high heels’ loses the diminutive folkloric name.

f312b7bde4a8db3d59c8788c3f2b845132bcbcc7.summary: Once in Lötsch'n, on which Huob I no longer know, a young married couple had a small child, and it fell mortally ill.

notes.label: Huob
notes.text: a farm holding, homestead, or landed allotment; the narrator no longer remembers which one in Lötsch'n.

notes.label: Fägfür
notes.text: dialect for Fegefeuer, ‘purgatory’; the child says its earthly suffering served half an hour of punishment on its father’s behalf.

notes.label: Lötscher Mundart
notes.text: ‘Lötschen dialect,’ the German dialect of the Lötschental in Valais in which the account was told.

notes.label: Das lidend Chindli im Todbett
notes.text: Valais German for ‘the suffering little child on its deathbed,’ with Chindli an affectionate diminutive for a child.

2eada215e28db8a83c9afa313228da61d07fb876.summary: The people of Lenk once wished to build a bridge at the Sulzy, and things were then as they so often are: they had no money.

1af769504c9f1b3697430d1315b78c0949c9e668.summary: Not long after the murderer Peschol and his band of rogues had been hanged according to their deserts, the young people, that merry rabble, arranged a secret revel in the Fanoischi and made merry.

notes.label: Muoter Tschegg
notes.text: an obscure Valais-dialect protective name in Peschol’s list of the traveler’s four companions, apparently corresponding to the light carried alongside the cat, dog, and rooster; the closest literal sense and cultural referent are genuinely uncertain.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: a historical small-denomination coin used in German-speaking Central Europe, including Swiss territories; its value varied by period and place, and here its ritual importance as the godchild’s sole burial gift matters more than a modern conversion.

f0e45716fec0ba31b4ba278978c2dccc9ba3a2f5.summary: A man passed a gallows from which a criminal hung. He called upward: ‘Had you lived better, you would not be up there now.’ The one addressed then began to speak: ‘Within three days from today, you will answer to me for those words in the Valley of Josaphat.’

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

notes.label: Göttikind
notes.text: a godchild, especially in Swiss German usage; the continuing ritual bond allows the dead child to advocate for the godparent.

notes.label: Göttigeschenk
notes.text: a gift from a godfather to a godchild; the dead child says that accepting the shoes created an obligation it must now repay dearly.

18821e11ce6911d27e52860dd16a7cdaa4515c35.summary: Once there was a farmer who lived in the middle of a great forest. Before his house stretched a meadow full of flowers, where the finest grass anyone could ever find grew.

notes.label: Orco
notes.text: an Italian and Ticinese folktale term for an ogre-like supernatural monster; here it murders the princess’s family, seeks to force her into marriage, and guards the Sun Castle.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical German title or form of address for a young nobleman or gentleman; the bird queen and the Orco use it for Vittorino after his long quest.

bcb2c1deba25812e3beb874f56dd5fa24218b3a2.summary: Where the Hudelmoos lies today, a city once stood. It sank into the depths, presumably as just punishment for sins committed there.

notes.label: Hudelmoos
notes.text: the proper name of the moor where the city is said to have sunk; Moos in Swiss place-names commonly means bog or marsh rather than moss alone.

bf005e7d1822166d24e7ba5e1833e4c3676d060e.summary: There seems to be something not quite right around Lake Bichelsee, which is neither easy nor difficult to find on a map because it is so very small.

e1aceda03c2417bcc76dd6c9307722ae4fa05bb5.summary: A man from Bristen often went over to Frentschenberg z'Stubeten. A man of Frentschenberg knew this and, one night when the other was returning home from his Stubeten, lay down across the narrow path.

notes.label: z'Stubeten
notes.text: an Alemannic expression for going on an evening household or courtship visit in the Stube; here it explains the man's habitual nighttime journey to Frentschenberg.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: the inflected form of Stubete, a traditional evening household or courtship visit; the prankster waits for the visitor's return from one.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: a young man making a customary evening courtship visit, related to the practice of Kiltgang; the word identifies the frightened traveler by the purpose of his journey.

d0bd60e3cb11a698cb87de19b933f0c7654c2b20.summary: Not very long ago three sisters lived in Räzüns, one of whom, Nonna (Anna), had a thoroughly respectable young man as her “Schatz”—sweetheart.

notes.label: Schatz
notes.text: literally ‘treasure,’ a customary German term of affection meaning sweetheart or beloved; throughout the tale it identifies Nonna's young suitor.

notes.label: Jung-Volk
notes.text: literally the ‘young folk,’ the local community of unmarried or marriageable rural youths whose customary evening visits frame the courtship.

notes.label: versorgt
notes.text: here not ‘provided for’ but put away securely in the place where the magical bottle was kept, as Jecklin's own gloss explains.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Jesus Christus
notes.text: the German form ‘Jesus Christ’; writing the sacred name in place of his own disperses the witches and leaves their membership book behind.

3a81cead9369fb09232a26608b433fce49898683.summary: A man from Grabs served as a soldier in Holland. One night, he longed to know how matters stood at home.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

b6e1c680ee924719840d065e403fb7cc55ac661c.summary: The many Erdmännchen that lived around Zurzach in former times dwelt partly in whole clans and partly alone in the rock caves on both banks of the Rhine.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean helpers; here they form named communities around Zurzach and are devout churchgoers.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Mette
notes.text: a traditional late-night or very early Catholic office or service; here the bell summons the Erdmännchen to an early-morning service in Zurzach rather than to an ordinary daytime Mass.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a small, narrow, flat-bottomed boat traditionally used on Swiss rivers, especially the Rhine; the supernatural shoes resemble tiny boats at both ends.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: communal land held or used collectively by a village, comparable to a common; here the travelers must cross the whole shared tract of woods and fields.

f5ce6afcbc944416adc0872f7602cb1e68582510.summary: A hundred years ago, there was a little swineherd in a great kingdom. One noon he sat wearily beside the field and saw the plowmen in the distance sitting at their meal, busily spooning, slicing, and pouring, while he himself felt a tremendous hunger and yet was to receive nothing before evening.

ee635dfe60f84ce7169c7b72a3063cbe5581a85d.summary: Around the middle of the sixteenth century, the Swiss helped fight out many wars of religion in France and elsewhere.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-confederates,’ the historical self-designation for members of the Swiss Confederacy; it carries a stronger sense of sworn political fellowship than simply ‘Swiss.’

notes.label: Alpenkantone
notes.text: ‘Alpine cantons,’ here especially the Catholic cantons of central Switzerland whose troops served the Catholic side.

notes.label: fünf alten Orte
notes.text: literally ‘five old places,’ the early confederate cantons Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, and Zug; Ort was a historical term for a member polity of the Confederacy.

notes.label: Weinmonat
notes.text: literally ‘wine month,’ an old German name for October, the month of the grape harvest.

notes.label: Gevattersleute
notes.text: people bound as godparents, sponsors, or intimate ritual kin; the king uses the familial term warmly for his Swiss protectors.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss spelling of Banner, the cantonal or regimental standard whose loss would mean profound dishonor.

notes.label: Bündner
notes.text: a person from Graubünden, historically the territory of the Three Leagues; Stuppa's regional identity is emphasized in the anecdote.

notes.label: Reislaufen
notes.text: the historical Swiss practice of going abroad for paid military service, especially in organized mercenary regiments.

notes.label: Schweizergarde
notes.text: the Swiss Guard, the Catholic Swiss corps serving the pope in Rome; the name refers to an institution rather than Swiss guards in general.

notes.label: sächste Buech Moses
notes.text: literally ‘Sixth Book of Moses’ in Bernese dialect, sächste Buech Moses refers to a legendary grimoire associated with forbidden magic and easy wealth; the edition the boys possessed and its contents are unspecified.

notes.label: Reiti
notes.text: Reiti here appears to name an upper rack, loft, or roof-space in the tailor’s house where the haunting rumbles; its exact architectural meaning is uncertain.

notes.label: Chunscht
notes.text: Chunscht is a Bernese dialect form for the masonry stove or kitchen hearth in which the book is burned; the source does not specify its exact construction.

d649380fec9439dc92fad72360d6330ae8ba616b.summary: A sawmill has stood in the Aufeld since ancient times. A man once lived there who played music for the young people's dancing at Fasnacht and the Kirchweih.

notes.label: Fasnacht
notes.text: the pre-Lenten carnival season, a customary time for community dancing and music.

notes.label: Kirchweih
notes.text: the annual church-dedication festival or parish fair, another major occasion for village dancing.

notes.label: Säge-Giger
notes.text: literally the ‘sawmill fiddler’; Giger is a regional form of Geiger, and the dead musician's worksite and instrument become his ghost-name.

notes.label: Sagebach
notes.text: the sawmill stream in which the drunken fiddler freezes to death; the spelling distinguishes it from Säge in the title.

notes.label: heiligen Zeit
notes.text: an inflected form of ‘holy season,’ the period before Christmas when the dead fiddler's music is heard.

notes.label: Dorflinde
notes.text: the village linden tree, a traditional communal landmark; the source identifies the old Mosnang linden as the end of the ghost's route.

a50211eedd73dbe4083b43ce9cf5b624e112c420.summary: The Bornhund, a black dog with a collar, is named Bruno. Whenever the weather changes, he descends from the upper rocks of the Bornberg to the Aare.

notes.label: Bornhund
notes.text: the spectral ‘Born dog’ associated with the Bornberg; in this account the collared black dog named Bruno foretells changes in the weather and death and is even said to fly across the Aare.

notes.label: Sägehund
notes.text: literally the ‘sawmill dog,’ a spectral black poodle named for Aarburg’s Säge district and its sawmill; the source title supplies the umlauted form, while the historical body’s Sagehund appears to be an unaccented or transcription variant.

notes.label: Namensbüchlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little name book,’ glossed by the source as an old ABC primer; the ghostly dog carries it through the districts around Aarburg on New Year’s night, but the story does not explain its ritual purpose.

notes.label: Wendelbaum
notes.text: a large rotating shaft or main axle in historical mill machinery; its catastrophic breaking marks the reputedly dishonest overseer’s death.

6652ee70c474c35a32e02894e1207eeacc3c316c.summary: A tailor who liked to parade in velvet and silk, court young women, and be wherever things were especially wild and merry once went across the fields to a baptismal feast.

notes.label: About this telling

1f3371ca73e1e83434ceb940fa51e6ef01e031d6.summary: High in the alpine pastures of Isenfluh—a very remote little village that seems pasted to a rock rising above the Lütschine—there lived a tailor.

9853d4949abb368011432cd457aadb5b47ff3d2f.summary: As soon as the Feierabendglocke sounds and the herds of the quiet Alpine valley have returned home from pasture, the Talgeist begins his wandering. —

notes.label: Feierabendglocke
notes.text: the bell marking the end of the working day; its sounding also marks the herds’ return and the spirit’s departure.

notes.label: Talgeist
notes.text: literally “valley spirit,” the wandering apparition whose monthly circuit defines the story.

notes.label: Scalära-Tobel
notes.text: the Scalära ravine, described as an abode of numerous spirits; Tobel denotes a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gully.

notes.label: Heuberge
notes.text: literally “hay mountains,” upland meadow districts used for cutting and gathering mountain hay.

notes.label: Pudel
notes.text: the German word for poodle; the retained form marks one of the Talgeist’s named supernatural shapes.

notes.label: Cur
notes.text: the historical form used here for Chur, the capital of Graubünden.

notes.label: Tal-Bülli
notes.text: one variant of the spirit’s local nickname; the narrative also gives Tal-Brülli and Talwaldbrülli, forms connected with bellowing or roaring in the valley.

notes.label: z'hengert
notes.text: a regional expression for going on an evening social visit or courtship visit; the exact social purpose of this young man’s walk is left unstated.

notes.label: Gügel
notes.text: the local name of a place or rise above Molinis where the young man meets the fiery apparition.

notes.label: Tal-Brülli
notes.text: the dialect form used in the apparition’s taunt, approximately “valley howler” or “valley roarer”; it is a variant of Tal-Bülli.

notes.label: Häsch' jetz a mol de Tal-Brülli gsäha!
notes.text: Swiss German for “Now have you finally seen the Tal-Brülli?”; the dialect taunt answers the young man’s repeated wish.
notes.anchor: Häsch' jetz a mol de Tal-Brülli gsäha!

notes.label: Talwaldbrülli
notes.text: an expanded variant of the spirit’s nickname, approximately “valley-forest howler”; the source does not explain why the name varies.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or presiding official of a canton, district, or historical jurisdiction; the precise office varied by place and period.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: boundary markers or surveyed property bounds, not Märchen meaning fairy tales; the former official repeatedly examines them on local estates.

notes.label: Vorder-Schanvigg
notes.text: the lower or front part of the historical Schanfigg valley district, where the future Landammann settled.

7e99662f6df6635350986e3323e3f484f59437c7.summary: In the Canton of Lucerne, a wild valley gorge is called the Enziloch. Because of its wildness, popular imagination fills it with the spirits of all those who, rich and powerful in life, abused their power and wealth to oppress the poor, weak, and dependent.

notes.label: Enziloch
notes.text: literally the ‘Enzi hole’ or gorge, the wild Lucerne ravine serving as a place of punishment; the exact meaning of Enzi is not explained in the source.

notes.label: Talherren
notes.text: literally ‘valley lords,’ the condemned spirits of powerful men who oppressed vulnerable people in life; in ‘einen neuen Talherren,’ Talherren is the weak-masculine accusative singular of Talherr, while the plural is also Talherren.

0b02ebd9a368c7689bb330b2bbbb410d33a76822.summary: A Kobolt is said to have lived in the Tamina Gorge. This legend owes its origin to the following account by a chamois hunter.

notes.label: Kobolt
notes.text: the source’s spelling for a kobold, an uncanny household or nature spirit; here it behaves as a dangerous mountain being, while the wider term can cover less hostile spirits.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, sturdy hunting rifle or carbine associated with Alpine marksmen; the exact firearm model is not specified.

869496b837178e444df1e1c17a3ef62ade877e76.summary: These are two of the most beautiful forests in Upper Valais, where magnificent, gigantic firs spread mysterious darkness even in broad daylight.

notes.label: Taubenwald
notes.text: literally ‘Dove Forest,’ one of the two named Upper Valais forests whose darkness and disorienting spirits prompted the building of a chapel.

notes.label: St. Antoni-Wald
notes.text: literally ‘St. Anthony's Forest,’ the second named Upper Valais forest associated with nocturnal bewilderment and a protective chapel.

b7f2b5fa625826a5d2c68bb7b7a3b58c0b75b118.summary: In a village of Upper Valais, one brother did not want to allow the other to marry because the latter had chosen as his bride a person the former disliked; when no other dissuasion helped, he even gave him poison.

fb0020582c5b6b61a663164720d5d35173de4af0.summary: On a lovely spring day, a man from Mädris went with his boy, I. F.

notes.label: Maiensäss
notes.text: a mid-elevation seasonal farm or pasture occupied chiefly in spring and autumn between the valley holding and the high Alp; here it lies in the Gigerberge and is the base for the boy's excursion.

61999827c73aef8756450965659b3d846c4aca7f.summary: Two girls from Tegerfelden were walking home together from gathering grass.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Schlosshase
notes.text: literally ‘castle hare,’ the local bewitched or spectral hare associated with the ruined castle; the story hints that it is a witch in animal form but does not state the identity outright.

c62cbeb8f6770bcc3959fdd491eae6042ca62ac9.summary: At the beginning of the ninth century, marshes and forests still enclosed the Akronian and Venetian waters, and a large part of the land lay uncultivated and desolate.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Uhrenbüschel
notes.text: the source’s unusual term for a cluster or sheaf carried by a priest of Ceres, probably ears of grain appropriate to the agricultural goddess; the spelling and exact object are uncertain.

notes.label: Herodul
notes.text: an older form of hierodule, a temple servant or sacred slave in an ancient cult; here the figure dances and gestures before the image of Isis, but rank and gender are not specified.

notes.label: Iststempel
notes.text: the form printed near the end for the temple previously called the Isistempel; it appears to be a textual or typographical variant, and the translation preserves it without asserting a separate deity or building.

82ea621f231406d9d1c8528ffcded5954ff40ea2.summary: A girl from Twann was once making hay in a meadow not far from the Schlossfluh on Lake Biel when a stranger approached her, handsome and splendidly dressed.

notes.label: Schlossfluh
notes.text: literally ‘castle crag’ or ‘castle cliff’; Fluh is a Swiss landscape word for a steep rock face or crag, here the supernatural rock above Twann that opens into the tempters' hall.

d6d9a7deaf73f48b0eda9c0aa02f75d82e0206cc.summary: A quarter-hour outside Vättis lies the Gaspus estate. In former times, witches' dances were also held there.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Männli
notes.text: literally ‘little man’; to do the Männli is an animal trick of sitting or standing upright in a begging, humanlike posture.

notes.label: Viehtreiber
notes.text: a cattle drover who drives livestock over distance, explaining the hunter's later journey from Switzerland to Milan.

a16b3caaa4c7c25e9ed0578d6ae45394093f78d0.summary: Anyone wishing today to travel to the sunny south, to Italy, ‘where the myrtle stands still and the laurel rises high,’ as the poet sings so beautifully, simply boards the railway and in a flash passes through the Gotthard mountains.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: pack-animal drivers and carriers who transported goods across Alpine passes; they were central to traffic over the Gotthard before modern roads and railways.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: a German-Swiss name for Romance-speaking lands; here it means Italian-speaking country south of the Gotthard, not a modern political jurisdiction.

notes.label: stiebenden Steg
notes.text: the source's inflected form of stiebender Steg, literally the ‘spraying’ or ‘mist-whipped walkway,’ an exposed early path through the Schöllenen beside the foaming Reuss.

notes.label: Urner
notes.text: the people of the canton of Uri; the legend celebrates their communal cunning in outwitting the Devil.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: the traditional open-air assembly in which eligible cantonal citizens vote directly on public business.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional title of the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity; here he both leads the assembly and negotiates the bargain.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Teufelsbrücke
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's Bridge,’ the Uri name for the bridge across the Schöllenen gorge whose construction this legend attributes to a bargain with the Devil.

notes.label: Teufelsstein
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's Stone,’ the enormous boulder below Göschenen that the Devil intended to use against the bridge.

e2f523d0b95204dc94a0f8670b04158ac87bd648.summary: At Wabern near Bern, there formerly stood a mighty glacial erratic of gneiss known by the name Teufelsbürde.

notes.label: Teufelsbürde
notes.text: literally ‘Devil’s burden,’ the traditional name of the gneiss boulder said to have fallen when divine lightning stopped Satan; it identifies both the landmark and its legendary origin.

d9095672dc24d2f11e51286799072d4027d648c3.summary: The little village of Mellikon lies in the Zurzach district near the Rhine.

notes.label: Teufelsloch
notes.text: literally ‘Devil’s Hole,’ the local name for the deep, unfillable rocky sinkhole on the Neuburgerhalde; the legend explains it as the collapse left when the underground little folk depart.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like subterranean beings of German-speaking Swiss folklore; here their underground cooking sustains the fertility and prosperity of the land above.

d4d8b728561b4f582d4a0d01ed07def077b58d9b.summary: In the southeastern head of the Melchtal, between firs and the Aabach at the foot of the Glogghüs and Ärzegg, lies the green Hochalp or Wildi Melchsee, with a Sennendorf and a chapel in which worship is held for the Älplern during summer.—A mirror-bright Alpsee heightens the charm of the scene.

notes.label: Hochalp
notes.text: a high-elevation seasonal pasture, here used as an alternate name for the Wildi Melchsee pastoral settlement.

notes.label: Wildi Melchsee
notes.text: the historic local form for Melchsee-Frutt's high-pasture and lake area; Wildi marks the upper or wild locality rather than describing the lake as ferocious.

notes.label: Sennendorf
notes.text: literally ‘dairymen's village,’ a cluster of seasonal Alpine huts occupied by Sennen and their households or crews.

notes.label: Älplern
notes.text: an inflected plural of Älpler, people who live or work seasonally on an Alp and attend the chapel's summer services.

notes.label: Alpsee
notes.text: a high-pasture mountain lake, here the mirror-bright water beside the chapel.

notes.label: Teufelssprung
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's leap,’ both the stone's name and the leap that leaves the hoof marks when the Devil misses the chapel.

notes.label: Tossen
notes.text: a regional word for a rocky prominence, crag, or projecting height from which the Devil is said to jump.

notes.label: Geissfüsse
notes.text: goat's feet or cloven goat hooves, the traditionally diabolical footprints impressed in the stone.

5de84b954f55759f2607a87ecae9dd951f2ce848.summary: A short Wegstunde outside Vals-Platz, close beside the road to Lugnez, the traveler finds a large upright block of rock, on whose summit a little fir tree quite merrily enjoys its existence. — Among the Valser it is known by the name Teufelsstein. — A legend is told of it:

notes.label: Wegstunde
notes.text: an old measure of travel distance based on approximately an hour’s walk; a short Wegstunde indicates somewhat less than that distance from Vals-Platz.

notes.label: Vals-Platz
notes.text: the central settlement of Vals; Platz distinguishes the village center from the wider valley and municipality.

notes.label: Valser
notes.text: the people or residents of Vals; they remember Schenni as their protector and tell both explanations of the rock.

notes.label: Teufelsstein
notes.text: literally “Devil’s Stone,” the split upright boulder whose marks are attributed to the Devil, Schenni, and in the alternate account the Holy Virgin.

notes.label: überhöhen
notes.text: Jecklin’s quoted regional verb for outdoing, overpowering, or getting the better of someone; the Devil seeks to surpass Schenni and displace his authority.

d40e3ba692d15c37d542abf194a5b014222abd9d.summary: On the Belalpe above Naters, often visited by travelers and surely the loveliest in all Valais both for its airy, beautiful situation and its magnificent views, a gently roaring stream flows through the middle of the charming Alpine valley.

notes.label: Belalpe
notes.text: the historic form of Belalp, the high pasture and settlement above Naters where the marked stone lies.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: an inflected form of Alp, a high seasonal pasture and dairying landscape rather than simply a mountain peak.

notes.label: Kühmatte
notes.text: literally ‘cow meadow,’ the broad, nearly level grazing ground through which the glacier-fed stream runs.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or cluster of herding and dairying buildings; this one has nearly thirty huts and a chapel.

notes.label: Steg
notes.text: a footbridge or narrow crossing, used here both for the bridge and the locality around it.

notes.label: Teufelstritt
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's step’ or ‘Devil's footprint,’ the foot-shaped impression left in the flat stone by the supernatural leap.

notes.label: Riesigen Horn
notes.text: the named mountain point from which the Devil takes his first gigantic step; the historical spelling is retained.

notes.label: Brigerzehnen
notes.text: the historical Zehnden, or district, of Brig; the Devil's stride is imagined as spanning the whole regional jurisdiction.

notes.label: Rüffel
notes.text: the source's quoted name for a tourist destination at Zermatt, likely the Riffel area; the older or humorous spelling is retained because the precise intended site is uncertain.

e4179b16fc74bd6f0a83abf362faead9894ef6d5.summary: At the upper end of Lake Zurich, where a bridge crosses the blue water, lies the old little town of Rapperswil, almost opposite the small, delightful islands of Ufenau and Lützelau.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘confederates’ or ‘oath-comrades,’ members and troops of the Old Swiss Confederacy; ‘Swiss’ alone would lose the story’s political and historical flavor.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss spelling of Banner, the military standards representing the named cantons.

notes.label: Lamparter
notes.text: an older regional form meaning Lombards or people from Lombardy; the source immediately supplies that identification.

notes.label: Heumonat
notes.text: literally ‘hay month,’ a traditional name for July and a reference to midsummer heat.

notes.label: Büchsen
notes.text: early guns or cannon; in this siege list the exact size and type are not specified.

notes.label: Blyden
notes.text: large medieval stone-throwing siege engines, broadly comparable to trebuchets; exact construction varied.

notes.label: Tummlern
notes.text: siege devices in the source’s historical list, probably mobile throwing or assault machines; the precise form intended is uncertain.

notes.label: Katzen
notes.text: literally ‘cats,’ here a name for covered siege shelters or related assault engines, not animals.

notes.label: Handwerken
notes.text: literally ‘handworks,’ a broad historical term here for hand-operated siege equipment or tools rather than ordinary crafts.

notes.label: Schirmen
notes.text: protective screens or mantlets used to shelter attackers during a siege.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: diminutive of ‘fountain’; the narrator jokingly treats the flowing wine taps as little red fountains.

notes.label: Estrich
notes.text: in Swiss usage an attic or upper floor space; the defenders open the structure above the cellar to pour down boiling liquid.

626a2fa3212e9afef725a8a400550604fcf8bb49.summary: In the Oberfeld between Kulm and Zetzwil there once stood the town of Hegenau, which perished in an earthquake.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

42a3395b9e9f3798e3ad4b012fb67958371909d9.summary: If the thorn standing in the middle of the Birrfeld dies, a battle will occur there whose stream of blood will drive the mill at Mülligen for three days and rise above the fetlocks of horses.

notes.label: About this telling

2c332834e2f818996da351ef6cf5863f82af7bc9.summary: Many, many years ago, three journeymen left their beautiful hometown of Rapperswil on Lake Zurich in the canton of St.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

9159fc0a5220cc44aeb0312ede94f438c79fbaca.summary: Once, three young men from Rapperswil were far from home and stopped in the evening with an old motherly woman beside the road.

notes.label: Kapuzinerglöckchen
notes.text: literally ‘little Capuchin bell,’ the bell associated with the Capuchin establishment in Rapperswil whose familiar sound reveals that the young men are home.

notes.label: Morgenmette
notes.text: morning matins, an early liturgical office announced by the bell.

notes.label: Handwerksgesellen
notes.text: trained craft journeymen who have completed apprenticeship and travel for work and experience; their wandering places the second group far from Rapperswil.

notes.label: Hurdenfelde
notes.text: literally ‘Hurden field,’ the open ground near Hürden where the transported travelers awaken and erect the three memorial crosses.

69134f87ffef24469fca213dcc8bf4d507f9c114.summary: When one leaves Rapperswil by the famous bridge, passes through the Schwyz village of Hurden, and steps out of it onto the field, three wooden crosses stand alone beside the road.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

00bf5a9ec47eced1aa1a9be849cdcc5adbd64ba2.summary: On Vasecla, a high mountain peak in the Graue Hörner, stand three crosses: two of iron and one of yew wood.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical coin denomination used in Switzerland and neighboring German-speaking lands; the passage distinguishes whole and half Batzen offerings, but its value varied by canton and period and should not be given a fixed modern conversion.

notes.label: Bündnerblutzger
notes.text: a small historical coin associated with Graubünden; the compound identifies a Bündner or Grisons form of the Blutzger, whose precise value varied, and here it records the regional origin of pilgrims’ offerings.

b6672614e0498cab9a94e3f7de5d96beb3934b24.summary: According to another legend, Catillon had three pretty daughters who offered a large basket full of eggs for sale at every weekly market in Boll or Fribourg.

notes.label: Kiltgänger
notes.text: a young man attending an evening courtship visit or social gathering, related to the custom of Kiltgang; here he is one of the daughters' suitors.

notes.label: Kilter
notes.text: a participant in the same Kiltgang courtship custom; the source switches from Kiltgänger to this shorter regional form for the man who eats the magical fat.

notes.label: Kratten
notes.text: a large carrying basket, often worn or carried for farm produce; the comic transformation makes the suitor produce a full basket's quantity of eggs.

72e3301c8d0f63cda885c0c9753e372e642d4946.summary: According to popular belief, the dragon—a flying serpent—dwells unseen in steep and inaccessible mountains; naturally, no one can claim ever to have seen one. (In recent years, however, one is said to have been seen in the Mörel area.) This monster gnaws and devours the mountains' veins of gold,…

notes.label: Moosguffer
notes.text: the local Saas name for a great accumulation of landslide boulders on the valley floor; the element Guffer denotes rough rock debris in Alpine usage, while the exact derivation of the full place-name is not explained in the source.

notes.label: Täschguffer
notes.text: the corresponding local name for a mass of landslide rubble in the Zermatt valley near Täsch; it is invoked as a regional parallel to the Moosguffer, and the source gives no more precise geological definition.

afa6948f0f8f40d8233912ef3a43953455902d31.summary: which can be seen on a wall of a house on the Stalden in Bürglen, where a billeted Frenchman was murdered during the Franzosenzeit, cannot be washed away or eradicated.

notes.label: Franzosenzeit
notes.text: literally the ‘French period,’ the regional historical name for the era of French invasion, occupation, and political upheaval around 1798; the tale does not give the soldier’s date or the exact circumstances of his billeting.

c6f25b213753c52d046197e2a96d880c0f235b45.summary: A loving pair of parents rejoiced at the happy birth of a handsome, healthy little boy.

notes.label: Die häig scho äs Paar Aïgä g'macht!
notes.text: Uri dialect for an exclamation such as ‘What a pair of eyes it made!’; the source emphasizes the black cat's glaring, uncanny expression rather than supplying a literal measurement.
notes.anchor: Die häig scho äs Paar Aïgä g'macht!

notes.label: Ich ha nit chennä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘I couldn't do it’ or ‘I wasn't able’; the child reports his failed attempt without apparently understanding the supernatural danger.

notes.label: Dillbaum
notes.text: a regional building term for a heavy beam supporting or bordering the Dill, a barn's boarded floor or hayloft; one variant places the cat and rope on this beam instead of a tree.

notes.label: Ruossdiele
notes.text: literally a soot-darkened loft floor or boarded level above the hearth or stable area; another variant locates the episode at a beam there, though the building's exact arrangement is not described.

e6772f8ac9e0e93c71ccb71f4893ca64a1b56b10.summary: At the back of the Källi, a farmer had slaughtered an animal and thrown the entrails onto the manure heap.

notes.label: Doktor Dubi
notes.text: the byname of a locally renowned herbal healer and cunning man, not necessarily a university-trained physician; he recognizes and counters the fox-women’s magic.

6a74b7072d56a60c188145ecbff755dc1de7aed3.summary: In ancient times, three giants lived near Iseltwald on Lake Brienz. They were tremendously strong and dressed in wolf and bear skins.

notes.label: About this telling

d27f729efcb4f26d95c740a1f19e613016a9c784.summary: Something strange once happened at Wolhusen in Lucerne territory. In former times a castle stood there, inhabited by a malicious Zwingherr.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: a coercive feudal lord or petty tyrant; the repeated title emphasizes rule by force rather than identifying a neutral castle owner.

notes.label: Ziehrind
notes.text: literally a draft bovine, the farmer's single ox or cow used for pulling loads and plainly inadequate for the huge trunk.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Hüh und Hott
notes.text: traditional German-speaking teamster calls directing draft animals one way or the other, comparable to ‘gee’ and ‘haw’; here they accompany the magical team's climb.

3a353ba19e92d922dc5eac51cf0bbf299b7a807d.summary: Many years ago, very wasteful and mischievous alpine hands lived on the Ruhegg Alp above Flums.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the head dairyman responsible for milk and cheesemaking on a Swiss alp; ‘alpine dairyman’ is the closest English role, but it does not fully convey the Senn’s traditional authority within the seasonal pasture household.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the Senn’s assistant in a Swiss alpine dairying household; ‘assistant dairyman’ is close, though duties and rank varied by region and pasture.

notes.label: Joggäli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Jakob, roughly ‘little Jackie,’ used here for two alpine hands and the hollow log they mockingly baptize; retaining it preserves the name shared by all three and the tale’s wordplay.

notes.label: Knochli
notes.text: literally a diminutive related to ‘little bone,’ the alternative local name given to Joggäli in another version of the sacrilege; the source does not explain why the name differs or how it relates to the flaying motif.

5e0297a2dd23df73ba6ea02f74f72f92d8a5dee6.summary: People relate that one evening, the priest Alois Regli of Wassen († 1879) was returning late from Meien.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: traditional boundary lines or their physical boundary markers; the dead officials confess to falsifying them to transfer land unjustly to relatives.

notes.label: Landsmarcher
notes.text: local boundary officials or surveyors responsible for establishing and maintaining the Marchen; the title uses an English plural while the exact source term remains visible in the prose.

64270d21e77b230e2c0911001322ffa907ed38f3.summary: Once there were three little hens. The mother was called White, and her children were Gray and Black.

notes.label: About this telling

4b9a1931ed76a80f09ff4e742fc7787211980ec0.summary: 1. At the boundary between Seelisberg and Emmetten, three men in old-fashioned dress often appeared, wearing red waistcoats, short trousers, buckled shoes, and tricorn hats.

notes.label: March
notes.text: a Swiss regional word for a territorial or property boundary, boundary line, or its markers; both episodes place the uncanny men directly on that legally and folklorically charged limit.

notes.label: Weltsmannen
notes.text: literally ‘world-men,’ an Uri expression apparently describing men of immense or superhuman size; the witness says he could have walked upright between their legs, but the term’s exact regional nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: Marcher
notes.text: regional boundary-walkers or men associated with establishing and recording a March, a territorial boundary; here the gigantic apparitions solemnly retrace the border, though the source does not identify their precise former office or offense.

7c8385d362f2cb6e66065c7840abee3683fa58e1.summary: In former times, the healing springs of Baden stood under the protection and supervision of three white women.

notes.label: Verenenbad
notes.text: literally ‘Verena's bath,’ the healing spring at Baden associated with Saint Verena and especially with fertility, childbirth, and children's health.

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

notes.label: Verenenloch
notes.text: literally ‘Verena's hole,’ the older, plainer name for the same spring or bathing place before it was called the Verenenbad.

notes.label: die drei Mareien
notes.text: literally ‘the three Marys,’ the local collective name for the three white female guardians of Baden's springs; the form may evoke Christian holy women while continuing an older spring-guardian tradition, but the source does not identify them individually.

7faaec1c32103885912fc2e71afa2220d9d3d9bd.summary: At one time the village of Issert narrowly escaped a dreadful disaster. Above the village, a torrent bed descends toward the Dranse.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Ortsvorsteher
notes.text: local heads or municipal leaders charged with acting on the village's behalf; the story does not specify their number or exact legal office.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Teufelsblock
notes.text: literally the “Devil's Block,” the villagers' name for the great rock around which the unseen spirits work to destroy Issert.

notes.label: Stemme, Nikolas, und schieb
notes.text: the spirit's command, “Brace yourself, Nicholas, and push”; it directs the unseen Nicholas to help force the great rock downhill.

notes.label: Gesegnetem
notes.text: a substantivized adjective meaning “something blessed” or “blessed stuff”; the spirit uses the deliberately nonspecific word for the consecrated plant dust scattered over the rock.

notes.label: Stumme
notes.text: the source's historical substantivized term for people unable to speak; the tale treats three such villagers as embodiments of innocence and supernatural guardians, without supplying any diagnosis or other description.

35aa173f83a7e5a78dee401db1c46efd7e3e00df.summary: Once there was a girl who, for as long as she could remember, had seen her father only in sorrow.

notes.text: The source bibliography ends with the incomplete word ‘Mit’ (‘With’); the English field preserves that truncation as ‘With’ rather than silently supplying missing material.

9ab28126cf13b817dfee2a2c13375d10948f1f34.summary: On the Fideris Heuberge stood a little house in which three sisters lived. One of them was snow-white, beautiful, and good; another was an evil black witch; the third was half white and half black, half good and half evil.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Küchlein
notes.text: small cakes, fritters, or pastries, often fried in regional usage; the source contrasts their color and flour but does not specify the recipe or cooking method, so no single English food name is exact.

d57a740bb163c7182fdb2c4034de06dca807191f.summary: On the Alp Niederbauen near Emmetten in Unterwalden lie the Höllenlöcher, two chasms that disappear deep into the mountain and are said to reach down into the underworld.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Niederbauen
notes.text: the Niederbauen high seasonal pasture above Emmetten where the entrances to the underworld are located.

notes.label: Höllenlöcher
notes.text: literally ‘hell holes,’ the two deep mountain chasms believed to descend into the underworld.

notes.label: Unterwaldner Landestracht
notes.text: the regional dress and colors of Unterwalden, identifying the vast sleeping army as local liberators.

notes.label: 1800 und nu meh, nu meh!
notes.text: ‘1800 and now more, now more’ or ‘and still longer, still longer’; the dialect phrase extends the sleepers' waiting beyond the named year but is deliberately indefinite.

notes.label: roten Turm
notes.text: the ‘red tower’ in the canton of Schwyz where the sleeping army is prophesied first to appear.

notes.label: Emmenfeld
notes.text: the field or plain by Emmen near Lucerne to which the liberators will drive the enemy.

notes.label: Sankt Jakobsplatz
notes.text: St. James's Square or field, the final named point of the prophetic campaign; the exact historical site intended is not further specified.

b049588bdc13b160677b2ce5ea7125cc2922a8ae.summary: a) One day a goat boy on Seelisberg lost a goat and searched diligently for it.

notes.label: Tellen
notes.text: a regional plural built from Tell, here denoting the three sleeping founding heroes associated with the Rütli tradition rather than three people all literally named William Tell; the variants identify them collectively with the three Eidgenossen.

notes.label: wiä spat dass' syg
notes.text: dialect for asking how late it was; in this supernatural-sleeper context the answer gives year and day rather than an hour, so it asks where the present age stands in time.

notes.label: Äs isch noch ä chlei z'fruoh
notes.text: dialect for ‘It is still a little too early’; the sleeper means that the appointed crisis for the heroes’ awakening has not yet arrived.

notes.label: Wildheuer
notes.text: Alpine laborers who cut wild hay on steep, uncultivated mountain slopes, a hazardous traditional occupation; their use of the cavern grounds the legendary place in a working landscape.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: literally ‘oath-comrades’ or confederates, the traditional term for the founders and members of the Swiss Confederation; here it specifically means the three legendary founding confederates.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. notes.text: literally the ‘Portner boys’ or young men, the traditional collective name of the three powerful brothers associated with the Fuhrport at Spiringen.

notes.label: Fuhrport
notes.text: the exact name of the old property or locality at Spiringen; the footnote links it for centuries with the Gisler family but does not derive the name or make the brothers Gislers.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; the brothers drink it freshly boiled and rub it on their bodies as part of their legendary regimen for strength.

notes.label: Schwinget
notes.text: a contest of Schwingen, the traditional Swiss wrestling style in which opponents grip special breeches and try to throw one another; the giant turns this public challenge into a lethal match.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; he summons the brothers to defend Uri’s honor.
