notes.text: a large Alpine dairy or cheese-making cauldron; the depth to which each brother drinks the Anken from it becomes the mother’s measure of strength.

notes.label: Bsetzisteine
notes.text: paving or cobblestones forming the Bsetzi road surface; tearing them from the street is the giant’s first display of power.

notes.label: Röhrli
notes.text: a diminutive regional name for the salt container or barrel given to the strongman; the diminutive is comic because its contents weigh seven Zentner.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight whose exact mass varied by place and period; the seven-Zentner salt load is prodigious, but it should not be assigned a falsely precise modern weight.

notes.label: Beckli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small basin, bowl, or cup; this variant measures the extra Anken drunk by Karli, but the vessel’s capacity is not stated.

notes.text: a Swiss Alpine word for a shallow cave or shelter beneath an overhanging rock; here the goatherd sits under one when he sees the hidden door.

notes.label: Letten
notes.text: a regional word for clay, loam, or sticky earth; here the boy plants his staff in it beside the supernatural doorway.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: literally ‘goat boy,’ a young goatherd; here it identifies the witness who later swears to his vision before authorities.

88edae1ec193f81d9e8b20e96a191ddbcfac4ffa.summary: According to folk belief, in a wild mountain region of Switzerland around the Vierwaldstättersee there is a cleft in the rock where the country's three liberators, called the drei Telle, lie sleeping.

notes.text: literally ‘Lake of the Four Forest Cantons,’ the German and Swiss name for Lake Lucerne; its founding-canton associations reinforce the legend's theme of national deliverance.

notes.label: drei Telle
notes.text: literally ‘three Tells’; Telle is a regional plural of the surname Tell, and the expression turns the single national hero William Tell into a trio of sleeping liberators who will return in a crisis.

notes.text: a Swiss German term for a clucking or brooding hen; here it is the suspected transformed shape of the banished three-legged horse.

514441d484d99afcec0607ca495a9a9035048f65.summary: Once a little man from Grächen developed a fierce craving for apples and thought, “I’ll go over to the Dörfji this evening; I recently saw a tree there with splendid red apples.” The man set out at night for the Dörfji and secretly gathered as many of those apples as he could carry away.

notes.label: Dörfji
notes.text: Dörfji is the Valais dialect diminutive for a little village, the location of the apple tree; the settlement’s exact identity is unspecified.

notes.label: Tregi
notes.text: Tregi denotes the man’s carried load or carrying apparatus for the apples; its exact form and relationship to the straps are uncertain.

notes.label: Kalputraner-Briggu
notes.text: Kalputraner-Briggu is the dialect name for the Kalpetran bridge on the route toward Grächen; the tale does not specify which historical bridge structure is meant.

notes.label: Chriz
notes.text: Chriz is the dialect form of ‘cross,’ here the wayside cross at a fork where making its sign triggers remorse; the cross’s exact location and form are unspecified.

notes.label: Juogsu
notes.text: Juogsu is glossed by the source with ‘shoulder’ and appears to denote the shoulders or yoke-like shoulder straps used to lift the load; its exact morphology and equipment are uncertain.

notes.label: Puggul
notes.text: Puggul is the dialect word for the back, onto which the man tries to hoist the apples; its exact pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Bescha
notes.text: Bescha denotes the Evil One who had secretly helped carry the stolen apples; its literal derivation and exact dialect nuance are uncertain.

notes.label: Tiful
notes.text: Tiful is the Valais dialect form of ‘Devil,’ credited with making the stolen load easy to carry away but not to return; its exact Stalden pronunciation is uncertain.

4bce66e2d175aaa6952bc1877fd171c0dad2ee53.summary: An Erdmännchen was deeply fond of a good girl in Escholzmatt, in the fine land of Entlebuch, and truly wished to see her happy.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth-man,’ a dwarf-like subterranean helper in Swiss folk belief; here he advises the bride, heals her, and controls a wish-granting tinderbox, but no single English creature name conveys the same regional identity.

notes.text: a large silver crown thaler used in parts of central Europe, here filling the supernatural basin that makes the couple wealthy; coin standards varied by issuer and period, so its exact value in the tale is uncertain.

4601b3b7dccdd4b9d57744b1fa6e7545ab9e05b8.summary: On the southern side of the village of Talheim in the Jura, in the Brugg district, west of the road leading across the Schlatt and the Gislifluh toward Aarau, lies the Herdflühlein.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name for a nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; here the witch’s roaming spirit takes cat form and sits on the farmhands’ hearts until turning her sleeping body prevents its return.

3030db7aae6bc27e3796f4160367431b7e155a84.summary: When the woodworm, called a Totänührli in Göscheneralp, can be heard in the walls, people say, ‘The Toggeli tängelet,’ and it is generally said that fine weather will follow.

notes.label: Totänührli
notes.text: literally a ‘little death clock,’ the Göscheneralp name for the wood-boring insect whose tapping is interpreted as a weather sign or omen of death; the source calls it a woodworm and does not establish a modern species.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for the nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; here it appears cat-like during an episode resembling sleep paralysis and is then associated with tapping inside the wall.

notes.label: tängelet
notes.text: an Uri verb for the light rhythmic hammering or tapping associated with peening a scythe and, by comparison, the woodworm's knock; retaining it preserves the wordplay that links the invisible worker, the Tangelstock, and the wall sound.

notes.label: Tangelstock
notes.text: the small anvil or block used when peening and sharpening a scythe blade; the searchers first run to it because the sound resembles someone performing that work.

d66bfde73f1618c4ff228cb6de0ab7de5686e502.summary: Two girls were sleeping in a chamber at Schattdorf. The Toggeli came upon one of them, and in her oppression the girl reached toward her breast and got a Patsch—a soft lump—into her hands.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a Swiss German night spirit, nightmare being, or oppressive household goblin; here it manifests as a tangible mass upon the sleeping girl's chest and then leaves no trace.

notes.label: Patsch
notes.text: a regional word here for a soft, shapeless lump or handful seized from the girl's chest; the source compares its feel to a fat kitten but does not identify a stable form.

notes.label: pluderlind
notes.text: Uri dialect for extremely soft, tender, or yielding; the uncanny mass feels as soft as a well-fed young kitten.

5f33c9dda9cedfdc4c2aa06d3ad2f9c8cab6547f.summary: A man from Spiringen who had long been tormented by the Toggeli felt it creeping across his bed one night.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for the nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; this account treats it as a small bodily presence that can be trapped in bedding and escape through a hole in the wall.

19ea5173df4cc99ea7ac4b395c82bc04b30caad5.summary: 1. An unmarried man was often oppressed by the Toggeli; it was a dreadful torment for him.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name most often used for a nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; here trapping its passage transforms or reveals it as a woman who becomes a wife, so the tale deliberately blurs spirit, supernatural woman, and human household member.

notes.label: Toggäli
notes.text: the Uri dialect form used by the departing wife for the same Toggeli; preserving it marks her self-identification in the children's farewell message.

notes.label: Niderland
notes.text: literally a ‘lower land,’ the uncanny destination to which the Toggeli wife returns through the wall or floor hole; it may suggest a lower country, distant lowlands, or a supernatural elsewhere, and should not automatically be read as the modern Netherlands.

59eb0d3b041cfd80848e9e200eb4904287f48ba9.summary: Strange tales are still circulated about the so-called Nachttoggi, though less often than formerly, when it paid its troublesome visits to many a person almost regularly every night.

notes.label: Nachttoggi
notes.text: literally a “night Toggi,” the Valais name for a nocturnal pressure-spirit blamed for waking paralysis, crushing weight, and breathlessness; it resembles nightmare beings elsewhere, but the source treats its exact nature and shape as uncertain.

notes.label: Toggi
notes.text: a Swiss regional name for the oppressive supernatural being that sits on a sleeper’s heart; the closest English parallels are a nightmare spirit or sleep-paralysis hag, though the tale also gives it possible animal forms.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

df8bd405c9c47f0225c463eb303ea324e51e060c.summary: A crooked, stone-old woman lived in a small pitch-black hut near Langer Mansie.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here they trade stories about the spirit's nighttime activity.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Milchgaden
notes.text: a dairy storage room or small building where milk and milk vessels are kept on an Alp; here it is one of the places the old woman haunts.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially thick or rich cream; here the old witch mysteriously always has a supply when a farmer's cow yields none.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a Bernese Oberland name here given to the crooked female spirit of the cave; related Toggi forms can denote bogeys or oppressive spirits, but this story gives her a distinct local biography.

notes.label: Toggiloch
notes.text: literally the ‘Toggeli hole,’ the cave below the Oberlaubhorn named for the condemned female spirit; here it shelters people and goats but allows the Toggeli to steal milk.

notes.label: Horemaa
notes.text: literally something like ‘horn man,’ an obscure invocatory name in the recovery charm addressed to the Toggeli; its exact identity or relationship to the female spirit is not explained.

86c55b52e360033eff83081274a1ca4e9fe07889.summary: Northeast of the church of St. Carlo near Puschlav rises a mighty block of rock that threatens at every moment to tumble down.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the historical German name for Val Poschiavo, the southern Graubünden valley in which the rock stands.

notes.label: Sasso delle Torriglie
notes.text: the Italian place-name of the boulder, glossed by Jecklin as Türmchen-Stein, or “little-tower stone.”

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Dialen
notes.text: a regional name for female Alpine nature beings or fairies; this tale says its hostile fairies lived like Dialen but were not friendly toward people.

notes.label: leidwerchige
notes.text: an older regional adjective glossed by Jecklin as “malicious”; literally it suggests creatures that work harm or bring trouble.

30ec001b254e713c47f6f68d98a6e3cae5e8d350.summary: Above Naters on the Furka road lies the hamlet of Weingarten, in vineis. This place is not unknown in Valais history, because Landsgemeinden and council assemblies were held there; it was also the ancestral seat of a family mentioned in history as de Vineis or Weingartner.

notes.label: Landsgemeinden
notes.text: Landsgemeinden are traditional open-air assemblies of eligible citizens used for communal or cantonal decision-making; the exact jurisdiction and procedure of the meetings held at Weingarten are uncertain.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Stutt
notes.text: this Valais term is glossed by the source as a support and here marks the post or structural prop beside which the treasure lay; its exact position and construction are uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Handwanne
notes.text: the quoted term appears to denote a hand-carried trough, litter, or similar conveyance used to bring the broken man home; its precise form and literal local meaning are uncertain.

notes.label: Totebaum
notes.text: literally ‘death-tree’ or ‘dead-person’s tree,’ a Bernese regional name for a coffin; in this divination tale it appears as an omen of the young woman’s death, and its figurative force is stronger than the plain English word coffin.

ee34b68266416b49c5d011df660dea0c4f9f9b17.summary: A small brook flows beside the churchyard at St. Stephan.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Totenbächlein
notes.text: literally ‘little brook of the dead,’ the churchyard stream whose unexplained whitening is taken as a death omen for the parish.

a646a6363c4cd1b293bece9a2cf452a024542010.summary: a) At the time when ‘Pül und Pest’ reigned, the Totenfuhre had to travel every day from Wald and Gibelflüh and the surrounding farms, which then belonged to the parish of Hochdorf, over the Wirtle to the burial ground, always carrying one or more dead.

notes.label: Pül und Pest
notes.text: the source's paired phrase for an epidemic time; Pest clearly means plague, while the precise local sense of Pül is uncertain and may name another pestilential illness, so the wording is retained rather than over-specified.

notes.label: Totenfuhre
notes.text: literally ‘dead-person transport’ or ‘corpse cart journey,’ the wagon service carrying plague victims to burial; it can refer to both the vehicle's load and the grim trip.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Bildstöcklcin
notes.text: the source's spelling of Bildstöcklein, a small wayside devotional shrine or image monument; it marks where the corpse lay.

notes.label: Totenbodenwald
notes.text: literally ‘dead-ground forest,’ the local woodland name explained by the corpse lost there during the plague.

1dfe9c4d751a726ef5f72d439ee8d3c40eca2210.summary: Several years ago, a man named Johann Jos. Volken died in Bellwald and appeared four times to his son-in-law Fabian Ritz.

notes.label: Voralpe
notes.text: a lower or preliminary Alpine pasture used in the seasonal movement between the home settlement and the high alp; here it is where the dead man first appears, though the source does not specify whether Voralpe is a generic pasture stage or a particular named locality.

notes.label: Lagel
notes.text: a regional cask, keg, or carried vessel for wine and by extension its measure; the deceased owes payment for one Lagel, but the container’s capacity and whether the word means vessel or quantity are not stated.

notes.label: Federtaler
notes.text: literally a ‘feather thaler,’ named here as a church payment or coin that the dead man collected and secretly kept; its exact denomination, purpose, and the reason for the name are uncertain from the account.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Fasten-Temperwoche
notes.text: the Lenten Ember Week, one of the Catholic quarterly periods of fasting and prayer; here it supplies the liturgical time of the procession, though the story does not give the exact calendar date.

notes.label: Totengang
notes.text: literally a ‘going of the dead,’ the named procession and prescribed route along which deceased people continue to walk; it can mean both the spectral company and its passage, and here even a released soul must join it before attaining heavenly joy.

notes.label: Neptissin
notes.text: an archaic or regional female kinship word, closest here to a niece or younger female relative of Fabian Ritz; the spelling leaves the precise degree of relationship uncertain.

84ba93c84600e2acc300ace95f454cf3b55fb485.summary: In ancient times—and still in our own day—blue lights, sometimes smaller and sometimes larger, are said to be seen not infrequently on dark nights, either in open fields, beside buildings, or even inside them.

notes.label: Totenlichter
notes.text: literally ‘lights of the dead’ or ‘death lights,’ blue, twittering apparitions believed to foretell a death in the family connected with the place where they appear; the singular is Totenlicht.

0a81abe2a5d69e01741052bf9add97ea7fb2b21a.summary: An hour above the beautiful church village of Unterbäch lies a small hamlet of black huts called Im Holz, which is inhabited for only a few months in summer.

notes.label: Im Holz
notes.text: literally “in the wood,” the name of the seasonally inhabited hamlet above Unterbäch where the supernatural dance occurs.

notes.label: Talglicht
notes.text: a lamp or candle burning animal fat or tallow, the young man's ordinary light in the winter hut.

notes.label: Eiskerzen
notes.text: literally “ice candles,” meaning the little icicles hanging from the dead dancers' clothing, hair, and fingers.

notes.label: Totentanz
notes.text: literally “dance of the dead” or “Dance of Death,” here the actual nocturnal dance of spirits rather than only the European artistic motif.

notes.label: Herzgespiel
notes.text: an intimate older term for a sweetheart or beloved, used by the young man when he recognizes Kathri.

notes.label: Aletschgletscher
notes.text: the Aletsch Glacier, from which Kathri says she comes to undergo her penance.

notes.label: Quatembern
notes.text: the recurring Ember Days of the Christian calendar; the dead must dance at these appointed penitential times.

1dff83b78a48d23e1f7fc88ace2129b3798fc7a6.summary: Many people claim to have heard the Totentrommel, even some who are still alive today.

notes.label: Totentrommel
notes.text: literally the ‘drum of the dead,’ an unseen, moving drum whose muffled old marches accompany spectral processions in Valais belief; the account treats it as an audible omen and guide to the dead without specifying whether the drum has a visible player or material form.

notes.label: Waller
notes.text: an older regional word for pilgrims or wayfarers on pilgrimage; the peaceful dead move in an ordered company like quiet pilgrims.

notes.label: Beckelein
notes.text: a diminutive for a little basin or bowl; the daughter carries it to collect the pearl-like tears her mother continues to shed.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk” or “people of the dead,” the ordered midnight procession of the deceased returning past their former homes.

fdb2c599b4706e682a3d0896d23d63eee12399c8.summary: In a house in Closters, an old man lived alone. One night he heard a strange humming and murmuring before his house.

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of present-day Klosters in Graubünden.

notes.label: G'wundrigi
notes.text: Swiss German for curiosity or inquisitiveness; it is the impulse that makes the old man peer outside despite the strange sounds.

notes.label: Läuferli
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for a small sliding pane or sash within a window, and hence the opening through which the man peers at the approaching procession.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” a regional name for a spectral procession of the dead; the living people seen among it are marked for death.

e6663c5c08be26ed28ad39f48a8ebae12438637c.summary: In the year 1841, Frau Ott died suddenly in Grüsch of a stroke, in the midst of preparations for a journey.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead people” or “host of the dead,” a nocturnal procession whose appearance and grave-digging foretell a death in the household.

06f676ca12196ee4a9e6f78fc9a875e7ddd501d8.summary: Two young men from Montbiel went to Platz, in Closters, for a “Hengert,” or evening social gathering.

notes.label: Hengert
notes.text: a traditional evening social gathering or visit for conversation and companionship; the source glosses it as Abendunterhaltung, and the young men are returning from one late at night.

notes.label: Doggi-Loch
notes.text: the local name of the shorter route taken by one young man; Loch can mean a hole, hollow, gap, or constricted place, while the source does not explain Doggi or the site’s precise form.

notes.label: Büel
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for a hill or rounded rise; here it forms part of the quoted local house and route descriptions “on the Büel” and “at the Büel.”

notes.label: Äujer-Brücke
notes.text: the local bridge-name where the two young men meet again; Brücke means bridge, but the source gives no secure explanation of Äujer.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” the regional name for a collective procession or company of the dead; here only one traveler can see its black figures, while the other hears and feels their passage.

f40544f0b9e3b24aea4bd0d513a6fa5699b9e8df.summary: “It was on the evening before Christmas Day in the year 1620 (during the Austrian fighting in Bünden) when I was at the home of my Gevatter, Christen Dysli in Maladers.

notes.label: Bünden
notes.text: Jecklin’s shortened historical form of Graubünden, the territory in which the account places the Austrian fighting of 1620 and 1622.

notes.label: Gevatter
notes.text: an older kinship and address term for a godparent or someone connected through baptismal sponsorship; the exact ritual relationship between the narrator and Christen Dysli is not stated.

notes.label: G'vatt'rin
notes.text: a contracted regional feminine counterpart to Gevatter, used here for Stina (Christine); it can mean a godmother or a woman connected through baptismal sponsorship, but the precise relationship is not specified.

notes.label: Gwechte
notes.text: a regional word for a drifted or accumulated mass of snow, potentially blocking or threatening passage through the ravine; the source supplies the broader gloss “heaped mass of snow.”

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided Alpine ravine or gorge, often containing a stream; the narrator fears that driven snow may have accumulated there.

notes.label: Baldiron
notes.text: the personal name attached in Graubünden’s historical memory to the feared leader of invading Austrian forces; in this narrative he is a human wartime enemy, not a folkloric being.

notes.label: Schanvigg
notes.text: Jecklin’s historical spelling of Schanfigg, the Graubünden valley later overrun by the soldiers described in the account.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” a spectral company or procession of the dead; its sounds at both villages foreshadow the people later killed there.

64dde0b0e3594a2935c5b9a6f739d22eea3d2ce9.summary: The now-deceased J. Brüesch of Jenins had from time to time been obliged in his youth to help his father perform the night-watchman’s office and Messmer-Dienst.

notes.label: Messmer-Dienst
notes.text: sacristan or sexton service, including practical care of the church and its bells; the younger Brüesch assists his father with this work as well as the night watch.

notes.label: wind und weh
notes.text: a regional idiom for becoming dizzy, faint, or thoroughly unwell; the ghostly congregation’s confused murmuring overwhelms both witnesses.

notes.label: wegmachen
notes.text: literally to make oneself away; the source glosses it as fleeing from the church, which the frightened son tries to do.

notes.label: schlecht
notes.text: here the quoted word means sick or nauseated rather than morally bad; the smell of decay nearly overcomes the two men.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” the spectral congregation containing both deceased people and living people whose future deaths may be foreshadowed.

notes.label: Jeninser-Kirche
notes.text: literally the Jenins church; the adjectival form Jeninser identifies the village community whose church and tower the father and son serve.

d5a2bb5af07aad449303e6f468a32d851ba9f562.summary: Once the plague raged in the Prätigäu, and a distinguished family fled to a remote mountain estate, leaving a servant behind.

notes.label: Prätigäu
notes.text: Jecklin's historical spelling of Prättigau, the Graubünden valley in which the plague procession appears.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally the ‘dead folk,’ a supernatural procession showing living people in the order in which death will soon claim them.

e469ef57bf1f76a8e88b1b6c9d4b9b3de5c6d391.summary: If someone spends the night on certain autumn nights on the Alpe Novai, after the cattle have gone home from the Alpe, he sees a man come up from the Käsekeller of the Alphütte wearing a Sennenlederkappe and with his shirtsleeves rolled up.

notes.label: Alpe
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and working settlement; Novai is deserted after the cattle descend in autumn.

notes.label: Käsekeller
notes.text: the cheese cellar in which the Alp’s cheeses are stored and matured.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: the working hut on the seasonal high pasture, containing the hearth and cheese cellar.

notes.label: Sennenlederkappe
notes.text: the leather cap of a Senn or Alpine dairyman, identifying the man who rises from the cheese cellar.

notes.label: grausam laid
notes.text: a dialect phrase indicating a terribly sorrowful, pitiable, or grim expression; its precise emotional shade is not further resolved by the source.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead people” or “host of the dead,” the nocturnal procession that descends to claim someone destined to die.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker after whom the death-host sings its psalm-like song.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Neuen
notes.text: literally a “new one,” glossed by the source as a Todesgeweihter—someone marked or destined for death—whom the procession goes to fetch.

6f9e59dbb3ecc82b804c0eba2bd3e1212bbe44d1.summary: The Totenvolk moves through the village at night in long funeral processions.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally ‘dead folk,’ the regional name for the nocturnal procession containing both the departed and living people marked for imminent death.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: children born during the Fronfasten, the quarterly Ember fasts; Swiss folk belief often credited them with second sight, which here lets them see the Totenvolk.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night folk,’ an alternative name for the same spectral procession, emphasizing when it travels rather than who belongs to it.

7cc0181fcea12578622cd24b92ad5ce287cc9b3e.summary: In Valens, late in the evening, people sometimes saw ‘the Totenwibli’ slip into houses, where someone then unfailingly died.

notes.label: Totenwibli
notes.text: literally a ‘little death woman’ or ‘little woman of the dead,’ the regional female death-omen seen entering a house shortly before an inhabitant dies; the diminutive does not make her harmless.

878e69a4a7f80783e8b550522ae4cea78ea739ec.summary: In a Christian community, there is scarcely a more pleasant and indispensable furnishing than beautiful, harmonious tower bells.

notes.label: Convoco, Laudo, Voco, Depello, Nuntio, Ploro, Arma, Deum, Vivos, Nubila, Laeta, Rogos
notes.text: a Latin bell inscription assembled from verbs and objects meaning approximately ‘I gather, praise, summon, dispel, announce, and mourn—arms, God, the living, clouds, joys, and funeral pyres’; the compressed ordering allows several associations rather than one unambiguous sentence.
notes.anchor: Convoco, Laudo, Voco, Depello, Nuntio, Ploro, Arma, Deum, Vivos, Nubila, Laeta, Rogos

6e0a1f1eae58cadc41972b0900379aa835053c2c.summary: A woman went from the village of Flums toward the house on the Grossberg near St.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

53c4eea42f7ed21d57385dd9b5e39a1f95976e6f.summary: In olden times—so people say in Glarus—a splendid little milk-producing grass grew all the way up to the highest ridges.

notes.label: Stäfle
notes.text: a Glarus Alemannic plural for the successive stations, terraces, or pasture levels of an alp; the farmers can leave the lower levels to dance but must remain at the upper ones to milk.

notes.label: Tüfel
notes.text: Glarus Alemannic for ‘devil’; the farmers’ careless wish that he take the grass causes its degeneration.

notes.label: Mutteri
notes.text: the local name for the exceptionally rich high-altitude fodder grass that yields abundant milk; its precise botanical identification is uncertain.

notes.label: Fideri
notes.text: the local name for the inferior grass said to replace Mutteri after the farmers’ curse; the closest botanical equivalent is uncertain.

42d1648eef402a776c8c929505ceebc518bfcc48.summary: 1. Two councilors from the Reuss Valley, swords at their sides, were returning from a council meeting.

notes.label: z'Stubätägah
notes.text: Uri dialect for going to a Stubete, a customary evening visit or social gathering often associated with courtship, conversation, music, or shared work; the source does not specify Albin’s particular purpose.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

ed60713edba9cc41eda56598045cb80746beb7cb.summary: On the road from Niederbipp to Bannwil in the northern part of the canton of Bern lies a small beech wood.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: historically ‘heathens’ or non-Christians, but in Swiss place-lore it can also mean ancient, pre-Christian, foreign, or vanished people; here it names mysterious aristocratic revenants rather than a reliable historical community.

6375526d48ac1e9bf19a2f310734bd0dafd32a61.summary: Two traveling journeymen had walked together for an entire day without reaching a village, so they had no choice but to spend the night in the forest.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

ef831d806d988fc213ba55ebdc2bd257a64c5e44.summary: On Alp Wolzen, little flowers grow in a hollow that can be found nowhere else.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alp Wolzen
notes.text: the named high alpine pasture above Nesslau where the flowers and guarded treasure are found; Alp denotes a summer pasture and farmstead.

notes.label: der Böse
notes.text: literally ‘the Evil One,’ a traditional euphemism for the Devil that avoids naming him directly.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the alpine herdsman and dairyman responsible for livestock and cheesemaking on an Alp.

notes.label: SG
notes.text: the standard abbreviation for the canton of St. Gallen, used in the parenthetical location attached to the title.

e811ab2061e4231317114bc698cc5b616f6a1dd1.summary: Sparse remains of Hardegg Castle can still be seen on the “Härdli.” In our fathers’ time, a woman sometimes sat there at night upon a chest of money.

notes.label: Härdli
notes.text: a local diminutive place-name, roughly ‘little hard ground’ or ‘small height,’ marking the remains of Hardegg Castle; the exact topographic origin is uncertain.

5e9a1fa049635d8a817eaf80c83efdb42f69d689.summary: In a beautiful clearing amid a great beech forest, a man once found a heap of brightly gleaming gold.

notes.label: About this telling

d9bc69daa3515461098172ad04d91d049bc289bb.summary: 1. A rich farmer had three daughters and a farmhand, all of whom he kept under very strict discipline.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the first farmhand hides in one, while later versions use related compounds for particular barn spaces.

notes.label: Hafen
notes.text: an older regional word for a pot or earthenware vessel, not the modern German word for a harbor; the treasure is carried and buried in these containers.

notes.label: Das Gäld müeß da sy und da blybä, bis Einä, wo-n-äs rots Mäntäli a'het, uf-ämä wyßä Geißbock, wo keis schwarzes Häärli und nur dry Bei het, drymal drüff hin- und härfahrt!
notes.text: the exact Uri-dialect treasure-binding formula; its elaborate conditions require a red-cloaked rider and a spotless white, three-legged billy goat to cross the hiding place three times.
notes.anchor: Das Gäld müeß da sy und da blybä, bis Einä, wo-n-äs rots Mäntäli a'het, uf-ämä wyßä Geißbock, wo keis schwarzes Häärli und nur dry Bei het, drymal drüff hin- und härfahrt!

notes.label: Eisenchessli
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for a small iron Chessi, kettle, cauldron, or pot; this one serves as the buried money container rather than a dairy vessel.

notes.label: Kitziböckli
notes.text: an Alemannic double diminutive for a young male goat or little kid-buck; the heirs raise it for seven years after removing one leg.

notes.label: Grebel
notes.text: a regional digging or farm implement, probably a hoe, mattock, or similar tool; the source names it beside a shovel but does not establish its exact form.

notes.label: Schafgädemli
notes.text: literally a ‘little sheep Gaden,’ a small barn, stall, or hay-storage structure associated with sheep; the traveler sleeps in its warm hay.

notes.label: Untergaden
notes.text: the lower or livestock level of a traditional Gaden beneath its upper hay-storage space; the farmer buries his treasure in its floor.

notes.label: diä sind eiswägs wider chu! Ä b'hiät-is, wiä heig das afah rumplä-n- und g'wirbä-n-i dem Gädemli innä!
notes.text: the narrator’s exact Uri-dialect exclamation, ‘they came straight back! God preserve us, how it began to rumble and whirl inside that little Gaden’; it preserves both the protective religious interjection and the violent uncanny sound.
notes.anchor: diä sind eiswägs wider chu! Ä b'hiät-is, wiä heig das afah rumplä-n- und g'wirbä-n-i dem Gädemli innä!

notes.label: Barnen
notes.text: an interior level or hay-storage area in an Uri stable or barn; the source does not specify its precise construction, but it is large enough for the beggar to sleep there.

cd372685f303890870cb56c002989582770cc3a4.summary: A very poor man from Sils was obliged to have a wall built beside his house.

notes.label: Haselnussmann
notes.text: literally the ‘hazelnut man,’ the story's temporary nickname for the poor discoverer after the enchanted nuts first become gold in his pocket.

b49ac2f2ecec13dc2dd19e37bf396c95d103f80a.summary: On the Brigerberg, at the Bleikinen, the rich treasure of ninety-nine knights is said to lie hidden.

notes.label: Temperkind
notes.text: a local historical label applied to the poor girl; its exact social or personal meaning is unclear from this story, so it is retained rather than normalized into an unsupported description.

notes.label: Louis d'or
notes.text: historical French gold coins, here called old and Spanish by the collector; that combination may reflect loose folk nomenclature rather than a precise numismatic identification.

01aa68095ffddef26b79027872198b076b5c4640.summary: On the Furka road, which leads from Uri’s Urseren Valley over into Valais and passes the mighty Rhône Glacier, lies the little village of Weingarten.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Zwerchsack
notes.text: literally a ‘crosswise sack’ and closest here to a traveler’s shoulder bag or pack worn across the back; it belongs to the older Alemannic travel vocabulary, while the story does not specify its exact shape.

notes.label: Heimwesen
notes.text: a Swiss term for a home holding or farmstead, usually the dwelling together with its attached agricultural property; here Niggi Eggel enlarges it and buys more land, but its precise legal extent is unstated.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

3bf8580bb50142bc9c4e92cc8b934c066d59004a.summary: After Easter, a man was walking through the brush near the Strättlingen Tower on Lake Thun when he saw a maiden sitting there.

21cdf4c106d0c3788a48cae062a17888dfa651b3.summary: In the Brestenegg, a small wood at the crossroads between the villages of Suhr and Hunzenschwil, where those who died in a terrible epidemic were buried, an iron treasure chest lies deep in the ground.

notes.label: About this telling

61cc4280059e7191d856d8fc1f1ec44c7fc56e63.summary: On the hill rising east of Reinach and today covered with deciduous forest, a city stood in Roman times whose houses were built entirely of wood.

notes.label: Schauthaler
notes.text: large display or presentation thalers valued for their appearance as well as silver content; here the word emphasizes the impressive coins in the spectral chest, though their exact minting is not identified.

92d2528af21c9eca91b5340669c7e86b05d7c873.summary: Every visitor climbing to Grasburg must notice the small horizontal cave entering the southern side of the first building's wall.

notes.label: Burgbühl
notes.text: literally ‘castle hill,’ the local mound or hill at Lenk where a parallel treasure-wagon story is told.

notes.label: Emmenthaler
notes.text: the historical spelling for a person from the Emmental; here it identifies the itinerant confidence man who calls himself a treasure digger.

notes.label: Schatzgräber
notes.text: literally ‘treasure digger,’ placed in quotation marks because the Emmenthaler is presented not as a successful magician but as a swindler.

4bff9b58e28d00d5901754c74e9bd4fe6b9a7d91.summary: In the territory of the municipality of Sevelen stands the ruin of Herrenberg, in which, according to popular belief, great treasures might still be found.

notes.label: Wedel
notes.text: a named calendar or almanac sign that the treasure diggers await before beginning their rite; its exact astronomical or calendrical meaning in this St. Gallen usage is genuinely uncertain.

notes.label: obsigänt
notes.text: a Swiss German almanac term most closely meaning the moon in its ascending course, used here as a favorable condition for treasure magic; the source does not establish whether local practice distinguished this from waxing, so some uncertainty remains.

e964cedc0ea8a19f68b21f1415efc51bf37850c3.summary: If you have ever walked from the Bötzberg over the Adlisberg into the Ueberthal, you will have seen how everything around the Oelbach is dug through and torn up.

notes.label: Ueberthal
notes.text: the source's older spelling of the local Überthal valley reached over the Adlisberg from Bötzberg.

notes.label: Oelbach
notes.text: the historic spelling of the Ölbach, the stream below the supposed castle and treasure workings.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a ‘Sunday child,’ someone born on Sunday and traditionally believed to possess second sight; the earthworks are said to be evident even without that gift.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: literally a ‘quarter,’ here a fiery object or measure-shaped apparition rolling above the stream; the source does not explain its physical form.

58a1805ee1f85319266017f6c497fc954050bc09.summary: The summit of the Burghaldenberg in the Fricktal was once surrounded by the stately walls and towers of a robber baron's castle.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Wünschelruthe
notes.text: historical spelling of Wünschelrute, a divining rod; the Capuchin uses it to locate the buried treasure rather than water, reflecting a traditional ritual use beyond well-finding.

notes.label: Glücksort
notes.text: literally the ‘luck spot,’ the auspicious place selected for digging; consecrated candles and a ring of mysterious ash ritually protect this point from the treasure's hostile spirit.

notes.label: Burghaldengeist
notes.text: literally the ‘castle-slope spirit,’ the surviving supernatural presence at the Burghaldenberg; after the treasure ritual fails, its cry remains a local omen of hail.

4158bbbeb0d5c8078f3e2e005435eb9120c8abc2.summary: A farmer near Aarburg reported the following. Within my memory, a poor man lived in a small hut on the Bornberg.

notes.label: Heidenloch
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ hole,’ this is the folk-name of the Bornberg cave believed to enter the treasure vaults; its archaeology, historical naming, and actual connection are uncertain.

2d75c8a0650ebb1ecc28fbb999f7b75d816c2dd8.summary: 1. A narrow rock cave called Schwarzbälmli or Rynächtloch extends deep into the Rynächtfluh between Schattdorf and Erstfeld, and beside it, a spring-fed stream rolls its pure, clear water along at a sluggish pace.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little woman,’ often used in these Uri legends for a female apparition; here it names the cursed treasure guardian but does not define her supernatural class.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the second version locates the cursed maiden and her treasure on the Franzen Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term for a shallow cave, rock shelter, or overhanging cliff recess; here it refers back to the Rynächt cave approached by a religious procession.

889978b2b7872b90061bc207602eed00ccd6d747.summary: On the low hill of Stavel (Puschlav), where Pedenale Castle formerly stood and where in the end only a few remnants of wall and the rubble of the shattered castle could still be seen, one could notice at the summit of the hill a grille set obliquely into the wall.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the historical German name for Val Poschiavo, the southern Graubünden valley containing Stavel and Pedenale.

cf178722542ef33226fca8063cff9252a7a80bb4.summary: Beside the ruins of Olzate Castle near Poschiavo stands a small old house in which a little red dog has repeatedly been seen lying upon a chest and staring with terribly large eyes.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

6dc2f81cb50e19c2b049b31baa47c2cf795a8baf.summary: Many years ago, as night was falling, two young people, one of whom was a Temperkind, stood near this castle and spoke with each other of how a treasure was also said to be hidden here.

notes.label: Temperkind
notes.text: a person believed to have been born during one of the Ember periods and therefore able to perceive spirits, treasure apparitions, or hidden phenomena; the associated birth dates and gifts vary regionally.

notes.label: was nit sy soll, schickt sich nit wohl
notes.text: Valais dialect for roughly ‘what is not meant to be does not turn out well’; the frightened youths use the proverb to resign themselves to the redemption and treasure they failed to accept.
notes.anchor: was nit sy soll, schickt sich nit wohl

9346b71895f427dc1a10edffbb2a704435b19bdc.summary: a) ‘The old people said that there had once been a forge in the lowest passage of the castle, and even in my youth one part of it still bore that name,’ an 80-year-old man from Seedorf tells me.

notes.label: ä Schnäggästägä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘a snail staircase,’ the regional image for a spiral staircase winding down into the earth.

notes.label: Heiteri
notes.text: Uri dialect for daylight, brightness, or the visible light from the opening above; losing it marks the point at which every treasure seeker turns back.

notes.label: Versteckis
notes.text: the Swiss German children’s game of hide-and-seek; both treasure sightings arise while children explore the castle during the game.

notes.label: d'Schmittä
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘the forge’; it is the traditional name of the ground-floor passage where traces of a former smithy and the three treasure pots were seen.

notes.label: G'stapäliär
notes.text: an obscure dialect form that most likely denotes a scapular or related small devotional object worn by the child; the source’s spelling leaves the exact item uncertain, but touching some personal possession to the treasure is the operative belief.

notes.label: Nastiächli
notes.text: Uri dialect for a little handkerchief; it is offered as another personal object that could have been touched to the treasure to keep it from disappearing.

notes.label: Ringä, Ringä, Rosä
notes.text: the local wording of a children’s ring-game rhyme, broadly comparable to ‘Ring-a-ring o’ roses’; the source preserves only this refrain, not a complete verse.

notes.label: Brösmeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a crumb, speck, or tiny fragment; no one can find even the least particle of the apparent gold.

176038343dae087f31cae8c1e8790baf39211f91.summary: A poor shoemaker who had been working in a field near Campell Castle went inside the castle walls to enjoy his meager midday meal in the shade.

notes.label: About this telling

86d1b38a092e6c2ce3622b204109db6e77f2cd33.summary: In the hill on which Felsberg Castle once stood, there is said to be a chamber containing a great chest filled with all manner of precious objects; among them is a golden set of skittles.

notes.label: Frohnfasten
notes.text: an older regional form of Fronfasten, the quarterly Ember fasts or Ember days in the Christian calendar; the lord’s recurring penance takes place during them.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: literally lords who compel or oppress, a condemnatory name for former seigneurial rulers; the golden skittle set is described as their plaything.

67b6d94afa1de69b24f6ce0d46aeb9cd61470327.summary: Every fifty years, a maiden dressed in white is said to walk in Friednau Castle, wearing medieval garments and a great ring of keys at her side; she is said to bring into the sun the treasures lying in the underground vaults. — But if a curious observer appears, the maiden and all the beautiful things vanish.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

0cf5b7bf3d0fb4b100e08e4fe26ff1e2789718f4.summary: My mother's sister and her husband once went on pilgrimage to Einsiedeln. At the landing stage in Brunnen, a dark-complexioned Wybervölchli joined them and said that they had a treasure in their house that she would reveal to them if the woman gave her the dangling gold earrings and, I believe, the…

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little woman’; in this telling it marks the dark-complexioned stranger as an outsider and can carry a dismissive or othering tone, but it does not identify a specific ethnicity.

notes.label: Totäschidälä
notes.text: literally a little death's-head or tiny human skull; it appears magically inside the egg, and the source does not say whether it is a real object, an image, or an apparition.

notes.label: Duplen
notes.text: a regional plural for gold doubloons or similar high-value gold coins; the exact denomination and mint are not specified.

notes.label: Maryeli
notes.text: an affectionate Alemannic diminutive of the girl's name Marie or Maria; it identifies the innocent child chosen to address the spirit.

notes.label: Dechizipfel
notes.text: Uri dialect for the corner or tip of a blanket or coverlet; the mother tells Maryeli to offer it so the spirit will not touch and burn the child's bare hand.

notes.label: G'schäry und G'rimpel
notes.text: an expressive Uri dialect pairing for screaming, clamor, rattling, and confused commotion; the exact sounds are not separated, but they accompany the spirit's disappearance.

12cbe5fb03bbeec3093ef1b3144afcdce70ca66e.summary: One day, a white maiden appeared before Kapfenstein Castle to children at play.

notes.label: Schlossjungfer
notes.text: literally “castle maiden,” a supernatural young woman bound to a castle and its treasure; here completing her gift without interruption would also release her suffering soul.

ce76173dd538652b9693f3346cf30a2a05ec8436.summary: Above the beautiful episcopal Meyerei called “Muliniira” near Trimis stand the remains of Rauh-Aspermont Castle, where a treasure is said to lie that a man once wished to obtain.

notes.label: Meyerei
notes.text: an estate or farm administered for a landholder; here it is the bishop's property near Trimis, identified by its local name Muliniira.

notes.label: Muliniira
notes.text: the quoted local name of the episcopal Meyerei below Rauh-Aspermont; Jecklin gives no further explanation, so it is not translated conjecturally.

notes.label: reinen Jungfrauen
notes.text: literally ‘pure maidens’; in the treasure-raising condition, the phrase demands three sexually chaste unmarried women.

notes.label: Glückshafen
notes.text: literally a ‘fortune pot,’ historically a lottery or tombola prize pot; Jecklin uses it figuratively for the hoped-for treasure cache the man sets out to raise.

notes.label: gute
notes.text: literally ‘good’ or ‘virtuous’; the story's insinuating quotation marks question whether one daughter still met the demanded standard of chastity.

98ef84b382d60e07dce6025e91f08a81d54e1416.summary: Just as one enters the village of Stans from Stansstad, an old building stands on the right side of the road.

notes.label: Höfli
notes.text: a diminutive of Hof, meaning a small estate, manor, or farmstead; here it is the later local name of the former Rosenburg Castle, not simply a little courtyard.

77784259ea8dd171e6f3ac96cd0d92f565dfde50.summary: Once the poor tenant farmer’s children brought a whole lapful of splendid gold coins into the room and related that, while they were playing in the castle courtyard, a large black man wearing a white tasselled cap on his head had come out of the cellar, given the coins to them, and told them to play with them.

notes.label: Schlösslein Apro
notes.text: the source’s diminutive name for the small castle or manor of Apro; the children find its treasure in the courtyard, but the tale gives no architectural or historical description.

ee5d05ae8046213f716126c727e342f0d642421f.summary: Once there lived a poor man. In the greatest need and unable to find work, he could no longer even sustain his life.

notes.label: Alphütte
notes.text: an alpine herdsman's or cheesemaker's hut on a high pasture, here containing the fire pit where the treasure is sought.

notes.label: Blumalp
notes.text: the named alpine pasture on the Stanserhorn where the dream directs the poor man; Alp denotes a high summer pasture and its farmstead.

notes.label: Beinhaus
notes.text: an ossuary or charnel house where exhumed bones are kept on consecrated ground; returning the skull there releases its soul.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

e7aafd873cc9eaa0ddef13f2fca4d3fcac1d647e.summary: From time immemorial, legend has said that much money and treasure lies buried and hidden in the church at Closters.

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for present-day Klosters in Graubünden.

1d4dfd72ed5b5fa2afed4f8280e3a0f9ad4cd773.summary: Not very far below the pilgrimage chapel in Theel, in the so-called Priest’s Wood, a treasure is said to lie hidden in a small hollow.

d0e5cc4992a7376e469730b56e54eff50809fe9b.summary: Many rich treasures lie hidden in a mountain by Gerzensee. All these treasures are loaded on a great four-wheeled wagon whose rattling and creaking can be heard quite clearly at certain times.

notes.label: Geisterbanner
notes.text: literally a ‘spirit binder,’ a ritual specialist believed able to command, banish, or constrain spirits; he accompanies the farmer to manage the supernatural danger, though the broken silence draws him into the mountain too.

add098a82fd482d08c16446b93616601e824b0c1.summary: In the cellar of the Möttelischloss, also called Sulzberg Castle, lies an enormous buried treasure guarded by two wonderfully beautiful maidens, each of whom keeps a large dog beside her.

notes.label: Möttelischloss
notes.text: the local name of the castle also identified as Schloss Sulzberg; Schloss means ‘castle,’ while Mötteli is a proper historical name rather than a description of the treasure.

c6d0846a0bdcfe4aaa108310923c706af0718264.summary: On the Schwalmis in Isental, an entire ship full of money is hidden in the ground.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, grazing rights, livestock, and dairy work, not simply a mountain peak; Bolgen is the named pasture on which nine seasons of disciplined service are required.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

174a54148419af053044b32c59702c42859a439d.summary: Where the so-called great house at Sisikon now stands, there is said once to have been a castle from which the “Jütz of Sisikon” originated, a family that emigrated to Schwyz in the 16th century.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; Buggi and Urwängi are described as privately held Alp properties belonging to the wealthy Jütz family.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

82ffccdb0ffa98c935d001adec3eacbd85540f2b.summary: Near Rohrbach by Huttwil in the canton of Bern lie the ruins of three castles; one of them is called the Old Castle.

notes.label: Capuchin friars

499e5946268e53322f5c5f152bcb30906c9f700d.summary: In wartime, the old convent is once said to have hidden the monstrance and other precious objects.

notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

7a6a10455c9b6f232764626c31644416b3c959b4.summary: Near Strahlegg Castle, the hoof of a packhorse once happened to strike a gleaming gold coin from the earth, and the Säumer walking behind it found a considerable treasure there.

notes.label: Säumer
notes.text: a pack-train carrier who led laden animals over Alpine trade routes; he walks behind the packhorse whose hoof exposes the coin.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a historical bailiff, steward, governor, or lord's territorial official; here he asserts his lord's claim to the discovered treasure.

notes.label: Fideris-Bad
notes.text: the historic spa or baths associated with Fideris; Bad in this place-name means a bathing or mineral-spring establishment, not ‘bad’ in the English sense.

7964d51f4bd3af88b9d1a672c924fffb1747ce36.summary: A little shepherd boy was tending sheep on the Blüemlisalp. He sat beside a willow bush.

notes.label: Blüemlisalp
notes.text: literally ‘little-flower Alp’ or ‘flower Alp,’ the name of a high seasonal pasture; Alp denotes the pastoral landscape and its working ground, not merely a mountain summit.

455d91f37fc331a71ecc193b7f65438d764eecab.summary: It was around the end of the 18th century when a man who lived near the church in Closters came home late from work one evening.

notes.label: Closters
notes.text: the historical spelling used by the source for Klosters in Prättigau; the church, house, and former monastery are located there.

notes.label: z'Nacht
notes.text: Swiss German for the evening meal or supper; the man’s inability to see the meal begins the haunting.

notes.label: Täubi
notes.text: a Swiss dialect word for rage or furious agitation; the source itself glosses the man as enraged when he believes his household has mocked him.

notes.label: Schlapin
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Schlappin, the high valley and route by which the man travels from Klosters toward Montafon.

notes.label: Montavon
notes.text: a historical German form of Montafon, the neighboring valley in present-day Vorarlberg; the two Catholic priests and the transferred treasure are located there.

notes.label: im Winkel
notes.text: literally ‘in the corner,’ the traditional house-name that the narrator says remained in use at the time of writing.

notes.label: Schäfli-Guler
notes.text: Hans Guler’s local byname; Schäfli is a diminutive of ‘sheep,’ but the source does not explain why he bore it.

notes.label: Weiss-Mönch
notes.text: literally ‘white monk,’ the source’s name for the white-clad monastic apparition repeatedly seen in the converted cellar.

8eb990f8b8f5ce0495d571b679edf69083d5acd5.summary: a) The learned Uri Landammann Dr. K.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate or head of government of a Swiss canton or rural polity; Dr. K. Lusser is identified by this historical office.

notes.label: Hiena
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for the bail or swinging handle of a kettle; the diggers reach this part of the buried cauldron before the storm drives them away.

notes.label: Alpkessel
notes.text: the great cauldron used in an Alpine dairy, especially for heating milk and making cheese; imagining one filled with money gives the treasure a distinctly pastoral vessel.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive or dialect form of Kessel, a kettle or cauldron; here it is the vessel said to be full of treasure.

notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

d508994c0446e5e02644e6b91842d932b030558c.summary: A rich lord owned a large, beautiful Alp. But an evil doom lay upon it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, grazing rights, livestock, and dairy-working community, not simply a mountain peak; the curse has deprived this valuable holding of workers.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alpknecht
notes.text: a hired male farmhand serving with livestock and dairy work on an Alp; the fearless applicant succeeds where every previous worker disappeared.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: a substantial herd of cattle together with the seasonal Alpine dairy operation that manages it; the exact number of animals in this magnificent herd is not given.

notes.label: Grebel
notes.text: a regional digging implement such as a hoe, mattock, or grubber; touching either it or the shovel would have triggered the spirit's lethal test.

notes.label: Häfen
notes.text: in this Alpine German context, large pots, cauldrons, or vessels rather than harbor basins; the three containers of gold are assigned to Masses, the poor, and the farmhand.

8b51a539195471be4fc50764c441500443a9de54.summary: In one of the so-called charcoal gardens opposite Amsteg, which have now partly been converted into meadowland and bear their name because charcoal was formerly burned there, a treasure had lain buried since the time of the French.

697846cc30e7d38beb05e8befb21ea2e3acd197f.summary: a) According to the revelation of a fahrender Schüler, there are three gold mines on the upper Lungenstutz in the Maderanertal, near the place where the great wooden cross stood only a few decades ago.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a recurring folklore figure credited with occult learning and knowledge of hidden treasure; here he reveals that three gold deposits exist without giving their precise locations.

notes.label: Stümpler
notes.text: a regional label for poor smallholders, cottagers, or people eking out a modest living in the Maderanertal; the source does not define their exact legal or occupational status.

notes.label: Wildheuer
notes.text: people who cut wild hay on steep, remote mountain slopes beyond ordinary meadows, a dangerous and distinctively Alpine livelihood.

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: Swiss Alpine crystal seekers or mineral hunters who enter rock faces and cavities in search of valuable specimens; here they and their children are portrayed as poor mountain workers.

notes.label: Trychelchüehli
notes.text: a little cow wearing a Trychel, the characteristic hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; the diminutive identifies the treasure-finding animal but its age and size remain unstated.

notes.label: Kegelries
notes.text: a complete set of skittles or ninepins, often appearing as a golden treasure in Swiss legend; this version offers it as an alternative form of the buried wealth.

a78c79fa6fb3e0122be3e66a467d5796e5252c1f.summary: 1. On the Oppli-Egg[1] between Opplital and Wylerlaue, three chests of gold lie buried in the ground.

notes.label: Egg
notes.text: in Alemannic place-names, a ridge, edge, or projecting rise rather than the English word ‘egg’; Oppli-Egg names the treasure site between Opplital and Wylerlaue.

b68f45d8d132673cb22e57b6330bf26e1d2b3dca.summary: The Siwiboden lies in the north of the Saas valley on the eastern mountainside.

notes.label: Mattwaldalpe
notes.text: the Alpine pasture of Mattwald, separated from Siwiboden by the Mattwald stream; the compound Alpe means a seasonal high-pasture estate, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its pastoral economy; the curse explains why this broad and apparently well-soiled grazing land remains poor in fodder.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Rittmahl
notes.text: literally ‘riding meal’ or ‘knights' ride meal,’ a place-name explained by the troop of knights stopping to dine; the derivation is explicitly folk legend rather than documented etymology.

875541637bc1f36cca41671b4c9d4c9a5d7e8efe.summary: At Hirnisbühl, near the notorious Galgenhölzli by Nebikon, Philip Lünz was once clearing land when his Karst struck a pot shaped like one of our bronze cooking pots.

notes.label: Galgenhölzli
notes.text: literally the ‘little gallows wood,’ a locally notorious grove near Nebikon whose execution-site associations make it an ominous place for buried treasure.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a heavy hoe or mattock used for breaking and clearing soil; Philip's strike with the tool exposes the enchanted vessel.

0ef98d543a7db65343c6cb2d860c94428920fe03.summary: A farmer from Kirchdorf in the Siggen Valley had suddenly become astonishingly rich without being able to give any clear reason for it, thereby arousing his neighbors' suspicion.

notes.label: About this telling

0ff773c91cd737d7eb047ac5d76fddf1b06d7391.summary: A fahriger Schüler came to a hunter in Gurtnellen and said that he would go for a time to the Nidersee on the Leutschachalp, whereupon the lake would begin to roar tremendously.

notes.label: fahriger Schüler
notes.text: an older regional form related to fahrender Schüler, literally an itinerant student; in Alpine legend such a figure is often understood as a wandering scholar with occult or magical knowledge, as the promised treasure-raising suggests here.

190115a6c911587aea0d6471342f586cd824f041.summary: It was winter. One evening, sleds guided by strong youths sped swiftly down the slope near Waltensburg; many a youth had his girl sitting behind him on the sled.

notes.label: Burgfräulein
notes.text: literally “castle maiden,” an enchanted noble maiden associated with a ruined castle and its buried treasure; here her rescuer must withstand apparitions within magic circles until the real morning bell.

notes.label: Jörgenburg
notes.text: the castle ruin called Jörgenberg in the title and Jörgenburg in the story; the two forms refer to the same legendary site near Waltensburg.

384226e63ccf7813eccd9c25a272cb6c25c174ba.summary: On Tannen, a high and wild Alp in Obwalden belonging to the Kilcher of Kerns, there is a cave whose end no one has ever been able to reach.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working landscape rather than simply a mountain; Tannen is the named wild Alp containing the treasure cave.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kilcher
notes.text: parishioners or people belonging to a church parish; here the Kilcher of Kerns collectively hold or use the Alp of Tannen.

95372c429cdbeac087a6395fe483230b89ed7cb7.summary: A convent once stood on the “Chiteboden” below the chapel at Schönbrunn in the canton of Zug.

notes.label: Chiteboden
notes.text: the local ground-name below the Schönbrunn chapel where the convent and treasure are said to have been; Boden means ground or a level tract, but the Chite element is unexplained.

d887b5ca8af3e6c3f0bed845240d40c6bc7dfdf0.summary: On the right bank of the Rhine between Laufenburg and Bünzgen, in the rocky valley of the Antlesbach, hammer works are said to have stood until the Thirty Years' War, and ruins of walls and slag in the ground still speak for it.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, traditional quarterly periods of Catholic fasting and prayer; their liminal timing makes hidden treasure visible.

notes.label: Besegnung
notes.text: ritual blessing or making protective signs while reciting sacred formulas; the neighbors believe it would have driven the demonic guardian from the treasure.

024089f9c9453243a8921306dbd491f57110fe91.summary: Not far from the Felsenbach, where a little road branches from the Prätigau highway toward Malans, a citizen of Malans was once walking along that road toward his home village on a dark evening.
