81397d36c6d3a3cb7ff38d16ffd3d7ddb31c5137.summary: On an Alp in the Reuss valley, the cattle were never left in peace. People attributed it to a witch.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation, not simply any alpine landscape; here it is the grazing farm afflicted by the witch.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working seasonally with livestock on an Alp; here they summon the surrounding population to encircle the witch.

notes.label: Ronen
notes.text: an Uri regional word explicitly glossed by the collector as a tree stump or trunk remnant; the witch has assumed its apparent form.

52d86720add81974f88f4c24a9d80fce945f579f.summary: At every new moon, a black dog and a butcher appear in the ruins of Trostburg Castle, accompanied by loud clamor and shouting.

notes.label: Bifang
notes.text: a historical land-name for an enclosed or specially bounded piece of cultivated land or holding; here it names the site of an abandoned farmstead reached by the apparitions.

ac267d9c3091fa3d056cec0b8a91e98ee476d86f.summary: Between the villages of Gebisdorf and Birmensdorf, not far to the right of the Baden highway, stands the Gebisdorf Weintrotte in a meadow, an old, half-ruined building.

notes.label: Weintrotte
notes.text: a building housing a traditional winepress and the work associated with grape pressing; Trotte can name both the press and its press-house.

notes.label: Trottengeister
notes.text: plural ‘winepress spirits,’ blamed for reopening the press-house door whenever people lock it.

notes.label: Most
notes.text: freshly pressed and often fermenting fruit juice, here grape must produced during the wine harvest; it is not necessarily finished wine and, in other Swiss contexts, can also mean cider.

notes.label: Gueten Obig, ihr Hêre, es chömed no meh derige, und i bi denn de Choch!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Good evening, gentlemen; more of this kind are coming, and then I shall be the cook!’; the little spirit’s comic warning suggests more uncanny figures will follow, while the ladle marks his claimed role.
notes.anchor: Gueten Obig, ihr Hêre, es chömed no meh derige, und i bi denn de Choch!

notes.label: Trottengeist
notes.text: literally a ‘winepress spirit,’ a supernatural inhabitant of a Trotte or press-house; here the title uses the singular for the comic gray apparition.

9033d9ffe61df5b9cb09a59c234305d209a23a3d.summary: In former times, no citizen dared press grapes at night in the Frick Gemeindstrotte.

notes.label: Gemeindstrotte
notes.text: the municipality's communal grape-press building or press facility, shared under local arrangements rather than privately owned.

notes.label: Mostbütten
notes.text: large vats holding Most, the freshly pressed and fermenting grape juice or must; the spirit spoils it by adding water.

notes.label: Pressbett
notes.text: the bed or platform of a traditional wine press upon which the grapes or pressing assembly rest.

notes.label: Trotte
notes.text: a traditional grape press or the building housing it; in this story it names both the haunted communal press and another press lower in the village.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Weidsack
notes.text: a hunter's game bag or hunting pouch carried at the body; Weid here relates to hunting, not pasture.

notes.label: Dreiröhrenhut
notes.text: literally a ‘three-tube hat,’ an old regional hat form probably referring to a three-cornered or otherwise folded hat; its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Viertel
notes.text: literally ‘quarter,’ here apparently a traditional vessel or unit used as a comparison for the victim's enormously swollen head; the source does not specify which local Viertel measure is intended.

notes.label: Unterdörfer
notes.text: inhabitants of the lower part of the village, acting together as a neighborhood group.

notes.label: Kapuziner
notes.text: Capuchin friars, members of the Catholic Franciscan reform order, summoned here for their perceived power to exorcise the spirit.

notes.label: Mistbahre
notes.text: literally ‘manure bier,’ a farm litter or stretcher normally used to carry dung, repurposed to bear the captured spirit in its kettle.

notes.label: Schlosse
notes.text: the local name of a section of Frick; despite its resemblance to Schloss, the source explicitly uses it as the name of part of the village.

notes.label: Laube
notes.text: here a covered porch, gallery, or open-sided space attached to a house, beneath which the red dog disappears.

notes.label: Schwemme
notes.text: a watering or washing place where horses enter water; the sound of four horses there describes the apparition's noisy approach.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a gray or white horse, ridden by one of the spirit's manifestations in the brook.

notes.label: Anstand
notes.text: a hunter's stationary waiting place or concealed stand for watching game.

notes.label: Luder
notes.text: carrion or animal material placed as bait for predators; here the hunter uses a ham bone to lure foxes.

notes.label: Trottengeist
notes.text: literally ‘wine-press spirit,’ a haunting associated with a Trotte, the communal building and machinery used to press grapes.

ee4db8ebf2af0cbcc2b3a90c96792ff6e5004b5a.summary: The wine-rich village of Oberflachs has several Trotten, all of which stand deserted outside the autumn season except for one; for as long as the people of Oberflachs can remember, this one has always been inhabited by the Trottentier.

notes.label: Trotten
notes.text: wine-press houses or the presses within them, especially active during the autumn grape harvest.

notes.label: Trottentier
notes.text: literally ‘wine-press beast,’ the spectral animal haunting an Oberflachs press house; the body text uses the older spelling Trottenthier.

notes.label: Trottmeister
notes.text: the master or supervisor of a communal wine press, here remembered as dishonest in measuring grapes and must.

notes.label: Dorfthier
notes.text: literally ‘village beast,’ an animal-shaped supernatural double of the appointed night watchman; Thier is an older spelling of Tier.

notes.label: Dorf-Ammann
notes.text: a village magistrate or chief local official; the legend treats one former officeholder as a possible identity of the apparition.

5345b2dcbc0f1e48d19f0361bd923d64337649e7.summary: On the ruins of the great Roman city of Vindonissa [Windisch] in Aargau, near today’s little town of prophets, Brugg, there once lived a holy hermit named Teutbert.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

22047250906161d5fd9c423996226ae0a8824fd7.summary: Between the municipalities of Tersnaus and Camuns lies a steep, desolate Tobel called the Tränen-Tobel.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a steep, narrow Alpine ravine or gorge, often cut by a torrent; the tragedy and the voices heard afterward give this one its name.

notes.label: Tränen-Tobel
notes.text: literally “Tears Gorge” or “Gorge of Tears,” named for the weeping and calling said to rise from the lost sledders’ ravine.

notes.label: geschlittet
notes.text: an older regional verb meaning to travel or play on a sled; here a moonlight sledding party loses control above the gorge.

33fca10186b7b6509654290c6d57e37fef159997.summary: On the spot where the Turtmann Glacier now spreads its blue burdens of ice, there once lay the loveliest alp in the valley, called Blüemlisalp.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman and dairyman in charge of cattle and cheese-making on a high summer pasture; here the sinful Senn’s conduct explains the glacier’s destruction of the alp.

0c53f54b9624c3e6cfadf268098482ac0ebdabc7.summary: It seems to me as though it were yesterday that old Nef, our neighbor, told us about the Tuutier.

notes.label: Tuutier
notes.text: the regional name of a shape-shifting haunting creature whose seven animal forms each have their own cry; the name likely evokes its calling sound, but its exact literal derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Wickvögel
notes.text: a local or supernatural bird name linked in the tale to the cry Wie witt; the precise bird species, if any, is uncertain.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: an evening household gathering for spinning, music, sociability, or courtship; here the boy is traveling to such a gathering. The two dialect cries were translated by sense.

c7969574be3316e32b0f20946335a2bff19be521.summary: Die beide Brüeder — The Two Brothers

notes.label: Die beide Brüeder
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the two brothers’; the unstandardized grammar is part of the source title and its oral register.

notes.label: hüscht
notes.text: a traditional directional command to a draft animal, contrasted with hott; the pair figuratively describes two people pulling a household in opposing directions, though exact left-right assignments vary regionally.

notes.label: hott
notes.text: a traditional directional command to a draft animal, contrasted with hüscht; here it represents the other brother pulling the household the opposite way.

notes.label: Schlössli
notes.text: a diminutive meaning a little castle or manor; it names the new residence facing Altburg, not necessarily a major fortress.

notes.label: dr alt Chib u dr Verbauscht
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the old quarrel and entrenched bad blood or obstinacy; the exact nuance of Verbauscht is uncertain, but the phrase describes the brothers’ unresolved hostility.

notes.label: Armerischt
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a crossbow, corresponding to standard German Armbrust; the weapon hangs on the wall until one brother uses it to shoot the other.

516c16c38ff616b2973abdbf9673f854c1a1c2b4.summary: There once was a king who had two wondrously beautiful daughters. e8a3666ca58a4ce8db2c725d0f91f559fce35da4.summary: Once there were two herders who drove their herds onto unlike pastures. One let his livestock graze only on stony, barren ground so that abundance would not make them unruly and difficult for him to herd.

notes.label: Wiedehopf
notes.text: the hoopoe; its German name and repeated hüp! call are used to explain the first herder’s transformed bird cry.

notes.label: hüp! hüp!
notes.text: an imitative command sounding like ‘hop, hop!’ and the hoopoe’s call, eternally used by the transformed herder to summon his livestock.

notes.label: Rohrdommel
notes.text: the bittern, a marsh bird whose booming call is interpreted here as the second herder’s Oha!

notes.label: Oha!
notes.text: an exclamation used to halt or check animals, heard in the call of the transformed herder’s bittern.

85df3e1fc2c358a10fd9607f6b4dbe7ef25fe70c.summary: The two Wartburg castles in Aargau stand near the little town of Aarburg on two neighboring, graceful mountain peaks and can be seen from far away through the Winen and Aare valleys.

notes.label: Sälischloss
notes.text: the local name of the surviving castle above Aarburg, literally a diminutive ‘Säli castle’; the legend contrasts it with the ruined Wartburg on the neighboring height.

035407a62892eaa7befeeb5b538fd34d4ff56d4c.summary: “Two of us half-grown girls were tending goats in the Meiental. Two women came along, pressed tightly against one another as though welded together.

notes.label: Tschööpchen
notes.text: diminutive regional plural for short women's jackets or bodices; here the white garments reach halfway down the back, but their precise cut is not described.

notes.label: Stössli
notes.text: the narrator's comparison for the red pieces projecting beneath the sleeves, perhaps small cuffs, tabs, or padded sleeve ends; the exact garment feature is genuinely uncertain from this description.
