notes.text: Uri regional usage for destructive mountain torrents or debris-laden flood flows rushing down gullies; here the weather witches are associated with several such flows during a violent storm.

970f8aebb701a55edfbcfab1d0461debd4057a93.summary: a) There was once a man who never had enough money. One day he saw yellow-bellied newts in the water.

notes.label: Meer
notes.text: literally ‘sea,’ but here the source explicitly identifies it as the local name for a marshy place near Andermatt rather than an ocean or lake.

notes.label: Tyfelisieder
notes.text: Uri dialect for a ‘little-devil boiler’ or ‘boiler of little devils,’ the mocking nickname given to the man who mistakes the newts in his kettle for demons.

notes.label: ds Tyfälisyders
notes.text: the dialect household or family-name form derived from Tyfelisieder; it marks the man’s descendants as the family of ‘the little-devil boiler,’ not as people who literally practice the rite.

notes.label: Hagstecken
notes.text: sturdy stakes used in a Hag, a fence or enclosure; here they serve as improvised weapons against the advancing newts.

notes.label: Helfer
notes.text: a historical Swiss Catholic title for an assistant priest or curate; the account distinguishes Wassen’s Helfer from the parish priest summoned afterward.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

9f23d5e71aff937a5fd264e1f9b685ee74b650f1.summary: On the Tschiertschen Alp of Farur lies a little valley called the Täli. Many people there have heard fiddle-playing, and it was so beautiful that everyone who heard it had to go where the music seemed to come from; yet the invisible musician was always in a different place from where one expected to find him.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its livestock-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Farur is the named Tschiertschen Alp containing the little valley.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Täli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Tal, ‘valley’; it means a little valley and also serves as this place's proper name.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or cattle tender, especially one working with cattle in an Alpine pastoral setting.

notes.label: Gruben
notes.text: literally pits or hollows, here a quoted local terrain-name below the Gürgaletsch rather than a mine identified by the source.

notes.label: Curwalden
notes.text: Jecklin's historical spelling of Churwalden; the source preserves the older local form in Johann Fleisch's attribution.

notes.label: Täli-Giger
notes.text: literally the ‘little-valley fiddler’; Giger is a regional word for a fiddler, and the name belongs to the invisible musician who compels dancing.

notes.label: sturm
notes.text: a dialect adjective that Jecklin glosses as betäubt, ‘dazed’ or ‘stunned’; it describes the dancer's prolonged exhaustion and disorientation.

73bd8c34a0e3120d48ba49b335ef40f72c572bb9.summary: From the Töber to the Weinburg, the Töberhund can be seen at night, a most unwelcome companion that constantly moans and growls and looks about terribly with its fiery eyes.

notes.label: Töberhund
notes.text: literally the ‘Töber dog,’ the fiery-eyed spectral hound haunting the route between the Töber and Weinburg; the source itself links Töber with toben, ‘to rage,’ fitting the creature's moaning, growling pursuit.

6b6c64a14b2df531e41a97982a0948e1851f7d3f.summary: The highest hill on the left side of the Aargau Wigger valley, situated between the villages of Brittnau and Strengelbach, is called the Childberg.

notes.label: Töst
notes.text: the Aargau regional name of the supernatural hunter elsewhere called Türst, leader of a Wild Hunt and omen of violent or prolonged weather; the spelling identifies this local version rather than a separate ordinary word.

notes.label: Türstengjaid
notes.text: Lucerne dialect for ‘Türst’s hunt,’ the regional Wild Hunt led by Türst; Gjaid is a dialect form of ‘hunt,’ and the term links the Childberg Töst to a wider central-Swiss tradition.

7089cf4dd9d3018d591e33b578bc13c9cef0cd60.summary: The Türrlidokter was a wonder-working physician in Unterwalden.[1] A man from Uri’s Isental from whom a thief had stolen a substantial quantity of meat once sought his help and asked him to show him the thief.

notes.label: Türrlidokter
notes.text: the dialect byname of a reputed wonder-working physician in Unterwalden, identified by the source’s footnote as Kaspar Josef Christen of Wolfenschiessen; the name’s derivation is not explained.

notes.label: Tirrlilahli
notes.text: a mocking diminutive form of Türrlidokter used by the skeptical girl and pointedly repeated by the doctor; its belittling force matters more here than a literal expansion of the nickname.

e9b12062913dbd194d4f60fcbb3b5b4e7c044459.summary: St. Georgenberg near Bärschis is separated from the opposite Brügenkopf by a deep saddle, which gives it its beautiful, open position and broad view.

notes.label: ughürig Brunnä
notes.text: dialect for the ‘uncanny well’ or ‘monstrous spring,’ the water-filled Roman grotto believed to conceal treasure and a penitent soul.

notes.label: VI. Buch Mofis
notes.text: the source's spelling of the ‘Sixth Book of Moses,’ a legendary grimoire believed to contain powerful conjurations rather than a biblical book; Mofis likely reflects typographic or historical spelling.

c59df335458afbc78cdf9fc2e067332322898f56.summary: Several people in Bristen—for this was only a few decades ago—saw a fox at night for a time in the Paradiesli and elsewhere around the church; it often came across as far as Frentschenberg.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

09ffec7ee5db738db691b7692227d30feb467b85.summary: It is often related of the Nachtvolk that they stopped in cattle sheds, cut meat from one head of cattle, and ate it, although afterward nothing could be noticed amiss with the animal—unless, through some clumsiness, a little bone had gone missing.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night people,’ a folkloric company of nocturnal supernatural beings rather than an ordinary group of people; traditions differ on whether they are spirits, the dead, or uncanny wanderers.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman who tends cattle and traditionally makes cheese on a high summer pasture; the role combines herdsman, milker, and cheesemaker, so no single English job title is exact.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

705c5948675cbdc5743bbb3d4d6157734c029bb9.summary: A man from Schattdorf was reading from a book. Suddenly, a raven flew in through the open window, and it could no longer be driven away.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e5032da2daee774f6dd96c05cf62a90b23595509.summary: Late one evening, a “Frohnfastenkind” was riding from the village of Grüsch toward his home at Malans.

notes.label: Frohnfastenkind
notes.text: a person born during the Frohnfasten or Ember fast period, traditionally credited with special perception or powers concerning spirits.

notes.label: dunkeln Buche
notes.text: literally the “dark beech,” a solitary named tree and the site of one of the murderer’s crimes.

notes.label: Lanquart
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for the Landquart River.

notes.label: Malanser-Säge
notes.text: the sawmill associated with Malans, where the terrified horse briefly slows.

notes.label: Ecken-Bovel
notes.text: the locally named and ill-reputed second murder site along the route.

notes.label: Muckerei
notes.text: balking, restiveness, or stubborn misbehavior by the horse; the exact movement is shown by its refusal and anxious passage.

notes.label: Rüfe
notes.text: a debris-flow channel, torrent scar, or stony wash; the pursuing apparition finally remains behind there.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a “Sunday child,” a person born on Sunday and traditionally believed to possess luck or the ability to perceive and release spirits.

3e760d0720077cd87cd8dba70de96d38fb8d6b3d.summary: A teamster from Diepoldsau often collected his last load from the quarry at Monstein late in the evening.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c3738505519e2131791eb91ead5b96648c4a810a.summary: People formerly spoke a great deal about underground passages. As reported above, one is said to have led from the house of Kastlan Gasser in Naters to Urnäfass Castle; another from a house in Glis to beneath the church there, behind the altar of Georg Supersaxo; another from Höllenmatte to beneath…

notes.label: Kastlan
notes.text: a Valais form of Kastellan, a historical castellan or district official with administrative and judicial authority; here it is Gasser's title, not part of his given name.

0c0230f4079c838934dbd2a5af3049622e6f8e00.summary: That same herdsman who, up on Tamunz, deliberately let a small herd of cattle plunge to its death must carry it up through the Boggries to the very top amid sighs and gasps, and then, with a shuddering laugh, let it roll back down again.

notes.text: In the dialect, erfallä luh was interpreted as deliberately letting the cattle fall to their death, and joulä as howling or yodeling.

f7b3c3ea9e5ce34c6d87f1d9908820f073793314.summary: Long ago in Laufenburg, a hardworking maid served a wealthy widow. Since her husband’s death, the woman had sought to devote herself entirely to the quiet virtues of charity and had plentiful alms distributed through her maid.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

014ae23276af543903ddc317a0669e021194c2e0.summary: Among the arts of magic and witchcraft, as the people generally believe, are also the skill and power of g'stellen, that is, holding thieves fast with the stolen goods until either the owner or the person who performed g'stellen releases them again.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: g'stellen
notes.text: literally ‘to set’ or ‘to fix’; in this Valais belief it is the magical act of immobilizing a thief together with the stolen goods until the owner or spell-worker releases the thief, with the story leaving the exact rite unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senntumsgeteilen
notes.text: the closest sense is co-sharers in an alpine dairy enterprise or herd; the compound joins Senntum, an alpine dairying or herd unit, with Geteilen, people holding a joint share, while the precise legal and property arrangement is not stated here.

notes.label: Alpenvogt
notes.text: literally an ‘alpine bailiff’ and closest here to an elected alpine steward; the office carried responsibility for communal pasture or dairy property, though its exact duties and authority varied by locality.

76ed6a61b553c3361e72a49aad5172c9fc0093eb.summary: At that time, people also spoke of a spirit that occasionally made its presence known in the Plasselbschlund.

notes.label: Plasselbschlund
notes.text: the Plasselb gorge or ravine, the Fribourg landscape in which the little monster makes its presence known; Schlund evokes a narrow, throat-like chasm.

notes.label: Spielmännlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little musician’ or ‘little player,’ another locally known spirit with which the stronger bear-like being is compared but not identified.

notes.label: Ungeheuerlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little monster,’ an intentionally diminutive name for the small but exceptionally strong, fiery-eyed spirit.

notes.label: Kilt
notes.text: a traditional nighttime courting visit, especially associated with rural Alpine communities; the brothers use it in a taunt about the spirit's supposed amorous outing.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name for a nightmare or pressure spirit associated with oppressive nocturnal visitations; here the taunters treat it as the Ungeheuerlein's companion.

notes.label: Fantumli
notes.text: glossed by the source as a frivolous girl; the diminutive is part of the brothers' coarse courting taunt.

notes.label: Milchsuppenjäger
notes.text: literally a ‘milk-soup hunter,’ a mocking name that belittles someone as timid, soft, or fit only for easy quarry.

notes.label: Grossmarcher
notes.text: Josi Brügger's regional byname, identifying him as the large or prominent man from Gross March or the March locality; the source does not resolve whether size, place, or both motivated it.

notes.label: trätschen
notes.text: to trudge or shuffle away; the spirit tells the drunken brothers to drag themselves home and sleep off their intoxication.

notes.label: Föppeler
notes.text: a mocker, teaser, or trickster; the insult aptly describes a spirit that humiliates the boastful fighters from out of reach in the treetop.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

d6cb636113d0524e4320b0d87949f45f01194f6e.summary: Ask in Luthern for the shortest way to Sumiswald, and you will be told to go over Scheidegg.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal livestock pasture and dairying settlement where travelers can obtain milk and butter.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Unholde
notes.text: a malignant or monstrous supernatural being; this Scheidegg entity controls destructive weather when offended.

cdef0dcafd049ba78706c62de54189c2e5649b50.summary: Along the upper course of the Reuss, shepherd boys drove goats into the mountains.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Alphörner
notes.text: plural of Alphorn, the long wooden horn associated with Alpine herding and signaling; the tale says the ox's horns became battle instruments richly bound in silver.

notes.label: Wälschen
notes.text: an older German-speaking Swiss label for Romance-language neighbors or peoples, here apparently enemy forces to the west or south; its exact historical referent is not specified and the term can carry an othering tone.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Uri bull,’ an emblematic bull associated with the canton of Uri; although the story's champion is called an ox, its horns are linked to Uri's heraldic and martial tradition.

ff5735aaaf72b521db1c11360d37bb3e1881e44e.summary: Not far from the little town of Sargans, on the Rieter toward the railway station, lies a large spring hole called the Urtel.

notes.label: Rieter
notes.text: wet meadows or marshland, the plural regional form associated with Riet; here it identifies the low ground near Sargans station.

notes.label: Urtel
notes.text: the local name of the supposedly bottomless spring hole near Sargans; the story connects it with the lost city's name Ordelium, but does not establish a certain etymology.

notes.label: Historical Swiss measures
notes.text: Historical Swiss units varied by place and period; the same name could represent different amounts. A fathom or Klafter is a length measure, while a Juchart measures land. The translation retains historical units without assigning a falsely exact modern conversion.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland

5d934d94e44a36bc30b4209e52c1cbf0607b556f.summary: In Monbiel, a wildes Männlein likewise tended the household cows for years.

notes.label: wildes Männlein
notes.text: literally a “little wild man,” a small supernatural mountain dweller that tends cattle but avoids human homes; the term overlaps with wild folk and dwarfs, though the story gives Uzy an individual name.

notes.label: Schoppen
notes.text: a historical drinking measure and the vessel holding that amount, varying by region and period and often roughly a third to half a liter; here it denotes the serving of Veltliner wine rather than a standardized modern volume.

notes.label: Uzystein
notes.text: literally “Uzy’s stone,” the local name of the meeting place where the wildes Männlein received cattle and gifts; the tale explains the name through Uzy, but does not establish whether the name predates the legend.

081fe8522cedac96e5c95b00dc40905f65cfad3c.summary: At night, a large black dog can often be seen shambling through the streets of Mels with a rattling noise.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

8a1df0157e937268762c0748e916179fff0f8ee4.summary: For many years Vilters and Wangs were embroiled in a boundary dispute over pasture and forest in the Valeistobel.

notes.label: Valeistobel
notes.text: the Valeis ravine; Tobel is a Swiss and southern German word for a steep, often wooded mountain gully or gorge.

notes.label: Stösse
notes.text: here a regional legal and topographic term for the points where boundaries meet or for the contested boundary locations themselves; the source immediately glosses them as disputed localities.

notes.label: Alpkamm
notes.text: literally ‘Alp ridge,’ a ridge carrying high-elevation summer pasture rather than simply any mountain crest.

notes.label: Valeisloch
notes.text: literally ‘Valeis hole’ or ‘Valeis opening,’ the named place from which the spectral dog begins its prescribed journey.

notes.label: Valeishund
notes.text: literally ‘Valeis dog,’ the name of the one-eyed spectral black dog condemned to retrace the route associated with the disputed Valeis boundary judgment.

notes.label: Markt- und Tanzlaube
notes.text: literally ‘market and dance hall’; Laube here denotes a roofed or open-sided civic structure used for public market and dancing functions, not a garden arbor.

notes.label: Gwunder
notes.text: Swiss German for curiosity, often with the sense of prying or nosiness; the ghost distinguishes practical need from dangerous supernatural curiosity.

notes.label: Markenwesen
notes.text: the boundary matter or boundary case, encompassing the disputed demarcation and the legal judgment rather than a commercial affair.

74aa79c5feaac03a6d3474f887f3dca359f9b9c3.summary: Devoutly believing people place a high value on the innocence of baptized children and readily attribute supernatural power to it.

notes.label: Bozen
notes.text: regional uncanny beings or bogey-like spirits; the source sets them beside haunting spirits as threats believed powerless in the company of an innocent baptized child, without describing their appearance more precisely.

notes.label: armen Seele
notes.text: literally ‘poor soul,’ an inflected Catholic folk designation for a suffering soul undergoing purification; here such a soul is believed to be released and to escort a dead innocent child to heaven.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

0505155a7e6d16214ec7781f68e35baa8d557fde.summary: On a hill between the villages of Grandson and Montagny, in the wine-rich land of Vaud, there stands amid somber fir trees an old oak said to have been planted by the Confederates when they defeated the Duke of Burgundy there.

notes.label: Donnerskatz
notes.text: Johannes’s comic near-oath combines ‘Donner’ (thunder) with ‘Katze’ (cat); it conveys a startled curse whose playful force has no exact English equivalent.

notes.label: Donnerssabel
notes.text: a parallel comic near-oath combining ‘Donner’ (thunder) with ‘Sabel’ or ‘Säbel’ (saber); its humorous, exasperated tone is more important than a literal English compound.

5e148075c98de79962c3c3a2843ca40c1a3c867f.summary: In Thurgau, close to the Zürich border, lies Lake Bichelsee beside the village of the same name.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

99b26fff77270da712161bb8d2ef505dcb825ccb.summary: There was a time when it was still customary for people to go about their business on high Charfreitag as on a weekday; a church service was indeed held, but afterward everyone was permitted to resume his work.

notes.label: Charfreitag
notes.text: the historical spelling used in the source for Karfreitag, Good Friday; “high” Charfreitag emphasizes the solemn holy day on which the peasant nevertheless works.

notes.label: Talschaft
notes.text: a valley community understood as both a geographic district and its body of inhabitants; spring is said to enter the whole valley district.

97e98e2875bd4254f0d970914d02c670327388ab.summary: ‘In earlier times those Venediger used to travel about the country; they were fine, knowledgeable Mandli!’

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetian,’ but in Alpine treasure lore a mysterious foreign mineral seeker credited with recognizing hidden ores and stones and often with magical knowledge or travel; the tale also links him directly with Venice.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Swiss German for a little man, using the characteristic -li diminutive; here it names the small Venediger without making him childlike.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd’s milk processing and cheesemaking and often for directing the seasonal hut; English has no exact equivalent for the full role.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, dairy work, and working community, not simply a mountain peak; Chammli is the principal summer setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Zuhirt
notes.text: a junior or assistant herdsman on an Alp who helps tend the cattle under the senior pastoral workers; the source distinguishes him from the Senn but does not specify all his duties.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working on a seasonal high-mountain pasture; here the term collectively names the dairy and herding workers.

notes.label: Trychelchüeh
notes.text: cows wearing Trycheln, large hammered sheet-metal livestock bells with a sound distinct from cast bells; the valuable stone is compared with one beautiful bell cow.

notes.label: Chibäli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a little Kübel or pail; here the black vessel holds cheese rennet, the one Alp provision from which the stranger received nothing.

notes.label: Bristenstäfeli
notes.text: the named uppermost Stäfeli near the Seeli, a small grazing level or seasonal station within an Alp; the diminutive may refer to its size or familiar local usage.

notes.label: Zottermandli
notes.text: literally a ragged or tatter-clad little man in Uri dialect; it describes the Venediger’s poor appearance without identifying a separate folkloric species.

notes.label: Gutterli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small bottle or flask; it contains the restorative liquid used during the magical journey.

notes.label: Vinediger
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Venediger used in the final variant for the same legendary mineral seeker.

notes.label: Vinedig
notes.text: the Uri dialect name for Venice; the spelling helps preserve the oral form in which the Vinediger invites the Senn to his city.

3315416c02fa96258481916df09457dc642ccaa4.summary: In the Canton of Glarus, many stories are told about Fahrende Schüler who come from Venice to the Alps in a single night, fill a sack with stones, and return home just as quickly.

notes.label: Fahrende Schüler
notes.text: plural of Fahrender Schüler, literally ‘wandering scholars’; in Alpine folklore they are itinerant learned or magical figures credited with secret knowledge and extraordinary travel.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a Venetian, but in Alpine mining and treasure lore the name often denotes a mysterious Venetian mineral seeker or magician who gathers valuable stones and can travel preternaturally fast; this tale also links him directly with Venice.

3400bf070f2919ebfcf5604c56d312d62cdb1d56.summary: Every year a Venediger appeared in Sörenberg at the sources of the Little Emme, which flows through the Entlebuch and is known to carry gold-bearing sand—for Venediger were found everywhere,

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetian’; in Alpine mining lore it denotes a mysterious foreign mineral prospector or gold-seeker, conventionally associated with Venice, though such figures were not necessarily historical Venetians.

85ffe69f6c7328e88d913a4966b21fa50339845e.summary: a) In the middle of the Arni Alp above Engelberg lies the Arni-Loch, a cave.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture together with its huts and working landscape, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Arni-Loch
notes.text: literally the ‘Arni hole,’ the locally named treasure cave in the Arni Alp above Engelberg.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally a Venetian, but in Alpine legend a mysterious foreign mineral seeker believed to locate hidden ore and treasure through secret knowledge.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially its herders and dairy workers; here they fear entering the treasure cave.

notes.label: Handbube
notes.text: a young, low-ranking alpine helper who performs general manual tasks; he is bold enough to accompany the Venediger.

notes.label: Noggel
notes.text: a historical regional and derogatory label for a person regarded as intellectually disabled or mentally impaired; it reflects the source's language, not an acceptable modern designation.

febbe00167780c72972d234468a1b72490d3862f.summary: On the Alp Casanna in the Prättigau, and in the area surrounding the Alp, the mountains contained much mineral wealth and especially veins of gold.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated grazing grounds or buildings, not simply a mountain peak; Casanna is the named Alp in this story.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bündner
notes.text: people from Graubünden, or the Grisons; the term carries the regional identity of emigrants and traders from that Swiss canton.

notes.label: laufenden Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling student,’ a folkloric wandering scholar credited with occult learning, divination, and knowledge of hidden treasure; the German phrase appears inflected in the source.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Venedigern
notes.text: the tale's inflected plural for Venediger, mysterious foreign prospectors—often imagined as Venetians—who know the locations of Alpine ores and hidden gold in Central European mining folklore.

ba3eb7090c7370ad79a28d951d2034e50ad60914.summary: At the time of the Milanese wars, a Venetian once entertained a young man from Weisstannen in the most splendid fashion.

notes.label: Chrütermandli
notes.text: Swiss German for a ‘little herb man,’ an itinerant herbalist or herb gatherer; the diminutive -li and dialect Chrüter give the mysterious Venetian a familiar Alpine guise.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a magical viewing device that reveals distant people and places across the Alps.

notes.label: Chly-z-Obet
notes.text: a local Swiss German name for the evening household blessing or prayer; the exact phrase is retained because its literal elements do not fully convey the devotional custom.

9730480498b3016173dc97b95b5df627e42111b6.summary: During the Milanese wars, a Venetian once entertained a young Weisstanner with the finest food and drink.

notes.label: Weisstanner
notes.text: a person from Weisstannen in the canton of St. Gallen; it is a local demonym, not a reference to a white fir tree despite the place-name’s literal appearance.

notes.label: Kräutermännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little herb man,’ an itinerant diminutive figure associated with gathering or trading herbs; here the mysterious traveler later reveals himself as the Venetian host.

notes.label: Bergspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘mountain mirror,’ a magical seeing device that lets the homesick traveler view his distant family; it should not be understood as an ordinary mirror placed on a mountain.

notes.label: Chli z'Obet
notes.text: literally a ‘little something in the evening,’ a light evening meal or snack in Swiss German domestic life; the exact foods and whether this was before or after a main supper are not specified.

f284259f2a62ab82c33cbac849eb9042a08dc89d.summary: During the summer a Wybervölchli often came to Brunni and begged. The people willingly gave her generous alms of Zieger, Geisskäse, and Anken.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person,’ sometimes familiar or disparaging; the beggar is later revealed riding the destructive torrent as a witch.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, often made from the whey remaining after another cheese; it is one of the Alpine foods given as alms.

notes.label: Geisskäse
notes.text: goat’s-milk cheese; the retained Swiss compound identifies a specific part of the community’s dairy alms.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; the abundant early-summer store is threatened by the beggar’s revenge.

notes.label: Wartet nur! ych wil-i im Nahsummer ä Schwirrä schlah, das-er nu am-mi dänket!
notes.text: the beggar’s exact dialect threat to strike them with such harm in the late summer that they will think only of her; Schwirrä denotes a damaging blow, trick, or calamity without a single precise English equivalent.
notes.anchor: Wartet nur! ych wil-i im Nahsummer ä Schwirrä schlah, das-er nu am-mi dänket!

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: the plural of an Uri word for destructive debris flows or torrents of rock, mud, and water; they roar down with the hailstorm and subside when the bell rings.

notes.label: Koosi
notes.text: the source’s name for the largest oncoming torrent, explicitly glossed there as a Rübi; its narrower literal sense or physical composition is not established.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Wybervolch
notes.text: an archaic collective or dismissive dialect form for a female person or female folk; here it names the second witch working the reel above the spinner.

notes.label: Lunnä! äs lyttet z'Schwandä!
notes.text: the reel-worker’s exact dialect alarm, ‘Listen! It is ringing at Schwanden!’; the consecrated chapel bell breaks the witches’ storm-working power.

notes.label: d'Grossmüetter St. Annä
notes.text: literally ‘Grandmother St. Anna,’ reflecting St. Anne’s traditional role as the mother of Mary and thus Christ’s grandmother; the witch grudgingly names her protective power.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

bd097427923b8f173e8ac1740744e24e9c25ae69.summary: Once the sixty or more cows of a Sente have been driven into the high-fenced and usually roofed Stofel, or milking place, the farmhands prepare to milk.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: a regional form of Sennten, the organized Alpine dairy herd and its pastoral unit.

notes.label: Stofel
notes.text: a fenced, often roofed Alpine milking place or pasture station; the source also glosses it as the Melteplatz.

notes.label: Kornspreuel
notes.text: chaff or husks from grain found between the cows' hooves, uncanny because the animals are on a high Alp rather than in harvested fields.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: ohä
notes.text: a traditional herding call used to halt or steady cattle; the timely cry stops the panicked herd.

notes.label: Viehrücken
notes.text: the cattle's sudden collective rush or unexplained movement away from the milking enclosure, interpreted either as supernatural panic or herd behavior.

notes.label: Hintersäss
notes.text: the rear or higher seasonal station of an Alp, one of the successive grazing and hut areas used during the summer.

notes.label: Wams
notes.text: a close-fitting jacket or jerkin; magically stabbing the garment transfers the wound to the supposed sorcerer.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the assistant Senn or second Alpine dairyman working under or beside the chief herdsman.

f44fe08a48704e08f28b8ad979ed9a8a74308194.summary: A young, merry shoemaker in Suhr owned a large glass bottle that lacked nothing but its bottom.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions

notes.label: Dorfthier
notes.text: the source’s older spelling of ‘village beast,’ the mocking lifelong byname given to the shoemaker after his fake haunting was exposed.

8e0bfa9e6074fa9a9265ccb37f3591299cecb017.summary: One evening, the pastor of Auenstein and his wife were walking home from the village of Rupperswil.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8abea90a875e96cd12c891f50e8c5bfd20ddab1a.summary: From the village fountain known as the Schwefelbrunnen, the Obwasser formerly ran down a roadside ditch into the village brook flowing from Winterfingen.

notes.label: Obwasser
notes.text: overflow or surplus water carried away from a village fountain; here it ran from the Schwefelbrunnen into an open roadside channel.

notes.label: Roßbächli
notes.text: literally “little horse brook,” the local name for the former muddy open drain; Bächli is the Swiss diminutive of brook or stream.

notes.label: Frohnfastentagen
notes.text: the traditional Ember fast days observed at recurring points in the church year; the apparition is tied to these calendrical days rather than to ordinary fasting in general.

a7506a0d714cbc780794b2a48958663fad29d31a.summary: Muri-Langdorf is divided into Oberdorf, Mitteldorf, and Unterdorf—the upper, middle, and lower village districts.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

92c23b1f7078839fe93000275ff4e960a2af868c.summary: The village of Hospental is said to have stood in ancient times on the other bank of the Reuss, at ‘Tendlen.’ From there, the pack trail climbed toward the Bätz and then descended through the Brigg forest.

notes.label: chly Heer
notes.text: Uri dialect for the ‘little priest’ or ‘little cleric’; Heer is a regional respectful designation for a priest, and chly may refer to stature or serve as a distinguishing byname rather than belittlement.

notes.label: Talgemeinde
notes.text: the political assembly or corporate community of a Swiss valley; Ursern’s traditional meeting place supports the memory of settlement and public space on the Reuss’s western bank.

22b070a4f30fa4ee1214df2a3dc21232ad85bcd7.summary: The St. Theodul is probably the highest mountain pass in our Switzerland.

notes.label: Hochalpe
notes.text: a very high Alpine pasture or high-mountain inhabited zone used seasonally; in the old man's warning it names the entire elevated setting that worsening snow and glacier conditions make uninhabitable.

e8d62cb36d6d1bf4820bf45a48c7df8c8cc0b4f2.summary: The Stubetiknaben in particular have tales to tell of this creature. During their nocturnal outings on field and forest paths—but preferably in the villages—a pig unexpectedly joins them, and they can rid themselves of it only with the greatest difficulty.

notes.label: Stubetiknaben
notes.text: young unmarried men who attend a Stubete, a traditional evening social gathering in a farmhouse parlor, often involving courtship, music, or communal work.

notes.label: Kobolde
notes.text: plural of Kobold, mischievous or dangerous spirits; the narrator applies the term to the uncanny sow and its piglets.

d98da1600002280f5f0c32668155accf9e919951.summary: Herrengässli is the name given to that part of the village of Wettingen in which the monastic clergy of the nearby Wettingen Stift owned several houses.

notes.label: Herrengässli
notes.text: literally ‘little gentlemen's lane,’ the Wettingen quarter associated with houses owned by the nearby monastery's clergy.

notes.label: Stift
notes.text: a collegiate or monastic religious foundation and its institutional property; here it refers to Wettingen Abbey rather than a simple charitable fund.

notes.label: Dorfpudel
notes.text: literally ‘village poodle,’ the regular-route black ghost dog believed to embody a person who died by suicide.

notes.label: Bachflotschi
notes.text: a local name for the splashing brook creature, probably from words evoking wetness, sloshing, or splattering; witnesses disagree about its shape even though it is generally called a dog.

c109ee2d1a0a74260a8a8d9ea5ff314f9902d9e7.summary: When, about 50–60 years ago, the avalanche swept out over the house at Blüemlismatt during the night, a voice was heard crying: ‘Hinecht chumi-n-i und nah hundert Jahrä chumi-n-i wider’—‘Tonight I am coming, and after a hundred years I shall come again.’

notes.label: Hinecht chumi-n-i und nah hundert Jahrä chumi-n-i wider
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Tonight I am coming, and after a hundred years I shall come again’; the avalanche speaks as a recurring being, while the source preserves hundred as a number word rather than the digits 100.
notes.anchor: Hinecht chumi-n-i und nah hundert Jahrä chumi-n-i wider

eea5853c86bca94e68fbcfc14153eed343e76ef6.summary: Among many others, the following legend shows how far belief in witchcraft, when it was in full bloom, could climb into foolishness and absurdity:

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

5a95a7ff88eb31e52b22f9bb2666a0ea6a62a79b.summary: Below the Schweigacher at Unterschächen, a traveler was overtaken by a terrible earthquake.

notes.label: Helgenstöckli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small wayside devotional shrine, image-post, or niche bearing a holy image; this one originally held a wooden Pietà and was later replaced by a stone niche.

33d55a9b73776a3debf10ee82988cdba5de9d169.summary: The wilda Mannli were much wiser than other people in many matters, and the Vättnerbergers learned a great deal from them, including how to fell timber.

notes.label: wilda Mannli
notes.text: St. Gallen Alemannic for ‘wild little men’; these folkloric mountain beings teach the Vättnerbergers a safer way to fell trees, and ‘wild’ here signals their nonhuman, uncultivated nature rather than mere savagery.

a1520f5df4bf08f5ead85a649ec6141676f33238.summary: Near the town of Zofingen, a hill in the Finkenhard forest is called Schloss Finkenstein.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a coarse Alpine conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones resemble nail heads; the legend treats the outcrop as the castle's petrified final wall.

notes.label: Landluegi
notes.text: the local name of the supernatural huntsman who surveys the countryside at night; luege is Swiss German for looking or watching, so the name suggests one who looks over the land.

notes.label: Lochluegenjäger
notes.text: the related hunter-name cited by the source; it combines Jäger, hunter, with a local luege or lookout formation whose exact place-sense is not explained here.

notes.label: Weidschrei
notes.text: a hunter's field or hunting cry; mocking the spectral leader's call brings the punishment of lameness.

notes.label: Hafen
notes.text: an older regional word for a pot or earthenware vessel; one treasure seeker sits upon it inside the conjuring circle.

notes.label: Christoffelgebet
notes.text: a prayer or charm associated with Saint Christopher, used here as part of a prohibited treasure-conjuring rite rather than ordinary devotion.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small Swiss coin denomination; the Devil grants the conjurers only one, provoking their ruinous dispute.

notes.label: Schellenwerk
notes.text: Bern's historical penal labor institution or prison; the name evokes the bells worn by prisoners, and the source glosses it as a Zuchthaus.

notes.label: Rothenburger
notes.text: the spectral castle lords associated with Rothenburg whose posthumous drilling and cannon fire continue their feuding character.

notes.label: W. Jagd
notes.text: the source's abbreviation for the Wilde Jagd, the Wild Hunt; it denotes a supernatural nocturnal procession of hunters, riders, noise, and hounds.

notes.label: Gutes Heer
notes.text: literally the ‘Good Host’ or ‘Good Army,’ a regional euphemistic name for a supernatural procession related to the Wild Hunt; ‘good’ is propitiatory rather than proof that the host is harmless.

notes.label: Dietewart
notes.text: the named principal point of the old rampart, explained by the story as Dietrichs Warte, ‘Dietrich's watch,’ in mocking reference to the feared enemy.

notes.label: W. Jäger
notes.text: the source abbreviates the adjective as W.; the parallel W. Jagd later in the same account and the supernatural-hunt context indicate Wilder Jäger, ‘Wild Hunter,’ though the source never expands the initial explicitly.

42bc96822c3a7973fb617cab183d5ff13f6ab776.summary: During those long famine years of the Swedish War, the Rhine region of Aargau suffered unspeakably.

notes.label: Meiler
notes.text: a Meiler is a carefully stacked and covered charcoal kiln or mound tended by a charcoal burner; its exact dimensions and construction here are uncertain.

notes.label: Jungferngraben
notes.text: literally ‘maidens’ ravine,’ this is the woodland place-name linked to the three treasure maidens; its exact boundary and relationship to Wachletä are uncertain.

notes.label: Wachletä-Jumpfere
notes.text: this Aargau name means approximately ‘maidens of Wachletä’ and identifies the singing white women of the local hollow; the place-name’s origin and the beings’ exact identity are uncertain.

447770607e2dcb39e541e39244f88eb79ee92f14.summary: Late one evening, guests were still sitting together in a village inn, entertaining one another with ghost stories.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e98203364f5458f8e962d72825f523bfeeb6dbbf.summary: Higher deities are imagined traveling in vehicles; even their riding is still understood by our dialect as a mere Fahrt, or vehicular journey, just as the older language called the two- and four-horse wagon reita and the driver reitweko.

notes.label: Fahrt
notes.text: a journey made by vehicle; the author notes that dialect extends this idea even to the gods' riding.

notes.label: reita
notes.text: an early Germanic word cited for a two- or four-horse wagon, part of the antiquarian argument linking riding and vehicular travel.

notes.label: reitweko
notes.text: an early Germanic word cited for a wagon driver or charioteer.

notes.label: Schlofts, Kinda, da schwari woag'n wird glei vabei foarn
notes.text: Austrian regional speech meaning ‘sleep, children, the heavy wagon will soon pass by,’ used to frighten wakeful children.
notes.anchor: Schlofts, Kinda, da schwari woag'n wird glei vabei foarn

notes.label: Hêrewagen
notes.text: a regional name for the Great Bear or Big Dipper constellation, understood as the celestial wagon of the deity.

notes.label: Cherwagen
notes.text: a variant regional name for the same celestial wagon constellation.

notes.label: Hörrwagen
notes.text: Scheuchzer's form of the wagon constellation's name, associated in his account with a whirlwind.

notes.label: Woenswagen
notes.text: a Netherlandic name meaning Woden's wagon for the Great Bear constellation.

notes.label: Wodanswagen
notes.text: the parallel name ‘Wodan's wagon’ for the same constellation.

notes.label: Heerwagen
notes.text: literally ‘host wagon,’ the name used in the quoted Bernese verse for the starry wagon beside the Great Bear.

notes.label: Leiterwagen
notes.text: a traditional wagon with ladder-like slatted sides; both the peaceful monastery vehicle and later vehicle of damnation take this form.

notes.label: Waogenpat
notes.text: the Baltrum name for the Milky Way as a wagon track, preserving the vehicle image in dialect.

notes.label: Kaupat
notes.text: the Groningen name ‘cow path’ for the Milky Way, connected by the author with a divine wagon drawn by cattle.

notes.label: Frû Waogen
notes.text: ‘Lady Wagon,’ a named goddess associated in the comparative tradition with Wodan's vehicle.

notes.label: Christkindlein
notes.text: the little Christ Child figure who distributes gifts and sings of the gold-and-silver wagon in Silesian custom.

notes.label: Langwied
notes.text: the long rear coupling pole or extension of a wagon, on which extra passengers cling when the Fribourg spirit wagon is overcrowded.

notes.label: Römerweg
notes.text: literally ‘Roman road,’ a name for the route of the crystal coach; the author equates the related Romweg with the Milky Way.

notes.label: Romweg
notes.text: literally ‘road to Rome,’ identified here as another regional name for the Milky Way.

notes.label: Christnachtskutsche
notes.text: literally ‘Christmas-night coach,’ the supernatural vehicle said to stand beneath Eldena monastery.

notes.label: Wütischen Heer
notes.text: an older printed form referring to the furious or Wild Host, illustrated by Geiler with an inverted man in a great wagon.

notes.label: dem Tüfel ab dem Charre g'heit
notes.text: Swiss regional speech for ‘fallen off the Devil's cart,’ said of a thoroughly wicked person.
notes.anchor: dem Tüfel ab dem Charre g'heit

notes.label: Hellwagen
notes.text: literally ‘hell wagon,’ the damned form of the divine vehicle recurring in supernatural processions.

notes.label: Hexenwiese
notes.text: literally ‘witches' meadow,’ the Pratteln location where an empty black coach foretells death or bad weather.

notes.label: Schimmelritter
notes.text: literally a knight or rider on a gray-white horse, the Liestal apparition whose voice sounds like a crowd or falling water.

notes.label: W. Heeres
notes.text: the title's abbreviation for Wilden Heeres, the Wild Host, whose supernatural wagon is compared with divine, stellar, festive, and damned vehicles.

5827d558095bca28b992bb7ff2956a127d4c08cc.summary: About a quarter of an hour from Rohrbach, near Huttwil in the canton of Bern, there still stands the ruin of a former castle called the Old Castle.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: oppressive or tyrannical lords, especially feudal castle rulers remembered as enriching themselves through coercion; the word carries a moral judgment stronger than the neutral ‘noblemen.’

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: German for gray horses whose coats often appear white; the four matching horses, all from one mother, satisfy the treasure legend's highly specific magical condition.

notes.label: Hü in Gottes Namen!
notes.text: a driving cry meaning roughly ‘Gee-up, in God's name!’; speaking it breaks the required silence, and even invoking God does not save the treasure seeker from the taboo's consequence.

82337f53097f499ea1de34270e23e45b09c0eceb.summary: In the rocks and crags of the Almende belonging to the little Zug village of Walchwil, the Bergmandli once lived.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: communal land held or used collectively by a village, comparable to a common; here it includes Walchwil’s shared rocky and wooded land.

notes.label: Bergmandli
notes.text: literally “little mountain men,” small supernatural Alpine beings associated with caves, crafts, hidden wealth, and aid or punishment; the form is regional and more culturally specific than the generic English “dwarfs.”

notes.label: Metzelsuppe
notes.text: the communal meal or feast associated with slaughtering a pig, at which fresh pork and slaughter products were served; it is not merely a bowl of soup.

notes.label: Bergmännlein
notes.text: literally “little mountain men,” a diminutive variant used here for the same Walchwil beings called Bergmandli elsewhere; retaining it preserves the source’s shift in wording.

notes.label: Bergmännchen
notes.text: literally “little mountain men,” another diminutive form for the beings; here it occurs in the historical passage that rationalizes the legend rather than in a separate modern identification.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: an outdated and often offensive historical German exonym for Romani and Sinti people; it is retained because the 1862 source uses the label in a skeptical rationalization of the dwarfs, not as a neutral modern identification.

notes.label: Kessler
notes.text: itinerant kettle-makers, coppersmiths, or metal menders; in the historical passage it names an occupation stereotypically assigned to the people labeled Zigeuner.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: little earth-dwelling beings of Swiss and Alemannic folklore, comparable to dwarfs or subterranean helpers; here it is another name for the Walchwil Bergmandli.

notes.label: Heidengass
notes.text: literally “heathens’ lane,” a local path-name traditionally associated here with the dwarfs; Heiden in old place-names can mark legendary pre-Christian or ancient inhabitants rather than a precise historical population.

notes.label: Heidenstube
notes.text: literally “heathens’ room,” a local place-name for a site associated with the dwarfs; Stube suggests an enclosed chamber or room-like space.

notes.label: Herdmandliloch
notes.text: a local cave-name meaning approximately “little earth-men’s hole” or “dwarf cave”; its dialect form links the site specifically to the legendary small beings.

1c27c4990315f779d4e0fe9864ef8e7de4161d64.summary: In the “Espen,” a small patch of Allmend meadowland near the Getschwyler chapel in the municipality of Spiringen, forest hermits formerly lived.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held village land used under shared local rights, often as meadow or pasture; here Espen is a small piece of such common meadowland near the chapel, not an ordinary privately owned field.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally a ‘forest brother,’ a lay religious hermit or recluse living outside a formal monastery; the devotional title does not mean someone's biological brother, and this tale recasts the last hermit as a teacher of sorcery.

notes.label: Rütteli
notes.text: a diminutive related to Rütti, land cleared for cultivation or pasture; the 1749 record grants the Waldbruder a small plot by his house, but its exact size and tenure are not specified.

notes.label: b'stellen
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb for magically stopping, binding, or immobilizing a person; the apprentices use a thread device to prevent people from walking, and no exact English verb captures both the physical arrest and the spell.

notes.label: Strassmeister-Heer
notes.text: the local byname of the priest Peter Alois Arnold; Heer is an older respectful title for a clergyman, while the reason he was called Strassmeister, approximately ‘road master,’ is not explained.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar’; in German-speaking Alpine folklore this is an itinerant learned figure often credited with occult or magical arts, not merely an ordinary student, and here it is an alternate description of the Waldbruder.

notes.label: Streiwipinggel
notes.text: an opaque Uri dialect plural for objects the apprentices make fly from the shady side of the valley to the sunny side; the story does not securely identify what the objects are, so their form is not guessed at.

notes.label: Der hätt etz oi bi mym Eich, noch nitt so gleitig miäßä chu!
notes.text: an Uri dialect complaint meaning approximately ‘By my oath, he did not need to come quite so quickly now!’; bi mym Eich functions as a softened oath and the exact force of the whole remark is regional.
notes.anchor: Der hätt etz oi bi mym Eich, noch nitt so gleitig miäßä chu!

notes.label: Fadenchlungeli
notes.text: a diminutive Uri dialect word for a small ball, coil, or tangle of thread; tightening and unwinding its thread magically binds and releases a chosen person, while its precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Spratzli
notes.text: the local name or nickname of a person in Unterschächen whom the boys repeatedly immobilized by magic; the source gives no identity or reliable literal derivation.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

ad077def8e8a214e0ce9c1adf4f5f39ecda69f13.summary: In the Fellibergen, in the municipality of Gurtnellen, stands the Waldbruderchäppeli.

notes.label: Waldbruderchäppeli
notes.text: the local diminutive name for the ‘forest brother’s little chapel’; it identifies a specific devotional building in the Fellibergen rather than a generic woodland chapel.

notes.label: Brudergädemli
notes.text: literally the brother’s little Gädemli, a small hut, chamber, shed, or farm outbuilding associated here with the Waldbruder; the source does not specify its exact construction.

notes.label: Riedmatterig
notes.text: a local collective family or household designation for the narrator’s Riedmatter forebears; the precise grammatical formation and range of people included are not explained.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the source says only that this one was large and built where the Brudergädemli had stood.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ an older regional name for a religious hermit or lay recluse living apart from ordinary society; the story leaves the brother’s formal ecclesiastical status uncertain and ultimately treats him as a spirit.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Chäppeli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a small chapel; here it is the place where the unseen Waldbruder celebrates Mass.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: Swiss German for a goat boy, a young herder charged with taking goats out to pasture; his pastoral work brings him past the chapel each morning.

b3435372e7fc6d5a28530f7987242ce56a0deeef.summary: The Bergleutlein, neither males nor females, have ever done anyone any harm unless they were provoked to the utmost and most sensitive degree.

notes.label: Bergleutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little mountain people,’ a collective name for small supernatural Alpine beings of both sexes; the diminutive suggests size, not childishness.

notes.label: Waldfenka
notes.text: the singular local name for a female forest being of the helpful little folk; the source equates her kind with Waldmuttern, but the name's precise derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Waldmuttern
notes.text: literally ‘forest mothers,’ an alternate plural name for the Waldfenka beings around Churwalden; ‘mothers’ signals female forest figures rather than necessarily biological motherhood.

notes.label: Waldfenken
notes.text: the plural of Waldfenka used for the forest beings collectively; their later bad reputation is presented as an unfair generalization from this retaliatory killing.

fc3bdd5816246bb475d996cae7aeab16591fb9a6.summary: Anyone who dies a violent death must ‘wander’ as a spirit after death until the number of years that person would otherwise have lived is complete.

notes.label: Gumpen
notes.text: a deep pool or hollow in a stream or riverbed, often scoured beneath falling water; here its changing depth makes the bathing place deadly.

notes.label: Flühnen
notes.text: a regional plural related to Fluh, meaning steep rock faces, cliffs, or rocky slopes; here it locates the ghost's shelter behind the pool.

notes.label: viertelmäss
notes.text: literally ‘quarter-measure-sized,’ invoking an old liquid or dry measure to describe the witness's grotesquely swollen head; the regional Maß varied, so the phrase conveys prodigious size rather than an exact modern volume.

notes.label: Wandelzeit
notes.text: literally ‘wandering time,’ the remaining span for which a person who dies violently must return as a spirit; here it equals the unrealized portion of the drowned youth's expected life.

debc24312a6e65000d5349cb30947991f78811ec.summary: In the Stockwald near Birgisch, parish of Naters, people tell of a Botzen (spirit) that is said often to have been seen and heard.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Botzen
notes.text: an inflected form of Boze, a Valais dialect name for a bogey, haunting spirit, or frightening supernatural being; here it denotes the human-shaped wanderer of the Stockwald.

notes.label: Giesswasser
notes.text: a local term for a rushing torrent, spillwater, or intermittent mountain stream; here the little bridge over it marks the limit the men do not dare cross.

notes.label: Botzenbrüggelte
notes.text: literally the ‘little Boze bridge,’ using a Valais diminutive for the bridge associated with the wandering spirit; here the narrator reports crossing it without an encounter.

notes.label: Botzenwald
notes.text: literally ‘Boze forest,’ the woodland named for the haunting spirit; here it forms part of the narrator's skeptical personal route.

notes.label: Wanderbotzen
notes.text: the inflected form of Wanderbotze used for the wandering spirit in the body text; it refers to the same being, with the final n reflecting German case grammar rather than a different creature.

notes.label: Wanderbotze
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering Boze,’ the local title for a restless Valais spirit that repeatedly follows the same path; here its cheerful yodel turns into lamentation.

fdd65b465d701864416092e6542ee12c0cf1f5f1.summary: Since ancient times, three human skulls have been kept in the chapel at Gerligen, a small village between Ballwil and Eschenbach.

notes.label: Tauner
notes.text: a poor day laborer or cottager who owned little or no farmland and worked for daily wages; the term signals the man's modest rural social position.

ec81af2b77dda8d93916b640023c2dad3d0fa3b1.summary: A large male figure is painted on the wall of a house in Lungern. When the bells ring at three o'clock in the afternoon on Good Friday to mark the death of Jesus, this man goes to the church fountain to drink water.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b882fdfca0142da09f0caed20c131e5b54f65358.summary: In the municipalities of Andwil and Gaiserwald, the ewige Jude, or Wandering Jew, once appeared as a stone-old little man in torn clothing.

notes.label: ewige Jude
notes.text: literally ‘eternal Jew,’ the German name for the Christian Wandering Jew legend in which a Jewish figure is condemned to roam for an offense against Jesus; it is a historically antisemitic folklore motif and must not be understood as a factual description of Jewish people or belief.

378eab0a5cf1e8d8c6609133fc144b2346f48f11.summary: A restless being, half man and half ghost, came one day, when it was raining terribly, to the Platz (Savien) and was hospitably invited into a house there.

notes.label: Platz
notes.text: the local place designation used for the settlement or central inhabited place in Savien; it should not be read merely as an abstract English “place.”

notes.label: Gebse
notes.text: a broad wooden dairy vessel or tub used in Alpine milk handling; the being hurls the boiling whey from one Gebse to another without spilling it.

11983aad3e8e64eec4ff32f1805f579375e280ed.summary: "I am an old man," an elderly man in Törbel once told me. "I have seen many things that only Temperkinder can see.

notes.label: Temperkinder
notes.text: children or people believed to be born during Ember times and therefore able to perceive spirits and hidden phenomena; the associated birth dates and gifts vary regionally.

notes.label: Kruterna
notes.text: a Valais regional term for the small cultivated plot crossed by the light; its exact land-use sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Almein
notes.text: a regional form of Allmend, communally held or used land; here it identifies the legal and agricultural status of the plot.

c49be768017ac02b8d9f2f53696a6b09bbc442c9.summary: “Be quiet, the gentlemen are walking about!” was formerly a common saying throughout the country when one wished to call someone who spoke too suggestively to a more respectful tone. (Melch.

notes.label: Rathsherren
notes.text: archaic spelling for councilmen or civic magistrates; their official robes and former town hall identify them as members of a historical local council, although their offices are not specified.

f405b931cf425488ff0e5e09aace8fc4a7674d08.summary: The hamlet of Deinikon in the Zug municipality of Baar is the place where, in 1531, peace was negotiated and concluded between the Reformed and the five old Catholic cantons.

notes.label: Büni
notes.text: the local name of the small rise at Deinikon where the peace was concluded; it may relate to Bühne, an elevated platform, but functions here as a place-name.

notes.label: Schimmelreiter
notes.text: literally ‘white-horse riders,’ mounted ghosts condemned to repeat a nocturnal circuit.

notes.label: dur Gottswillen
notes.text: dialect for ‘for God’s sake,’ the conventional religious appeal made while begging alms.

01a55c77168856f58f213eb8f91133f5da099b72.summary: The fields between Schupfart and Obermumpf, two neighboring Fricktal villages, are broad, rising hillside farms.

notes.label: Almende
notes.text: communal land held or used collectively by a village, comparable to a common; here it is Obermumpf’s wooded shared land, whose precise historical access rights are not stated.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Wanzenschneider
notes.text: the local name of Obermumpf’s ghostly tailor, associated in the tale with the Wanzengraben; although the compound can look literally like “bug tailor,” the first element functions here as a place-name and its deeper derivation is uncertain.

be32f25df6f07b733769c369be11f80fde9758a4.summary: In one war, bees were loosed upon the enemy, and in this way the battle was won.

5bbee55583e7b1c2e29bf425a35410ac9cd3a92f.summary: In the lower part of the Malun Alp spreads the beautiful Dreierwald. It is not rarely swept by an uncanny, shrill whistling, especially toward the time when people begin to speak of the Vonalpfahrt, but only at night.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; here Malun is both the cattle’s summer ground and the place from which they descend.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Vonalpfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal descent of people, cattle, and equipment from an Alp at the end of summer pasturing; here the forest’s whistling warns that the herd must come down early, while the ceremony and route are not described.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle and dairy work on a seasonal Alp; he recognizes the warning and later brings down the equipment, though his exact authority over the herd is not detailed.

58684e10736111f6ca830ce7bfde7b0d46c900fe.summary: Not far from Lake Thun, behind the Ralligen vineyard, lies the place called the Einöde.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ dwarf-like beings of German-speaking Alpine folklore who dwell in or beneath the earth; here they act as benevolent guardians by warning the town before the mountain collapses.

notes.label: spiti Fluh
notes.text: dialect for the ‘pointed cliff’ or ‘pointed rock face’; Fluh is a Swiss and Alemannic topographic word, and the split formation is the immediate source of the rockslide.

notes.label: Schlegel und Wege si kalte
notes.text: the prepared text's third warning line is textually uncertain. A clearer traditional variant reads Schlegel und Weggen si ghalten, meaning that mallets and wedges are held ready, imagery consistent with the Erdmännchen splitting the rock.

notes.label: Stampach
notes.text: the local stream or place toward which the warning tells Roll's inhabitants to evacuate; the source does not give a fuller modern identification.

44a61e9f3e70c0191fc9d6f60d596e65fc614fa8.summary: In the Heldtobel, not far from Waldkirch toward Bernhardzell, where a path formerly crossed the brook, a young, slender washerwoman once washed and “flatterte” with desperate intensity whenever people passed by.

notes.label: flatterte
notes.text: the source’s quoted verb probably describes beating, flapping, or otherwise vigorously working the laundry as the apparition washes; its precise regional technique and meaning are uncertain.

2d074398cb27933b05be9b67f6134563119e6f33.summary: Between the now-abandoned footbridge that crossed the Alpbach — the path now runs much farther up into the alp — and the waterfall spraying farther above, an old woman sometimes does her washing with the most industrious activity on the sunny side of the stream bank.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: children born during one of the traditional Ember fast periods, believed in Swiss folklore to possess second sight and perceive spirits invisible to others; the exact calendrical reckoning and attributed gifts varied locally.

e339f72b850a3556d3d85528a66d7af5eed5dfe6.summary: Near Lisighaus, a little white-clad woman could be seen at night washing at a fountain.
