989505c234f2d8965e03d5ece6a8a2540566d2ce.summary: It was after the Feast of the Assumption when a little farm boy from the village of Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz set out to make his way home to his remote little village of Untersyten.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Ankenbabeli
notes.text: a Swiss nickname meaning roughly ‘Butter Barbara,’ combining Anken, ‘butter,’ with a diminutive form of Barbara; it identifies the woman in Schmiedgasse who receives the butter delivery.

notes.label: Traggabel
notes.text: literally a ‘carrying fork,’ a forked or framed back-carrying implement used to support bundled goods; the tale treats it as the boy’s ordinary transport gear, though its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Brandeggtöneli
notes.text: an affectionate local name meaning roughly ‘little Tony of Brandegg,’ combining a place or household name with the diminutive Töneli; it marks the child by local origin rather than giving a formal surname.

notes.label: Vogel Huppert
notes.text: the named uncanny bird haunting the Waldweg; Vogel means ‘bird,’ while Huppert is a regional name whose literal derivation is uncertain, and the being disorients the boy through unseen wings and sighing.

notes.label: Mooskartoffelacker
notes.text: literally a ‘moss- or bog-potato field,’ a potato plot on peaty or marshy ground; in the fog, an alder bush deceptively looks like a woman weeding such a plot.

notes.label: Troglosenwasserfrau
notes.text: singular ‘water woman of the Troglosen,’ one of the pale, green-eyed female spirits bound to the local marsh and river; the compound is a regional designation, not a separate species established outside this tale.

notes.label: Troglosensihl
notes.text: the local stretch or branch of the Sihl flowing through the Troglosen wetland; the compound joins the place-name Troglosen with the river name Sihl.

notes.label: Wasserfrauen
notes.text: literally ‘water women,’ female supernatural beings associated with rivers, lakes, and marshes; these beings resemble water spirits more than ordinary women living beside the water.

notes.label: Jesus Heiland!
notes.text: literally ‘Jesus, Savior!’ a Catholic invocation cried for protection at the moment of supernatural danger; it functions as more than a casual expression of surprise.

notes.label: Vrenelisgärtlein
notes.text: literally ‘little Vreneli’s garden,’ the traditional name of a conspicuous ice- or snow-covered Alpine landmark visible beyond the valley; it is not an ordinary cultivated garden.

notes.label: Schlagenschlucht
notes.text: the local gorge on Brandeggtöneli’s route home; Schlucht means ‘gorge,’ while the precise origin of Schlagen in this place-name is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Troglosenwasserfrauen
notes.text: plural ‘water women of the Troglosen,’ the local spirits whose redeeming flower grants supernatural song; their souls remain bound in its root until Judgment Day when the attempt fails.

788aa70bfce00dab739022b5d8563c1b0a128cf6.summary: In Obwalden legend, the Wassermann survived into the present century, deftly and smoothly luring children to the water.

notes.label: Wassermann
notes.text: literally a ‘water man,’ the male water spirit who entices children to the water and pulls them beneath it.

notes.label: Höggema
notes.text: the Obwalden name for the Wassermann, associated by the source with his Hacke or hook; the form makes the hooked implement the being's defining feature.

993d7d1c8bb752210b10bf9c6d814783e1738e03.summary: This must have happened in Attinghausen. A mother there had an impudent son who feared nothing.

notes.label: Bäuzi
notes.text: an Uri name for a frightening bogey, specter, or dark uncanny being; here it appears as a black figure, but the source does not identify its form more precisely.

notes.label: Rüesstili
notes.text: an Uri house feature associated with soot and positioned above the cooking place, apparently a hearth ledge, shelf, beam, or soot-darkened flue structure; its exact construction is not described.

7153843551b45957d7b6fa09836034fc3dab965a.summary: A woman had a son so wayward that she despaired over him. He played the worst tricks on her, and in her sorrow and grief she no longer knew how she might set him on the right path.

notes.label: Goldzechinen
notes.text: the source’s historical German form for gold zecchins, high-value coins associated with Venice and other Italian mints; the magic donkey drops them near the gate of Hell.

notes.label: Schlaraffenland
notes.text: the German folk Land of Cockaigne, an imagined realm of effortless plenty; the boy feels he has entered it when the donkey produces gold.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a historical large silver coin-name from which the English word dollar ultimately derives; its precise value varied by place and period, so no modern sum is imposed.

a59e1afff27ab47196cf5749f35149f198049aec.summary: Even today, at the White Cross inn in Olten, people point out a hall in which some four-and-twenty counts and barons of the Froburg line held their customary gatherings; all of them could travel there from their castles and return while the sun was shining.

notes.label: auf Burg
notes.text: literally ‘at/on the castle,’ the traditional field-name for the land surrounding the scant remains of Froburg; it survives after the building itself has vanished.

notes.label: Dürst
notes.text: a regional Swiss name for the supernatural leader of the Wild Hunt, here a rider on a white horse; ‘wild huntsman’ conveys his role, but the name’s literal derivation and its relationship to other local hunt leaders remain uncertain.

6562baf17cfb641530be0dab87ffc96ad18b03f1.summary: Once, while the Husenfränzel family in Meien were working at the hay in magnificent fair weather, a woman wearing a red-striped short skirt and a straw hat came up the lane, stopped, and said: ‘Iähr meeget de nu eppä-n-ä chly uf Rickä-n-innä ha, äs chennt de nu eiswägs ander Wätter…

notes.label: Iähr meeget de nu eppä-n-ä chly uf Rickä-n-innä ha, äs chennt de nu eiswägs ander Wätter gä
notes.text: Uri dialect warning that the haymakers may still have work or hay to bring in before the weather turns markedly worse; several words are highly local, so the English rendering is deliberately approximate rather than a claim of exact idiomatic equivalence.
notes.anchor: Iähr meeget de nu eppä-n-ä chly uf Rickä-n-innä ha, äs chennt de nu eiswägs ander Wätter gä

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri regional word for a violent debris-laden torrent or flood; here it roars down the small valley after the hailstorm and buries the meadows, not merely a stream of clear water.

085d4c032a2ea1cd79359fb915551c82aa40a9c7.summary: About half a century ago, or somewhat more, a woodshed and washhouse were built beside the rectory in Seedorf.

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin denomination and small unit of money whose value varied by canton and period; here it is offered as a modest alms, and no fixed modern equivalent is implied.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.text: an Uri word for sheets or household linen laid out to dry; the passage does not identify the particular type of linen more narrowly.

8876ac3505574d4e2c57f30045d02474ad887b7a.summary: Once on Baberg, it is said, a strange woman came into the Alp hut and asked for food and drink, and old Schipfer gave her plenty to eat and drink.

notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working community, not simply a mountain; the stranger receives hospitality in its working hut before causing the storm.

3131166ac0d80efc96e2b621ef763c987710755c.summary: On Golzer, there lived a mother with three daughters; they were all witches.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little woman’; here it refers to the mother accused of weather magic, with a familiar or mildly belittling tone rather than defining a supernatural species.

c1bdb3101d556a323814d732059d4d344d88cbdd.summary: She came from Wyler, a black figure, and walked through the Wylertal and across Blüemlismatt as far as Buchen, where she rested.

notes.label: G'hirmi
notes.text: an Uri term that can name a rest taken while carrying a load, an established stopping place, or a small shelter; here it is the witch’s resting point, but the passage does not describe a structure.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow or torrent carrying earth, stones, and water down a slope; this one descends the Opplital after the weather witch’s passage, but its exact material is not specified.

09a0323153b5bded307bcc049f3797568202f609.summary: 1. One day, not yet a hundred years ago, an old Müetterli came to Bommatter's Rössli in Schattdorf.

notes.label: Müetterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Mutter, literally ‘little mother’ or ‘old mother’; here it is a familiar designation for an elderly woman, not a claim of kinship.

notes.label: Rössli
notes.text: literally ‘little horse,’ a common Swiss inn name; here it names Bommatter's establishment in Schattdorf rather than an animal.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for rich cream skimmed from milk; Bommatter's refusal to surrender both the cream and the remaining skimmed milk provokes the stranger.

notes.label: Sacklumpli
notes.text: literally a little scrap or rag of sackcloth; the woman flourishes or waves it as she departs, though the source does not explain its role in raising the storm.

notes.label: B'hänki
notes.text: a dialect designation here for feared women believed able to work harmful weather magic; ‘witches’ is the closest contextual sense, but the word's precise derivation and range are uncertain.

b67ec38c5e776d8bb37bab55b20621e8d2fc3454.summary: The Messmer Math. Camenisch in Räzüns was once supposed to ring “zum Wetter” at St.

notes.label: Messmer
notes.text: the church sexton or sacristan, whose duties here include ringing the bell against dangerous weather.

notes.label: zum Wetter
notes.text: literally “for the weather,” the customary ringing of a church bell to avert or break an approaching storm, flood, or destructive weather-working.

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally “God’s acre,” a traditional term for the churchyard or burial ground threatened by the flood.

notes.label: Barlott
notes.text: a witches’ assembly or company; the source supplies both German senses parenthetically.

notes.label: seduvrei, seduvrei avon ehe la piertga da Paul conta
notes.text: the source’s local-language witches’ cry, glossed there as “let us finish before the sow of Paul sings,” meaning before St. Paul’s bell sounds.

notes.label: Maiensässe
notes.text: the source’s inflected form of Maiensäss, a seasonal spring and early-summer pasture with huts between the valley farm and the high Alp.

notes.label: Tschuncons
notes.text: the pasture’s local name, parenthetically glossed by the source as “Five-Corner.”

notes.label: la Crap dellas Strias
notes.text: the Romansh name glossed by the source as “the Witches’ Stone,” preserving the block’s local identity and its association with the thwarted witches.

46b75c15b8f68a8fde62e4e613d6410f4560434e.summary: A woman on Camana was just making cheese and had the kettle of milk over the fire, where the milk was beginning to grow hot.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a small male member of the wild forest or mountain beings called Fänggen in Alpine tradition; here it possesses weather knowledge that the human family lacks, but the story does not otherwise describe its nature.

notes.label: Gebsi
notes.text: a Graubünden dialect name for a bowl, basin, or open dairy vessel; here the Fänggenmannli asks for a larger one so the hot milk can be swirled and cooled quickly, but its material and exact form are unspecified.

acca85af34c4c4b06df9e49d1a13c9982427300a.summary: ‘One morning—at the time I was still a Schulmeitli—I was driving the goats up toward the Kilchberge.

notes.label: Schulmeitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a schoolgirl; the diminutive places the 91-year-old narrator’s eyewitness encounter in her childhood.

notes.label: hennd eißter äso pfnätzget
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the two goats kept snuffling, snorting, or sneezing in alarm; the exact animal sound has no single English equivalent.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: a debris flow or rubble-laden mountain torrent; the source does not specify whether this event was primarily water, mud, or rock.

notes.text: literally a ‘changing thaler,’ a magical coin that steals or draws other money back into its owner’s cashbox.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss variant of the church office also known as Siegrist, meaning a sacristan or sexton; here he rings the specially consecrated charnel-house bell during storms.

notes.text: the source’s name for the iron wedge-and-ring fitting driven into the stone so a rope can control it; the exact hardware form and wider regional usage are not stated.

notes.text: regional forestry terms for beams or heavy timbers and logs intended for sawing; they illustrate the sort of winter hauling rope the witch uses.

c30176bce2c5f1097c5794cf463d519dd110bc29.summary: When the dew descends into the valleys in the evening and the Sennen water their herds at the fountain, when night envelops the valley and the last bell tone has died away, a voice can be heard in the depths of the Engstligen valley beside the road to Adelboden.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine dairy herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheese-making on high pastures; here their evening routine marks the hour when the ghost's lament begins.

notes.label: Änneli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Anna, with -li marking smallness or endearment; here the form is part of the doomed young woman's customary name.

notes.label: Alp

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; here a lightning strike beside the narrow path on the Fluh precedes the merchant's fatal fall.

notes.label: Landtag
notes.text: a historical territorial or cantonal assembly and court; here it is convened to judge Franz, though the story does not specify its precise jurisdiction or procedure.

a9e7320019e814915ae97b41d13b2c2d70ffccbe.summary: In the Schächental, no one can versenken the water—make it sink away—not even with mercury.

notes.label: versenken
notes.text: literally ‘to cause to sink,’ used here in a specialized folk-belief statement about making spring or well water disappear, supposedly even by mercury; the source omits an explicit grammatical subject, so the exact imagined procedure remains uncertain.

notes.label: Brünnelein
notes.text: a diminutive of Brunnen, here a small spring or fountain of clear flowing water rather than necessarily a deep dug well; it is the beggar’s miraculous gift.

notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

7525f2f4d6ec612d24b06bc96cb0bdeed8b291e8.summary: At the time when Josef Maria Arnold—a tall, stately gentleman with splendid eyes who always wore a white tasselled cap—was still serving as chaplain in Göscheneralp (1806 – †1849), it happened one day that, in the most magnificent weather and beneath a brilliantly clear sky, a strange and unknown…

notes.text: the high Alpine valley and seasonal-pasture landscape above Göschenen from which headwaters of the Reuss descend; Alp here denotes a working mountain-pasture region, not merely a summit.

78b7099e2c968f426fb2b733c8c2f28ed83e5a57.summary: “A girl from Bolzbach,” my storyteller continues, “once climbed toward the Gygenstäfeli to fetch Süffi.

notes.label: Süffi
notes.text: an Uri dairying term for a thin whey or whey-like liquid produced during cheesemaking; the exact processing stage and consistency meant here are not specified.

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: an Uri regional, often disparaging name for a strange, disreputable, or uncanny female figure; the title construes this one as a Wetterhexe, but the word itself does not define a supernatural species.

notes.label: Zeine
notes.text: a regional word for a shallow woven carrying or market basket, here balanced on the woman’s head; its exact size and material are not specified.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture with its huts and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; the girl reaches a small Alp shelter before the hail begins.

4daabc704744099d26b99decfcb985271c058682.summary: The Buchgatter on Aarau's Hungerberg is the boundary as far as the neighboring village of Erlinsbach was formerly permitted to drive its grazing livestock.

notes.label: Buchgatter
notes.text: the named gate or boundary at Aarau's Hungerberg, likely a ‘beech gate’ in literal formation; it marked the former limit of Erlinsbach's livestock-grazing rights.

notes.label: Wetterhut
notes.text: literally a ‘weather hat,’ the distinctive broad headwear of a vanishing weather prophet; seeing its wearer foretells sustained fair conditions.

notes.label: Schinnhut
notes.text: a broad historical hat woven from split willow rods or similar basketry, as the source itself explains; the Küttigen apparition wears one in rainy weather.

notes.label: Muet
notes.text: the name of the broad-hatted supernatural leader in the local riddle; the source associates him with the Muetisheer, but the name's derivation and wider mythological identity remain uncertain.

notes.label: Muetisheer
notes.text: the spectral host or Wild Hunt commanded by Muet; the rhyme exaggerates its countless followers as more numerous than fir branches.

519300cbe4afd04aabddedb998712794a87919f1.summary: Baschi’s Babä at Stalden and other people in Gurtnellen almost always saw an unknown man come from Nyw-Gadä and disappear into the large, ancient house at Stalden whenever the weather broke.

notes.label: Babä
notes.text: an Uri familiar name or byname for an older woman or female relative, possibly a grandmother; the source identifies her through Baschi but does not state their exact kinship, so the regional term is retained rather than resolved more narrowly.

notes.label: Wildmanndli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild man,’ an Alpine diminutive for a humanlike wilderness being associated with forests and remote pasture country; this variant follows the same route as the weather apparition and gives a jubilant call.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or cry used to hail across distance, celebrate, or answer another caller; it is related to yodeling but not identical with sustained yodel song.

notes.label: Holzwitteren
notes.text: the regional name of the place or structure behind which the Wildmanndli hides near the old house; it appears connected with wood storage or work, but the source does not describe its exact form or function.

notes.label: Wettermanndli
notes.text: literally ‘little weather man,’ the local name for the unknown small male apparition seen whenever the weather worsens; the story does not say whether he causes or merely foretells the change.

9a8d710298b83de793763843a26c71c63fd13c60.summary: Wildampfern and Alplen are two small Stafel belonging to the Intschialp on the Geissberg above Gurtnellen.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a grazing level, seasonal station, or cluster of herding and dairying buildings within an Alp; Wildampfern and Alplen are two such stations belonging to Intschialp.

notes.label: Wildmanndli
notes.text: literally a ‘little wild man,’ a small wild or mountain being in Alpine folklore; here its cries warn of bad weather, though the final episode does not establish what was heard.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a piercing Alpine whoop or sustained call used across mountain distances; in these accounts the uncanny call serves as a warning of snow and avalanches rather than an ordinary human greeting.

notes.label: Wettermanndli
notes.text: literally ‘little weather man,’ the local name for an unseen or small male weather-being whose cries foretell storms and avalanches; the final account leaves its identity uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally ‘poor soul,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for a departed soul still needing prayer and release, often understood as a soul in purgatory; it is one of several possible identities proposed for the warning cry.

notes.label: The poor souls
notes.text: In Catholic belief, a person who dies in God’s grace may still undergo purification before entering heaven. Prayers for the dead belong to that belief. A tale’s ghostly appearance or demand for help is its own folkloric treatment of the idea.

notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a little man; both weather-beings are described with this familiar but supernatural form.

notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Did you not see the Wättermanndli?’; Wättermanndli is the dialect spelling used in the witnesses’ recurring weather question.

notes.label: Wettermännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little weather man,’ the source-title form for a small male weather-being whose appearance and cries foretell rain, snow, or misfortune; the accounts do not decide whether it causes weather, predicts it, or is an enchanted human soul.

notes.text: high mountain masses or rugged upland areas, glossed by the source itself as the mountains; the animals are removed from them before snowfall.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. notes.label: Güpfi
notes.text: the pointed crown, peak, or little summit of the Wettermanndli’s hat; the exact historical hat construction is not described.

notes.label: Sturm
notes.text: the source’s quoted regional word for the broad projecting part of the weather hat, apparently its brim; it should not be read here in the ordinary sense ‘storm.’

notes.label: staflen
notes.text: to occupy and work a Stafel, a seasonal station or level of an Alp; the being uses the hut when the pastoral workers are absent.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal ceremonial and practical movement of people and livestock up to the Alp in spring or early summer; the skeptical men visit before that ascent.

notes.text: an unexplained local name for a small seat, block, ledge, or feature associated with the Senn; the Manndli reaches it to watch the last autumn traveler, but the source gives no exact construction.

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or carrying cry, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; here the supernatural cry foretells bad weather rather than expressing ordinary joy.

8203e23997cd78fb36d28f85180d33cfba19ba4f.summary: Above Wettingen, a dragon is said to have had its cave. The cave is inaccessible, and therefore no one knows whether the dragon may still be living inside it.

notes.text: in the source's historical spelling, literally the ‘village beast,’ a generalized local dragon or stream monster for which individual villages had their own stories.

notes.text: the long beam or pole used to bind and secure a load, especially hay, on a wagon; comparing the dragon's body to one gives rural readers a familiar measure of its great length.

notes.text: the holder, sheath, or water-filled container in which a mower carries a whetstone.

fcabb06782c5cc24a9ed59128ad70ad6823365ea.summary: In the Münstertal, the people were at the height of haymaking. Not a cloudlet was visible far or wide that might have foretold rain, and they made eager use of the magnificent weather. — The hay already lay in heaps ready for loading when suddenly a snow-white cloud came racing up, settled over the…

notes.label: Tyroler
notes.text: the source’s historical spelling for a man from Tyrol; he is working as a seasonal farm laborer and recognizes the cloud as supernatural.

notes.label: Die sollen nochmal kimme
notes.text: a Tyrolean dialect challenge meaning “Let them come again”; kimme corresponds to standard German kommen, “to come.”

notes.label: Schnätz
notes.text: a dialect name here for a small cutting implement or knife carried in a side pocket; the story establishes that it can be thrown and lodge in wood, but does not specify its exact blade form.

notes.label: Passauer
notes.text: a person associated here with the historically magical Passauer Kunst, which was credited with power over weapons and bodily harm; the comparison marks the Tyroler’s artful throw, though the source does not explain the precise connection.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of an Alpine or German-speaking house, where the Tyroler recognizes his Schnätz.

notes.label: Schwarzkünstler
notes.text: literally a practitioner of the “black art,” meaning a sorcerer or worker of harmful magic; the husband unknowingly applies it to the Tyroler.

notes.label: weisse Kunst
notes.text: literally the “white art,” a form of magic contrasted with black magic; the wife went to the Münstertal to learn it.

notes.label: heimschen
notes.text: a regional verb for acknowledging, claiming, or taking something home; here it means reclaiming the thrown Schnätz as one’s own.

notes.label: Buffet
notes.text: a household sideboard or cupboard; the husband keeps and displays the loaded pistol there.

eccbf6322f57243a9718bd1240c947610b55269a.summary: Every day a poor Geissbub drove his herd of goats up to the Arpsee. Once, at midday, when he opened his little black leather satchel to eat his meal, three white birds flew in and settled on the lake.

notes.text: a Swiss German expression for a goatherd boy, literally a goat boy; he tends the village herd and prefers that life in Valais to the swans’ distant land.

notes.label: Arpsee
notes.text: the local lake to which the Geissbub drives his goats and where the three enchanted white birds appear; the source supplies no more precise identification.

notes.text: the name of the distant land from which the princess comes; the tale does not locate it geographically or explain the name.

notes.text: literally ‘bands,’ narrow ledges or grassy strips running across steep mountain rock where chamois can graze; the source does not specify their width.

4695ed264ff54206332979ec8213001f2e720202.summary: It was a star-clear September night. Theodul, the Gemsjäger, had set out as early as two o’clock in the morning.

d298f7e36aaa4d563f565b73f30bc7685efc1a13.summary: It was in gray antiquity when a courageous rider wished to travel from the Bernese country across into Valais.

notes.label: lauter Sand
notes.text: ‘nothing but sand’; lauter functions here as ‘entirely’ or ‘nothing but’ and supplies the first half of the tale's folk etymology.

notes.label: lauter Brunnen
notes.text: ‘nothing but springs or fountains’; Brunnen can mean a spring as well as a constructed well, and the phrase supplies the second half of Lauterbrunnen.

notes.label: Lauterbrunnen
notes.text: the Bernese valley name explained in the legend as a fusion of lauter, ‘nothing but,’ and Brunnen, ‘springs’; this is a narrative folk etymology rather than a linguistic proof.

8fa616ce80160da92c3c904790db56feedd4dee2.summary: In the Eisten near Stalden, on the eastern side of the valley, a laboriously and boldly constructed Wasserleite carries the water of the Vispa for well over one and a half hours to irrigate the meadows of Staldenried.

notes.label: Wasserleite
notes.text: a constructed irrigation channel carrying mountain water across slopes, especially important in the dry inner valleys of Valais; it may include open channels and artificial crossings.

notes.label: Meadow irrigation
notes.text: Some Swiss meadows were watered through managed channels rather than rainfall alone. Maintaining channels and sharing their flow required coordinated local work. Conflicts over diverted water therefore concern both property and the hay needed to feed livestock.

notes.label: Wasserfuhr
notes.text: literally ‘water conveyance,’ another regional term for the irrigation watercourse and the managed movement of water through it.

notes.label: Känel
notes.text: plural or collective form for wooden troughs, flumes, or channel sections that carry irrigation water across difficult terrain.

notes.label: Bergruffinen
notes.text: unstable mountain gullies, erosion channels, or debris-slide ravines; the historical regional form is uncommon, and the precise terrain feature can vary.

notes.label: Gitzlein
notes.text: a diminutive for a young goat or kid; the apparently innocent white animal shape is the disguise adopted by Satan in the tale.

notes.label: Eistertal
notes.text: the valley associated with Eisten; Tal means ‘valley,’ and the local place-name is retained.

4dfead81a272e2d57867dbf759aebf5b5d3f7b0c.summary: It was late one evening when the men of the village of Peist left the municipal assembly.

notes.text: Jecklin’s quoted regional expression for the young men’s noisy, boisterous roaming through the village lanes rather than an actual storm.

notes.text: a historical Alpine name for an aromatic, nutritious pasture herb, generally associated with Alpine lovage; here it signifies exceptionally rich grazing, though the source does not give a botanical identification.

notes.text: literally ‘a Klafter in length,’ using a historical span roughly based on a person’s outstretched arms; the source gives no locally standardized modern measurement.

4adec86c7af5b7f6b84388d7526f8d74207b838e.summary: There was once a mother and a little boy living alone in a small house. But the mother was not kind, could not bear the Büebli at all, and gave him as many blows as she pleased.

notes.label: Büebli
notes.text: an affectionate Alemannic diminutive meaning a little boy; the title contrasts the child’s kindness and vulnerability with his mother’s cruelty.

notes.label: Läff
notes.text: the dialect body-part word for what the bear uses to carry the child; the immediate context establishes that function but does not securely distinguish its mouth or jaws from a paw, so the exact anatomy remains open.

notes.label: Chrättli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small basket, especially one used to carry provisions; the mother lowers the bear’s bread and milk in it from the house gallery.

notes.label: Gvätterliwaar
notes.text: small gifts or treats associated with a Gvatter, a godparent or familiar family sponsor; here the word broadly covers the toys, devotional pictures, and coin that delight the child.

notes.label: Helgeli
notes.text: small religious pictures or holy cards, common devotional keepsakes and children’s gifts; the diminutive -li marks their small size.

notes.label: Züriguldi
notes.text: a Zurich gulden, named in dialect as a distinctive coin from Zurich; the child values the bright new coin above the bear’s other gifts.

notes.label: Chasperli
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive of Chasper or Kaspar; it is the grown boy’s name when he reassures his frightened mother.

03fddd24da65160587a422603a4ca84f87f49f9a.summary: High in the Nanzertal lies a small but beautiful Alp that is still counted among the best in the Vispertal.

notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman or cheesemaker; in this story he abuses the younger herdsman and envies his supernatural gift.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: one of the successive seasonal pasture levels or stations of an Alp; the cattle and workers move from the grazed-out lower Staffel to the upper one.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senne, the old-fashioned male Alpine dairy workers who enter the lower hut at night.

notes.label: Sennerinnen
notes.text: female Alpine dairy workers; the apparition includes women in distinctive historical Valais clothing.

notes.label: Walliserhut
notes.text: literally “Valais hat,” the high, stiff regional women's headwear worn by the supernatural Sennerinnen.

notes.label: Graui
notes.text: literally “the gray one,” the cow's familiar name; her restored body retains the wound corresponding to the flesh the boy ate.

notes.label: rechte Milch
notes.text: literally “right” milk, meaning proper, wholesome, or unaccursed milk in contrast to the fermented and cursed choices offered by the spirit.

notes.label: Alpkraut
notes.text: the aromatic vegetation or herbage of the high pasture, heavy with dew at daybreak.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical honorific for a young nobleman or untitled member of the lesser nobility; here it is the title of the humane lord Albin von Silinen.

notes.text: Swiss German for butter; here the lord's promise of Anken on the widow's bread is a metaphor enacted by placing the document that frees her farm from dues upon it.

5923dab8711fffa17738e5fbd4a76cf8db3780f3.summary: Not very long ago in Erstfeld, several young men were making merry in the house of two strikingly pretty, young, perfectly healthy girls.

0abbaf26c8cf53d301975954250d2dff7f61d260.summary: When the people of Wangs repaired the alpine fence before the Alpfahrt to their Gamidaur pasture, an unknown but vigorous-looking man came to them and offered to perform the duties of a Senn during the coming summer without pay or complaint.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial and practical seasonal drive of people and cattle up to the high summer pasture; it denotes more than an ordinary journey.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman who tends cattle and traditionally makes cheese on a high summer pasture; the role combines herdsman, milker, and cheesemaker, so no single English job title is exact.

notes.label: Alpgenossen
notes.text: members of the cooperative community holding rights and duties in a shared alpine pasture; they are not merely companions on the mountain.

notes.label: Sente
notes.text: the organized herd or cattle procession moving to or from an alpine pasture, sometimes including the wider dairying unit; English ‘herd’ does not carry all of these associations.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: the assistant or subordinate Senn in an alpine dairying team; the role is more specific than a general farmhand.

10459ea8b6ccf358ed8a6036497b3edd3fe83582.summary: For many summers in succession, a Fänggenmannli tended the Heimkühe at Conters without ever accepting any reward.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a “little Fängg man,” a male wild forest or mountain being in Alpine tradition; as in other gift-of-clothing tales, his service ends once he receives human clothes.

notes.label: Heimkühe
notes.text: cows kept in connection with the home village and brought daily to pasture, in contrast to a herd remaining on a distant high Alp for the season.

notes.label: Weidelamâ
notes.text: an uncertain dialect form in the cowherd’s couplet, approximately a “pasture fellow” or herdsman; in context, his new clothes make him consider himself too fine to keep herding cows.

bf95ef48b08b99aa523ba8775ce365e43de7c3f5.summary: On dark, stormy nights, a ghostly procession called the wildes Heer often passes through the valleys and over the heights of our land.

notes.label: wildes Heer
notes.text: literally ‘Wild Host’ or ‘Wild Army,’ the spectral procession better known across Germanic folklore as the Wild Hunt; here it travels through Bernese valleys and lodges in Alpine buildings, and ‘host’ conveys a company rather than a modern military unit.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and cheese-making on a high pasture; here each Senn is the solitary keeper confronted by the ghostly company.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night people,’ a regional folklore name for the uncanny nocturnal company; in this story it overlaps with the wildes Heer, but the terms need not be exact synonyms in every tradition.

notes.label: Die wildi Jagd im Fuhrebärg
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘the Wild Hunt on the Fuhrebärg’; the spectral procession follows a former full-moon route from the common pasture.

notes.label: Jaghüng
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘hunting dogs’; the supernatural hounds suddenly surround Hani and paralyze him, though the source does not describe their appearance.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

notes.text: a regional Bernese name for the spectral leader or embodiment of the Wild Hunt; here it identifies the mounted huntsman haunting the Schwendelberg, though the term’s precise etymology is uncertain.

notes.text: the Bernese Alemannic form of ‘Schwendelberg’; the dialect name anchors the closing verse in the Guggisberg region.

notes.label: Guggisbärg
notes.text: the Bernese Alemannic form of ‘Guggisberg’; it names the wider district in which the legend is said to be known.

ba1238d3eb3e929d9b9c5608ff12e466d8873d4e.summary: A farmer and miller in that vicinity once allowed one of his farmhands to go home to his family in the evening.

notes.text: a regional Bernese name for the leader or embodiment of the Wild Hunt, a terrifying nocturnal supernatural procession; spellings and local conceptions vary across Switzerland.

notes.text: literally the ‘recruitment of the Thürst,’ the belief that the spectral hunter conscripts a living person into his following; here the farmhand participates while his body apparently remains in bed.

d141581622efd7d70ee1126974acf71e450c5f23.summary: In the mountains of Grindelwald, a strange call is often heard around midnight.

notes.label: Sennhirt
notes.text: a compound for an Alpine dairyman-herder, combining Senn's cheesemaking role with livestock care; he knows the ritual precaution required for the nocturnal host's passage.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: the high seasonal pasture with its cattle, buildings, and work community; the Sennhirt leaves it temporarily in the herder boys' care.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Melkhaus
notes.text: literally ‘milking house,’ the Alpine dairy building through whose open gates the supernatural riders must be allowed to pass.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an inflected form of Senn, the senior Alpine dairyman or cattle herder; it refers to the same Sennhirt after he leaves.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often violent Alpine downslope wind; its heat and roar make the Wild Hunt's approach resemble an unnatural mountain storm.

notes.label: Friesen
notes.text: literally ‘Frisians,’ the name shouted for the riders crossing the Scheidegg; whether it recalls a historical troop, a folkloric host, or a locally transformed name is not explained.

07e24241f4fa674a4db6be85a25043ada7782a1a.summary: Who could forget the road from Zurzach to Kaiserstuhl, the way it formerly went uphill and downhill as though from heaven into hell?

notes.label: Batzen
notes.text: a historical Swiss coin denomination; here four Batzen specifies the meager amount of hay bought, but its value varied by place and period.
The source’s interrupted curse is preserved. Wildjäger in the title denotes the supernatural Wild Huntsman.

07163ddf40d96853faa165abd833949711af149b.summary: Above Vilters lies the Wild Lake. If stones are thrown into it, it begins to rage, and storms and severe thunderstorms arise.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2eba115142c274d795e65b70e556f5a3cd124024.summary: On an Alp, a wild little man lived on fairly familiar terms with the Senn and received from him many things that gave him pleasure; in return, he was very devoted to the Senn.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, an Alp is a high seasonal pasture and its associated dairy-working place, not simply any mountain; the precise extent of the pasture in this telling is unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: a Senn is the specialist dairyman responsible for livestock and cheesemaking on a Swiss Alp; the character’s exact rank and duties beyond this episode are uncertain.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: here Schotte means the whey left after cheesemaking, a product associated with Alpine dairying; the lost second preparation alluded to by the legend is explicitly uncertain.

3b3bdbe232f8b83d0f55d5676704dee76c161acc.summary: In the so-called Glassauer Forest there were once many wilde Lütli. They wanted no dealings with the farmers and, on the contrary, harmed them wherever they could and wished; this in turn made the valley people angry and harsh toward the inhabitants of cave and forest.

notes.label: wilde Lütli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little wild people,’ the cave- and forest-dwelling beings described in the tale.

notes.label: Waldweiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little forest women,’ a diminutive name for female wild-folk beings rather than ordinary women living in the woods.

notes.label: Holz-Mueterli
notes.text: literally ‘little wood mother,’ a regional name for the curious female forest being whom the farmer traps in the split timber.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: wild Alpine beings in Graubünden folklore; here the whole group answers the Holz-Mueterli’s cry and chases the farmer.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a narrow, steep-sided Alpine ravine or gorge, often containing a stream; the Glassauer Tobel adjoins the forest.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Mann, ‘man’; in the title it names the little wild men of local Alpine folklore.

97777949cce1f4c7291cc74bd6b4716951907ab3.summary: A man from Klosters had lost his newborn baby, and an ugly changeling had been laid in the cradle in its place.

notes.label: Bôschga
notes.text: an unexplained Graubünden landscape name or dialect designation that the changeling claims to have seen alternate five times between meadow and forest; its precise location and literal derivation are not established by the source.

notes.label: Guckhäfeli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for tiny cooking pots or little vessels; the changeling jokingly interprets the half eggshells arranged on the hearth as an unprecedented number of pots.

notes.label: Fängge
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alpine name for a wild, giant-like, or ogre-like supernatural being; here one has stolen the human infant and returns it when the changeling reveals its great age.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘little man,’ here a wild supernatural being rather than an ordinary short man; the diminutive can sound familiar without making the being childlike.

88e1d52ccc579e502f8ae23b6330338279d53758.summary: In olden times, accidents often occurred throughout the land during tree felling.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man’; here it denotes one of the wild, diminutive mountain or forest beings credited with knowledge that humans lack, rather than merely a small human man.

notes.label: Gemschen
notes.text: a dialectal diminutive of Gemse, ‘chamois’; the comparison suggests the being's quick, nimble, goatlike leaps on difficult ground.

84323aa895415ae147c667a97c10ed0072d7031f.summary: At the Houses, as the place is called, far back in the Safien valley, a woman was once making cheese.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ a diminutive often used for small Alpine supernatural beings; this wild Männlein knows the mountain weather better than the skeptical dairywoman.

notes.label: Gebsi
notes.text: a Graubünden dialect word for a bowl, basin, or open vessel; the little man asks for a larger one so the hot milk will cool more quickly.

8859f9660b2e236da871318d10fd0d4be8e1318e.summary: In Safien, people still know and point out the place where the wild Männlein lived with his wife.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little man,’ here one of the elusive wild people believed to inhabit Alpine rocks and assist or reward humans.

notes.label: Z'wilta Mannlis Balma
notes.text: Safien dialect for ‘at the wild little man's Balma,’ the traditional name of the overhanging rock shelter where the couple lived.

notes.label: Balma
notes.text: a Romansh and Alpine place-word for a cave or shelter beneath an overhanging rock; the source explicitly describes this formation.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonally used high-mountain pasture with its huts and working landscape, not merely a mountain peak.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Völklein
notes.text: literally a ‘little people,’ the collective folk name for the wild beings; their constant running distinguishes them from humans.

notes.label: Weiblein
notes.text: literally a ‘little woman’ or ‘little wife,’ the feminine counterpart of Männlein; here she is the wild mother delivered of twins.

35469bf7437af4f5fa9919769ab149b3f7e8ddfe.summary: Another legend from this region—the southern part of Fribourg—relates:

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2b773b0a1326183f7a76cfb92fd0031cde4b40bf.summary: At the time when dear simplicity was still customary in our country, it once happened that the sworn official Val.

notes.label: Wild-Mannli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild man’ in Swiss German, an Alpine folkloric being associated here with mountain herds and wiser practical judgment than the villagers; ‘wild man’ is close, but the diminutive and local character would be lost.

39f59f5445be599d62c13479e67ba7e0bbcd443f.summary: Just as people learned from the Fänggen how to bore Teuchel, they learned many other useful methods and practical tricks from them as well.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: the plural of Fängg, a wild Alpine being in Graubünden folklore; here the beings are credited with practical woodland knowledge.

notes.label: Teuchel
notes.text: regional German for bored wooden pipes or conduits, traditionally made from logs; another tale says people learned the boring technique from the Fänggen.

notes.label: Wild-Mannli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild man’ in Swiss German, a diminutive name for an Alpine wild-folk being rather than an ordinary small man.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Mann, ‘man’; here it is the shortened name for the same Wild-Mannli.

notes.label: Wildlütli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little wild people,’ another affectionate or diminutive collective name for the Alpine wild folk.

notes.label: ung'fällig
notes.text: a dialect word glossed by the source as ‘unfortunate’; in this context it means suffering an accident while felling timber.

d376476143ec90231cc27d7d5ec00d6208bbe2aa.summary: In the southern part of the canton of Fribourg, the Taunabach flows through a landscape of mountains and valleys that several hundred years ago was the haunt of a wild hunter who carried on his restless activity every Saturday, especially during hunting season.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the prayer bell, commonly the evening Angelus bell, after whose ringing the supernatural hunt begins.

notes.label: Voralp
notes.text: a lower or preliminary Alpine pasture used before or after the highest summer grazing season; the hunter pauses there before midnight.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: Alpine herdsmen and dairymen who must keep absolutely quiet while the wild hunter occupies their pasture.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Vorsatz
notes.text: a lower or early-season pasture section associated with the Alpine holding; the hunter ravages its farm structures when disturbed.

notes.label: Staffel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or farmstead, including its hut and cattle buildings, rather than merely the stable itself.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd, specifically the inexperienced young worker who mocks the approaching supernatural hunter's cry.

notes.label: Nachtjäger
notes.text: literally ‘night hunter,’ the local nocturnal form of the wild hunter leading the spectral chase.

notes.label: Gewild
notes.text: an older collective word for hunted game; by daylight the supposed quarry has vanished, leaving only blood, hair, and tracks.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: wilde Heer
notes.text: the Wild Host, a noisy supernatural procession closely related to the Wild Hunt; the title uses Heer, ‘host or army,’ although the episode focuses on one hunter and his hounds.

a3b936abd2e2c7999400da015105f7fbec5603c4.summary: Centuries ago, a hunter ranged the woods around Zofingen and Brittnau. If he had killed no hare throughout the entire day, the Devil still had to drive one out for him on his journey home in the places called Vor dem Wald and Strengelbach.

notes.label: Wilde Jagd
notes.text: the Wild Hunt, a supernatural nocturnal procession of hunters, hounds, airborne noise, and dangerous demands; changes in weather announce its passage here.

536fefb093a27439b8f5a9318693ad3fc4fa6560.summary: In various places, wilden Männlein have tended people’s cattle, driving them to pasture and home again.

notes.label: wilden Männlein
notes.text: inflected German for ‘wild little men,’ folkloric nonhuman helpers associated with Alpine pastures; in Maladers one tends cattle for simple food until unexpectedly offered full milk.

notes.label: Männlein
notes.text: literally ‘little man’; the shortened final reference still denotes the same Alpine helper, not an ordinary small human.

notes.label: wildes Männlein
notes.text: the singular form, ‘wild little man’; the being’s departure after a change in payment resembles traditions in which helpful spirits leave when their customary treatment is altered.

c1bede04783cf0a382a51a577eaf9949d0027756.summary: East of the small town of Puschlav rises the gigantic Sassalbo. At its foot, deep caves penetrate the mountain’s interior, and these were formerly inhabited by “Wilden.”

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the historical German name for Val Poschiavo, the southern Graubünden valley dominated here by Sassalbo.

notes.label: Wilden
notes.text: literally “wild ones” or “wild people,” the large, hairy cave-dwellers of the tale; the plural is retained because no single English folklore category captures them.

notes.label: Salvanghi
notes.text: the popular local name given to the Wilden, related to Romance words for wild or woodland beings; the precise language form and classification are not specified by Jecklin.

notes.label: Wilde
notes.text: the singular form of Wilden; grammatical context identifies this one as female and unusually protective toward the lost boys.

notes.label: gnan, gnan, carn da cristian
notes.text: the local Romance-language cry that Jecklin glosses as “it smells of Christian flesh here”; its spelling is preserved as printed.

notes.label: Alpe Sassiglione
notes.text: the named high pasture to which the male Wilde descends; Alpe here means the seasonal grazing and dairy-working place, not a mountain peak.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: the dairy hut on an Alp where milk is processed and cheese is made.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled Alpine dairymen or head herdsmen responsible for cattle and cheesemaking during the summer pasture season.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people working or living seasonally on an Alp; here it refers to the dairy crew completing its work in the presence of the Wilde.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: a regional word for whey, the liquid remaining after curds are removed during cheesemaking, as Jecklin’s gloss confirms.

c940dbf277c1349c0e69715e2b3a33d82d30c6da.summary: At the Stöckhof near Egliswil, the farmer lodged a Capuchin friar making his appointed begging rounds and was still chatting with him before bedtime when a distant din announced the Wildes Heer.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Wildes Heer
notes.text: literally the ‘Wild Host,’ a regional form of the Wild Hunt whose noisy nocturnal passage must not be challenged; the tale does not identify its leader.

notes.label: Läusterli
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for a small window opening, shutter, or hinged panel; the parenthetical ‘window shutter’ comes from the source, while its exact construction is unstated.

notes.label: Du rîist i der Nacht
notes.text: dialect for ‘you ride in the night,’ the first line of the boy’s mocking verse addressed to the passing host.

notes.label: De Tüfel het di g'macht!
notes.text: dialect for ‘the Devil made you,’ a taunt that associates the rider with demonic origin.

notes.label: Du rîtist wie ne Schnîder
notes.text: dialect for ‘you ride like a tailor,’ using a traditional mocking comparison whose exact insult is not explained.

notes.label: De Tüfel holt di wieder!
notes.text: dialect for ‘the Devil take you back,’ completing the boy’s provocative stanza.

notes.label: witt du mit mer strîte
notes.text: dialect for ‘if you wish to quarrel with me,’ the spectral rider’s direct response to the mockery.

notes.label: se chast au mit mer rîte!
notes.text: dialect for ‘then you can ride with me too,’ a threat immediately fulfilled when the boy is carried from the window.
notes.anchor: se chast au mit mer rîte!

57283da24c99598b83a5c79455a8a137eb827895.summary: At Conters, too, a wildes Männlein tended the cows for a long time. Then, when people once gave it a suit of clothes and it had put them on, it likewise grew proud, tossed the herding staff high into the air, and sang:

notes.label: wildes Männlein
notes.text: literally a ‘wild little man,’ a small Alpine folklore being rather than an ordinary feral human; in tales of this type, receiving human clothing makes the being proud or frees it from tending livestock.

notes.label: Weideleman
notes.text: dialect for a pasture-man or herdsman; the being uses the word in its song to reject its former lowly work after receiving clothes.

e8d916fd9dae7dbc457d8deac3bbb5da86eb6d43.summary: About thirty years ago, a man lived in Oberflachs who, because he knew very well how to handle wine, was given supervision of the municipality’s Zehntenkeller and was therefore called the Wildi-Küfer.

notes.label: Zehntenkeller
notes.text: literally ‘tithe cellar,’ a communal cellar for wine collected as a tithe or levy.

notes.label: Wildi-Küfer
notes.text: literally ‘Wildi cooper,’ the byname of the man placed over the communal wine cellar; Küfer is a cooper or cellar worker, while Wildi appears to be a family or local name.

notes.label: Tausen
notes.text: plural of Tause, a regional wine measure or carrying vessel glossed by the source as half a bucket.

notes.label: Tause
notes.text: singular form of the regional wine measure or vessel the cooper carries on his back.

notes.label: Gülle
notes.text: Swiss German for liquid manure or slurry, which the thief pretends to pour beside the tree as fertilizer.

notes.label: Taglohn
notes.text: day labor paid by the day, the basis on which the narrator’s cousin worked for the cooper’s family.

cd135490b12065c2c8c127010eccac146993528d.summary: On the southeastern side of the great Windgälle rises a strange mass of rock that, seen from some distance, resembles a man standing upright.

notes.label: Wildmannli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild man,’ the hunters' name for the man-shaped rock and, by extension, the irreverent hunter petrified there; the diminutive can be familiar or descriptive and does not necessarily make him tiny.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

8fc0564634646cd1dd894018c7e6ed503e104643.summary: Near the two ponds outside the city of Baden, directly opposite the brickworks there, a chapel called the Rad-kappeli stood on the Bandstrasse several decades ago.

notes.label: Rad-kappeli
notes.text: literally ‘little Rad chapel,’ with Kappeli a Swiss German diminutive of chapel; Rad is the local name element and is not explained by the source.

notes.label: Markstein
notes.text: a boundary stone marking a legal or territorial division; here it is distinguished by a granite cross.

notes.label: Marti, Marti, wotisch für en armi Seel bete!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Marti, Marti, would you pray for a poor soul?’; the unseen request reflects Catholic ideas of helping a suffering soul through prayer, addressed here to a man who later consults a Reformed pastor.
notes.anchor: Marti, Marti, wotisch für en armi Seel bete!

notes.label: Steuermeier
notes.text: an older local office title, approximately a tax steward, fiscal administrator, or collector; its exact duties could vary by community and period.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosing barrier, here high enough that the man is thrown over it.

notes.label: Donner hol!
notes.text: literally ‘thunder take [it/you],’ a dialectal exclamation or softened curse expressing shock.

notes.label: Es het mi e so en Siebechetzer do abe gheit!
notes.text: Swiss German meaning approximately ‘such a Siebechetzer threw me down here’; Siebechetzer names or abuses the unseen force, but its literal derivation and precise regional sense are uncertain.
notes.anchor: Es het mi e so en Siebechetzer do abe gheit!

notes.label: Donner hol, es het domole numme ne kei Wind gnappet!
notes.text: a dialectal insistence that there was not even the slightest movement of wind; the source explicitly explains that not a single leaf moved, emphasizing that no ordinary gust caused the fall.
notes.anchor: Donner hol, es het domole numme ne kei Wind gnappet!

6a32d3455632a9b741592be7003959be3d9b9177.summary: Will-o’-the-wisps appear most often at the time of the new moon, when the weather tends to change, and so the farmer regards them as good prophets of the weather.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

74f29646acb06e8bf3752ff1a3daa36dc5e570cd.summary: A girl from Zermatt who had grown up at Aroleid found that region altogether too wild, so she wandered down the valley and through the country.

notes.label: Z’Pfinggo-Pfi
notes.text: a Valais dialect form referring to the Pfyn or Pfynwald country; in the woman's rhyme it is the otherworldly place where she must endlessly separate the water she mixed into her wine.

notes.label: Pfinggo-Pfi
notes.text: the shortened form of the same Valais place-name used in the narrator's closing warning; the story turns a real regional landscape into the adulteress's place of punishment.

8262a509081d5ada9623f21a2dfd6bac4a53b905.summary: One evening, a man fetched wine from the inn for his wife, who had just given birth.

notes.label: Nachtleutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little night people,’ nocturnal supernatural beings presented here as a company of dwarfs or good little folk; their gift remains abundant only while the encounter is kept secret.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

8e050832c073d32530cfa328ba1b81e3de51728e.summary: In Zizers there still lives a peaceable married couple—he is called Hans, she Uschi (Ursula)—who in the year 1874 had “already sold,” that is, promised, the wine still in the Bütte (wine vat).

notes.label: Uschi
notes.text: a familiar Swiss German form of the given name Ursula.

notes.label: Bütte
notes.text: a large open vat; here the parenthetical source gloss specifies a wine vat holding the fermenting wine.

notes.label: Trester
notes.text: grape pomace—the skins, seeds, and stems left after pressing or fermentation.

notes.label: abziehen
notes.text: literally to draw off; in winemaking it means transferring the clear wine away from sediment or pomace.

notes.label: Zuber
notes.text: a large tub or vat used as a traditional capacity reference; the buyer expects enough wine to fill six of them.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: a historical liquid measure whose exact local volume could vary; only about ten measures remain in this comic account.

0e7dbb2015f827a4dc1167395688a3d06e96e35c.summary: The little Winon River near Beromünster—perhaps an ancient Vienna—rises near Neudorf and flows through a valley covered with firs, the Winonholz, toward the Lucerne border near Maihausen.

notes.label: Winonholzfräuli
notes.text: literally the little lady of the Winon Wood, the local name used to address the wandering maiden.

notes.label: Kräze
notes.text: a regional name for an itching skin eruption or scabies-like affliction; the exact diagnosis is uncertain.

47fc8266e2115ac09729f7d3335b76ae8ec3a549.summary: Wirtle is the name of the hill between Ballwil and Hochdorf over which the valley road has passed for centuries.

notes.label: Räf
notes.text: a traditional Swiss carrying frame or open-backed pack used to transport loads on foot; ‘pack frame’ is the closest English term, but its construction and the load carried here are not specified.

notes.label: Wirtletier
notes.text: literally the ‘Wirtle animal,’ the local name for an indistinct black, dog-like creature haunting the Wirtle hill and causing a dangerous wound; ‘Wirtle beast’ is close, but the account leaves its exact form and nature uncertain.

9d6934b65be5a91b4dbf9b2906723f1853228ff6.summary: The inhabitants of the municipality of Tenna caught a large bear that had done great harm to their herds.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Mann, ‘man’; here it denotes the little wild man who advises the villagers.

notes.label: ’S grusigst ist, lent na hürötha
notes.text: a Swiss German joke meaning ‘The most horrible punishment is: let him marry’; its deliberately cynical view of marriage becomes the tale's proverb.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: a diminutive name for a male member of the Fänggen, the wild folk of Graubünden tradition; the being appears here as a proverbial wise man.

b8e47cb9e010cc8ea55dcaba42f3f4fe10060ca2.summary: Far back in the Schanfigg Valley, above the little village of Arosa and lovely Schwellisee, an old Ziernüßlibaum stands alone.

notes.label: Ziernüßlibaum
notes.text: a local name for a nut-bearing Swiss stone pine, corresponding to the Arven mentioned around it; the exact historical spelling is retained because the solitary tree is the cave's landmark.

notes.label: Arven
notes.text: Swiss stone pines, culturally characteristic high-Alpine trees; all but the single Ziernüßlibaum have vanished for half an hour's distance around the site.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a ‘Sunday child,’ someone born on a Sunday and traditionally believed to possess special luck or supernatural perception; only such a person can find the key and entrance.

notes.label: Plümpe
notes.text: a large Alpine cattle bell, generally among the largest bell types hung on cows; choosing the golden one grants magnificent livestock but little happiness.

notes.label: Küehjer
notes.text: an Alpine cowherd or cattle-tender, closely associated with seasonal dairying; his occupational love of livestock explains his choice of the Plümpe.

notes.label: Sennenleben
notes.text: literally ‘Senn life,’ the merry seasonal life of Alpine dairymen and herders on the high pastures; the tale contrasts its appeal with the wiser choice of redeeming the maiden.

ddd8f8c9e8cceb2f2f91cf6b6962c2da7dae1963.summary: It is an old Zellata (legend) that the Wissle, or Herumjini, cannot bear whistling.

notes.label: Zellata
notes.text: a Valais dialect word for a legend or traditional tale; the source itself supplies Sage as its closest standard German gloss.

notes.label: Wissle
notes.text: a regional name for small supernatural beings living among stones or scree; here they hate whistling, swarm from holes, and tear the man's coat apart, while their exact appearance remains undescribed.

notes.label: Herumjini
notes.text: another Valais name for the same or closely related stone-dwelling beings called Wissle; here the singular Herumji is imagined peering from beside every rock, and the relationship between the two labels is not further defined.

notes.label: Steirischu
notes.text: a local topographic word for a stony scree or rock field; here the man sleeps beside it, though the exact landform intended by the dialect is uncertain.

notes.label: Rischina
notes.text: a Valais term for a scree slope, stone run, or mass of fallen rock; here its holes are the dwellings from which the Wissle emerge.

notes.label: Herumji
notes.text: the singular form corresponding to Herumjini, one individual of the stone-dwelling little people; here the frightened man imagines a head beside every stone.

notes.label: Tschopo
notes.text: a Valais dialect word for an outer garment, glossed in the source as overcoat, jacket, or vest; here the man sacrifices it as a decoy so the Wissle tear cloth rather than him.

3464a199aafbfe7db4330888f94b4d2f4d4473f5.summary: The Wißmaidli fir was an old tree near Oberflachs, now felled; the Wißmaidli spring is nearby.

notes.label: Wißmaidli
notes.text: an Aargau form meaning approximately ‘white maiden’ or ‘little white maiden’; it names both the fir and nearby spring and may allude to the enchanted castle maiden, though the source does not explicitly equate the names.

notes.label: Junker
notes.text: a historical title for a young or lesser nobleman; here it identifies the father of the enchanted Schenkenberg maiden.

5c47da2ee110564c73693c08380ffd58901ff8b7.summary: In a house in Oberuzwil, whenever milk was boiled, it “separated.” Someone advised that the next time milk was boiled and began to rise, it should be stirred with a birch switch until it settled again.

notes.label: anrichten
notes.text: in this St. Gallen tale, the woman’s plea to anrichten the milk appears to mean to stop, settle, restore, or otherwise set the bewitched milk right; the ordinary German verb has several other meanings, so the precise local magical sense is uncertain.

91f3b46f2da589e3590e504b6d6c9d9993fa3622.summary: In the Haslenholz toward Lehn, a woman wrapped in ragged clothes teased passersby, especially women.

notes.label: Bösgatter
notes.text: literally ‘evil gate’ or ‘wicked barrier,’ the local name of the gate or barrier where the ragged apparition disappears.

a8025588ba6c5730a263af912f00d26eeb382910.summary: In one region, newborn children were always being killed, and when they were examined, a little wound like one made by a Gufen was found on their heads.

notes.label: Gufen
notes.text: an Alemannic word for a pin or large needle; here it is the weapon that leaves the fatal wound on each newborn’s head, but its exact size is not specified.

15d6aa2d4b225e024831fd5acd47195b644ba467.summary: There was once a husband whose wife often went dancing at night. For a long time the man did not notice, because whenever she went out she put a broom in the bed beside him.

a7ba99f01d95b3d8f3ef598104d0fe74f8766e11.summary: When the people of Schattdorf were trying to hang the new great bell in the church tower, they could not manage it at all; the bell simply would not go in.

notes.text: an Alemannic place-name meaning approximately ‘little church field’; it identifies the nearby spot from which the suspected witch watches, not part of the bell itself.

notes.label: Guschi

c6505ecb6fe7880f48cfd54090e9c1b8ff383faa.summary: At the time when there was still much talk of witches and Strideln and their mischief, the community of Zermatt held a Gemeintrunk.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a seasonal station, level, or group of huts and pasture within an Alp; here it is the upland place where the sheep and old hut are located, though its exact extent is unstated.

notes.text: a grammatical or regional form of Alp, meaning a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its livestock operation rather than simply a mountain; the girls climb there to guard the sheep.

fac66ff3f9b45ba8b94c41a31fd30446d8f2befb.summary: A man once walked uphill through Sapün-Dörfli above Langwies with one of his finest cattle when a little old woman came pattering up to him, looked at the animal, and stroked its back with her right hand while saying, “Das ist doch en' hübschi Mähni.” Then she walked quickly away.

c8af861d49af53df9704f27425d3d6db5be1c0c5.summary: Once two men from Closters were returning home from the Davos market. Night had long since fallen when they reached the so-called Ried-Loch, beside the path that descends from the so-called Black Lake and joins the road.

notes.label: g'spässig

10743d6d3799e617238600d5292f9581edbcb1cb.summary: Surrounded on every side by lush herbs, up here there is a level little spot where nothing ever grows green or blossoms, because in former times witches and evil spirits held their nocturnal gatherings there.

notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its associated pastoral operation, not simply any mountain; the Wangser Alpen and Gafarra are such Alpine pasture places.

notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

1097cec806b07f4b0d5f118d7d91ce6523591b90.summary: On the right side of the Almenser-Tobel is a sparse meadow near a mill. This basin-shaped meadow owes its more specific name, Pro da Scadella (also Prau; from Latin Pratum; “Bowl Meadow”), to its bowl-like hollow.

notes.label: Almenser-Tobel
notes.text: the local ravine by Almens; Tobel is a regional word for a steep, narrow gorge or stream-cut valley.

notes.label: Pro da Scadella
notes.text: a local Romance or Romansh meadow-name glossed by the source as “Bowl Meadow,” referring to the meadow’s hollowed shape; Prau and Latin Pratum are given as related forms.

notes.text: a seasonal intermediate mountain holding, with pasture and buildings used between the valley farm and the high summer Alp.

617dd2957fe0cc04b1b80ed355f2897b241eb8b4.summary: A Schierser who had his cattle at Rahl, a “Gadenstatt” above Fanas, for the “Vor-Winterung” and was feeding them there heard dreadful screaming in the yard before the stalls for a long time one night.

notes.label: Gadenstatt
notes.text: a mountain holding or seasonal farmstead characterized by its barns and stalls; the source itself glosses it as a Berggut, or mountain farm.

notes.label: Vor-Winterung

notes.label: Schmalvieh

0e5f95a6dff68bc18641cb1b1f40382734771935.summary: Women hermits, forest sisters, or Beguines once lived on the high rock that bears the very unusual pilgrimage chapel of Saint George near Bärschis, probably built on the ruins of a Roman fortress.

ed3a5a39d2842f2c74c05200c78fac462ea540bd.summary: Very often in the wild hunt of the gods, a woman has either a co-leading or dominant rank, or else a suffering part.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: a female wild-hunt or winter spirit of central Swiss folklore; the plural-like form can name both the leading woman and the beings ritually hunted.

notes.label: Grosskellerin
notes.text: literally ‘great cellar-mistress’ or senior female steward, one regional title for the dominant woman in the wild host; the precise office imagined is uncertain.

notes.label: Pfaffengälere
notes.text: another local name for the woman in the wild host, apparently containing Pfaffe, ‘cleric,’ but its second element and literal sense are uncertain.

notes.label: Streggelenjagen
notes.text: literally ‘hunting the Streggelen,’ a noisy midwinter custom and supernatural frame in which an unseen eighth rider joins the sled party.

notes.label: Türsts
notes.text: the genitive form of Türst, a leader or embodiment of the central Swiss Wild Hunt; the boys invoke his name during their dangerous sled ride.

notes.label: Berner Neutaler
notes.text: old Bernese ‘new thalers,’ large silver coins whose buried treasure finances the promised chapel.

0ee1a2614896b90c555fe3cf846ebd3a132d0076.summary: At Ennetmoos near Stans, "a dreadful and pitiful screaming" is often heard up and down the Pfaffenkellergraben.

notes.text: apparently a pastime of kneading or working clay; the source itself marks the interpretation Lehm kneten with uncertainty.

notes.label: Luzernerbieterin
notes.text: a woman in the characteristic dress of the rural Lucerne territory or its market-going countrywomen; the exact costume reference is not described.

aef918aa9334158060b641d546151a88e409931a.summary: On the Galgenbächlein between Sarnen and Sachseln, the wild spirit-woman rides over hill and dale on a “hellish monster,” screaming so loudly that she can be heard for miles around.

notes.label: Mohre
notes.text: a regional word for a sow, explicitly glossed as Sau in the source; it should not be confused here with the unrelated modern German word referring to a Moor.

notes.label: Grosskellerin
notes.text: literally something like “great cellar-mistress” or senior female steward, a regional title for the dominant woman in the Wild Host; the precise office imagined by the name is uncertain.

notes.label: Su, su!
notes.text: a traditional call used to summon or urge pigs; in the tale it reinforces the spirit-woman’s imagined porcine form.

notes.label: Nachtbub
notes.text: literally a “night lad,” meaning a young man roaming outdoors at night, often for nocturnal courting or revelry; the exact reason for his being out is not stated.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a regional term for a barn, stable, storehouse, or enclosed farm outbuilding; the exact type of rural structure here is not specified.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: a female Wild Host or winter spirit of central Swiss folklore; the plural-looking form can name both the leading woman and related beings, and traditions vary from place to place.

104b8f19daaf7f99796c726c2ae4e08f6c867054.summary: On the Hostris—that is to say, Hochgesträss, because the ancient road once ran here along the Wigger—lie several Jucharten of farmland called the Holderacker.

notes.label: Jucharten
notes.text: plural of Juchart, a traditional Swiss measure of land based on the area that could be plowed in a day; its exact size varied by region and period.

notes.label: Schöpferschmied-Anneli
notes.text: Anneli is the familiar Swiss-German diminutive of Anna; the compound identifies her through the local smith's household or byname and is retained as the tale's identifying name.

31e11bfe3b91df251b4a7ed9dc546d331927b053.summary: On Streggelnnacht, men from Triengen went into the Oelerhölzli, the beechwood above the village, to hunt and capture the Streggeln.

notes.label: Streggelnnacht
notes.text: this Lucerne-area name denotes the ritual night on which people hunted the Streggeln; its calendar date and exact relationship to other winter masquerade nights are uncertain.

notes.label: Streggelen
notes.text: this is the singular name used for the captured female Wild Hunt or witchlike being; her precise folkloric identity and relationship to the plural Streggeln are uncertain.

notes.label: Ragöri
notes.text: this unexplained name is called toward the sack during the mock hunt and receives the apparition’s answer; its referent, etymology, and role in the game are uncertain.
