ff2d919cb696d0f84c0a66e2b5e9bdb8407878d9.summary: At Schwarzenberg in Schorried near Alpnach, people know that an extraordinarily large billy goat appears there with a catlike animal sitting between its horns.

notes.label: wilden Heere
notes.text: the inflected form of wildes Heer, the ‘Wild Host’ or ‘Wild Hunt,’ a spectral nocturnal procession whose cries are often explained through ambiguous call-and-response phrases.

c0dcdb631f47bd1cd2686bf6f8f1c9894963118e.summary: On one of the Alpen on the Sigriswil Rothorn, a thriving boy once slept beside his herd.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, meaning the high seasonal mountain pastures and their working landscapes rather than mountains in general; the boy is tending his herd on one of these pastures at the Rothorn.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

d036881ed41d567adc77cf8f5af18996bc29d8c3.summary: In former times, the dark-haired Walliser very often came over the Rawil to the Lenk fair with their mules.

notes.label: Walliser
notes.text: German for people of Valais; here it identifies the Catholic neighbors who cross the Rawil and become the people of Lenk's legendary opponents.

notes.label: Rawil
notes.text: the high Rawil Pass linking the Lenk area with Valais; it carries trade, raiders, the recovered cattle, and both pursuing groups.

notes.label: Melchtern
notes.text: plural of a regional vessel for milking or holding milk, generally a wooden milk pail or tub; these coopered goods form part of the Lenk-Valais trade.

notes.label: Brenten
notes.text: plural of Brente, a tall wooden carrying vessel, often fitted for transport on the back and used for milk or other liquids in Alpine regions.

notes.label: Fähnlein
notes.text: literally a ‘little banner,’ and historically the company serving under it; the people of Lenk carry theirs into the wider war of religion.

notes.label: Ammann
notes.text: a local magistrate, chief official, or community head; identifying Greda as his daughter places her within Lenk's civic leadership.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; Siegfried moves from one dangerous rocky vantage to another while hunting.

notes.label: Gewild
notes.text: an older collective term for wild game animals; the precise species Siegfried watches for is not stated.

notes.label: Treichel
notes.text: a large, heavy livestock bell made from hammered sheet metal rather than cast like a traditional bell; Siegfried uses its deep herd sound as deception and then throws the largest through the tavern window.

50178bbdd4784a833b0393ece66dd8756ce3e8bd.summary: Between Endingen and Degerfelden is a bridge that is dangerous to cross at night; a ghost is said to block the way.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e357bb9dc0f1d50ebb60f7907cb453c7145c24cb.summary: High in the ice fields of the Bernese Oberland, in the midst of a glacier, is a wondrous vault of ice that perfectly resembles the interior of a church.

notes.label: Eiskirche
notes.text: literally ‘ice church,’ the glacier cavern whose natural forms resemble a complete church and were once credited with healing; its current existence and exact location are unknown.

7b0e0f53562206567ede0da1235d365f1f9fd3de.summary: During the Council at Basel, several clergymen walked out beyond the city into a little wood called the Bruderholz so that they might discuss some disputed points.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

caebf2d19524f080d38f0e3a89307420aa83a511.summary: A poor woodcutter working not far from the ruins of Bischofsstein Castle once saw something sparkling and shining among the old masonry like gold, silver, or precious stone.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4a90d54b596e4b479babcd4687c352c87406e29a.summary: In the Walenhütten Vorsass, an Alpine herdsman is said to have lived long ago who liked the herding life so well that he once declared that if he could remain on the mountain forever, he had no wish to enter heaven.

notes.label: Vorsass
notes.text: a pre-Alpine or intermediate seasonal pasture with huts, used between the valley farm and the higher Alp; ‘lower pasture’ is the closest concise English sense, but its altitude and role vary regionally.

5f937545c282a22049bf332721a4ada72ac55845.summary: Slander has been inventive in every age. According to the legend, a distinguished and wealthy gentleman of Brig is also said once to have experienced it.

notes.label: Pensionen, Fried- und Gemeingelder
notes.text: historical public revenues or payments, including foreign-service pensions, peace monies, and communal funds; the exact administrative categories varied in old Valais, so the source terms are retained rather than treated as modern personal pensions.

8510327697ff5ec5ded908c3fa8b04f841abb593.summary: High in the forest is a pond from which the village stream flows. At night, a marrow-piercing scream is often heard there.

notes.label: Wuetihee
notes.text: a local name connected by the collector with the memory of Wodan's raging host or Wild Hunt; in this localized account, the uncanny cry is reinterpreted as that of a woman condemned to haunt the pond after drowning her child.

d6743b5009c11c22057830ed053dc36e2364de8f.summary: A barn once stood in the Zelg below Rieden. Its owner kept his livestock there to feed and tend them.

notes.label: Zelg
notes.text: one field section in the traditional three-field rotation system, and by extension the named cultivated area below Rieden.

notes.label: Wunderkräutlein
notes.text: literally ‘little wonder herb,’ the medicinal plant delivered by the toad spirit to heal the chronic wound.

notes.label: Bresthafte
notes.text: an archaic term for an afflicted or infirm person; here it describes the man suffering from the open leg wound.

notes.label: Hausgeist
notes.text: a household spirit, benevolent in this account and embodied by the remedy-bearing toad.

notes.label: Hausgeister
notes.text: household spirits in the plural, said no longer to appear because the modern age has ceased to believe in them.

6f5df64da9d1c251c7b1a27ac54629c6c6456bf7.summary: At Christmas one hears the Wuotië high in the air, a wild outcry coming from the southeast.

notes.label: Wuotië
notes.text: the St. Gallen name for a wild airborne Christmas outcry approaching from the southeast; it resembles regional Wild Hunt traditions, but this brief source does not securely explain the name, participants, or derivation.

fa327849e067994e943d76dc91dcb7dc05daec84.summary: The Stadtthier in Kaiserstuhl bears the names above. It appears as a dog and as a Schwarzwälder-Hotzenmann—that is, in the beautifully archaic costume of the farmers from the neighboring County of Hauenstein on the Upper Rhine in Baden near Waldshut.

notes.label: Stadtthier
notes.text: literally ‘town animal,’ an old label here for Kaiserstuhl's local supernatural being; it may appear as a dog or a man, so ‘animal’ does not exhaust its form.

notes.label: Schwarzwälder-Hotzenmann
notes.text: a man of the Hotzenwald in the southern Black Forest wearing the region's distinctive traditional costume; here the town spirit assumes that human appearance.

notes.label: Wälderma
notes.text: dialect for ‘forest man’ or ‘man from the wooded country,’ one name or form of Kaiserstuhl's local spirit; the source also calls it Rhima and does not fully distinguish the names.

notes.label: Babeli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Barbara; here it is the familiar name of the old woman at the customs house who treats the visiting spirit as well known.

notes.label: Rhima
notes.text: another local name for Kaiserstuhl's shape-changing town spirit, perhaps related to the Rhine setting; the source supplies no secure etymology or clear distinction from Wälderma.

73f65810e6d965d9925950681ec63c9d1b1393e6.summary: 1. a) On the Mettenenalp in Unterschächen, an old woman was often observed who was called the Wängiguschi because she always went through Mettenen to the Alp Wängi.

notes.label: Wängiguschi
notes.text: the local name for a ragged, female weather apparition associated with Alp Wängi; its appearance foretells hail or misfortune, while the source leaves its identity and the precise derivation of Guschi uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: a central Swiss dialect label for an uncanny, disreputable, or witch-like female figure; here it is the shortened name for the weather-bringing Wängiguschi rather than a precise class of being.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person,’ sometimes familiar or dismissive in tone; here it describes the ragged female apparition without establishing whether it is human or ghostly.

notes.label: Fürscheibe
notes.text: an Uri term for an apron-like front cloth or garment panel; this apparition wears a red one with red stockings in an old-fashioned costume.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source’s name for a large, broad-brimmed hat worn by the apparition; its exact historical construction is not explained.

notes.label: Schlätterchorb
notes.text: a large regional carrying basket worn on the back; the source gives neither its exact woven construction nor what the Wängiguschi carries inside it.

notes.label: Helgenstöckli
notes.text: a diminutive wayside shrine containing a holy image or devotional cross; the footnote explains how the Abraham image came to this particular shrine around 1900/1901.

05e93e3723247cb6aecfc6a037009700c9755317.summary: The Wäschebach rises in a wooded upland meadow belonging to the village of Birri in the Freiamt, waters the meadows of Aristau, and, after a short course, empties into the Reuss.

notes.label: Wäscherli
notes.text: literally a diminutive “little washer”; here it is the local name of a white-clad, streamside apparition that attacks passersby, and the source does not identify it more narrowly as a washerwoman, water spirit, or ghost.

8705162b8defccad7c05eba3567f8a81302f2bfb.summary: The Wässermann once cheated his neighbors over water rights and has wandered ever since.

notes.label: Wässermann
notes.text: literally a ‘water man,’ here the revenant of someone who dishonestly deprived neighbors of water rights, rather than the more usual water-dwelling spirit.

notes.label: G'hei
notes.text: the source's abbreviated local place-name for the area from which the black apparition approaches; its full form is not supplied.

56875e68e7f452267f0101b6ea8a388ea0452723.summary: 1. Whenever people heard a Jauchzer coming from the Beerdli, those at the Ronastutz and in Fellenen would say, “Aha!

notes.label: Jauchzer
notes.text: a high, ringing Alpine whoop or cry, related to but distinct from sustained yodeling; the Wättermanndli’s call is answered by the witnesses and treated as a warning of bad weather.

notes.label: Wättermanndli
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘little weather man,’ a hat-wearing supernatural figure whose Jauchzer, appearance, and staff at the hut foretell bad weather; the source does not say whether he is a weather spirit, a haunting soul, or another kind of being.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle, milk work, and cheesemaking on a seasonal high pasture; the narrator’s role places him in charge of the hut’s pastoral routine, including the prayer call.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

2037b08095b8d507256ec1341217c6ebcef253b7.summary: A boy once fell asleep beneath the branches of a gigantic fir tree near the ruins of Heidenburg, on the road from Obersaxen to Tavanasa.

notes.label: Windsbraut
notes.text: literally “wind bride,” a traditional German personification of a violent whirlwind or raging gale; its imagined struggle conveys the host’s confused roar.

notes.label: Wütende Heer
notes.text: literally the “raging host,” a regional name for the spectral airborne procession more broadly known as the Wild Hunt; the boy recognizes it from earlier stories.

1f8b83e9f13a8e743be98542c832a2b84c272929.summary: A farmer’s son visited his bride. The path led across fields and meadows, including a place where things were not safe.

notes.label: wütende Heer
notes.text: literally the ‘raging host,’ a St. Gallen name for the airborne supernatural company related to the Wild Hunt; here it sounds like countless pursuing birds and imposes a precise bodily taboo on anyone who turns to look, while no visible leader or members are described.

a1e1c48154485a2353cf737e37ba168645fa3533.summary: From the Rotental between Hasli and Grindelwald and across the Scheidegg, one often hears the roaring of the raging host, or Wütisheer, as it is called here.

notes.label: Wütisheer
notes.text: the local name for the ‘raging host,’ a Wild Hunt procession heard crossing the Bernese mountains, especially during the Christmas season.

notes.label: Westfriesen
notes.text: the source's name for mighty giants regarded as primordial inhabitants of the land; it resembles ‘West Frisians,’ but the legend treats it as a local race-name rather than explaining a historical Frisian connection.

notes.label: Melkhaus
notes.text: an alpine milking and dairy house; its gates must remain open so the supernatural procession can pass without harming the building.

c8b20a4e2a7887e20e0d7cd2c589dd74a5a14464.summary: Between Hasli and Grindelwald, one often hears from the direction of the Rotental the roaring of the gray Talherren or of the Wütisheer.

notes.label: Talherren
notes.text: literally ‘valley lords,’ the gray beings whose roaring is identified with the Wütisheer; their rank, appearance, and relationship to the other spirits are not explained.

notes.label: Wütisheer
notes.text: a regional name for the Wild Hunt or raging spectral host that travels noisily through the night, especially around Christmas; the source associates it with the cursed dead of the Rotental.

notes.label: Westfriesen
notes.text: the tale’s name for mighty giants who lead the procession; although the word resembles ‘West Frisians,’ the source gives no geographic or historical explanation.

notes.label: Melkhaus
notes.text: the milking or dairy house on the mountain pasture; its doors must be opened to let the spectral procession pass, though the building’s exact layout is unstated.

b2a210b7c39fc0cdc923d8335cc92fc9c7a395c5.summary: Once there was a young duke who was so devout and God-fearing that he would have preferred to die at once and journey to Heaven.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

fb2d3a61ce6bb73fb98833eb2603ae3949d0261a.summary: Another time, around midnight, a thoroughly tipsy young man from Plaffeien made his way through the lane toward Plasselb.

notes.label: kilten
notes.text: the traditional Swiss custom of a young man making a nighttime courtship visit to a young woman's window or home; here the drunken visitor is on his way to such a meeting.

notes.label: Gassentätscher
notes.text: a regional name for Plaffeien's shape-changing night ghost, literally suggesting something that pads, slaps, or blunders through the lanes; here it appears as a fire-spitting dog and crushing burden.

notes.label: Geissalp
notes.text: literally ‘goat Alp,’ a high seasonal pasture associated with goats; here its imagined fat cows serve only as a humorous measure of the ghost's supernatural weight, and the exact place intended is not identified.

0ee401823635e41baee0b1f8e15491284bea2cab.summary: Two boys were talking with each other about treasure hunting: "The Devil has the treasures in his power."—"Then he must bring us money."—"Yes, but the person to whom the Jaggi must bring money must not be very good."—"God be praised, that would be me."

notes.label: Jaggi
notes.text: a Valais dialect name here used for the Devil or a devilish treasure-bringer; related regional uses can denote a bogey or masked figure.

2e2ef21d429c0453a4539afecf4768e44c0e0b13.summary: Even now, people in the mountains believe in certain places that the Marflu of the marmots comes from their eating a particular herb before hibernation.

notes.label: Marflu
notes.text: a Valais-dialect name for the profound winter sleep attributed to marmots and, in this tale, imitated disastrously by a man; the closest sense is ‘hibernation’ or ‘deep sleep,’ but the word’s literal derivation and the exact physiological folk belief are uncertain.

notes.label: Ziberlisturm
notes.text: the Bernese-dialect name of the cooked dish the woman hides; it appears to be a local food name, but its ingredients and exact literal sense are not established by the story, so the name is retained.

notes.label: Nachtlütli
notes.text: literally ‘little night people’ in Swiss German, here benevolent knee-high household or farm helpers who leave permanently when slighted; ‘night folk’ conveys the words but not the beings’ local folkloric identity.

3f8dd17e24a88c3548ce66dca309e34486204990.summary: Soon lit by the sun’s bright gleam,

notes.label: Galanda
notes.text: the mountain overlooking the Chur Rhine valley; the poem personifies it as a ruler above the forests, valleys, and young Rhine.

notes.label: Mutternen
notes.text: a regional form in the name-family for alpine spignel, a valued milk-producing fodder plant.

notes.label: Ritz
notes.text: a Graubünden German name for alpine plantain, Plantago alpina, paired with Muttern as nourishing pasture fodder.

notes.label: Ziprion
notes.text: the legendary milk-rich herb at the center of the poem; after it is cursed and omitted from the hunter’s blessing, it withers outside but retains thick white sap within.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen responsible for the herd and milk work; in the enchanted former Alp, beautiful maidens occupy their place.

notes.label: Sennerinnen
notes.text: female Alpine dairy and pasture workers; the poem’s Sennerinnen join the witches’ dance and bring the curse upon the Ziprion.

notes.label: Hexenboden
notes.text: literally ‘witches’ ground,’ the named high-mountain dancing place where black grass is said to mark the nocturnal gathering.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Sennerin
notes.text: singular of Sennerinnen, a female Alpine dairy worker; the youngest remains with the hunter after the others call her back to milk.

notes.label: Flühe
notes.text: a Swiss plural for steep rock faces, cliffs, or crags; dawn is already shining on them when the Sennerin is summoned away.

notes.label: Muttern
notes.text: another regional form for alpine spignel; the hunter’s counter-blessing preserves Muttern and Ritz but accidentally omits Ziprion.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the curse destroys this pastoral world.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

9c2ca77025353d8a7c791752083e1bd46c73c153.summary: Years ago, a Senne, a Zu-Senne, and the Schreiber stayed on the Tamins-Grossalp.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: the dairyman responsible for livestock and cheese-making on an Alp; the source distinguishes him from the subordinate Zu-Senne.

notes.label: Zu-Senne
notes.text: an assistant dairyman or second Senn on an Alpine dairy farm; the title identifies the worker responsible for repeatedly retrieving the missing cow.

notes.label: Schreiber
notes.text: literally ‘scribe’ or ‘writer,’ here the title of the third worker named on the Alp; Jecklin does not describe his precise pastoral or accounting duties.

notes.label: Tamins-Grossalp
notes.text: the large communal or principal Alp associated with Tamins; Grossalp denotes the larger high-pasture operation, not a mountain named ‘Great Alp.’

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its livestock, buildings, and dairy-working operation, not simply a mountain peak; the entire herd ranges across it.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

8b1c762171eb578393e9f1a89d4e65ea58a34336.summary: In those dark times when individuals even in Switzerland still presumed to exercise unlimited dominion over the bodies and souls of their fellow human beings, a Hagheer, or Zwingherr, lived in the region near Wald.

notes.label: Hagheer
notes.text: the local title or name used for the same tyrannical lord whom the source glosses as a Zwingherr; the story does not securely establish the word's exact derivation.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: literally a ‘coercive lord,’ an oppressive ruler who uses a castle and arbitrary power to dominate a subject population; the term belongs to Swiss liberation-legend vocabulary.

notes.label: Zwingburg
notes.text: literally a ‘coercion castle,’ a fortress built to impose or maintain a lord's control over the surrounding population, not merely a defensible residence.

notes.label: Trämeln
notes.text: a regional plural for massive logs, trunks, or heavy lengths of timber laid out for working.

notes.label: Hexenschuss
notes.text: literally ‘witch's shot,’ the ordinary German folk term for a sudden attack of lumbago or sharp lower-back pain; the carpenter only pretends to suffer it as part of his ruse.

notes.label: Hagheernburg
notes.text: literally the ‘Hagheer's castle,’ the tale's compound name for the planned fortress of oppression whose construction is prevented.

notes.label: Zwingherrschaft
notes.text: literally ‘coercive lordship,’ meaning tyrannical domination by a Zwingherr rather than governance under ordinary law.

5a1f930633fecb9d80bbb33c7a2ac206014131bd.summary: Zwingherren or Twingherren are said to have inhabited most castles in the Canton of Bern.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: plural of Zwingherr, literally coercive or oppressive lords, a legendary name for castle rulers remembered as tyrants; the term evokes feudal domination but is not a precise rank.

notes.label: Twingherren
notes.text: a spelling variant of Zwingherren rooted in the Swiss legal term Twing or Zwing for local jurisdiction; here it likewise denotes oppressive castle lords, though the passage does not distinguish the two forms.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a Swiss term for a deep, dug well or shaft-well, literally a draw-well; here it becomes both the tyrant’s grave and the hiding place of his treasure, while its exact construction is unstated.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: literally an oppressive or coercive lord, the legendary tyrant of Wartenstein; it describes his remembered conduct more than a formally documented noble title.

98148238dba70486925516ab33e5a7175b13d473.summary: There was once a Zwingburg in Wolhusen. One day its lord rode past a farmhouse and saw a magnificent tree trunk lying there.

notes.label: Zwingburg
notes.text: literally a ‘coercion castle,’ a stronghold associated in Swiss historical memory with domination and arbitrary lordly power; the term frames the castle as an instrument of oppression.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: literally a ‘coercing lord,’ an oppressive or tyrannical castle lord who abuses feudal power; it is a moral characterization, not merely a neutral noble title.

bb022ebb911222b057f57a451bd123490ecbefa7.summary: One afternoon on the Flums Alp called Fursch, the cattle and dairying equipment had been moved down from the upper Säss to the lower one.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Säss
notes.text: one of the seasonal stations or levels of an Alp, with its own hut and grazing ground; the herd moves from the upper to the lower Säss.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for the cattle and cheese-making operation.

notes.label: Baschi
notes.text: a Swiss familiar form of Sebastian used here as the cowherd boy's name.

notes.label: Tril
notes.text: the raised sleeping platform or bunk used by Alpine farmhands in the herdsman's hut.

notes.label: sennen
notes.text: to carry out a Senn's Alpine dairying work, especially milking and cheese-making.

notes.label: Es ist nit suber in dr Hüttä; i gschmöggä Minschäbluot!
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for ‘it is not clean in the hut; I smell human blood!’; the spirits detect the hidden living boy.
notes.anchor: Es ist nit suber in dr Hüttä; i gschmöggä Minschäbluot!

notes.label: Där, wo uf der Tril lit, söll ahä chu und mit Wohrheit sägä, was er do ztuä heb; es ward em dinn nüt Leids gschieh!
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect promising that the person on the sleeping platform will not be harmed if he comes down and tells the truth.
notes.anchor: Där, wo uf der Tril lit, söll ahä chu und mit Wohrheit sägä, was er do ztuä heb; es ward em dinn nüt Leids gschieh!

notes.label: Zwingnagel
notes.text: a lowly Alpine helper or underling compelled to do unwanted work; Baschi humbly applies the obscure regional term to himself, and the title makes it central to the tale.

notes.label: Ich bi nu an armä Zwingnagel, und üsärä Senn hat mi gnötiget, no in dr Nacht vu do si Mälchstuohl z' holä
notes.text: Baschi's dialect explanation that he is only a poor underling forced by the Senn to fetch the stool at night; his truthful humility earns the gift.
notes.anchor: Ich bi nu an armä Zwingnagel, und üsärä Senn hat mi gnötiget, no in dr Nacht vu do si Mälchstuohl z' holä

notes.label: Stofel
notes.text: an Alpine pasture station or its cluster of hut and working ground, here the lower place to which Baschi returns for milking.

notes.label: Chunnst indli ämol, du glampätä Hösi!
notes.text: a mocking dialect greeting roughly meaning ‘are you finally coming, you clumsy fool?’; Hösi literally evokes a rabbit but functions here as an insult.
notes.anchor: Chunnst indli ämol, du glampätä Hösi!

notes.label: Obersässhütle
notes.text: the little hut at the upper Säss, where Baschi meets the spirits; the final -le is diminutive.

notes.label: Gepsenlatten
notes.text: slats or racks used to hold Gepsen, shallow wooden dairy bowls or milk vessels; the cruel Senn's pieces are displayed on this equipment.

3196220cd91ae216f795d4a6c81598eefd3e0b61.summary: In ancient times, around haymaking season, a young dwarf once came to the people at Obegg near Zweisimmen, sat down beside the haymakers, and watched their diligent work as though he too wished to learn it.

notes.label: Zyland
notes.text: the source identifies Zyland as Daphne mezereum, or mezereon, believed to open hidden treasure vaults; the exact ritual use, dialect etymology, and historical breadth of that belief are uncertain.

844ff15171682e2dc626bffb8a0063027a7aa240.summary: High above the left bank of the Rhine in Graubünden rises the Calanda mountain chain.

notes.label: Zyprion
notes.text: the local name for the once-valuable Alpine fodder herb cursed in this legend; afterward it remains pale and milky-looking when broken, but cattle refuse to eat it, and the source does not provide a secure modern botanical identification.

notes.label: Muttern
notes.text: a valued aromatic Alpine pasture herb, generally identified with Alpine motherwort or mutellina; the hunter's blessing saves it from the dairywoman's curse.

notes.label: Ritz
notes.text: a local pasture-plant name paired with Muttern and likewise saved by the hunter; the source does not describe it well enough for a secure modern species identification.

notes.label: Milcherkraut
notes.text: literally ‘milk herb,’ a cattle-forage plant associated with rich milk production; the source lists it among the herbs of the formerly fertile Calanda heights.

notes.label: Hexenboden
notes.text: literally ‘witches' ground,’ the high-mountain dancing place where black grass still marks the dairywomen's nocturnal gatherings.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

97cb887ff47833d8b8ef33d889ee359c58f0b954.summary: In former times there were many Zössler in the fields; they formed entire chains and leapt after one another.

notes.label: Zössler
notes.text: a regional variant of Züsler, denoting fiery or uncanny wandering spirits; in this brief account they form long chains in the fields and leap after one another, but their exact appearance is not described.

28207ce46221cacb132ebeefee13933f7e5d59fe.summary: On the holy night, someone saw two ‘Zössler’ walking across the bridge in the Töbeli.

notes.label: Zössler
notes.text: a regional variant of Züsler, denoting fiery or uncanny wandering spirits; these two appear headless on the holy night with a one-eyed fiery dog.

8e549a29464f7d9f96ff1531f3532acfb0eff10b.summary: Many centuries ago, a poor boy once came running from the Zurich countryside to Zurzach and begged outside the Ox Inn.

notes.label: Züriheiri
notes.text: a colloquial and disparaging generic nickname for a man from the Zurich region, combining Züri with Heiri, the Swiss German form of Heinrich; in the tale it becomes the immigrant boy's enduring name.

notes.label: Zürichbieter
notes.text: a person from the historical territory or countryside of Zurich, not necessarily from the city itself.

notes.label: Zurzacher Messen
notes.text: the great commercial fairs of Zurzach, whose visiting merchants and crowds create the economic opportunity through which the stable boy prospers.

notes.label: Gabenholz
notes.text: literally ‘gift wood,’ a customary allotment of firewood or timber distributed from communal forests to entitled local citizens.

notes.label: Ausbürger
notes.text: here a resident who lacks full citizenship or communal-right status in the locality; the precise legal privileges attached to the historical status could vary.

notes.label: Zurzacherbann
notes.text: the territory under Zurzach's communal jurisdiction or forest rights; Bann denotes a legally bounded district as well as the authority exercised within it.

notes.label: Grüt
notes.text: the local name of the forest district where the theft and murder occur; it may be related to cleared or scrubby ground, but the source treats it simply as a place-name.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a communal warden charged with guarding the legally bounded forest and its use rights.

notes.label: Reiswellen
notes.text: tightly bound bundles of brushwood or thin branches used as fuel, rather than waves in the modern English sense.

notes.label: Hag-Gertel
notes.text: a curved hedge or brushwood billhook, glossed by the source as a Faschinenmesser; it is both the thief's working tool and the murder weapon.

notes.label: Gertel
notes.text: a regional word for the same curved chopping or billhook tool called Hag-Gertel earlier in the tale.

notes.label: Blutgericht
notes.text: literally ‘blood court,’ a court possessing high or capital jurisdiction, including authority to impose a death sentence.

notes.label: Schwörfinger
notes.text: literally ‘oath fingers,’ the three fingers raised or used in the traditional German-speaking oath gesture; here they are placed into the victim's wound during an ordeal-like proof of guilt.

0fdbb8cab8240f2fae812a9cd346c35e14def4a1.summary: Old Spörri, who died at the beginning of the 19th century, had a Reckzug—five horses used to haul ships upward from Lake Zürich through the Linth into Lake Walen—and could therefore feed his horses only at night.

notes.label: Reckzug
notes.text: the team of horses and associated towing operation used to haul vessels against the current between Lake Zürich and Lake Walen.

notes.label: Züsler
notes.text: a fiery or smoldering revenant whose name is related to züseln, to smolder or burn weakly; here its heat leaves finger marks in the shingle.

notes.label: Reckerei
notes.text: the historic regional trade of towing or hauling boats along the Linth, for which Benken was a center.

f6083394b5285af37e18eaec96fa5973c7566cd0.summary: In former times, a Züsler made the road across the Bendelhöhe unsafe. With his magical light, he led travelers astray so that they could find their bearings again only at dawn.

notes.label: Züsler
notes.text: a regional name for a misleading light-spirit or fiery apparition that rides travelers; the exact derivation is uncertain.

c050bee449cdb40c61bccb8fbe992f437a26b11a.summary: In a deep ravine near Rieden, a timber thief atones for his crimes as a Züsler.

notes.label: Züsler
notes.text: a regional St. Gallen name for a wandering light-bearing revenant or will-o'-the-wisp-like figure; here a man who stole timber must roam with a lantern in punishment, while the alternative account rationalizes the lights as living travelers.

1a9897c935ead035bb78753b4f2928db3573a72a.summary: Near the so-called "little village," below the parish church in Emd, a large, solidly built, tower-like house with several rooms, halls, and spacious living quarters stood at the edge of a rock.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

60b958e60d949cc53c8277fc4d829a040bb815a5.summary: Directly before Wartburg, magnificently situated on the Töss and reduced to ruin by the vindictiveness of Queen Agnes of Hungary, rises the no-longer-existing castle of Pfungen, an ancient structure that, if the chronicle can be trusted, was the court and favorite castle of Duke Gottfried of…

notes.label: Äckelmümmelisbrunnen
notes.text: the full-size variant meaning ‘Äckelmümmeli’s fountain’; the legend links the local name to the saint called Priminius in this source.

notes.label: Neckelmümmeli
notes.text: the alternate folk name for the miracle-working figure at the spring; the narrator identifies him with Saint Priminius, but the shift between Neckel- and Äckel- remains unexplained.

notes.label: Äckelmümmelisbrünneli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive place-name, approximately ‘Äckelmümmeli’s little spring or fountain’; it preserves the folk figure’s name and the affectionate diminutive Brünneli rather than identifying an ordinary unnamed well.

f10bc14e2272ea7b647a18e5c91bd5112707bb2b.summary: Beside the deep bed of the Thur between Kengelbach and Loretto lies the Äuli, a solitary farmstead.

notes.label: Äuli
notes.text: a diminutive place-name related to Au, an alluvial meadow or riverside flat; here it names the isolated farmstead by the Thur.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Betläuten
notes.text: the ringing that calls people to prayer, especially the Angelus bell; the dog appears before this protective devotional signal.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Äulihund
notes.text: literally ‘dog of the Äuli,’ the spectral boundary-walker identified with the farmer who tried to defraud his neighbor.

0b7717c7aa4f074c296f26035644df9d76be7182.summary: Not far from Flums, by the little chapel above the Seez, the "Äuliwibli" wanders about in shirtsleeves.

notes.label: Äuliwibli
notes.text: a diminutive Alemannic name for a little woman associated with an Au or riverside meadow; here it is the local apparition whose sight causes swelling, and no single English creature-name carries those associations.

72d47057e187fc48cd33e5df64be654319b0e33a.summary: This valley specter holds sway in Oberhof and Wölfliswil down toward Wittnau throughout the whole valley, as far as the Oerkenbächlein runs, and makes itself known in almost countless shapes and manifestations.

notes.label: Örkentier
notes.text: literally the ‘Oerken creature,’ the shape-changing valley specter associated with the Oerken stream; accounts disagree whether it is the ghost of a local farmer or a Swedish soldier, and its forms include a horse, a man, and an unseen obstructing force.

notes.label: frischem Feuer
notes.text: literally ‘fresh fire,’ newly struck flame used here as a protective countermeasure; the mill hand circles his immobilized wagon three times after lighting his tobacco, and the horses can move again.

notes.label: Chaischen
notes.text: a regional diminutive of chaise, meaning a small carriage; the judge turns this vehicle around and leads it backward with the horse's eyes covered to pass the spirit's barn.

2a1900651af92198c1662ba2f3843af34b27a18b.summary: When Mühli-Leart, or Mill-Leonhard, who died many years ago, was still young and nosed around the house in the manner of boys, he found a worm-eaten book in an old trough on the upper floor.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

1aca1056d30d2efbeec2cf5d51a72ccbccf3ff59.summary: I have always heard this told too: In Attinghausen, from Heeräzwy to Regliberg, there was in olden times a broad, beautiful stretch of level land with magnificent farms, and above it there were fine mountain farms reaching up toward Seewli.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

87f31e7e49bee72dafb18e97f8e3ed615b4877c4.summary: A spirit in the “Fürstenalpe” above Trimis, which has belonged to the Bishop of Chur since ancient times, had commanded each successive group of Sennen to say a formula over the herds entrusted to them every evening before going to sleep, in the “drei höchsten Namen,” or else things would go badly for them.

notes.label: Fürstenalpe
notes.text: literally the “Prince’s Alp,” the episcopal high pasture above Trimis where the spirit imposes the nightly observance.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine dairymen who manage cattle and dairy work during the high-pasture season.

notes.label: drei höchsten Namen
notes.text: literally the “three highest names,” a protective Christian formula likely invoking divine persons or sacred names; Jecklin does not spell the names out.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: the hired Alpine hands or herdsmen working under the Senn on the high summer pasture.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the head Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for the cattle and milk production on an Alp.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the seasonal journey taking people and livestock up to the high pasture, and by extension the opening of the summer Alp season.

notes.label: Bazger
notes.text: an Alpine crew role named but not defined by Jecklin; he is distinguished from both the Senn and the other Alpknechte, so the more precise duty remains uncertain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Schmalz
notes.text: rendered here in its Alpine dairy sense as melted or clarified fat, likely butterfat; the source makes being boiled in it one of the punishments.

notes.label: büchlen
notes.text: to blow an alphorn as a signal; here the condemned Senn must blow until his lungs burst, hoping the call will bring rescue.

5f5a6c70130445a2ec946f5c002c0d84207db6a4.summary: Only a few years ago, the Jostä-Chaspi family at Küpfen in the municipality of Spiringen owned, among their other sheep, a Chilber—a young female sheep that had never given birth—which in the evening could be driven into the stable only by force.

notes.label: Chilber
notes.text: an Uri husbandry term explicitly defined by the source as a young female sheep that has not yet given birth; the term marks its age and reproductive status rather than simply meaning any ewe.

notes.label: flamändere
notes.text: a Schächen Valley euphemism for cursing, as the source's footnote explains; the softened word still precedes a command that folklore treats as dangerously literal.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Hörige
notes.text: a woman in hereditary or legally dependent service to a lord or institution, here the Abbey of Einsiedeln; the historical status was unfree or serf-like rather than ordinary employment alone.

notes.label: Teufelsbrücke
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's Bridge,’ the local bridge-name on the Sihl beside the house associated with Paracelsus.

notes.label: Schweizerlandesart
notes.text: literally ‘the manner of the Swiss land,’ Paracelsus's phrase for a temperament he characterizes as rough rather than subtly fashioned.

notes.label: Rastus
notes.text: one popular Einsiedeln distortion of the name Theophrastus, used for Paracelsus in oral tradition.

notes.label: Raster
notes.text: another local distortion of Theophrastus and the form most often used for the magician in this account.

notes.label: Erast
notes.text: a third local shortened or altered form of Theophrastus recorded among the country people.

notes.label: Degen
notes.text: a sword or long thrusting sidearm, often closer to a rapier than a broad sword; here it is Paracelsus's magical weapon.

notes.label: Degenknopf
notes.text: literally ‘sword knob,’ the pommel of the Degen, said to contain the four elements and possess transmuting power.

notes.label: Gegenzauber
notes.text: literally ‘counter-magic’ or ‘counterspell,’ the antidotal magic that fails when the neighbors interrupt Paracelsus.

1853754989bd286a521f33863e9022db219a5f4f.summary: One morning, a farmer found three cows in two chains in his stable. He sought advice from the Capuchin friar.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

3587d0b62d5a8fdfd7949c45084bedb8d91dfd94.summary: Once, while the young men of Selzach, in Solothurn’s Leberberg district, were playing on their skittles ground, three strange bearded men stepped into their midst and challenged them to a match.

notes.label: Maß
notes.text: a historical German-speaking liquid measure and, by extension, a serving vessel of that capacity; its exact local volume varied, so the wager is best understood as a substantial measure of wine per throw rather than a modern standardized liter.

340036d42fb35da6f85800dc8c0358cb873dde51.summary: In the upper Saas Valley toward Monte Moro, three dragons lived in a mountain above Almagell.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

b220f31ae5f3f57dfd3a712ed267efdd4771f592.summary: At the time when influenza was raging in Unterschächen in 1918 and had already claimed many victims, it happened one day that the Sigrist, while at his work, saw three hands on the cemetery wall.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan, responsible for practical church and cemetery duties; his work places him at the cemetery when the omen appears.

7d933ef527881e44e7f6c2c8679dc3c8676fe0eb.summary: Near the Strättlingen Tower by Spiez Castle on Lake Thun, a man was walking through the brush after Easter when he saw a maiden sitting there.

notes.label: Säwidemünze
notes.text: the source's name for the lowest-valued coin into which the black beans turn; its exact denomination and the word's derivation are uncertain.

notes.label: Strättlinger Jungfer
notes.text: literally the ‘Strättlingen maiden,’ the supernatural young woman attached to the tower and castle landscape who distributes the treasure beans.

notes.label: Schatzbohen
notes.text: the input title's form for ‘treasure beans’; the body uses Bohnen, so Bohen is best treated as a title spelling or possible transcription variant rather than a distinct bean name.

6c89098f350c68b534b4babc9f2b3ec6caec2265.summary: Between Oberwil and Brütten in the canton of Zürich lies a field called Steinmürli.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

e2aab0e5b6dd1645ba8ca80abb6a80c7e0bd506f.summary: In the castle ruins at Weissenburg in the Simmental, a boy saw three linen sheets, “Lilache,” spread out.

notes.label: Lilache
notes.text: a Swiss German plural for linen sheets or bed sheets, corresponding to standard German Leintücher; here they display differently colored treasure pieces and vanish selectively with the guardian dog.

11d58337c154a45dda6e479590790d4b38bee34f.summary: A knight's castle is said once to have stood behind the Hertenstein near Baden.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

a7b763d1e96134a058ef38f7616fddf3ea40738f.summary: Three Handwerksburschen, who had never seen one another before in their lives, met entirely by chance while traveling in search of work.

notes.label: Handwerksburschen
notes.text: traveling journeymen craftsmen who traditionally moved from place to place in search of work and experience; the three strangers meet while on such a journey.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a small Swiss coin and the centime unit of the Swiss franc; having not a single Rappen emphasizes the craftsmen’s complete lack of money.

notes.label: Ränzel
notes.text: a small traveling knapsack or pack, here containing only the journeymen’s badly tattered underclothes.

notes.label: Kratzfuss
notes.text: an elaborate scraping bow made by drawing one foot backward; the black gentleman’s courtly gesture immediately precedes the revelation of his hoofprint.

notes.label: Feuerbesen
notes.text: a hearth broom used to sweep embers or coals together; the Devil turns the stolen implement into the revelers’ supernatural light.

fd6fee6f5314ef887d9ad25aeaf7524cb710f103.summary: A young married couple were saddened that no children had been granted to them.

notes.label: Schurzfell
notes.text: the protective leather apron worn by a blacksmith at the forge; Hannes throws it aside when he abandons his work and home.

notes.label: Draufgeld
notes.text: an additional payment, bonus, or item added on top of an agreement; after Hannes chooses advice instead of wages, the master gives him the horse as this extra consideration.

notes.label: Wegzehrung
notes.text: food provisions for a journey; the master gives Hannes the unopened loaf for sustenance on the road, though it ultimately contains his wages.

notes.label: Handwerksburschen
notes.text: traveling journeymen or young craftsmen moving between places of work; Burschen here does not mean untrained boys.

notes.label: Schmied-Hannes
notes.text: literally “Smith Hannes,” the village byname identifying Hannes by his trade; the innkeeper uses it without recognizing the returned man.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, understood as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection and a sacramental participation in his sacrifice. The word can name a service offered for a particular person, rather than simply a sermon or a gathering.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: the Eucharist and Mass

notes.label: Gemeinderat
notes.text: the municipal or communal council; it sponsors the village feast honoring the young priest's first Mass.

notes.label: Gastfreundschaft
notes.text: literally “guest-friendship,” meaning generous hospitality extended to a guest or stranger rather than an existing personal friendship; the approved source contains a soft line-break hyphen within the word.

notes.label: Heller
notes.text: a historical small coin of very low value; the statement that not one Heller is missing means the hidden gold equals every part of Hannes's twenty-year wage.

notes.label: Stumpebäse
notes.text: literally a stump- or worn-down broom, placed as a counter-charm in three corners but powerless against ordinary damp weather.

notes.label: Bohnere
notes.text: the floor or area being polished or worked with wax, likely a wooden room floor whose condition suffered in the persistent wet; the precise household sense is dialectal.

notes.label: Dokter
notes.text: dialect for doctor, here a folk adviser at Chalberbach who prescribes the broom charm.

1cf75bb1ca54742874aeb6381895265ffa041fdf.summary: An innkeeper would not believe that an ä-n-ändiri Wält¹—another world—existed.

notes.label: äs gäb de-n-ä-n-Ewigkeit
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘there is indeed an eternity’; the newly dead innkeeper announces what he has learned, while the inserted n sounds reflect connected local speech.

notes.label: ä-n-ändiri Wält
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘another world’ or the world beyond death; the skeptical innkeeper denies its existence, and the source footnote records the related form Dië äner, änder Wält.

8bf981a770399489adda40d228fee0bf48806e14.summary: Once, Doctor Schmon intended to walk down the mountain at night. When he reached the area between Freudenberg and Spillberg, he heard someone call:

notes.label: Dökterli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little doctor,’ using the familiar or teasing diminutive -li for Doctor Schmon in the supernatural rhyme.

notes.label: Hasenpanier
notes.text: literally ‘hare's banner,’ a historical idiom for fleeing or taking to one's heels in fear; the mock-military image reinforces the doctor's timidity.

964a9130e6cc879e61b6b355a8210e176c56bf9d.summary: According to folk belief in Obwalden, toads were enchanted people. Many were therefore very afraid of the animal.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f05e2c5ab83038caaebc8964c9a845bab7eb1aa5.summary: Whenever the carter Peter Schmied had to drive from Laufenburg to Basel—and that happened every week—his wife continually begged him to bring her a market gift for once.

notes.label: Zwilchsacke
notes.text: the inflected historical form of Zwilchsack, a sack made from strong two-thread twill cloth, used here to carry the captured frogs.

notes.label: Goldfüchse
notes.text: literally ‘gold foxes,’ a colloquial or playful term here for the gleaming gold coins into which the toads transform.

642912cd9d8a496161eb88f685509a921bb0a3f3.summary: a) More rarely, the Toggeli is understood to be a creature belonging to the race of dwarfs; most often it means the Nachtmahr, an elfin thing imagined as a fiend.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name most often used here for a nightmare or pressure spirit that sits on sleepers, though the source notes that it can also mean one of the dwarf-like little folk; its forms and identity vary among the episodes.

notes.label: Nachtmahr
notes.text: the oppressive supernatural “mare” behind the older sense of nightmare, believed to press on a sleeper's chest; it denotes a being, not merely a bad dream.

notes.label: Doggkelin
notes.text: R. Cysat's older spelling of the being later called Toggeli; his account presents it as either an animal or spirit in feline form.

notes.label: Wirtel
notes.text: a spindle whorl, the weighted disk used in hand spinning; hung on a cradle, its clatter was meant to divert the Toggeli into spinning instead of attacking the child.

notes.label: Gotte
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a godmother; the kin-like bond makes the revelation that she is the attacking Toggeli especially disturbing.

notes.label: Werchhechel
notes.text: a flax heckle, a board or comb set with sharp iron teeth for dressing flax fibers; its dangerous points form the protective trap in the story.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Zigge
notes.text: a light playful blow or tap; the accompanying dialect rhyme calls it a Nachtzigge and jokingly wishes the cat-shaped Toggeli upon the other child.

b86663af27e48621e3174b4881d9e1f0f659686a.summary: It is often observed that goats and kids lose the hair over the rump and then appear smoothly shorn in places; people then say, ‘The Toggäli has shorn them.’

notes.label: Toggäli
notes.text: the dialect spelling used in the reported saying for the same Toggeli being; the account attributes the goats' shorn-looking hair loss to it without describing how the act occurs.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name for an oppressive night spirit, bogey, or uncanny being; the title uses this spelling for what is blamed for mysterious bare patches on goats.

aa5a3fcaafea68c25ab95ed3379a4f0a9962ef60.summary: ‘Toggäli Fyrlibrand, gim-mer ä goldigä Zant, ich gib d'r ä beinigä!’—‘Toggäli Firebrand, give me a golden tooth; I will give you one of bone!’ the children say when they throw a lost tooth into the fire.

notes.label: Toggäli Fyrlibrand, gim-mer ä goldigä Zant, ich gib d'r ä beinigä!
notes.text: the tooth-losing rhyme in Uri dialect, literally asking Toggäli Firebrand for a golden tooth in exchange for the child’s ‘bone’ tooth.
notes.anchor: Toggäli Fyrlibrand, gim-mer ä goldigä Zant, ich gib d'r ä beinigä!

notes.label: Toggäli, Toggäli, Fyrlibrand, gim-mer ä nywä Zant!
notes.text: the Wassen children’s Uri-dialect rhyme asking Toggäli Firebrand for a new tooth while they trace a trembling reflection of sunlight.
notes.anchor: Toggäli, Toggäli, Fyrlibrand, gim-mer ä nywä Zant!

notes.label: Toggäli, Toggäli, nimm äu äs Chlee, ich nihmä-n-äu eis!
notes.text: an Uri-dialect game formula meaning ‘Toggäli, Toggäli, take a clover leaf too; I shall take one too’; the performed disappearance makes the being the imagined recipient.
notes.anchor: Toggäli, Toggäli, nimm äu äs Chlee, ich nihmä-n-äu eis!

notes.label: Toggälichlee
notes.text: literally ‘Toggeli clover,’ the name of a children’s sleight-of-hand game in which a clover leaf seems to vanish from a knife; the source does not state that the leaf must have any special number of leaflets.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name used broadly for an uncanny little being and, in many other accounts, a nightmare or pressure spirit; in these children’s rhymes it receives teeth or clover and is more playful than terrifying.

c77791a0624b9e472218f01a541243e99e4c96ce.summary: In Mr. Muther's horse stable in Wassen, the mane of one of the horses was found braided into small, very tight plaits every morning.

notes.label: Fuchsli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a small chestnut or reddish-brown horse; this one has an unusually whitish mane that shows the tight supernatural braids clearly.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper level of a barn or stable used for hay or storage; stairs beside the horse's stall lead up to it.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a Swiss German night spirit, nightmare being, or oppressive household goblin, often blamed for tangling hair and horses' manes; here its activity continues even when the horse is moved.

61e48d9fb97c15e1c8401b598aeb29f9f40071b4.summary: A poor man from Rans who was looking for dry wood near the Geitzbach ravine on Buchserberg fell over a rock and broke a leg.

notes.label: Männchen
notes.text: literally ‘little man,’ here a wild supernatural being whose dismissive comparison makes toothache sound worse than a broken leg; the source does not classify it more precisely as dwarf, spirit, or forest being.

61ca288a47d5aec0961c99ada08cee3b4728bcb7.summary: A quarter of an hour beyond the village of Unterschächen in the little land of Uri, sweet, cold bathing water springs from beneath a rock.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

bf43c87c3b9091c8b859837b27597db50fd5d23c.summary: Half an hour northeast of Grabs, on the valley floor, lie several properties bearing the name Gula.

notes.label: Irrkraut
notes.text: literally ‘straying herb,’ a folkloric plant believed to make anyone who steps on it lose direction and wander in circles; here it offers an alternative explanation to witchcraft, while no precise botanical species is identified.

953d1dcfbdb39c1843c6df6c33459f6824a47e9a.summary: 1. A fahrender Schüler said that the Hubel at the Pfaffensprung concealed a precious treasure and was worthy of being wound about with a garland.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally an ‘itinerant scholar’ or ‘traveling student,’ but in Alpine legend a wandering learned practitioner able to perceive concealed treasure.

notes.label: Hubel
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a rounded hill, knoll, or mound; the two Hubel references identify the elevated site beside the Pfaffensprung considered both for treasure and for the church foundation.

431896f5f2bb6c065713682ab60645cbc3749fc8.summary: Near the village of Bellikon is a cave about which the people still tell many events.

notes.label: Zwilchsack
notes.text: this is a sack made of strong twill or ticking into which the treasure seeker loads gold; its exact size and textile construction are uncertain.

4e766c859b7a9b0c62a689b2e4c9e56ac3e1058b.summary: Frau Brand in the village of Spiringen claimed to have experienced the following: Several of us children amused ourselves with all kinds of games ‘between the Stöcken’ on Alp Wängi (on the northern slope of the Kinzig Pass).

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, together with its huts and working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; Wängi is the named Alp where the children play and the subterranean passage briefly opens.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

88ee6d6df1632c69d29dbfe985efe240d9da9c21.summary: In times not long past, one finds people—and I myself have known many of them—who set their whole heart, mind, and spirit, together with all their goods and possessions, upon digging for treasure.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

3cedcffecac392b0315eff3845e4a0276ccfee9a.summary: A fahrender Schüler once came to Attinghausen. As happens, the conversation turned to all manner of subjects, and the people also told him about the castle’s treasure.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar’; in German-speaking Alpine folklore this is an itinerant learned figure often credited with occult or magical arts, not merely an ordinary student, although the source does not identify his training or powers.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a girl or young woman; here it denotes the half-grown girl whose curiosity leads the stranger to show her the treasure, while the precise age nuance is approximate.

notes.label: under ds Hinder, gottmerchytt, äs wär nur da sicher
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘under the backside—God preserve us, only there would it be safe’; the narrator inserts the protective exclamation while describing the Devil hiding treasure beneath himself, and the spelling and word division reflect the oral transcription.
notes.anchor: under ds Hinder, gottmerchytt, äs wär nur da sicher

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: an Alpine Swiss German word for a large kettle or cauldron, often the vessel used in cheese-making; here it contains treasure beneath a hazel shrub, and the source does not specify its material or size.

bba0980ef5c1152529e5fc6484abc7b5beaf9aa5.summary: This cave is known through the beautiful legend of Schrutan Winkelried, the dragon slayer.

notes.label: Schrutan Winkelried
notes.text: the legendary Nidwalden dragon slayer associated with the cave near Ennetmoos; he is distinct from Arnold von Winkelried of the Sempach battle tradition.

notes.label: gesonnt
notes.text: literally ‘sunned’ or exposed to light; in treasure lore, the guarded hoard is temporarily brought out or made accessible at a sacred time, though the source does not explain the precise action.

3e0d452ae2a6a6df3853db3e1963665c5e50c963.summary: Two hunters named Schrötenthaler once went hunting on the high Rialt. As they passed one of the castle ruins there, they suddenly noticed an open iron door in the masonry, although they had never seen it on any of the many times they had passed the same place before.

notes.label: Rialt
notes.text: the local height bearing castle ruins where the enchanted treasure appears; the tale provides no more precise identification of the site.

94248712e0b857bc60b43fc1fdc7371dd8332426.summary: In the Fehden in the forest at Attinghausen, a chest full of money is hidden beneath a great slab of rock.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

4dc7475fce87893687b7d4fa892feb19535d2b1a.summary: 1. On the Bristenstock, a Geissbub found his way by a strange route into a deep cave, a chamber of Strahlen that he had never seen before.

notes.label: Geissbub
notes.text: a boy who tends goats; the repeated figure is an Alpine child herder whose ordinary work brings him to the vanishing treasures.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: in Swiss Alpine mineral lore, crystals or crystal points found in rock cavities and near glaciers; the accounts use the word for specimens of several colors and kinds, not rays of light.

notes.label: Gand
notes.text: an Alpine scree field, stony waste, or slope covered with loose rock; two crystal finds appear in this rough terrain on the Bristenstock.

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine crystal seeker or mineral hunter who searches rock cavities for valuable specimens; the man in episode 3 is also a hunter.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; episode 4 and the source footnote identify this Alpine livelihood without specifying every worker’s exact task.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, together with its huts and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; several crystal finds are embedded in that working environment.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Fräßchessli
notes.text: a small copper cooking kettle used by Älpler; the source footnote says rice porridge, Fänz, and similar foods are served and eaten from it, and the story uses one to catch dripping gold.

notes.label: Cheeräli
notes.text: the narrator’s dialect word for the small golden-yellow objects beneath the stone, described as shirt-button-sized and shining like gold Napoleon coins; their material, shape, and a secure Standard German equivalent remain uncertain.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: literally ‘wild hay,’ grass cut on steep, remote mountain slopes outside ordinary meadows; harvesting it was dangerous seasonal work, and the men discover the crystal cleft while mowing.

notes.label: Grebel
notes.text: a regional digging implement, probably a hoe, mattock, or similar tool; it accompanies a pointed iron on the return search, but the source does not identify its exact form.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small barn, shed, farm outbuilding, or chamber; the man enters it for privacy, but the source does not identify its exact use.

notes.label: Bätti
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive for a rosary or set of prayer beads; here it could be thrown over the coins as a blessed devotional object to keep the treasure from disappearing.

notes.label: Krontaler
notes.text: a large silver crown thaler familiar in Switzerland and neighboring regions; the account calls the coins old but does not specify their mint, date, or exact value.

notes.label: Heidägmyr
notes.text: Uri dialect for Heidengemäuer, approximately ‘heathen masonry,’ the local name for extremely old walls and earth holes attributed to vanished ore-mining people; it is a folk-archaeological label, not proof of the builders’ identity.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or non-Christians, but in Alpine folk vocabulary it can mark something ancient, uncanny, foreign, or attributed to a vanished people; the story does not establish the miners’ historical religion or ethnicity.

notes.label: Gofä
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for children or youngsters, often with a colloquial tone; here they play among the castle ruins and unknowingly handle treasure.

notes.label: Fünfliber
notes.text: the popular Swiss name for five-franc coins, literally ‘five-livre’ pieces; the children stack and roll them before the money changes into stone.

notes.label: Fänz
notes.text: an Alpine flour-and-butter dish explicitly named in the source footnote; regional recipes and consistency can vary.

notes.label: Süffi
notes.text: a thin whey or whey-like liquid produced during cheesemaking; the source footnote says it is served in a Fräßmuttli but does not specify the precise production stage or consistency.

notes.label: Fräßmuttli
notes.text: a regional Alpine table vessel used here to serve coffee, milk, and Süffi; the source contrasts it with the copper Fräßchessli but does not describe its material, size, or exact shape.

efa75e1a5cbde24ea0c1f5fd0ce1113b1b7da82c.summary: Montas Castle stood on Maria near Schiers, and at certain times its last owner is said to ride around the castle hill on his Schimmel during a stormy night. — If a “Sonntagskind” happens to see him and dares seize the horse’s bridle, the child is led into the underground passage, where great treasures are found.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a white or gray horse; the dead castle owner rides one on stormy nights.

notes.label: Sonntagskind
notes.text: literally a “Sunday child,” a person born on Sunday and traditionally believed to possess luck or the ability to perceive and release spirits.

notes.label: Schierser-Knabe
notes.text: a boy from Schiers, identified by his home community.

notes.label: Weisshaselstaude
notes.text: a white-hazel shrub or bush; the boy sleeps beneath it when the treasure appears.

6189ace94a3ad2f4de51c147ddc567685e17ddab.summary: In the Lusser house in Altdorf, which had formerly belonged to the highly respected Landammann Thaddäus Schmid, money and jewelry were buried in the cellar at the time of the invasion by the Russians and French.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a canton or district in the old Swiss political order, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; both Thaddäus Schmid and Johann Zumbrunnen bear the title here.

e7ec8718c91c4c8a15cc0587a47efb57cc56933b.summary: Tribächli is the name today of a forest on the heights of the Lindenberg, where white maidens once came out of the water and appeared to children gathering strawberries.

notes.label: Tribächli
notes.text: a local place-name for a Lindenberg woodland once associated with white water maidens; Bächli can mean ‘little stream,’ but the full name’s derivation is not supplied.

345c86c1a660159513fe190ab2da155de45fbe8e.summary: The Binzenhof is a pleasant country estate situated near Aarau on the Distelberg below the Gönhard forest.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d3a857f1719b7b5a0b9cfb0adc5e375788de7105.summary: One evening in Schiers, a man told a gathering that until then he had never believed in witchcraft, yet something curious had indeed happened to him that evening.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Bissen
notes.text: wedges or chocks in the fastening; the man knocks them out before he can free the chained cows.

notes.label: Hengert
notes.text: a traditional evening social gathering or visit for conversation and companionship; the man tells both versions of his supposed witchcraft there.

93e1fc353eab00f05938baf975ff76c6085bffff.summary: “I am certainly not superstitious, and yet something happened to me that did not proceed by natural means,” Stega-Leart (Leonhard), who was widely known as a freethinker, told me.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f32755359e779f1bac9ad426073079d11a533200.summary: A farmer was once mowing his meadow when a man came along the road, wished him ‘ds Zyt a,’ and asked why he chose to torment and exhaust himself so.

notes.label: ds Zyt a
notes.text: a dialect greeting or good wish offered to someone at work, literally invoking ‘the time’; the source does not supply a clean conventional English equivalent.

notes.label: Mattli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small meadow; the farmer says he cannot simply leave it standing unmown.

notes.label: b'stellt
notes.text: an Uri dialect form for being magically stopped, fixed, or immobilized; each sorcerer can impose and undo the condition.

notes.label: b'stellen
notes.text: the corresponding verb ‘to immobilize by magic’; the farmer turns the stranger’s trick back upon him.

notes.label: Bann
notes.text: a supernatural binding, prohibition, or spell; when it is lifted, the long-immobilized stranger collapses.

720ba2ad1c97cd7f7681dfb7d1b63a58a574401a.summary: Tüfeli im Äcke — Little Devils at the Neck

notes.label: Tüfeli im Äcke
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘little devil at the neck’ or nape; the visionary board reveals one clinging to every dancer, though ordinary sight cannot perceive them.

notes.label: Totebäumli
notes.text: literally a ‘little dead-person tree,’ a regional euphemistic name here for the small coffin in which an unbaptized child had lain; a knotted board from it becomes a supernatural viewing device.

notes.label: Tüfelsgäld
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘Devil’s money’; the magically gathered fern seed becomes wealth only through a dangerous encounter that resembles a diabolical contract.

notes.label: Sant Johannisnacht
notes.text: St. John’s Night, the midsummer feast eve traditionally associated with fires, plants, treasure, and heightened supernatural power; local dating customs can differ.

notes.label: Farnsome
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘fern seed’; because ferns visibly produce no flowers or seeds, folklore treated their supposed seed as rare, invisible, and magically potent.

notes.label: Dümpfe cheut er i eui linggi Hang
notes.text: a difficult dialect sentence cautiously rendered as ‘you can dip into your left hands’; in the context of signing the stranger’s book, it probably alludes to using blood from the left hand, but the exact omitted object and action are uncertain.
notes.anchor: Dümpfe cheut er i eui linggi Hang

notes.label: Toggiburg
notes.text: a dialect form of Toggenburg, the eastern Swiss region where the pursuing man finally disappears; it is a place-name, not a literal ‘defiant castle.’

notes.label: Tüfelswärch
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Devil's work’; it names both the supernatural trick with the wire-filled straw and the hare that lures the boys away from their companion.

61d719165c043d2f469945e03e43f46a87232ff0.summary: The Türst hunted throughout the Canton of Lucerne, usually with dogs. In Kriens, the now-vanished Klausengass was his route.

notes.label: Türst
