notes.text: a regional name for the leader or embodiment of the nocturnal Wild Hunt in central Switzerland, traveling with a spectral host of dogs and sometimes pigs; the figure’s precise origin and form vary from place to place.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss German term for a church sexton or sacristan; his proximity to bells and sacred space matters when a straggling hunt-dog must wait between prayer bells.

notes.label: Gespänlein
notes.text: a diminutive for a little companion or member of a team or host; here it is the spectral puppy separated from the Türst’s pack, not necessarily an ordinary draft animal.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Bresten
notes.text: a regional term for disease, affliction, or damage among livestock; the exact ailment caused when the protective panel is removed is not specified.

notes.label: Nachtjäger
notes.text: literally ‘night hunter,’ an alternate name for the Türst as leader of the nocturnal spectral hunt.

notes.label: Gfert
notes.text: an older word for the equipment, commotion, or accompanying apparatus of a hunt; the quotation groups it with dogs and horn-blowing, and the precise scope is broad.

notes.label: Gjägd
notes.text: dialect for the hunt or hunting activity; the older quotation compares the specter’s noise with equipment used by human hunters.

notes.label: ’s Irrlig’Spor
notes.text: dialect approximately meaning ‘the straying track,’ the name for the spectral pigs or their misleading trail at Escholzmatt; stepping in it causes supernatural disorientation.

notes.label: Betglockenzeit
notes.text: the time marked by the prayer bell, commonly morning or evening; the Türst’s little dogs are immobilized between one such bell-time and the next.

notes.label: Gim m’r mis Gragöri use
notes.text: dialect for ‘give me back my Gragöri,’ the great spectral dog’s demand for the stranded puppy; Gragöri is the puppy’s personal name or call-name, whose further significance is uncertain.

notes.label: Drei Schritt rechts uf d’ Site!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘three steps to the right’; the warning formula tells a traveler exactly how to clear the oncoming Wild Hunt’s path.
notes.anchor: Drei Schritt rechts uf d’ Site!

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: the local female supernatural figure invoked and mocked by the sledding boys; the brief source shows her as a long-legged shadow that follows them but does not securely explain her name, origin, or wider character.

notes.label: Frau Fischte
notes.text: a rhyming or variant form paired with Frau Faschte in the boys' mocking challenge; the source does not establish whether it is a second name, deliberate distortion, or nonsense rhyme.

notes.label: Uf dr Chaltenegg
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘on the Chaltenegg,’ a ridge or hillside place-name whose first element suggests coldness.

notes.label: wildi Jagd
notes.text: dialect for the ‘Wild Hunt,’ the roaring airborne procession of spirits heard crossing the ridge at night.

5ce0ebe016572328f5f81d4e03cdb3bacf2a7eba.summary: Uf em Arni — On the Arni

notes.label: Uf em Arni
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “on the Arni,” the upland setting named in the tale; Arni is a local place-name associated with seasonal pasture, while its exact boundaries and derivation are not given.

notes.label: Arnihütte
notes.text: the seasonal Alpine hut on the Arni, used for herding and dairy work; it is haunted only after the workers and livestock leave, and the building’s exact arrangement is unspecified.

notes.label: War
notes.text: a Bernese dialect word apparently referring here to the herd or cattle collective that occupies the pasture; the closest sense is “livestock,” but the term’s precise local range is uncertain.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the Alpine herders and dairymen who live and work on seasonal high pastures; their departure leaves the Arnihütte open to the spirit.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

5a22a73f8a352010a5e249fd8d8ab9276a294034.summary: Uf em Hingerarni — On the Hingerarni

notes.label: Uf em Hingerarni
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “on the Hingerarni,” the named upland or farm setting of the tale; Hingerarni itself is a local place-name, and the passage does not establish its exact boundaries or literal derivation.

notes.label: Verdingbueb
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a boy placed out by contract to work in another household, often in conditions now associated with Switzerland’s history of coerced or exploitative child labor; here it marks Röthlisbärger’s poor youth, though his exact arrangement is unstated.

741c3d663aa8bca048535ed5968b30c5bff9fd39.summary: Uf em Hunze — Up on the Hunze

notes.label: Uf em Hunze
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘up on the Hunze’ or ‘on the Hunze’; Hunze is the local height or area containing the uncanny dancing place, and the source varies between Hunze and Hunzen in inflected use.

notes.label: Mäss
notes.text: a traditional measure or measuring vessel; saying that Spilejoggi's head was ‘like a Mäss’ conveys an extreme swollen or heavy-headed condition after the encounter, but the comparison's exact physical sense is uncertain.

notes.label: nid sufer
notes.text: literally ‘not clean’ in Bernese German, a folk expression meaning that a place is supernaturally uncanny, haunted, or unsafe rather than physically dirty; Spilejoggi applies it to the woods by the dancing place and Schlosschnubel.

b526435f571d2aa7dc4277f4b3f7870164b89fc7.summary: Uf em Steihufe u drum ume — On the Steihufe and Around It

notes.label: Uf em Steihufe u drum ume
notes.text: dialect for ‘on the Steihufe and around it’; Steihufe is retained as the local terrain-name, while its literal formation suggests a stony tract or holding but is not explained.
notes.anchor: Uf em Steihufe u drum ume

notes.label: Wolfsgruebe
notes.text: the plural of Wolfsgrube, literally ‘wolf pits,’ traps or pits historically associated with catching wolves; the source says only that two lie beside the route.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: literally ‘little woman’ or ‘little lady,’ with the Alemannic diminutive -li; here it is an uncanny female figure digging with a golden hoe.

notes.label: Nochtsemi
notes.text: apparently a local district, farm group, or settlement-name whose men show the narrator the grave mounds; the dialect passage does not supply a secure literal derivation.

notes.label: Zwingherr
notes.text: an oppressive or tyrannical lord, a stock figure attached to ruined castles in Swiss legend; the term emphasizes coercive rule rather than merely noble rank.

notes.label: Sodloch
notes.text: literally a deep well-hole or shaft; the lord's daughter and then the lord leap into it, but the source does not describe whether it held water.

notes.label: Rütschelebammert
notes.text: a local personal byname for the man who tried to enter the cave; its literal derivation and whether it refers to an office, family, or nickname remain unclear.

e374979a1cb48808276d3ad54aa7145b70121b57.summary: Above the Schwäbischen Meer, Lake Constance, around the Säntis range, lies the green Appenzell country.

notes.label: Schwäbischen Meer
notes.text: the source’s inflected form of ‘Swabian Sea,’ a traditional German name for Lake Constance; the source immediately identifies the lake for readers.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, especially a herder or dairy worker; here the term characterizes the Appenzell fighters through their mountain livelihood.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Letzimauer
notes.text: a defensive barrier wall or fortified closure across a valley route, part of the Swiss Letzi tradition; the Stoß wall blocks the advancing army but is breached.

notes.label: Föhnsturm
notes.text: a storm driven by the warm, dry Alpine Föhn wind; the image compares flying helmets to nests torn loose in such a gale.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn, storage building, or hay structure in Alpine and southern German usage; here it refers back to the hay barn set alight behind Rotach.

bb243060ef3fbf5fb062adfa781143b1e06354b5.summary: was formerly punished by cutting off the right hand, old people from various parts of the canton assert; and even some 35 years ago a man from Isental said to a boy who had committed this offense: ‘They would now have the right to cut off your right hand.’

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

43b4648ec385360d66ea8fe7eaff14b896d099c6.summary: According to legend, underground passages connected Attinghausen Castle with the residential tower at Schweinsberg, and that tower with the convent in Seedorf.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Ankenwage
notes.text: literally the ‘butter scales,’ a named butter-weighing or market point in Altdorf; the tale places a covered shaft exit and signaling bell there, but does not describe the installation’s exact form.

notes.label: Unger dr Walkibrügg
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘under the Walki Bridge’; retaining it preserves the tale’s local place-label and spoken form.

notes.label: Walkibrügg
notes.text: the local Bernese name of the bridge, with ‘Brügg’ meaning bridge; ‘Walki’ is the associated place or works name and is not safely translatable.

notes.label: Gluggere
notes.text: a clucking or broody hen; here the word identifies the creature-like sound ‘Glugg, glugg, glugg’ heard beneath the stove.

5d91ea5a1714ea4ddeff4ed8cfbc006543c5929a.summary: In the Canton of Bern lies a forest called Bannholz where remarkable grave antiquities are found, especially the Unghür-Hubel in the middle of the forest, on the road between Heitern and the Süri near Laupen.

notes.label: Bannholz
notes.text: a protected or regulated communal woodland placed under a Bann, a legal restriction on use; here it is the forest containing the mound, while the specific historic restrictions are not stated.

notes.label: Unghür-Hubel
notes.text: Swiss German for an “uncanny-creature mound” or “monster hill,” with Hubel meaning a rounded hillock; it names the archaeological-looking mound, but the tale does not identify any particular Unghür associated with it.

notes.label: Fuss
notes.text: the historical German foot measure, whose exact length varied by territory before metric standardization; the stated 30 Fuss therefore conveys approximate height rather than a directly standardized modern measurement.

notes.label: Unghürschloss
notes.text: literally “uncanny-creature castle” or “monster castle,” an alternative local name for the mound because building remains occur on its summit; Schloss may evoke a castle without proving that the structure was one.

notes.label: Aschentuch
notes.text: literally an “ash cloth,” a cloth used in connection with ashes or lye-making; here the Devil spreads money on it in the sun, but the object’s precise household form and magical significance are not explained.

notes.label: Mühlicharer
notes.text: a mill carter or wagoner who transports goods for a mill; the dialect compound combines Mühli, ‘mill,’ with a form of carter or driver.

notes.label: Bättlermanndli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive meaning a little beggar man; his cat-gray appearance and impossibly heavy sack mark him as more than an ordinary traveler.

notes.label: Wehrsteine
notes.text: stones belonging to a weir, bridge approach, or river-control structure; the exact arrangement in the Rüegsauschachen landscape is not explained.

notes.label: Mühliross
notes.text: a mill horse used for hauling the mill's loads; even four such working horses cannot move the supernatural sack.

notes.label: unnötigi Almuese wo-n-i zsämebättlet ha
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘needless alms that I have begged together’; the little man's answer explains why the sack bears such moral and supernatural weight.

notes.label: Unnötig zsämebättleti Almuese
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘needlessly begged-together alms’; the phrase names the impossibly heavy burden and carries the story's criticism of soliciting charity without need.

6cfe385728e856adab1641b7ed3ca9b3951843bb.summary: On an alpine pasture in Schwyz, the herdsmen had forgotten something when they moved away, and one of them had to return to the abandoned hut and fetch the missing object.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

fb9a12478f13db64c3e34266503cb92498923652.summary: A wild little man stayed in Portels and made himself useful to the farmers through all kinds of services.

notes.label: essed de Chriesiblägel underem Bank
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘eat the cherry mess beneath the bench’; Chriesiblägel is a disparaging word for the cooked, crushed, or messy cherry dish used to insult the wild helper, and the exact consistency is not specified.

cb2253baa519d0b52def8b234bc4bfb10609e288.summary: a) Two young men from Schattdorf went z'Gass to three pretty girls in Bürglen.

notes.label: z'Gass
notes.text: a Swiss German expression for paying an evening social or courting visit; the two young men visit the three unmarried women under rules that conceal the women's Saturday flight.

notes.label: Stube
notes.text: the principal heated living room of a German-speaking Alpine house; the visitors watch the women groom themselves and read the magic book there.

notes.label: Obä-n-üß und niänä-n-a
notes.text: Uri dialect literally suggesting ‘up and out, and against nowhere’; it is the safe broom-flight formula that carries the speaker through the chimney without collision.

notes.label: Chämi üff und niänä-n-a
notes.text: Uri dialect for a variant such as ‘up the chimney and against nowhere’; the exact grammar is formulaic, but its function is to guarantee unobstructed flight.

notes.label: Obä-n-üß und z'allä-n-Ortä-n-a
notes.text: the mistaken Uri dialect formula, roughly ‘up and out and against every place’; by replacing nowhere with every place, the speaker makes himself collide with every surface.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for girls or young women; the narrative first presents the three as courting partners and then reveals their participation in the witches' gathering.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Betenläuten
notes.text: the ringing of the prayer or Angelus bell, which marks a protective morning hour; in variant b the battered traveler lands only when it sounds.

notes.label: Obä-n-üß und niänä-n-a bis i d'Stadt Wiän
notes.text: an expanded flight formula meaning roughly ‘up and out, touching nowhere, as far as the city of Vienna’; this version supplies the destination omitted by the shorter charm.
notes.anchor: Obä-n-üß und niänä-n-a bis i d'Stadt Wiän

notes.label: Salbe hiär und Salbe da
notes.text: the opening of a rhyming Uri magic formula, ‘Ointment here and ointment there’; its second line sends the rider out the chimney without touching anything.

4c044e58bc12795ed110cdc16fca2fab6858cc48.summary: At Birchi, in the very first or second little house on the old road as one enters the Isental from Seedorf or Isleten, there once lived two unmarried women of a somewhat peculiar nature.

notes.label: Chämi üff und niänä-n-a
notes.text: an Uri dialect witch’s flight formula, approximately ‘Up the chimney and nowhere against!’; in this story it propels the young man safely out through the chimney and far across the world, while the precise spatial force of niänä-n-a remains uncertain.

aa3974d6e1050587d4c6928491f4339da444785a.summary: The ruins of destroyed Urgiss upon the little mountain below Densbüren cover a large iron chest filled with money.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

2f8cb2238fe1a97a703f759806d6c67b0b96d2b8.summary: Urispiegel and the Devil on the Stove

notes.label: Urispiegel
notes.text: this Bernese tale-name adapts the trickster name Eulenspiegel with an apparent reference to Uri and identifies the human who outwits the Devil; whether it denotes a distinct local figure or only a localized name is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

52934723ba2beda9378f30a4083b36dcaeed23e4.summary: The origins of belief in magic reach back into pagan antiquity. The figure of the Devil, by contrast, as popular belief depicts him, properly appears only after the introduction of Christianity.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Urispiegel
notes.text: Urispiegel is a local trickster figure whose name echoes the broader Eulenspiegel tradition, here bluffing the Devil in a carrying contest; his supposed origin and relationship to other tricksters are uncertain.

notes.label: Tüfel
notes.text: Tüfel is the Bernese dialect form of ‘Devil,’ fooled here into believing Urispiegel can carry an entire group of logs; its exact pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Trämel
notes.text: Trämel are logs or heavy cut tree trunks lying beside the forest road, one of which the Devil lifts; their size and intended use are unspecified.

notes.label: Wid
notes.text: a Wid is a flexible withe or twisted wooden tie, which Urispiegel claims is the only use he has for logs that small; the intended object he pretends to bind is left unspecified.

1a06e40daf9b3648695b6d2448a9ec49e5cf3c9b.summary: This castle stands opposite Supersaxo Castle, with the Kelchbach flowing between them. — Only the strong tower of Urnäfass Castle remains.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

1c0fa3404def933ea54bd7a229c5304c94feff16.summary: In the previous century, people in Urseren told the French traveler Ramond that this valley, now poor in timber, had formerly been richly planted with fir trees and had otherwise been a true paradise as well.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘traveling scholar,’ a traditional German-speaking folklore figure imagined as a wandering student versed in forbidden learning or magic; here he destroys Urseren’s woods through fire and sorcery, while the story does not specify whether he is human, demonic, or merely reputed to be a magician.

notes.label: Bannwald
notes.text: literally a forest placed under a ban or legal protection, especially an Alpine protective forest preserved to shield settlements and routes from avalanches and other hazards; here it is Urseren’s last surviving woodland, though the exact historical restrictions on its use are not stated.

dbc702bbe59faca9ff80531e3a92923446ed4dea.summary: In the 18th century, people in Ursern told the French traveler Ramond that this valley, now poor in timber, had formerly been richly covered with fir trees and had otherwise been a true paradise.

notes.label: fahriger Schüler
notes.text: an older regional form related to fahrender Schüler, literally an itinerant student; in Alpine legend such a figure is a wandering scholar credited with occult or magical knowledge, here used to destroy the valley’s woods.

notes.label: Bannwald
notes.text: a forest placed under legal protection, especially an Alpine protective forest maintained to shield settlements and routes from avalanches and related hazards; the legend presents it as Ursern’s scant surviving woodland.

b4f06706ac2d2db30ef2e5e2469f3a8cb782d003.summary: Uznaberg Castle belonged to the Counts of Toggenburg, who took the liberty of seizing and plundering merchants from Zurich.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

f401e8af27145d29e717d02fbf3ec4f297582f13.summary: At Mombiel near Klosters, a Fänggenmannli tended the Heimkühe for years. He too never came as far as the livestock owners’ dwellings, but waited beside a large stone above the hamlet and took charge of his herd there.

notes.label: Fänggenmannli
notes.text: literally a ‘little Fängg man,’ a small male member of the wild forest or mountain beings called Fänggen; ordinary categories such as dwarf or goblin would narrow the tradition too much.

notes.label: Heimkühe
notes.text: cows kept near the home settlement rather than sent to a remote high Alp; Uzy collects and tends this local herd without entering the owners’ houses.

notes.label: Schöppli
notes.text: a Swiss diminutive for a small serving or measure of wine; Uzy cautiously drinks the whole portion, while its exact volume is unstated.

notes.label: Mannli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive meaning ‘little man’; here it refers back to the Fänggenmannli without defining him as an ordinary human.

notes.label: Uzy
notes.text: the Fänggenmannli’s recorded personal name; the source provides no secure literal derivation, but the nearby Uzystein preserves it.

71efb6be39c934fd07146b3f10a944a5b0c48cad.summary: No one knows how long ago there was a town on the Chilpel, or Kilchberg, near Schötz on the Luthern, another near Grosswangen, and another in Nebikon.

notes.label: Chilpel
notes.text: the local name identified parenthetically with Kilchberg, literally a church hill; the source treats it as a place-name connected with a vanished town.

notes.label: Käppeli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive for a small chapel or wayside shrine; the surviving structure helps mark the claimed western extent of ancient Willisau.

8b252d5c830fa5bea1f71390b6a1c73964257aa6.summary: Below the church at Neuheim in the canton of Zug, on the Unterhausmatte, a women's convent is said to have stood in former times.

notes.label: Unterhausmatte
notes.text: a local field-name below the church at Neuheim; Matte is a Swiss and southern German word for a meadow or grass field.

notes.label: Krebsbach
notes.text: the local stream name beside the Kuzelrüti, literally ‘crayfish brook.’

notes.label: Kuzelrüti
notes.text: a local place-name near the Baarburg; Rüti commonly denotes land cleared from woodland, while the meaning of the first element is not explained by the source.

5aa54af48042e17927e0f848b29eace526f7586b.summary: At the beginning of the eleventh century, between 1020 and 1025, Altdorf and a large part of Bürglen and Schattorf are said to have perished.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

fed5efb8bb6b6f63a2e3e60458767342da78e6a9.summary: A rooster lived in a house for seven years and laid an egg in the horse manure.

notes.label: About this telling

f5838aa9165530780154d7910d77fdab12f8387c.summary: The hare in the Langenhag appears between Klingnau and Ober-Endingen by day and night and remains fearlessly in place.

notes.label: Stadtbann
notes.text: the legally bounded territory or jurisdiction of a town, here formerly marked by an oak.

b5927052a29a34a94f0ed06d1c7c0ed6eba86ebe.summary: As long as my grandfather served at Wuechswil in the canton of Lucerne, he knew a boy who was once given a shotgun to shoot the hare that regularly ate the vegetable field bare.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

c5287dde36839cb9c866949f601024c768629d55.summary: Schwarzwasserstelz Castle, situated in the Rhine below Kaiserstuhl, formerly belonged to a Baron von Tschudi.

notes.label: Hasenfrauen
notes.text: literally ‘hare-women,’ women believed able to appear as hares or use a hare-form in witchcraft; this Kaiserstuhl episode identifies the animal as an old woman but does not explain how the transformation or reflected shot works.

a6fa125e7703ba1b17bce4cda04ec53407eb277a.summary: a. At night, on the Zurzach road by the place called the Brünneli, an enormous man lies crosswise over the way; one must step across him.

notes.label: Brünneli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Brunnen, a small spring, fountain, or well; here it is the named roadside site of the first apparition.

notes.label: Nachthund
notes.text: literally ‘night dog,’ a spectral dog whose noise drives a family away and whose circuit follows chapel lands.

notes.label: Gotteshöfe
notes.text: literally ‘God's farms,’ landed estates endowed to a religious institution; the Nachthund patrols the former chapel properties.

notes.label: Schinnhut
notes.text: the source's local name for the apparition's exceptionally large hat; its precise construction and the sense of Schinn are not explained.

notes.label: Dorfpudel
notes.text: literally ‘village poodle,’ the local form of the supernatural village dog that accompanies the two men as far as running water.

notes.label: Angerhund
notes.text: literally a dog of the village green or common meadow; its howling brings bodily harm to anyone who looks out.

notes.label: Schlosshund
notes.text: literally ‘castle dog,’ a spectral dog associated here with weather prediction rather than an ordinary watchdog.

notes.label: Dorfhund
notes.text: literally ‘village dog,’ the recurring Aargau apparition attached to a settlement, route, castle, or punishment tradition.

notes.label: Tüfelsgässli
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little Devil's lane’; -li is diminutive, and the name marks the Muri Dorfhund's route.

notes.label: Dorfthier
notes.text: historical spelling of ‘village beast,’ a shape-changing local apparition rather than a normal domestic animal.

notes.label: Langböri
notes.text: the proper local name of Densbüren's dog-or-bull apparition; the story does not explain the name's literal derivation.

notes.label: Strassenhund
notes.text: literally ‘road dog,’ the posthumous form of a corrupt road builder who now foretells weather.

notes.label: Bornhund
notes.text: the spectral ‘Born dog’ associated with the Bornberg; its bell collar sounds before changes in the weather.

notes.label: W. Jäger
notes.text: the source abbreviates the adjective as W.; the supernatural-hunt context indicates Wilder Jäger, ‘Wild Hunter,’ though the initial is not expanded in this entry.

notes.label: Baschishund
notes.text: the named Wallbach house spirit in dog form, interpreted as a pagan nobleman guarding a buried war chest; Baschi is a local personal-name form.

notes.label: Büngerte
notes.text: a regional form meaning orchard or enclosed fruit-tree plot; here it identifies the limit of the Tegerfelden dog's route.

notes.label: chretzen
notes.text: the source's verb for carrying the monster over one's shoulder like a back-basket; the gloss is supplied by the historical text itself.

notes.label: Trübelhund
notes.text: literally a ‘grape-cluster dog’ or vineyard dog, the proverbial name for a howling spectral hound among the vines.

notes.label: Rochelenmoor
notes.text: the local name for a dog-or-cat apparition between Obermumpf and Schupfart; its literal derivation is not securely explained here.

notes.label: Pudelhund
notes.text: literally ‘poodle dog,’ one route-dependent name for the same changing apparition called Rochelenmoor elsewhere.

notes.label: Bachpflätschi
notes.text: a local compound for a splashing or wet stream-being; it names the apparition when it follows a particular route near Schupfart.

notes.label: Pflätschi
notes.text: the shortened regional name for a wet or splashing apparition; a related being roams the neighboring village of Hellikon.

notes.label: Jonenthier
notes.text: historical spelling of ‘Jonen beast,’ the many-shaped apparition associated with both the Jonen waters and the upper Freiamt.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: the historical Aargau region of the Freie Ämter, or Free Bailiwicks, not a generic administrative office.

notes.label: Zofinger-Stadtthier
notes.text: the ‘Zofingen town beast,’ a huge black dog whose appearance during the holy nights causes illness or injury.

notes.label: Mättelithier
notes.text: the Niederwil name for the supernatural dog, probably associated by the account with castle bailiff Metteli; -li is diminutive, but the creature is not small.

notes.label: Rollenthier
notes.text: literally a ‘rolling beast’ or a beast named for rolling noise or motion; it is an alternate name for the Mättelithier, and the account does not resolve the nuance.

notes.label: Mättelihund
notes.text: the ‘Mätteli dog,’ another name for the Niederwil apparition whose name the source links with castle bailiff Metteli.

notes.label: The Landvogt
notes.text: The historical Swiss bailiff, or Landvogt, represented a ruling authority in a district and could exercise judicial, financial, administrative, and military powers. The title carries broader authority than the modern American use of “bailiff” for a court officer.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Landvogt

notes.label: Bachpfaddli
notes.text: a local name for the stream-side apparition beneath the bridge; Bach means stream, while the precise sense of Pfaddli is uncertain in this form.

notes.label: Bachpflotschi
notes.text: an alternate name for the Bachpfaddli, evoking a wet, splashing stream-being; passers sometimes see two girls in the water instead.

4a5cd9d332bc1a409a4bc94062de4a407140cfd0.summary: The Zusenne on the Casana-Alpe took refuge beneath a rock during a thunderstorm and waited there until the rain had passed.

notes.label: Zusenne
notes.text: the subordinate dairyman or assistant to the senior Senn on an Alpine dairy pasture; he helps tend the cattle and make dairy products.

notes.label: Casana-Alpe
notes.text: the Casana Alpine pasture; Alpe here means a high summer-grazing and dairying area rather than simply a mountain peak.

b399f34ef27b9bfcdfe62cf7372798b35253b39e.summary: Our mountains are rich in ore. In former times, the Venediger knew this; they came here and gathered precious stones in their sacks.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians,’ but in Alpine legend a class of mysterious foreign mineral seekers, treasure finders, and eventually sorcerers; the collector explicitly explains how Venice's wealth and the strangers' skill merged with dwarf lore.

notes.label: Taler
notes.text: a large historical silver coin; streets paved with Taler coins are an extravagant image of Venice's legendary wealth, not a precise statement of denomination or date.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: welsch
notes.text: a German-speaking Swiss label for Romance-speaking, non-German, or broadly foreign people and things; its scope shifts by region and can sound distancing, which the collector uses to explain how unknown miners became exoticized.

0902b232654b03e3bdea9788d3b97c7e5c8ce9f0.summary: At various places in the Toggenburg, most notably near Wildenburg in Wildhaus, the Venediger found rich treasures of gold.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: literally ‘Venetians,’ but in Alpine folklore it often denotes mysterious foreign prospectors believed to find hidden mineral wealth by secret or magical knowledge; the term can refer either to actual Italians or to this legendary class of treasure seekers.

notes.label: Landrat
notes.text: here the Toggenburg territorial council acting as a judicial authority; depending on period and region, the same term can denote a legislative or governing council.

3c4a45bebaf2d1effbfeb35deef83e505888a4e3.summary: In former times, the Venediger had a reputation for trading in little devils called spiritus familiares, or familiar spirits.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine legend, a name for supposedly Venetian or southern prospectors and occult practitioners credited with secret knowledge of ores and spirits; ‘Venetians’ gives the geographic association but not this regional folkloric role, whose historical basis is uncertain.

066250d59746c55925a89cee490be0320446ad02.summary: Belief in the wondrous city of Venice was once deeply rooted among the people of Uri.

notes.label: Waisenvogt
notes.text: a public guardian or administrative officer responsible for the legal and financial interests of orphans and other wards; here the official intervenes paternalistically in the adult man's affairs, but the account does not state his exact statutory authority.

f05370200c4146e55618f24f3ff8ae30ef301cd9.summary: On the Eigenalp at the Gand in Bürglen, diseases and all kinds of misfortune repeatedly afflicted the livestock.

notes.label: Gespenst
notes.text: a ghost, spectral apparition, or other haunting being; the account does not describe its appearance, only the harm attributed to it.

notes.label: Barnen
notes.text: an interior level or hay-storage area in an Uri stable or barn; the nine nails are driven there, though its exact construction is not specified.

notes.label: Vernageln
notes.text: literally to nail up, nail shut, or magically ‘nail down’; the title names a gradual nine-night binding remedy against the being blamed for livestock losses.

ebbd3472702fcd82d641171966a1d346e7cc4db6.summary: In former times, at the western end of the village, there lived a married couple who were at odds with each other.

notes.label: Verzich
notes.text: a dialect cry most likely corresponding to standard German verzeih, ‘forgive [me]’; the dead husband calls for forgiveness because he died unreconciled, though the spelling can also suggest verzichten, ‘to renounce,’ so its precise nuance is uncertain.

2a95265f085a830283e18409d0c4899937e95a8a.summary: A lord of Strättlingen on Lake Thun once found himself at the court of the Duke of Burgundy.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

9f6ccab535d9f61e9e548f5e8a80772d47766ac9.summary: One spring they drove up to the Surenen Alp much too early. On the first evening, as the Älpler sat together in the hut, the shovels and Grebel tools began to rumble and rattle, and a voice cried, ‘Vill z'friëh, vill z'friëh!’ Indeed, the next day brought snowy weather and became so cold that they had to leave the Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy-working landscape; going ‘up’ to it and later leaving it are seasonal livestock movements, not ordinary mountain excursions.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live and work seasonally with livestock on an Alp; their shared hut and early ascent place the warning within Alpine pastoral practice.

notes.label: Grebel
notes.text: a regional farm or digging implement, probably a hoe, mattock, or similar tool; the source names it beside shovels but gives too little context to identify its exact form.

notes.label: Vill z'friëh
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘much too early’; the repeated supernatural warning judges the herders’ premature spring ascent, which the next day’s snow forces them to reverse.

notes.label: Vo chline Lütli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of little people,’ referring to diminutive supernatural visitors who reward hospitality.

notes.label: chlini Lütli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘little people,’ the two wandering beings refused lodging until they reach the smithy.

notes.label: Riegeli
notes.text: a small bar, bolt, or piece of the smithy’s locking hardware; either it or a lock serves as a protective token for Eriswil.

a3f6e9299724ff37163e3d043bb3b831b753f9db.summary: Vo de drei Chüeiher uf em Enzi (The Three Cowherds on the Enzi)

notes.label: Chüeiher
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for cowherds or men tending cattle; the form conveys the rural dialect voice of the account.

notes.label: Vo de drei Chüeiher uf em Enzi
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of/from the three cowherds on the Enzi’; the exact dialect title is retained because Enzi is a local place-name and Chüeiher is a regional occupational word.
notes.anchor: Vo de drei Chüeiher uf em Enzi

notes.label: Enzi
notes.text: a local upland place-name in the Trub region of the Emmental; English readers should understand it as the named grazing area, not as a translated common noun.

notes.label: Rafen
notes.text: a dialect word for a roof rafter or heavy roof beam; here the blow against it opens the survivor's head wound.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional title of a cantonal chief magistrate; Tresch's plague cure is offered as a Swiss comparison to the bleeding cowherd.

afb91b91447bd277c589c5fdf821fc1e9bb135d3.summary: Vo de drü Mannen im Flüehli — Of the Three Men in the Little Cliff

notes.label: Vo de drü Mannen im Flüehli
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of the three men in the little cliff’; the title locates the penitential vision inside a small rock face near the Altburg.
notes.anchor: Vo de drü Mannen im Flüehli

notes.label: Flüehli
notes.text: diminutive of Flueh, meaning a little cliff, rock face, or rocky rise; it is treated as a hollow supernatural place visible from the stream.

notes.label: gruchset
notes.text: a dialect verb for grunting, groaning, or making a rough throaty noise; the exact quality of the repeated sound is not further described.

notes.label: Füiffränkler
notes.text: Swiss German for five-franc coins; the miser’s endless forced exchange turns familiar money into an instrument of punishment.

notes.label: Vo de Schnabellüt
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of the beak-people,’ subterranean bird-headed humanoids connected by the collector with a medieval poem.

notes.label: Schnabellüt
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘beak-people,’ the local plural form.

notes.label: Wosch zu de Schnabellüten abe?
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Do you want to go down to the beak-people?’—a teasing question asked of someone digging deeply.

notes.label: Schnabelleuten
notes.text: standard-German inflected plural for ‘beak-people,’ used in the collector’s literary comparison.

6669f31bee2b569a228f9158adbb4adb6ac16ef9.summary: Vo dr Brunscht z’Schmiedige — Of the Conflagration at Schmidigen

notes.label: Brunscht
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a major destructive fire or conflagration, used here for the historically remembered burning at Schmidigen rather than an ordinary hearth fire.

notes.label: Cheigel
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the game of skittles or ninepins; the impious players stage it with food and imitate the thunderstorm that later destroys the inn.

notes.label: Mütschi
notes.text: a regional name for small bread rolls or compact loaves; the oral version makes halved Mütschi into pins, while the quoted chronicle appears to make them thrown objects, so their exact role varies between tellings.

notes.label: Zweupfünger
notes.text: dialect for ‘two-pounders,’ probably two-pound bread loaves used as skittle balls in the oral account; the source does not independently specify their ingredients or shape.

dce2af736d3f17ddc5da8e9f05e8ef6a73a06edb.summary: Vo dr Färbergweid us — From the Färbergweid

notes.label: Vo dr Färbergweid us
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘from the Färbergweid,’ naming the pasture from which the storm-being approaches.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: the local name of the roaring or storm-associated beast that sweeps hay into the air; its compound elements and exact imagined shape are uncertain.

notes.label: Äs isch nümm sufer
notes.text: literally ‘it is no longer clean,’ an idiom meaning conditions or weather no longer look clear or safe; the farmer recognizes the warning before the hay is taken.

notes.label: Gable
notes.text: dialect for a fork or pitchfork, which the servants try to throw into the swiftly moving phenomenon.

notes.label: gleitig
notes.text: dialect for quick, nimble, or moving at speed; it explains why striking the being with a fork is difficult.

notes.label: Vo dr Müllerschtochter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of the miller's daughter,’ the title of the curing-and-marriage tale.

notes.label: Müllerschtochter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘miller's daughter,’ the bewitched woman whose hidden cure the boy overhears.

notes.label: Chuppele Häxen
notes.text: a little group, cluster, or gathering of witches; Chuppele conveys an indefinite bunch rather than a formal coven.

notes.label: Hörli us em Stiel
notes.text: literally a ‘little horn out of the stalk/stem,’ said to come from a snow-white horse; the dialect remedy's exact anatomical or botanical object is unclear, so the phrase is retained.

notes.label: im Hangumdräihe
notes.text: literally in the turning of a hand, meaning immediately or in no time at all.

notes.label: füregi Mur
notes.text: a fiery wall; the boy's prayer creates this protective barrier that prevents the witches from bewitching him.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

f8c09e148ee6e19a3e90d78509b4d0f36a58fa07.summary: Vo dr Schlossschür (Of the Castle Barn)

notes.label: Vo dr Schlossschür
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of’ or ‘from the castle barn’; the title refers to a surviving farm building traditionally said to have belonged to the vanished castle.

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a Swiss German field, vineyard, or woodland watchman charged with guarding rural property; here one of the brothers living at the Barn serves in that role.

notes.label: Gutsche
notes.text: a Swiss German form of Kutsche, meaning a coach or carriage; here an unseen supernatural vehicle rattles up the hollow lane at night.

notes.label: Dolder
notes.text: a dialect word for the crown or upper tuft of a tree; here the sound begins high in a fir before something armored seems to fall.

5aa91be9363b527827084af1700a47a03b369369.summary: Once there were a man and a woman. Whenever the man could put aside a few Batze, he placed them in the cupboard, laughed, and said, “That is something for an old man.” By this he meant that he would use the money when he was old.

notes.label: Batze
notes.text: plural of Batzen, a historical Swiss and south German coin or small sum of money whose value varied by place and period; here it simply means the husband’s modest savings.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Frau, meaning “little wife,” “dear wife,” or simply “woman” in a familiar register; the husband’s use can sound patronizing as well as affectionate, and the exact tone is ambiguous.

notes.label: Vo eifältige Fraueline
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “of simple little women” or “about foolish women”; the diminutive has a familiar tone, while the tale uses “simple” in the older sense of naive or gullible.

5713706e2e770793f035576af9b3fe0afd0694ec.summary: Vo re Chünigstochter — About a King's Daughter

notes.label: Vo re Chünigstochter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘about a king's daughter’; the entire tale is recorded in dialect, and this original title is retained beside its English gloss.

notes.label: Hanterchsbursche
notes.text: a dialect form of Handwerksbursche, a traveling journeyman craftsman; such young tradesmen traditionally traveled to gain experience after apprenticeship.

notes.label: bsägnet
notes.text: Bernese dialect for making a protective blessing over oneself, probably including the sign of the cross; in the story this religious act prevents the Devil from reaching the traveler.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Mur
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘wall’; it is not a physical wall here but the supernatural barrier that the Devil sees around the blessed traveler.

efc3704a7b68e266fe92c95f388c1810c7ebc5a2.summary: Vo re Häx u ihrem Chrott

notes.label: Vo re Häx u ihrem Chrott
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of a witch and her toad,’ with Chrott denoting a toad rather than an ordinary frog.
notes.anchor: Vo re Häx u ihrem Chrott

notes.label: Chrott
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a toad; the repeated term identifies the witch's supernatural source of eggs.

notes.label: hasligs Rüetli
notes.text: a little hazel switch, used here as the magical implement that forces the toad to lay eggs.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

c5db920d265a3d6414b53ee03003095e22bfd874.summary: Vo ren unghüürige Chueh — Of a Monstrous Cow

notes.label: Vo ren unghüürige Chueh
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of a monstrous, enormous, or uncanny cow’; unghüürig can carry several overlapping senses, and the animal’s supernatural nature is implied rather than explained.

notes.label: Chäser
notes.text: Swiss German for a cheesemaker; the narrator identifies the man by this later occupation but does not state whether he owned or managed the dairy.

notes.label: Triebbueb
notes.text: a young boy employed to drive or move livestock; the source gives no further detail about his age, pay, or exact responsibilities.

notes.label: e Fuehr
notes.text: a Bernese dialect expression for a difficult business, struggle, or commotion with someone or something; here it describes the repeated trouble with the strange cow, not necessarily a wagonload.

notes.label: brevsti
notes.text: dialect for the finest, most imposing, or strongest-looking one; the cow’s exact distinguishing quality is not specified.

notes.label: e Chuppele
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a bunch, group, or whole cluster of people; the number involved is not stated.

notes.label: Schorloch
notes.text: a low opening or gutter-hole in a cattle stall, likely used for drainage or manure removal; the exact local construction through which the cow escapes is not described.

notes.label: Vo Sargnegel
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of coffin nails,’ the magically charged objects used to lame a horse.

notes.label: Sargnegel
notes.text: Swiss German plural for coffin nails, believed to carry the contagious power of death from coffin or bier.

notes.label: Kumission
notes.text: dialect for the commission or official requisitioning board expected to take military horses.

notes.label: Springete
notes.text: Bernese German for traditional youthful dancing or leaping gatherings; the narrator contrasts them with modern dancing, so ‘dance’ alone is too narrow.

notes.label: Springplatz
notes.text: literally ‘leaping place’ or ‘dance place,’ the forest clearing named for the former Springete held there.

notes.label: im Verschleikte
notes.text: covertly, hidden away, or in concealment; the gatherings were arranged so outsiders would not notice.

notes.label: Uzit
notes.text: an out-of-the-way or off-hours time suited to secrecy; the exact dialect time reference is uncertain.

notes.label: Springet
notes.text: singular form of Springete, one such traditional dancing or leaping gathering.

notes.label: Uberegi
notes.text: a moment or figure in the gathering when participants crossed or passed one another; the exact dance action is uncertain.

notes.label: Bänger
notes.text: colored ribbons or bands woven into the girls’ long braids.

notes.label: Blüemeler
notes.text: literally someone associated with a little flower, the byname earned by tying a flower into the girl’s braid.

notes.label: z’Chile
notes.text: literally ‘to church’; going to church together is a discreet dialect expression here for marrying.

notes.label: Vo Wirtslüte
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of innkeepers’ or ‘about innkeeping people’; the title introduces linked traditions about a dishonest innkeeper and his wife returning after death.

notes.label: Wirti
notes.text: Bernese German for a female innkeeper or the innkeeper's wife; her repeated confession reenacts her theft from horses and adulteration of wine.

notes.label: Bare
notes.text: Bernese German for a manger or feeding rack; taking hay from it deprived stabled guests' horses of feed that had been paid for.

notes.label: Schoppe
notes.text: regional liquid measures or drinking portions, here three of wine and one of water; exact volumes varied, and the point is the innkeeper's fraudulent mixture.

notes.label: Moss
notes.text: the dialect form of Mass or Maß, a larger historical liquid measure; the ghost confesses that three Schoppe of wine plus one of water were sold as a full Moss.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Uflot
notes.text: the source's dialect comparison for the snorting spirit, apparently an animal or creature known for forceful snorting; its exact referent is uncertain.

notes.label: Chrützer
notes.text: a small historical coin, related to Kreuzer; the Capuchin says he paid for the turnip by placing one in the hole from which he pulled it.

notes.label: Härmli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a stoat or ermine; the escaping spirit's nimble climbing is compared with this small predator even while it takes the form of a green woodpecker.

notes.label: Saarbaum
notes.text: the dialect name of the tree into whose hole the Capuchin binds the spirit; the precise tree species intended is uncertain from this source.

notes.label: Gütterli
notes.text: a small glass bottle or vial; in the alternate account, the Capuchin confines the spirit in this portable vessel.

notes.label: Reiti
notes.text: the part of the building or masonry being rebuilt when Murersepp seals the spirit's bottle into the wall; the exact architectural feature is not explained.

notes.label: Gutter
notes.text: a dialect form for a glass bottle, the larger or non-diminutive counterpart of Gütterli; after accidental release, the spirit is confined in it again and buried in the streambed.

ad72c3706d73809b13b2a85d372712b19d7c9181.summary: Vom alte Buume — About Old Buume

notes.label: Vom alte Buume
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘about old Buume’; Buume is the devout man’s identifying name or byname rather than the ordinary German word Baum, ‘tree.’

notes.label: Ungerdorf
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the ‘lower village,’ a locally understood part of the settlement whose precise modern boundary is not supplied.

notes.label: Ihelüte
notes.text: the ringing-in of church bells that calls worshipers into the service; Buume remains outside while both living and dead congregants are entering.

notes.label: Totehof
notes.text: literally ‘yard of the dead,’ a dialect name for the churchyard or cemetery whose wall Buume uses as his waiting place.

notes.label: Verlüten
notes.text: the concluding or completed peal of the church bells; the exact local sequence of bells is not detailed, but Buume waits until this ringing has finished.

83907de13169c857e14753a5de2377f724e82484.summary: Vom alte Füürglöggli — Of the Old Fire Bell

notes.label: Vom alte Füürglöggli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘of the old little fire bell’; Füürglöggli is an affectionate diminutive for the small bell used to sound a fire alarm.

notes.label: Füürglöggli
notes.text: a little fire-alarm bell; the legend gives the old bell a speaking voice and traces its movement among Sant Urbe, Gumiswil, Huttwil, and Rohrbach.

notes.label: Gumiswil
notes.text: the dialect form of Gondiswil used by this Bernese source; Huttel in the same passage is likewise a dialect form of Huttwil.

notes.label: ’s isch mer, wie wen i nid zahlt wär!
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘I feel as though I had not been paid!’; the repeated phrase imitates what listeners heard in the bell's ringing and prompts the quarrel over it.
notes.anchor: ’s isch mer, wie wen i nid zahlt wär!

bc46df5a11e6234fe756b213c0f18815e2b2301a.summary: Vom arme Bueb (Of the Poor Boy)

notes.label: Vom arme Bueb
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of the poor boy’; the exact dialect title preserves the storyteller's regional voice.

notes.label: Altburg
notes.text: literally ‘old castle,’ the named castle hill or ruin around which the boy must walk at midnight to receive money.

notes.label: Vom Brüeltier
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘of the bellowing beast’; Brüel imitates its terrible cry, while Tier means animal or beast.

notes.label: Brüeltier
notes.text: literally ‘bellowing beast,’ the clawed weather-night creature whose cry resembles a goat being slaughtered; its exact shape is not described.

notes.label: unghüürig
notes.text: dialect for uncanny, monstrous, or deeply unsettling; it characterizes the whole region when the being roams.

notes.label: Matten
notes.text: grass or hay meadows across which the Brüeltier approaches in darkness and rough weather.

notes.label: brüelet
notes.text: dialect for bellows, roars, or cries loudly; the sound gives the creature its name.

notes.label: Kilte
notes.text: a nighttime social or courtship gathering, often involving visiting and games; the cards reveal what the frightened group had been doing.

notes.label: tätsche
notes.text: to slap, smack, or thump against something; the creature strikes the window and catches on its frame.

notes.label: bim Düner
notes.text: a mild dialect oath, ‘by thunder’; it lends emphatic oral-storytelling force to the claim about the claws.

979dbf950b6c886bc6388868535db1745f3d535e.summary: Vom Bärewirt z’Bärn — The Bear Innkeeper of Bern

notes.label: Bärewirt
notes.text: literally ‘Bear innkeeper,’ the keeper of a Bear-named inn in Bern; the tale uses the designation almost as the wealthy lender’s name.

notes.label: Vom Bärewirt z’Bärn
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘about the Bear innkeeper in Bern’; Bär is ‘bear,’ but here Bärewirt identifies the proprietor of an inn named for the Bear rather than an innkeeper who is literally a bear.

notes.label: Gisnauﬂueh
notes.text: the local cliff or rock face at Gisnau near Burgdorf; Flueh is a Swiss term for a steep rocky face, and the cliff opens here as an entrance to the realm of the dead.

notes.label: Chünde
notes.text: a Bernese dialect nominal form connected with announcing or making something known; here it names the supernatural death-sign in which Sameli's returning voice announces his death at sea. ‘Death-sign’ is contextual rather than a universal one-word equivalent.

notes.label: Hanischulmeischterbueb
notes.text: Bernese dialect, approximately ‘the Hani schoolmaster’s boy/son,’ used as the local identity of a man credited with weather magic and extraordinary military feats; the text heading also records the spelling Hanischuelmeischterbueb, and whether Hani is a personal, household, or place-related name is not established by the source.

c948853867d77f479c0219a55ec5a5f7a1c7362b.summary: Vom Rütscheleschnieder — Of the Rütschele Tailor

notes.label: Rütscheleschnieder
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the Rütschele tailor, apparently a local byname formed from a place, household, or personal name plus Schnieder, ‘tailor’; the source does not explain Rütschele.

notes.label: Taunermanndli
notes.text: a diminutive for a poor cottager, smallholder, or day laborer of the Tauner social class; the man supports himself partly through winter woodland work, but his exact status is uncertain.

notes.label: gwedelet
notes.text: Bernese dialect for making Wellen, tied bundles or faggots of brushwood used as fuel; it describes the tailor’s winter work.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a little woman, often used for a female supernatural being; here she invisibly disrupts the tailor’s tools and bundles.

notes.label: Wällen
notes.text: dialect plural for tied bundles or faggots of brushwood; the Fraueli repeatedly knocks them over.

notes.label: e Lugi agä
notes.text: Bernese dialect for telling someone a lie or feeding him a false story; the farmer intends to expose or tease the tailor rather than deceive him for gain.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a regional word here apparently referring to earth, soil, or clods lifted by a whirlwind in the field; the exact material and singular-plural sense are uncertain.

notes.label: Höseler
notes.text: a dialect word for a timid, hesitant, or cowardly fellow; the farmer admits that the tailor outdoes him in answering the invented story.

bb90a4c1dbea5ec2f0b54428d941dd70d55f11dd.summary: Vom Schmied u vom Doggeli (Of the Blacksmith and the Doggeli)

notes.label: Vom Schmied u vom Doggeli
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of the blacksmith and the Doggeli’; the exact dialect title is retained because Doggeli has no single English equivalent.

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a Swiss nocturnal pressure spirit or nightmare-being believed to sit upon, oppress, or torment sleepers; tales may identify it with a witch whose body bears injuries inflicted on its disguised form.

c88a9e1ecc074074b4298f8ede7a694e1261d16f.summary: Vom schwarze Hung — Of the Black Dog

notes.label: Vom schwarze Hung
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘of the black dog’; Hung is the regional form of Hund, and the unstandardized title preserves the oral register.

notes.label: Toggiburg
notes.text: a dialect form of Toggenburg used for the locality in the narrator’s account; the exact branch road and modern spelling of Ungerausel are not clarified.

notes.label: Pfruendschür
notes.text: a benefice or parsonage barn associated with church property or a clerical living; it serves as the landmark where the dog blocks the road.

notes.label: Gring
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for the head, often with a rough or colloquial tone; the father’s unexplained swelling follows the encounter.

notes.label: wie-n-es Mäss
notes.text: dialect meaning approximately ‘like a measuring vessel’ or ‘as large as a measure’; the exact vessel and intended size comparison are not specified.

notes.label: Velolatärne
notes.text: Swiss German for a bicycle lantern; the modern-looking comparison explains the supernatural brightness of the dog’s eyes for the source’s contemporary readers.

941323b2e24acbef8b86ce4186f209bb2bc0a3ab.summary: Vom schwarze Ma uf em Lürligrot — The Black Man on the Lürligrot

notes.label: Vom schwarze Ma uf em Lürligrot
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘of/about the black man on the Lürligrot’; the title ties the supernatural helper and treasure guardian to a named high pasture.
notes.anchor: Vom schwarze Ma uf em Lürligrot

notes.label: Lürligrot
notes.text: the local pasture or ridge-name where repeated accidents make herding dangerous; its exact literal derivation is not established by the source.

notes.label: War
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the livestock or herd entrusted to a herdsman; the precise mix of animals is not stated.

notes.label: Azeiger
notes.text: the dialect form of Anzeiger, a local advertisement sheet or newspaper in which the farmers announce the vacant herding position.

notes.label: Chohlebrönner
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘charcoal burner’; Sami mistakes or mockingly addresses the coal-black apparition as a charcoal worker.

notes.label: Ziegermilch
notes.text: the liquid associated with making Zieger whey cheese, closest here to whey or a whey-based drink; Sami shares it as the evening meal.

notes.label: ehrigs Häfeli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a little earthenware pot; it emerges from the cellar ground with the sack of money.

notes.label: Zwilchsack
notes.text: a sack made of Zwilch, a strong twilled fabric traditionally used for durable work clothes and bags; here it is filled with money.

b0c9b3826ba176243fba1f14a1bf3e74ae288eff.summary: Legends everywhere know how to tell of hidden treasures. In dangerous times of war, people probably often buried money in safe places, and chance discoveries, such as the one reported from the Ellmegg near Huttwil, continually nourished belief in hidden treasure.

notes.label: War
notes.text: a dialect collective for a farmer’s livestock or stock of animals, not the English word ‘war.’

notes.label: Verdingbueb
notes.text: a boy contracted or placed out to live and work for a farming household, often under conditions of poverty and limited power; the institution could overlap with foster care, indenture, and child labor.

notes.label: Vom Verdingbueb uf em Ällmig
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘about the contract boy on the Ällmig’; the title identifies a child or youth placed with a farmer for labor and maintenance.

notes.label: Ällmig
notes.text: the local dialect place-name for the hill associated in the commentary with the Ellmegg near Huttwil; it may echo Allmend or communal-land vocabulary, but the source does not establish the etymology.

notes.label: Hoger
notes.text: a dialect word for a hill, rise, or rounded height; the Ällmig is the named Hoger beside the route.

notes.label: Gläck
notes.text: a livestock lick or feed mixture, evidently containing salt and flour in this story; regional recipes and spellings vary.

notes.label: Fuetterchübel
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a feed bucket or pail; its salt-and-flour contents accidentally or instinctively break the enchantment over the treasure.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a barn chamber, stable bay, or agricultural storage space; the boy hides the money in an old cupboard there, but the exact room within the farm building is not specified.

notes.label: i d’Hüpple
notes.text: an obscure dialect phrase indicating that the farmer took his daughter sharply to task, questioned, or cornered her; its literal image and exact local nuance are uncertain.

notes.label: Gredi
notes.text: an orderly, proper, or acceptable state of affairs; the farmhand says matters can still be set right once wealth is the only obstacle.

notes.label: d’Milch ganz abe glo
notes.text: literally ‘let the milk all the way down,’ an idiomatic image for the farmer finally relenting or yielding completely; the precise proverbial nuance is uncertain, but the next clause confirms he no longer objects.

notes.label: Seelne
notes.text: a regional plural meaning souls; the commentary imagines the souls of greedy people becoming evil spirits that continue guarding buried wealth.

notes.label: Wasedokter
notes.text: literally the ‘Wasen doctor,’ the name for Zürcher Ueli in his role as a local folk healer, diviner, and cunning man who diagnoses witchcraft, finds lost beings and objects, and compels thieves.

notes.label: Sunnewirbelbletter
notes.text: dialect for the leaves of a folk-medicinal plant used here to make a drink against harm blamed on a witch; the source does not identify the plant securely enough for a modern botanical equivalent.

notes.label: Läufterli
notes.text: a small opening, sliding window, or little window panel; Ueli opens it and quietly consults an unseen informant before locating the missing husband.

notes.label: Sant Johannisblueme
notes.text: literally ‘Saint John's flower,’ a traditional medicinal-herb name usually associated with Saint John's wort; tea made from it is prescribed for the girl's recurring behavior.

notes.label: Hörnlima
notes.text: literally the ‘little horned man,’ a dialect name for a horned supernatural being, commonly the Devil; the hidden being knows that the boy is eavesdropping in the hayloft.

notes.label: Hurrlibueb
notes.text: literally a ‘whirling boy,’ an image for something that spins and hums furiously; Ueli's wheel sympathetically torments the boys until they return his cider barrel.

notes.label: Winge
notes.text: the source's dialect name for the sawyer's stolen implement or possession; the short anecdote does not identify the object precisely enough for a confident English replacement.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Stächpalm
notes.text: the dialect name for holly; its magically hidden branches are placed above the stable door as a protective healing charm.

8b9c418748e88a7799692fca127b1f7089a21be0.summary: Vom wisse Riter im Längwäg — The White Rider on the Längwäg

notes.label: wisse Riter
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘white rider’; it names the mounted nocturnal apparition rather than merely describing a rider's clothing.

notes.label: Längwäg
notes.text: a local Bernese place or road name, literally ‘long way/road’; the apparition's route is tied to this named landscape feature.

notes.label: Galgelöli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive place-name closest to ‘little gallows hill/place’; it marks the end from which the rider comes.

notes.label: Dorniggütsch
notes.text: a local destination place-name on the rider's route; its exact modern identification and literal formation are uncertain, so it is retained without inventing a gloss.

notes.label: Vom wisse Vögeli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘about the little white bird’; Vögeli is an affectionate diminutive, and the commentary interprets the heavenly bird as a soul and divine messenger.

notes.label: Aschtränzen
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form of Astränzen, referring to masterwort, an Alpine medicinal plant used in traditional plague lore; the source does not specify its preparation.

notes.label: Bibernäll
notes.text: Bernese dialect for Bibernelle, generally burnet saxifrage or a related medicinal pimpernel; the herb commonly appears in German-language plague rhymes as a protective remedy.

notes.label: Ärdspiegel
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘earth mirror,’ a divinatory mirror prepared through contact with crossroads and the dead or, in a second method, with a woodpecker's nest; it reveals hidden knowledge or groundwater.

notes.label: Chrüzwäg
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a crossroads, a liminal place widely associated in European folk belief with spirits, magic, burial, and divination.

notes.label: Tüfeli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive plural for ‘little devils’; despite their frightening arrival, they cannot harm the person standing on the buried mirror.

notes.label: Buechegrotjoggi
notes.text: the local nickname of the man who attempts the rite; Joggi is a familiar form of Jakob, while the source does not securely explain the Buechegrot element.

notes.label: Totebäumli
notes.text: literally a ‘little death-tree,’ a dialect and folkloric name for a coffin, recalling the hollowed wooden trunk or boards from which it was made.

notes.label: Kreuzwege
notes.text: the standard-German plural of crossroads used in the source's commentary; these places are treated as powerful boundaries in popular belief.

notes.label: Feldspiegel
notes.text: literally ‘field mirror,’ an older German name for a telescope or field glass; the author suggests distant reports of the optical instrument shaped belief in the magical mirror.

notes.label: Grüenspächt
notes.text: dialect for the green woodpecker; the informant says he knows no corresponding procedure involving this bird.

notes.label: Schwarzspächt
notes.text: dialect for the black woodpecker; placing the mirror in its nesting hollow is said to give the mirror power to reveal underground water.

notes.label: Bammert
notes.text: a regional form related to Bannwart, a field, woodland, or vineyard watchman; in the title it identifies the old-fashioned local apparition rather than merely describing any guard.

notes.label: Taunerli
notes.text: a diminutive regional term for a poor cottager or day laborer with little land; it conveys both the resident’s low economic status and the tale’s sympathetic tone.

notes.label: Dreizopfehuet
notes.text: an old-fashioned regional hat name, probably referring to tricorn-like headwear; it marks the apparition as belonging to an earlier period, but its exact construction is not described by the source.

notes.label: Bammertheiri
notes.text: the local name of the apparition, combining Bammert with the personal name Heiri, a dialect form of Heinrich; the source identifies him as a former resident but gives no further biography.

5a087148bc75d310418c197de5fbe0832b76357f.summary: Witches and sorcerers transform themselves into animals, but the soul too often takes animal form.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Vome Ching u re Schlange
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “about a child and a snake”; the retained tale title signals the source’s dialect voice, while Ching can mean a child without specifying sex.

notes.label: Boti
notes.text: a child-language or Bernese dialect form for bread or a little piece of bread; here the child urges the snake to eat bread as well as milk, though the precise diminutive nuance is uncertain.

notes.label: Mämmi
notes.text: a child-language or Bernese dialect word for milk or milky food; here it contrasts with Boti in the child’s invitation, but its exact nursery register may vary.

notes.label: Seelentier
notes.text: literally “soul-animal,” a folkloric animal form in which a human soul, especially an ancestral or deceased family soul, may appear; here it interprets the household snake, although the narrator presents this as a scholarly reading of the legend.

notes.label: Fürspräch
notes.text: a Bernese German word for an advocate or legal spokesman; here it denotes a lawyer whose success in every lawsuit is morally suspect and whose ability to speak fails after death.

notes.label: Füürblatte
notes.text: literally the ‘fire slab,’ the hearthstone or plate at the household fire; the dead advocate's black-dog apparition repeatedly sits there, bringing the supernatural visitation into the center of the home.

75b42d4a8131f6a1bdb2cf2e84ea4c40942ab559.summary: Vomene schwarze Ma — Of a Black Man

notes.label: Vomene schwarze Ma
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘of a black man’; the schwarze Ma who claims the careless reader is a customary dark, indirect representation of the Devil.

notes.label: schwarze Ma
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘black man,’ used here as a euphemistic name for the Devil rather than as a description of human ethnicity.

notes.label: wo meh het chönne
notes.text: literally someone ‘who could do more,’ a cautious folk euphemism for a person believed to command magic or forbidden knowledge.

notes.label: Büechli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a little book; in this legend, reading the owner's unexplained book acts like opening a book of magic and summons the claimant.

notes.label: Mäss Hirsch
notes.text: a measure of millet, using Hirsch as a regional word for millet rather than the animal ‘deer’; scattering the tiny grains into a woodpile gives the supernatural claimant an impossible sorting task.

notes.label: Hirsch
notes.text: the regional grain-name meaning millet in this context; the lad is rescued because the Devil must pick every scattered grain back out of the woodpile.

notes.label: Vorzeiche
notes.text: Bernese dialect for Vorzeichen, an omen or warning sign; here the church clock’s abnormal striking foretells Huttwil’s fire.

notes.label: Chilezit
notes.text: Bernese dialect for the church clock or its time-striking mechanism; its repeated ‘stuttering’ is the acoustic omen heard before the disaster.

notes.label: Heidesiegerischt
notes.text: a mocking dialect expression meaning approximately a ‘heathen sacristan’ or pagan bell-ringer supposedly behind the faulty striking; Siegerischt is a regional form for sacristan, while the joke’s precise local nuance is uncertain.

e213d7f67edb015770752b4900b5fa2980ac3265.summary: Below the Albis Pass, in the secluded and pleasant Knonaueramt, which also has a merry nickname, lies a quiet mountain lake, the Türlersee.

notes.label: Knonaueramt
notes.text: the historical Zurich district centered on Knonau, also known as the Säuliamt; Amt here means an administrative territory rather than an office or job.

notes.label: fahrende Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘wandering scholars,’ itinerant learned men who in German-language folklore are often credited with occult arts; here they use magic to dig the drainage trench, and the label does not necessarily mean ordinary schoolchildren.

notes.label: Firn
notes.text: old, compacted granular snow that has survived at least one melt season and is intermediate between fresh snow and glacial ice; here the accumulating snow hardens into Firn before becoming a glacier.

notes.label: Vrenelis Gärtlein
notes.text: literally ‘little Vreneli's garden,’ the traditional name of the glacier feature on the Glärnisch where Frau Vrene becomes a pillar of ice; Vreneli is an affectionate diminutive of Verena, while Gärtlein is ‘little garden.’

47837a36b961c9454d7d3e531f288cdd1072b79b.summary: Formerly, this summit was a garden belonging, together with several rich alpine pastures, to a herdsman who had a daughter named Vreneli.

notes.label: Gärtli
notes.text: the Swiss German diminutive of Garten, ‘garden’; in the place-name Vreneli’s Gärtli it means ‘Vreneli’s little garden’ and preserves the local name attached to the summit.

c87a4ca11bb2a27aefe3b4d2b07da70805362351.summary: Opposite old Toggenburg stood Waldegg Castle, of which only sparse remains survive.

notes.label: Burgstock
notes.text: a local topographic name for the castle hill or elevated site associated with a fortification; here the visible holes are interpreted as remains of wells, but the archaeology is not established by the tale.

75b9b745b77320738f6acd3f797f0846dfb423ac.summary: Gedeon of Färnigen in the Meien Valley, who liked to cleanse his throat with a little glass of schnapps, was on his way home from the village one evening.

notes.label: Bundesfusel
notes.text: literally and disparagingly ‘federal rotgut,’ a Swiss nickname for cheap, poor-quality spirits associated with the Confederation; here it is the drink whose bottle keeps Gedeon trapped in his circular night walk.
