bb77d0a07b816fd72c94e638c8778ab309dda8f0.summary: When the castle was built, the Zwingherren had the mortar mixed with pure wine; that is why it remains as hard as iron today.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: literally coercive or oppressive lords, a polemical Swiss term for castle-holding rulers who denied local freedom; here their extravagant use of wine explains Wartau's mortar.

ada80ce2d90d26d03e5ef1ce1344d9e0251bc1fc.summary: Warum dr Totewage chunnt — Why the Death Wagon Comes

notes.label: Totewage
notes.text: the dialect compound meaning ‘death wagon’ or ‘wagon of the dead,’ a supernatural funeral-like vehicle associated with people denied ordinary burial and rest.

notes.label: Warum dr Totewage chunnt
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘why the death wagon comes’; the tale explains the supernatural wagon through a suicide and an irregular burial.

notes.label: Legistück
notes.text: an obscure dialect term for the substitute object or weight placed in the coffin in place of the secretly buried body; its precise material and literal derivation are not recoverable from this brief source.

notes.label: Totebäumli
notes.text: literally a ‘little dead-person tree,’ a regional euphemistic name for a coffin, traditionally made from a hollowed or boarded wooden form; here it receives the Legistück rather than the body.

notes.label: Chilehof
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘churchyard,’ the consecrated burial ground beside the church; the account contrasts it with the separate place once assigned to suicides.

notes.label: Schlossjungfer
notes.text: literally a ‘castle maiden,’ a recurring female castle apparition often associated with treasure, seasonal appearances, or weather omens; this one washes at the village fountain.

notes.label: Wäscherli
notes.text: literally a diminutive ‘little washer’; here it is both the pond's name and the name implied for the old-fashioned female washing apparition who appears before bad weather.

notes.label: Schinnhut
notes.text: a broad hat made of woven willow or similar basketry, part of the apparition's old regional costume; the source itself supplies the material explanation.

notes.label: Jüppe
notes.text: a traditional woman's garment whose precise form varied by region; here it is described as short and is part of the washer's old-fashioned dress.

notes.label: Schaube
notes.text: here a heavily pleated Deckelmütze or flat-topped cap; Schaube could name different outer garments elsewhere, so the source's parenthetical costume definition controls this context.

notes.label: Altammann
notes.text: a former Ammann, the local chief magistrate or senior communal officeholder; the title identifies the witness's civic standing rather than his personal name.

notes.label: Bündelmaideli
notes.text: literally a ‘little bundle maiden,’ the local name of a female apparition used here also to frighten disobedient children; the source gives no further account of her bundle or origin.

notes.label: Bergfridli
notes.text: the familiar diminutive name of a male mountain or woodland weather spirit whose calls foretell changes in the weather; the text connects him with Fridolin, patron of the Fricktal.

notes.label: Waschjungfer
notes.text: literally a ‘washing maiden,’ a female water- or fountain-side apparition seen washing, wringing, or spreading linen at night.

notes.label: Strähl-Anneli
notes.text: Anneli ‘of the comb,’ from Swiss German strähle, to comb; the name evokes a female apparition associated with combing, though this brief entry preserves only her memory as an uncanny figure.

notes.label: Spinnmütterli
notes.text: literally the ‘little spinning mother,’ a diminutive female spirit-name associated with spinning and here blamed for upsetting a vineyard worker's manure basket.

notes.label: Bachmaidschi
notes.text: literally a ‘little brook girl,’ the local female water apparition who moves as a blue flame over the stream during Fronfasten.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember Days, the traditional quarterly fasting periods in the Christian calendar; Alpine and Swiss legends frequently treat their nights as times of heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Bühl
notes.text: a southern German and Swiss word for a hill or rounded rise; here it describes a cone-shaped mound resembling an old castle site.

notes.label: Züber
notes.text: a large wooden tub or vat; the unseen sound of one being set at the fountain is the wife's only perception of the water-fetching apparition.

notes.label: Müselifräuli
notes.text: the ‘little lady of the Müseli,’ a local spring-side apparition who combs and washes herself, displays shimmering clothes, and sings while measuring them.

notes.label: Müseri
notes.text: a variant local name connected by the source with Müseli and a spirit at Gebistorf; the exact relationship between the place-name, the spirit-name, and Moos or marsh is not resolved in the entry.

notes.label: Moosweibchen
notes.text: literally a ‘little moss or marsh woman,’ a regional female nature-spirit label used here as an alternative characterization of the Müselifräuli.

notes.label: Bränzhaube
notes.text: a traditional black gauze cap with a radiating wire rim, explicitly described as part of the Old Cook's costume.

notes.label: Goller
notes.text: a square-cut shoulder and neck covering or broad collar that covers the breast and upper back, part of traditional women's dress.

notes.label: Jüpplein
notes.text: a diminutive form of Jüppe; here the source explicitly identifies it as a black bodice laced over the breast.

notes.label: Brisnestel
notes.text: the decorative or functional lacing cord used to fasten the bodice across the breast; the precise spelling reflects the historical source.

notes.label: Rubelhaar
notes.text: shaggy or tousled hair; here it describes the little ghost-dog's white, rough coat, with the source itself glossing the word as zottig.

notes.label: Rüfenmaul
notes.text: an enormous, likely swollen or distorted mouth received as supernatural punishment after addressing the spirit; the precise physical sense of Rüfen in this compound is uncertain.

2c7ff2c0743679b7e72ac4dd84c02f1e90fc3b75.summary: In former times, every Seckelbub could supposedly lay and lift a ban, if the stories one hears are true.—Five men from Isental stood in front of the Alpine hut at Bolgen, ready to go down into the valley.

notes.label: Seckelbub
notes.text: a dismissive Uri label for an ordinary boy or young fellow; the passage says that even such a youth once supposedly knew magical binding and counter-binding, while the word's exact age and social nuance remain uncertain.

f63eb7fac3e335dde261b3ece6bb228c4183fffa.summary: On the road from Leuggern to Neuenthal, one comes at the Trottenbach to the old footbridge leading over the ravine.

notes.label: Hafen
notes.text: an older southern German and Swiss word for a pot or earthenware vessel; the spirit’s roar sounds hollow as if issuing from one.

8d8f809387ede811123331776e3bb7fe8ed26960.summary: 1. Three poor hunters from the area around Amsteg entered a cave on the Bristenstock that extended deep into the mountain.

notes.label: Miär brüchet d's Herrgotts Sunnä nytt
notes.text: literally ‘we do not need the Lord God’s sun’ in Uri dialect; the boast means that the hunters’ gold lets them pay for artificial light, and its irreverent pride explains the treasure’s disappearance.
notes.anchor: Miär brüchet d's Herrgotts Sunnä nytt

5850eb0896539d5981436b5e01b244be5ef3bf38.summary: When Mathilde Rämi of Attinghausen was a young girl, she once went into the Bodenwald with a friend to gather wood.

notes.label: Gertel
notes.text: a Swiss billhook or heavy hooked knife used for cutting brush and wood; forgetting it leaves the girls without their customary tool in the forest.

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: an Uri regional, often disparaging name for an old woman or uncanny female figure; Mathilde identifies this one as a witch, but the title preserves the possibility of a weather demon.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source’s regional name for the apparition’s hat; its exact historical style, material, and the first element’s derivation are uncertain, while its faded appearance matches her clothing.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

d9c945a681e504143b074677002c89dce0353b77.summary: An 80-year-old widow from Seedorf tells—yes, the pure, certain truth; you can surely believe me!

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held or used land, often meadow, pasture, or open ground belonging to a local community rather than a private owner; the women cross Seedorf’s Allmend.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: an Uri regional, often disparaging label for an old, disreputable, or uncanny female figure; here the woman’s appearance and the immediate destructive hail imply witch-like power without defining her nature.

notes.label: Zeintli
notes.text: a diminutive of the regional Zeine, a handled or carrying basket often made of wicker; this old figure wears one on her head in place of a hat, but its contents and construction are unstated.

notes.label: Pfaffächälleri
notes.text: the narrator’s dialect form of Pfaffenkellerin, a historical and disparaging regional label for a clergyman’s female housekeeper or supposed illicit partner; Central Swiss legend also uses it for an uncanny or witch-like woman.

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: the plural of an Uri word for destructive debris flows or torrents of rock, mud, and water; the hailstorm releases them across the landscape and destroys the paths.

389c6d8208616153469b486b293355aa352f664e.summary: 1. On Alp Gornern it happens now and then that the Alp workers hear “someone” approaching in heavy wooden shoes across the stable's Bsetzi and climbing the ladder as far as the hay door.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the spirits' sounds are tied to work and weather at Gornern, Galtenebnet, Seenalp, and Spilau.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Bsetzi
notes.text: a paved or cobbled yard or standing area beside a stable; the weather spirit's heavy wooden soles are repeatedly heard crossing this hard surface.

notes.label: Nischt
notes.text: the sleeping nest, bunk, or bed space in an Alpine hut where the frightened worker takes refuge; the source does not describe its exact construction.

b971733218228a4def1c02dc60ec41cd023cfd44.summary: 1. My father related that he had been in service on the Felliberg at Gurtnellen.

notes.label: g'sywlet
notes.text: a dialect verb for the children's activity also called Sywli 'tribä; the source supplies no rules, and any exact identification of the game would be uncertain.

notes.label: Sywli 'tribä
notes.text: literally something like ‘driving the little sow,’ the alternate local name for the children's game; the animal image may belong to the game's name rather than describe actual livestock.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: hay cut from uncultivated, often steep and remote mountain grassland; gathering it is a distinctively Alpine and dangerous seasonal task, and Michael Nell falls while mowing it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture and its seasonal livestock-and-dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the repeated weeping accompanies the workers' descent from Wängi.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy production on an Alp; the omen says he will serve one further summer before dying.

notes.label: Betruf
notes.text: a traditional Alpine prayer call projected over the pasture to invoke divine protection for people, livestock, and the Alp; the unseen voice answers the Senn's final seasonal call.

notes.label: Betruf or Alpine blessing
notes.text: This is a protective prayer called or chanted over an Alp at the end of the working day. Herders ask God, Mary, and saints to protect people and animals through the night; the custom belongs to the seasonal herding community.

source.label: Swiss Inventory of Living Traditions: Betruf

b4a45ddc125eb434f883d3f22b7ebffa11e5288c.summary: Barthli Flütsch in St. Antönien once wished to go to his mountain meadow “very early” in the morning to make hay, and ordered his “Alte” (wife) to wake him at four o’clock and by then have “z'Morget” (breakfast) ready for him.

notes.label: Barthli
notes.text: the familiar diminutive of Bartholomäus used for Barthli Flütsch.

notes.label: Alte
notes.text: literally “old woman,” but here the husband’s colloquial designation for his wife; the source explicitly glosses it as Frau.

notes.label: z'Morget
notes.text: Swiss German for breakfast, literally the morning meal.

notes.label: 's Zit
notes.text: dialect for the clock or timepiece; the source explains that it has not been running.

notes.label: Gang nu
notes.text: Swiss German for “Just go”; the source inserts its own High German gloss before Uschi continues.

notes.label: i weck' Di sicher
notes.text: Swiss German for “I’ll surely wake you”; Uschi sends Barthli to bed before operating the clock by hand.

notes.label: Schlafgaden
notes.text: a sleeping chamber or small sleeping structure attached to an Alpine farm building; the source glosses it as Schlafgemach.

notes.label: Uschi
notes.text: a familiar Swiss German form of the given name Ursula.

notes.label: trüllte
notes.text: a regional verb meaning twisted or rolled; Uschi twists the lamp wicks while she sits awake.

notes.label: Döchte
notes.text: the source’s historical plural form for lamp wicks.

notes.label: Unschligg
notes.text: tallow or rendered animal fat prepared as fuel for the lamp.

notes.label: Ofenbank
notes.text: the bench built beside or around the room’s masonry stove, a customary warm seat in an Alpine household.

notes.label: Perpendikel
notes.text: the historical term for a clock pendulum; Uschi moves it throughout the night to keep time.

notes.label: Wer hätti denn triiba sölla
notes.text: Swiss German for “Who would have kept it going then?”; her reply explains why tending the broken clock prevented her from making breakfast.

notes.label: Weiber-List
notes.text: literally “women’s” or “wives’ cunning”; the historical title uses an archaic term for women and frames Uschi’s practical solution as a comic trick.

8b5814c3fbf6e8307b203fcba882033e73e70dc3.summary: The farm called Weiberlist at Oberkirch is rightly named. A farmer from there once entered into a pact with the Devil for money and pleasure and, after the agreed term had passed, was to belong body and soul to the Evil One.

notes.label: Weiberlist
notes.text: literally ‘woman's cunning,’ both the farm name and the source's gendered name for the wife's ingenuity; the historical word Weiber is dismissive by modern standards, but retaining the place-name preserves the legend's naming explanation.

4e0913524208a86c9ab492959ce388109d9f89d0.summary: A mighty Weisstanne is said to have stood upon the site where the village church now stands before its foundation stone was laid; hence the name of the village and valley.

notes.label: Weisstanne
notes.text: the silver fir, Abies alba, literally ‘white fir’; the tale derives the place-name from a mighty specimen that stood before the church was founded.

notes.label: Weihtannen
notes.text: the title's form of the village and valley name; the legend explains it through a Weisstanne, although the spelling difference shows that this is a folk etymology rather than certain linguistic history.

8e2e1e43b3f7d9fc9533c29659f33aee75a134df.summary: Only a few remains of this old castle survive, left behind by its former destruction.

notes.label: Natisserfeld
notes.text: literally the ‘Naters field,’ the historic cultivated plain associated with Naters; it is a local place-name rather than the name of a separate settlement.

notes.label: Zwingherrn
notes.text: plural of Zwingherr, literally ‘coercive lords,’ meaning oppressive castle rulers or tyrannical feudal lords in Swiss historical and legendary vocabulary.

79627934c047a8d79031fa7782e838a284ec57d8.summary: A fahrender Schüler once stopped at the Hältäli in the Maderan Valley. He noticed that the farmer went about dejectedly and that the family, with its numerous crowd of children, had hired the best cook of all—namely hunger.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a wandering scholar or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning, magic, and secret knowledge rather than an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Weisshaslen
notes.text: literally a ‘white hazel,’ the unusual treasure-marking shrub on which the mistletoe grows; the source does not securely identify a modern botanical species or explain why it is white.

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: a magical mandrake or mandrake familiar believed to bring money and occult power; the informant does not know whether the farmer found one or literal money, so both possibilities remain.

7944b352f1d0bb6bc92b2a961107f0f60843184a.summary: Welen eh bim Gattertöri? — Who Is There by the Little Gate?

notes.label: Gattertöri
notes.text: a diminutive for the little door or gate in a pasture fence; crossing it becomes the precise boundary of the farmer's escape.

notes.label: Welen eh bim Gattertöri?
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘who is there by the little gate?’; the farmer mockingly echoes an owl-like call and nearly gives the unseen caller a chance to claim him.

notes.label: Chutz
notes.text: a Bernese word for an owl; its three cries can be heard as an ordinary bird or as the voice of the pursuing supernatural being.

notes.label: hesch Zit gha
notes.text: literally ‘you had time’ or ‘you were in time’; in context, the voice means that the farmer escaped just soon enough and otherwise would have belonged to it.

920b25f6961e2985480fed62e7209fbc32e33e83.summary: Once the devil came to Strättlingen Castle disguised as a needy pilgrim. Because it was very cold, the lord of the castle, Wernhard, took pity on him and sent him his own cloak so that he could cover his nakedness.

notes.label: Lamparten
notes.text: an older German name for Lombardy or northern Italy, used here as the place of Wernhard's imprisonment.

notes.label: fahrender Spielmann
notes.text: an itinerant minstrel, musician, or entertainer who traveled from place to place; Wernhard adopts this low-status identity to enter his own castle unnoticed.

71b7a5df8be2084618528bdaaf12976be41743e8.summary: In the middle of the previous century, a citizen named Cugniet crossed the little Saint John’s Bridge in the city of Fribourg one night.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

8f2ce8872fc2e5556f9d72b163074418df7ba277.summary: Around 1590, the hermit Peter Cunert, a native of the county of Rotenburg, lived near Horw in the Bruderhäuschen.

notes.label: Bruderhäuschen
notes.text: literally ‘little brother-house,’ the small hermitage occupied by the Waldbruder near Horw.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held or used land, often pasture or open ground belonging to a local community rather than a private owner.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Käpeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a small chapel; the repeated local form makes the sacred shelter part of the route.

notes.label: Gatter
notes.text: a gate or barred passage, often in a fence controlling access to pasture or common land.

notes.label: Bildstöckli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small wayside devotional shrine, image-post, or sacred marker.

notes.label: Allmendkäpeli
notes.text: literally ‘little chapel on the common land,’ combining Allmend with the diminutive Käpeli.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ a male religious hermit living apart from ordinary settlement; Bruder is a devotional title, not a claim that he is someone's sibling.

notes.label: Jakobi
notes.text: the feast day of St. James used as a traditional calendar marker; the source dates the report to the Saturday following that feast.

29a9640ad8e42f0ae877cf26be7a5acc3f6dac93.summary: Near Gams, in the Toggenburg municipality of Wildhaus in the canton of St. Gallen, the ruins of Wildenburg Castle stand on a rock.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine legend, a name for supposedly Venetian or southern prospectors credited with secret knowledge of mountain ores and often feared as sorcerers; ‘Venetians’ gives the geographic origin but not this regionally specific folkloric role, whose historical basis is uncertain.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

d4fb6e6842d09347195054cfbbcf2196fb5fee3d.summary: 1. Not very many years ago, an avalanche descended from the Gross Windgällen across Bernetsmatt and the Golzersee as far as the Stössialp.

notes.label: äs Gäräli
notes.text: Uri dialect for a small hairnet or snood of the kind historically worn by women; its appearance on the avalanche identifies the witch's supposed magical remnant.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri landscape term for a destructive debris flow, earth slide, or torrent of loose material; the executed witch is said to have left an object through which this and the paired Laui could do harm.

notes.label: Laui
notes.text: Swiss German for an avalanche or destructive slide; the confession pairs it with Rübi as the two mountain disasters empowered by the witch's object.

notes.label: Weibervolk
notes.text: an archaic and often disparaging Alemannic collective word for a woman or womenfolk; the narrator uses it for the solitary traveler later identified as a witch, so the English retains the social coloring rather than reducing it to a neutral label.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the strange tools and personal objects appear between it and the isolated house.

notes.label: Wirzägrebel
notes.text: a regional name for a hoe or cultivating tool used around Wirz, cabbage or Swiss chard; the exact head shape is not described, but the source separately mentions its short handle.

notes.label: Halb
notes.text: an uncertain Uri tool-word that context identifies as the short haft or handle fitted both to the Wirzägrebel and the broad axe.

notes.label: Strähl
notes.text: Swiss German for a comb, especially a hair comb; women's hair remains caught in this one among the witch's supposed belongings.

notes.label: glockenpfennigganze
notes.text: an unusual historical adjective describing the square windowpane as wholly intact or proverbially complete; its literal formation and any connection to a Glockenpfennig are uncertain.

notes.label: Finkensohlen
notes.text: soles from Finken, soft house shoes or slippers in Swiss German usage; the detached pair is found among the objects deposited by the storm.

notes.label: Bitzi
notes.text: a regional land-name for a small enclosed plot, orchard, or field; here it identifies the rear holding at Erstfeld where the avalanche boulder lies.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

bca3b9fdd39d400f6697512d43dddf9de700d7fd.summary: My cousin told me of supernatural beings that come through the high air and produce storms and bad weather, or come swimming through the water and cause floods.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

d83753d15541aac377654e8839a2bfed3bdf99bc.summary: In no. 120, it is claimed that a high road once ran along the ridge of the Küttigen Jura, passable by horse and wagon, from the mountains behind down to Biberstein on the Aare.

notes.label: Karrenwege
notes.text: literally ‘cart roads,’ the name given to otherwise inexplicable track-like formations across remote high rock in the forest cantons.

notes.label: Scheideweg
notes.text: a dividing way, crossroads, or boundary route; the author interprets high passes as divine paths marking the separation of landscapes and worlds.

notes.label: Götterwagen
notes.text: literally ‘chariot of the gods,’ a mythic name for a remote mountain summit understood as a deity's road or point of ascent.

notes.label: Rosswagen
notes.text: literally ‘horse wagon,’ the proper name of a Tyrolean mountain used as another example of landscape imagined through vehicle lore.

notes.label: Teufelskarrweg
notes.text: literally ‘Devil's cart road,’ the name for a deeply cut rock formation along Lake Thun attributed to supernatural traffic.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Wagenlücke
notes.text: literally ‘wagon notch,’ the high cleft on the Säntis whose impossible roadway-like setting invites mythic explanation.

notes.label: Sodbrunnen
notes.text: a deep draw-well or shaft well; the golden wagon on the Emmenhorn lies hidden within one rather than an open fountain.

notes.label: Bärlisgrub
notes.text: literally something like ‘little bear's pit,’ the title of the separately numbered explanation cited by Rochholz; its exact referent is outside this story.

Her spell was: ‘Durs Chämmi uf und niene a!—Up through the chimney and touch nowhere!’ Another person who had watched but had not understood the spell correctly wanted to ride after her, but said: ‘Durs Chämmi uf und überall a!—Up through the chimney and strike…

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Durs Chämmi uf und niene a!
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for ‘up through the chimney and touch nowhere,’ a precisely worded flight spell whose negative command ensures safe passage.
notes.anchor: Durs Chämmi uf und niene a!

notes.label: Durs Chämmi uf und überall a!
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for ‘up through the chimney and against everything,’ the misheard version that makes the broom strike every obstacle.

4395ccacdae68bde177eb0e70f50350bc532a086.summary: When the milk will not turn to butter, one should take Stryten and lay it crosswise beneath the Barren, and likewise upon the stand where the Milchmutte rests.

notes.label: Stryten
notes.text: this is the ritual material laid crosswise when milk will not butter; its plant, object, spelling, and exact identity are uncertain.

notes.label: Barren
notes.text: in this dairy context, Barren denotes a rack, bench, or support beneath which the charm is laid; its exact form is uncertain.

notes.label: Milchmutte
notes.text: this regional compound denotes the vessel or tub holding milk on its stand; its capacity and construction are unspecified.

22ca9d75cbef0c0e6d65854bd7e204d9f8413f40.summary: In ancient times, as I have often heard tell, a man from the Schächental was once walking home from Altdorf at night up through the Hellgässli when an elderly man came running across his path from a side lane.

notes.label: G'hirmiplatte
notes.text: the local name of a slab or flat place at Vorfrutt near the Klausen Pass; G'hirmi can denote a resting place, load-setting stop, or shelter in Uri usage, but the source does not describe this particular site's form or the sin committed there.

notes.label: Loherstei
notes.text: a Bernese dialect term for the stone the farmer illicitly moved, evidently a boundary or landmark stone; Stei means ‘stone,’ while the precise local sense of Loher is not explained in the source.

c56075a178e1e4474fa909101981ed181488d3da.summary: The Meye- or Eyesee behind Sörenberg rests upon gold. The Little Emme takes it from there and carries it far away.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and milk work on a seasonal high pasture; Bürkli’s work gives him repeated access to the little lake, though his precise duties are not stated.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.label: Gulden
notes.text: a historical florin-denominated currency used across central Europe and Switzerland; the source gives the payment as 25 Gulden without specifying mint, weight, or modern value.

notes.label: Gulden and florins
notes.text: Gulden and florin name historical currencies associated originally with the gold coin of Florence, and later with different coins and accounting units. Their value depended on place and period. They are not modern Swiss francs, and the tale’s amount has no single reliable conversion into dollars.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Gulden

notes.label: Emmengold
notes.text: literally ‘Emme gold,’ the gold said to be carried from the Meye- or Eyesee by the Little Emme river; the tale does not distinguish placer gold from other gold-bearing stones.

notes.label: Bränz
notes.text: a regional name for strong distilled liquor or schnapps; the young men bring it to sustain their courage while waiting for the treasure spirit.

dd1be3f4318724ce509b3905c622970353bf66e8.summary: Whoever pledges himself to the Devil has his portrait hung in hell, and if he considers breaking the pact, the Prince of Hell need only pierce the portrait with a knife, and the faithless man is dead.

notes.label: Freemasonry
notes.text: Swiss Freemasonry belongs to the history of fraternal lodges and their private rituals. Legends can attach occult suspicions to such groups; a tale’s accusation should not be treated as a factual account of what lodge members did.

source.label: Swissinfo on Swiss Freemasonry

f571bb0d87e7aaa66a7abb22f4222eb4060fb025.summary: In ancient times, an entire host of warriors came across the sea from Egypt to Valais.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Blüemliberg
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘little-flower mountain,’ the extraordinarily rich high pasture crossed by Longinus.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Strüdlen
notes.text: female uncanny beings or witches in Alpine folklore; the exact local distinction from Hexen is not explained.

notes.label: die Lengg
notes.text: the story’s older or dialect name for the Lenk, explained through folk etymology as a memorial to Longinus.

bd715e54040b34d7b1a73e9ba7901c48d80709f2.summary: Once, as I passed several slender, tall-growing Aspen and watched the strange trembling of their leaves, which begin rustling at the slightest breath of air, I said to an old man accompanying me: ‘What a strange tree this is!

notes.label: Aspen
notes.text: the source's plural form referring to several aspen trees; it should be read as German plural rather than the English place-name Aspen.

notes.label: Aspe
notes.text: an older German and regional name for the aspen tree, whose flattened leaf stalks make its foliage tremble in the slightest breeze; the legend gives that natural trait a Christian moral origin.

05ec775bb2d2f5ad649a815962489fd4770709bb.summary: Boys from Merenschwand are taunted in other villages with the nickname Speckbuben.

notes.label: Speckbuben
notes.text: literally “bacon boys,” a teasing collective nickname for the boys of Merenschwand; the tale derives it from hidden pork found among greasy swaddling cloths, while the historical reach of the nickname is not established.

notes.label: Dorfloos
notes.text: the local name of Merenschwand’s uncanny village apparition, elsewhere appearing as a pig; the narrator explicitly rejects it as the source of Speckbuben, and the exact sense of Loos in this ghost-name remains uncertain.

51b6a5ef24c4f08c2a9f22a7ed2826fa22f2e183.summary: Saint Verena once knelt in prayer before her cell near Solothurn, including in her prayer all who had strayed from the path of truth and virtue and threatened to fall directly into the power of evil.

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: Verena is a saint especially associated with Zurzach in Aargau. Her regional cult gives local stories of healing, charitable care, and holy places a setting that would have been familiar to the collector’s readers.

source.label: Bad Zurzach parish

66b9440a3a902c853e9a9887fda02977b2e0f1c0.summary: In the Lucerne region, a man contracted with the Devil to build a bridge in exchange for whatever crossed it first when it was finished.

notes.label: Kreuzer
notes.text: The Kreuzer was a historical small-denomination coin used in parts of Switzerland and neighboring lands. Its value varied across monetary systems; in some Swiss systems it counted as one quarter of a Batzen. A named coin in a tale is therefore not a modern cent with a fixed national value.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Kreuzer

2953c41941038e14c6ea74ea2f875e75ebf3caa8.summary: Josef Baumann of the Meiental (d. 1909 at about eighty years of age) repeatedly heard the following story from his father Johann, a farmer at Färnigen who died in the forties of the preceding century:

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: bstellt
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb for being supernaturally stopped, held, confronted, or placed under a power; the passage says people were affected near the grave but does not specify the exact experience.

notes.label: Steingand
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine term for a steep field or slope of loose stones and scree; the misleading light draws travelers upward into this hazardous terrain.

notes.label: Seelensonntage
notes.text: literally ‘Sundays of the Souls,’ recurring Catholic parish observances for the dead; the exact local rite is not described here, but their institution is said to end the haunting.

2b6669ef178c263cb9e38db0c54e67993c9d9657.summary: A boy wished to buy a bread roll from a woman but would not take it at her proposed price, so she said: "Then fly up and cry ‘cuckoo’!" At that, the boy flew away as our cuckoo.

notes.label: About this telling

129e04b0b9bc896cb4f57650c1ac9e1841799b74.summary: When Bishop Salomon, builder of St. Magnus Church, once visited the monastery of Gallus from his episcopal seat in Constance, he brought with him a maiden named Wiborada, who was known for her virtues.

notes.label: About this telling

f0f22ef9c3ce2e12f3b46c19725e00d8324b5731.summary: On Semelenberg near the Hirschensprung, the little castle of Wichenstein stood inside a rock cave.

notes.label: Hirschensprung
notes.text: literally ‘stag's leap,’ the dramatic Rhine Valley gorge and local landmark near the cave castle.

notes.label: Buschkleppern
notes.text: bush-ranging robbers or highwaymen who ambushed travelers from cover; the inflected plural form is retained from the source.

notes.label: Rofahans
notes.text: Hans's local byname, likely combining a farm, family, or place-name Rofa with Hans; the exact reference is uncertain.

notes.label: Oberrieter
notes.text: an inhabitant of Oberriet in the St. Gallen Rhine Valley.

38ad744144dfb7e8c008c19ff18f736fcaeff4b6.summary: A certain Hänzli, whose origins and homeland no one knew, was a Sennenhirt for many summers on the Bachalp near Erschmatt.

notes.label: Hänzli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Hans, roughly ‘little Hans’; here it is the familiar name of the mysterious herdsman later blamed for theft and haunting.

notes.label: Sennenhirt
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman associated with the seasonal care of cattle and dairy work on a high pasture; the compound combines Senn with Hirt, ‘herdsman.’

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a seasonal high-mountain pasture and its working settlement rather than simply a mountain; the cattle losses and later haunting occur across two neighboring Alps.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Alpstaffel
notes.text: a level or station within an Alpine pasture system, commonly including its cluster of working huts and enclosures; rocks are hurled down into this occupied area.

notes.label: Kässpende
notes.text: literally a ‘cheese donation,’ an endowed charitable or religious distribution of cheese; the annual Easter Monday gift to Ferden's poor serves here as the community's remedy for the haunting.

08f85c09021b70f84591ab7a73312fead55a749f.summary: On a steep slope, far back in a ravine, there was once a little house; people called it the Crow’s Nest.

notes.text: The dialect syntax in the reference to the earlier Äschlismatt story is genuinely ambiguous; the phrase about the cat is translated literally as going down the girl’s throat.

5db97c32f741d7f34f4ddd79e27a779d579f11d6.summary: Wider bi Spinnere — Again at the Spinner’s

notes.label: Wider bi Spinnere
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for “again at the spinner’s” or “another tale at the spinner’s”; the title links this episode to related spinning-room legends and preserves the source’s dialect voice.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally “Lady Fast” or “Mrs. Fasting,” a southwestern German-speaking and Swiss female bogey who enforces seasonal and late-night work taboos; here she tests women spinning after hours, though her relationship to Lent and older supernatural figures remains debated.

notes.label: widligs Härdöpfelchörbli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a small potato basket that is porous, wickerwork, or otherwise unable to hold water; the clever spinner assigns Frau Faschte an impossible task, while widligs has a locally nuanced sense not fully recoverable here.

notes.label: Haschpel
notes.text: a Bernese dialect form of Haspel, a reel or winder used to wind yarn; Frau Faschte turns the ordinary spinning tool into the instrument of the woman’s punishment.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the quarterly Catholic Ember fasts and their associated days; the trial testimony treats each set as a time for supernatural travel, while the exact day within the observance is not specified.

notes.label: Frau Fasten
notes.text: literally “Lady Fast” or “Lady Lent,” the standardized form used by the commentator for the punitive female seasonal being; the source equates her with Frau Holt and closely relates her to Frau Venus, but these identifications are interpretive.

notes.label: Wie dr Spahr heiritet
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic that can be heard as ‘how Spahr rode home’ through hei ritet, while resembling standard German ‘how Spahr marries’; the story concerns his supernatural ride home, so the English gloss follows that contextual sense.

notes.label: Chilchsturm
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘church tower’; Spahr reveals that his flying horse stumbled against the one at Kirchberg.

f4a54a7adee27c40ac0132648d2098cfbcfeb7c6.summary: Wie me am Tüfel cha wehre

notes.label: Wie me am Tüfel cha wehre
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘how one can ward off the Devil.’
notes.anchor: Wie me am Tüfel cha wehre

notes.label: Heuet
notes.text: the haymaking season or hay harvest, usually early summer.

notes.label: Schutz
notes.text: a dialect word for a gunshot or report, here fired periodically as protection.

notes.label: Schütz
notes.text: the inflected or variant dialect form for the shots being fired.

notes.label: Tafel
notes.text: the printed dialect form in the farmer’s speech, evidently referring to the Tüfel or Devil; whether it reflects pronunciation or a textual error is uncertain.

b62be9ac6f53c3be1f63cb56c5f999dd8e4f9a50.summary: Wie ’s Galgelölitier chunnt — How the Galgelölitier Comes

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: a dialect variant of Galgenlölitier, the name of an airborne animal apparition; Galge suggests ‘gallows’ and Tier ‘animal,’ but Löli and the creature's precise form remain uncertain.

notes.label: Wie ’s Galgelölitier chunnt
notes.text: dialect for ‘how the Galgelölitier comes,’ introducing a local account of the creature scattering a field's crop; the exact name is retained because its middle element is obscure.

notes.label: Wärch
notes.text: processed or drying fiber plants—commonly flax or hemp—spread on the meadow; the passage does not specify which fiber crop is intended.

notes.label: Wie’s eim cha goh
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘what can happen to a person’ or ‘how things can go for someone’; the idiomatic title introduces an uncanny roadside encounter.

notes.label: Möntschelieb
notes.text: a Bernese dialect expression for a human-shaped being or apparition; here it flies through the air with a calf’s head, and the precise supernatural category is uncertain.

notes.label: Galgelölitier
notes.text: literally something like ‘gallows-little-light animal,’ a local name for an uncanny creature associated with a ghostly gallows light; the witnesses identify the apparition only tentatively.

49639e04211946b672c37777dcbf8fdd71110040.summary: The long Kestenberg, covered with beautiful beech forest, bears the two castles of Wildegg and Brunnegg at its western and eastern ends.

aa855847fddc7d0fe5fbb819e9a948c38bff9658.summary: Not far from Gambs in the canton of St. Gallen lie the remains of Wildenburg Castle.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: oppressive feudal lords or tyrants, a recurring Swiss legendary type condemned to haunt their former castles.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: legendary Venetian or foreign mineral seekers credited in Alpine tradition with secret knowledge of ores, crystals, and hidden riches; the term need not identify ordinary residents of Venice.

notes.label: die weisse Ziegenkrautblume
notes.text: ‘the white goat-herb flower,’ a magical treasure-finding plant; the source gives the folk name but does not securely identify a botanical species.

43c42efaafd080e07f4ecf5487461bb105a49daa.summary: The Vogt at Wildenburg had a maid. She was the beloved of a young man who lived nearby, but she was never permitted to visit him.

notes.label: Vogt
notes.text: a Vogt was a bailiff or castle governor, here the title of Wildenburg’s oppressive lords; their exact jurisdiction and dates are uncertain.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: a Senn is an Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy production, here victimized by castle raids; the individual workers and Alps are unspecified.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Ziegerkrautblume
notes.text: literally a ‘Zieger-herb flower,’ this rare white magical plant opens the treasure vault and controls the spirits; its identification with the printed botanical name and actual species is uncertain.

notes.label: Uftue
notes.text: this Alemannic cry means ‘open up’ and is heard from the trapped soldier inside the stone labyrinth; its exact pronunciation is uncertain.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Kobolde
notes.text: Kobolde are German-speaking place or household spirits, here the punished lords guarding treasure in monstrous form; their distinction from the simultaneously named gnomes is uncertain.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: this plural denotes oppressive lords ruling by coercion, transformed after death into treasure guardians; their identities and historical basis are uncertain.

notes.label: Venediger
notes.text: in Alpine folklore, Venediger are mysterious outsiders associated with Venice, minerals, treasure, and magic; whether these figures reflect real migrants or legendary specialists is uncertain.

notes.label: Irrwische
notes.text: Irrwische are wandering ghost lights or will-o’-the-wisps, used here to describe the luminous dwarfs; whether literal lights were part of the local tradition is uncertain.

notes.label: Quatember
notes.text: Quatember denotes the quarterly Ember fasts of the Christian calendar, treated as heightened times of haunting; which seasonal observance is intended is unspecified.

f46b0384067cb79942ab770781027fe18919b24c.summary: On the eastern side of the Siluner-Ruck, or Seln, in the Kuhfirsten mountain chain—now called the Churfirsten—a cave lies in a rock wall between Silun and Breitenalp.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or herder living near the cave.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Wildenmannlisloch
notes.text: the unhyphenated cave name used in the body, ‘little wild men’s cave.’

notes.label: Wildmännchen
notes.text: little wild men, dwarf-like cave inhabitants who help neighboring Alpine herders.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, Alpine dairymen or herders.

notes.label: schoren
notes.text: to clear manure or muck from a stable, as glossed by the source.

notes.label: Wildweiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little wild woman,’ a female member of the cave-dwelling folk who needs a midwife.

notes.label: Rauchloch
notes.text: literally ‘smoke hole,’ a deep opening that releases weather-making vapors.

notes.label: Wetterloch
notes.text: literally ‘weather hole,’ a comparable mountain opening associated with changing weather.

notes.label: Hinter-Risi-Manndli
notes.text: literally something like ‘little man behind the scree slide,’ a scarlet-coated fiddling spirit; the place element Hinter-Risi is retained.

notes.label: Wildenmannlis-Loch
notes.text: literally ‘little wild men’s hole,’ the title’s regional name for the extensive cave dwelling.

91ec89f5d18f5ef2dd3061a52a000ee0e8653b4b.summary: Not far from the houses on the Buchserberg lies the Wildenmannslöchli, a rock cave that many say extends half an hour into the mountain.

notes.label: Wildenmannslöchli
notes.text: literally ‘little wild-man hole,’ the diminutive local name of the cave near the Buchserberg houses where wild little men are said to live.

notes.label: wilden Männli
notes.text: Swiss German-inflected plural for ‘wild little men,’ diminutive mountain or earth beings with subterranean domestic activities.

notes.label: Kübel
notes.text: tubs, pails, or large containers whose rumbling is heard during the beings' underground bread making; the exact baking vessel is not specified.

notes.label: Wecken
notes.text: small shaped bread rolls or loaves, one of the forms in which the clay ‘bread’ appears.

notes.label: Zelten
notes.text: flat cakes or festive breads; regional recipes vary, but here they too are made supernaturally from red clay.

c7a12149f82e0b7ddeb561174ae0be1290e4b3f6.summary: Even today, in the villages at the foot of the Galanda, one hears the saying:

notes.label: hät's Wild-Mann li g'seit
notes.text: Swiss German for “the Wild-Mannli said”; the source prints an internal space in Mann li, which is preserved in this quoted form.

notes.label: Wild-Mannli
notes.text: literally “little wild man,” the helpful hairy being who tends the farmer’s cattle except when driven into hiding by the wind.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, dry, often powerful Alpine downslope wind; in this tale it forces the wild beings to abandon all work and seek cover.

notes.label: Fänggen
notes.text: a regional plural for wild, hairy mountain or forest beings; Jecklin uses it as the broader class to which the Wild-Mannli belongs.

notes.label: Wildmallnli
notes.text: the title’s local spelling for a little wild man, a hairy Alpine or woodland being; the body uses the variant Wild-Mannli.

dae777452c69a85ed21c606ae377b3556a7c5bdb.summary: On the Tüfelisalp at the Churfirsten is a deep cave furnished with stone benches and tables.

notes.label: Tüfelisalp
notes.text: literally approximately ‘little-devil Alp,’ the high pasture containing the first described cave; the name need not imply that the helpful inhabitants are devils.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture with its livestock, huts, and work; the little mountain people freely herd cattle there.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Wildmannlisloch
notes.text: literally ‘little wild men's hole,’ the great cave associated with a helpful dwarf people; alternate source spellings include Wildemannloch.

notes.label: Wildmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wild men,’ dwarf-like cave dwellers who help neighboring Alpine workers rather than threatening them.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the senior Alpine dairymen or cattle herders whom the cave beings assist.

notes.label: schoren
notes.text: a regional stable task, probably scraping, cleaning, or arranging bedding and manure; the precise action is not defined by the collector.

notes.label: Wildweiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little wild woman,’ a female member of the cave people who requires a human midwife.

notes.label: Wildemannloch
notes.text: an alternate form of Wildmannlisloch, ‘wild-man cave’; it refers to the same or closely associated cave system in a later account.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder; attempts by two Sennen to repay the beings with food and clothes cause them to vanish.

notes.label: Allermannsharnisch
notes.text: literally ‘everyman's armor,’ the protective Alpine plant Allium victorialis; this account explains its roots as transformed dwarfs.

9254084a0154650f0d02d8ee5eeeffbb5fd534fb.summary: Überchumen i ächt au eine u wele?—Will I really get one too, and which one?

notes.label: Überchumen i ächt au eine u wele?
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘Will I really get one too, and which one?’—a question about whether the speaker will obtain a spouse and who that person will be.
notes.anchor: Überchumen i ächt au eine u wele?

notes.label: Angereesenacht
notes.text: the local name of a night used for marriage divination; the excerpt describes its ritual but does not identify the calendar date or securely explain the name.

notes.label: Müsli, Müsli
notes.text: the opening words of a Swiss German tooth-exchange rhyme meaning ‘Little mouse, little mouse.’ The full verse asks the mouse to give the child a new tooth in exchange for the old one and is spoken three times at the hearth.

notes.label: Seelentierchen
notes.text: literally ‘little soul animal,’ an animal form in which a soul or ancestral spirit is imagined to appear; here it explains the mouse's role in the tooth rite.

cb67b07f377e002c8f5f573ccff6c1b725c0bda1.summary: According to popular belief, will-o'-the-wisps performed their nocturnal dance as ‘fürige Manne’ because during their lifetimes, they had moved boundary stones and thereby robbed their neighbors.

notes.label: fürige Manne
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘fiery men,’ the personified local interpretation of will-o'-the-wisps as punished boundary thieves; the collector juxtaposes this belief with competing scientific explanations.

86873dc5442f823519660a365562515db826ffaf.summary: The road between Sonnental (Tscherlach) and Bärschis is also said not always to be entirely safe.

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: literally the ‘prayer bell,’ a church bell rung at an appointed devotional hour; its consecrated sound dispels the misleading fiery lights.

notes.label: Windspiel
notes.text: in these Bernese accounts, a dialect name for a whirlwind understood as a supernatural force; it should not be read in the standard German sense of a sighthound or merely a decorative ‘wind play.’

notes.label: Süidräck! Süidräck!
notes.text: a coarse Bernese ritual cry, literally ‘sow filth’ or ‘pig dirt,’ shouted while casting a sharp object into the whirlwind; its force is apotropaic abuse rather than a polite descriptive phrase.

notes.label: Tschöttelichappe
notes.text: a Bernese dialect name for a cap with a tassel or dangling tuft; recovering this personal item, rather than the hay, is what the speaker demands from the whirlwind.

notes.label: Süicheib
notes.text: a forceful Bernese insult addressed to the whirlwind, literally something like ‘sow-carrion’ or ‘swine rogue’; the precise English strength is context-dependent, so the original curse is retained.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a Swiss German name for an oppressive nightmare-being or small malicious spirit; the comparison places the whirlwind’s magic among familiar forms of local supernatural danger.

f86606137666c27a1847328ce11772dd2dda448f.summary: If a Windspiel can arise beneath a wagon already fully loaded with sheaves, it lifts the wagon into the air and then scatters the entire load in every direction.

notes.label: Windspiel
notes.text: literally ‘wind play,’ used here for a whirlwind or dust devil capable of lifting a loaded harvest wagon; in other contexts the German word can mean a sighthound or wind toy, neither of which is intended here.

notes.label: Freiamt
notes.text: the historical and present regional name for the southeastern part of Aargau; here it locates Nesselnbach and should not be read literally as a ‘free office.’

notes.label: Säukegel
notes.text: a coarse rural insult literally referring to a pig-shaped lump of animal dung or droppings; here it is shouted repeatedly at the whirlwind, apparently as a verbal counter-charm, though the tale does not explain why it works.

7dae94bab5f0749699207855ef04285395f7fae1.summary: A young Bernese man near Langenthal in Upper Aargau did not believe in the spectral nature of the Windsbraut.

notes.label: Windsbraut
notes.text: literally ‘bride of the wind,’ a traditional personification of the whirlwind as a female or spectral being; the warning hand confirms the belief the young man mocked.

notes.label: Windspiel
notes.text: literally ‘wind play,’ a local name for a passing whirlwind or dancing gust imagined here as a supernatural manifestation rather than ordinary weather.

f9f798ab9957d517a4d397fc4023207697dbd7c0.summary: During the thirties of the 19th century, while workers near Intschi were engaged in building the new Gotthard road, they saw many a Lagel of the finest Italian wine being carried down the old Ried road on the opposite side of the narrow Reuss Valley.

notes.label: Lagel
notes.text: a small cask or transport barrel, especially one used for carrying wine along Alpine routes; the workers watch the Italian wine pass beyond their reach.

731b712ef2d4e02ec547aadf0e5e826a584cce1e.summary: There is said to have been a vineyard in Gumpisch beyond the Tällä in former times.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a destructive debris flow or torrent carrying earth, stones, and water; this one is said to have transported fir trees upright in their soil and destroyed the vineyard.

671861335139ccd3524bc9118270be340a2c6126.summary: In the municipality of Beinwil on the Hallwilersee, a large field on the mountainside bears the name Wingart, meaning vineyard.

notes.label: Wingart
notes.text: a regional and historical form of Weingarten, ‘vineyard,’ preserved as the field-name at Beinwil even though the account describes no surviving vines.

notes.label: Karst
notes.text: a heavy pronged grubbing hoe or mattock used to work the soil; the hollow sound beneath it reveals the buried vault, and it is unrelated here to the limestone-landscape sense of karst.

notes.label: Schwabenstiefel
notes.text: literally ‘Swabian boots,’ the local name given to the apparition’s leather boots rising above the thighs; the source does not explain whether the label refers to a precise historical style or a broader regional stereotype.

notes.label: Kronentaler
notes.text: crown thalers, large historical silver coins; the black-clad figure winnows them in a basket like grain, marking the buried site as a place of supernatural wealth.

dcad97791df562616187389924cdfa244f0d6000.summary: At the time when people began to clear and clean the forests of Switzerland, a hideous serpent and dreadful dragon, called a Lindwurm in the Swiss annals, was found in the land of Unterwalden.

notes.label: Lindwurm
notes.text: a great serpent-like dragon of Germanic and Alpine legend, often less winged or leonine than later heraldic dragons; its blood remains deadly after defeat.

notes.label: Ödweiler
notes.text: literally ‘desolate hamlet,’ the village name explained by the dragon's depopulation of the area.

ea4ca2dfa1886c57dd1082afd4aca13a1a293643.summary: On the Frauenhalde, situated toward the woods by the little village of Kienberg in the Frickthale, there still live Erdweibchen regarded as wise and holy women.

notes.label: Frauenhalde
notes.text: literally ‘women's slope,’ the wooded hillside near Kienberg where the wise earth women live.

notes.label: Frickthale
notes.text: older inflected spelling of Fricktal, the Aargau Rhine-region valley containing Kienberg.

notes.label: Erdweibchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth women,’ subterranean female beings regarded as wise, holy, and healing.

notes.label: Erdmännchen
notes.text: literally ‘little earth men,’ the corresponding beings at Densbüren who also withdraw after humans investigate their feet.

notes.label: Schak
notes.text: the local form of the name Jacques, explicitly glossed in the source.

notes.label: Heilkräutlein
notes.text: a little healing herb placed upon a poor injured boy by the Erdweibchen.

notes.label: Wiss Ampeisse
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘white ants’; the dialect name becomes the title for the insects interpreted as the dead children's souls.

notes.label: Ampeisse
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ants; in this story their white color and emergence at the hearth make them manifestations of the dead children.

notes.label: Büri
notes.text: a Bernese feminine form for a woman farmer or farm wife; the compressed second occurrence is retained because the clause's exact physical meaning is unclear.

notes.label: Githung
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a profoundly greedy, miserly person; here it characterizes the woman who begrudges everyone everything.

notes.label: im Verschleikte
notes.text: Bernese dialect meaning secretly, furtively, or under concealment; it marks that the children were killed out of public sight.

notes.label: unger em Härd
notes.text: literally ‘under the hearth’ in the printed dialect; the compressed clause does not make clear whether it describes the Büri's position, remains, or a corrupt reading, so the phrase is retained rather than silently resolved.

notes.label: Seelentierchen
notes.text: literally ‘little soul-animals/creatures,’ a folkloric interpretive term for small animals or insects understood as embodied or returning souls.

4fe18754cea246eed69a64b8ed35b51ca669e4e5.summary: 1. Every ten years, an unknown woman came onto an Alp in the canton of Glarus, wandered among the cows, and then patted the finest cow on the muzzle, saying, ‘That really is a lovely little cow!’ This animal was then always doomed to destruction.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, together with its huts and dairy-working landscape, not simply a mountain peak; the first witch’s periodic attack is tied to this cattle-grazing setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Schellenkuh
notes.text: literally a ‘bell cow,’ a leading or prominent cow wearing the herd’s large bell; the witch singles her out as the herd passes along the Axenstrasse.

notes.label: Schapf
notes.text: a regional vessel or quantity measure for milk; the witch praises the cow as producing one full Schapf, but the source gives neither its exact form nor capacity.

ff4cbc566ed21a43422d10853ecbe5607340e230.summary: 1. About half a century ago, a peculiar Weibervolk wandered through the mountain holdings of Bürglen.

notes.label: Weibervolk
notes.text: an archaic and often disparaging Alemannic collective word for a woman or womenfolk; the account uses it to other a vulnerable itinerant woman before identifying her as Vinzenzia Megnet.

notes.label: Grissäste
notes.text: regional wording for conifer branches used to cover the body on the cart, probably fir or spruce boughs; the precise tree species is not secure from the account.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person’; here it carries the same suspicious, belittling tone applied to another itinerant woman.

notes.label: ds Tügg-Annäli
notes.text: a dialect byname meaning approximately ‘little Annie of the tufa’; it identifies the itinerant seller by the Tüggkugeln she carries rather than supplying a family name.

notes.label: Zeintli
notes.text: a diminutive of regional Zeine, a handled carrying basket often made of wicker; it contains the stone balls offered for sale, but its size and weave are not stated.

notes.label: Tüggkugeln
notes.text: regional wording for rounded pieces or balls of Tügg, explicitly glossed by the source as Tuff, tufa stone; selling them is suspected of being a pretext for entering homes.

2928ac0faafc4ce1883dae4f9ece0efe03019592.summary: A boy went on Stubeten visits to two girls in the little land of Uri who were no longer very young.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: plural or inflected use of Stubete, a traditional evening visit or social gathering in a farmhouse room; such visits could involve courtship, conversation, music, or communal work.

notes.label: Zum Kamin aus und nirgends an
notes.text: the witches' flight formula, literally ‘out through the chimney and nowhere against’; it instructs the enchanted ride to pass cleanly through without striking anything, which the boy fails to reproduce correctly.
notes.anchor: Zum Kamin aus und nirgends an

975569f8bd1f91dd3597e7590ed0226b1fb9aace.summary: a) Two farmhands belonging to Prosper Bär of Schattdorf—a wealthy farmer who also owned a field in the neighboring municipality of Bürglen—had spent an evening visiting three girls in Bürglen.

notes.label: Grotzli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small, stunted, or scrubby fir or spruce; here the wind-driven little conifer is believed to embody or conceal the witch.

notes.label: Meitli
notes.text: Swiss German for a girl or young woman, using the characteristic -li diminutive; here it describes the two unusual young women without necessarily implying that they are children.

notes.label: Wusch
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a loose wisp, bundle, or tuft; here it is a compact mass of hay spinning in the wind and believed to be the witch’s form.

notes.label: Bätti
notes.text: an Uri Catholic name for a rosary or string of prayer beads; throwing one into the whirlwind is presented as a protective act alongside throwing tools.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a barn bay, livestock shelter, hay store, or farm outbuilding; the exact barn layout in which the chained cows become entangled is not stated.

6b49109a9bb0762c7b4d3a1ef73be323896dce4c.summary: At home in Staldenried, people once held a certain young woman to be a witch who enchanted the livestock.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

6f03a8a29db91da5c8951fa0ef61a2f99ffc531f.summary: At Häggrigen, a mother was busy melting down a Chessi full of Anken. It had already begun to liquefy when a strange old Müetterli entered the kitchen with her hair loose and hanging down over her head and begged for some Anken.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large cauldron, commonly used in Alpine dairying; here it is filled with Anken rather than milk for cheese.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for butter; here more than twenty pounds of it seethe supernaturally and are lost.

notes.label: Müetterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Mutter, literally ‘little mother’ or ‘old mother’; here it is a familiar designation for an elderly woman, not a claim of kinship.

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a low, broad wooden dairy vessel; the source does not specify its capacity, and the bewitched Anken continues boiling after being poured into it.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

81d20ea79eccb2bfcd43dcfe268a52fa96f2ebf6.summary: If one stands a broom upright at the door, witches cannot come in.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Schwarzmeisterwurzeln
notes.text: roots burned or smoked as a folk counter-charm against witches; the historical plant name is retained because the brief source does not identify the species securely enough for a modern botanical equivalent.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Swiss coin and the hundredth part of a franc; the claim that a witch owes 7 Rappen of daily damage measures her supernatural obligation in a deliberately small, everyday sum.

notes.label: Schrätteliszöpfe
notes.text: literally ‘Schrätteli braids,’ tangles or mats in horses' manes attributed to a Schrätteli, a regional nightmare or oppressive night-spirit; English readers may know the related motif as elf-locks or witches' knots.

notes.label: Hexen streiche
notes.text: literally ‘witch tracks’ or ‘witch marks,’ a source spelling for circular meadow patches attributed to witches' dancing.

notes.label: Hexenringe
notes.text: literally ‘witch rings,’ circular growth patterns in grass that folklore interprets as places where witches danced; the natural phenomenon is often called a fairy ring in English.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: the Ember fasts or Ember days, the quarterly Catholic fast periods traditionally associated here with heightened supernatural activity.

notes.label: Geißböcklein
notes.text: a little billy goat; seeing one reflected or revealed inside a woman's eyes is presented as a sign that she is a witch, drawing on the goat's demonic associations in Christian folklore.

482f641209fff4f5e87c8ad1105a047249a6b4b8.summary: In Rapperswil in 1609, Salome Schörpf of Mels was beheaded as a witch and then burned.

aa59707fe5207c313bf21d279d5a606cc3509a03.summary: 1. A woman once came to Pastor Bissig († 1911) in Seedorf and offered potted flowers for sale.

notes.label: Eja, im Namä Jesus cha-n-ä ja abnä'
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘Well, in the name of Jesus I can surely take it from her’; invoking the sacred name prevents direct transfer rather than overcoming the barrier.

notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

notes.label: Pfaffächällärä
notes.text: a strongly disparaging Uri expression for women associated with priests, witches, or priest-household women; the exact compound and target are locally colored, so the term remains visible rather than being reduced to a neutral ‘witches.’

notes.label: Jää, vorem G'wichnä-n- und vor heiligä Nämä und vor güetä Gidankä hennt-s'Respäk, d'Pfaffächällärä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the Pfaffächällärä respect or fear consecrated things, holy names, and good thoughts; the formula summarizes the legend’s protective theology.

notes.label: Hättisch g'seit, so nimm's i Gottsnamä, sä wärisch de scho drüffchu, was es g'sy wär
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘If you had said, “Take it in God’s name,” you would soon have discovered what she was’; the advice treats the sacred formula as a test of a suspected witch.

notes.label: Alp

notes.label: Zum Teufel, drei Brode habe ich bei mir!
notes.text: the man's German exclamation, ‘To the Devil! I have three loaves with me!’; the tale says the utterance breaks the witches' binding power but does not explain why invoking the three loaves releases him.
notes.anchor: Zum Teufel, drei Brode habe ich bei mir!

notes.label: Lungnez
notes.text: Jecklin's German form of the Graubünden valley now generally called Lumnezia; the story places the witches' stable between Morissen and Villa.

notes.label: Chamois

notes.label: Maijen
notes.text: a decorative sprig, small bouquet, or plume worn on a woman’s hat; the chamois leaves this personal ornament behind, allowing the hunters to identify the transformed woman, but the source does not specify its plant material.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the chief magistrate of a Swiss canton or rural polity, an office with broader authority than an ordinary mayor; Frau Landammann here means the officeholder’s wife rather than a separate title she holds.

notes.label: Krachen
notes.text: an Alpine German word for a deep cleft, ravine, or rocky chasm; the chamois falls into one so confined and deep that only a strip of skirt remains visible.

32f8b23f8b9a3816a7593a23ecfbe60fa807d2d9.summary: Late one night a farmer passed the ruined stable whose surroundings are called Sand, about half an hour from Meierhof.

notes.label: wind und weh
notes.text: a regional expression for becoming dizzy, sick, distressed, or faint; the source conveys the farmer’s bodily and emotional overwhelm without fixing one precise symptom.

notes.label: Ribe
notes.text: a Nidwalden name, also given as Rübe, for a descending mass of earth and debris imagined as a witch’s vehicle as well as a landslide; the tale’s Hexenriebe is the halted slide, while the precise natural distinction from other debris flows is unstated.

notes.label: Wetterglöcklein
notes.text: literally a ‘little weather bell,’ a consecrated chapel bell rung to avert storms, hail, and harmful spirits; here its sound stops the witch-driven landslide, reflecting a Central Swiss protective bell custom.

notes.label: Steinibach-Hündli
notes.text: literally the ‘little dog of Steinibach,’ the witch’s mocking or resentful nickname for the chapel’s Wetterglöcklein because it ‘barks’; the phrase personifies the bell, not an actual dog.

notes.label: Beinhausglöggli
notes.text: dialect for the ‘little ossuary bell,’ a bell specifically made and rung against hail-producing witchcraft; the passage does not describe its size, inscription, or precise location beyond the ossuary association.

notes.label: gross Mohr
notes.text: literally ‘the great Moor,’ an unexplained Willisau name in the witch’s list of protective sounds, probably a local bell or other loudly sounding object; the source only says that it wheezes, so its identity remains genuinely uncertain.
