ae1c6160e618135f5a8ed821356d89a50e7d96b5.summary: Stocks and gallows—that is, the higher jurisdiction—belonged to the territorial lord, formerly the Counts of Werdenberg and later the governor from Glarus.

notes.label: Schelmenwegli
notes.text: literally ‘little rogues’ path,’ the diminutive local name of the steep route reserved for leading accused or condemned criminals to the castle without crossing the town’s jurisdiction.

ac6035306100d4227d686211216b919570c7800c.summary: Wittnauer Hans was still very small when his father fell to his death in a quarry.

notes.label: Wittnauer
notes.text: a person from Wittnau in Aargau; the regional demonym functions as part of Hans’s identifying name.

notes.label: He so nu so denn!
notes.text: a Swiss German expression of reluctant assent, roughly ‘well, all right then’; the miserly cousin growls it before agreeing to try Hans as a herder.

notes.label: Spunten
notes.text: the bung or stopper closing the hole of a barrel; because the robbers had knocked it out, air could enter and Hans did not suffocate.

notes.label: Spuntloch
notes.text: the bunghole or opening left by the removed Spunten; Hans sees the stunned robber through this small aperture.

notes.label: Obertenne
notes.text: the upper threshing floor, barn bay, or storage level of a Swiss farm building; Hans enters it from behind the house and hides among sheaves above the robbers.

notes.label: Garbenloch
notes.text: literally ‘sheaf hole,’ an opening through which bundled grain or hay could be moved between levels of a barn; Hans falls through it into the room below.

notes.label: Ankenschnitten
notes.text: slices of bread prepared or spread with Anken, the Swiss German word for butter; the robbers want honey as a sweet accompaniment.

notes.label: Küherbuben
notes.text: cowherd boys or young cattle tenders; the ending uses the term to emphasize Hans’s rise from an impoverished farm servant to an independent landowner.

ce8f483e1f2b4537415931ef8818cae1356a3bb7.summary: When the pagan deities succumbed to victorious Christianity and the inhabitants of Vaud also swore allegiance to the new doctrine, the vanquished gods' resentment against their former followers was so great that, through the elements over which they had not yet entirely lost power, they sought to…

notes.label: Rigou, hai ousson!
notes.text: a locally recorded Romance-language command glossed by the collector as ‘River, rise up!’; its exact dialect, spelling, and word-by-word analysis are uncertain, but it summons the Rhône's destructive flood.

notes.label: Saint Maurice
notes.text: Saint Maurice is associated with the Theban Legion and with the abbey at Saint-Maurice in Valais. References to him belong to a regional tradition of Christian martyrdom and devotion; the particular miracle remains the collector’s telling.

source.label: Abbey of Saint-Maurice

8c74836805d8f8a27c4f9221e17fb81515c65b2b.summary: Toward evening, a woman from Wassen went to Silenen to see Doctor Lussmann on behalf of a gravely ill neighbor.

notes.label: bärsianen
notes.text: the source’s dialect adjective for the uncanny woman’s dress; its material, color, or regional style cannot be established securely from this account, so the exact form is retained rather than guessed.

789baf52c6010ea9d44c8e594868d6d3834233e5.summary: In the church at Buochs, the women of Ennetbürgen in Unterwalden go zum Opfer—to make their offering—before the men because, according to an old legend, in the year 1315 they attacked a troop of the Austrian army that had entered the Kropfgasse and drove it to flight.

notes.label: zum Opfer
notes.text: to go forward for the church offertory or presentation of an offering; the local order, women before men, is explained as an honor commemorating the women's legendary defense of Ennetbürgen.

833c2bca8035f0e25aa6e388f46f0060dfe23971.summary: According to country people's belief, beautiful women made themselves a pleasure garden in the forest meadows not far from the little town of Brugg.

notes.label: Beijel (Bühl)
notes.text: the local name of the women's forest pleasure garden; Bühl is an older word for a hill or rise, reflected in the story's title Frauenhügel, ‘women's hill.’

30d09c3e4b35cd5948f1e9c72ea7866c3b242243.summary: The mountains were wondrous once. Between the jagged peaks, where rigid seas of ice spread today, lay lovely valleys whose green meadows were strewn with the adornment of brilliantly colored flowers.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Bergsennen
notes.text: Bergsennen are Alpine dairymen and herders working with cattle on high seasonal pastures, here magnified along with the legendary landscape; their exact household or labor organization is unspecified.

7f4890285834ac23c67cce9b4d056a1a02d423b1.summary: a) From ancient times, a Bethäuslein stood on the gravel hill east of Urswil, where the 14 Nothhelfer were venerated.

notes.label: Bethäuslein
notes.text: a diminutive ‘little prayer house’ or wayside devotional building; the shining directs the blind knight to restore it as a larger chapel.

notes.label: 14 Nothhelfer
notes.text: the Fourteen Holy Helpers, a traditional group of saints invoked collectively against illness and danger; the source retains the numeral and older spelling.

notes.label: Bodenzinse
notes.text: hereditary or long-term ground rents charged upon land; transferring them gives the chapel a continuing source of maintenance income.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

source.label: History of the Swiss Capuchins

notes.label: Bildstock
notes.text: a small freestanding wayside shrine or image pillar, here built of stone with a Marian image and a resting bench; it is more specific than a generic monument.

3fbd6ed0ab214e4b6a1fa2c6b512cca9196c0305.summary: It was Pentecost when a sudden violent storm arose at sea and threatened at every moment to swallow the ship.

notes.label: Capuchin friars
notes.text: The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscan religious order. In Swiss communities their work included preaching and pastoral care. The friar in a legend therefore belongs to a recognizable religious institution, even when the telling gives him extraordinary powers.

9b82d0100ac1785e931faea2a099bef54bb241c4.summary: At the beginning of the hay and Emd harvest, late in the evening one not infrequently hears “dängeln” (sharpening scythes) in several hamlets or farmsteads of the Puschlav valley.

notes.label: Emd
notes.text: the second cutting of hay, or the finer aftermath hay harvested after the first hay crop.

notes.label: dängeln
notes.text: to sharpen a scythe by hammering its cutting edge thin on a small anvil; the ringing work sound is central to the haunting.

notes.label: Dängeln
notes.text: the noun formed from dängeln, meaning the hammer-sharpening of scythes.

notes.label: Puschlav
notes.text: the traditional German name for the Poschiavo valley, a southern Graubünden valley with strong Italian cultural influence.

notes.label: Strenge
notes.text: literally severity, strictness, or rigor; in this quoted moral explanation it suggests excessive harshness or work discipline, but its precise local nuance is not stated.

notes.label: Quartane
notes.text: a traditional local grain measure and container; its loose iron rings produce the reported tic, tic, tic during winnowing.

notes.label: Kornmaass
notes.text: the historical spelling of Kornmaß, a grain measure; the parenthetical explanation identifies the Quartane as the measure formerly used.

notes.label: rinnen
notes.text: literally to run, flow, or trickle; here grain is allowed to stream slowly from the measure onto cloth so the wind can remove the chaff.

notes.label: Uberträttig
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German form meaning a transgression, violation, or improper crossing of a customary boundary; working after the accepted evening stopping time risked supernatural consequences.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: literally ‘Lady Fast’ or ‘Woman of the Fast,’ a female folkloric enforcer associated with fasting-season and household-work taboos; the exact local character may overlap with wider Perchta-like traditions.

f3832bbbdae44d52950beed116d6aa3b180ff58a.summary: In the Rhine valley, Wotan’s raging host is called “Wuatahee” or “Wuatihee.” The “Klagweh” is distinguished from it.

notes.label: Wuatahee
notes.text: a Rhine-valley name for Wotan’s raging supernatural host or Wild Hunt; the spelling evokes Wüetisheer, the furious army.

notes.label: Wuatihee
notes.text: an alternate regional spelling of Wuatahee for the same Wild Hunt host.

notes.label: Klagweh
notes.text: literally something like ‘lamenting woe,’ a distinct airborne apparition characterized by endlessly sorrowful sounds.

notes.label: Wärber
notes.text: Wärber are military recruiters, here using the declaration and enlistment payment to claim dancers as recruits; their unit and legal powers are unspecified.

notes.label: Wärber bim Tanz
notes.text: literally ‘recruiters at the dance’ in Bernese dialect, Wärber bim Tanz names the attempted enlistment through a staged dance; the incident’s date and military authority are unspecified.

notes.label: Bärghans
notes.text: Bärghans is the strong young man’s dialect nickname, approximately ‘Mountain Hans’; his full name and home are uncertain.

notes.label: Chuutzemischt
notes.text: Chuutzemischt is a dialect oath or exclamation of angry disbelief; its literal derivation, strength, and exact pronunciation are uncertain.

notes.label: Handgäld
notes.text: Handgäld is the enlistment bounty or earnest money whose acceptance could bind a recruit, secretly slipped into Hans’s pocket; the sum and legal validity are unspecified.

notes.label: Wätter azeige
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘to announce’ or ‘foretell weather’; here humanlike apparitions appear immediately before sudden storms.

notes.label: uf dr Stör
notes.text: a traditional expression for an artisan working temporarily at a customer's home or farm rather than in a fixed workshop; here the narrator's father is returning from such work on the Liemberg.

notes.label: Grebli
notes.text: a Bernese Swiss German diminutive for a small ditch, trench, or gully; here a plank bridges it, causing the witness to look down and lose sight of the apparition.

notes.label: Drufabe het ’s Wätter gänderet
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘After that, the weather changed’; the commentary identifies it as a formulaic ending attached to tales of returning spirits.

notes.label: Müsli
notes.text: here the Bernese diminutive for a little mouse, not the cereal called muesli in English.

notes.label: Wätter u Müsli mache
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘making weather and little mice’; both storm-making and creating crop-eating mice are treated as forms of witchcraft.

notes.label: Luzärner
notes.text: Swiss German for a man or person from Lucerne; the outsider interprets both the mouse and storm as Zürcher Ueli's magic.

notes.label: Zürcher Ueli
notes.text: literally ‘Zurich Ueli,’ a man named Ueli identified by his Zurich association; the source does not clarify whether Zürcher is a nickname, origin label, or family designation.

notes.label: Chatzerschwang
notes.text: a local route or place-name crossed on the way home; the source supplies no explanation of its component meanings or exact location.

notes.label: Jo, jo
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘yes, yes,’ used here as a knowing acknowledgment before the visitor states his conclusion.

notes.label: chan er Müsli mache, chan er au Wätter mache!
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘if he can make mice, he can also make weather!’; the parallel wording links two harms traditionally attributed to witches.
notes.anchor: chan er Müsli mache, chan er au Wätter mache!

80ba00c3dfe6e4198fb0b88f2c166e3a9ebbe4d6.summary: The Wüetihö is a many-legged black animal shaped like a cat, though considerably larger.

notes.label: Wüetihö
notes.text: the local name for a many-legged black, catlike night creature said to travel over fields and even through the air; the brief source does not explain the name or securely identify it with another folkloric being.

b6a9867e0a574264e773fd1cee9f05e34ef2f09d.summary: Above Eisten in Meien, the small children were alone at home one day in an old black cottage while their parents worked on a remote property.

notes.label: b'segnen
notes.text: an Uri dialect verb meaning to bless or make a protective sign of blessing over someone; the mother's habitual act shields the children from the threatening woman while she is away.

9c0e53e31c7d396a28edf4e7c9dfa89053f39a35.summary: One night a Senn at Gufern could find no peace at all in his hut; something kept waking him from sleep.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy work on a seasonal high pasture; the title identifies the man’s occupation, not merely any farmhand.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gliger
notes.text: a regional sleeping place in an Alpine hut, often a simple bunk, hay bed, or straw bed; the source does not specify its construction here.

notes.label: Halbtürli
notes.text: literally a ‘little half-door,’ the small half-height or divided door of the Alpine hut; the dark creature crouches upon this architectural feature.

b333e1da4c97b972e545d81bd08aa63f604bb62e.summary: ‘Chählä-n-Alois was a brutal man,’ an old resident of Gurtnellen relates. ‘One evening, as he went home heavily drunk, he climbed up to the window of our house on the Stalden, mocked and jeered at the specter in the Leidloch, which he had to pass, and boasted that this evening he would certainly show it who was master.

notes.label: Chählä-n-Alois
notes.text: a local house-name or byname construction identifying Alois through Chählä; the exact family, farm, or place relationship expressed by the inserted -n- is not explained.

notes.label: i 'Klüs gnu
notes.text: a dialect phrase for being taken in a constricting grip, trap, or affliction; the spirit’s precise action in the Leidloch is not described, but the lasting injury to Alois’s leg shows that it is more than a verbal rebuke.

notes.label: Z'spettlä-n-erlydet's nitt
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the uncanny being ‘does not tolerate being mocked’; the proverb-like formula warns that quiet passage is safe but ridicule or attack provokes retaliation.

notes.label: der Präzis
notes.text: literally ‘the precise one,’ the narrator Johann Tresch’s recorded byname; it may praise his exactness or identify him locally, but the source gives no further explanation.

0cdbdabad7af81d0b5214060fc0f16bc747d646d.summary: Above Pisciadella is a place containing nothing but the ruins of buildings, and to this day that place is called la Rovina (“the ruin”).

notes.label: la Rovina
notes.text: a local Romance place-name literally meaning “the ruin”; it designates the site of building remains above Pisciadella.

884748637ef8686181ecd2d4b111936c2c023831.summary: This was told at Hergiswil. In a house, a Ziberlisturm—porridge—had just been served when several familiar Heidenweiblein were seen approaching.

notes.label: Ziberlisturm
notes.text: a regional porridge dish; Sturm suggests a heap or mass, and hiding it from supernatural guests produces the proverbial rebuke.

notes.label: Heidenweiblein
notes.text: literally ‘little heathen women,’ a historical folk label for mysterious female beings imagined as remnants of an earlier people; it marks supernatural otherness rather than a precise religion.

notes.label: Ziberli
notes.text: the title's regional food-name, related in the tale to Ziberlisturm; the source identifies the dish only as a porridge, so its precise ingredients remain uncertain.

279bfcd31a29f4326f31f9c482a452ad2124f262.summary: A weary, heavily burdened little old woman who wanted to sit down and rest was threatened with Verlochen by a band of Zigeuner to which she belonged.

notes.label: Verlochen
notes.text: literally something like putting into a hole or burying, here a threatened way of disposing of an elderly person; whether the tale imagines burial alive, killing followed by burial, or another act is not stated securely.

notes.label: Zigeuner
notes.text: a historical and now derogatory German exonym often applied to Roma and Sinti, but also used indiscriminately for itinerant outsiders; it is retained to expose the source's hostile stereotype, and the tale does not establish the group's identity or validate its accusation.

eef6eb23d507cd972ce2106ad52647b4d13848a3.summary: As is well known, the Reformer Ulrich Zwingli was a preacher in Einsiedeln between 1516 - 1518.

notes.label: Pilgrimage to Einsiedeln
notes.text: Einsiedeln is a Benedictine abbey and an important Catholic pilgrimage destination. A journey there in a story can be an act of religious devotion, petition, or thanksgiving, rather than ordinary travel.

source.label: Einsiedeln Abbey

notes.label: Brül
notes.text: a local place-name in Einsiedeln for the open ground from which Zwingli is said to have leapt; the precise older landscape sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Ketzerboden
notes.text: literally ‘heretic's ground,’ the place-name said to commemorate where the Reformer landed after his miraculous escape.

26651ba7c274ec6c390129666773795fbc16bcbb.summary: Züsler—fiery men and movers of boundary markers—were often seen here. Usually, it is Fronfastenkinder who see such things.

notes.label: Züsler
notes.text: a regional name for a fiery wandering spirit, often understood as a dead boundary-marker mover doing penance; the word evokes glowing or smoldering fire.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: literally ‘Ember-tide children,’ people born during the quarterly Ember fasts who were traditionally believed able to perceive spirits and other supernatural phenomena.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming

notes.label: Z’förchte mache
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘to make someone afraid’ or ‘to frighten someone’; the exact dialect title frames the boys' disguise as an imitation of a feared figure.

notes.label: Frau Faschte
notes.text: the dialect name of the uncanny female apparition called Frau Fasten in the commentary; the source does not explain whether the name relates to fasting or to a local figure.

notes.label: Mösli
notes.text: a diminutive place-name meaning a small moor or marshy spot, where the boys stage their prank.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; at Rütschelen, the apparition emerges from one.

notes.label: Z’Leimiswil
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘at/in Leimiswil,’ marking the locality where the silent spectral procession is seen.

notes.label: Hohlen
notes.text: the local name or dialect plural for hollow ways or sunken lanes through which the procession descends; the precise route is not further identified.

notes.label: Totebäumli
notes.text: literally ‘little dead tree’ or ‘little death tree,’ the object carried at the head of the procession; it may denote a funerary marker or death-associated little tree, but the short account leaves its form ambiguous.

notes.label: Z’Urschebech
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘at/in Urschebech,’ the local place-name attached to the witness and the apparition; the source does not explain its literal derivation.

notes.label: Lichezug
notes.text: Bernese dialect for a funeral procession; here it is a supernatural procession whose sight makes the witness lose his hair.

notes.label: Totenheer
notes.text: literally ‘army/host of the dead,’ the long spectral company following the death wagon.

notes.label: Nachtvolk
notes.text: literally ‘night people,’ the Graubünden name for a nocturnal spectral procession compared with the Bernese Totenheer.

notes.label: Gratzug
notes.text: a Valais spectral procession, literally a ‘ridge procession’ or possibly a historically altered compound; the exact etymology is debated, so the source's comparative name is retained.

74c4266ee5adf3a122b002f28886fdd5c59e9c5a.summary: a) In 1629, the parish church at Giswil was flooded after a violent thunderstorm and buried beneath debris together with the whole beautiful meadow country.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

notes.label: Lauwi
notes.text: an Obwalden place and dialect word for a destructive mountain torrent or debris flow; in these accounts it names both the watercourse and the dangerous flood phenomenon.

notes.label: Lauwitier
notes.text: literally the ‘Lauwi beast,’ a supernatural animal believed to race ahead of the swollen Lungerer torrent with rubble and thunderous noise.
