notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Mutte
notes.text: a regional word for a trough or similarly hollow vessel; the witch uses one as her uncanny boat upon the flood crest.

notes.label: Ahabach-Ma
notes.text: dialect for the ‘Ahabach man,’ Dallenwil's locally named male flood or stream spirit; the brief source preserves the name but gives no further description.

notes.label: Überschwemmer
notes.text: literally ‘flood-bringers’ or ‘inundators,’ a collective title for the supernatural beings and creatures said to ride before destructive Obwalden flood torrents.

a30a60626182c1ddf9a0989e43575c887c798ba0.summary: ‘Hesch ghulfe jage…’ — ‘Did You Help with the Hunt…’

notes.label: Hesch ghulfe jage
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘Did you help with the hunt?’; the supernatural hunter turns the mocker's participation into a demand that he gnaw the thrown bone.

notes.label: Grossätti
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for grandfather or grandfatherly elder; he is named as the teller of the household account.

notes.label: Taunermannli
notes.text: a diminutive for an impoverished rural cottager or day laborer; the affectionate -li form describes Rabijobbi's humble status and person.

notes.label: Süidürscht
notes.text: a Bernese regional name for a noisy Wild Hunt-like aerial procession; the source compares it with other Dürscht forms and associates its sound with migratory birds.

notes.label: Dürscht
notes.text: the shorter form used for the supernatural hunt or its leader; its exact etymology is uncertain, but it is not the ordinary German word for thirst.

notes.label: Hescht ghulfe jage
notes.text: the opening of the dialect threat, ‘You helped with the hunt’; the following line says that the mocker can now help gnaw the thrown bone.

notes.label: Vorstuehl
notes.text: the source's dialect name for the seat or chair from which the mocker falls; its exact furniture form is not described.

notes.label: NachtlütIi
notes.text: literally ‘little night people,’ the source's local comparison for nocturnal beings corresponding to the forest women hunted in other traditions.

notes.label: Hungsdürscht
notes.text: a named variant of the Dürscht procession; the source lists it without explaining the first element securely.

notes.label: Vogeldürscht
notes.text: literally a ‘bird Dürscht,’ the variant most transparently connected with flocks of migrating birds heard overhead at night.

e082ba267d1e25f8cb5fb7922f23830b64bd8d48.summary: One summer, a Bettlermandli went about the mountains of Bürglen and the Schächen Valley, but the people gave him too little, and he said he would yet play them a Schwirren.

notes.label: Bettlermandli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little male beggar or begging man; the form can be familiar or disparaging and does not by itself establish that he is supernaturally small.

notes.label: Schwirren
notes.text: part of a local idiom for dealing someone a harmful trick, blow, or piece of mischief; here the Bettlermandli's threat is followed by the destructive storm, but the word's exact nuance is not defined.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri Alpine term for a violent debris-laden mountain torrent or flow of water, earth, and rock; the tale personifies it as something voices can ride and steer.

notes.label: Leit', leit'!
notes.text: the exact dialect command ‘Guide it, guide it!’ or ‘Steer it, steer it!’ shouted by one voice riding the Rübi.

notes.label: Santä-Toni-Sywli
notes.text: the traditional Uri nickname for St. Anthony's little chapel bell; Sywli literally suggests a little sow or piglet, and its ‘squealing’ is the bell heard from the storm.

notes.label: I mag nimmä g'leitä, ds Santä-Toni-Sywli gysset
notes.text: the exact dialect reply ‘I can guide it no longer; the Santä-Toni-Sywli is squealing’; the protective chapel bell's ringing has broken the riders’ power.
notes.anchor: I mag nimmä g'leitä, ds Santä-Toni-Sywli gysset

bd092891a061f27775aac312cdbd98be1e0e492d.summary: According to legend, one of the lords of Grasburg had an excellent horse that he named ‘Wels,’ probably not without intending an allusion to the political party then so powerful in Germany.

notes.label: Stell di Wels!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘stop yourself, Wels!’ or ‘brace, Wels!’—the rider's desperate command to his horse; the source also hears a political pun in the horse's name, likely alluding to the German Welf faction, but prints Wels.

notes.label: Oele
notes.text: the source's local place-name below the vertical sandstone cliff on the old Fribourg road; its exact modern referent is not explained in the account.

notes.label: ’s Chalb a dr Firscht
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘the calf at the roof ridge’; it names the suspended protective object whose presence prevents further calf deaths.

notes.label: Firscht
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for the ridge or ridgepole of a roof; the calf is hoisted there as an apotropaic object.

notes.label: Chüeiherhütte
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for a cowherd’s hut or cattleman’s Alpine shelter; its hidden location contains the bound calf charm.

notes.label: uehebannet
notes.text: Bernese Alemannic for ‘bound up there by a ban or spell’; it explains why the thin thread cannot be loosened, though the exact magical rite is not described.

notes.label: ’s Chilchli z’Frybech
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the little church at Freibach,’ preserving the diminutive Chilchli and the dialect form of the place-name.

notes.label: Rain
notes.text: here a slope, bank, or raised strip of ground, not rainfall; it locates the former chapel above the path.

notes.label: Moos
notes.text: here marshy or boggy ground, not simply botanical moss; it names the low-lying landscape near the chapel site.

notes.label: Eselsise
notes.text: Swiss German for donkey shoes or small horseshoes fitted to a donkey, reportedly found among the chapel-site stones.

notes.label: Chinglibrünnli
notes.text: literally ‘little children's spring’ or ‘little child spring,’ a diminutive fountain-name; the text itself stresses that the true reason for the name is unknown.

notes.label: Zilete
notes.text: rows, files, or processional lines of people; the old witnesses see whole ordered groups traveling toward the vanished chapel.

notes.label: Brudersami
notes.text: a regional form meaning brotherhood or confraternity, here the religious association founded by smiths and later opened to other men and women.

notes.label: ’s Doggeli
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the Doggeli,’ a nightmare spirit that enters sleeping rooms and presses upon the chest.

notes.label: Doggeli
notes.text: a regional name for an oppressive night spirit, comparable to the nightmare mare or Alp.

notes.label: Unghüürli
notes.text: a little monster, uncanny creature, or diminutive horror.

notes.label: Ote
notes.text: dialect for breath; the Doggeli’s pressure leaves sleepers unable to breathe.

e2647e4898969f5c9d04d45f02e9bf404e8a4fc2.summary: ’s Fraueli a dr Sossaugass (The Little Woman on Sossau Lane)

notes.label: ’s Fraueli a dr Sossaugass
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the little woman on Sossau Lane’; Fraueli is an often affectionate diminutive of Frau, but here it names an ugly weather-associated apparition rather than an endearing figure.

notes.label: strübere
notes.text: a Bernese dialect verb for the weather turning rough, gusty, or squally; here the apparition's arrival signals such unsettled conditions, while the exact mix of wind and precipitation is not specified.

notes.label: Spinnhuppele
notes.text: a rare Bernese dialect comparison for gray, tufted clumps associated with spiders or cobwebs; here it describes the little woman's face, but the source does not define the object precisely enough to choose between web-tufts, dust-clumps, or a spider-related growth.

5e937490fef704cac7309db28e09f5a5bd6569ce.summary: ’s Fraueli bi dr Lushütte — The Little Woman by the Lushütte

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive of Frau, closest to ‘little woman’; in this story it is the local name for an uncanny female apparition and does not imply a child.

notes.label: ’s Fraueli bi dr Lushütte
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the little woman by the Lushütte’; the diminutive can sound familiar but here names an ugly, selectively visible weather-demonic figure, while Lushütte is retained as the local hut name.

notes.label: Gusti
notes.text: a regional term for young cattle, especially a heifer or young bovine; the passage does not make the animals’ exact age or sex fully clear.

notes.label: Wätterluft
notes.text: literally ‘weather-air,’ a dialect expression for the wind or atmospheric force of an approaching storm; here it signals the Fraueli’s weather-demonic character.

notes.label: D’Luft isch voll vo Geischter; we me se ums gsäch! Sie hei chum Platz näbenangere.
notes.text: Bernese dialect meaning ‘The air is full of spirits, if only one could see them; they scarcely have room beside one another’; it summarizes the regional soul-belief that the dead move invisibly in wind and air.
notes.anchor: D’Luft isch voll vo Geischter; we me se ums gsäch! Sie hei chum Platz näbenangere.

75fa8dcd78c81c0a567fc25ca261403a9e024862.summary: ’s Fraueli mit em Rächeli — The Little Woman with the Little Rake

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: an affectionate or diminutive Swiss German form meaning a little woman; here it names the female being who emerges from the tree.

notes.label: ’s Fraueli mit em Rächeli
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘the little woman with the little rake’; both diminutives make the apparition sound small and familiar even though the source leaves her identity and purpose unexplained.

notes.label: Rächeli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small rake; the source specifies that the apparition's characteristic implement is made of wood.

notes.label: Chappeli
notes.text: a Bernese diminutive for a small chapel; it serves as the first local landmark on the route to the apparition's hollow tree.

notes.label: ’s Füür banne
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘to bind’ or magically contain the fire; in this legend it is a protective folk practice that forces a spreading blaze to rise straight up instead of reaching neighboring houses. The wording names supernatural containment rather than ordinary firefighting.

notes.label: ’s Galgelölitier
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘the Galgelöli animal’ or ‘Galgelöli beast,’ the elusive rushing monster named for the little wood where it manifests.

notes.label: ’s Galgelöli
notes.text: the dialectal name of the little wood near Madiswil; the source does not explain the place-name's derivation.

notes.label: Hunzerügge
notes.text: a local ridge-name on the apparition's route, with Rügge corresponding to ‘ridge’ or ‘back’; the first element is unexplained.

notes.label: Unghüür
notes.text: Swiss German for a monster, uncanny creature, or monstrous being, emphasizing that the Galgelölitier is not an ordinary animal.

notes.label: d’Bisig
notes.text: a dialectal local place or direction toward which the creature usually travels; its precise referent is not explained in the source.

notes.label: Charfriti
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for Good Friday, a sacred day on which the men's hunting makes their encounter especially transgressive or ominous.

notes.label: Viel Jages u weni Fos
notes.text: literally ‘much hunting and little catch,’ a dialect expression for great effort yielding little prey or reward.

notes.label: Güegi
notes.text: here a mood of cocky good spirits, boastfulness, or overconfidence after the apparently successful hunt; its exact shade is regional.

notes.label: Galgelöli, wo bischt?
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Galgelöli, where are you?’; calling the being's name provokes the impossible answer from inside the captured sack.

notes.label: Galgelöli i Hämelersch Sack inne
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Galgelöli inside Hämeler's sack,’ the first version of the supernatural reply; the surname spelling varies across the tale's versions.

notes.label: was gischt, was hescht
notes.text: a dialect idiom meaning at top speed, pell-mell, or as fast as possible; it conveys the hunters' panicked flight.

notes.label: Galgelöli, wo bisch?
notes.text: a slightly different dialect spelling of ‘Galgelöli, where are you?’ in the second and third versions.

notes.label: Galgelöli i Hämerlersch Sack inne
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘Galgelöli inside Hämerler's sack,’ the second version's reply, preserving its distinct surname form.

notes.label: Burdi
notes.text: Swiss German for a burden or carried load; the stolen sack becomes supernaturally heavy as lead.

notes.label: I Hämerlesch Sack inne!
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘inside Hämerle's sack!’; this is the third version's shortened reply and another historical spelling of the name.

notes.label: Gringe
notes.text: Swiss German plural for heads, often with a coarse or grotesque tone; witnesses claim the escaped creature had six or seven of them.

notes.label: ’s Liecht i dr Lohäule
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the light in the Lohäule,’ naming a recurring luminous apparition near the Altburg.

notes.label: Chüehweid
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘cow pasture,’ the place from which the mysterious light approaches.

notes.label: ’s Lingge Hannes
notes.text: Bernese Swiss German for ‘left-handed Hannes’ or ‘Hannes the left-hander,’ a descriptive nickname using Hannes as a familiar form of Johannes.

notes.label: Vierteli
notes.text: literally ‘little quarters,’ probably small allotted parcels, shares, or usufruct rights that formed part of Hannes's meager livelihood; the precise local institution is uncertain.

notes.label: Johrholz
notes.text: Bernese dialect for ‘year-wood,’ an annual allotted entitlement to firewood or timber from communal woodland.

notes.label: Bündteli
notes.text: a dialect diminutive for a small travel bundle or bindle, containing the emigrant's few belongings.

notes.label: Urähnigrossätti
notes.text: an elaborately compounded Bernese kinship term for a very remote male ancestor, approximately a great-great-grandfather.

notes.label: Bärnbiet
notes.text: the Bernese region or territory, literally the ‘Bern country,’ rather than only the city of Bern.

notes.label: Wannebach
notes.text: the local stream or hollow where Hannes cuts the ritual hazel switch after returning home.

notes.label: Haslehag
notes.text: a hazel hedge or enclosure, the landmark beside which the required one-year forked switch grows.

notes.label: Chilezit
notes.text: literally ‘church time,’ here the hour sounded by the church clock at midnight.

notes.label: Altburg
notes.text: literally ‘old castle,’ the fortified site Hannes must circle three times before the treasure doors appear.

notes.label: lätz Hufe
notes.text: dialect for the ‘wrong heap’ and possibly also the ‘left-hand heap’; the warning exploits lätz as ‘wrong’ or ‘left.’

a0be9f80c4be5bbbbcea5ea44a19d279aba4cde0.summary: ’s Meitli vor em Spiegel — The Girl before the Mirror

notes.label: ’s Meitli vor em Spiegel
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the girl before the mirror’; Meitli is the familiar Swiss diminutive word for a girl.

notes.label: z’Predig
notes.text: Bernese dialect for going ‘to the sermon,’ meaning to the church service.

notes.label: Müetti
notes.text: an affectionate Swiss German diminutive for mother, comparable to ‘Mummy’ or ‘Mama.’

notes.label: Äs lütet zsäme
notes.text: Bernese German for ‘the bells are ringing together,’ the church-bell signal summoning worshippers to the service.

notes.label: Mira
notes.text: a dialect interjection of dismissal or indifference, approximately ‘for all I care’ or ‘never mind’; here it introduces the girl's irreverent retort.

67650cdec98d6b139a828d4a65d1d68eca15266e.summary: ’s Weierli brätsche — Beating the Water in the Little Pond

notes.label: ’s Weierli brätsche
notes.text: a Bernese dialect phrase meaning to strike or beat the water in the little pond; Weierli is a diminutive of pond and brätsche conveys beating rather than ordinary splashing, but this brief account does not explain the act's purpose or ritual significance.

6c8fe4f5b15a194bcfbf0c187bce5101a7a4de95.summary: In olden times, the so-called ’s Wibli vo Steckbore came to church every year to celebrate Christmas there.

notes.label: ’s Wibli vo Steckbore
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘the little woman of Steckborn,’ the name attached to a Christmas church visitor, a bell saying, and a children’s street call; the source itself reports that this may be a reshaping of another local name.

notes.label: ’s Wibli vo Steckawege
notes.text: the alternative dialect name proposed by the narrator, ‘the little woman of Steckawege’; it is linked to a route called Stecken Wegen, but the exact modern place-name and whether the folk etymology is correct remain uncertain.

notes.label: ’s Wibli vo Steckawege kunnt!
notes.text: Alemannic for ‘the little woman of Steckawege is coming!’; people say it on seeing the old Christmas traveler’s light along the route.

69be6700344fc8b473715d991e4774fdf54a1baf.summary: In Ennetbühl, on the bridge spanning the Mühletobel, one sees the Bruggfräuli at night.

notes.label: Bruggfräuli
notes.text: literally ‘little bridge-woman’ in Swiss Alemannic; it is the shortened local name repeatedly used for the white female apparition at the Mühletobel bridge.

notes.label: ’s wiss Bruggfräuli
notes.text: St. Gallen dialect for ‘the white little bridge-woman’; Fräuli is an affectionate or diminutive feminine form, and here names a harmless moonlit bridge apparition rather than an ordinary woman.

34260c03927ec83f80a09f1806aa8204e85adf2a.summary: A dreadful storm poured down over Bürglen. The rain fell with a roar, and streams large and small raged on every side.

notes.label: Rübi
notes.text: an Uri term for a destructive, debris-laden mountain torrent or flow; each witch unleashes one during the storm and rides with it down the slope.

notes.label: Rübenen
notes.text: the source's plural form of Rübi for the two debris flows; their stopping when the church bells ring gives the flood event its supernatural reading.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

cff5e7140f77a5d539bdb208746e60033f8ca290.summary: The treasure in the little castle at Seedorf is guarded by the Evil One; but on Good Friday, or also on Palm Sunday, ‘during the Passion he must leave it, he must flee.’ ‘From the Schopfli where we lived, every Good Friday my mother saw an animal as large as a calf come out through the castle gate…

notes.label: Schopfli
notes.text: a diminutive of Schopf, a shed, lean-to, or small outbuilding, here used for the family’s home or named homestead; the exact structure from which the mother watches is uncertain.

5fb431f29023d0912f4b8856aca1306be5c371ae.summary: 1. At Wischenwassern in Guretzmettlen in the Meien Valley, something often threw pebbles at the Älpler.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: a person living or working seasonally on an Alp, tending livestock and participating in its pastoral economy; here the plural refers to workers pelted with stones at Wischenwassern.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its huts, livestock, and working landscape, not simply a mountain; stones repeatedly strike a particular place on the Gornern Alp.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Helgenstöckli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small wayside devotional shrine, image-post, or niche bearing a holy image; the stone shower surrounds the traveler near this landmark without striking him.

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

99d2f2077a667d8bc808a4cfca7ce8ea8f50f4e7.summary: In ancient times our Alp pastures extended much higher and were used far more intensively than they are today.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its grazing rights, livestock, huts, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; the account describes the former extent and intensity of these pastoral holdings.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working on a seasonal high-mountain pasture; here they collectively manage the cattle beyond the Märcht.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: a full organized Alpine cattle herd or cattle-and-dairy unit under pastoral management, not merely an unstructured group of cows; the entire Sennten is lost in the disaster.

notes.label: Märcht
notes.text: an Alpine regional word for a boundary or boundary line and also the local name attached to this divide; the source locates the old grazing ground beyond it without defining its exact course.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: an Alpine German term for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; the frightened herd plunges over one more than 100 meters high.

notes.label: Trinkelkuh
notes.text: the leading cow wearing a Trinkel or Trychel, a large hammered sheet-metal livestock bell; the herdsman grabs her bell strap in an attempt to turn the whole following herd.

fbfd5c1889fabbd5f97ccacc1914f0dca95a787f.summary: There was once a young herdsman who wished to marry and knew three sisters, each as beautiful as the others, so that choosing was difficult for him and he could not decide to give any one of them preference.

notes.label: The cheese test
notes.text: The mother uses three ways of cutting cheese to judge household thrift: eating the rind, discarding edible cheese, or trimming carefully.

source.label: Jacob Grimm and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Haus-Märchen, seventh edition, volume II (Göttingen: Dieterich, 1857), KHM 155, p. 287, Die Brautschau.

notes.label: Edition and spelling
notes.text: This is KHM 155 in the Grimms' 1857 seventh edition. The catalogue transcription modernizes spellings such as heirathen, Rath and that; the short description appended by the catalogue is omitted from the story.

source.label: Jacob Grimm and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Haus-Märchen, seventh edition, volume II (Göttingen: Dieterich, 1857), KHM 155, p. 287, Die Brautschau.

0510de7be9d94f6f462e9fbc5f84fd05dda436d1.summary: When the heavy iron cross was to be placed atop the high, slender steeple of the parish church in Spiringen, a criminal condemned to death was entrusted with this life-threatening task and promised that his life would be spared if he succeeded.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

ec5d929c30d068b51f5312244dffefa25ce54e80.summary: A jovial young fellow whom I knew well, and who was almost always whistling and whooping to himself, was walking along the Rynächt one night.

notes.label: Gässli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little lane or narrow way; here it leads from the Rynächt toward communal land opposite the Bälmli.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held or used land, often meadow, pasture, or open ground belonging to a local community rather than a private owner.

notes.label: Communal grazing rights
notes.text: Grazing on a shared Alp was governed by membership and defined rights. These could limit whose animals used the pasture and how many could be kept there. A boundary or an extra animal could therefore affect the livelihood of an entire group of households.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Alpine grazing rights

notes.label: Betglocke
notes.text: the prayer bell, whose morning ringing repeatedly ends the spirits’ nighttime power in these accounts.

notes.label: z'Stubeten
notes.text: to go on a Stubeten, an evening social or courting visit traditionally made to a household; the expression does not mean merely visiting a public inn.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: an evening household gathering or courting visit in Alpine custom; several men meet spirits while returning from one.

notes.label: Häägglä
notes.text: a local finger-hooking strength contest resembling finger wrestling; the challengers lock hands or fingers, which explains the three broken middle fingers.

notes.label: Ratsherr
notes.text: a member of a local or cantonal council; the historical Swiss civic office is more specific than a generic adviser.

notes.label: Schindäli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small shingle, splinter, or thin piece of wood; the councilman prudently offers it instead of touching the redeemed spirit’s hand.

notes.label: Ungeheuer
notes.text: in the narrator’s local supernatural taxonomy, a troublesome uncanny being distinct from a Gespenst; the narrator insists on the distinction but cannot define its exact nature.

notes.label: Gespenst
notes.text: a ghost or spectral apparition; the narrator says Gespenster are more harmful, malicious, and difficult to redeem than Ungeheuer.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a regional word for an orchard, homestead plot, or named farm property; here it identifies the dwelling place on the Vorder Mühlebach.

notes.label: Stübli
notes.text: a diminutive of Stube, the small heated parlor or living room into which the being carries the child.

notes.label: Grotzen
notes.text: a regional landscape term for rough conifer growth, stunted trees, roots, or woody scrub; the source does not identify the vegetation more narrowly.

notes.label: Schwinget
notes.text: a wrestling bout in the Swiss Schwingen tradition; the word makes the spirit’s attack sound like a recognized folk contest even though its outcome is deadly.

notes.label: Tschopen
notes.text: a regional term for a man’s jacket or short coat; Spittler removes it with his hat and vows never to put it on again.

notes.label: Nacht-büebähosä
notes.text: literally the trousers of a Nachtbub, a young man making nighttime social or courting visits; the spirit treats the garment as the only thing preventing it from grinding the wearer like stones.

notes.label: Hosenlupf
notes.text: literally a ‘trouser lift,’ a traditional Swiss wrestling move or bout based on gripping and throwing an opponent by the clothing.

notes.label: Nachtbub
notes.text: literally a ‘night lad,’ a young man who goes out after dark for revelry or courting visits; the term can be teasing or disapproving rather than a claim of criminal conduct.

notes.label: Betenläuten
notes.text: the ringing that calls the community to prayer; like the Betglocke and Ave, it marks the dawn boundary at which the apparition loses power.

notes.label: Ave
notes.text: the bell-ringing for the Ave Maria or Angelus; its first note makes the wrestling Gespenst disappear.

notes.label: ä Güegä
notes.text: Uri dialect for a beetle or small bug; the bizarre creature emerges from Franz Zurfluh’s nose and then vanishes from a glass.

notes.label: Gspor
notes.text: dialect for tracks, traces, or a trail; the snow shows only Arnold’s own marks and the disturbance of his unseen struggle.

notes.label: Mit diër wil-i scho schwingä! Lüegä wil-i, ob-i nitt stercher syg ass dü!
notes.text: Bifängler-Hansi’s exact Uri-dialect challenge, ‘I will wrestle with you! I want to see whether I am not stronger than you!’
notes.anchor: Mit diër wil-i scho schwingä! Lüegä wil-i, ob-i nitt stercher syg ass dü!

notes.label: Heer und Dokter
notes.text: literally ‘priest and doctor’ in this Uri usage; the paired expression calls for both spiritual and medical aid after the supernatural wrestling match.

notes.label: Butzenscheiben
notes.text: old bull’s-eye or bottle-glass windowpanes whose thick centers and greenish glass make the view partly opaque.

notes.label: Hüss-Jumpfärä!
notes.text: a nighttime suitor’s traditional call to the ‘house maiden’ at a woman’s window; here it summons an uncanny woman instead.

notes.label: Achseln zu putschen
notes.text: literally to bump or shove shoulders, a former strength contest among Nachtbuben; the source explains the custom but not a fixed set of rules.

notes.label: Blagg
notes.text: a harsh dialect insult for an unpleasant, ugly, or contemptible female figure; its precise shade is uncertain, so the source word remains in the challenge.

notes.label: Englischer Gruss
notes.text: the Angelic Salutation, traditionally the Ave Maria; fervently praying it makes the attacking apparition vanish.

notes.label: Dorfen
notes.text: nighttime village-going, social visiting, or courting; the narrator wonders whether the experience made the young man abandon the custom, while its exact local practice is not further described.

notes.label: Historical wording
notes.text: These accounts correspond to entries 759–772 of the 1929 volume. The catalogue uses Arzt where the historical transcription has the older dative form Arzte; the sense is unchanged.

source.label: Josef Müller, Sagen aus Uri, volume 2, edited by Hanns Bächtold-Stäubli (Basel: G. Krebs, 1929), nos. 759–772, pp. 183–189.

84e026a701650a57841b185d7c63cf7fc4c09931.summary: 1. a) Heitmenegg is a sunny Alp in the Schächen valley at the foot of the rugged Windgällenstock.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture together with its seasonal livestock, dairy work, huts, and workers; Heitmenegg and Etzlialp are complete summer farming operations, not simply mountain scenery.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the senior Alpine dairyman responsible for cheesemaking and often for directing the other seasonal workers; in these variants he is the master who disguises himself to frighten a junior boy.

notes.label: Nischt
notes.text: the sleeping nest, bunk, or bed space in an Alpine hut; the Senn takes the horse blanket from it, but its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Büebli
notes.text: an affectionate or diminutive Swiss German word for a little boy; here the adjective marks the timid junior worker whom the Senn intends to frighten.

notes.label: Kähle
notes.text: a local topographic word for a steep channel, gully, or ravine; the disguised Senn slides down its stony slope, but the feature’s exact size is not given.

notes.label: Kreuzfingerring
notes.text: literally a ‘cross finger-ring,’ a ring bearing a cross or used as a Christian protective sign; its survival identifies the vanished Senn, although the story does not explain its precise devotional use.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: the people living and working seasonally with livestock on an Alp; here they are the hut community that recognizes the Senn’s ring and searches for him.

notes.label: Handbub
notes.text: a junior male helper or general hand in an Alp’s dairying and herding workforce; here he repeatedly fetches water for the Senn.

notes.label: Bräntä
notes.text: a regional wooden vessel or carrying tub worn on the back for transporting milk, water, or another liquid; here the Handbub takes it to the stream for water.

notes.label: Handbueb
notes.text: an Uri spelling variant of Handbub, the junior male Alp helper who throws the stone back at his disguised master.

notes.label: Alpgnof
notes.text: a parenthetical name or source designation attached to this variant; the record does not explain whether it is a place, household name, or narrator identifier, so its precise reference remains uncertain.

notes.label: Schnitzeldecke
notes.text: a patchwork covering made, as the source explains, from scraps or ends of woolen cloth; the Senn uses it as a ghost disguise.

notes.label: Tinder
notes.text: a local title for a junior herding or Alp worker in the Ursern variant; the source distinguishes him from the Hirt but does not state his exact duties.

notes.label: Holy water and blessings
notes.text: Catholic blessings often use prayer together with a gesture or a material sign, including the cross or holy water. The tales can extend these practices into protection from uncanny beings; that supernatural episode belongs to the story, rather than a guarantee made by the Church.

source.label: Catholic Catechism: blessings and sacramentals

notes.label: Handknab
notes.text: another regional form for a junior male farm or Alp hand; at Römerstalden he is the water-carrier obstructed by the disguised Senn.

6aedd58e14932514c32b6701bade1f154f088022.summary: At Obergadmen behind Sisikon, one friend once said to another: ‘When I am dead one day, I will come sleep beside you.’ And indeed, it was not long before he died.

notes.label: Chan-i chu schlafä?
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘May I come sleep?’ or ‘May I come and sleep beside you?’; the compressed wording recalls the dead friend’s promise, and the immediate opening of the door makes the living man’s attempted consent consequential.

863d63ca1146cfe583b1bf9693833b1d492a7a7c.summary: 1. Three priests had disputed a great deal with one another about eternity.

notes.label: Maitli
notes.text: an Uri spelling of Meitli, Swiss German for girls or young women; here the two friends make the dangerous promise about returning after death.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper level, loft, or hay floor of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding; here it is used as a sleeping place beside the hay door.

notes.label: Gnäu
notes.text: Uri dialect related to genau, carrying the sense of exact, strict, severe, or close; paired with a warning finger and reports of judgment, it suggests rigorous accounting, but no single English word captures the utterance fully.

notes.label: gnäu
notes.text: the lower-case Uri form of Gnäu, meaning exact, strict, severe, or close; here the paired phrase hert und gnäu says that conditions in the afterlife are hard and rigorously exacting.

notes.label: Zäi
notes.text: Uri dialect for tough, tenacious, hard, or unyielding; the collector glosses it with standard German zähe, and it serves as a variant of the warning Gnäu.

notes.label: Spitzli
notes.text: literally little points, tips, or pointed ornaments; paired with Chrüsäli in a purgatorial verse, it may refer to fashionable adornments, but the exact objects being condemned are uncertain.

notes.label: Chrüsäli
notes.text: literally little curls, frills, or crimped ornaments; the purgatorial verse probably targets decorative fashion, but the source does not identify the exact garment or hairstyle.

notes.label: Fäckfyr
notes.text: an Uri dialect form of Fegefeuer, purgatorial fire; in Catholic folk belief it is the place or condition of purification where the dead suffer before release.

notes.label: Büttig
notes.text: an Uri regional term for a craftsman’s workshop or workroom; the source itself glosses it as Werkstatt, and here it is the carpenter’s shop.

0d6d7c51b565a47e00add99305d62955a7ac870b.summary: Not far from Andermatt lies a large white block of stone. Many years ago, a house is said to have stood on that spot, inhabited by an old woman.

notes.label: Nidelgret
notes.text: literally ‘Cream Gret,’ combining Nidel, ‘cream,’ with Gret, a short form of Margret; it is the byname of the old woman whose magically abundant cream leads to her imprisonment in stone.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for rich cream skimmed from milk; its impossible abundance from a single cow establishes Nidelgret's reputation and later kills the greedy herdsman.

notes.label: Sommerfahrt
notes.text: literally ‘summer journey,’ the seasonal drive of cattle to high pasture and a period of abundant Alpine milk production.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cattle herder or cowherd, particularly one working with dairy cattle; here he spies on Nidelgret, copies her charm, and greedily enlarges its demand.

notes.label: Gebs
notes.text: a shallow wooden dairy vessel used for holding milk or cream; exact shapes and spellings vary regionally.

notes.label: Hexengut
notes.text: literally ‘witches' goods’ or ‘witch-property,’ part of the cream-gathering charm; its function overlaps with Sennenzoll and is not explained separately.

notes.label: Sennenzoll
notes.text: literally the ‘Senn's toll,’ a supposed portion taken from every cow; the charm presents supernatural dairy theft as a customary due.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairy herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on a high pasture; the final sentence applies this role-name to the greedy Küher.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Niedergret
notes.text: the title's spelling of the old woman's byname; the body consistently gives Nidelgret, so the difference is preserved as a source variation rather than silently corrected.

b8e16e83a00340d1b14804b5fe338bb0d2c93126.summary: a) On the tower in the Dörfli at Silenen, according to the tradition attested by several people, there formerly stood a wooden house, which is certainly correct.

notes.label: Landvögte
notes.text: plural of Landvogt, a territorial bailiff or governor exercising delegated authority in the older Swiss political order; the tradition groups them with coercive lords.

notes.label: Zwingherren
notes.text: coercive feudal lords or tyrannical castle-holders, from a word associated with compulsion; the stories portray forced deliveries, waste, and claimed sexual rights over subjects' wives.

notes.label: Trägänä
notes.text: loads or carrying containers of eggs, probably baskets, trays, or loads borne with a carrying device; the exact vessel is uncertain, but the plural emphasizes the quantity demanded.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

273a116b7dd56d7130e197a60eacb5e80e84de3f.summary: Older people still speak often of Süffibalzi, an eccentric, harmless vagabond who traveled through the canton of Uri about half a century ago and lived on people's charity.

notes.label: Süffibalzi
notes.text: the man's local nickname, derived in the source from his fondness for Ziegersüffi; the Balzi element may echo a personal name, but its precise formation is not explained.

notes.label: Ziegersüffi
notes.text: an Uri dish based on Ziger, the Swiss whey-cheese or curd product, prepared in a soft or soupy form; the exact recipe is not given, and adding rennet causes the fatal fermentation in the tale.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: an Alpine cattle herd understood as a managed, often bell-bearing dairy collective; Süffibalzi humorously recreates one from toy cows and lice.

notes.label: Stäfel
notes.text: a seasonal station, level, or cluster of buildings within an Alpine pasture system; the source uses it as a destination but does not define its exact local extent at Alpgnof.

0d7c8f2ce65d1801163f16473314c6f769c1d606.summary: 1. Maxä-Toni's Sepp of Bürglen related: One day our young farmhand was tending the cows on Alp Mättädall at the foot of the Rosstock.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high seasonal mountain pasture and its livestock-and-dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; Mättädall is the named Alp where the boy tends cattle.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Gwätti
notes.text: an Uri dialect word apparently denoting a joint, notch, or recess in the barn's timberwork where the glowing stone is lodged; the source does not identify the exact structural feature, so its closest physical equivalent is uncertain.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: literally ‘rays,’ a traditional Swiss Alpine term for rock crystals or crystal points sought in the mountains; here one exceptional crystal makes the whole collection shine, though the source does not identify its mineral species.

notes.label: The parish
notes.text: A parish is an enduring local religious community, historically responsible for worship and pastoral care within a larger church organization. Its territory need not be identical to the civil village. Parish membership could shape where people attended services and which church served an outlying settlement.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: parish communities

fe85d3a95c0fa1099bc55fb555d9858a385ee7ad.summary: High in the Teiftal on the slope of the Bristenstock, a Karfunkel shone brightly enough to be seen for hours' journey around.

notes.label: Karfunkel
notes.text: the legendary carbuncle, imagined as a precious red gemstone that shines with its own fiery light; this mountain stone is visible across the Reuss valley and supernaturally defends itself from seekers.

d9cb736886046f91b66e89ce4ee79dc813380ca3.summary: a) In a Heimkuhalpeli, entirely apart from the other people, lived a Wybervölchli who seldom went out, never fetched provisions, and yet lived well.

notes.label: Heimkuhalpeli
notes.text: a diminutive Alpine term for a small pasture or holding used by home-kept cows; the source gives the pastoral setting but not its precise tenure or distance from the settlement.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person,’ sometimes familiar or dismissive; here it labels the solitary suspected witch without securely indicating her age or stature.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially the rich layer skimmed from milk; the witch steals it from Alpine dairy cellars and converts her magic into an impossible supply.

notes.label: Anken
notes.text: the traditional Swiss German word for butter; it is both the product created in the witch’s churn and the inherited store that repeatedly returns.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Witch accusations
notes.text: Swiss witch persecutions affected both women and men. Accusations included harm to people, livestock, and crops through magic. A legend may present an accused person as a real witch; that is the telling’s claim and should not be treated as proof about a historical person.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: witch persecutions

notes.label: Züsiliächtli
notes.text: an Uri diminutive for a tiny flickering or glimmering light seen in the witch’s hut; its exact fuel, color, and magical function are not described.

notes.label: Ankenkübel
notes.text: a large tub or churn for making Anken; the story describes the witch working the vessel but not its precise mechanism.

notes.label: Stämpfel
notes.text: a regional diminutive for a pestle, plunger, or churn-dasher inserted into the Ankenkübel; its exact construction is not specified.

notes.label: Lüzifer, vor Raphael, Schneeveegel, Läckdafis, Pumpis a' diä Wyggä
notes.text: the witch’s exact repeated incantation. Lüzifer and Raphael resemble the names Lucifer and Raphael, while the remaining words and the formula’s literal syntax are too uncertain to normalize without invention.
notes.anchor: Lüzifer, vor Raphael, Schneeveegel, Läckdafis, Pumpis a' diä Wyggä

notes.label: Büebli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a little boy; here it names the tiny pitch-black being produced from the churn rather than establishing that it is a human child.

notes.label: Schibel
notes.text: an uncertain Uri quantity word, apparently a lump, batch, or substantial portion; the source does not establish how much Anken the witch removes.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working seasonally with livestock on an Alp, especially its herders and dairy workers; they discover that their milk has already been skimmed.

813c8758c8ef420e367bc2a4a4384f9d950c2d86.summary: is said to have been so wealthy that a member of the monastery traveling from Seedorf to Jerusalem could spend every evening (or every second evening) on property belonging to his religious house.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

3b46c0e20813662133375169cfc6321989143a24.summary: A little boy and a girl who had gone out to pick strawberries lost their way in the forest near Conters.

notes.label: Waldfängge
notes.text: literally a forest Fängge, one of the wild beings associated with Alpine woods and mountains; the account locates this one in a cave near Conters.

notes.label: Waldfänggin
notes.text: the feminine form for a female forest Fängge; unlike her man-eating husband, she pities the lost children and leads them safely home.

notes.label: Fängge
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alpine name for a wild, giant-like, or ogre-like supernatural being; this male Fängge is explicitly a devourer of children.

notes.label: A small transcription difference
notes.text: Jecklin's 1874 printing says ihre Noth ('their distress'); the catalogue transcription has Not without ihre. Spelling and punctuation have also been modernized. The telling otherwise follows the complete page-30 account.

source.label: Dietrich Jecklin, Volksthümliches aus Graubünden, part I (Zürich: Orell Füssli, 1874), p. 30, Der Fängge als Menschenfresser.

7252b0f85891f45dba6405ab6882fdef3fc147db.summary: A miser ordered that the money he had scraped together be placed in his coffin after his death, and this was done.

notes.label: About this telling
notes.text: The German genre Sage often ties an extraordinary event to a named place, time, or witness. Such details establish the telling’s local authority, but do not independently verify the event. The source credit identifies the recorded version preserved here.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland: Sagen und Legenden

cb61f932fe8f1237e160f6bd68174dc1d05108ed.summary: a) Old Biäl-Leni-Chaspi of Unterschächen often claimed that enough money was verlochet—hidden away—beneath the little chapel at Äsch.

notes.label: verlochet
notes.text: an Alpine German verb meaning concealed, stowed, or hidden away, especially underground; the old man claims ample money is cached beneath the later chapel.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar’ or student, a recurring German-speaking folklore figure credited with occult learning and secret knowledge; here he reveals the buried gold's location and number of vessels.

notes.label: Häfen
notes.text: in this Alpine German context, large pots, cauldrons, or vessels rather than modern harbor basins; three of them are said to be filled with gold.

notes.label: Gott b'hiät-is davor
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘God preserve us from it’; the protective aside distances narrator and listener from naming or encountering the living Devil.

notes.label: Frechlinge
notes.text: bold, brazen, or foolhardy fellows; the source characterizes the three treasure seekers by their daring, with a disapproving shade that ‘brave men’ would miss.

7800f8fc12d3922e4cbd7d0febc1346bb6cf1aee.summary: Many hundreds of years ago, when giants still existed, there were once two brothers in Scarl.

notes.label: Scarl
notes.text: Jecklin's historical spelling for the Lower Engadine village now generally written S-charl; the source form is retained as a place-name.

notes.label: The ending
notes.text: Although the title names two brothers, this printed telling follows the younger one and ends with his wedding. The older brother's further fate is not given on pages 120–121.

source.label: Dietrich Jecklin, Volksthümliches aus Graubünden, part II (Chur: Jost & Albin, 1876), H. Märchen, no. 1, pp. 120–121, Die zwei Brüder und die vier Riesen.

8bf0829bf9494d9b9b6a589a091f564ceba1090a.summary: 1. ‘At that time I was serving in the house of Mr.

notes.label: Landammann
notes.text: the traditional chief magistrate or presiding official of a Swiss canton or rural polity; Xaver Arnold’s title situates the remembered house in Altdorf’s civic history.

d6a1aec9a78729046692a60ae9639d669a6bda48.summary: 1. A young man wished to raise a treasure guarded by a ghost.

notes.label: Grebel
notes.text: a regional digging implement such as a hoe, mattock, or grubber; the young man first excavates with it and the shovel, then must strike the guardian animals.

notes.label: Chrott
notes.text: Uri dialect for a toad; this prose form names the monstrous animal charged to guard the Fronalp treasure.

notes.label: vergaumä
notes.text: Uri dialect for watching over, guarding, or keeping custody of something; the toad's assigned task is to prevent access to the treasure.

notes.label: Mülärä
notes.text: an uncertain dialect personal or house-name associated with the treasure, possibly a feminine Miller or Müller designation; the source calls the figure verschwignä, taciturn or secretive, but gives no further identity.

notes.label: fahrändä Schueler
notes.text: Uri dialect for a fahrender Schüler, literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a folklore figure credited with occult learning and secret knowledge; here he is also described as shrewd and experienced.

notes.label: Krott
notes.text: the verse's form of the dialect word for a toad; the rhyme magnifies her to the size of an oven with pane-like eyes.

notes.label: Taapen
notes.text: a regional plural for paws, feet, or broad limbs; the giant toad beckons with them, though the source does not specify their exact shape.

notes.label: Judsfad
notes.text: the historical local place-name above the Rotgand at Meien, apparently containing an older ethnic label for a Jewish person; readers should recognize the period wording rather than treat it as neutral current usage.

notes.label: Franzosenzeit
notes.text: literally the ‘French period,’ the regional historical name for the era of French invasion, occupation, and political upheaval around 1798; the tale dates the hidden treasure only to that general period.

2d09df6d877d09334db7209e56a8471b1ebd54ec.summary: 1. Whenever the devout Senn of an Alp in Meien called out the Gospel of St.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the lead Alpine dairyman responsible for cattle and dairy work; in the first account, his religious duty includes projecting the Gospel call across the Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its hut, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain; the Senn's Gospel call and both fatal encounters occur within that pastoral setting.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Folle
notes.text: an Uri Alpine object or feature through which the Senn projects the Gospel of St. John, likely a funnel-like dairy implement used as a speaking horn; its exact construction is not identified in the passage.

notes.label: Handknab
notes.text: a junior male Alpine worker or dairyman's assistant; the role is subordinate to the Senn and herdsman, but its exact duties here are not stated.

4b5ddc2e6fef9b96e77854e7eb3c08d2f7f4cccf.summary: On the little hill where Dingten Castle once stood, a silver-bright spring bubbles out of the rock.

notes.label: Lee
notes.text: the source’s word for the body of water within the mountain; the historical Note later calls it a See, a lake, so the context supports an underground lake while the exact form Lee remains uncertain.

notes.label: Brünnlein
notes.text: a small natural spring or fountain; in this legend it is the silver-bright water named for Magdhilde and a place where she bathes and foretells weather changes.

notes.label: Jungfernbrunnen
notes.text: literally the ‘Maidens’ Spring,’ the traditional name of the clear, cold spring in the Langholz forest connected with three murdered maidens.

notes.label: Hollenteiche
notes.text: ponds associated with Holla or Holle in traditions about the supernatural source of newborn children; the nearby historical discussion connects them with children’s springs rather than with infernal ‘hell ponds.’

notes.label: Kleinkinderbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘little-children’s springs’ or ‘infants’ wells,’ folkloric waters from which newborn children were said to be fetched and brought to their parents.

notes.label: Hollabrunn
notes.text: the spring-name in the closing children’s rhyme, associated in the historical note with the belief that a nursewoman fetches newborn children from water; the source rhyme is textually irregular, so no missing words are invented.

notes.label: Magdhildenbrünnlein
notes.text: the named little spring or fountain near Dingten associated with the maiden Magdhilde; Brünnlein is the diminutive of Brunnen and may mean either a small spring or a small fountain.

notes.label: The 1862 source resolves a reading
notes.text: Rochholz's original page 143 reads See, meaning a lake, where the catalogue has Lee. The preserved translation follows that catalogue spelling. Read the opening as an underground lake inhabited by maidens; the digitized printing now resolves the uncertainty recorded in the earlier translation note. The catalogue also drops in from the closing rhyme: the printing says find’t ein Kind’l in der Sunn.

source.label: Ernst Ludwig Rochholz, Naturmythen. Neue Schweizersagen (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1862), section 6, no. 14, p. 143, including the quoted portion of the author's note.

notes.label: Story and historical commentary
notes.text: The short story ends with Magdhilde appearing before a change in the weather, followed by the informant Jak. Matter's name. The material introduced as Note is Rochholz's nineteenth-century commentary. Its links to Saint Ursula, Holla and children fetched from springs are the collector's interpretation. They should be read separately from the villagers' account. The catalogue quotes that note through its nursery rhyme; Rochholz's subsequent biblical and medieval comparisons are outside this excerpt.

source.label: Ernst Ludwig Rochholz, Naturmythen. Neue Schweizersagen (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1862), section 6, no. 14, p. 143, including the quoted portion of the author's note.

notes.label: Edition and transcription
notes.text: The story and quoted commentary come from Naturmythen. Neue Schweizersagen, published in Leipzig in 1862. The catalogue updates spelling and punctuation, uses dort for dorten and adds the labels Legend from Dingten and Note. The original wording and the existing English translation are preserved here, with these differences made explicit.

source.label: Ernst Ludwig Rochholz, Naturmythen. Neue Schweizersagen (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1862), section 6, no. 14, p. 143, including the quoted portion of the author's note.

799cb78e486abb39bba8bb0bbf24abd92bcf2684.summary: When the Alpen lie buried beneath the weight of winter snow, people and livestock have descended into the valley, and, in the snowbound huts, the men carve wooden wares by the light of a flickering Kienspan while the women ply the old-fashioned spindle, the reign of the mountain spirits begins.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, the high-mountain summer pastures and working landscapes abandoned during winter, not simply the Alps as a mountain chain.

notes.label: Alpine summer farming
notes.text: An Alp is a high seasonal grazing area. Families and hired herders moved livestock uphill for summer, cared for the animals, and made dairy products there. A hut in these stories is often a workplace away from the permanent village, rather than a vacation cabin.

source.label: UNESCO: Alpine pasture season

notes.label: Kienspan
notes.text: a resin-rich pinewood splint burned as a small household light before modern lamps.

notes.label: Household spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns prepared fibers into yarn; weaving turns yarn into cloth. In historical Swiss households, textile work could also provide income through merchants who supplied materials and bought the finished work. The spinning room could therefore combine domestic labor with economic and social life.

source.label: Swiss National Museum: textile work in the household

notes.label: Tobeln
notes.text: plural of Tobel, steep, narrow ravines or gorges in Swiss and southern German usage; the mountain spirits gather in these rocky clefts.

notes.label: Chamois
notes.text: The chamois is a mountain-dwelling hoofed animal adapted to steep Alpine terrain. Its presence places the hunt in a demanding mountain environment. The animal’s supernatural behavior, if any, is part of the tale.

source.label: Swiss National Park

notes.label: Strahler
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine crystal seeker or mineral hunter who enters rock cavities in search of specimens.

notes.label: Strahlen
notes.text: literally ‘rays,’ a traditional Alpine term for rock crystals; the story treats them as the mountain spirits' finest adornment.

notes.label: The verified 1910 telling
notes.text: This is the complete account on page 42 of Hartmann's Berner Oberland in Sage und Geschichte, volume I: Sagen. Its printed title is Die Geister auf der Jungfrau. The catalogue updates spelling and punctuation, uses niedrigen for niederen and has welcher where the printing reads welchen. The sequence and content of the telling are preserved.

source.label: Hermann Hartmann, Berner Oberland in Sage und Geschichte, I: Sagen (Bümpliz: Benteli, 1910), p. 42, Die Geister auf der Jungfrau; Universitätsbibliothek Bern, MUE H XXXV 173.

notes.label: Hartmann's own source credit
notes.text: Under this paragraph Hartmann credits C. Vogt, Im Gebirg und auf den Gletschern. That line is absent from the catalogue transcription. The dated witness used for this page is Hartmann's 1910 printing; the source credit alone does not establish the wording or date of an earlier Vogt edition.
